# Algorithms and Data Structures in Go

This guide is for readers who know basic Go variables, functions,
loops, and types. It teaches how to represent data, choose a method,
and explain why a solution works.

Study one lesson at a time: replay its trace on paper, run its code,
then change an input and predict the result. Read the relevant
selection guidance in C before choosing a method from B. The
[practice plan](INTERVIEW_PREP_PLAN.md) supplies exercises.

Coverage: every listed lesson is complete, from A.1.1 through A.20.4,
B.1.1 through B.39.5, and C.1.1 through C.16.4.

## A. Data structures

### A.1 Arrays and slices

#### A.1.1 Fixed arrays and dynamic slices

##### Problem and contract

You need to keep values in order and read or change a value by its
position. A fixed array has a length in its type, such as `[3]int`.
A slice, such as `[]int`, describes a variable-length view of an
underlying array. Positions start at zero; a length of three permits
indexes 0, 1, and 2. Duplicates keep their positions.

The example below demonstrates the ownership problem that appears
when two slices share storage. Given the array `[10, 20, 30]`, make
an independent array copy, change an element through a slice, append
within available capacity, then append beyond it. Finally make an
independent slice copy. The expected outcome distinguishes which
writes reach the original array and which remain private.

Prerequisites are basic Go assignment, calls, and printing. No
concurrent access occurs. Allocation must fit available memory.
Invalid dynamic indexes or slice bounds panic; the example uses only
valid bounds. This lesson makes no timing or allocation-size promise.

##### Mental model

An array value contains its elements. Assigning an array copies those
elements. A slice value instead describes a starting position,
length, and capacity. Assignment copies that description and can
leave two views sharing the same elements. This sharing is aliasing.

Length counts currently accessible elements. Capacity counts slots
from the view's start to its permitted storage limit. For
`view := backing[:2]` on a three-element array, `len(view)` is 2 and
`cap(view)` is 3. `view[1]` means "read the second visible element,"
which is `backing[1]`. `view[2]` is invalid despite spare capacity.
The range `[:2]` includes index 0 and excludes index 2; this is a
half-open range.

Appending returns a slice with the new length. If space remains,
it writes into the existing array; otherwise it allocates a new
array and copies the visible elements. Always keep the returned
slice. Growth capacity is unspecified: the old view's length does
not grow, and old aliases do not follow newly allocated storage.

##### Worked walkthrough

Input is `[10, 20, 30]`. Expected final values are
`backing = [10, 99, 7]`, `arrayCopy = [10, 20, 30]`,
`grown = [55, 99, 7, 8]`, and `detached = [66, 99, 7, 8]`.

Initial state: the array literal creates `backing = [10, 20, 30]`.
No copies or views exist yet.

1. Decision: assign `arrayCopy := backing`, then take
   `view := backing[:2]` and `alias := view`. Array assignment copies
   the three integers; both slice assignments refer to the original
   storage.
   After: `arrayCopy = [10, 20, 30]`; `view` and `alias` both show
   `[10, 20]`, with length 2 and capacity 3.
   Known correct: the array copy is independent; both views share
   the first two slots of `backing`.

2. Decision: set `view[1] = 99`. Index 1 is below length 2, so this
   writes the second shared slot.
   After: `backing = [10, 99, 30]`; both views show `[10, 99]`;
   `arrayCopy` still holds `[10, 20, 30]`.
   Known correct: element writes are visible through other views of
   the same slot, but cannot alter the independent array copy.

3. Decision: evaluate `view = append(view, 7)`. The requested length
   is 3, equal to capacity 3, so the existing third slot is reused.
   After: `view = [10, 99, 7]`, length 3, capacity 3;
   `backing = [10, 99, 7]`; `alias` still shows `[10, 99]`.
   Known correct: the append overwrote the original 30, but only the
   returned slice acquired length 3. The alias length remains 2.

4. Decision: evaluate `grown := append(view, 8)`. The requested
   length 4 exceeds capacity 3, so a new array receives the three
   visible values and then 8. Set `grown[0] = 55`.
   After: `grown = [55, 99, 7, 8]`, length 4, capacity at least 4;
   `view` and `backing` remain `[10, 99, 7]`.
   Known correct: `grown` has different storage, so its element
   write cannot reach `backing`. Its exact capacity is irrelevant.

5. Decision: allocate `detached` with length `len(grown)`, copy all
   four integers, then set `detached[0] = 66`. Copying to newly
   allocated storage guarantees independence without relying on
   whether an append happens to grow.
   After: `detached = [66, 99, 7, 8]`; `grown` stays `[55, 99, 7, 8]`.
   Known correct: every expected final value has been established.
   No operations remain; printing exposes these values and exits.

Focused boundary: let `empty` be a nil `[]int`. Its length and
capacity are zero. `empty = append(empty, 5)` needs length 1, so it
obtains storage and returns `[5]`; the original nil value has no
element that could be overwritten. Reading `empty[1]` now panics:
the first invalid index equals its length, 1.

Counterexample to "append always makes a private copy": start with
`backing = [1, 2, 3]` and `short := backing[:1]`. Appending 9 needs
length 2, which fits capacity 3. The write changes `backing` to
`[1, 9, 3]`. The first mistaken decision was treating spare capacity
as independent storage; use an explicit copy when ownership matters.

##### Implementation

This is a complete Go program using only the standard library. Save
the block as a temporary `main.go` and run it with `go run`. All
mutation is local; its only external effect is printing. Comments
identify the operations in the walkthrough.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	// An array owns its elements directly. Assignment therefore copies
	// all three integers, so later writes to backing cannot change
	// arrayCopy.
	backing := [3]int{10, 20, 30}
	arrayCopy := backing

	// A slice is only a view of an array. view and alias get separate
	// slice descriptions, but both descriptions point at backing.
	view := backing[:2]
	alias := view
	// This write reaches the shared second slot, so all views of that
	// slot observe 99. arrayCopy remains independent.
	view[1] = 99
	fmt.Println(backing, arrayCopy, view, alias)

	// view has one unused slot in backing. append reuses that capacity,
	// overwrites backing[2], and returns a view that includes the slot.
	view = append(view, 7)
	fmt.Println(backing, view, alias)

	// A fourth value cannot fit. append therefore allocates new storage,
	// which is why changing grown no longer changes backing or view.
	grown := append(view, 8)
	grown[0] = 55
	fmt.Println(backing, view, grown)

	// When ownership must be guaranteed, allocate the destination and
	// copy every visible element instead of relying on append to grow.
	detached := make([]int, len(grown))
	copy(detached, grown)
	detached[0] = 66
	fmt.Println(grown, detached)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[10 99 30] [10 20 30] [10 99] [10 99]
[10 99 7] [10 99 7] [10 99]
[10 99 7] [10 99 7] [55 99 7 8]
[55 99 7 8] [66 99 7 8]
```

##### Why it works

Every slice used here satisfies `0 <= len <= cap`. An element write
is valid only below its length. Assignment preserves this relation
while copying either an array's elements or a slice's description.
That distinction explains the independent `arrayCopy` and the shared
`alias` after the first step.

Each append returns a description that includes the new element.
The first append stays within capacity, and the second exceeds it;
the reuse and allocation rules therefore determine exactly which
array is written. No assumption about a growth multiplier is needed.
The explicit copy covers four elements because both source and
destination have length 4. For these integer elements there are no
nested references that could preserve sharing.

This is a finite sequence of operations, so it terminates after
printing. If the same demonstration used slices of slices, copying
the outer elements would still share inner arrays; independence here
depends on the element type as well as the outer allocation.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

For `n` integer elements, indexing reads or writes one slot and slice
assignment copies a fixed-size description: O(1) work. Array
assignment and copying all elements take O(n) work and require O(n)
destination storage. Creating a subslice does not copy its elements.

Appending one value with capacity available takes O(1) work.
Appending when full copies the visible elements, requiring O(n) work
and a new allocation. Repeated single-element appends normally cost
O(1) amortized per append under geometric capacity growth: earlier
cheap appends pay for occasional copies. This is a runtime cost
model, not a language timing guarantee or a fixed doubling rule.

A slice of length 1 can keep a much larger backing array reachable.
Returning that view avoids copying but may retain O(n) storage.
Copying just the required values trades immediate work for shorter
storage lifetime. For this fixed example, all sizes and costs are
constant; generalized copying costs depend on element count.
The printed output also takes work proportional to values printed.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty: nil and non-nil empty slices both have length zero and can
  be appended to. `make([]int, 0)` is non-nil; a nil slice compares
  equal to nil. Do not use that distinction as an element count.
- Length versus capacity: `make([]int, 0, 3)[0]` panics because its
  length is zero. Append first or make a positive length; capacity
  alone never permits an indexed read or write.
- One slot: `[1]int{4}` has only index 0. Index 1 is invalid, even
  when a loop mistakes `<= len(values)` for `< len(values)`.
- Lost length: a function that appends to a slice parameter must
  return the result if the caller needs the new length. Passing the
  slice copies its description, so the caller's length stays old.
- Restricting growth: `backing[:2:2]` has length and capacity 2.
  Appending must allocate, but assigning index 0 still writes the
  shared original array. A capacity limit is not a complete copy.
- Copy length: copying `[4, 5]` into a zero-length slice with spare
  capacity copies zero elements. `copy` uses lengths; allocate the
  required destination length and check its result when truncation
  is possible.
- Duplicates, negatives, and zero are ordinary integer elements.
  `[0, -1, -1]` keeps its order; no arithmetic overflow arises from
  assignment. Negative dynamic lengths or invalid bounds panic;
  impossible allocations are outside the successful contract.
- Array assignment copies elements, not recursively referenced
  objects. An array of pointers still refers to the same pointed-to
  objects after assignment. The integer example avoids that case.
- Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts later elements if
  order must be preserved. Fast indexing does not make those shifts
  constant-time.

##### When to choose it

Use an array for a fixed number of slots whose count is part of the
type, such as three coordinates. Use a slice for input of varying
length, sequential scans, and frequent indexed reads. Reserve known
capacity when collecting results, while retaining the returned
slice after every append.

If the workload repeatedly removes from the front, a queue with a
moving head avoids repeatedly shifting every remaining value. If
the workload asks whether arbitrary values exist, a hash set avoids
scanning the slice for each lookup. Those alternatives address
specific operations; a slice remains useful for ordered output.

Next study [matrices](#a12-multidimensional-arrays-and-matrices)
for nested slices. Practice input
mutation with [Remove Element](
problems/solved_easy_leetcode_0027_remove_element.go).
Language contracts are defined by the Go specification's
[array types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Array_types),
[slice types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_types),
[slice expressions](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_expressions), and
[append and copy](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Appending_and_copying_slices).

#### A.1.2 Multidimensional arrays and matrices

##### Problem and contract

A grid needs two positions: a row and a column. Before writing a
grid algorithm, decide whether all rows must have the same length
and whether changing one row can affect another. Read
[arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) first.

A matrix is a rectangular grid. A Go `[2][3]int` contains two array
values of three integers each; its shape is fixed in its type. A
`[][]int` contains slice descriptions, so its rows can have different
lengths or share storage. A rectangular shape is a contract that
your code must establish, not a guarantee of `[][]int`.

Our operation transposes an integer matrix: input cell at row 1,
column 2 becomes output cell at row 2, column 1. Given R rows of
C columns, return C independent rows of R columns without changing
the input. Repeated and negative values keep their corresponding
positions; this operation performs no arithmetic on values.

Reject unequal row lengths with an error and a nil result. Accept
nil or empty input and return a non-nil empty result. Accept rows
of length zero, including nil rows, and return an empty result.
`[][]int` alone cannot record how many columns a zero-row result
would have. Use explicit dimensions if that distinction matters.
Allocations must fit available memory; no concurrent mutation occurs.

##### Mental model

The first index chooses a row; the second chooses an element inside
that row. `matrix[1][2]` means "the third integer in the second row."
It is valid only if both indexes satisfy their respective lengths.

First validate every row against the first row's width. Then allocate
one new output row for each input column. Copy each input cell to
the output using swapped positions. Fresh allocation for every row
prevents a write in one output row from changing another row.

Keep the roles separate: `rowCount` and `columnCount` are counts;
`row` and `column` are zero-based positions. Output row `column`
stores the input column with that number. Processing stops after
every input row and every cell within it have been visited.

##### Worked walkthrough

Input and expected output:

```text
input rows                 output rows
row 0: [1 2 3]             row 0: [1 4]
row 1: [4 5 6]             row 1: [2 5]
                           row 2: [3 6]
```

Initial state: `rowCount = 2`; the input is unchanged. Output does
not exist yet.

1. Decision: input is nonempty, so read `columnCount = 3` from the
   first row. Row 0 has length 3 and row 1 has length 3. Both match.
   After: validation succeeds with shape 2 by 3.
   Known correct: every input cell with `row < 2` and `column < 3`
   exists. No output allocation or copying has happened yet.

2. Decision: allocate three output row descriptions, then allocate
   two integer slots separately for output rows 0, 1, and 2.
   After: output is `[[0,0],[0,0],[0,0]]`.
   Known correct: these zeros are initialized placeholders. The rows
   have the required size and share no element storage.

3. Decision: visit input row 0 in column order. Copy input `[0][0]`
   value 1 to output `[0][0]`, value 2 at `[0][1]` to output `[1][0]`,
   and value 3 at `[0][2]` to output `[2][0]`.
   After: output is `[[1,0],[2,0],[3,0]]`; input row 0 is exhausted.
   Known correct: the first slot of each output row is confirmed.
   The second slots remain uncomputed placeholders.

4. Decision: visit input row 1. Copy value 4 at `[1][0]` to output
   `[0][1]`, value 5 at `[1][1]` to output `[1][1]`, and value 6 at
   `[1][2]` to output `[2][1]`.
   After: output is `[[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]`; input row 1 is exhausted.
   Known correct: every output slot contains its corresponding
   input value. Input cells have only been read.

5. Decision: there are no more input rows. Return the output and
   a nil error.
   After: the caller receives `[[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]`.
   Known correct: the shape and every transposed position meet the
   contract, with independent output storage.

Focused failure: input `[[1,2],[3]]` sets width 2. Row 0 matches,
but row 1 has length 1, so validation returns nil and an error before
allocation. Without validation, copying column 1 of row 1 would
index past that row's end.

Counterexample to reusing one output row: for `[[1,2],[3,4]]`,
suppose both output rows refer to the same `[0,0]`. Copying 1 writes
its first slot; copying 2 to the other row's first slot overwrites
that same slot. Both rows now start with 2 instead of 1 and 2.
Allocating each row independently prevents the first wrong write.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program uses `fmt` for errors and printing. Save it
as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. The function returns new
storage or an error; only `main` prints.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func transposeInts(matrix [][]int) ([][]int, error) {
	// Empty input has no first row from which to learn the width. Return
	// the promised non-nil empty result before evaluating matrix[0].
	rowCount := len(matrix)
	if rowCount == 0 {
		return make([][]int, 0), nil
	}

	// A [][]int may be ragged. Check every row against the first row so
	// failure cannot leave a partly built transpose.
	columnCount := len(matrix[0])
	for row, values := range matrix {
		if len(values) != columnCount {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("row %d has wrong width", row)
		}
	}

	// Columns become rows. Allocate one independent row per input
	// column; shared rows would make later writes overwrite each other.
	transposed := make([][]int, columnCount)
	for column := range transposed {
		transposed[column] = make([]int, rowCount)
	}

	// Visit each input cell once. Swapping row and column sends it to
	// one output position required by the transpose contract.
	for row, values := range matrix {
		for column, value := range values {
			transposed[column][row] = value
		}
	}
	return transposed, nil
}

func main() {
	// A non-square matrix makes reversed dimensions visible: two input
	// rows must become three output rows.
	matrix := [][]int{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}}
	transposed, err := transposeInts(matrix)
	// This example uses valid input, so an error means its assumptions
	// implementation no longer agree with the stated contract.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(transposed)
}
```

Expected output is `[[1 4] [2 5] [3 6]]`.

##### Why it works

Validation establishes equal row lengths before any cell access.
Output allocation uses the opposite dimensions: its row index is
an input column, and its column index is an input row. All writes
are consequently within the allocated lengths.

Initially no copied positions are confirmed. After each assignment,
all previously visited input positions still have their correct
output values: two distinct input positions cannot become the same
position merely by swapping their coordinates. The new assignment
therefore adds one correct cell without invalidating an earlier one.

Both loops advance through finite slice lengths. At termination,
every input cell has been visited exactly once, so every output
cell is correct. New row allocations ensure independence from the
input and from each other. Empty dimensions contain no cells to
copy; returning an empty result satisfies the documented convention.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let R be the number of input rows and C their common width. For
nonempty input, checking the shape reads R lengths. Allocation
creates C row descriptions and R times C integer slots; copying
visits every cell once. Work is O(R + C + R*C), or O(R*C) when both
dimensions are positive. With R positive and C zero, validation
still costs O(R). Nil or empty input returns in O(1) work.

Output storage is O(C + R*C), counting its row descriptions as well
as elements. Auxiliary storage beyond the output is O(1); there is
no recursion or intermediate matrix. Bad width at row 0 is impossible
because it defines the width. A mismatch at row 1 exits after two
checks; the worst rejection checks R rows. Allocation and printing
costs are separate from those early error paths.

An outer-slice copy would be cheaper than a full transpose but would
share rows and preserve the original shape. It does not satisfy this
operation's result or ownership contract.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil input and `[][]int{}` both produce a non-nil empty result.
  Accessing row 0 before the empty check would panic.
- `[][]int{nil, []int{}}` is a valid two-row, zero-column input.
  Its transpose logically has zero rows and two columns, but
  `[][]int` cannot record a column count when it has no rows.
  Explicit dimensions are needed to retain that shape.
- `[[7]]` returns `[[7]]` in independent storage. A single row
  `[[7,8]]` becomes `[[7],[8]]`; a single column `[[7],[8]]`
  becomes `[[7,8]]`. Square-only tests miss dimension errors.
- `[[1,2],[3]]` is rejected as traced above. Iterating the first
  row's width without checking later rows is unsafe.
- `[[0,-2],[0,-2]]` becomes `[[0,0],[-2,-2]]`. Equal or negative
  values do not change the index mapping; zero is valid data.
- Changing result `[0][0]` must not change the input or another
  output row. Reusing a row allocation violates this guarantee.
- An input may itself contain shared rows. Read-only traversal is
  still safe; the returned rows are fresh. Concurrent input writes
  are excluded, since reading while another goroutine writes would
  need synchronization.
- Large matrices require enough memory for input and output at the
  same time. This function copies values, so it cannot satisfy an
  in-place requirement. Value overflow is irrelevant: no values
  are added or multiplied.

##### When to choose it

Use nested slices when row-oriented access and readable coordinates
matter, or when you actually want variable-length rows. Validate a
rectangle when the algorithm requires one. Fixed nested arrays suit
small dimensions known in the type and give array-copy semantics.

Choose a [flat array](#a14-flat-storage-and-multidimensional-indexing)
when explicit dimensions and a single element allocation are useful.
Choose [sparse rows](#a13-sparse-matrices) when most cells are zero
and processing should visit only stored entries. Neither choice
removes the need to state shape and ownership.

For grid practice see the
[matrix question family](#b16-grid-and-matrix-questions). The Go
specification defines
[array types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Array_types)
and [slice types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_types); A.1.1 explains
their copying behavior.

#### A.1.3 Sparse matrices

##### Problem and contract

A dense grid spends a slot on every zero. When almost all cells are
zero, keep only nonzero cells and enough information to find their
positions. Read [matrices](#a12-multidimensional-arrays-and-matrices)
first; this lesson uses the same rectangular input convention.

Convert an R-by-C integer matrix into compressed sparse row storage,
usually called CSR or CRS. Store nonzero values in row order, with
increasing column positions within each row. Zero means a real
numeric zero and is omitted. Each coordinate appears once; equal
values at different coordinates remain separate entries. Preserve
the input and return newly owned storage.

Reject ragged input with an error. Nil and empty input mean zero
rows and zero columns. Zero-width rows are valid and retain their
row count in the result. Reject a row count too large to represent
R+1 row boundaries. Other allocations must fit available memory.
The returned slices are an educational representation: callers must
preserve their invariants if they modify them. No concurrent
mutation is allowed.

##### Mental model

Keep three slices and the column count. `values` holds only nonzero
integers. At the same entry position, `columnByEntry` identifies the
original column. `rowOffsets` contains one boundary per row plus
a final boundary after all entries.

For example, `rowOffsets[2] = 1` means "row 2's entries start at
storage position 1." Row 2's end is `rowOffsets[3]`. A row occupies
the half-open entry range from its start up to, excluding, its end.
Equal adjacent boundaries describe an empty row, not a missing row.

Start the boundaries with zero. Scan each dense row left to right:
skip zero, or append a value and its column together. After the
whole row, append the number of values stored so far as its end.
Stop after all rows. The result avoids storing zero values, although
converting from dense input still requires inspecting every cell.

##### Worked walkthrough

Input has three rows and four columns:

```text
row 0: [0 5 0  0]
row 1: [0 0 0  0]
row 2: [7 0 0 -2]

expected rowOffsets:    [0 1 1 3]
expected columnByEntry: [1 0 3]
expected values:        [5 7 -2]
```

Initial state: validate row lengths 4, 4, and 4 against width 4.
Set `columnCount = 4`, `rowOffsets = [0]`, `columnByEntry = []`,
and `values = []`. The boundary zero starts row 0 before any entries.

1. Decision: scan row 0. Column 0 has zero, so skip it. Column 1
   has 5, so append column 1 and value 5. Columns 2 and 3 are zero
   and are skipped. Append `len(values) = 1` as the row end.
   After: offsets `[0,1]`, columns `[1]`, values `[5]`.
   Known correct: entry 0 represents exactly cell `[0][1] = 5`;
   row 0's entry range is `[0,1)`.

2. Decision: scan row 1's columns 0 through 3. All four values are
   zero, so append no entries. Still append the current value count
   1 as the row end.
   After: offsets `[0,1,1]`, columns `[1]`, values `[5]`.
   Known correct: row 1's range `[1,1)` is empty. Its position is
   preserved even though it has no stored values.

3. Decision: row 2 column 0 has 7, so append column 0 and value 7.
   Columns 1 and 2 are zero and skipped. Column 3 has -2, so append
   column 3 and value -2. Append value count 3 as the row end.
   After: offsets `[0,1,1,3]`, columns `[1,0,3]`, values `[5,7,-2]`.
   Known correct: row 2's range `[1,3)` contains entries 1 and 2,
   representing columns 0 and 3. All earlier rows remain correct.

4. Decision: no rows remain, so return the three slices and width 4.
   After: the result matches every expected slice.
   Known correct: the final boundary 3 equals the value count; each
   row can be decoded without reading the dense input.

To decode row 2, read offsets 1 and 3, then inspect entries 1 and 2:
column 0 holds 7 and column 3 holds -2. Unstored columns 1 and 2
are zero, yielding `[7,0,0,-2]`. Querying column 2 therefore returns
zero after finding no matching stored column; absence is valid data.

Counterexample to omitting an empty row's boundary: storing offsets
`[0,1,3]` for this input makes the second stored range appear to
belong to row 1. The first incorrect decision is skipping the end
boundary after row 1. Boundaries count rows even when values do not.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program prints the representation above. Save it
as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. `compressRows` returns newly
allocated slices; it neither modifies nor retains the input rows.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type sparseRows struct {
	// columnCount preserves the width even when every value is zero.
	columnCount int
	// rowOffsets[r]:rowOffsets[r+1] selects row r's stored entries.
	rowOffsets []int
	// Matching positions in these slices hold a column and its value.
	columnByEntry []int
	values        []int
}

func compressRows(matrix [][]int) (sparseRows, error) {
	// rowOffsets needs one more item than the number of rows. Reject the
	// only row count for which that length would overflow int.
	maxInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	if len(matrix) == maxInt {
		return sparseRows{}, fmt.Errorf("too many rows")
	}

	// Use the first row to define the width, then validate every row
	// before building output, so failure returns no partial data.
	columnCount := 0
	if len(matrix) > 0 {
		columnCount = len(matrix[0])
	}
	for row, values := range matrix {
		if len(values) != columnCount {
			return sparseRows{}, fmt.Errorf("ragged row %d", row)
		}
	}

	// The first zero says that row 0 starts before any stored entry. It
	// also makes a matrix with no rows unambiguous.
	compressed := sparseRows{
		columnCount: columnCount,
		rowOffsets:  []int{0},
	}
	for _, rowValues := range matrix {
		// Scan columns from left to right. Store only nonzero values, while
		// recording each original column so its position is not lost.
		for column, value := range rowValues {
			if value == 0 {
				continue
			}
			compressed.columnByEntry = append(
				compressed.columnByEntry, column,
			)
			compressed.values = append(compressed.values, value)
		}
		// The current entry count is the exclusive end of this row and the
		// start of the next. Empty rows deliberately repeat the boundary.
		compressed.rowOffsets = append(
			compressed.rowOffsets, len(compressed.values),
		)
	}
	return compressed, nil
}

func main() {
	// The empty middle row proves that repeated offsets preserve a row
	// even though that row contributes no value or column entry.
	matrix := [][]int{
		{0, 5, 0, 0},
		{0, 0, 0, 0},
		{7, 0, 0, -2},
	}
	compressed, err := compressRows(matrix)
	// The literal is rectangular, so an error would contradict the
	// stated input and should stop the demonstration immediately.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(compressed.rowOffsets)
	fmt.Println(compressed.columnByEntry)
	fmt.Println(compressed.values)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[0 1 1 3]
[1 0 3]
[5 7 -2]
```

##### Why it works

Initially both entry slices have length zero and the sole boundary
is zero. Before each row, all previous rows have exactly one end
boundary and contain precisely their nonzero cells.

Skipping a zero preserves that statement because omitted cells mean
zero. Appending a nonzero and its column at the same entry position
preserves their correspondence. The left-to-right scan orders those
columns and cannot duplicate a coordinate. Appending the value count
after every row records exactly where the next row starts, including
when no new values were appended.

All loops advance through finite input slices. At termination,
there are R+1 nondecreasing boundaries, the last equals the entry
count, and both entry slices have equal length. Every nonzero cell
can be reconstructed from its row range and stored column; all
others reconstruct as zero. Fresh appends hold integer copies,
so subsequent input writes cannot change the representation.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let R be the row count, C the common column count, K the number of
nonzero cells, and K_row the number stored in a particular row.
Validation reads R row lengths; conversion reads R*C cells and
appends K entries and R boundaries. Under the usual amortized slice
growth model, total work is O(1 + R + R*C), even when K is tiny.
An unrepresentable boundary count is rejected in O(1). The best
ragged error path discovers a mismatch at row 1; the worst checks all
R rows. More zeros reduce storage, not dense-input scanning.

The returned representation uses O(1 + R + K) storage, including
two K-entry slices and R+1 boundaries. Slice growth can temporarily
retain old and new arrays during copying; under geometric growth
this remains O(1 + R + K) peak additional storage. Outside result
construction, loop state is O(1). The dense input still exists
throughout conversion and uses O(R + R*C) storage itself.

Locating a row's range is O(1); scanning it takes O(K_row), and
scanning all stored cells takes O(R + K). A point lookup can scan
that row, or use binary search on its ordered columns. Dense storage
instead gives direct O(1) point access without searching. Inserting
a new entry into CSR may shift later entries and update later row
boundaries, taking O(R + K) worst-case work.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input yields width 0, offsets `[0]`, and no entries. Without
  the initial zero, there would be no start boundary.
- A row count equal to the largest `int` is rejected because the
  result would need one more boundary than an `int` can count.
- Three empty rows yield `[0,0,0,0]` offsets. Three all-zero rows of
  width 4 yield the same offsets but width 4; dimensions distinguish
  these different shapes.
- A single nonzero `[[9]]` yields offsets `[0,1]`, columns `[0]`,
  values `[9]`. A single zero yields `[0,0]` and no entries.
- The empty middle row in the trace must keep its repeated boundary.
  Empty last rows need repeated final boundaries for the same reason.
- `[[4,4]]` stores two entries with columns `[0,1]`. Deduplicating
  equal values would lose a coordinate.
- Negative integers are stored normally, including the smallest
  representable `int`; conversion does no value arithmetic.
- A coordinate-list input could repeat coordinates. This converter
  accepts dense rows, so it never encounters that ambiguity. A
  separate coordinate-list constructor must define whether to sum,
  overwrite, or reject duplicates before claiming this format.
- Ragged `[[0,1],[2]]` is rejected before construction. Rectangular
  validation remains necessary even if the short row is all zero.
- If zero means a meaningful recorded event rather than absence,
  omitting it loses information. Use a representation with explicit
  presence information for that contract.
- If all cells are nonzero, storing their column indexes adds cost
  with little benefit. Sparse does not mean smaller for every input.

##### When to choose it

Choose CSR for a mostly zero matrix whose rows will be scanned many
times with few structural updates. A million-column row containing
two nonzeros then needs two value visits rather than a million cell
visits after conversion. Conversion pays off only if later work or
storage savings justify its initial dense scan.

For frequent coordinate insertion, a map keyed by row and column
avoids shifting a packed suffix, at the cost of hashing and unordered
iteration. A coordinate list is convenient for building a matrix;
CSR is convenient once row groups are stable. For dense data or
frequent point reads, use [nested storage](
#a12-multidimensional-arrays-and-matrices) or
[flat storage](#a14-flat-storage-and-multidimensional-indexing).

The [Netlib compressed row storage description](
https://netlib.org/linalg/html_templates/node91.html) supplies the
standard format and attribution. This lesson uses zero-based entry
positions and explicitly omits zero values.

#### A.1.4 Flat storage and multidimensional indexing

##### Problem and contract

You want a rectangular grid in one contiguous integer slice rather
than a collection of row slices. The cost is that you must translate
row and column positions into one storage position. Read
[matrices](#a12-multidimensional-arrays-and-matrices) first.

Create a zero-filled grid from nonnegative row and column counts.
Return an error for negative dimensions or a product too large for
`int`; allocation must also fit available memory. Keep dimensions
explicit, so a zero-row, five-column grid retains both counts.
The example's fields are private to its package and are not modified
after construction, except for element writes to `values`.

The `index` method returns a storage position and true for an
in-bounds coordinate. It returns `(0, false)` for an invalid one;
the caller must check the boolean because position zero is valid.
Values are integers in row order, including duplicates and zeros.
No input is consumed or mutated; construction owns new storage.
No concurrent mutation occurs.

##### Mental model

Place all of row 0 first, then all of row 1, and so on. This is
row-major order. With three columns, each complete row occupies
three slots. To reach row 1, skip three slots; to reach its column
2, skip two more. The storage position is `1*3 + 2 = 5`.

In general, `row*columnCount + column` is the number of complete
earlier rows' cells plus the offset within this row. The multiplier
`columnCount` is the row stride: the distance between row starts.
For a valid flat position and positive column count, integer
division recovers the row and remainder recovers the column.
For position 5, `5/3 = 1` and `5%3 = 2`.

Allocation remembers row count, column count, and the one element
slice. A checked coordinate determines the next indexed access;
index translation itself does not move or copy elements. Higher
dimensions repeat the idea using the product of later dimensions
as each stride. Every product must fit before using it as a size.

##### Worked walkthrough

Create a 2-by-3 grid, fill it in row order with 1 through 6, find
cell `(1,2)`, then change it through a row view. Expected final
storage is `[1,2,3,4,5,9]`; its last slot represents `(1,2)`.

Initial state: dimensions are 2 and 3; no storage is allocated yet.

1. Decision: both dimensions are nonnegative. Check that 3 does not
   exceed the largest `int` divided by 2, so their product fits.
   Allocate six zeroed integer slots.
   After: dimensions `(2,3)`, values `[0,0,0,0,0,0]`.
   Known correct: the slice has exactly one slot per coordinate;
   the zeros are initialized data, not results of the fill loop.

2. Decision: fill row 0. Its start is `0*3 = 0`. Columns 0, 1, 2
   map to positions 0, 1, 2; write values 1, 2, 3 in that order.
   After: values `[1,2,3,0,0,0]`.
   Known correct: every row-0 coordinate is filled, and row 1's
   slots remain unchanged.

3. Decision: fill row 1. Its start is `1*3 = 3`. Columns 0, 1, 2
   map to positions 3, 4, 5; write 4, 5, 6.
   After: values `[1,2,3,4,5,6]`; both loops have exhausted their
   row and column ranges.
   Known correct: all six coordinates are represented exactly once.

4. Decision: call `index(1,2)`. Check `0 <= 1 < 2` and
   `0 <= 2 < 3`, then compute `1*3 + 2 = 5`. Divide and take the
   remainder of 5 by 3 to decode the coordinate.
   After: position 5, decoded row 1 and column 2, value 6.
   Known correct: the forward and reverse translations agree.

5. Decision: take row 1's range `[3:6]`, then set its column 2 to 9.
   The view shares the original slice, so it writes position 5.
   After: row view `[4,5,9]`, values `[1,2,3,4,5,9]`.
   Known correct: only coordinate `(1,2)` changed. The demonstration
   prints this result and exits.

Focused rejection: `index(0,3)` on this grid fails because column 3
equals the column count. Computing `0*3+3 = 3` before checking each
coordinate would silently access row 1 column 0, even though flat
position 3 is within the slice. Checking only the flat bound is wrong.

Counterexample to multiplying by the row count: `(1,0)` would map
to `1*2+0 = 2`, which already represents `(0,2)`. The first incorrect
write would overwrite row 0's last cell. The stride is the number
of columns in a row, not the number of rows in the grid.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program uses `fmt` for errors and printing. Save
it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. The bit expression computes
the largest platform `int`; the adjacent comment explains it.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type flatGrid struct {
	// Coordinates use the two counts; values uses one row-major slice.
	rowCount    int
	columnCount int
	values      []int
}

func newFlatGrid(rows, columns int) (flatGrid, error) {
	// Negative dimensions cannot describe a grid. Reject them before the
	// overflow check divides by rows or any allocation is attempted.
	if rows < 0 || columns < 0 {
		return flatGrid{}, fmt.Errorf("negative dimension")
	}
	// Build the largest int without assuming a word size. Compare
	// against maxInt/rows before computing the possibly unsafe product.
	maxInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	if rows > 0 && columns > maxInt/rows {
		return flatGrid{}, fmt.Errorf("dimension product overflow")
	}
	// One flat allocation owns every cell. A fresh slice has zero in
	// each position, matching the grid's initial value contract.
	return flatGrid{
		rowCount:    rows,
		columnCount: columns,
		values:      make([]int, rows*columns),
	}, nil
}

func (grid flatGrid) index(row, column int) (int, bool) {
	// Check coordinates separately. Merely checking the computed flat
	// offset would let a column spill into the following row.
	if row < 0 || row >= grid.rowCount {
		return 0, false
	}
	if column < 0 || column >= grid.columnCount {
		return 0, false
	}
	// Each complete earlier row contributes columnCount cells. The
	// constructor's product check and these bounds keep this sum safe.
	return row*grid.columnCount + column, true
}

func main() {
	grid, err := newFlatGrid(2, 3)
	// Fixed positive dimensions should succeed. Stop if construction no
	// longer honors that assumption.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	// Fill logical rows left to right. index translates every pair to
	// the next physical slice position, exposing row-major order.
	nextValue := 1
	for row := 0; row < grid.rowCount; row++ {
		for column := 0; column < grid.columnCount; column++ {
			position, ok := grid.index(row, column)
			if !ok {
				panic("loop produced invalid coordinate")
			}
			grid.values[position] = nextValue
			nextValue++
		}
	}

	// For a positive width, division finds the complete rows before an
	// offset and the remainder finds its column inside the row.
	position, ok := grid.index(1, 2)
	if !ok {
		panic("expected coordinate to exist")
	}
	decodedRow := position / grid.columnCount
	decodedColumn := position % grid.columnCount
	fmt.Println(position, decodedRow, decodedColumn)

	// Slice the second row's half-open range. This is a shared view,
	// so changing its last element must also change grid.values.
	rowStart := grid.columnCount
	rowEnd := rowStart + grid.columnCount
	rowView := grid.values[rowStart:rowEnd]
	rowView[2] = 9
	fmt.Println(grid.values)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
5 1 2
[1 2 3 4 5 9]
```

##### Why it works

The division guard checks the product before multiplication. When
rows is zero, the product is zero and division is skipped. For
positive rows and nonnegative columns, `columns <= maxInt/rows`
implies the allocated element count fits `int`.

Each valid row occupies `[row*C, (row+1)*C)`, with C columns. These
row ranges are disjoint and consecutive. A column below C therefore
selects exactly one position in that row. The largest valid position
is `R*C-1`, within the allocated slice; checking both coordinates
also excludes invalid positions that happen to land in another row.

During filling, earlier visited positions contain 1 through the
number of completed writes. The next coordinate maps to the next
storage slot, so each write extends this correct prefix. Both loops
stop at their dimension counts and fill every cell exactly once.
The final row view refers to slots 3 through 5, so its index 2
changes only flat slot 5. For zero-width grids there are no valid
coordinates, and reverse division must never be attempted.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let R and C be the dimensions, and N their product. Construction
checks two dimensions and allocates and zeroes N integer slots:
O(1 + N) work, O(N) output storage, O(1) auxiliary state. An invalid
size exits in O(1) without allocation. Coordinate translation uses
constant arithmetic and no allocation: O(1) work and storage.

The example fill writes N cells and uses O(1) auxiliary storage.
It also iterates R outer-loop positions even if C is zero, so its
general cost is O(1 + R + N). The literal demonstration uses
positive dimensions. A row view costs O(1); copying a row instead
would cost O(C) work and new storage. Printing every element costs
work proportional to N.

One element allocation removes per-row element allocations and
keeps neighboring row-major cells adjacent. This can help locality,
but speed depends on access order and the machine; it is not a
universal timing guarantee. A view of one row retains the entire
element allocation. Frequent column scans use nonadjacent slots;
column-major storage can better match that workload.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- `(0,5)` and `(3,0)` both allocate zero elements but keep different
  dimensions. Every coordinate is rejected. Dividing a position
  by a zero column count would panic and is outside valid decoding.
- `(1,1)` has one valid coordinate `(0,0)`, mapping to position 0.
  Returning zero as an error sentinel without a boolean would
  confuse this valid position with failure.
- Row -1, column -1, row R, or column C is invalid. Checking only
  the computed position misses the `(0,3)` failure traced above.
- A product exceeding the largest `int` is rejected before `make`.
  Multiplying first could wrap and make the size check meaningless.
  A product that fits may still exceed available memory; the code
  does not promise to recover from allocation failure.
- Zero, negative, repeated, and extreme integer cell values are
  preserved by indexing. Dimension arithmetic and cell arithmetic
  are different: this operation does no arithmetic on stored values.
- Appending to `rowView` can overwrite the next row if capacity
  permits. Use a full slice expression to limit append capacity, or
  copy to obtain full independence; see A.1.1. Direct writes still
  reach shared storage even with a capacity limit.
- Copying a `flatGrid` value copies its slice description, not all
  cells. Make and copy `values` explicitly for independent ownership.
- Changing dimensions after construction breaks the index proof.
  Keep the representation private behind checked operations in a
  reusable package rather than exposing mutable shape fields.

##### When to choose it

Choose flat storage for dense fixed-shape grids with many coordinate
accesses or sequential row scans. Explicit dimensions represent empty
shapes without ambiguity, and a single element allocation simplifies
passing all cells to a function expecting `[]int`.

Choose [nested rows](#a12-multidimensional-arrays-and-matrices) when
rows have independent lengths or must be replaced separately. Choose
[CSR](#a13-sparse-matrices) when most cells are zero and traversing
only nonzeros matters. A transposed view can swap coordinate roles
without copying, but it shares storage and changes the stride rules;
it is a different contract from A.1.2's independent transpose.

The Go specification defines [integer arithmetic](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Integer_operators) and
[slice expressions](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_expressions).
For applications, see the
[grid and matrix questions](#b16-grid-and-matrix-questions).

### A.2 Strings

#### A.2.1 Bytes, runes, and character sequences

##### Problem and contract

You need to count or slice text without splitting an encoded symbol.
First decide what one item means: a byte, a Unicode code point, or
a displayed character. Those are different units. Read
[array and slice indexing](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices)
before this lesson.

A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes. A byte is an integer
from 0 through 255. Its bytes cannot be changed through the string.
Unicode assigns numbers called code points; a `rune` is Go's
`int32` alias used to represent one of those numbers.
UTF-8 encodes a valid code point using one to four bytes. A displayed
character can combine several code points, so counting runes does
not always count what a reader sees as characters.

Our function accepts a string containing valid UTF-8 and returns
the byte start of each rune followed by the final byte length.
An invalid encoding returns a nil slice and an error. Empty input
returns `[0]`: the sole boundary is also the end. Preserve input,
order, duplicates, and exact encoding; do not normalize text or
combine displayed characters. Returned offsets refer to this input
string, not to an independently edited version. Allocations must fit
available memory, including one extra end boundary.

##### Mental model

`len(text)` counts bytes, and `text[byteOffset]` returns one byte.
A `range` loop over a string instead decodes runes and reports each
rune's starting byte offset. A rune ordinal is its zero-based
position in the decoded sequence, not its starting byte offset.

For `"A\u00e9\U0001f642"`, A uses one byte, the e with acute accent
uses two, and the smiling face uses four. There are seven bytes but
three runes. Rune number 2 starts at byte 3, not byte 2.

Build `boundaries` in encounter order. `boundaries[2] = 3` means
"the third rune starts at byte position 3." Once the end boundary
is appended, rune number 2 occupies `text[3:7]`. The range includes
byte 3 and excludes byte 7, matching Go's half-open slice notation.
Validate first so that decoding never silently substitutes an
invalid sequence with the replacement code point U+FFFD.

##### Worked walkthrough

Input is `"A\u00e9\U0001f642"`. Expected boundaries are `[0,1,3,7]`.
The Unicode escapes specify code points; they do not appear as
literal backslashes in the input's bytes.

```text
byte offset:     0   1   2   3   4   5   6
hex byte:       41  c3  a9  f0  9f  99  82
rune ordinal:    0   1       2
code point:    0041 00e9    1f642
end boundary:                                7
```

Initial state: input has byte length 7; `boundaries` has not been
allocated. No rune boundaries have been confirmed yet.

1. Decision: `utf8.ValidString` checks all seven bytes. Their
   sequences encode U+0041, U+00E9, and U+1F642, so validation
   succeeds. Allocate an empty result slice.
   After: `boundaries = []`; input is unchanged.
   Known correct: decoding can now enumerate original code points
   without replacement caused by malformed input.

2. Decision: the first `range` iteration begins at byte 0 and
   decodes U+0041. Append its starting offset, 0.
   After: `boundaries = [0]`; the next rune begins at byte 1.
   Known correct: rune ordinal 0 begins at byte 0. Its final slice
   end is not stored yet.

3. Decision: decode bytes 1 and 2 as U+00E9. Append start offset 1;
   advancing two bytes moves the decoder to byte 3.
   After: `boundaries = [0,1]`; the next rune begins at byte 3.
   Known correct: rune 0 occupies `[0:1]`, and rune 1 starts at 1.

4. Decision: decode bytes 3 through 6 as U+1F642. Append start 3;
   advancing four bytes reaches the input length, 7.
   After: `boundaries = [0,1,3]`; decoding has no bytes remaining.
   Known correct: rune 1 occupies `[1:3]`, and rune 2 starts at 3.

5. Decision: `range` is exhausted. Append byte length 7 as the end
   boundary and return with a nil error.
   After: `boundaries = [0,1,3,7]`; rune count is `4-1 = 3`.
   Known correct: every adjacent boundary pair selects exactly
   one complete rune, including the final range `[3:7]`.

Focused failure: `"A\xffB"` contains an invalid UTF-8 byte at
offset 1. Validation rejects it before constructing any offsets.
Without validation, `range` reports U+FFFD at byte 1 and continues
at byte 2. That recovery is useful for tolerant display, but violates
this function's strict-input contract.

Counterexample to slicing by rune ordinal: rune number 2 in the
ordinary input starts at byte 3. Taking `text[2:3]` instead selects
only byte `a9`, the trailing byte of the previous rune. It produces
invalid UTF-8. Translate the ordinal through the boundary slice.

##### Implementation

This complete program uses `fmt` and `unicode/utf8`. Save it as
`main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It prints byte and rune counts,
boundaries, and each complete rune. `%+q` prints non-ASCII content
as escapes so the output does not depend on font rendering.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"unicode/utf8"
)

func runeByteBoundaries(text string) ([]int, error) {
	// A range loop silently replaces malformed bytes with U+FFFD. Reject
	// them first so every reported boundary refers to the original text.
	if !utf8.ValidString(text) {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("input is not valid UTF-8")
	}

	// Ranging over a string reports the byte offset where each decoded
	// rune begins. Save those offsets in reading order.
	boundaries := make([]int, 0)
	for byteOffset := range text {
		boundaries = append(boundaries, byteOffset)
	}
	// len(text) is the exclusive end of the final rune. Appending it
	// gives empty input the single boundary [0].
	boundaries = append(boundaries, len(text))
	return boundaries, nil
}

func main() {
	// These runes use one, two, and four bytes, making byte offsets
	// visibly different from rune ordinals.
	text := "A\u00e9\U0001f642"
	boundaries, err := runeByteBoundaries(text)
	// This literal is valid UTF-8, so an error contradicts the example.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(text), len(boundaries)-1)
	fmt.Println(boundaries)

	// Each neighboring pair forms a half-open byte range for one rune.
	// ordinal names the rune's logical position, not a byte position.
	for ordinal := 0; ordinal+1 < len(boundaries); ordinal++ {
		start := boundaries[ordinal]
		end := boundaries[ordinal+1]
		fmt.Printf("%d:%+q\n", ordinal, text[start:end])
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
7 3
[0 1 3 7]
0:"A"
1:"\u00e9"
2:"\U0001f642"
```

##### Why it works

Validation establishes that every input byte belongs to a valid
UTF-8 sequence. String iteration then visits exactly the start of
each sequence, in increasing byte order. Initially the result has
no starts; each iteration appends the next true start without
changing any earlier one. The decoder always advances by at least
one byte, so the finite string is eventually exhausted.

Appending the byte length closes the last sequence. Therefore each
adjacent pair surrounds one complete rune, and there is one more
boundary than runes. Empty input has no iterations and ends with
`[0]`, preserving that count relation. This establishes safe rune
slices, not safe displayed-character slices: multiple runes may
belong to one displayed character.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let B be the input byte count and R its rune count. Validation scans
up to B bytes; successful decoding scans them again and appends R+1
integers. Under ordinary amortized slice growth, total work is
O(1 + B), with O(1 + R) output storage. Construction can transiently
hold old and new result arrays while growing, remaining O(1 + R)
under geometric growth. Other working state is O(1).

Malformed input can fail early or after O(B) validation work and
allocates no boundary result. For valid input, preprocessing pays
for O(1) lookup of any rune's byte range later. If you only scan
once, a direct `range` loop avoids storing all offsets. Repeatedly
rescanning from the start to find each rune would revisit earlier
bytes; a long ASCII string would take quadratic total work.

Go does not promise whether slicing a string copies its bytes.
An implementation may share storage, so a small substring can keep
a larger original allocation reachable. Code must not rely on
either copying or sharing. The offset slice stores only integers
and does not keep the input alive. Printing the example is
additional work proportional to its displayed output.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- `""` yields `[0]` and rune count 0. Do not append both an initial
  zero and a final zero for empty input; that would invent one rune.
- `"aa"` yields `[0,1,2]`. Equal values still have separate starts;
  a set of rune values cannot represent their positions or count.
- `"\U0001f642"` yields `[0,4]`. Its sole rune occupies four bytes;
  byte length 4 is not rune count 4.
- `"\x00A"` yields `[0,1,2]`. Zero is valid string data and does not
  terminate a Go string. Treating it as an end marker loses A.
- A valid `"\ufffd"` yields `[0,3]` and is accepted. Seeing U+FFFD
  alone does not prove invalid input; the explicit UTF-8 validation
  distinguishes encoded replacement characters from malformed bytes.
- Both `"\u00e9"` and `"e\u0301"` can display an accented e, but
  their boundaries are `[0,2]` and `[0,1,3]`. They are different
  byte strings with one and two runes. Normalization means choosing
  a consistent code-point sequence for equivalent text. It would be
  a separate contract, not an automatic effect of string comparison.
- A displayed character may be a grapheme cluster, meaning several
  code points treated together for text editing. Emoji sequences
  can have this property too. Neither byte iteration nor `[]rune`
  conversion supplies grapheme segmentation.
- `text[len(text)]` is out of bounds even though `len(text)` is a
  valid exclusive slice end. The last boundary marks an end, not
  another rune start.
- For very large strings, the offset result needs R+1 integer
  slots, not B bytes. Stream once with `range` if storing every
  boundary exceeds your memory budget.

##### When to choose it

ASCII represents its 128 code points using one byte each. Use bytes
for an ASCII-only alphabet or a byte-oriented protocol.
Use decoded runes when the problem explicitly defines items as
Unicode code points. Keep a boundary index when many later queries
need rune positions but must return slices of the original encoding.

For cursor movement or displayed-character reversal, first define
grapheme boundaries; the rune model above is insufficient. For
arbitrary binary strings, skip UTF-8 interpretation and keep byte
semantics. Choose the unit from the contract before choosing an
algorithm such as the [substring methods](
#b5-contiguous-subarrays-and-substrings).

Continue with [editable buffers](#a22-mutable-character-buffers).
The Go specification owns [string types](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#String_types) and
[range behavior](https://go.dev/ref/spec#For_range).
[UTF-8 validation](https://pkg.go.dev/unicode/utf8#ValidString)
defines the acceptance check. Rob Pike's
[Go strings article](https://go.dev/blog/strings) explains the
distinction between bytes, code points, and characters.
For displayed-character boundaries, see Unicode's
[text segmentation standard](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/).

#### A.2.2 Mutable character buffers

##### Problem and contract

You need to change text at specific positions while preserving the
original string. A Go string cannot be modified by indexed writes.
Convert to a mutable buffer, apply edits, then construct a result
string. First read [text units](
#a21-bytes-runes-and-character-sequences)
and [slice ownership](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices).

Our operation reverses the code-point order of a valid UTF-8 string.
It returns the reversed string and a nil error, or `""` and an error
for malformed UTF-8. Empty input returns `""` successfully. Preserve
every code point, including duplicates and zero, without changing
the input or normalizing it. This is not displayed-character
reversal: combining marks may move away from their original bases.
Allocation must fit available memory; no concurrent mutation occurs.

##### Mental model

A `[]byte` buffer supports byte edits. A `[]rune` buffer supports
code-point edits after decoding. The conversion determines what an
index means: `characters[1]` in a rune slice selects the second code
point regardless of how many bytes its UTF-8 encoding used.

Validate the input, then decode it into `codePoints := []rune(text)`.
Keep `left` at the first unresolved position and `right` at the last.
Swap those code points, then move both positions inward. Positions
outside this unresolved range are already in their final places.
Stop when the positions meet or cross; encode the slice back into
an immutable string.

Conversion produces an editable representation independent of the
input string. Assigning another variable to that slice afterward
does share storage, as A.1.1 explains. Conversion to a result string
preserves the current contents even if the buffer is later edited.
These are observable ownership guarantees; a compiler may eliminate
unnecessary physical copies when behavior remains the same.

##### Worked walkthrough

Input is `"A\u00e9\U0001f642B"`. Expected result is
`"B\U0001f642\u00e9A"`: reverse four code points, not eight bytes.

Initial state: no buffer exists. The input is eight bytes encoding
U+0041, U+00E9, U+1F642, and U+0042, in that order.

1. Decision: UTF-8 validation succeeds. Decode the four code points
   into a rune slice; initialize `left = 0`, `right = 3`.
   After: buffer `[U+0041,U+00E9,U+1F642,U+0042]`, unresolved
   positions 0 through 3.
   Known correct: every rune equals its original input code point.
   No position is fixed in the reversed result yet.

2. Decision: `0 < 3`, so exchange positions 0 and 3. Move `left`
   to 1 and `right` to 2, removing the settled outer positions.
   After: buffer `[U+0042,U+00E9,U+1F642,U+0041]`, unresolved
   positions 1 through 2.
   Known correct: positions 0 and 3 hold the last and first input
   runes, exactly where they belong in reversed order.

3. Decision: `1 < 2`, so exchange positions 1 and 2. Move `left`
   to 2 and `right` to 1.
   After: buffer `[U+0042,U+1F642,U+00E9,U+0041]`; the unresolved
   range is empty because the positions have crossed.
   Known correct: both outer pairs now have their reversed values.

4. Decision: `2 < 1` is false. Encode the buffer as UTF-8 and return
   it with a nil error.
   After: result `"B\U0001f642\u00e9A"`; input is unchanged.
   Known correct: every original code point appears at its opposite
   position, and the complete result remains valid UTF-8.

Focused middle case: `"abc"` decodes to `[a,b,c]`, with positions
0 and 2. Swap a and c to get `[c,b,a]`; both positions move to 1.
Since `1 < 1` is false, b stays in the middle. No extra swap occurs.
Empty input gives `left = 0`, `right = -1`; the loop never indexes
the slice. A single rune similarly needs no swap.

Counterexample to reversing bytes: `"\u00e9"` has bytes `c3 a9`.
Swapping its two bytes produces `a9 c3`, which is invalid UTF-8,
although reversing one code point should leave it unchanged.
The first wrong decision is selecting bytes as the editable unit.

##### Implementation

This complete program uses `fmt` and `unicode/utf8`. Save it as
`main.go` and run `go run main.go`. Only `main` prints; the function
performs local buffer edits and returns a new immutable value.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"unicode/utf8"
)

func reverseCodePoints(text string) (string, error) {
	// Converting malformed bytes to runes would replace them with U+FFFD
	// and lose the original input. Reject that lossy case first.
	if !utf8.ValidString(text) {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("input is not valid UTF-8")
	}
	// []rune makes every code point one addressable element, even when
	// whether its UTF-8 encoding occupied one byte or several.
	codePoints := []rune(text)
	left := 0
	right := len(codePoints) - 1

	// Everything outside [left, right] is already in its final reversed
	// position. Swap the two unresolved ends, then shrink that interval.
	for left < right {
		codePoints[left], codePoints[right] =
			codePoints[right], codePoints[left]
		left++
		right--
	}
	// Converting the finished rune slice back to string re-encodes its
	// points as valid UTF-8 and returns immutable text.
	return string(codePoints), nil
}

func main() {
	// Unequal byte widths make it clear that the function reverses code
	// points rather than individual UTF-8 bytes.
	text := "A\u00e9\U0001f642B"
	reversed, err := reverseCodePoints(text)
	// Valid literal input means an error would contradict the setup.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("%+q\n", reversed)
}
```

Expected output is `"B\U0001f642\u00e9A"`.

##### Why it works

Validation prevents conversion from replacing malformed byte
sequences. The rune buffer therefore starts with exactly the input
code points. Initially every position is unresolved, so the claim
that all outside positions are correct holds without any work.

At each iteration, `left` and `right` are opposite positions in the
original sequence. Swapping them places each rune at its reversed
destination. Earlier settled positions are untouched. Moving both
indexes inward preserves the claim and reduces the unresolved
length by two. It eventually reaches zero or one; a sole middle
rune is already in its correct position. Encoding then represents
that proven sequence as a string.

This proof concerns code-point positions only. `"e\u0301x"` reverses
to `"x\u0301e"`; the combining acute accent now follows x. Correct
rune reversal can therefore be incorrect for a text editor's
displayed-character contract.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let B be the input byte count and R its rune count. Validation and
decoding inspect O(B) bytes. The loop performs floor(R/2) swaps;
encoding visits R runes and writes B bytes because the same code
points have only changed order. Total successful work is O(1 + B).
There is no faster successful path for already reversed or all-equal
input: validation and conversion still inspect the input.

The rune buffer needs O(R) auxiliary storage; each element is an
`int32`. The returned UTF-8 string needs O(B) output storage. Both
can be live during encoding, so peak additional storage is O(B + R).
No recursion is used. Invalid input returns during validation with
no rune buffer or output construction, after O(B) worst-case work.

A byte buffer avoids rune decoding for an ASCII-only contract and
uses one byte per element. It is also right for arbitrary binary
data. For Unicode code-point edits, smaller byte storage does not
justify splitting encoded sequences. Repeated immutable string
reconstruction for every swap would repeatedly copy the whole
result; one mutable buffer avoids that repeated work.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- `""` and `"Z"` return unchanged. With empty input, `right = -1`
  is safe because the loop condition prevents any access.
- `"abba"` returns `"abba"`; equal values still pass through the
  same swaps. Equality is not a reason to stop before inner work.
- `"\x00A"` reverses to `"A\x00"`. Zero is a normal code point,
  not a terminator. A byte-oriented end marker would truncate it.
- `"\xff"` is rejected. Converting directly to `[]rune` would
  replace it with U+FFFD and lose the original byte, making a claim
  of byte-preserving reversal false.
- `"\ufffd"` is valid input and stays unchanged. It is different
  from the malformed-byte case despite similar possible display.
- Rune reversal breaks some displayed characters, as the combining
  mark example demonstrates. Grapheme segmentation requires a
  separate Unicode-aware method and contract.
- `[]byte("cat")` followed by changing index 0 to `'b'` produces
  `"bat"` without changing `"cat"`. After saving `string(buffer)`,
  changing buffer index 1 to `'u'` produces `"but"` in the buffer;
  the saved string remains `"bat"`.
- Assigning `alias := buffer` shares the buffer. Edits through
  `alias` also change `buffer`; make and copy when both mutable
  versions must evolve independently.
- Inserting one rune shifts later positions in a rune slice.
  An old byte-boundary index from A.2.1 is also stale after edits
  that change encoding widths. Rebuild indexes for the edited text.
- A very large ASCII input expands to four-byte rune slots during
  conversion. Use the contract's byte semantics when sufficient;
  rune conversion is not free just because the source is ASCII.

##### When to choose it

Choose an editable byte or rune buffer when the algorithm must
overwrite, swap, or compact existing positions. The decisive choice
is the text unit promised by the problem. Reversing ASCII DNA bases
can use bytes; reversing Unicode code points needs rune-aware work.

When you only append output pieces, a
[string builder](#a23-string-builders) avoids exposing editable
positions and fits the construction workflow. When you only read,
string iteration avoids allocating a mutable copy. The
[palindrome methods](#b8-palindromes-and-string-transformations)
apply related position logic under their own contracts.

The Go specification defines [string and slice conversions](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Conversions_to_and_from_a_string_type).
Use [UTF-8 validation](https://pkg.go.dev/unicode/utf8#ValidString)
for the strict input policy demonstrated here.

#### A.2.3 String builders

##### Problem and contract

You need to assemble output from pieces as you discover them. If
every append rebuilds an immutable string, earlier output may be
copied repeatedly. A builder keeps a growing construction buffer
and exposes the result as a string. Read
[string units](#a21-bytes-runes-and-character-sequences) and
[slice growth](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) first.

Our function joins nonempty string pieces in their original order,
placing the chosen separator only between retained pieces. Keep
duplicates and exact bytes; do not trim whitespace or validate
UTF-8. Empty or nil input, or input containing only empty pieces,
returns `""`. An empty separator simply concatenates retained pieces.
Inputs are unchanged, and the returned string is immutable.

The total output and allocations must fit `int` and available
memory. One goroutine owns the local builder. A non-zero builder
must not be copied by value; keep it local or pass a pointer when
sharing it with a helper. Allocation failures are outside this
function's successful contract.

##### Mental model

Keep `output`, a zero-value `strings.Builder`, and `wroteAny`, a
boolean meaning "at least one nonempty piece has been appended."
An empty piece changes neither state. Before a nonempty piece,
append the separator only when `wroteAny` is already true. Then
append the piece and mark the flag true. Stop after all pieces and
call `String` to obtain the result.

The builder's length counts accumulated bytes, not runes or pieces.
It is append-oriented and does not offer arbitrary indexed edits.
Its exact capacity is not part of the result contract. `Grow(n)`
can reserve room for n additional bytes when a safe size is known;
it does not append n zero bytes or change the length.

For comparison, repeatedly joining four one-byte pieces with `+`
can construct prefixes of lengths 1, 2, 3, and 4. Each later step
may copy the earlier prefix again. A construction buffer can retain
earlier bytes across appends until capacity needs to grow.

##### Worked walkthrough

Input pieces are `["", "go", "", "rust", "go"]`; separator is
`"|"`. Expected result is `"go|rust|go"`, with ten bytes.

Initial state: zero-value `output` has empty contents and length 0;
`wroteAny = false`. No input pieces have been processed.

1. Decision: piece 0 is empty, so skip it before any separator or
   piece write.
   After: output `""`, length 0, `wroteAny = false`.
   Known correct: the processed prefix contains no retained pieces
   and therefore contributes no output or separator.

2. Decision: piece 1 is `"go"`. Since `wroteAny` is false, do not
   append a separator. Append its two bytes and set the flag true.
   After: output `"go"`, length 2, `wroteAny = true`.
   Known correct: the first retained piece has no leading separator.

3. Decision: piece 2 is empty; skip it without writing anything.
   After: output `"go"`, length 2, `wroteAny = true`.
   Known correct: an empty middle piece has not created an extra
   separator or erased the record of an earlier retained piece.

4. Decision: piece 3 is `"rust"`, and `wroteAny` is true. Append
   `"|"`, reaching length 3, then `"rust"`, reaching length 7.
   After: output `"go|rust"`, length 7, `wroteAny = true`.
   Known correct: exactly one separator joins the two retained
   pieces. Their bytes and order match the input.

5. Decision: piece 4 is `"go"`. Append `"|"` to reach length 8,
   then `"go"` to reach length 10; keep `wroteAny` true.
   After: output `"go|rust|go"`, length 10.
   Known correct: the duplicate piece is preserved as a separate
   retained occurrence with one separator before it.

6. Decision: no pieces remain. Return `output.String()`.
   After: result is `"go|rust|go"`.
   Known correct: every retained piece occurs once in order, with
   separators between pieces and none at either end.

Focused empty case: `["", ""]` skips both pieces. The flag stays
false, the builder stays empty, and `String()` returns `""`.
With `["go", "rust"]` and an empty separator, the separator write
has length zero and the result is `"gorust"`.

Counterexample to using the original piece index for separators:
on `["", "go"]`, testing `pieceIndex > 0` before writing `"go"`
would add a leading `"|"`. The first wrong decision confuses earlier
input positions with earlier retained pieces. `wroteAny` records
the fact actually needed by the contract.

##### Implementation

This complete program uses `fmt` and `strings`. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. `Builder.WriteString` documents that it
returns the full byte length and a nil error, so these calls need
no error branch. Only `main` prints; construction stays local.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)

func joinNonemptyPieces(pieces []string, separator string) string {
	// A zero-value Builder is ready to use and grows one output buffer.
	// Keep one instance because copying a used Builder is invalid.
	var output strings.Builder
	// wroteAny means output already contains a retained piece. It is
	// the exact condition for writing a separator before the next one.
	wroteAny := false
	for _, piece := range pieces {
		// Reject an empty piece before writing it or a separator. This
		// prevents leading, trailing, and doubled separators.
		if piece == "" {
			continue
		}
		if wroteAny {
			output.WriteString(separator)
		}
		// Append the retained text, then remember that future pieces need a
		// separator. Input position alone cannot provide that fact.
		output.WriteString(piece)
		wroteAny = true
	}
	// String exposes the completed immutable result. No more writes
	// builder occur after this point.
	return output.String()
}

func main() {
	// End and middle empty pieces exercise every skip position.
	pieces := []string{"", "go", "", "rust", "go"}
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", joinNonemptyPieces(pieces, "|"))
}
```

Expected output is `"go|rust|go"`.

##### Why it works

Initially no pieces are retained, so an empty output with a false
flag is correct. After every processed input prefix, maintain that
the builder contains exactly its nonempty pieces joined by the
separator, and the flag states whether that sequence is nonempty.

Skipping an empty piece preserves both facts. For the first
nonempty piece, the false flag prevents a leading separator. For
each later nonempty piece, the true flag adds exactly the separator
needed to extend the sequence. Appending the unchanged piece bytes
preserves order and duplicates. Each loop iteration consumes one
input piece, so the loop terminates after the finite slice ends.
The invariant then describes the complete required result.

The builder's API preserves returned strings as immutable values.
A later append through the same correctly used builder cannot
rewrite an earlier returned string's contents. This does not allow
copying a non-zero builder: its internal ownership rules must still
be respected.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let P be the number of input pieces and L the output byte length,
including separators. Inspecting pieces takes O(P) work. Appending
writes each output byte, with occasional buffer growth copying
earlier bytes. Under the usual amortized growth model, total work
is O(1 + P + L). All-empty input still examines P pieces but needs
no output buffer. Output construction uses O(L) byte storage;
loop state beyond construction is O(1).

Repeatedly concatenating P equal nonempty pieces into an accumulating
string can copy a growing prefix each time: for fixed piece length,
the total copied length grows quadratically with P. The builder
avoids that repeated-prefix workload. A fixed expression such as
`first + ":" + second` does not imply the same repeated-loop cost.

In the installed Go 1.26.5 implementation, checked on 2026-10-30,
`String()` exposes the accumulated bytes without a final byte copy.
The result can therefore retain spare buffer capacity. Keeping a
short result after a large `Grow` may retain a large allocation.
Growth can also temporarily hold old and new buffers, still O(L)
under ordinary growth when capacity was not over-reserved. These
allocation details are implementation observations, not a promise
of a particular capacity or allocation count from the public API.

Use `strings.Join` when every existing piece should be kept. It
handles separators directly; this custom loop exists because empty
pieces must be filtered. Streaming to an `io.Writer` can avoid
retaining the whole result, but adds write-error and partial-output
behavior that this in-memory function does not have.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil pieces, an empty slice, and `["", ""]` return `""`. A loop
  that starts with `pieces[0]` would panic on the first two inputs.
- `["", "go", ""]` returns `"go"`. Index-based separator logic
  creates leading or trailing punctuation instead of filtering.
- `["go", "go"]` returns `"go|go"` with separator `"|"`.
  Deduplicating pieces would change the contract.
- A whitespace piece `" "` is nonempty and remains present.
  Trimming it would silently turn a byte-preserving join into a
  different operation.
- `["a", "b"]` with separator `"::"` yields `"a::b"`; separator
  length need not be one. With `""`, the result is `"ab"`.
- `["\xff", "\x00"]` with separator `"|"` yields bytes
  `ff 7c 00`. `WriteString` copies bytes without UTF-8 validation;
  use A.2.1's validation policy if your output must be Unicode text.
- After writing `"a"`, take `snapshot := output.String()`, then
  append `"b"`. The builder reads `"ab"`, while `snapshot` remains
  `"a"`. After `Reset`, the builder is empty; saved strings remain
  unchanged. Do not assume Reset preserves a reusable allocation.
- Copying a used builder with assignment and then writing through
  the copy violates its API contract. Go 1.26.5 detects such a write
  and panics. Pass `*strings.Builder` to helpers instead of a value.
- `Grow(-1)` panics. A size estimate must be nonnegative and must
  not overflow while being calculated. This implementation avoids
  a speculative preallocation calculation altogether.
- Very large output still needs memory for all L bytes. A builder
  removes repeated-prefix copying, not the output storage cost.

##### When to choose it

Use a builder when one owner appends pieces while generating output,
especially when filtering or formatting decisions happen inside a
loop. Use `strings.Join` for an existing slice whose every element
belongs in the result; joining `["", "go"]` directly intentionally
keeps the empty first element and gives `"|go"` with separator `"|"`.

Use a [mutable buffer](#a22-mutable-character-buffers) when later
steps must edit earlier positions. Use a direct concatenation for
a small fixed expression, and an `io.Writer` when output should be
sent incrementally instead of kept as one string. The destination
and required edit operations decide which representation fits.

The standard library owns [strings.Builder](
https://pkg.go.dev/strings#Builder), its
[WriteString guarantee](
https://pkg.go.dev/strings#Builder.WriteString),
and [strings.Join](https://pkg.go.dev/strings#Join).
The implementation observation above was verified against the
installed Go 1.26.5 `strings/builder.go`, not inferred from timing.

### A.3 Linked lists

#### A.3.1 Singly linked lists

##### Problem and contract

A sequence sometimes needs cheap insertion or removal after a known
element. A singly linked list stores each value in a node with a
pointer to the next node. The head points to the first node; the last
node points to nil. Read [slice ownership](
#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) and
[Go pointer basics](https://go.dev/tour/moretypes/1) first.

Our operation removes the first node whose integer value equals a
target. It returns the possibly changed head and whether removal
