values. Each pop reads the corresponding boundary, removes one
position, and leaves the other positions in their former order.

When full, growth copies offset 0 to new index 0, offset 1 to index 1,
and so on. It therefore preserves logical order while changing only
physical positions. Resetting head to 0 reestablishes the same
invariant in the larger storage before the pending push continues.

`wrapIndex` produces the mathematical modulo result without first
forming a sum that might overflow. Each ordinary operation has a
fixed number of steps; a growth loop advances through exactly the old
size and terminates. End queries read but do not change the invariant.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be current size and M be the greatest size reached since the
current backing allocation was created. Pops and end queries take
O(1) time. A push is O(1) without growth and O(N) when full because
growth copies N values. Doubling makes a sequence of pushes amortized
O(1) per push: intervening insertions pay for each larger copy.

Immediately after growth, capacity is between N and a constant
multiple of N. Because the deque never shrinks, later pops can leave
capacity much larger than current size. Retained storage is O(M),
operations use O(1) temporary storage, and growth temporarily holds
O(N) old values plus the new allocation. The `values` method uses
O(N) output storage.

A linked deque avoids resize copies but allocates nodes and stores two
links per value. A fixed circular deque gives strict capacity and
constant operation work but must reject insertions when full.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- The zero-value deque has no slots. Grow before the first modulo or
  the program divides by zero.
- Empty pops and end queries return zero and false. A stored zero
  returns zero and true.
- One value is both front and back. Either pop must restore the same
  canonical empty state with size 0 and head 0.
- Full wrapped storage must copy in logical order during growth.
  Copying the physical slice `[5,2,3,4]` directly would rotate values.
- Push front at head 0 wraps directly to `capacity - 1`; every other
  head decrements normally. Blind subtraction can produce -1, while
  add-then-modulo arithmetic can overflow at extreme capacities.
- Pop back decreases size but does not move head. Moving both ends
  would skip the current front.
- Near the integer limit, doubling would overflow even when one more
  element still fits. Growth clamps to the largest `int`; a push that
  would exceed that element count is outside the stated contract.
- The deque never shrinks. A burst can retain a large backing array;
  add an explicit shrink policy only when memory behavior requires it.

##### When to choose it

Choose a deque when both the oldest and newest pending values need
constant-time access: sliding-window candidates, 0-1 breadth-first
search, work stealing, and palindrome comparisons are examples.

Use a queue when only front removal and back insertion are needed; its
smaller API makes invalid end choices impossible. Use a stack when
only one end matters. Use a priority queue when value priority, not
position, selects the next removal.

The ordinary operation family follows the authoritative [Design
Circular Deque](https://leetcode.com/problems/design-circular-deque/)
problem, while this implementation grows instead of rejecting on
full. The [0-1 BFS](#b132-0-1-bfs-deque-and-distance-array)
and [monotonic deque](#a54-monotonic-deques) show two applications.

#### A.5.3 Array-backed and linked queues

##### Problem and contract

An unbounded logical queue can store values in contiguous array
storage or in separately allocated linked nodes. Both must expose the
same first-in, first-out behavior even though their memory and growth
costs differ.

Our two integer queues support enqueue, dequeue, front, size, and a
front-to-back snapshot. Their zero values are ready to use. Empty
dequeue and front return zero and false. Duplicates and zero are
valid. Operations mutate only the selected queue, and allocation must
fit memory. Methods require a non-nil queue pointer. Unsynchronized
concurrent access is excluded.

The array-backed version appends at the physical end, advances a head
index on dequeue, and occasionally compacts when at least half of its
stored slice is a discarded prefix. The linked version retains head
and tail pointers. Read [dynamic slices](
#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices), [singly linked lists](
#a31-singly-linked-lists), and [queue order](
#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) first.

##### Mental model

For the array-backed queue, `values[head:]` is the complete logical
queue. Positions before head are consumed holes, not members. Enqueue
appends after every live value. Dequeue reads at head and advances it.
Compaction copies only the live suffix into a new slice and resets
head to 0; logical order does not change.

For the linked queue, head is the oldest node and tail is the newest.
Enqueue links a new node after tail. Dequeue moves head to its next
node. When the last node leaves, tail must also become nil.

In either representation, values from front to back are exactly the
successful enqueues not yet dequeued, in their original order. The
next dequeue can only return the oldest one.

##### Worked walkthrough

Apply the same operations to both queues: enqueue 4, 7, and 9;
dequeue; enqueue 11; then drain. Expected dequeue order is
`[4,7,9,11]`, and both queues end empty.

Initial state: the array slice is nil with head 0. Linked head and
tail are nil. Both sizes are 0.

1. Decision: enqueue 4, 7, and 9. Append each array value. Link each
   new node after the linked tail, setting both ends on the first.
   After: both logical orders are `[4,7,9]` and sizes are 3.
   Known correct: enqueue order is preserved, with 4 oldest and 9
   newest.

2. Decision: dequeue the front. The array reads index 0 and advances
   head to 1. The linked queue moves head from node 4 to node 7 and
   detaches node 4.
   After: both return 4 and contain `[7,9]`.
   Known correct: exactly the oldest value left; retained order is
   unchanged.

3. Decision: the array has one consumed position out of three, less
   than half, so it does not compact. Enqueue 11 by appending; link
   node 11 after the linked tail.
   After: array storage is `[0,7,9,11]` with head 1; both logical
   orders are `[7,9,11]`.
   Known correct: the hole is outside the logical suffix and 11 is
   newest in both queues.

4. Decision: dequeue 7. Array head becomes 2, so two of four stored
   positions are discarded; copy live suffix `[9,11]` into a new
   slice and reset head to 0. Linked head moves to node 9.
   After: both return 7 and contain `[9,11]`.
   Known correct: compaction changed storage positions, not order.

5. Decision: dequeue 9. In the array queue, advancing head leaves
   one hole and one live value, so compact `[11]` and reset head.
   In the linked queue, move head from node 9 to node 11.
   After: both return 9 and contain `[11]`; returned order so far is
   `[4,7,9]`.
   Known correct: compaction again preserves the sole live value,
   which is both the oldest and newest remaining item.

6. Decision: dequeue 11. The array has no remaining suffix, so reset
   its slice and head. The linked head becomes nil, so clear tail.
   After: returned order is `[4,7,9,11]`; both queues are empty.
   Known correct: every value left in enqueue order exactly once, and
   neither representation keeps a stale logical end.

7. Decision: try one more dequeue and front query on each queue.
   After: every operation returns zero and false without mutation.
   Known correct: empty is observable without confusing it with a
   queued zero, so processing stops.

Focused duplicate case: enqueue 5 twice and dequeue twice returns 5
twice; node identity or array position distinguishes occurrences.
Focused reuse case: after complete drain, either queue can enqueue
again from its canonical empty state.

Counterexample to a linked queue with only a head pointer: enqueue
would have to traverse every node to find the back. The first wrong
decision is discarding the tail information needed for O(1) append.

##### Implementation

This complete program runs both representations through the same
operation sequence. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type sliceQueue struct {
	// Live values occupy [head, len(values)); earlier slots are retired.
	values []int
	head   int
}

func (queue *sliceQueue) enqueue(value int) {
	// Appending places the new value after all live values, at the back.
	queue.values = append(queue.values, value)
}

func (queue *sliceQueue) dequeue() (int, bool) {
	// head equal to length means no live value remains. The slice may
	// still contain retired slots, so len alone is not the queue size.
	if queue.head == len(queue.values) {
		return 0, false
	}
	value := queue.values[queue.head]
	// Clear references held by the retired slot, then move the logical
	// front one position right without shifting every remaining value.
	queue.values[queue.head] = 0
	queue.head++

	remaining := len(queue.values) - queue.head
	if remaining == 0 {
		// Release drained storage and restore the zero-value state.
		queue.values = nil
		queue.head = 0
	} else if queue.head >= remaining {
		// Reclaim the prefix only after retired slots occupy at least half.
		// This bounds retained waste without copying after every dequeue.
		compacted := append([]int(nil), queue.values[queue.head:]...)
		queue.values = compacted
		queue.head = 0
	}
	return value, true
}

func (queue *sliceQueue) front() (int, bool) {
	// The first live slice position is the logical front.
	if queue.head == len(queue.values) {
		return 0, false
	}
	return queue.values[queue.head], true
}

func (queue *sliceQueue) size() int {
	// Subtract retired prefix slots from the physical slice length.
	return len(queue.values) - queue.head
}

func (queue *sliceQueue) snapshot() []int {
	// Copy so callers cannot mutate the queue through shared storage.
	return append([]int(nil), queue.values[queue.head:]...)
}

type linkedQueue struct {
	// head is oldest, tail is newest, and size counts the linked nodes.
	head *queueNode
	tail *queueNode
	size int
}

type queueNode struct {
	value int
	next  *queueNode
}

func (queue *linkedQueue) enqueue(value int) {
	node := &queueNode{value: value}
	// The first node becomes head. Later nodes follow the old tail
	// so existing FIFO order is preserved.
	if queue.tail == nil {
		queue.head = node
	} else {
		queue.tail.next = node
	}
	// Both branches make node the newest value.
	queue.tail = node
	queue.size++
}

func (queue *linkedQueue) dequeue() (int, bool) {
	// A nil head is the linked representation of empty.
	if queue.head == nil {
		return 0, false
	}
	removed := queue.head
	// Expose the next-oldest node before detaching the former head.
	queue.head = removed.next
	removed.next = nil
	queue.size--
	if queue.head == nil {
		// Removing the final node must clear tail as well as head.
		queue.tail = nil
	}
	return removed.value, true
}

func (queue *linkedQueue) front() (int, bool) {
	// Head stores the oldest value and is unchanged by this read.
	if queue.head == nil {
		return 0, false
	}
	return queue.head.value, true
}

func (queue *linkedQueue) snapshot() []int {
	// Copy nodes from head to tail into their logical FIFO order.
	result := make([]int, 0, queue.size)
	for node := queue.head; node != nil; node = node.next {
		result = append(result, node.value)
	}
	return result
}

func main() {
	// Run the same history through both representations and compare each
	// externally visible result.
	array := &sliceQueue{}
	linked := &linkedQueue{}
	for _, value := range []int{4, 7, 9} {
		array.enqueue(value)
		linked.enqueue(value)
	}

	arrayValue, arrayOK := array.dequeue()
	linkedValue, linkedOK := linked.dequeue()
	fmt.Println(arrayValue, arrayOK, linkedValue, linkedOK)

	array.enqueue(11)
	linked.enqueue(11)
	fmt.Println(array.snapshot(), linked.snapshot())

	// Include the first removed value, then drain the remaining values
	// to prove both queues preserve the complete insertion order.
	arrayOrder := []int{arrayValue}
	linkedOrder := []int{linkedValue}
	for array.size() > 0 {
		value, _ := array.dequeue()
		arrayOrder = append(arrayOrder, value)
	}
	for linked.size > 0 {
		value, _ := linked.dequeue()
		linkedOrder = append(linkedOrder, value)
	}
	fmt.Println(arrayOrder)
	fmt.Println(linkedOrder)

	// One extra dequeue demonstrates their matching empty behavior.
	_, arrayOK = array.dequeue()
	_, linkedOK = linked.dequeue()
	fmt.Println(arrayOK, linkedOK)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
4 true 4 true
[7 9 11] [7 9 11]
[4 7 9 11]
[4 7 9 11]
false false
```

##### Why it works

For the slice queue, the live suffix from head to the slice end is the
logical queue. Append places a value after that suffix. Dequeue
removes its first value by advancing head. Compaction copies the
suffix in the same increasing-index order, so resetting head changes
no logical position.

For the linked queue, following next links from head reaches every
value in enqueue order and ends at tail. Enqueue attaches one new node
after tail. Dequeue removes head and exposes its successor. Clearing
tail when the successor is nil makes both ends agree with empty.

Both invariants hold initially and survive each operation, so each
dequeue returns the oldest unremoved enqueue. Every method has bounded
local work except compaction or snapshot traversal, whose loops or
copies cover a finite live suffix.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be current size. In Go 1.26.5, slice enqueue is amortized O(1)
under geometric append growth.
Most slice dequeues take O(1); a compaction takes O(N), but waiting
until holes occupy at least half makes dequeue amortized O(1) across a
sequence. Live values and the temporary copy use O(N) storage.

Linked enqueue, dequeue, and front perform O(1) pointer operations.
Each enqueue allocates one node, and N values retain O(N) nodes plus
one pointer per value. Allocation and garbage collection add runtime
cost outside the link count.

Both snapshots take O(N) time and O(N) output storage. The slice has
better locality but may retain spare capacity. Linked nodes avoid
bulk copies but use more metadata and scattered allocations.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Both zero values are valid empty queues. Empty dequeue and front
  return zero and false without indexing or dereferencing nil.
- Enqueue 0 then dequeue returns zero and true. Test the boolean.
- After the last linked dequeue, clear both head and tail. A stale
  tail would attach the next node to an object outside the new queue.
- Do not reslice as `values = values[1:]` forever when elements
  contain pointers; a long-lived backing array can retain consumed
  objects.
- Compact only the live suffix and reset head. Copying the entire
  physical slice would put consumed holes back into the queue.
- Compacting after every dequeue can repeatedly copy a long live
  suffix and approach quadratic total work. Wait until consumed holes
  number at least as many as remaining values.
- A linked queue without tail makes enqueue O(N). A queue with tail
  but no sole-node cleanup leaves inconsistent empty state.
- Copying either mutable queue struct can share slice storage or node
  chains. Define ownership instead of mutating copies independently.

##### When to choose it

Choose an array-backed queue for compact storage, good locality, and
typical in-process traversal workloads. Choose linked nodes when
stable nodes or avoidance of occasional bulk copies outweighs
allocation and pointer overhead.

Choose a fixed [circular buffer](#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers)
when a capacity bound is part of the contract. Choose a deque when
both ends change, or a priority queue when ordering depends on a key.
Go's [`container/list`](https://pkg.go.dev/container/list) can back a
linked queue, though a typed private node avoids interface values.

The [breadth-first search](
#b122-breadth-first-search-adjacency-list-and-queue) and
[Kahn topological sort](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) are core queue
applications.

#### A.5.4 Monotonic deques

##### Problem and contract

For every contiguous window of K integers, return its maximum. For
values `[1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7]` and K equal to 3, the windows have
maxima `[3,3,5,5,6,7]`.

Scanning all K values for every window repeats work and can take
O(NK) time for N input values. We need to retain only positions that
can still become the maximum of the current or a later window.

Our function accepts any integer values without mutating them. Window
size must be from 1 through N; zero, negative, larger-than-input, and
empty-input window requests return an error. Duplicate maxima use the
newest equal position internally, but only maximum values are
returned.

Read [double-ended queues](#a52-double-ended-queues) and
[monotonic stacks](#a42-monotonic-stacks) first.

##### Mental model

Keep a deque of candidate indices. Their indices increase from front
to back, while their looked-up values strictly decrease. Read front
index 4 for value 5 as "5 is the greatest value still eligible for
the current window."

At each input index, first remove front indices left of the window.
Then remove back indices whose values are less than or equal to the
current value. They can never win again: the current value is at
least as large and remains eligible longer. Push the current index at
the back.

Once the first full window ends, the value at the front is its
maximum. Expiry needs the front because indices age in increasing
order; dominance needs the back because values decrease in that
direction.

The implementation stores at most K candidate indices in a fixed
circular buffer. Head and count give its logical front and size.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use values `[1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7]` with K equal to 3. Expected output
is `[3,3,5,5,6,7]`. Deque snapshots show `index:value` from front to
back.

Initial state: candidate deque and output are empty. The first result
is emitted only after processing index 2.

1. Decision: index 0 has value 1. Nothing expires or is dominated;
   push `0:1`.
   After: deque `[0:1]`; output `[]`.
   Known correct: index 0 is the only candidate, but no full window
   exists yet.

2. Decision: value 3 at index 1 dominates back value 1. Pop `0:1`,
   then push `1:3`.
   After: deque `[1:3]`; output `[]`.
   Known correct: index 0 cannot beat 3 before index 1 expires.

3. Decision: value -1 does not dominate 3, so push `2:-1`. The first
   full window covers indices 0 through 2; emit front value 3.
   After: deque `[1:3,2:-1]`; output `[3]`.
   Known correct: the front is the greatest eligible value in the
   complete window.

4. Decision: at index 3 the expiry boundary is 0, so index 1 remains.
   Value -3 dominates nothing; push `3:-3` and emit 3.
   After: deque `[1:3,2:-1,3:-3]`; output `[3,3]`.
   Known correct: all candidates lie in window 1 through 3 and values
   decrease from front to back.

5. Decision: at index 4, expiry boundary is 1, so remove front
   `1:3`. Value 5 then dominates `3:-3` and `2:-1`; pop both and push
   `4:5`. Emit 5.
   After: deque `[4:5]`; output `[3,3,5]`.
   Known correct: every older position is expired or permanently
   dominated by the newer 5.

6. Decision: value 3 at index 5 does not dominate 5; push it and emit
   front value 5.
   After: deque `[4:5,5:3]`; output `[3,3,5,5]`.
   Known correct: 5 remains eligible and greater than the new value.

7. Decision: value 6 at index 6 dominates back values 3 and 5. Pop
   both, push `6:6`, and emit 6.
   After: deque `[6:6]`; output `[3,3,5,5,6]`.
   Known correct: the newer 6 outlasts and exceeds both removed
   candidates.

8. Decision: value 7 at index 7 dominates 6. Replace it with `7:7`
   and emit 7, then stop at the input end.
   After: deque `[7:7]`; output `[3,3,5,5,6,7]`.
   Known correct: one maximum was emitted for every complete window,
   matching the required result.

Focused equality case: values `[4,4]` with K 2 discard index 0 when
index 1 arrives. The maximum remains 4, and the newer equal candidate
stays eligible longer. Focused K 1 case emits each input value.

Counterexample to expiring after emission: for `[9,1,2]` with K 2,
index 0 is outside the second window. Emitting before removal would
wrongly return 9 instead of 2. The first wrong decision is querying a
candidate before confirming it is still eligible.

##### Implementation

This complete program implements the walkthrough and invalid-input
path. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It allocates the
result and a K-slot candidate buffer but does not mutate input.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func wrapIndex(start, offset, capacity int) int {
	// Wrap by subtracting the distance to the physical end. This avoids
	// forming start+offset, which could overflow before modulo.
	distanceToEnd := capacity - start
	if offset >= distanceToEnd {
		return offset - distanceToEnd
	}
	return start + offset
}

func windowMaximums(
	values []int,
	windowSize int,
) ([]int, error) {
	// A window must contain a value and fit entirely in input. Reject an
	// invalid size before using it in allocation arithmetic.
	if windowSize <= 0 || windowSize > len(values) {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("window size must be from 1 through %d",
			len(values))
	}

	// This circular deque stores indexes still able to become a maximum.
	// Values decrease front to back, so front is always strongest.
	candidateIndices := make([]int, windowSize)
	candidateHead := 0
	candidateCount := 0
	maximums := make(
		[]int,
		0,
		len(values)-windowSize+1,
	)

	for index, value := range values {
		// An index at or left of this boundary no longer belongs to the
		// window ending at index. Remove expired candidates from the front.
		expiryBoundary := index - windowSize
		for candidateCount > 0 &&
			candidateIndices[candidateHead] <= expiryBoundary {
			candidateHead = wrapIndex(
				candidateHead,
				1,
				windowSize,
			)
			candidateCount--
		}

		// Remove back candidates no greater than the new value. They expire
		// earlier and can never beat this newer value in a future window.
		for candidateCount > 0 {
			backPosition := wrapIndex(
				candidateHead,
				candidateCount-1,
				windowSize,
			)
			backIndex := candidateIndices[backPosition]
			if values[backIndex] > value {
				// A greater value stays useful and preserves decreasing
				// candidate order, so pruning stops here.
				break
			}
			candidateCount--
		}

		// Append the new index after every stronger retained candidate.
		insertPosition := wrapIndex(
			candidateHead,
			candidateCount,
			windowSize,
		)
		candidateIndices[insertPosition] = index
		candidateCount++

		if index >= windowSize-1 {
			// The first complete window ends at windowSize-1. The deque front
			// is its greatest live value by the maintained order.
			frontIndex := candidateIndices[candidateHead]
			maximums = append(maximums, values[frontIndex])
		}
	}
	return maximums, nil
}

func main() {
	// This input exercises expiry and repeated back pruning.
	values := []int{1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7}
	maximums, err := windowMaximums(values, 3)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(maximums)

	// A zero-width call demonstrates explicit boundary rejection.
	_, err = windowMaximums(values, 0)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[3 3 5 5 6 7]
true
```

##### Why it works

Before each result, candidate indices are inside the current window
and increase from front to back, while their values strictly decrease.
The front is therefore the greatest retained value.

Expiry removes only indices that cannot belong to the current or any
later window. During back removal, a discarded candidate is no greater
than the current value and expires earlier, so it can never become a
future maximum. These removals preserve every candidate that might
still win. Pushing current preserves increasing indices and strict
value decrease.

Any current-window value absent from the deque was either expired or
dominated by a newer, at-least-as-large retained value. Thus the front
is the window maximum when emitted.

Each iteration advances the input index. Every index is pushed once,
removed at most once from the front or back, and never reinserted, so
both inner loops and the complete scan terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be input length and K be window size. Every index enters and
leaves the deque at most once, so the scan takes Theta(N) time in the
best, average, and worst cases. Modulo and comparisons are constant
work per deque action.

The circular candidate buffer uses O(K) auxiliary storage. The output
contains `N - K + 1` integers and uses that much separate storage.
Invalid input returns before either allocation.

A direct scan uses O(1) auxiliary storage but O(NK) time. A heap gives
O(N log K) time and needs a way to discard expired entries. The
monotonic deque is linear because it permanently removes dominated
candidates.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty values with any K are rejected because no positive window can
  fit. K 0, negative K, and K greater than N also return an error.
- K 1 returns a new slice equal in values to the input. No alias is
  returned, so later result changes do not mutate input.
- K equal to N emits exactly one maximum after the final input value.
- Equal values pop the older index with `<=` dominance. Keeping both
  is correct but wastes candidate capacity and obscures the invariant.
- Expire before dominance and emission. Otherwise an out-of-window
  maximum can be returned once too often.
- Store indices, not only values. Expiry depends on position even when
  duplicate values are indistinguishable.
- Use a loop for back removal. One large value may dominate every
  current candidate, as value 5 does in the walkthrough.
- Allocate K candidate slots only after validating K. Modulo by zero
  would panic on an invalid window size.
- Compute wrapped positions without first adding two large indexes;
  `wrapIndex` avoids overflow before applying the circular rule.

##### When to choose it

Choose a monotonic deque for a maximum or minimum over every moving
fixed-width window when values become permanently irrelevant after a
newer value dominates them. Sliding ranges and streaming extrema fit.

Do not use it for arbitrary range queries, changing historical values,
or several unrelated aggregates. Use a heap when candidates have
other priorities, or a range-query structure for arbitrary intervals.

The walkthrough follows the authoritative [Sliding Window Maximum](
https://leetcode.com/problems/sliding-window-maximum/) problem. The
[window-extrema family](
#b55-window-extrema-monotonic-deque) applies the same invariant, and
[monotonic stacks](#a42-monotonic-stacks) handle one-directional
nearest-value queries without expiry from the opposite end.

#### A.5.5 Double-ended priority queues

##### Problem and contract

A deque removes by position, but some workloads must repeatedly access
or remove either the smallest or largest value regardless of arrival
order. A double-ended priority queue provides insert, peek minimum,
peek maximum, delete minimum, and delete maximum.

Our integer structure accepts duplicates and extreme values. Peek and
delete operations return zero and false when empty; zero remains valid
data. Equal values are separate inserted items, though deleting either
equal occurrence has the same observable integer result.

The implementation assigns each item a unique 64-bit ID. Insert
returns false without mutation if the next ID would wrap. Allocation
and every live or physical record count must fit `int`. Operations
require a non-nil queue pointer. They mutate private heap storage;
even a peek may discard obsolete internal records while leaving the
logical values unchanged. Concurrent access requires synchronization.

The zero-value structure is ready to use. This entry defines the
needed heap behavior locally; read
[heaps and priority queues](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) for the
general representation and operations.

##### Mental model

Store every inserted item in two binary heaps: a min-heap exposes the
smallest value, and a max-heap exposes the largest. Give both copies
the same ID. A map records which IDs are still live.

Deleting from one heap removes that copy and marks its ID dead. The
other heap may still contain its obsolete copy, called a tombstone.
Before reading either root, repeatedly pop roots whose IDs are dead.
The first live min-heap root is the minimum; the first live max-heap
root is the maximum.

Lazy deletion avoids searching a heap for the counterpart. To bound
retained tombstones, rebuild both heaps from live items when either
heap has more stale records than live records plus a small constant.
Rebuilding preserves values and IDs but removes all tombstones.

At every public boundary, the live-ID map is the logical collection.
Each live item has one copy in each heap; dead copies may remain only
until cleanup or rebuild.

##### Worked walkthrough

Insert 4, 1, 7, and another 1. Peek both ends, delete one minimum and
the maximum, then peek again. Expected observations are initial
minimum 1, maximum 7, deleted values 1 and 7, then minimum 1 and
maximum 4.

Initial state: both heaps and the live-ID map are empty; logical size
is 0. IDs begin at 0.

1. Decision: insert 4 as item `4#0`. Push the same item into both
   heaps and mark ID 0 live.
   After: live values `[4]`; both roots are `4#0`; size 1.
   Known correct: the sole live item is both minimum and maximum.

2. Decision: insert `1#1`, `7#2`, and `1#3` by the same rule.
   After: all four IDs are live. The min root is `1#1` and max root
   is `7#2`; the second 1 remains a distinct item.
   Known correct: each heap contains every live item and orders its
   own requested extreme at the root.

3. Decision: peek minimum and maximum. Both roots have live IDs, so
   return values 1 and 7 without logical mutation.
   After: live values and size remain unchanged.
   Known correct: heap-root order establishes both requested extremes.

4. Decision: delete minimum. Pop `1#1` from the min-heap, remove ID 1
   from the live map, and reduce size. Its max-heap copy becomes a
   tombstone but is not the max root.
   After: live items are `4#0`, `7#2`, and `1#3`; returned value is 1.
   Known correct: exactly one duplicate occurrence became dead.

5. Decision: delete maximum. Max root `7#2` is live, so pop it and
   remove ID 2. Its min-heap counterpart becomes a tombstone.
   After: live items are `4#0` and `1#3`; returned value is 7.
   Known correct: no live value is smaller than 1 or larger than 4.

6. Decision: peek both ends. The current roots needed for the answers
   are live, so return minimum 1 and maximum 4.
   After: logical values remain `[1,4]`; size is 2.
   Known correct: tombstones cannot be returned because every root is
   checked against the live map first, so the walkthrough stops.

Focused duplicate case: inserting 5 twice gives different IDs.
Deleting minimum once leaves one live 5, which is still both extremes.
Focused empty case: all four peek or delete operations return zero and
false when no live ID exists.

Counterexample to pairing heaps only by value: after inserting two 1s,
deleting one cannot identify which counterpart became obsolete. The
first wrong decision is treating equal occurrences as one item instead
of sharing a unique identity between their two heap copies.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. It uses Go's `container/heap` package and
keeps tombstone storage bounded with rebuilding.

```go
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
)

type priorityItem struct {
	value int
	// id distinguishes duplicate values and identifies lazy deletions.
	id uint64
}

type minimumHeap []priorityItem

func (items minimumHeap) Len() int {
	return len(items)
}

func (items minimumHeap) Less(left, right int) bool {
	// Equal values leave in insertion order; smaller IDs are older.
	if items[left].value == items[right].value {
		return items[left].id < items[right].id
	}
	return items[left].value < items[right].value
}

func (items minimumHeap) Swap(left, right int) {
	items[left], items[right] = items[right], items[left]
}

func (items *minimumHeap) Push(value any) {
	// Only this queue calls heap.Push, always with a priorityItem.
	*items = append(*items, value.(priorityItem))
}

func (items *minimumHeap) Pop() any {
	// container/heap moves its chosen root to the last slot before Pop.
	old := *items
	lastIndex := len(old) - 1
	item := old[lastIndex]
	// Clear the retired slot before shrinking retained backing storage.
	old[lastIndex] = priorityItem{}
	*items = old[:lastIndex]
	return item
}

type maximumHeap []priorityItem

func (items maximumHeap) Len() int {
	return len(items)
}

func (items maximumHeap) Less(left, right int) bool {
	// Reverse value order. IDs still make older duplicates leave first.
	if items[left].value == items[right].value {
		return items[left].id < items[right].id
	}
	return items[left].value > items[right].value
}

func (items maximumHeap) Swap(left, right int) {
	items[left], items[right] = items[right], items[left]
}

func (items *maximumHeap) Push(value any) {
	// The queue owns this heap and supplies only priorityItem values.
	*items = append(*items, value.(priorityItem))
}

func (items *maximumHeap) Pop() any {
	// container/heap moves the selected root to the slice end first.
	old := *items
	lastIndex := len(old) - 1
	item := old[lastIndex]
	old[lastIndex] = priorityItem{}
	*items = old[:lastIndex]
	return item
}

type doubleEndedPriorityQueue struct {
	// Both heaps hold the same items in opposite orders. The map says
	// which IDs are still logically present after lazy deletion.
	minimums     minimumHeap
	maximums     maximumHeap
	liveItemByID map[uint64]struct{}
	nextID       uint64
	size         int
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) insert(value int) bool {
	// IDs must never repeat while stale heap copies may still exist.
	if queue.nextID == ^uint64(0) {
		return false
	}
	if queue.liveItemByID == nil {
		// Lazily allocate so the zero-value queue is immediately usable.
		queue.liveItemByID = make(map[uint64]struct{})
	}
	item := priorityItem{value: value, id: queue.nextID}
	// Mark the ID live before publishing either heap copy.
	queue.nextID++
	queue.liveItemByID[item.id] = struct{}{}
	heap.Push(&queue.minimums, item)
	heap.Push(&queue.maximums, item)
	queue.size++
	return true
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) discardDeadMinimums() {
	// A deletion from the max heap leaves a stale copy in the min heap.
	// Pop stale roots until the root ID is live or the heap is empty.
	for len(queue.minimums) > 0 {
		item := queue.minimums[0]
		if _, live := queue.liveItemByID[item.id]; live {
			return
		}
		heap.Pop(&queue.minimums)
	}
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) discardDeadMaximums() {
	// Mirror cleanup for items previously deleted through min order.
	for len(queue.maximums) > 0 {
		item := queue.maximums[0]
		if _, live := queue.liveItemByID[item.id]; live {
			return
		}
		heap.Pop(&queue.maximums)
	}
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) peekMinimum() (int, bool) {
	// Logical size, not heap length, defines emptiness because the
	// heaps may retain stale copies.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		return 0, false
	}
	queue.discardDeadMinimums()
	// Nonzero logical size guarantees cleanup will expose one live root.
	return queue.minimums[0].value, true
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) peekMaximum() (int, bool) {
	// Remove stale roots before trusting the maximum heap's first item.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		return 0, false
	}
	queue.discardDeadMaximums()
	return queue.maximums[0].value, true
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) deleteMinimum() (int, bool) {
	// Clean first so the removed heap root is the smallest live item.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		return 0, false
	}
	queue.discardDeadMinimums()
	item := heap.Pop(&queue.minimums).(priorityItem)
	// Removing the ID makes the matching maximum-heap copy stale.
	delete(queue.liveItemByID, item.id)
	queue.size--
	queue.maybeRebuild()
	return item.value, true
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) deleteMaximum() (int, bool) {
	// This is symmetric: clean max order, then invalidate the min copy.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		return 0, false
	}
	queue.discardDeadMaximums()
	item := heap.Pop(&queue.maximums).(priorityItem)
	delete(queue.liveItemByID, item.id)
	queue.size--
	queue.maybeRebuild()
	return item.value, true
}

func (queue *doubleEndedPriorityQueue) maybeRebuild() {
	// Each heap needs one copy per live item; any excess is stale.
	staleMinimums := len(queue.minimums) - queue.size
	staleMaximums := len(queue.maximums) - queue.size
	maxInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	allowedStale := maxInt
	// Rebuild when stale storage exceeds live size plus a cushion. Guard
	// the addition so the threshold itself cannot overflow.
	if queue.size <= maxInt-16 {
		allowedStale = queue.size + 16
	}
	if staleMinimums <= allowedStale &&
		staleMaximums <= allowedStale {
		// Storage is proportional to useful state; keep cheap laziness.
		return
	}

	// Every live ID has a min-heap copy. Filter that heap, then copy the
	// live set into both orderings and restore heap structure.
	liveItems := make([]priorityItem, 0, queue.size)
	for _, item := range queue.minimums {
		if _, live := queue.liveItemByID[item.id]; live {
			liveItems = append(liveItems, item)
		}
	}
	queue.minimums = minimumHeap(
		append([]priorityItem(nil), liveItems...),
	)
	queue.maximums = maximumHeap(
		append([]priorityItem(nil), liveItems...),
	)
	heap.Init(&queue.minimums)
	heap.Init(&queue.maximums)
}

func main() {
	// Duplicate 1 values verify that IDs preserve independent copies.
	queue := &doubleEndedPriorityQueue{}
	for _, value := range []int{4, 1, 7, 1} {
		if !queue.insert(value) {
			panic("priority queue item IDs exhausted")
		}
	}
	minimum, minimumOK := queue.peekMinimum()
	maximum, maximumOK := queue.peekMaximum()
	fmt.Println(minimum, minimumOK, maximum, maximumOK)

	minimum, minimumOK = queue.deleteMinimum()
	// Delete opposite ends so each heap receives one stale counterpart.
	fmt.Println(minimum, minimumOK)
	maximum, maximumOK = queue.deleteMaximum()
	fmt.Println(maximum, maximumOK)

	minimum, minimumOK = queue.peekMinimum()
	maximum, maximumOK = queue.peekMaximum()
	fmt.Println(minimum, minimumOK, maximum, maximumOK)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
1 true 7 true
1 true
7 true
1 true 4 true
```

##### Why it works

Each successful insert creates one ID, records it live, and places
identical items into heaps whose roots are respectively smallest and
largest by value. Thus every live item is represented in both
orderings. Rejected insertion changes nothing.

Deleting one extreme first removes dead roots, so the selected root is
live and is the requested extreme among all live items. Removing its
ID from the map makes both copies logically absent. Its counterpart
may remain physically, but root cleanup prevents any dead item from
being observed. Peek applies the same cleanup without changing live
IDs.

A rebuild copies exactly items whose IDs are live into both heaps and
reestablishes both heap invariants. It therefore removes storage only,
not logical values. After any cleanup, the first live root supplies
the correct extreme.

Every heap operation terminates on a finite slice. Root cleanup
removes one tombstone per iteration, and rebuilding scans a finite
heap. A tombstone may remain if no later operation exposes it, but the
rebuild rule keeps the number of retained stale records bounded.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be live item count. The rebuild rule keeps each physical heap at
no more than about `2N + 16` items after deletions, so retained
storage is O(N) plus a small constant. Two heaps and the live-ID map
use O(N) space. Each live item contributes two heap records and one
map entry; bounded tombstones add O(N) records.

Insert performs two heap pushes and takes O(log(N + 1)) time. A delete
normally takes O(log(N + 1)). A single cleanup or rebuild can take
different work: popping N tombstones can take O(N log(N + 1)), while
scanning live records and calling `heap.Init` rebuilds in O(N).
Each tombstone is removed once, and rebuilding requires accumulated
stale work. Across an operation sequence, delete and cleanup cost
amortized O(log(N + 1)), assuming expected O(1) map membership.

Peek is O(1) when its root is live. Its worst single call may clean
many tombstones, but that cleanup has the same amortized bound. A
single min-max heap can give stricter bounds with less duplicated
storage, at the cost of more complex ordering and repair logic.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty peeks and deletes return zero and false before indexing a
  heap. Inserting zero then peeking returns zero and true.
- Duplicate values need separate IDs. Removing one 5 must leave the
  other 5 live in both logical orderings.
- Extreme integers are compared directly; no negation is used for the
  max-heap, so the minimum integer cannot overflow.
- Clean dead roots before every peek or delete. Checking only during
  deletion can let a peek expose an obsolete value.
- Mark the shared ID dead after popping the chosen live root. Removing
  a heap record without updating the map leaves its counterpart live.
- Lazy deletion without rebuilding can retain memory proportional to
  total historical inserts instead of current size.
- Rebuild from live IDs, then call `heap.Init` for both orderings. A
  copied heap slice is not automatically heap-ordered for the other
  comparison.
- When the next ID is the largest `uint64`, insert returns false
  before incrementing it. This prevents wraparound from reusing an
  old ID.
- Copying the structure shares heap slices and a live map. Keep one
  owner or implement an explicit deep copy.

##### When to choose it

Choose a double-ended priority queue when each step may need either
numeric extreme: bounded scheduling, median-adjacent maintenance, and
algorithms that alternately trim low and high outliers are examples.

Use an ordinary min-heap or max-heap when only one extreme matters.
Use a deque when arrival position, not value, chooses removal. Use a
balanced ordered multiset when arbitrary ordered lookup and deletion
are also required.

Go's authoritative [`container/heap`](
https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap) documentation defines the heap
interface and operation costs used by this implementation. The
[two-heaps composite](#a143-two-heaps) covers streaming-median
partitioning with different invariants.

### A.6 Hash maps and hash sets

#### A.6.1 Direct-address tables

##### Problem and contract

When every valid key is a small integer in a known range, the key can
select storage directly. A direct-address table avoids hashing and
collision handling by giving every possible key its own slot.

Our table maps integer keys from 0 through `keyLimit - 1` to strings.
Construction requires a positive key limit and returns an error
otherwise. Put inserts or replaces a value and reports whether the key
already existed. Get and delete report presence separately from the
string, so an empty string remains valid. Out-of-range operations
return an error without mutation.

The table owns its slices, assumes allocation succeeds, and excludes
unsynchronized concurrent access. Operations require a non-nil table
returned by the constructor. Key limit and every key must fit Go's
`int`. Read [arrays and slices](
#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) first.

##### Mental model

Use the key itself as a slice index. Slot 5 answers only questions
about key 5; no other key can share it. A values slice holds strings,
and a parallel occupied slice states whether each slot belongs to the
map.

Read `values[5] == ""` together with `occupied[5] == true` as "key 5
is present and maps to the empty string." The boolean distinguishes
that fact from an unused slot, whose string also has the zero value.

Put validates the index, writes the value, and marks the slot
occupied. Get validates and reads the two parallel slots. Delete
clears both and decrements size only when the key was present.

At every operation boundary, occupied key K is true exactly when K is
in the table, and its value is stored at values index K.

##### Worked walkthrough

Create a table for keys 0 through 7. Put `2 -> "two"` and `5 -> ""`,
read key 5, replace key 2 with `"TWO"`, delete key 2, then reject key
8. The final table contains only key 5.

Initial state: both slices have length 8. Every occupied entry is
false, every string is empty, and size is 0.

1. Decision: key 2 is valid and unoccupied. Write `"two"` at values
   index 2, mark occupied index 2, and increase size.
   After: key 2 maps to `"two"`; size is 1; replaced is false.
   Known correct: the one present key owns its exact-key slot.

2. Decision: key 5 is valid and unoccupied. Write the empty string,
   mark its occupied slot, and increase size.
   After: keys 2 and 5 are present; size is 2.
   Known correct: occupied index 5 preserves presence even though the
   stored value equals the string zero value.

3. Decision: get key 5. Its occupied entry is true, so return the
   value at index 5, true, and no error.
   After: result is `""`, true, nil; the table is unchanged.
   Known correct: presence and value have not been conflated.

4. Decision: put `2 -> "TWO"`. Key 2 is already occupied, so replace
   its value without changing size and report replaced true.
   After: key 2 maps to `"TWO"`; key 5 maps to `""`; size remains 2.
   Known correct: one key still owns one slot and one current value.

5. Decision: delete key 2. Save `"TWO"`, clear its string and occupied
   entries, and decrement size.
   After: deletion returns `"TWO"` and true; only key 5 remains.
   Known correct: a later get of key 2 returns absent, while key 5 is
   unaffected.

6. Decision: get key 8. Valid indices stop at 7, so return an error
   before reading either slice.
   After: size remains 1 and key 5 remains present.
   Known correct: invalid input caused no partial mutation, completing
   the required sequence.

Focused boundary case: key 0 and key 7 select the first and last
slots. Key -1 and key 8 are invalid. Focused missing delete: deleting
valid but absent key 3 returns an empty string, false, and no error.

Counterexample to using the string zero value as the only absence
marker: after storing `5 -> ""`, get cannot tell present-empty from
missing. The first wrong decision is asking one field to encode both
payload and membership.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. Construction allocates two fixed slices;
successful valid operations do not resize table storage.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type directAddressTable struct {
	// A key is its slice index. occupied separates a stored empty string
	// from a key that has no entry.
	values   []string
	occupied []bool
	size     int
}

func newDirectAddressTable(
	keyLimit int,
) (*directAddressTable, error) {
	// A positive limit creates the half-open key range [0, keyLimit).
	if keyLimit <= 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("key limit must be positive")
	}
	return &directAddressTable{
		// Parallel slices give each key a value slot and a presence
		// bit without hashing or collision handling.
		values:   make([]string, keyLimit),
		occupied: make([]bool, keyLimit),
	}, nil
}

func (table *directAddressTable) validateKey(key int) error {
	// Check before indexing; negative indexes and the
	// exclusive upper bound would both panic.
	if key < 0 || key >= len(table.values) {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"key %d is outside [0,%d)",
			key,
			len(table.values),
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func (table *directAddressTable) put(
	key int,
	value string,
) (bool, error) {
	// Invalid input leaves values, presence bits, and size unchanged.
	if err := table.validateKey(key); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	replaced := table.occupied[key]
	// Write both parallel facts. Only a newly present key increases the
	// number of stored entries; replacement preserves size.
	table.values[key] = value
	table.occupied[key] = true
	if !replaced {
		table.size++
	}
	return replaced, nil
}

func (table *directAddressTable) get(
	key int,
) (string, bool, error) {
	// Validate before reading the presence bit at key.
	if err := table.validateKey(key); err != nil {
		return "", false, err
	}
	if !table.occupied[key] {
		// Absence is successful lookup information, not an input error.
		return "", false, nil
	}
	return table.values[key], true, nil
}

func (table *directAddressTable) delete(
	key int,
) (string, bool, error) {
	// As with get, an out-of-range key is an error and changes nothing.
	if err := table.validateKey(key); err != nil {
		return "", false, err
	}
	if !table.occupied[key] {
		// Deleting an absent valid key is a no-op reported by found=false.
		return "", false, nil
	}
	value := table.values[key]
	// Save the result before clearing both facts. Clearing the value
	// releases any string data retained only by this slot.
	table.values[key] = ""
	table.occupied[key] = false
	table.size--
	return value, true, nil
}

func main() {
	// Eight slots admit keys 0 through 7; key 8 tests the boundary.
	table, err := newDirectAddressTable(8)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	// Store normal and empty values. occupied must distinguish
	// that empty value from an absent key.
	replaced, err := table.put(2, "two")
	fmt.Println(replaced, err)
	replaced, err = table.put(5, "")
	fmt.Println(replaced, err)

	// Read empty, replace key 2 without growing size, then delete
	// it and confirm its presence bit was cleared.
	value, found, err := table.get(5)
	fmt.Printf("%q %v %v\n", value, found, err)
	replaced, err = table.put(2, "TWO")
	fmt.Println(replaced, err)
	value, found, err = table.get(2)
	fmt.Printf("%q %v %v\n", value, found, err)

	value, found, err = table.delete(2)
	fmt.Printf("%q %v %v\n", value, found, err)
	value, found, err = table.get(2)
	fmt.Printf("%q %v %v\n", value, found, err)

	// The exclusive upper bound is invalid and must not change size.
	_, _, err = table.get(8)
	fmt.Println(err != nil, table.size)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
false <nil>
false <nil>
"" true <nil>
true <nil>
"TWO" true <nil>
"TWO" true <nil>
"" false <nil>
true 1
```

##### Why it works

Construction gives every valid key exactly one distinct index. All
occupied entries start false, so the representation initially matches
an empty map.

Successful put writes the requested value to the key's unique slot and
marks that same slot present. It increments size only on a transition
from absent to present. Get returns a value only when the parallel
occupied entry proves membership.

Successful delete clears exactly the requested key's unique slot and
decrements size once. Missing deletion changes nothing. Validation
rejects every index outside the allocated universe before access, so
invalid operations preserve the representation.

No two valid keys share a slot. Therefore the local slot invariant for
every key implies the complete map contract. Each operation has a
fixed, finite number of slice accesses and terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let U be the number of possible keys and N the number currently
present. Construction zeroes two U-entry slices, taking Theta(U) time
and O(U) retained storage. Put, get, and delete each take Theta(1)
worst-case time and O(1) temporary storage.

Storage depends on U, not N. Ten present keys in a universe of one
billion would still require one billion value and presence slots. In
return, lookup has no hash calculation, collision chain, probe, or
distribution assumption.

A boolean set needs only one presence table. Small counters can store
counts directly when zero unambiguously means absent. A packed bit set
reduces membership storage when values are only present or absent.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Key limit 0 or negative returns an error before allocation. A table
  with no valid key would make every operation fail.
- Keys 0 and `keyLimit - 1` are valid. Key -1 and keyLimit return an
  error without indexing a slice.
- Empty string is valid data. Use the occupied slice rather than a
  payload sentinel to distinguish it from missing.
- Replacing an existing key leaves size unchanged. Incrementing on
  every put makes size count operations instead of present keys.
- Deleting a missing valid key returns false and leaves size
  unchanged. Decrementing unconditionally can make size negative.
- Clearing a deleted string drops that reference, allowing its backing
  bytes to be reclaimed when no other references remain.
- For a known range `[minimum, maximum]`, translate key K to checked
  offset `K - minimum`. Computing an unchecked offset can overflow or
  index outside the table.
- Copying the table struct shares both slice backings. Keep one owner
  or implement a deep copy before independent mutation.

##### When to choose it

Choose direct addressing when the key universe is small, stable, and
dense enough to allocate up front: byte tables, weekday states, board
cells, and bounded problem values are common examples.

Do not choose it for sparse identifiers, arbitrary strings, or a key
range much larger than the number of entries. A hash table spends
storage on present entries plus capacity rather than every possible
key; an ordered tree also supports sorted traversal.

The fixed byte table in the solved Longest Substring Without Repeating
Characters archive, listed in the [problem index](problems/README.md),
uses direct addressing because its contract bounds characters to 256
byte values. The [packed bit vectors](
#a131-packed-bit-vectors) compress boolean direct-address tables.

#### A.6.2 Separate chaining and open addressing

##### Problem and contract

A hash function maps many possible keys into a smaller array of bucket
indices. Different keys can select the same index, called a collision.
A correct hash table must preserve every collided key and still find,
reject as duplicate, or delete the requested one.

We will build two fixed-size integer sets. A separate-chaining set
stores a slice of keys at each bucket and can grow chains without a
limit derived from the bucket count. An open-addressing set stores
keys inside one slot array and follows a linear probe sequence;
insertion returns an error when no reusable slot remains.

Both constructors require positive storage size. Add reports whether
a new key was inserted. Contains and remove report membership. Keys
may be negative, zero, duplicated, or extreme integers. Neither set
preserves insertion order. Allocation must fit memory, and concurrent
access requires synchronization. Operations require a non-nil set
returned by its constructor, and item counts must fit `int`.

Read [direct-address tables](#a61-direct-address-tables) first.

##### Mental model

For this lesson, the hash index is the key's remainder modulo storage
size, adjusted into the nonnegative index range. With five positions,
keys 1, 6, and -4 all select index 1. This deliberately simple hash
makes the collision visible.

Separate chaining treats a bucket as a small collection. Add scans
that one chain for a duplicate before appending. Contains scans for an
equal key. Remove deletes only the matching chain element.

Open addressing keeps one slot per physical position. Starting at the
hash index, linear probing checks the next position and wraps around.
A slot is never used, occupied, or deleted. Never-used ends an
unsuccessful search. Deleted, also called a tombstone, does not end
it, because a collided key may have been placed later.

Open insertion remembers the first tombstone but continues until it
finds the key or a never-used slot. This prevents inserting a
duplicate that appears later in the same probe sequence.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use five buckets and slots. Add keys 1, 6, and -4; remove 6; then add
11. All four keys hash to index 1. A dot is never-used and `x` is a
tombstone.

Initial state: five chains are empty. Open slots are
`[.,.,.,.,.]`. Both sizes are 0.

1. Decision: add key 1. Chain bucket 1 has no duplicate, so append 1.
   Open slot 1 is never used, so occupy it.
   After: chain 1 is `[1]`; open slots are `[.,1,.,.,.]`.
   Known correct: both sets contain exactly key 1.

2. Decision: add key 6. It hashes to 1 but differs from chain key 1,
   so append it. Open slot 1 is occupied by 1; probe slot 2 and
   insert.
   After: chain 1 is `[1,6]`; open slots are `[.,1,6,.,.]`.
   Known correct: collision handling retained both distinct keys.

3. Decision: add key -4. Normalized remainder is 1. Append after
   scanning the chain. In open storage, probe occupied slots 1 and 2,
   then insert at slot 3.
   After: chain 1 is `[1,6,-4]`; open slots are `[.,1,6,-4,.]`.
   Known correct: negative hashing selects a valid index and all three
   colliding keys remain findable.

4. Decision: remove key 6. Delete it from the chain. In open storage,
   probe from 1, find it at 2, and mark that slot deleted rather than
   never-used.
   After: chain 1 is `[1,-4]`; open slots are `[.,1,x,-4,.]`.
   Known correct: 6 is absent, while probing through tombstone 2 still
   reaches live key -4 at slot 3.

5. Decision: add key 11. Chain bucket 1 lacks it, so append. Open
   probing sees key 1, remembers tombstone 2, continues past key -4,
   and stops at never-used slot 4. Insert into remembered slot 2.
   After: chain 1 is `[1,-4,11]`; open slots are `[.,1,11,-4,.]`.
   Known correct: tombstone reuse saved capacity, and the continued
   search proved 11 was not already present.

6. Decision: query 6 and -4. Both searches reject 6 and find -4.
   After: no storage changes; results agree across representations.
   Known correct: collision, deletion, and tombstone reuse all
   preserve set membership, completing the sequence.

Focused duplicate case: adding 1 again returns false and changes no
size. Focused full case: an open table with every slot occupied and no
matching key returns an error after exactly its capacity probes.

Counterexample to marking a removed open slot never-used: after step
4, contains -4 would stop at slot 2 and incorrectly return false. The
first wrong decision is erasing evidence that the probe sequence once
continued beyond that position.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. The remainder hash is educational, not a
general-purpose integer-mixing function. The display-only
`bucketKeys` helper requires a valid bucket index.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strconv"
)

func normalizedIndex(key, storageSize int) int {
	// A Go remainder keeps the dividend's sign. Add storageSize when the
	// key is negative so every key maps into [0, storageSize).
	index := key % storageSize
	if index < 0 {
		index += storageSize
	}
	return index
}

func wrapIndex(start, offset, capacity int) int {
	// Wrap without first forming start+offset, which could overflow int.
	distanceToEnd := capacity - start
	if offset >= distanceToEnd {
		return offset - distanceToEnd
	}
	return start + offset
}

type chainedSet struct {
	// Each bucket stores every key whose normalized index selects it.
	buckets [][]int
	size    int
}

func newChainedSet(bucketCount int) (*chainedSet, error) {
	// Positive bucket count makes normalization and indexing safe.
	if bucketCount <= 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("bucket count must be positive")
	}
	return &chainedSet{
		buckets: make([][]int, bucketCount),
	}, nil
}

func (set *chainedSet) add(key int) bool {
	// Hashing chooses a bucket, not a unique slot. Search that collision
	// chain first so set insertion never creates a duplicate.
	bucketIndex := normalizedIndex(key, len(set.buckets))
	bucket := set.buckets[bucketIndex]
	for _, storedKey := range bucket {
		if storedKey == key {
			return false
		}
	}
	// No equal key exists, so append one member and count
	// the absent-to-present transition.
	set.buckets[bucketIndex] = append(bucket, key)
	set.size++
	return true
}

func (set *chainedSet) contains(key int) bool {
	// Only keys in the normalized bucket can match; scan it fully.
	bucketIndex := normalizedIndex(key, len(set.buckets))
	for _, storedKey := range set.buckets[bucketIndex] {
		if storedKey == key {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

func (set *chainedSet) remove(key int) bool {
	// Locate the exact key inside its collision chain.
	bucketIndex := normalizedIndex(key, len(set.buckets))
	bucket := set.buckets[bucketIndex]
	for index, storedKey := range bucket {
		if storedKey != key {
			continue
		}
		// Shift the suffix left to preserve bucket order, clear the retired
		// slot, and shorten the stored bucket exactly once.
		copy(bucket[index:], bucket[index+1:])
		bucket[len(bucket)-1] = 0
		set.buckets[bucketIndex] = bucket[:len(bucket)-1]
		set.size--
		return true
	}
	return false
}

func (set *chainedSet) bucketKeys(bucketIndex int) []int {
	// Copy so diagnostics cannot mutate the set's internal bucket.
	return append([]int(nil), set.buckets[bucketIndex]...)
}

type probeState uint8

const (
	// neverUsed ends a search; deleted must not, because later keys
	// may have crossed that slot before it became a tombstone.
	neverUsed probeState = iota
	occupied
	deleted
)

type probeSlot struct {
	key   int
	state probeState
}

type probingSet struct {
	// slots stores keys inline; size counts only occupied slots.
	slots []probeSlot
	size  int
}

func newProbingSet(capacity int) (*probingSet, error) {
	// A positive capacity bounds every probe and permits normalization.
	if capacity <= 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("capacity must be positive")
	}
	return &probingSet{
		slots: make([]probeSlot, capacity),
	}, nil
}

func (set *probingSet) add(key int) (bool, error) {
	// Probe from the key's home. Remember the first tombstone, but keep
	// searching until neverUsed proves no duplicate lies later.
	start := normalizedIndex(key, len(set.slots))
	firstDeleted := -1
	for step := 0; step < len(set.slots); step++ {
		index := wrapIndex(start, step, len(set.slots))
		slot := set.slots[index]
		switch slot.state {
		case occupied:
			// A live equal key means the set already contains this value.
			if slot.key == key {
				return false, nil
			}
		case deleted:
			// Save the earliest tombstone until duplicate search completes.
			if firstDeleted == -1 {
				firstDeleted = index
			}
		case neverUsed:
			// No key in this probe sequence can occur beyond neverUsed. Insert
			// into an earlier tombstone when available, or insert here.
			if firstDeleted != -1 {
				index = firstDeleted
			}
			set.slots[index] = probeSlot{
				key:   key,
				state: occupied,
			}
			set.size++
			return true, nil
		}
	}
	if firstDeleted != -1 {
		// A full traversal found no duplicate or neverUsed slot, but a
		// tombstone can still hold the new key.
		set.slots[firstDeleted] = probeSlot{
			key:   key,
			state: occupied,
		}
		set.size++
		return true, nil
	}
	// Every physical slot is occupied and no tombstone is reusable.
	return false, fmt.Errorf("open-addressing set is full")
}

func (set *probingSet) contains(key int) bool {
	// Probe at most capacity positions so a full table always stops.
	start := normalizedIndex(key, len(set.slots))
	for step := 0; step < len(set.slots); step++ {
		index := wrapIndex(start, step, len(set.slots))
		slot := set.slots[index]
		if slot.state == neverUsed {
			// Insertion stops here, so the key cannot occur later.
			return false
		}
		if slot.state == occupied && slot.key == key {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

func (set *probingSet) remove(key int) bool {
	// Follow the same probe sequence used by add and contains.
	start := normalizedIndex(key, len(set.slots))
	for step := 0; step < len(set.slots); step++ {
		index := wrapIndex(start, step, len(set.slots))
		slot := set.slots[index]
		if slot.state == neverUsed {
			return false
		}
		if slot.state == occupied && slot.key == key {
			// Leave a tombstone; later collided keys must
			// remain reachable through this position.
			set.slots[index] = probeSlot{state: deleted}
			set.size--
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

func (set *probingSet) display() []string {
	// Render all states so the walkthrough exposes probe history.
	result := make([]string, len(set.slots))
	for index, slot := range set.slots {
		switch slot.state {
		case occupied:
			result[index] = strconv.Itoa(slot.key)
		case deleted:
			result[index] = "x"
		case neverUsed:
			result[index] = "."
		}
	}
	return result
}

func main() {
	// Five buckets make 1, 6, and -4 collide after normalization.
	chained, err := newChainedSet(5)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	probing, err := newProbingSet(5)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	for _, key := range []int{1, 6, -4} {
		// Insert the same keys into both collision strategies.
		chained.add(key)
		if _, err := probing.add(key); err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
	}
	fmt.Println(chained.bucketKeys(1))
	fmt.Println(probing.display())

	// Remove the middle collision. Chaining shifts; probing must
	// leave a tombstone so -4 remains discoverable.
	fmt.Println(chained.remove(6), probing.remove(6))
	fmt.Println(chained.bucketKeys(1))
	fmt.Println(probing.display())

	// Key 11 has the same home and should reuse the tombstone
	// only after confirming that no live 11 already exists.
	chainedAdded := chained.add(11)
	probingAdded, err := probing.add(11)
	fmt.Println(chainedAdded, probingAdded, err)
	fmt.Println(chained.bucketKeys(1))
	fmt.Println(probing.display())
	fmt.Println(
		chained.contains(6),
		probing.contains(6),
		chained.contains(-4),
		probing.contains(-4),
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 6 -4]
[. 1 6 -4 .]
true true
[1 -4]
[. 1 x -4 .]
true true <nil>
[1 -4 11]
[. 1 11 -4 .]
false false true true
```

##### Why it works

For chaining, every key is stored only in the bucket selected by its
normalized hash. Add checks that entire bucket before appending;
contains and remove scan the same bucket. Therefore a key is present
exactly when that bucket contains one equal entry.

For open addressing, insertion and lookup follow the same bounded
probe sequence. An occupied matching slot proves presence. A
never-used slot proves absence because insertion would have stopped at
that position before placing the key later in the sequence.

Deletion leaves a tombstone, so it cannot create a false stopping
point for keys placed later. Insertion remembers a tombstone but keeps
searching for a duplicate; when absence is established, reusing the
earliest tombstone preserves reachability and adds exactly one key.

Every chain scan ends at its finite slice length. Every open operation
checks at most the slot capacity, so collision-heavy or full searches
still terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be item count, B the chain bucket count, C the open slot
capacity, and P the total retained capacity of all bucket slices.
Chaining retains O(B + P) storage. Without deletions, geometric slice
growth keeps P in O(N); deletions in this implementation do not shrink
the backing arrays. With well-distributed hashes, expected chain
length is about N divided by B, giving expected O(1) operations when
the load ratio stays bounded. If every key lands in one bucket, an
operation takes O(N) worst-case time.

Open addressing retains O(C) storage and has better locality. With a
good hash and a load ratio safely below one, add, contains, and remove
take expected O(1) time. A clustered, tombstone-heavy, or nearly full
table may probe all C slots, so worst-case time is O(C).

This fixed open table never resizes. Production tables usually grow
and rehash live keys before probe sequences become long. Rehashing is
O(N) for that operation but can support amortized expected O(1)
updates across a sequence.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Zero or negative bucket count or capacity returns an error before
  any modulo operation, avoiding division by zero.
- Negative key -4 with size 5 has remainder -4 in Go; adding 5 gives
  valid index 1. Using the raw remainder would index negatively.
- Duplicate add returns false without increasing size or adding a
  second chain or slot entry.
- Removing a missing key returns false and leaves size unchanged.
- Open deletion must write a tombstone, not never-used, or later
  collided keys become unreachable.
- Open insertion must search beyond the first tombstone for a
  duplicate, then reuse that tombstone only after absence is known.
- A full open table checks exactly C slots and returns an error. An
  unbounded probe loop would never find a never-used slot.
- Compute a wrapped probe position without first adding two large
  indexes; `wrapIndex` avoids overflow before wraparound.
- The remainder hash clusters arithmetic patterns such as keys spaced
  by C. Real tables use a mixing hash and resize policy appropriate to
  their key type and adversarial risk.
- Iteration order is not part of either set contract. Storage or
  resize changes may reorder keys.

##### When to choose it

Use separate chaining when variable bucket sizes or deletion without
tombstones matter more than per-bucket allocation and slice overhead.
Use open addressing when compact storage and locality matter and load
can be kept below capacity.

In ordinary Go code, prefer the built-in map unless custom storage or
teaching goals justify implementing a table. The language specifies
map behavior, not a particular collision strategy. The official
[Go maps article](https://go.dev/blog/maps) explains presence checks,
deletion, key rules, and that implementation details are unspecified.

Practice lookup with [Two Sum](
problems/solved_easy_leetcode_0001_two_sum.go). The
[membership](#b12-membership-tracking-hash-set) and
[complement lookup](#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) families apply
hash tables without reimplementing their storage.

#### A.6.3 Multisets and frequency maps

##### Problem and contract

A set records whether a value is present. Some tasks also need its
multiplicity: how many copies are present. A multiset, also called a
bag, stores that count. A frequency map is the usual representation:
each key is a value and its mapped integer is the multiplicity.

Our word bag starts empty and stores string values. `add` and `remove`
accept a positive amount or return an error without mutation. Removal
also fails without mutation when fewer copies exist than requested.
`count` returns zero for a missing word. `total` counts all copies,
while `distinct` counts keys with positive multiplicity.

The empty string is a valid word. The caller must use the constructor,
and all counts and their sum must fit in Go's `int`. The bag retains
the strings used as keys and excludes unsynchronized concurrent
access. Read [hash-table collision handling](
#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) first.

##### Mental model

Treat each map entry as a labeled counter. Reading
`countByWord["apple"] == 3` means the bag contains three copies of
`"apple"`. A missing map key reads as zero, which is exactly the
missing multiplicity.

Only positive counters belong in the map. Adding increases one counter
and the total. Removing decreases both; when a counter reaches zero,
delete its key. The map length is therefore the distinct count without
a second field.

At every operation boundary, each stored count is positive, it
equals the number of copies of that word, and `total` is the sum of
all stored counts.

##### Worked walkthrough

Start empty. Add two apples, add one pear, add one apple, remove two
apples, remove the pear, then try to add zero apples. The final bag
has one apple.

Initial state: `countByWord` is `{}`, `total` is 0, and `distinct` is
0.

1. Decision: add `"apple"` by 2. The amount is positive and the
   missing counter reads as 0, so store `0 + 2`.
   After: counts are `{apple:2}`; total is 2; distinct is 1.
   Known correct: both copies are represented by one positive counter.

2. Decision: add `"pear"` by 1. Its current count is 0, so create a
   second positive counter.
   After: counts are `{apple:2, pear:1}`; total is 3; distinct is 2.
   Known correct: the counters and total describe all three copies.

3. Decision: add `"apple"` by 1. Its counter already exists, so
   replace 2 with 3 rather than creating another key.
   After: counts are `{apple:3, pear:1}`; total is 4; distinct is 2.
   Known correct: duplicate values change multiplicity, not key count.

4. Decision: remove two apples. Three are available, so store the
   positive remainder `3 - 2` and reduce total by 2.
   After: counts are `{apple:1, pear:1}`; total is 2; distinct is 2.
   Known correct: exactly the requested copies disappeared.

5. Decision: remove one pear. Its remainder is zero, so delete the map
   key instead of storing a zero counter.
   After: counts are `{apple:1}`; total is 1; distinct is 1.
   Known correct: map length still counts positive-frequency words.

6. Decision: add zero apples. Zero is not a positive amount, so return
   an error before reading or writing a counter.
   After: counts remain `{apple:1}`; total and distinct remain 1.
   Known correct: failure caused no partial mutation, completing the
   required sequence.

Focused shortage case: removing two apples from the final bag returns
an error because only one exists. Focused representation case: adding
one empty string creates the valid entry `{"":1}`.

Counterexample to storing only membership: after step 1, a set says
only that apple is present. The first wrong decision is discarding the
count, so one later removal would incorrectly make both copies absent.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. The program prints logical observations
rather than ranging over the map, whose iteration order is
unspecified.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type wordBag struct {
	// Each map value counts one word; total counts copies of all words.
	countByWord map[string]int
	total       int
}

func newWordBag() *wordBag {
	// Writes require a non-nil map, so construction initializes it once.
	return &wordBag{
		countByWord: make(map[string]int),
	}
}

func (bag *wordBag) add(word string, amount int) error {
	// Reject invalid changes before either stored count can
	// change. The contract assumes successful sums fit in int.
	if amount <= 0 {
		return fmt.Errorf("add amount must be positive")
	}

	// A missing key reads as zero, so one addition handles a new
	// word and extra copies of an existing word.
	bag.countByWord[word] += amount
	bag.total += amount
	return nil
}

func (bag *wordBag) remove(word string, amount int) error {
	// Validate the whole request before mutating either stored fact.
	if amount <= 0 {
		return fmt.Errorf("remove amount must be positive")
	}
	current := bag.countByWord[word]
	// Refuse a negative multiplicity. Missing words have count zero
	// and are rejected by the same comparison.
	if amount > current {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"remove %d %q: only %d present",
			amount,
			word,
			current,
		)
	}

	// Keep only positive counters so map length equals the number of
	// distinct words. A zero count is represented by an absent key.
	remaining := current - amount
	if remaining == 0 {
		delete(bag.countByWord, word)
	} else {
		bag.countByWord[word] = remaining
	}
	// The request was fully satisfied, so total loses the same number of
	// copies as the word-specific counter.
	bag.total -= amount
	return nil
}

func (bag *wordBag) count(word string) int {
	// Go's zero value for a missing key is the required absent count.
	return bag.countByWord[word]
}

func (bag *wordBag) distinct() int {
	// Because zero counts are deleted, map length is the distinct count.
	return len(bag.countByWord)
}

func main() {
	bag := newWordBag()

	// Apply changes that exercise new words and repeated words.
	fmt.Println(bag.add("apple", 2))
	fmt.Println(bag.add("pear", 1))
	fmt.Println(bag.add("apple", 1))
	fmt.Println(bag.count("apple"), bag.total, bag.distinct())

	fmt.Println(bag.remove("apple", 2))
	fmt.Println(bag.remove("pear", 1))
	fmt.Println(bag.count("pear"), bag.total, bag.distinct())

	// A rejected update occurs before mutation, so observations remain
	// identical to the preceding state.
	err := bag.add("apple", 0)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
	fmt.Println(bag.count("apple"), bag.total, bag.distinct())
}
```

Expected output:

```text
<nil>
<nil>
<nil>
3 4 2
<nil>
<nil>
0 1 1
true
1 1 1
```

##### Why it works

The constructor creates an empty map and zero total, so there are no
stored zero or negative counts and the total equals the empty sum.

Successful add increases exactly the requested word's counter and the
total by the same positive amount. Every other counter is unchanged,
so the representation continues to match all multiplicities.

Successful remove first proves enough copies exist. A positive
remainder stays as the new count; a zero remainder removes the key.
Subtracting the same amount from total preserves the sum invariant.
Every failure returns before mutation.

Each method performs a finite number of map operations and terminates.
Because the invariant holds after every successful or failed update,
`count`, `total`, and map length return the promised observations.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let K be the number of distinct words and L the byte length of the
word used by an operation. Under the usual well-distributed
hash-table assumption, add, remove, and count take expected Theta(L)
time: hashing the string reads its bytes, then table access is
expected constant time. Go's language specification does not promise
a map complexity bound. `total` and `distinct` take Theta(1) time.

The map retains O(K) entries plus references to the distinct key
bytes. It may retain more backing storage than the live entries need.
Each operation uses O(1) auxiliary storage apart from possible map
growth during insertion.

A frequency map avoids storing every duplicate separately. It also
makes count lookup direct, but it does not preserve insertion order or
support ordered predecessor and range queries.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A missing word has count zero. Using two-value lookup is optional
  when zero and missing have the same meaning.
- The empty string is a valid map key. Reject it only when the domain,
  not the representation, forbids it.
- Adding zero or a negative amount returns an error. Accepting it
  could create a stored zero or make a count negative.
- Removing more copies than exist returns an error before mutation.
  Clamping to zero would hide an invalid request and corrupt total.
- Removing the final copy deletes the key. Keeping a zero entry makes
  map length disagree with the distinct count.
- Increment total by amount, not by one. Otherwise `add("apple", 2)`
  immediately breaks the sum invariant.
- Counts can overflow `int`; this contract requires the caller to keep
  each count and the total representable.
- Ranging over a Go map does not promise insertion or sorted order.
  Sort copied keys when deterministic presentation is required.

##### When to choose it

Choose a frequency map when duplicates affect the answer: inventory,
word counts, anagram checks, resource consumption, and sliding-window
multiplicity are recognizable cases.

Use a set when only present or absent matters. Use a direct-address
counter array when keys come from a small dense range. Use an ordered
multiset when the workload asks for the smallest value, predecessor,
or range counts as well as multiplicity.
