Practice the invariant with [Valid Anagram](
problems/easy_leetcode_0242_valid_anagram.go), [Ransom Note](
problems/easy_leetcode_0383_ransom_note.go). The [problem index](
problems/README.md) also lists the reviewed Longest Substring Without
Repeating Characters archive.

The [frequency-counting family](
#b11-frequency-counting-hash-map) applies this representation to
interview problems.

#### A.6.4 Composite keys and custom hashes

##### Problem and contract

Some lookups depend on several values together. A route price may be
identified by origin, destination, and stop count; none of those
fields alone selects the record. A composite key groups the fields
into one logical identity.

Our route table maps `routeKey` values to travel minutes. Every string
and `int` value is a valid key field. Construction requires a positive
bucket count. Put inserts or replaces an exact key and reports whether
it replaced one. Get returns minutes and presence separately. Hash
collisions must not merge unequal routes.

The table owns its bucket slices but retains string data referenced by
keys. Bucket allocation must fit memory, integer arithmetic follows
Go's unsigned wraparound rules, and access is not synchronized.
Operations require a non-nil table returned by the constructor, and
the entry count must fit `int`. Read [separate chaining](
#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) first.

##### Mental model

Read `routeKey{"A", "BC", 0}` as one tuple: from A to BC with zero
stops. Equality asks whether all three corresponding fields match.
Changing even one field creates a different key.

A hash compresses the tuple into an integer, then modulo chooses a
candidate bucket. It is only a locator, not proof of identity. The
table scans that bucket and compares the complete stored key before
reading or replacing a value.

The hash processes a canonical field sequence: origin length and
bytes, destination length and bytes, then stop count. Including field
lengths distinguishes the sequences `("A", "BC")` and
`("AB", "C")`, which naive concatenation would both encode as
`"ABC"`.

The essential hash law is one-way: equal keys must produce equal
hashes. Unequal keys may collide and share a bucket because equality
checks keep their entries separate.

##### Worked walkthrough

Create two buckets. Insert routes `("A", "BC", 0) -> 90` and
`("AB", "C", 0) -> 80`, replace the first value with 85, then insert
`("A", "BC", 1) -> 110`. The first two hashes are 85974545592091 and
86013270075031. Both are odd, so modulo 2 selects bucket 1 and
deliberately exercises a collision.

Initial state: buckets are `[[], []]` and size is 0.

1. Decision: hash `("A", "BC", 0)`. Its bucket is 1, whose chain is
   empty, so append the key and 90 minutes.
   After: bucket 1 contains `[(A,BC,0):90]`; size is 1.
   Known correct: the only exact key maps to its inserted value.

2. Decision: hash `("AB", "C", 0)`. Its full hash differs from the
   first route's, but modulo 2 also selects bucket 1. The complete
   keys differ, so append rather than replace.
   After: bucket 1 contains both routes with values 90 and 80; size is
   2.
   Known correct: the collision preserved two distinct identities.

3. Decision: put `("A", "BC", 0) -> 85`. Hashing reaches bucket 1,
   and the first complete key is equal, so replace only its minutes.
   After: the values are 85 and 80; size remains 2.
   Known correct: an update changed one value, not membership.

4. Decision: get each collided key. Both start in bucket 1; full-key
   comparisons select 85 for the first and 80 for the second.
   After: both queries return their value, true; storage is unchanged.
   Known correct: a shared bucket did not make the keys
   interchangeable.

5. Decision: put `("A", "BC", 1) -> 110`. The changed stop count is
   part of equality and hashing, so insert a third key.
   After: size is 3 and the new key maps to 110.
   Known correct: changing one component creates a separate route.

6. Decision: get `("BC", "A", 0)`. No equal entry exists in its
   selected bucket, so return zero and false.
   After: size remains 3 and all inserted routes are unchanged.
   Known correct: field order matters and the missing query caused no
   mutation, completing the sequence.

Focused failure case: construction with zero buckets returns an error
before allocation or modulo. Focused duplicate case: putting the same
three fields again replaces minutes and leaves size unchanged.

Counterexample to using concatenation as the map key: `"A" + "BC"`
and `"AB" + "C"` both produce `"ABC"`. The first wrong decision is
discarding field boundaries, so the second route replaces the first
before collision handling can help.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. Its deterministic polynomial hash makes the
trace reproducible; it is not hardened against adversarial keys.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

const routeHashMultiplier uint64 = 131

type routeKey struct {
	// All three comparable fields participate in route identity.
	origin      string
	destination string
	stops       int
}

type routeEntry struct {
	key     routeKey
	minutes int
}

type routeTable struct {
	// Each bucket is a collision chain; size counts exact distinct keys.
	buckets [][]routeEntry
	size    int
}

func newRouteTable(bucketCount int) (*routeTable, error) {
	// A positive count makes later modulo selection defined.
	if bucketCount <= 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("bucket count must be positive")
	}
	return &routeTable{
		buckets: make([][]routeEntry, bucketCount),
	}, nil
}

func mixRouteField(hash uint64, value string) uint64 {
	// Mix length before bytes to preserve field boundaries. Without it,
	// tuples ("A", "BC") and ("AB", "C") form one byte stream.
	hash = hash*routeHashMultiplier + uint64(len(value))
	for byteIndex := 0; byteIndex < len(value); byteIndex++ {
		// Unsigned overflow deliberately wraps during hash mixing.
		hash *= routeHashMultiplier
		hash += uint64(value[byteIndex]) + 1
	}
	return hash
}

func hashRoute(key routeKey) uint64 {
	// Visit fields in a fixed order. Equal tuples therefore perform the
	// same operations and must produce equal hashes.
	hash := uint64(17)
	hash = mixRouteField(hash, key.origin)
	hash = mixRouteField(hash, key.destination)
	// stops has a fixed integer width, so a separate mix step is
	// enough to distinguish it from the preceding string bytes.
	hash *= routeHashMultiplier
	hash += uint64(key.stops)
	return hash
}

func (table *routeTable) bucketIndex(key routeKey) int {
	// Modulo reduces the hash to the table's valid bucket range.
	hash := hashRoute(key)
	return int(hash % uint64(len(table.buckets)))
}

func (table *routeTable) put(
	key routeKey,
	minutes int,
) bool {
	// Hashing narrows the work to one collision chain.
	bucketIndex := table.bucketIndex(key)
	bucket := table.buckets[bucketIndex]

	// Exact struct equality, not hash or bucket, confirms identity.
	// Replace that entry and leave the distinct-key count unchanged.
	for entryIndex := range bucket {
		if bucket[entryIndex].key != key {
			continue
		}
		bucket[entryIndex].minutes = minutes
		return true
	}

	// No exact key exists, so append a separate collided entry and count
	// one new logical mapping.
	table.buckets[bucketIndex] = append(
		bucket,
		routeEntry{key: key, minutes: minutes},
	)
	table.size++
	return false
}

func (table *routeTable) get(key routeKey) (int, bool) {
	// Search the selected chain and confirm every component through key
	// equality. bool still distinguishes a stored zero-minute value.
	bucketIndex := table.bucketIndex(key)
	for _, entry := range table.buckets[bucketIndex] {
		if entry.key == key {
			return entry.minutes, true
		}
	}
	return 0, false
}

func main() {
	// Two buckets make collisions visible in a small printed example.
	table, err := newRouteTable(2)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	first := routeKey{
		// These boundaries differ from second even though concatenated
		// text would be the same "ABC".
		origin:      "A",
		destination: "BC",
		stops:       0,
	}
	second := routeKey{
		origin:      "AB",
		destination: "C",
		stops:       0,
	}
	fmt.Println(hashRoute(first), table.bucketIndex(first))
	fmt.Println(hashRoute(second), table.bucketIndex(second))

	// Distinct colliding keys append; an equal key replaces in place.
	fmt.Println(table.put(first, 90), table.size)
	fmt.Println(table.put(second, 80), table.size)
	fmt.Println(table.put(first, 85), table.size)

	minutes, found := table.get(first)
	fmt.Println(minutes, found)
	minutes, found = table.get(second)
	fmt.Println(minutes, found)

	// Changing only stops still creates a third composite key.
	withStop := routeKey{
		origin:      "A",
		destination: "BC",
		stops:       1,
	}
	fmt.Println(table.put(withStop, 110), table.size)
	missing := routeKey{
		origin:      "BC",
		destination: "A",
		stops:       0,
	}
	minutes, found = table.get(missing)
	fmt.Println(minutes, found)

	// Zero buckets are rejected before modulo or indexing can occur.
	_, err = newRouteTable(0)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
85974545592091 1
86013270075031 1
false 1
false 2
true 2
85 true
80 true
false 3
0 false
true
```

##### Why it works

The constructor creates a finite, nonempty bucket array. Equal
`routeKey` values contain the same field values, so `hashRoute`
processes the same lengths, bytes, and stop count and returns the same
hash. They therefore always select the same bucket.

Put scans that complete bucket. If it finds an equal key, replacing
only the value preserves membership and size. If it finds none,
appending creates exactly one new mapping and increases size once.
Unequal keys with the same bucket remain separate entries.

Get computes the same bucket and returns a value only after exact-key
equality succeeds. If the finite scan ends, no equal key can be stored
elsewhere because equal keys must select this bucket. It safely
returns absent. Every loop is bounded by one finite chain, so each
operation terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be entry count, B bucket count, P total retained bucket
capacity, and L the greatest total key-byte length examined by one
operation.
Hashing costs Theta(L). With well-distributed hashes and bounded
`N / B`, expected lookup or put time is Theta(L). If all entries share
one bucket and their string fields require full comparison, worst-case
time is O(NL).

The table retains O(B + P) entry storage plus references to key bytes.
Without deletions, geometric slice growth keeps P in O(N). A put may
allocate when its bucket grows; other work uses O(1) auxiliary
storage. This fixed table never resizes, so a growing load increases
chains.

Composite keys avoid nested maps and keep identity rules in one type.
Custom tables add control over equality, hashing, and storage, but
they also add collision, resizing, and adversarial-input
responsibilities.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Zero or negative bucket count returns an error before modulo. A zero
  divisor would panic in `bucketIndex`.
- Empty strings, negative stops, and zero minutes are valid under this
  representation contract. Domain validation belongs at its boundary.
- Replacing an equal key leaves size unchanged. Comparing only the
  hash could replace an unequal collided key.
- Equal keys must hash alike. If equality preserves case but hashing
  folds it, unequal case variants merely collide. If equality folds
  case but hashing preserves it, keys considered equal can select
  different buckets and become unreachable.
- Unequal keys may have equal hashes. A collision is expected data,
  not permission to skip exact equality.
- Concatenating variable-length fields loses boundaries. Use a typed
  key or a canonical encoding with lengths or unambiguous tags.
- A struct is a built-in map key only when all fields are comparable.
  A slice field makes the struct ineligible; arrays remain comparable
  when their element type is comparable.
- Pointer fields compare addresses, not pointed-to contents. Choose
  value fields when logical identity depends on the contents.
- Unsigned hash overflow is intentional and deterministic here. The
  hash is educational and predictable, so hostile inputs can cluster.

##### When to choose it

Choose a composite key when lookup identity naturally forms a tuple:
grid coordinates, graph edges, cache variants, locale plus path, or a
fixed-size frequency signature.

In ordinary Go code, prefer a built-in map such as
`map[routeKey]int`. Go automatically hashes comparable structs and
arrays. Use a custom table only when you need different equality,
specialized storage, or another data structure's hash interface.

For adversarially robust custom hashing, use the standard
[`hash/maphash`](https://pkg.go.dev/hash/maphash) package rather than
this teaching hash. Its `Comparable` function hashes comparable values
with a per-table seed while preserving the equality-to-hash rule. The
[Go map specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Map_types) defines the
key comparability requirement.

Practice a fixed-array composite signature with [Group Anagrams](
problems/medium_leetcode_0049_group_anagrams.go). The
[memoization](#b201-memoization-map-and-recursion) and
[bitmask DP](#b207-bitmask-dp-state-table) families use composite
state keys in larger algorithms.

### A.7 Trees

#### A.7.1 Binary trees

##### Problem and contract

Some data branches into two independent parts instead of continuing
through one next element. A binary tree represents that shape with a
root node and up to two ordered child links, called left and right.
The links may be absent, and values need not be sorted or unique.

Given a proper binary tree of integers, our functions return preorder,
inorder, postorder, and level-order traversals. Each node appears once
in each result. A nil root returns an empty result. Traversal does not
mutate nodes or transfer ownership.

A proper tree is finite and acyclic, the root has no parent, and every
other node has exactly one parent. Shared children and cycles are
outside the contract because they form a graph, not a tree. Read
[linked ownership](#a31-singly-linked-lists) and [queues](
#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) first.

##### Mental model

Each node stores a value and two links. A nil link means that side has
no child. A node together with everything reachable below it is a
subtree. A node with no children is a leaf.

Depth-first traversal completely handles one subtree before the next.
The point at which it records the current node defines the order:

- Preorder records node, then left subtree, then right subtree.
- Inorder records left subtree, node, then right subtree.
- Postorder records left subtree, right subtree, then node.

Breadth-first traversal, also called level order, keeps a queue. It
removes the earliest pending node, records it, then appends its left
and right children. The root has depth 0; each child has depth one
greater than its parent. Tree height is the greatest node depth, while
some problem statements instead count nodes on the longest path.

For every active recursive call, the current node names the exact
subtree still being handled. For the queue, every pending node has
been discovered but not yet recorded.

##### Worked walkthrough

Traverse this tree. The expected preorder is `[4,2,1,3,7,9]`, inorder
is `[1,2,3,4,7,9]`, postorder is `[1,3,2,9,7,4]`, and level order is
`[4,2,7,1,3,9]`.

```text
        4
       / \
      2   7
     / \   \
    1   3   9
```

Initial state: all three depth-first outputs are empty. The first call
is responsible for the subtree rooted at 4.

1. Decision: enter node 4. Preorder records 4 before either child,
   then recursion chooses the left subtree rooted at 2.
   After: preorder is `[4]`; inorder and postorder are empty; node 2
   is active.
   Known correct: preorder has recorded every entered ancestor before
   its unresolved descendants.

2. Decision: enter node 2, record it in preorder, and choose its left
   child 1. Node 1 has nil children, so record 1 in all three
   positions and return to node 2.
   After: preorder is `[4,2,1]`; inorder is `[1]`; postorder is `[1]`.
   Known correct: leaf 1 is complete, while node 2 still has a right
   subtree.

3. Decision: record node 2 in inorder, then enter leaf 3. Record 3 in
   preorder, inorder, and postorder; after it returns, record node 2
   in postorder.
   After: preorder is `[4,2,1,3]`; inorder is `[1,2,3]`;
   postorder is `[1,3,2]`.
   Known correct: the entire subtree rooted at 2 is complete in every
   order.

4. Decision: the left subtree of 4 is complete, so record 4 in
   inorder and enter its right child 7. Node 7 has no left child, so
   record 7 in inorder immediately after its preorder entry.
   After: preorder is `[4,2,1,3,7]`; inorder is `[1,2,3,4,7]`;
   postorder remains `[1,3,2]`.
   Known correct: only the subtree rooted at 9 and pending postorder
   ancestors remain.

5. Decision: enter leaf 9, record it in all three positions, return,
   then record 7 and 4 in postorder as their subtrees finish.
   After: preorder is `[4,2,1,3,7,9]`; inorder is
   `[1,2,3,4,7,9]`; postorder is `[1,3,2,9,7,4]`.
   Known correct: every node is complete once in every depth-first
   order.

6. Decision: start breadth first with queue `[4]`. Remove 4, record
   it, and append children 2 and 7 from left to right.
   After: level order is `[4]`; queue is `[2,7]`.
   Known correct: depth 0 is complete and depth 1 is pending in order.

7. Decision: remove 2 and 7 in queue order. Record them; append 1 and
   3 from node 2, then 9 from node 7.
   After: level order is `[4,2,7]`; queue is `[1,3,9]`.
   Known correct: depths 0 and 1 are complete, and all depth-2 nodes
   are pending left to right.

8. Decision: remove leaves 1, 3, and 9. None has children to append.
   After: level order is `[4,2,7,1,3,9]`; queue is empty.
   Known correct: no discovered node remains, so all four traversals
   match the required result.

Focused boundary case: a nil root returns four empty outputs without
dereferencing it. A one-node tree returns its value in every order.

Counterexample to treating a binary tree as sorted: node 7 may have
right child 1 in an ordinary binary tree. The first wrong decision is
discarding a subtree based on value before a search-tree invariant has
been established.

##### Implementation

This complete program builds the pictured tree and prints all four
orders. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type treeNode struct {
	value int
	left  *treeNode
	right *treeNode
}

type depthFirstOrders struct {
	// Nodes are recorded before, between, or after child visits.
	preorder  []int
	inorder   []int
	postorder []int
}

func appendDepthFirst(
	node *treeNode,
	orders *depthFirstOrders,
) {
	// A nil pointer is an empty subtree, so it contributes no value
	// and ends this recursive branch.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}

	// Record before children for preorder, between them for inorder, and
	// after both for postorder. Calls visit left before right.
	orders.preorder = append(orders.preorder, node.value)
	appendDepthFirst(node.left, orders)
	orders.inorder = append(orders.inorder, node.value)
	appendDepthFirst(node.right, orders)
	orders.postorder = append(orders.postorder, node.value)
}

func collectDepthFirst(root *treeNode) depthFirstOrders {
	// One accumulator lets each visit append to all three
	// sequences without walking the tree three separate times.
	var orders depthFirstOrders
	appendDepthFirst(root, &orders)
	return orders
}

func collectLevelOrder(root *treeNode) []int {
	// Empty input has no level and returns a non-nil empty result.
	if root == nil {
		return []int{}
	}

	// The slice is a queue. nextNodeIndex separates processed nodes
	// from nodes waiting in breadth-first order.
	queue := []*treeNode{root}
	order := make([]int, 0)
	nextNodeIndex := 0
	for nextNodeIndex < len(queue) {
		// Remove the front by advancing the index, without shifting
		// remaining slice elements.
		node := queue[nextNodeIndex]
		nextNodeIndex++
		order = append(order, node.value)
		// Enqueue left before right to keep each level in tree order.
		if node.left != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.left)
		}
		if node.right != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.right)
		}
	}
	return order
}

func main() {
	// This asymmetric tree exercises missing children and both sides:
	// 4 has children 2 and 7; 2 has 1 and 3; 7 has only right child 9.
	root := &treeNode{
		value: 4,
		left: &treeNode{
			value: 2,
			left:  &treeNode{value: 1},
			right: &treeNode{value: 3},
		},
		right: &treeNode{
			value: 7,
			right: &treeNode{value: 9},
		},
	}

	orders := collectDepthFirst(root)
	fmt.Println(orders.preorder)
	fmt.Println(orders.inorder)
	fmt.Println(orders.postorder)
	fmt.Println(collectLevelOrder(root))
	fmt.Println(collectLevelOrder(nil))
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[4 2 1 3 7 9]
[1 2 3 4 7 9]
[1 3 2 9 7 4]
[4 2 7 1 3 9]
[]
```

##### Why it works

For depth first, a nil subtree correctly contributes no node. Assume
the recursive calls return each child subtree in the requested order.
Recording the current value before both calls, between them, or after
both produces exactly preorder, inorder, or postorder for the larger
subtree. This establishes the claim from leaves up to the root.

For level order, the queue initially contains only the depth-0 root.
Removing a node before appending its children keeps every earlier
depth ahead of every later depth. Appending left before right
preserves left-to-right order within a depth. Each reachable node is
appended by its unique parent exactly once and later removed once.

A proper finite tree makes recursive calls descend toward nil and
makes the queue eventually empty. At termination every reachable node
has therefore been recorded once in each promised order.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be node count, H the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf
path, and W the maximum nodes at one depth. Each traversal reads each
node once and takes Theta(N) time. The three depth-first outputs store
3N integers, and their recursion uses O(H) auxiliary stack space.

The level-order output stores N integers. This implementation also
retains an N-entry queue slice because it advances an index rather
than reusing removed slots, so its auxiliary storage is O(N). A
circular queue can reduce live queue storage to O(W).

A balanced tree has H in Theta(log N); a one-sided chain has H in
Theta(N). Recursion expresses the shape directly, but an explicit
stack avoids depending on call-stack growth for a very deep tree.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A nil root returns empty output. Reading `root.value` before the nil
  check panics.
- A leaf visits two nil subtrees and still appears exactly once in
  each order. Appending on every call would add nonexistent nodes.
- Duplicate values are separate nodes. Tracking visited values would
  incorrectly skip equal-valued nodes.
- A node with only a right child still processes its empty left side
  before the right. Swapping the links changes traversal meaning.
- A one-sided tree can make recursion depth N. Use an explicit stack
  when input depth may exhaust the available call stack.
- A cycle never reaches a nil base case, and a shared child is visited
  once per incoming link. Reject such inputs or use graph traversal
  with node identity tracking instead.
- The indexed queue retains every appended pointer until return. Do
  not claim O(W) auxiliary storage for this exact implementation.

##### When to choose it

Choose a binary tree when each item has distinct left and right roles:
expression operands, decision branches, hierarchical partitions, and
tree-shaped problem input are common signals.

Use a binary search tree only when the ordering invariant is part of
the contract. Use an array-backed heap when the shape is complete and
only an extreme value matters. Use a general rooted tree when a node
may have more than two children, and a graph when sharing or cycles
are valid.

Practice traversal and shape reasoning with [Maximum Depth](
problems/easy_leetcode_0104_maximum_depth_of_binary_tree.go) and the
[tree problem index](problems/README.md). The
[depth-first](#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) and
[breadth-first](#b112-breadth-first-traversal-queue) families apply
these orders to interview tasks.

#### A.7.2 Binary search trees

##### Problem and contract

Searching every node of an arbitrary binary tree wastes its shape when
keys could instead direct the search. A binary search tree, or BST,
maintains a strict order: every key in a node's left subtree is less
than the node key, and every key in its right subtree is greater.

Our unbalanced BST is a mutable set of Go `int` values. Insert adds a
missing value and returns true; a duplicate returns false without
mutation. Contains reports membership. Remove deletes a present value
and returns true; a missing value returns false without mutation.
Inorder traversal returns every stored value in increasing order.

The zero-value tree is empty and ready to use. The tree owns its
nodes, does not expose stable node identities, and excludes
unsynchronized concurrent access. Methods require a non-nil tree
pointer. Comparisons do not overflow. Read
[binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) first.

##### Mental model

At a node, comparison eliminates one whole subtree. A smaller target
can occur only on the left; a larger target can occur only on the
right; equality finishes the search. Insert follows the same path and
attaches a new leaf at the first nil link.

Each visited node also narrows an implicit valid interval. Going left
adds an upper bound; going right adds a lower bound. The ordering rule
applies to every descendant, not only to immediate children.

Deletion reconnects the remaining tree according to node shape:

- A leaf becomes nil.
- A node with one child is replaced by that child.
- A node with two children copies the smallest key in its right
  subtree, called its inorder successor, then removes that successor
  from its old position.

At every operation boundary, keys are unique and an inorder traversal
is strictly increasing. Search paths contain every location where the
requested key could legally appear.

##### Worked walkthrough

Insert `8,3,10,1,6,14,4,7,13`, query 7 and 5, reject duplicate 6,
then remove leaf 1, one-child node 14, and two-child root 8. Finally,
try to remove missing 42.

Initial state: the root is nil and the set is empty.

1. Decision: insert 8 at the nil root. For 3, compare `3 < 8` and use
   the nil left link. For 10, compare `10 > 8` and use the nil right
   link. Insert 1 by following left from 8 and 3. Insert 6 by going
   left from 8 and right from 3. Insert 14 by going right from both
   8 and 10. Insert 4 by following `8 -> 3 -> 6` and then left;
   insert 7
   along the same path and then right. Insert 13 by following
   `8 -> 10 -> 14` and then left.
   After:

   ```text
           8
          / \
         3   10
        / \    \
       1   6    14
          / \   /
         4   7 13
   ```

   Inorder is `[1,3,4,6,7,8,10,13,14]`.
   Known correct: every inserted key lies within all ancestor bounds.

2. Decision: search for 7. Since `7 < 8`, go left; since `7 > 3`
   and `7 > 6`, go right twice; equality at 7 finishes the search.
   For 5, follow `8 -> 3 -> 6 -> 4 -> nil` by comparing less than
   8, greater than 3, less than 6, and greater than 4.
   After: results are true and false; the tree is unchanged.
   Known correct: each discarded subtree is entirely on the wrong side
   of the target.

3. Decision: insert 6. Comparisons follow `8 -> 3 -> 6`; equality
   reports a duplicate before allocation.
   After: insertion returns false and inorder is unchanged.
   Known correct: the strict ordering invariant still represents a
   set.

4. Decision: remove 1 by following left from 8 and 3. Node 1 has no
   children, so replace its parent link with nil.
   After: inorder is `[3,4,6,7,8,10,13,14]`.
   Known correct: only key 1 disappeared; all remaining ancestor
   bounds still hold.

5. Decision: remove 14 by following right from 8 and 10. It has only
   left child 13, so replace 14 with 13.
   After: inorder is `[3,4,6,7,8,10,13]`.
   Known correct: 13 was already greater than every ancestor that now
   leads to it.

6. Decision: remove root 8, which has two children. The smallest key
   in its right subtree is 10. Copy 10 to the root, then detach the
   old 10; its right child 13 takes that old position.
   After:

   ```text
          10
          / \
         3   13
          \
           6
          / \
         4   7
   ```

   Inorder is `[3,4,6,7,10,13]`.
   Known correct: the successor is above every left key and no greater
   than any key remaining on the right.

7. Decision: remove 42. Comparisons follow right links
   `10 -> 13 -> nil`, so report missing.
   After: removal returns false and inorder remains
   `[3,4,6,7,10,13]`.
   Known correct: the failed search exhausted the only legal path and
   caused no mutation, completing the sequence.

Focused boundary case: removing the only node makes the root nil.
Focused extreme case: minimum and maximum `int` keys need only direct
comparison; no `value - 1` bound arithmetic is required.

Counterexample to checking only parent and child: root 10 with left
child 5 and that child's right child 12 passes local comparisons but
is not a BST. The first wrong decision is forgetting the upper bound
10 while descending below node 5.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type searchNode struct {
	value int
	left  *searchNode
	right *searchNode
}

type searchTree struct {
	root *searchNode
}

func (tree *searchTree) insert(value int) bool {
	// The first value becomes root because no ordering constraint exists
	// yet beyond the value itself.
	if tree.root == nil {
		tree.root = &searchNode{value: value}
		return true
	}

	// At each node, search-tree order rules out one whole subtree.
	// Stop at equality or the nil child link where this value belongs.
	node := tree.root
	for {
		switch {
		case value < node.value:
			// The right subtree is too large for this insertion.
			if node.left == nil {
				node.left = &searchNode{value: value}
				return true
			}
			node = node.left
		case value > node.value:
			// Every value in the left subtree is too small for this insertion.
			if node.right == nil {
				node.right = &searchNode{value: value}
				return true
			}
			node = node.right
		default:
			// The set contract rejects duplicate keys without mutation.
			return false
		}
	}
}

func (tree *searchTree) contains(value int) bool {
	// Follow the only subtree that can still contain value. Reaching nil
	// proves the search path ended without equality.
	for node := tree.root; node != nil; {
		switch {
		case value < node.value:
			node = node.left
		case value > node.value:
			node = node.right
		default:
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

func detachMinimum(node *searchNode) (*searchNode, int) {
	// The first node without a left child is minimum. Return its right
	// child to preserve values greater than that minimum.
	if node.left == nil {
		return node.right, node.value
	}
	var minimum int
	// Reconnect the changed left subtree while recursion unwinds.
	node.left, minimum = detachMinimum(node.left)
	return node, minimum
}

func removeNode(
	node *searchNode,
	value int,
) (*searchNode, bool) {
	// A nil search path proves the value is absent and changes no links.
	if node == nil {
		return nil, false
	}
	if value < node.value {
		// Only the left subtree can contain a smaller target. Reattach the
		// returned subtree root in case removal changed it.
		var removed bool
		node.left, removed = removeNode(node.left, value)
		return node, removed
	}
	if value > node.value {
		// Symmetrically, a greater target can occur only on the right.
		var removed bool
		node.right, removed = removeNode(node.right, value)
		return node, removed
	}

	// The target matches. With at most one child, promote it; all
	// its values already satisfy the removed node's surrounding bounds.
	if node.left == nil {
		return node.right, true
	}
	if node.right == nil {
		return node.left, true
	}

	// With two children, the right minimum is next larger. Detach
	// it from the right, then reuse its value at this position.
	var successor int
	node.right, successor = detachMinimum(node.right)
	node.value = successor
	return node, true
}

func (tree *searchTree) remove(value int) bool {
	// removeNode may replace root, so keep its returned pointer.
	var removed bool
	tree.root, removed = removeNode(tree.root, value)
	return removed
}

func appendInorder(node *searchNode, values *[]int) {
	// Empty subtrees contribute nothing to sorted traversal.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}
	appendInorder(node.left, values)
	// Left values are smaller and right values greater, so recording the
	// node between them produces increasing order.
	*values = append(*values, node.value)
	appendInorder(node.right, values)
}

func (tree *searchTree) inorderValues() []int {
	values := make([]int, 0)
	appendInorder(tree.root, &values)
	return values
}

func main() {
	// This history covers leaf, one-child, two-child, duplicate, and
	// absent operations.
	var tree searchTree
	for _, value := range []int{
		8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13,
	} {
		if !tree.insert(value) {
			panic("unexpected duplicate")
		}
	}

	fmt.Println(tree.inorderValues())
	fmt.Println(tree.contains(7), tree.contains(5))
	fmt.Println(tree.insert(6))
	fmt.Println(tree.remove(1), tree.inorderValues())
	fmt.Println(tree.remove(14), tree.inorderValues())
	fmt.Println(tree.remove(8), tree.inorderValues())
	fmt.Println(tree.remove(42), tree.inorderValues())
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14]
true false
false
true [3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14]
true [3 4 6 7 8 10 13]
true [3 4 6 7 10 13]
false [3 4 6 7 10 13]
```

##### Why it works

The empty tree satisfies strict ordering. Insert and contains compare
at each node. The invariant proves that the rejected subtree cannot
contain the target, so following the selected child preserves every
possible location. Insertion at nil adds one leaf within all bounds;
equality leaves the unique-key set unchanged.

Removal uses the same safe search path. Removing a leaf or promoting
an only child preserves all ancestor bounds already satisfied by that
subtree. With two children, the right-subtree minimum is greater than
every left key and less than every other right key. Moving it to the
deleted position and detaching its old node preserves strict order
without duplicating the successor.

Inorder recursively emits every left key, then the node, then every
right key, so the invariant makes its result strictly increasing.
Every search or recursive call descends one level in a finite tree and
therefore terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be node count and H the number of nodes on the longest
root-to-leaf path. Contains, insert, and remove take O(H) time. A root
hit or empty-tree result takes Theta(1); a balanced shape gives
Theta(log N), while a one-sided shape gives Theta(N).

Successful insert allocates one node; its other auxiliary storage is
O(1). Iterative contains uses O(1) storage. Recursive remove uses O(H)
call-stack space and allocates no replacement nodes. Inorder takes
Theta(N) time, O(H) auxiliary stack space, and O(N) output storage.

Unlike a sorted slice, a BST inserts without shifting later values.
Unlike a hash set, it preserves order for minimum, successor, and
range operations. This implementation does not balance itself, so
insertion order controls whether those benefits retain logarithmic
height.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- An empty tree reports contains and remove false. A first insert must
  update the root rather than a nonexistent parent.
- A duplicate returns false. Sending equal keys consistently left or
  right would create duplicates and make the strict invariant false.
- Removing the root must assign the returned subtree to `tree.root`.
  Updating only a local node variable leaves the old root reachable.
- A two-child removal must delete the copied successor from its old
  position. Copying without detaching creates a duplicate key.
- The successor may have a right child. `detachMinimum` promotes that
  child instead of discarding its subtree.
- Minimum and maximum `int` values are valid. Bounds expressed by
  subtraction or sentinels can overflow or reject an extreme key.
- Checking only `left < node < right` misses deeper violations such as
  12 inside the left subtree of 10. Carry ancestor bounds or verify
  that inorder is strictly increasing.
- Sorted insertion such as `1,2,3,4` creates height N. Use a balanced
  tree when worst-case operation bounds matter.
- External pointer mutation could violate ordering. Keep nodes owned
  by the tree or validate after untrusted construction.

##### When to choose it

Choose a BST for a dynamic ordered set or map when searches, inserts,
deletes, and ordered traversal all matter. It is especially useful as
the base idea behind balanced search trees and augmented rank trees.

Use a hash table when only exact membership matters and ordering does
not. Use a sorted slice for mostly static data and cache-friendly
binary search. Use the next [balanced-search-tree lesson](
#a73-balanced-search-trees) when adversarial or sorted updates require
guaranteed logarithmic height.

Practice the global invariant with [Validate Binary Search Tree](
problems/medium_leetcode_0098_validate_binary_search_tree.go) and the
[tree problem index](problems/README.md). The
[search-tree validation](#b114-search-tree-validation-bounds-or-stack)
and [rank-query](#b1111-search-tree-rank-queries-subtree-counts)
families build on strict ordering and inorder traversal.

#### A.7.3 Balanced search trees

##### Problem and contract

An ordinary binary search tree can become a one-sided chain when keys
arrive in sorted order. Its searches then inspect every node. A
balanced search tree limits height so each comparison still discards a
large part of the remaining keys.

This lesson builds a static height-balanced BST from a strictly
increasing slice of unique `int` values. A nil or empty slice produces
an empty tree. Unsorted or duplicate input returns an error before any
node is allocated. The builder does not mutate or retain the slice.
The result owns newly allocated nodes. The caller must not mutate the
input concurrently with construction. Contains reports membership
without mutation; concurrent tree mutation is excluded.

Height in this lesson counts nodes: an empty tree has height 0 and a
leaf has height 1. Height-balanced means the two child heights differ
by at most one at every node. Dynamic insertion and deletion are
outside this contract; later lessons cover mechanisms that restore
balance after updates. Read [binary search trees](
#a72-binary-search-trees) first.

##### Mental model

The middle value of a sorted range separates smaller values on its
left from larger values on its right. Make that value the subtree
root, then repeat independently for the two half-open index ranges.

For range `[lower, upper)`, compute
`middle = lower + (upper - lower) / 2`. The upper endpoint is
excluded. When the range length is even, integer division chooses the
upper of the two middle values. Empty ranges become nil links.

Every recursive range contains exactly the values for one subtree.
Choosing its middle keeps left and right element counts within one,
while sorted order establishes the BST invariant.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build from `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]`, then search for 7 and missing 8. The
expected tree has height 3 and level order `[4,2,6,1,3,5,7]`.

Initial state: validation has not read any adjacent pair, no node is
allocated, and the active range will be `[0,7)`.

1. Decision: validate each adjacent pair. Every earlier value is
   strictly less than the next, so construction may proceed.
   After: all seven values are known to be sorted and unique; the tree
   is still empty.
   Known correct: any index split will put smaller values before the
   root and larger values after it.

2. Decision: range `[0,7)` has middle index
   `0 + (7 - 0) / 2 = 3`, whose value is 4. Allocate root 4 and assign
   `[0,3)` to its left and `[4,7)` to its right.
   After: root 4 exists; both child ranges contain three values.
   Known correct: every pending left value is less than 4 and every
   pending right value is greater.

3. Decision: `[0,3)` chooses index 1, value 2. Its ranges `[0,1)` and
   `[2,3)` create leaves 1 and 3; their child ranges are empty.
   After: the left subtree is `2` with children 1 and 3.
   Known correct: it is a height-2 BST containing exactly values 1, 2,
   and 3.

4. Decision: `[4,7)` chooses index 5, value 6. Its one-value ranges
   create leaves 5 and 7.
   After:

   ```text
          4
        /   \
       2     6
      / \   / \
     1   3 5   7
   ```

   Known correct: both root subtrees have height 2, and every node has
   child-height difference 0.

5. Decision: search for 7. Compare `7 > 4`, then `7 > 6`, then equal
   at 7. For 8, compare greater than 4, 6, and 7, then follow 7's
   nil right link.
   After: results are true and false; the tree is unchanged.
   Known correct: each comparison discarded the subtree whose sorted
   range cannot contain the target.

6. Decision: compute height from leaves upward. Leaves return 1,
   nodes 2 and 6 return 2, and root 4 returns 3.
   After: reported height is 3 and level order is
   `[4,2,6,1,3,5,7]`.
   Known correct: all recursive ranges and searches have terminated,
   completing the required result.

Focused even case: `[1,2]` chooses index 1, so root 2 has left child
1; heights differ by one. Focused failure case: `[1,1,2]` returns an
error at the equal pair before allocating a root.

Counterexample to plain sorted insertion: inserting 1 through 7 into
the unbalanced BST from A.7.2 creates a height-7 right chain. The
first wrong decision is preserving arrival order when the complete
sorted set is already available for midpoint construction.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type balancedNode struct {
	value int
	left  *balancedNode
	right *balancedNode
}

func buildBalancedRange(
	values []int,
	lower int,
	upper int,
) *balancedNode {
	// The half-open range [lower, upper) is empty when its bounds meet.
	if lower == upper {
		return nil
	}

	// Choose the middle value as root. Computing the remaining distance
	// before adding lower avoids the overflow risk of (lower+upper)/2.
	middle := lower + (upper-lower)/2
	// Values before middle are smaller; later ones are greater. The two
	// recursive ranges exclude middle and differ in size by at most one.
	return &balancedNode{
		value: values[middle],
		left: buildBalancedRange(
			values,
			lower,
			middle,
		),
		right: buildBalancedRange(
			values,
			middle+1,
			upper,
		),
	}
}

func buildBalancedSearchTree(
	values []int,
) (*balancedNode, error) {
	// Strict increase supplies search-tree order and unique keys.
	// Validate everything before allocating a partial tree.
	for index := 1; index < len(values); index++ {
		if values[index-1] >= values[index] {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"values must be strictly increasing",
			)
		}
	}
	return buildBalancedRange(values, 0, len(values)), nil
}

func containsBalanced(root *balancedNode, target int) bool {
	// Ordering lets each comparison discard the wrong-side subtree.
	for node := root; node != nil; {
		switch {
		case target < node.value:
			node = node.left
		case target > node.value:
			node = node.right
		default:
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

func heightInNodes(node *balancedNode) int {
	// An empty subtree contributes zero nodes to a root-to-leaf path.
	if node == nil {
		return 0
	}
	leftHeight := heightInNodes(node.left)
	rightHeight := heightInNodes(node.right)
	// The current node adds one above the taller child path.
	return 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight)
}

func levelOrderBalanced(root *balancedNode) []int {
	// Preserve the function's non-nil empty-result contract.
	if root == nil {
		return []int{}
	}
	queue := []*balancedNode{root}
	values := make([]int, 0)
	// nextIndex advances the queue front. Children append after all
	// node already waiting at the current or earlier level.
	for nextIndex := 0; nextIndex < len(queue); nextIndex++ {
		node := queue[nextIndex]
		values = append(values, node.value)
		// Enqueue left before right to preserve within-level order.
		if node.left != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.left)
		}
		if node.right != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.right)
		}
	}
	return values
}

func main() {
	// Seven sorted values form three complete levels around value 4.
	root, err := buildBalancedSearchTree(
		[]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7},
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(levelOrderBalanced(root))
	fmt.Println(heightInNodes(root))
	fmt.Println(
		containsBalanced(root, 7),
		containsBalanced(root, 8),
	)

	// Duplicates violate strict ordering; nil input is a valid empty
	// sequence and therefore builds an empty tree.
	_, err = buildBalancedSearchTree([]int{1, 1, 2})
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
	empty, err := buildBalancedSearchTree(nil)
	fmt.Println(empty == nil, err)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[4 2 6 1 3 5 7]
3
true false
true
true <nil>
```

##### Why it works

Validation establishes strict increase before construction. For any
nonempty range, the middle value is greater than every value in the
left range and less than every value in the right range. Assuming the
recursive calls build valid child BSTs, attaching them under the
middle value therefore builds a valid BST for the whole range.

The two child range sizes are equal or consecutive. By induction,
midpoint trees built from consecutive sizes have equal heights or
heights differing by one: crossing a power-of-two size boundary can
increase only the larger height. Therefore every node satisfies this
lesson's child-height bound.

Contains uses the BST invariant to keep the only subtree that could
hold the target. A range shrinks to a strict subrange on every build
call, and search descends one level each step. Finite input therefore
makes both processes terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length. Validation reads one adjacent pair for each
index from 1 through N minus 1, and construction allocates and
initializes N nodes. Total build time is Theta(N), and the tree
retains O(N) storage. Balanced recursion uses O(log N) auxiliary
stack space.

Contains takes O(log N) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary storage.
Height calculation and level-order output each take Theta(N) time.
Height uses O(log N) stack space; this indexed level-order queue uses
O(N) auxiliary storage and returns O(N) output.

The builder spends linear work once to guarantee logarithmic searches.
It does not support cheap updates: inserting into the source slice and
rebuilding costs O(N). Dynamic balanced trees spend extra metadata and
restructuring work to preserve height after each update.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty input both produce a nil root and no error. Reading a
  midpoint before checking an empty range would index out of bounds.
- One value becomes a height-1 leaf. Returning height 0 for it would
  mix edge-count and node-count conventions.
- Even ranges use the upper middle because of integer division.
  Either middle can balance the tree, but tests and serialization
  must use one stated rule consistently.
- Duplicate or descending adjacent values return an error before node
  allocation. Building first would leave an unusable partial result.
- Use `lower + (upper-lower)/2`, not `(lower+upper)/2`; the former
  avoids overflowing large valid indices.
- Do not keep a slice into the input as node storage if callers may
  mutate it. This builder copies each integer into an owned node.
- A balanced root alone is insufficient. Every subtree must satisfy
  the child-height bound.
- This static builder does not make later pointer insertion balanced.
  Use a dynamic balancing algorithm when updates are part of the
  contract.

##### When to choose it

Choose midpoint construction when sorted unique data is available as
a batch and will receive many searches but few or no updates. It gives
a deterministic shallow BST without rotation metadata.

Use binary search on the sorted slice when tree nodes add no needed
behavior; contiguous storage is usually simpler and more cache
friendly. Use [AVL or red-black trees](
#a75-avl-and-red-black-trees) for dynamic updates, and a B-tree family
when storage blocks or database pages matter.

Practice this exact conversion through the [tree problem index](
problems/README.md), which lists Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search
Tree. The [search-tree validation](
#b114-search-tree-validation-bounds-or-stack) family checks the global
ordering invariant after construction.

#### A.7.4 General rooted trees

##### Problem and contract

Many hierarchies do not have exactly two child roles. A department can
contain any number of teams, and a directory can contain any number of
entries. A general rooted tree stores an ordered collection of child
links at each node instead of fixed left and right links.

Given a proper rooted tree of string labels, our functions return
preorder labels, labels grouped by depth, and subtree node counts. A
nil root returns empty traversals and count zero. Duplicate labels are
valid because nodes, not label text, define identity. Traversal does
not mutate nodes.

The root has no parent, every other node has exactly one parent, every
child entry is nonnil, and the structure is finite and acyclic. Shared
children, nil child entries, and cycles are outside the contract. The
caller owns the nodes and child slices and must not mutate them during
traversal. Read [binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) first.

##### Mental model

Each node stores an ordered slice of actual children. Reading
`node.children[1]` means the second child in that node's local order;
it says nothing about the child's depth or a global index. An empty or
nil child slice makes the node a leaf.

Preorder records a node, then completely visits each child subtree
from slice index 0 upward. Level order keeps a queue, so all nodes at
one depth are recorded before their children at the next depth.

Subtree size is a bottom-up summary. A node counts itself once, then
adds the already-defined size of every child subtree. For each active
call, the current node identifies exactly one disjoint subtree.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build this organization. Expected preorder is
`[company,engineering,platform,product,sales,field,operations]`.
Expected levels from depth 0 through depth 2 are:

```text
[[company],
 [engineering,sales,operations],
 [platform,product,field]]
```

The full size is 7 and engineering's subtree size is 3.

```text
company
|- engineering
|  |- platform
|  \- product
|- sales
|  \- field
\- operations
```

Initial state: preorder is empty. The first recursive call is
responsible for the subtree rooted at company.

1. Decision: record company, then choose child index 0, engineering.
   Record engineering and choose its child index 0, platform.
   After: preorder is `[company,engineering,platform]`; platform has
   no pending children.
   Known correct: every recorded parent precedes its recorded
   children, and later sibling subtrees remain unresolved.

2. Decision: return from platform and choose engineering child index
   1, product. Product is a leaf; after it returns, engineering has no
   more children.
   After: preorder is
   `[company,engineering,platform,product]`.
   Known correct: engineering's complete subtree occupies one
   contiguous preorder segment.

3. Decision: choose company child index 1, sales. Record sales and its
   only child field, then choose company child index 2, operations.
   After: preorder is
   `[company,engineering,platform,product,sales,field,operations]`.
   Known correct: every node is recorded once in parent-before-child,
   sibling-index order.

4. Decision: start level order with queue `[company]`. Remove company,
   record depth 0, and append all three children in slice order.
   After: levels are `[[company]]`; queue is
   `[engineering,sales,operations]`.
   Known correct: depth 0 is complete and all depth-1 nodes are
   pending in local order.

5. Decision: remove the three depth-1 nodes. Record their labels;
   append platform and product from engineering, field from sales, and
   nothing from operations.
   After: levels add `[engineering,sales,operations]`; queue holds
   `[platform,product,field]`.
   Known correct: depths 0 and 1 are complete, and depth 2 is pending.

6. Decision: remove the three leaves and append no children.
   After: levels add `[platform,product,field]`; the queue is empty.
   Known correct: level order has grouped every node by its depth.

7. Decision: compute sizes bottom up. Each leaf returns 1;
   engineering returns `1 + 1 + 1 = 3`, sales returns 2, operations
   returns 1, and company returns `1 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 7`.
   After: full size is 7 and engineering size is 3.
   Known correct: disjoint child subtrees plus the parent account for
   every node exactly once, completing the required results.

Focused boundary case: nil returns preorder `[]`, levels `[]`, and
size 0. Focused duplicate case: two different leaf nodes labeled
`"field"` both appear because traversal follows links, not a label
set.

Counterexample to using fixed left and right fields: company has three
children. The first wrong decision is forcing operations into a deeper
level or sibling chain, which changes the represented parent-child
relationship unless an explicit conversion convention is added.

##### Implementation

This complete program builds the pictured organization and prints the
three promised observations. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type rootedNode struct {
	label    string
	children []*rootedNode
}

func appendRootedPreorder(
	node *rootedNode,
	labels *[]string,
) {
	// Nil is an empty subtree and ends this branch without a label.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}
	// Preorder records the parent before children in their stored
	// left-to-right order.
	*labels = append(*labels, node.label)
	for _, child := range node.children {
		appendRootedPreorder(child, labels)
	}
}

func rootedPreorder(root *rootedNode) []string {
	// One result slice accumulates the recursive traversal.
	labels := make([]string, 0)
	appendRootedPreorder(root, &labels)
	return labels
}

func labelsByDepth(root *rootedNode) [][]string {
	// Preserve a non-nil empty outer result for an empty tree.
	if root == nil {
		return [][]string{}
	}

	// A nil marker follows every depth. Nodes before that marker belong
	// to the same currentLevel; their children wait behind it.
	queue := []*rootedNode{root, nil}
	levels := make([][]string, 0)
	currentLevel := make([]string, 0)
	nextIndex := 0
	for nextIndex < len(queue) {
		// Advance a queue head rather than shifting the backing slice.
		node := queue[nextIndex]
		nextIndex++
		if node == nil {
			// The marker closes one level. Add another only when
			// child nodes are still waiting, avoiding an endless marker loop.
			levels = append(levels, currentLevel)
			currentLevel = make([]string, 0)
			if nextIndex < len(queue) {
				queue = append(queue, nil)
			}
			continue
		}
		// Record this level's label, then enqueue children in their listed
		// order so the next depth keeps parent and sibling order.
		currentLevel = append(currentLevel, node.label)
		queue = append(queue, node.children...)
	}
	return levels
}

func rootedSubtreeSize(node *rootedNode) int {
	// An empty subtree contains zero nodes.
	if node == nil {
		return 0
	}
	size := 1
	// Count the current node once, then add each disjoint child subtree.
	for _, child := range node.children {
		size += rootedSubtreeSize(child)
	}
	return size
}

func main() {
	// Build a three-depth company tree with unequal child counts.
	platform := &rootedNode{label: "platform"}
	product := &rootedNode{label: "product"}
	field := &rootedNode{label: "field"}
	engineering := &rootedNode{
		label:    "engineering",
		children: []*rootedNode{platform, product},
	}
	sales := &rootedNode{
		label:    "sales",
		children: []*rootedNode{field},
	}
	operations := &rootedNode{label: "operations"}
	company := &rootedNode{
		label: "company",
		children: []*rootedNode{
			engineering,
			sales,
			operations,
		},
	}

	// Compare depth-first order, grouped levels, and subtree sizes.
	fmt.Println(rootedPreorder(company))
	fmt.Println(labelsByDepth(company))
	fmt.Println(
		rootedSubtreeSize(company),
		rootedSubtreeSize(engineering),
	)
	// Empty input exercises every traversal's explicit base case.
	fmt.Println(
		rootedPreorder(nil),
		labelsByDepth(nil),
		rootedSubtreeSize(nil),
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[company engineering platform product sales field operations]
[[company] [engineering sales operations] [platform product field]]
7 3
[] [] 0
```

##### Why it works

Preorder records the current node once, then processes each child
subtree in the slice's order. By the recursive claim, each child call
records exactly that disjoint subtree. Their concatenation after the
parent is therefore the required preorder.

For level order, the queue begins with the root and an end-of-depth
marker. Nodes before the marker are exactly one depth. Processing them
appends their children after that marker, in parent and child order.
Replacing each consumed marker only when nodes remain creates exactly
one output slice per nonempty depth.

Subtree size starts at one for the current node. Each recursive child
result counts one disjoint child subtree, so their sum counts every
node in the current subtree once. Proper finite-tree preconditions
make all recursion reach leaves and make the queue empty, so every
function terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be node count, H the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf
path, and W the greatest node count at one depth. A nonempty proper
tree has N minus one child links; an empty tree has none. Preorder and
subtree size each take Theta(N) time and O(H) auxiliary call-stack
space. Preorder returns O(N) labels.

Level order takes Theta(N) time and returns O(N) labels across its
level slices. This implementation's indexed queue retains O(N) node
and marker entries; a circular queue can reduce live queue storage to
O(W). The tree itself retains O(N) nodes and child references, plus
any unused capacities in child slices.

The child slice represents arbitrary branching directly and preserves
sibling order. Compared with fixed child fields, it adds one slice
header per node and may allocate separately as children are appended.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A nil root returns empty traversals and size zero. Appending a level
  before checking nil would incorrectly return one empty level.
- Nil and empty child slices both mean leaf. A slice containing a nil
  entry violates the contract and would make the marker-based queue
  mistake that entry for an end-of-depth marker.
- Duplicate labels identify different nodes. Deduplicating by label
  loses valid subtrees; use pointer identity only when detection is
  required.
- Child order is observable. Iterating children backward reverses
  sibling order in both preorder and level order.
- A shared child has two parents and is counted twice. A cycle never
  reaches a leaf. Validate untrusted graph-like input before using
  tree traversal.
- Appending to a shared children slice can mutate aliases or replace
  its backing array. Define one owner or deep-copy before independent
  modification.
- Recursion depth is H. An explicit stack is safer when a one-child
  chain may exhaust available call-stack resources.

##### When to choose it

Choose a general rooted tree for arbitrary-branching hierarchies with
one owner per node: organizations, syntax trees, menus, categories,
and directory-like models are common examples.

Use a binary tree when left and right have distinct meaning. Use a
flat parent-ID table when persistence and database queries matter more
than pointer traversal. Use a graph when nodes may have multiple
parents or cycles.

The [tree problem index](problems/README.md) supplies traversal and
subtree practice. The [subtree aggregation](
#b113-subtree-aggregation-recursive-return-values), [lowest common
ancestor](#b116-lowest-common-ancestor-tree-or-ancestor-table), and
[serialization](
#b117-serialization-and-deserialization-queue-or-stack) families build
on rooted-tree ownership and traversal order.

#### A.7.5 AVL and red-black trees

##### Problem and contract

A dynamic search tree must repair the height damage caused by each
insertion. AVL and red-black trees preserve the binary-search ordering
invariant while rotating local links to prevent a long chain. They
differ in how strictly they define balance.

This lesson implements two insertion-only sets of Go `int` values: an
AVL tree and a left-leaning red-black tree, abbreviated LLRB. Their
zero values are empty. Insert returns true for a new key and false for
a duplicate without mutation. Contains and inorder traversal do not
mutate the trees. Deletion is outside this lesson's contract.

Both trees own their nodes and exclude unsynchronized concurrent
access. Callers receive values, not node pointers, so rotations do not
promise stable node positions. Methods require a non-nil tree pointer.
Read [binary search trees](
#a72-binary-search-trees) and [balance](
#a73-balanced-search-trees) first.

##### Mental model

An AVL node stores its subtree height. Its balance factor is
`left height - right height` and must be -1, 0, or 1. After recursive
insertion, update heights from the changed leaf upward. A factor 2 or
-2 identifies the first damaged ancestor.

A rotation changes links without changing inorder order. A left-left
or right-right shape needs one rotation. A left-right or right-left
shape first rotates the child toward a straight line, then rotates the
ancestor the other way.

An LLRB node stores the color of its incoming parent link. A red link
glues two keys into one conceptual 3-node. In the corresponding 2-3
tree, one logical node holds one or two keys and therefore has two or
three child ranges. A black link moves down one logical level. The
root is black, red links lean left, consecutive red links are
forbidden, and every root-to-nil path has the same number of black
links.

LLRB insertion repairs a returned subtree in this order: rotate a lone
red right link left, rotate two consecutive red left links right, then
flip colors when both children are red. At every operation boundary,
inorder keys are strictly increasing and the structure's own balance
invariants hold.

##### Worked walkthrough

Insert `30,10,20,40,50,25` into both trees. Then reject duplicate 20
and query 25 and missing 99. Both final inorder results are
`[10,20,25,30,40,50]`.

Initial state: both roots are nil.

AVL diagrams label nodes by key. LLRB diagrams append `B` for a black
incoming link and `R` for a red incoming link.

1. Decision: insert 30 as each root, then insert 10 to its left.
   AVL heights are 1 at node 10 and 2 at node 30. In the LLRB tree,
   10 has a red incoming link under black root 30.
   After: both trees contain 10 and 30 without a balance violation.

   ```text
   AVL             LLRB
       30              30B
      /               /
     10              10R
   ```

   Known correct: ordering is strict and every balance bound holds.

2. Decision: insert 20. The AVL path is `30 -> 10 -> right`, creating
   a left-right shape at 30. Rotate left at 10, then right at 30.
   In LLRB, 20 first becomes the red right child of red node 10.
   Rotate that right link left, making 20 the red parent of 10. At
   node 30, two consecutive red left links now require a right
   rotation. The resulting node 20 has two red children, so flip all
   three colors and finally force the root black.
   After: both roots are 20 with children 10 and 30; AVL height is 2,
   and all three LLRB nodes are black.

   ```text
   AVL             LLRB
        20              20B
       /  \            /   \
     10    30        10B   30B
   ```

   Known correct: rotations preserved inorder `[10,20,30]` while
   restoring both balance schemes.

3. Decision: insert 40 and then 50. AVL insertion of 50 makes the
   subtree at 30 right-right heavy, so rotate left at 30. LLRB
   insertion of 40 rotates its lone red right link above node 30.
   Inserting 50 then gives node 40 two red children, so flip their
   colors. The resulting red right link from 20 to 40 rotates left,
   making 40 the black root.
   After: AVL root 20 has right subtree 40 with children 30 and 50.
   LLRB root is 40, with red left child 20 and black right child 50.

   ```text
   AVL                    LLRB
        20                      40B
       /  \                    /   \
     10    40                20R   50B
          /  \              /   \
         30  50           10B   30B
   ```

   Known correct: both trees contain the same five ordered keys even
   though their legal balanced shapes differ.

4. Decision: insert 25. AVL path `20 -> 40 -> 30 -> left` makes root
   20 right-left heavy. Rotate right at 40, then left at 20. LLRB adds
   25 as a red left child of black node 30 without another repair.
   After:

   ```text
   AVL                    LLRB
          30                    40B
         /  \                  /   \
       20    40              20R   50B
      / \     \              / \
    10  25    50           10B 30B
                                  /
                                25R
   ```

   Known correct: AVL balance factors are within one; the LLRB root is
   black, red links lean left, and black path counts agree.

5. Decision: insert duplicate 20. Each comparison reaches an equal
   key and returns false before allocation or repair.
   After: both shapes and sizes are unchanged.

   ```text
   AVL                    LLRB
          30                    40B
         /  \                  /   \
      [20]   40             [20R]  50B
      / \     \              / \
    10  25    50           10B 30B
                                  /
                                25R
   ```

   Brackets mark the equal node where duplicate insertion stops.
   Known correct: both structures still represent sets.

6. Decision: query 25 and 99. Search follows ordinary BST comparisons;
   25 is found and 99 reaches nil on the right.
   After: both trees return true for 25 and false for 99.

   ```text
   AVL search paths
   25: 30 -> 20 -> 25 -> found
   99: 30 -> 40 -> 50 -> nil

   LLRB search paths
   25: 40B -> 20R -> 30B -> 25R -> found
   99: 40B -> 50B -> nil
   ```

   Known correct: no query mutated metadata or links, completing the
   required sequence.

Focused single-rotation case: inserting `3,2,1` into AVL creates a
left-left shape and one right rotation. Focused color case: every LLRB
insert forces the returned root black, including the first node.

Counterexample to updating height before recursive insertion: the
parent still sees the old child height and misses the first imbalance.
The first wrong decision is checking metadata before the changed
subtree has returned.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type avlNode struct {
	value int
	// height counts nodes on the longest path starting here.
	height int
	left   *avlNode
	right  *avlNode
}

type avlTree struct {
	root *avlNode
}

func avlHeight(node *avlNode) int {
	// Empty children have height zero, making leaf height one.
	if node == nil {
		return 0
	}
	return node.height
}

func updateAVLHeight(node *avlNode) {
	// Recompute only after child links and child heights are final.
	node.height = 1 + max(
		avlHeight(node.left),
		avlHeight(node.right),
	)
}

func rotateAVLLeft(top *avlNode) *avlNode {
	// Promote the right child and move its left subtree into top's open
	// right link. Search-tree order is preserved across all three parts.
	newTop := top.right
	top.right = newTop.left
	newTop.left = top
	// top changed first and is now lower, so update it before newTop.
	updateAVLHeight(top)
	updateAVLHeight(newTop)
	return newTop
}

func rotateAVLRight(top *avlNode) *avlNode {
	// Mirror the rotation: promote left and transfer its right side.
	newTop := top.left
	top.left = newTop.right
	newTop.right = top
	updateAVLHeight(top)
	updateAVLHeight(newTop)
	return newTop
}

func insertAVLNode(node *avlNode, value int) (*avlNode, bool) {
	// A new leaf has no children and therefore height one.
	if node == nil {
		return &avlNode{value: value, height: 1}, true
	}
	var inserted bool
	// Ordinary search-tree comparisons choose the only possible subtree.
	if value < node.value {
		node.left, inserted = insertAVLNode(node.left, value)
	} else if value > node.value {
		node.right, inserted = insertAVLNode(node.right, value)
	} else {
		// Duplicate insertion leaves links and heights unchanged.
		return node, false
	}
	if !inserted {
		return node, false
	}

	// The changed child has returned with correct metadata. Refresh this
	// node, then repair it if one side is more than one level taller.
	updateAVLHeight(node)
	balance := avlHeight(node.left) - avlHeight(node.right)
	if balance > 1 {
		// A value right of the left child makes a bend. Straighten
		// that child first, then perform the outer right rotation.
		if value > node.left.value {
			node.left = rotateAVLLeft(node.left)
		}
		return rotateAVLRight(node), true
	}
	if balance < -1 {
		// Mirror the same reasoning for a right-left bend.
		if value < node.right.value {
			node.right = rotateAVLRight(node.right)
		}
		return rotateAVLLeft(node), true
	}
	return node, true
}

func (tree *avlTree) insert(value int) bool {
	// A rotation may replace the subtree root, including the whole root.
	var inserted bool
	tree.root, inserted = insertAVLNode(tree.root, value)
	return inserted
}

func (tree *avlTree) contains(value int) bool {
	// Balance changes height, not search-tree order, so directed
	// lookup still rules out one subtree per comparison.
	for node := tree.root; node != nil; {
		if value < node.value {
			node = node.left
		} else if value > node.value {
			node = node.right
		} else {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

type linkColor bool

const (
	black linkColor = false
	red   linkColor = true
)

type redBlackNode struct {
	value int
	color linkColor
	left  *redBlackNode
	right *redBlackNode
}

type redBlackTree struct {
	root *redBlackNode
}

func isRed(node *redBlackNode) bool {
	// Nil links count as black; only a non-nil red link is red.
	return node != nil && node.color == red
}

func rotateRedBlackLeft(top *redBlackNode) *redBlackNode {
	// Promote a red right link left. The promoted node inherits the
	// old incoming color, while the demoted node becomes red below it.
	newTop := top.right
	top.right = newTop.left
	newTop.left = top
	newTop.color = top.color
	top.color = red
	return newTop
}

func rotateRedBlackRight(top *redBlackNode) *redBlackNode {
	// Mirror rotation removes two consecutive left-leaning red links.
	newTop := top.left
	top.left = newTop.right
	newTop.right = top
	newTop.color = top.color
	top.color = red
	return newTop
}

func flipRedBlackColors(node *redBlackNode) {
	// Move a temporary four-node split up by toggling the parent and
	// two red children. Callers use this only when both children exist.
	node.color = !node.color
	node.left.color = !node.left.color
	node.right.color = !node.right.color
}

func insertRedBlackNode(
	node *redBlackNode,
	value int,
) (*redBlackNode, bool) {
	// Insert red leaves so existing black path counts do not change.
	if node == nil {
		return &redBlackNode{value: value, color: red}, true
	}
	var inserted bool
	// Comparisons select one child; equality rejects duplicates.
	if value < node.value {
		node.left, inserted = insertRedBlackNode(node.left, value)
	} else if value > node.value {
		node.right, inserted = insertRedBlackNode(node.right, value)
	} else {
		return node, false
	}
	if !inserted {
		return node, false
	}

	// A red right link must lean left.
	if isRed(node.right) && !isRed(node.left) {
		node = rotateRedBlackLeft(node)
	}
	if isRed(node.left) && isRed(node.left.left) {
		// Two red links in a row need a right rotation at their top.
		node = rotateRedBlackRight(node)
	}
	if isRed(node.left) && isRed(node.right) {
		// Two red children represent a full temporary four-node; split it.
		flipRedBlackColors(node)
	}
	return node, true
}

func (tree *redBlackTree) insert(value int) bool {
	// Rotations may replace root. Force it black so its incoming
	// virtual link never contributes a red-red violation.
	var inserted bool
	tree.root, inserted = insertRedBlackNode(tree.root, value)
	if tree.root != nil {
		tree.root.color = black
	}
	return inserted
}

func (tree *redBlackTree) contains(value int) bool {
	// Colors do not affect key order, so lookup follows BST rules.
	for node := tree.root; node != nil; {
		if value < node.value {
			node = node.left
		} else if value > node.value {
			node = node.right
		} else {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

func appendAVLInorder(node *avlNode, values *[]int) {
	// Left, node, right gives sorted order; nil contributes nothing.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}
	appendAVLInorder(node.left, values)
	*values = append(*values, node.value)
	appendAVLInorder(node.right, values)
}

func appendRedBlackInorder(
	node *redBlackNode,
	values *[]int,
) {
	// Red-black colors change balance only, not inorder key order.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}
	appendRedBlackInorder(node.left, values)
	*values = append(*values, node.value)
	appendRedBlackInorder(node.right, values)
}

func avlInorder(root *avlNode) []int {
	values := make([]int, 0)
	appendAVLInorder(root, &values)
	return values
}

func redBlackInorder(root *redBlackNode) []int {
	values := make([]int, 0)
	appendRedBlackInorder(root, &values)
	return values
}

func avlLevelOrder(root *avlNode) []int {
	// A growing indexed queue emits nodes one level at a time.
	if root == nil {
		return []int{}
	}
	queue := []*avlNode{root}
	values := make([]int, 0)
	for nextIndex := 0; nextIndex < len(queue); nextIndex++ {
		node := queue[nextIndex]
		values = append(values, node.value)
		if node.left != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.left)
		}
		if node.right != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.right)
		}
	}
	return values
}

func redBlackLevelOrder(root *redBlackNode) []string {
	// Include node colors so the balancing representation is visible.
	if root == nil {
		return []string{}
	}
	queue := []*redBlackNode{root}
	values := make([]string, 0)
	for nextIndex := 0; nextIndex < len(queue); nextIndex++ {
		node := queue[nextIndex]
		color := "B"
		// Nil is not queued; live red nodes override the black label.
		if node.color == red {
			color = "R"
		}
		values = append(
			values,
			fmt.Sprintf("%d%s", node.value, color),
		)
		if node.left != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.left)
		}
		if node.right != nil {
			queue = append(queue, node.right)
		}
	}
	return values
}

func main() {
	// This sequence triggers AVL rotations and matching red-black
	// link rotations and color flips.
	var avl avlTree
	var redBlack redBlackTree
	for _, value := range []int{30, 10, 20, 40, 50, 25} {
		if !avl.insert(value) || !redBlack.insert(value) {
			panic("unexpected duplicate")
		}
	}
	// Matching inorder output shows that both trees store the same set;
	// level order exposes their different valid balanced shapes.
	fmt.Println(avlInorder(avl.root))
	fmt.Println(redBlackInorder(redBlack.root))
	fmt.Println(avlLevelOrder(avl.root), avl.root.height)
	fmt.Println(redBlackLevelOrder(redBlack.root))
	fmt.Println(avl.insert(20), redBlack.insert(20))
	fmt.Println(avl.contains(25), avl.contains(99))
	fmt.Println(
		redBlack.contains(25),
		redBlack.contains(99),
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[10 20 25 30 40 50]
[10 20 25 30 40 50]
[30 20 40 10 25 50] 3
[40B 20R 50B 10B 30B 25R]
false false
true false
true false
```

##### Why it works

Recursive insertion first preserves BST order by placing a new leaf on
the comparison path. AVL height updates then expose any first ancestor
whose child heights differ by two. Single or double rotations preserve
inorder order and reduce that difference; updating the lower node
before the new top restores exact stored heights.

For LLRB insertion, a new key begins as a red leaf, so it does not
increase black path count immediately. The three fix-ups translate
temporary right-leaning or 4-node shapes back into the canonical 2-3
tree representation. Rotations preserve inorder order, color movement
preserves black path counts, and forcing the root black completes the
invariants.

Contains relies only on the shared BST invariant. Each recursive
insert descends to nil and performs bounded local repair while
returning. Contains descends one child per comparison. Finite height
therefore makes every operation terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be key count and H tree height. AVL balance implies
H = O(log N) because the minimum nodes for successive heights grow at
least as fast as a Fibonacci recurrence. Red-black equal black heights
and the ban on consecutive red links make any path at most twice a
shortest black-only path, also giving H = O(log N).

Insert and contains therefore take O(log N) worst-case time. Both
recursive insertions use O(log N) stack space and allocate one node on
success. Each rotation and color flip is O(1). The trees retain O(N)
nodes; AVL stores a height per node, while red-black stores a color.

AVL's stricter height bound can shorten searches. Red-black trees
permit more height variation and often require less rebalancing across
mixed insertion and deletion workloads. This LLRB variant uses a
smaller set of symmetric cases than a conventional parent-pointer
red-black implementation.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- The first inserted node has AVL height 1 and must finish black in
  LLRB. Leaving a red root violates the public invariant.
- A duplicate returns false without allocating or changing metadata.
  Rebalancing an equal key can hide a broken duplicate policy.
- Update AVL heights after changing child links, and update the lower
  rotated node before the new top. Reversing that order stores stale
  height.
- A left-right or right-left shape needs two rotations. Applying only
  the outer rotation preserves ordering but not balance.
- LLRB fix-up order matters. Rotate a lone red right link before
  testing consecutive red left links and splitting two red children.
- Color belongs to the incoming link even though the code stores it on
  the child node. Treating it as an intrinsic key color confuses what
  a rotation must copy.
- This code does not implement deletion. Removing a node with ordinary
  BST deletion would violate height or black-path invariants.
- External link or metadata mutation can invalidate either tree. Keep
  node ownership inside the data structure.

##### When to choose it

Choose AVL or red-black trees when a dynamic ordered set or map needs
worst-case logarithmic search and insertion. Prefer AVL when lookup
latency and a tighter height bound dominate; prefer red-black when a
