```go
) (*ternaryNode, bool) {
	// Add ternary node while preserving the representation invariant.
	letter := word[byteIndex]
	if node == nil {
		node = &ternaryNode{letter: letter}
	}

	var inserted bool
	switch {
	case letter < node.letter:
		// Alternatives stay at the same input position.
		node.left, inserted = insertTernaryNode(
			node.left,
			word,
			byteIndex,
		)
	case letter > node.letter:
		node.right, inserted = insertTernaryNode(
			node.right,
			word,
			byteIndex,
		)
	case byteIndex+1 < len(word):
		// Equality alone consumes the current input byte.
		node.middle, inserted = insertTernaryNode(
			node.middle,
			word,
			byteIndex+1,
		)
	case node.terminal:
		return node, false
	default:
		node.terminal = true
		inserted = true
	}
	return node, inserted
}

func (tree *ternaryTree) insert(word string) (bool, error) {
	// Validate before recursion so failure cannot add a prefix.
	if err := validateTernaryText(word); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	if len(word) == 0 {
		if tree.emptyWord {
			return false, nil
		}
		tree.emptyWord = true
		return true, nil
	}

	var inserted bool
	tree.root, inserted = insertTernaryNode(
		tree.root,
		word,
		0,
	)
	return inserted, nil
}

func (tree *ternaryTree) contains(word string) bool {
	// Follow the lookup rule for the requested item without changing
	// state.
	if validateTernaryText(word) != nil {
		return false
	}
	if len(word) == 0 {
		return tree.emptyWord
	}

	node := tree.root
	byteIndex := 0
	for node != nil {
		letter := word[byteIndex]
		switch {
		case letter < node.letter:
			node = node.left
		case letter > node.letter:
			node = node.right
		case byteIndex+1 == len(word):
			return node.terminal
		default:
			byteIndex++
			node = node.middle
		}
	}
	return false
}

func (tree *ternaryTree) hasPrefix(prefix string) bool {
	// Follow the lookup rule for prefix without changing state.
	if validateTernaryText(prefix) != nil {
		return false
	}
	if len(prefix) == 0 {
		return true
	}

	node := tree.root
	byteIndex := 0
	for node != nil {
		letter := prefix[byteIndex]
		switch {
		case letter < node.letter:
			node = node.left
		case letter > node.letter:
			node = node.right
		case byteIndex+1 == len(prefix):
			return true
		default:
			byteIndex++
			node = node.middle
		}
	}
	return false
}

func appendTernaryWords(
	node *ternaryNode,
	prefix string,
	words *[]string,
) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}
	appendTernaryWords(node.left, prefix, words)

	word := prefix + string(node.letter)
	if node.terminal {
		*words = append(*words, word)
	}
	appendTernaryWords(node.middle, word, words)
	appendTernaryWords(node.right, prefix, words)
}

func (tree *ternaryTree) words() []string {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	words := make([]string, 0)
	if tree.emptyWord {
		words = append(words, "")
	}
	appendTernaryWords(tree.root, "", &words)
	return words
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	var tree ternaryTree
	for _, word := range []string{
		"cat",
		"cap",
		"bat",
		"car",
		"ca",
		"dog",
	} {
		inserted, err := tree.insert(word)
		if err != nil || !inserted {
			panic("unexpected insertion failure")
		}
	}
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", tree.words())
	fmt.Println(
		tree.contains("car"),
		tree.contains("can"),
		tree.hasPrefix("ca"),
		tree.hasPrefix("do"),
		tree.hasPrefix("cow"),
	)

	inserted, err := tree.insert("cat")
	fmt.Println(inserted, err == nil)
	_, err = tree.insert("c!")
	fmt.Println(err != nil, tree.hasPrefix("c!"))
	inserted, err = tree.insert("")
	fmt.Println(inserted, err == nil, tree.contains(""))
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", tree.words())
}
```

Expected output:

```text
["bat" "ca" "cap" "car" "cat" "dog"]
true false true true false
false true
true false
true true true
["" "bat" "ca" "cap" "car" "cat" "dog"]
```

##### Why it works

At a node for one input position, its left subtree contains only lower
candidate bytes and its right subtree only higher candidate bytes.
The middle subtree contains continuations after matching the node
byte. These facts hold initially for nil.

Insertion preserves them by sending a lower or higher byte to the
corresponding subtree without changing position. Equality associates
the current byte with the node and advances exactly once. Marking a
node terminal after the final equality adds exactly that complete word
without changing longer continuations.

Exact and prefix lookup make the same comparisons, so every discarded
subtree contains the wrong byte at the current position. Exact lookup
accepts only a terminal final match. Prefix lookup accepts any final
match because the reached node exists only as part of a stored word.
Inorder traversal emits lower alternatives first, then a word and its
longer continuations, then higher alternatives, which is precisely
byte-lexicographic order.

Every left or right move descends through a finite comparison tree.
Every middle move consumes one byte. A nil link, duplicate terminal,
or final match returns, so insertion and lookup terminate. Validation
before mutation makes rejection atomic.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let L be input byte length, P be allocated node count, and D be the
maximum stored word length. For the fixed 26-byte alphabet, each input
position can compare with at most 26 distinct node bytes. Insert,
contains, and prefix lookup therefore take O(26L), written O(L), time.
Actual constants depend on the left/right shape and insertion order.

A successful insert allocates at most L nodes. Recursive insertion
uses O(L) stack space because the alphabet bound is constant;
iterative queries use O(1) auxiliary space. Retained storage is O(P),
with one byte, three pointers, and one terminal flag per node.

The display traversal visits P nodes. Building immutable prefix
strings can copy up to D bytes at a node, so this simple helper takes
O(PD) time and cumulatively allocates O(PD) string bytes in the worst
case. Along one recursive path, as many as O(D^2) non-output
prefix bytes can remain live, plus O(D) stack frames. Returned word
strings occupy O(R) output bytes, where R is their total length.

A TST avoids a fixed child array and avoids a map per node. It pays
for extra comparisons, three pointers per byte node, and shape
sensitivity. It also leaves unary middle chains uncompressed, unlike
a radix tree.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty string uses `emptyWord`; no byte node can represent zero
  consumed bytes. Empty prefix remains true even in an empty tree.
- A word can be a prefix of another. With `a` and `at`, node `a` is
  terminal and still has a middle continuation.
- Duplicate `cat` returns false without changing nodes. Allocating a
  second terminal path would violate set semantics.
- Invalid `c!` is rejected before recursion. Rejecting only after
  inserting `c` could expose a path from a failed operation.
- Left and right moves do not advance `byteIndex`. Advancing on
  `p < t` loses the unmatched `p` from `cap`.
- Equality must advance before using `middle`. Comparing the same byte
  again can loop or place later bytes at the wrong position.
- Inorder needs the original prefix for left and right, but the
  extended word for middle. Reusing the extended value on the right
  produces words with an extra byte.
- Sorted insertion can skew same-position alternatives. The alphabet
  cap preserves O(L) asymptotics here, but comparison constants grow.
- This contract uses bytes, not Unicode characters. UTF-8, uppercase,
  and punctuation are invalid.

##### When to choose it

Choose a TST when prefix operations and lexicographic traversal
matter, the alphabet is sparse enough to waste fixed arrays, and
avoiding a map at every node is useful. It can work well for
dictionaries with many shared prefixes.

Use a [plain trie](#a91-prefix-trees) for the simplest predictable
small-alphabet lookup. Use a [compressed radix tree](
#a92-compressed-radix-trees) when long unary paths dominate memory.
Use a hash set for exact membership alone or a sorted slice for static
ordered data. The [BST lesson](#a72-binary-search-trees) owns the
ordering invariant reused by each TST comparison level.

### A.10 Graphs

#### A.10.1 Directed and undirected graphs

##### Problem and contract

Trees give each non-root node one parent, but many relationships have
multiple routes, cycles, or no connection at all. A graph represents
items as vertices and pairwise relationships as edges. The first
choice is whether each relationship has a direction.

Our mutable simple graph fixes vertices as integers in `[0, V)` at
construction. A directed edge `u -> v` permits movement from `u` to
`v` only. An undirected edge `u - v` permits both directions. Edges
carry no weights in this lesson.

`addEdge` returns true for a new edge, false with nil error for a
duplicate, and an error for an invalid endpoint or self-loop. Errors
cause no mutation. Parallel edges and self-loops are outside this
simple-graph contract. `edgeCount` counts logical edges, so one
undirected edge counts once even though it is stored twice.

`hasEdge` returns false for invalid endpoints. `outNeighbors` returns
a sorted copy or an error for an invalid vertex. `inDegrees` returns
one incoming-arc count per vertex. The constructor rejects a negative
vertex count. The zero value is a valid empty undirected graph; use
the constructor to choose direction or create vertices. Methods
require a non-nil graph pointer, and the logical edge count must fit
`int`.

The graph owns its slice and maps, while returned neighbor slices are
independent copies. Copying a graph value would share its internal
slice and maps. Unsynchronized concurrent use is outside the contract.

##### Mental model

A graph is commonly written `G = (V, E)`: `V` is the vertex set and
`E` is the edge set. Here, storage position `outgoing[u]` is a set of
all vertices `v` for which movement from `u` to `v` is allowed.

Read `outgoing[0] = {1, 2}` as: "vertex 0 has outgoing edges to 1 and
2." In a directed graph, that fact says nothing about edges back to 0.
In an undirected graph, adding `{0, 1}` stores both `outgoing[0][1]`
and `outgoing[1][0]` so either endpoint sees the same relationship.

An ordered pair `(u, v)` represents directed edge `u -> v`; reversing
it generally produces a different edge. An unordered pair `{u, v}`
represents one undirected edge; reversing its input order is the same
edge.

For directed graphs, outdegree is the number of outgoing neighbors,
while indegree counts other vertices' arcs into a vertex. For this
loop-free undirected graph, both views equal ordinary degree. Each
undirected edge contributes one adjacency entry at each endpoint, so
the sum of degrees is twice the logical edge count.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use vertices `[0, 1, 2, 3]`. First add directed edges `0 -> 1`,
`1 -> 2`, `2 -> 0`, and `0 -> 2`. Then add undirected edges with the
same first three endpoint pairs.

Initial state: both graphs have four vertices, four nil adjacency
maps, and zero logical edges. Vertex 3 is isolated.

1. Decision: add directed `0 -> 1`. Both endpoints are valid and
   distinct; the arc is absent, so create set 0, insert 1, and
   increase logical edge count to one. Do not update set 1.
   After: directed adjacency is `[[1], [], [], []]`.
   Known correct: movement from 0 to 1 exists, while `1 -> 0` does
   not.

2. Decision: add `1 -> 2` and `2 -> 0`, creating a directed cycle
   `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0`. Add `0 -> 2` as a second outgoing choice from
   0.
   After: adjacency is `[[1,2], [2], [0], []]`; edge count is four.

   ```text
   0 ----> 1
   |       |
   v       v
   2 --back to 0

   3 (isolated)
   ```

   Known correct: each listed arc appears exactly once, cycles are
   allowed, and isolated vertex 3 remains represented.

3. Decision: query both orientations of endpoints 0 and 1.
   `outNeighbors(0)` returns sorted copy `[1,2]`.
   `hasEdge(0, 1)` is true; `hasEdge(1, 0)` is false. Count incoming
   arcs by scanning every stored adjacency entry.
   After: the copied neighbors are `[1,2]`, and indegrees are
   `[1,1,2,0]` for vertices 0 through 3.
   Known correct: vertex 2 receives arcs from 0 and 1, independently
   of its one outgoing arc to 0.

4. Decision: in the undirected graph, add `{0,1}`, `{1,2}`, and
   `{2,0}`. For each new logical edge, store the opposite endpoint in
   both sets but increase edge count only once.
   After: adjacency is `[[1,2], [0,2], [0,1], []]`; count is three.

   ```text
   0 ----- 1
    \     /
      \ /
       2        3 (isolated)
   ```

   Known correct: every stored adjacency has its reciprocal, so either
   endpoint can traverse each relationship.

5. Decision: add undirected edge with reversed input `(1, 0)`. Entry
   `outgoing[1][0]` already exists, so return `(false, nil)` and leave
   count three. Try endpoint 4, then self-loop `(2, 2)`; validation
   rejects both before map mutation.
   After: adjacency and edge count remain unchanged.
   Known correct: reversal is a duplicate, and both invalid operations
   are atomic, completing every contract branch.

Focused boundary: a graph with zero vertices is valid and has empty
adjacency. An isolated vertex such as 3 still belongs to `V` even
though it never appears in another vertex's set.

Counterexample to storing an undirected edge only as
`outgoing[u][v]`: after adding `{0,1}`, a search beginning at 1 would
not see neighbor 0. The first wrong action is treating an unordered
relationship as one ordered arc; reciprocal storage restores the
contract.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Maps provide set
semantics; snapshots sort copied neighbor values for deterministic
output. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Directed and undirected graphs.
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

type simpleGraph struct {
	directed  bool
	outgoing  []map[int]struct{}
	edgeCount int
}

func newSimpleGraph(
	vertexCount int,
	directed bool,
) (*simpleGraph, error) {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial simple graph state.
	if vertexCount < 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex count %d is negative",
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	return &simpleGraph{
		directed: directed,
		outgoing: make(
			[]map[int]struct{},
			vertexCount,
		),
	}, nil
}

func (graph *simpleGraph) validateVertex(vertex int) error {
	// Reject input outside the vertex contract before mutation.
	if vertex < 0 || vertex >= len(graph.outgoing) {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex %d is outside [0, %d)",
			vertex,
			len(graph.outgoing),
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func (graph *simpleGraph) addEdge(
	from int,
	to int,
) (bool, error) {
	// Validate every endpoint before allocating either adjacency set.
	if err := graph.validateVertex(from); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	if err := graph.validateVertex(to); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	if from == to {
		return false, fmt.Errorf(
			"self-loop at vertex %d is not allowed",
			from,
		)
	}
	if _, exists := graph.outgoing[from][to]; exists {
		return false, nil
	}

	if graph.outgoing[from] == nil {
		graph.outgoing[from] = make(map[int]struct{})
	}
	graph.outgoing[from][to] = struct{}{}
	if !graph.directed {
		// Reciprocal storage gives both endpoints the same edge.
		if graph.outgoing[to] == nil {
			graph.outgoing[to] = make(map[int]struct{})
		}
		graph.outgoing[to][from] = struct{}{}
	}
	graph.edgeCount++
	return true, nil
}

func (graph *simpleGraph) hasEdge(from int, to int) bool {
	// Follow the lookup rule for edge without changing state.
	if graph.validateVertex(from) != nil {
		return false
	}
	if graph.validateVertex(to) != nil {
		return false
	}
	_, exists := graph.outgoing[from][to]
	return exists
}

func sortedNeighborValues(
	neighborSet map[int]struct{},
) []int {
	// Copy and sort neighbors so map iteration cannot change output.
	neighbors := make([]int, 0, len(neighborSet))
	for neighbor := range neighborSet {
		neighbors = append(neighbors, neighbor)
	}
	sort.Ints(neighbors)
	return neighbors
}

func (graph *simpleGraph) outNeighbors(
	vertex int,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Copy and sort neighbors for deterministic output.
	if err := graph.validateVertex(vertex); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return sortedNeighborValues(graph.outgoing[vertex]), nil
}

func (graph *simpleGraph) adjacency() [][]int {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	values := make([][]int, len(graph.outgoing))
	for vertex := range graph.outgoing {
		values[vertex] = sortedNeighborValues(
			graph.outgoing[vertex],
		)
	}
	return values
}

func (graph *simpleGraph) inDegrees() []int {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	degrees := make([]int, len(graph.outgoing))
	// Every stored arc contributes once to its destination.
	for from := range graph.outgoing {
		for to := range graph.outgoing[from] {
			degrees[to]++
		}
	}
	return degrees
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	directed, err := newSimpleGraph(4, true)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	for _, edge := range [][2]int{
		{0, 1},
		{1, 2},
		{2, 0},
		{0, 2},
	} {
		added, addErr := directed.addEdge(edge[0], edge[1])
		if addErr != nil || !added {
			panic("unexpected directed edge failure")
		}
	}
	fmt.Println(directed.adjacency(), directed.edgeCount)
	neighbors, err := directed.outNeighbors(0)
	fmt.Println(neighbors, err == nil)
	fmt.Println(
		directed.hasEdge(0, 1),
		directed.hasEdge(1, 0),
	)
	fmt.Println(directed.inDegrees())

	undirected, err := newSimpleGraph(4, false)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	for _, edge := range [][2]int{
		{0, 1},
		{1, 2},
		{2, 0},
	} {
		added, addErr := undirected.addEdge(
			edge[0],
			edge[1],
		)
		if addErr != nil || !added {
			panic("unexpected undirected edge failure")
		}
	}
	fmt.Println(undirected.adjacency(), undirected.edgeCount)
	fmt.Println(
		undirected.hasEdge(0, 1),
		undirected.hasEdge(1, 0),
	)

	added, err := undirected.addEdge(1, 0)
	fmt.Println(added, err == nil, undirected.edgeCount)
	_, err = undirected.addEdge(0, 4)
	fmt.Println(err != nil, undirected.edgeCount)
	_, err = undirected.addEdge(2, 2)
	fmt.Println(err != nil, undirected.edgeCount)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[[1 2] [2] [0] []] 4
[1 2] true
true false
[1 1 2 0]
[[1 2] [0 2] [0 1] []] 3
true true
false true 3
true 3
true 3
```

##### Why it works

Initially every adjacency set is empty, so it represents no edges.
For a directed insertion, adding `to` only to `outgoing[from]` creates
exactly ordered pair `(from, to)`. For an undirected insertion, adding
both reciprocal entries creates exactly unordered pair `{from, to}`.
Increasing `edgeCount` once therefore counts logical edges in either
mode.

Duplicate detection occurs before mutation. In directed mode it
checks the requested ordered pair. In undirected mode the reciprocal
invariant means either orientation finds the same existing
relationship. Full endpoint and self-loop validation before
allocation makes errors atomic.

`hasEdge` reads the defining set entry. Neighbor snapshots enumerate
exactly one outgoing set and sort only their copied output. Scanning
every stored arc increments precisely its destination's indegree. In
undirected mode, reciprocal arcs make that same count equal ordinary
degree.

Every loop ranges over a finite vertex slice or finite adjacency map,
and each operation returns after bounded validation and updates, so
all methods terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count, E be logical edge count, A be stored arc count,
D be one requested vertex's outdegree, and Delta be maximum outdegree.
Here A equals E for directed graphs and 2E for undirected graphs.

Construction takes Theta(V) time and O(V) slice storage; maps allocate
lazily. Assuming expected constant-time Go map access, `addEdge` and
`hasEdge` take expected O(1) time. A successful addition stores one or
two map entries and may allocate their maps.

`outNeighbors` copies D integers and sorts them, taking O(D log D)
time, O(D) output storage, and O(log D) sorting stack space.
`inDegrees` takes Theta(V + A) time and returns O(V) counts. A
complete adjacency snapshot uses O(V + A) output space and
O(V + A log Delta) time for copying and per-vertex sorting.

Retained graph storage is O(V + A). Maps give expected constant-time
duplicate checks but add hashing and allocation overhead. Arrays or
bit sets can be better for dense graphs; flat edge lists can be better
when iteration matters more than neighbor lookup.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Zero vertices is valid; adjacency is empty. Adding any edge then
  fails endpoint validation without allocating a map.
- Vertex 3 is isolated but still present. Deriving vertices only from
  edges would silently lose it.
- Endpoint -1 or V is invalid. Validate both endpoints before adding
  either half of an undirected edge.
- Directed edge `(0,1)` is not the same as `(1,0)`. Undirected
  reversal is a duplicate because both map entries already exist.
- A self-loop such as `(2,2)` is rejected here. Silently accepting it
  would change degree counting and violate this simple-graph contract.
- An undirected edge is stored twice but counted once. Incrementing
  count for each map write reports `2E` logical edges.
- Returned neighbors are sorted copies. Returning a map or internal
  slice would expose representation mutation and unstable order.
- Copying the graph shares maps and the slice backing array. Keep one
  owner or implement a deep copy before independent mutation.

##### When to choose it

Choose directed edges for one-way relationships such as dependencies,
web links, state transitions, or permissions. Choose undirected edges
for mutual relationships such as physical roads usable both ways,
friendship, or interchangeable network links.

Decide direction from the relationship contract before selecting a
traversal algorithm. The next [weighted-graph lesson](
#a102-weighted-and-unweighted-graphs) adds edge costs. The
[representation lesson](
#a103-adjacency-lists-matrices-and-edge-lists) compares storage, while
[multigraphs and self-loops](#a105-multigraphs-and-self-loops) changes
the duplicate and loop rules deliberately.

#### A.10.2 Weighted and unweighted graphs

##### Problem and contract

If every connection is interchangeable, a path with fewer edges is a
natural notion of "shorter." Real connections often have different
travel times, prices, capacities, or risks. A weighted graph attaches
a value to each edge, and the problem must define how those values
combine.

Our teaching graph is directed and simple, with fixed vertices in
`[0, V)`. Each edge has a nonnegative `int64` cost. `addEdge` returns
true for a new edge, false with nil error for a duplicate, and an
error for an invalid endpoint, self-loop, or negative cost. A
duplicate does not replace its original cost. Errors cause no
mutation.

`pathCost` accepts a nonempty vertex sequence. One vertex is a valid
zero-edge path with zero cost. Every consecutive pair must be a stored
edge. The method returns hop count and the sum of costs, or an error
for an invalid vertex, missing edge, empty path, or `int64` overflow.
It evaluates a supplied path; it does not search for an optimal one.

The zero value is an empty graph. The graph owns its maps and does not
expose mutable edge storage. Copying a graph value would share the
slice and maps. Methods require a non-nil graph pointer;
unsynchronized concurrent use is outside the contract.
Read [directed and undirected graphs](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) first.

##### Mental model

An unweighted graph answers only whether an edge exists. Treating each
edge as cost 1 makes a path's cost equal its number of edges, called
its hop count. Path `[0,1,3]` has two hops.

A weighted adjacency entry stores both destination and edge cost. Read
`outgoing[0][2] = 2` as: "edge `0 -> 2` exists and contributes cost 2
when a path uses it." For additive costs, path cost is the sum of each
consecutive edge:

```text
cost([0,2,1,3]) = cost(0,2) + cost(2,1) + cost(1,3)
                  = 2 + 2 + 1
                  = 5
```

Hop count and weighted cost answer different questions. A two-edge
path can cost more than a three-edge path. The units also matter:
adding minutes is meaningful, while treating bandwidth as an additive
cost usually is not; a capacity path may use a minimum instead.

This implementation permits zero-cost edges but rejects negative
costs. That range fits algorithms such as Dijkstra's later, but the
representation itself is not a proof that any particular shortest-path
algorithm applies.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use vertices `[0,1,2,3]` and directed cost edges
`0 -> 1:9`, `0 -> 2:2`, `2 -> 1:2`, `1 -> 3:1`, and `2 -> 3:8`.
Compare paths `[0,1,3]` and `[0,2,1,3]`.

Initial state: four nil adjacency maps contain no edges or costs.

1. Decision: validate and add every edge. For `0 -> 1:9`, store value
   9 under destination 1 in source map 0. Repeat for the other four
   distinct endpoint pairs.
   After:

   ```text
   0: [{to:1 cost:9} {to:2 cost:2}]
   1: [{to:3 cost:1}]
   2: [{to:1 cost:2} {to:3 cost:8}]
   3: []
   ```

   Known correct: every map entry records exactly one edge and its
   immutable nonnegative cost.

2. Decision: view the graph as unweighted. Path `[0,1,3]` has two
   consecutive edges, while `[0,2,1,3]` has three. Fewer hops favors
   the first path.
   After: hop counts are 2 and 3.
   Known correct: ignoring weights makes each existing edge contribute
   exactly one.

3. Decision: evaluate `[0,1,3]` with weights. Edge `0 -> 1` adds 9;
   edge `1 -> 3` adds 1. Neither addition overflows.
   After: total cost is 10 with two hops.
   Known correct: both consecutive edges exist and the running total
   equals their cost sum.

4. Decision: evaluate `[0,2,1,3]`. Add costs 2, then 2, then 1.
   After: total cost is 5 with three hops.
   Known correct: the three-hop path is cheaper than the two-hop path,
   so an unweighted answer need not minimize weighted cost.

5. Decision: add zero-cost edge `3 -> 0`; zero is valid, so insertion
   succeeds. Retry `0 -> 1` with cost 4; the endpoint pair already
   exists, so return false and keep cost 9. Reject negative cost -1
   before allocation. Evaluate missing edge path `[3,2]` and return an
   error without a partial result.
   After: only `3 -> 0:0` joins the five original edges.
   Known correct: zero, duplicate, invalid, and missing-edge branches
   all follow the contract.

Focused boundary: a one-vertex path such as `[2]` has zero hops and
zero cost because it traverses no edge. An empty sequence is invalid
because it does not identify even a starting vertex.

Counterexample to using fewest hops on a weighted graph: choosing
`[0,1,3]` after seeing two hops commits to cost 10, while the
three-hop alternative costs 5. The first wrong decision discards edge
costs before defining what "shortest" means.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Snapshots sort edges
by destination for deterministic output. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Weighted and unweighted graphs.
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
	"sort"
)

type costEdge struct {
	to   int
	cost int64
}

type costGraph struct {
	outgoing []map[int]int64
}

func newCostGraph(vertexCount int) (*costGraph, error) {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial cost graph state.
	if vertexCount < 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex count %d is negative",
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	return &costGraph{
		outgoing: make([]map[int]int64, vertexCount),
	}, nil
}

func (graph *costGraph) validateVertex(vertex int) error {
	// Reject input outside the vertex contract before mutation.
	if vertex < 0 || vertex >= len(graph.outgoing) {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex %d is outside [0, %d)",
			vertex,
			len(graph.outgoing),
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func (graph *costGraph) addEdge(
	from int,
	to int,
	cost int64,
) (bool, error) {
	// Validate the complete edge before changing adjacency state.
	if err := graph.validateVertex(from); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	if err := graph.validateVertex(to); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	if from == to {
		return false, fmt.Errorf(
			"self-loop at vertex %d is not allowed",
			from,
		)
	}
	if cost < 0 {
		return false, fmt.Errorf(
			"cost %d is negative",
			cost,
		)
	}
	if _, exists := graph.outgoing[from][to]; exists {
		return false, nil
	}

	if graph.outgoing[from] == nil {
		graph.outgoing[from] = make(map[int]int64)
	}
	graph.outgoing[from][to] = cost
	return true, nil
}

func (graph *costGraph) pathCost(
	path []int,
) (int, int64, error) {
	// Keep path cost in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if len(path) == 0 {
		return 0, 0, fmt.Errorf("path is empty")
	}
	// Validate every vertex before examining consecutive edges.
	for position, vertex := range path {
		if err := graph.validateVertex(vertex); err != nil {
			return 0, 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"path position %d: %w",
				position,
				err,
			)
		}
	}

	total := int64(0)
	edgeIndex := 0
	for edgeIndex+1 < len(path) {
		from := path[edgeIndex]
		to := path[edgeIndex+1]
		cost, found := graph.outgoing[from][to]
		if !found {
			return 0, 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d -> %d is missing",
				from,
				to,
			)
		}
		if cost > math.MaxInt64-total {
			return 0, 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"path cost overflows int64",
			)
		}
		total += cost
		edgeIndex++
	}
	return len(path) - 1, total, nil
}

func sortedCostEdges(
	edgesByDestination map[int]int64,
) []costEdge {
	// Reorder values using the comparison rule defined above.
	destinations := make(
		[]int,
		0,
		len(edgesByDestination),
	)
	for destination := range edgesByDestination {
		destinations = append(destinations, destination)
	}
	sort.Ints(destinations)

	edges := make([]costEdge, 0, len(destinations))
	for _, destination := range destinations {
		edges = append(edges, costEdge{
			to:   destination,
			cost: edgesByDestination[destination],
		})
	}
	return edges
}

func (graph *costGraph) adjacency() [][]costEdge {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	values := make([][]costEdge, len(graph.outgoing))
	for vertex := range graph.outgoing {
		values[vertex] = sortedCostEdges(
			graph.outgoing[vertex],
		)
	}
	return values
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	graph, err := newCostGraph(4)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	for _, edge := range []struct {
		from int
		to   int
		cost int64
	}{
		{from: 0, to: 1, cost: 9},
		{from: 0, to: 2, cost: 2},
		{from: 2, to: 1, cost: 2},
		{from: 1, to: 3, cost: 1},
		{from: 2, to: 3, cost: 8},
	} {
		added, addErr := graph.addEdge(
			edge.from,
			edge.to,
			edge.cost,
		)
		if addErr != nil || !added {
			panic("unexpected edge failure")
		}
	}
	fmt.Println(graph.adjacency())

	firstHops, firstCost, err := graph.pathCost(
		[]int{0, 1, 3},
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	secondHops, secondCost, err := graph.pathCost(
		[]int{0, 2, 1, 3},
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(firstHops, firstCost)
	fmt.Println(secondHops, secondCost)

	added, err := graph.addEdge(3, 0, 0)
	fmt.Println(added, err == nil)
	added, err = graph.addEdge(0, 1, 4)
	fmt.Println(added, err == nil)
	_, err = graph.addEdge(3, 2, -1)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
	_, _, err = graph.pathCost([]int{3, 2})
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[[{1 9} {2 2}] [{3 1}] [{1 2} {3 8}] []]
2 10
3 5
true true
false true
true
true
```

##### Why it works

Each stored map entry associates one ordered endpoint pair with
exactly one immutable cost. Validation precedes allocation, and
duplicate detection leaves the existing entry untouched, so every
successful insertion preserves the simple directed graph contract.

For a supplied path, position validation establishes that every map
lookup is in range. Each loop iteration reads exactly the next
consecutive edge and adds its cost once. The running total therefore
equals the sum of the processed prefix. The overflow guard proves the
next nonnegative addition is representable before performing it.

At termination, `len(path)-1` is the number of consecutive pairs and
the total is their complete cost sum. A missing edge or overflow
returns an error rather than a partial metric. The loops advance
through finite slices, so insertion helpers and path evaluation
terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count, E be stored edge count, L be vertices in the
supplied path, and D be one vertex's outdegree. Construction takes
Theta(V) time and O(V) slice storage, with maps allocated lazily.

Assuming expected constant-time Go map access, edge insertion takes
expected O(1) time and one map entry of retained storage. `pathCost`
validates L vertices and reads L - 1 edges, taking Theta(L) expected
time and O(1) auxiliary space.

The display snapshot copies and sorts each adjacency set. One row
takes O(D log(D + 1)) time and O(D) output storage. Across the graph
it takes O(V + E log(Delta + 1)) time and O(V + E) output storage,
where Delta is maximum outdegree. Retained graph storage is O(V + E).

Compared with an unweighted adjacency set, every edge stores a cost
and path algorithms must combine it correctly. Weight precision,
overflow, sign, and units become part of the contract. A separate edge
type is clearer than parallel destination and cost slices that can
drift out of alignment.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A one-vertex path `[2]` returns `(0, 0, nil)`. An empty path returns
  an error because it lacks a start vertex.
- Zero-cost `3 -> 0` is valid. Testing `cost <= 0` would incorrectly
  reject it.
- Negative cost -1 is rejected by this implementation. Accepting it
  would require selecting algorithms whose guarantees allow negatives.
- Duplicate `0 -> 1:4` returns false and keeps original cost 9.
  Silently replacing it would contradict insert-only semantics.
- Missing edge path `[3,2]` errors. Adding only vertex costs or
  skipping the absent pair would report a path that does not exist.
- Summing `math.MaxInt64` and 1 must error before addition. Checking
  overflow afterward is too late for fixed-width arithmetic.
- Weight units must agree. Adding a price to a duration produces a
  number without a useful path meaning.
- This graph rejects self-loops and parallel edges. Models needing
  either must define how their costs and duplicates behave.

##### When to choose it

Use an unweighted graph when every edge represents the same unit step
and the objective is fewest hops. Use a weighted graph when edge
values change the objective, such as travel time, price, distance, or
risk.

Before choosing an algorithm, determine whether weights are additive,
whether zero or negative values occur, and whether the goal is
minimum, maximum, or another aggregation. The [shortest-path family](
#b13-shortest-paths-and-minimum-travel-costs) owns algorithm
selection.
The preceding [direction lesson](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) owns edge orientation, while the
next [representation lesson](
#a103-adjacency-lists-matrices-and-edge-lists) compares storage forms.

#### A.10.3 Adjacency lists, matrices, and edge lists

##### Problem and contract

The same graph can be stored in forms that favor different work.
Traversals repeatedly ask for one vertex's neighbors. Dense-graph
queries may ask whether a particular edge exists. Other algorithms
sort or scan every edge globally. No single representation makes all
three operations equally cheap.

Our builder receives a fixed vertex count and simple undirected edges.
Vertices are integers in `[0, V)`. It rejects a negative count,
invalid endpoint, self-loop, or duplicate, including a reversed
duplicate. It validates all input before constructing three equivalent
views:

- a sorted adjacency list with reciprocal neighbor entries;
- a symmetric Boolean adjacency matrix;
- a lexicographically sorted edge list of canonical pairs `u < v`.

Zero vertices and an empty edge set are valid. The builder does not
mutate or retain the input edge slice. Returned views own their nested
slices, but copying a view value shares those slices. Mutating one
view after construction can break equivalence; this lesson treats them
as read-only. Unsynchronized concurrent mutation is outside the
contract.

Exact edge queries return false for invalid vertices or self-pairs.
Read [directed and undirected graphs](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) first.

##### Mental model

Suppose vertex 0 connects to 1 and 3.

An adjacency list stores:

```text
adjacencyList[0] = [1, 3]
```

Read that row as "the neighbors reached directly from 0." Sorting lets
exact lookup binary-search the row. An undirected edge appears in two
rows, once at each endpoint.

An adjacency matrix stores one cell for every ordered endpoint pair:

```text
adjacencyMatrix[0][3] = true
```

The row index selects the first endpoint and the column selects the
second. Undirected symmetry requires both `[0][3]` and `[3][0]` true.
Most cells are false when the graph is sparse.

An edge list stores each logical relationship once:

```text
edgeList = [[0,1], [0,3], ...]
```

Canonical `u < v` order makes `{3,0}` the same key as `{0,3}`. The
list is compact and easy to sort globally, but finding all neighbors
of one vertex may inspect every edge unless another index is built.

The vertex count remains separate metadata in every form. An isolated
vertex has an empty list row and an all-false matrix row but appears
in no edge-list pair.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build all three forms for vertices `[0,1,2,3,4]` and edges
`{0,1}`, `{0,3}`, `{1,2}`, and `{2,3}`. Vertex 4 is isolated.

Initial state: the input edge slice is unchanged; no output storage
has been allocated.

1. Decision: validate each endpoint and reject self-pairs.
   Canonicalize every edge so its smaller endpoint comes first. Insert
   the canonical pair into a temporary set to detect both ordinary and
   reversed duplicates.
   After: canonical pairs are `[[0,1], [0,3], [1,2], [2,3]]`.
   Known correct: all four pairs are unique, in range, and represent
   exactly the input's unordered relationships.

2. Decision: sort canonical pairs, allocate five list rows and a
   five-by-five matrix. For `{0,1}`, append 1 to row 0 and 0 to row 1;
   set matrix cells `[0][1]` and `[1][0]`. Repeat for every pair, then
   sort each neighbor row.
   After:

   ```text
   list:   [[1,3], [0,2], [1,3], [0,2], []]
   matrix: [01010, 10100, 01010, 10100, 00000]
   edges:  [[0,1], [0,3], [1,2], [2,3]]
   ```

   Known correct: all forms encode four logical edges and retain
   isolated vertex 4 through their separate vertex count.

3. Decision: query edge `{0,3}`. Binary-search sorted list row 0 and
   find 3. Read matrix cell `[0][3]` as true. Canonicalize to `[0,3]`
   and find that pair in the edge list.
   After: all three queries return true.
   Known correct: the representations agree on a present edge through
   their own lookup rules.

4. Decision: query missing edge `{0,2}`. List row 0 has `[1,3]`,
   matrix cell `[0][2]` is false, and no canonical pair `[0,2]`
   exists.
   After: all three queries return false.
   Known correct: absence is represented consistently rather than by a
   matrix sentinel that could collide with a valid value.

5. Decision: independently try reversed duplicate inputs `{0,1}` and
   `{1,0}`, invalid endpoint 5, and self-loop `{2,2}`. Each build
   validates before output allocation and returns an error.
   After: no partial representation is returned for any invalid input.
   Known correct: duplicate, range, and loop failures are atomic.

Focused boundary: with five vertices and no edges, the list has five
empty rows, the matrix has 25 false cells, and the edge list is empty.
With zero vertices, all three outer collections are empty.

Counterexample to inferring V from the largest edge endpoint: the
largest endpoint here is 3, so inference would construct only four
vertices and silently lose isolated vertex 4. Vertex membership and
edge membership are separate facts.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Matrix rows use `0`
and `1` strings to keep snapshots compact. Save it as `main.go` and
run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Adjacency lists, matrices, and
// edge lists. Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

type graphRepresentations struct {
	adjacencyList   [][]int
	adjacencyMatrix [][]bool
	edgeList        [][2]int
}

func canonicalUndirectedEdge(
	first int,
	second int,
) [2]int {
	// Evaluate canonical undirected edge without changing the maintained
	// state.
	if second < first {
		first, second = second, first
	}
	return [2]int{first, second}
}

func buildGraphRepresentations(
	vertexCount int,
	inputEdges [][2]int,
) (graphRepresentations, error) {
	// Build graph representations in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	if vertexCount < 0 {
		return graphRepresentations{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex count %d is negative",
			vertexCount,
		)
	}

	// Validate into new canonical storage before allocating views.
	canonicalEdges := make([][2]int, 0, len(inputEdges))
	seen := make(map[[2]int]struct{}, len(inputEdges))
	for inputIndex, inputEdge := range inputEdges {
		first := inputEdge[0]
		second := inputEdge[1]
		if first < 0 || first >= vertexCount {
			return graphRepresentations{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d has invalid vertex %d",
				inputIndex,
				first,
			)
		}
		if second < 0 || second >= vertexCount {
			return graphRepresentations{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d has invalid vertex %d",
				inputIndex,
				second,
			)
		}
		if first == second {
			return graphRepresentations{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d is a self-loop",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}

		canonical := canonicalUndirectedEdge(first, second)
		if _, duplicate := seen[canonical]; duplicate {
			return graphRepresentations{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d is a duplicate",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
		seen[canonical] = struct{}{}
		canonicalEdges = append(canonicalEdges, canonical)
	}

	// Canonical ordering makes the edge-list snapshot deterministic.
	sort.Slice(
		canonicalEdges,
		func(firstIndex int, secondIndex int) bool {
			first := canonicalEdges[firstIndex]
			second := canonicalEdges[secondIndex]
			if first[0] != second[0] {
				return first[0] < second[0]
			}
			return first[1] < second[1]
		},
	)

	// Build reciprocal list entries and symmetric matrix cells.
	adjacencyList := make([][]int, vertexCount)
	adjacencyMatrix := make([][]bool, vertexCount)
	for row := range adjacencyMatrix {
		adjacencyMatrix[row] = make([]bool, vertexCount)
	}
	for _, edge := range canonicalEdges {
		first := edge[0]
		second := edge[1]
		adjacencyList[first] = append(
			adjacencyList[first],
			second,
		)
		adjacencyList[second] = append(
			adjacencyList[second],
			first,
		)
		adjacencyMatrix[first][second] = true
		adjacencyMatrix[second][first] = true
	}
	for vertex := range adjacencyList {
		sort.Ints(adjacencyList[vertex])
	}

	return graphRepresentations{
		adjacencyList:   adjacencyList,
		adjacencyMatrix: adjacencyMatrix,
		edgeList:        canonicalEdges,
	}, nil
}

func (views graphRepresentations) validPair(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Evaluate valid pair without changing the maintained state.
	vertexCount := len(views.adjacencyList)
	return first >= 0 && first < vertexCount &&
		second >= 0 && second < vertexCount &&
		first != second
}

func (views graphRepresentations) listHasEdge(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Expose has edge in logical order without changing source.
	if !views.validPair(first, second) {
		return false
	}
	neighbors := views.adjacencyList[first]
	position := sort.SearchInts(neighbors, second)
	return position < len(neighbors) &&
		neighbors[position] == second
}

func (views graphRepresentations) matrixHasEdge(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Keep matrix has edge in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if !views.validPair(first, second) {
		return false
	}
	return views.adjacencyMatrix[first][second]
}

func (views graphRepresentations) edgeListHasEdge(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Keep edge list has edge in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if !views.validPair(first, second) {
		return false
	}
	wanted := canonicalUndirectedEdge(first, second)
	for _, edge := range views.edgeList {
		if edge == wanted {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

func (views graphRepresentations) matrixRows() []string {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	rows := make([]string, len(views.adjacencyMatrix))
	for rowIndex, matrixRow := range views.adjacencyMatrix {
		row := make([]byte, len(matrixRow))
		for column, present := range matrixRow {
			row[column] = '0'
			if present {
				row[column] = '1'
			}
		}
		rows[rowIndex] = string(row)
	}
	return rows
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	views, err := buildGraphRepresentations(
		5,
		[][2]int{
			{0, 1},
			{0, 3},
			{1, 2},
			{2, 3},
		},
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(views.adjacencyList)
	fmt.Println(views.matrixRows())
	fmt.Println(views.edgeList)
	fmt.Println(
		views.listHasEdge(0, 3),
		views.matrixHasEdge(0, 3),
		views.edgeListHasEdge(0, 3),
	)
	fmt.Println(
		views.listHasEdge(0, 2),
		views.matrixHasEdge(0, 2),
		views.edgeListHasEdge(0, 2),
	)

	_, duplicateErr := buildGraphRepresentations(
		3,
		[][2]int{{0, 1}, {1, 0}},
	)
	_, endpointErr := buildGraphRepresentations(
		5,
		[][2]int{{0, 5}},
	)
	_, loopErr := buildGraphRepresentations(
		5,
		[][2]int{{2, 2}},
	)
	fmt.Println(
		duplicateErr != nil,
		endpointErr != nil,
		loopErr != nil,
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[[1 3] [0 2] [1 3] [0 2] []]
[01010 10100 01010 10100 00000]
[[0 1] [0 3] [1 2] [2 3]]
true true true
false false false
true true true
```

##### Why it works

Validation and canonicalization create one unique pair for each input
relationship. Because no output view exists yet, any error returns
without partial state. Sorting changes only pair order, not edge
membership.

For every canonical `{u,v}`, construction appends each endpoint to the
other's list and marks both matrix orientations. It retains the pair
once in the edge list. Thus list membership, a true matrix cell, and
edge-list pair membership are equivalent statements about the same
logical edge. No other entries are added.

All outer collections use the explicit vertex count, so empty rows
preserve isolated vertices. List sorting makes binary search valid;
matrix indexing names the endpoints directly; canonicalization makes
either query orientation match the one edge-list pair.

Every validation, construction, sort, and query loop ranges over a
finite input or allocated collection. The methods therefore terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count, E be logical edge count, D be a queried
vertex's degree, and Delta be maximum degree. Validation takes
expected O(E) time and O(E) temporary set storage. Sorting canonical
edges takes O(E log(E + 1)) time.

Allocating the matrix takes Theta(V^2) time and storage. Filling the
list and matrix takes Theta(E) time; sorting all list rows takes
O(E log(Delta + 1)). Total build time is
O(V^2 + E log(E + 1) + E log(Delta + 1)). All three retained views
together use O(V^2 + V + E) storage. The builder's temporary set is
O(E) auxiliary storage beyond the returned views.

For an exact edge query, this sorted-list implementation takes
O(log(D + 1)), the matrix takes Theta(1), and the linear edge-list
scan takes O(E). Enumerating one vertex's neighbors takes Theta(D)
from the list, Theta(V) from a matrix row, and Theta(E) by scanning
the edge list.

Adjacency lists fit sparse graphs and neighbor-heavy traversals.
Matrices spend quadratic space for constant-time edge tests and simple
dense operations. Edge lists are compact for global edge scans and
sorting, but need an index for fast per-vertex work. Keeping several
forms speeds mixed workloads but consumes memory and requires every
mutation to update all views consistently.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Zero vertices produces three empty outer collections. A positive V
  with no edges still needs V list and matrix rows.
- Isolated vertex 4 appears through V, an empty list row, and an
  all-zero matrix row. It cannot be inferred from the edge list.
- Reversed pair `{1,0}` duplicates `{0,1}`. Detect duplicates after
  canonicalization, not before.
- Endpoint -1 or V is invalid. Validate before matrix indexing to
  avoid a panic or partial list update.
- Self-loop `{2,2}` is rejected by this contract. A loop-supporting
  matrix would use its diagonal and would need explicit degree rules.
- Undirected list and matrix updates are reciprocal. Writing only one
  orientation silently turns traversal into a directed graph.
- A false matrix cell is absence, not weight zero. Weighted matrices
  need a separate presence bit or a sentinel outside valid weights.
- Mutating only one returned view breaks equivalence. Treat the result
  as read-only or centralize every update behind one owner.
- A dense graph makes a list approach V^2 entries anyway; a
  matrix may then be simpler and more compact in practice.

##### When to choose it

Choose an adjacency list when most possible edges are absent and
algorithms repeatedly enumerate neighbors. Choose a matrix when V is
small enough for quadratic storage and exact edge queries or dense
algebra dominate. Choose an edge list when algorithms process edges
globally, such as sorting them by weight.

The preceding [weight lesson](#a102-weighted-and-unweighted-graphs)
explains what an edge value means. The [direction lesson](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) explains reciprocal storage.
[Reverse adjacency](#a107-reverse-adjacency-and-residual-graphs) adds
an index for incoming edges, while the [graph algorithm
families](#b12-reachability-components-and-graph-cycles) use these
representations according to their access pattern.

#### A.10.4 Bipartite graphs and directed acyclic graphs

##### Problem and contract

Some graph algorithms need more than direction and weights; they need
a structural promise. An undirected bipartite graph can split vertices
into two groups with every edge crossing between groups. A directed
acyclic graph, or DAG, has no directed cycle. These are independent
properties for different graph models, not two names for one shape.

Our bipartite classifier accepts a fixed vertex count and undirected
endpoint pairs. It returns a deterministic color 0 or 1 for every
vertex when a valid split exists. Each disconnected component's
smallest uncolored vertex starts with color 0. A self-loop makes the
result non-bipartite. Repeated edges are allowed and do not change the
answer.

Our DAG classifier accepts directed endpoint pairs and returns one
topological order: every edge's source appears before its destination.
It returns false when a directed cycle prevents such an order. Initial
zero-indegree vertices enter in numeric order; outgoing edges are
processed in input order. Multiple correct orders may exist.

Both functions reject a negative vertex count or invalid endpoint.
They validate the complete input before classification, do not mutate
or retain the edge slice, and return no partial witness on failure.
Zero vertices is valid for both properties. Read the [direction
lesson](#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) first.

##### Mental model

For bipartite classification, `color[v]` stores which side contains
vertex `v`: 0, 1, or -1 while unassigned. An edge requires opposite
colors. Breadth-first search starts a component at 0, assigns each new
neighbor `1 - color[v]`, and rejects an edge whose endpoints already
have the same color.

The colors record path-length parity from the component start: even
distance gets color 0 and odd distance gets color 1. An odd cycle
returns to its start after flipping color an odd number of times, so
one edge must conflict. Even cycles can remain bipartite.

For DAG classification, `indegree[v]` stores how many incoming edges
from not-yet-emitted vertices remain. A zero count means the vertex
can come next without placing any predecessor after it. Emitting that
vertex removes its outgoing edges and may expose more zero counts.
This is Kahn's topological-order method.

If all vertices are emitted, the order witnesses a DAG. If work stops
early, every remaining vertex has a remaining predecessor. Following
predecessors in a finite graph must eventually repeat a vertex, which
proves a directed cycle.

##### Worked walkthrough

Classify undirected graph edges `{0,1}`, `{0,3}`, `{2,1}`, `{2,3}`,
and `{4,5}` over vertices `[0,1,2,3,4,5]`. Then add `{1,3}` to create
an odd cycle. Separately classify directed edges
`0->2`, `1->2`, `1->3`, `2->4`, `3->4`, and `4->5`; then add `5->1`.

Initial state: every bipartite color is -1. DAG indegrees are not yet
computed. Both output sequences are empty.

1. Decision: start undirected component at vertex 0 with color 0 and
   queue `[0]`. Pop 0; uncolored neighbors 1 and 3 receive color 1 and
   enter the queue.
   After: colors are `[0,1,-1,1,-1,-1]`; queue is `[1,3]`.
   Known correct: both processed edges from 0 cross between colors.

2. Decision: pop 1. Neighbor 0 already has opposite color; assign
   uncolored neighbor 2 color 0. Pop 3 and observe that both neighbors
   0 and 2 have opposite color. The first component is complete.
   After: colors are `[0,1,0,1,-1,-1]`; queue is exhausted.
   Known correct: every edge among vertices 0 through 3 crosses the
   partition, including the even cycle `0-1-2-3-0`.

3. Decision: vertex 4 is the next uncolored start, so assign 0. Its
   neighbor 5 receives 1. All vertices are now colored.
   After: colors are `[0,1,0,1,0,1]`; return true.

   ```text
   0(0) ----- 1(1)       4(0) ----- 5(1)
    |           |
    |           |
   3(1) ----- 2(0)
   ```

   Known correct: disconnected components need no relationship between
   their arbitrary color names, only opposite endpoints per edge.

4. Decision: classify again after adding `{1,3}`. The earlier search
   assigns both 1 and 3 color 1; their new edge demands opposite
   colors, so reject.
   After: return false with no partial color slice.

   ```text
   0(0) ----- 1(1)
    \          |
      \        | new edge joins equal colors
        3(1) --+
   ```

   Known correct: edges `0-1`, `1-3`, and `3-0` form an odd cycle.

5. Decision: count the directed example's incoming edges. Vertices 0
   and 1 have indegree 0; vertices 2 through 5 have counts
   `[2,1,2,1]`. Enqueue `[0,1]`.
   After: order is empty and queue is `[0,1]`.
   Known correct: only vertices with no un-emitted predecessors are
   ready.

6. Decision: emit 0, reducing indegree 2 from 2 to 1. Emit 1; its
   edges reduce indegrees of 2 and 3 to zero, so enqueue them in input
   order. Emit 2, then 3; vertex 4 reaches zero only after both.
   Finally emit 4 and then 5.
   After: order is `[0,1,2,3,4,5]`; six vertices were emitted.

   ```text
   0 ---> 2 ---> 4 ---> 5
          ^      ^
          |      |
   1 -----+----> 3
   ```

   Known correct: every directed edge points from an earlier position
   to a later one, so return true.

7. Decision: add `5->1`. Now only vertex 0 initially has indegree
   zero.
   Emitting it reduces vertex 2 but does not release the cycle
   `1->3->4->5->1`; the queue empties after one vertex.
   After: emitted count 1 is less than V; return false and no order.

   ```text
   1 ---> 3 ---> 4 ---> 5
   ^                       |
   +-----------------------+

   remaining cycle has no zero-indegree vertex
   ```

   Known correct: incomplete emission is a cycle witness, not a
   partial topological answer.

8. Decision: call either classifier with endpoint 6. Full validation
   finds it outside `[0,6)` before adjacency allocation.
   After: return an error and no witness.
   Known correct: malformed input is distinct from a well-formed graph
   that simply lacks the requested property.

Focused boundaries: an empty graph and a one-vertex graph are both
bipartite and acyclic. A self-loop is simultaneously an odd cycle of
length one in the undirected view and a directed cycle in the DAG
view.

Counterexample to rejecting every cycle as non-bipartite: the square
`0-1-2-3-0` has a cycle but admits colors `[0,1,0,1]`. Odd parity, not
cycle existence alone, causes the color conflict.

Counterexample to judging a DAG from its undirected shape: edges
`0->1`, `0->2`, and `1->2` form an undirected triangle but have
topological order `[0,1,2]`. Direction determines whether a cycle
returns to its start.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs both walkthroughs. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Bipartite graphs and directed
// acyclic graphs. Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func validateGraphEdges(
	vertexCount int,
	edges [][2]int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the graph edges contract before mutation.
	if vertexCount < 0 {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex count %d is negative",
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	for edgeIndex, edge := range edges {
		for endpointIndex, vertex := range edge {
			if vertex < 0 || vertex >= vertexCount {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %d endpoint %d is invalid",
					edgeIndex,
					endpointIndex,
				)
			}
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func bipartiteColors(
	vertexCount int,
	edges [][2]int,
) ([]int, bool, error) {
	// Keep bipartite colors in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if err := validateGraphEdges(vertexCount, edges); err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}
	adjacency := make([][]int, vertexCount)
	for _, edge := range edges {
		first := edge[0]
		second := edge[1]
		adjacency[first] = append(adjacency[first], second)
		adjacency[second] = append(adjacency[second], first)
	}

	colors := make([]int, vertexCount)
	for vertex := range colors {
		colors[vertex] = -1
	}
	queue := make([]int, 0, vertexCount)
	for start := 0; start < vertexCount; start++ {
		if colors[start] != -1 {
			continue
		}
		colors[start] = 0
		queue = queue[:0]
		queue = append(queue, start)

		// A queued vertex has a fixed color before its edges run.
		queueHead := 0
		for queueHead < len(queue) {
			vertex := queue[queueHead]
			queueHead++
			for _, neighbor := range adjacency[vertex] {
				if colors[neighbor] == -1 {
					colors[neighbor] = 1 - colors[vertex]
					queue = append(queue, neighbor)
					continue
				}
				if colors[neighbor] == colors[vertex] {
					return nil, false, nil
				}
			}
		}
	}
	return colors, true, nil
}

func topologicalOrder(
	vertexCount int,
	edges [][2]int,
) ([]int, bool, error) {
	// Keep topological order in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if err := validateGraphEdges(vertexCount, edges); err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}
	adjacency := make([][]int, vertexCount)
	indegrees := make([]int, vertexCount)
	for _, edge := range edges {
		from := edge[0]
		to := edge[1]
		adjacency[from] = append(adjacency[from], to)
		indegrees[to]++
	}

	queue := make([]int, 0, vertexCount)
	for vertex, indegree := range indegrees {
		if indegree == 0 {
			queue = append(queue, vertex)
		}
	}
	order := make([]int, 0, vertexCount)
	queueHead := 0
	for queueHead < len(queue) {
		vertex := queue[queueHead]
		queueHead++
		order = append(order, vertex)

		// Removing these arcs exposes newly ready destinations.
		for _, neighbor := range adjacency[vertex] {
			indegrees[neighbor]--
			if indegrees[neighbor] == 0 {
				queue = append(queue, neighbor)
			}
		}
	}
	if len(order) != vertexCount {
		return nil, false, nil
	}
	return order, true, nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	bipartiteEdges := [][2]int{
		{0, 1},
		{0, 3},
		{2, 1},
		{2, 3},
		{4, 5},
	}
	colors, bipartite, err := bipartiteColors(
		6,
		bipartiteEdges,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(bipartite, colors)

	oddCycleEdges := append(
		append([][2]int(nil), bipartiteEdges...),
		[2]int{1, 3},
	)
	colors, bipartite, err = bipartiteColors(
		6,
		oddCycleEdges,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(bipartite, colors)

	dagEdges := [][2]int{
		{0, 2},
		{1, 2},
		{1, 3},
		{2, 4},
		{3, 4},
		{4, 5},
	}
	order, acyclic, err := topologicalOrder(6, dagEdges)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(acyclic, order)

	cycleEdges := append(
		append([][2]int(nil), dagEdges...),
		[2]int{5, 1},
	)
	order, acyclic, err = topologicalOrder(6, cycleEdges)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(acyclic, order)

	_, _, err = topologicalOrder(
		6,
		[][2]int{{0, 6}},
	)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
true [0 1 0 1 0 1]
false []
true [0 1 2 3 4 5]
false []
true
```

##### Why it works

For bipartite classification, a component start has even path parity
and color 0. Whenever an edge discovers a vertex, assigning the
opposite color matches one more edge and therefore flips parity. A
previously colored neighbor with the opposite color is consistent.
The invariant survives every processed edge.

If a same-color edge appears, the two BFS-tree paths to its endpoints
have the same parity; joining them with that edge forms an odd closed
walk and contains an odd cycle. Conversely, if no conflict appears,
the returned color sets partition every vertex and every input edge
crosses between them, which is exactly bipartiteness.

For topological ordering, each indegree initially counts all incoming
edges. After some vertices are emitted, decrementing precisely their
outgoing edges leaves each count equal to incoming edges from the
remaining graph. A zero-count vertex has no remaining predecessor, so
appending it cannot violate any edge order.

If V vertices are emitted, each edge source was removed before its
destination became eligible, so the result is topological. If emission
stalls, every remaining vertex has a remaining predecessor; following
those predecessors in a finite set repeats a vertex and proves a
directed cycle. Both queue heads advance at most V times, so the
classifiers terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count and E be edge occurrence count, including
repeated edges. Validation, adjacency construction, and each
classification take Theta(V + E) time. Each function stores adjacency
with one entry per directed edge or two per undirected edge, plus O(V)
colors, counts, queues, and output. Total auxiliary and output storage
is O(V + E).

Two-coloring returns a useful partition but only for undirected
bipartiteness. Kahn's method returns a useful dependency order but
needs indegrees and is specific to directed acyclicity. A depth-first
implementation can classify the same structures with recursion and
different witness or ordering behavior.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Zero vertices returns true with an empty witness for both classes.
  A lone isolated vertex gets bipartite color 0 and topological order
  `[0]`.
- Disconnected components require new starts. Coloring only from 0
  would leave component `{4,5}` unclassified.
- A repeated edge adds repeated adjacency and indegree entries but
  preserves both answers because every occurrence is processed.
- An undirected self-loop colors one endpoint opposite to itself and
  returns non-bipartite. A directed self-loop prevents full emission.
- An even cycle can be bipartite. Reject only a same-color edge, not
  every previously visited neighbor.
- On a bipartite conflict, return no partial colors. Callers must not
  mistake tentative assignments for a valid partition.
- A DAG may have many topological orders. Tests should verify every
  edge goes forward unless the contract fixes the same queue policy.
- In Kahn's method, decrement indegree once per stored occurrence.
  Deduplicating only one of adjacency or indegree can release a vertex
  too early or never release it.
- An incomplete topological order is failure, not a usable prefix.
  Compare emitted count with V before returning success.
- Invalid endpoints are errors, distinct from property failure on a
  valid graph.

##### When to choose it

Look for bipartite structure when vertices must split into two
compatible roles, such as workers and jobs, or when constraints say
neighboring items need opposite states. Odd-cycle conflicts rule it
out.

Look for a DAG when edges encode prerequisites, irreversible state
transitions, or computation dependencies. A topological order enables
dependency scheduling and one-pass dynamic programming. The
[reachability and cycle family](
#b12-reachability-components-and-graph-cycles) owns broader traversal
selection, while [valid task ordering](
#b14-dependencies-and-valid-task-ordering) develops topological
applications. The [direction lesson](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) remains the prerequisite for
interpreting either edge model.

#### A.10.5 Multigraphs and self-loops

##### Problem and contract

A simple graph collapses an endpoint pair into one relationship and
often rejects an edge from a vertex to itself. Some models need
several roads between the same cities, repeated transactions between
accounts, or a state transition back to the same state. A multigraph
preserves parallel edge occurrences, and a self-loop has equal
endpoints.

Our mutable undirected multigraph fixes vertices in `[0, V)`. Every
valid `addEdge(u, v)` adds one logical occurrence, even when the same
pair or loop already exists. `removeEdge` removes one occurrence and
returns false with nil error when none exists. Invalid endpoints
return an error without mutation.

`multiplicity(u, v)` reports the number of logical edges for that
unordered pair. One non-loop edge contributes one to each endpoint's
degree. One self-loop contributes two to its vertex's degree because
both edge ends are incident there. `edgeCount` counts logical edge
occurrences once. Counts and degree are required to fit in Go `int`.

The zero value is a valid graph with zero vertices. The graph owns its
slice and maps; snapshots are copies. Copying a graph value would
share the internal slice and maps. Methods require a non-nil graph
pointer; unsynchronized concurrent use is outside the contract. Read
[directed and undirected graphs](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) first.

##### Mental model

Storage position `multiplicityByNeighbor[u][v]` is a count, not a
Boolean. Read value 2 at `[0][1]` as: "two separate undirected edge
occurrences connect vertices 0 and 1." For distinct endpoints, the
same count is stored reciprocally at `[1][0]`.

A loop at vertex 1 uses only entry `[1][1]`; writing a reciprocal copy
would address the same map cell and accidentally double its
multiplicity. Logical storage and degree contribution differ:

```text
one edge 0-1:  degree(0) += 1, degree(1) += 1
one loop 1-1:  degree(1) += 2
```

Degree counts incident edge ends. Every undirected edge has exactly
two ends, including a loop whose ends meet the same vertex. Therefore
the sum of all degrees remains `2 * edgeCount`.

Removing one edge decrements its count. A count of one disappears from
the maps after removal; a larger count remains with one fewer
occurrence. Distinct endpoints update two reciprocal entries, while a
loop updates one entry.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use vertices `[0,1,2]`. Add edge `0-1` twice, loop `1-1` once, and
edge `1-2` once. Then remove one `0-1` occurrence and try failures.

Initial state: three nil neighbor maps contain no counts; logical edge
count is zero.

1. Decision: add `0-1`. Allocate maps 0 and 1, set reciprocal counts
   to 1, and increase `edgeCount`. Add `0-1` again; increment both
   entries to 2 and increase count again.
   After: multiplicity `(0,1)` is 2; logical edge count is 2.
   Known correct: the endpoint pair retains two distinct occurrences
   instead of collapsing to a Boolean edge.

2. Decision: add loop `1-1`. Increment map entry `[1][1]` once and
   increase logical edge count once. Do not perform a reciprocal write
   because both endpoints name the same entry.
   After: loop multiplicity is 1; logical edge count is 3.
   Known correct: exactly one loop was added even though it has two
   incidences for later degree calculation.

3. Decision: add `1-2`, storing reciprocal count 1. Compute degrees.
   Vertex 0 sees two occurrences to 1, so degree 2. Vertex 1 sees two
   to 0, loop contribution 2, and one to 2, so degree 5. Vertex 2 has
   degree 1.
   After: degrees are `[2,5,1]`; edge count is 4.

   ```text
   0 == two parallel edges == 1 -- one edge -- 2
                              |
                              +-- one loop --+
   degrees: 0=2, 1=2+2+1=5, 2=1
   ```

   Known correct: degree sum 8 equals twice four logical edges.

4. Decision: remove one `0-1`. Both reciprocal counts fall from 2 to
   1; neither map entry disappears. Decrease logical edge count once.
   After: edge count is 3 and degrees are `[1,4,1]`.

   ```text
   0 -- one remaining edge -- 1 -- one edge -- 2
                              |
                              +-- one loop --+
   degrees: 0=1, 1=1+2+1=4, 2=1
   ```

   Known correct: one parallel occurrence remains and degree sum 6 is
   still twice the edge count.

5. Decision: remove missing edge `0-2`; its count is zero, so return
   false without mutation. Try endpoint 3; validation fails before any
   count lookup or update.
   After: edge count and snapshot remain unchanged.
   Known correct: missing and invalid outcomes are distinct and
   atomic.

Focused boundaries: removing a count-one non-loop deletes both map
entries. Removing a count-one self-loop deletes only `[v][v]`. A graph
with vertices but no edges gives every vertex degree zero.

Counterexample to computing degree as the sum of stored counts: at
vertex 1, entries `{0:2, 1:1, 2:1}` sum to 4, but correct degree is 5.
The first wrong decision counts the loop once rather than counting its
two incident ends.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Each snapshot row is
sorted by neighbor. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Multigraphs and self-loops.
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

type multiNeighbor struct {
	vertex       int
	multiplicity int
}

type undirectedMultiGraph struct {
	multiplicityByNeighbor []map[int]int
	edgeCount              int
}

func newUndirectedMultiGraph(
	vertexCount int,
) (*undirectedMultiGraph, error) {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial undirected multi
	// graph state.
	if vertexCount < 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex count %d is negative",
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	return &undirectedMultiGraph{
		multiplicityByNeighbor: make(
			[]map[int]int,
			vertexCount,
		),
	}, nil
}

func (graph *undirectedMultiGraph) validateVertex(
	vertex int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the vertex contract before mutation.
	vertexCount := len(graph.multiplicityByNeighbor)
	if vertex < 0 || vertex >= vertexCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"vertex %d is outside [0, %d)",
			vertex,
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func (graph *undirectedMultiGraph) addEdge(
	first int,
	second int,
) error {
	// Validate both endpoints before changing either count.
	if err := graph.validateVertex(first); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if err := graph.validateVertex(second); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[first] == nil {
		graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[first] = make(map[int]int)
	}
	graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[first][second]++
	if first != second {
		// Only distinct endpoints need a reciprocal map entry.
		if graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[second] == nil {
			graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[second] = make(map[int]int)
		}
		graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[second][first]++
	}
	graph.edgeCount++
	return nil
}

func decrementMultiplicity(
	counts map[int]int,
	neighbor int,
) {
	// Read the maintained count without changing state.
	if counts[neighbor] == 1 {
		delete(counts, neighbor)
		return
	}
	counts[neighbor]--
}

func (graph *undirectedMultiGraph) removeEdge(
	first int,
	second int,
) (bool, error) {
	// Remove edge while preserving the remaining representation.
	if err := graph.validateVertex(first); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	if err := graph.validateVertex(second); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	if graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[first][second] == 0 {
		return false, nil
	}

	decrementMultiplicity(
		graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[first],
		second,
	)
	if first != second {
		decrementMultiplicity(
			graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[second],
			first,
		)
	}
	graph.edgeCount--
	return true, nil
}

func (graph *undirectedMultiGraph) multiplicity(
	first int,
	second int,
) (int, error) {
	// Read the maintained count without changing state.
	if err := graph.validateVertex(first); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
	if err := graph.validateVertex(second); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
	return graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[first][second], nil
}

func (graph *undirectedMultiGraph) degree(
	vertex int,
) (int, error) {
	// Read the maintained count without changing state.
	if err := graph.validateVertex(vertex); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
	degree := 0
	for neighbor, count := range graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[vertex] {
		if neighbor == vertex {
			// A loop contributes both of its ends at this vertex.
			degree += 2 * count
			continue
		}
		degree += count
	}
	return degree, nil
}

func sortedMultiNeighbors(
	counts map[int]int,
) []multiNeighbor {
	// Copy and sort neighbors for deterministic output.
	vertices := make([]int, 0, len(counts))
	for vertex := range counts {
		vertices = append(vertices, vertex)
	}
	sort.Ints(vertices)

	neighbors := make([]multiNeighbor, 0, len(vertices))
	for _, vertex := range vertices {
		neighbors = append(neighbors, multiNeighbor{
			vertex:       vertex,
			multiplicity: counts[vertex],
		})
	}
	return neighbors
}

func (graph *undirectedMultiGraph) adjacency() [][]multiNeighbor {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	values := make(
		[][]multiNeighbor,
		len(graph.multiplicityByNeighbor),
	)
	for vertex := range graph.multiplicityByNeighbor {
		values[vertex] = sortedMultiNeighbors(
			graph.multiplicityByNeighbor[vertex],
		)
	}
	return values
}

func (graph *undirectedMultiGraph) degrees() []int {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	values := make([]int, len(graph.multiplicityByNeighbor))
	for vertex := range values {
		degree, err := graph.degree(vertex)
		if err != nil {
			panic("validated vertex became invalid")
		}
		values[vertex] = degree
	}
	return values
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	graph, err := newUndirectedMultiGraph(3)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	for _, edge := range [][2]int{
		{0, 1},
		{0, 1},
		{1, 1},
		{1, 2},
	} {
		if err := graph.addEdge(edge[0], edge[1]); err != nil {
			panic(err)
		}
	}
	fmt.Println(graph.adjacency(), graph.edgeCount)
	parallelCount, err := graph.multiplicity(0, 1)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	loopCount, err := graph.multiplicity(1, 1)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(parallelCount, loopCount)
	fmt.Println(graph.degrees())

	removed, err := graph.removeEdge(0, 1)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(removed, graph.edgeCount)
	fmt.Println(graph.adjacency())
	fmt.Println(graph.degrees())

	removed, err = graph.removeEdge(0, 2)
	fmt.Println(removed, err == nil)
	removed, err = graph.removeEdge(0, 3)
	fmt.Println(removed, err != nil, graph.edgeCount)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[[{1 2}] [{0 2} {1 1} {2 1}] [{1 1}]] 4
2 1
[2 5 1]
true 3
[[{1 1}] [{0 1} {1 1} {2 1}] [{1 1}]]
[1 4 1]
false true
false true 3
```

##### Why it works

Initially every pair has multiplicity zero. Adding a distinct-endpoint
edge increments both reciprocal entries, so they stay equal and encode
one more logical occurrence. Adding a loop increments its one map cell
once. In either case, increasing `edgeCount` once matches the added
logical edge.

Removal first proves an occurrence exists. Decrementing the same cells
reverses one addition, and deleting a zero-count entry changes no
remaining multiplicity. Missing or invalid removals return before any
write, so the invariants and count remain unchanged.

Degree sums one incidence for each non-loop occurrence at the vertex
and two for each loop. Thus every logical edge contributes exactly two
across all vertices, proving the degree-sum identity. Snapshot helpers
copy counts and sort only their output.

All map and slice loops are finite. Each add or remove performs
bounded validation and at most two map updates, so every method
terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count, E be logical edge occurrence count, A be
stored nonzero map-entry count, and D be one vertex's
distinct-neighbor count. Construction takes Theta(V) time and O(V)
slice storage.

Assuming expected constant-time Go map access, add, remove, and
multiplicity query take expected O(1) time. Degree takes Theta(D) time
and O(1) auxiliary space. Retained storage is O(V + A); aggregating
parallel occurrences can use much less space than storing E records.

A snapshot row copies and sorts D entries in O(D log(D + 1)) time and
O(D) output storage. Across all rows, snapshot work is
O(V + A log(Delta + 1)), where Delta is maximum distinct-neighbor
count, and output storage is O(V + A).

Count aggregation loses per-edge identity, order, weight, and
metadata. When those facts matter, store separate edge records with
stable IDs and keep an endpoint index in addition to the records.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Two additions of `0-1` produce multiplicity 2. A Boolean set would
  silently collapse one logical edge.
- Loop `1-1` is stored once but contributes two to degree 1. Writing a
  reciprocal update to the same cell would create multiplicity 2.
- Removing one of two parallel edges leaves count 1. Deleting the pair
  immediately would lose the remaining occurrence.
- Removing missing `0-2` returns false; it must not create a negative
  count or decrement `edgeCount`.
- Invalid endpoint 3 returns an error before either reciprocal update.
- When the last non-loop occurrence is removed, delete both reciprocal
  entries. Leaving one side breaks undirected symmetry.
- The contract requires counts and degrees to fit in `int`. A system
  that can exceed that bound needs checked wider counters.
- In a directed multigraph, a loop contributes one to indegree and
  one to outdegree; do not reuse the undirected degree calculation
  blindly.
- Copying the graph shares maps. Independent mutation requires a deep
  copy of every row.

##### When to choose it

Choose a multigraph when repeated relationships change the answer:
parallel transport routes, repeated events, or separate channels
between the same endpoints. Allow self-loops when staying at the same
state is a real transition or when the domain records reflexive
events.

Use a simple graph when only endpoint connectivity matters; collapsing
parallel occurrences then reduces storage and avoids accidental double
counting. Use the [weighted-graph lesson](
#a102-weighted-and-unweighted-graphs) when one edge value matters, and
the [representation lesson](
#a103-adjacency-lists-matrices-and-edge-lists) when choosing storage.
The next [implicit-graph lesson](
#a106-implicit-graphs-and-state-spaces) generates neighbors instead of
storing edge occurrences.

#### A.10.6 Implicit graphs and state spaces

##### Problem and contract

A graph can exist even when no input lists its vertices and edges. A
