Focused side-one case: a side-1 root is already one cell. Changing it
sets the leaf directly, with no midpoint or child allocation. Focused
empty query: `[1,1) x [0,4)` has zero width and returns zero.

Counterexample to assigning midpoint coordinates to the low child:
point `(2,0)` in the side-4 root belongs to `[2,4) x [0,2)`. Sending
it left stores it under `[0,2)`, so later lookup follows the correct
high child and falsely reports unoccupied. The `>= midpoint` rule
prevents the first wrong branch.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Recursive calls are
bounded by `log2(sideLength)`. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Quadtrees and octrees. Function
// comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type orthantNode struct {
	children      []*orthantNode
	occupied      bool
	occupiedCount int
}

type orthantTree struct {
	dimensions int
	sideLength int
	root       *orthantNode
}

func newOrthantTree(
	dimensions int,
	sideLength int,
) (*orthantTree, error) {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial orthant tree state.
	if dimensions != 2 && dimensions != 3 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"dimensions must be 2 or 3",
		)
	}
	if sideLength <= 0 ||
		sideLength&(sideLength-1) != 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"side length must be a positive power of two",
		)
	}

	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	cellCount := 1
	for axis := 0; axis < dimensions; axis++ {
		if sideLength > maximumInt/cellCount {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"cell count exceeds int capacity",
			)
		}
		cellCount *= sideLength
	}
	return &orthantTree{
		dimensions: dimensions,
		sideLength: sideLength,
		root:       &orthantNode{},
	}, nil
}

func (tree *orthantTree) validatePoint(
	point [3]int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the point contract before mutation.
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		if point[axis] < 0 ||
			point[axis] >= tree.sideLength {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"axis %d coordinate %d is outside [0, %d)",
				axis,
				point[axis],
				tree.sideLength,
			)
		}
	}
	for axis := tree.dimensions; axis < len(point); axis++ {
		if point[axis] != 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"unused axis %d must be zero",
				axis,
			)
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func (tree *orthantTree) validateBox(
	minimum [3]int,
	maximum [3]int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the box contract before mutation.
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		if minimum[axis] < 0 ||
			minimum[axis] > maximum[axis] ||
			maximum[axis] > tree.sideLength {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"axis %d range [%d, %d) is invalid",
				axis,
				minimum[axis],
				maximum[axis],
			)
		}
	}
	for axis := tree.dimensions; axis < len(minimum); axis++ {
		if minimum[axis] != 0 || maximum[axis] != 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"unused axis %d must be zero",
				axis,
			)
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func (tree *orthantTree) regionVolume(sideLength int) int {
	// Compute the geometric measure from valid coordinates.
	volume := 1
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		volume *= sideLength
	}
	return volume
}

func (tree *orthantTree) split(
	node *orthantNode,
	childSideLength int,
) {
	// Keep split in one helper so callers use one rule.
	childCount := 1 << tree.dimensions
	childVolume := tree.regionVolume(childSideLength)
	node.children = make([]*orthantNode, childCount)
	for childIndex := range node.children {
		child := &orthantNode{occupied: node.occupied}
		if node.occupied {
			child.occupiedCount = childVolume
		}
		node.children[childIndex] = child
	}
	// Internal nodes derive their value from children.
	node.occupied = false
}

func (tree *orthantTree) childLocation(
	regionOrigin [3]int,
	childSideLength int,
	point [3]int,
) (int, [3]int) {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	childIndex := 0
	childOrigin := regionOrigin
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		midpoint := regionOrigin[axis] + childSideLength
		if point[axis] >= midpoint {
			childIndex |= 1 << axis
			childOrigin[axis] = midpoint
		}
	}
	return childIndex, childOrigin
}

func (tree *orthantTree) originForChild(
	regionOrigin [3]int,
	childSideLength int,
	childIndex int,
) [3]int {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	childOrigin := regionOrigin
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		if childIndex&(1<<axis) != 0 {
			childOrigin[axis] += childSideLength
		}
	}
	return childOrigin
}

func (tree *orthantTree) mergeIfUniform(
	node *orthantNode,
) {
	// Combine compatible parts while preserving their invariant.
	firstChild := node.children[0]
	if firstChild.children != nil {
		return
	}
	value := firstChild.occupied
	for _, child := range node.children[1:] {
		if child.children != nil || child.occupied != value {
			return
		}
	}
	node.children = nil
	node.occupied = value
}

func (tree *orthantTree) setNode(
	node *orthantNode,
	regionOrigin [3]int,
	regionSideLength int,
	point [3]int,
	occupied bool,
) {
	// Apply the requested change, then repair derived state.
	if node.children == nil && node.occupied == occupied {
		return
	}
	if regionSideLength == 1 {
		node.occupied = occupied
		if occupied {
			node.occupiedCount = 1
		} else {
			node.occupiedCount = 0
		}
		return
	}

	childSideLength := regionSideLength / 2
	if node.children == nil {
		tree.split(node, childSideLength)
	}
	childIndex, childOrigin := tree.childLocation(
		regionOrigin,
		childSideLength,
		point,
	)
	tree.setNode(
		node.children[childIndex],
		childOrigin,
		childSideLength,
		point,
		occupied,
	)

	// The sum remains valid whether or not children can merge.
	node.occupiedCount = 0
	for _, child := range node.children {
		node.occupiedCount += child.occupiedCount
	}
	tree.mergeIfUniform(node)
}

func (tree *orthantTree) setOccupied(
	point [3]int,
	occupied bool,
) error {
	// Apply the requested change, then repair derived state.
	if err := tree.validatePoint(point); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	tree.setNode(
		tree.root,
		[3]int{},
		tree.sideLength,
		point,
		occupied,
	)
	return nil
}

func (tree *orthantTree) isOccupied(
	point [3]int,
) (bool, error) {
	// Evaluate is occupied without changing the maintained state.
	if err := tree.validatePoint(point); err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	node := tree.root
	regionOrigin := [3]int{}
	regionSideLength := tree.sideLength
	for node.children != nil {
		childSideLength := regionSideLength / 2
		childIndex, childOrigin := tree.childLocation(
			regionOrigin,
			childSideLength,
			point,
		)
		node = node.children[childIndex]
		regionOrigin = childOrigin
		regionSideLength = childSideLength
	}
	return node.occupied, nil
}

func maximum(first int, second int) int {
	// Compute the requested item from the state without mutating it.
	if first > second {
		return first
	}
	return second
}

func minimum(first int, second int) int {
	// Compute the requested item from the state without mutating it.
	if first < second {
		return first
	}
	return second
}

func (tree *orthantTree) countNode(
	node *orthantNode,
	regionOrigin [3]int,
	regionSideLength int,
	queryMinimum [3]int,
	queryMaximum [3]int,
) int {
	// Compute node from the state without mutating it.
	intersectionVolume := 1
	fullyCovered := true
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		regionMaximum :=
			regionOrigin[axis] + regionSideLength
		intersectionStart := maximum(
			regionOrigin[axis],
			queryMinimum[axis],
		)
		intersectionEnd := minimum(
			regionMaximum,
			queryMaximum[axis],
		)
		if intersectionStart >= intersectionEnd {
			return 0
		}
		intersectionVolume *=
			intersectionEnd - intersectionStart
		if queryMinimum[axis] > regionOrigin[axis] ||
			queryMaximum[axis] < regionMaximum {
			fullyCovered = false
		}
	}
	if fullyCovered {
		return node.occupiedCount
	}
	if node.children == nil {
		if node.occupied {
			return intersectionVolume
		}
		return 0
	}

	childSideLength := regionSideLength / 2
	count := 0
	for childIndex, child := range node.children {
		childOrigin := tree.originForChild(
			regionOrigin,
			childSideLength,
			childIndex,
		)
		count += tree.countNode(
			child,
			childOrigin,
			childSideLength,
			queryMinimum,
			queryMaximum,
		)
	}
	return count
}

func (tree *orthantTree) countOccupied(
	minimum [3]int,
	maximum [3]int,
) (int, error) {
	// Compute occupied from the state without mutating it.
	if err := tree.validateBox(minimum, maximum); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
	return tree.countNode(
		tree.root,
		[3]int{},
		tree.sideLength,
		minimum,
		maximum,
	), nil
}

func countReachableNodes(node *orthantNode) int {
	// Compute reachable nodes from the state without mutating it.
	count := 1
	for _, child := range node.children {
		count += countReachableNodes(child)
	}
	return count
}

func (tree *orthantTree) reachableNodeCount() int {
	// Keep reachable node count in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return countReachableNodes(tree.root)
}

func mustSet(
	tree *orthantTree,
	point [3]int,
	occupied bool,
) {
	// Run the operation and stop if the fixed example fails.
	if err := tree.setOccupied(point, occupied); err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
}

func mustCount(
	tree *orthantTree,
	minimum [3]int,
	maximum [3]int,
) int {
	// Run the operation and stop if the fixed example fails.
	count, err := tree.countOccupied(minimum, maximum)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	return count
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	quadtree, err := newOrthantTree(2, 4)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	for _, point := range [][3]int{
		{0, 0, 0},
		{1, 0, 0},
		{0, 1, 0},
		{1, 1, 0},
		{3, 3, 0},
	} {
		mustSet(quadtree, point, true)
	}
	lowerMinimum := [3]int{0, 0, 0}
	lowerMaximum := [3]int{2, 2, 0}
	fmt.Println(
		quadtree.root.occupiedCount,
		quadtree.reachableNodeCount(),
	)
	fmt.Println(
		mustCount(quadtree, lowerMinimum, lowerMaximum),
	)

	mustSet(quadtree, [3]int{1, 1, 0}, false)
	fmt.Println(
		quadtree.root.occupiedCount,
		mustCount(quadtree, lowerMinimum, lowerMaximum),
		quadtree.reachableNodeCount(),
	)
	mustSet(quadtree, [3]int{1, 1, 0}, true)
	fmt.Println(
		quadtree.root.occupiedCount,
		mustCount(quadtree, lowerMinimum, lowerMaximum),
		quadtree.reachableNodeCount(),
	)
	first, err := quadtree.isOccupied([3]int{3, 3, 0})
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	second, err := quadtree.isOccupied([3]int{2, 3, 0})
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(first, second)
	err = quadtree.setOccupied([3]int{4, 0, 0}, true)
	fmt.Println(err != nil, quadtree.root.occupiedCount)

	octree, err := newOrthantTree(3, 2)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	mustSet(octree, [3]int{0, 0, 0}, true)
	mustSet(octree, [3]int{1, 1, 1}, true)
	fmt.Println(
		octree.root.occupiedCount,
		mustCount(
			octree,
			[3]int{0, 0, 0},
			[3]int{1, 1, 1},
		),
	)
	for x := 0; x < 2; x++ {
		for y := 0; y < 2; y++ {
			for z := 0; z < 2; z++ {
				mustSet(octree, [3]int{x, y, z}, true)
			}
		}
	}
	fmt.Println(
		octree.root.occupiedCount,
		octree.reachableNodeCount(),
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
5 9
4
4 3 13
5 4 9
true false
true 5
2 1
8 1
```

##### Why it works

Initially, the root is one uniform false leaf, so it represents every
cell in the domain exactly once and its count is zero. Assume each
leaf uniformly represents its region, sibling regions are disjoint
and cover their parent, and every stored count is exact.

Splitting replaces one uniform region by all four or eight midpoint
children with the same value. Those children partition the parent, so
the represented cells and count do not change. Midpoint comparisons
select exactly one child on every active axis, making one root-to-cell
path unique.

The recursive update changes only that path. At side length 1 it sets
the requested cell. Recomputing sums gives each ancestor the exact
count of its disjoint children. Merging equal leaf children is safe
because their union is uniform; removing their links changes only the
representation. The update invariant is therefore preserved.

For a range query, an empty intersection contributes no requested
cell. A fully covered node contributes its exact stored count. A
partially covered uniform leaf contributes precisely the product of
overlap lengths on every axis. Otherwise, child regions partition the
partial intersection, so adding their recursively correct results
counts each requested occupied cell once.

Every split halves a positive power-of-two side. After
`log2(sideLength)` splits, side length is 1, so updates terminate.
Queries either stop at a pruning rule or descend the same finite tree.
Validation runs before an update reaches the root, proving rejected
operations cannot mutate it.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let D be dimension 2 or 3, S be side length, H be `log2(S)`, B be
`2^D`, V be `S^D` unit cells, and M be the number of reachable nodes.
Here B is 4 for a quadtree and 8 for an octree.

Construction validates D, S, and V in O(D) time, then allocates one
root. Point lookup visits at most H internal nodes, taking O(DH) time
and O(1) auxiliary space. With fixed D, this is O(H).

An idempotent update that stops at a uniform root takes O(1) time. A
worst-case update visits H levels, may allocate B children per split,
and inspects B children per possible merge. It takes O(BH) time,
allocates O(BH) nodes, and uses O(H) call-stack space. Because D is at
most 3, B is a fixed factor.

A full-cover, no-overlap, or uniform-leaf range query can finish in
O(D) time at the root. In the worst case, a partial query visits all M
nodes and spends O(DM) time with O(H) call-stack space. It returns one
integer and allocates no output collection.

The retained tree uses O(M) nodes and child pointers. A completely
refined tree has V cell leaves and a geometric number of internal
nodes, so M is O(V). Merging drops child references, making those
nodes eligible for garbage collection; it does not promise immediate
memory release.

A dense Boolean array always uses Theta(V) cell storage and offers
direct point access. This tree is valuable only when large uniform
regions keep M much smaller than V. Pointer-rich nodes and child
slices can cost more than a dense grid for noisy data.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Side length 1 is both root and cell. Updating it must not divide by
  two or allocate zero-sized children.
- Side lengths 3 or 0 are rejected. Repeated halving relies on a
  positive power of two; padding or uneven child bounds need a
  different contract.
- Point coordinate S is outside `[0,S)`, while a query maximum may
  equal S because that boundary is exclusive.
- If any query axis has equal minimum and maximum, the box is empty
  and returns zero. A minimum greater than maximum is invalid.
- In 2D, `[3]int{x,y,1}` is rejected. Silently ignoring z would let
  distinct caller inputs address the same cell.
- A coordinate equal to the midpoint takes the high child. Using `>`
  instead of `>=` sends boundary cells into a region that does not
  contain them.
- Splitting an occupied leaf must initialize every child as occupied
  with the correct volume. Default-false siblings would erase cells
  other than the updated point.
- Recompute a parent count before merging. Keeping only the changed
  child's count loses occupied cells in siblings.
- Merge only when every child is a leaf with the same value. Equal
  counts do not imply equal cell layouts, and merging internal
  children can destroy detail.
- A fully covered node returns its stored count. A partially covered
  occupied leaf returns intersection volume, not the full node count.
- Idempotent updates stop before splitting. Repeatedly setting the
  same point should not grow the tree.
- Validate a point before mutation. Discovering an invalid unused axis
  after splitting would violate atomic failure.
- `S^D` must fit `int` because counts and intersection volumes use
  `int`. The constructor checks multiplication before performing it.
- Recursion depth is H, not M. Very large allowed side lengths can
  still make allocation fail even though the arithmetic is valid.

##### When to choose it

Choose a region quadtree for large 2D rasters with broad uniform
areas, such as binary maps or image masks. Choose an octree for the
analogous 3D voxel workload. They support adaptive detail, point
changes, and box pruning while preserving exact unit-cell values.

Use a flat grid when the domain is small, dense, or noisy enough that
nearly every cell needs a leaf. Use a hash set when only sparse
occupied points and exact membership matter; it avoids empty regions
but offers little geometric range pruning.

Use a [k-d tree](#a172-k-d-trees) for an irregular point collection
and nearest-neighbor or point-range search. Use an [R-tree](
#a174-r-trees) for stored rectangles with overlap and nonuniform
extents. Use a 2D prefix sum when the grid is static and only
rectangular counts matter.

This implementation assumes fixed integer bounds and exact cells.
Floating coordinates, moving objects, unbounded growth, and loose
object bounds need explicit subdivision and placement policies.

Samet's [quadtree survey](
https://doi.org/10.1145/356924.356930) develops recursive spatial
decomposition. Meagher's [octree encoding paper](
https://doi.org/10.1016/0146-664X(82)90104-6) applies the eight-way
hierarchy to three-dimensional geometry.

#### A.17.2 k-d trees

##### Problem and contract

You have points in a small number of dimensions and need to answer
many geometric queries. Scanning every point is simple, but it
repeats work even when a whole region cannot affect the answer. A
k-dimensional tree, usually written k-d tree, divides points with one
coordinate at a time so a query can reject some subtrees at once.

This lesson builds a static k-d tree for one through eight dimensions.
Each point uses a `[8]int64`. Only the first k coordinates are active;
every unused coordinate must be zero. Active coordinates belong to
`[-500000000,500000000)`. The constructor validates all points,
copies them, and assigns each point a stable input ID equal to its
slice index. Duplicate points remain separate entries with separate
IDs.

The tree supports two read-only operations. A range search returns the
IDs of points inside an axis-aligned, half-open box. On each axis,
`minimum <= coordinate < maximum`. Results are sorted by ID and are
owned by the caller. An empty box returns a non-nil empty slice.

A nearest-neighbor search returns the input ID and exact squared
Euclidean distance of the closest point. Squared distance avoids
square roots without changing which distance is smaller. Equal
distances are resolved by the smaller input ID. An empty tree returns
ID 0, distance 0, `found == false`, and no error.

Point queries use the same coordinate interval as stored points. Box
boundaries may use either domain endpoint, so each boundary belongs to
`[-500000000,500000000]`. Invalid dimensions, coordinates, unused
components, or box bounds return errors. The constructor validates
everything before allocating the tree. A query error returns no
partial result and cannot change the tree.

The coordinate and dimension limits make every accepted squared
distance fit in `int64`. The greatest coordinate difference is
999999999, and the sum of eight squared differences is less than the
largest `int64`.

The tree is immutable after construction. Independent queries may run
concurrently, and each range query owns its result slice. Allocation
failure is outside the contract. Copying the tree value would share
nodes. Methods require a non-nil tree pointer returned by the
constructor; a zero tree is not initialized. Read [binary search
trees](#a72-binary-search-trees) and [multidimensional indexing](
#a14-flat-storage-and-multidimensional-indexing) first.

##### Mental model

Imagine placing a flat cutting plane through the points. At depth 0,
compare x coordinates; at depth 1, compare y; continue through the k
active axes and then cycle back to x. The point at the median becomes
the node on the cutting plane. Points before it go left; points after
it go right.

For a node whose split axis is `axis`, every left-subtree point has
`point[axis] <= node.point[axis]`, and every right-subtree point has
`point[axis] >= node.point[axis]`. Equality can occur on either side
because duplicate coordinates are allowed. Other coordinates do not
obey that node's ordering rule.

Each node remembers one copied point, its stable input ID, its split
axis, and two child links. Choosing a median at every subtree keeps
the two side counts within one. Cycling axes prevents the same
coordinate from controlling every level.

A range query first tests the node's complete point. It visits the
left subtree only when `minimum[axis] <= splitCoordinate`; otherwise
every left point is below the box. It visits the right subtree only
when `maximum[axis] > splitCoordinate`; otherwise every right point
is at or beyond the excluded maximum.

A nearest query descends first toward the side containing the query.
After that side returns, the squared distance from the query to the
split plane is a lower bound for every point on the other side. If
that bound is greater than the best complete distance, the other side
cannot win. Equality must still be searched because it may contain an
equal-distance point with a smaller ID.

The split plane supplies only one-coordinate information. The code
does not store subtree bounding boxes, so some queries still visit
many nodes. A balanced shape limits recursion depth; it does not
guarantee that geometric pruning will be strong.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build a two-dimensional tree from these points. The number at the left
is the stable input ID:

```text
0: (2,3)   1: (5,4)   2: (9,6)
3: (4,7)   4: (8,1)   5: (7,2)
```

The range query is `[3,9) x [1,5)`, whose expected IDs are
`[1,4,5]`. The nearest query is `(9,2)`, whose expected result is ID 4
at squared distance 2.

Initial state: construction has copied the six points. No caller slice
or result slice is retained or shared.

1. Decision: sort the root entries by x, then use coordinates and ID
   to break ties. Their ID order is `0,3,1,5,4,2`; choose upper
   median ID 5 at `(7,2)` and split on x.
   After: IDs `0,3,1` are pending on the left and IDs `4,2` on the
   right.
   Known correct: every left x is at most 7, every right x is at least
   7, and each side differs in size by at most one.

2. Decision: at depth 1, sort each side by y. The left median is ID 1
   at `(5,4)`, with ID 0 left and ID 3 right. The right median is ID 2
   at `(9,6)`, with ID 4 left.
   After: the finite tree is:

   ```text
             5:(7,2) split x
            /                 \
      1:(5,4) split y     2:(9,6) split y
       /       \             /
   0:(2,3)  3:(4,7)      4:(8,1)
   ```

   Known correct: each recursive side has its own median and the next
   axis; every input ID occurs exactly once.

3. Decision: test root ID 5 against the box. Both `3 <= 7 < 9` and
   `1 <= 2 < 5` hold, so collect ID 5. Because `3 <= 7` and `9 > 7`,
   both x sides might contain matches.
   After: collected traversal IDs are `[5]`; both children are
   pending.
   Known correct: the root is included once, and neither subtree was
   pruned without a split-axis proof.

4. Decision: on the left, ID 1 is inside and is collected. ID 0 fails
   because x is 2; ID 3 fails because y is 7. On the right, ID 2 fails
   both the exclusive x maximum and y maximum. Its left child ID 4 is
   inside. The box maximum y is 5, not greater than ID 2's split value
   6, so no right child could qualify.
   After: traversal collected `[5,1,4]`; sorting by stable ID returns
   `[1,4,5]`.
   Known correct: every visited point was tested on both active axes,
   and every skipped region lies wholly outside one box boundary.

5. Decision: begin nearest search for `(9,2)` at ID 5. Its squared
   distance is `2*2 + 0*0 = 4`. Since query x is greater than 7,
   search the right child before the left.
   After: best is `(ID 5,distance 4)` and the right subtree is active.
   Known correct: the best record is the closest tested point, with
   the smallest tested ID on a tie.

6. Decision: ID 2 has distance 16 and cannot replace the best. Query y
   is below 6, so visit its left child ID 4. Its distance is
   `1*1 + 1*1 = 2`, so replace the best. The y-plane distance at ID 2
   is 16, greater than 2, so its other side cannot win.
   After: best is `(ID 4,distance 2)` and the right subtree is
   finished.
   Known correct: every point pruned below ID 2 has y difference at
   least 4, already exceeding the complete best distance.

7. Decision: back at ID 5, the x-plane distance is `2*2 = 4`. It is
   greater than best distance 2, so prune the whole left subtree and
   stop.
   After: return ID 4, squared distance 2, and `found == true`.
   Known correct: an unseen left point has x at most 7, so its x
   difference alone is at least 2 and its full distance cannot improve
   or tie the winner.

8. Decision: build two duplicate points `(1,1)` with IDs 0 and 1. The
   box `[1,2) x [1,2)` crosses equal split coordinates, so search both
   possible sides. Nearest query `(1,1)` gives both distance 0 and
   keeps ID 0.
   After: the range result is `[0,1]`; nearest returns ID 0 and
   distance 0.
   Known correct: coordinates do not replace stable identity, and tie
   order is independent of traversal order.

9. Decision: query an empty tree, then query coordinate 500000000 in a
   nonempty tree. The empty valid query has no candidate. The endpoint
   equals the exclusive point limit, so validation rejects it before
   search.
   After: the empty result has `found == false`; the invalid query
   returns an error and the tree is unchanged.
   Known correct: absence is separate from ID 0, and invalid input
   cannot produce or partially expose a candidate.

Counterexample to pruning the far side when plane distance equals the
best: use IDs `0:(0,0)`, `1:(0,10)`, and `2:(1,1)`, with ID 1 as the
x-splitting root, then query `(1,0)`. The near point ID 2 has distance
1. The plane distance is also 1, and far point ID 0 ties at distance 1
but has the smaller ID. A strict `<` branch returns the wrong ID;
`<=` preserves the tie rule.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. It uses only `fmt` and
`sort`. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates k-d trees. Function comments
// connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

const (
	kdMaximumDimensions = 8
	kdCoordinateLimit   = int64(500_000_000)
)

type kdPoint [kdMaximumDimensions]int64

type kdEntry struct {
	point      kdPoint
	inputIndex int
}

type kdNode struct {
	entry kdEntry
	axis  int
	left  *kdNode
	right *kdNode
}

type kdTree struct {
	dimensions int
	root       *kdNode
}

func validateKDDimensions(dimensions int) error {
	// Reject input outside the kd dimensions contract before mutation.
	if dimensions < 1 || dimensions > kdMaximumDimensions {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"dimensions must be in [1, %d]",
			kdMaximumDimensions,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func validateKDPoint(
	dimensions int,
	point kdPoint,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the kd point contract before mutation.
	for axis := 0; axis < dimensions; axis++ {
		if point[axis] < -kdCoordinateLimit ||
			point[axis] >= kdCoordinateLimit {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"axis %d coordinate is outside [%d, %d)",
				axis,
				-kdCoordinateLimit,
				kdCoordinateLimit,
			)
		}
	}
	for axis := dimensions; axis < len(point); axis++ {
		if point[axis] != 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"unused axis %d must be zero",
				axis,
			)
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func kdEntryLess(
	first kdEntry,
	second kdEntry,
	axis int,
	dimensions int,
) bool {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	if first.point[axis] != second.point[axis] {
		return first.point[axis] < second.point[axis]
	}
	for comparedAxis := 0; comparedAxis < dimensions; comparedAxis++ {
		if first.point[comparedAxis] !=
			second.point[comparedAxis] {
			return first.point[comparedAxis] <
				second.point[comparedAxis]
		}
	}
	return first.inputIndex < second.inputIndex
}

func buildKDNode(
	entries []kdEntry,
	dimensions int,
	depth int,
) *kdNode {
	// Build kd node in the order required by the lesson contract.
	if len(entries) == 0 {
		return nil
	}
	axis := depth % dimensions
	sort.Slice(entries, func(firstIndex int, secondIndex int) bool {
		return kdEntryLess(
			entries[firstIndex],
			entries[secondIndex],
			axis,
			dimensions,
		)
	})
	medianIndex := len(entries) / 2
	return &kdNode{
		entry: entries[medianIndex],
		axis:  axis,
		left: buildKDNode(
			entries[:medianIndex],
			dimensions,
			depth+1,
		),
		right: buildKDNode(
			entries[medianIndex+1:],
			dimensions,
			depth+1,
		),
	}
}

func newKDTree(
	points []kdPoint,
	dimensions int,
) (*kdTree, error) {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial kd tree state.
	if err := validateKDDimensions(dimensions); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	for _, point := range points {
		if err := validateKDPoint(dimensions, point); err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
	}

	entries := make([]kdEntry, len(points))
	for inputIndex, point := range points {
		entries[inputIndex] = kdEntry{
			point:      point,
			inputIndex: inputIndex,
		}
	}
	return &kdTree{
		dimensions: dimensions,
		root: buildKDNode(
			entries,
			dimensions,
			0,
		),
	}, nil
}

func (tree *kdTree) validateBox(
	minimum kdPoint,
	maximum kdPoint,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the box contract before mutation.
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		if minimum[axis] < -kdCoordinateLimit ||
			minimum[axis] > kdCoordinateLimit ||
			maximum[axis] < -kdCoordinateLimit ||
			maximum[axis] > kdCoordinateLimit ||
			minimum[axis] > maximum[axis] {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"axis %d box boundary is invalid",
				axis,
			)
		}
	}
	for axis := tree.dimensions; axis < len(minimum); axis++ {
		if minimum[axis] != 0 || maximum[axis] != 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"unused axis %d must be zero",
				axis,
			)
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func (tree *kdTree) appendRangeMatches(
	node *kdNode,
	minimum kdPoint,
	maximum kdPoint,
	inputIndices *[]int,
) {
	// Use maintained boundaries to answer this range query.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}
	inside := true
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		coordinate := node.entry.point[axis]
		if coordinate < minimum[axis] ||
			coordinate >= maximum[axis] {
			inside = false
			break
		}
	}
	if inside {
		*inputIndices = append(
			*inputIndices,
			node.entry.inputIndex,
		)
	}

	splitCoordinate := node.entry.point[node.axis]
	if minimum[node.axis] <= splitCoordinate {
		tree.appendRangeMatches(
			node.left,
			minimum,
			maximum,
			inputIndices,
		)
	}
	if maximum[node.axis] > splitCoordinate {
		tree.appendRangeMatches(
			node.right,
			minimum,
			maximum,
			inputIndices,
		)
	}
}

func (tree *kdTree) rangeSearch(
	minimum kdPoint,
	maximum kdPoint,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Use maintained boundaries to answer this range query.
	if err := tree.validateBox(minimum, maximum); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	inputIndices := make([]int, 0)
	for axis := 0; axis < tree.dimensions; axis++ {
		if minimum[axis] == maximum[axis] {
			return inputIndices, nil
		}
	}
	tree.appendRangeMatches(
		tree.root,
		minimum,
		maximum,
		&inputIndices,
	)
	sort.Ints(inputIndices)
	return inputIndices, nil
}

type kdNearestCandidate struct {
	inputIndex      int
	squaredDistance int64
	found           bool
}

func kdSquaredDistance(
	first kdPoint,
	second kdPoint,
	dimensions int,
) int64 {
	// Keep kd squared distance in one helper so callers use one rule.
	var total int64
	for axis := 0; axis < dimensions; axis++ {
		difference := first[axis] - second[axis]
		total += difference * difference
	}
	return total
}

func (tree *kdTree) searchNearest(
	node *kdNode,
	query kdPoint,
	best *kdNearestCandidate,
) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for nearest without changing state.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}
	distance := kdSquaredDistance(
		node.entry.point,
		query,
		tree.dimensions,
	)
	if !best.found || distance < best.squaredDistance ||
		(distance == best.squaredDistance &&
			node.entry.inputIndex < best.inputIndex) {
		best.inputIndex = node.entry.inputIndex
		best.squaredDistance = distance
		best.found = true
	}

	difference := query[node.axis] -
		node.entry.point[node.axis]
	nearChild := node.right
	farChild := node.left
	if difference < 0 {
		nearChild = node.left
		farChild = node.right
	}
	tree.searchNearest(nearChild, query, best)
	planeDistance := difference * difference
	if planeDistance <= best.squaredDistance {
		tree.searchNearest(farChild, query, best)
	}
}

func (tree *kdTree) nearest(
	query kdPoint,
) (int, int64, bool, error) {
	// Compute the requested ordered or extreme result.
	if err := validateKDPoint(tree.dimensions, query); err != nil {
		return 0, 0, false, err
	}
	best := kdNearestCandidate{}
	tree.searchNearest(tree.root, query, &best)
	return best.inputIndex,
		best.squaredDistance,
		best.found,
		nil
}

func mustKDTree(
	points []kdPoint,
	dimensions int,
) *kdTree {
	// Run the operation and stop if the fixed example fails.
	tree, err := newKDTree(points, dimensions)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	return tree
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	points := []kdPoint{
		{2, 3},
		{5, 4},
		{9, 6},
		{4, 7},
		{8, 1},
		{7, 2},
	}
	tree := mustKDTree(points, 2)
	inputIndices, err := tree.rangeSearch(
		kdPoint{3, 1},
		kdPoint{9, 5},
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(inputIndices)

	inputIndex, distance, found, err := tree.nearest(
		kdPoint{9, 2},
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(inputIndex, distance, found)

	duplicateTree := mustKDTree(
		[]kdPoint{{1, 1}, {1, 1}},
		2,
	)
	inputIndices, err = duplicateTree.rangeSearch(
		kdPoint{1, 1},
		kdPoint{2, 2},
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(inputIndices)
	inputIndex, distance, found, err =
		duplicateTree.nearest(kdPoint{1, 1})
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(inputIndex, distance, found)

	emptyTree := mustKDTree(nil, 2)
	inputIndex, distance, found, err =
		emptyTree.nearest(kdPoint{})
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(inputIndex, distance, found)
	_, _, _, err = tree.nearest(
		kdPoint{kdCoordinateLimit, 0},
	)
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 4 5]
4 2 true
[0 1]
0 0 true
0 0 false
true
```

##### Why it works

Construction sorts each subtree by its chosen axis and a deterministic
tie order. The median becomes the node. Therefore every entry placed
on the left is no greater on that axis, and every entry on the right
is no less. Recursive calls apply the same fact on the next axis.
Each call removes one median, so every input entry appears once and
construction terminates.

For range search, assume the split invariant holds. If the box minimum
is greater than the split coordinate, every left point is smaller than
the minimum on that axis and is outside. Otherwise the left side may
contain a match and is searched. If the box maximum is at most the
split coordinate, every right point is at or beyond the half-open
maximum and is outside. Otherwise the right side may contain a match.
Every unpruned node is tested on all axes, so the algorithm includes
exactly the matching IDs. Final sorting establishes the output order.

For nearest search, the best record initially represents no tested
point. Testing a node replaces it exactly when that node has smaller
distance or the same distance and smaller ID. Thus it always holds
the required winner among tested nodes.

After searching the near side, any point on the far side differs from
the query along the split axis by at least the query-to-plane
distance. Its complete squared distance is at least the square of that
one difference. A plane distance strictly greater than the best
therefore proves no far point can improve or tie the result. When it
is less or equal, searching preserves the possibility of a closer
point or a smaller-ID tie. At termination, every unvisited subtree
has this proof, so the best tested point is the global answer.

Each recursive query advances to a child. The finite balanced tree
ends at nil links, so both searches terminate. Validation precedes
descent, and no query writes a node, preserving the construction
invariants and atomic failure behavior.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of points, K the active dimension count, H the
tree height, R the number of range results, and V the number of nodes
a query visits. Median splitting gives `H = O(log N)` for a nonempty
tree.

Construction copies N points. This clear implementation sorts again in
every recursive subtree. Comparisons can inspect K coordinates on
ties, so construction takes `O(K*N*log^2(N))` time and O(N) retained
tree-and-entry storage. With K limited to eight, time is commonly
written `O(N*log^2(N))`. Node recursion and in-place sorting add
O(log N) auxiliary stack space beyond the copied entries and nodes.
Presorting or linear-time median selection can reduce construction
work, but needs a more involved representation.

An empty range exits after O(K) validation. A nonempty range spends
O(KV) testing visited points, then O(R log R) sorting returned IDs.
Its worst case is `O(KN + R log R)` time. It uses O(H) traversal
stack, O(log R) sorting stack, and O(R) caller-owned output storage.

Nearest search spends O(KV) time, returns fixed-size state, and uses
O(H) stack space. A root-only case takes O(K); the worst case visits
all points and takes O(KN). Balance guarantees logarithmic stack
depth, not average logarithmic query time. Point distribution,
dimension count, and query location determine pruning.

Exact integer distance and deterministic IDs make answers
reproducible. The fixed `[8]int64` value keeps nodes simple but stores
eight words even for a two-dimensional tree. The read-only design
makes ownership and concurrent queries straightforward, but insertions
or deletions require rebuilding or a different balancing policy.

As K grows, many split planes can remain close enough to search. This
is the curse of dimensionality: geometric indexes lose discrimination
and a flat scan can become simpler and comparably fast.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- An empty input is valid. Nearest returns `found == false`, while a
  range query returns a non-nil empty slice. Treating ID 0 alone as
  absence would confuse an empty tree with the first stored point.
- One point becomes the root. Both child searches end at nil, and a
  matching range must return its stable ID 0.
- Duplicate points are separate entries. Deduplicating by coordinates
  loses input identity, range multiplicity, and the smallest-ID tie.
- Equal split coordinates may occur on both sides. Range search must
  use `minimum <= split` for the left and `maximum > split` for the
  right; stricter comparisons miss boundary duplicates.
- A half-open box with any equal endpoints is empty. It returns an
  owned empty slice. A minimum greater than its maximum is invalid.
- Stored coordinates and point queries accept -500000000 but reject
  500000000. A box boundary may equal either endpoint because the
  upper boundary is not itself a stored coordinate.
- With K equal to 2, `[8]int64{1,2,3}` is invalid. Ignoring the third
  component would make distinct caller values address the same point.
- Squaring arbitrary `int64` differences can overflow silently. The
  stated coordinate and K limits are part of correctness, not merely a
  sample-data suggestion.
- Nearest search must visit the far side when plane distance equals
  the best. The walkthrough's counterexample shows that a smaller-ID
  tie can live there.
- Compare squared distances consistently. Comparing one squared value
  with one unsquared value makes the pruning inequality meaningless.
- The constructor must copy before recursive sorting. Sorting the
  caller's slice would violate ownership and visibly reorder input.
- Range results are sorted after traversal. Exposing traversal order
  makes the API depend on build details and median choices.
- A balanced tree can still scan every point. Repeated coordinates,
  broad boxes, high dimensions, or a large nearest radius weaken split
  plane pruning.
- This implementation is static. Appending a leaf without rebalancing
  can destroy the height guarantee; rebuild or use a dynamic
  structure.

##### When to choose it

Choose a k-d tree for a mostly static set of points in a small number
of dimensions when exact axis-aligned range or nearest-neighbor
queries are repeated. Location points in two dimensions and modest
feature vectors are recognizable examples. The build cost is useful
when it replaces many full scans.

Use a flat scan for a small point set, one query, or enough dimensions
that pruning rarely removes work. Use a grid or spatial hash when the
domain divides naturally into fixed cells and exact cell lookup
matters. Use a [quadtree or octree](
#a171-quadtrees-and-octrees) when uniform spatial regions, not just
irregular points, are the compressible unit.

Use an [R-tree](#a174-r-trees) for rectangles or objects with extent;
a k-d node stores a point and does not directly organize overlapping
boxes. Sorting by one coordinate is also simpler for a one-off range
query. The [nearest-neighbor question family](
#b307-nearest-neighbor-queries-k-d-tree-advanced) points back to this
primary implementation.

This exact version favors deterministic teaching behavior over dynamic
updates or approximate results. Large production workloads may add
subtree bounds, bulk-loading policies, rebuilding thresholds, or an
approximation budget, each with a new contract.

Bentley's original [k-d tree paper](
https://doi.org/10.1145/361002.361007) introduces the multidimensional
binary search tree and its associative-search motivation.

#### A.17.3 Interval trees

##### Problem and contract

You have many intervals on one number line and must repeatedly report
every interval that overlaps a query interval. Scanning all stored
intervals answers one query, but repeats work on regions that cannot
overlap later queries. An interval tree groups intervals around
carefully chosen coordinates so a query can skip whole groups.

This lesson builds a static centered interval tree. Every stored
interval is a nonempty half-open range `[start,end)` of `int64`
coordinates, so `start < end`. The constructor validates the complete
input, copies it, and assigns each interval a stable input ID equal to
its slice index. Equal intervals remain separate entries.

`overlaps(queryStart,queryEnd)` returns every stored ID whose interval
overlaps the half-open query. Two nonempty half-open intervals overlap
exactly when both of these inequalities hold:

```text
stored.start < queryEnd
queryStart < stored.end
```

The query may be empty, with equal endpoints; it then returns a
non-nil empty slice. A reversed query is invalid. Results are sorted
by input ID and owned by the caller. All `int64` endpoints are valid
because the implementation compares them without subtracting or
averaging them.

An empty stored collection is valid. An empty or reversed stored
interval is invalid because it would not describe an object with
positive extent. Invalid construction returns a nil tree and an
error. Invalid queries return no partial result and cannot change the
tree. Allocation failure is outside the contract.

The tree is immutable after construction, exposes no nodes, and does
not retain the input slice. Independent queries are safe concurrently,
and each returned slice is independent. The zero value is a valid
empty tree. Methods require a non-nil tree pointer; copying a tree
value shares immutable nodes. Read [binary search trees](
#a72-binary-search-trees) and [balanced search trees](
#a73-balanced-search-trees) first.

##### Mental model

Each node chooses one coordinate called its center. Stored intervals
are divided into three disjoint groups:

- An interval with `end <= center` belongs entirely to the left.
- An interval with `start > center` belongs entirely to the right.
- Every other interval contains the center and stays at this node.

The node keeps two sorted slices of its center-crossing intervals: one
by increasing start and one by decreasing end. Both slices contain the
same stable IDs. They duplicate entry records, not logical intervals.

Choose the median stored start as the center. The interval owning that
start must cross the center because its end is greater than its start.
At most half the intervals can be entirely left, because their starts
precede the median. At most half can be entirely right, because their
starts follow it. Recursing therefore produces logarithmic height.

A query entirely left of a center has `queryEnd <= center`. Every
interval stored at that node already ends beyond the center, so only
its start can prevent overlap. Scan increasing starts until one is at
or beyond the excluded query end, then recurse left.

A query entirely right has `queryStart >= center`. Every interval at
the node starts at or before the center, so only its end can prevent
overlap. Scan decreasing ends until one is at or before the included
query start, then recurse right.

Otherwise, `queryStart < center < queryEnd`. The query contains the
center, so every interval stored at that node overlaps it. Report the
whole node group and recurse into both children. A nil child ends that
path.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build a tree from these seven intervals. The number at the left is the
stable input ID:

```text
0: [1,5)    1: [2,3)    2: [4,8)    3: [6,10)
4: [8,9)    5: [11,13)  6: [0,2)
```

The main query is `[3,9)`, whose expected IDs are `[0,2,3,4]`.
A focused query `[1,2)` should return `[0,6]`.

Initial state: validation has established that every stored interval
is nonempty. The constructor has copied the seven values and assigned
IDs 0 through 6.

1. Decision: sort starts as `0,1,2,4,6,8,11` and choose median 4 as
   the root center. IDs 0 and 2 contain 4, so store them at the root.
   IDs 1 and 6 end at or before 4; IDs 3, 4, and 5 start after 4.
   After: root order by start is `[0,2]`; its left work is `[1,6]`
   and its right work is `[3,4,5]`.
   Known correct: every interval is in exactly one group, and both
   child groups contain at most half the original entries.

2. Decision: choose median start 2 for the left group. Store ID 1 at
   that center and send ID 6 left, where center 0 stores it. Choose
   median start 8 for the right group. Store IDs 3 and 4 there and
   send ID 5 right, where center 11 stores it.
   After: the constructed tree is:

   ```text
                   center 4: IDs 0,2
                  /                 \
        center 2: ID 1       center 8: IDs 3,4
         /                              \
   center 0: ID 6                 center 11: ID 5
   ```

   Known correct: each child repeats the same partition rule, every
   node has a crossing interval, and every ID is stored once.

3. Decision: query `[3,9)` at center 4. Since `3 < 4 < 9`, every
   root interval overlaps. Collect IDs 0 and 2, then search both
   children.
   After: collected traversal IDs are `[0,2]`; centers 2 and 8 are
   pending.
   Known correct: both reported intervals contain coordinate 4, which
   is inside the query.

4. Decision: at center 2, query start 3 is to the right. Scan ID 1 in
   decreasing-end order. Its end equals 3, so `end <= queryStart` and
   the scan stops. Recurse right, which is nil.
   After: the left side contributes no IDs and is complete.
   Known correct: `[2,3)` only touches `[3,9)` at excluded boundary 3;
   center-2 left intervals end no later and cannot overlap either.

5. Decision: at center 8, the query contains the center. Collect IDs
   3 and 4 and search both children. Its right child has center 11.
   There, query end 9 is left of the center; ID 5 starts at 11, so the
   increasing-start scan stops immediately.
   After: traversal collected `[0,2,3,4]`; sorting leaves the same ID
   order and returns it.
   Known correct: all four reported intervals satisfy both overlap
   inequalities, and every pruned group fails one of them.

6. Decision: query `[1,2)` at root center 4. Scan root intervals by
   increasing start: ID 0 starts at 1 and overlaps; ID 2 starts at 4,
   so stop. Recurse left to center 2. Its ID 1 starts at the excluded
   query end 2, so stop and recurse left to center 0. Scan decreasing
   ends there; ID 6 ends at 2, which is greater than query start 1, so
   collect it.
   After: traversal IDs `[0,6]` sort to `[0,6]`.
   Known correct: the trace exercised both one-sided orderings and
   treated touching end 2 consistently with half-open intervals.

7. Decision: build duplicate intervals `[5,7)` with IDs 0 and 1, then
   query `[5,6)`. Both cross the chosen center and both are reported.
   Query `[5,5)` separately; it is empty, so return before traversal.
   After: duplicate result is `[0,1]`; empty result is a non-nil `[]`.
   Known correct: stable identity preserves duplicates, while an empty
   query contains no coordinate that could belong to an overlap.

8. Decision: try reversed query `[9,3)` and stored interval `[4,4)`.
   Their endpoint orders violate the query and storage contracts.
   After: both operations return errors; no tree or node changes.
   Known correct: validation completes before construction or query
   traversal exposes any partial result.

Counterexample to closed-interval comparisons: stored `[2,3)` and
query `[3,9)` do not overlap. Testing `stored.end >= queryStart`
incorrectly accepts equality at 3. The strict condition
`queryStart < stored.end` prevents that first wrong decision.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs both traced queries and focused cases.
It uses only `fmt` and `sort`. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Interval trees. Function comments
// connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

type interval struct {
	start int64
	end   int64
}

type intervalEntry struct {
	interval   interval
	inputIndex int
}

type intervalNode struct {
	center  int64
	byStart []intervalEntry
	byEnd   []intervalEntry
	left    *intervalNode
	right   *intervalNode
}

type intervalTree struct {
	root *intervalNode
}

func intervalStartLess(
	first intervalEntry,
	second intervalEntry,
) bool {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	if first.interval.start != second.interval.start {
		return first.interval.start < second.interval.start
	}
	if first.interval.end != second.interval.end {
		return first.interval.end < second.interval.end
	}
	return first.inputIndex < second.inputIndex
}

func intervalEndGreater(
	first intervalEntry,
	second intervalEntry,
) bool {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	if first.interval.end != second.interval.end {
		return first.interval.end > second.interval.end
	}
	if first.interval.start != second.interval.start {
		return first.interval.start < second.interval.start
	}
	return first.inputIndex < second.inputIndex
}

func buildIntervalNode(
	entries []intervalEntry,
) *intervalNode {
	// Build interval node in the order required by the lesson contract.
	if len(entries) == 0 {
		return nil
	}

	// A median start guarantees one crossing entry and balanced sides.
	starts := make([]int64, len(entries))
	for entryIndex, entry := range entries {
		starts[entryIndex] = entry.interval.start
	}
	sort.Slice(starts, func(firstIndex int, secondIndex int) bool {
		return starts[firstIndex] < starts[secondIndex]
	})
	center := starts[len(starts)/2]

	leftEntries := make([]intervalEntry, 0)
	rightEntries := make([]intervalEntry, 0)
	crossingEntries := make([]intervalEntry, 0)
	for _, entry := range entries {
		if entry.interval.end <= center {
			leftEntries = append(leftEntries, entry)
		} else if entry.interval.start > center {
			rightEntries = append(rightEntries, entry)
		} else {
			crossingEntries = append(
				crossingEntries,
				entry,
			)
		}
	}

	// Opposite orderings let one-sided queries stop at one boundary.
	byStart := append([]intervalEntry(nil), crossingEntries...)
	byEnd := append([]intervalEntry(nil), crossingEntries...)
	sort.Slice(byStart, func(firstIndex int, secondIndex int) bool {
		return intervalStartLess(
			byStart[firstIndex],
			byStart[secondIndex],
		)
	})
	sort.Slice(byEnd, func(firstIndex int, secondIndex int) bool {
		return intervalEndGreater(
			byEnd[firstIndex],
			byEnd[secondIndex],
		)
	})

	return &intervalNode{
		center:  center,
		byStart: byStart,
		byEnd:   byEnd,
		left:    buildIntervalNode(leftEntries),
		right:   buildIntervalNode(rightEntries),
	}
}

func newIntervalTree(
	intervals []interval,
) (*intervalTree, error) {
	// Finish validation before allocating or reordering copied entries.
	for inputIndex, current := range intervals {
		if current.start >= current.end {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"interval %d must have start less than end",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
	}

	entries := make([]intervalEntry, len(intervals))
	for inputIndex, current := range intervals {
		entries[inputIndex] = intervalEntry{
			interval:   current,
			inputIndex: inputIndex,
		}
	}
	return &intervalTree{
		root: buildIntervalNode(entries),
	}, nil
}

func (tree *intervalTree) appendOverlaps(
	node *intervalNode,
	queryStart int64,
	queryEnd int64,
	inputIndices *[]int,
) {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	if node == nil {
		return
	}

	if queryEnd <= node.center {
		// Stored intervals end beyond center; only starts can fail.
		for _, entry := range node.byStart {
			if entry.interval.start >= queryEnd {
				break
			}
			*inputIndices = append(
				*inputIndices,
				entry.inputIndex,
			)
		}
		tree.appendOverlaps(
			node.left,
			queryStart,
			queryEnd,
			inputIndices,
		)
		return
	}

	if queryStart >= node.center {
		// Stored intervals start by center; only ends can fail.
		for _, entry := range node.byEnd {
			if entry.interval.end <= queryStart {
				break
			}
			*inputIndices = append(
				*inputIndices,
				entry.inputIndex,
			)
		}
		tree.appendOverlaps(
			node.right,
			queryStart,
			queryEnd,
			inputIndices,
		)
		return
	}

	// The query contains center, so every stored interval overlaps it.
	for _, entry := range node.byStart {
		*inputIndices = append(
			*inputIndices,
			entry.inputIndex,
		)
	}
	tree.appendOverlaps(
		node.left,
		queryStart,
		queryEnd,
		inputIndices,
	)
	tree.appendOverlaps(
		node.right,
		queryStart,
		queryEnd,
		inputIndices,
	)
}

func (tree *intervalTree) overlaps(
	queryStart int64,
	queryEnd int64,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	if queryStart > queryEnd {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"query start must not exceed query end",
		)
	}
	inputIndices := make([]int, 0)
	if queryStart == queryEnd {
		return inputIndices, nil
	}
	tree.appendOverlaps(
		tree.root,
		queryStart,
		queryEnd,
		&inputIndices,
	)
	sort.Ints(inputIndices)
	return inputIndices, nil
}

func mustIntervalTree(
	intervals []interval,
) *intervalTree {
	// Run the operation and stop if the fixed example fails.
	tree, err := newIntervalTree(intervals)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	return tree
}

func mustOverlaps(
	tree *intervalTree,
	queryStart int64,
	queryEnd int64,
) []int {
	// Run the operation and stop if the fixed example fails.
	inputIndices, err := tree.overlaps(queryStart, queryEnd)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	return inputIndices
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	tree := mustIntervalTree(
		[]interval{
			{start: 1, end: 5},
			{start: 2, end: 3},
			{start: 4, end: 8},
			{start: 6, end: 10},
			{start: 8, end: 9},
			{start: 11, end: 13},
			{start: 0, end: 2},
		},
	)
	fmt.Println(mustOverlaps(tree, 3, 9))
	fmt.Println(mustOverlaps(tree, 1, 2))

	duplicateTree := mustIntervalTree(
		[]interval{
			{start: 5, end: 7},
			{start: 5, end: 7},
		},
	)
	fmt.Println(mustOverlaps(duplicateTree, 5, 6))
	emptyResult := mustOverlaps(tree, 5, 5)
	fmt.Println(emptyResult, emptyResult != nil)

	_, queryErr := tree.overlaps(9, 3)
	_, intervalErr := newIntervalTree(
		[]interval{{start: 4, end: 4}},
	)
	fmt.Println(queryErr != nil, intervalErr != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[0 2 3 4]
[0 6]
[0 1]
[] true
true true
```

##### Why it works

At construction, choosing a median start guarantees that at least its
own nonempty interval crosses the center. The three partition tests
are disjoint and exhaustive: an interval is wholly left, wholly right,
or contains the center. Recursion applies the same fact to each child,
so every input ID is stored at exactly one node.

An entirely left interval has a start below the median start; an
entirely right interval has a start above it. Neither child can
contain more than half the current entries. Each recursive call also
removes at least one crossing interval. Construction therefore
terminates with height O(log N).

For a left-side query, every node-stored interval has
`stored.end > center >= queryEnd > queryStart`. Its end condition is
already true, so it overlaps exactly when `stored.start < queryEnd`.
Increasing-start order reports precisely that prefix. Every right
subtree interval starts beyond the center and cannot overlap, so only
the left subtree remains possible.

The right-side case is symmetric. Every node-stored start is at or
before `center <= queryStart < queryEnd`, so decreasing-end order
reports exactly the prefix with `stored.end > queryStart`. A left
subtree interval ends no later than the center and cannot overlap.

When a query contains the center, both it and every node-stored
interval contain that coordinate, so all those intervals overlap.
Either child can still overlap the part of the query on its side and
must be searched. Thus every report is valid and every pruned group is
impossible. Each query call moves to a child and the finite tree ends
at nil, proving termination. Sorting the collected IDs establishes the
promised output order.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the stored interval count, R the reported count, and H the
tree height. Median-start partitioning gives `H = O(log N)` for a
nonempty tree.

This readable constructor sorts starts again in each recursive
subproblem. Across one depth, subproblems contain at most N entries;
across H depths, construction takes `O(N*log^2(N))` time. Sorting
the crossing lists adds at most O(N log N), which does not change that
bound. Presorting and partition-preserving techniques can build more
quickly but require a more involved representation.

The tree retains O(N) nodes and entries. Each interval occurs in the
two orderings of exactly one node, so the constant storage factor is
two entry records plus partition metadata. Temporary construction
slices use O(N) peak space, and recursion uses O(log N) stack space.

Before final ID sorting, a nonempty query takes O(log N + R) time.
One-sided steps follow one child and scan only reported entries plus a
stopping boundary. A step that searches both children reports at least
one interval from that node, so branching can be charged to output.
The implementation then spends O(R log R) time to make IDs stable.

An empty query returns in O(1) time. A nonempty query uses O(log N)
recursion stack and O(R) output storage; standard sorting adds
`O(log(1+R))` stack space. A query that reports every interval must
spend Theta(N) time on output even when the tree prunes perfectly.

This static design gives compact, deterministic queries and safe
concurrent reads. It pays two local orderings per interval and
rebuilds when the collection changes. A dynamic interval tree needs
balanced updates and maintained secondary ordering or augmentation.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input builds a nil root. Any nonempty query returns a non-nil
  empty slice without dereferencing it.
- One interval is stored at the root center equal to its start. A
  matching query returns ID 0; a touching query at its end does not.
- Equal intervals keep separate IDs. Deduplicating them changes report
  multiplicity and violates stable input identity.
- `[2,3)` and `[3,4)` only touch. Using `<=` in both overlap tests
  reports a false match; half-open overlap needs two strict tests.
- Empty query `[5,5)` is valid and returns no IDs. Stored `[5,5)` is
  invalid because stored objects must have positive extent.
- Query start equal to a center takes the right-side branch. Left
  intervals end at or before that coordinate and cannot overlap it.
- Query end equal to a center takes the left-side branch. Right
  intervals begin after the center and cannot overlap it.
- The center is a median start, not an arithmetic midpoint. Computing
  `(start+end)/2` can overflow `int64` and does not bound child sizes.
- Both node orderings must contain the same IDs. Omitting an interval
  from one silently loses it for queries approaching from that side.
- Stop the increasing scan at `start >= queryEnd` and the decreasing
  scan at `end <= queryStart`. Reversing either equality admits a
  touching interval.
- Sort final IDs explicitly. Traversal order depends on centers and
  local endpoint order, not the public stable-ID contract.
- Copy input before partitioning. Retaining or rearranging the caller
  slice violates ownership and makes later mutation observable.
- If all intervals share one coordinate, one root list stores all of
  them. Reporting all overlaps is necessarily linear in the output.
- This implementation is static. Inserting into one local list without
  rebalancing can invalidate height and ordering guarantees.

##### When to choose it

Choose an interval tree for a mostly static one-dimensional collection
when many queries must report the actual intervals that overlap a
range. Calendar spans, genomic ranges, and time-window records are
recognizable workloads when their endpoint semantics match the
contract.

Use a flat scan for a small collection or one query. For an offline
batch of known intervals and queries, sorting endpoints and sweeping
once may avoid a retained tree. Use an augmented balanced BST when
insertions and deletions are essential and the required query contract
fits its augmentation.

A [segment tree](#a124-segment-trees) organizes coordinate segments
for aggregates and range updates; this interval tree stores interval
objects and reports their IDs. Use a [k-d tree](#a172-k-d-trees) for
multidimensional points and the next [R-tree](#a174-r-trees) for
rectangles or objects with spatial extent in multiple dimensions. The
[interval question family](
#b17-intervals-scheduling-and-event-processing) covers offline and
scheduling alternatives.

Edelsbrunner's [publication archive](
https://pub.ista.ac.at/~edels/Papers/) lists the original 1980 report
on dynamic data structures for orthogonal intersection queries.

#### A.17.4 R-trees

##### Problem and contract

You need to store two-dimensional objects with width and height, then
repeatedly report every object whose rectangle overlaps a query
rectangle. A k-d tree represents points, and a one-dimensional
interval tree represents spans on one line. Neither directly captures
objects whose extents matter on both axes.

An R-tree groups nearby rectangles and covers each group with one
minimum bounding rectangle, abbreviated MBR. A query can reject a
group when its MBR does not overlap the query. Unlike a fixed grid,
group boundaries come from the stored objects and may overlap.

This lesson implements a mutable two-dimensional R-tree. A rectangle
is the half-open region
`[minimumX,maximumX) x [minimumY,maximumY)`. Stored rectangles need
positive width and height. Every boundary belongs to
`[-1000000000,1000000000]`. These limits keep every width, height,
area, union area, and enlargement exact in `int64`.

`insert` validates a rectangle, stores a value copy, and returns a
stable item ID. IDs begin at zero and follow successful insertion
order. Equal rectangles receive separate IDs. Invalid insertion
returns an error before changing the tree or consuming an ID.

`search` accepts a valid rectangle with either dimension possibly
empty. An empty query returns a non-nil empty slice. A nonempty query
returns every stored ID whose rectangle overlaps it, sorted by ID. Two
rectangles overlap only when their half-open interiors overlap on both
axes. The returned slice belongs to the caller.

Each node holds at most four entries. Every non-root node holds at
least two. The root may be an empty leaf or contain fewer entries. All
leaves remain at the same depth. Overflow uses a deterministic
quadratic split. The heuristic affects grouping and query work, not
which answers are correct.

This implementation supports insertion and search, but not deletion
or bulk loading. It owns all nodes and mutates on each successful
insertion. Queries do not mutate, but concurrent access with an
insertion needs external synchronization. Allocation failure is
outside the contract. Copying the tree value would share nodes.
Methods require a non-nil tree pointer returned by `newRTree`; a zero
tree is not initialized. Read [balanced search trees](
#a73-balanced-search-trees), [k-d trees](#a172-k-d-trees), and
[interval trees](#a173-interval-trees) first.

##### Mental model

A leaf entry stores one object rectangle and its stable ID. An
internal entry stores a child pointer and that child's exact MBR. Read
bounds `[0,10) x [1,5)` as: "every object below this link is inside
that rectangle." The MBR may cover empty space.

Insertion descends one child per level. For each candidate child,
compute how much its MBR area would grow to include the new rectangle.
Choose the smallest enlargement. Break ties by smaller current area,
then fewer child entries, then earlier entry order. After insertion,
replace every MBR on the return path with the exact child union.

A fifth entry overflows a node. Quadratic splitting first chooses the
two seed entries that waste the most area if placed in one MBR:

```text
waste = area(union) - area(first) - area(second)
```

Each seed starts a group. Among unassigned entries, choose the one
whose two possible enlargement costs differ most; that decision is
hardest to postpone. Put it in the group needing less enlargement.
Break ties by smaller group area, fewer entries, then the first group.
If one group needs every remaining entry to reach minimum fill two,
reserve them for that group.

One group replaces the overflowing node and the other becomes its
sibling. The parent receives a new sibling entry. Overflow can then
propagate toward the root. If the root splits, create a new root over
both siblings; this is the only way tree height increases.

Search checks every entry whose rectangle overlaps the query. At an
internal node, overlap means the child may contain a match, so
descend. At a leaf, the entry rectangle is exact, so report its ID.
Overlapping MBRs can require several paths, and an MBR overlap can be
a false positive that disappears only at a leaf.

##### Worked walkthrough

Insert these rectangles in ID order. The notation lists x range, then
y range:

```text
0: [0,2) x [0,2)     1: [3,5) x [0,2)
2: [0,2) x [3,5)     3: [3,5) x [3,5)
4: [8,10) x [0,2)    5: [8,10) x [3,5)
6: [4,6) x [1,4)
```

Query `[4,5) x [1,2)` should return `[1,6]`. Query
`[7,8) x [1,2)` should return no IDs even though it overlaps both root
MBRs. Query `[1,4) x [1,4)` should return `[0,1,2,3]`.

Initial state: the root is an empty leaf. Maximum fill is four and
minimum non-root fill is two. The next successful insertion receives
ID 0.

1. Decision: insert IDs 0 through 3 into the leaf root. No insertion
   exceeds capacity, so no split is needed.
   After: the root leaf holds four exact object entries and has height
   1.
   Known correct: every stored entry has its insertion ID. The root
   exception permits one through four entries.

2. Decision: insert ID 4. Five entries overflow the root. Quadratic
   seed selection chooses IDs 2 and 4: their union has area 50, their
   own areas total 8, and waste is 42, the largest pair value.
   Assigning the others by enlargement produces top group `[2,3]`
   with MBR `[0,5) x [3,5)` and bottom group `[4,1,0]` with MBR
   `[0,10) x [0,2)`.
   After: a new internal root points to two leaf siblings. Its height
   is now two, and both leaves meet minimum fill.
   Known correct: the split stored every ID exactly once, each parent
   entry is the exact union of its child, and leaf depths still agree.

3. Decision: insert ID 5. Expanding the top MBR costs 10 area units;
   expanding the bottom costs 30. Choose the top leaf and update its
   MBR to `[0,10) x [3,5)`.
   After: top IDs are `[2,3,5]`; bottom IDs remain `[4,1,0]`.
   Known correct: the chosen leaf now contains the new rectangle, and
   both root MBRs exactly cover their child entries.

4. Decision: insert ID 6. Either root MBR would grow by 20. Both
   leaves have equal area and entry count, so the final tie picks the
   earlier top entry. Its MBR becomes `[0,10) x [1,5)`.
   After: top IDs are `[2,3,5,6]`; bottom IDs are `[4,1,0]`.
   Their MBRs overlap in `[0,10) x [1,2)`.
   Known correct: capacity remains four, and deterministic tie rules
   make the demonstrated shape reproducible.

5. Decision: search `[4,5) x [1,2)`. It overlaps both root MBRs, so
   descend into both leaves. Only ID 6 overlaps in the top leaf; only
   ID 1 overlaps in the bottom leaf.
   After: traversal collects `[6,1]`; sorting returns `[1,6]`.
   Known correct: every reported leaf rectangle satisfies all four
   strict overlap comparisons, and no overlapping MBR was mistaken for
   a final answer.

6. Decision: search `[7,8) x [1,2)`. Both root MBRs overlap again.
   In the top leaf, ID 6 ends at x 6 and ID 5 begins at x 8. In the
   bottom leaf, ID 4 begins at x 8; the other entries end earlier.
   After: both paths finish without a leaf match and return `[]`.
   Known correct: an MBR is only a conservative cover; searching a
   false-positive path cannot create a false-positive result.

7. Decision: search `[1,4) x [1,4)`. Both root paths are possible.
   Exact leaf checks accept IDs 0, 1, 2, and 3. ID 6 starts at the
   excluded x maximum 4, while IDs 4 and 5 begin at x 8.
   After: sorted result is `[0,1,2,3]`.
   Known correct: touching at x 4 is excluded consistently, and every
   actual overlap from either branch is present.

8. Decision: insert the same rectangle twice into a separate tree and
   query it. Then search an empty-width rectangle. Finally try a
   zero-area stored rectangle and a reversed query.
   After: duplicates return IDs `[0,1]`; the empty query returns a
   non-nil `[]`. Both invalid operations return errors without
   mutation.
   Known correct: identity, empty-query behavior, and failure
   atomicity all match the contract.

Counterexample to returning an internal MBR as a match: step 6
overlaps both root MBRs but no object. The first wrong decision would
be treating a group cover as stored geometry. An MBR overlap
authorizes descent; only a leaf rectangle authorizes an output ID.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. The rectangle literals
in `main` follow the declared field order: minimum x, minimum y,
maximum x, maximum y. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates R-trees. Function comments connect
// each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

const (
	rTreeMaximumEntries  = 4
	rTreeMinimumEntries  = 2
	rTreeCoordinateLimit = int64(1_000_000_000)
)

type rectangle struct {
	minimumX int64
	minimumY int64
	maximumX int64
	maximumY int64
}

type rTreeEntry struct {
	bounds rectangle
	child  *rTreeNode
	itemID int
}

type rTreeNode struct {
	leaf    bool
	entries []rTreeEntry
}

type rTree struct {
	root       *rTreeNode
	nextItemID int
}

func newRTree() *rTree {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial r tree state.
	return &rTree{root: &rTreeNode{leaf: true}}
}

func validateRectangle(
	bounds rectangle,
	allowEmpty bool,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the rectangle contract before mutation.
	coordinates := [...]int64{
		bounds.minimumX,
		bounds.minimumY,
		bounds.maximumX,
		bounds.maximumY,
	}
	for coordinateIndex, coordinate := range coordinates {
		if coordinate < -rTreeCoordinateLimit ||
			coordinate > rTreeCoordinateLimit {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"coordinate %d is outside [%d, %d]",
				coordinateIndex,
				-rTreeCoordinateLimit,
				rTreeCoordinateLimit,
			)
		}
	}
	if bounds.minimumX > bounds.maximumX ||
		bounds.minimumY > bounds.maximumY {
		return fmt.Errorf("rectangle boundaries are reversed")
	}
	if !allowEmpty &&
		(bounds.minimumX == bounds.maximumX ||
			bounds.minimumY == bounds.maximumY) {
		return fmt.Errorf("stored rectangle must have positive area")
	}
	return nil
}

func rectangleIsEmpty(bounds rectangle) bool {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	return bounds.minimumX == bounds.maximumX ||
		bounds.minimumY == bounds.maximumY
}

func rectangleArea(bounds rectangle) int64 {
	// Compute the geometric measure from valid coordinates.
	width := bounds.maximumX - bounds.minimumX
	height := bounds.maximumY - bounds.minimumY
	return width * height
}

func rectangleUnion(
	first rectangle,
	second rectangle,
) rectangle {
	// Keep rectangle union in one helper so callers use one rule.
	result := first
	if second.minimumX < result.minimumX {
		result.minimumX = second.minimumX
	}
	if second.minimumY < result.minimumY {
		result.minimumY = second.minimumY
	}
	if second.maximumX > result.maximumX {
		result.maximumX = second.maximumX
	}
	if second.maximumY > result.maximumY {
		result.maximumY = second.maximumY
	}
	return result
}

func rectanglesOverlap(
	first rectangle,
	second rectangle,
) bool {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	return first.minimumX < second.maximumX &&
		second.minimumX < first.maximumX &&
		first.minimumY < second.maximumY &&
		second.minimumY < first.maximumY
}

func rectangleEnlargement(
	current rectangle,
	added rectangle,
) int64 {
	// Keep rectangle enlargement in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return rectangleArea(rectangleUnion(current, added)) -
		rectangleArea(current)
}

func entriesBounds(entries []rTreeEntry) rectangle {
	// Keep entries bounds in one helper so callers use one rule.
	bounds := entries[0].bounds
	for _, entry := range entries[1:] {
		bounds = rectangleUnion(bounds, entry.bounds)
	}
	return bounds
}

func chooseRTreeChild(
	node *rTreeNode,
	added rectangle,
) int {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	bestIndex := 0
	bestEnlargement := rectangleEnlargement(
		node.entries[0].bounds,
		added,
	)
	bestArea := rectangleArea(node.entries[0].bounds)
	bestEntryCount := len(node.entries[0].child.entries)
	for entryIndex := 1; entryIndex < len(node.entries); entryIndex++ {
		entry := node.entries[entryIndex]
		enlargement := rectangleEnlargement(
			entry.bounds,
			added,
		)
		area := rectangleArea(entry.bounds)
		entryCount := len(entry.child.entries)
		if enlargement < bestEnlargement ||
			(enlargement == bestEnlargement &&
				(area < bestArea ||
					(area == bestArea &&
						entryCount < bestEntryCount))) {
			bestIndex = entryIndex
			bestEnlargement = enlargement
			bestArea = area
			bestEntryCount = entryCount
		}
	}
	return bestIndex
}

type rTreeSplitGroup struct {
	entries []rTreeEntry
	bounds  rectangle
}

func (group *rTreeSplitGroup) add(entry rTreeEntry) {
	// Add the requested item while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	if len(group.entries) == 0 {
		group.bounds = entry.bounds
	} else {
		group.bounds = rectangleUnion(
			group.bounds,
			entry.bounds,
		)
	}
	group.entries = append(group.entries, entry)
}

func pickRTreeSeeds(entries []rTreeEntry) (int, int) {
	// Keep pick r tree seeds in one helper so callers use one rule.
	bestFirst := 0
	bestSecond := 1
	bestWaste := rectangleArea(
		rectangleUnion(entries[0].bounds, entries[1].bounds),
	) - rectangleArea(entries[0].bounds) -
		rectangleArea(entries[1].bounds)
	for firstIndex := 0; firstIndex < len(entries); firstIndex++ {
		secondIndex := firstIndex + 1
		for secondIndex < len(entries) {
			waste := rectangleArea(
				rectangleUnion(
					entries[firstIndex].bounds,
					entries[secondIndex].bounds,
				),
			) - rectangleArea(entries[firstIndex].bounds) -
				rectangleArea(entries[secondIndex].bounds)
			if waste > bestWaste {
				bestFirst = firstIndex
				bestSecond = secondIndex
				bestWaste = waste
			}
			secondIndex++
		}
	}
	return bestFirst, bestSecond
}

func absoluteInt64(value int64) int64 {
	// Keep absolute int64 in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if value < 0 {
		return -value
	}
	return value
}

func pickRTreeNext(
	entries []rTreeEntry,
	assigned []bool,
	firstBounds rectangle,
	secondBounds rectangle,
) int {
	// Keep pick r tree next in one helper so callers use one rule.
	bestIndex := -1
	var bestDifference int64
	for entryIndex, entry := range entries {
		if assigned[entryIndex] {
			continue
		}
		firstEnlargement := rectangleEnlargement(
			firstBounds,
			entry.bounds,
		)
		secondEnlargement := rectangleEnlargement(
			secondBounds,
			entry.bounds,
		)
		difference := absoluteInt64(
			firstEnlargement - secondEnlargement,
		)
		if bestIndex == -1 || difference > bestDifference {
			bestIndex = entryIndex
			bestDifference = difference
		}
	}
	return bestIndex
}

func firstRTreeGroupPreferred(
	entry rTreeEntry,
	first *rTreeSplitGroup,
	second *rTreeSplitGroup,
) bool {
	// Apply the documented comparison or boundary rule.
	firstEnlargement := rectangleEnlargement(
		first.bounds,
		entry.bounds,
	)
	secondEnlargement := rectangleEnlargement(
		second.bounds,
		entry.bounds,
	)
	if firstEnlargement != secondEnlargement {
		return firstEnlargement < secondEnlargement
	}
	firstArea := rectangleArea(first.bounds)
	secondArea := rectangleArea(second.bounds)
	if firstArea != secondArea {
		return firstArea < secondArea
	}
	if len(first.entries) != len(second.entries) {
		return len(first.entries) < len(second.entries)
	}
	return true
}

func assignRemainingRTreeEntries(
	entries []rTreeEntry,
	assigned []bool,
	group *rTreeSplitGroup,
) {
	// Keep assign remaining r tree entries in one helper so callers use
	// one rule.
	for entryIndex, entry := range entries {
		if !assigned[entryIndex] {
			group.add(entry)
			assigned[entryIndex] = true
		}
	}
}

func splitRTreeNode(node *rTreeNode) *rTreeNode {
	// Keep split r tree node in one helper so callers use one rule.
	entries := append([]rTreeEntry(nil), node.entries...)
	firstSeed, secondSeed := pickRTreeSeeds(entries)
	assigned := make([]bool, len(entries))
	assigned[firstSeed] = true
	assigned[secondSeed] = true
	firstGroup := rTreeSplitGroup{}
	secondGroup := rTreeSplitGroup{}
	firstGroup.add(entries[firstSeed])
	secondGroup.add(entries[secondSeed])
	remaining := len(entries) - 2

	for remaining > 0 {
		// Reserve every remaining entry when a group needs minimum fill.
		if len(firstGroup.entries)+remaining ==
			rTreeMinimumEntries {
			assignRemainingRTreeEntries(
				entries,
				assigned,
				&firstGroup,
			)
			break
		}
		if len(secondGroup.entries)+remaining ==
			rTreeMinimumEntries {
			assignRemainingRTreeEntries(
				entries,
				assigned,
				&secondGroup,
			)
			break
		}

		nextIndex := pickRTreeNext(
			entries,
			assigned,
			firstGroup.bounds,
			secondGroup.bounds,
		)
		if firstRTreeGroupPreferred(
			entries[nextIndex],
			&firstGroup,
			&secondGroup,
		) {
			firstGroup.add(entries[nextIndex])
		} else {
			secondGroup.add(entries[nextIndex])
		}
		assigned[nextIndex] = true
		remaining--
	}
```
