- Duplicate 6 and missing 42 return the original root. Copying the
  path on a no-op is logically correct, but wastes memory and breaks
  the pointer-identity contract used here.
- A leaf removal returns nil; a one-child removal returns its child.
  Copying or mutating that surviving subtree is unnecessary.
- Removing a two-child node must copy the entire path to a deep
  successor. Copying only the matched node and mutating node 10 while
  removing successor 9 would corrupt the old version.
- When the successor is the immediate right child, `removeMinimum`
  returns that child's right subtree. Leaving the successor in place
  creates a duplicate key.
- Minimum and maximum `int` values are valid. Comparisons are safe;
  bounds such as `value-1` or sentinel arithmetic can overflow.
- Sorted inserts `1,2,3,4` create a height-4 chain. Persistence does
  not provide balancing. Recursive updates can exhaust the call stack
  on a sufficiently deep adversarial tree.
- Copying a `persistentIntSet` value copies only its root and size,
  not its nodes. This is safe only because nodes remain unexported and
  no method mutates them.
- `values` must allocate its own slice. Returning internal mutable
  storage would let a caller change a snapshot's observable contents.
- Publishing a root to another goroutine still needs normal Go
  synchronization. Immutability prevents later node races; it does not
  make an unsynchronized handoff safe.
- Persistence here is not a database guarantee. Process exit loses all
  versions unless a separate serialization layer stores them.

##### When to choose it

Choose path copying when updates touch a narrow route through a linked
structure and the program needs snapshots, undo, speculative branches,
time-travel queries, or updates from old states. Persistent search and
segment trees are especially natural because one operation already
visits only one or a few root-to-leaf paths.

Use the mutable [BST](#a72-binary-search-trees) when only the newest
state matters and allocation would add needless cost. Use a balanced
tree when adversarial updates require bounded height. Use a full copy
when the structure is tiny or most nodes change anyway. An operation
log plus replay can reduce retained memory when old queries are rare,
but reconstructing a version then costs replay time.

Fat nodes and bounded-change node-copying transformations store
versioned changes within nodes and can improve asymptotic update
space, at the cost of more complex access and update rules. This
lesson deliberately uses direct immutable path copying so every
version is represented by an ordinary root and ordinary child
pointers.

The [persistent segment-tree lesson](
#a127-dynamic-and-persistent-segment-trees-advanced) applies the same
sharing rule to range queries. Continue with [persistent lists and
stacks](#a192-persistent-lists-and-stacks), where updating the front
can share an entire tail, and then [versioned maps](
#a193-versioned-maps).

Driscoll, Sarnak, Sleator, and Tarjan's foundational [paper](
https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0000(89)90034-2) defines partial and full
persistence and develops systematic node-copying techniques. Its
stronger balanced-tree transformations achieve bounds beyond this
simple O(H)-allocation implementation.

#### A.19.2 Persistent lists and stacks

##### Problem and contract

Suppose several computations begin from the same stack state and then
push or pop independently. Copying every stored value for each branch
preserves the old states but repeats an unchanged suffix. Mutating one
linked stack is cheap, but destroys the state that another branch may
still need.

This lesson implements a fully persistent stack of Go `int` values.
`push` may start from any version and returns a new version with one
new top. `pop` returns the top value, the remaining version, and true.
On empty, it returns zero, the exact input version, and false. `peek`
observes the top with the same zero-and-boolean convention.

Duplicates, zero, negative values, and extreme integers are ordinary
data. Last-in, first-out order is the only ordering rule. The zero
value is an empty usable stack. Each version stores its size, and
`valuesTopFirst` returns a non-nil caller-owned slice in top-to-bottom
order.

Nodes are immutable after construction and are not exposed. Versions
may share nodes and may be read concurrently after safe publication;
the code does not synchronize publication of handles. Persistent here
means that old in-memory values remain usable, not that process exit
preserves them on disk. Valid versions are finite acyclic chains built
only by these methods.

Read [singly linked lists](#a31-singly-linked-lists), [ordinary
stacks](#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks), and [path copying](
#a191-path-copying-trees) first.

##### Mental model

An immutable singly linked list already has the operations of a stack:

- Prepend, often called `cons`, is stack push.
- Reading the head is stack peek.
- Returning the tail is stack pop without the removed value.

A version is one top pointer and one size. Push allocates a new head
whose next pointer names the old top. Pop does not delete or detach
anything. It returns a handle whose top is the old head's next
pointer. Every older node remains unchanged and can be shared.

The walkthrough creates four nodes:

```text
node A: 10 -> nil
node B: 20 -> A
node C: 30 -> B
node D: 99 -> A

version one top   = A
version two top   = B
version three top = C
branch top        = D
```

Read `node B: 20 -> A` as "this version has 20 on top, followed by
the complete older version beginning at node A." Version three and the
branch have distinct new prefixes but eventually share node A.

Unlike a tree update, a front update changes no path below the root.
Push needs one new node; pop needs none. This advantage is specific to
the front. Appending to an immutable singly linked list cannot change
its last node, so it must copy the entire left list before linking the
right list.

##### Worked walkthrough

Starting empty, push 10, 20, and 30. Pop the three-value version,
then branch from the one-value version by pushing 99. Expected live
versions include `[30,20,10]`, `[20,10]`, `[10]`, and `[99,10]`.

Initial state: `empty.top` is nil, size is 0, and its values are `[]`.

1. Decision: push 10. Allocate node A with value 10 and next nil; put
   A in a new size-1 handle.
   After: version one is `[10]`; empty remains `[]`.
   Known correct: A is the sole and therefore newest unpopped value.

2. Decision: push 20 from version one. Allocate B with value 20 and
   next A; do not copy or alter A.
   After: version two is `[20,10]`; version one remains `[10]`.
   Known correct: B is newest, and its shared tail is exactly the old
   version in its original order.

3. Decision: push 30 from version two. Allocate C with value 30 and
   next B.
   After: version three is `[30,20,10]`; C's next pointer is identical
   to version two's top pointer.

   ```text
   version three top -> C:30 -> B:20 -> A:10 -> nil
   version two top ----------^       |
   version one top ------------------+
   empty top ------------------------------------> nil
   ```

   Known correct: the new version adds only 30 before all prior
   values.

4. Decision: pop version three. Read 30, then use `C.next`, which is
   B, as the top of a new size-2 handle. Do not clear C's next
   pointer.
   After: return 30, true, and restored values `[20,10]`. Version
   three still reads `[30,20,10]`.
   Known correct: B is pointer-identical to version two's top, so pop
   exposes the exact older tail without changing either version.

5. Decision: return to version one and push 99. Allocate D whose next
   pointer is A.
   After: the branch is `[99,10]`; versions two and three still
   contain 20 and 30, while the branch does not.

   ```text
   version three -> C:30 -> B:20 -> A:10 -> nil
   version two -----------> B:20 ---^
   version one -------------------> A:10
   branch -------> D:99 ----------> A:10
   ```

   Known correct: updating an old handle created an independent branch
   and shared only its unchanged base.

6. Decision: peek at the branch. Its top is D, so return 99 and true
   without changing any handle or node.
   After: the branch remains `[99,10]`.
   Known correct: the observed value is the newest unpopped branch
   value.

7. Decision: traverse each requested snapshot from its top to nil,
   appending values to a new slice.
   After: the program prints version three, the restored version, the
   branch, and version one in their separate top-to-bottom orders.
   Known correct: each traversal followed exactly one version's chain;
   shared nodes contributed the same suffix wherever reached.

8. Decision: compare C's next with B and the restored top with B; both
   are identical. Finally, pop empty and take its failure branch.
   After: both pointer checks are true. Empty pop returns zero, false,
   and an unchanged size-0 version; processing stops.
   Known correct: sharing is real, and the valid empty boundary
   neither allocates nor underflows size.

Focused one-value case: popping `[10]` returns 10 and an empty
version, while the original `[10]` remains queryable. Focused
duplicate case: pushing 7 twice creates two nodes; successive pops
return 7 twice.

Counterexample to mutable pop: assigning `C.next = nil` to "detach"
the popped node would change version three from `[30,20,10]` to
`[30]`. The first wrong decision is applying an ephemeral-list cleanup
rule to a node that an old version still owns. Persistent pop changes
only the returned handle.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Persistent lists and stacks.
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type persistentStackNode struct {
	value int
	next  *persistentStackNode
}

type persistentStack struct {
	top  *persistentStackNode
	size int
}

func (stack persistentStack) push(value int) persistentStack {
	// The new head owns one node and shares the immutable old tail.
	return persistentStack{
		top: &persistentStackNode{
			value: value,
			next:  stack.top,
		},
		size: stack.size + 1,
	}
}

func (stack persistentStack) pop() (
	int,
	persistentStack,
	bool,
) {
	// Remove the requested item while preserving the remaining
	// representation.
	if stack.top == nil {
		return 0, stack, false
	}

	// Reusing the old tail restores the version below this top.
	return stack.top.value, persistentStack{
		top:  stack.top.next,
		size: stack.size - 1,
	}, true
}

func (stack persistentStack) peek() (int, bool) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for the requested item without changing
	// state.
	if stack.top == nil {
		return 0, false
	}
	return stack.top.value, true
}

func (stack persistentStack) valuesTopFirst() []int {
	// Expose top first in logical order without changing source.
	values := make([]int, 0, stack.size)
	for node := stack.top; node != nil; node = node.next {
		values = append(values, node.value)
	}
	return values
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	var empty persistentStack
	versionOne := empty.push(10)
	versionTwo := versionOne.push(20)
	versionThree := versionTwo.push(30)

	popped, restored, ok := versionThree.pop()
	branch := versionOne.push(99)

	fmt.Println(versionThree.valuesTopFirst())
	fmt.Println(popped, ok, restored.valuesTopFirst())
	top, ok := branch.peek()
	fmt.Println(top, ok, branch.valuesTopFirst())
	fmt.Println(versionOne.valuesTopFirst())
	fmt.Println(
		versionThree.top.next == versionTwo.top,
		restored.top == versionTwo.top,
	)
	emptyValue, emptyAfter, ok := empty.pop()
	fmt.Println(emptyValue, ok, emptyAfter.size)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[30 20 10]
30 true [20 10]
99 true [99 10]
[10]
true true
0 false 0
```

##### Why it works

For every version, maintain this invariant: following `size` next
pointers from top yields exactly its unpopped values from newest to
oldest, then reaches nil; no reachable node will ever be modified. The
zero value satisfies the invariant with no nodes and size 0.

Push constructs one node whose value is newest and whose next pointer
reaches the complete old sequence. Increasing size by one therefore
describes exactly the new chain. Since the old top and its descendants
are untouched, the input version keeps its invariant.

On nonempty pop, the top holds exactly the newest value. Its next
pointer starts the remaining sequence, and decrementing size describes
that tail. Returning a different handle without changing the node
preserves both the old and new versions. On empty pop, returning the
input handle and false preserves the empty invariant.

Peek reads the first value without changing any state. Traversal
visits nodes in top-to-bottom order and writes them only into
caller-owned output. Every traversal step follows one next pointer in
a finite chain, so it reaches nil after size steps and terminates.

These arguments depend only on the input handle, not on it being the
newest version. Any old version can therefore be pushed or popped, so
the structure is fully persistent.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Push, pop, and peek each perform a fixed number of reads, writes to a
new handle, or pointer assignments. Their best, average, and worst
times are Theta(1); no amortized assumption is involved. Push
allocates and retains one node. Pop and peek allocate no nodes and use
O(1) temporary storage.

One version containing N values reaches N nodes and uses O(N) storage.
Across all retained branches, P successful pushes create exactly P
nodes, and K retained handles store K pointer-and-size pairs. Shared
nodes count once, so total retained representation is O(P + K). Nodes
unique to discarded versions become collectible once no live top can
reach them.

`valuesTopFirst` takes Theta(N) time, O(N) caller-owned output space,
and O(1) auxiliary space beyond that output. Its iterative traversal
does not consume recursive stack space.

The same representation is less efficient away from the front. Looking
up zero-based position J takes Theta(J + 1) time. Replacing that value
copies the first J + 1 nodes before sharing the untouched suffix.
Appending a left list of length L to another immutable list takes
Theta(L) time and L new nodes, then shares the right list. Reversing
takes Theta(N) time and N new nodes.

Compared with a mutable slice stack, this design avoids resize copies
and makes snapshots cheap, but allocates on every push and has poorer
memory locality. It is a poor substitute for a random-access
persistent vector or a catenable sequence when those operations define
the workload.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty pop returns zero, false, and the exact empty version.
  Decreasing size before checking top would underflow the logical
  count.
- Empty peek returns zero and false. Zero pushed as data returns zero
  and true, so callers must inspect the boolean.
- Empty `valuesTopFirst` returns a non-nil empty caller-owned slice.
  Returning nil would also have length zero, but would break this
  output contract.
- Popping the sole node returns an empty new handle, but the one-node
  input remains `[value]`. Clearing the old node would violate this.
- Duplicate values occupy separate nodes. Deduplicating two pushed 7s
  would change the stack abstraction into a set.
- Minimum and maximum `int` values need no sentinels or arithmetic and
  are returned unchanged.
- Copying a `persistentStack` value copies only its top and size. This
  shallow copy is safe because every reachable node stays immutable.
- Size must equal the number of reachable nodes. Forgetting to
  increment or decrement it can make snapshot capacity wrong and
  falsifies the representation invariant even if traversal still
  prints values.
- `valuesTopFirst` must allocate a fresh slice. Reusing exposed
  mutable output could let one caller change another snapshot's
  observation.
- A generic stack does not make mutable payloads immutable. If a node
  stores a slice, map, or pointer, callers need copying or an
  ownership rule for the referenced object as well as for the node.
- Appending by changing the shared last node corrupts every version
  that reaches it. Copy the left spine or choose a catenable
  representation.
- Safe concurrent reads still require synchronized publication of
  each handle. Immutability prevents later node writes, not data races
  while transferring the handle.
- These versions are not durable records. Serialize them separately if
  they must survive process failure.

##### When to choose it

Choose a persistent stack or front-oriented list when computations
need cheap snapshots, undo states, speculative branches, parser
contexts, or depth-first paths. A push or pop changes only the
accessible front, so each branch costs at most one node rather than a
full copy.

Use the mutable [stack](#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks) when only
the latest state matters and slice locality is more valuable than old
versions. Use a slice or persistent vector for frequent indexing. Use
a catenable list, rope, or sequence tree when concatenation is
central; a singly linked persistent list must copy its left operand.

The preceding [path-copying tree](#a191-path-copying-trees) copies a
search path because updates occur below the root. Continue with
[versioned maps](#a193-versioned-maps), which apply persistence to
keyed lookup. The mutable [singly linked list](
#a31-singly-linked-lists) shows why detaching nodes belongs only to an
ephemeral ownership contract.

Chapter 2 of Okasaki's [Purely Functional Data Structures](
https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511530104.003) presents copying and
sharing for lists and search trees, maps `cons`, head, and tail to
stack operations, and derives the linear copying cost of immutable
list concatenation.

#### A.19.3 Versioned maps

##### Problem and contract

A program may need a key-value map before and after each edit. Cloning
every entry for every version costs time and memory proportional to
the whole map. Mutating one Go map is cheaper, but destroys the state
that snapshots, undo, or speculative branches still need.

This lesson builds a fully persistent map from string keys to `int`
values. `put` may start from any version. It inserts a missing key or
replaces that key's value in a new version. Putting the same mapping
again returns the exact input root. `remove` returns a new version and
true for a present key; a missing key returns the exact input version
and false.

The zero-value map is empty and usable. Copying a version handle is
safe: the copies name the same immutable root and can branch
independently through later method calls.

`get` returns `(value, true)` for a present key and `(0, false)` for a
missing key. Zero is valid data, so callers must inspect the boolean.
Keys are exact Go strings: empty and invalid UTF-8 strings are
allowed, and byte-distinct strings are different keys. Each version
records its entry count.

`entriesByKey` returns every mapping in Go's bytewise string order in
a non-nil, caller-owned slice. It exposes no mutable node storage.
Nodes and their child slices never change after construction, so
versions may share them and may be read concurrently after safe handle
publication.

This teaching implementation uses a stable 64-bit FNV-1a hash and a
16-way bitmap-compressed hash array mapped trie, or HAMT. FNV is not a
cryptographic or adversarially secure hash. Exact key checks preserve
correctness under collisions, but collision-heavy input can hurt time.

Read [hash collisions](#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing),
[binary tries](#a93-binary-tries-for-integer-keys), and
[path copying](#a191-path-copying-trees) first. Persistent means old
in-memory roots remain usable; it does not imply disk durability or
transactions.

##### Mental model

Hash a key once, then read four hash bits at each trie depth. Four
bits select one of 16 logical child slots. A 64-bit hash therefore
supplies at most 16 chunks. This implementation consumes the
least-significant chunk first.

A branch stores two related values:

- A 16-bit bitmap says which logical slots exist.
- A dense child slice stores only those children, in slot order.

For logical slot S, form `bit = 1 << S`. If the bitmap does not
contain that bit, the slot is absent. Otherwise its dense slice
position is:

```text
popcount(bitmap & (bit - 1))
```

`bit - 1` has ones only below slot S. The population count therefore
states how many present children precede S. With logical slots 5 and
12 present, bitmap `0x1020` has two bits but the dense slice has
length 2: slot 5 is at position 0 and slot 12 is at position 1.

A leaf stores one full hash and one or more exact key-value entries.
Usually it has one entry. Distinct keys with the same complete 64-bit
hash share a collision leaf and are distinguished by key comparison.
No collision can create a false lookup result.

Leaves stay shallow until two different hashes need separation. The
trace keys have these first two chunks:

```text
key   hash suffix   depth 0   depth 1
"a"   ...8c         c          8
"q"   ...bc         c          b
"b"   ...a5         5          a
```

Keys `"a"` and `"q"` share root slot `c` and split at the next level.
Key `"b"` uses root slot 5. A put or removal copies only the visited
branches, their dense child slices, and the changed leaf. Every child
outside that path remains pointer-shared with the old root.

##### Worked walkthrough

Starting empty, put `a=1`, `q=2`, and `b=3`. Replace `q` with 20,
branch from the `a=1` version with `b=99`, and remove `a` from the
updated three-key version.

Initial state: the root is nil, size is 0, and entries are `[]`.

1. Decision: put `a=1`. The root is empty, so compute `hash("a")`
   and create one leaf. No branch is needed while the hash is unique.
   After: version one is `[{a 1}]`, with a leaf root and size 1.
   Known correct: the leaf contains exactly the requested key, full
   hash, and value; empty remains unchanged.

2. Decision: put `q=2` into version one. Its full hash differs from
   `a`, but both depth-0 chunks are `c`. Create a root branch whose
   bitmap is `0x1000`, then descend its only child. At depth 1, chunks
   8 and `b` differ, so create a branch with bitmap `0x0900`. Its
   dense children are `[a-leaf,q-leaf]` at positions 0 and 1.
   After: version two is `[{a 1} {q 2}]`; version one's leaf is
   intact.
   Known correct: both paths consume their shared chunk once, then
   choose distinct occupied slots that lead to the exact entries.

3. Decision: put `b=3`. Its first chunk is 5. Root bit 5 is absent;
   `popcount(0x1000 & 0x001f)` is 0, so insert the new leaf at dense
   position 0. Copy the root slice and retain its old slot-`c` child
   at position 1. The new root bitmap is `0x1020`.
   After: version three is `[{a 1} {b 3} {q 2}]`. Version two still
   has only `a` and `q`.

   ```text
   root bitmap slots {5,12}
      +-- slot 5,  dense index 0 -> leaf b=3
      +-- slot 12, dense index 1 -> inner slots {8,11}
                                      +-- 8  -> leaf a=1
                                      +-- 11 -> leaf q=2
   ```

   Known correct: bitmap order agrees with dense order, and the entire
   unchanged `a`/`q` subtrie is shared.

4. Decision: put `q=20` into version three. Root slot `c` maps to
   dense position 1. At the next branch, slot `b` also maps to
   position 1.
   The exact key matches, so create a replacement leaf with value 20.
   Copy the two branch nodes and their child slices on the return
   path; reuse the `a` and `b` leaves.
   After: updated is `[{a 1} {b 3} {q 20}]`; version three still maps
   `q` to 2, and both sizes remain 3.

   ```text
   shared leaves: a=1, b=3

   version three root -> copied-path source -> q=2 leaf
   updated root       -> copied new path     -> q=20 leaf
   ```

   Known correct: only the chosen mapping changed in the new root, and
   every old or off-path node retained its prior contents.

5. Decision: return to version one and put `b=99`. Chunks `c` and 5
   differ immediately, so create a two-child root sharing the old
   `a` leaf and holding one new `b` leaf.
   After: the branch is `[{a 1} {b 99}]`; it contains no `q` mapping.

   ```text
   version one: a=1
      +-- version two: a=1, q=2
      |      +-- version three: a=1, b=3, q=2
      |             +-- updated: a=1, b=3, q=20
      |
      +-- branch: a=1, b=99
   ```

   Known correct: an old version accepted an independent update, so
   version history can branch rather than only move forward.

6. Decision: remove `a` from updated. Follow root slot `c`, then inner
   slot 8 at dense position 0. Delete the `a` leaf. The inner branch
   now has only the `q` leaf, so collapse it to that leaf. Copy the
   root with its `b` leaf and new `q` child.
   After: removal returns true and `[{b 3} {q 20}]`. Updated remains
   `[{a 1} {b 3} {q 20}]`.
   Known correct: one exact key disappeared, empty paths were pruned,
   and no surviving mapping or historical version changed.

7. Decision: get `q` through version three and updated. Both hashes
   choose chunks `c,b`; their terminal leaves hold values 2 and 20.
   After: the lookups return `2,true` and `20,true` without mutation.
   Known correct: a version root selects the mapping visible at that
   point in history even when most nodes are shared.

8. Decision: put `q=20` into updated. The exact leaf already stores
   20, so return the same root while recursion unwinds. Remove missing
   key `"missing"`; its first absent bit proves failure, so again
   return the same root.
   After: root identity checks are true; missing removal returns
   false, and the program stops.
   Known correct: both no-op paths preserve size, allocate no copied
   path, and leave every version unchanged.

Focused collision case: tests force distinct keys `"first"` and
`"second"` to use hash `0x1234`. Both occupy one collision leaf, exact
lookup finds each, and removing one retains the other.

Counterexample to indexing the dense slice by logical slot: after step
3, root slot 12 is dense position 1, not index 12. Reading child 12
would panic or select unrelated storage. The first wrong decision is
ignoring that the bitmap compresses absent slots; population count is
the required conversion.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. It uses only the standard library.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Versioned maps. Function comments
// connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math/bits"
	"sort"
)

const mapChunkBits = 4

const mapChunkLevels = 64 / mapChunkBits

const mapChunkMask uint64 = (1 << mapChunkBits) - 1

type versionedMapEntry struct {
	key   string
	value int
}

type versionedMapNode struct {
	hash     uint64
	entries  []versionedMapEntry
	bitmap   uint16
	children []*versionedMapNode
}

type versionedMap struct {
	root *versionedMapNode
	size int
}

func hashString(key string) uint64 {
	// Follow the lookup rule for string without changing state.
	const offsetBasis uint64 = 14695981039346656037
	const prime uint64 = 1099511628211
	hash := offsetBasis
	for byteIndex := 0; byteIndex < len(key); byteIndex++ {
		hash ^= uint64(key[byteIndex])
		hash *= prime
	}
	return hash
}

func hashChunk(hash uint64, depth int) uint16 {
	// Follow the lookup rule for chunk without changing state.
	shift := uint(depth * mapChunkBits)
	return uint16((hash >> shift) & mapChunkMask)
}

func childPosition(bitmap uint16, childBit uint16) int {
	// Bits below this slot count its dense-array predecessors.
	earlierBits := bitmap & (childBit - 1)
	return bits.OnesCount16(earlierBits)
}

func newVersionedMapLeaf(
	hash uint64,
	key string,
	value int,
) *versionedMapNode {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial versioned map leaf
	// state.
	return &versionedMapNode{
		hash: hash,
		entries: []versionedMapEntry{{
			key:   key,
			value: value,
		}},
	}
}

func mergeVersionedMapLeaves(
	first *versionedMapNode,
	second *versionedMapNode,
	depth int,
) *versionedMapNode {
	// Combine compatible parts while preserving their invariant.
	if depth >= mapChunkLevels {
		panic("different hashes exhausted every chunk")
	}
	firstSlot := hashChunk(first.hash, depth)
	secondSlot := hashChunk(second.hash, depth)
	firstBit := uint16(1) << firstSlot
	secondBit := uint16(1) << secondSlot
	if firstSlot == secondSlot {
		child := mergeVersionedMapLeaves(
			first,
			second,
			depth+1,
		)
		return &versionedMapNode{
			bitmap:   firstBit,
			children: []*versionedMapNode{child},
		}
	}

	children := []*versionedMapNode{first, second}
	if secondSlot < firstSlot {
		children[0], children[1] = children[1], children[0]
	}
	return &versionedMapNode{
		bitmap:   firstBit | secondBit,
		children: children,
	}
}

func insertVersionedMapChild(
	children []*versionedMapNode,
	position int,
	child *versionedMapNode,
) []*versionedMapNode {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	result := make([]*versionedMapNode, len(children)+1)
	copy(result, children[:position])
	result[position] = child
	copy(result[position+1:], children[position:])
	return result
}

func replaceVersionedMapChild(
	children []*versionedMapNode,
	position int,
	child *versionedMapNode,
) []*versionedMapNode {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	result := append([]*versionedMapNode(nil), children...)
	result[position] = child
	return result
}

func putVersionedMapNode(
	node *versionedMapNode,
	depth int,
	hash uint64,
	key string,
	value int,
) (*versionedMapNode, bool, bool) {
	// Add versioned map node while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	if node == nil {
		return newVersionedMapLeaf(hash, key, value), true, true
	}
	if node.entries != nil {
		if node.hash != hash {
			newLeaf := newVersionedMapLeaf(hash, key, value)
			return mergeVersionedMapLeaves(
				node,
				newLeaf,
				depth,
			), true, true
		}
		for entryIndex, entry := range node.entries {
			if entry.key != key {
				continue
			}
			if entry.value == value {
				return node, false, false
			}
			entries := append(
				[]versionedMapEntry(nil),
				node.entries...,
			)
			entries[entryIndex].value = value
			return &versionedMapNode{
				hash:    hash,
				entries: entries,
			}, false, true
		}

		entries := make(
			[]versionedMapEntry,
			len(node.entries)+1,
		)
		copy(entries, node.entries)
		entries[len(node.entries)] = versionedMapEntry{
			key:   key,
			value: value,
		}
		return &versionedMapNode{
			hash:    hash,
			entries: entries,
		}, true, true
	}

	slot := hashChunk(hash, depth)
	childBit := uint16(1) << slot
	position := childPosition(node.bitmap, childBit)
	if node.bitmap&childBit == 0 {
		newChild := newVersionedMapLeaf(hash, key, value)
		return &versionedMapNode{
			bitmap: node.bitmap | childBit,
			children: insertVersionedMapChild(
				node.children,
				position,
				newChild,
			),
		}, true, true
	}

	newChild, added, changed := putVersionedMapNode(
		node.children[position],
		depth+1,
		hash,
		key,
		value,
	)
	if !changed {
		return node, false, false
	}
	return &versionedMapNode{
		bitmap: node.bitmap,
		children: replaceVersionedMapChild(
			node.children,
			position,
			newChild,
		),
	}, added, true
}

func (version versionedMap) put(
	key string,
	value int,
) versionedMap {
	// Add the requested item while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	hash := hashString(key)
	newRoot, added, changed := putVersionedMapNode(
		version.root,
		0,
		hash,
		key,
		value,
	)
	if !changed {
		return version
	}
	newSize := version.size
	if added {
		newSize++
	}
	return versionedMap{root: newRoot, size: newSize}
}

func getVersionedMapNode(
	node *versionedMapNode,
	depth int,
	hash uint64,
	key string,
) (int, bool) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for versioned map node without changing
	// state.
	for node != nil {
		if node.entries != nil {
			if node.hash != hash {
				return 0, false
			}
			for _, entry := range node.entries {
				if entry.key == key {
					return entry.value, true
				}
			}
			return 0, false
		}

		slot := hashChunk(hash, depth)
		childBit := uint16(1) << slot
		if node.bitmap&childBit == 0 {
			return 0, false
		}
		position := childPosition(node.bitmap, childBit)
		node = node.children[position]
		depth++
	}
	return 0, false
}

func (version versionedMap) get(key string) (int, bool) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for the requested item without changing
	// state.
	return getVersionedMapNode(
		version.root,
		0,
		hashString(key),
		key,
	)
}

func removeVersionedMapChild(
	children []*versionedMapNode,
	position int,
) []*versionedMapNode {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	result := make([]*versionedMapNode, len(children)-1)
	copy(result, children[:position])
	copy(result[position:], children[position+1:])
	return result
}

func removeVersionedMapNode(
	node *versionedMapNode,
	depth int,
	hash uint64,
	key string,
) (*versionedMapNode, bool) {
	// Remove versioned map node while preserving the remaining
	// representation.
	if node == nil {
		return nil, false
	}
	if node.entries != nil {
		if node.hash != hash {
			return node, false
		}
		entryIndex := -1
		for index, entry := range node.entries {
			if entry.key == key {
				entryIndex = index
				break
			}
		}
		if entryIndex == -1 {
			return node, false
		}
		if len(node.entries) == 1 {
			return nil, true
		}

		entries := make(
			[]versionedMapEntry,
			len(node.entries)-1,
		)
		copy(entries, node.entries[:entryIndex])
		copy(entries[entryIndex:], node.entries[entryIndex+1:])
		return &versionedMapNode{
			hash:    hash,
			entries: entries,
		}, true
	}

	slot := hashChunk(hash, depth)
	childBit := uint16(1) << slot
	if node.bitmap&childBit == 0 {
		return node, false
	}
	position := childPosition(node.bitmap, childBit)
	newChild, removed := removeVersionedMapNode(
		node.children[position],
		depth+1,
		hash,
		key,
	)
	if !removed {
		return node, false
	}

	if newChild != nil {
		if len(node.children) == 1 && newChild.entries != nil {
			return newChild, true
		}
		return &versionedMapNode{
			bitmap: node.bitmap,
			children: replaceVersionedMapChild(
				node.children,
				position,
				newChild,
			),
		}, true
	}
	if len(node.children) == 1 {
		return nil, true
	}

	children := removeVersionedMapChild(
		node.children,
		position,
	)
	if len(children) == 1 && children[0].entries != nil {
		return children[0], true
	}
	return &versionedMapNode{
		bitmap:   node.bitmap &^ childBit,
		children: children,
	}, true
}

func (version versionedMap) remove(
	key string,
) (versionedMap, bool) {
	// Remove the requested item while preserving the remaining
	// representation.
	newRoot, removed := removeVersionedMapNode(
		version.root,
		0,
		hashString(key),
		key,
	)
	if !removed {
		return version, false
	}
	return versionedMap{
		root: newRoot,
		size: version.size - 1,
	}, true
}

func (version versionedMap) entriesByKey() []versionedMapEntry {
	// Keep entries by key in one helper so callers use one rule.
	entries := make([]versionedMapEntry, 0, version.size)
	var collect func(*versionedMapNode)
	collect = func(node *versionedMapNode) {
		if node == nil {
			return
		}
		if node.entries != nil {
			entries = append(entries, node.entries...)
			return
		}
		for _, child := range node.children {
			collect(child)
		}
	}
	collect(version.root)
	sort.Slice(entries, func(first int, second int) bool {
		return entries[first].key < entries[second].key
	})
	return entries
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	var empty versionedMap
	versionOne := empty.put("a", 1)
	versionTwo := versionOne.put("q", 2)
	versionThree := versionTwo.put("b", 3)
	updated := versionThree.put("q", 20)
	branch := versionOne.put("b", 99)
	withoutA, removed := updated.remove("a")

	fmt.Println(versionOne.entriesByKey())
	fmt.Println(versionThree.entriesByKey())
	fmt.Println(updated.entriesByKey())
	fmt.Println(branch.entriesByKey())
	fmt.Println(removed, withoutA.entriesByKey())
	oldValue, oldOK := versionThree.get("q")
	newValue, newOK := updated.get("q")
	fmt.Println(oldValue, oldOK, newValue, newOK)
	same := updated.put("q", 20)
	fmt.Println(same.root == updated.root)
	missing, removed := updated.remove("missing")
	fmt.Println(removed, missing.root == updated.root)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[{a 1}]
[{a 1} {b 3} {q 2}]
[{a 1} {b 3} {q 20}]
[{a 1} {b 99}]
true [{b 3} {q 20}]
2 true 20 true
true
false true
```

##### Why it works

Maintain three representation facts. Every branch bitmap has one set
bit per child, its child slice is ordered by logical slot, and its
length equals the bitmap population count. Every leaf entry has the
leaf's full hash, and keys within a collision leaf are unique.
Finally, no published node or backing slice is ever modified.

The empty root satisfies all three facts. Lookup consumes one chunk
at each branch. A zero bitmap bit proves the requested hash path is
absent.
For a one bit, counting earlier bits gives exactly the dense position
because the slice contains precisely those earlier occupied slots.
At a leaf, full-hash and exact-key comparison proves presence or
absence even when two keys collide.

Putting into nil creates one valid leaf. A different hash is separated
at the first differing chunk; different 64-bit hashes must differ
within 16 chunks. A same-hash key either replaces its own copied entry
or joins the finite collision bucket. As recursion returns, every new
branch replaces one child in a newly allocated slice and preserves
the other ordered children. A same mapping returns the old nodes
unchanged.

Removal follows the same unique hash path. Removing a collision entry
copies the remaining entries. Removing the last leaf clears its branch
bit and dense child together. Empty branches disappear; a branch with
one leaf may collapse because the leaf checks its complete hash and no
longer needs the skipped chunk positions. Surviving entries and bitmap
positions remain consistent.

Because updates write only new nodes and slices, an old root reaches
exactly its old graph. The reasoning does not depend on choosing the
newest root, so any version can be queried or updated. This
establishes full persistence.

Recursion advances one of at most 16 hash chunks, then scans a finite
collision bucket. Traversal visits a finite node graph, and sorting
handles a finite output slice. Every operation therefore terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let L be the key length in bytes, D = 16 the maximum trie depth,
B = 16 the branch width, C the matching full-hash collision-bucket
size, and N the entry count in one version.

Hashing takes Theta(L) time. After that, get visits at most D branches
and scans at most C collision entries, for O(L + D + C) time and O(1)
auxiliary space. Under a well-distributed 64-bit hash, C is normally
constant, so expected time is O(L). If N distinct keys share one full
hash, worst-case lookup is O(L + N).

Put and remove perform the same search and use O(D) recursion space.
A changed update copies at most D nodes and, at each branch, at most B
child pointers. It may also copy C collision entries. Its time and
new retained storage are O(L + D*B + C). Since D and B are fixed here,
the usual expected bound is O(L), but hash computation and allocation
remain real costs. A same-value put or missing removal allocates no
nodes after its search.

Across K retained versions, total storage is the first root's graph,
K handles, and every copied path still reachable from those roots.
Sharing prevents a full O(N) clone per edit, but frequently updated
paths and long-lived old roots still retain memory until collection.

`entriesByKey` visits O(N) leaves and entries, then
comparison-sorts the result in O(N log N) time. It uses O(N)
caller-owned output space,
O(D) traversal stack space, and the sorting routine's bounded internal
stack. Sorting affects only the new output slice, never trie storage.

This 16-way design favors visible arithmetic. Production HAMTs often
use 32-way nodes, pack entries beside children, cache hashes, provide
temporary mutable builders, or use CHAMP layouts for better locality.
A persistent ordered tree costs logarithmic comparisons but supports
sorted traversal and range queries without a final sort.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty get and remove return zero/false and the unchanged nil root.
  Empty `entriesByKey` returns a non-nil empty caller-owned slice.
- Key `""` is valid and hashes its zero bytes from the offset basis.
  Treating empty as a missing sentinel would lose a real mapping.
- Stored value 0 returns `0,true`; missing returns `0,false`. Ignoring
  the boolean confuses data with absence.
- Replacing `q=2` with `q=20` keeps size 3. Incrementing on every put
  would make size disagree with reachable entries.
- Putting `q=20` again returns the exact old root. Copying a no-op
  path is correct by value but wastes memory and violates this
  contract.
- Different keys may have the same full hash. Comparing only hashes
  overwrites one key or reports false presence; collision leaves must
  compare exact keys.
- Slot 0 uses bit 1, so `bit - 1` is zero and its dense position is 0.
  Counting the selected bit too creates an off-by-one index.
- A branch update must allocate a new child slice. Appending into
  spare capacity of a shared slice can mutate an older version
  invisibly.
- Removal must clear the bitmap bit and dense child at the same
  logical slot. Updating only one makes every later dense position
  incorrect.
- A one-child branch can collapse only when its child is a leaf.
  Dropping a branch above another branch would skip a hash depth and
  route later lookups with the wrong chunk.
- Equivalent-looking Unicode strings with different byte encodings are
  different keys. Normalize before put when the application requires
  canonical text equivalence.
- FNV-1a is deterministic but not collision-resistant. Use a seeded,
  adversarially appropriate hash at untrusted boundaries; every
  version must nevertheless use one consistent algorithm and seed.
- A generic map with slice, map, or pointer values needs a payload
  ownership rule. Immutable trie nodes do not freeze referenced data.
- Concurrent reads need safe root publication. This structure provides
  neither synchronized writes nor process-crash durability.

##### When to choose it

Choose a persistent HAMT when keyed lookup, replacement, deletion,
snapshots, and branching versions all matter, while sorted order does
not. Configuration states, compiler environments, undo histories, and
speculative computations often reuse most mappings between versions.

Use Go's mutable map when only the latest state matters; it avoids the
copied-node and version-lifetime overhead. Clone a whole map when maps
are tiny and simplicity dominates. Use an overlay change log when
writes are frequent but historical reads are rare enough to tolerate
replay or periodic compaction.

Use a persistent balanced search tree when range queries,
predecessor, or ordered iteration matter. Use a database's
multi-version concurrency control when versions need transactions,
cross-process coordination, retention policy, and durable recovery;
an in-memory HAMT supplies none of those operational guarantees.

The [hash-table lesson](#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing)
owns ordinary collision and load-factor behavior. The [path-copying
lesson](#a191-path-copying-trees) owns the general immutable-update
proof. The next [rank/select lesson](
#a201-rank-and-select-bit-vectors) uses bitmap population counts for a
different purpose.

Bagwell's original [Ideal Hash Trees](
https://lampwww.epfl.ch/papers/idealhashtrees.pdf) introduces HAMTs,
progressive hash-bit traversal, bitmap-compressed child arrays, and
population-count indexing. This lesson adds immutable path copying,
finite 64-bit collision buckets, and version handles to that core.

### A.20 Succinct and specialized structures (advanced)

#### A.20.1 Rank and select bit vectors

##### Problem and contract

A packed bit vector answers whether one position is 0 or 1. Some
algorithms also need to translate between positions and occurrence
numbers. Repeatedly scanning from the beginning wastes the same
counting work on every query.

For a static string of N ASCII bits, `rank(bitValue,end)` counts the
chosen bit in the half-open prefix `[0,end)`. The chosen bit is 1 when
`bitValue` is true and 0 when it is false. Valid ends satisfy
`0 <= end <= N`; an invalid end returns an error.

`selectBit(bitValue,ordinal)` returns the position of the occurrence
whose zero-based number is `ordinal`. A negative or missing ordinal
returns `(-1,false)`. For example, in `10110`, the 1 bits are at
positions `[0,2,3]`, so selecting 1 occurrence 1 returns position 2.
For every valid occurrence k, this convention makes rank and select
agree:

```text
rank(true, selectBit(true, k) + 1) = k + 1
```

Construction accepts only bytes `'0'` and `'1'`. Malformed input
returns no index. Empty input is valid. The constructor copies bits
into owned words, exposes no slices, and the finished index never
mutates. Read-only queries are safe concurrently after safe pointer
publication. Queries require a non-nil pointer returned by the
constructor; a zero index is not initialized. Copying an initialized
index value would share immutable slices and is safe.

This lesson implements a practical sampled index, not a formally
succinct one. A succinct rank/select representation stores an
arbitrary N-bit vector plus only `o(N)` extra bits, meaning the extra
space becomes a vanishing fraction of N. Fixed 512-bit sampling in Go
has small constant overhead but still uses `O(N)` extra bits
asymptotically.

Read [packed bit vectors](#a131-packed-bit-vectors), [multiword bit
sets](#a132-multiword-bit-sets), and [prefix sums](
#a121-prefix-sum-arrays) first. They own the packing, padding, and
prefix-count ideas reused here.

##### Mental model

Rank is a prefix-count query. Store the total number of 1 bits before
each 512-bit superblock. A superblock contains eight 64-bit words.
To count 1 bits before `end`:

1. Jump to the stored count before `end`'s superblock.
2. Population-count, or count the 1 bits in, each complete word before
   `end` in that block.
3. Mask and count only the low bits before `end` in its final word.

At most seven complete words and one partial word are counted after
the jump. Zero rank needs no second directory: among `end` positions,
`end - rank1(end)` positions are zero.

Select reverses that question. Binary-search the superblock ending
counts for the first block containing the requested occurrence.
Subtract the count before that block, scan its at most eight words,
then locate the remaining set bit inside one word. For zero select,
complement the word and immediately mask away padding beyond N.

Index i is stored at bit `i % 64` of word `i / 64`, with lower logical
indices in lower word bits. This makes population count over a low-bit
mask equal the number of chosen positions in a logical prefix.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build this 517-bit input:

```text
"1011010010" + 502 zero bits + "10101"
```

Its 1 positions are `[0,2,3,5,8,512,514,516]`. Query both ranks at
end 515, select 1 occurrence 6, select 0 occurrence 507, then try a
missing occurrence and malformed inputs.

Initial state: no words or directory exist. The input length is 517,
and all query results are unresolved.

1. Decision: pack positions 0 through 511 into words 0 through 7.
   The first ten characters set offsets 0, 2, 3, 5, and 8 in word 0,
   giving `0x12d`; the following 502 zeros leave words 1 through 7
   clear. Pack the final `10101` into offsets 0, 2, and 4 of word 8,
   giving `0x15`.
   After: there are nine words; unused high bits of word 8 are zero.
   Known correct: every input position has the same logical index as
   its packed word and offset, and no padding bit represents input.

2. Decision: build counts at 512-bit boundaries. Before superblock 0
   the count is 0. Its eight words contain 5 ones, so the count before
   superblock 1 is 5. Word 8 adds 3, so store terminal count 8.
   After: the directory is `[0,5,8]`.
   Known correct: entry j counts all ones before superblock j, and the
   terminal entry counts every one in the vector.

3. Decision: rank 1 at ends 0 and 517. End 0 uses directory count 0
   and no word bits. End 517 starts with 5, then counts all five valid
   bits of word 8 and adds 3.
   After: the ranks are 0 and 8.
   Known correct: the empty and full half-open prefixes obey the same
   boundary rule.

4. Decision: rank at end 515. This end is in superblock 1 and word 8.
   Start from 5, then mask local offsets `[0,3)`, whose bits are `101`
   and contain 2 ones. Thus 1 rank is 7; zero rank is `515 - 7 = 508`.
   After: return 7 for ones and 508 for zeros.
   Known correct: these counts cover exactly positions `[0,515)` and
   exclude positions 515 and 516.

5. Decision: select 1 occurrence 6. Superblock 0 ends with only 5
   ones, while superblock 1 ends with 8, so the target is in block 1.
   Subtract its starting count: `6 - 5 = 1`, the second local one.
   Word 8 is `10101`; clear its lowest set bit, then the next lowest
   set bit is offset 2.
   After: return global position `512 + 2 = 514` and true.
   Known correct: exactly six 1 bits precede position 514, and that
   position is also 1.

6. Decision: select 0 occurrence 507. Before position 512 there are
   `512 - 5 = 507` zeros, so the target is the first zero in block 1.
   Complement word 8 and mask to its five valid bits, producing local
   candidates `01010`; the first is offset 1.
   After: return position 513 and true.
   Known correct: exactly 507 zeros precede position 513, and padding
   played no part in the search.

7. Decision: select 1 occurrence 8. The terminal count is 8, so valid
   ordinals stop at 7. Reject before searching. Rank end 518 exceeds
   N, and constructor input `10x` contains an invalid byte at index 2.
   After: select returns `-1,false`; both invalid inputs return
   errors.
   Known correct: failed operations expose no partial result or index,
   and the immutable valid index remains unchanged.

Focused empty case: an empty vector has no words and directory `[0]`.
Both ranks at end 0 return 0, while every select returns `-1,false`.

Counterexample to complementing without a tail mask: a 65-bit
all-zero vector has one valid bit in its second word. Raw complement
makes its 63 padding bits look selectable, so zero occurrence 65 would
incorrectly return position 65. Masking to the one valid bit proves
that ordinal 65 is missing.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. It uses only the standard library.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Rank and select bit vectors.
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math/bits"
	"sort"
	"strings"
)

const bitsPerRankWord = 64
const wordsPerRankSuperblock = 8

type rankSelectBitVector struct {
	length                   int
	words                    []uint64
	onesBeforeEachSuperblock []int
}

func lowBitMask(bitCount int) uint64 {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	if bitCount == bitsPerRankWord {
		return ^uint64(0)
	}
	if bitCount == 0 {
		return 0
	}
	return (uint64(1) << bitCount) - 1
}

func newRankSelectBitVector(
	bitString string,
) (*rankSelectBitVector, error) {
	// Relate the key to its position in sorted order.
	wordCount := len(bitString) / bitsPerRankWord
	if len(bitString)%bitsPerRankWord != 0 {
		wordCount++
	}
	words := make([]uint64, wordCount)
	for bitIndex := 0; bitIndex < len(bitString); bitIndex++ {
		switch bitString[bitIndex] {
		case '0':
			continue
		case '1':
			wordIndex := bitIndex / bitsPerRankWord
			bitOffset := bitIndex % bitsPerRankWord
			words[wordIndex] |= uint64(1) << bitOffset
		default:
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"bit %d is %q; want '0' or '1'",
				bitIndex,
				bitString[bitIndex],
			)
		}
	}

	superblockCount := wordCount / wordsPerRankSuperblock
	if wordCount%wordsPerRankSuperblock != 0 {
		superblockCount++
	}
	onesBefore := make([]int, superblockCount+1)
	runningOnes := 0
	superblockIndex := 0
	for superblockIndex < superblockCount {
		onesBefore[superblockIndex] = runningOnes
		firstWord := superblockIndex * wordsPerRankSuperblock
		lastWord := firstWord + wordsPerRankSuperblock
		if lastWord > len(words) {
			lastWord = len(words)
		}
		for wordIndex := firstWord; wordIndex < lastWord; wordIndex++ {
			runningOnes += bits.OnesCount64(words[wordIndex])
		}
		superblockIndex++
	}
	onesBefore[superblockCount] = runningOnes

	return &rankSelectBitVector{
		length:                   len(bitString),
		words:                    words,
		onesBeforeEachSuperblock: onesBefore,
	}, nil
}

func (vector *rankSelectBitVector) validateEnd(end int) error {
	// Reject input outside the end contract before mutation.
	if end < 0 || end > vector.length {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"end %d is outside [0, %d]",
			end,
			vector.length,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func (vector *rankSelectBitVector) rank(
	bitValue bool,
	end int,
) (int, error) {
	// Relate the key to its position in sorted order.
	if err := vector.validateEnd(end); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	wordIndex := end / bitsPerRankWord
	superblockIndex := wordIndex / wordsPerRankSuperblock
	ones := vector.onesBeforeEachSuperblock[superblockIndex]
	firstWord := superblockIndex * wordsPerRankSuperblock
	scannedWord := firstWord
	for scannedWord < wordIndex {
		ones += bits.OnesCount64(vector.words[scannedWord])
		scannedWord++
	}
	bitsInPartialWord := end % bitsPerRankWord
	if bitsInPartialWord != 0 {
		partialMask := lowBitMask(bitsInPartialWord)
		ones += bits.OnesCount64(
			vector.words[wordIndex] & partialMask,
		)
	}
	if bitValue {
		return ones, nil
	}
	return end - ones, nil
}

func (vector *rankSelectBitVector) bitsBeforeSuperblock(
	superblockIndex int,
) int {
	// Keep bits before superblock in one helper so callers use one rule.
	firstWord := superblockIndex * wordsPerRankSuperblock
	// A terminal sample may follow the final partial superblock.
	if firstWord >= len(vector.words) {
		return vector.length
	}
	return firstWord * bitsPerRankWord
}

func (vector *rankSelectBitVector) countBeforeSuperblock(
	bitValue bool,
	superblockIndex int,
) int {
	// Compute before superblock from the state without mutating it.
	ones := vector.onesBeforeEachSuperblock[superblockIndex]
	if bitValue {
		return ones
	}
	return vector.bitsBeforeSuperblock(superblockIndex) - ones
}

func (vector *rankSelectBitVector) validWordMask(
	wordIndex int,
) uint64 {
	// Evaluate valid word mask without changing the maintained state.
	firstBit := wordIndex * bitsPerRankWord
	validBitCount := vector.length - firstBit
	if validBitCount > bitsPerRankWord {
		validBitCount = bitsPerRankWord
	}
	return lowBitMask(validBitCount)
}

func selectedBits(
	word uint64,
	validMask uint64,
	bitValue bool,
) uint64 {
	// Narrow candidates until the requested ordered item remains.
	if bitValue {
		return word & validMask
	}
	return ^word & validMask
}

func selectSetBit(word uint64, ordinal int) int {
	// Each clear removes the lowest remaining selected position.
	for skipped := 0; skipped < ordinal; skipped++ {
		word &= word - 1
	}
	return bits.TrailingZeros64(word)
}

func (vector *rankSelectBitVector) selectBit(
	bitValue bool,
	ordinal int,
) (int, bool) {
	// Narrow candidates until the requested ordered item remains.
	if ordinal < 0 {
		return -1, false
	}
	superblockCount :=
		len(vector.onesBeforeEachSuperblock) - 1
	totalCount := vector.countBeforeSuperblock(
		bitValue,
		superblockCount,
	)
	if ordinal >= totalCount {
		return -1, false
	}

	// Find the first superblock whose ending prefix owns the target.
	superblockIndex := sort.Search(
		superblockCount,
		func(candidate int) bool {
			endingCount := vector.countBeforeSuperblock(
				bitValue,
				candidate+1,
			)
			return endingCount > ordinal
		},
	)
	remaining := ordinal - vector.countBeforeSuperblock(
		bitValue,
		superblockIndex,
	)
	firstWord := superblockIndex * wordsPerRankSuperblock
	lastWord := firstWord + wordsPerRankSuperblock
	if lastWord > len(vector.words) {
		lastWord = len(vector.words)
	}
	for wordIndex := firstWord; wordIndex < lastWord; wordIndex++ {
		candidates := selectedBits(
			vector.words[wordIndex],
			vector.validWordMask(wordIndex),
			bitValue,
		)
		wordCount := bits.OnesCount64(candidates)
		if remaining >= wordCount {
			remaining -= wordCount
			continue
		}
		bitOffset := selectSetBit(candidates, remaining)
		return wordIndex*bitsPerRankWord + bitOffset, true
	}
	panic("rank/select directory disagrees with packed words")
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	bitString := "1011010010" +
		strings.Repeat("0", 502) +
		"10101"
	vector, err := newRankSelectBitVector(bitString)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}

	fmt.Println(vector.length, len(vector.words))
	fmt.Printf("%#x %#x\n", vector.words[0], vector.words[8])
	fmt.Println(vector.onesBeforeEachSuperblock)
	onesAtZero, err := vector.rank(true, 0)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	onesAtEnd, err := vector.rank(true, vector.length)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(onesAtZero, onesAtEnd)
	ones, err := vector.rank(true, 515)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	zeros, err := vector.rank(false, 515)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(ones, zeros)
	onePosition, oneFound := vector.selectBit(true, 6)
	fmt.Println(onePosition, oneFound)
	zeroPosition, zeroFound := vector.selectBit(false, 507)
	fmt.Println(zeroPosition, zeroFound)
	missingPosition, missingFound := vector.selectBit(true, 8)
	fmt.Println(missingPosition, missingFound)

	_, invalidEndErr := vector.rank(true, 518)
	fmt.Println(invalidEndErr)
	_, invalidBitErr := newRankSelectBitVector("10x")
	fmt.Println(invalidBitErr)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
517 9
0x12d 0x15
[0 5 8]
0 8
7 508
514 true
513 true
-1 false
end 518 is outside [0, 517]
bit 2 is 'x'; want '0' or '1'
```

##### Why it works

Maintain three facts. Word bit `i % 64` equals logical bit i in word
`i / 64`. Every directory entry equals the number of 1 bits before
its superblock. Every padding bit after N is zero and is excluded by
the final-word mask.

Packing establishes the first and third facts. Directory construction
starts with zero before the first block and adds every word's exact
population count before recording the next boundary. Induction over
superblocks therefore establishes the second fact, including the
terminal total.

A rank query begins with the exact count before its block. Complete
word counts cover the next disjoint 64-bit ranges, and the low-bit
mask covers exactly the remaining range before end. Their union is
`[0,end)`, with no overlap. Subtracting one rank from end counts every
other position, so zero rank is also exact.

For select, prefix counts never decrease. The first superblock whose
ending count exceeds ordinal must contain that occurrence; all prior
blocks contain too few. Subtracting the starting count gives its local
ordinal. Skipping whole-word counts preserves that ordinal among the
remaining words. Clearing one lowest selected bit per skipped local
occurrence leaves the requested one lowest, so trailing-zero count
returns its offset. Tail masking prevents padding from entering this
argument for zero select.

Construction loops over finite input, words, and superblocks. Rank
scans at most eight words. Select's binary search shrinks a finite
range, its word scan has at most eight iterations, and its bit loop
has at most 63. Every operation terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be logical bit count, W = ceil(N/64) packed words, and
S = ceil(W/8) superblocks. Construction reads N input bytes and W
words, taking Theta(N) time. It retains W 64-bit words and S + 1 Go
`int` counts.

Rank reads one directory entry and population-counts at most eight
words. With fixed 64-bit words and 512-bit superblocks, it takes
Theta(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space. This includes zero rank,
which performs one subtraction.

A successful select binary-searches S superblocks, scans at most eight
words, and clears at most 63 set bits in one word. It takes
O(log S) time and O(1) auxiliary space. A negative or out-of-range
ordinal fails in Theta(1) time after reading the terminal total.

The packed payload uses `64*W` bits, at most 63 more than N. On a
64-bit Go target, one eight-byte directory count per 512 payload bits
adds about 12.5 percent for a large vector, plus one terminal count
and slice headers. Because that ratio is constant, this executable
index is compact but not formally succinct.

Theoretical directories can support rank and select in O(1) word-RAM
time with `o(N)` extra bits, but need more levels, lookup tables, or
specialized broadword code. This example favors a locally auditable
bridge from prefix counts to those structures.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input builds no words and directory `[0]`. Only rank end 0 is
  valid; all selects return `-1,false` without binary search.
- End 0 counts an empty prefix, while end N counts the full vector.
  Treating end as inclusive makes every nonempty rank off by one.
- Select ordinals are zero-based. In `10110`, ordinal 1 names the
  second 1 at position 2, not the first one at position 0.
- All-zero input has no selectable 1; all-one input has no selectable
  0. Check the terminal total before searching.
- A final partial word contains padding. Complementing it for zero
  select without `validWordMask` returns nonexistent positions.
- Lengths 64, 512, and their multiples end exactly at word or block
  boundaries. Do not index a nonexistent partial word when its size
  is zero.
- Malformed input such as `10x` returns no index. Treating every byte
  other than `'1'` as zero silently accepts corrupted data.
- Directory entries count bits before a block. Mixing that boundary
  convention with an inclusive prefix double-counts its first word.
- The structure is static. Mutating a packed word without rebuilding
  later directory totals makes rank and select disagree.
- Go strings are byte sequences. This constructor accepts ASCII bit
  bytes, not Unicode digits or textual separators.
- Returning internal word or directory slices would let callers break
  immutability and query safety. Keep them private or return copies.

##### When to choose it

Choose a rank/select bit vector when a static Boolean sequence is
queried often in both directions: "how many marked positions precede
this boundary?" and "where is marked occurrence k?" Succinct trees,
FM-indexes, wavelet trees, and compressed integer encodings use these
translations as navigation primitives.

Use a plain packed bit set when membership and population count are
enough. Use a prefix count per position when memory is unimportant and
the simplest O(1) rank is preferable. For a sparse set of K positions,
store sorted positions: select is direct and rank is a binary search,
using O(K) machine words rather than N bits.

Use a Fenwick or segment tree when bits change between queries; this
static directory otherwise needs rebuilding. Compressed bitmap
formats are often better for very sparse or clustered large universes.
Use a production succinct library when `N + o(N)` space or constant
time select is a requirement rather than an educational goal.

The [multiword bit-set lesson](#a132-multiword-bit-sets) owns packing
and tail masks. The [prefix-sum lesson](#a121-prefix-sum-arrays) owns
the boundary-count invariant. The next [wavelet-tree lesson](
#a202-wavelet-trees) uses rank to translate a range between levels.

Jacobson's [Space-efficient static trees and graphs](
https://doi.org/10.1109/SFCS.1989.63533) develops rank/select
directories with sublinear extra bits. Kurpicz's [Engineering Compact
Data Structures for Rank and Select Queries on Bit Vectors](
https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.01149) states the modern half-open rank
definition and studies practical directory tradeoffs. Raman, Raman,
and Rao's [Succinct Indexable Dictionaries](
https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.0552) gives constant-time rank/select under
near-information-theoretic space bounds for indexable dictionaries.

#### A.20.2 Wavelet trees

##### Problem and contract

Suppose a static integer sequence must answer three different kinds
of question: read the value at one position, count a value in a
prefix, and find the k-th smallest value inside a subrange. Keeping
the original slice gives constant-time access, but rank scans a prefix
and range selection repeatedly scans or sorts overlapping values.

This lesson builds a balanced wavelet tree over a copied sequence.
`access(index)` returns the value at zero-based index `index`.
`rank(value,end)` counts occurrences of `value` in the half-open
prefix `[0,end)`; a value absent from the alphabet has rank zero.

`kthSmallest(start,end,ordinal)` examines `[start,end)` and counts
duplicates separately. Its ordinal is zero-based: ordinal 0 returns
the minimum, and ordinal `end-start-1` returns the maximum. Invalid
indices, ends, ranges, and ordinals return errors. Empty construction
is valid, but empty ranges contain no selectable ordinal. Zero is a
valid stored value, so callers must inspect query errors.

Every Go `int` value is valid, including duplicates, negatives, and
the minimum and maximum integers. Construction neither mutates nor
retains the input slice. The tree owns its alphabet and prefix arrays,
exposes no mutable storage, and never changes after construction.
Read-only queries are safe after safe pointer publication. Queries
require a non-nil pointer returned by `newWaveletTree`; a zero tree is
not initialized. Copying an initialized tree value would share only
immutable nodes and slices and is safe.

This teaching version stores one `int` prefix count per routing bit.
It demonstrates wavelet-tree navigation but is not compressed. A
production succinct wavelet tree replaces those arrays with packed
rank/select bit vectors.

Read [prefix sums](#a121-prefix-sum-arrays) and [rank/select bit
vectors](#a201-rank-and-select-bit-vectors) first. The rank/select
lesson owns half-open bit-prefix translation; this lesson applies that
translation at every alphabet level.

##### Mental model

First sort the distinct values into an alphabet. Replace each value
conceptually with its alphabet rank, preserving comparisons without
using the numeric distance between values. This order-preserving map
is coordinate compression. For `[7,1,7,3,5,1,4,7]`, the alphabet is:

```text
rank:    0  1  2  3  4
value:   1  3  4  5  7
```

Each node owns a half-open alphabet-rank interval and the stable
subsequence of values in that interval. Stable means values keep their
relative order from the parent. Split the interval at its middle:
lower ranks route left and upper ranks route right.

The node remembers the routing sequence through `rightBefore`:

```text
rightBefore[i] = right routes among positions [0,i)
```

The route at local position i is right exactly when
`rightBefore[i+1] - rightBefore[i]` equals 1. A parent boundary i maps
to child boundaries like this:

```text
right boundary = rightBefore[i]
left boundary  = i - rightBefore[i]
```

Read root entry `rightBefore[4] = 2` as: "two of the first four input
values route right." Thus parent boundary 4 becomes boundary 2 in
both child subsequences.

Access follows the route bit for one local position. Rank already
knows the target value's root-to-leaf path and translates one prefix
boundary at every node. Range selection translates both boundaries,
counts how many range values went left, then chooses the child that
contains the requested ordinal. A leaf owns one alphabet rank, so its
value is the answer.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build the tree for values `[7,1,7,3,5,1,4,7]`. Then access index 4,
rank value 7 before end 6, and find ordinal 3 in range `[1,7)`. The
expected answers are 5, 2, and 4.

Initial state: the input order is unchanged, no alphabet or nodes
exist, and every query is unresolved.

1. Decision: sort and deduplicate a copy. The values become alphabet
   `[1,3,4,5,7]` with ranks 0 through 4. Map the input to ranks
   `[4,0,4,1,3,0,2,4]`.
   After: numeric extremes and gaps have become a compact ordered
   universe `[0,5)`.
   Known correct: equal values share one rank, and comparing ranks
   gives the same less-than result as comparing original values.

2. Decision: split root interval `[0,5)` at rank 2. Ranks 0 and 1 go
   left; ranks 2, 3, and 4 go right. In input order, routing bits are
   `10101011`, so cumulative right counts are
   `[0,1,1,2,2,3,3,4,5]`.
   After: the stable left sequence is `[1,3,1]`; the stable right
   sequence is `[7,7,5,4,7]`.
   Known correct: every input value occurs in exactly one child, and
   each parent boundary maps to its two child boundaries by rank.

3. Decision: continue until each alphabet interval has one rank. The
   left child splits `[1,3,1]` into value 1 versus value 3 with prefix
   `[0,0,1,1]`. The right child splits value 4 from `[7,7,5,7]` with
   prefix `[0,1,2,3,3,4]`. That latter subsequence splits value 5
   from value 7 with prefix `[0,1,2,2,3]`.
   After: five leaves represent values 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7.

   ```text
   root [1,3,4,5,7]: [7 1 7 3 5 1 4 7]
      +-- left [1,3]: [1 3 1]
      |      +-- [1]: [1 1]
      |      +-- [3]: [3]
      +-- right [4,5,7]: [7 7 5 4 7]
             +-- [4]: [4]
             +-- right [5,7]: [7 7 5 7]
                    +-- [5]: [5]
                    +-- [7]: [7 7 7]
   ```

   Known correct: every root-to-leaf path narrows the ordered alphabet
   while preserving the local order needed by later range mappings.

4. Decision: access input index 4. At the root, counts change from 2
   to 3 across boundaries 4 and 5, so route right and map index 4 to
   right-local index 2. The right child also routes local index 2
   right and keeps local index 2. The next node routes it left and
   maps it to local index 0.
   After: reach the value-5 leaf and return 5.

   ```text
   root index 4 -> right-local index 2
   [4,5,7] index 2 -> right-local index 2
   [5,7] index 2 -> left-local index 0 -> value 5
   ```

   Known correct: each mapped local index names the same original
   occurrence inside the chosen stable subsequence.

5. Decision: rank value 7 at end 6. Value 7 always follows the right
   path. Root prefix entry 6 maps the end to 3. The right child's
   entry 3 keeps it at 3, and the final node's entry 3 maps it to 2.
   After: return 2.

   ```text
   root end 6 -> right end 3
   [4,5,7] end 3 -> right end 3
   [5,7] end 3 -> value-7 end 2
   ```

   Known correct: the leaf prefix contains exactly the two 7 values
   at original indices 0 and 2, both before end 6.

6. Decision: select ordinal 3 in `[1,7)`, whose values are
   `[1,7,3,5,1,4]`. At the root, three range values went left. Since
   ordinal 3 is not below that count, route right and subtract 3,
   leaving ordinal 0 in right-local range `[1,4)`.
   After: the unresolved candidates are `[7,5,4]`, seeking their
   smallest value.
   Known correct: all three discarded left values are smaller than
   every remaining value, so subtracting their count preserves order.

7. Decision: in right-local range `[1,4)`, one value goes to the
   value-4 left child and two go right. Ordinal 0 is below left count
   1, so map boundaries to `[0,1)` and descend left.
   After: reach value 4 and return it.
   Known correct: sorted range values are `[1,1,3,4,5,7]`, whose
   zero-based ordinal 3 is 4; selection terminates at its leaf.

8. Decision: rank missing value 2, access index 8, and select ordinal
   0 from empty range `[3,3)`. Alphabet search proves 2 absent, while
   the index and ordinal checks reject the other two queries before
   traversal.
   After: missing rank returns 0; both invalid queries return errors.
   Known correct: failure does not inspect a nonexistent node or
   change the immutable tree.

Focused uniform case: `[4,4,4]` has one alphabet value, so the root is
already a leaf. Access returns 4, rank of 4 is the requested valid
prefix length, and every valid range ordinal selects 4 without a
routing array.

Counterexample to unstable partitioning: sorting each child sequence
would keep its values but destroy their parent-relative positions.
The first wrong decision occurs when root right sequence
`[7,7,5,4,7]` is reordered to `[4,5,7,7,7]`; mapped range `[1,4)` no
longer represents the right-routed values from original range `[1,7)`.
Stable partitioning is required for boundary translation.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`. It uses only the standard library.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Wavelet trees. Function comments
// connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

type waveletNode struct {
	alphabetStart int
	alphabetEnd   int
	rightBefore   []int
	left          *waveletNode
	right         *waveletNode
}

type waveletTree struct {
	root     *waveletNode
	alphabet []int
	length   int
}

func distinctSortedValues(values []int) []int {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	sortedValues := append([]int(nil), values...)
	sort.Ints(sortedValues)
	distinctValues := make([]int, 0, len(sortedValues))
	for _, value := range sortedValues {
		if len(distinctValues) == 0 ||
			distinctValues[len(distinctValues)-1] != value {
			distinctValues = append(distinctValues, value)
		}
	}
	return append([]int(nil), distinctValues...)
}

func buildWaveletNode(
	valueRanks []int,
	alphabetStart int,
	alphabetEnd int,
) *waveletNode {
	// Build wavelet node in the order required by the lesson contract.
	if len(valueRanks) == 0 {
		return nil
	}
	node := &waveletNode{
		alphabetStart: alphabetStart,
		alphabetEnd:   alphabetEnd,
	}
	if alphabetEnd-alphabetStart == 1 {
		return node
	}

	alphabetMiddle := alphabetStart +
		(alphabetEnd-alphabetStart)/2
	// Prefix counts translate parent boundaries into each child.
	node.rightBefore = make([]int, len(valueRanks)+1)
	for valueIndex, valueRank := range valueRanks {
		node.rightBefore[valueIndex+1] =
			node.rightBefore[valueIndex]
		if valueRank >= alphabetMiddle {
			node.rightBefore[valueIndex+1]++
		}
	}

	rightCount := node.rightBefore[len(valueRanks)]
	leftRanks := make([]int, 0, len(valueRanks)-rightCount)
	rightRanks := make([]int, 0, rightCount)
	// Appending in encounter order preserves range coordinates.
	for _, valueRank := range valueRanks {
		if valueRank < alphabetMiddle {
			leftRanks = append(leftRanks, valueRank)
		} else {
			rightRanks = append(rightRanks, valueRank)
		}
	}
	node.left = buildWaveletNode(
		leftRanks,
		alphabetStart,
		alphabetMiddle,
	)
	node.right = buildWaveletNode(
		rightRanks,
		alphabetMiddle,
		alphabetEnd,
	)
	return node
}

func newWaveletTree(values []int) *waveletTree {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial wavelet tree state.
	alphabet := distinctSortedValues(values)
	valueRanks := make([]int, len(values))
	for valueIndex, value := range values {
		valueRanks[valueIndex] = sort.SearchInts(
			alphabet,
			value,
		)
	}
	return &waveletTree{
		root: buildWaveletNode(
			valueRanks,
			0,
			len(alphabet),
		),
		alphabet: alphabet,
		length:   len(values),
	}
}

func (tree *waveletTree) access(index int) (int, error) {
	// Keep access in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if index < 0 || index >= tree.length {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"index %d is outside [0, %d)",
			index,
			tree.length,
		)
	}
	node := tree.root
	localIndex := index
	// Each route remaps the same occurrence into child coordinates.
	for node.alphabetEnd-node.alphabetStart > 1 {
		rightBeforeIndex := node.rightBefore[localIndex]
		rightThroughIndex := node.rightBefore[localIndex+1]
		if rightThroughIndex > rightBeforeIndex {
			localIndex = rightBeforeIndex
			node = node.right
		} else {
			localIndex -= rightBeforeIndex
			node = node.left
		}
	}
	return tree.alphabet[node.alphabetStart], nil
}

func (tree *waveletTree) rank(
	value int,
	end int,
) (int, error) {
	// Relate the key to its position in sorted order.
	if end < 0 || end > tree.length {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"end %d is outside [0, %d]",
			end,
			tree.length,
		)
	}
	valueRank := sort.SearchInts(tree.alphabet, value)
	if valueRank == len(tree.alphabet) ||
		tree.alphabet[valueRank] != value {
		return 0, nil
	}

	node := tree.root
	localEnd := end
	// Follow the value while translating the prefix boundary.
	for node.alphabetEnd-node.alphabetStart > 1 {
		alphabetMiddle := node.alphabetStart +
			(node.alphabetEnd-node.alphabetStart)/2
		rightCount := node.rightBefore[localEnd]
		if valueRank >= alphabetMiddle {
			localEnd = rightCount
			node = node.right
		} else {
			localEnd -= rightCount
			node = node.left
		}
	}
	return localEnd, nil
}

func (tree *waveletTree) validateRange(
	start int,
	end int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the range contract before mutation.
	if start < 0 || start > tree.length {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"start %d is outside [0, %d]",
			start,
			tree.length,
		)
	}
	if end < start || end > tree.length {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"end %d is outside [%d, %d]",
			end,
			start,
			tree.length,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func (tree *waveletTree) kthSmallest(
	start int,
	end int,
	ordinal int,
) (int, error) {
	// Compute the requested ordered or extreme result.
	if err := tree.validateRange(start, end); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
	rangeLength := end - start
	if ordinal < 0 || ordinal >= rangeLength {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"ordinal %d is outside [0, %d)",
			ordinal,
			rangeLength,
		)
	}

	node := tree.root
	localStart := start
	localEnd := end
	// Lower-half count decides which child owns the ordinal.
	for node.alphabetEnd-node.alphabetStart > 1 {
		rightStart := node.rightBefore[localStart]
		rightEnd := node.rightBefore[localEnd]
		leftStart := localStart - rightStart
		leftEnd := localEnd - rightEnd
		leftCount := leftEnd - leftStart
		if ordinal < leftCount {
			localStart = leftStart
			localEnd = leftEnd
			node = node.left
		} else {
			ordinal -= leftCount
			localStart = rightStart
			localEnd = rightEnd
			node = node.right
		}
	}
	return tree.alphabet[node.alphabetStart], nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int{7, 1, 7, 3, 5, 1, 4, 7}
	tree := newWaveletTree(values)
	fmt.Println(tree.alphabet)
	fmt.Println(tree.root.rightBefore)

	value, err := tree.access(4)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(value)
	count, err := tree.rank(7, 6)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(count)
	selected, err := tree.kthSmallest(1, 7, 3)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(selected)
	missingCount, err := tree.rank(2, tree.length)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(missingCount)

	_, accessErr := tree.access(8)
	_, emptyRangeErr := tree.kthSmallest(3, 3, 0)
	fmt.Println(accessErr != nil, emptyRangeErr != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 3 4 5 7]
[0 1 1 2 2 3 3 4 5]
5
2
4
0
true true
```

##### Why it works

Maintain three node facts. Its alphabet interval contains exactly its
possible values. Its local sequence is the stable filter of the
parent sequence for that interval. Finally, `rightBefore[i]` counts
right routes in local prefix `[0,i)`.

The root contains the whole sequence and alphabet. Construction sends
each local value to exactly the child containing its alphabet rank,
