every position below `runStart` belongs to one complete classified
run, and `duplicates` contains exactly the length-at-least-two values
from those runs, once each and ascending.

The inner loop advances `runEnd` across exactly the positions equal to
`sortedValues[runStart]`. It stops at the first different value or the
slice boundary, so subtraction gives the complete run length. A value
occurs at least twice exactly when that length is at least two.
Appending once or excluding it therefore classifies the run correctly.

Assigning `runStart = runEnd` preserves the invariant and advances by
at least one position. Both indexes are bounded by the finite slice
length, so both loops terminate. At outer-loop termination every run
is classified; the invariant then gives the required complete result.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length and R the number of distinct duplicated
values returned. Copying costs Theta(N) time and O(N) owned storage.
Scanning costs Theta(N) time even though the loops are nested: every
sorted index is crossed by one run, not by every run. Building the
result takes amortized Theta(R) append work and O(R) output storage.

Under the standard comparison-sort model, sorting N integers takes
O(N log N) comparisons, so sorting dominates the overall O(N log N)
time bound. The `slices.Sort` API guarantees ascending order but does
not publish a complexity contract; code that requires one as an API
guarantee must own or pin the sorting implementation.

The current standard-library implementation sorts the owned slice in
place. Its internal stack is smaller than the O(N) copy, so auxiliary
storage is O(N), dominated by `sortedValues`; output remains separate
at O(R). Nil input takes Theta(1) work. The mandatory copy and scan
give Omega(N) work for nonempty input even if the sorter recognizes an
already ordered slice. No distribution-independent average case is
claimed.

If mutation is allowed, sorting the input directly removes the O(N)
copy but changes caller-visible order. If the input is already sorted,
the run scan alone is Theta(N) and needs O(1) auxiliary state beyond
the output.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil, empty, and one-value inputs return a non-nil empty result. The
  outer guard must run before reading `sortedValues[runStart]`.
- An all-unique input such as `[-1,0,3]` returns empty after three
  singleton runs; output length is not the distinct count.
- `[5,5,5,5]` returns `[5]`. Appending once per equal pair would
  incorrectly return three copies of 5.
- Already sorted and reverse-sorted inputs produce the same ascending
  duplicate output. Correctness cannot depend on initial order.
- Zero and negative values sort normally. No numeric sentinel marks a
  run boundary; `runEnd` and slice length do.
- Signed extremes must be compared directly. A comparator based on
  subtraction can overflow and reverse their order.
- Test `runEnd < len(sortedValues)` before indexing at `runEnd`. The
  last run otherwise reads one position past the slice.
- Initialize `runEnd = runStart + 1`. Starting it at `runStart` can
  count the same position incorrectly or fail to advance.
- Set `runStart = runEnd`, not `runStart++`. Jumping skips repeated
  output and ensures total scan work stays linear.
- Sort the copy, not `values`, when input preservation is promised.
  Slice assignment alone would still share the caller's array.
- `slices.Sort` need not be stable for this task. Equal integers have
  no separate identity or payload whose relative order must survive.
- Concurrent input writes are excluded; copying during a write is not
  a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose sorting and scanning when ordered duplicate output is useful,
the input is already sorted or may be copied or reordered, and a
deterministic comparison order is preferable to hash lookup. Grouping
also makes run lengths, unique values, and neighboring comparisons
available for later logic.

Use [membership tracking](#b12-membership-tracking-hash-set) when only
the earliest repeat matters and expected linear time is preferable.
Use [frequency counting](#b11-frequency-counting-hash-map) when exact
counts or first-appearance order matter. Use [bounded-value counting](
#b14-bounded-value-counting-array) when keys lie in a small dense
integer range.

The [comparison-sorting lesson](
#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) compares sorting algorithms rather
than this duplicate application. Practice scanning equal runs with
[Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array](
https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array/)
and duplicate-aware sorting with [3Sum](
problems/medium_leetcode_0015_3sum.go).

The standard-library [`slices.Sort` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort) defines ascending order for integers.
Its [current source](https://go.dev/src/slices/sort.go) shows the
in-place implementation used by this environment; treat source-level
cost details as version-dependent, not a language guarantee.

#### B.1.4 Bounded-value counting (array)

##### Problem and contract

Many counting problems promise that every value belongs to a small
integer universe. That promise can replace a hash map with a slice:
the value itself selects the counter to increment.

Given a finite `[]int` and a nonnegative `valueLimit`, return a new
count slice of length `valueLimit`. For every valid value `v`, output
index `v` must equal the number of times `v` occurs. Valid input
values occupy the half-open range `[0,valueLimit)`, so the output also
includes zero counters for values that never occur.

A negative limit or any out-of-range value returns a nil result and a
non-nil error. Nil or empty input with a valid limit succeeds. In
particular, an empty input with limit zero returns a non-nil empty
slice. The function does not mutate the input. Allocation must fit
memory, and concurrent input mutation is excluded.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) and
[direct-address tables](#a61-direct-address-tables) first. The table
lesson owns the general data structure; this lesson applies the same
indexing fact to linear frequency problems.

##### Mental model

Treat the count slice as a histogram with one bucket per possible
value. For `valueLimit = 5`, the indices are 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4.
Reading `counts[3] == 2` means exactly two input values equal 3.

First validate the limit and every input value. Only then allocate
`counts`. Go initializes each new integer element to zero, so every
bucket correctly describes the empty processed prefix.

Scan the input again. When the next value is `v`, increment only
`counts[v]`. No search, hash calculation, or collision resolution is
needed: the range contract proves that `v` is already a valid index.

After any processed prefix, bucket `v` equals the number of copies of
`v` in that prefix. Buckets for absent values remain zero. Completing
the scan turns that prefix fact into the requested full histogram.

##### Worked walkthrough

Count `[3,0,3,1,4,3,1]` with `valueLimit = 5`. The expected result is
`[1,2,0,3,1]`: value 0 occurs once, value 1 twice, value 2 zero times,
value 3 three times, and value 4 once.

Initial state: the input belongs to the caller. No output has been
allocated, and no input position has been accepted yet.

1. Decision: validate limit 5, then inspect all seven values. Each is
   at least zero and less than 5.
   After: the whole input is known to fit indices 0 through 4; no
   slice has been allocated or mutated.
   Known correct: every later `counts[value]` access will be in
   bounds.

2. Decision: allocate five integer counters after validation succeeds.
   After: `counts = [0,0,0,0,0]`; the processed prefix is empty.
   Known correct: every bucket equals its value's zero occurrences in
   the empty prefix.

3. Decision: process value 3 at input index 0 and increment bucket 3.
   After: `counts = [0,0,0,1,0]`; the processed prefix is `[3]`.
   Known correct: bucket 3 records the one 3, and all other prefix
   frequencies are zero.

4. Decision: process value 0 at index 1 and increment bucket 0.
   After: `counts = [1,0,0,1,0]`; the prefix is `[3,0]`.
   Known correct: exactly the new value's counter changed from zero to
   one.

5. Decision: process values 3 and 1 at indices 2 and 3 in order.
   After: `counts = [1,1,0,2,0]`; four positions are processed.
   Known correct: the counters sum to four, and each bucket matches
   its frequency in `[3,0,3,1]`.

6. Decision: process the remaining values 4, 3, and 1.
   After: `counts = [1,2,0,3,1]`; return that new slice while the
   input remains `[3,0,3,1,4,3,1]`.
   Known correct: all seven positions are represented once, including
   zero occurrences for value 2, so the complete contract holds.

Focused empty case: nil input with limit 4 skips both scans and
returns `[0,0,0,0]`. Focused empty-universe case: nil input with
limit zero returns a non-nil empty slice, while any value with limit
zero is invalid.

Counterexample to allocating `len(values)` counters: input `[4]` with
limit 5 needs bucket 4 even though its length is one. Indexing a
one-element slice by 4 panics. The universe size, not the observation
count, determines the histogram length.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, empty-input, and
invalid-input cases. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.
Validation finishes before allocation or indexing.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Bounded-value counting (array).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func countBoundedValues(
	values []int,
	valueLimit int,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	if valueLimit < 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("value limit must not be negative")
	}
	for index, value := range values {
		if value < 0 || value >= valueLimit {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"value %d at index %d is outside [0,%d)",
				value,
				index,
				valueLimit,
			)
		}
	}

	counts := make([]int, valueLimit)
	for _, value := range values {
		counts[value]++
	}
	return counts, nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int{3, 0, 3, 1, 4, 3, 1}
	counts, err := countBoundedValues(values, 5)
	fmt.Println(counts, err)
	fmt.Println(values)

	emptyCounts, err := countBoundedValues(nil, 4)
	fmt.Println(emptyCounts, err, emptyCounts != nil)

	invalidCounts, err := countBoundedValues(
		[]int{1, 5, 2},
		5,
	)
	fmt.Println(invalidCounts == nil, err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 2 0 3 1] <nil>
[3 0 3 1 4 3 1]
[0 0 0 0] <nil> true
true true
```

##### Why it works

Validation proves every input value is a legal index before the
function allocates or accesses `counts`. If validation fails, the
function returns nil immediately, so no partial histogram escapes.

After allocation and before counting, every bucket is zero. This is
the correct frequency for every value in the empty processed prefix.
Maintain this invariant before each counting iteration: for every
`v` in `[0,valueLimit)`, `counts[v]` equals the number of copies of
`v` in the already processed prefix.

The next input value is some valid `v`. Incrementing `counts[v]` adds
the one new copy of `v`; leaving every other bucket unchanged is
correct because the new item has no other value. The invariant is
therefore preserved for the prefix extended by one position.

Each validation and counting iteration advances once through a finite
slice. Both loops terminate after at most N iterations. When counting
ends, the processed prefix is the full input, so the invariant proves
every returned frequency. A bucket cannot exceed `len(values)`, so a
valid input cannot overflow an `int` counter.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length and K be `valueLimit`. Validation reads N
values, allocation initializes K counters, and counting reads N values
again. Every successful call therefore takes Theta(N + K) time. The
second scan doubles a constant factor, not the asymptotic bound.

The returned histogram occupies O(K) output space. Beyond that output,
the function uses O(1) auxiliary state and no recursion. The input and
output do not share element storage.

A negative limit fails in Theta(1) time. An invalid value at position
P fails after Theta(P + 1) validation work and allocates no histogram.
Successful best, average, and worst cases have the same Theta(N + K)
bound because the contract requires reading every input and returning
all K buckets.

Unlike a map, the slice has no expected-time qualification, hashing,
or collision behavior. Its cost depends on the whole universe K even
when only a few values occur. A million buckets for three observed
values is usually worse than storing three map entries.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Limit zero accepts only empty input and returns a non-nil empty
  slice. Calling `make([]int, 0)` satisfies that output contract.
- Value zero is the first valid bucket. It is data, not an empty or
  missing sentinel.
- For a positive limit, value `valueLimit - 1` is the last valid
  bucket. Value `valueLimit` and every negative value must be rejected
  before indexing.
- Absent valid values must retain zero counters. Omitting those slots
  changes a dense histogram into a different, sparse result shape.
- Allocate K counters, not N counters. Input length says how many
  observations exist, not which indices must be addressable.
- Validate the limit before calling `make`; a negative slice length
  panics instead of returning the promised error.
- Validate every value before the counting pass. Indexing first can
  panic and can leave a partially changed result during refactoring.
- Do not append counters while scanning. Bucket position is the value,
  so the slice needs its final length before increments begin.
- Two passes are still linear. Combining validation and counting is
  possible, but then invalid input does work on a result that must be
  discarded and complicates the no-partial-result story.
- Allocation failure is outside this contract. At a system boundary,
  cap an untrusted K before attempting to reserve K integers.
- For a signed range `[minimum,maximum]`, use a checked offset
  `value - minimum` and a checked range width. Unchecked subtraction
  can overflow; the direct-address lesson owns that extension.
- Concurrent writes to `values` race with both scans. The function
  does not synchronize or produce an atomic snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose bounded counting when values are integers in a small, known,
dense universe and exact frequencies matter. Byte histograms, school
grades, small status codes, lowercase-letter counts after validation,
and counting-sort buckets are common examples.

Use [frequency counting](#b11-frequency-counting-hash-map) for sparse,
large, negative, string, or otherwise arbitrary keys. Use [membership
tracking](#b12-membership-tracking-hash-set) when only presence or the
first repeat matters. Use [sorting and scanning](
#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) when arbitrary integers must be
grouped in order and O(N log N) comparison work is acceptable.

Use the full [direct-address table](#a61-direct-address-tables) when
each key owns a payload or needs insert, get, and delete operations.
This counting pattern needs only integer counters whose zero value
already means no occurrences.

Practice fixed-alphabet counting with [Valid Anagram](
problems/easy_leetcode_0242_valid_anagram.go) and [Ransom Note](
problems/easy_leetcode_0383_ransom_note.go). The authoritative
[Go specification on slices](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Making_slices_maps_and_channels) defines the
storage created by `make`; its [zero-value section](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#The_zero_value) specifies the initial integer
zeros used by the histogram.

#### B.1.5 Boyer-Moore majority vote (counters)

##### Problem and contract

A strict majority is a value that occupies more than half of all
positions. Counting every distinct value finds it, but the map may
grow with the input. Boyer-Moore majority vote keeps only one
candidate and one balance. It cancels occurrences of different
values.

Given a finite `[]int`, return its strict majority and true. If no
strict majority exists, return `(0,false)`. For N values, a majority
must occur more than `floor(N/2)` times; exactly half is not enough.
Here `floor` means round down to a whole number. At most one value can
satisfy that threshold.

Every `int` is valid, including zero, negatives, and the signed
extremes. Nil and empty input return `(0,false)`. The function reads
nonempty input twice, does not mutate it, and allocates no per-input
storage. Concurrent input mutation is excluded.

Read [frequency counting](#b11-frequency-counting-hash-map) first.
That lesson owns exact per-value counters; this entry deliberately
answers only the stricter yes-or-no majority question with constant
auxiliary state.

##### Mental model

Imagine repeatedly removing two positions whose values differ. Each
removed pair can contain at most one copy of any proposed majority.
A true majority has more copies than all other values combined, so
unequal pairs cannot remove every copy of it.

The algorithm performs that cancellation without storing the pairs.
`candidate` names the one kind of unmatched value currently retained.
`balance` says how many unmatched copies of it remain. Reading
`candidate == 2` and `balance == 3` means the processed prefix can be
split into unequal-value pairs plus three unmatched 2s.

When balance is zero, the next value becomes the candidate with
balance one. A matching value increases the balance. A different
value forms one conceptual pair with an unmatched candidate copy, so
the balance decreases.

If a majority exists, the surviving candidate must be that majority.
If no majority exists, some value may still survive. Therefore a
second scan counts the candidate and accepts it only when its count is
strictly greater than `len(values)/2`.

##### Worked walkthrough

Find the strict majority of `[1,2,3,2,2,2,2]`. The length is 7, so a
majority needs more than `floor(7/2) = 3` copies. The expected result
is `(2,true)` because 2 occurs five times.

Initial state: `balance = 0`; the candidate is irrelevant. No input
position has been processed, and no conceptual pair exists.

1. Decision: index 0 holds 1 and balance is zero, so retain 1 as the
   candidate with balance one.
   After: candidate 1; balance 1; unmatched values `[1]`.
   Known correct: the prefix `[1]` is zero unequal pairs plus one
   unmatched 1.

2. Decision: index 1 holds 2, different from candidate 1. Cancel it
   with the unmatched 1.
   After: balance 0; conceptual pair `(1,2)`; no unmatched value.
   Known correct: both processed positions belong to one unequal pair.

3. Decision: index 2 holds 3 and balance is zero, so retain 3 as the
   new candidate.
   After: candidate 3; balance 1; unmatched values `[3]`.
   Known correct: the earlier unequal pair remains canceled, and the
   only unpaired position holds 3.

4. Decision: index 3 holds 2, different from candidate 3. Cancel the
   two values.
   After: balance 0; pairs are `(1,2)` and `(3,2)`.
   Known correct: the first four positions are partitioned into two
   unequal pairs with no unmatched position.

5. Decision: index 4 holds 2 and balance is zero, so choose 2 as the
   candidate with balance one.
   After: candidate 2; balance 1; one unmatched 2.
   Known correct: every earlier position remains paired, and the new
   position is the only unmatched one.

6. Decision: indices 5 and 6 also hold 2. Each matches the candidate,
   so increase the balance once for each position.
   After: candidate 2; balance 3; three unmatched 2s; the first scan
   is exhausted.
   Known correct: all seven positions are two unequal pairs plus three
   unmatched copies of candidate 2.

7. Decision: scan the original input again and count candidate 2.
   Its count is 5, and `5 > 7/2` is true.
   After: return `(2,true)`; the input remains
   `[1,2,3,2,2,2,2]`.
   Known correct: verification proves the surviving candidate crosses
   the strict threshold, so it is the unique majority.

Focused no-majority case: `[1,2,3]` cancels 1 with 2 and ends with
candidate 3 and balance one. Verification finds only one copy, and
`1 > 3/2` is false, so the result is `(0,false)`. Focused empty case:
nil input returns `(0,false)` before reading a position.

Counterexample to trusting the first-pass survivor: `[1,2,3]` leaves
3 unmatched even though every value occurs once. The first wrong
decision is treating "not canceled" as "more than half." Cancellation
can nominate only a possible majority; the second scan proves it.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, no-majority, and
zero-majority cases. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.
It uses only equality and counters, so extreme integers need no
special arithmetic.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Boyer-Moore majority vote
// (counters). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func findStrictMajority(values []int) (int, bool) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for strict majority without changing state.
	if len(values) == 0 {
		return 0, false
	}

	// Cancel unequal pairs while retaining one unmatched value kind.
	candidate := 0
	balance := 0
	for _, value := range values {
		if balance == 0 {
			candidate = value
			balance = 1
			continue
		}
		if value == candidate {
			balance++
			continue
		}
		balance--
	}

	// A survivor is only a candidate until its full count is checked.
	candidateCount := 0
	for _, value := range values {
		if value == candidate {
			candidateCount++
		}
	}
	if candidateCount <= len(values)/2 {
		return 0, false
	}
	return candidate, true
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	majority, found := findStrictMajority(
		[]int{1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2},
	)
	fmt.Println(majority, found)

	majority, found = findStrictMajority([]int{1, 2, 3})
	fmt.Println(majority, found)

	majority, found = findStrictMajority([]int{0, 1, 0})
	fmt.Println(majority, found)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
2 true
0 false
0 true
```

##### Why it works

After every processed prefix in the first scan, maintain this
invariant: the prefix can be partitioned into pairs of unequal values
and exactly `balance` unmatched copies of `candidate`. When balance is
zero, there are no unmatched copies and the stored candidate does not
matter. This holds for the empty prefix.

With zero balance, retaining the next value creates one unmatched copy
and establishes the invariant. With positive balance and a matching
value, adding one unmatched candidate copy preserves it. With positive
balance and a different value, pairing that value with one unmatched
candidate copy removes one of each and decreases balance. These are
all possible first-scan branches, so the invariant is preserved.

Suppose value M is a strict majority. Every unequal pair contains at
most one M, while the input contains more Ms than non-M values. Some M
must remain unmatched after every possible unequal pairing. The
invariant says all unmatched values equal the final candidate, so that
candidate must be M.

Without a strict majority, the invariant makes no frequency promise
about a survivor. The second scan counts the candidate exactly and
returns true only when its count exceeds `len(values)/2`. Thus it
accepts every real majority and rejects every false candidate.

Each loop advances through a finite slice and terminates after N
iterations. Candidate count and balance never exceed N, which is an
`int` slice length, so neither counter can overflow for valid input.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length. For nonempty input, nomination examines N
values and verification examines N values, so successful and
no-majority calls both take Theta(N) time. Empty input takes Theta(1).
There is no input-dependent average-case improvement because this
contract always verifies a nonempty candidate.

The function retains two counters and one candidate, uses O(1)
auxiliary space, and returns a scalar result using O(1) output space.
It allocates no map, copied slice, recursion stack, or other per-input
storage.

If the caller's contract guarantees a majority, the verification pass
may be omitted: nomination alone is Theta(N) time and O(1) space. For
arbitrary input, omitting verification changes the contract and can
return a false majority.

Frequency counting also takes expected O(N) time for integer keys but
retains O(D) map entries for D distinct values and provides all exact
counts. Sorting a copy uses O(N) copied storage and O(N log N)
comparison work. Boyer-Moore saves storage by discarding every fact
except what can still identify a strict majority.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty input return `(0,false)`. Reading `values[0]` to seed
  the candidate before checking length would panic.
- A singleton such as `[7]` returns `(7,true)` because one is greater
  than `floor(1/2)`, which is zero.
- `[1,1,2,2]` has two copies of each value. Two is exactly half of
  four, not more than half, so verification must return false.
- `[0,1,0]` returns `(0,true)`. The boolean distinguishes a real zero
  majority from the no-majority result `(0,false)`.
- All-equal input `[5,5,5]` grows balance to three and verifies 5. A
  large balance still records an unmatched surplus, not the exact
  count until the second scan.
- The first candidate need not survive. In the walkthrough, 1 and 3
  are canceled before 2 becomes the final candidate.
- Test balance zero before comparing with the stored candidate. When
  balance is zero, that old value is irrelevant and the next value
  must start a new unmatched group.
- On a mismatch with positive balance, decrement only the balance.
  Replacing the candidate immediately breaks the unequal-pair model.
- Verify with `candidateCount > len(values)/2`. Testing greater than
  or equal accepts exact halves; testing `2*candidateCount` can
  overflow on theoretical maximum-length slices.
- Negative and extreme integers are ordinary values. Compare them for
  equality rather than subtracting them.
- Verification requires replaying the input. A one-shot stream can
  nominate a candidate in one pass but cannot confirm arbitrary input
  without replay, retained data, or an external count.
- Concurrent writes between or during scans can invalidate both the
  pairing and verification facts. The function requires a stable
  input slice.

##### When to choose it

Choose Boyer-Moore when the question asks for a value occurring more
than half the time and constant auxiliary space matters. Election-like
votes, dominant labels, and the Majority Element interview problem are
recognizable forms.

Do not use it for the mode, plurality winner, exact frequencies, or a
threshold below one half. A value can be most frequent without being a
strict majority. Use [frequency counting](
#b11-frequency-counting-hash-map) when those counts matter, or
[bounded-value counting](#b14-bounded-value-counting-array) for a
small dense integer universe.

If input can be reordered or copied, [sorting and scanning](
#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) can group all values but costs more
work or mutation. Below the one-half threshold, multiple values may
qualify, so one Boyer-Moore candidate is not sufficient.

Practice the guaranteed-majority form with [Majority Element](
problems/easy_leetcode_0169_majority_element.go). That problem permits
omitting verification because its input promise supplies the missing
proof; this general function keeps verification for untrusted input.
The authors' [majority-vote explanation](
https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~moore/best-ideas/mjrty/index.html) and the
original [MJRTY paper](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~boyer/mjrty.pdf)
describe the algorithm and its history.

#### B.1.6 Missing values by placement (slice)

##### Problem and contract

Finding a missing value by repeated membership scans can compare the
same input positions many times. When N input positions imply a useful
value range of 1 through N, each useful value can instead mark its own
presence by occupying a designated slice index.

Given a finite `[]int`, return the smallest positive integer absent
from it. Duplicates, zero, negatives, and values larger than the input
length are valid. Nil and empty input return 1. For example,
`[3,4,-1,1]` returns 2.

The function rearranges the input slice in place and does not preserve
order. It does preserve the same multiset: no value is added, removed,
or changed. It allocates no per-input storage. The input length N must
permit `N + 1` to fit in `int`, and concurrent mutation is excluded.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) first
for indexing, swapping, mutation, and ownership. This entry applies
placement to one missing-value problem; it does not replace the later
general study of array rearrangement.

##### Mental model

For a slice of length N, useful values are 1 through N. Value `v`
belongs at index `v - 1`: value 1 belongs at index 0, and value N
belongs at index `N - 1`. For example, in a four-element slice, value
4 belongs at index 3.

The answer must lie in 1 through `N + 1`. If any value from 1 through
N is absent, the smallest such value is the answer. If all N are
present, the N positions are already occupied by them, so `N + 1` is
absent.

At each `currentIndex`, inspect its value. Ignore it and advance when
it is outside 1 through N. Otherwise compute its `homeIndex` as
`value - 1`. If that home already contains the value, advance; this
covers both a correctly placed copy and an extra duplicate.

If the home contains something else, swap the current value into its
home. Do not advance yet: the displaced value now at `currentIndex`
has not been classified. When placement ends, scan from index 0. The
first index not holding `index + 1` reveals the smallest missing
positive.

##### Worked walkthrough

Find the first missing positive in `[3,4,-1,1]`. Its length is 4, so
values 1 through 4 have homes at indices 0 through 3. The expected
answer is 2.

Initial state: `values = [3,4,-1,1]` and `currentIndex = 0`. No home
has been established by the algorithm.

1. Decision: index 0 holds 3, whose home is `3 - 1 = 2`. Index 2
   holds -1 rather than 3, so swap indices 0 and 2. Keep the current
   index at 0 afterward.
   After: `values = [-1,4,3,1]`; index 2 is a correct home.
   Known correct: value 3 is present and permanently represented at
   its unique home; the displaced -1 still needs classification.

2. Decision: index 0 now holds -1, which is not between 1 and 4
   inclusive. It cannot fill a home, so advance.
   After: `values = [-1,4,3,1]`; `currentIndex = 1`.
   Known correct: index 0 has no useful value to place, while the home
   for 3 remains correct.

3. Decision: index 1 holds 4, whose home is index 3. Index 3 holds 1,
   so swap indices 1 and 3 and recheck index 1.
   After: `values = [-1,1,3,4]`; homes for 3 and 4 are correct.
   Known correct: the displaced 1 remains unclassified, and no correct
   home was disturbed.

4. Decision: index 1 now holds 1, whose home is index 0. Index 0 holds
   -1, so swap indices 1 and 0 and recheck index 1.
   After: `values = [1,-1,3,4]`; homes for 1, 3, and 4 are correct.
   Known correct: every useful value encountered so far occupies its
   own home; the displaced -1 remains to be skipped.

5. Decision: skip -1 at index 1. At indices 2 and 3, values 3 and 4
   already occupy their homes, so advance after each. Stop when
   `currentIndex` reaches 4.
   After: placement is complete with `values = [1,-1,3,4]`.
   Known correct: every useful value present in the input occupies its
   home. No unclassified index remains.

6. Decision: scan homes from the start. Index 0 correctly holds 1,
   but index 1 does not hold 2.
   After: return 2; the caller's slice remains `[1,-1,3,4]`.
   Known correct: 1 is present, 2 is absent, and no smaller positive
   value can be missing.

Focused duplicate case: `[1,1]` leaves the first 1 at index 0. At
index 1, the extra 1 finds its home already filled, so the algorithm
advances instead of swapping equal values forever. The scan returns 2.
Focused empty case: nil input performs neither loop and returns
`N + 1 = 1`.

Counterexample to advancing after every swap: on `[3,4,-1,1]`, place
4 at index 3 and advance past index 1. The displaced 1 never reaches
index 0, leaving `[-1,1,3,4]`; the scan then incorrectly returns 1.
The first wrong decision is abandoning a displaced, unclassified
value. Recheck the same current index after a swap.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, duplicate, and
empty cases. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It mutates
the supplied slices and prints their resulting arrangements.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Missing values by placement
// (slice). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func firstMissingPositive(values []int) int {
	// Place useful values and recheck every displaced value.
	for currentIndex := 0; currentIndex < len(values); {
		value := values[currentIndex]
		if value <= 0 || value > len(values) {
			currentIndex++
			continue
		}

		homeIndex := value - 1
		// A filled home also stops duplicates from swapping forever.
		if values[homeIndex] == value {
			currentIndex++
			continue
		}

		// Do not advance: the displaced value is not classified yet.
		values[currentIndex], values[homeIndex] =
			values[homeIndex], values[currentIndex]
	}

	// The first incorrect home identifies the smallest missing value.
	for index, value := range values {
		if value != index+1 {
			return index + 1
		}
	}
	return len(values) + 1
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int{3, 4, -1, 1}
	fmt.Println(firstMissingPositive(values))
	fmt.Println(values)

	duplicates := []int{1, 1}
	fmt.Println(firstMissingPositive(duplicates))
	fmt.Println(duplicates)

	fmt.Println(firstMissingPositive(nil))
}
```

Expected output:

```text
2
[1 -1 3 4]
2
[1 1]
1
```

##### Why it works

First, the answer lies in 1 through `N + 1`. There are only N input
positions. If some value in 1 through N is absent, one of those values
is the answer; if none is absent, all N positions contain those N
distinct values and `N + 1` is absent.

During placement, a swap writes value `v` to its unique home `v - 1`.
That home was not already correct, because the equality guard would
have advanced instead. A later different value cannot target the same
home, and a duplicate `v` finds the home filled and advances. Thus a
correct home is never disturbed.

Every placement-loop iteration either advances `currentIndex` or
permanently fills at least one new correct home. There are N indices
and N homes, so there can be at most N advances and N swaps. The loop
therefore terminates.

A swap only exchanges existing elements, so it preserves the multiset.
Because the loop rechecks every displaced value, each useful original
value is either placed in its home or finds a duplicate already there.
At termination, every present value `v` in 1 through N therefore
occupies index `v - 1`.

Consider the first scan index whose value is not `index + 1`. All
earlier homes prove their smaller positive values are present. If
`index + 1` were present, placement would have put a copy in this
home, so the mismatch proves it absent. Returning it is correct.

If every home matches, all values 1 through N are present. The initial
range argument proves `N + 1` is then the smallest missing positive.
The scan advances through a finite slice, so it also terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length. Placement advances across N indices and
performs at most N swaps; each check or swap takes constant work. The
final scan examines between one and N positions for nonempty input.
The whole function therefore takes Theta(N) time in its best, average,
and worst cases; placement must classify every input index even when
the final scan returns immediately. Empty input takes Theta(1).

The function keeps only indices and one value, using O(1) auxiliary
space and O(1) scalar output space. It allocates no result collection
or recursion stack. Each swap performs two element writes, so the
number of writes is also O(N).

This storage bound depends on permission to reorder the input. Copying
first would preserve the caller's order but add Theta(N) copy work and
O(N) auxiliary storage. A hash set also preserves the input and gives
expected Theta(N) lookup work, while retaining O(N) values.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty input return 1. Reading index 0 first would panic.
- `[1]` returns 2; `[2]` returns 1. A one-position input exercises
  both the filled-home and missing-first-home results.
- `[1,2,3]` fills every home and returns 4. Returning N after a full
  scan would repeat a present value; the required result is `N + 1`.
- Zero, negatives, and values above N have no useful home. For
  `[-1,0,8]`, skip all three and return 1.
- Check the useful range before computing `value - 1`. Subtracting
  from the minimum integer can overflow, and indexing a negative or
  too-large home panics.
- Value N belongs at index `N - 1`; value `N + 1` is outside the
  homes. Mixing values with zero-based indices causes off-by-one
  errors.
- Duplicates need the `values[homeIndex] == value` guard. Swapping the
  two 1s in `[1,1]` forever makes no progress.
- Recheck `currentIndex` after a swap. Advancing can skip the
  displaced value, as the walkthrough counterexample demonstrates.
- A swap is permitted only when the target is not already correct.
  This makes every swap fill a new home and supplies the linear bound.
- The final arrangement is not sorted and is not stable. The function
  promises only the same multiset and correct homes for useful values.
- The input-length precondition ensures `len(values) + 1` cannot
  overflow the returned `int`. A wider result type or explicit error
  is required if that precondition cannot be guaranteed.
- Concurrent input writes can undo a home or race with the scan. The
  algorithm requires exclusive mutation for the call.

##### When to choose it

Choose placement when useful values map one-to-one onto a dense index
range, the task asks which value is missing or duplicated, and input
reordering is allowed. The clues here are the range 1 through N, the
home conversion `value - 1`, and a constant-auxiliary-space target.

Use a hash set when the input must remain unchanged or values have no
compact home range. Use [bounded-value counting](
#b14-bounded-value-counting-array) when a separate K-slot histogram is
allowed and exact counts matter. Sort a copy when ordered grouping is
useful and O(N log N) comparison work is acceptable.

Sum or XOR shortcuts fit narrower contracts such as exactly one
missing value from a known duplicate-free range. They do not solve
this contract with arbitrary negatives, large values, and duplicates.

Practice the exact pattern with [First Missing Positive](
https://leetcode.com/problems/first-missing-positive/description/).
The [slice lesson](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) owns Go's
indexing and mutation rules; this application relies on them while
adding the value-to-home invariant.

### B.2 Pairs, triplets, and target sums

#### B.2.1 Complement lookup (hash map)

##### Problem and contract

Checking every pair repeats comparisons: for each position, a nested
scan asks whether some later value completes the target. A hash map
can remember earlier values, so the current position needs one
complement lookup instead.

Given a finite `[]int` and an `int` target, find two distinct indices
whose values have the mathematical sum target. If several pairs exist,
return the pair with the smallest second index; among pairs with that
second index, return the smallest first index. Indices are returned in
ascending order. Mathematical sum means exact arithmetic without
machine overflow.

If no pair exists, return `(-1,-1,false)`. Nil, empty, and one-value
inputs have no pair. Every `int` value and target is valid, including
signed extremes. The function checks complement subtraction before
performing it, so overflow cannot create a false lookup key.

The input is read but not mutated. The local map may allocate and must
fit memory. Concurrent input mutation is excluded. Read [hash-table
collision handling](#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) and
[membership tracking](#b12-membership-tracking-hash-set) first. Those
entries own hash storage and lookup timing; this entry maps a value to
its earliest index.

##### Mental model

At index `i` with value `v`, the needed complement is `target - v`.
For target 7 and value -3, the complement is 10 because
`10 + (-3) = 7`.

Keep `earliestIndexByValue`. Each key is an earlier input value, and
its mapped integer is that value's smallest index. Reading
`earliestIndexByValue[10] == 0` means value 10 first appeared at index
0 in the already processed prefix.

Look up the complement before storing the current value. A found key
forms a pair with an earlier, distinct index. If it is absent, store
the current value only when the map does not already contain it; this
preserves the earliest index for deterministic tie-breaking.

Subtraction needs one boundary check. If the exact mathematical
complement is below the smallest `int` or above the largest `int`, no
earlier `int` can equal it. Skip that lookup, but still remember the
current value because it may complement a later position.

The left-to-right scan makes the first found second index the smallest
possible one. The map's earliest stored index then makes the first
index smallest among pairs ending there.

##### Worked walkthrough

Find a pair in `[10,-2,7,-3]` with target 7. The expected result is
`(0,3,true)` because indexes 0 and 3 hold 10 and -3.

Initial state: `earliestIndexByValue = {}` and the next position is
index 0. No earlier pair exists.

1. Decision: index 0 holds 10, so the complement is `7 - 10 = -3`.
   The map has no -3. Store `10 -> 0` and advance.
   After: map `{10:0}`; next index 1.
   Known correct: no pair ends at index 0, and 10's earliest index is
   available to later positions.

2. Decision: index 1 holds -2, so the complement is 9. It is absent;
   store `-2 -> 1` and advance.
   After: map `{10:0,-2:1}`; next index 2.
   Known correct: no pair ends below index 2, and the map records
   every distinct earlier value at its earliest index.

3. Decision: index 2 holds 7, so the complement is 0. It is absent;
   store `7 -> 2` and advance.
   After: map `{10:0,-2:1,7:2}`; next index 3.
   Known correct: every pair whose second index is below 3 has been
   rejected, and all three earlier values are available for lookup.

4. Decision: index 3 holds -3, so the complement is 10. The map finds
   10 at earliest index 0.
   After: return `(0,3,true)` without storing -3; the input remains
   `[10,-2,7,-3]`.
   Known correct: the indices are distinct, their values sum to 7,
   and every smaller second index was already rejected.

Focused equal-value case: for `[3,3]` and target 6, index 0 finds no
earlier 3 and is then stored. Index 1 finds that earlier 3 and returns
`(0,1,true)`; checking before insertion prevents self-pairing. Focused
no-pair case: `[1,2]` with target 10 exhausts the scan and returns
`(-1,-1,false)`.

Focused overflow case: let `maximumInt` be the largest `int`. For
`[-1,0,maximumInt]` and target `maximumInt`, index 0 would need
`maximumInt + 1`, which is unrepresentable, so lookup is skipped and
-1 is stored. Later, `maximumInt` needs complement 0 and returns
`(1,2,true)`.

Counterexample to storing before lookup: on `[3]` with target 6,
storing `3 -> 0` first makes the same iteration find index 0 and
return `(0,0,true)`. That reuses one element twice. The map must
describe only the strictly earlier prefix at lookup time.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, equal-value,
no-pair, and overflow cases. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`. It leaves each input slice unchanged.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Complement lookup (hash map).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func checkedComplement(target, value int) (int, bool) {
	// Derive signed bounds without assuming a 32- or 64-bit int.
	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	minimumInt := -maximumInt - 1
	if value > 0 && target < minimumInt+value {
		return 0, false
	}
	if value < 0 && target > maximumInt+value {
		return 0, false
	}
	return target - value, true
}

func findEarliestTargetPair(
	values []int,
	target int,
) (int, int, bool) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for earliest target pair without changing
	// state.
	earliestIndexByValue := make(map[int]int)

	// Match only against earlier positions, then remember this one.
	for secondIndex, value := range values {
		complement, representable := checkedComplement(
			target,
			value,
		)
		if representable {
			firstIndex, found := earliestIndexByValue[complement]
			if found {
				return firstIndex, secondIndex, true
			}
		}

		// Keep the earliest index for deterministic tie-breaking.
		if _, exists := earliestIndexByValue[value]; !exists {
			earliestIndexByValue[value] = secondIndex
		}
	}
	return -1, -1, false
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	first, second, found := findEarliestTargetPair(
		[]int{10, -2, 7, -3},
		7,
	)
	fmt.Println(first, second, found)

	first, second, found = findEarliestTargetPair(
		[]int{3, 3},
		6,
	)
	fmt.Println(first, second, found)

	first, second, found = findEarliestTargetPair(
		[]int{1, 2},
		10,
	)
	fmt.Println(first, second, found)

	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	first, second, found = findEarliestTargetPair(
		[]int{-1, 0, maximumInt},
		maximumInt,
	)
	fmt.Println(first, second, found)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
0 3 true
0 1 true
-1 -1 false
1 2 true
```

##### Why it works

Before processing index `i`, maintain two facts: the map contains the
earliest index of every distinct value in `values[0:i]`, and no valid
pair has a second index below `i`. Both hold for the empty prefix.

If the exact complement is representable and present, its mapped index
is below `i`. The two distinct positions have values whose exact sum
is target, so returning them is valid. The scan order proves this
second index is the earliest possible, and the stored earliest index
proves the stated tie-break.

If the complement is absent, no earlier value completes the current
one. An unrepresentable complement also cannot equal an earlier `int`.
Adding the current value only when absent extends the map with its
earliest index while preserving existing earlier indices. Thus both
invariant facts hold for the next position.

For positive `value`, subtraction underflows exactly when
`target < minimumInt + value`. For negative `value`, it overflows
exactly when `target > maximumInt + value`. Each boundary addition is
itself representable because its added value points inward from the
corresponding extreme. If neither condition holds, `target - value`
is safe and exact.

Each nonreturning iteration advances one position, so the loop either
returns or terminates after N values. On exhaustion, the invariant
says every possible second index failed, proving no pair exists.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length, P the number of positions examined before
return, and D the distinct values stored. Each position performs
constant arithmetic and an expected constant-time map lookup and
possible insertion. Under the usual hash-table assumption, time is
expected Theta(P).

For inputs of length at least two, a match at index 1 gives Theta(1)
best-case work relative to N. Exhaustion or a match at the last index
takes expected Theta(N) worst-case work. A distribution-independent
average case is not meaningful. Go specifies map behavior but no
worst-case constant-time bound.

The map retains O(D) key-index entries and may reserve more internal
capacity than its live count. Checked subtraction and the scalar
result use O(1) additional space. The function allocates no input or
output slice and does not recurse.

Checking every unordered pair uses O(1) auxiliary space but takes
Theta(N squared) time when no early pair is found. Sorting value-index
records enables two pointers in O(N log N) comparison work and O(N)
copied storage. Complement lookup trades O(D) map storage for expected
linear early-exit work while preserving original indices.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil, empty, and one-value inputs return `(-1,-1,false)`. No two
  distinct indices exist.
- `[3,3]` with target 6 returns `(0,1,true)`. Lookup before insertion
  permits two occurrences while rejecting self-pairing.
- `[0,0]` with target 0 also succeeds. Zero is a map key, not an
  absence sentinel; use the map lookup boolean.
- Multiple answers follow the explicit tie-break. For `[1,4,2,3]`
  and target 5, return `(0,1,true)` before considering `(2,3)`.
- Preserve the first index for each value. On `[1,1,4]` with target 5,
  overwriting `1 -> 0` with `1 -> 1` returns the wrong tied pair.
- Do not test `earliestIndexByValue[complement] != 0`. Index 0 is
  valid; the two-value map lookup distinguishes it from absence.
- Check subtraction before evaluating `target - value`. Go signed
  integer arithmetic wraps modulo the word size instead of reporting
  an error, which can produce a false complement key.
- An unrepresentable complement cannot be an `int`, but the current
  value must still be stored for later positions.
- Minimum and maximum integers can form a valid pair: their exact sum
  is -1. Direct equality lookup avoids adding them in Go.
- The algorithm never ranges over the map. Unspecified map iteration
  order cannot affect the deterministic result.
- Concurrent input mutation is excluded. The map represents a prefix
  of one stable input order, not a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose complement lookup for one target pair in an unsorted sequence
when original indices matter and expected linear time is preferable to
a nested scan. Subtraction turns the two-value condition into one map
membership question per position.

Use [two pointers after sorting](
#b22-two-pointers-after-sorting-slice) when values are already sorted
or map storage is undesirable. Use [counting pairs](
#b25-counting-pairs-frequency-map) when the result is the number of
pairs rather than one deterministic pair. Larger tuple sizes need
additional structure, such as sorting or meet-in-the-middle tables.

Practice the unique-answer version in the completed [Two Sum archive](
problems/solved_easy_leetcode_0001_two_sum.go) and the authoritative
[Two Sum statement](https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum/). The
[Go maps article](https://go.dev/blog/maps) defines the built-in map
operations used here; the hash-table lesson owns their storage model.

#### B.2.2 Two pointers after sorting (slice)

##### Problem and contract

Sorted values make pair elimination possible. Instead of remembering
every earlier value in a map, compare the smallest and largest
remaining values. Their sum proves that one endpoint cannot belong to
any solution still under consideration.

Given a finite `[]int` sorted in nondecreasing order and an `int`
target, return two distinct zero-based indices whose values have the
exact mathematical sum target. Nondecreasing means each value is at
least the value before it, so duplicates are allowed.

If several pairs exist, return the one with the smallest left index;
among pairs with that left index, return the largest right index. If
no pair exists, return `(-1,-1,false)`. Nil, empty, and one-value
inputs have no pair.

Every `int` value and target is valid. Pair-sum comparison checks for
signed overflow before addition. The function does not mutate or
allocate from the input, and concurrent input mutation is excluded.
Sorted order is a precondition and is not validated; unsorted input is
outside the contract.

Read [sorting and scanning](#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) first for
copying and ordering, then [complement lookup](
#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) for the unsorted map alternative.
This entry owns the inward endpoint decision once sorted order exists.

##### Mental model

Keep `leftIndex` at the smallest remaining value and `rightIndex` at
the largest. The inclusive interval `[leftIndex,rightIndex]` contains
every index that might still participate in a solution.

Compare the endpoints with the target using exact arithmetic:

- If their sum equals the target, return the endpoints.
- If their sum is too small, discard the left endpoint by
  incrementing `leftIndex`. Pairing that smallest value with any
  smaller right value can only make the sum no larger.
- If their sum is too large, discard the right endpoint by
  decrementing `rightIndex`. Pairing that largest value with any
  larger left value can only make the sum no smaller.

Stop without a pair when the pointers meet or cross. Distinct indices
require `leftIndex < rightIndex`; equality would reuse one element.

The comparison helper detects a positive overflow as greater than
every `int` target and a negative underflow as less than every `int`
target. It returns -1 for a sum below target, 0 for equality, and 1
for a sum above target. It adds the endpoints only when their sum is
representable.

##### Worked walkthrough

Search `[-10,-4,1,3,9,20]` for target 5. The expected result is
`(1,4,true)` because -4 plus 9 equals 5.

Initial state: `leftIndex = 0` at -10 and `rightIndex = 5` at 20. All
six indices remain eligible.

1. Decision: compare the endpoint sum `-10 + 20 = 10` with target 5.
   It is too large, so discard right index 5.
   After: active interval `[0,4]`, with endpoints -10 and 9.
   Known correct: 20 cannot form target 5 because even pairing it with
   the smallest value produced 10; every other partner is no smaller.

2. Decision: compare `-10 + 9 = -1` with 5. It is too small, so
   discard left index 0.
   After: active interval `[1,4]`, with endpoints -4 and 9.
   Known correct: -10 cannot form target 5 because even its largest
   remaining partner produced -1; every smaller partner is no larger.

3. Decision: compare `-4 + 9 = 5` with the target. They are equal.
   After: return `(1,4,true)`; the input remains
   `[-10,-4,1,3,9,20]`.
   Known correct: the two indices are distinct and exact. Every
   discarded endpoint was proved unable to participate in a solution.

Focused no-pair case: for `[-2,0,4]` and target 3, sum 2 is too small,
so move left from -2 to 0. Sum 4 is then too large, so move right from
4 to 0. The pointers meet and the function returns `(-1,-1,false)`.

Focused duplicate case: `[3,3]` with target 6 starts at distinct
indices 0 and 1 and returns `(0,1,true)`. Focused extreme case: the
minimum and maximum integers have exact sum -1, so those two sorted
values return `(0,1,true)` without overflowing.

Counterexample to moving right when the sum is too small: for
`[1,2,4,8]` and target 10, the initial sum 9 is too small.
Decrementing right makes the sum even smaller and misses `2 + 8`.
The first wrong decision discards the only large enough partner;
increment left instead.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, duplicate,
no-pair, and extreme cases. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`. It assumes each input slice is already sorted and
leaves it unchanged.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Two pointers after sorting
// (slice). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func comparePairSumToTarget(
	leftValue int,
	rightValue int,
	target int,
) int {
	// Derive signed bounds without assuming a 32- or 64-bit int.
	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	minimumInt := -maximumInt - 1

	// An overflowing sum is above every int target.
	if rightValue > 0 && leftValue > maximumInt-rightValue {
		return 1
	}
	// An underflowing sum is below every int target.
	if rightValue < 0 && leftValue < minimumInt-rightValue {
		return -1
	}

	pairSum := leftValue + rightValue
	switch {
	case pairSum < target:
		return -1
	case pairSum > target:
		return 1
	default:
		return 0
	}
}

func findTargetPairInSorted(
	values []int,
	target int,
) (int, int, bool) {
	// Sorted order makes one endpoint impossible after each comparison.
	leftIndex := 0
	rightIndex := len(values) - 1
	for leftIndex < rightIndex {
		comparison := comparePairSumToTarget(
			values[leftIndex],
			values[rightIndex],
			target,
		)
		switch {
		case comparison < 0:
			leftIndex++
		case comparison > 0:
			rightIndex--
		default:
			return leftIndex, rightIndex, true
		}
	}
	return -1, -1, false
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	left, right, found := findTargetPairInSorted(
		[]int{-10, -4, 1, 3, 9, 20},
		5,
	)
	fmt.Println(left, right, found)

	left, right, found = findTargetPairInSorted(
		[]int{3, 3},
		6,
	)
	fmt.Println(left, right, found)

	left, right, found = findTargetPairInSorted(
		[]int{-2, 0, 4},
		3,
	)
	fmt.Println(left, right, found)

	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	minimumInt := -maximumInt - 1
	left, right, found = findTargetPairInSorted(
		[]int{minimumInt, maximumInt},
		-1,
	)
	fmt.Println(left, right, found)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
1 4 true
0 1 true
-1 -1 false
0 1 true
```

##### Why it works

Maintain this invariant before each comparison: every valid pair not
yet ruled out uses two distinct indices inside the inclusive active
interval `[leftIndex,rightIndex]`. Initially the interval contains the
whole input, so the invariant holds.

If the endpoint sum is too small, sorted order makes every value at or
left of `rightIndex` no greater than the right endpoint. Pairing the
left endpoint with any eligible partner therefore remains too small.
Discarding only `leftIndex` preserves every possible pair.

If the sum is too large, every value at or right of `leftIndex` is no
smaller than the left endpoint. Pairing any eligible partner with the
right endpoint therefore remains too large. Discarding only
`rightIndex` is safe. Equality directly proves a valid distinct pair.

The same eliminations establish the tie-break. A left index advances
only after every possible partner for it is ruled out, so the returned
left index is smallest. For that left index, larger right indices have
already been proved too large, so the returned right index is largest.

Each nonreturning iteration moves one pointer inward. Their distance
starts below N and decreases by one, so the loop terminates after at
most `N - 1` comparisons. If the pointers meet, the invariant and the
distinct-index requirement prove no pair remains.

The comparison helper is exact. If positive addition would overflow,
the mathematical sum exceeds `maximumInt` and is therefore above any
`int` target. Negative underflow similarly puts the sum below any
target. The guard boundaries are representable, and ordinary addition
runs only when its result fits in `int`.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length and P be the number of endpoint comparisons.
Each comparison either returns or removes one endpoint, so
`P <= N - 1` for N at least one. A pair at the initial endpoints takes
Theta(1) best-case time. Pointer exhaustion takes Theta(N) worst-case
time. No distribution-independent average case is claimed.

The function retains two indices, one comparison result, and fixed
arithmetic state. It uses O(1) auxiliary space and O(1) scalar output
space, performs no allocation, and does not recurse. The input remains
unchanged.

These bounds exclude obtaining sorted order. For unsorted input,
copying and sorting costs O(N log N) comparison work and O(N) copied
storage under the standard comparison-sort model. Returning original
indices also requires carrying each value's original index through
the sort.

A hash map avoids sorting and takes expected O(N) time with O(N)
storage. Binary-searching a complement for every index uses O(1)
auxiliary state on an already sorted slice but takes O(N log N) time;
two pointers share information across searches and scan only once.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil, empty, and one-value inputs return `(-1,-1,false)`. With nil
  or empty input, `rightIndex` starts at -1, but the loop guard
  prevents an index access.
- `[3,3]` with target 6 succeeds because the pointers occupy distinct
  indices. Using `leftIndex <= rightIndex` can pair one 3 with itself.
- Multiple answers use the stated tie-break. `[1,2,3,4,5]` with target
  6 returns endpoints `(0,4)`, not the inner pair `(1,3)`.
- Sorted order is mandatory. On unsorted `[4,1,3]` with target 4, the
  endpoint decisions can miss indices 1 and 2; the function does not
  detect this contract violation.
- Move left only when the sum is too small and right only when it is
  too large. Reversing either move cannot bring the sum toward target.
- Compare before adding extreme integers. Positive overflow can appear
  negative after machine addition and cause movement in the wrong
  direction; negative underflow has the symmetric failure.
- Do not compare with `(leftValue + rightValue) - target`. The sum or
  later subtraction can overflow; use the checked boundaries first.
- The function returns zero-based indices. A one-based judge adapter
  must add one to both only after a pair is found.
- Concurrent input mutation can break sorted order during the scan.
  The function requires one stable snapshot for the call.

##### When to choose it

Choose inward two pointers when values are already sorted, only one
target pair is needed, and constant auxiliary space matters. The key
clue is monotonicity: moving left can only raise the sum, while moving
right can only lower it.

Use [complement lookup](#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) when input is
unsorted, original indices matter, and O(N) map storage is acceptable.
Sort a copy first when only the values matter and O(N log N) setup is
acceptable. Use [counting pairs](#b25-counting-pairs-frequency-map)
when every qualifying pair or its multiplicity must be counted.

Practice the exact sorted-input form in [Two Sum II](
problems/medium_leetcode_0167_two_sum_ii_input_array_is_sorted.go) and
the authoritative [problem statement](
https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted/).
The [sorting-and-scanning lesson](
#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) owns copy and ordering details; this
entry relies only on the order they establish.

#### B.2.3 Meet in the middle (slices and hash maps)

##### Problem and contract

Some exact searches have too many choices for one full enumeration,
but each complete choice can be split into two independent halves.
Meet in the middle enumerates the halves separately and joins
compatible partial results.

Given at most 40 `int64` values and an `int64` target, find one subset
of input indices whose values have the exact mathematical sum target.
Each index may be selected zero or one time. Return selected
zero-based indices in ascending order, a found flag, and an error.

The empty subset is valid, so target zero returns a non-nil empty
index slice. Duplicate and negative values are valid because choices
refer to positions, not distinct values. No solution returns
`(nil,false,nil)`. Invalid input returns `(nil,false,error)`.

This implementation splits the input by index. It returns the
solution with the smallest numeric left-half mask; among solutions
with that mask, it uses the smallest numeric right-half mask. A mask's
bit `k` says whether offset `k` in that half is selected.

All subset sums formed entirely inside either half must fit in
`int64`. The function checks that rule while enumerating and rejects
the input if any such sum overflows. It also rejects more than 40
values before allocating exponential storage.

The function reads but does not mutate the input. A successful result
owns a new index slice. Allocation must fit memory, and concurrent
input mutation is excluded.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) for
indexing and ownership, [hash-table collisions](
#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) for expected map costs,
and [complement lookup](#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) for the
two-value form of the same matching idea.

##### Mental model

Split N positions at `middleIndex = N / 2`. The left half has L
positions and the right half has R positions, where `L + R = N`.
Every full subset now has exactly one L-bit mask and one R-bit mask.

Enumerate a half's sums in numeric mask order. Start with sum zero for
mask 0. For each new value, freeze the old sum count, then append that
value to every old sum. The old entries are masks whose new bit is
zero; the appended entries are the same masks with that bit set.
Consequently, the slice index is also the mask.

Build `rightMaskBySum`. Its key selects a right-half sum and its value
stores the smallest mask that produces that sum. Reading
`rightMaskBySum[7] == 6` means right mask 6, binary `110`, selects
offsets 1 and 2 and those values total 7. Keep the first mask for a
repeated sum because enumeration visits masks in increasing order.

Then scan left sums in mask order. A left sum `leftSum` needs
`target - leftSum` from the right. If that subtraction is
representable and the map contains the result, the two masks form a
complete solution. Decode their set bits into original indices and
stop. If the complement is outside `int64`, no stored right sum can
equal it, so skip that left mask rather than wrapping the subtraction.

This is the meet: neither half knows the complete answer while being
enumerated. The hash lookup joins two partial choices whose stored
facts satisfy the full target equation.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use values `[8,-3,5,2,11,-4]` and target 12. Split before index 3:
the left values are `[8,-3,5]`, and the right values are
`[2,11,-4]`. The expected indices are `[0,1,4,5]` because
`8 + -3 + 11 + -4 = 12`.

Masks below are written with the newest bit on the left. For example,
left mask `011` selects offsets 0 and 1.

Initial state: both sum slices are absent, the right map is empty,
and no left mask has been tested.

1. Decision: enumerate the left half. Start with `[0]`. Processing 8
   appends `[8]`; processing -3 appends `[-3,5]`; processing 5
   appends `[5,13,2,10]` to the four prior entries.
   After: left sums by masks `000` through `111` are
   `[0,8,-3,5,5,13,2,10]`.
   Known correct: entry m is the sum selected by the three bits of
   left mask m; every left subset appears once.

2. Decision: enumerate the right half by the same doubling rule.
   Processing 2 gives `[0,2]`; 11 extends it to `[0,2,11,13]`;
   -4 appends `[-4,-2,7,9]`.
   After: right sums by masks `000` through `111` are
   `[0,2,11,13,-4,-2,7,9]`.
   Known correct: every right subset appears once, and all stored sums
   are exact `int64` values.

3. Decision: visit right masks from 0 through 7 and store the first
   mask for each sum. These eight sums are distinct in this example.
   After: the map contains `0:0`, `2:1`, `11:2`, `13:3`, `-4:4`,
   `-2:5`, `7:6`, and `9:7`.
   Known correct: each map entry names the smallest right mask with
   that sum.

4. Decision: left mask `000` has sum 0 and needs 12. The map lacks
   12, so advance to the next left mask.
   After: no result; left mask 0 is ruled out.
   Known correct: no right subset can complete left mask 0.

5. Decision: left mask `001` has sum 8 and needs 4. The map lacks 4,
   so advance.
   After: no result; left masks 0 and 1 are ruled out.
   Known correct: neither tested left choice can reach target 12.

6. Decision: left mask `010` has sum -3 and needs 15. The map lacks
   15, so advance.
   After: no result; left masks 0 through 2 are ruled out.
   Known correct: every numerically smaller left mask has been tested
   against all right choices through its sum lookup.

7. Decision: left mask `011` has sum 5 and needs 7. The map returns
   right mask 6, binary `110`. Decode left bits 0 and 1 as original
   indices 0 and 1; decode right bits 1 and 2 as indices 4 and 5.
   After: return `[0,1,4,5]`, true, and nil error.
   Known correct: the four values total 12. Left mask 3 is the first
   matching left mask, and right mask 6 is its smallest matching mask.

Focused empty case: nil values with target 0 produce sum zero for both
mask-0 halves. The lookup succeeds and decoding returns a non-nil
empty slice. Nil values with target 1 instead exhaust the one left
mask and return `(nil,false,nil)`.

Focused overflow case: `[0,maximumInt64,1]` splits as `[0]` and
`[maximumInt64,1]`. Building the right sum for mask `11` would add 1
to `maximumInt64`, so enumeration returns an error before matching.

Counterexample to one full mask: 40 values have about one trillion
full masks, but two 20-value halves have about one million masks each.
The split does not make the search polynomial; it halves the exponent
that controls each enumeration.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the ordinary, empty, no-solution,
overflow, and size-limit cases. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`. It uses only the standard library and leaves every
input slice unchanged.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Meet in the middle (slices and
// hash maps). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

const (
	maximumSubsetValues = 40
	maximumInt64        = int64(1<<63 - 1)
	minimumInt64        = int64(-1 << 63)
)

func checkedInt64Addition(
	left int64,
	right int64,
) (int64, bool) {
	// Shift the relevant bound inward before Go can wrap the sum.
	if right > 0 && left > maximumInt64-right {
		return 0, false
	}
	if right < 0 && left < minimumInt64-right {
		return 0, false
	}
	return left + right, true
}

func checkedInt64Subtraction(
	left int64,
	right int64,
) (int64, bool) {
	// Positive subtraction can underflow; negative can overflow.
	if right > 0 && left < minimumInt64+right {
		return 0, false
	}
	if right < 0 && left > maximumInt64+right {
		return 0, false
	}
	return left - right, true
}

func enumerateSubsetSums(values []int64) ([]int64, error) {
	// Keep enumerate subset sums in one helper so callers use one rule.
	capacity := 1 << len(values)
	subsetSums := make([]int64, 1, capacity)
	for valueIndex, value := range values {
		// Freeze the old length: appends create the masks whose new bit
		// is one, in the same order as the masks whose bit is zero.
		previousCount := len(subsetSums)
		for subsetIndex := 0; subsetIndex < previousCount; subsetIndex++ {
			subsetSum, representable := checkedInt64Addition(
				subsetSums[subsetIndex],
				value,
			)
			if !representable {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"subset sum overflows at half index %d",
					valueIndex,
				)
			}
			subsetSums = append(subsetSums, subsetSum)
		}
	}
	return subsetSums, nil
}

func indicesFromMasks(
	leftMask uint64,
	rightMask uint64,
	middleIndex int,
	totalValues int,
) []int {
	// Keep indices from masks in one helper so callers use one rule.
	selectedIndices := make([]int, 0, totalValues)
	for bitOffset := 0; bitOffset < middleIndex; bitOffset++ {
		if leftMask&(uint64(1)<<bitOffset) != 0 {
			selectedIndices = append(
				selectedIndices,
				bitOffset,
			)
		}
	}
	rightCount := totalValues - middleIndex
	for bitOffset := 0; bitOffset < rightCount; bitOffset++ {
		if rightMask&(uint64(1)<<bitOffset) != 0 {
			selectedIndices = append(
				selectedIndices,
				middleIndex+bitOffset,
			)
		}
	}
	return selectedIndices
}

func findSubsetWithTarget(
	values []int64,
	target int64,
) ([]int, bool, error) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for subset with target without changing
	// state.
	if len(values) > maximumSubsetValues {
		return nil, false, fmt.Errorf(
			"got %d values; maximum is %d",
			len(values),
			maximumSubsetValues,
		)
	}

	// Split by index so every original subset has one mask per half.
	middleIndex := len(values) / 2
	leftSums, err := enumerateSubsetSums(values[:middleIndex])
	if err != nil {
		return nil, false, fmt.Errorf("enumerate left half: %w", err)
	}
	rightSums, err := enumerateSubsetSums(values[middleIndex:])
	if err != nil {
		return nil, false, fmt.Errorf("enumerate right half: %w", err)
	}

	// The first mask for a sum is its smallest numeric mask.
	rightMaskBySum := make(map[int64]uint64)
	for rightMask, rightSum := range rightSums {
		if _, exists := rightMaskBySum[rightSum]; !exists {
			rightMaskBySum[rightSum] = uint64(rightMask)
		}
	}

	// Scan left masks in increasing order for a stored complement.
	for leftMask, leftSum := range leftSums {
		neededRightSum, representable :=
			checkedInt64Subtraction(target, leftSum)
		if !representable {
			continue
		}
		rightMask, found := rightMaskBySum[neededRightSum]
		if found {
			indices := indicesFromMasks(
				uint64(leftMask),
				rightMask,
				middleIndex,
				len(values),
			)
			return indices, true, nil
		}
	}
	return nil, false, nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	indices, found, err := findSubsetWithTarget(
		[]int64{8, -3, 5, 2, 11, -4},
		12,
	)
	fmt.Println(indices, found, err, indices == nil)

	indices, found, err = findSubsetWithTarget(nil, 0)
	fmt.Println(indices, found, err, indices == nil)

	indices, found, err = findSubsetWithTarget(
		[]int64{2, 4, 8},
		7,
	)
	fmt.Println(indices, found, err, indices == nil)

	_, _, overflowErr := findSubsetWithTarget(
		[]int64{0, maximumInt64, 1},
		maximumInt64,
	)
	fmt.Println(overflowErr != nil)

	tooManyValues := make([]int64, maximumSubsetValues+1)
	_, _, sizeErr := findSubsetWithTarget(tooManyValues, 0)
	fmt.Println(sizeErr != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[0 1 4 5] true <nil> false
[] true <nil> false
[] false <nil> true
true
true
```

The final Boolean on each of the first three lines reports whether
the returned slice is nil. It distinguishes the valid empty solution
from the nil no-solution result.

##### Why it works

After processing k values in one half, maintain this enumeration
invariant: `subsetSums` has length `2^k`, and entry m is the exact sum
selected by the k low bits of mask m. It holds initially for k = 0:
mask 0 selects nothing and has sum zero.

Before adding the next value, `previousCount` freezes the old
`2^k` entries. Those entries keep the new bit zero. Appending the new
value to each old sum produces the same masks with bit k set, at
indexes `2^k` through `2^(k+1) - 1`. Checked addition either preserves
an exact `int64` sum or rejects the input. Induction proves both half
sum slices enumerate every mask exactly once and in numeric order.

After building the right map, maintain this fact: each key is a
reachable right sum, and its value is the smallest mask producing
that sum. The first encountered mask establishes the entry. Ignoring
later duplicate sums preserves the smaller mask.

Every full subset splits uniquely into one left mask and one right
mask, and its total is `leftSum + rightSum`. Therefore a subset totals
target exactly when its right sum equals `target - leftSum`. If a
solution exists, scanning reaches its left mask and the map contains a
right mask with the required sum. The function then returns a valid
subset. If the scan exhausts, no possible left-right pair satisfies
the equation.

Increasing left-mask order makes the first match use the smallest
matching left mask. The map's invariant supplies the smallest right
mask for that left sum, establishing the stated tie-break. Decoding
low bits before high bits, and left before right, returns indices in
ascending order.

For addition with positive `right`, overflow occurs exactly when
`left > maximumInt64 - right`. With negative `right`, underflow occurs
exactly when `left < minimumInt64 - right`. Each boundary expression
moves inward from its extreme, so the boundary calculation itself is
representable.

For subtraction with positive `right`, underflow occurs exactly when
`left < minimumInt64 + right`. With negative `right`, overflow occurs
exactly when `left > maximumInt64 + right`. If a mathematical
complement is unrepresentable, it cannot equal any `int64` map key;
skipping it loses no solution under the validated half-sum contract.

For accepted input, each enumeration loop runs once per value and its
inner bound is frozen and finite. Each half has at most 20 values, so
neither sum slice exceeds `2^20` entries. Map construction, left
scanning, and mask decoding are also finite. The function therefore
terminates. Oversized input terminates before a shift or allocation.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the value count, `L = floor(N / 2)`, and `R = N - L`.
Generating the halves appends `2^L - 1` and `2^R - 1` sums, so it
takes Theta(`2^L + 2^R`) arithmetic work. This implementation always
finishes both enumerations before matching, even when target zero has
an immediate empty solution.

Let U be the number of distinct right sums. Building U map entries and
probing once for each left mask takes expected
Theta(`2^R + 2^L`) time under the usual hash-table assumption. Go does
not promise worst-case constant-time map operations, so no stronger
hashing worst-case or distribution-independent average is claimed.

The two sum slices retain Theta(`2^L + 2^R`) `int64` values. The map
retains O(U) sum-mask entries, with implementation-dependent bucket
overhead. Mask decoding takes Theta(N) time and uses O(1) scalar
state. It allocates the caller-owned result with capacity N, so output
storage is O(N) even when the selected subset is small. The input is
not copied.

Rejecting N greater than 40 takes Theta(1) time and allocates no
exponential storage. For every accepted input, best and worst
enumeration work have the same exponential order; matching may stop
after one left lookup or inspect all `2^L` left masks.

Incremental brute-force enumeration over all positions needs
Theta(`2^N`) time and O(N) mask state; recomputing every subset sum
adds an N factor. Meet in the middle reduces the exponent in time but
pays exponential storage. It remains unsuitable when N is much larger
than 40.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil or empty input with target 0 returns a non-nil empty slice and
  true. Returning false forgets that selecting no index is a subset.
- Nil input with target 1 returns nil, false, and nil error. There is
  one possible mask, but its sum zero does not match.
- `[4,4]` with target 8 selects both positions. Equal values are
  distinct choices; deduplicating the input changes the problem.
- Negative values need no special branch. `[7,-2,-5]` can reach -7
  with indices 1 and 2 because the map stores signed sums.
- `[2,4,8]` with target 7 returns no solution after all left masks.
  Absence is not an invalid-input error.
- Target zero intentionally prefers the empty subset because masks 0
  are numerically smallest. A caller requiring a nonempty subset needs
  a different contract and must exclude the double-zero-mask match.
- More than 40 values is rejected before `1 << len(values)`. Moving
  the check after enumeration can overflow a shift or request
  impractical storage.
- A half sum outside `int64` returns an error even if some other
  subset would hit the target. Silently wrapping it can invent a
  false map key or hide a real mathematical sum.
- A complement outside `int64` is skipped, not wrapped. For target
  `maximumInt64` and left sum -1, `maximumInt64 + 1` cannot be a right
  map key.
- Freeze `previousCount` before appending. Looping to the growing
  slice length keeps consuming newly appended entries and no longer
  performs one bounded doubling step.
