- Use the map lookup Boolean. Right mask 0 is a valid stored value, so
  testing `rightMaskBySum[needed] != 0` misses the empty right subset.
- Keep the first mask for a repeated right sum. Overwriting it changes
  the deterministic smallest-mask result.
- Decode half masks with half-relative bit offsets. Forgetting to
  add `middleIndex` to right offsets returns positions from the wrong
  half.
- The 40-value limit keeps every mask below 20 bits, so conversion
  from a slice index to `uint64` and every decode shift are safe.
- Concurrent input mutation is excluded. Enumeration requires one
  stable value at every index for the whole call.

##### When to choose it

Choose meet in the middle for an exact subset or combination search
when N is moderate, roughly 30 to 40 here, and enumerating all `2^N`
choices is too slow. It is especially useful when values may be
negative or very large, so a table indexed by attainable target
magnitude would be impractical.

Use direct subset enumeration for small N when exponential storage
is not justified. Use the [subset-sum dynamic programming
lesson](#b203-knapsack-and-subset-sum-dp-table-or-bit-set) when
reachable sums fit a compact range. Backtracking is preferable when
ordering the choices gives strong, sound pruning. Use
[complement lookup](#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) or
[sorted two pointers](#b22-two-pointers-after-sorting-slice) when
exactly two indices must be selected; enumerating all half subsets
would solve a broader problem than required.

The classic method is due to Horowitz and Sahni. Their original
[partition and knapsack paper](
https://www.cise.ufl.edu/~sahni/papers/computingPartitions.pdf)
develops the split-enumeration improvement and analyzes its storage
tradeoff. Its [journal record and DOI](
https://doi.org/10.1145/321812.321823) identify the 1974 Journal of
the ACM publication. The [Go maps article](https://go.dev/blog/maps)
documents the lookup and presence operations used by the join.

#### B.2.4 Generalized k-sum (sorted slice and recursion)

##### Problem and contract

Pair search asks for two values with one target sum. Generalized
k-sum asks for a fixed number of values, commonly three or four, and
must usually return every distinct value combination rather than stop
after the first match.

Given a finite `[]int64`, a tuple size K from 2 through 12, and an
`int64` target, return every unique K-value combination whose exact
mathematical sum is target. Each input position may be used at most
once. A repeated value can appear several times in a combination only
when the input supplies that many occurrences.

Values inside each combination are nondecreasing. Combinations are
returned in lexicographic order: compare their first unequal values,
and the one with the smaller value comes first. For example,
`[-2,0,0,2]` precedes `[-1,0,0,1]` because -2 is smaller than -1.

No combination returns a non-nil empty outer slice and nil error. A
valid K greater than the input length has the same result. K below 2
or above 12 returns `(nil,error)`. The upper bound makes recursion
depth explicit; this algorithm is already impractical for large K.

Every input value and target in `int64` is valid. Intermediate
residual targets and pair sums use `math/big.Int`, so exact arithmetic
does not wrap even when a partial sum lies outside `int64`.

The function sorts an owned copy and leaves the caller's input order
unchanged. Every returned inner slice and the outer slice belong to
the caller. Allocation must fit memory, and concurrent input mutation
is excluded.

Read [sorting and scanning](#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) for
copying, ordering, and duplicate groups. Read [sorted two pointers](
#b22-two-pointers-after-sorting-slice) for the pair base case. This
entry owns the recursive reduction from K values to two.

##### Mental model

Sort a copy first. A recursive frame remembers four facts:

- `startIndex` is the first position this frame may use.
- `valuesNeeded` is how many more values the result requires.
- `target` is the exact sum those remaining values must make.
- `selectedValues` is the sorted prefix already chosen.

Reading a frame with `startIndex = 2`, `valuesNeeded = 3`, target 2,
and prefix `[-2]` means: choose three positions from indexes 2 onward
whose values total 2, then append them after -2.

When more than two values are needed, try each possible next position
that leaves enough positions for the rest. Choosing value x creates a
child that starts one position later, needs one fewer value, and needs
target minus x. Append x to the tentative prefix before the call, then
remove it after the child returns. This removal is backtracking.

Equal adjacent values at the same recursion depth create identical
value prefixes, so try only the first. Deeper frames may still choose
later equal occurrences. This distinction removes duplicate outputs
without confusing equal values with the same input position.

At `valuesNeeded = 2`, stop recursing. Put one pointer at each end of
the remaining sorted range. An exact pair sum below target discards
the whole equal-value group on the left; a sum above target discards
the equal group on the right. Equality copies the selected prefix and
pair into the output, then skips both groups.

The residual target is a `big.Int`. Its arithmetic methods store the
answer in their receiver, so every child uses a fresh receiver. That
keeps the parent's target unchanged when the child returns.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use values `[1,0,-1,0,-2,2]`, K = 4, and target 0. The expected
combinations are `[-2,-1,1,2]`, `[-2,0,0,2]`, and
`[-1,0,0,1]`, in that order.

Initial state: the caller's values are unsorted, no prefix is chosen,
the exact residual target is 0, and the output is empty.

1. Decision: copy and sort because recursion and duplicate skipping
   require adjacent equal values, but the caller keeps its order.
   After: sorted copy `[-2,-1,0,0,1,2]`; original input unchanged;
   root frame `(start 0, need 4, target 0, prefix [])`.
   Known correct: every original occurrence has one position in the
   sorted copy, and choosing increasing positions cannot reuse one.

2. Decision: at the root, choose index 0 value -2. It is the first
   candidate at this depth and leaves five positions for three values.
   Subtracting -2 makes the child target 2.
   After: child frame `(start 1, need 3, target 2, prefix [-2])`.
   Known correct: every four-value combination beginning with -2 now
   corresponds to one three-value completion of exact sum 2.

3. Decision: choose child index 1 value -1. The base case now needs
   two values totaling 3 from indexes 2 through 5. Pointers begin at
   values 0 and 2; their sum 2 is too small. Skip both adjacent zeros
   on the left. Values 1 and 2 then sum to 3, so emit the prefix and
   pair and skip both matched value groups.
   After: output `[[-2,-1,1,2]]`; the pair pointers meet; restore the
   three-value prefix to `[-2]`.
   Known correct: `[-2,-1,1,2]` is unique, and no pair before it in
   the remaining range can total 3.

4. Decision: the three-value frame next chooses index 2 value 0 and
   needs a pair totaling 2 from indexes 3 through 5. Endpoint values
   0 and 2 match immediately, so emit them. After returning, index 3
   is another 0 at the same depth, so skip that duplicate prefix.
   After: output
   `[[-2,-1,1,2],[-2,0,0,2]]`; the -2 branch is exhausted.
   Known correct: the branch contains both unique completions starting
   with -2, and choosing the second 0 first would repeat the latter.

5. Decision: restore the root prefix, choose root index 1 value -1,
   and recurse with target 1. The child chooses its first 0 at
   index 2.
   In the pair range, 0 plus 2 is too large, so discard 2; 0 plus 1
   then matches. Emit the combination and skip the second same-depth
   zero anchor after backtracking.
   After: output also contains `[-1,0,0,1]`; root prefix is restored.
   Known correct: every combination beginning with -1 is represented
   once, and the new result follows both -2 results lexicographically.

6. Decision: choose root index 2 value 0, the last root position that
   leaves three later values. Its only three-value branch cannot make
   residual 0 from `[0,1,2]`. No later root index leaves enough
   values.
   After: return
   `[[-2,-1,1,2],[-2,0,0,2],[-1,0,0,1]]` and nil error.
   Known correct: every possible first value and every unique child
   prefix has been exhausted, so no target combination is missing.

Focused duplicate case: five copies of 2 with K = 4 and target 8
return `[[2,2,2,2]]`. Each depth can use a later occurrence, while
same-depth skipping prevents five index selections from appearing as
the same value result repeatedly.

Focused exact-arithmetic case: K = 4, target `maximumInt64`, and
values `[minimumInt64,maximumInt64,maximumInt64,1]` use all four
positions.
After choosing `minimumInt64`, the residual is `2^64 - 1`, outside
`int64`, but `big.Int` preserves it and the valid result is found.

Counterexample to deduplicating the whole input: replacing
`[2,2,2,2]` with `[2]` before searching makes the valid four-value
combination impossible. Skip equal choices only at one recursion
depth; do not erase the occurrences that deeper frames may consume.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves the
input, compares signed extremes exactly, distinguishes empty output
from nil, and rejects invalid K. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`. It uses only the standard library.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Generalized k-sum (sorted slice
// and recursion). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"slices"
)

const maximumTupleSize = 12

func comparePairSum(
	leftValue int64,
	rightValue int64,
	target *big.Int,
) int {
	// Use a fresh receiver because big.Int arithmetic mutates it.
	pairSum := new(big.Int).SetInt64(leftValue)
	pairSum.Add(pairSum, big.NewInt(rightValue))
	return pairSum.Cmp(target)
}

func appendUniquePairs(
	sortedValues []int64,
	startIndex int,
	target *big.Int,
	selectedValues []int64,
	results *[][]int64,
) {
	// Expose unique pairs in logical order without changing source.
	leftIndex := startIndex
	rightIndex := len(sortedValues) - 1
	for leftIndex < rightIndex {
		leftValue := sortedValues[leftIndex]
		rightValue := sortedValues[rightIndex]
		comparison := comparePairSum(
			leftValue,
			rightValue,
			target,
		)

		switch {
		case comparison < 0:
			// Equal left values make the same too-small sum.
			for leftIndex < rightIndex &&
				sortedValues[leftIndex] == leftValue {
				leftIndex++
			}
		case comparison > 0:
			// Equal right values make the same too-large sum.
			for leftIndex < rightIndex &&
				sortedValues[rightIndex] == rightValue {
				rightIndex--
			}
		default:
			// Copy the path so later backtracking cannot change output.
			combination := make(
				[]int64,
				0,
				len(selectedValues)+2,
			)
			combination = append(combination, selectedValues...)
			combination = append(
				combination,
				leftValue,
				rightValue,
			)
			*results = append(*results, combination)

			// Skip both value groups after emitting this unique pair.
			for leftIndex < rightIndex &&
				sortedValues[leftIndex] == leftValue {
				leftIndex++
			}
			for leftIndex < rightIndex &&
				sortedValues[rightIndex] == rightValue {
				rightIndex--
			}
		}
	}
}

func collectUniqueKSum(
	sortedValues []int64,
	startIndex int,
	valuesNeeded int,
	target *big.Int,
	selectedValues []int64,
	results *[][]int64,
) {
	// Expose unique k sum in logical order without changing source.
	if len(sortedValues)-startIndex < valuesNeeded {
		return
	}
	if valuesNeeded == 2 {
		appendUniquePairs(
			sortedValues,
			startIndex,
			target,
			selectedValues,
			results,
		)
		return
	}

	lastStartIndex := len(sortedValues) - valuesNeeded
	chosenIndex := startIndex
	for chosenIndex <= lastStartIndex {
		chosenValue := sortedValues[chosenIndex]
		if chosenIndex > startIndex &&
			chosenValue == sortedValues[chosenIndex-1] {
			chosenIndex++
			continue
		}

		// A fresh target keeps the caller's residual unchanged.
		chosenBig := big.NewInt(chosenValue)
		nextTarget := new(big.Int).Sub(target, chosenBig)
		selectedValues = append(selectedValues, chosenValue)
		collectUniqueKSum(
			sortedValues,
			chosenIndex+1,
			valuesNeeded-1,
			nextTarget,
			selectedValues,
			results,
		)

		// Restore the path before trying the next value.
		selectedValues = selectedValues[:len(selectedValues)-1]
		chosenIndex++
	}
}

func uniqueKSum(
	values []int64,
	tupleSize int,
	target int64,
) ([][]int64, error) {
	// Keep unique k sum in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if tupleSize < 2 || tupleSize > maximumTupleSize {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"tuple size must be between 2 and %d",
			maximumTupleSize,
		)
	}

	results := make([][]int64, 0)
	if tupleSize > len(values) {
		return results, nil
	}

	// Sort an owned copy so equal values are adjacent without mutation.
	sortedValues := append([]int64(nil), values...)
	slices.Sort(sortedValues)
	selectedValues := make([]int64, 0, tupleSize-2)
	collectUniqueKSum(
		sortedValues,
		0,
		tupleSize,
		big.NewInt(target),
		selectedValues,
		&results,
	)
	return results, nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int64{1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2}
	results, err := uniqueKSum(values, 4, 0)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(results)
	fmt.Println(values)

	maximumInt64 := int64(1<<63 - 1)
	minimumInt64 := int64(-1 << 63)
	extremeResults, err := uniqueKSum(
		[]int64{maximumInt64, minimumInt64, 0},
		2,
		-1,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(extremeResults)

	noResults, err := uniqueKSum(
		[]int64{1, 2, 3},
		3,
		100,
	)
	fmt.Println(noResults, err, noResults == nil)

	_, invalidErr := uniqueKSum(values, 1, 0)
	fmt.Println(invalidErr != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[[-2 -1 1 2] [-2 0 0 2] [-1 0 0 1]]
[1 0 -1 0 -2 2]
[[-9223372036854775808 9223372036854775807]]
[] <nil> false
true
```

The `false` confirms that an ordinary no-result return is non-nil.
The final `true` confirms that K = 1 is rejected.

##### Why it works

Maintain this recursion invariant: `selectedValues` contains values
from distinct, strictly increasing sorted indexes before `startIndex`;
it is nondecreasing; `valuesNeeded` more positions must be chosen; and
their exact required sum is the frame's target. At the root, the
prefix is empty, all positions are available, K values are needed, and
the required sum is the original target, so the invariant holds.

Choosing index i appends its value, changes the next available index
to `i + 1`, decreases the needed count by one, and subtracts the value
from the exact residual. These updates preserve all four invariant
facts. Restoring the prefix length after the child returns recreates
the parent's state before its next choice.

When two values remain, sorted order makes the endpoint decision safe.
If the endpoint sum is too small, pairing the same left value with any
smaller right value is also too small, so its whole duplicate group is
impossible. The symmetric argument safely discards a right group when
the sum is too large. Equality satisfies the residual exactly, so
appending the pair completes a target-sum K-tuple.

Completeness follows by induction on `valuesNeeded`. Any valid
combination has some first available index. The loop tries its value,
and the child invariant describes exactly the remaining suffix. For
equal same-depth candidates, every suffix available after a later
occurrence is also available after the earliest occurrence. Skipping
later ones therefore cannot remove a unique value combination. The
two-pointer base is complete by its endpoint eliminations.

The same-depth skip and pair-group skips also prove uniqueness. Two
branches cannot begin with the same value at the same prefix, and one
pair scan emits each endpoint-value pair once. Every recursion level
chooses values in ascending order, so combinations are internally
sorted. Increasing candidate order and increasing left endpoints make
the outer result lexicographic.

Every subtraction and addition stores its result in a fresh
`big.Int`, so it is mathematically exact and cannot mutate an ancestor
target. Copying the selected prefix before output separates each
result from later backtracking.

Each recursive call reduces `valuesNeeded`, which starts at most 12,
until the two-value base. Within a frame, `chosenIndex` increases and
is bounded by `lastStartIndex`. In the base, at least one pointer
moves after every comparison. All paths and loops are finite, so the
function terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length, K the requested tuple size, and S the
number of returned combinations. Copying takes Theta(N) time and
space. Sorting the copy takes O(N log N) comparison work before the
search.

The recursion chooses K - 2 prefix values. There are at most
O(`N^(K-2)`) such prefix states, and each base call scans at most N
positions. The search therefore takes O(`N^(K-1)`) comparisons in the
worst case for fixed K. Skipped duplicates can greatly reduce the
actual state count, but no input-independent average is claimed.

Writing the output takes Theta(S*K) element copies and retains
Theta(S*K) result storage. The sorted copy uses O(N) auxiliary space.
The selected prefix, recursion stack, and live residual targets use
O(K) entries or objects. K is capped at 12, so each exact residual
uses only a small fixed number of machine words for `int64` inputs.

The implementation creates temporary `big.Int` values for recursive
subtraction and pair comparison. They avoid overflow but add
allocation and arithmetic constants compared with a problem whose
numeric constraints prove native addition safe.

Invalid K and K greater than N exit before copying or sorting, in
Theta(1) time. For valid K no larger than N, all results are required,
so finding one match does not stop the search. On duplicate-heavy
input, same-depth skipping can reduce search work toward O(N*K), but
sorting and output costs still apply.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil or empty input with K = 2 returns a non-nil empty result. There
  are too few positions, but the request itself is valid.
- A valid K greater than N returns empty without sorting. Treating it
  as malformed confuses an impossible search with an invalid tuple
  size.
- K = 1, K = 0, negative K, and K = 13 return nil plus an error. The
  recursive contract and its bounded depth cover only 2 through 12.
- `[2,2,2,2,2]`, K = 4, target 8 returns one `[2,2,2,2]`. Global
  deduplication misses it; no duplicate skipping emits it repeatedly.
- `[-1,0,1,2,-1,-4]`, K = 3, target 0 returns exactly
  `[[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]]` in lexicographic order.
- `[1,2,3]`, K = 3, target 100 returns empty after exhausting its one
  possible tuple. No result is not an arithmetic or validation error.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` values sum to -1. Native addition wraps
  before comparison; `big.Int` returns the exact pair.
- A recursive residual can exceed `int64` even when the final sum
  fits, as the focused four-extreme case shows. Checking only pair
  addition is insufficient.
- `lastStartIndex = N - valuesNeeded` is inclusive. Stopping before it
  misses the final prefix that leaves exactly enough remaining values;
  continuing after it explores a branch that cannot reach length K.
- Skip an equal anchor only when `chosenIndex > startIndex`. Comparing
  with the previous global position at every depth can skip the first
  valid value in a child range.
- After a matched pair, skip both endpoint groups. Moving only one
  pointer can emit the same value pair again from duplicate positions.
- `big.Int` methods mutate their receiver. Using the frame's target as
  the subtraction destination corrupts sibling branches; allocate a
  fresh result as the implementation does.
- Restore `selectedValues` after every recursive return, including
  an empty child. Otherwise one branch's value leaks into the next
  branch.
- Copy the selected prefix into a result. Appending a view of the live
  path lets later backtracking overwrite a previously emitted tuple.
- Results contain values, not original indices. A problem requiring
  index tuples needs value-index records and its own duplicate rule.
- Sorting the caller's slice would violate the ownership contract.
  Copy before `slices.Sort`, as the implementation does.
- Concurrent input mutation is excluded while copying. The function
  does not provide a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose generalized k-sum when K is small and fixed, all unique value
combinations are required, and sorting enables both duplicate control
and a linear two-value base. Three-sum and four-sum are the common
signals.

Use a specialized three-sum loop when K is always three; it expresses
the same anchor-plus-two-pointer invariant with less recursion and
fewer temporary exact-integer objects. Use [complement lookup](
#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) when K = 2, input is unsorted, and
original indices matter. Use [meet in the middle](
#b23-meet-in-the-middle-slices-and-hash-maps) for one fixed- or
variable-cardinality subset on moderate N when reducing the exponent
matters more than enumerating every unique value tuple.

Use backtracking when additional constraints provide strong pruning
or order matters. Use dynamic programming when only existence or a
count is needed and the target range is compact; materializing every
combination has unavoidable output cost.

Practice the K = 3 specialization in the repository's unsolved
[3Sum exercise](problems/medium_leetcode_0015_3sum.go). The official
[4Sum statement](https://leetcode.com/problems/4sum/) supplies the
walkthrough instance. The Go [slices documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort) defines the in-place sort used on the
copy. The [multi-precision integer documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/math/big#Int) defines exact `Int` arithmetic and
its receiver-mutation rule.

#### B.2.5 Counting pairs (frequency map)

##### Problem and contract

Finding one target-sum pair can stop at the first match. Counting all
pairs cannot: duplicate values may create many distinct pairs of
positions even though they form the same pair of values.

Given a finite `[]int64` and an `int64` target, return the number of
unordered index pairs `(leftIndex,rightIndex)` such that
`leftIndex < rightIndex` and the values have the exact mathematical
sum target. Each pair uses two distinct positions. Two pairs are
different when either index differs.

For `[1,1,5,5]` and target 6, the answer is 4: either 1 position can
pair with either 5 position. The result counts index multiplicity,
not merely the distinct value pair `(1,5)`.

The result type is `uint64`. If the exact count exceeds its maximum,
the function returns zero and an error instead of wrapping. Nil,
empty, and one-value inputs return zero and nil error. Every `int64`
value and target is valid.

Complement subtraction is checked before it is performed. An exact
complement outside `int64` cannot match an input value and is skipped.
The function reads but does not mutate the input. Its local map may
allocate and must fit memory. Concurrent input mutation is excluded.

Read [frequency counting](#b11-frequency-counting-hash-map) for the
prefix-counter pattern and [complement lookup](
#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) for finding one pair. This entry owns
the multiplicity calculation that counts every matching index pair.

##### Mental model

Scan values from left to right and treat the current position as the
right endpoint of every new pair. Keep `earlierCountByValue`. Its key
selects an input value, and its `uint64` value says how many positions
with that value occur strictly before the current index.

Reading `earlierCountByValue[1] == 2` at a current value 5 means there
are two distinct earlier positions that each form a target-6 pair
with this 5. Add 2 to `pairCount`, not 1.

At current value v, compute the exact complement `target - v`. If it
fits in `int64`, add its earlier frequency to the result. A missing
map key reads as zero, which is correct because stored frequencies are
always positive.

Only after counting pairs ending at the current position, increment
the frequency of v. This order makes the map describe a strict prefix
and prevents one position from pairing with itself.

Stop after the final position. Every unordered pair has one later
endpoint, so this scan gives every pair exactly one moment when it can
be counted.

##### Worked walkthrough

Count target-6 pairs in `[1,5,1,5,3,-1,7]`. The four combinations of
the two 1 positions with the two 5 positions contribute 4, and the
-1 and 7 positions contribute 1, so the expected count is 5.

Initial state: `earlierCountByValue = {}`, `pairCount = 0`, and the
next right endpoint is index 0.

1. Decision: index 0 holds 1 and needs complement 5. Its earlier
   count is zero, so add nothing; then record this 1.
   After: count 0; frequencies `{1:1}`; next index 1.
   Known correct: no pair can end at the first position, and the map
   describes exactly the processed prefix.

2. Decision: index 1 holds 5 and needs 1. The map reads `1 -> 1`, so
   add one pair, then record this 5.
   After: count 1; frequencies `{1:1,5:1}`; next index 2.
   Known correct: pair `(0,1)` is the only target pair ending at or
   before index 1.

3. Decision: index 2 holds 1 and needs 5. One earlier 5 contributes
   one new pair. Add it, then raise 1's frequency from one to two.
   After: count 2; frequencies `{1:2,5:1}`; next index 3.
   Known correct: pairs `(0,1)` and `(1,2)` are counted once each.

4. Decision: index 3 holds 5 and needs 1. Two earlier 1 positions
   produce pairs `(0,3)` and `(2,3)`, so add two, then record the
   second 5.
   After: count 4; frequencies `{1:2,5:2}`; next index 4.
   Known correct: every combination of processed 1 and 5 positions is
   counted; value multiplicity has not been collapsed into one match.

5. Decision: index 4 holds 3 and also needs 3. The earlier count is
   zero, so add nothing before recording the first 3.
   After: count 4; frequencies `{1:2,5:2,3:1}`; next index 5.
   Known correct: the current 3 did not pair with itself because it
   entered the map only after the lookup.

6. Decision: index 5 holds -1 and needs 7. No earlier 7 exists, so
   add nothing and record -1.
   After: count 4; frequencies `{1:2,5:2,3:1,-1:1}`; next index 6.
   Known correct: every target pair with right endpoint below 6 is
   already included, and all earlier values retain exact frequencies.

7. Decision: index 6 holds 7 and needs -1. Its earlier frequency is
   one, so add one and record 7.
   After: count 5; all seven positions are represented in the map.
   Known correct: pair `(5,6)` is the fifth match. No later endpoint
   remains, so return 5 and nil error.

Focused equal-value case: `[3,3,3,3]` with target 6 adds earlier
frequencies 0, 1, 2, and 3. The result is 6, equal to the number of
ways to choose two of four positions.

Focused complement-boundary case: for
`[minimumInt64,0,maximumInt64]` and target `maximumInt64`, the first
value would need `2^64 - 1`, so lookup is skipped but the value is
still recorded. The final value needs 0 and produces the one valid
pair `(1,2)`.

Counterexample to a presence set: on `[1,1,5,5]`, a set can add only
one match for each 5 and returns 2. The first incorrect update ignores
that the complement 1 occupies two earlier positions. Store a
frequency, not a Boolean.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, equal-value,
extreme-complement, empty, and count-overflow-boundary cases. Save it
as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It uses only the standard
library and leaves every input slice unchanged.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Counting pairs (frequency map).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

const (
	maximumInt64  = int64(1<<63 - 1)
	minimumInt64  = int64(-1 << 63)
	maximumUint64 = uint64(1<<64 - 1)
)

func checkedInt64Subtraction(
	left int64,
	right int64,
) (int64, bool) {
	// Positive subtraction can underflow; negative can overflow.
	if right > 0 && left < minimumInt64+right {
		return 0, false
	}
	if right < 0 && left > maximumInt64+right {
		return 0, false
	}
	return left - right, true
}

func checkedUint64Addition(
	left uint64,
	right uint64,
) (uint64, bool) {
	// maximumUint64-right is the largest safe left operand.
	if left > maximumUint64-right {
		return 0, false
	}
	return left + right, true
}

func countTargetPairs(
	values []int64,
	target int64,
) (uint64, error) {
	// Compute target pairs from the state without mutating it.
	earlierCountByValue := make(map[int64]uint64)
	var pairCount uint64

	// Before insertion, the map describes only earlier positions.
	for rightIndex, value := range values {
		complement, representable := checkedInt64Subtraction(
			target,
			value,
		)
		if representable {
			matchingEarlier := earlierCountByValue[complement]
			nextPairCount, fits := checkedUint64Addition(
				pairCount,
				matchingEarlier,
			)
			if !fits {
				return 0, fmt.Errorf(
					"pair count exceeds uint64 at index %d",
					rightIndex,
				)
			}
			pairCount = nextPairCount
		}

		// Record this position only after counting pairs ending here.
		earlierCountByValue[value]++
	}
	return pairCount, nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	pairCount, err := countTargetPairs(
		[]int64{1, 5, 1, 5, 3, -1, 7},
		6,
	)
	fmt.Println(pairCount, err)

	pairCount, err = countTargetPairs(
		[]int64{3, 3, 3, 3},
		6,
	)
	fmt.Println(pairCount, err)

	pairCount, err = countTargetPairs(
		[]int64{minimumInt64, 0, maximumInt64},
		maximumInt64,
	)
	fmt.Println(pairCount, err)

	pairCount, err = countTargetPairs(nil, 0)
	fmt.Println(pairCount, err)

	_, countFits := checkedUint64Addition(maximumUint64, 1)
	fmt.Println(countFits)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
5 <nil>
6 <nil>
1 <nil>
0 <nil>
false
```

The final false demonstrates that adding one beyond the maximum count
is rejected. The counting function uses the same helper before every
result update.

##### Why it works

Before processing index i, maintain two invariant facts. First,
`earlierCountByValue[x]` equals the number of occurrences of x in the
strict prefix `values[0:i]`. Second, `pairCount` equals the number of
valid pairs whose right index is below i. Both hold initially because
the prefix is empty and contains no pair.

For current value v, every new valid pair ending at i must use an
earlier value equal to `target - v`. If that complement is
representable, its map frequency is exactly the number of such
earlier positions. Adding the frequency therefore counts all and only
new pairs ending at i.

If the exact complement is outside `int64`, no input value can equal
it, so zero new pair ends at i. In either case, incrementing v after
the addition makes the map exactly describe `values[0:i+1]`. All old
pairs remain counted, so both invariant facts hold for the next index.

Every unordered pair has one unique larger index. The iteration for
that index counts it once, and no other iteration can count the same
two positions. When the scan ends at N, the invariant says
`pairCount` covers every valid pair in the full input.

For positive v, `target - v` underflows exactly when
`target < minimumInt64 + v`. For negative v, it overflows exactly when
`target > maximumInt64 + v`. The boundary expressions move inward and
are themselves representable.

Unsigned result addition overflows exactly when
`pairCount > maximumUint64 - matchingEarlier`. The subtraction is
always representable, so checking that boundary before addition
prevents wraparound. On failure, returning zero with an error matches
the stated no-partial-result contract.

Each iteration advances one finite slice position and performs no
nested scan. The loop therefore terminates after N iterations. A map
frequency cannot overflow `uint64`: it never exceeds the slice length,
and Go slice lengths fit in `int`, whose supported widths are no wider
than `uint64`.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length and D the number of distinct values. Every
position performs fixed-width arithmetic, one expected constant-time
map read, one expected constant-time map update, and one checked count
addition. The function therefore takes expected Theta(N) time under
the usual hash-table assumption.

Unlike a find-one search, counting must inspect all N positions even
when the first two form a pair. Best and worst scan counts are both N
for a given input length. Go does not promise worst-case constant-time
map operations, and no distribution-independent average beyond the
hashing assumption is claimed.

The map retains D `int64` keys and `uint64` frequencies, using O(D)
auxiliary space plus implementation-dependent bucket overhead. The
scalar result, complement, and counters use O(1) space. There is no
recursion, input copy, or output collection.

A nested comparison of every unordered index pair uses O(1)
auxiliary space but Theta(N squared) time. Sorting a copy and scanning
equal-value groups takes O(N log N) comparison work and O(N) copied
storage. If the input is already sorted and mutation is allowed, the
grouped two-pointer alternative can count in Theta(N) time with O(1)
auxiliary state.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil, empty, and one-value inputs return `(0,nil)`. No two distinct
  positions exist, and the range loop performs no unsafe access.
- `[0,0,0,0,0]` with target 0 returns 10 by adding frequencies 0
  through 4. Zero is an ordinary key, not an absence marker.
- `[3,3,3,3]` with target 6 returns 6. Looking up before incrementing
  prevents self-pairing and naturally implements `4 choose 2`.
- `[1,1,5,5]` with target 6 returns 4, not one distinct value pair and
  not two presence matches. Each occurrence combination is an answer.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` form target -1 without addition.
  Directly adding them is unsafe when other extreme pairs are
  considered.
- `[maximumInt64,maximumInt64]` with target -2 returns zero. Wrapped
  machine addition would produce -2 and invent a false pair.
- An unrepresentable complement skips only the lookup. Still increment
  the current value because it may complement a later position.
- Look up before incrementing. Reversing the order makes `[3]` with
  target 6 count the single position as a pair with itself.
- Do not store only presence. The walkthrough's second 5 must add two,
  not one.
- A missing map key safely reads as frequency zero because the code
  never stores zero frequencies. No presence Boolean is needed here.
- Check `uint64` addition before updating the result. Silent wrap can
  turn a very large positive count into a plausible small answer.
- On count overflow the function returns zero and an error, not the
  valid partial count accumulated before the failing right endpoint.
- The map never needs iteration, so unspecified map iteration order
  cannot affect the deterministic scalar result.
- Concurrent input mutation is excluded. The map summarizes one
  stable prefix, not a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose a prefix frequency map when the question asks how many index
pairs meet an equality, input is unsorted, and O(D) map storage is
acceptable. The key clue is multiplicity: one current value may match
many earlier positions with the same complement.

Use [complement lookup](#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) when only one
deterministic pair is needed; stopping early avoids unnecessary work.
Use [sorted two pointers](#b22-two-pointers-after-sorting-slice) when
the input is already ordered or map storage is undesirable, but count
whole duplicate groups rather than advancing one position at a time.
Use [generalized k-sum](
#b24-generalized-k-sum-sorted-slice-and-recursion) when fixed tuples
larger than two and their actual value combinations are required.

The completed [Two Sum archive](
problems/solved_easy_leetcode_0001_two_sum.go) is a find-one contrast
that uses the same complement equation. The [frequency-map owner](
#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) explains mutable counter semantics.
The official [Go maps article](https://go.dev/blog/maps) documents
missing-key zero values and map update operations used here.

### B.3 Ordering, ranking, and selection

#### B.3.1 Comparison sorting (slice)

##### Problem and contract

Many records have no useful numeric bucket or direct index. They can
still be ordered when a comparison answers which of two records comes
first. Comparison sorting treats that answer as its only knowledge of
the keys.

Given a finite slice of candidate records, return every record ranked
by these keys in order:

1. Higher `score` first.
2. For equal scores, lexicographically smaller `name` first.
3. For equal scores and names, smaller `submissionID` first.

Scores are arbitrary `int64` values, names are arbitrary Go strings,
and submission IDs are arbitrary `uint64` values. Exact duplicate
records remain duplicated. The comparison regards them as equivalent;
their relative positions are not promised because `slices.SortFunc`
is unstable.

The function returns a newly allocated slice and leaves the input
order unchanged. Nil and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice.
Record values are copied, while their immutable string data may remain
shared. Allocation must fit memory, and concurrent input mutation is
excluded. There is no malformed record and therefore no error result.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) for
copying and ownership. The earlier [sorting and scanning application](
#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) groups integers after sorting; this
entry owns the general comparison contract and multi-key ordering.

##### Mental model

A comparator takes `left` and `right` and returns:

- a negative number when left must come before right;
- zero when the ordering treats them as equivalent;
- a positive number when left must come after right.

Compare keys lexicographically: ask the highest-priority question and
return as soon as it differs. Only a tie reaches the next key. Reading
`compareCandidates(Mina-91-4,Ari-91-2) > 0` means the scores tie, but
`"Mina"` follows `"Ari"`, so Mina belongs later.

Descending score does not require subtraction or negation. Reverse
the operands to `cmp.Compare`: comparing `right.score` with
`left.score` returns a negative result when left has the larger score.
Names and submission IDs use ordinary left-to-right ascending
comparison.

The comparator must be a strict weak ordering. In plain terms, no
record precedes itself, reversing two records reverses the sign,
chains such as A before B and B before C imply A before C, and
equivalence is consistent. A sort cannot repair contradictory answers.

Copy the records, then let `slices.SortFunc` reorder that copy. Its
internal comparison and swap schedule is intentionally unspecified;
the observable promise is that no later record compares before the
record immediately preceding it.

##### Worked walkthrough

Rank these records, written as `name-score-ID`:

```text
Mina-91-4, Ari-91-2, Ari-91-1, Zoe-87-3, Bo-100-5
```

The expected order is Bo, Ari ID 1, Ari ID 2, Mina, then Zoe.

Initial state: the caller owns the five records in their supplied
order. No output storage exists.

1. Decision: allocate five output positions and copy every record
   because the library sort mutates the slice it receives.
   After: both slices contain
   `[Mina-91-4,Ari-91-2,Ari-91-1,Zoe-87-3,Bo-100-5]`, but their
   record arrays are distinct.
   Known correct: later swaps can change only the output order.

2. Decision: apply the three comparison keys. Bo's score 100 places
   it before every score 91 or 87. Among score-91 records, both Ari
   names precede Mina; between the Aris, ID 1 precedes ID 2. Mina's
   score 91 places it before Zoe's 87.
   After: the required ordering constraints are
   `Bo < Ari-1 < Ari-2 < Mina < Zoe`.
   Known correct: every tie has advanced to the next key, and every
   unequal higher-priority key has stopped comparison immediately.

3. Decision: call `slices.SortFunc` with that comparator. The library
   may compare and swap records in a version-dependent sequence; its
   contract uses the same ordering constraints regardless of sequence.
   After: output is
   `[Bo-100-5,Ari-91-1,Ari-91-2,Mina-91-4,Zoe-87-3]`.
   Known correct: the library produces a sorted permutation under a
   valid strict weak ordering; no record was added or removed.

4. Decision: verify adjacent records with the comparator. Bo versus
   Ari-1 returns negative by score; Ari-1 versus Ari-2 returns
   negative by ID; Ari-2 versus Mina returns negative by name; Mina
   versus Zoe returns negative by score.
   After: return the ranked copy; the input remains in its initial
   order.
   Known correct: every adjacent pair respects a transitive ordering,
   so every earlier result belongs no later than every following one.

Focused empty case: nil input allocates and returns a non-nil
zero-length slice. Sorting it performs no comparison.

Focused extreme case: records scored `minimumInt64` and
`maximumInt64` put the maximum first. Reversing comparator operands is
exact; computing `minimumInt64 - maximumInt64` would overflow and can
reverse the intended answer.

Focused equivalence case: two records with identical name, score, and
ID both remain. The comparator returns zero. Because this sort is
unstable, their original relative identity would be unspecified if a
record carried additional unranked payload.

Counterexample to an inconsistent tie rule: if equal-score records
always return negative instead of comparing names, both
`compare(Ari,Mina)` and `compare(Mina,Ari)` say the left record comes
first. No single order can satisfy both claims. Comparators must
return zero or continue to a consistent tie-break.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves the
input, handles score extremes, and demonstrates the non-nil empty
result. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It uses the
standard `cmp` and `slices` packages.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Comparison sorting (slice).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"cmp"
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)

type candidate struct {
	name         string
	score        int64
	submissionID uint64
}

func compareCandidates(left, right candidate) int {
	// Reverse the operands for descending score without negating.
	if byScore := cmp.Compare(right.score, left.score); byScore != 0 {
		return byScore
	}
	if byName := cmp.Compare(left.name, right.name); byName != 0 {
		return byName
	}
	return cmp.Compare(left.submissionID, right.submissionID)
}

func rankCandidates(values []candidate) []candidate {
	// Sort an owned copy because SortFunc mutates its argument.
	ranked := make([]candidate, len(values))
	copy(ranked, values)
	slices.SortFunc(ranked, compareCandidates)
	return ranked
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []candidate{
		{name: "Mina", score: 91, submissionID: 4},
		{name: "Ari", score: 91, submissionID: 2},
		{name: "Ari", score: 91, submissionID: 1},
		{name: "Zoe", score: 87, submissionID: 3},
		{name: "Bo", score: 100, submissionID: 5},
	}
	ranked := rankCandidates(values)
	fmt.Println(ranked)
	fmt.Println(values)

	maximumInt64 := int64(1<<63 - 1)
	minimumInt64 := int64(-1 << 63)
	extremes := rankCandidates([]candidate{
		{name: "low", score: minimumInt64, submissionID: 2},
		{name: "high", score: maximumInt64, submissionID: 1},
	})
	fmt.Println(extremes)

	empty := rankCandidates(nil)
	fmt.Println(empty, empty == nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[{Bo 100 5} {Ari 91 1} {Ari 91 2} {Mina 91 4} {Zoe 87 3}]
[{Mina 91 4} {Ari 91 2} {Ari 91 1} {Zoe 87 3} {Bo 100 5}]
[{high 9223372036854775807 1} {low -9223372036854775808 2}]
[] false
```

The second line confirms that the input order did not change. The
final false confirms that the empty result is not nil.

##### Why it works

The comparator implements the contract one key at a time. Unequal
scores decide immediately in descending order. Equal scores reach
ascending name comparison. Only equal scores and names reach ascending
submission ID comparison. A zero result therefore means all three
ordering keys are equal.

Each component uses the built-in order of one ordered Go type. Such an
order is irreflexive and transitive. Lexicographically composing the
three components preserves those properties: the first component that
differs decides both directions, while exact ties consistently move to
the next component. The comparator is therefore a strict weak order;
in fact, it totally orders distinct key triples.

`slices.SortFunc` promises to sort its argument according to a valid
comparator. Supplying the proved comparator therefore produces a
permutation in the requested order. Sorting changes positions but
does not create or delete records, so duplicates remain duplicated.

The function gives the library a newly allocated copy. All reordering
is confined to that copy, proving input preservation. The returned
slice owns its record array; copied strings remain safe to share
because Go strings are immutable values.

The input is finite, the comparator has bounded straight-line control
flow, and the standard-library sort terminates under its comparator
contract. Copying and sorting an empty slice are both valid, so the
same reasoning covers every input size.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the record count and B be the maximum number of name bytes a
single string comparison examines before finding a difference or
ending. Copying N records takes Theta(N) time and creates the O(N)
returned record array. It copies string headers, not name bytes.

This example was verified with Go 1.26.5. That implementation uses
pattern-defeating quicksort, small-range insertion sort, and a
heapsort fallback after repeated bad partitions. It makes
O(N log N) comparator calls in the worst case and uses O(log N)
call-stack space while reordering the returned slice in place. Those
algorithm details are version-dependent, not part of the `SortFunc`
API contract.

A score or ID decision costs O(1). A tied score can require a string
comparison costing O(B), so the full worst-case work is
O(N log N * B), plus the initial copy. When most scores differ, the
name cost is usually avoided. No distribution-independent average is
claimed.

For N distinct arbitrary keys, every comparison-only algorithm needs
Omega(N log N) comparisons in the worst case: a decision tree must
distinguish N factorial possible permutations. This lower bound does
not apply when an algorithm exploits more key structure than pairwise
order, as counting and radix sorting do.

Nil and singleton inputs require Theta(N) copying and no meaningful
ordering work. Already ordered inputs may take fewer comparisons in
the current adaptive implementation, but exact best-case behavior is
version-dependent. The unstable function avoids a stability promise;
use the stable variant when preserving equal-record order is required.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice. Returning nil
  would violate the explicit result-shape contract.
- One record is copied and returned unchanged; no comparison is
  needed.
- Exact duplicate records are retained. Sorting orders elements; it
  does not deduplicate them.
- Equal scores compare names before IDs. Returning zero after the
  score tie leaves Mina and Ari equivalent and violates the ranking
  contract.
- Equal scores and names compare IDs. Reversing that final comparison
  silently reverses the two Ari records in the walkthrough.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` scores are valid. Do not subtract scores
  or negate a score to simulate descending order; either can overflow.
- Go's built-in string comparison is not locale-aware collation. Case,
  accents, normalization, and invalid UTF-8 bytes follow Go string
  ordering, not a user's language rules.
- Return zero only when all ranked keys tie. Calling distinct records
  equivalent permits their relative order to vary in an unstable sort.
- A comparator must not depend on call count, random state, or mutable
  external data. The library may ask about pairs in any order and may
  repeat comparisons.
- `SortFunc` mutates its slice. Slice assignment alone still shares
  the caller's array; allocate and copy before sorting.
- The returned record array is independent, but string bytes may be
  shared. Strings are immutable; a record containing mutable slices or
  maps would need a documented shallow- or deep-copy policy.
- `SortFunc` does not preserve the input order of equivalent records.
  Use `slices.SortStableFunc` when that order is part of the contract.
- Concurrent input mutation during copying is excluded. The function
  does not provide a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose comparison sorting when all N records need a total or weak
order and the keys expose comparison but not a small dense universe.
Multi-field records, strings, large integers, and caller-defined
priority rules are common signals.

Use [counting and radix sorting](
#b32-counting-and-radix-sorting-arrays) when integer or digit
structure permits linear passes and its extra storage is acceptable.
Use [quickselect](#b33-quickselect-slice) when only one rank is
needed. Use [top-k selection](
#b34-top-k-selection-heap) when only a small prefix matters; fully
sorting all N records performs unnecessary ordering work.

Choose the later algorithm-specific lessons when implementation
constraints decide the method: [merge sort](
#b36-merge-sort-slice-and-buffer) for stable buffered merging,
[quicksort](#b37-quicksort-slice-and-partition-bounds) for
partitioning, [heapsort](#b38-heapsort-array-backed-heap) for an
in-place worst-case bound, and [elementary sorts](
#b39-insertion-and-selection-sort-slice) for tiny or educational
inputs.

The official [`slices.SortFunc` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#SortFunc) defines comparator signs, strict
weak ordering, and instability. The [Go 1.26.5 sorting source](
https://go.dev/src/slices/sort.go) identifies the implementation used
for the stated version-dependent costs. NIST's [comparison-sort
definition](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/comparisnsrt.html)
contrasts this model with sorts that exploit a restricted key
universe.

#### B.3.2 Counting and radix sorting (arrays)

##### Problem and contract

Comparison sorting learns about keys by comparing pairs. Fixed-width
integers expose more structure: each key is a short sequence of
bounded digits. Counting sort can order one digit, and radix sort can
compose those digit passes into a full order.

Given a finite `[]int32`, return all its values in ascending signed
order. Every `int32` is valid, including the minimum, maximum,
negatives, zero, and duplicates. Nil and empty inputs return a
non-nil empty slice.

The function returns a newly allocated slice and does not change the
input. The returned element storage belongs to the caller. Allocation
must fit memory, and concurrent input mutation is excluded. There is
no malformed public input and therefore no error result.

This implementation uses least-significant-digit radix sort. It
examines four bytes from least significant to most significant. Each
byte is in `[0,256)`, so a stable counting-sort pass can order it with
256 counters.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) and
[bounded-value counting](#b14-bounded-value-counting-array) first.
The bounded-counting lesson owns dense histograms. This entry owns
stable placement, digit composition, and signed-key transformation.

##### Mental model

Think of a 32-bit key as four base-256 digits. Sorting first by the
least significant byte seems backward, but stability carries every
decision already made. When a later pass groups equal current bytes,
it preserves their earlier low-byte order.

One counting pass has three phases:

1. Count how many values have each byte digit.
2. Convert counts into each digit's first output index.
3. Scan input left to right, place each value at its digit's next
   index, and advance that index.

The third phase makes the pass stable. Two values with the same digit
leave the pass in the order in which they entered it. After byte zero,
the values are ordered by one byte. After byte one, they are ordered
by the low two bytes. Four passes order all 32 bits.

Ordinary unsigned byte order does not match signed order. Converting
`int32` to `uint32` puts negative values after nonnegative values.
Flip the top bit before extracting bytes:

```text
ordered key = uint32(value) XOR 0x80000000
```

This maps the signed range monotonically onto the unsigned range.
Minimum `int32` maps to `0x00000000`, -1 maps to `0x7fffffff`, zero
maps to `0x80000000`, and maximum `int32` maps to `0xffffffff`.

Keep two equally sized owned slices. One is the current order and the
other receives the next stable pass. Swap their roles after each pass;
do not copy all elements back between passes.

##### Worked walkthrough

Sort:

```text
[258,-1,2,256,-258,0,1,-256]
```

The expected signed order is:

```text
[-258,-256,-1,0,1,2,256,258]
```

Initial state: copy the input into `current` and allocate an equally
long `buffer`. The caller's input remains separate. Every value is
viewed through its sign-flipped ordered key.

1. Decision: count and stably place by byte zero, the least
   significant byte. Digit `00` receives 256, 0, and -256 in their
   input order. Digit `02` receives 258 and 2 in their input order.
   After: `[256,0,-256,1,258,2,-258,-1]`.
   Known correct: the sequence is stably ordered by its lowest byte;
   equal low-byte values retain their prior order.

2. Decision: swap slice roles and stably place by byte one. Digit
   `00` receives 0, 1, and 2; digit `01` receives 256 and 258;
   digits `fe` and `ff` receive the remaining negative values.
   After: `[0,1,2,256,258,-258,-256,-1]`.
   Known correct: byte one is ordered, and stability preserves byte
   zero order inside each equal-byte-one group.

3. Decision: place by byte two. The five nonnegative ordered keys
   have byte `00`; the three negative ordered keys have byte `ff`.
   After: `[0,1,2,256,258,-258,-256,-1]`.
   Known correct: the first three key bytes are ordered even though
   this pass happens not to change the sequence.

4. Decision: place by byte three, the most significant byte. Negative
   ordered keys have top byte `7f`; these examples' nonnegative keys
   have top byte `80`. Stability preserves the lower-three-byte order
   inside each group.
   After: `[-258,-256,-1,0,1,2,256,258]`.
   Known correct: all four bytes are ordered, which is the complete
   sign-adjusted key, so signed values are ascending.

5. Decision: return `current` after the fourth role swap.
   After: the returned slice has the sorted values, while the input is
   still `[258,-1,2,256,-258,0,1,-256]`.
   Known correct: the result is a sorted permutation in independent
   storage.

Focused signed-boundary case: sorting minimum `int32`, maximum
`int32`, zero, and -1 returns minimum, -1, zero, maximum. Their
ordered keys are `00000000`, `7fffffff`, `80000000`, and `ffffffff`.

Focused stability case: byte zero orders `[1,0]` as `[0,1]`. Both
values have byte one equal to zero. A stable byte-one pass preserves
`[0,1]`; an unstable pass may reverse it and destroy the work of the
first pass.

Counterexample to counting the complete key directly: an `int32` key
has `2^32` possible values. A counter for every possible key makes
the universe cost dominate ordinary inputs. Four passes reuse only
256 counters per digit.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves the
input, handles signed extremes, and demonstrates the non-nil empty
result. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Counting and radix sorting
// (arrays). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

const (
	byteCount = uint(4)
	radix     = 256
	signBit   = uint32(1) << 31
)

func orderedKey(value int32) uint32 {
	// Flipping the sign bit maps signed order to unsigned order.
	return uint32(value) ^ signBit
}

func byteDigit(value int32, byteIndex uint) uint8 {
	// Keep byte digit in one helper so callers use one rule.
	shift := byteIndex * 8
	return uint8(orderedKey(value) >> shift)
}

func stableByteCountingPass(
	input []int32,
	output []int32,
	byteIndex uint,
) {
	// Keep stable byte counting pass in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	if len(input) != len(output) {
		panic("counting pass slice lengths differ")
	}
	if byteIndex >= byteCount {
		panic("counting pass byte index is out of range")
	}

	var countByDigit [radix]int
	for _, value := range input {
		digit := byteDigit(value, byteIndex)
		countByDigit[digit]++
	}

	var nextIndexByDigit [radix]int
	nextIndex := 0
	for digit, count := range countByDigit {
		nextIndexByDigit[digit] = nextIndex
		nextIndex += count
	}

	// Left-to-right placement preserves input order within a digit.
	for _, value := range input {
		digit := byteDigit(value, byteIndex)
		outputIndex := nextIndexByDigit[digit]
		output[outputIndex] = value
		nextIndexByDigit[digit]++
	}
}

func radixSortInt32(values []int32) []int32 {
	// Keep radix sort int32 in one helper so callers use one rule.
	current := make([]int32, len(values))
	copy(current, values)
	buffer := make([]int32, len(values))

	for byteIndex := uint(0); byteIndex < byteCount; byteIndex++ {
		stableByteCountingPass(current, buffer, byteIndex)
		current, buffer = buffer, current
	}
	return current
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int32{
		258,
		-1,
		2,
		256,
		-258,
		0,
		1,
		-256,
	}
	sorted := radixSortInt32(values)
	fmt.Println(sorted)
	fmt.Println(values)

	extremes := radixSortInt32([]int32{
		-1 << 31,
		1<<31 - 1,
		0,
		-1,
	})
	fmt.Println(extremes)

	empty := radixSortInt32(nil)
	fmt.Println(empty, empty == nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[-258 -256 -1 0 1 2 256 258]
[258 -1 2 256 -258 0 1 -256]
[-2147483648 -1 0 2147483647]
[] false
```

The second line confirms that sorting did not change the input. The
final false confirms that the empty result is not nil.

##### Why it works

First prove the key transformation. For a nonnegative `int32` value
x, flipping the zero sign bit adds `2^31`. For a negative x,
conversion to `uint32` gives `x + 2^32`; flipping its set sign bit
subtracts `2^31`. In both cases, the mathematical transformed value
is `x + 2^31`. Adding one constant is strictly increasing, so unsigned
ordered-key order is exactly signed `int32` order.

Now consider one counting pass. After counting, `countByDigit[d]`
equals the number of input values with digit d. The prefix sum stored
in `nextIndexByDigit[d]` is the total count of all smaller digits, so
it is the first output index reserved for d. Those adjacent reserved
ranges are disjoint and together contain exactly N positions.

During placement, maintain this invariant: every already read input
value occupies the next free position in its digit's range, and
unread values have enough remaining positions. Placing the next value
at its recorded index and advancing that one index preserves the
invariant. Because input is read left to right, equal-digit values
enter their range in input order. The completed pass is therefore a
stable ordering by its selected byte and is a permutation of input.

Every count and output index is at most N, which already fits Go's
`int` because N is a slice length. Valid byte indexes are zero through
three, so their shift counts are zero, eight, 16, and 24. Every array
access and shift is therefore within its established bound.

For the radix composition, maintain this invariant after pass p:
`current` is ordered by bytes p through zero, treating byte p as the
most significant among those processed, and equal processed-byte
keys retain input order. The byte-zero counting pass establishes the
base case. The next stable pass groups values by its new byte; inside
one group it preserves the already correct lower-byte order. This
proves the invariant by induction.

After pass three, all four bytes of every transformed key have been
processed. The keys are therefore in unsigned ascending order. The
transformation proof converts that statement to signed ascending
order. Every pass preserves the multiset, so the output is also a
permutation of the input.

The initial copy separates caller and result storage. The two pass
slices are distinct, and swapping their headers changes only their
roles. The internal panics encode programmer invariants: each pass
must receive equal lengths and one of the four valid byte indexes.
`radixSortInt32` always satisfies both conditions.

Each pass has three finite loops: two over N values and one over 256
digits. The outer loop advances through exactly four bytes. All loops
are bounded, so the function terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of values, R be the radix 256, and P be the four
bytes per key. One pass performs Theta(N + R) work: count N values,
scan R counters, and place N values. All passes take
Theta(P * (N + R)) time. With fixed `int32`, P and R are constants,
so this is Theta(N) time.

The implementation always performs all four passes. For nonempty
inputs, its best, average, and worst cases therefore have the same
Theta(N) bound, including already sorted input. Empty input takes
Theta(1) time for the four fixed 256-counter scans. Neither bound
depends on a favorable key distribution.

The returned current slice uses O(N) output space. At peak, the other
slice uses O(N) auxiliary space, and the two 256-entry counter arrays
use O(R) auxiliary space. After return, the unused buffer is no
longer retained. Slice-role swaps take O(1) time and storage.

General counting sort over a complete universe of size U takes
Theta(N + U) time and O(U) counter space. Radix sort trades P passes
for the smaller digit universe R. Choosing a larger radix reduces P
but enlarges and initializes the counter arrays; choosing a smaller
radix does the reverse.

Unlike comparison sorting, the algorithm reads key digits. It is not
subject to the comparison-only Omega(N log N) lower bound. For small
N, comparison sorting may still be faster because it has less setup,
smaller fixed storage, and a standard-library implementation.

This least-significant-digit form needs stable passes and an O(N)
placement buffer. More specialized in-place radix methods exist, but
their invariants and movement costs are more complex. The clear
buffered form is often preferable unless memory measurements require
another design.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice. Four passes over
  empty slices are valid, and their 256-counter scans remain bounded.
- One value passes through all four buffers and returns unchanged.
- Duplicate values remain duplicated. Their relative identity is not
  observable for plain integers, but pass stability is still required
  for the radix proof.
- Minimum and maximum `int32` are valid. The sign-bit transform maps
  them to the endpoints of the unsigned range without arithmetic
  overflow.
- Omitting the sign-bit flip puts all nonnegative values before all
  negative values. Raw unsigned order is not signed ascending order.
- Flipping every bit reverses order; flip only the sign bit to rotate
  the two signed halves while preserving order inside each half.
- Process bytes from least significant to most significant for this
  stable-pass proof. Reversing that direction makes later low-byte
  passes override more significant decisions.
- Each pass must be stable. Filling a digit's reserved range from the
  end while scanning left to right reverses equal-digit values.
- Convert counts to starting indexes before placement. A raw count is
  a range length, not an output position.
- Keep input and output pass slices distinct. Writing into the slice
  being scanned can overwrite a value that has not been counted or
  placed yet.
- Swap slice headers after every pass. Swapping elements pairwise or
  copying the whole buffer back adds unnecessary Theta(N) work per
  pass.
- Byte extraction here is numeric shifting, so it does not depend on
  the computer's memory endianness. Reading raw memory bytes would
  need an explicit endianness contract.
- `byteIndex` is an internal program state, not caller data. The
  helper panics on an impossible index or unequal slice lengths so a
  programming error cannot silently corrupt the result.
- Changing the public type to `int` without changing the number of
  passes is wrong on 64-bit platforms. Fixed-width keys make digit
  count and sign-bit position explicit.
- Concurrent writes to the input race with the initial copy. The
  function does not provide a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose counting sort when keys occupy a small dense universe and the
counter array is reasonable. Choose least-significant-digit radix
sort when keys have a fixed number of bounded digits, stable passes
are available, and O(N) auxiliary storage is acceptable. Large
batches of fixed-width integers, byte strings of fixed length, and
records with fixed-width integer keys are common signals.

Use [comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) when keys
offer only a comparator, the dataset is small, or simpler library code
matters more than a linear asymptotic bound. Use [bucket sort](
#b310-bucket-sort-bucket-arrays) when values distribute into ranges
that receive their own local ordering. Use [merge sort](
#b36-merge-sort-slice-and-buffer) when a general stable comparison
order is required.

For variable-length strings, decide how a missing digit sorts and
whether bytes, Unicode code points, or locale-aware units define the
key. This fixed-width integer implementation does not silently extend
to those contracts.

NIST's [counting-sort definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/countingsort.html) describes counts,
running totals, and final placement. Its [radix-sort definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/radixsort.html) describes stable
least-significant-part passes and identifies counting sort as a pass
method. The Go specification's [numeric conversion rules](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Conversions_between_numeric_types) define the
signed-to-unsigned conversion used by `orderedKey`.

#### B.3.3 Quickselect (slice)

##### Problem and contract

Sometimes one sorted position matters but the order of every other
value does not. Finding a median, percentile boundary, or one contest
rank does not inherently require a fully sorted slice.

Given a finite `[]int64` and a zero-based `rank`, return the value at
that position in ascending sorted order. Rank zero asks for the
smallest value, and rank `len(values)-1` asks for the largest. Equal
values occupy separate sorted positions, so `[2,2,7]` has value 2 at
both ranks zero and one.

Equivalently, a returned value x has at most `rank` input values
strictly below x and more than `rank` values at most x. The function
returns only x; it does not return a sorted or partitioned slice.

A rank outside `[0,len(values))` returns zero and a non-nil error.
Nil and empty input therefore have no valid rank. Zero itself is a
valid selected value, so callers must inspect the error rather than
using zero as a missing sentinel.

Every `int64` value is valid. The function partitions a newly
allocated copy and leaves the input unchanged. Its temporary storage
is no longer retained by the function after return. Allocation must
fit memory, and concurrent input mutation is excluded.

This deterministic Quickselect chooses the middle physical index of
the current range as its pivot. That choice makes the walkthrough
reproducible, but it does not promise a median value or a worst-case
linear running time.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) and
[comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) first. Comparison
sorting owns complete ordering; this entry owns selecting one rank by
partitioning only the ranges that can still contain it.

##### Mental model

Imagine where the requested value would sit after a full sort, but do
not perform that sort. Keep an inclusive active range
`[left,right]`. The requested global rank lies inside this range.
Values discarded before `left` are smaller than every active value;
values discarded after `right` are greater than every active value.

Choose one pivot value from the active range. A three-way partition
rearranges that range into adjacent half-open regions:

```text
[left,lessEnd)              values below pivot
[lessEnd,greaterStart)      values equal to pivot
[greaterStart,right+1)      values above pivot
```

No region is internally sorted. Its boundary is enough. If `rank` is
below `lessEnd`, only the less-than region can contain the answer. If
`rank` is at least `greaterStart`, only the greater-than region can
contain it. Otherwise the rank lies in the equal band, so the pivot
value is the answer.

The partition scan itself remembers four regions:

```text
less | equal | unknown | greater
```

`lessEnd` starts the equal region, `scanIndex` starts the unknown
region, and `greaterStart` starts the greater region. A smaller value
is swapped to `lessEnd`, then both left boundaries advance. An equal
value advances only `scanIndex`. A greater value is swapped just
before `greaterStart`; `scanIndex` stays because the value swapped in
from the unknown region has not been classified yet.

The scan stops when the unknown region is empty. Quickselect then
discards two of the three regions and repeats only when the requested
rank is outside the equal band.

##### Worked walkthrough

Find zero-based rank 4, the fifth-smallest value, in:

```text
[7,2,9,4,2,8,5,1,6]
```

The fully sorted order would be `[1,2,2,4,5,6,7,8,9]`, so the
expected answer is 5. Quickselect will establish that value without
ordering the rest.

Initial state: `rank = 4`. The caller owns the displayed input. No
working storage or active range exists yet.

1. Decision: validate that 4 lies in `[0,9)`, copy all values, and
   set the active range to inclusive indexes `[0,8]`.
   After: `working = [7,2,9,4,2,8,5,1,6]`, `left = 0`, and
   `right = 8`; the input remains separate.
   Known correct: only the copy may be rearranged, and the requested
   sorted position lies in the active range.

2. Decision: the midpoint index is 4, whose pivot value is 2.
   Partition the active range. At scan index 0, 7 is greater, so swap
   it with the last unknown value 6 and keep scanning index 0. Six is
   also greater, so swap it with 1; now 1 is smaller, so grow the less
   region. Values equal to 2 grow the middle region. Repeating the
   same rules empties the unknown region.
   After: `working = [1,2,2,4,8,5,9,6,7]`. The bands are
   `[0,1) < 2`, `[1,3) == 2`, and `[3,9) > 2`.
   Known correct: final sorted ranks zero through two are represented
   by the first two bands, while rank 4 must be in the greater band.

3. Decision: `rank 4 >= greaterStart 3`, so discard both bands at
   or below the pivot and set `left = 3`. Keep `right = 8`.
   After: the active range is `[3,8]`, containing
   `[4,8,5,9,6,7]`; indexes below 3 need no further ordering.
   Known correct: every discarded value is smaller than every active
   value, so none can occupy global rank 4.

4. Decision: the new midpoint index is 5, whose value is 5.
   Partition indexes 3 through 8. Value 4 grows the less region.
   Values 8, 7, 6, and 9 grow the greater region, with each swapped-in
   value inspected before the scan advances. The pivot forms the
   equal band.
   After: `working = [1,2,2,4,5,9,6,7,8]`. Within the active range,
   `[3,4) < 5`, `[4,5) == 5`, and `[5,9) > 5`.
   Known correct: index 4 belongs to the pivot's equal band; internal
   order in the greater band is irrelevant.

5. Decision: `lessEnd 4 <= rank 4 < greaterStart 5`, so stop and
   return the pivot value 5.
   After: the result is 5 with nil error. The caller's input remains
   `[7,2,9,4,2,8,5,1,6]`.
   Known correct: four values occupy lower sorted positions and every
   remaining value is at least 5, so 5 is exactly rank 4.

Focused duplicate case: selecting rank 2 from `[4,2,4,4,1]` returns
4. One partition around 4 can create the equal band covering sorted
ranks 2 through 4; the algorithm stops without revisiting each copy.

Focused invalid case: selecting rank zero from nil input returns zero
and an error before allocating or partitioning. The same zero result
with nil error is possible for valid input `[-1,0,1]` at rank one.

Counterexample to treating the midpoint index as a median value: for
`[0,3,5,7,6,4,2,1]` and rank 1, this exact implementation visits
active sizes 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1. The first pivot choice is at
the middle index, but its value 7 is nearly extreme. Index position
does not reveal value rank in an unordered slice.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves the
input, handles duplicates and signed extremes, and demonstrates rank
failure. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Quickselect (slice). Function
// comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func partitionByPivotIndex(
	values []int64,
	left int,
	right int,
	pivotIndex int,
) (int, int) {
	// Separate the active range around its chosen boundary.
	if left < 0 || left > right || right >= len(values) {
		panic("partition bounds are invalid")
	}
	if pivotIndex < left || pivotIndex > right {
		panic("pivot index is outside the active range")
	}

	pivotValue := values[pivotIndex]
	// The four ranges are less, equal, unknown, and greater.
	lessEnd := left
	scanIndex := left
	greaterStart := right + 1

	for scanIndex < greaterStart {
		switch {
		case values[scanIndex] < pivotValue:
			// Grow the less region and preserve the equal region.
			values[lessEnd], values[scanIndex] =
				values[scanIndex], values[lessEnd]
			lessEnd++
			scanIndex++
		case values[scanIndex] > pivotValue:
			// Grow the greater region from the right boundary.
			greaterStart--
			values[scanIndex], values[greaterStart] =
				values[greaterStart], values[scanIndex]
			// Inspect the swapped-in value before advancing.
		default:
			// An equal value extends the middle region.
			scanIndex++
		}
	}
	return lessEnd, greaterStart
}

func selectKthSmallest(
	values []int64,
	rank int,
) (int64, error) {
	// Narrow candidates until the requested ordered item remains.
	if rank < 0 || rank >= len(values) {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"rank %d is outside [0,%d)",
			rank,
			len(values),
		)
	}

	// Partition an owned copy so selection preserves caller order.
	working := make([]int64, len(values))
	copy(working, values)
	left := 0
	right := len(working) - 1

	for left <= right {
		// Only this range can contain the requested sorted position.
		pivotIndex := left + (right-left)/2
		pivotValue := working[pivotIndex]
		lessEnd, greaterStart := partitionByPivotIndex(
			working,
			left,
			right,
			pivotIndex,
		)

		switch {
		case rank < lessEnd:
			// The requested rank lies in the smaller-value region.
			right = lessEnd - 1
		case rank >= greaterStart:
			// The requested rank lies in the larger-value region.
			left = greaterStart
		default:
			return pivotValue, nil
		}
	}

	panic("valid rank escaped the active range")
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int64{7, 2, 9, 4, 2, 8, 5, 1, 6}
	selected, err := selectKthSmallest(values, 4)
	fmt.Println(selected, err)
	fmt.Println(values)

	duplicate, err := selectKthSmallest(
		[]int64{4, 2, 4, 4, 1},
		2,
	)
	fmt.Println(duplicate, err)

	extreme, err := selectKthSmallest(
		[]int64{1<<63 - 1, -1 << 63, 0},
		1,
	)
	fmt.Println(extreme, err)

	invalid, err := selectKthSmallest(nil, 0)
	fmt.Println(invalid, err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
5 <nil>
[7 2 9 4 2 8 5 1 6]
4 <nil>
0 <nil>
0 true
```

The second line confirms that selection did not change the input. The
fourth line shows that zero can be a valid result, while the final
true distinguishes an invalid rank.

##### Why it works

First prove the partition. Before each scan iteration, maintain four
facts: `[left,lessEnd)` contains values below the pivot;
`[lessEnd,scanIndex)` contains values equal to it;
`[scanIndex,greaterStart)` is unclassified; and
`[greaterStart,right+1)` contains values above it. All four facts hold
initially because the first three known regions are empty.

For a smaller scanned value, swapping with `lessEnd` puts that value
in the less region. If the equal region was nonempty, the displaced
value is equal and becomes its new last member after both boundaries
advance. For an equal value, advancing only the scan extends the equal
region. For a greater value, decrementing `greaterStart` and swapping
puts it in the greater region. The swapped-in value remains unknown,
so leaving `scanIndex` fixed preserves every fact.

Every partition iteration reduces the unknown-region length by one:
the smaller and equal branches advance `scanIndex`, while the greater
branch decreases `greaterStart`. The scan terminates with no unknown
values, and the four facts imply the returned three-way partition.
Because the pivot came from the active range, its equal band is
nonempty.

For selection, maintain this outer invariant: `rank` lies in
`[left,right]`; values before `left` are smaller than every active
candidate; and values after `right` are greater than every active
candidate. It holds for the initial full copy.

After partitioning, every value in the less band precedes every pivot
copy in sorted order, and every greater-band value follows them. With
the outer invariant, the three band boundaries are also global sorted
rank boundaries. If `rank < lessEnd`, no equal or greater value can
occupy the requested position, so moving `right` left is safe. If
`rank >= greaterStart`, no less or equal value can occupy it, so
moving `left` right is safe. Both changes preserve the outer
invariant.

If rank lies in the equal band, the number of smaller values places
the whole band at exactly those sorted positions. Returning the pivot
therefore satisfies the contract. Otherwise, the nonempty equal band
is discarded with at least one position, so the active range strictly
shrinks. A finite range can shrink only finitely many times, proving
outer-loop termination.

Rank validation occurs before allocation. Copying before the first
partition confines every swap to `working`, proving input
preservation. Direct comparisons handle all `int64` values without
subtraction or overflow.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length. Copying always takes Theta(N) time and
uses O(N) auxiliary storage. A partition of an active range of length
M takes Theta(M) time and O(1) additional storage.

If every pivot ends the search or leaves an active range at most a
fixed fraction of the previous one, partition work is a geometric
sum `N + cN + c^2N + ...` for some `c < 1`. It totals Theta(N).
Including the mandatory copy, the best case and every such balanced
case take Theta(N) time.

With this deterministic midpoint-index pivot, an adversarial
arrangement can discard only one value per partition. The work then
is `N + (N-1) + ... + 1`, which is Theta(N squared). The focused
eight-value counterexample exhibits that pattern. No
