distribution-independent average bound is claimed for this pivot
rule.

All-equal input takes one Theta(N) partition because the equal band
covers the complete range. Duplicate-heavy input can similarly shrink
faster than a two-way partition that handles pivot copies one at a
time.

The working copy is O(N) auxiliary space and no output collection is
retained; the returned value and loop state use O(1) space. An API
allowed to rearrange caller input could remove the copy and use O(1)
auxiliary space, but it would have a different mutation contract.

Uniformly random pivot selection gives expected Theta(N) partition
work when choices are independent of the input, while retaining a
quadratic worst case. A median-of-medians pivot can guarantee
worst-case linear selection but adds grouping and pivot-selection
work. The later
[randomized Quickselect lesson](#b315-randomized-quickselect-slice)
owns the probabilistic guarantee.

An invalid rank returns in Theta(1) time before allocation. Full
sorting takes O(N log N) comparisons but also supplies every rank and
the complete order; Quickselect deliberately computes less.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty input reject every rank. Entering the loop with
  `right = -1` would obscure the real caller error, so validate first.
- One value accepts only rank zero and returns that value after one
  partition. Rank one is already outside the half-open valid range.
- Rank is zero-based. Rank 4 means the fifth value; treating it as
  one-based returns the fourth or rejects the final valid rank.
- `[4,2,4,4,1]` at rank 2 returns 4. A two-way partition that does
  not collect equals may revisit pivot copies and degrade badly on
  duplicate-heavy input.
- All equal values produce an equal band spanning the active range.
  Continuing after that partition can fail to shrink and loop forever.
- Zero with nil error is a selected value. Only the error
  distinguishes it from the zero returned for an invalid request.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` compare directly. Subtracting a pivot
  from a value to choose a branch can overflow and reverse the result.
- `left + (right-left)/2` avoids overflowing `left + right`. The
  indexes are valid slice positions, so their difference fits `int`.
- A middle index is not a median value. The adversarial example makes
  active sizes decrease by one and exposes the quadratic worst case.
- On the greater-than branch of the partition scan, do not advance
  `scanIndex`. The swapped-in value has not yet been classified.
- `greaterStart` is the first greater position, not the last equal
  position. Use `rank >= greaterStart` for the right-side decision.
- The less and greater regions need not be internally sorted. Sorting
  either one wastes work that selection never observes.
- Returning `working[rank]` before rank enters the equal band is
  wrong; physical position has no sorted meaning until partition
  boundaries prove it.
- Partitioning the caller's slice directly violates this contract.
  Copy first unless an in-place API explicitly permits mutation.
- Concurrent input mutation can race with the initial copy. The
  function does not provide a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose Quickselect for one or a few ranks from an unsorted in-memory
batch when rearranging a private copy is acceptable and complete order
would be wasted. Median, percentile cutoff, and one kth-smallest query
are recognizable signals.

Use [comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) when every
rank, sorted iteration, or many later rank queries are needed. Use
[top-k selection](#b34-top-k-selection-heap) when the actual smallest
or largest K values must all be retained, especially for a stream.
Use an [order-statistic tree](#a77-order-statistic-trees) when updates
and rank queries interleave.

Use deterministic median-of-medians when a linear worst-case bound is
worth its extra implementation cost. Use the later randomized variant
when expected linear work is acceptable and inputs may defeat a fixed
pivot rule. If input is already sorted and remains static, direct
indexing answers every valid rank in O(1) time.

NIST defines the [kth-element selection problem](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/selectkth.html) and identifies
partition-based selection. Its [Select entry](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/select.html) describes the stronger
median-of-medians pivot variant. Oxford's record for Hoare's original
[Algorithm 65: Find](
https://www.cs.ox.ac.uk/publications/publication8194-abstract.html)
preserves the source of the partition-selection family.

#### B.3.4 Top-k selection (heap)

##### Problem and contract

A request for the largest few values does not need the complete order
of a much larger input. Sorting every value establishes comparisons
between items that will never appear in the result.

Given a finite `[]int64` and an integer `count`, return exactly the
largest `count` values in descending order. Duplicates occupy separate
result positions. For example, the largest three values of
`[9,4,9,2]` are `[9,9,4]`, not `[9,4]`.

Count zero is valid and returns a non-nil empty slice without scanning
the input. Count equal to `len(values)` returns every value in
descending order. A negative count or one greater than the input
length returns nil and a non-nil error.

Every `int64` value is valid, including signed extremes. The function
reads but does not mutate the input and returns newly allocated
storage. Allocation must fit memory, and concurrent input mutation is
excluded. Equal values have no identity or stability beyond their
multiplicity and descending value order.

Read [min-heaps and max-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) first.
That lesson owns heap representation and repair. This entry owns the
fixed-size selection invariant: retain only the largest K values seen
so far, with their weakest member exposed at a min-heap root.

The function processes one finite batch and returns its final result.
The later [streaming top-k lesson](#b233-streaming-top-k-heap) owns a
long-lived structure that accepts updates and answers repeated
queries.

##### Mental model

Keep a min-heap containing at most K values. Although the request is
for largest values, the minimum among the retained values is the one
that matters next: it is the weakest current member and the first one
to replace when a better value arrives.

Read `retained[0] == 8` in a full size-three heap as: "the processed
prefix has three retained values, all at least 8; 8 is the current
cutoff." A new value 2 cannot enter that prefix's largest three. A
new value 14 can enter, and the cutoff 8 must leave.

For each input value:

1. If the heap holds fewer than K values, push the value. No candidate
   can be discarded before K positions are filled.
2. If the heap is full and the value is at most its root, discard the
   value. K processed values are already at least as large.
3. If the heap is full and the value exceeds its root, pop the root
   and push the new value. The heap again contains K candidates.

Equality in the second rule is safe because results distinguish only
values, not occurrences. Replacing one root 8 with a new 8 would
produce the same top-K multiset.

The heap slice is not sorted. After the scan, repeatedly pop its
minimum. These values arrive from smallest selected to largest
selected. Fill the output from right to left so its observable order
is descending.

##### Worked walkthrough

Find the largest three values in:

```text
[5,1,9,3,14,8,2,14]
```

The expected result is `[14,14,9]`. The walkthrough shows the actual
heap slice used by Go's `container/heap`; only index zero has a global
ordering promise.

Initial state: `count = 3`, the input is unmodified, and `retained` is
an empty min-heap with capacity three.

1. Decision: push 5 because the heap has fewer than three values.
   Push 1, which rises to the root. Push 9, which remains a child.
   After: heap slice is `[1,5,9]`; all three slots are filled.
   Known correct: the heap contains every processed value, so it is
   exactly the largest three of prefix `[5,1,9]`; root 1 is weakest.

2. Decision: inspect 3. The heap is full and `3 > root 1`, so pop 1
   and push 3.
   After: heap slice is `[3,9,5]`; retained values are `{3,5,9}`.
   Known correct: discarded 1 is below all three retained values, so
   it cannot belong to the prefix's largest three.

3. Decision: inspect 14. Because `14 > root 3`, replace 3 with 14.
   After: heap slice is `[5,9,14]`.
   Known correct: `{5,9,14}` is the largest-three multiset of the
   processed prefix, and root 5 is its cutoff.

4. Decision: inspect 8. Because `8 > root 5`, replace 5 with 8.
   After: heap slice is `[8,14,9]`.
   Known correct: the retained multiset is `{8,9,14}`; sibling order
   14 then 9 does not violate the min-heap property.

5. Decision: inspect 2. Because `2 <= root 8`, discard it without a
   heap operation.
   After: heap remains `[8,14,9]`.
   Known correct: each of the three retained values is at least 8, so
   2 cannot enter the largest three.

6. Decision: inspect the final 14. Because `14 > root 8`, replace 8.
   After: heap slice is `[9,14,14]`; the input scan is exhausted.
   Known correct: the heap contains exactly the input's largest-three
   multiset, including both occurrences of 14.

7. Decision: allocate three result positions. Pop 9 into result index
   2, pop 14 into index 1, and pop the final 14 into index 0.
   After: result is `[14,14,9]`; the temporary heap is empty.
   Known correct: every selected value appears once and reverse
   placement converts ascending pops into descending output.

Focused zero case: nil input with count zero returns a non-nil empty
slice and nil error. The function does not access a heap root or scan
an input value.

Focused full case: input `[-1,2,-1]` with count three returns
`[2,-1,-1]`. Keeping all values is valid; heap extraction supplies
the promised descending order.

Counterexample to using a max-heap: retain 5 and 1 for K = 2, then
process 9 and 8. A max-heap exposes strongest value 5 first, so after
admitting 9 its root is 9. Comparing 8 with that root discards 8 and
can leave 1, producing `{9,1}` instead of `{9,8}`. The first wrong
decision pops strongest value 5 when 9 arrives instead of weakest
value 1. The root must expose the weakest retained value, which
requires a min-heap here.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves the
input, handles zero and full counts, and demonstrates invalid count
failure. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It uses only
the standard library.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Top-k selection (heap). Function
// comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
)

type minimumInt64Heap []int64

func (values minimumInt64Heap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(values)
}

func (values minimumInt64Heap) Less(first, second int) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	return values[first] < values[second]
}

func (values minimumInt64Heap) Swap(first, second int) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	values[first], values[second] = values[second], values[first]
}

func (values *minimumInt64Heap) Push(item any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	value := item.(int64)
	*values = append(*values, value)
}

func (values *minimumInt64Heap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	current := *values
	lastIndex := len(current) - 1
	value := current[lastIndex]
	current[lastIndex] = 0
	*values = current[:lastIndex]
	return value
}

func largestK(values []int64, count int) ([]int64, error) {
	// Compute k from the state without mutating it.
	if count < 0 || count > len(values) {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"count %d is outside [0,%d]",
			count,
			len(values),
		)
	}
	if count == 0 {
		return make([]int64, 0), nil
	}

	retained := make(minimumInt64Heap, 0, count)
	for _, value := range values {
		// The root is the weakest of the largest values retained.
		if len(retained) < count {
			heap.Push(&retained, value)
			continue
		}
		if value <= retained[0] {
			continue
		}
		heap.Pop(&retained)
		heap.Push(&retained, value)
	}

	// Minimum pops filled from the end produce descending output.
	result := make([]int64, len(retained))
	for remaining := len(result); remaining > 0; remaining-- {
		value := heap.Pop(&retained).(int64)
		result[remaining-1] = value
	}
	return result, nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int64{5, 1, 9, 3, 14, 8, 2, 14}
	selected, err := largestK(values, 3)
	fmt.Println(selected, err)
	fmt.Println(values)

	all, err := largestK([]int64{-1, 2, -1}, 3)
	fmt.Println(all, err)

	empty, err := largestK(nil, 0)
	fmt.Println(empty, err, empty == nil)

	invalid, err := largestK(values, 9)
	fmt.Println(invalid == nil, err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[14 14 9] <nil>
[5 1 9 3 14 8 2 14]
[2 -1 -1] <nil>
[] <nil> false
true true
```

The second line confirms that input order is unchanged. The false
confirms that a valid empty result is not nil. The final line confirms
that an excessive count returns nil plus an error.

##### Why it works

Maintain this scan invariant after every processed prefix: the heap
contains exactly the largest `min(count,prefix length)` values of that
prefix as a multiset, and its root is the smallest retained value.
The empty prefix and empty heap establish the invariant.

Before the heap reaches count values, pushing the next value keeps
every processed value, so the multiset statement remains true. The
heap package restores its property, making the root the new minimum.

Once the heap is full, suppose the next value is at most the root.
Every retained value is at least the root and therefore at least the
new value. Discarding the new occurrence leaves a valid choice of the
largest K values, including the same multiplicity when values tie.

If the next value exceeds the root, it belongs above the current
cutoff. The root is no larger than any other retained value, so it is
the one retained occurrence that must leave. Popping it and pushing
the new value produces exactly the largest K values of the extended
prefix and restores the root property.

At scan termination, the prefix is the complete input, so the heap
contains the requested multiset. `heap.Pop` returns its minimum each
time. Writing successive minima into result positions K - 1 through
zero makes every earlier output at least every later output, proving
descending order without changing multiplicity.

The input loop advances once per finite input value. Every heap repair
moves through a finite tree. Extraction reduces heap length by one on
each iteration, so all phases terminate.

Validation precedes allocation and root access. The only pushed items
are `int64`, so the private interface assertions are guaranteed. The
heap stores copied integer values, and all mutation stays inside its
owned slice, proving input preservation.

The retained slice begins empty, which already satisfies the heap
invariant. No `heap.Init` call is needed before its first
package-level push.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be input length and K be `count`. When K = 0, the function
returns in Theta(1) time with O(1) output metadata and does not scan N
values. Invalid counts also fail in Theta(1) time without allocation.

For positive K, the scan examines all N values. The heap never exceeds
K entries. A root comparison takes Theta(1); a push, pop, or repair
takes O(log(K + 1)) time. Building the retained heap, processing
replacements, and popping K results together take at most
O(N log(K + 1)) time.

The best case for positive K is Theta(N): equal values can require no
repair swaps, and the scan and output still visit N and K positions.
The worst case is Theta(N log(K + 1)). Actual work depends on how
often new values cross the cutoff and how far heap repairs travel, so
no distribution-independent average is claimed.

The retained heap uses O(K) auxiliary storage. The returned slice
uses O(K) output storage. Both coexist during extraction, so peak
additional storage is O(K), with distinct heap and output arrays. The
input is never copied in full.

When K is much smaller than N, this avoids the O(N log N) comparisons
of full sorting. When K = N, the upper bound becomes O(N log N), and a
standard sort is usually simpler. If descending output is unnecessary,
returning an unordered copy of the final heap can avoid K pop repairs,
but the result would have a different contract.

Quickselect can identify the K-value boundary in expected linear time
with a randomized pivot, then the selected region can be sorted in
O(K log K) time. The heap approach instead gives deterministic
O(N log(K + 1)) worst-case work and naturally processes values one at
a time.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil input accepts only count zero and returns a non-nil empty slice.
  Count one is invalid before any root access.
- Count zero on a nonempty input returns immediately. Scanning anyway
  and reading `retained[0]` panics because no heap slot may exist.
- Count one keeps the maximum value. The one-item min-heap root is
  both the weakest and strongest retained value.
- Count N retains every occurrence, then pops them into descending
  order. Rejecting equality with N loses a valid full-result case.
- `[4,4,4,2]` with K = 2 returns `[4,4]`. Deduplicating input or
  storing a set returns too few positions.
- A new value equal to the root may be discarded only because result
  identity and stability are outside the contract. Records with
  tie-breaking fields need a full comparator and explicit tie policy.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` values compare directly. Subtraction is
  unnecessary and could overflow.
- Use a min-heap for largest K. A max-heap exposes the strongest item,
  so comparing against its root can discard a value that should
  replace the true weakest item.
- The heap slice is only partially ordered. Returning it directly
  does not satisfy the descending-output contract.
- Fill output from right to left while popping minima. Filling from
  left produces ascending rather than descending output.
- The `heap.Interface` method `Pop` removes the last slice slot. The
  package moves the logical root there before calling it. Removing
  index zero inside the method corrupts the package's repair protocol.
- `Push` and `Pop` need pointer receivers because they change slice
  length. Value receivers would update only copied slice headers.
- Only `int64` values enter this private heap. Passing another dynamic
  type to `heap.Push` would panic at the assertion and is outside the
  public function's path.
- Clearing the removed slot is harmless for `int64` and becomes
  important when heap elements contain pointers that should not stay
  retained in spare capacity.
- Concurrent writes to input race with the scan. The function does
  not provide a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose a size-K heap when an unsorted batch is much larger than K,
the actual K values are required, and a deterministic worst-case
bound matters. It also adapts directly to inputs that arrive one at a
time because it never needs future values.

Use [Quickselect](#b33-quickselect-slice) when only one rank or an
unordered boundary is needed and partitioning a private batch is
acceptable. Use [comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice)
when K is near N or complete order will serve later work. Use the
later [streaming lesson](#b233-streaming-top-k-heap) when the retained
state must survive between calls.

For smallest K, reverse the design: keep a size-K max-heap so its root
is the largest, weakest retained value. For records, define a strict
weak ordering over every ranking and tie-breaking field before
choosing the heap direction.

Go's authoritative [`container/heap` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap) defines the root, interface, and
push/pop protocol used here. NIST's [priority-queue definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/priorityque.html) defines the
insert, find-minimum, and delete-minimum operations that support the
selection invariant.

#### B.3.5 Merging sorted sources (heap or pointers)

##### Problem and contract

Several sources may already be sorted even though their combined
order is not. Concatenating them preserves every value but can place a
large value from one source before a small value from another. Sorting
the concatenation repeats ordering work that each source has already
done.

Given a finite `[][]int64`, return one nondecreasing slice containing
every value from every source exactly once. Each source must already
be nondecreasing. Empty sources, a nil outer slice, duplicates, and
signed extremes are valid.

If a source decreases between adjacent positions, return nil and an
error identifying the source and later position of the first observed
decrease. If the sum of source lengths cannot fit in Go's `int`,
return nil and an error before heap or output allocation. Allocation
of an otherwise valid result must fit memory.

Equal values retain their order within one source. Across sources,
the implementation gives the lower source index priority; position
breaks any remaining tie. The returned values alone do not expose
that provenance, but the rule makes record-oriented adaptations
deterministic.

The function reads but does not mutate or retain the sources. It
returns a newly allocated, non-nil slice, including for no values.
Concurrent source mutation during validation or merging is excluded.

For exactly two sources, two indexes are enough: compare both current
heads and advance the one emitted. For an arbitrary number of
sources, a min-heap finds the least current head without scanning
every source after every output.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) and
[min-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) first. This lesson owns
merging already sorted sources. The next [merge-sort lesson](
#b36-merge-sort-slice-and-buffer) owns recursively creating sorted
runs before merging them.

##### Mental model

Each nonexhausted source has one frontier value: its first value not
yet emitted. Because a source is sorted, every later value in that
source is at least its frontier. Therefore the smallest frontier
across all sources is the smallest value remaining anywhere.

Represent one frontier as:

```text
(value, sourceIndex, valueIndex)
```

Reading `(4,1,1)` means value 4 at position 1 of source 1 is that
source's next unmerged value. The heap compares value first, then
source index, then position. It contains at most one candidate for
each nonexhausted source.

Pop the minimum candidate and append its value to the result. That
source's next position, if one exists, becomes its new frontier and is
pushed into the heap. Other sources do not move. Stop when the heap is
empty, which means every source is exhausted.

For two sources, the heap would hold at most two items and its
logarithmic factor is only a constant. Two explicit indexes express
the same frontier rule with less machinery: emit the smaller head,
advance its index, and append the other suffix after one source ends.

##### Worked walkthrough

Merge four sources, one of them empty:

```text
source 0: [1,4,4,10]
source 1: [-2,4,9]
source 2: []
source 3: [0,4,11]
```

The expected result is:

```text
[-2,0,1,4,4,4,4,9,10,11]
```

Frontiers below are written in priority order for readability. The
actual heap slice promises only that its minimum is at index zero.
In the trace, `s1` means source index 1 and `i0` means value index 0.

Initial state: no source has been validated, no result or heap exists,
and the total output length is unknown.

1. Decision: validate adjacent values in every source and sum lengths
   with an overflow check. All sources are nondecreasing, total length
   is 10, and three sources are nonempty. Create one head candidate
   for each of those sources and initialize the heap.
   After: result is empty; frontiers in priority order are
   `(-2,s1,i0)`, `(0,s3,i0)`, and `(1,s0,i0)`.
   Known correct: each candidate is the least unmerged value of its
   source, and empty source 2 has no candidate.

2. Decision: pop `(-2,s1,i0)`, append -2, and advance source 1 to
   its next value 4 at index 1.
   After: result is `[-2]`; frontiers are `(0,s3,i0)`, `(1,s0,i0)`,
   and `(4,s1,i1)`.
   Known correct: -2 was the least frontier and therefore the least
   value remaining anywhere; source 1 again has exactly one frontier.

3. Decision: pop `(0,s3,i0)`, append 0, and push source 3's next
   candidate `(4,s3,i1)`.
   After: result is `[-2,0]`; frontiers are `(1,s0,i0)`,
   `(4,s1,i1)`, and `(4,s3,i1)`.
   Known correct: output is nondecreasing, and every unmerged source
   value is at least one displayed frontier.

4. Decision: pop `(1,s0,i0)`, append 1, and push `(4,s0,i1)`.
   After: result is `[-2,0,1]`; the three frontiers all have value 4,
   ordered by source indexes 0, 1, and 3.
   Known correct: all values below 4 have been emitted, and the tie
   rule identifies the next source without changing value order.

5. Decision: pop source 0's first 4 and push its next 4. Source 0
   still wins the tie, so pop that second 4 and push 10. Then pop the
   4 from source 1 and push 9, followed by source 3's 4 and 11.
   After: result is `[-2,0,1,4,4,4,4]`; frontiers are
   `(9,s1,i2)`, `(10,s0,i3)`, and `(11,s3,i2)`.
   Known correct: all four equal occurrences were preserved in the
   deterministic source order, and every new frontier is at least 4.

6. Decision: pop and append 9; source 1 becomes exhausted, so push
   nothing. Pop 10 and exhaust source 0. Pop 11 and exhaust source 3.
   After: result is `[-2,0,1,4,4,4,4,9,10,11]`; heap is empty.
   Known correct: each pop was the least remaining frontier, and no
   source has an unmerged position.

7. Decision: observe the empty heap and return the result.
   After: all input sources remain in their original order and the
   returned slice owns its storage.
   Known correct: the output is a nondecreasing permutation of all ten
   input occurrences, so the complete contract holds.

Focused empty case: nil sources produce no candidates and return a
non-nil empty slice. A mixture of nil and empty inner slices behaves
the same.

Focused failure: sources `[[1,5,3],[2,4]]` fail while validating
source 0 at index 2 because `3 < 5`. The function returns nil and an
error before creating a heap or partial result.

Counterexample to consuming one source after choosing it: with
sources `[1,100]` and `[2,3]`, emitting 1 is correct. Emitting 100
immediately afterward is the first wrong decision because the other
frontier 2 is smaller. Push successor 100 back into the shared
frontier comparison before choosing again.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves source
storage, returns a non-nil empty result, and demonstrates validation
failure. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It uses only
the standard library.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Merging sorted sources (heap or
// pointers). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
)

type mergeCandidate struct {
	value       int64
	sourceIndex int
	valueIndex  int
}

type mergeCandidateHeap []mergeCandidate

func (candidates mergeCandidateHeap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(candidates)
}

func (candidates mergeCandidateHeap) Less(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	if candidates[first].value != candidates[second].value {
		return candidates[first].value < candidates[second].value
	}
	if candidates[first].sourceIndex !=
		candidates[second].sourceIndex {
		return candidates[first].sourceIndex <
			candidates[second].sourceIndex
	}
	return candidates[first].valueIndex <
		candidates[second].valueIndex
}

func (candidates mergeCandidateHeap) Swap(first, second int) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	candidates[first], candidates[second] =
		candidates[second], candidates[first]
}

func (candidates *mergeCandidateHeap) Push(item any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	candidate := item.(mergeCandidate)
	*candidates = append(*candidates, candidate)
}

func (candidates *mergeCandidateHeap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	current := *candidates
	lastIndex := len(current) - 1
	candidate := current[lastIndex]
	current[lastIndex] = mergeCandidate{}
	*candidates = current[:lastIndex]
	return candidate
}

func mergeSortedSources(
	sources [][]int64,
) ([]int64, error) {
	// An all-one uint shifted right yields the platform's maximum int.
	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	totalLength := 0
	nonemptyCount := 0
	for sourceIndex, source := range sources {
		for valueIndex := 1; valueIndex < len(source); valueIndex++ {
			if source[valueIndex] < source[valueIndex-1] {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"source %d decreases at index %d",
					sourceIndex,
					valueIndex,
				)
			}
		}
		if len(source) > maximumInt-totalLength {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("merged length exceeds int")
		}
		totalLength += len(source)
		if len(source) > 0 {
			nonemptyCount++
		}
	}

	// Only the current head of each nonempty source enters the heap.
	candidates := make(mergeCandidateHeap, 0, nonemptyCount)
	for sourceIndex, source := range sources {
		if len(source) == 0 {
			continue
		}
		candidates = append(candidates, mergeCandidate{
			value:       source[0],
			sourceIndex: sourceIndex,
			valueIndex:  0,
		})
	}
	heap.Init(&candidates)

	merged := make([]int64, 0, totalLength)
	for len(candidates) > 0 {
		candidate := heap.Pop(&candidates).(mergeCandidate)
		merged = append(merged, candidate.value)

		// The successor becomes this source's only frontier item.
		nextIndex := candidate.valueIndex + 1
		source := sources[candidate.sourceIndex]
		if nextIndex < len(source) {
			heap.Push(&candidates, mergeCandidate{
				value:       source[nextIndex],
				sourceIndex: candidate.sourceIndex,
				valueIndex:  nextIndex,
			})
		}
	}
	return merged, nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	sources := [][]int64{
		{1, 4, 4, 10},
		{-2, 4, 9},
		{},
		{0, 4, 11},
	}
	merged, err := mergeSortedSources(sources)
	fmt.Println(merged, err)
	fmt.Println(sources)

	empty, err := mergeSortedSources(nil)
	fmt.Println(empty, err, empty == nil)

	invalid, err := mergeSortedSources([][]int64{
		{1, 5, 3},
		{2, 4},
	})
	fmt.Println(invalid == nil, err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[-2 0 1 4 4 4 4 9 10 11] <nil>
[[1 4 4 10] [-2 4 9] [] [0 4 11]]
[] <nil> false
true true
```

The second line confirms that no source changed. The false confirms a
valid empty result is non-nil. The final line confirms that a decrease
returns nil plus an error.

##### Why it works

Validation proves each source is nondecreasing before the function
allocates candidates or output. It also proves their total length fits
an output slice index. On failure, no partially merged result escapes.

Maintain this merge invariant: output is nondecreasing and contains
exactly the consumed prefix of every source; each nonexhausted source
has exactly one heap candidate, its first unconsumed value; and an
exhausted source has none. After initialization, output and every
consumed prefix are empty, while each nonempty source contributes its
index-zero value, so the invariant holds.

Within a nonexhausted sorted source, its frontier is no greater than
any later unconsumed value. The minimum heap candidate is therefore
no greater than any unconsumed value in any source. Appending it
preserves output order and consumes exactly that position.

If the popped source has a successor, pushing that successor
restores its one-candidate frontier. If not, omitting a push correctly
marks the source exhausted. No other source changes, so every part of
the invariant survives the iteration.

Equal candidate values are all safe minima. Comparing source and
position only selects a deterministic one; it cannot disturb numeric
order. At termination the heap is empty, so the invariant implies
every source is exhausted. Output then contains every occurrence
exactly once and remains nondecreasing.

Each iteration consumes one previously unconsumed value, so exactly N
iterations empty all finite sources. Heap repairs operate on at most
one candidate per nonempty source and also terminate. The algorithm
therefore cannot stall or duplicate a position.

All candidates and output elements are copied values. Source indexes
only read input storage during the call, and the returned slice has
its own array. This proves mutation and ownership claims.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let S be the number of sources, A the number of nonempty sources, and
N the total number of values. Validation visits S source headers and
N values in Theta(S + N) time. Initializing a heap of A first values
takes O(A) time.

The merge performs N heap pops and N - A heap pushes. The heap never
contains more than A candidates, so the worst-case total is
Theta(S + N log(A + 1)) time. Favorable heap layouts can stop repairs
early, giving Theta(S + N) best-case work. No distribution-independent
average is claimed.

The returned slice uses O(N) output storage. The candidate heap uses
O(A) auxiliary storage, including its candidate records. Loop state
uses O(1) additional space, and the implementation has no recursion.

With exactly two sources, two indexes merge in Theta(N) time with
O(1) auxiliary frontier storage, in addition to output. A heap is
unnecessary for that fixed-width frontier. With many sources, scanning
all A heads per output costs O(N*A), while the heap reduces each
choice to O(log(A + 1)).

Repeatedly merging sources into one growing intermediate can copy
early values many times and take O(N*S) work in a skewed order. A
balanced pairwise merge tree takes O(N log(S + 1)) work and may be
attractive for parallel in-memory merging. The heap method produces
one output pass and also works when sources are read incrementally.

An invalid source fails during validation after its inspected prefix
and allocates neither heap nor output. A total-length overflow fails
before addition and allocation. Physical allocation failure remains
outside the function's recoverable contract.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil or zero sources return a non-nil empty slice. `heap.Init` and
  the merge loop both accept the empty candidate heap.
- Any number of empty inner sources contribute no candidate and no
  output value. Pushing a placeholder zero invents data.
- One nonempty source still returns a copy. Returning the source slice
  directly would let result mutation change caller-owned storage.
- Source `[1,5,3]` is invalid at index 2. Merging without validation
  can emit 5 before 3 and silently violate output order.
- Equal values inside and across sources remain separate occurrences.
  Deduplication would change the required multiset.
- Equal cross-source heads use lower source index first. A comparator
  that gives contradictory tie answers can violate heap assumptions.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` compare directly. Subtracting values in
  `Less` can overflow and reverse their order.
- Keep only one candidate per nonexhausted source. Pushing every value
  is correct but expands auxiliary storage from O(A) to O(N) and loses
  the benefit of already sorted sources.
- After popping a candidate, push its successor before the next pop.
  Consuming that source immediately can skip a smaller head elsewhere.
- The heap array itself is not sorted. Only its root is guaranteed to
  be the next frontier; the walkthrough's priority lists are an
  explanatory view.
- `heap.Interface.Pop` removes the final slot after the package moves
  the logical minimum there. Removing index zero in the method breaks
  the package protocol.
- Check `maximumInt - totalLength` before adding a source length.
  Adding first can wrap and request an invalid output capacity.
- The function validates and later reads each source again. Concurrent
  mutation can invalidate the earlier proof and creates a data race.

##### When to choose it

Choose a heap-based multiway merge when several independently sorted
sources must become one sorted stream or slice and only their current
heads fit naturally in memory. Sorted database runs, log shards, and
external-sort runs are common signals.

Use two pointers for exactly two in-memory sources. Use the next
[merge-sort lesson](#b36-merge-sort-slice-and-buffer) when one
unsorted slice must first be divided and ordered. Use [comparison
sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) when inputs are not already
sorted and no run structure can be reused.

Linked lists use the same frontier proof but advance node pointers
instead of slice indexes. Practice two-source merging in the completed
[Merge Two Sorted Lists archive](
problems/solved_easy_leetcode_0021_merge_two_sorted_lists.go), array
merging in [Merge Sorted Array](
problems/solved_easy_leetcode_0088_merge_sorted_array.go), and
multiway merging in the unsolved [Merge k Sorted Lists exercise](
problems/hard_leetcode_0023_merge_k_sorted_lists.go).

NIST's [merge definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/merge.html) specifies a sorted
permutation of sorted inputs. Its [ideal-merge entry](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/idealmerge.html) describes retaining
source heads in a heap. Go's [`container/heap` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap) defines the initialization and
minimum-pop operations used here.

#### B.3.6 Merge sort (slice and buffer)

##### Problem and contract

An unsorted slice has no ready-made runs to merge. Here, a run is one
contiguous range that is already sorted. Merge sort creates such
runs: a one-record range is sorted, and two adjacent sorted ranges
can be combined into a larger one. Repeating that rule builds a
complete ordering from the bottom of the recursion up.

Given a finite slice of records with an `int64` key and a string
label, return every record in ascending key order. The sort is stable:
records with equal keys retain their relative input order. Labels do
not affect ordering, so they make that stability visible.

Every key and label is valid. Duplicate records remain duplicated.
Nil and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice.
There is no malformed public input and therefore no error result.

The function leaves the input order unchanged and returns an
independent record array. Record values are copied; their immutable
string data may remain shared. Allocation must fit memory, and
concurrent input mutation is excluded.

This implementation is top-down merge sort. It copies the input once,
allocates one equally sized work buffer, recursively sorts half-open
ranges, and reuses the buffer for every merge. Its internal merge
helper panics if its two slices or range bounds violate programmer
invariants; the public function never supplies such a state.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices),
[comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice), and
[merging sorted sources](
#b35-merging-sorted-sources-heap-or-pointers) first. The preceding
merge lesson owns already sorted independent sources. This lesson
owns recursively creating adjacent sorted runs inside one slice.

##### Mental model

Treat a half-open range `[start,end)` as one sorting job. Its length
is `end - start`. Length zero or one is already sorted, so it is the
base case. A longer range splits at:

```text
middle = start + (end-start)/2
```

That produces adjacent ranges `[start,middle)` and `[middle,end)`.
Neither overlaps the other, and together they cover the original
range. Recursive calls sort both halves before the current call
merges them.

During a merge, `left` points to the first unmerged record in the left
run, `right` points to the first unmerged record in the right run, and
`write` points to the next buffer position:

```text
[start,left)       consumed from the left run
[left,middle)      unconsumed left run
[middle,right)     consumed from the right run
[right,end)        unconsumed right run
[start,write)      merged prefix in the buffer
```

Both unconsumed runs are sorted. Their two front records are therefore
the only candidates for the next smallest record. Copy the smaller
one to `buffer[write]` and advance its pointer. When keys tie, copy
the left record. The left run came from earlier input positions, so
this choice preserves stable order.

Once either run is empty, copy the other run's suffix. The buffer
range now contains a stable sorted permutation of both runs. Copy it
back to `values[start:end]`, making that larger range ready for its
parent call. One buffer is safe to reuse because recursive children
finish before their parent writes, and each merge touches only its
own range.

##### Worked walkthrough

Sort these records, written as `key-label`:

```text
4-A, 2-B, 4-C, 1-D, 3-E
```

The expected stable result is:

```text
1-D, 2-B, 3-E, 4-A, 4-C
```

Initial state: the caller owns the five records in their displayed
order. No sorted copy or work buffer exists.

1. Decision: allocate a five-record result array, copy the input, and
   allocate a five-record buffer. Sort range `[0,5)`.
   After: `values` is `[4-A,2-B,4-C,1-D,3-E]`; the input has separate
   storage and remains unchanged.
   Known correct: all later reordering is confined to the owned copy,
   and range `[0,5)` covers every record exactly once.

2. Decision: split `[0,5)` at index 2 into `[0,2)` and `[2,5)`.
   Split `[0,2)` at 1. Its two length-one ranges contain `4-A` and
   `2-B`, so both are base cases.
   After: the first pending merge has left run `[4-A]` and right run
   `[2-B]`.
   Known correct: both runs are sorted, disjoint, and together contain
   exactly the original first two records.

3. Decision: compare 4 with 2, write `2-B`, then copy the remaining
   `4-A`. Copy buffer range `[0,2)` back into `values`.
   After: `values` is `[2-B,4-A,4-C,1-D,3-E]`.
   Known correct: `[0,2)` is a sorted permutation of its original
   records, and no position outside that range changed.

4. Decision: sort `[2,5)` by splitting it at 3. Range `[2,3)` is the
   base record `4-C`. Split `[3,5)` at 4, compare keys 1 and 3, write
   `1-D`, then copy `3-E` from the remaining right run.
   After: the right-side runs are `[4-C]` and `[1-D,3-E]`;
   `values[3:5]` is `[1-D,3-E]`.
   Known correct: each displayed run is sorted, and together they
   contain exactly the records originally in `[2,5)`.

5. Decision: merge `[4-C]` with `[1-D,3-E]`. Compare 4 with 1 and
   write `1-D`; compare 4 with 3 and write `3-E`; then copy `4-C`.
   Copy the buffer range back.
   After: `values` is `[2-B,4-A,1-D,3-E,4-C]`, with `[2,5)` sorted.
   Known correct: the right half is a stable sorted permutation of its
   three original records.

6. Decision: merge final runs `[2-B,4-A]` and `[1-D,3-E,4-C]`.
   Compare their front keys in this order:

   ```text
   2 versus 1 -> write 1-D
   2 versus 3 -> write 2-B
   4 versus 3 -> write 3-E
   4 versus 4 -> write 4-A from the left run
   left empty -> copy 4-C
   ```

   After: buffer range `[0,5)` is
   `[1-D,2-B,3-E,4-A,4-C]`.
   Known correct: each choice was the smallest remaining front; at the
   equal-key choice, earlier input record `4-A` stayed before `4-C`.

7. Decision: copy buffer range `[0,5)` back and return the sorted
   slice.
   After: result is `[1-D,2-B,3-E,4-A,4-C]`; caller input remains
   `[4-A,2-B,4-C,1-D,3-E]`.
   Known correct: the result is a stable sorted permutation of every
   input record and owns its record array.

Focused empty case: nil input allocates two zero-length slices. Range
`[0,0)` reaches the base case and returns a non-nil empty result.

Focused equal case: `[2-first,2-second,2-third]` remains in exactly
that order. Recursive stability preserves ties inside each half, and
left-first tie handling preserves ties that cross a split.

Counterexample to using `<` for the left choice: in the final merge
above, keys `4-A` and `4-C` tie. Choosing the right record on equality
writes `4-C` before `4-A`. The keys remain sorted, but the promised
stable order is broken at that decision.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves input,
shows stable ties and signed extremes, and returns a non-nil empty
result. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Merge sort (slice and buffer).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type mergeRecord struct {
	key   int64
	label string
}

func mergeStableRuns(
	values []mergeRecord,
	buffer []mergeRecord,
	start int,
	middle int,
	end int,
) {
	// Combine compatible parts while preserving their invariant.
	if len(values) != len(buffer) {
		panic("merge slices have different lengths")
	}
	if start < 0 || start > middle || middle > end ||
		end > len(values) {
		panic("merge range is invalid")
	}

	left := start
	right := middle
	write := start
	for left < middle && right < end {
		if values[left].key <= values[right].key {
			buffer[write] = values[left]
			left++
		} else {
			buffer[write] = values[right]
			right++
		}
		write++
	}
	for left < middle {
		buffer[write] = values[left]
		left++
		write++
	}
	for right < end {
		buffer[write] = values[right]
		right++
		write++
	}
	copy(values[start:end], buffer[start:end])
}

func mergeSortRange(
	values []mergeRecord,
	buffer []mergeRecord,
	start int,
	end int,
) {
	// Combine compatible parts while preserving their invariant.
	if end-start <= 1 {
		return
	}
	middle := start + (end-start)/2
	mergeSortRange(values, buffer, start, middle)
	mergeSortRange(values, buffer, middle, end)
	mergeStableRuns(values, buffer, start, middle, end)
}

func stableMergeSort(values []mergeRecord) []mergeRecord {
	// Keep stable merge sort in one helper so callers use one rule.
	sorted := make([]mergeRecord, len(values))
	copy(sorted, values)
	buffer := make([]mergeRecord, len(values))
	mergeSortRange(sorted, buffer, 0, len(sorted))
	return sorted
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []mergeRecord{
		{key: 4, label: "A"},
		{key: 2, label: "B"},
		{key: 4, label: "C"},
		{key: 1, label: "D"},
		{key: 3, label: "E"},
	}
	sorted := stableMergeSort(values)
	fmt.Println(sorted)
	fmt.Println(values)

	ties := stableMergeSort([]mergeRecord{
		{key: 2, label: "first"},
		{key: 2, label: "second"},
		{key: 2, label: "third"},
	})
	fmt.Println(ties)

	extremes := stableMergeSort([]mergeRecord{
		{key: 1<<63 - 1, label: "high"},
		{key: -1 << 63, label: "low"},
	})
	fmt.Println(extremes)

	empty := stableMergeSort(nil)
	fmt.Println(empty, empty == nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[{1 D} {2 B} {3 E} {4 A} {4 C}]
[{4 A} {2 B} {4 C} {1 D} {3 E}]
[{2 first} {2 second} {2 third}]
[{-9223372036854775808 low} {9223372036854775807 high}]
[] false
```

The second line confirms that input order did not change. The third
line exposes stable equal-key order. The final false confirms that the
empty result is not nil.

##### Why it works

Prove by induction on range length that `mergeSortRange` replaces its
range with a stable sorted permutation of the records that entered
that range and changes no position outside it.

For length zero or one, the function returns immediately. Such a
range is already sorted, its only possible record keeps its position,
and nothing is written. This establishes the base case.

For a longer range, `middle` creates two shorter, disjoint ranges that
exactly cover the parent. By the induction hypothesis, the two
recursive calls leave both halves stably sorted and preserve their
records. It remains to prove the merge.

Maintain this merge invariant: `buffer[start:write]` is a stable
sorted sequence containing exactly the records consumed from the two
runs, while `left` and `right` identify their first unconsumed
records. Initially no record is consumed and the buffer prefix is
empty, so the invariant holds.

Because each run is sorted, its front is no greater than anything
later in that run. The smaller of the two fronts is therefore a
smallest remaining record. Copying it extends sorted order and
consumes exactly one record. If keys tie, either is numerically valid,
but the left record occupied an earlier input position than every
record in the right run. Choosing left preserves their relative order.

When one run is exhausted, every record in the other suffix is at
least the last written record and is already in stable order. Copying
that suffix completes a stable sorted permutation of both runs. The
copy-back changes only `[start,end)`, proving the induction step.

At the top call, the range is the entire copied slice. The inductive
claim therefore proves the returned ordering, permutation, and
stability guarantees. The initial copy proves input preservation and
independent record-array ownership.

Every non-base call uses two ranges strictly shorter than its own.
Repeated integer halving reaches length one, so recursion terminates.
Each merge-loop iteration advances exactly one input pointer and
`write`, so the number of unconsumed records decreases by one. At most
`end - start` records can be consumed. All loops and calls therefore
terminate.

The helper checks that value and buffer lengths match and that
`0 <= start <= middle <= end <= len(values)`. The sort creates equal
lengths once and derives every child boundary inside its parent, so
all buffer indexes and copy ranges are valid.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the record count. Splitting forms a balanced recursion tree
with `ceil(log2(N))` nontrivial levels when N is greater than one.
Across one level, merge ranges are disjoint and contain O(N) records.
Each merged record is written once to the buffer and once back to the
result slice.

The recurrence is `T(N) = T(floor(N/2)) + T(ceil(N/2)) + Theta(N)`,
so sorting takes Theta(N log N) time. This implementation always
merges both halves, even when their boundary keys are already ordered.
For growing N, its best, average, and worst cases are therefore all
Theta(N log N). The initial copy and buffer initialization add
Theta(N), which does not change that bound.

Merging two runs of total length M makes at most M - 1 key comparisons
and always performs M buffer writes plus M copy-back writes. No key
subtraction is used, so signed extremes do not change the work or risk
overflow.

The returned record array uses O(N) output storage. The reusable
buffer uses O(N) auxiliary storage during the call. Balanced recursion
uses O(log N) stack frames, each with constant scalar state. Excluding
the required returned array, peak auxiliary space is O(N); including
it, the call owns two O(N) record arrays at peak. The buffer becomes
unreachable after return.

Allocating a new temporary slice inside every merge would create
O(N log N) total allocation volume even though live storage can remain
O(N). Reusing one full-size buffer keeps allocation count and peak
storage predictable. Alternating source and destination roles can
avoid copy-back at each level, but its ownership and recursion
invariants are harder to teach.

An in-place stable merge sort can reduce extra array storage, but its
merge logic and movement costs are substantially more complex. Linked
list merge sort can relink nodes with O(log N) recursive stack space,
but it gives up the slice locality and indexing used here.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice. The base range is
  `[0,0)`, so recursion performs no indexing.
- One record is copied and returned unchanged. It needs no comparison
  or merge, but result storage must still be independent.
- Already sorted and reverse-sorted inputs both take Theta(N log N)
  here because every recursion level still merges and copies back.
- Equal keys retain input order. Use `<=` for the left choice; `<`
  selects the right record on a tie and makes the sort unstable.
- Equal records remain duplicated. A sort changes order, not
  multiplicity.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` keys compare directly. Subtracting keys
  to choose a side can overflow and reverse the decision.
- Use half-open ranges consistently. Mixing an inclusive `end` with
  these loops can skip the last record or index one past the slice.
- Compute `middle` as `start + (end-start)/2`. It remains inside the
  validated range and matches the half-open length calculation.
- Stop at length zero or one. Recursing on a length-one range without
  a base case repeats the same boundaries forever.
- Sort both halves before merging. A frontier comparison is valid only
  when each remaining run is already sorted.
- After one run ends, copy the complete other suffix. Stopping the
  merge early silently drops records.
- Copy the buffer range back before returning to the parent. Otherwise
  the parent reads the old unsorted values.
- Reuse buffer positions only after child calls return. Concurrently
  merging overlapping parent and child ranges would corrupt both.
- Allocate the buffer with the full result length. A zero-capacity
  append buffer does not support direct indexing by original position.
- Slice assignment alone shares the input array. Allocate and copy
  before recursive reordering to preserve caller-owned storage.
- Record copying is shallow. Strings are immutable, but records with
  slices, maps, or pointers need an explicit deep-ownership contract.
- The helper panics only for an internal programming error. Do not
  turn an impossible range into a silent return that hides corruption.
- Recursion depth is logarithmic for this balanced split. A different
  split rule that removes one record at a time can create depth N.
- Concurrent input mutation races with the initial copy. The function
  does not create a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose merge sort when stable comparison ordering is required,
Theta(N log N) worst-case time matters, and an O(N) work buffer is
acceptable. Records with meaningful equal-key input order and linked
lists that merge cheaply are common fits. The same divide-sort-merge
shape also underlies external sorting, where runs live outside memory.

Use [comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) and the
standard library for routine production sorting; Go's
[`slices.SortStableFunc`](https://pkg.go.dev/slices#SortStableFunc)
directly promises to retain equal-element order. Implement merge sort
when its invariant is the subject, a stable worst-case bound is part
of the design, or custom run handling justifies owning the algorithm.

Use [counting or radix sorting](
#b32-counting-and-radix-sorting-arrays) when fixed-width key structure
supports linear passes. Use [quicksort](
#b37-quicksort-slice-and-partition-bounds) when in-place partitioning
is more important and its stability tradeoff is acceptable. Use
[heapsort](#b38-heapsort-array-backed-heap) for O(1) auxiliary array
space with a worst-case comparison bound, but without stability.

The earlier [sorted-source merge lesson](
#b35-merging-sorted-sources-heap-or-pointers) is the right tool when
the runs already exist; do not pay to build them again. The later
[external merge-sort lesson](
#b371-external-merge-sort-sorted-runs-and-heap)
owns limited-memory run generation and multiway disk merging.

NIST's [merge-sort definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/mergesort.html) describes recursive
splitting, sorting, and merging with Theta(N log N) time. Its
[merge definition](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/merge.html)
formalizes the left-first equal choice and the sorted-permutation
result used in the proof. The official
[`slices.SortStableFunc` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#SortStableFunc) states Go's library-level
stable-order guarantee.

#### B.3.7 Quicksort (slice and partition bounds)

##### Problem and contract

Sorting every value does not require building and copying separate
sorted runs. Another approach chooses one pivot value, groups smaller
and larger values around it, and repeats the same job inside those
groups. Once the groups are individually sorted, their established
boundaries put the whole range in order.

Given a finite `[]int64`, return every value in nondecreasing order.
Every `int64` is valid, including duplicates and signed extremes. Nil
and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice. There is no malformed
public input and therefore no error result.

The function leaves caller order unchanged and returns an independent
element array. Allocation must fit memory, and concurrent input
mutation is excluded.

This deterministic teaching implementation chooses the middle
physical index of each active half-open range as its pivot. That makes
the walkthrough reproducible, but the pivot value need not be near
the median. The sort has quadratic worst-case time.

Partitioning is three-way: values below, equal to, and above the pivot
form separate bands. Sorting is not stable. Plain equal integers have
no visible identity, but a record adaptation may reorder equal-key
records.

The implementation recursively sorts a no-larger strict band: the
shorter one, or either one when their lengths tie. It loops over the
other band. This control flow preserves Quicksort's ordering work
while limiting recursive stack depth to O(log N), even when pivot
choices are consistently poor. Internal helpers panic on invalid
program-generated ranges or pivot indexes; the public function never
supplies them.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices),
[comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice), and
[Quickselect](#b33-quickselect-slice) first. Quickselect owns stopping
after the requested rank enters a pivot band. This lesson owns sorting
both strict bands and managing their recursion bounds.

##### Mental model

Each sorting job owns a half-open range `[start,end)`. A range of
length zero or one is already sorted. For a longer range, choose:

```text
pivotIndex = start + (end-start)/2
pivotValue = values[pivotIndex]
```

The subtraction form avoids index overflow, but a physical middle
position says nothing about the pivot's rank among the values.
Partition the range into:

```text
[start,lessEnd)              values below pivot
[lessEnd,greaterStart)       values equal to pivot
[greaterStart,end)           values above pivot
```

No strict band is internally sorted yet. The equal band is finished:
all its values are interchangeable under integer order, and every
value in the left band belongs before it while every value in the
right band belongs after it.

The partition scan maintains four adjacent regions:

```text
less | equal | unknown | greater
```

`lessEnd` separates less from equal. `scanIndex` is the first unknown
position. `greaterStart` separates unknown from greater. A smaller
value swaps into `lessEnd`, then both left boundaries advance. An
equal value advances only `scanIndex`. A greater value swaps just
before `greaterStart`; `scanIndex` stays because its swapped-in value
has not been classified.

After partitioning, both strict bands need the same sorting job. The
code recursively processes whichever band is no larger. It then
changes `start` or `end` and continues the larger band in the current
stack frame. The recursive choice controls stack depth; it does not
change which values are eventually sorted.

##### Worked walkthrough

Sort:

```text
[4,1,3,2,5,8,5,6,7]
```

The expected result is:

```text
[1,2,3,4,5,5,6,7,8]
```

Initial state: the caller owns the displayed slice. No working copy
or active sorting range exists.

1. Decision: allocate and copy nine values, then sort `[0,9)`. Its
   middle index is 4, so pivot value is 5. Values 4, 1, 3, and 2 grow
   the less band. The first 5 grows the equal band. At index 5, value
   8 swaps with the final unknown value 7; keep index 5 fixed. Seven
   swaps with 6, then 6 swaps with the second 5. That swapped-in 5 is
   equal, so advance and stop when unknown becomes empty.
   After: working values are `[4,1,3,2,5,5,6,7,8]`. Bands are
   `[0,4) < 5`, `[4,6) == 5`, and `[6,9) > 5`.
   Known correct: both pivot copies are at their final value band;
   only `[0,4)` and `[6,9)` still need internal sorting.

2. Decision: the strict-band lengths are 4 and 3, so recursively sort
   smaller range `[6,9)` first. Its middle index 7 holds pivot 7.
   Partition `[6,7) < 7`, `[7,8) == 7`, and `[8,9) > 7`.
   After: `[6,9)` is `[6,7,8]`; each strict band has length one.
   Known correct: the right band of the original pivot is fully sorted
   because both of its strict bands are base ranges.

3. Decision: return to the original frame and continue its larger
   band by setting `end = 4`. The current range is `[0,4)`, containing
   `[4,1,3,2]`; its middle index 2 holds pivot 3. Partition it.
   Value 4 swaps with final unknown value 2, which is then classified
   as smaller. Value 1 is smaller, 3 is equal, and 4 is greater.
   After: working values are `[2,1,3,4,5,5,6,7,8]`. New bands are
   `[0,2) < 3`, `[2,3) == 3`, and `[3,4) > 3`.
   Known correct: indexes 2 through 8 now hold their final sorted
   suffix; only prefix `[2,1]` remains unordered.

4. Decision: the right strict band has length one and is smaller than
   the left band's length two. Recurse on `[3,4)`, which immediately
   returns. Continue `[0,2)` in the same frame. Its middle index 1
   holds pivot 1. Value 2 swaps with pivot 1, which is then classified
   equal; value 2 belongs in the greater band.
   After: working values are `[1,2,3,4,5,5,6,7,8]`. The final bands
   are empty `< 1`, `[0,1) == 1`, and `[1,2) > 1`.
   Known correct: the only remaining strict band has one value and is
   already sorted.

5. Decision: recurse on the empty left band and continue the one-value
   right band. Its length is not greater than one, so the loop stops.
   All pending calls return.
   After: the working copy remains `[1,2,3,4,5,5,6,7,8]`.
   Known correct: every strict band reached a base range, while every
   equal band stayed between smaller and larger sorted values.

6. Decision: return the working copy.
   After: result is `[1,2,3,4,5,5,6,7,8]`; caller input remains
   `[4,1,3,2,5,8,5,6,7]`.
   Known correct: the result is a nondecreasing permutation of the
   input and owns its element array.

Focused empty case: nil input creates a non-nil zero-length working
slice. Range `[0,0)` skips the loop and returns safely.

Focused duplicate case: `[4,4,4,4]` forms one equal band spanning the
whole range. One partition finishes the sort; neither strict band
contains work.

Counterexample to treating the middle index as a median value: for
`[0,2,4,6,7,5,3,1]`, this implementation's continued larger bands
have sizes 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, and 2. Each chosen pivot is extreme in
its active range. The first pivot is physical index 4 but value 7,
the maximum, so the first partition leaves seven values on one side.
That repeated imbalance causes quadratic work.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough, preserves caller
order, handles duplicates and signed extremes, and returns a non-nil
empty result. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Quicksort (slice and partition
// bounds). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func partitionAroundPivot(
	values []int64,
	start int,
	end int,
	pivotIndex int,
) (int, int) {
	// Separate the active range around its chosen boundary.
	if start < 0 || start >= end || end > len(values) {
		panic("partition range is invalid")
	}
	if pivotIndex < start || pivotIndex >= end {
		panic("pivot index is outside the partition range")
	}

	pivotValue := values[pivotIndex]
	// These boundaries separate less, equal, unknown, and greater.
	lessEnd := start
	scanIndex := start
	greaterStart := end
	for scanIndex < greaterStart {
		switch {
		case values[scanIndex] < pivotValue:
			values[lessEnd], values[scanIndex] =
				values[scanIndex], values[lessEnd]
			lessEnd++
			scanIndex++
		case values[scanIndex] > pivotValue:
			greaterStart--
			values[scanIndex], values[greaterStart] =
				values[greaterStart], values[scanIndex]
			// The swapped-in value is still unknown.
		default:
			scanIndex++
		}
	}
	return lessEnd, greaterStart
}

func quickSortRange(values []int64, start int, end int) {
	// Use maintained boundaries to answer this range query.
	if start < 0 || start > end || end > len(values) {
		panic("quicksort range is invalid")
	}

	for end-start > 1 {
		pivotIndex := start + (end-start)/2
		lessEnd, greaterStart := partitionAroundPivot(
			values,
			start,
			end,
			pivotIndex,
		)

		leftLength := lessEnd - start
		rightLength := end - greaterStart
		// Recurse on a no-larger band to bound stack depth.
		if leftLength < rightLength {
			quickSortRange(values, start, lessEnd)
			// Continue on the larger band in this stack frame.
			start = greaterStart
		} else {
			quickSortRange(values, greaterStart, end)
			// Continue on the larger band in this stack frame.
			end = lessEnd
		}
	}
}

func quickSortCopy(values []int64) []int64 {
	// Partition an owned copy so caller order remains unchanged.
	sorted := make([]int64, len(values))
	copy(sorted, values)
	quickSortRange(sorted, 0, len(sorted))
	return sorted
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int64{4, 1, 3, 2, 5, 8, 5, 6, 7}
	sorted := quickSortCopy(values)
	fmt.Println(sorted)
	fmt.Println(values)

	equal := quickSortCopy([]int64{4, 4, 4, 4})
	fmt.Println(equal)

	extremes := quickSortCopy([]int64{
		1<<63 - 1,
		0,
		-1 << 63,
	})
	fmt.Println(extremes)

	empty := quickSortCopy(nil)
	fmt.Println(empty, empty == nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 2 3 4 5 5 6 7 8]
[4 1 3 2 5 8 5 6 7]
[4 4 4 4]
[-9223372036854775808 0 9223372036854775807]
[] false
```

The second line confirms that input order did not change. The final
false confirms that the empty result is not nil.

##### Why it works

First prove the partition. Before every scan iteration, maintain four
facts: `[start,lessEnd)` holds values below the pivot;
`[lessEnd,scanIndex)` holds values equal to it;
`[scanIndex,greaterStart)` is unknown; and
`[greaterStart,end)` holds values above it. Initially all known bands
are empty, so the facts hold.

For a smaller scanned value, swapping it with `lessEnd` places it in
the less band. If an equal band existed, its first value moves to the
scan position; advancing both boundaries keeps that value equal. For
an equal value, advancing only `scanIndex` extends the equal band. For
a greater value, decreasing `greaterStart` and swapping places that
value in the greater band. The swapped-in value remains unknown, so
holding `scanIndex` preserves every fact.

Each iteration shrinks the unknown band by one: the smaller and equal
branches advance `scanIndex`, while the greater branch decreases
`greaterStart`. When the scan stops, no unknown value remains and the
returned boundaries describe exactly the three promised bands.

The pivot value was read from inside the active range. At least that
occurrence therefore enters the equal band, making it nonempty even
if swaps move the original pivot position.

Now prove sorting by induction on range length. Length zero or one is
already sorted. For a longer range, partitioning preserves every value
and establishes that all left-band values are below every equal-band
value, which is below every right-band value. Both strict bands are
shorter because the equal band is nonempty.

By the induction hypothesis, processing the left and right strict
bands sorts each one without changing values outside it. Whether a
band is reached by a recursive call or the loop does not affect that
claim; both invoke the same range operation. Concatenating the sorted
left band, the equal band, and the sorted right band produces a sorted
permutation of the parent range. The top range is the whole copied
slice, so the returned result satisfies the contract.

Every partition finishes because its unknown band loses one position
per iteration. Every subsequent strict band omits a nonempty equal
band and is therefore shorter than its parent. The loop and recursive
calls can descend through only finitely many lengths, proving sorting
termination.

For stack depth, the recursive call receives the no-larger strict
band. The two strict lengths sum to at most M - 1 for a parent length
M, so that band has length at most `floor((M-1)/2)`. Each added frame
therefore at least halves the recursive problem. The larger band may
shrink by only one, but the loop handles it without adding a frame.

Range checks establish `0 <= start <= end <= len(values)` before
sorting. Partition runs only for length greater than one, and its
middle calculation stays inside the nonempty range. Direct value
comparison handles signed extremes without subtraction or overflow.

The initial copy confines every swap to returned storage. Partition
swaps preserve the multiset, so copying plus the induction proof also
establishes input preservation and independent result ownership.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of values. Partitioning a range of length M scans
exactly M classifications. Each classification performs at most two
key comparisons, one optional swap, and constant boundary updates, so
it takes Theta(M) time and O(1) non-stack space.

When distinct-value pivots split ranges by a fixed fraction, each
recursion-tree level processes O(N) values and there are O(log N)
levels. The work is Theta(N log N). Under a random-order model where
each nontrivial pivot rank behaves like a uniform random choice, the
expected work is Theta(N log N). That expectation depends on the
stated input-distribution assumption.

With consistently extreme pivots, partition lengths are
`N, N-1, ..., 2`. Their sum is Theta(N squared). The focused
eight-value input demonstrates this worst-case pattern. A middle
physical index does not prevent it.

The three-way equal band changes the best case. All N equal values
finish after one partition, so sorting work is Theta(N). Duplicate
heavy inputs can similarly remove many values at once. There is no
distribution-independent average bound for the deterministic pivot
rule.

Copying the input takes Theta(N) time and creates the O(N) returned
array. Inside that copy, partitioning uses O(1) scalar space. The
smaller-side rule limits stack use to O(log N) for N greater than one,
even in the worst case. Balanced distinct partitions use
Theta(log N) frames, while an all-equal partition uses O(1). Excluding
the returned array, worst-case auxiliary space is O(log N). Including
output, the function owns O(N) storage.

A conventional implementation that recursively calls both bands can
use O(N) stack frames after extreme pivots. Tail-looping the larger
band avoids that failure without improving its quadratic comparison
work.

Random pivot selection makes adversarial arrangement independent of
the pivot choices and gives expected Theta(N log N) time, while still
allowing a quadratic sequence of unlucky choices. Median-of-three,
small-range insertion sort, and an introspective heapsort fallback are
common engineering refinements, but each needs its own verified
contract and cost analysis.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice. Range `[0,0)`
  skips pivot selection and performs no unsafe indexing.
- One value returns unchanged. The length-one range is already a base
  case and needs no partition.
- `[4,4,4,4]` finishes in one partition. A two-way method that leaves
  equals in strict bands may repeatedly process pivot copies.
- Duplicate values remain duplicated. Partitioning rearranges
  occurrences; it does not deduplicate them.
- This sort is unstable. Adapting it to records can swap a later
  equal-key record before an earlier one even though keys are sorted.
- Minimum and maximum `int64` compare directly. Subtracting the pivot
  from a value can overflow and reverse a branch.
- `start + (end-start)/2` avoids adding two potentially large indexes.
  Valid half-open bounds make the difference and result safe.
- A middle index is not a median value. The adversarial example's
  first middle pivot is the maximum, leaving a seven-value band.
- On a greater value, do not advance `scanIndex`. The element swapped
  from the unknown region has not been classified.
- Decrease `greaterStart` before swapping. It names the first position
  reserved for the greater band and keeps index `end` untouched.
- The equal band must be excluded from both later ranges. Including it
  can prevent shrinkage on all-equal input and recurse forever.
- Partition boundaries do not sort a strict band. Returning after one
  partition leaves `[4,1,3,2]` unordered in the walkthrough.
- Sort both strict bands. Quickselect follows only the band containing
  one rank, but complete sorting cannot discard the other band.
- Recurse on the no-larger band and loop over the larger one.
  Reversing those roles restores O(N) worst-case stack depth.
- An empty strict band does not finish the whole parent range. Its
  call returns, while the loop must continue the nonempty band.
- Half-open `end` is excluded. Passing it as a pivot index or reading
  `values[end]` is out of bounds.
- Internal invalid ranges panic because they are programming errors.
  Silently returning would hide a lost or overlapping partition.
- Partition the owned copy, not caller storage. Slice assignment alone
  shares an array and would violate the mutation contract.
- Concurrent mutation can race with the initial copy. The function
  does not provide a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose Quicksort when teaching or controlling partition-based sorting,
when data is held in a random-access slice, and when in-place
reordering of owned storage is valuable. Three-way partitioning is
especially useful when duplicate keys may be common.

For routine Go sorting, prefer the standard library's
[`slices.Sort`](https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort). Its public contract
is the dependency; a hand-written teaching Quicksort should not
replace a maintained library implementation without measured need.

Use [merge sort](#b36-merge-sort-slice-and-buffer) when stability and
Theta(N log N) worst-case work justify an O(N) buffer. Use the next
[heapsort lesson](#b38-heapsort-array-backed-heap) when O(1) auxiliary
array storage and a worst-case comparison bound matter more than
stability. Use [Quickselect](#b33-quickselect-slice) when only one
rank is needed; sorting both outer bands then performs unnecessary
work.

For tiny or nearly sorted ranges, [insertion sort](
#b39-insertion-and-selection-sort-slice) can have lower overhead.
Production hybrids often switch methods, randomize or sample pivots,
and fall back after repeated imbalance.

NIST's [Quicksort definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/quicksort.html) describes pivot
partitioning, recursive sorting, typical logarithmic-level work, and
the quadratic worst case. Hoare's original 1962
[`Quicksort` paper](
https://academic.oup.com/comjnl/article-abstract/5/1/10/395338)
records the algorithm's in-place recursive design. The official
[`slices.Sort` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort) defines
the library alternative used for ordinary ordered Go values.

#### B.3.8 Heapsort (array-backed heap)

##### Problem and contract

Quicksort can spend quadratic time when pivots repeatedly split badly.
Merge sort avoids that case but uses an extra linear buffer. Heapsort
offers another tradeoff: arrange the values as a max-heap, then remove
the maximum into its final position until the array is sorted.

Given a finite `[]int64`, return every value in nondecreasing order.
Every `int64` is valid, including duplicates and signed extremes. Nil
and empty inputs return a non-nil empty slice. There is no malformed
public input and therefore no error result.

The function leaves caller order unchanged and returns an independent
element array. It creates that copy before heap construction, then
reorders the copy in place. Allocation must fit memory, and concurrent
input mutation is excluded.

This implementation is not stable. Equal integers have no visible
identity, but adapting the swaps to records may reverse equal-key
records. Comparisons use values directly and never subtract them.

The implementation uses bottom-up max-heap construction followed by
repeated root extraction. It is fully iterative, so heap repair uses
no recursive stack. Its internal sift helper panics on invalid
program-generated bounds; the public function never supplies them.

Read [arrays and slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) and
[min-heaps and max-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) first. The
heap lesson owns complete-tree indexing and priority-queue updates.
This lesson owns turning one heap into a complete sorted order with a
shrinking prefix and growing suffix.

##### Mental model

The working slice has two adjacent regions, where N is its length:

```text
[0,heapEnd)       max-heap of values not yet placed
[heapEnd,N)       sorted suffix in final positions
```

In a zero-based binary heap, index `i` has children `2*i + 1` and
`2*i + 2` when those indexes are below `heapEnd`. A max-heap requires
every parent to be at least both children. Its root is therefore the
largest value in the heap prefix.

Build that heap from the bottom up. With Go integer division, indexes
at or beyond `heapEnd/2` are leaves and need no repair. Process the
remaining parent indexes in reverse order. When one parent sifts
down, both of its child subtrees are already heaps.

For `heapEnd = 6`, indexes 3, 4, and 5 are leaves. Index 2 is the last
parent because `2 < 6/2`; its left child is index 5. Index 3 is a leaf
because `3 < 6/2` is false. Check the leaf boundary before computing
`2*i + 1`; this also prevents child-index overflow.

Sift-down compares both children and chooses the larger. If the parent
already matches or exceeds that child, it exceeds both and repair is
finished. Otherwise swap with the larger child and continue from that
position. Choosing the larger child is what repairs both child links
at the old parent position.

After construction, swap the maximum at index 0 with index
`heapEnd - 1`. The maximum has reached its final position. Decrease
`heapEnd`, excluding that position from future heap work, then sift
the new root down inside only the remaining prefix. Repeating until
the prefix length is one grows a sorted suffix from right to left.

##### Worked walkthrough

Sort:

```text
[4,10,3,5,1,8]
```

The expected result is:

```text
[1,3,4,5,8,10]
```

Initial state: the caller owns the displayed slice. No working copy,
heap prefix, or sorted suffix exists.

1. Decision: allocate and copy the six values. Begin bottom-up heap
   construction at the last parent, index 2. Its only child at index 5
   stores 8, which exceeds parent value 3, so swap them.
   After: working values are `[4,10,8,5,1,3]`.
   Known correct: index 2 now roots a max-heap; indexes 3 through 5
   were leaves before repair and remain valid heaps.

2. Decision: process parent index 1. Value 10 already exceeds children
   5 and 1, so do not swap. Process root index 0. Compare children 10
   and 8, choose 10, and swap with 4. At index 1, compare children 5
   and 1, choose 5, and swap again.
   After: working values are `[10,5,8,4,1,3]`; `heapEnd = 6`.
   Known correct: every parent is at least its children, so the full
   prefix is a max-heap and root 10 is its maximum.
