- The table retains the entire input, and a longest substring aliases
  it. Keeping either result can retain a much larger allocation.
- The product guard prevents `int` overflow, not memory exhaustion.
  Quadratic storage becomes impractical long before integer overflow
  on ordinary machines.

##### When to choose it

Choose the full table when one fixed text receives many palindrome
range queries or when later transitions repeatedly need exact interval
facts. [Palindrome partitioning](
#b85-palindrome-partitioning-backtracking-or-dp-table) is the central
example: each cut decision can consult one precomputed substring cell.

Use [center expansion](
#b81-two-pointers-and-center-expansion-string) for one simple longest
query when constant auxiliary space matters. Use [Manacher's
algorithm](#b84-manachers-algorithm-radius-arrays) for every center
radius or one longest answer under a linear-time requirement.

Use a [palindromic tree](#a165-palindromic-trees) when the workload is
online or asks for distinct palindrome values and occurrence counts.
Use generic [interval DP](
#b205-interval-dp-two-dimensional-table) when a problem combines
smaller intervals by several split positions rather than merely
removing equal endpoints.

Go defines strings as byte sequences and indexing as byte access in
the [string type specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#String_types).
The [slice specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_types)
defines the contiguous Boolean storage retained by the table.

#### B.8.3 Edit distance and subsequences (DP table)

##### Problem and contract

Find the minimum number of single-byte edits that transform one whole
string into another, and return one optimal edit script. This lesson
owns unit-cost Levenshtein edit distance. Later entries own direct
subsequence questions, including [longest common subsequence](
#b253-longest-common-subsequence-dp-table).

`editDistance(source,target)` permits four alignment steps:

- match equal bytes, consuming both at cost zero;
- replace one source byte with one target byte at cost one;
- delete one source byte at cost one; or
- insert one target byte at cost one.

The result contains the minimum edit count and a forward script. A
match is included in the script so the complete alignment can be
replayed, but it does not add to the distance. Matches and
replacements consume one source byte and emit one target byte.
Deletion consumes without emitting; insertion emits without
consuming.

Several optimal scripts may exist. Backtracking chooses a match when
available, then replacement, deletion, and insertion in that order.
This tie rule makes the returned script deterministic; it does not
claim that one optimal alignment is semantically preferable.

Both inputs are arbitrary byte strings. The function does not decode
UTF-8, normalize text, fold case, ignore punctuation, transpose
neighbors, search for a substring, or assign custom operation costs.
The source and target remain unchanged. The returned step slice owns
new storage and does not retain either input, because each step stores
copied byte values.

Empty strings are valid. Transforming empty source into M target bytes
uses M insertions; transforming N source bytes into empty target uses
N deletions. Two empty strings have distance zero and an empty script.

The function returns an error before table allocation if either prefix
dimension or their product cannot fit `int`. A smaller allocation may
still exhaust memory; allocation failure is outside the contract.

Read [flat table indexing](
#a14-flat-storage-and-multidimensional-indexing) before the row-major
implementation. Read [byte and rune semantics](
#a21-bytes-runes-and-character-sequences) before changing the compared
unit.

##### Mental model

Create a table with N+1 source-prefix rows and M+1 target-prefix
columns. State `distance[I][J]` means:

```text
the minimum cost to transform source[:I] into target[:J]
```

I and J are byte counts, not final byte indexes. Thus cell `[2][3]`
compares the first two source bytes with the first three target bytes.
In flat row-major storage its position is `2*(M+1)+3`.

Row zero transforms empty source into target prefixes, so its values
are 0 through M insertions. Column zero transforms source prefixes
into empty target, so its values are 0 through N deletions.

For a positive cell, consider how an alignment reaches it:

- diagonal consumes both last bytes; its extra cost is zero when they
  match and one when replacement is required;
- the cell above deletes the last source byte, adding one; or
- the cell to the left inserts the last target byte, adding one.

Store the minimum of those three complete predecessor costs. Fill rows
from shorter source prefixes to longer ones and columns from shorter
target prefixes to longer ones. Every predecessor is then final before
the current cell reads it.

After filling, begin at `[N][M]`. Choose a predecessor whose value
plus its step cost equals the current value, using the declared tie
order.
Record the corresponding step and move to that predecessor. This walks
from the end of the alignment to its beginning, so reverse the steps
before returning them.

The zero-cost match steps, read forward, form a common subsequence:
they occur in increasing order in both inputs while other bytes may be
skipped or replaced. They are not necessarily a longest common
subsequence because this recurrence optimizes edit cost and allows a
one-cost replacement. B.25.3 uses a different state objective.

##### Worked walkthrough

Transform `kitten` into `sitting`. The expected distance is three:
replace `k` with `s`, replace `e` with `i`, and insert final `g`.

```text
source byte positions: 0 1 2 3 4 5
source:               k i t t e n
target byte positions: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6
target:                s i t t i n g
```

Initial state: N is 6 and M is 7. No dimensions are checked, no table
exists, and no edit prefix is confirmed.

1. Decision: check and allocate `(6+1)*(7+1) = 56` integer cells.
   Initialize row zero to `[0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7]` and column zero to
   `[0,1,2,3,4,5,6]`.
   After: every empty-prefix pair has its insertion or deletion count;
   all positive-by-positive cells remain zero placeholders.
   Known correct: transforming empty to J bytes needs exactly J
   insertions, and transforming I bytes to empty needs I deletions.

2. Decision: fill cell `[1][1]` for `k` and `s`. Diagonal replacement
   costs `0+1 = 1`; deletion costs `1+1 = 2`; insertion costs
   `1+1 = 2`. Store one.
   After: the first positive cell is 1.
   Known correct: replacing `k` with `s` is cheaper than deleting and
   then inserting. All three possible final step kinds were compared.

3. Decision: finish row `k`, then row `ki`. At `[2][2]`, final bytes
   `i` and `i` match, so the diagonal cost stays `[1][1] = 1`; delete
   and insert alternatives cost at least two.
   After: rows are `[1,1,2,3,4,5,6,7]` and
   `[2,2,1,2,3,4,5,6]` after their column-zero cells.
   Known correct: every prefix pair through source `ki` has its
   minimum cost. The match extends the earlier `k`-to-`s` replacement
   for free.

4. Decision: fill rows for `kit` and `kitt`. Equal final `t` bytes use
   zero-cost diagonals at `[3][3]` and `[4][4]`.
   After: those rows are `[3,3,2,1,2,3,4,5]` and
   `[4,4,3,2,1,2,3,4]`.
   Known correct: the two ordered `t` matches preserve distance one;
   all cells to their right and left have also considered three moves.

5. Decision: in row `kitte`, cell `[5][5]` compares `e` with `i`.
   Replacement from `[4][4]` costs two; deletion and insertion each
   cost three. Store two, then finish the row.
   After: row is `[5,5,4,3,2,2,3,4]`.
   Known correct: two replacements transform `kitte` into `sitti`;
   no cheaper predecessor reaches that prefix pair.

6. Decision: fill final row `kitten`. Cell `[6][6]` matches `n` for
   zero extra cost, giving two. At `[6][7]`, insertion from `[6][6]`
   costs three and beats the other predecessors.
   After: final row is `[6,6,5,4,3,3,2,3]`; the full table is:

   ```text
             ""  s  i  t  t  i  n  g
   ""         0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
   k          1  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
   ki         2  2  1  2  3  4  5  6
   kit        3  3  2  1  2  3  4  5
   kitt       4  4  3  2  1  2  3  4
   kitte      5  5  4  3  2  2  3  4
   kitten     6  6  5  4  3  3  2  3
   ```

   Known correct: every prefix pair is final; bottom-right value three
   is the minimum cost for the complete strings.

7. Decision: backtrack from `[6][7] = 3`. The left cell `[6][6] = 2`
   plus insertion cost one matches, so record `insert g`. At `[6][6]`,
   equal `n` bytes and equal diagonal value select `match n`.
   After: position is `[5][5]`; reverse-order steps are
   `[insert g, match n]`.
   Known correct: those steps explain the optimal final `ng`
   alignment, and the unresolved prefix pair has distance two.

8. Decision: at `[5][5]`, diagonal `[4][4] = 1` plus replacement
   selects `replace e -> i`. Then equal diagonals select `match t`,
   `match t`, and `match i`. At `[1][1]`, select `replace k -> s`.
   After: position reaches `[0][0]`; the reverse-order script is
   `[insert g, match n, replace e->i, match t, match t, match i,
   replace k->s]`.
   Known correct: each move explains its current cell and strictly
   decreases at least one prefix length, so no suffix remains.

9. Decision: reverse the steps and replay them from the source start.
   Replacement emits `s`, matches emit `itt`, replacement emits `i`,
   match emits `n`, and insertion emits `g`.
   After: output is `sitting`; three non-match steps were used.
   Known correct: the script transforms the complete source into the
   complete target and its edit count equals the bottom-right minimum.

The matched bytes `i`, `t`, `t`, and `n` spell common subsequence
`ittn`. This trace does not prove it is a longest common subsequence;
that is not the optimized state.

Focused empty cases: `"" -> "abc"` follows row zero and returns three
insertions. `"abc" -> ""` follows column zero and returns three
deletions. `"same" -> "same"` follows only zero-cost diagonals and
returns distance zero with four match steps.

Focused tie: `"ab" -> "ba"` has distance two. Two replacements and a
delete-match-insert alignment are both optimal. The tie rule chooses
the two replacements. Its match sequence is empty even though `a` or
`b` is a common subsequence of length one, so edit-script matches are
not automatically an LCS.

Focused arbitrary bytes: `[0,255] -> [0,1,255]` matches byte zero,
inserts byte one, and matches byte 255, for distance one.

Counterexample to resolving the first mismatch greedily: for
`"ab" -> "b"`, replacing `a` with `b` and then deleting the original
`b` costs two. The optimal first action deletes `a`, exposing the
zero-cost `b` match for total one. The table preserves both alignments
until their complete prefix costs can be compared.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program computes the table, reconstructs the ordinary
example, and runs empty, equal, and arbitrary-byte cases. Save it as
`main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Edit distance and subsequences (DP
// table). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type editKind string

const (
	matchByte   editKind = "match"
	replaceByte editKind = "replace"
	deleteByte  editKind = "delete"
	insertByte  editKind = "insert"
)

type editStep struct {
	kind       editKind
	sourceByte byte
	targetByte byte
}

type editResult struct {
	distance int
	steps    []editStep
}

func checkedGridCellCount(rows int, columns int) (int, error) {
	// Compute grid cell count with an overflow check instead of
	// wrapping.
	if rows <= 0 || columns <= 0 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("table dimensions must be positive")
	}
	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	if columns > maximumInt/rows {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("edit table exceeds int capacity")
	}
	return rows * columns, nil
}

func minimumOfThree(first int, second int, third int) int {
	// Return the smallest candidate without changing any input value.
	minimum := first
	if second < minimum {
		minimum = second
	}
	if third < minimum {
		minimum = third
	}
	return minimum
}

func editDistance(
	source string,
	target string,
) (editResult, error) {
	// Keep edit distance in one helper so callers use one rule.
	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	if len(source) == maximumInt ||
		len(target) == maximumInt {
		return editResult{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"prefix dimension exceeds int capacity",
		)
	}

	sourcePrefixCount := len(source) + 1
	targetPrefixCount := len(target) + 1
	cellCount, err := checkedGridCellCount(
		sourcePrefixCount,
		targetPrefixCount,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return editResult{}, err
	}
	distanceByPrefixes := make([]int, cellCount)
	position := func(sourceLength int, targetLength int) int {
		return sourceLength*targetPrefixCount + targetLength
	}

	// Empty prefixes require one insertion or deletion per byte.
	for sourceLength := 1; sourceLength <= len(source); {
		distanceByPrefixes[position(sourceLength, 0)] =
			sourceLength
		sourceLength++
	}
	for targetLength := 1; targetLength <= len(target); {
		distanceByPrefixes[position(0, targetLength)] =
			targetLength
		targetLength++
	}

	// Each cell extends already solved shorter prefix pairs.
	for sourceLength := 1; sourceLength <= len(source); {
		for targetLength := 1; targetLength <= len(target); {
			cellPosition := position(
				sourceLength,
				targetLength,
			)
			diagonalPosition := position(
				sourceLength-1,
				targetLength-1,
			)
			deletePosition := position(
				sourceLength-1,
				targetLength,
			)
			insertPosition := position(
				sourceLength,
				targetLength-1,
			)
			deleteCost :=
				distanceByPrefixes[deletePosition] + 1
			insertCost :=
				distanceByPrefixes[insertPosition] + 1
			diagonalCost :=
				distanceByPrefixes[diagonalPosition]
			if source[sourceLength-1] !=
				target[targetLength-1] {
				diagonalCost++
			}
			distanceByPrefixes[cellPosition] =
				minimumOfThree(
					diagonalCost,
					deleteCost,
					insertCost,
				)
			targetLength++
		}
		sourceLength++
	}

	// Backtracking prefers match, replace, delete, then insert.
	reversedSteps := make([]editStep, 0)
	sourceLength := len(source)
	targetLength := len(target)
	for sourceLength > 0 || targetLength > 0 {
		cellPosition := position(sourceLength, targetLength)
		cellDistance := distanceByPrefixes[cellPosition]
		if sourceLength > 0 && targetLength > 0 {
			diagonalPosition := position(
				sourceLength-1,
				targetLength-1,
			)
			diagonalDistance :=
				distanceByPrefixes[diagonalPosition]
			sourceByte := source[sourceLength-1]
			targetByte := target[targetLength-1]
			if sourceByte == targetByte &&
				cellDistance == diagonalDistance {
				reversedSteps = append(
					reversedSteps,
					editStep{
						kind:       matchByte,
						sourceByte: sourceByte,
						targetByte: targetByte,
					},
				)
				sourceLength--
				targetLength--
				continue
			}
			if cellDistance == diagonalDistance+1 {
				reversedSteps = append(
					reversedSteps,
					editStep{
						kind:       replaceByte,
						sourceByte: sourceByte,
						targetByte: targetByte,
					},
				)
				sourceLength--
				targetLength--
				continue
			}
		}

		if sourceLength > 0 {
			deletePosition := position(
				sourceLength-1,
				targetLength,
			)
			deleteDistance :=
				distanceByPrefixes[deletePosition]
			if cellDistance == deleteDistance+1 {
				sourceByte := source[sourceLength-1]
				reversedSteps = append(
					reversedSteps,
					editStep{
						kind:       deleteByte,
						sourceByte: sourceByte,
					},
				)
				sourceLength--
				continue
			}
		}

		if targetLength == 0 {
			return editResult{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"edit table has no valid predecessor",
			)
		}
		insertPosition := position(
			sourceLength,
			targetLength-1,
		)
		insertDistance :=
			distanceByPrefixes[insertPosition]
		if cellDistance != insertDistance+1 {
			return editResult{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"edit table has no valid predecessor",
			)
		}
		targetByte := target[targetLength-1]
		reversedSteps = append(
			reversedSteps,
			editStep{
				kind:       insertByte,
				targetByte: targetByte,
			},
		)
		targetLength--
	}

	// Backtracking produced the alignment from its end to its start.
	for left, right := 0, len(reversedSteps)-1; left < right; {
		reversedSteps[left], reversedSteps[right] =
			reversedSteps[right], reversedSteps[left]
		left++
		right--
	}
	finalPosition := position(len(source), len(target))
	finalDistance := distanceByPrefixes[finalPosition]
	return editResult{
		distance: finalDistance,
		steps:    reversedSteps,
	}, nil
}

func printStep(step editStep) {
	// Expose step in logical order without changing source.
	switch step.kind {
	case matchByte:
		fmt.Printf("match %q\n", step.sourceByte)
	case replaceByte:
		fmt.Printf(
			"replace %q -> %q\n",
			step.sourceByte,
			step.targetByte,
		)
	case deleteByte:
		fmt.Printf("delete %q\n", step.sourceByte)
	case insertByte:
		fmt.Printf("insert %q\n", step.targetByte)
	}
}

func mustEdit(source string, target string) editResult {
	// Run the operation and stop if the fixed example fails.
	result, err := editDistance(source, target)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	return result
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	result := mustEdit("kitten", "sitting")
	fmt.Println(result.distance)
	for _, step := range result.steps {
		printStep(step)
	}

	fmt.Println(mustEdit("", "abc").distance)
	fmt.Println(mustEdit("abc", "").distance)
	fmt.Println(mustEdit("same", "same").distance)

	binarySource := string([]byte{0, 255})
	binaryTarget := string([]byte{0, 1, 255})
	fmt.Println(
		mustEdit(binarySource, binaryTarget).distance,
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
3
replace 'k' -> 's'
match 'i'
match 't'
match 't'
replace 'e' -> 'i'
match 'n'
insert 'g'
3
3
0
1
```

The first number and seven steps are the `kitten` alignment. The final
four numbers cover insertion-only, deletion-only, exact-match, and
arbitrary-byte cases.

##### Why it works

Interpret the table as a shortest-path grid. Cell `[I][J]` is a node
for one pair of prefixes. A diagonal edge consumes both final bytes
and costs zero for equality or one for replacement. A downward edge
consumes the next source byte as a deletion and costs one. A rightward
edge emits the next target byte as an insertion and costs one.

The initialized top row and left column are correct because only one
edge direction is available when the other prefix is empty. Assume
all cells before `[I][J]` in row-major fill order contain shortest
path costs. Every path entering `[I][J]` must use exactly one of its
diagonal, upper, or left edges. Adding that edge's cost to its already
optimal predecessor therefore covers every possible final operation.
Taking the minimum gives the shortest cost for the current prefixes.

All three predecessors have a smaller row or column and are filled
before the current cell. Induction over the row-major order proves
every cell, including `[N][M]`. Both fill loops advance bounded prefix
counts. Checked positive dimensions and product bounds keep every flat
position inside the allocated slice and prevent loop-counter overflow.

During backtracking, the recurrence guarantees at least one
predecessor whose value plus step cost equals the current cell. The
tie order picks one such edge without changing optimal cost. A
diagonal reduces both prefix lengths. Deletion reduces the source
length; insertion reduces the target length. Every move therefore
approaches `[0][0]`, so
backtracking terminates after at most N+M steps.

The recorded edges run from target end to start. Reversal puts them in
source-consumption order. Each step then performs exactly the
alignment operation represented by its edge. Replay consumes all
source bytes and emits exactly all target bytes. Non-match edge count
equals the bottom-right distance, proving that the returned script is
optimal.

Inputs are only indexed, never changed. Step values copy bytes into a
new slice, so the result script has independent ownership.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be source byte length and M target byte length. Allocation
zeroes (N+1)(M+1) integer cells, and filling visits each
positive-prefix cell. Best, average, and worst successful fill time
are all Theta((N+1)(M+1)); byte equality changes edge costs, not the
visited grid.

Backtracking and reversal each take O(N+M) time in the worst case. The
returned alignment has at most N+M steps, so it uses O(N+M) output
storage. The temporary full distance table uses
Theta((N+1)(M+1)) auxiliary storage and is released after return.
Other working state is O(1).

If only the numeric distance is required, each row depends only on the
previous row and its own left cell. Two rolling rows reduce auxiliary
space to O(min(N,M)) after orienting the shorter string as columns.
Discarding old rows loses direct backtracking information, so it
cannot return this script without recomputation or a
divide-and-conquer reconstruction method.

The full table stores one `int` cost per prefix pair, so its quadratic
memory has a substantial constant factor. Memory is often the
practical limit before arithmetic overflow. The guard proves the cell
count fits `int`; it does not promise that physical memory is
available.

A unit replacement changes one byte for cost one; modeling that same
change as deletion plus insertion would cost two. Weighted edit
distance changes the edge costs. Allowing adjacent transposition adds
another predecessor and state condition; that is a different distance,
not a small output-format change.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty-to-empty returns zero and no steps. Starting fill loops at
  zero can overwrite this base with an invented edit.
- `"" -> "abc"` needs row-zero values 0, 1, 2, 3. Leaving them at
  zero incorrectly makes every target prefix free.
- `"abc" -> ""` needs column-zero values 0, 1, 2, 3. Initializing only
  the top row breaks deletion-only transformations.
- Equal bytes use a zero-cost diagonal, not replacement cost one.
  `"same" -> "same"` must remain distance zero.
- Mismatched bytes compare replacement, deletion, and insertion.
  Greedily replacing fails on `"ab" -> "b"` as traced above.
- Prefix count I addresses byte `I-1`. Indexing byte I shifts every
  comparison and panics at the final prefix.
- The flat stride is M+1, the target prefix count. Multiplying by M
  overlaps rows and corrupts base-column values.
- Backtracking must test equality between current and predecessor
  cost, not merely choose the numerically smallest neighboring cell.
  Each edge has its own added cost.
- Optimal scripts need not be unique. Tests that demand another valid
  script conflict with the declared match-replace-delete-insert rule.
- `"ab" -> "ba"` costs two here. Treating adjacent transposition as
  one operation silently changes the metric to a Damerau-style model.
- The source-to-target script is directional even though unit-cost
  distance is symmetric. Reversing the arguments changes insertions to
  deletions and may choose a different tied alignment.
- Match steps form a common subsequence but not necessarily a longest
  one. Reusing this table as an LCS result confuses two objectives.
- Byte zero, byte 255, and malformed UTF-8 are ordinary values. A rune
  edit contract requires decoding and byte-offset mapping; grapheme
  edits additionally require text segmentation.
- The dimension guard prevents integer overflow, while ordinary memory
  exhaustion remains outside the successful contract.

##### When to choose it

Choose unit-cost edit distance when the question asks how many local
insertions, deletions, or replacements separate two complete
sequences.
Keep the full table when an actual alignment or edit script is needed.
Use rolling rows when only the numeric distance matters and memory is
the binding limit.

Use [longest common subsequence](
#b253-longest-common-subsequence-dp-table) when the objective is to
retain the greatest ordered set of equal items, not minimize a model
that includes replacement. Use [subsequence checking](
#b251-subsequence-checking-two-pointers) when one sequence only needs
to be confirmed inside another; its linear two-pointer scan avoids a
quadratic table.

Use [exact string matching](
#b72-kmp-matching-prefix-function-array) when edits are forbidden. Use
[wildcard or regex matching](
#b79-wildcard-and-regex-matching-dp-table-or-automaton) when pattern
syntax, rather than edit cost, defines acceptable text. Weighted,
transposition-aware, banded, or thresholded distance requires a
contract and recurrence tailored to those operations.

Wagner and Fischer's [string-correction paper](
https://doi.org/10.1145/321796.321811) gives the product-time dynamic
programming framework and connects it to common subsequences. Go's
[string type specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#String_types)
defines the byte indexing used here.

#### B.8.4 Manacher's algorithm (radius arrays)

##### Problem and contract

Compute the maximal palindrome around every possible center of one
static string in linear time. Use those radii to return one longest
palindromic substring without the repeated comparisons made by
independent center expansion.

`manacher` accepts an arbitrary byte string and returns two arrays of
length N:

- `odd[center]` counts the center byte plus matching byte pairs around
  it. Radius R represents range `[center-R+1,center+R)` and length
  `2*R-1`.
- `even[center]` counts matching pairs around the gap immediately
  before `center`. Radius R represents range
  `[center-R,center+R)` and length `2*R`.

Every nonempty odd radius is at least one. An even radius may be zero.
The gap before byte zero has radius zero. There is no array entry for
the gap after byte N-1; that final gap cannot center a nonempty
palindrome, so no positive result is lost.

Each radius describes the maximal palindrome at that exact center.
Smaller palindromes of the same parity and center are implicit: reduce
the radius while it remains positive. The arrays do not enumerate
every substring separately, because one all-equal text can contain a
quadratic number of palindromic occurrences.

The second result contains the longest value, its half-open byte
range, and `found = true` for nonempty input. Empty input returns
empty radius arrays and `("",0,0,false)`. Equal maximum lengths use
the earliest source start.

The input is not changed. Both radius arrays own new integer storage;
the longest string shares the immutable input bytes. Byte zero, byte
255, and malformed UTF-8 are valid data. There is no normalization,
case folding, or grapheme interpretation. Slice allocation must fit
available memory; allocation failure is outside the contract.

Read the [center-expansion owner](
#b81-two-pointers-and-center-expansion-string) first for odd and even
centers, maximality, ranges, and the earliest-start tie. Compare the
[palindrome table](#b82-palindrome-dynamic-programming-table) when
many explicit interval facts matter more than linear preprocessing.

##### Mental model

Run one left-to-right pass for odd centers and another for even gaps.
Within one pass, remember the half-open range
`[windowStart,windowEnd)` of the processed palindrome reaching
farthest right. Call it the active window. It is not necessarily the
longest palindrome seen; its right boundary is what can prove facts
about later centers.

If a new center lies outside the active window, begin with only the
parity's base radius: one for odd or zero for even. If it lies inside,
reflect it across the window's center:

```text
odd mirror = windowStart + (windowEnd - 1 - center)
even mirror = windowStart + (windowEnd - center)
```

The formulas differ because an odd center is a byte while an even
center is a gap. The subtraction is performed before addition so the
calculation never needs the potentially overflowing sum of both window
boundaries.

Symmetry proves that bytes around the mirror also match around the new
center, but only while they remain inside the active window. The
known right-side room is `windowEnd-center`. Initialize the new radius
to the smaller of the mirror radius and this available radius.

Then compare only the next pair outside that confirmed core. Continue
while both positions exist and their bytes match. The first mismatch
or boundary makes the radius maximal. If its range ends farther right
than the active window, replace the window. Compare this maximal range
with the saved longest range using length and earliest start.

The reuse is the essential improvement: a center fully contained in a
known palindrome can inherit many equal pairs without reading them
again. Clipping prevents inherited symmetry from making claims beyond
the only boundary the active window has proved.

##### Worked walkthrough

Compute radii for `abacaba`. The expected odd radii are
`[1,2,1,4,1,2,1]`, every even radius is zero, and the longest range is
the whole string `[0,7)`.

```text
byte position:  0 1 2 3 4 5 6
byte:           a b a c a b a
```

Initial state: allocate two seven-element zero arrays. No center is
processed, best is not found, and the odd active window is `[0,0)`.

1. Decision: odd center zero starts with radius one. Expansion would
   read position -1, so stop. Store `odd[0] = 1`, producing `[0,1)`.
   After: odd window is `[0,1)`; best is `a` at `[0,1)`.
   Known correct: center zero's maximal odd palindrome is one byte,
   and it is the only processed candidate.

2. Decision: center one is outside the exclusive window end. Start at
   one, compare positions zero and two (`a == a`), and grow to radius
   two. The next pair crosses the left boundary.
   After: `odd[1] = 2`; range `[0,3)` becomes window and best.
   Known correct: `aba` is maximal at center one, and the active
   window now proves its symmetry through exclusive end three.

3. Decision: center two is inside `[0,3)`. Its odd mirror is
   `0+(3-1-2) = 0`. Mirror radius one and available radius one agree,
   so inherit one. Next bytes at positions one and three are `b` and
   `c`, so expansion stops.
   After: `odd[2] = 1`; window and best remain `[0,3)`.
   Known correct: inherited center byte was proved by symmetry, and
   the first new comparison proved that no larger radius works.

4. Decision: center three equals the window end, so begin at one.
   Compare pairs `(2,4)`, `(1,5)`, and `(0,6)`; they are `a/a`,
   `b/b`, and `a/a`. Radius reaches four, then both bounds end.
   After: `odd[3] = 4`; window and best become `[0,7)`.
   Known correct: `abacaba` is maximal around center three and reaches
   the farthest possible right boundary.

5. Decision: center four mirrors center two. Inherit radius one;
   positions three and five are `c` and `b`, so stop.
   After: `odd[4] = 1`; the full-string window stays active.
   Known correct: center four is maximal, and no right extension was
   found.

6. Decision: center five mirrors center one. Mirror radius two equals
   the available radius two, so inherit it. The next right position is
   seven, outside the input. Center six similarly inherits radius one
   from center zero and reaches the boundary.
   After: odd radii are `[1,2,1,4,1,2,1]`; best stays `[0,7)`.
   Known correct: every odd center is maximal. The last two centers
   reused all comparisons that fit inside the active window.

7. Decision: reset the active window and scan even gaps. Every
   adjacent pair in `abacaba` differs; the gap before zero also has no
   left byte.
   After: even radii are `[0,0,0,0,0,0,0]`; best is unchanged.
   Known correct: every even center fails its first possible pair, so
   no nonempty even palindrome exists.

8. Decision: both passes are exhausted, so return the arrays and best.
   After: result is `("abacaba", 0, 7, true)`.
   Known correct: every odd byte center and every even gap center has
   one maximal radius, and best compared all positive candidates.

Focused clipping and even reuse: `aaaa` has odd radii `[1,2,2,1]` and
even radii `[0,1,2,1]`. During the odd pass at center three, active
window `[1,4)` mirrors center one with radius two, but only
`4-3 = 1` unit remains. Clipping to one avoids claiming invalid range
`[2,5)`. During the even pass, gap two expands to radius two and
window `[0,4)`; gap three mirrors gap one and safely inherits radius
one.
The longest result is `[0,4)`.

Focused even answer: `cbbd` has even radii `[0,0,1,0]`. Gap two lies
between the `b` bytes and yields range `[1,3)`, so longest is `bb`.

Focused tie: `babad` has radius two at odd centers one and two,
representing `bab` and `aba`. Equal length keeps earlier `[0,3)`.

Focused empty and binary cases: empty input returns empty arrays and
no longest value. Bytes `[0,255,0]` produce odd radii `[1,2,1]` and
return whole range `[0,3)` regardless of UTF-8 validity.

Counterexample to copying a mirror without clipping: at odd center
three in `aaaa`, copying mirror radius two would claim end five in a
four-byte string. The first wrong decision is trusting symmetry beyond
active end four. Taking the minimum with available radius one keeps
the inherited range inside established evidence.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program prints an odd-centered example, an
even-centered example, tie and all-equal results, empty input, and
arbitrary bytes. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Manacher's algorithm (radius
// arrays). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type palindromeRadii struct {
	odd  []int
	even []int
}

type palindromeResult struct {
	value string
	start int
	end   int
	found bool
}

func isBetterPalindromeRange(
	start int,
	end int,
	bestStart int,
	bestEnd int,
	bestFound bool,
) bool {
	// Evaluate is better palindrome range without changing the
	// maintained state.
	if !bestFound {
		return true
	}
	length := end - start
	bestLength := bestEnd - bestStart
	return length > bestLength ||
		length == bestLength && start < bestStart
}

func manacher(text string) (palindromeRadii, palindromeResult) {
	// Keep manacher in one helper so callers use one rule.
	textLength := len(text)
	radii := palindromeRadii{
		odd:  make([]int, textLength),
		even: make([]int, textLength),
	}
	best := palindromeResult{}

	// The half-open window is the rightmost odd palindrome found.
	windowStart := 0
	windowEnd := 0
	for center := 0; center < textLength; center++ {
		radius := 1
		if center < windowEnd {
			mirror := windowStart +
				(windowEnd - 1 - center)
			availableRadius := windowEnd - center
			radius = radii.odd[mirror]
			if radius > availableRadius {
				radius = availableRadius
			}
		}

		// Only comparisons beyond the known mirror region are new.
		for center-radius >= 0 &&
			center+radius < textLength &&
			text[center-radius] == text[center+radius] {
			radius++
		}
		radii.odd[center] = radius
		palindromeStart := center - radius + 1
		palindromeEnd := center + radius
		if palindromeEnd > windowEnd {
			windowStart = palindromeStart
			windowEnd = palindromeEnd
		}
		if isBetterPalindromeRange(
			palindromeStart,
			palindromeEnd,
			best.start,
			best.end,
			best.found,
		) {
			palindromeValue :=
				text[palindromeStart:palindromeEnd]
			best = palindromeResult{
				value: palindromeValue,
				start: palindromeStart,
				end:   palindromeEnd,
				found: true,
			}
		}
	}

	// The even center is the gap before the center index.
	windowStart = 0
	windowEnd = 0
	for center := 0; center < textLength; center++ {
		radius := 0
		if center < windowEnd {
			mirror := windowStart +
				(windowEnd - center)
			availableRadius := windowEnd - center
			radius = radii.even[mirror]
			if radius > availableRadius {
				radius = availableRadius
			}
		}

		// Compare the next pair outside the confirmed even core.
		for center-radius-1 >= 0 &&
			center+radius < textLength &&
			text[center-radius-1] ==
				text[center+radius] {
			radius++
		}
		radii.even[center] = radius
		palindromeStart := center - radius
		palindromeEnd := center + radius
		if palindromeEnd > windowEnd {
			windowStart = palindromeStart
			windowEnd = palindromeEnd
		}
		if radius > 0 && isBetterPalindromeRange(
			palindromeStart,
			palindromeEnd,
			best.start,
			best.end,
			best.found,
		) {
			palindromeValue :=
				text[palindromeStart:palindromeEnd]
			best = palindromeResult{
				value: palindromeValue,
				start: palindromeStart,
				end:   palindromeEnd,
				found: true,
			}
		}
	}

	return radii, best
}

func printLongest(text string) {
	// Compute the requested ordered or extreme result.
	_, result := manacher(text)
	fmt.Printf(
		"%q %d %d %t\n",
		result.value,
		result.start,
		result.end,
		result.found,
	)
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	oddExample, oddResult := manacher("abacaba")
	fmt.Println(oddExample.odd)
	fmt.Println(oddExample.even)
	fmt.Printf(
		"%q %d %d %t\n",
		oddResult.value,
		oddResult.start,
		oddResult.end,
		oddResult.found,
	)

	evenExample, evenResult := manacher("cbbd")
	fmt.Println(evenExample.odd)
	fmt.Println(evenExample.even)
	fmt.Printf(
		"%q %d %d %t\n",
		evenResult.value,
		evenResult.start,
		evenResult.end,
		evenResult.found,
	)

	printLongest("babad")
	printLongest("aaaa")
	printLongest("")
	printLongest(string([]byte{0, 255, 0}))
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 2 1 4 1 2 1]
[0 0 0 0 0 0 0]
"abacaba" 0 7 true
[1 1 1 1]
[0 0 1 0]
"bb" 1 3 true
"bab" 0 3 true
"aaaa" 0 4 true
"" 0 0 false
"\x00\xff\x00" 0 3 true
```

The first three lines show both `abacaba` arrays and its longest
result. The next three show `cbbd`; the remaining lines cover ties,
repetition, empty input, and arbitrary bytes.

##### Why it works

Prove each parity pass by increasing center. The active window is a
confirmed palindrome with the greatest exclusive right end among all
processed centers. Before any center, the empty window satisfies that
claim.

For a center outside the window, only its parity's base palindrome is
known. Direct expansion compares every additional symmetric pair, so
the stored radius is maximal. Updating the window only for a farther
end preserves the rightmost-window invariant.

For a center inside the window, reflect it to an already processed
center. Because the active range is palindromic, every mirrored pair
strictly inside it has an equal pair around the new center. If the
mirror radius ends before the window boundary, the whole radius is
safe. If it reaches beyond the opposite boundary, symmetry proves only
the portion through `windowEnd`. The minimum of mirror radius and
available radius is therefore confirmed and never too large.

Expansion begins immediately outside that confirmed core. Every
successful comparison adds one equal pair. A mismatch proves no larger
palindrome can use this center; a boundary proves no larger in-range
candidate exists. Thus the final radius is maximal. Replacing the
window only when this candidate ends farther right preserves the
invariant for the next center. The same reasoning applies to byte
centers and gap centers, with their respective mirror formulas.

Every nonempty palindrome has exactly one odd byte center or one even
gap center. The two passes therefore contain its center, and that
center's maximal radius contains it. Comparing every maximal range by
length and earliest start finds the required global longest result.
Empty input has no center, so leaving `found` false is correct.

Each loop advances its center to N and stops. Each expansion moves one
pair outward and is bounded by input ends. Therefore the procedure
terminates. The boundary-derived range formulas keep every text slice
inside `[0,N)`.

For the linear bound, each center performs constant mirror work and at
most one failing byte comparison. The right byte of every successful
explicit comparison is at or beyond the active right end. Each such
comparison advances the candidate end, and the later window update
advances `windowEnd` by the same aggregate distance. That boundary
increases at most N times per pass. Two passes therefore perform O(N)
comparisons and work.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input byte count. Two N-element integer slices are
allocated and zeroed, and both passes visit N centers. The amortized
comparison argument above bounds all expansions by O(N). For nonempty
input, best, average, and worst successful time are Theta(N); byte
distribution changes reuse locations, not the asymptotic bound. Empty
input returns in Theta(1) time.

The two returned radius arrays use Theta(N) output storage. The
longest descriptor uses O(1) output storage and aliases the input
bytes. Apart from returned arrays, the algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary
state and no recursion. Keeping the longest value alive may retain a
much larger input allocation.

The arrays compactly represent all centered palindromes. An all-equal
text has Theta(N^2) palindromic occurrences, but each center needs
only one maximal radius; smaller same-center radii are implicit.
Listing every occurrence explicitly would require quadratic output
regardless of preprocessing speed.

Independent [center expansion](
#b81-two-pointers-and-center-expansion-string) uses O(1) auxiliary
space and is simpler, but its worst case is Theta(N^2). The
[palindrome table](#b82-palindrome-dynamic-programming-table) stores
Theta(N^2) interval facts and answers direct interval queries without
center conversion.

Another Manacher formulation inserts separators between bytes and uses
one radius array. It scans one transformed coordinate system but needs
space for roughly twice as many positions and a collision-safe way to
distinguish separators. Separate odd and even arrays keep original
byte coordinates and cannot collide with input values.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input returns two length-zero arrays and no longest value.
  Code that initializes best from byte zero panics before either pass.
- One byte returns odd `[1]`, even `[0]`, and range `[0,1)`. Odd
  radius zero would lose the center byte itself.
- `cbbd` needs gap two in the even array. Scanning only odd centers
  misses `bb`; treating `even[center]` as the gap after center shifts
  its range by one.
- Gap zero and the unrepresented gap after N-1 cannot have positive
  radii because one side is empty. Their absence does not lose a
  nonempty palindrome.
- Clip inherited radius to `windowEnd-center`. The `aaaa`
  counterexample otherwise produces an out-of-bounds range.
- The odd mirror is `L+(R-1-center)`; the even mirror is
  `L+(R-center)`. Reusing one formula shifts a mirror and can read an
  unprocessed or wrong center.
- The active window is the processed palindrome ending farthest right,
  not the globally longest palindrome. Replacing it only by length
  destroys the symmetry needed near the scan frontier.
- Update the active window only when a candidate end is greater.
  Replacing it for an equal end is unnecessary and complicates which
  mirrors are already processed.
- A mirrored radius proves only the part inside the active palindrome.
  Explicit comparison must resume at its first unproved pair, not at
  radius one or after skipping an extra pair.
- `babad` requires earliest-start tie handling separate from the
  active window update. Rightmost reach and returned-answer order are
  different objectives.
- Byte zero and byte 255 are ordinary input. A separator byte chosen
  from the input alphabet can collide in a transformed-string variant;
  the two-array implementation has no sentinel.
- UTF-8 code points may span several indexes. Rune or grapheme radii
  require changing the item sequence and mapping results to byte
  offsets.
- Compute mirrors with subtraction before addition as in the code.
  Writing `L+R-center` can overflow even when every boundary fits
  `int`.
- Radius arrays own their storage, while the longest value shares the
  input. Clone the value when it must not retain the source
  allocation.
- Slice sizes that fit `int` can still exceed available memory;
  allocation failure is outside the successful contract.

##### When to choose it

Choose Manacher's algorithm when one static sequence needs every
maximal center radius, one longest palindrome under a strict linear
bound, or many later queries that can be translated into center and
required radius. The decisive clue is repeated symmetric work across
overlapping centers.

Use [center expansion](
#b81-two-pointers-and-center-expansion-string) for a small input, a
simple baseline, or when constant auxiliary space matters more than
the quadratic worst case. Use [palindrome DP](
#b82-palindrome-dynamic-programming-table) when downstream transitions
are most naturally expressed as arbitrary interval cells.

Use a [palindromic tree](#a165-palindromic-trees) for append-oriented
processing, distinct palindrome values, suffix links, or occurrence
counts. Manacher radii group occurrences by center; they do not merge
equal values or maintain an online index.

Manacher's [original 1975 paper](
https://doi.org/10.1145/321892.321896) introduced the linear-time
palindrome method. This lesson uses the modern odd/even radius
formulation. Go's [string type specification](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#String_types) defines the byte indexing and
immutable input used here.

#### B.8.5 Palindrome partitioning (backtracking or DP table)

##### Problem and contract

Split one byte string into contiguous, nonempty pieces so every piece
is a palindrome, and return every possible split. A partition keeps
the original byte order and uses every byte exactly once. For `aab`,
the two results are `[a,a,b]` and `[aa,b]`.

`palindromePartitions` accepts at most 16 bytes. A longer input
returns
`nil` plus an error before allocating the dynamic-programming table.
The bound matches the canonical problem and makes exhaustive output a
deliberate part of the API rather than an unbounded accident.

The function compares arbitrary bytes. It does not decode UTF-8,
normalize text, fold case, or ignore punctuation. The empty string has
one valid partition: the empty sequence of pieces. It therefore
returns
a non-nil outer slice containing one non-nil empty inner slice.

Results use depth-first order with the earliest next cut tried first.
For `aaa`, the order is `[a,a,a]`, `[a,aa]`, `[aa,a]`, then `[aaa]`.
Each cut pattern appears once. The outer slice and every inner slice
belong to the caller. Piece strings are sliced from the input; no
independent byte copy is promised.

Read [palindrome dynamic programming](
#b82-palindrome-dynamic-programming-table) first. That entry owns the
interval recurrence and flat table representation. This lesson reuses
those facts as constant-time guards and owns the enumeration state,
backtracking rule, output order, and exponential-output tradeoff.

##### Mental model

First build a Boolean table. For input length N, the cell at
`start*N + endInclusive` answers this sentence:

```text
text[start:endInclusive+1] is a palindrome
```

For example, in `aab`, cell `[0][1]` is true because `aa` is a
palindrome, while `[1][2]` is false because `ab` is not. Fill start
positions from right to left. Then the interior cell beginning at
`start+1` is already final when an enclosing interval needs it.

After preprocessing, imagine a decision tree. One search frame stores:

- `start`, the first byte not yet assigned to a piece; and
- `path`, the chosen palindromic pieces that exactly cover
  `text[:start]`.

At that frame, try every half-open range `[start,end)` in increasing
end order. A false table cell rejects the range. A true cell permits
three actions: append that substring to `path`, search from `end`,
then
remove the appended piece. Removing it restores the parent state and
is the backtracking step.

When `start == N`, the path covers the whole input. Copy it into the
results before returning. The copy matters because the live path is
immediately shortened and reused for sibling choices.

For empty input, the root already has `start == N == 0`. Emitting the
empty path is not a special mathematical exception: it is the same
completion rule used by every nonempty partition.

##### Worked walkthrough

Partition `aab`. The expected ordered result is
`[[a,a,b],[aa,b]]`.

Initial state: N is 3, no table cell has been computed, `path` is
empty, and no partition has been emitted.

1. Decision: fill the table from start two down to zero. The one-byte
   cells for `a`, `a`, and `b` are true. Cell `[0][1]` for `aa` is
   also true; `ab` and `aab` are false.
   After: the true ranges are `[0,1)`, `[0,2)`, `[1,2)`, and `[2,3)`.
   Known correct: every true cell satisfies equal endpoints and a true
   or empty interior; every needed interior was computed first.
2. Decision: enter the root with `start = 0`. Try end one first.
   Range `[0,1)` is true, so append `a` and recurse from one.
   After: `path = [a]`; bytes `[0,1)` are assigned; `[1,3)` remains.
   Known correct: the path is palindromic and exactly covers
   `text[:1]`.
3. Decision: at start one, try end two. Range `[1,2)` is true, so
   append the second `a` and recurse from two.
   After: `path = [a,a]`; only byte range `[2,3)` remains.
   Known correct: both pieces are true table intervals and cover
   `text[:2]` without a gap or overlap.
4. Decision: at start two, range `[2,3)` is the only candidate and is
   true. Append `b` and recurse to start three.
   After: `path = [a,a,b]` and `start == N`.
   Known correct: the path is a complete palindromic partition of all
   three bytes.
5. Decision: copy `[a,a,b]` into the result, return, and remove `b`.
   No later end exists at start two, so return again and remove the
   second `a`.
   After: result is `[[a,a,b]]`; the restored frame has
   `start = 1` and `path = [a]`.
   Known correct: the emitted inner slice is independent of the live
   path, and the parent state is exactly as it was before its choice.
6. Decision: the start-one frame next tests end three. Cell `[1][2]`
   describes `ab` and is false, so skip it. The frame is exhausted;
   return to the root and remove its first `a`.
   After: root state is `start = 0`, `path = []`, with end one fully
   explored.
   Known correct: no partition beginning with the first one-byte `a`
   remains, because every possible next end was tested.
7. Decision: the root tries end two. Cell `[0][1]` is true for `aa`,
   so append it. At start two, append the true piece `b` and reach the
   base case.
   After: copy `[aa,b]`; results are `[[a,a,b],[aa,b]]`.
   Known correct: this is the only branch whose first cut is at two,
   and it is distinct from the first-cut-at-one branch.
8. Decision: backtrack to the root and test end three. `aab` is not a
   palindrome, so skip it. No root choice remains.
   After: return `[[a,a,b],[aa,b]]` and nil error.
   Known correct: every possible first cut and every permitted child
   cut has been exhausted in the declared order.

Focused repeated-backtracking case: `aaa` first reaches `[a,a,a]`.
It then removes the final `a`, chooses `aa` at start one, and emits
`[a,aa]`. After restoring the root, it explores `[aa,a]` and `[aaa]`.
This produces all four cut patterns without sharing mutable paths.

Focused empty case: N is zero, so the table has zero cells and the
root immediately copies its zero-length path. The result is `[[]]`,
not `[]`; one way exists to partition zero bytes into zero pieces.

Counterexample to a greedy longest-first rule: on `aab`, choosing
`aa` first returns `[aa,b]` but misses `[a,a,b]`. A shortest-first
rule
has the symmetric failure. Enumeration must return after one complete
branch and continue with the parent's other choices.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program runs the ordinary and repeated-backtracking
cases, the empty identity, arbitrary bytes, and oversized rejection.
Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Palindrome partitioning
// (backtracking or DP table). Function comments connect each
// operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)

const maximumPalindromePartitionBytes = 16

func buildPalindromeCells(text string) []bool {
	// Build palindrome cells in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	size := len(text)
	cells := make([]bool, size*size)

	// Descending starts make every shorter interior ready first.
	for start := size - 1; start >= 0; start-- {
		for endInclusive := start; endInclusive < size; endInclusive++ {
			interiorIsPalindrome := endInclusive-start < 2
			if !interiorIsPalindrome {
				interiorPosition :=
					(start+1)*size + endInclusive - 1
				interiorIsPalindrome = cells[interiorPosition]
			}
			cells[start*size+endInclusive] =
				text[start] == text[endInclusive] &&
					interiorIsPalindrome
		}
	}
	return cells
}

func palindromePartitions(text string) ([][]string, error) {
	// Keep palindrome partitions in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if len(text) > maximumPalindromePartitionBytes {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"input has %d bytes; maximum is %d",
			len(text),
			maximumPalindromePartitionBytes,
		)
	}

	palindromeCells := buildPalindromeCells(text)
	partitions := make([][]string, 0)
	path := make([]string, 0, len(text))
	var collectFrom func(int)
	collectFrom = func(start int) {
		if start == len(text) {
			// Copy the live path before later backtracking changes it.
			partition := make([]string, len(path))
			copy(partition, path)
			partitions = append(partitions, partition)
			return
		}

		// Increasing ends choose the earliest next cut first.
		for end := start + 1; end <= len(text); end++ {
			position := start*len(text) + end - 1
			if !palindromeCells[position] {
				continue
			}

			path = append(path, text[start:end])
			collectFrom(end)
			// Restore the parent's path before its next choice.
			path = path[:len(path)-1]
		}
	}

	collectFrom(0)
	return partitions, nil
}

func printPartitions(text string) {
	// Expose partitions in logical order without changing source.
	partitions, err := palindromePartitions(text)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", partitions)
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	printPartitions("aab")
	printPartitions("aaa")
	printPartitions("")

	binaryText := string([]byte{0, 255, 0})
	binaryPartitions, err := palindromePartitions(binaryText)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(
		len(binaryPartitions),
		[]byte(binaryPartitions[1][0]),
	)

	_, err = palindromePartitions(strings.Repeat("a", 17))
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[["a" "a" "b"] ["aa" "b"]]
[["a" "a" "a"] ["a" "aa"] ["aa" "a"] ["aaa"]]
[[]]
2 [0 255 0]
true
```

The first two lines show deterministic branch order. The third shows
the empty identity. The fourth confirms that byte zero and byte 255
form an ordinary palindrome around their center. The final true value
confirms rejection of 17 bytes.

##### Why it works

First prove the table correct. Process starts from N-1 down to zero.
One-byte intervals are true because one byte reads the same in both
directions. For two bytes, equal endpoints are sufficient because the
interior is empty. A longer interval is palindromic exactly when its
endpoints agree and its interior
`[start+1,endInclusive)` is palindromic. That interior's row begins at
a larger start, so descending-start order computed it before the
enclosing cell reads it. Induction over processed starts therefore
proves every upper-triangle cell.

For the search, maintain this invariant at entry to every frame:
`path` contains nonempty palindromic substrings that occur in order,
without gaps or overlaps, and concatenate to `text[:start]`. It holds
at the root because an empty path covers the empty prefix.

A permitted range `[start,end)` is nonempty and palindromic by its
table cell. Appending it extends the covered prefix to `text[:end]`,
so the child invariant holds. When the child returns, shortening the
path by one restores the exact parent invariant for the next end.

If `start == N`, the invariant says the path covers all input bytes,
so every emitted result is sound. Conversely, consider any valid
partition. Its first piece has some end that the root loop tries, and
its table cell is true. Applying the same argument to each remaining
piece follows one search branch to that exact partition. Thus every
valid partition is emitted.

Different branches first disagree at one chosen end, so they
represent different cut patterns. Each frame tries every end once,
proving no cut pattern is duplicated. Increasing ends and depth-first
completion also prove the declared order: all results under an earlier
next cut appear before any result under a later next cut.

Every recursive call increases `start` by at least one, so depth is at
most N. Every frame's end increases through a finite range, and N is
at most 16. The search terminates. Copying at the base separates
completed results from the path restoration that follows.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the byte count, P the number of returned partitions, and C
the total number of string pieces across all P partitions. For
example, `aab` has P = 2 and C = 5.

The DP phase allocates N squared Boolean cells and computes the
N(N+1)/2 cells on or above the diagonal. Its time and retained
preprocessing space are Theta(N^2), independent of byte values.

The search inspects a table cell for each candidate end at every
reachable prefix. Its exact work depends on which intervals are
palindromes. Copying completed paths costs Theta(C). With N bytes,
there are at most `2^(N-1)` cut patterns, and each has at most N
pieces. Worst-case total time is Theta(N * `2^N`) after preprocessing.
All-equal input reaches that bound because every cut pattern is valid
and writing all piece headers already takes Theta(N * `2^N`) time. No
content-independent average is claimed.

The output retains P inner slice headers and C string headers, for
Theta(P + C) output space. Piece construction does not request byte
copies, so retaining the output may retain input storage. The table,
recursion stack, and live path use Theta(N^2 + N) auxiliary space.
The outer and inner result slices are owned copies; changing their
elements cannot change sibling partitions.

The 16-byte bound limits P to 32,768. It does not promise that every
environment has enough memory for every successful allocation; memory
exhaustion remains outside the contract. Oversized input takes
Theta(1) time and allocates neither the table nor results.

Checking each candidate with inward pointers would remove the table
but spend up to O(N) extra work per candidate. The table pays
quadratic space once to make every branch guard O(1). Memoizing only
the search by `start` is not a direct replacement: different live
prefixes need separate output construction even when their remaining
suffix matches.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input returns `[[]]`. Returning `[]` says no partition exists,
  which breaks the recursion identity used by a completed suffix.
- One byte returns `[[text]]`. The root chooses its only nonempty
  range and then reaches the base case.
- `abc` returns `[[a,b,c]]`. Having no multi-byte palindrome does not
  mean no solution; every one-byte substring is palindromic.
- Sixteen equal bytes return 32,768 partitions. This is valid maximum
  output, not a reason to stop after finding one decomposition.
- Seventeen bytes return nil plus an error before `size*size` or any
  result allocation. Moving validation after preprocessing defeats the
  resource boundary.
- Use `end-1` to translate half-open `[start,end)` into the table's
  inclusive endpoint. Reading column `end` shifts the interval and can
  index past the final byte.
- Two equal bytes need no stored interior cell. Looking up
  `[start+1][end-1]` for `aa` addresses a lower-triangle placeholder.
- Try every end, not only the shortest or longest true range. Either
  greedy choice loses a valid `aab` result.
- Append before recursion and remove exactly one piece afterward.
  Failing to restore the path leaks one sibling's choice into another.
- Copy the path at the base. Appending the live slice header can let
  later backtracking overwrite a partition that was already emitted.
- Return immediately after emitting. Continuing the end loop with
  `start == N` would compute a table position for an empty suffix.
- Increasing ends define output order. Reversing the loop can remain
  complete but violates this contract and the demonstrated output.
- Byte zero, byte 255, and malformed UTF-8 are ordinary data. A rune
  or grapheme contract requires a different item sequence and offset
  mapping.
- Piece strings come from slicing the input, and no independent copy
  is promised. Clone them when byte ownership or release of a much
  larger source allocation matters.
- Case and punctuation remain significant. Preprocessing them changes
  both equality and how pieces map to the original source.

##### When to choose it

Choose this method when every palindrome decomposition is required and
the input is small enough for exponential output. The useful signal is
not merely the word "partition": each boundary is a choice, invalid
pieces can be rejected locally, and every valid choice sequence must
be materialized.

Use [palindrome dynamic programming](
#b82-palindrome-dynamic-programming-table) alone when the workload
asks
many interval questions but not every decomposition. Use a minimum-cut
DP when only the fewest pieces or cuts are required; enumerating all
partitions solves a much larger problem. Use [center expansion](
#b81-two-pointers-and-center-expansion-string) or
[Manacher's algorithm](
#b84-manachers-algorithm-radius-arrays) when the goal is one longest
palindrome rather than a split of the whole input.

Checking palindromes on demand can be preferable when memory is tight
and the input is tiny. The [general backtracking lesson](
#b191-subsets-and-permutations-backtracking-and-path) broadens the
choose, recurse, restore pattern beyond strings. This entry remains
the primary owner of palindrome-partition output and interval guards.

The canonical [Palindrome Partitioning problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/palindrome-partitioning/) specifies all
partitions and the 16-character maximum. This lesson broadens its
alphabet to arbitrary bytes and defines empty-input behavior. Go's
[string specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#String_types) defines
the immutable byte sequence, indexing, and slicing semantics used by
the implementation.

#### B.8.6 Character reorganization (counts and heap)

##### Problem and contract

Rearrange every byte of one string so equal bytes never occupy
adjacent positions. Return the rearranged string and `found = true`
when that is possible. Return `("", false)` when no valid ordering
exists.

`reorganizeBytes` accepts any addressable Go string, including empty
and malformed UTF-8 strings. It compares bytes without normalization
or case folding. The result contains exactly the same byte
multiplicities as the input. It does not mutate the immutable input.

Empty input returns `("", true)`: the empty ordering violates no
adjacency rule. One byte also succeeds. A failed nonempty input and a
successful empty input both have an empty string value, so callers
must inspect the Boolean.

Several valid outputs may exist. This function is deterministic. At
each position it chooses the eligible byte with the greatest remaining
count. Equal counts use the smaller numeric byte. The previously
emitted byte is ineligible for exactly one turn. For `aaabbc`, these
rules return `ababac`.

The returned string is a new result value. Internal count and heap
storage belongs only to the call. Allocation failure for an
addressable input remains outside the successful contract, and
unsynchronized mutation of memory used to construct the input is
outside ordinary Go string semantics.

Read [multisets and frequency maps](
#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) for multiplicity invariants and
[min-heaps and max-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) for priority
repair. This lesson owns the one-turn cooldown and the feasibility
argument that connects counts to a valid schedule.

##### Mental model

Count each possible byte in a 256-cell direct-address array. Reading
`countByByte['a'] == 3` means that three `a` bytes still need
positions.
The byte alphabet is small and dense, so an array gives direct lookup
without map hashing or iteration order.

Let N be the input length and M the largest count. M copies need at
least M-1 other bytes between them:

```text
x _ x _ x ... _ x
```

There are N-M other bytes. Reorganization is possible exactly when
`N-M >= M-1`, or equivalently `M <= ceil(N/2)`. Compute the ceiling as
`N/2 + N%2` so `N+1` cannot overflow.

For feasible input, put one record per distinct byte in a heap. A
record stores the byte and how many copies remain. Greater remaining
count has greater priority; a smaller byte wins a tie.

One record named `held` stays outside the heap. It represents the byte
most recently appended. Because it is absent, the next pop cannot
repeat that byte. After popping and appending a different byte,
decrement its count, reinsert the old held record if it still has
copies, then hold the newly appended record.

The heap therefore answers two questions together: which bytes are
currently legal, and which legal byte is most urgent. Stop when the
heap is empty. The feasibility invariant guarantees that the held
record then has no copies left and exactly N bytes were emitted.

##### Worked walkthrough

Reorganize `aaabbc`. The counts are `a:3`, `b:2`, and `c:1`; the
deterministic result is `ababac`.

Initial state: no byte is counted, no feasibility decision has been
made, the heap and result are empty, and `held` has count zero.

1. Decision: count all six bytes. The largest count is 3, while the
   maximum allowed count is `6/2 + 6%2 = 3`, so continue.
   After: counts are `a:3`, `b:2`, `c:1`; the result is empty.
   Known correct: every input byte is represented once in the counts,
   and the necessary feasibility bound holds at equality.
2. Decision: push each positive count. Greater counts outrank smaller
   counts, so `a:3` is at the root ahead of `b:2` and `c:1`.
   After: heap priorities are `(a:3, b:2, c:1)`; `held` is empty.
   Known correct: every unscheduled byte is eligible initially, and
   the root is the most urgent deterministic choice.
3. Decision: pop `a:3`, append `a`, decrement it to 2, and hold it.
   There is no older held record to reinsert.
   After: result is `a`; heap contains `b:2, c:1`; held is `a:2`.
   Known correct: output counts plus pending counts equal the input,
   and `a` cannot be selected in the next turn.
4. Decision: pop `b:2`, append `b`, decrement it to 1, then reinsert
   the old `a:2` because `b` now separates it from the previous `a`.
   After: result is `ab`; heap contains `a:2, c:1`; held is `b:1`.
   Known correct: adjacent bytes differ, and every byte in the heap is
   eligible after the last output `b`.
5. Decision: pop `a:2`, append `a`, decrement it to 1, and reinsert
   held `b:1`.
   After: result is `aba`; heap contains `b:1, c:1`; held is `a:1`.
   Known correct: `a` was most urgent, and holding it prevents an
   immediate fourth-position `a`.
6. Decision: `b:1` and `c:1` tie, so pop smaller byte `b`. Append it,
   reduce its count to zero, and reinsert `a:1`.
   After: result is `abab`; heap contains `a:1, c:1`; held is `b:0`.
   Known correct: the tie rule is satisfied and zero-count `b` will
   not return to the heap.
7. Decision: `a:1` wins the next tie against `c:1`. Append `a`; the
   zero-count held `b` is not reinserted.
   After: result is `ababa`; heap contains `c:1`; held is `a:0`.
   Known correct: all three input copies of `a` have been emitted with
   a different byte between every pair.
8. Decision: pop and append `c`, leaving both its count and the heap
   empty. Check the held count and result length.
   After: return `("ababac", true)`; held count is 0 and length is 6.
   Known correct: every count is exhausted, the result is a
   permutation, and all five adjacent pairs differ.

Focused impossible case: `aaab` has M = 3 and N = 4. Only one non-`a`
byte exists, but two separators are required. Since
`3 > 4/2 + 4%2`, the function returns `("", false)` before building
the heap or result.

Focused tie case: `aabbcc` always chooses the smaller byte among equal
eligible counts and returns `abcabc`. Heap layout itself may vary, but
the complete comparison makes every pop deterministic.

Focused arbitrary-byte case: bytes `[0,0,255]` return
`[0,255,0]`. Byte zero needs no sentinel treatment, and byte 255 is an
ordinary array index.

Counterexample to repeatedly popping the global maximum without a
cooldown: `aaabbc` begins by popping `a:3`, then `a:2`, producing the
invalid prefix `aa`. The first wrong decision is making the just-used
byte eligible before another byte has separated it.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program runs the ordinary case, count ties, a small
success, impossible input, empty input, and arbitrary bytes. Save it
as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Character reorganization (counts
// and heap). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
)

type byteCount struct {
	value     byte
	remaining int
}

type byteCountHeap []byteCount

func (queue byteCountHeap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(queue)
}

func (queue byteCountHeap) Less(
	firstIndex int,
	secondIndex int,
) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	first := queue[firstIndex]
	second := queue[secondIndex]
	if first.remaining != second.remaining {
		return first.remaining > second.remaining
	}
	return first.value < second.value
}

func (queue byteCountHeap) Swap(
	firstIndex int,
	secondIndex int,
) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	queue[firstIndex], queue[secondIndex] =
		queue[secondIndex], queue[firstIndex]
}

func (queue *byteCountHeap) Push(item any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	*queue = append(*queue, item.(byteCount))
}

func (queue *byteCountHeap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	items := *queue
	lastIndex := len(items) - 1
	item := items[lastIndex]
	items[lastIndex] = byteCount{}
	*queue = items[:lastIndex]
	return item
}

func reorganizeBytes(text string) (string, bool) {
	// Keep reorganize bytes in one helper so callers use one rule.
	var countByByte [256]int
	maximumCount := 0
	for position := 0; position < len(text); position++ {
		value := text[position]
		countByByte[value]++
		if countByByte[value] > maximumCount {
			maximumCount = countByByte[value]
		}
	}

	// A dominant byte needs a different byte in every internal gap.
	maximumAllowed := len(text)/2 + len(text)%2
	if maximumCount > maximumAllowed {
		return "", false
	}

	queue := make(byteCountHeap, 0, len(countByByte))
	for integerValue, count := range countByByte {
		if count == 0 {
			continue
		}
		heap.Push(&queue, byteCount{
			value:     byte(integerValue),
			remaining: count,
		})
	}

	result := make([]byte, 0, len(text))
	held := byteCount{}
	for queue.Len() > 0 {
		current := heap.Pop(&queue).(byteCount)
		result = append(result, current.value)
		current.remaining--

		// One intervening byte makes the previous value eligible again.
		if held.remaining > 0 {
			heap.Push(&queue, held)
		}
		held = current
	}

	// The feasibility check makes leftover held work unreachable.
	if held.remaining != 0 || len(result) != len(text) {
		return "", false
	}
	return string(result), true
}

func printReorganization(text string) {
	// Expose reorganization in logical order without changing source.
	result, found := reorganizeBytes(text)
	fmt.Printf("%q %t\n", result, found)
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	printReorganization("aaabbc")
	printReorganization("aabbcc")
	printReorganization("aab")
	printReorganization("aaab")
	printReorganization("")

	binaryText := string([]byte{0, 0, 255})
	binaryResult, found := reorganizeBytes(binaryText)
	fmt.Println([]byte(binaryResult), found)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
"ababac" true
"abcabc" true
"aba" true
"" false
"" true
[0 255 0] true
```

The two empty strings have different Boolean meanings. The last line
confirms that the algorithm uses bytes rather than a text-only
alphabet.

##### Why it works

First prove the feasibility test. If one byte occurs M times, placing
those copies without adjacency needs at least M-1 other bytes as
separators. Exactly N-M other bytes exist. Therefore every valid
result must satisfy `M-1 <= N-M`, which rearranges to
`M <= ceil(N/2)`.

For sufficiency, describe a remaining-state invariant. Let `previous`
be the last emitted byte. Its remaining count must be no greater than
the total remaining count of all other bytes, because every future
copy
of `previous` needs an earlier different byte. Any other byte may have
at most one more remaining copy than all bytes different from it,
because it is eligible for the next position.

The initial feasibility test establishes the second inequality for
every byte; there is no previous byte yet. Suppose the invariant holds
and the heap chooses eligible byte X with the greatest count. Removing
one X makes X the new previous byte. Its old inequality loses one from
both its count and the total, producing exactly the stronger
previous-byte inequality.

The old previous byte becomes ordinary. Its former stronger inequality
implies the ordinary one after total remaining decreases by one. For
any other unchosen byte Y, only its number of other remaining bytes
decreases. The ordinary inequality could fail only if Y formerly had
one more copy than all other bytes combined. Such a Y would be the
unique greatest eligible count, so the heap would have chosen Y rather
than X. Thus every unchosen byte also preserves its inequality.

The held record is exactly the new previous byte and remains outside
the heap. Every popped byte is therefore different from the last
output byte. Reinsertion occurs only after that different byte has
been
appended, so every adjacent pair differs.

Each append decreases the total remaining count by one. If work
remained only in `held`, the stronger previous-byte inequality would
require its positive count to be at most zero, a contradiction. Thus a
feasible run cannot empty the heap early. It performs exactly N
iterations, exhausts every original count, and terminates with a valid
permutation.

The full heap comparison orders first by remaining count and then by
byte value. Heap operations preserve that ordering, so the chosen
sequence also satisfies the deterministic tie rule.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input byte count and U the number of distinct byte
values.
Here `0 <= U <= 256` and `U <= N` for nonempty input.

Counting takes Theta(N) time and scans the full input even when the
eventual answer is impossible. Building the heap with U pushes takes
O(U log(U+1)) time. A successful run performs N pops and at most N-1
reinserts, each taking O(log(U+1)) time. Total time is therefore
O(N log(U+1)) after absorbing U into N. Because U is at most 256, this
is also O(N) for the fixed byte alphabet.

No distribution-independent average bound is needed. Impossible input
returns after Theta(N) counting time without allocating the heap or
result. Empty input takes Theta(1) time. Successful input must spend
Theta(N) time writing its N-byte result even when heap repair is
cheap.

The 256 counters use fixed O(1) storage relative to N. The heap
retains
O(U) records. The result builder holds N bytes, and converting it to a
string may require another N-byte allocation, so peak construction
storage is O(N+U); the returned output retains Theta(N) bytes.

A direct counter array is ideal for bytes but fixes the alphabet size.
Rune input needs a map from rune to count and a heap of runes, plus a
separate decision about normalization and result offsets. Sorting all
N bytes by count could also find a layout, but the heap expresses the
changing eligibility and urgency directly.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input returns `("", true)`, while `aa` returns `("", false)`.
  Ignoring `found` makes these distinct outcomes indistinguishable.
- One byte returns itself. Its count one equals the allowed ceiling
  one, and the held record is exhausted after the sole pop.
- `aab` is feasible because `ceil(3/2) = 2`. Using only `N/2` as the
  limit would reject this valid odd-length case.
- `aaab` is impossible because three copies need two separators but
  only `b` is available. A heap cannot repair a failed count bound.
- All distinct bytes are valid. Their counts tie, so numeric byte
  order
  determines the complete output.
- Do not push zero-count records. They could be popped after real work
  and append bytes that never occurred in the input.
- Pop before reinserting `held`. Reinserting first makes the previous
  byte eligible immediately and can produce the invalid prefix `aa`.
- Decrement the selected record once per append. Decrementing on both
  pop and reinsertion loses a byte; forgetting it can prevent
  termination.
- Reinsert only a positive held count. Zero-count records are
  finished,
  not pending work.
- `container/heap` is a min-heap according to `Less`. Returning true
  for a greater count intentionally makes it the package's minimum and
  therefore the next popped record.
- Compare byte values after equal counts. Omitting the tie comparison
  may preserve validity but loses deterministic output.
- The interface methods `Push` and `Pop` contain type assertions and
  assume calls through `container/heap` with `byteCount` records.
  Passing another type would panic and is outside the private helper's
  use.
- `N/2 + N%2` computes the ceiling without evaluating `N+1`, which
  could overflow at the largest representable string length.
- Byte zero is valid data, not an empty-record sentinel. The held
  record's remaining count, not its byte value, indicates absence.
- UTF-8 characters can occupy several bytes. Reorganizing bytes can
  split encodings and produce invalid text; use a rune or grapheme
  contract when textual characters are the required unit.

##### When to choose it

Choose count-plus-heap reorganization when all items must be emitted,
equal items cannot be adjacent, and the active priority changes after
every choice. The same one-turn cooldown pattern appears in schedulers
that prohibit immediately repeating a task type.

Use a fixed-position placement method when only this byte problem is
needed and the smallest constants matter: placing the most frequent
byte into alternating positions can achieve linear time without a
heap. Use a queue with release times when equal items must be K
positions apart rather than merely nonadjacent.

Use [frequency counting](#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) without a
heap when the task only compares multiplicities. Use a
[max-heap](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) without cooldown when
repeated
selection of the same value is allowed.

The canonical [Reorganize String problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/reorganize-string/) specifies the
adjacency goal and empty-string failure sentinel for lowercase input.
This lesson broadens the alphabet to bytes and adds a Boolean so empty
success remains distinct. Go's [`container/heap` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap) defines the interface, root
ordering,
and logarithmic push and pop bounds used here. The [string type
