  contract. Enforce a separate node limit when input is untrusted.

##### When to choose it

Choose visit history when memory is available and you want simple
local reasoning, the exact first repeated state, or visit-step
diagnostics. The same pattern detects recurrence in any deterministic
state transition whose states are comparable map keys.

Choose [fast and slow pointers](
#b102-fast-and-slow-pointers-linked-list) when O(1) auxiliary space is
decisive and the input is a one-successor path. Choose a bounded step
limit when the contract asks only whether processing exceeds a budget,
not whether a structural cycle exists.

Practice the Boolean form with the local [Linked List Cycle](
problems/easy_leetcode_0141_linked_list_cycle.go) exercise. The
canonical [Linked List Cycle](
https://leetcode.com/problems/linked-list-cycle/) and
[Linked List Cycle II](
https://leetcode.com/problems/linked-list-cycle-ii/) problems define
the Boolean and entry contracts. Go specifies
[map key and lookup behavior](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Map_types) and
[two-value index expressions](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Index_expressions).

#### B.10.4 Intersection by pointer switching (node pointers)

##### Problem and contract

Find the first node reachable from two singly linked-list heads by
following `next`. Intersection means pointer identity: both paths
reach the same node, not merely nodes with equal values. Read
[singly linked lists](#a31-singly-linked-lists) and
[node-pointer transformations](
#b101-reversal-splicing-and-merging-node-pointers) first.

`intersectionNode(first, second)` returns the first shared node, or
nil when the paths are disjoint. Nil is valid for either head. If the
heads are identical, that head is the answer. If one head begins
inside the other list, the shorter list's head is the answer.

Both inputs must be finite acyclic chains. Once acyclic singly linked
paths share a node, their deterministic next links give them the same
remaining suffix; they cannot separate again. Therefore a nonempty
intersection has one well-defined first shared node.

Node values may repeat and play no part in the result. The function
only reads links, allocates no collection or data node, and returns a
pointer into caller-owned storage. Both topologies must remain stable
during the call. Cycles and unsynchronized concurrent mutation are
outside the contract.

##### Mental model

Start one pointer at each head. On an ordinary node, move to its next
node. On nil, cross to the other list's head. Thus each pointer walks
one combined route:

```text
fromFirst:  first list -> nil -> second list
fromSecond: second list -> nil -> first list
```

Nil is a boundary position, not a node in either list. Switching only
when the current pointer is nil makes crossing that boundary one loop
update. Both pointers must update independently on every iteration.

Suppose the first list has P unique nodes before the shared suffix,
the second has Q, and the suffix has S nodes. The first pointer pays
for P, then S, the nil boundary, and Q before it reaches the shared
entry on its crossed route. The second pays for Q, then S, the same
boundary, and P. These totals are equal:

```text
P + S + 1 + Q = Q + S + 1 + P
```

If the unique prefixes have equal length, the pointers meet at the
entry on their first pass. Otherwise, switching cancels their length
difference. For disjoint lists, both combined routes end at nil, so
nil becomes their common stopping state.

Compare the pointers at the start of each loop. Equality at a node is
the answer; equality at nil means no intersection. No length counter
or visited set is needed.

##### Worked walkthrough

Let the first path be
`A1 -> A2 -> C1 -> C2 -> nil`. Let the second be
`B1 -> B2 -> B3 -> C1 -> C2 -> nil`. C1 and C2 are the same node
objects in both paths. The expected result is pointer C1.

Initial state: `fromFirst = A1` and `fromSecond = B1`. The pointers
are unequal, and neither has crossed a nil boundary.

```text
A1 -> A2 --+
            v
            C1 -> C2 -> nil
            ^
B1 -> B2 -> B3
```

1. Decision: A1 and B1 are distinct, so move both to their next
   nodes.
   After: `fromFirst = A2`; `fromSecond = B2`.
   Known correct: no shared node has been skipped because A1 and B1
   were compared before either pointer moved.
2. Decision: A2 and B2 are distinct. Move to C1 and B3.
   After: `fromFirst = C1`; `fromSecond = B3`.
   Known correct: the first pointer has entered the shared suffix,
   while the second still has one unique node.
3. Decision: C1 and B3 are distinct. Move to C2 and C1.
   After: `fromFirst = C2`; `fromSecond = C1`.
   Known correct: moving at the same speed preserves their one-step
   offset inside the acyclic shared suffix.
4. Decision: C2 and C1 are distinct. Move to nil and C2.
   After: `fromFirst = nil`; `fromSecond = C2`.
   Known correct: the first route has finished its own list; the
   second pointer still follows its original route.
5. Decision: nil and C2 differ. Cross `fromFirst` to B1 and move
   `fromSecond` from C2 to nil.
   After: `fromFirst = B1`; `fromSecond = nil`.
   Known correct: each pointer has now reached its own nil boundary.
6. Decision: B1 and nil differ. Move `fromFirst` to B2 and cross
   `fromSecond` to A1.
   After: `fromFirst = B2`; `fromSecond = A1`.
   Known correct: both pointers are on their crossed routes.
7. Decision: B2 and A1 are distinct. Move to B3 and A2.
   After: `fromFirst = B3`; `fromSecond = A2`.
   Known correct: each pointer is now one update from the shared
   entry, so their earlier offset is gone.
8. Decision: B3 and A2 are distinct. Move both pointers to C1.
   After: `fromFirst = C1`; `fromSecond = C1`.

   ```text
   first route:  A1 A2 C1 C2 nil B1 B2 B3 C1
   second route: B1 B2 B3 C1 C2 nil A1 A2 C1
                                             ^ meet
   ```

   Known correct: both combined routes have paid the same total
   prefix distance and now reach the shared entry together.
9. Decision: the loop condition sees identical pointers, so stop and
   return C1.
   After: the result is the exact first shared node; no link changed.
   Known correct: every earlier compared pair was distinct, and C1
   begins the common suffix.

Focused disjoint case: use `X -> nil` and
`Y -> Z -> nil`, with all nodes distinct. The loop-start states are
`(X,Y)`, `(nil,Z)`, `(Y,nil)`, `(Z,X)`, then `(nil,nil)`. Both nil
pointers compare equal, so the function returns nil without reading a
field through nil.

Focused immediate case: when both heads are C1, the initial loop
condition is already false. The function returns C1 with no pointer
updates.

Counterexample to comparing values: distinct heads `A(7) -> nil` and
`B(7) -> nil` have equal values but no shared node. Returning A or B
at the first comparison invents an intersection. The correct decision
compares `A == B`, which is false.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program runs the ordinary, disjoint, same-head, and
nil cases. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. The finder
does not mutate either list; only setup code allocates nodes.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Intersection by pointer switching
// (node pointers). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type listNode struct {
	value int
	next  *listNode
}

func intersectionNode(
	first *listNode,
	second *listNode,
) *listNode {
	// Keep intersection node in one helper so callers use one rule.
	fromFirst := first
	fromSecond := second

	for fromFirst != fromSecond {
		// Crossing to the other head equalizes both total routes.
		if fromFirst == nil {
			fromFirst = second
		} else {
			fromFirst = fromFirst.next
		}

		if fromSecond == nil {
			fromSecond = first
		} else {
			fromSecond = fromSecond.next
		}
	}
	return fromFirst
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	sharedTail := &listNode{value: 40}
	sharedHead := &listNode{
		value: 30,
		next:  sharedTail,
	}
	first := &listNode{
		value: 10,
		next: &listNode{
			value: 20,
			next:  sharedHead,
		},
	}
	second := &listNode{
		value: 11,
		next: &listNode{
			value: 21,
			next: &listNode{
				value: 22,
				next:  sharedHead,
			},
		},
	}

	found := intersectionNode(first, second)
	fmt.Println(found.value, found == sharedHead)

	disjointFirst := &listNode{value: 5}
	disjointSecond := &listNode{value: 5}
	fmt.Println(
		intersectionNode(disjointFirst, disjointSecond) == nil,
	)
	fmt.Println(
		intersectionNode(sharedHead, sharedHead) == sharedHead,
	)
	fmt.Println(intersectionNode(nil, second) == nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
30 true
true
true
true
```

##### Why it works

First establish the shape fact. If both paths reach node C, then both
next steps read the one field `C.next`. By induction, every later node
is shared. In finite acyclic lists, the intersection is therefore an
entire suffix with one first node.

Let the first and second lengths be M and N. Before each loop test,
`fromFirst` is at the state for the completed-update count on route
`first -> nil -> second -> nil`; `fromSecond` is at the same-numbered
state of `second -> nil -> first -> nil`. The update branches move
each pointer to exactly its next route state, so this statement holds
initially and after every iteration.

If the lists share a suffix, let P and Q be their unique-prefix
lengths and S the shared-suffix length. Thus `M = P + S` and
`N = Q + S`. When P equals Q, both pointers reach the entry after P
updates. Distinct nodes in the unique prefixes cannot compare equal,
so this is their first meeting.

When P and Q differ, the pointers enter the suffix at different times
and keep that nonzero offset while both move one edge per update.
Acyclicity prevents the later pointer from wrapping around to catch
the earlier one. After crossing, `fromFirst` reaches the entry after
`M + 1 + Q` updates. `fromSecond` reaches it after
`N + 1 + P` updates. Both counts equal `P + Q + S + 1`, so the loop
stops at the entry. It cannot stop at a later shared node because both
pointers compare equal as soon as they reach the entry.

If the lists are disjoint, no nonnil states on their routes can be
equal. Each route contains M plus N nodes and one internal nil
boundary. After at most `M + N + 1` updates, both pointers are at the
final nil. The loop then stops and returns nil. The same bound proves
termination for intersecting inputs; an earlier equality only stops
the loop sooner.

The function never assigns a `next` field. Returning a nonnil pointer
therefore returns the original shared node and preserves both input
topologies.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let M and N be the two node counts. Each iteration performs two
constant-time pointer updates. The loop performs at most
`M + N + 1` iterations, so worst-case time is Theta(M + N). Disjoint
lists with unequal lengths can reach that bound.

When the heads are already identical, including two nil heads, best
case time is Theta(1). Other shapes can also stop before traversing
both combined routes. Without a distribution over list shapes, there
is no meaningful general average-case bound.

The function keeps four pointers and uses O(1) auxiliary space. It
allocates no nodes, map, output collection, or recursion frames. The
returned pointer is O(1) output and aliases caller-owned data. The
construction code in the example has separate linear allocation
cost.

Length alignment is another O(M + N)-time, O(1)-space method. Count
both lengths, advance the longer path by their difference, then move
both pointers together. It is useful when the lengths are needed for
other work, but it needs explicit counting and alignment phases.

A visited-node map gives expected O(M + N) time under ordinary hash
table assumptions and O(M) auxiliary space when storing the first
path. Its membership reasoning is direct and can retain diagnostics,
but pointer switching achieves this narrow contract without storage.
The Go specification defines map behavior, not an asymptotic hash
bound.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Two nil heads return nil before any update. One nil head also
  returns nil after the combined routes finish.
- Identical nonnil heads return that head immediately. Advancing
  before comparing would miss this zero-prefix intersection.
- If `second` points at an internal node of `first`, that second head
  is the entry. The method does not require both unique prefixes to be
  nonempty.
- A shared last node is a valid one-node suffix. Both pointers must
  compare that node before advancing to nil.
- Equal, duplicate, zero, negative, and extreme values do not imply
  intersection. Compare `*listNode` values, never `node.value`.
- Go pointer equality means the same pointed-to variable or two nil
  pointers. `listNode` has nonzero size, so the specification's
  special allowance for distinct zero-size variables does not apply.
- Reset a nil pointer to the other head, not its own head. Resetting
  it to its own head merely repeats the original length difference.
- Update both pointers independently. Making the second update an
  `else if` branch can freeze it whenever the first pointer crosses a
  boundary and break the equal-route argument.
- This code switches when the pointer itself is nil. Switching at a
  tail uses a different route convention; mixing the two conventions
  invalidates this trace and proof.
- Return the node pointer, not its value. A value cannot identify the
  shared object when duplicates exist.
- A cycle violates the contract. A pointer may never reach the nil
  boundary, so termination and the unique-suffix proof no longer
  hold. Detect cycles first and define cyclic intersection separately.
- Concurrent link mutation can change a route between reads and
  invalidate the result. Synchronize access or use an immutable
  snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose pointer switching when two finite acyclic singly linked paths
must be tested for a shared node, topology must remain unchanged, and
O(1) auxiliary space matters. The clues are node-reference identity,
different possible prefix lengths, and a result that is one node or
nil.

Choose length alignment when lengths or tail pointers are already
available or useful afterward. Choose a visited map when extra memory
is acceptable and retaining which nodes were seen aids diagnostics.
Do not apply this method unchanged to cyclic lists, value-based
overlap, doubly linked structures with multiple routes, or sequences
that do not share node identity.

Review [cycle detection with memory](
#b103-cycle-detection-with-memory-hash-set) when acyclicity is not
guaranteed. The canonical [Intersection of Two Linked Lists](
https://leetcode.com/problems/intersection-of-two-linked-lists/)
problem defines the identity and unchanged-topology contract. The Go
specification defines [pointer equality](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Comparison_operators) and
[pointer types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Pointer_types).

#### B.10.5 Copying random pointers (map or interleaved nodes)

##### Problem and contract

Deep-copy a linked list whose nodes have both `next` and `random`
pointers. `next` orders the list. `random` may point to any node in
that list, including the same node, or may be nil. Read
[singly linked lists](#a31-singly-linked-lists),
[hash tables](#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing), and
[node splicing](
#b101-reversal-splicing-and-merging-node-pointers) first.

A correct result contains exactly one new node for each original. The
copy preserves values and the complete edge relationship: if original
X points to original Y through either field, copy x points to copy y
through the same field. No copied pointer may lead to an original
node. After a successful return, the source has exactly its original
values and links, so later changes to either list are independent.

`copyWithMap(head)` uses an explicit original-to-copy map and never
mutates the source. `copyByInterleaving(head)` temporarily inserts
each copy after its original, uses that adjacency as the mapping, then
separates the two lists and restores the source. Both return nil for
nil input.

The `next` chain must be finite and acyclic. Every nonnil `random`
target must belong to that chain. Values may repeat and may use any
`int` value. The functions assume those preconditions rather than
validating them, and all required allocations must succeed.

Concurrent mutation is outside both contracts. Interleaving also
requires exclusive access even from readers because its temporary
`next` links are observable. It guarantees restoration on normal
return, not after a panic during its mutation window.

##### Mental model

The hard part is translating identity. Copying an integer is direct;
copying `A.random = C` requires knowing which new node represents C.
A shallow struct copy is wrong because it preserves pointers to the
old nodes.

The map method remembers the translation explicitly. The map
`copyByOriginal` uses an original pointer as its key and stores the
corresponding copied pointer. Read `copyByOriginal[B] = b` as:
"original B is represented by new node b." A first pass creates every
copy. A second pass translates both outgoing edges through the map.
Creating all nodes first is necessary because a random edge may point
forward to a node not yet visited.

The map includes `nil -> nil`. Therefore both assignments use the
same rule without a special nil branch:

```text
copy.next   = copyByOriginal[original.next]
copy.random = copyByOriginal[original.random]
```

Interleaving stores the same translation in the list temporarily. It
uses three passes:

1. Insert copy x immediately after every original X, producing
   `X -> x -> Y -> y` along `next`.
2. For `X.random = Y`, assign `x.random = Y.next`. Y's successor is
   y because every original now sits beside its copy.
3. Restore every original `next` edge and connect each copy to the
   next copy.

Save the next original before inserting or separating. Otherwise an
update can lose the unprocessed suffix or make traversal visit copies
as if they were originals.

##### Worked walkthrough

Copy three originals with this state:

```text
next:    A(7) -> B(13) -> C(11) -> nil
random:  A -> C, B -> A, C -> B
```

The expected result has new nodes `a -> b -> c -> nil`, values
7, 13, and 11, and random edges `a -> c`, `b -> a`, and `c -> b`.
The original A, B, and C must keep all their links.

Initial state: for the map method,
`copyByOriginal = {nil:nil}`. No copy node exists yet.

1. Decision: A has no counterpart. Allocate new node a with value 7
   and nil links, then store `A:a`.
   After: map is `{nil:nil,A:a}`; a has nil next and random.
   Known correct: A has exactly one distinct value-equal counterpart.
2. Decision: advance through original `next` to B. Allocate b with
   value 13 and store `B:b`.
   After: map is `{nil:nil,A:a,B:b}`; copied links remain unset.
   Known correct: A and B have distinct counterparts; C is unresolved.
3. Decision: advance to C. Allocate c with value 11 and store `C:c`.
   After: the map also contains `C:c`; every original has a copy.
   Known correct: any valid next or random target can now translate.
4. Decision: revisit A. Its targets are B and C, so assign
   `a.next = copyByOriginal[B]` and
   `a.random = copyByOriginal[C]`.
   After: `a.next = b`; `a.random = c`.
   Known correct: both of a's edges reproduce A's relationships using
   only new nodes.
5. Decision: B targets C through next and A through random. Translate
   both map lookups.
   After: `b.next = c`; `b.random = a`.
   Known correct: copies a and b now have their final outgoing edges.
6. Decision: C has nil next and random target B. Translate both.
   After: `c.next = nil`; `c.random = b`.
   Known correct: all copied edges match the complete source state.
7. Decision: the second pass reaches nil. Return
   `copyByOriginal[A]`, which is a.
   After: result is `a -> b -> c`; the source was never written.
   Known correct: all three result nodes are new and no result edge
   points into the source.

Now run interleaving on the same unchanged source.

Initial state: for interleaving, the next chain is
`A -> B -> C -> nil`; all copy nodes are unallocated.

1. Decision: save B, allocate a, set `A.next = a` and `a.next = B`,
   then continue from saved B.
   After: next chain is `A -> a -> B -> C -> nil`.
   Known correct: a is adjacent to A and the unprocessed suffix still
   begins at B.
2. Decision: insert b after B while preserving C.
   After: chain is `A -> a -> B -> b -> C -> nil`.
   Known correct: A and B are paired; C remains reachable.
3. Decision: insert c after C and preserve its nil successor.
   After: chain is `A -> a -> B -> b -> C -> c -> nil`.
   Known correct: every original is followed by its unique copy.
4. Decision: A's random target is C. Because `C.next = c`, assign
   `a.random = C.next`.
   After: `a.random = c`; next links stay interleaved.
   Known correct: a's random edge reaches C's copied counterpart.
5. Decision: B targets A, so assign `b.random = A.next`.
   After: `b.random = a`.
   Known correct: both processed random edges stay inside the copy.
6. Decision: C targets B, so assign `c.random = B.next`.
   After: `c.random = b`; all copied random edges are final.
   Known correct: every source random relationship is translated.
7. Decision: for pair A/a, save `a.next = B`, restore `A.next = B`,
   and set `a.next = B.next`, which is b.
   After: from A the chain is `A -> B -> b -> C -> c`; from a it is
   `a -> b -> C -> c`. Only the first pair is separated.
   Known correct: A's next edge is restored and a reaches the next
   copy b.
8. Decision: for B/b, save C, restore `B.next = C`, and set
   `b.next = C.next`, which is c.
   After: from A the chain is `A -> B -> C -> c`; the copy chain is
   `a -> b -> c -> nil`.
   Known correct: A and B are restored; a and b have final next edges.
9. Decision: for C/c, the saved next original is nil. Restore
   `C.next = nil` and keep `c.next = nil`.
   After: source is `A -> B -> C -> nil`; copy is
   `a -> b -> c -> nil`.
   Known correct: both next chains are completely separated, and
   random links were unaffected by separation.
10. Decision: no original remains. Return saved copy head a.
    After: both lists encode the expected state with disjoint nodes.
    Known correct: the source is restored and the deep copy is final.

Focused nil case: the map contains only `nil:nil`, and its return
lookup yields nil. Interleaving returns before any write. Focused
self-reference: for one node X with `X.random = X`, interleaving makes
`X -> x`, then assigns `x.random = X.next = x` before separation.

Counterexample to a shallow copy: assigning `x := *X` copies pointer
bits, so `x.random` still targets an original. The first wrong
decision is treating an identity relationship like an integer value.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program runs both methods on the walkthrough input.
`listState` prints `[value, randomIndex]`, using -1 for nil, and is
only a display helper. Save the program as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Copying random pointers (map or
// interleaved nodes). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type randomNode struct {
	value  int
	next   *randomNode
	random *randomNode
}

func copyWithMap(head *randomNode) *randomNode {
	// Create an independent copy of the requested state.
	copyByOriginal := map[*randomNode]*randomNode{
		nil: nil,
	}

	// Allocate every counterpart before translating forward edges.
	for original := head; original != nil; original = original.next {
		copyByOriginal[original] = &randomNode{
			value: original.value,
		}
	}

	// Translate each source edge through the completed correspondence.
	for original := head; original != nil; original = original.next {
		copy := copyByOriginal[original]
		copy.next = copyByOriginal[original.next]
		copy.random = copyByOriginal[original.random]
	}
	return copyByOriginal[head]
}

func copyByInterleaving(head *randomNode) *randomNode {
	// Create an independent copy of the requested state.
	if head == nil {
		return nil
	}

	// Put each copy immediately after its original counterpart.
	for original := head; original != nil; {
		nextOriginal := original.next
		copy := &randomNode{
			value: original.value,
			next:  nextOriginal,
		}
		original.next = copy
		original = nextOriginal
	}

	// A random target's adjacent successor is its copied counterpart.
	for original := head; original != nil; {
		copy := original.next
		if original.random != nil {
			copy.random = original.random.next
		}
		original = copy.next
	}

	copyHead := head.next
	// Restore original links while separating the copied chain.
	for original := head; original != nil; {
		copy := original.next
		nextOriginal := copy.next
		original.next = nextOriginal
		if nextOriginal == nil {
			copy.next = nil
		} else {
			copy.next = nextOriginal.next
		}
		original = nextOriginal
	}
	return copyHead
}

// Encode random targets by next-chain index for readable output.
func listState(head *randomNode) [][2]int {
	// Expose state in logical order without changing source.
	nodes := make([]*randomNode, 0)
	indexByNode := make(map[*randomNode]int)
	for current := head; current != nil; current = current.next {
		indexByNode[current] = len(nodes)
		nodes = append(nodes, current)
	}

	state := make([][2]int, len(nodes))
	for index, node := range nodes {
		randomIndex := -1
		if node.random != nil {
			mappedIndex, exists := indexByNode[node.random]
			if !exists {
				panic("random pointer leaves list")
			}
			randomIndex = mappedIndex
		}
		state[index] = [2]int{node.value, randomIndex}
	}
	return state
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	third := &randomNode{value: 11}
	second := &randomNode{value: 13, next: third}
	first := &randomNode{value: 7, next: second}
	first.random = third
	second.random = first
	third.random = second

	mapped := copyWithMap(first)
	interleaved := copyByInterleaving(first)
	fmt.Println(listState(first))
	fmt.Println(listState(mapped))
	fmt.Println(listState(interleaved))
	fmt.Println(first.next == second, first.random == third)
	fmt.Println(mapped != first, mapped.random != third)
	fmt.Println(interleaved != first, interleaved.random != third)
	fmt.Println(
		copyWithMap(nil) == nil,
		copyByInterleaving(nil) == nil,
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[[7 2] [13 0] [11 1]]
[[7 2] [13 0] [11 1]]
[[7 2] [13 0] [11 1]]
true true
true true
true true
true true
```

##### Why it works

For the map method's first pass, maintain this invariant: every
visited original has exactly one distinct new counterpart in
`copyByOriginal`, with the same value and initially nil links; no
unvisited original has a map entry. It holds for the empty prefix.
Each iteration allocates one node, records it under the current
original pointer, and advances along the unchanged next chain, so the
invariant is preserved. Finite acyclicity makes the pass terminate
after all N originals.

Before each second-pass iteration, all originals have counterparts,
and every earlier copy has both edges translated. The current next
and random targets are either nil or map keys by the precondition.
Looking them up therefore returns exactly the corresponding copies.
After N iterations every copied edge matches its source edge. Each
map value was newly allocated, so copies are distinct from originals;
the function never writes the source.

For interleaving phase one, the processed prefix alternates each
original with one new same-value copy. Each copy points to the next
original, and the unprocessed suffix retains its old chain. Saving
`nextOriginal` before insertion and advancing to it preserves this
invariant. After N iterations every original X is followed by copy x.

During phase two, that adjacency remains unchanged. For any nonnil
random target Y, `Y.next` is y by phase one's invariant. Assigning
`x.random = Y.next` therefore translates exactly the random edge.
Advancing through `x.next` reaches the next original and processes
each pair once.

During phase three, the processed original prefix is restored and the
processed copy prefix is separated with correct next edges. The
unprocessed suffix remains interleaved. At pair X/x, `x.next` saves
the next original Y. Restoring `X.next = Y` repairs the source. If Y
exists, its current successor is y, so `x.next = Y.next` extends the
copy chain; if Y is nil, x is the copied tail. This preserves the
invariant and advances to Y.

After the third N-step pass, all original next edges are restored and
all copies form their own next chain. Original random edges were never
changed, and copied random edges already target copies. The saved
copy head therefore satisfies the deep-copy contract. Each phase
advances to a later original in a finite acyclic chain, proving
termination.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of source nodes. Every successful method must
allocate and initialize N output nodes, so nonempty copying requires
Theta(N) output work and Theta(N) output storage.

The map method makes two N-node passes and performs a constant number
of map operations per node. Under the ordinary expected constant-time
hash-map model, it takes expected Theta(1 + N) time. Go specifies map
behavior but not its hashing strategy or asymptotic operation bound,
so that expectation is not a language guarantee. The map retains
N plus one logical entries and implementation-dependent bucket slack,
using O(N) auxiliary space in addition to the N output nodes.

Interleaving makes three N-node passes with fixed pointer work, taking
Theta(1 + N) time. It uses O(1) auxiliary space beyond the N required
output nodes. Nil takes Theta(1) for either method. For a nonempty
input, every node must be copied, so there is no useful
input-dependent best, average, or worst distinction beyond the
map-operation assumption.

The map method leaves source links unchanged throughout and is easier
to audit. Its correspondence-map idea generalizes when paired with a
traversal for structures whose edges do not provide a single ordering.
Interleaving removes the map but temporarily doubles the next-chain
length, needs exclusive mutation access, performs an extra pass, and
is not restoration-safe if execution panics midway.

Recursive memoization can copy the graph reachable through both edge
types, but it still needs an O(N) map and may use O(N) call-stack
space. Serializing random targets as indices and rebuilding works
when an indexed external representation is available; the direct
pointer-only contract supplies no such indices.

The example's `listState` helper separately uses O(N) maps, slices,
and output. Those diagnostic costs are not part of either copy
algorithm.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil returns nil. The map method's explicit `nil:nil` entry makes
  its head lookup and nil-edge translations use the ordinary rule;
  interleaving returns before reading `head.next`.
- One node with nil random produces one new node with both links nil.
  One node pointing randomly to itself must produce `x.random = x`,
  not `x.random = X`.
- Forward, backward, and self random edges are all valid. Allocate all
  map counterparts or all interleaved copies before translating them.
- Random edges may form cycles even though `next` may not. All
  algorithm passes traverse only `next`, so random cycles do not
  affect termination.
- Duplicate and extreme values are ordinary payload. Key the map by
  `*randomNode`; keying by value merges distinct equal-valued nodes.
- A shallow struct assignment copies old `next` and `random` pointers.
  New storage alone does not make the pointer graph a deep copy.
- In map phase two, translate both fields. Copying next correctly but
  leaving random nil loses part of the source state.
- In interleaving phase one, advance to saved `nextOriginal`, not the
  newly written `original.next`. The latter is the copy and causes
  copies of copies or an unbounded loop.
- Do not assign random edges before every original has an adjacent
  copy. A forward target would still lead to another original.
- During separation, save `copy.next` before restoring the original,
  and obtain the next copy from `nextOriginal.next` while that pair is
  still woven. Reversing those operations can lose a chain.
- A `next` cycle violates the precondition and can make either method
  loop forever. Detect or reject it before copying when input is not
  trusted.
- A random target outside the next chain violates the precondition.
  A map lookup can translate the missing key to nil, while
  interleaving can follow an unrelated `next`; validate membership
  when this is a real input possibility.
- Readers can observe the interleaved source between phases. Use the
  map method when the source cannot be exclusively owned for the call.
- An allocation panic during interleaving phase one can leave inserted
  copies in the source. Use the map method when restoration across
  recoverable failures is required.

##### When to choose it

Choose the map method by default when clarity, source immutability
during the call, or generalization to arbitrary pointer graphs matters
more than linear auxiliary storage. It is the safer choice for shared
or externally observed lists.

Choose interleaving only when the source is a finite acyclic next
chain, every random target belongs to it, exclusive temporary mutation
is acceptable, and O(1) auxiliary space is a real constraint. It does
not reduce the required N output allocations.

Use the local [Copy List with Random Pointer](
problems/medium_leetcode_0138_copy_list_with_random_pointer.go)
exercise to practice the contract. The canonical
[Copy List with Random Pointer](
https://leetcode.com/problems/copy-list-with-random-pointer/)
problem defines the deep-copy requirements. Go documents
[map key and lookup behavior](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Map_types) and
[pointer-key examples](https://go.dev/blog/maps).

#### B.10.6 Merge sorting lists (node pointers)

##### Problem and contract

Sort a singly linked list by changing `next` links instead of copying
values into an array. The result must contain every original node
exactly once in nondecreasing value order. Read the general
[merge-sort lesson](#b36-merge-sort-slice-and-buffer),
[stable node merging](
#b101-reversal-splicing-and-merging-node-pointers), and
[fast and slow pointers](#b102-fast-and-slow-pointers-linked-list)
first.

`mergeSortList(head)` is stable: nodes with equal values retain their
relative input order. It returns nil for nil and returns the identical
node for a one-node input. Values may repeat or use any `int` value.

The function consumes the input topology. It allocates no result
nodes, preserves every node's value and other payload, and returns the
new head. Callers must use that returned pointer. External aliases
still identify the same nodes but observe their new next links.

The input must be a finite acyclic next chain whose node count fits
`int`. Unsynchronized concurrent access is outside the contract. An
invalid cycle can prevent the counting pass from terminating.

This implementation is bottom-up merge sort. It uses iterative passes
of widths 1, 2, 4, and so on, avoiding recursion and its O(log N)
stack. Internal helpers require a positive run width and receive only
detached, sorted runs created by the sorter.

##### Mental model

A run is a consecutive chain already sorted in stable order. Every
one-node run is sorted. If two adjacent runs are sorted, the stable
merge from the earlier lesson can combine them into a run twice as
wide without moving values out of their nodes.

First count N nodes. Then rebuild the whole list in passes:

- At width W, take up to W nodes as `left`, up to W more as `right`,
  merge them, and append that merged run to the rebuilt prefix.
- `unmerged` points to the first node not yet assigned during this
  pass. `mergedTail` is the last node of the rebuilt prefix.
- `splitRun(head, W)` walks at most W nodes, cuts the last node's next
  link to nil, and returns the untouched remainder.
- `mergeStableRuns(left, right)` returns the merged head and tail, so
  the outer loop can append the next result in O(1) link work.

At the start of a width-W pass, the list is partitioned from its head
into stably sorted runs of W nodes, except possibly a shorter final
run. The pass combines adjacent pairs, creating the same partition
with width `2 * W`. Doubling W eventually makes one run cover all N
nodes.

During a merge, compare only the two run heads. Choose the smaller
value. On equality, choose `left`, because every left-run node
preceded every right-run node before this merge. Detach the selected
node, append it after the merge tail, and advance only its source.

The final width update uses a division guard rather than blindly
doubling. When `W > N / 2`, the completed pass already covers more
than N nodes per merged run, and doubling could only be unnecessary
or risk integer overflow.

##### Worked walkthrough

Sort these nodes, where the letter is non-key payload and exposes
stable identity:

```text
4-A -> 2-B -> 4-C -> 1-D -> 3-E -> nil
```

The expected result is:

```text
1-D -> 2-B -> 3-E -> 4-A -> 4-C -> nil
```

Initial state: the original head is A. No links have changed, and the
node count and first run width are not yet known.

1. Decision: traverse next links and count five nodes. Place a
   temporary sentinel before A and set `runWidth = 1`.
   After: `nodeCount = 5`; `mergedTail` and `unmerged` will be reset
   at the start of each pass.
   Known correct: width-one runs are individually sorted, and the
   sentinel is control state rather than result data.
2. Decision: in the width-one pass, cut left run `[4-A]` and right
   run `[2-B]`; save C as `unmerged`. Compare 4 with 2, select B,
   then attach remaining A.
   After: rebuilt prefix is `[2-B,4-A]`; `mergedTail = A`;
   `unmerged = C`.
   Known correct: the first two original nodes form one stable sorted
   run, and C through E remain available.
3. Decision: cut `[4-C]` and `[1-D]`, saving E. Select D before C and
   append that merged run after A.
   After: rebuilt prefix is `[2-B,4-A,1-D,4-C]`;
   `mergedTail = C`; `unmerged = E`.
   Known correct: the prefix contains two sorted two-node runs in
   their original run order.
4. Decision: E is the last width-one left run; its right run is nil.
   Merge returns E unchanged and appends it.
   After: width-one pass yields
   `[2-B,4-A,1-D,4-C,3-E]`; `unmerged = nil`.
   Known correct: all five nodes occur once in sorted runs of length
   at most two. Double the next width to two.
5. Decision: at width two, cut `[2-B,4-A]` and `[1-D,4-C]`, saving E.
   Merge front values in this order:

   ```text
   2 versus 1 -> D
   2 versus 4 -> B
   4 versus 4 -> A from the left run
   left empty -> C
   ```

   After: rebuilt prefix is `[1-D,2-B,4-A,4-C]`;
   `unmerged = E`.
   Known correct: the four-node run is sorted, and left-first equality
   keeps earlier A before equal-valued C.
6. Decision: append singleton E as the final width-two run.
   After: pass result is `[1-D,2-B,4-A,4-C,3-E]`.
   Known correct: all nodes occur once in runs of length at most four.
   Double the next width to four.
7. Decision: cut the first four nodes as the left run and E as the
   right run. Select D for `1 <= 3`, B for `2 <= 3`, then E for
   `4 > 3`; attach remaining A and C.
   After: pass result is `[1-D,2-B,3-E,4-A,4-C]`.
   Known correct: one stable sorted run now contains every input node.
8. Decision: completed width four is greater than `5 / 2`, so do not
   double. Stop and return `sentinel.next`, which is D.
   After: the returned chain matches the expected order; A still
   precedes C, and all five original node pointers remain present.
   Known correct: no further run exists to merge, and the width guard
   prevents an unnecessary or overflowing update.

Focused nil and singleton cases return before counting or mutation.
Focused incomplete pair: at width two, singleton E has no right run;
the merge returns E itself, so odd run counts need no placeholder.

Counterexample to choosing the right node on equality: in step 5,
using `<` instead of `<=` selects C before A. Values remain sorted,
but equal input nodes reverse order and violate stability at that
decision.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough and checks nil and
singleton identity. `label` is demonstration payload and does not
affect ordering. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Merge sorting lists (node
// pointers). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type listNode struct {
	value int
	label string
	next  *listNode
}

func splitRun(
	head *listNode,
	maximumLength int,
) *listNode {
	// Keep split run in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if maximumLength <= 0 {
		panic("run length must be positive")
	}
	if head == nil {
		return nil
	}

	tail := head
	length := 1
	for length < maximumLength && tail.next != nil {
		tail = tail.next
		length++
	}
	remainder := tail.next
	tail.next = nil
	return remainder
}

func mergeStableRuns(
	first *listNode,
	second *listNode,
) (*listNode, *listNode) {
	// Combine compatible parts while preserving their invariant.
	if first == nil && second == nil {
		return nil, nil
	}

	var sentinel listNode
	tail := &sentinel
	for first != nil && second != nil {
		var selected *listNode
		if first.value <= second.value {
			selected = first
			first = first.next
		} else {
			selected = second
			second = second.next
		}

		// Detach so the confirmed merged prefix ends at its tail.
		selected.next = nil
		tail.next = selected
		tail = selected
	}
	if first != nil {
		tail.next = first
	} else {
		tail.next = second
	}
	for tail.next != nil {
		tail = tail.next
	}
	return sentinel.next, tail
}

func mergeSortList(head *listNode) *listNode {
	// Combine compatible parts while preserving their invariant.
	if head == nil || head.next == nil {
		return head
	}

	nodeCount := 0
	for current := head; current != nil; current = current.next {
		nodeCount++
	}

	sentinel := &listNode{next: head}
	for runWidth := 1; runWidth < nodeCount; {
		mergedTail := sentinel
		unmerged := sentinel.next
		for unmerged != nil {
			left := unmerged
			right := splitRun(left, runWidth)
			unmerged = splitRun(right, runWidth)
			mergedHead, mergedEnd := mergeStableRuns(left, right)
			mergedTail.next = mergedHead
			mergedTail = mergedEnd
		}

		// Double only while the result still fits in int.
		if runWidth > nodeCount/2 {
			break
		}
		runWidth *= 2
	}
	return sentinel.next
}

func listOrder(head *listNode) []string {
	// Expose order in logical order without changing source.
	order := make([]string, 0)
	for current := head; current != nil; current = current.next {
		order = append(
			order,
			fmt.Sprintf("%d-%s", current.value, current.label),
		)
	}
	return order
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	fifth := &listNode{value: 3, label: "E"}
	fourth := &listNode{value: 1, label: "D", next: fifth}
	third := &listNode{value: 4, label: "C", next: fourth}
	second := &listNode{value: 2, label: "B", next: third}
	first := &listNode{value: 4, label: "A", next: second}

	sorted := mergeSortList(first)
	fmt.Println(listOrder(sorted))
	fmt.Println(sorted == fourth, first.next == third)

	single := &listNode{value: 7, label: "only"}
	fmt.Println(
		mergeSortList(nil) == nil,
		mergeSortList(single) == single,
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1-D 2-B 3-E 4-A 4-C]
true true
true true
```

The second line confirms the new head is original D and the earlier
equal-valued A still links to C. The last line confirms nil and
singleton identity behavior.

##### Why it works

First prove the stable merge rule. Before each comparison, the chain
through `tail` contains exactly the selected nodes in stable sorted
order, while `first` and `second` head the untouched sorted suffixes.
The smaller head is no greater than any later node in either suffix,
so selecting it is safe. On equality, the first-run node appeared
earlier in the input, so `<=` preserves stable order. Detaching and
appending consumes exactly that node and preserves the invariant.

When one run empties, the other suffix is already sorted. If the
merged prefix is nonempty, no suffix value is less than its confirmed
tail; if the prefix is empty, no lower bound is needed. Attaching the
suffix whole gives a stable sorted permutation of both runs. Scanning
it only finds the returned tail and does not change order. Each
comparison consumes one node, so the merge terminates.

Now prove the outer passes by induction on run width. Before the first
pass, the list's width-one partition is stably sorted. Suppose it
starts a pass partitioned into sorted width-W runs, except possibly a
shorter final run. `splitRun` cuts two consecutive, disjoint runs
without changing their internal order and leaves `unmerged` at the
next untouched node.

By the merge rule, those two runs become one stable sorted run of at
most `2 * W` nodes containing exactly their nodes. Linking it after
`mergedTail` extends the rebuilt prefix without losing or repeating a
node. The inner-loop invariant is therefore: the rebuilt prefix
contains completed stable runs of at most `2 * W`, and `unmerged`
begins every node not yet processed in pass-start order.

When `unmerged` becomes nil, that invariant covers all N nodes. Thus
the next pass may use width `2 * W`. Once a completed merged-run width
is at least N, the whole list is one stable sorted run. Returning the
sentinel's next link therefore gives the required head and order.

Every split either reaches nil or cuts after at most W nodes. Every
inner iteration consumes at least its nonempty left run, so a finite
pass terminates. Run widths are positive powers of two. If doubling
is still needed, `runWidth <= nodeCount / 2`, so doubling stays within
`int`; otherwise the guard stops after a pass already wide enough.
These facts prove all valid loops terminate.

No helper changes values or labels. Splitting and merging redirect
only next links among the original nodes, so the result preserves
exact node identity and introduces no data node.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the node count. Nil and one-node inputs take Theta(1). For a
larger list, counting takes Theta(N). There are `ceil(log2(N))` merge
passes. Within one pass, split scans and merges visit each node only a
constant number of times, so one pass is Theta(N).

Total best, average, and worst-case time is Theta(N log N) for growing
N. This implementation performs every pass even when the input is
already sorted; value order does not improve its bound. It compares
values directly, so minimum and maximum integers cannot overflow a
subtraction.

The sorter stores a node count, a run width, and a fixed number of
pointers. Its temporary sentinels are control values, not result
nodes. Because merge calls are iterative and nonoverlapping, only a
constant number of them are live. Auxiliary space is O(1), and the
returned head is O(1) output space. The result reuses all N input
nodes and allocates no output collection.

Top-down list merge sort uses fast and slow pointers to split each
subproblem and has the same Theta(N log N) time and stability rule. It
is shorter conceptually, but balanced recursion retains O(log N)
stack frames. Bottom-up sorting pays one counting pass and more run
bookkeeping to meet a strict constant-auxiliary-space goal.

Copying node pointers into a slice and using a library stable sort is
often simpler and may improve locality while sorting the slice, but it
uses O(N) auxiliary storage and must relink nodes afterward. Natural
merge sort can exploit already sorted runs; this fixed-width version
has simpler deterministic pass boundaries but is not adaptive.

The example's `listOrder` helper separately uses O(N) output-slice
space and string formatting. Those display costs are not part of the
sorter.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and one-node inputs return the identical head and perform no
  link write. Reading `head.next` without checking nil would panic.
- Two reversed nodes need one width-one merge. The selected second
  node becomes the returned head; callers must save it.
- An odd final run may have no right partner. Merging a nonnil left
  run with nil returns the same run and its actual tail.
- Duplicates are stable only when equality selects the left run. With
  `[2-A,2-B]`, using `<` produces B before A.
- Already sorted, reverse-sorted, all-equal, negative, zero, and
  extreme values follow the same pass schedule.
- `splitRun` must set the cut tail's next link to nil. Leaving runs
  connected lets a merge consume nodes belonging to later pairs.
- Save the remainder by splitting both runs before merging. Once
  merge rewiring begins, old run boundaries no longer describe the
  untouched suffix.
- Set `mergedTail = mergedEnd` after every pair. Reusing the old tail
  overwrites the preceding result link on the next append.
- Detach a selected merge node only after saving its source successor.
  Detaching first would lose the rest of that run.
- Return the sentinel's next node, not the original head. Sorting may
  move the original head into the middle or to the tail.
- Blindly applying `runWidth *= 2` can overflow and make the width
  nonpositive for a representable extreme count. Guard before
  doubling.
- A next cycle violates the contract and prevents the count from
  reaching nil. Detect a cycle first when topology is untrusted.
- External aliases observe the final rewiring. Concurrent readers can
  also observe temporarily detached runs, so exclusive mutation access
  is required.
- A recursive version uses O(log N) auxiliary stack even though it
  allocates no node array. Include call frames in space analysis.

##### When to choose it

Choose bottom-up list merge sort when data already lives in a singly
linked list, stable comparison order and Theta(N log N) worst-case
time are required, nodes should be reused, and auxiliary space must
remain constant.

Choose top-down list merge sort when simpler divide-and-conquer code
matters more than O(log N) stack space. Choose a slice and standard
library sorting when random access, cache locality, or routine
production maintenance matters more than a pointer-only workflow.
For small lists, insertion sort may be simpler despite its quadratic
worst case. For bounded integer keys, counting or radix techniques may
avoid the comparison-sorting lower bound at the cost of extra storage.

Practice with the local [Sort List](
problems/medium_leetcode_0148_sort_list.go) exercise. The canonical
[Sort List](https://leetcode.com/problems/sort-list/) problem states
the ordering and constant-space follow-up. NIST defines
[merge sort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/mergesort.html) and the
[stable left-first merge rule](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/merge.html).

#### B.10.7 Reordering and group reversal (node pointers)

##### Problem and contract

Some linked-list problems ask for a new node order without allowing a
new list of copied values. Two common forms are:

- reorder `L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln` into
  `L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> ...`; and
- reverse every complete consecutive group of `K` nodes while leaving
  a final group with fewer than `K` nodes unchanged.

Both operations change only `next` links. They must preserve every
node exactly once, preserve every stored value, and return an acyclic
list. That makes the problem a topology rewrite rather than a value
transformation.

This lesson assumes a finite, acyclic, singly linked list owned by the
caller for the duration of the mutation. Concurrent readers or writers
would observe temporary shapes and require synchronization outside
these functions.

The group function accepts every positive group size. A size larger
than the list simply leaves the list unchanged. A nonpositive size is
an invalid request: it returns the original head and an error before
changing any link.

##### Mental model

Alternating-end reordering has three phases:

1. Find the end of the first half. Starting `fast` at `head.next`
   leaves the first half one node longer when the length is odd.
2. Detach and reverse the second half. Detachment is important: it
   gives both halves a real `nil` boundary before weaving begins.
3. Alternate one node from the first half with one node from the
   reversed second half. Save both successor pointers before writing.

For five nodes, the split is `1 -> 2 -> 3` and `4 -> 5`. Reversing the
second half produces `5 -> 4`; weaving produces
`1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> 3`.

Complete-group reversal uses a sentinel before the head because the
first group can change the head. For each candidate group:

1. Scan exactly `K` links from `beforeGroup` to find `groupEnd`.
   If the scan reaches `nil`, return immediately without changing the
   incomplete suffix.
2. Remember `groupStart` and `afterGroup`.
3. Reverse links from `groupStart` through `groupEnd`. Initialize
   `previous` to `afterGroup`, so the old group start becomes the new
   tail and already points to the untouched suffix.
4. Connect `beforeGroup.next` to the old group end, which is now the
   group head. Move `beforeGroup` to the old group start.

The scan-before-write rule is the essential transaction boundary. It
proves that a complete group exists before any link in that group is
mutated.

##### Worked walkthrough

Reorder `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5`:

1. **Before:** `firstHalfEnd=1`, `fast=2`.
   **Decision:** move the slow pointer once and the fast pointer twice
   while two fast-path nodes remain. **After:** the first iteration
   gives `firstHalfEnd=2`, `fast=4`; the second gives
   `firstHalfEnd=3`, `fast=nil`. **Known correct:** the first half has
   three nodes and the second half has two.
2. **Before:** the list is still
   `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5`. **Decision:** save node `4`, set
   `3.next=nil`, and reverse from node `4`. **After:** the independent
   halves are `1 -> 2 -> 3` and `5 -> 4`.
   **Known correct:** every node is in exactly one acyclic half.
3. **Before:** `first=1` and `second=5`. **Decision:** save nodes `2`
   and `4`, then link `1 -> 5 -> 2`. **After:** the visible prefix is
   `1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 3`, and the remaining second-half node is `4`.
   **Known correct:** the first outside pair, nodes `1` and `5`, is in
   its final position.
4. **Before:** `first=2` and `second=4`. **Decision:** save node `3`
   and `nil`, then link `2 -> 4 -> 3`. **After:** the list is
   `1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> 3`. **Known correct:** all five original nodes
   occur once in alternating-end order.

```text
first half:    1 -> 2 -> 3
reversed half: 5 -> 4

merged:        1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> 3 -> nil
```

Reverse complete groups of three in
`1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8`:

1. **Before:** the sentinel points to node `1`.
   **Decision:** scan three nodes before writing. **After:**
   `groupStart=1`, `groupEnd=3`, and `afterGroup=4`.
   **Known correct:** nodes `1`, `2`, and `3` form a complete group.
2. **Before:** `previous=4` and `current=1`.
   **Decision:** redirect `1.next` to `4`, then `2.next` to `1`, then
   `3.next` to `2`. **After:** connect the sentinel to node `3`; the
   list starts `3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4`. **Known correct:** the first three
   nodes are reversed and remain connected to the suffix.
3. **Before:** `beforeGroup=1` and the suffix starts at node `4`.
   **Decision:** scan and reverse the complete group `4,5,6`.
   **After:** the list starts
   `3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 6 -> 5 -> 4 -> 7 -> 8`.
   **Known correct:** the first two complete groups are final.
4. **Before:** `beforeGroup=4` and only nodes `7,8` remain.
   **Decision:** scan for three nodes. **After:** the scan reaches
   `nil` before any write. **Known correct:** the incomplete suffix
   remains `7 -> 8`, so the whole result is correct.

```text
groups: [1 2 3] [4 5 6] [7 8]
          reverse   reverse   keep
result:  3 2 1     6 5 4     7 8
```

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Reordering and group reversal
// (node pointers). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type listNode struct {
	value int
	next  *listNode
}

func reverseList(head *listNode) *listNode {
	// Swap opposite positions while shrinking the unresolved interval.
	var reversed *listNode
	current := head
	for current != nil {
		nextCurrent := current.next
		current.next = reversed
		reversed = current
		current = nextCurrent
	}
	return reversed
}

func reorderAlternatingEnds(head *listNode) *listNode {
	// Keep reorder alternating ends in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	if head == nil || head.next == nil {
		return head
	}

	// Leave the first half one node longer when the length is odd.
	firstHalfEnd := head
	fast := head.next
	for fast != nil && fast.next != nil {
		firstHalfEnd = firstHalfEnd.next
		fast = fast.next.next
	}

	second := firstHalfEnd.next
	firstHalfEnd.next = nil
	second = reverseList(second)
	first := head

	// Alternate one node from each half until the shorter half ends.
	for second != nil {
		nextFirst := first.next
		nextSecond := second.next
		first.next = second
		second.next = nextFirst
		first = nextFirst
		second = nextSecond
	}
	return head
}

func reverseCompleteGroups(
	head *listNode,
	groupSize int,
) (*listNode, error) {
	// Swap opposite positions while shrinking the unresolved interval.
	if groupSize <= 0 {
		return head, fmt.Errorf("group size must be positive")
	}
	if head == nil || groupSize == 1 {
		return head, nil
	}

	sentinel := &listNode{next: head}
	beforeGroup := sentinel
	for {
		// Find a complete group before changing any of its links.
		groupEnd := beforeGroup
		for count := 0; count < groupSize; count++ {
			groupEnd = groupEnd.next
			if groupEnd == nil {
				return sentinel.next, nil
			}
		}

		groupStart := beforeGroup.next
		afterGroup := groupEnd.next
		previous := afterGroup
		current := groupStart
		for current != afterGroup {
			nextCurrent := current.next
			current.next = previous
			previous = current
			current = nextCurrent
		}

		// The old end is the new head; the old start is the new tail.
		beforeGroup.next = groupEnd
		beforeGroup = groupStart
	}
}

func listFromValues(values []int) *listNode {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	var head *listNode
	var tail *listNode
	for _, value := range values {
		node := &listNode{value: value}
		if head == nil {
			head = node
		} else {
			tail.next = node
		}
		tail = node
	}
	return head
}

func valuesFromList(head *listNode) []int {
	// Expose from list in logical order without changing source.
	values := make([]int, 0)
	for current := head; current != nil; current = current.next {
		values = append(values, current.value)
	}
	return values
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	reordered := reorderAlternatingEnds(
		listFromValues([]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}),
	)
	fmt.Println(valuesFromList(reordered))

	grouped, err := reverseCompleteGroups(
		listFromValues([]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}),
		3,
	)
	fmt.Println(valuesFromList(grouped), err)

	unchanged := listFromValues([]int{9, 10})
	returned, err := reverseCompleteGroups(unchanged, 0)
	fmt.Println(returned == unchanged, err != nil)
	fmt.Println(reorderAlternatingEnds(nil) == nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
[1 5 2 4 3]
[3 2 1 6 5 4 7 8] <nil>
true true
true
```

The sentinel is a temporary helper, not an output node. Both
successful operations return a list made from exactly the caller's
original nodes.

##### Why it works

For reordering, let the original length be `N`. The midpoint loop puts
`ceil(N/2)` nodes in the first half and `floor(N/2)` in the second.
Detaching the halves means their node sets are disjoint and their
combined node set is exactly the original one.

The reversal loop preserves this invariant: `reversed` contains the
already processed second-half nodes in reverse order, and `current`
starts the unprocessed suffix in original order. Moving one node from
`current` to `reversed` preserves every node and reduces the
unprocessed suffix by one. The loop terminates after the second-half
length, so the entire second half is reversed.

During weaving, the built prefix alternates first-half and reversed
second-half nodes in their required order. `first` begins the unused
first-half suffix and `second` begins the unused reversed-half suffix.
Each iteration consumes one node from each without changing either
saved successor. The second half is never longer, so when it is empty,
the first half has at most its odd-length middle node left. That node
is already attached. Thus every original node occurs exactly once in
the required order.

For group reversal, the initial scan makes one of two facts known. If
it reaches `nil`, fewer than `K` nodes remain and no link has changed;
returning preserves the required suffix. Otherwise, the closed region
from `groupStart` through `groupEnd` contains exactly `K` nodes.

Inside the bounded reversal, `previous` is the correctly reversed
processed prefix followed by `afterGroup`, while `current` begins the
unprocessed part of the group. Redirecting one `next` link moves one
node into the processed prefix. The loop stops exactly at
`afterGroup`, so it cannot consume a node from the next group.

After reversal, the old group end is its new head and the old group
start is its new tail. Connecting `beforeGroup.next` to the new head
restores the prefix boundary; initializing `previous` with
`afterGroup` already restored the suffix boundary. Moving
`beforeGroup` to the new tail establishes the same invariant for the
next iteration. Each successful iteration finalizes `K` more nodes,
and the last unsuccessful scan returns, so the outer loop terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

For a list of `N` nodes, alternating-end reordering uses three linear
passes: midpoint discovery, reversal of at most half the list, and
weaving. Best, average, and worst cases are Theta(N) for nontrivial
lists. Nil and one-node lists take Theta(1). Auxiliary space is O(1):
the function allocates no list nodes and keeps a fixed number of
pointers.

For a valid group size `K > 1`, complete-group reversal takes
Theta(N) time in the best, average, and worst cases. A node is visited
once by a group scan and at most once by a reversal. The final
incomplete suffix is only scanned. The sentinel is one constant-size
allocation, so auxiliary space is O(1). A nonpositive size, a nil
list, or `K=1` returns in Theta(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

These bounds exclude storage already occupied by the input nodes. The
example's conversion to and from slices is presentation code, not part
of either pointer algorithm.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Reordering without setting `firstHalfEnd.next=nil` can leave an old
  cross-half link in the structure. Later writes may create a cycle or
  make the same node reachable twice.
- Overwriting `first.next` or `second.next` before saving both
  successors loses the rest of a half.
- Starting the midpoint pointers differently changes which half owns
  the middle node. State the intended split and verify lengths two,
  three, four, and five.
- Reversing nodes before proving that a complete group exists mutates
  a short final group that should remain unchanged.
- Reversing until `nil` instead of stopping at `afterGroup` consumes
  later groups and destroys their boundary.
- Forgetting to reconnect the previous prefix to `groupEnd` leaves the
  newly reversed group unreachable.
- Advancing `beforeGroup` to the new group head is wrong. It must move
  to `groupStart`, the old head and new tail.
- A group size of zero can make progress logic meaningless. Reject all
  nonpositive sizes before mutation.
- Nil lists, singleton lists, `K=1`, `K=N`, `K>N`, odd lengths, and
  even lengths are distinct boundary cases worth testing.
- Tests should compare node identities and original values, not only
  resulting values. Duplicate values can hide lost or repeated nodes.

##### When to choose it

Use split-reverse-weave when the required order alternates between the
front and back of a singly linked list and node identity must be
preserved. The same phases also appear in palindrome checks, although
a read-only API may need to reverse the second half again to restore
the input.

Use scan-reverse-reconnect when each complete fixed-size block must be
reversed and a short suffix must stay untouched. It is especially
useful when the problem requires O(1) auxiliary space and changing
values is forbidden.

When not to choose it:

Do not mutate links when callers require the original topology after
the call, nodes may be shared by multiple lists, or concurrent access
is unsynchronized. Copy into new nodes or establish an ownership and
locking contract instead.

For a doubly linked list, an array, or a deque, use the structure's
own bidirectional operations. For production code where inputs are
small and O(N) extra memory is acceptable, collecting node pointers
in a slice may be easier to review than a dense in-place rewrite.

Do not use fixed-group reversal for value-based runs or groups whose
boundaries depend on content. Find and validate those boundaries under
their own contract before applying a bounded reversal.

Related material:

[B.10.1 Reversal, splicing, and merging](
#b101-reversal-splicing-and-merging-node-pointers) develops the
save-write-advance invariant and sentinel-based reconnection used
here.
[B.10.2 Fast and slow pointers](
#b102-fast-and-slow-pointers-linked-list) explains midpoint
conventions and their effect on even and odd splits.

Practice complete-group reversal with the local
[Reverse Nodes in k-Group](
problems/hard_leetcode_0025_reverse_nodes_in_k_group.go) exercise. The
canonical [Reorder List](
https://leetcode.com/problems/reorder-list/) and
[Reverse Nodes in k-Group](
https://leetcode.com/problems/reverse-nodes-in-k-group/) statements
define the two output orders and prohibit changing node values.

### B.11 Tree traversal, paths, and reconstruction

#### B.11.1 Depth-first traversal (stack or recursion)

##### Problem and contract

Many tree tasks must finish one child subtree before moving to the
next. Depth-first traversal provides that control flow. For a finite,
acyclic binary tree whose non-root nodes each have one parent, this
lesson returns three left-before-right orders:

- preorder records a node before either child;
- inorder records it after the left child but before the right; and
- postorder records it after both children.

The input may be nil, and values may repeat. A nil root returns three
non-nil empty slices. Every real node contributes its value once to
each order. The functions do not change values or child links.

The root has no parent. A cycle or shared child makes the structure a
graph and is outside this contract. Read [binary trees](
#a71-binary-trees) for the representation and
[stacks](#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks) for last-in,
first-out storage.

The recursive and iterative functions promise identical results. The
iterative form makes suspended work explicit, which is useful when a
tree may be too deep for a practical recursive call stack.

##### Mental model

A recursive call for one node has three observable moments:

1. Enter the node, before visiting its left child.
2. Resume after the left child, before visiting its right child.
3. Resume after the right child, just before returning.

Preorder records at moment 1, inorder at moment 2, and postorder at
moment 3. A nil child returns immediately and records nothing.

Recursion remembers the current node and return location in the call
stack. The iterative version stores the same facts in a slice of
frames. Each frame contains a node and one of these stages:

- `enter`: neither child has been handled;
- `between`: the left subtree is complete; or
- `exit`: both subtrees are complete.

Read `(4, between)` as: node 4's preorder event and entire left
subtree are complete; its inorder event is next, followed by its right
subtree. The top frame is always the next active call. A parent frame
stays below a child frame until that child is popped.

At `enter`, record preorder, advance the frame to `between`, and push
the left child if present. At `between`, record inorder, advance to
`exit`, and push the right child if present. At `exit`, record
postorder and pop the completed frame.

##### Worked walkthrough

Traverse this tree. The required preorder is `[8,4,6,10,9]`, inorder
is `[4,6,8,9,10]`, and postorder is `[6,4,9,10,8]`.

```text
        8
       / \
      4  10
       \  /
        6 9
```

The stack snapshots below run from bottom to top.

Initial state: the stack is `[(8,enter)]`; all outputs are empty.

1. Decision: the top frame is `(8,enter)`, so append 8 to preorder,
   advance its stage, and push left child 4.
   After: preorder is `[8]`; the stack is
   `[(8,between),(4,enter)]`.
   Known correct: node 8 has been recorded before every descendant.

2. Decision: enter node 4. Append 4 to preorder and advance its frame.
   Its left link is nil, so there is no child frame to push.
   After: preorder is `[8,4]`; the stack is
   `[(8,between),(4,between)]`.
   Known correct: the empty left subtree of 4 is already complete.

3. Decision: `(4,between)` means append 4 to inorder, advance to
   `exit`, and push right child 6.
   After: inorder is `[4]`; the stack is
   `[(8,between),(4,exit),(6,enter)]`.
   Known correct: node 4 follows its empty left subtree and precedes
   every node in its right subtree.

4. Decision: node 6 is a leaf. Across its next three stages, append 6
   to preorder, find no left child, append 6 to inorder, find no right
   child, append 6 to postorder, and pop it.
   After: preorder is `[8,4,6]`, inorder is `[4,6]`, postorder is
   `[6]`, and the stack is `[(8,between),(4,exit)]`.
   Known correct: leaf 6 is complete in all three orders.

5. Decision: `(4,exit)` has no unresolved child, so append 4 to
   postorder and pop its frame.
   After: postorder is `[6,4]`; the stack is `[(8,between)]`.
   Known correct: the entire subtree rooted at 4 is complete.

6. Decision: resume node 8 between its children. Append 8 to inorder,
   advance its frame to `exit`, and push right child 10.
   After: inorder is `[4,6,8]`; the stack is
   `[(8,exit),(10,enter)]`.
   Known correct: the left subtree and inorder event of 8 are final.

7. Decision: enter node 10. Append 10 to preorder, advance its frame,
   and push its left child 9.
   After: preorder is `[8,4,6,10]`; the stack is
   `[(8,exit),(10,between),(9,enter)]`.
   Known correct: node 10 precedes every node in its subtree.

8. Decision: process leaf 9 through `enter`, `between`, and `exit`,
   using the same three-event rule as leaf 6.
   After: preorder is `[8,4,6,10,9]`, inorder is `[4,6,8,9]`,
   postorder is `[6,4,9]`, and the stack is
   `[(8,exit),(10,between)]`.
   Known correct: leaf 9 is complete, while node 10 must still record
   its inorder and postorder events.

9. Decision: record node 10 in inorder, find no right child, then
   record it in postorder and pop it.
   After: inorder is `[4,6,8,9,10]`, postorder is `[6,4,9,10]`, and
   the stack is `[(8,exit)]`.
   Known correct: the entire right subtree of 8 is complete.

10. Decision: record node 8 in postorder and pop the final frame.
    After: postorder is `[6,4,9,10,8]`; the stack is empty.
    Known correct: no active subtree remains, so all three outputs are
    complete and may be returned.

The recursive version causes the same events. For example, its call
for node 4 records preorder, calls the nil left child, records
inorder, calls node 6, then records postorder after node 6 returns.

Focused nil case: no frame or recursive call is created, so all three
results are `[]`. Focused singleton case: node 5 advances through all
three stages without pushing a child and returns `[5]` in every order.

A plausible wrong iterative preorder pushes left child 4 and then
right child 10. Because the stack removes the newest item first, 10 is
visited next and the result starts `[8,10]`. Push right before left in
a preorder-only stack, or use the staged one-child-at-a-time method
shown here.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Depth-first traversal (stack or
// recursion). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type treeNode struct {
	value int
	left  *treeNode
	right *treeNode
}

type traversalOrders struct {
	preorder  []int
	inorder   []int
	postorder []int
}

func emptyTraversalOrders() traversalOrders {
	// Keep empty traversal orders in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return traversalOrders{
		preorder:  []int{},
		inorder:   []int{},
		postorder: []int{},
	}
}

func collectRecursive(root *treeNode) traversalOrders {
	// Expose recursive in logical order without changing source.
	orders := emptyTraversalOrders()
	var visit func(*treeNode)
	visit = func(node *treeNode) {
		// A nil child is an empty subtree with no visit event.
		if node == nil {
			return
		}

		// The three append positions define the three orders.
		orders.preorder = append(orders.preorder, node.value)
		visit(node.left)
		orders.inorder = append(orders.inorder, node.value)
		visit(node.right)
		orders.postorder = append(orders.postorder, node.value)
	}
	visit(root)
	return orders
}

type visitStage uint8

const (
	stageEnter visitStage = iota
	stageBetween
	stageExit
)

type traversalFrame struct {
	node  *treeNode
	stage visitStage
}

func collectIterative(root *treeNode) traversalOrders {
	// Expose iterative in logical order without changing source.
	orders := emptyTraversalOrders()
	if root == nil {
		return orders
	}

	// Each frame remembers where a paused recursive call resumes.
	stack := []traversalFrame{{node: root, stage: stageEnter}}
	for len(stack) > 0 {
		topIndex := len(stack) - 1
		frame := &stack[topIndex]
		switch frame.stage {
		case stageEnter:
			orders.preorder = append(
				orders.preorder,
				frame.node.value,
			)
			frame.stage = stageBetween
			if frame.node.left != nil {
				stack = append(stack, traversalFrame{
					node:  frame.node.left,
					stage: stageEnter,
				})
			}
		case stageBetween:
			orders.inorder = append(
				orders.inorder,
				frame.node.value,
			)
			frame.stage = stageExit
			if frame.node.right != nil {
				stack = append(stack, traversalFrame{
					node:  frame.node.right,
					stage: stageEnter,
				})
			}
		case stageExit:
			orders.postorder = append(
				orders.postorder,
				frame.node.value,
			)
			stack = stack[:topIndex]
		}
	}
	return orders
}

func equalValues(left []int, right []int) bool {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	if len(left) != len(right) {
		return false
	}
	for index := range left {
		if left[index] != right[index] {
			return false
		}
	}
	return true
}

func equalOrders(
	left traversalOrders,
	right traversalOrders,
) bool {
	// Keep equal orders in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return equalValues(left.preorder, right.preorder) &&
		equalValues(left.inorder, right.inorder) &&
		equalValues(left.postorder, right.postorder)
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	root := &treeNode{
		value: 8,
		left: &treeNode{
			value: 4,
			right: &treeNode{value: 6},
		},
		right: &treeNode{
			value: 10,
			left:  &treeNode{value: 9},
		},
	}

	recursive := collectRecursive(root)
	iterative := collectIterative(root)
	fmt.Println(recursive.preorder)
	fmt.Println(recursive.inorder)
	fmt.Println(recursive.postorder)
	fmt.Println(equalOrders(recursive, iterative))

	empty := collectIterative(nil)
	fmt.Println(empty.preorder, empty.inorder, empty.postorder)
}
```

Output:

```text
[8 4 6 10 9]
[4 6 8 9 10]
[6 4 9 10 8]
true
[] [] []
```

The complete program needs only Go's `fmt` package. Both collectors
return result slices that do not alias node storage and retain no tree
node pointer after returning.

##### Why it works

For recursion, consider any subtree. A nil subtree correctly produces
no value. For a non-nil node, assume each recursive child call returns
the correct three orders for that child subtree. The current call
places its value before both child results in preorder, between them
in inorder, and after both in postorder. Those are exactly the
definitions for the larger subtree. Starting with leaves establishes
the claim for the whole finite tree.

For iteration, the stack from bottom to top represents the active
recursive path. Each frame's stage states exactly which of its three
events and child subtrees are complete. Initially, the root at `enter`
matches a newly called recursive function.

An `enter` transition performs the recursive function's first append,
remembers the return point as `between`, and makes the left child the
next active call. A `between` transition performs the second append,
remembers `exit`, and activates the right child. An `exit` transition
performs the final append and returns by popping. Missing children
cause no push, exactly like an immediate recursive nil return. Thus
every iterative transition preserves the call-stack correspondence.

Each input node is pushed once. Its stage advances from `enter`
to `between` to `exit`, after which it is popped. Therefore there are
exactly three loop visits per node, the process terminates, and the
three event sequences equal the recursive traversals. Neither version
writes a node field, so the input topology and values are preserved.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the node count and `H` the number of nodes on the longest
root-to-leaf path. With amortized O(1) slice append, both collectors
perform three constant-work events per node, so nonempty best,
average, and worst running time is Theta(N). A nil tree takes
Theta(1).

Each result contains three slices totaling `3N` integers, which is
Theta(N) required output space. The recursive version also keeps at
most `H` active calls, so its auxiliary space is O(H). The iterative
version keeps at most `H` frames and also uses O(H) auxiliary space.
Its slice may allocate and copy existing frames while growing; those
allocations do not change the O(H) retained-space bound.

A balanced binary tree has `H` in Theta(log N). A one-sided tree has
`H=N`, making either representation use Theta(N) auxiliary space.
The iterative form moves that storage to an ordinary slice and avoids
relying on available call-stack resources; it does not improve the
asymptotic bound.

If only one order is required, store only that output and use a
specialized traversal. Returning all three orders is part of this
lesson's contract, not an inherent cost of depth-first search.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil input must return before dereferencing a node. This example
  returns three non-nil empty slices, not nil slices.
- A leaf still has all three events. Recording only when a child
  exists would omit it from one or more orders.
- Duplicate values represent distinct nodes. A `map[int]bool` visited
  set would wrongly merge equal-valued nodes.
- A right-only node performs its inorder event before entering the
  right child. Skipping the absent left child must not skip that
  event.
- In a last-in, first-out preorder stack that pushes both children,
  pushing left before right visits right first. Push in reverse
  desired order or use staged frames.
- Recording only when a frame is popped can produce postorder, but it
  loses the separate entry and between-child events needed for the
  other two orders.
- Popping a frame at `between` discards the pending right subtree.
  Advance it to `exit` and keep it below the right child instead.
