- A one-sided tree has depth `N`. Recursive code may exhaust practical
  call-stack resources even though its logic is correct.
- A cycle never finishes and a shared child appears once per incoming
  link. Those shapes violate the tree-shape precondition.
- Traversal should not modify child links. Snapshot-based tests can
  detect accidental rewiring even when output values look correct.

##### When to choose it

Choose depth first when a task can finish one subtree before its
sibling: checking shapes, evaluating expressions, enumerating paths,
or computing facts that depend on descendants are common signals.

Choose recursion when the tree depth is safely bounded and the
subproblem is naturally stated as "solve the left subtree, then the
right." Choose an explicit stack when depth may be large, traversal
must pause and resume, or the algorithm needs visible control over
entry and return events.

Choose preorder when a parent must be handled before descendants,
inorder when work belongs between ordered binary children, and
postorder when a parent depends on completed child work.

When not to choose it:

Use [breadth-first traversal](
#b112-breadth-first-traversal-queue) when depth order, nearest nodes,
or complete levels matter. Depth first can reach a deep leaf before a
shallower answer elsewhere.

Do not apply this tree traversal unchanged to graphs with cycles or
shared children. Graph DFS needs identity-based discovery state so a
vertex is not expanded repeatedly.

Use a simple loop for an array or linked list that has only one next
choice. Consider Morris traversal when O(1) auxiliary space is a hard
requirement and temporary link mutation is permitted. Morris traversal
has a more delicate ownership and restoration contract.

Related material:

[A.7.1 Binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) owns the node model and basic
order definitions. [A.4.1 Stacks](
#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks) explains the last-in, first-out
behavior used by explicit frames. The next lessons apply traversal to
[breadth-first levels](#b112-breadth-first-traversal-queue) and
[subtree aggregation](
#b113-subtree-aggregation-recursive-return-values).

Practice recursive depth first with [Maximum Depth of Binary Tree](
problems/easy_leetcode_0104_maximum_depth_of_binary_tree.go) and
paired traversal with [Same Tree](
problems/easy_leetcode_0100_same_tree.go). NIST defines
[tree traversal](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/treeTraversal.html)
and [depth-first search](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/depthfirst.html), including its
preorder, inorder, and postorder specializations.

#### B.11.2 Breadth-first traversal (queue)

##### Problem and contract

Some tree tasks need nodes grouped by distance from the root rather
than by subtree. Breadth-first traversal, also called level-order
traversal on a tree, visits depth 0 first, then depth 1, and so on. A
node's depth is the number of child links on its unique path from the
root.

Given a finite, acyclic binary tree whose non-root nodes each have one
parent, this lesson returns one integer slice per depth. The root is
at depth 0. Within each depth, values appear from left to right
according to the ordered child links. Duplicate values remain separate
entries.

A nil root returns a non-nil empty outer slice. The function does not
change any node value or child link and retains no node pointer after
returning. A cycle or shared child makes the structure a graph and is
outside this contract.

Read [binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) for the node model and
[queues](#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) for first-in, first-out
order. Contrast [depth-first traversal](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion), which finishes one
subtree before its siblings.

##### Mental model

The implementation represents the queue as two frontiers:

- `currentLevel` contains every node at one depth, left to right; and
- `nextLevel` collects their non-nil children for the next depth.

Read `currentLevel[1] = node 3` as: node 3 is the second node to
process at the current depth. Its index is an order within that depth,
not the node's depth or value.

Create `currentLevel` with only the root. For one outer iteration,
allocate an output row with the same length and start an empty
`nextLevel`. Scan `currentLevel` from index 0 upward. Record each
value, then append its left child followed by its right child when
present.

Do not make `nextLevel` current until the entire current frontier is
finished. That boundary prevents a child from being processed beside
its parent. Once the row is complete, append it to the result and
replace `currentLevel` with `nextLevel`. An empty new frontier ends
the traversal.

These two frontiers implement first-in, first-out order in batches.
Parents leave in left-to-right order, and their children enter in the
same parent order, with left before right.

##### Worked walkthrough

Traverse this sparse tree. The required result is
`[[1],[2,3],[4,5],[6]]`.

```text
        1
       / \
      2   3
       \ /
       4 5
      /
     6
```

Initial state: `currentLevel=[1]`, `levels=[]`, and no next frontier
has been built.

1. Decision: depth 0 contains one node. Record 1, then append its left
   child 2 and right child 3 to `nextLevel` in that order.
   After: commit row `[1]`; `levels=[[1]]` and
   `currentLevel=[2,3]`.
   Known correct: every depth-0 node is output, and all depth-1 nodes
   are pending from left to right.

2. Decision: at depth 1, process index 0, node 2. Record 2. Its left
   link is nil, so append only right child 4.
   After: the unfinished row is `[2,_]`; `nextLevel=[4]`; node 3 is
   still pending in `currentLevel`.
   Known correct: node 2 is the first depth-1 value, and node 4 is the
   first discovered depth-2 node.

3. Decision: process index 1, node 3. Record 3, append left child 5,
   and skip its nil right link. The current frontier is now exhausted.
   After: commit row `[2,3]`; `levels=[[1],[2,3]]` and
   `currentLevel=[4,5]`.
   Known correct: depth 1 is complete, and depth-2 order follows
   parent 2 before parent 3.

4. Decision: at depth 2, process node 4 first. Record 4 and append its
   left child 6; its right link is nil.
   After: the unfinished row is `[4,_]`; `nextLevel=[6]`; node 5 is
   still pending.
   Known correct: node 6 is the first and currently only depth-3 node.

5. Decision: process node 5. Record 5 and append no children. The
   current frontier is exhausted.
   After: commit row `[4,5]`; `levels=[[1],[2,3],[4,5]]` and
   `currentLevel=[6]`.
   Known correct: every depth through 2 is final, and depth 3 is
   pending in left-to-right order.

6. Decision: process leaf 6. Record it and append no children.
   After: commit row `[6]`; the result is
   `[[1],[2,3],[4,5],[6]]`, and `currentLevel=[]`.
   Known correct: every reachable node has been recorded once at its
   depth, and no child remains pending.

7. Decision: test the outer-loop condition. The current frontier is
   empty, so stop and return the accumulated rows.
   After: the returned value remains `[[1],[2,3],[4,5],[6]]`.
   Known correct: an empty frontier proves there is no deeper node.

Focused nil case: no frontier is created, so the result is `[]`.
Focused singleton case: current `[7]` produces row `[7]`, discovers no
child, and returns `[[7]]` after one outer iteration.

A plausible wrong approach appends children to the same level being
scanned without freezing its boundary. Its first incorrect decision
is treating node 2 as another depth-0 node immediately after node 1,
which flattens levels. Separate the next frontier, or capture the
current queue length before processing a level.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Breadth-first traversal (queue).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type treeNode struct {
	value int
	left  *treeNode
	right *treeNode
}

func valuesByLevel(root *treeNode) [][]int {
	// Expose by level in logical order without changing source.
	levels := make([][]int, 0)
	if root == nil {
		return levels
	}

	// The current frontier contains one whole depth in queue order.
	currentLevel := []*treeNode{root}
	for len(currentLevel) > 0 {
		levelValues := make([]int, len(currentLevel))
		nextLevel := make([]*treeNode, 0)
		for index, node := range currentLevel {
			levelValues[index] = node.value

			// Left before right preserves order within the next depth.
			if node.left != nil {
				nextLevel = append(nextLevel, node.left)
			}
			if node.right != nil {
				nextLevel = append(nextLevel, node.right)
			}

			// Release the processed pointer from this local queue.
			currentLevel[index] = nil
		}
		levels = append(levels, levelValues)
		currentLevel = nextLevel
	}
	return levels
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	root := &treeNode{
		value: 1,
		left: &treeNode{
			value: 2,
			right: &treeNode{
				value: 4,
				left:  &treeNode{value: 6},
			},
		},
		right: &treeNode{
			value: 3,
			left:  &treeNode{value: 5},
		},
	}

	fmt.Println(valuesByLevel(root))
	fmt.Println(valuesByLevel(nil))
}
```

Output:

```text
[[1] [2 3] [4 5] [6]]
[]
```

The program needs only Go's `fmt` package. Each output row owns an
integer backing array; it does not alias either frontier or the tree.

##### Why it works

At the start of each outer iteration, maintain this invariant:
`currentLevel` contains exactly all nodes at one depth, in
left-to-right order, and all earlier depths already appear correctly
in `levels`.

Initially, the root is the only depth-0 node, so the invariant holds.
Assume it holds for depth `D`. Scanning the frontier records every
depth-`D` node in its existing order. Every node at depth `D+1` is a
child of exactly one depth-`D` parent. Processing parents left to
right and appending each left child before its right child therefore
places every depth-`D+1` node into `nextLevel` exactly once and in the
required order.

Committing the completed row and promoting `nextLevel` reestablishes
the invariant for depth `D+1`. Each input node enters one frontier and
is processed once. Because the tree is finite, eventually no child is
appended, the next frontier is empty, and the loop terminates. At that
point the invariant says every reachable depth has been returned in
the promised order.

Only local slices are changed. Clearing a processed queue slot removes
that local reference; it does not write through the node pointer, so
the tree remains unchanged.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the node count, `W` the greatest number of nodes at any one
depth, and `D` the number of nonempty depths. With amortized O(1)
slice append, each node is recorded once and each of its two child
links is checked once. Nonempty best, average, and worst running time
is Theta(N); a nil tree takes Theta(1).

The result stores `N` integers and `D` slice headers, requiring
Theta(N+D) output space, which is Theta(N) for a nonempty tree. During
one iteration, the current and next frontiers contain at most the
widths of two adjacent depths, each no greater than `W`. Their live
node-pointer storage is therefore O(W). The output row is required
output, not auxiliary queue storage.

A one-sided tree has `W=1`, so queue storage is O(1) even though it
has `D=N` result rows. A perfect tree has `W` in Theta(N), so the
widest frontier requires Theta(N) auxiliary storage. Clearing
processed queue slots shortens pointer lifetime but does not change
these asymptotic bounds.

An indexed growing queue that never reuses or compacts its prefix may
retain all `N` appended pointers. A circular queue or these two
frontiers keeps live queue storage proportional to width instead.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil input returns a non-nil empty outer slice. Enqueuing a nil root
  and reading its value would panic.
- A singleton produces `[[value]]`, not `[value]`; the outer slice
  represents depths and the inner slice represents one level.
- Duplicate values are distinct nodes. Deduplicating by integer value
  drops valid output entries.
- Missing children are skipped. Enqueuing nil placeholders changes
  row widths and requires a different serialization contract.
- Appending right before left reverses siblings within the next level.
  Always enqueue children in the required output order.
- Processing until a growing queue becomes empty without a saved level
  boundary produces a flat breadth-first order, not grouped rows.
- Reusing one `levelValues` backing array without copying makes stored
  rows overwrite one another. Allocate or detach each committed row.
- Clearing `currentLevel[index]` is safe because it clears a local
  slice slot. Setting `node.left` or `node.right` to nil would corrupt
  the input tree.
- Repeatedly removing queue index 0 by copying the suffix can take
  Theta(N^2) time. Use a head index, circular queue, or frontiers.
- An indexed queue with a head but no compaction can retain all old
  pointers. Account for O(N), or use a width-bounded representation.
- A cycle never exhausts the frontier, and a shared child is appended
  more than once. Those inputs need graph BFS with discovery tracking.

##### When to choose it

Choose breadth first when the contract mentions levels, depth order,
nearest nodes by edge count, or the first result at minimum depth.
Level averages, right-side views, zigzag rows, and per-level maxima
all start from this frontier boundary.

The two-frontier form is especially clear when output is grouped by
depth. A single FIFO queue is equally suitable: capture its current
length before removing that many nodes, and leave newly appended
children for the next outer iteration.

When not to choose it:

Use depth first when work depends on completing a subtree, such as
postorder aggregation, and the tree is narrow enough that O(H) stack
space is preferable to an O(W) frontier. A shallow, very wide tree is
the clearest counterexample: breadth first may retain nearly half its
nodes at once.

Do not use plain breadth first for weighted shortest paths; edge count
is not total cost. Use a suitable weighted shortest-path algorithm.
For graphs with cycles or shared destinations, add identity-based
discovery state and mark a vertex when it is enqueued.

Do not use level-order traversal when an API requires preorder,
inorder, or postorder. Those contracts place parents relative to
subtrees rather than grouping equal depths.

[A.5.1 Queues](#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) owns FIFO mechanics,
while [A.7.1 Binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) owns the node and depth
model. [B.11.1 Depth-first traversal](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) contrasts
subtree-first processing with level-first processing.

Practice grouped output with [Binary Tree Level Order Traversal](
problems/medium_leetcode_0102_binary_tree_level_order_traversal.go),
then vary the per-level action with [Average of Levels](
problems/easy_leetcode_0637_average_of_levels_in_binary_tree.go) and
the zigzag exercise in the [tree problem index](problems/README.md).
The canonical [level-order problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-level-order-traversal/) uses
the same left-to-right row contract. NIST defines
[breadth-first search](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/breadthfirst.html) and identifies it
with level-order traversal on a tree.

#### B.11.3 Subtree aggregation (recursive return values)

##### Problem and contract

Many tree answers depend on facts from both children. Recomputing each
fact from the child nodes every time a parent needs it repeats work.
Subtree aggregation instead returns all reusable child facts together.

For a finite, acyclic binary tree whose non-root nodes each have one
parent, this lesson reports four facts about the root's whole subtree:

- `nodeCount` is the number of nodes;
- `leafCount` is the number with no children;
- `height` is the greatest number of nodes on a root-to-leaf path; and
- `heightBalanced` is true when, at every node, the two child heights
  differ by at most one.

Nil input returns count 0, leaf count 0, height 0, and balanced true.
A singleton returns `(1,1,1,true)`. Node values do not affect these
structural facts, so negative, extreme, and duplicate values behave
the same. The function does not mutate or retain the tree.

A cycle or shared child is outside the tree contract. Read
[binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) and [postorder depth first](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) first.

##### Mental model

Treat `summarizeSubtree(node)` as a precise question: "What are all
four promised facts about the subtree rooted here?" Each invocation
returns one `subtreeSummary`; it exposes no unfinished work.

The nil summary `(0,0,0,true)` is an identity for missing children.
Zero nodes, leaves, and height contribute nothing to a parent. Empty
must be balanced so that an actual leaf can be balanced.

For a non-nil node, recursively summarize the left child, then the
right child. Only after both returns are complete, combine them:

- nodes are `1 + left nodes + right nodes`;
- height is `1 + max(left height, right height)`;
- leaves are 1 for a leaf, otherwise the two child leaf counts; and
- balance requires both child summaries to be balanced and their
  heights to differ by at most one.

This is postorder computation: children produce facts before their
parent. Read `(4,2,3,true)` as "this subtree has four nodes, two
leaves, height three, and every node inside it is height-balanced."
The parent needs no pointer into that subtree after receiving the
summary.

Returning height together with balance matters. If a parent calls a
separate height traversal after checking each child, descendants are
visited again at every ancestor.

##### Worked walkthrough

Summarize this tree. Write a summary as
`S=(nodes,leaves,height,balanced)`. The required root result is
`(6,3,4,false)`.

```text
        8
       / \
      4  10
     / \
    2   6
   /
  1
```

Initial state: `summarizeSubtree(8)` is active, but neither child
summary is known.

1. Decision: the root cannot combine until its left child is complete,
   so recurse from 8 to 4, from 4 to 2, and from 2 to 1. Each ancestor
   pauses before its right-child call.
   After: the active path is `8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1`; no nonempty summary
   has returned yet.
   Known correct: every paused call owns one distinct ancestor subtree
   and waits only for a smaller child subtree.

2. Decision: node 1 has two nil children. Each returns
   `(0,0,0,true)`. Set leaf count to 1; the current node also makes
   node count and height 1.
   After: node 1 returns `(1,1,1,true)` to node 2.
   Known correct: the one-node subtree has one node, one leaf, height
   one, and equal child heights.

3. Decision: node 2 now has left summary `(1,1,1,true)`. Its right
   child is nil and returns `(0,0,0,true)`. Combine the two summaries.
   After: node 2 returns `(2,1,2,true)` to node 4.
   Known correct: nodes 2 and 1 are counted once; their height
   difference at node 2 is one.

4. Decision: node 4 has its left summary, so summarize right leaf 6.
   Both nil children of 6 return the identity summary.
   After: node 6 returns `(1,1,1,true)`; node 4 now has both child
   summaries.
   Known correct: every fact needed to combine node 4 is available,
   and neither child will be traversed again.

5. Decision: combine node 4 with left `(2,1,2,true)` and right
   `(1,1,1,true)`. Compute nodes `1+2+1=4`, leaves `1+1=2`, height
   `1+max(2,1)=3`, and height difference 1.
   After: node 4 returns `(4,2,3,true)` to node 8.
   Known correct: every node under 4 is represented once, and both
   child summaries and node 4 satisfy the balance rule.

6. Decision: the left subtree of 8 is complete, so summarize right
   leaf 10 from two nil identities.
   After: node 10 returns `(1,1,1,true)`; node 8 has both summaries.
   Known correct: all descendants of 8 are complete before the
   root combine, which is postorder.

7. Decision: combine left `(4,2,3,true)` and right
   `(1,1,1,true)`. Compute nodes `1+4+1=6`, leaves `2+1=3`, height
   `1+max(3,1)=4`, and height difference 2.
   After: node 8 returns `(6,3,4,false)`.
   Known correct: counts and height cover the whole tree; the root's
   difference of two is enough to make the whole tree unbalanced.

Focused nil case: the base case immediately returns `(0,0,0,true)`.
Focused singleton case: two nil identities combine at one node to
produce `(1,1,1,true)`.

Counterexample to separate height recomputation: on a four-node chain,
checking balance at the root rescans three descendants for height,
then the child rescans two, then the next rescans one. The first wrong
decision is discarding a child's height after computing it. Returning
height with balance changes repeated `3+2+1` work into one visit per
node.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Subtree aggregation (recursive
// return values). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type treeNode struct {
	value int
	left  *treeNode
	right *treeNode
}

type subtreeSummary struct {
	nodeCount      int
	leafCount      int
	height         int
	heightBalanced bool
}

func summarizeSubtree(root *treeNode) subtreeSummary {
	// Empty children contribute zero size and height and are balanced.
	if root == nil {
		return subtreeSummary{heightBalanced: true}
	}

	// Postorder returns complete child facts before combining them.
	left := summarizeSubtree(root.left)
	right := summarizeSubtree(root.right)

	height := left.height
	if right.height > height {
		height = right.height
	}
	height++

	leafCount := left.leafCount + right.leafCount
	if root.left == nil && root.right == nil {
		leafCount = 1
	}

	heightDifference := left.height - right.height
	if heightDifference < 0 {
		heightDifference = -heightDifference
	}
	heightBalanced := left.heightBalanced &&
		right.heightBalanced &&
		heightDifference <= 1

	return subtreeSummary{
		nodeCount:      1 + left.nodeCount + right.nodeCount,
		leafCount:      leafCount,
		height:         height,
		heightBalanced: heightBalanced,
	}
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	root := &treeNode{
		value: 8,
		left: &treeNode{
			value: 4,
			left: &treeNode{
				value: 2,
				left:  &treeNode{value: 1},
			},
			right: &treeNode{value: 6},
		},
		right: &treeNode{value: 10},
	}

	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", summarizeSubtree(root))
	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", summarizeSubtree(nil))
}
```

Output:

```text
{nodeCount:6 leafCount:3 height:4 heightBalanced:false}
{nodeCount:0 leafCount:0 height:0 heightBalanced:true}
```

The program needs only Go's `fmt` package. The returned summary is a
constant-size value containing no node pointer, so it neither aliases
nor prolongs the lifetime of the input tree.

##### Why it works

For a nil subtree, the returned values match the definitions directly:
there is no node, leaf, or path, and no node can violate balance.

Assume both recursive calls return correct summaries for their child
subtrees. Those subtrees are disjoint because every non-root input
node has one parent. Adding one for the current node therefore gives
the exact node count. A non-leaf's leaves are exactly the leaves of
its children; a leaf itself contributes one. Every root-to-leaf path
uses one current node followed by a path in one child, so one plus the
larger child height is exact.

The whole subtree is height-balanced exactly when the left subtree is
balanced, the right subtree is balanced, and the two child heights
differ by at most one. The returned boolean tests all three necessary
and sufficient conditions. Thus the combine produces a correct summary
for the current subtree. Induction from nil children proves the root
summary.

Every recursive call moves from a node to one of its child subtrees.
A finite acyclic tree eventually reaches nil. The unique-parent
contract means each node is called once, does constant combine work,
and returns, so the process terminates without rescanning a
descendant.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the node count and `H` the number of nodes on the longest
root-to-leaf path. The function visits every node once and performs
constant work after its two child calls. Nonempty best, average, and
worst running time is Theta(N); nil input takes Theta(1).

At most `H` non-nil calls are active along one root-to-leaf path. The
recursive call stack therefore uses O(H) auxiliary space. Each
returned summary and the final output use O(1) space; summaries from
completed siblings are held only while their parent combines them.

A balanced tree has `H` in Theta(log N). A one-sided chain has `H=N`
and uses Theta(N) stack space. An explicit postorder stack can move
that storage out of the call stack but cannot improve the O(H)
asymptotic bound for this dependency pattern.

If balance checking separately recomputes height at every node, a
balanced tree takes Theta(N log N) and a chain takes Theta(N^2).
Returning both facts in one summary restores Theta(N) work.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil must be balanced true. Returning false makes every leaf and then
  every nonempty tree falsely unbalanced.
- Height units must be fixed. This lesson counts nodes, so nil height
  is 0 and leaf height is 1; an edge-count convention uses different
  base values.
- A leaf count needs a leaf special case. Adding two nil leaf counts
  gives 0 unless the current leaf contributes 1.
- Checking only the current height difference is insufficient. A child
  may hide an unbalanced descendant even when the root's two heights
  differ by at most one; include both child balance flags.
- Returning only balance and later recomputing child heights recreates
  the quadratic chain case. Return all facts needed by ancestors.
- A one-sided tree of `N` nodes creates `N` active non-nil calls. Use
  an explicit stack when that depth can exceed practical call-stack
  resources.
- Duplicate or extreme node values do not affect this structural
  summary. Adding a numeric sum would require an explicit overflow
  contract.
- A cycle never reaches the nil base case, and a shared child is
  counted once per incoming link. Those inputs violate the tree
  precondition.
- Writing aggregate fields into the input nodes changes ownership and
  cache-invalidation requirements. This function deliberately returns
  values without mutation.

##### When to choose it

Choose recursive return-value aggregation when a subtree's answer can
be computed from its root and constant-size child answers. Counts,
heights, sums, minimum or maximum values, validity flags, and best
path fragments commonly have this form.

Return every fact the parent will reuse. A small named struct is
clearer than parallel unnamed return values when several fields must
stay consistent. Choose recursion when tree height is safely within
practical call-stack resources; otherwise simulate postorder with
explicit frames and store child summaries in those frames.

When not to choose it:

Use breadth first when the answer depends on complete depths or
minimum edge distance. Use top-down parameters when a child needs
ancestor context, such as a running path sum or allowed value bounds.
Some tasks need both directions and may require two passes or
rerooting dynamic programming.

For a mutable tree with many repeated queries, recomputing every
subtree after each update may be wasteful. Store aggregates in nodes
or an external index and update only affected ancestors, with a clear
consistency contract.

Do not recurse unchanged over graphs with cycles or shared children.
Use discovery state and, for an acyclic graph, memoize a vertex
summary when multiple parents reuse it.

defines [recursion](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/recursion.html)
as dividing into smaller parts and combining their solutions, and
[postorder traversal](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/postorderTraversal.html) as
processing child subtrees before their root.

#### B.11.4 Search-tree validation (bounds or stack)

##### Problem and contract

A binary tree is not a binary search tree merely because each child is
on the correct side of its parent. Every descendant must also satisfy
every relevant ancestor comparison.

This lesson validates a strict binary search tree, or BST. For every
node, all values in its left subtree must be smaller, all values in
its right subtree must be greater, and both subtrees must obey the
same rule. Duplicate values are invalid.

The input is a finite, acyclic binary tree whose non-root nodes each
have one parent. Nil and singleton trees are valid. Every Go `int`,
including `math.MinInt` and `math.MaxInt`, is a valid key. Validation
returns a boolean without changing or retaining any node.

Cycles and shared children are outside the tree contract. Read
[binary search trees](#a72-binary-search-trees) for the strict order
and [depth-first traversal](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) for recursion and
explicit stacks.

##### Mental model

The bounds method carries an exclusive interval from the ancestors.
A bound stores both an integer and an `exists` flag. The root starts
without either bound.

At value 15 with bounds `(10, none)`, read the state as: "this node
must be strictly greater than 10; no ancestor imposes an upper
limit." Reject a value less than or equal to an existing lower
bound, or greater than or equal to an existing upper bound.

After a node passes, its left child inherits the lower bound and uses
the node value as a new upper bound. Its right child uses the node
value as a new lower bound and inherits the upper bound. No `value-1`
or `value+1` arithmetic is needed.

The inorder method uses an equivalent fact: a strict BST's inorder
values are strictly increasing. An explicit stack reaches the next
smallest unvisited node by pushing the current left path. After
popping a node, compare it with the previously visited value, then
explore its right child.

`hasPrevious` says whether `previousValue` is meaningful. Without that
boolean, using an integer sentinel could reject a valid extreme key or
accept the first comparison for the wrong reason.

##### Worked walkthrough

Validate this tree. It is invalid even though every immediate child is
on the correct side of its parent.

```text
        10
       /  \
      5    15
          /  \
         6    20
```

The bounds method should reject node 6:

Initial state: node 10 has no lower or upper bound.

1. Decision: 10 has no bound to violate. Recurse left with no lower
   bound and exclusive upper bound 10.
   After: node 5 is active with interval `(none,10)`.
   Known correct: every value in this left subtree must be below 10.

2. Decision: 5 is below 10. Its nil children are valid, so its subtree
   returns true. Continue to the right child of 10 with lower bound 10
   and no upper bound.
   After: node 15 is active with interval `(10,none)`.
   Known correct: the whole left subtree is valid, and every value now
   examined must remain above 10.

3. Decision: 15 is above 10. Recurse to its left child with bounds
   `(10,15)` because that child must remain right of 10 and left of
   value 15. After: node 6 is active with both exclusive bounds.
   Known correct: both ancestor comparisons still constrain node 6;
   the nearer parent does not replace the lower bound from node 10.

4. Decision: compare 6 with lower bound 10. Since `6 <= 10`, reject
   immediately.
   After: node 15 and then node 10 return false; node 20 is not
   visited because boolean `&&` short-circuits.
   Known correct: one violated ancestor bound is sufficient to prove
   the whole tree is not a strict BST.

The stack method sees the same violation as an inorder decrease:

Initial state: `node=10`, `stack=[]`, and no previous value exists.

1. Decision: push the left path 10 then 5. Node 5 has no left child,
   so pop it as the next inorder value.
   After: accept 5 as the first value; set `previousValue=5`, and its
   right child is nil. The stack contains `[10]`.
   Known correct: 5 is the smallest visited value, and there is no
   earlier value to compare.

2. Decision: pop 10. Since `10 > 5`, accept it, remember 10, and move
   to right child 15.
   After: the accepted inorder prefix is `[5,10]`; `node=15`.
   Known correct: the visited prefix is strictly increasing.

3. Decision: push 15 and its left child 6, then pop 6 as the next
   inorder value. Compare it with previous value 10.
   After: `6 <= 10`, so return false with unvisited work still on the
   stack.
   Known correct: the inorder prefix `[5,10,6]` is not increasing,
   which is impossible for a strict BST.

Focused nil case: both methods exhaust no work and return true. For
`0` with children `math.MinInt` and `math.MaxInt`, optional bounds and
`hasPrevious` accept all three values. A duplicate child is rejected
by an equal bound or a non-increasing inorder comparison.

Counterexample to checking only immediate children is the main tree:
node 6 is less than parent 15, yet it lies in root 10's right subtree.
The first wrong decision is forgetting lower bound 10 when descending
through node 15.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Search-tree validation (bounds or
// stack). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

type treeNode struct {
	value int
	left  *treeNode
	right *treeNode
}

type valueBound struct {
	value  int
	exists bool
}

func validWithinBounds(
	root *treeNode,
	lower valueBound,
	upper valueBound,
) bool {
	// Evaluate valid within bounds without changing the maintained
	// state.
	if root == nil {
		return true
	}

	// Strict bounds carry every relevant ancestor comparison.
	if lower.exists && root.value <= lower.value {
		return false
	}
	if upper.exists && root.value >= upper.value {
		return false
	}

	current := valueBound{value: root.value, exists: true}
	return validWithinBounds(root.left, lower, current) &&
		validWithinBounds(root.right, current, upper)
}

func isStrictBSTWithBounds(root *treeNode) bool {
	// Evaluate is strict bst with bounds without changing the maintained
	// state.
	return validWithinBounds(root, valueBound{}, valueBound{})
}

func isStrictBSTWithInorder(root *treeNode) bool {
	// Expose keys in sorted inorder without changing the tree.
	stack := make([]*treeNode, 0)
	node := root
	var previousValue int
	hasPrevious := false

	for node != nil || len(stack) > 0 {
		// Reach the next smallest unvisited node.
		for node != nil {
			stack = append(stack, node)
			node = node.left
		}

		topIndex := len(stack) - 1
		node = stack[topIndex]
		stack = stack[:topIndex]
		if hasPrevious && node.value <= previousValue {
			return false
		}
		previousValue = node.value
		hasPrevious = true
		node = node.right
	}
	return true
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	invalid := &treeNode{
		value: 10,
		left:  &treeNode{value: 5},
		right: &treeNode{
			value: 15,
			left:  &treeNode{value: 6},
			right: &treeNode{value: 20},
		},
	}
	fmt.Println(
		isStrictBSTWithBounds(invalid),
		isStrictBSTWithInorder(invalid),
	)

	valid := &treeNode{
		value: 0,
		left:  &treeNode{value: math.MinInt},
		right: &treeNode{value: math.MaxInt},
	}
	fmt.Println(
		isStrictBSTWithBounds(valid),
		isStrictBSTWithInorder(valid),
	)
	fmt.Println(
		isStrictBSTWithBounds(nil),
		isStrictBSTWithInorder(nil),
	)
}
```

Output:

```text
false false
true true
true true
```

The program uses only Go's `fmt` and `math` packages. Both validators
are read-only and return as soon as they prove a violation.

##### Why it works

For bounds recursion, maintain this invariant: every value in the
current subtree must lie strictly inside the supplied ancestor bounds.
The unbounded root satisfies it. A node outside the interval directly
violates one ancestor relationship and is safely rejected.

When a node is inside its interval, adding its value as the left upper
bound exactly expresses that every left descendant must be smaller.
Adding it as the right lower bound expresses that every right
descendant must be greater. Inherited opposite bounds preserve all
older ancestor requirements. If both recursive calls succeed, every
node in both subtrees satisfies the complete strict BST rule.

For inorder, assume the visited prefix is strictly increasing and
`previousValue` is its greatest value. The stack returns nodes in
left-subtree, node, right-subtree order. Accepting only a value
greater than the previous one preserves the invariant. If a
comparison fails, the sequence is not strictly increasing and the
tree cannot be a strict BST.

Conversely, if the complete inorder sequence is strictly increasing,
then every value before a node, including its entire left subtree, is
smaller; every value after it, including its right subtree, is
greater. Thus success implies the global BST property, not merely
local order.

Each bounds call descends to a child. The iterative method pushes and
pops each node at most once. A finite acyclic tree therefore makes
both methods terminate after visiting at most all nodes.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the node count and `H` the number of nodes on the longest
root-to-leaf path. A valid tree requires both methods to inspect all
`N` nodes, taking Theta(N) time. An invalid tree may fail after
constant work, while a violation encountered last still takes
Theta(N); there is no useful input-independent average guarantee.

Bounds recursion keeps at most `H` calls and uses O(H) auxiliary stack
space. Iterative inorder keeps at most `H` node pointers and also uses
O(H) auxiliary space. Both return one boolean and allocate no output
proportional to `N`.

A balanced tree has `H` in Theta(log N), while a one-sided tree has
`H=N`. The explicit stack avoids recursive call-stack limits but has
the same asymptotic space requirement. Short-circuit rejection can
reduce work but does not improve the worst-case bound.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and singleton trees are valid because no pair can violate strict
  order.
- Equal values are invalid on either side. Using only `<` for the
  lower check or `>` for the upper check accidentally admits
  duplicates.
- `math.MinInt` and `math.MaxInt` are legal keys. Integer sentinels,
  `value-1`, or `value+1` can collide or overflow; store bound
  presence separately.
- The first inorder value has no predecessor. A `hasPrevious` flag
  distinguishes that state from a real previous value of zero or an
  extreme.
- A lower or upper bound can come from a distant ancestor. Replacing
  both bounds with the immediate parent's value misses deep
  violations.
- Inorder must compare strictly. Using `<` instead of `<=` in the
  rejection condition accepts duplicates.
- The iterative inner loop must push the entire left path. Moving
  right before popping the node skips the node's inorder position.
- Short-circuit failure may leave many nodes unvisited. Validation
  promises a boolean, not a complete list of every violation.
- A one-sided tree uses O(N) recursive calls or explicit stack
  entries. The iterative method avoids call-stack exhaustion, not
  linear depth.
- A cycle prevents termination and a shared child is visited twice.
  Those shapes violate the tree precondition.
- Neither validator repairs the input. Mutation by another goroutine
  during validation is outside the ownership contract.

##### When to choose it

Choose ancestor bounds when validation is naturally top down or the
recursive code can return immediately at the violating node. Bounds
also adapt directly to a different documented duplicate policy by
changing which endpoints are inclusive.

Choose iterative inorder when a sorted traversal is already useful,
when recursion depth is unsafe, or when adjacent ordered values feed
another calculation such as minimum difference. It validates strict
order without materializing an O(N) inorder slice.

When not to choose it:

Do not use local parent-child checks; they cannot see a descendant
that crosses an older ancestor boundary. Do not use strict validators
when the data structure deliberately permits duplicates on one side;
state that policy and adjust both bound and monotonicity comparisons.

For arbitrary binary trees, sorted order is not promised and failing
validation is not an error. For graphs with cycles or shared nodes,
first validate topology or use graph discovery state; these functions
assume a tree.

Use an explicit stack rather than bounds recursion when a one-sided
input may exceed practical call-stack resources. Use Morris inorder
only when O(1) auxiliary space justifies temporary tree mutation and a
strict restoration contract.

ordering invariant. [B.11.1 Depth-first traversal](

and explicit-stack mechanics used here.

problems/medium_leetcode_0098_validate_binary_search_tree.go). Once a

problems/easy_leetcode_0530_minimum_absolute_difference_in_bst.go)

https://leetcode.com/problems/validate-binary-search-tree/) states the
strict duplicate-free rule. NIST defines the same global
[binary-search-tree invariant](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/binarySearchTree.html) and
[inorder traversal](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/inorderTraversal.html).

#### B.11.5 Tree reconstruction (index map and recursion)

##### Problem and contract

Two traversal sequences can describe a binary tree without storing
child pointers. This lesson reconstructs the one binary tree whose
preorder and inorder traversals match the supplied integer slices.

The contract requires equal lengths, distinct values within each
slice, identical value sets, and mutually consistent orders. Empty
slices reconstruct a nil tree. Every Go `int` is a valid value. A
valid input returns freshly allocated nodes; an invalid input returns
a nil root and an error. The function neither changes nor retains the
input slices.

Distinct values matter because a value must identify one unambiguous
position in inorder. Under that rule, preorder plus inorder uniquely
determines the topology. Preorder alone does not: `[1,2]` can describe
root 1 with either a left child or a right child.

Read [binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) for the node model,
[depth-first traversal](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) for traversal order,
and [hash maps](#a6-hash-maps-and-hash-sets) for indexed lookup.

##### Mental model

Preorder visits each subtree root before that root's descendants.
Therefore the next unused preorder value is the root of the current
subtree. Inorder visits the left subtree, then the root, then the
right subtree. The root's inorder position consequently separates
the two child subtrees.

Build `inorderIndex` once, mapping each value to its inorder position.
This replaces a repeated linear search with an expected constant-time
lookup. Reject duplicate inorder values while building the map. A
second map rejects duplicate preorder values and verifies membership.
Equal lengths then imply that the two distinct value sets are equal.

The recursive helper owns a half-open inorder range `[left,right)` and
shares `nextPreorder`, the index of the next unconsumed root:

1. If `left == right`, the range is empty, so return nil without
   consuming preorder.
2. Consume the next preorder value as the root.
3. Look up its inorder position. It must lie inside the current range;
   otherwise the two orders are incompatible.
4. Build `[left,split)` as the left child, then
   `[split+1,right)` as the right child.

Left must be built before right because preorder lists an entire left
subtree before its right sibling. Half-open ranges represent empty
children without sentinel indices and make each child's ownership
explicit.

##### Worked walkthrough

Reconstruct this input:

```text
preorder = [3,9,20,15,7]
inorder  = [9,3,15,20,7]
```

Initial state: `inorderIndex` is
`{9:0,3:1,15:2,20:3,7:4}`, `nextPreorder=0`, and the first call owns
inorder range `[0,5)`.

1. Decision: consume preorder value 3. Its inorder split is 1, so
   allocate node 3 and define child ranges `[0,1)` and `[2,5)`.
   After: `nextPreorder=1`; build the left range first.
   Known correct: preorder identifies 3 as this subtree's root, while
   inorder places exactly value 9 to its left.

2. Decision: consume 9 for range `[0,1)`. Its split is 0. Both child
   ranges, `[0,0)` and `[1,1)`, are empty and return nil.
   After: node 9 is the completed left child of 3 and
   `nextPreorder=2`.
   Known correct: the one-position inorder range can contain only
   leaf 9.

3. Decision: resume node 3 and build its right range `[2,5)`.
   Consume 20, whose inorder split is 3.
   After: allocate node 20; its child ranges are `[2,3)` and
   `[4,5)`, and `nextPreorder=3`.
   Known correct: all three remaining inorder values belong below 20;
   split 3 assigns 15 left and 7 right.

4. Decision: build `[2,3)` from next preorder value 15. Its split is
   2, so both child ranges are empty.
   After: node 15 is the completed left child of 20 and
   `nextPreorder=4`.
   Known correct: the left range of 20 has been consumed exactly.

5. Decision: build `[4,5)` from value 7. Its split is 4 and both
   children are empty. Return node 7, then nodes 20 and 3.
   After: `nextPreorder=5`; every range and preorder value is
   consumed.
   Known correct: the constructed tree traverses as both original
   sequences.

The result is:

```text
        3
       / \
      9  20
         / \
        15  7
```

Focused empty case: `[0,0)` returns nil without indexing either slice.
A singleton consumes its only value and creates two empty child
ranges. Values `math.MinInt` and `math.MaxInt` need no special case
because values are map keys, not arithmetic bounds.

Same lengths and value sets are not sufficient. For preorder
`[1,2,3]` and inorder `[3,1,2]`, root 1 splits the first range at 1.
Its left child must come from inorder range `[0,1)`, but next preorder
value 2 has inorder index 2. The out-of-range split proves that no
tree has both traversals, so reconstruction returns an error.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Tree reconstruction (index map and
// recursion). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type treeNode struct {
	value int
	left  *treeNode
	right *treeNode
}

func reconstructFromPreorderInorder(
	preorder []int,
	inorder []int,
) (*treeNode, error) {
	// Expose keys in sorted inorder without changing the tree.
	if len(preorder) != len(inorder) {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("traversal lengths differ")
	}

	inorderIndex := make(map[int]int, len(inorder))
	for index, value := range inorder {
		if _, exists := inorderIndex[value]; exists {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("inorder repeats %d", value)
		}
		inorderIndex[value] = index
	}

	seenPreorder := make(map[int]bool, len(preorder))
	for _, value := range preorder {
		if seenPreorder[value] {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("preorder repeats %d", value)
		}
		seenPreorder[value] = true
		if _, exists := inorderIndex[value]; !exists {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("preorder value %d is absent", value)
		}
	}

	nextPreorder := 0
	var build func(int, int) (*treeNode, error)
	build = func(left int, right int) (*treeNode, error) {
		if left == right {
			return nil, nil
		}
		if nextPreorder == len(preorder) {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("preorder ended early")
		}

		rootValue := preorder[nextPreorder]
		nextPreorder++
		split := inorderIndex[rootValue]
		if split < left || split >= right {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"value %d is outside inorder range [%d,%d)",
				rootValue,
				left,
				right,
			)
		}

		root := &treeNode{value: rootValue}
		var err error
		root.left, err = build(left, split)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		root.right, err = build(split+1, right)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		return root, nil
	}

	root, err := build(0, len(inorder))
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	if nextPreorder != len(preorder) {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("preorder has unused values")
	}
	return root, nil
}

func collectTraversals(root *treeNode) ([]int, []int) {
	// Expose traversals in logical order without changing source.
	preorder := make([]int, 0)
	inorder := make([]int, 0)
	var visit func(*treeNode)
	visit = func(node *treeNode) {
		if node == nil {
			return
		}
		preorder = append(preorder, node.value)
		visit(node.left)
		inorder = append(inorder, node.value)
		visit(node.right)
	}
	visit(root)
	return preorder, inorder
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	root, err := reconstructFromPreorderInorder(
		[]int{3, 9, 20, 15, 7},
		[]int{9, 3, 15, 20, 7},
	)
	preorder, inorder := collectTraversals(root)
	fmt.Println(preorder)
	fmt.Println(inorder)
	fmt.Println(err)

	empty, err := reconstructFromPreorderInorder(nil, nil)
	fmt.Println(empty, err)

	_, err = reconstructFromPreorderInorder(
		[]int{1, 2, 3},
		[]int{3, 1, 2},
	)
	fmt.Println(err)
}
```

Output:

```text
[3 9 20 15 7]
[9 3 15 20 7]
<nil>
<nil> <nil>
value 2 is outside inorder range [0,1)
```

The program imports only `fmt`. `collectTraversals` demonstrates the
round trip; reconstruction itself does not need to traverse the
finished tree. A partial tree allocated before an error becomes
unreachable and is reclaimed by Go's garbage collector.

##### Why it works

Maintain two invariants for every call on `[left,right)`: the range
contains exactly the inorder values of the subtree being built, and
`preorder[nextPreorder]` is that nonempty subtree's root.

An empty range has no node, so returning nil is correct and preserves
the cursor. For a nonempty range, preorder's definition makes the next
value the root. Its unique inorder position divides the range into
exactly the values of the left and right subtrees.

The recursive left call receives the left partition. By induction on
range length, it constructs that subtree and consumes exactly its
preorder block. The cursor then points at the right subtree's root, so
the right call does the same for the right partition. Attaching both
results to the chosen root constructs exactly the current subtree.
Starting with `[0,N)` proves the complete tree has both requested
traversals.

The same argument proves uniqueness. The first preorder value forces
the root, its unique inorder position forces both child value sets,
and the rule repeats in each smaller range. No different root or split
is possible.

Before recursion, the two maps establish length, distinctness, and
set equality. During recursion, a split outside the owned range
detects inconsistent relative order. Every nonempty call consumes one
preorder value and recurses only on smaller disjoint ranges, so finite
input terminates after at most one nonempty call per value.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the common traversal length and `H` the reconstructed tree
height. Building and checking the maps scans each traversal once.
Reconstruction creates one node and performs one expected constant-
time map lookup per value. Valid input therefore takes expected
Theta(N) time. Go does not promise a strict worst-case bound for map
operations.

A length mismatch returns in Theta(1). Other invalid inputs can fail
early, but their worst case is expected Theta(N). Scanning the current
inorder range for every root instead of building a map takes
Theta(N^2) time on a one-sided tree.

The returned nodes require Theta(N) result space. Two maps retain
Theta(N) entries, and recursion keeps O(H) active calls, so auxiliary
space is O(N+H), which is O(N). A balanced result has
`H` in Theta(log N); a one-sided result has `H=N` and may exceed a
practical recursive call-stack limit.

The function passes slice headers and integer boundaries rather than
copying subslices. It allocates one node per accepted value, plus the
two validation maps. No output node aliases an input because inputs
contain values rather than nodes.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty traversals are valid and return a nil root. Indexing preorder
  before checking an empty range panics.
- Equal lengths do not prove equal sets or compatible order. Validate
  duplicates, membership, and each recursive split.
- Repeatedly scanning inorder makes a skewed case quadratic. Build the
  index map once.
- Slicing both traversals at every call can copy data and obscure
  which indices a call owns. Share slices and pass half-open bounds.
- The root's inorder position is excluded from both child ranges.
  Using `[left,split]` or `[split,right)` repeats the root and may not
  terminate.
- With a shared preorder cursor, build left before right. Reversing
  the calls consumes roots in the wrong order.
- Increment `nextPreorder` exactly once per nonempty call. Empty
  children consume no value.
- Values need not be sorted and may include integer extremes. Inorder
  describes topology here, not search-tree order.
- Reject duplicates before assigning map positions. Silently replacing
  an earlier index destroys the uniqueness premise.
- Return nil with an error after any invalid split. Do not expose a
  partially constructed tree as a valid result.
- Do not mutate the traversal slices to mark consumed values. A local
  cursor and bounds preserve caller ownership.
- Recursive depth equals tree height. A 3,000-node chain is logically
  valid but materially deeper than a balanced 3,000-node tree.

##### When to choose it

Use this pattern when distinct node identifiers arrive as preorder
and inorder traversals and the actual child-link topology is needed.
The same partition invariant works for inorder plus postorder: consume
postorder from the end and construct the right subtree before the
left.

The index-map pattern also helps when a recursive decomposition
repeatedly locates a unique delimiter inside fixed original storage.
Half-open bounds avoid copying and make empty partitions explicit.

When not to choose it:

Do not claim a unique result when values repeat unless inputs include
stable node identities or another disambiguating rule. A value-to-one-
index map discards duplicate positions.

Preorder plus postorder does not uniquely identify a general binary
tree: a single child can be either left or right. Extra shape rules,
such as every internal node having two children, change that contract.
A preorder serialization with explicit nil markers can instead encode
the complete shape by itself.

Use an iterative reconstruction when untrusted input can form a chain
deep enough to exhaust recursion resources. If callers already own a
tree and need only another traversal, traverse it directly rather than
reconstructing equivalent nodes.

#### B.11.6 Lowest common ancestor (tree or ancestor table)

##### Problem and contract

The lowest common ancestor, or LCA, of two nodes is their deepest
shared ancestor. A node counts as its own ancestor, so the LCA of a
node and one of its descendants is that node.

This lesson answers the same identity-based query in two ways:

- a postorder search handles one or a few queries directly; and
- a binary-lifting table preprocesses a stable tree for many queries.

The input is a finite, acyclic, rooted binary tree whose non-root
nodes each have one parent. Values may repeat; target pointers, not
values, identify nodes. A query succeeds only when both non-nil
targets belong to the tree. Both methods return the original LCA
pointer and a presence boolean without changing the tree.

The one-shot function retains nothing after returning. The table
retains every node pointer and describes the topology at build time.
Callers must therefore keep those nodes alive and must not rewire the
tree while using that table.

Read [binary trees](#a71-binary-trees) for ancestor terminology and
[postorder traversal](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) for
child-before-parent control flow.

##### Mental model

The one-shot search visits children before deciding about their
parent. Each call returns a candidate LCA and how many distinct
targets its subtree contains. Normally two targets are needed. If
both arguments point to the same node, only one identity is needed.

If a child subtree already found every needed target, its candidate
is deeper than the current node and can return unchanged. Otherwise,
add the left and right counts, then add one for each target identity
matched by the current node. The first call on the return path whose
count reaches `needed` returns its own node as the LCA. A final count
below `needed` means at least one target is absent.

For repeated queries, preprocessing assigns every node an integer ID
and records its depth and parent. The ancestor table obeys:

```text
up[k][v] = the 2^k-th ancestor of node v
```

The root names itself as every ancestor beyond the top. Row zero
stores parents. Each later row doubles a jump:

```text
up[k][v] = up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]
```

There are `bits.Len(N)` rows for `N` nonempty-tree nodes. To query two
IDs, lift the deeper node by the binary digits of the depth
difference. If the IDs then match, that node is the LCA. Otherwise
scan jump rows from largest to smallest. Whenever the two proposed
ancestors differ, move both nodes there. The final nodes are distinct
children of their LCA, so their immediate parent is the answer.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use this tree. Labels are values, but queries hold node pointers.

```text
          3
        /   \
       5     1
      / \   / \
     6   2 0   8
        / \
       7   4
```

First run the one-shot query for nodes 5 and 4.

Initial state: `needed=2`; no subtree has reported a target.

1. Decision: search the left child of node 5. Leaf 6 matches neither
   target and returns count zero.
   After: node 5 has no target from its left subtree.
   Known correct: no ancestor strictly inside subtree 6 can answer.

2. Decision: search node 2. Leaf 7 returns zero; leaf 4 matches the
   second target and returns count one.
   After: node 2 propagates count one and no candidate.
   Known correct: subtree 2 contains node 4 but not node 5.

3. Decision: combine both child counts at node 5, then compare the
   current pointer with the targets. Node 5 matches the first target.
   After: the total reaches two, so node 5 becomes the candidate.
   Known correct: node 5 contains both targets, and neither child
   subtree does.

4. Decision: return the complete candidate to root 3 without searching
   root 3's right subtree.
   After: the query returns node 5 with `found=true`.
   Known correct: an ancestor above an already complete candidate
   cannot be lower than that candidate.

Now query the table for nodes 6 and 8. Both have depth two.

Initial state: the two IDs are distinct and need no depth lift.

1. Decision: test the largest jumps first. Every jump of two or more
   edges reaches root 3 for both nodes, so do not take those jumps.
   After: the working IDs still name 6 and 8.
   Known correct: jumping both onto the same ancestor would pass or
   land on the LCA instead of staying below it.

2. Decision: at row zero, the proposed parents are 5 and 1. They
   differ, so move the working IDs to 5 and 1.
   After: both working nodes have root 3 as their immediate parent.
   Known correct: 5 and 1 remain in different branches below the LCA.

3. Decision: return the immediate parent of either working node.
   After: the table returns node 3.
   Known correct: the working nodes differ, while their parents are
   equal; that common parent is the deepest shared ancestor.

Focused cases: querying 5 and descendant 4 returns 5 after depth
equalization makes both IDs equal. Querying the same node twice
returns that node. A nil target, an external pointer with a duplicate
value, or a query against an empty tree returns nil and false.

A value-based map is a counterexample when two nodes both store 7.
It merges distinct identities and may return the wrong branch. Both
implementations below key membership by `*treeNode` instead.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Lowest common ancestor (tree or
// ancestor table). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math/bits"
)

type treeNode struct {
	value int
	left  *treeNode
	right *treeNode
}

func lowestCommonAncestorOnce(
	root *treeNode,
	first *treeNode,
	second *treeNode,
) (*treeNode, bool) {
	// Compute common ancestor once from the state without mutating it.
	if first == nil || second == nil {
		return nil, false
	}

	needed := 2
	if first == second {
		needed = 1
	}
	var search func(*treeNode) (*treeNode, int)
	search = func(node *treeNode) (*treeNode, int) {
		if node == nil {
			return nil, 0
		}

		ancestor, leftFound := search(node.left)
		if leftFound == needed {
			return ancestor, leftFound
		}
		ancestor, rightFound := search(node.right)
		if rightFound == needed {
			return ancestor, rightFound
		}

		found := leftFound + rightFound
		if node == first {
			found++
		}
		if second != first && node == second {
			found++
		}
		if found == needed {
			return node, found
		}
		return nil, found
	}

	ancestor, found := search(root)
	return ancestor, found == needed
}

type ancestorTable struct {
	nodes []*treeNode
	ids   map[*treeNode]int
	depth []int
	up    [][]int
}

type pendingNode struct {
	node     *treeNode
	parentID int
	depth    int
}

func buildAncestorTable(root *treeNode) ancestorTable {
	// Build ancestor table in the order required by the lesson contract.
	table := ancestorTable{
		nodes: make([]*treeNode, 0),
		ids:   make(map[*treeNode]int),
		depth: make([]int, 0),
	}
	if root == nil {
		return table
	}

	parents := make([]int, 0)
	stack := []pendingNode{{node: root, parentID: -1}}
	for len(stack) > 0 {
		last := len(stack) - 1
		pending := stack[last]
		stack = stack[:last]

		id := len(table.nodes)
		table.ids[pending.node] = id
		table.nodes = append(table.nodes, pending.node)
		table.depth = append(table.depth, pending.depth)
		parents = append(parents, pending.parentID)

		childDepth := pending.depth + 1
		if pending.node.right != nil {
			stack = append(stack, pendingNode{
				node:     pending.node.right,
				parentID: id,
				depth:    childDepth,
			})
		}
		if pending.node.left != nil {
			stack = append(stack, pendingNode{
				node:     pending.node.left,
				parentID: id,
				depth:    childDepth,
			})
		}
	}

	levelCount := bits.Len(uint(len(table.nodes)))
	table.up = make([][]int, levelCount)
	for level := range table.up {
		table.up[level] = make([]int, len(table.nodes))
	}
	for id, parentID := range parents {
		if parentID == -1 {
			parentID = id
		}
		table.up[0][id] = parentID
	}
	for level := 1; level < levelCount; level++ {
		for id := range table.nodes {
			halfway := table.up[level-1][id]
			table.up[level][id] = table.up[level-1][halfway]
		}
	}
	return table
}

func (table ancestorTable) lowestCommonAncestor(
	first *treeNode,
	second *treeNode,
) (*treeNode, bool) {
	// Compute common ancestor from the state without mutating it.
	firstID, firstExists := table.ids[first]
	secondID, secondExists := table.ids[second]
	if !firstExists || !secondExists {
		return nil, false
	}

	if table.depth[firstID] < table.depth[secondID] {
		firstID, secondID = secondID, firstID
	}
	distance := table.depth[firstID] - table.depth[secondID]
	for level := 0; distance > 0; level++ {
		if distance&1 == 1 {
			firstID = table.up[level][firstID]
		}
		distance >>= 1
	}
	if firstID == secondID {
		return table.nodes[firstID], true
	}

	for level := len(table.up) - 1; level >= 0; level-- {
		firstUp := table.up[level][firstID]
		secondUp := table.up[level][secondID]
		if firstUp != secondUp {
			firstID = firstUp
			secondID = secondUp
		}
	}
	return table.nodes[table.up[0][firstID]], true
}

func resultValue(node *treeNode, found bool) any {
	// Keep result value in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if !found {
		return "not found"
	}
	return node.value
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	nodes := make([]*treeNode, 9)
	for index, value := range []int{
		3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, 7, 4,
	} {
		nodes[index] = &treeNode{value: value}
	}
	nodes[0].left, nodes[0].right = nodes[1], nodes[2]
	nodes[1].left, nodes[1].right = nodes[3], nodes[4]
	nodes[2].left, nodes[2].right = nodes[5], nodes[6]
	nodes[4].left, nodes[4].right = nodes[7], nodes[8]

	table := buildAncestorTable(nodes[0])
	queries := [][2]*treeNode{
		{nodes[1], nodes[2]},
		{nodes[1], nodes[8]},
		{nodes[7], nodes[8]},
		{nodes[3], nodes[6]},
	}
	for _, query := range queries {
		once, onceFound := lowestCommonAncestorOnce(
			nodes[0],
			query[0],
			query[1],
		)
		indexed, indexedFound := table.lowestCommonAncestor(
			query[0],
			query[1],
		)
		fmt.Println(
			resultValue(once, onceFound),
			resultValue(indexed, indexedFound),
		)
	}

	missing := &treeNode{value: 5}
	_, onceFound := lowestCommonAncestorOnce(
		nodes[0],
		nodes[1],
		missing,
	)
	_, indexedFound := table.lowestCommonAncestor(
		nodes[1],
		missing,
	)
	fmt.Println(onceFound, indexedFound)
}
```

Output:

```text
3 3
5 5
2 2
3 3
false false
```

The program imports `fmt` and `math/bits`. The first column comes from
the one-shot search and the second from the table. An external node
with value 5 demonstrates that equality of values is not membership.

##### Why it works

For the one-shot method, maintain this invariant: a call's count is
the number of required target identities in that subtree, and a
non-nil candidate is the lowest node in that subtree containing all
of them. A nil subtree has count zero.

Assume the child calls satisfy the invariant. If one child already
contains every target, its LCA is strictly no higher than the current
node, so returning it preserves lowestness. Otherwise neither child
contains all targets. Adding their disjoint counts and current-node
matches gives the exact count for the larger subtree. When that sum
first reaches `needed`, the current node is the only place the targets
can meet and is therefore their LCA. At the root, a short count proves
that a target is absent.

For the table, induction on `k` proves `up[k][v]` is the `2^k`-th
ancestor: row zero is the parent, and two `2^(k-1)` jumps compose one
`2^k` jump. Binary decomposition therefore lifts the deeper query
node by exactly the depth difference without passing the shallower
depth.

After equalization, matching IDs are already the LCA. Otherwise the
descending row scan maintains two facts: the working nodes have the
same depth, and their LCA is strictly above both. A jump is taken only
when its destinations differ, so it never moves either node onto or
above the common ancestor. Considering every power from large to small
leaves the nodes as high as possible while still distinct. Their
parents must then be equal, and that parent is the LCA.

The recursive search descends through child links in a finite tree.
Preprocessing pushes each node once. Each query loop examines a finite
number of table rows, so both methods terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the node count, `H` the tree height in nodes, and `Q` the
number of queries. A one-shot query has Theta(1) best-case time for
nil targets or a matching singleton and Theta(N) worst-case time. It
may short-circuit after finding both targets, but there is no useful
input-independent average guarantee. Its recursive auxiliary space is
O(H).

Building the table enumerates `N` nodes, then fills Theta(log N) rows.
With expected constant-time Go map operations, it takes
Theta(N log N) time and retains Theta(N log N) integer table entries,
plus Theta(N) node, ID, and depth storage. Go does not promise a
strict worst-case map-operation bound. The iterative build stack holds
O(H) pending nodes. Empty input builds an empty table in Theta(1).

A table query uses expected Theta(1) best-case time for a same-node
query and expected Theta(log N) worst-case time for the row scan. Its
extra space is Theta(1), and there is no useful shape-independent
average guarantee. Across `Q` queries, direct search costs O(QN),
while the table costs expected
Theta(N log N + Q log N) in the worst case.

A balanced binary tree has `H` in Theta(log N); a chain has `H=N`.
The table build is iterative and avoids recursive depth, while the
one-shot function may exceed practical call-stack resources on a
long chain.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A node is its own ancestor. Querying a node with its descendant, or
  with itself, can return that node.
- Compare target pointers, not values. Duplicate values may identify
  different nodes.
- The common recursive shortcut that returns the first target found
  assumes both targets exist. Carry counts when absence is possible.
- When both target arguments are the same pointer, require one match,
  not two visits to the same node.
- Nil or external targets return nil and false. An external pointer
  does not become a member by sharing a stored value.
- Equalize depths before lifting both nodes. Otherwise they can never
  meet at corresponding ancestors.
- `up[k][v]` uses two row-`k-1` jumps. Advancing only one side of the
  recurrence stores the wrong distance.
- Scan query rows from largest to smallest. Small-first jumps can stop
  below the highest safe jump and complicate correctness.
- Jump both IDs only while their proposed ancestors differ. Jumping
  onto a common ancestor can pass the "just below LCA" state.
- After the descending scan, return the immediate parent, not either
  still-distinct working node.
- Making the root its own parent prevents missing-index sentinels from
  leaking into table lookups above the root.
- Allocate enough rows for the largest possible depth. `bits.Len(N)`
  covers every depth from zero through `N-1` in an `N`-node tree.
- The table intentionally retains node pointers. Account for that
  lifetime and do not query it concurrently with topology mutation.
- A chain gives the recursive method depth `N`. Use an iterative
  parent walk or preprocessing when stack depth is untrusted.
- Cycles never finish and shared children violate unique parent IDs.
  Both are outside the rooted-tree contract.

##### When to choose it

Use the postorder search for one query, a small number of queries, or
when retaining an index is undesirable. Its presence count is useful
when the problem does not guarantee that both targets exist.

Use binary lifting when one rooted tree is stable and many ancestor or
LCA queries must be answered. The same table can jump a node upward by
any requested distance represented in binary.

For many queries with stricter query-time requirements, an Euler tour
plus a range-minimum structure can support other LCA tradeoffs. For a
binary search tree, key ordering can guide a simpler root-down LCA
search; these methods deliberately make no search-tree assumption.

When not to choose it:

Do not build Theta(N log N) state for one cheap query. Conversely, do
not repeat a full-tree search for a large batch against an unchanged
tree.

Do not reuse an ancestor table after changing a child link, root, or
node membership. Its IDs, depths, and jumps describe the old topology;
rebuild it after structural changes. Value-only targets are also
insufficient when values can repeat.

These functions assume a tree. A directed acyclic graph can have
multiple parents and a different notion of lowest common ancestor;
cycles also invalidate traversal and preprocessing. Validate such
structures with graph-specific state and semantics.

[B.11.1 Depth-first traversal](

#b292-binary-lifting-ancestor-table) develops the table technique in

`medium_leetcode_0236_lowest_common_ancestor_of_a_binary_tree.go`
under `dsa/problems/`. The canonical [LeetCode 236 statement](
../REFERENCE_LINKS.md#leetcode-source-0236) specifies that a node is

[lowest common ancestor](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/lowestcommon.html). The University
