```go
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

const unreachableCost int64 = -1

type weightedEdge struct {
	to   string
	cost int64
}

type aStarResult struct {
	cost  int64
	path  []string
	found bool
}

type aStarItem struct {
	vertex         string
	costFromStart  int64
	estimatedTotal int64
	insertionOrder int
}

type aStarHeap []aStarItem

func (frontier aStarHeap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(frontier)
}

func (frontier aStarHeap) Less(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	if frontier[first].estimatedTotal !=
		frontier[second].estimatedTotal {
		return frontier[first].estimatedTotal <
			frontier[second].estimatedTotal
	}
	return frontier[first].insertionOrder <
		frontier[second].insertionOrder
}

func (frontier aStarHeap) Swap(first int, second int) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	frontier[first], frontier[second] =
		frontier[second], frontier[first]
}

func (frontier *aStarHeap) Push(value any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	item := value.(aStarItem)
	*frontier = append(*frontier, item)
}

func (frontier *aStarHeap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	items := *frontier
	lastIndex := len(items) - 1
	item := items[lastIndex]
	items[lastIndex] = aStarItem{}
	*frontier = items[:lastIndex]
	return item
}

func validateAStarInput(
	vertexOrder []string,
	adjacencyByVertex map[string][]weightedEdge,
	heuristicByVertex map[string]int64,
	start string,
	target string,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the a star input contract before mutation.
	// Build the exact vertex set first so duplicate labels cannot make
	// later adjacency and heuristic checks ambiguous.
	vertexSet := make(map[string]bool, len(vertexOrder))
	for vertexIndex, vertex := range vertexOrder {
		if vertexSet[vertex] {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"vertex %q repeats at index %d",
				vertex,
				vertexIndex,
			)
		}
		vertexSet[vertex] = true
	}
	// Every listed vertex needs one row, and every stored edge needs a
	// listed endpoint and a nonnegative cost.
	for _, vertex := range vertexOrder {
		edges, exists := adjacencyByVertex[vertex]
		if !exists {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"vertex %q has no adjacency row",
				vertex,
			)
		}
		for _, edge := range edges {
			if !vertexSet[edge.to] {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %q -> %q has an invalid endpoint",
					vertex,
					edge.to,
				)
			}
			if edge.cost < 0 {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %q -> %q has negative cost %d",
					vertex,
					edge.to,
					edge.cost,
				)
			}
		}
	}
	// Reject extra adjacency rows that do not belong to the vertex set.
	for vertex := range adjacencyByVertex {
		if !vertexSet[vertex] {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"adjacency row %q has no listed vertex",
				vertex,
			)
		}
	}
	// Both public endpoints must name vertices before search can start.
	if !vertexSet[start] {
		return fmt.Errorf("start %q is not a vertex", start)
	}
	if !vertexSet[target] {
		return fmt.Errorf("target %q is not a vertex", target)
	}

	// Finally require one nonnegative heuristic estimate per vertex.
	for _, vertex := range vertexOrder {
		estimate, exists := heuristicByVertex[vertex]
		if !exists {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"vertex %q has no heuristic",
				vertex,
			)
		}
		if estimate < 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"vertex %q has negative heuristic %d",
				vertex,
				estimate,
			)
		}
	}
	for vertex := range heuristicByVertex {
		if !vertexSet[vertex] {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"heuristic %q has no listed vertex",
				vertex,
			)
		}
	}
	if heuristicByVertex[target] != 0 {
		return fmt.Errorf("target heuristic must be zero")
	}

	// Consistency makes estimated totals nondecreasing along edges.
	for _, from := range vertexOrder {
		for _, edge := range adjacencyByVertex[from] {
			remaining := heuristicByVertex[edge.to]
			if edge.cost > math.MaxInt64-remaining {
				continue
			}
			allowed := edge.cost + remaining
			if heuristicByVertex[from] > allowed {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"heuristic is inconsistent at %q -> %q",
					from,
					edge.to,
				)
			}
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func checkedNonnegativeSum(
	first int64,
	second int64,
) (int64, bool) {
	// Compute nonnegative sum with an overflow check instead of
	// wrapping.
	if first > math.MaxInt64-second {
		return 0, false
	}
	return first + second, true
}

func reconstructAStarPath(
	parentByVertex map[string]string,
	vertexCount int,
	start string,
	target string,
	cost int64,
) (*aStarResult, error) {
	// Derive a star path from the validated state described above.
	reversed := []string{target}
	for vertex := target; vertex != start; {
		parent, exists := parentByVertex[vertex]
		if !exists {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"missing parent for %q",
				vertex,
			)
		}
		vertex = parent
		reversed = append(reversed, vertex)
		if len(reversed) > vertexCount {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("parent chain contains a cycle")
		}
	}

	path := make([]string, len(reversed))
	for index, vertex := range reversed {
		path[len(reversed)-1-index] = vertex
	}
	return &aStarResult{
		cost:  cost,
		path:  path,
		found: true,
	}, nil
}

func aStarShortestPath(
	vertexOrder []string,
	adjacencyByVertex map[string][]weightedEdge,
	heuristicByVertex map[string]int64,
	start string,
	target string,
) (*aStarResult, error) {
	// Compute the requested ordered or extreme result.
	if err := validateAStarInput(
		vertexOrder,
		adjacencyByVertex,
		heuristicByVertex,
		start,
		target,
	); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	if start == target {
		return &aStarResult{
			cost:  0,
			path:  []string{start},
			found: true,
		}, nil
	}

	bestCostByVertex := map[string]int64{start: 0}
	parentByVertex := make(map[string]string)
	settledByVertex := make(map[string]bool)
	frontier := aStarHeap{
		{
			vertex:         start,
			costFromStart:  0,
			estimatedTotal: heuristicByVertex[start],
			insertionOrder: 0,
		},
	}
	nextInsertionOrder := 1
	heap.Init(&frontier)

	for frontier.Len() > 0 {
		item := heap.Pop(&frontier).(aStarItem)
		knownCost, reached := bestCostByVertex[item.vertex]
		if !reached || item.costFromStart != knownCost {
			continue
		}
		if settledByVertex[item.vertex] {
			continue
		}
		settledByVertex[item.vertex] = true
		if item.vertex == target {
			return reconstructAStarPath(
				parentByVertex,
				len(vertexOrder),
				start,
				target,
				item.costFromStart,
			)
		}

		for _, edge := range adjacencyByVertex[item.vertex] {
			if settledByVertex[edge.to] {
				continue
			}
			candidate, representable := checkedNonnegativeSum(
				item.costFromStart,
				edge.cost,
			)
			knownDestination, destinationReached :=
				bestCostByVertex[edge.to]
			if !representable {
				if destinationReached {
					continue
				}
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"path cost overflows at %q -> %q",
					item.vertex,
					edge.to,
				)
			}
			if destinationReached &&
				candidate >= knownDestination {
				continue
			}
			estimatedTotal, representable :=
				checkedNonnegativeSum(
					candidate,
					heuristicByVertex[edge.to],
				)
			if !representable {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"estimated total overflows at %q",
					edge.to,
				)
			}

			// Strict improvement leaves any older heap item stale.
			bestCostByVertex[edge.to] = candidate
			parentByVertex[edge.to] = item.vertex
			heap.Push(&frontier, aStarItem{
				vertex:         edge.to,
				costFromStart:  candidate,
				estimatedTotal: estimatedTotal,
				insertionOrder: nextInsertionOrder,
			})
			nextInsertionOrder++
		}
	}
	return &aStarResult{
		cost:  unreachableCost,
		path:  make([]string, 0),
		found: false,
	}, nil
}

func zeroHeuristic(vertexOrder []string) map[string]int64 {
	// Keep zero heuristic in one helper so callers use one rule.
	estimates := make(map[string]int64, len(vertexOrder))
	for _, vertex := range vertexOrder {
		estimates[vertex] = 0
	}
	return estimates
}

func printAStarResult(result *aStarResult, err error) {
	// Expose a star result in logical order without changing source.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(result.cost, result.path, result.found)
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	vertexOrder := []string{
		"S", "A", "B", "C", "D", "T", "X",
	}
	adjacencyByVertex := map[string][]weightedEdge{
		"S": {{to: "A", cost: 4}, {to: "B", cost: 1}},
		"A": {{to: "C", cost: 2}, {to: "T", cost: 9}},
		"B": {{to: "A", cost: 1}, {to: "D", cost: 2}},
		"C": {{to: "T", cost: 2}},
		"D": {{to: "T", cost: 10}},
		"T": {},
		"X": {},
	}
	heuristicByVertex := map[string]int64{
		"S": 6,
		"A": 4,
		"B": 5,
		"C": 2,
		"D": 10,
		"T": 0,
		"X": 0,
	}

	result, err := aStarShortestPath(
		vertexOrder,
		adjacencyByVertex,
		heuristicByVertex,
		"S",
		"T",
	)
	printAStarResult(result, err)
	result, err = aStarShortestPath(
		vertexOrder,
		adjacencyByVertex,
		zeroHeuristic(vertexOrder),
		"A",
		"A",
	)
	printAStarResult(result, err)
	result, err = aStarShortestPath(
		vertexOrder,
		adjacencyByVertex,
		heuristicByVertex,
		"S",
		"X",
	)
	printAStarResult(result, err)

	invalidHeuristic := zeroHeuristic(vertexOrder)
	invalidHeuristic["A"] = 100
	_, heuristicErr := aStarShortestPath(
		vertexOrder,
		adjacencyByVertex,
		invalidHeuristic,
		"S",
		"T",
	)
	_, overflowErr := aStarShortestPath(
		[]string{"S", "A", "T"},
		map[string][]weightedEdge{
			"S": {{to: "A", cost: math.MaxInt64}},
			"A": {{to: "T", cost: 1}},
			"T": {},
		},
		map[string]int64{"S": 0, "A": 0, "T": 0},
		"S",
		"T",
	)
	fmt.Println(heuristicErr != nil, overflowErr != nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
6 [S B A C T] true
0 [A] true
-1 [] false
true true
```

The function validates and reads the caller's maps and slices but does
not mutate or retain them. The returned path owns its slice. Strings
may share immutable backing data with the input, which is normal for
Go strings. A caller that mutates a shared map concurrently must still
synchronize access or provide a snapshot.

##### Why it works

Every finite `g(v)` stored by the algorithm is the cost of a real path
from the start. This is initially true for the empty path to the
start. A relaxation extends an already real path by one real edge, so
the property is preserved. Parent assignments record those
extensions.

Consistency makes estimated totals monotone along an edge. If a route
reaches `u` with cost `g(u)` and continues through `(u,v)`, then:

```text
g(u) + h(u) <= g(u) + cost(u,v) + h(v)
```

Therefore a route cannot acquire a smaller lower bound merely by
moving one step. Because `h(target)=0`, a target heap item's `f` is
its actual discovered path cost.

To see why a settled cost is final, suppose the removed current vertex
`v` had a cheaper path that had not been recorded. On that cheaper
path, take the first unsettled vertex `x`; its predecessor was already
settled. Scanning that predecessor offered x a `g` no greater than the
path prefix. Repeated consistency along the remaining path from x to v
gives `h(x) <= suffix cost + h(v)`. Therefore x has a current heap key
strictly below `g(v)+h(v)`. The heap could not choose v first. This
contradiction proves that v's stored cost is final, so no settled
vertex needs to reopen.

When the target is removed, the same argument compares its actual
cost, `f(target)=g(target)`, with the lower bound of every pending
route. No pending route can produce a cheaper target path, so the
returned cost is optimal.

Only strict cost improvements push items. Each settled adjacency row
is scanned once, so finitely many edges cause finitely many pushes and
pops. The loop therefore terminates. Each parent is assigned while an
already settled vertex relaxes an unsettled one. Along the final
parent chain, settlement times strictly decrease, so the chain cannot
cycle; the explicit vertex-count bound also detects a broken
invariant.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `V` be the number of vertices, `A` the number of directed edges,
`R` the number of vertices actually settled, `A_R` the edges scanned
from them, `I` the number of heap insertions, and `L` the number of
vertices in the returned path. Go map access is expected `O(1)`.

On valid input, full validation costs `Theta(V + A)` because it checks
every vertex, edge, map key, heuristic, and consistency inequality.
An invalid map with extra keys also has work linear in those supplied
keys. During search, each settled row is scanned once. Each strict
relaxation pushes once, so `I <= A_R + 1`. A push or pop costs
`O(log I)`, including stale items. Search work is therefore
`O(R + A_R + I log I)` after validation, and total work is
`O(V + A + I log I)`. A common graph-only bound is
`O((V + A) log(A + 1))` for this lazy heap.

The fixed validation pass means even an excellent heuristic leaves the
whole function with a best-case lower bound of `Theta(V + A)`. The
heuristic can still greatly reduce settled rows, scanned edges, and
heap operations. With `h=0`, behavior is Dijkstra. A weak or
misleading but consistent heuristic can settle most reachable
vertices, so A* does not improve the asymptotic worst case. There is
no useful average case without a probability model for graphs and
heuristics.

The cost, parent, and settled maps use `O(V)` entries. The lazy heap
can hold `O(I)`, which is `O(A)` in the worst case. Excluding the
input and returned path, auxiliary memory is `O(V + A)` in the worst
case. Path reconstruction temporarily and finally uses `O(L)` space;
the final slice is output space. The printed output also takes
`Theta(L)` work.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Order by `g+h`, not by h alone. Ordering only by h is greedy
  best-first search and need not return a cheapest path.
- Relax with `g(current)+edge.cost`, not with the current `f`. The
  heuristic is a priority estimate, not cost already paid.
- Never overestimate under the admissibility contract. A value that
  merely points in a useful direction can make early target removal
  return a nonoptimal path.
- Check consistency if settled vertices never reopen. Admissibility
  alone does not justify this implementation's settled set.
- Stop when the target's current item is removed, not when the target
  is first discovered or pushed.
- Mark a vertex settled on current removal, not on insertion. A later
  route may strictly improve its tentative cost before removal.
- Skip lazy stale items. Without comparing the captured `g` with the
  cost map, old entries can rescan a row or corrupt parent reasoning.
- Update only on a strict improvement. Equal-cost updates can create
  needless duplicates and unstable parent choices around zero cycles.
- Validate `h(target)=0`. Otherwise the target key is not its actual
  route cost at the stopping point used by the proof.
- Distinguish a missing heuristic key from a stored zero. A one-value
  map lookup silently turns absence into zero.
- Check both `g+edge.cost` and `g+h` for overflow before storing or
  ordering them.
- Zero-cost edges, self-loops, cycles, and parallel edges are valid.
  Strict relaxation and settled checks must still ensure termination.
- Bound parent reconstruction and reject a missing link. Returning a
  partial path would hide a violated internal invariant.
- Validate before returning the zero-edge `start == target` result so
  malformed graph data is not silently accepted.
- The empty string is a valid vertex name. Map presence, not a string
  sentinel, determines whether it exists.
- Empty `vertexOrder` has no valid query. A nil adjacency row is valid
  for a listed vertex, while an absent row is not.
- Preserve deterministic ties when exact path output matters. This
  example uses adjacency order plus a heap insertion counter instead
  of relying on randomized Go map iteration.
- Unreachable is a successful search result with cost `-1`, nonnil
  empty path, and false. Invalid input returns nil and an error.
- Synchronize input maps shared with concurrent writers. Read-only
  algorithm code does not make concurrent map mutation safe.

##### When to choose it

Use A* when all of these are true:

- The query asks for one known target rather than every distance.
- Edge costs are nonnegative.
- A cheap, meaningful lower bound to the target is available.
- The graph or implicit state space is large enough that avoiding
  expansions matters.
- The heuristic can meet the consistency contract, or the algorithm
  is deliberately extended with correct reopen logic.

Grid routing is the standard example. With four-directional movement
and unit costs, Manhattan distance is consistent. Spatial routing can
use straight-line distance when no edge costs less than physical
distance. Puzzle search can use a lower bound on remaining moves. The
heuristic must be proved against the actual move and cost model rather
than chosen only because it seems correlated with progress.

When not to choose it:

Use Dijkstra when all distances from one source are needed, many
targets will reuse one traversal, or no useful heuristic is available.
With `h=0`, A* is correct but offers no search advantage.

Do not use this implementation with negative edges. Dijkstra's settled
invariant and A*'s proof both fail. Use Bellman-Ford or a problem-
specific method that supports negative costs and detects reachable
negative cycles.

Do not pass an admissible but inconsistent heuristic to an
implementation that never reopens settled vertices. Either derive a
consistent heuristic or use an A* variant whose state, stopping rule,
and proof explicitly support reopens. Changing the target usually also
changes `h`; a heuristic proved for one target is not automatically
valid for another.

Avoid a heuristic whose computation costs more than the expansions it
saves. For small graphs, the cost map and heap may be simpler and fast
enough without domain estimates.

Related material:

[A.8.1 Min-heaps and max-heaps](
#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) explains the heap invariant and Go
interface used by the frontier. [B.13.3 Dijkstra](
#b133-dijkstra-heap-or-scan-distance-array) owns the nonnegative
relaxation and lazy-entry pattern; A* changes the heap key from `g` to
`g+h`. [B.13.1 Unweighted BFS](
#b131-unweighted-bfs-queue-and-distance-array) is preferable when
every edge has equal cost and no heuristic is needed. [B.13.8
Bidirectional BFS](
#b138-bidirectional-bfs-two-frontiers-and-maps) reduces an unweighted
one-target search from both ends instead of using a cost lower bound.

Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael's original [A* paper](
https://doi.org/10.1109/TSSC.1968.300136) develops the formal
optimality conditions behind the heuristic order. Go's
[`container/heap` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap)
defines the interface and operation costs used by the example.

#### B.13.10 Bottleneck paths (heap or disjoint sets)

##### Problem and contract

Some routes are judged by their worst edge rather than by the sum of
all edges. Given an undirected graph with nonnegative edge costs, a
start, and a target, find the smallest possible value of the largest
edge on any route between them.

For a path with edge costs `[3,4,6,5]`, the **bottleneck cost** is 6.
The **minimum bottleneck path**, also called a **minimax path**, is a
path whose bottleneck is as small as possible. The output in this
lesson is that numeric cost, not the path itself.

This differs from ordinary shortest paths. A route with edges `[1,8]`
has total cost 9 and bottleneck 8, while `[5,5]` has total cost 10 and
bottleneck 5. Dijkstra with addition prefers the first route; a
minimax query must prefer the second.

The input contract is:

- `vertexOrder` lists every string vertex exactly once. The empty
  string is a valid name.
- Each `undirectedWeightedEdge` names two listed endpoints and one
  nonnegative `int64` cost. An undirected edge is listed once.
- Self-loops, parallel edges, zero costs, isolated vertices, and
  `math.MaxInt64` costs are valid.
- Both query endpoints must be listed. An empty graph has no valid
  query.

A reachable query returns the minimum bottleneck and `found=true`.
The valid zero-edge query from a vertex to itself has cost zero. A
disconnected pair returns cost `-1` and false. Because valid costs are
nonnegative, that sentinel cannot collide with an answer. Invalid
input returns the zero result and an error before either algorithm
searches.

The example gives two algorithms the same contract:

- a Dijkstra-like heap search that replaces addition with maximum;
- a sorted-edge threshold sweep using disjoint sets.

Both validate and read the input without mutating or retaining it.
The set version sorts an owned edge copy. Unsynchronized mutation of
shared input while either function reads it is outside the contract.

Read [Dijkstra](
#b133-dijkstra-heap-or-scan-distance-array) for lazy relaxation and
[disjoint sets](#a111-parent-and-size-arrays) for incremental
undirected connectivity.

##### Mental model

The heap version stores `bestCostByVertex[v]`, the smallest bottleneck
of any discovered route from start to `v`. Read
`bestCostByVertex["A"] == 4` as: "a discovered route reaches A, and
no discovered route to A has a largest edge below 4." Absence from
the map means not yet reached.

When a settled route of bottleneck `current` crosses an edge of cost
`edge`, the extended route has:

```text
candidate = max(current, edge)
```

The larger value is the worst edge seen so far. If `candidate`
strictly improves the destination, store it and push a new heap item.
The heap removes the smallest tentative bottleneck. Older items remain
as lazy duplicates and are skipped when their captured cost differs
from the map. The target is final when its current item is removed.

The start has bottleneck zero because every edge cost is nonnegative.
No addition occurs, so even `math.MaxInt64` is safe and no arithmetic
overflow is possible.

The disjoint-set version uses the threshold interpretation:

```text
There is a route with bottleneck at most W
exactly when start and target are connected
using only edges whose cost is at most W.
```

Sort an owned edge copy by increasing cost. Begin with one disjoint
set per vertex, then union each edge's endpoints. Immediately after an
edge of cost W first connects start and target, W is the answer. All
processed edges cost at most W, while the pair was disconnected before
the decisive union.

The heap approach builds adjacency because it explores outward from
the start. The set approach keeps the edge list because it processes
global thresholds. Disjoint sets do not retain an actual route; they
answer only whether the threshold graph is connected.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use vertices `S, A, B, C, T, X`. X is isolated. The undirected edges
are deliberately not in cost order:

```text
S-A(8) A-T(9) S-B(3) B-C(10)
B-A(4) C-T(5) A-C(6)
```

The required answer from S to T is 6, witnessed by
`S-B-A-C-T` with edge costs `[3,4,6,5]`.

Heap trace:

Initial state: `best[S]=0`; the heap contains `(S:0)`; no other vertex
has a discovered route.

1. Decision: remove current S at cost 0. Extend over `S-A(8)` and
   `S-B(3)`, taking the maximum with zero.
   After: `best[A]=8`, `best[B]=3`; heap priorities are
   `[(B:3),(A:8)]`.
   Known correct: both stored values describe real one-edge routes,
   and B has the smallest tentative bottleneck.

2. Decision: remove B at 3. `B-A(4)` gives
   `max(3,4)=4`, improving A from 8. `B-C(10)` first reaches C at 10.
   After: current entries are `A:4` and `C:10`; old `A:8` is stale.
   Known correct: route `S-B-A` has bottleneck 4, and no unsettled
   discovered vertex has a value below 4.

3. Decision: remove A at 4. `A-C(6)` improves C to 6, and `A-T(9)`
   first reaches T at 9. Edges back to settled S and B are skipped.
   After: current entries include `C:6` and `T:9`; `A:8` and `C:10`
   are stale.
   Known correct: `S-B-A-C` has bottleneck 6, while the known route
   to T has bottleneck 9.

4. Decision: remove C at 6. Crossing `C-T(5)` gives
   `max(6,5)=6`, so T improves from 9 to 6.
   After: current T is `(T:6)`; old `(T:9)` is stale.
   Known correct: the full route `S-B-A-C-T` has largest edge 6.

5. Decision: remove current T at 6 and stop.
   After: return `{cost:6, found:true}` without removing stale items.
   Known correct: every pending route has tentative bottleneck at
   least 6, so none can produce an answer below 6.

Disjoint-set trace:

Initial state: the sorted costs are `3,4,5,6,8,9,10`; every vertex is
its own component; S and T are disconnected.

1. Decision: process `S-B(3)` and union its endpoints.
   After: component `{S,B}` exists; all other vertices are separate.
   Known correct: the threshold-3 graph does not connect S to T.

2. Decision: process `B-A(4)` and merge A into S and B's component.
   After: `{S,B,A}` is one component; T remains separate.
   Known correct: no route using only edges of cost at most 4 reaches
   T.

3. Decision: process `C-T(5)` and union C with T.
   After: components include `{S,B,A}` and `{C,T}`.
   Known correct: the threshold-5 graph still separates the query
   endpoints, so every S-to-T route has an edge above 5.

4. Decision: process `A-C(6)`. It merges the two components, so check
   S and T immediately.
   After: S and T share a root; return cost 6.
   Known correct: processed edges supply `S-B-A-C-T`, while the
   threshold-5 state proved that no smaller bottleneck can work.

Focused cases expose the remaining branches:

- A valid query from A to A returns zero after complete validation.
- S to isolated X exhausts the heap or all edges and returns
  `{-1,false}`.
- Parallel edges of costs 5 and 0 let a route use the zero-cost edge.
  Strict improvement keeps the numeric answer stable.
- Self-loops never join different components and cannot lower the
  start's zero value.
- A single edge of cost `math.MaxInt64` returns that exact value; the
  algorithms compare costs but never add them.
- A negative cost, unknown endpoint, duplicate vertex, or missing
  query endpoint is rejected before `start == target` can return.

The `[1,8]` versus `[5,5]` counterexample identifies a common wrong
algorithm. Adding edge costs makes the first route win at 9. The first
incorrect decision is using `current + edge` during relaxation. The
bottleneck contract requires `max(current, edge)`, which gives 8 for
the first route and 5 for the second.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Bottleneck paths (heap or disjoint
// sets). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
	"sort"
)

const unreachableBottleneck int64 = -1

type undirectedWeightedEdge struct {
	first  string
	second string
	cost   int64
}

type bottleneckResult struct {
	cost  int64
	found bool
}

func validateBottleneckInput(
	vertexOrder []string,
	edges []undirectedWeightedEdge,
	start string,
	target string,
) (map[string]int, error) {
	// Reject input outside the bottleneck input contract before
	// mutation.
	indexByVertex := make(map[string]int, len(vertexOrder))
	for index, vertex := range vertexOrder {
		if _, exists := indexByVertex[vertex]; exists {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"vertex %q repeats at index %d",
				vertex,
				index,
			)
		}
		indexByVertex[vertex] = index
	}
	for edgeIndex, edge := range edges {
		if _, exists := indexByVertex[edge.first]; !exists {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d has invalid endpoint %q",
				edgeIndex,
				edge.first,
			)
		}
		if _, exists := indexByVertex[edge.second]; !exists {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d has invalid endpoint %q",
				edgeIndex,
				edge.second,
			)
		}
		if edge.cost < 0 {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"edge %d has negative cost %d",
				edgeIndex,
				edge.cost,
			)
		}
	}
	if _, exists := indexByVertex[start]; !exists {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("start %q is not a vertex", start)
	}
	if _, exists := indexByVertex[target]; !exists {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("target %q is not a vertex", target)
	}
	return indexByVertex, nil
}

func maxInt64(first int64, second int64) int64 {
	// Keep max int64 in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if first > second {
		return first
	}
	return second
}

type bottleneckNeighbor struct {
	vertex string
	cost   int64
}

type bottleneckItem struct {
	vertex string
	cost   int64
}

type bottleneckHeap []bottleneckItem

func (frontier bottleneckHeap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(frontier)
}

func (frontier bottleneckHeap) Less(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	if frontier[first].cost != frontier[second].cost {
		return frontier[first].cost < frontier[second].cost
	}
	return frontier[first].vertex < frontier[second].vertex
}

func (frontier bottleneckHeap) Swap(first int, second int) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	frontier[first], frontier[second] =
		frontier[second], frontier[first]
}

func (frontier *bottleneckHeap) Push(value any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	item := value.(bottleneckItem)
	*frontier = append(*frontier, item)
}

func (frontier *bottleneckHeap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	items := *frontier
	lastIndex := len(items) - 1
	item := items[lastIndex]
	items[lastIndex] = bottleneckItem{}
	*frontier = items[:lastIndex]
	return item
}

func buildUndirectedAdjacency(
	vertexOrder []string,
	edges []undirectedWeightedEdge,
) map[string][]bottleneckNeighbor {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	adjacencyByVertex := make(
		map[string][]bottleneckNeighbor,
		len(vertexOrder),
	)
	for _, vertex := range vertexOrder {
		adjacencyByVertex[vertex] = nil
	}
	for _, edge := range edges {
		adjacencyByVertex[edge.first] = append(
			adjacencyByVertex[edge.first],
			bottleneckNeighbor{
				vertex: edge.second,
				cost:   edge.cost,
			},
		)
		adjacencyByVertex[edge.second] = append(
			adjacencyByVertex[edge.second],
			bottleneckNeighbor{
				vertex: edge.first,
				cost:   edge.cost,
			},
		)
	}
	return adjacencyByVertex
}

func minimumBottleneckWithHeap(
	vertexOrder []string,
	edges []undirectedWeightedEdge,
	start string,
	target string,
) (bottleneckResult, error) {
	// Compute bottleneck with heap from the state without mutating it.
	if _, err := validateBottleneckInput(
		vertexOrder,
		edges,
		start,
		target,
	); err != nil {
		return bottleneckResult{}, err
	}
	if start == target {
		return bottleneckResult{cost: 0, found: true}, nil
	}

	adjacencyByVertex := buildUndirectedAdjacency(
		vertexOrder,
		edges,
	)
	// A stored value is the best discovered route bottleneck.
	bestCostByVertex := map[string]int64{start: 0}
	settledByVertex := make(map[string]bool)
	frontier := bottleneckHeap{{vertex: start, cost: 0}}
	heap.Init(&frontier)

	for frontier.Len() > 0 {
		item := heap.Pop(&frontier).(bottleneckItem)
		// Only a current minimum can settle a vertex.
		knownCost, reached := bestCostByVertex[item.vertex]
		if !reached || item.cost != knownCost {
			continue
		}
		if settledByVertex[item.vertex] {
			continue
		}
		settledByVertex[item.vertex] = true
		if item.vertex == target {
			return bottleneckResult{
				cost:  item.cost,
				found: true,
			}, nil
		}

		for _, neighbor := range adjacencyByVertex[item.vertex] {
			if settledByVertex[neighbor.vertex] {
				continue
			}
			// Extending a route preserves its largest edge.
			candidate := maxInt64(item.cost, neighbor.cost)
			knownNeighbor, neighborReached :=
				bestCostByVertex[neighbor.vertex]
			if neighborReached && candidate >= knownNeighbor {
				continue
			}

			// The new item leaves any older, larger item stale.
			bestCostByVertex[neighbor.vertex] = candidate
			heap.Push(&frontier, bottleneckItem{
				vertex: neighbor.vertex,
				cost:   candidate,
			})
		}
	}
	return bottleneckResult{
		cost:  unreachableBottleneck,
		found: false,
	}, nil
}

type indexDisjointSet struct {
	parentByIndex []int
	sizeByRoot    []int
}

func newIndexDisjointSet(elementCount int) *indexDisjointSet {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial index disjoint set
	// state.
	set := &indexDisjointSet{
		parentByIndex: make([]int, elementCount),
		sizeByRoot:    make([]int, elementCount),
	}
	for element := 0; element < elementCount; element++ {
		set.parentByIndex[element] = element
		set.sizeByRoot[element] = 1
	}
	return set
}

func (set *indexDisjointSet) findRoot(element int) int {
	// Follow parent links to the maintained representative.
	root := element
	for set.parentByIndex[root] != root {
		root = set.parentByIndex[root]
	}
	// Compression changes tree shape, not component membership.
	for element != root {
		parent := set.parentByIndex[element]
		set.parentByIndex[element] = root
		element = parent
	}
	return root
}

func (set *indexDisjointSet) union(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Combine memberships while preserving one copy of each member.
	firstRoot := set.findRoot(first)
	secondRoot := set.findRoot(second)
	if firstRoot == secondRoot {
		return false
	}
	// Keep the larger tree above the smaller tree.
	if set.sizeByRoot[firstRoot] < set.sizeByRoot[secondRoot] {
		firstRoot, secondRoot = secondRoot, firstRoot
	}
	set.parentByIndex[secondRoot] = firstRoot
	set.sizeByRoot[firstRoot] += set.sizeByRoot[secondRoot]
	set.sizeByRoot[secondRoot] = 0
	return true
}

func (set *indexDisjointSet) connected(
	first int,
	second int,
) bool {
	// Compare representatives to test component membership.
	return set.findRoot(first) == set.findRoot(second)
}

func minimumBottleneckWithSets(
	vertexOrder []string,
	edges []undirectedWeightedEdge,
	start string,
	target string,
) (bottleneckResult, error) {
	// Compute bottleneck with sets from the state without mutating it.
	indexByVertex, err := validateBottleneckInput(
		vertexOrder,
		edges,
		start,
		target,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return bottleneckResult{}, err
	}
	if start == target {
		return bottleneckResult{cost: 0, found: true}, nil
	}

	// Sort an owned copy so the caller's edge order is unchanged.
	sortedEdges := append([]undirectedWeightedEdge(nil), edges...)
	sort.SliceStable(
		sortedEdges,
		func(first int, second int) bool {
			return sortedEdges[first].cost <
				sortedEdges[second].cost
		},
	)
	set := newIndexDisjointSet(len(vertexOrder))
	startIndex := indexByVertex[start]
	targetIndex := indexByVertex[target]
	// The first threshold joining the query endpoints is optimal.
	for _, edge := range sortedEdges {
		merged := set.union(
			indexByVertex[edge.first],
			indexByVertex[edge.second],
		)
		if merged && set.connected(startIndex, targetIndex) {
			return bottleneckResult{
				cost:  edge.cost,
				found: true,
			}, nil
		}
	}
	return bottleneckResult{
		cost:  unreachableBottleneck,
		found: false,
	}, nil
}

func ordinaryBottleneckGraph() ([]string, []undirectedWeightedEdge) {
	// Keep ordinary bottleneck graph in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	vertexOrder := []string{
		"S", "A", "B", "C", "T", "X",
	}
	edges := []undirectedWeightedEdge{
		{first: "S", second: "A", cost: 8},
		{first: "A", second: "T", cost: 9},
		{first: "S", second: "B", cost: 3},
		{first: "B", second: "C", cost: 10},
		{first: "B", second: "A", cost: 4},
		{first: "C", second: "T", cost: 5},
		{first: "A", second: "C", cost: 6},
	}
	return vertexOrder, edges
}

func printBottleneckResult(
	result bottleneckResult,
	err error,
) {
	// Expose bottleneck result in logical order without changing source.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(result.cost, result.found)
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	vertexOrder, edges := ordinaryBottleneckGraph()
	result, err := minimumBottleneckWithHeap(
		vertexOrder,
		edges,
		"S",
		"T",
	)
	printBottleneckResult(result, err)
	result, err = minimumBottleneckWithSets(
		vertexOrder,
		edges,
		"S",
		"T",
	)
	printBottleneckResult(result, err)
	result, err = minimumBottleneckWithHeap(
		vertexOrder,
		edges,
		"A",
		"A",
	)
	printBottleneckResult(result, err)
	result, err = minimumBottleneckWithSets(
		vertexOrder,
		edges,
		"S",
		"X",
	)
	printBottleneckResult(result, err)

	invalidEdges := append(
		[]undirectedWeightedEdge(nil),
		edges...,
	)
	invalidEdges = append(
		invalidEdges,
		undirectedWeightedEdge{
			first:  "S",
			second: "T",
			cost:   -1,
		},
	)
	_, heapErr := minimumBottleneckWithHeap(
		vertexOrder,
		invalidEdges,
		"S",
		"T",
	)
	_, setErr := minimumBottleneckWithSets(
		vertexOrder,
		invalidEdges,
		"S",
		"T",
	)
	fmt.Println(heapErr != nil, setErr != nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
6 true
6 true
0 true
-1 false
true true
```

The heap's vertex tie-break makes equal-cost removal deterministic,
although only the numeric result is observable. Both functions return
their result by value and retain no caller storage. The internal
adjacency, sorted edge copy, maps, heap, and disjoint-set slices are
owned by the call.

##### Why it works

For the heap method, every stored finite value is the bottleneck of a
real route from start. The start's empty route has cost zero. A
relaxation extends a real route by one real edge and takes the
maximum, so the property survives every update.

Suppose the heap removes vertex `v` with current value B, but some
route to v has bottleneck C below B. On that cheaper route, choose the
first unsettled vertex x. Its predecessor was settled, so scanning
that edge offered x a candidate no greater than C: both the prefix
bottleneck and that edge cost are at most C. Thus x has a current heap
key below B, contradicting removal of v as the minimum. A settled
value is therefore final. When v is the target, its final value is the
required minimum bottleneck.

Strict improvements are the only pushes. Each settled adjacency row
is scanned once, so finitely many adjacency entries create finitely
many heap items. Every loop iteration removes one item; the heap
search terminates. Lazy stale items cannot change an answer because
the map already records the strictly smaller item that replaced them.

For the set method, after any processed prefix, two vertices share a
root exactly when processed edges contain a route between them. This
is true for the empty prefix. Unioning one edge merges exactly the two
components that edge connects, preserving the statement.

Because edges are processed in nondecreasing order, the decisive edge
of cost W proves a route using only costs at most W. Immediately
before that union, start and target were separate, so processed
cheaper edges did not connect them. In particular, no route with
bottleneck below W exists. W is both achievable and a lower bound, so
it is optimal.

The edge loop is finite. Union by size keeps parent trees shallow, and
every `findRoot` walk follows parents to a self-parented root. Path
compression changes only tree shape, not component membership, so all
set operations terminate and preserve connectivity.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `V` be the listed vertex count, `E` the undirected edge count,
`R` the number of vertices settled by the heap, `A_R` the adjacency
entries scanned from them, and `P` the number of strict improvements.
Each undirected edge creates two adjacency entries, so
`A_R <= 2E` and `P <= A_R`. Go map access is expected `O(1)`.

Validation costs `Theta(V+E)`. On a valid nontrivial heap query,
building adjacency also costs `Theta(V+E)`. The start and each strict
improvement create one push and eventual pop. Heap work is
`O((P+1) log(P+1))`, and scanning costs `Theta(R+A_R)`. Total heap
time is `O(V+E+(P+1)log(P+1))`, conventionally
`O((V+E)log(E+2))` in the worst case.

Validation fixes the valid-input best case at `Theta(V+E)`, including
`start == target`. A useful target may be settled before much of the
graph is explored, but all input edges were still validated and used
to build adjacency for a nontrivial query. There is no meaningful
average without a graph, weight, and query distribution.

The heap version stores adjacency in `Theta(V+E)` space, two state
maps in `O(V)`, and at most `O(P)` lazy items. Its auxiliary space is
`O(V+E)` in the worst case. The result uses constant output space.

The set version validates in `Theta(V+E)`, copies E edges, and sorts
them in `O(E log E)` comparison time. At most E unions and
connectivity checks cost `O(E alpha(V))` amortized, where `alpha` is
the inverse Ackermann function. Total worst-case time is
`O(V+E log E)`. Sorting happens before the early connectivity stop.

Its index map and disjoint-set arrays use `Theta(V)` space; the owned
sorted edge copy uses `Theta(E)`. Total auxiliary space is
`Theta(V+E)`, with constant-size output. If edges are already sorted
under an explicit input contract, the copy and sort policy can change,
but this function promises not to mutate caller order.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Extend with `max(current, edge)`, not addition. Addition solves a
  different objective and fails on `[1,8]` versus `[5,5]`.
- Use a min-heap of tentative bottlenecks. A max-heap settles the
  worst discovered route first and invalidates the finality proof.
- Stop when the target is removed as a current minimum, not when first
  discovered. T first appears at 9 in the trace and later improves to
  6.
- Skip stale lazy items. Old `A:8`, `C:10`, and `T:9` no longer match
  the cost map and must not rescan rows.
- Mark settled on current removal, not insertion. A and T both improve
  after their first heap insertion.
- Relax only strict improvements. Equal candidates change no numeric
  answer and can cause needless heap growth around zero-cost cycles.
- Sort edges in increasing cost for minimax. Descending order instead
  supports a maximum-capacity or widest-path threshold.
- Copy before sorting. `sort.SliceStable(edges, ...)` on the caller's
  slice would silently change observable input order.
- Union both endpoints before checking connectivity. Checking first
  delays the decisive edge and can return a larger threshold.
- Treat edges as undirected exactly once. Building only one adjacency
  direction loses valid routes; listing both directions duplicates
  work under this contract.
- Self-loops may appear twice in built adjacency but cannot improve a
  settled vertex or merge two components. They do not change output.
- Parallel edges remain distinct. The lower one may produce a strict
  improvement or connect components at an earlier threshold.
- Zero is a valid bottleneck for a zero-cost route and for
  `start == target`. Use the found flag rather than testing cost
  alone.
- `math.MaxInt64` is a valid answer. Avoid sentinel maxima and avoid
  subtracting costs inside a sort comparison.
- Validate the full input before `start == target`; an equal-endpoint
  query must not hide a negative edge or unknown vertex elsewhere.
- A nil edge slice is a valid graph with isolated listed vertices. A
  nil or empty vertex slice has no valid query.
- The empty string is a valid vertex. Two-value map lookup, not a
  nonempty-name test, establishes membership.
- Disconnected is `{cost:-1, found:false}` without an error. Invalid
  structure is the zero result plus an error.
- Disjoint sets lose route information. If a caller needs the actual
  route, retain a forest or use heap parents rather than inventing a
  path from component roots.
- Synchronize slices shared with concurrent writers. Copying for sort
  does not make an earlier concurrent read safe.

##### When to choose it

Choose a minimum bottleneck path when phrases such as these define the
objective:

- minimize the largest jump, slope, risk, latency, or required effort;
- find the smallest threshold that makes two states connected;
- choose a route whose worst edge is as mild as possible.

Use the heap version for one or a few endpoint queries, especially
when adjacency already exists, the target may be reached early, or a
path witness is needed. To return a witness, record a parent on each
strict improvement and reconstruct only after target settlement.

Use the sorted-edge set version when the graph is undirected, arrives
as an edge list, and only the threshold value or connectivity matters.
It is close to Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree process and is often
the cleanest proof for "first threshold that connects these
endpoints."

For many queries on one static graph, build a minimum spanning forest
once. The unique tree path between two connected vertices has the same
minimum possible bottleneck; preprocessing that forest for maximum
edge queries can avoid rerunning either single-query algorithm.

When not to choose it:

Use ordinary Dijkstra when the objective is the sum of edge costs.
The `[1,8]` versus `[5,5]` example proves that minimum sum and minimum
maximum can choose different routes.

Do not use the disjoint-set method for directed reachability. Union
makes connectivity symmetric: processing `A -> B` also makes B appear
connected to A. A directed minimax query can use the heap relaxation
with directed adjacency, but that is outside this input contract.

A **widest path** maximizes the minimum capacity edge. It is the dual
bottleneck problem, not this minimax-cost problem. It uses a max-first
selection rule and `min(current, edge)` extension rather than this
lesson's min-first heap and maximum extension.

Do not pass negative costs to this implementation. A generalized
minimax definition can support them, but the empty path then needs an
identity below every edge rather than zero, and `-1` cannot remain the
unreachable sentinel. This contract rejects that ambiguity.

For a small integer cost range, binary search over a threshold plus
BFS or DFS can be readable, but it repeats traversal work. For dynamic
edge deletions, ordinary disjoint sets cannot undo connectivity; use a
dynamic-connectivity or offline rollback technique designed for the
update model.

#### B.13.11 State-augmented paths (distance table and queue)

##### Problem and contract

Sometimes reaching the same vertex with different history creates
different futures. A route may have used a coupon, collected a key,
changed direction, crossed a limited number of walls, or arrived with
a particular parity. Marking only the vertex as visited merges states
that the problem must keep separate.

This lesson uses a directed graph in which every edge costs one step.
An edge either consumes no token or consumes one token. Given a
nonnegative token budget, a start, and a target, return the fewest
steps in any route that consumes at most that many tokens.

The search vertex is not merely original vertex `v`. It is the pair:

```text
(v, exact number of tokens used so far)
```

This construction is called a **state-augmented graph**, **expanded
state space**, or **product graph**. Ordinary breadth-first search can
then run over those pairs because every expanded transition still
costs one step.

The input contract is:

- `adjacency[v]` lists directed `tokenEdge` values from vertex `v`.
- Vertices are integer indices in `[0,V)`; start, target, and every
  edge endpoint must be valid.
- `consumesToken=false` is a free edge; true consumes exactly one
  token. All edges still add exactly one path step.
- The token budget must be nonnegative.
- Cycles, self-loops, parallel edges, isolated vertices, and nil or
  empty rows are valid. An empty graph has no valid query.

A reachable result contains the minimum step count and `found=true`.
An unreachable target returns `steps=-1` and false. A valid query from
a vertex to itself returns zero steps. Invalid input returns the zero
result and an error after validating the whole graph, even when start
equals target.

The function reads but does not mutate or retain the adjacency slices.
The result owns no input storage. Unsynchronized mutation of shared
rows during validation or search is outside the contract.

Read [implicit state spaces](
#a106-implicit-graphs-and-state-spaces) for complete state keys and
[unweighted BFS](#b131-unweighted-bfs-queue-and-distance-array) for
the FIFO shortest-path invariant.

##### Mental model

Let `distanceByState[v][u]` store the fewest steps discovered to reach
vertex `v` after consuming exactly `u` tokens. Read
`distanceByState[4][0] == 3` as: "a three-step route reaches vertex
4 without consuming a token." A value of `-1` means that exact pair
has not been discovered.

The queue stores the same complete pair. Removing state `(v,u)` and
inspecting edge `v -> w` produces:

```text
next tokens = u       for a free edge
next tokens = u + 1   for a consuming edge
```

Reject a consuming transition when `u` already equals the budget.
Otherwise, if `distanceByState[w][next tokens]` is still `-1`, assign
the current distance plus one and enqueue that full state. Mark before
enqueueing so each pair enters once.

Two entries for the same original vertex are intentionally different.
Reaching C in two steps with one token used may leave no resource for
the next edge. Reaching C in three steps with zero used may still be
the only feasible route to the target. The distance table preserves
both possibilities until FIFO order decides the fewest total steps.

The code reduces an excessive budget to `V-1`. Any shortest feasible
route can be made simple: if it repeats a vertex, delete the cycle
between two visits. That deletion shortens the route and cannot add
token consumption. A simple route has at most `V-1` edges, so it can
consume at most `V-1` tokens. The cap preserves every optimum and
prevents `maxTokens+1` overflow or pointless table columns.

The target may appear in several token columns. Return when the first
target state leaves the FIFO queue. All earlier queue states have no
larger step distance, so that target occurrence is minimum across all
allowed token counts.

##### Worked walkthrough

Name vertices `S=0`, `A=1`, `B=2`, `D=3`, `C=4`, `T=5`, and `X=6`.
The word `token` marks consuming edges:

```text
S: A(token), B(free)   D: C(free)
A: C(free)             C: T(token)
B: D(free)             T: []
X: []
```

With a one-token budget, the required answer from S to T is four
steps along `S-B-D-C-T`. The shorter `S-A-C-T` route needs two tokens
and is infeasible.

Initial state: `distance[S][0]=0`; all other table entries are `-1`;
the queue contains `[(S,0)]`.

1. Decision: remove `(S,0)`. Edge `S-A` consumes a token, so discover
   `(A,1)` at distance 1. Edge `S-B` is free, so discover `(B,0)` at
   distance 1. Mark both before enqueueing.
   After: queue `[(A,1),(B,0)]`; both distance entries are 1.
   Known correct: these are exactly the feasible one-edge states, in
   adjacency order.

2. Decision: remove `(A,1)` and follow free edge `A-C`.
   After: discover `(C,1)` at distance 2; queue is
   `[(B,0),(C,1)]`.
   Known correct: C is reachable quickly, but this state has spent the
   entire budget.

3. Decision: remove `(B,0)` and follow free edge `B-D`.
   After: discover `(D,0)` at distance 2; queue is
   `[(C,1),(D,0)]`.
   Known correct: every distance-1 state has been expanded before the
   distance-2 states can leave the queue.

4. Decision: remove `(C,1)`. Edge `C-T` consumes a token, but
   `1 == budget`, so reject that transition.
   After: queue is `[(D,0)]`; no target state exists.
   Known correct: the two-step arrival at C cannot legally continue
   to T under the one-token contract.

5. Decision: remove `(D,0)` and follow free edge `D-C`.
   After: discover `(C,0)` at distance 3 and enqueue it, even though
   `(C,1)` was already processed.
   Known correct: exact tokens used is part of identity; `(C,0)` has a
   different legal future from `(C,1)`.

6. Decision: remove `(C,0)`. Consuming `C-T` produces `(T,1)` within
   budget at distance 4.
   After: queue contains `[(T,1)]` and its table entry is 4.
   Known correct: `S-B-D-C-T` is a feasible four-edge route.

7. Decision: remove `(T,1)`. It is the first dequeued target state.
   After: return `{steps:4, found:true}`.
   Known correct: FIFO order processed every state at distances below
   4 first, so no shorter feasible target route exists.

Increasing the budget to two changes step 4: `(C,1)` can cross to
`(T,2)` at distance 3, and that target state leaves before the longer
zero-token detour finishes. The result becomes three.

The trace is also a counterexample to one Boolean per vertex. A
vertex-only BFS marks C when `(C,1)` arrives at distance 2. Its first
incorrect decision is then discarding later `(C,0)` as "already
visited." It reports unreachable even though the four-step route is
valid. The fix is not to delay marking; it is to mark the complete
pair on enqueue.

Focused cases cover the remaining branches:

- Start equal to target returns zero after graph validation.
- Target X is isolated, so the queue exhausts and returns
  `{-1,false}`.
- With budget zero, every consuming edge is skipped but free cycles
  and parallel edges remain valid.
- A self-loop can reach another token column, but each full pair still
  enters at most once.
- Parallel free and consuming edges to the same vertex may create two
  distinct states; neither is incorrectly merged.
- `maxTokens=math.MaxInt` is safely capped to `V-1` before allocation.
- A negative budget or invalid endpoint is rejected before any table
  or queue state is published.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates State-augmented paths (distance
// table and queue). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

const unreachableTokenDistance = -1

type tokenEdge struct {
	to            int
	consumesToken bool
}

type tokenPathResult struct {
	steps int
	found bool
}

type tokenState struct {
	vertex     int
	tokensUsed int
}

func validateTokenPathInput(
	adjacency [][]tokenEdge,
	maxTokens int,
	start int,
	target int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the token path input contract before
	// mutation.
	if maxTokens < 0 {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"maximum tokens %d is negative",
			maxTokens,
		)
	}
	vertexCount := len(adjacency)
	if start < 0 || start >= vertexCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"start %d is outside [0, %d)",
			start,
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	if target < 0 || target >= vertexCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"target %d is outside [0, %d)",
			target,
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	for vertex, edges := range adjacency {
		for _, edge := range edges {
			if edge.to < 0 || edge.to >= vertexCount {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %d -> %d has an invalid endpoint",
					vertex,
					edge.to,
				)
			}
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func usefulTokenBudget(
	vertexCount int,
	maxTokens int,
) int {
	// Keep useful token budget in one helper so callers use one rule.
	maximumUseful := vertexCount - 1
	if maxTokens < maximumUseful {
		return maxTokens
	}
	return maximumUseful
}

func newTokenDistanceTable(
	vertexCount int,
	tokenBudget int,
) [][]int {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial token distance table
	// state.
	distanceByState := make([][]int, vertexCount)
	for vertex := range distanceByState {
		distanceByState[vertex] = make(
			[]int,
			tokenBudget+1,
		)
		// -1 distinguishes unseen states from the zero-step start.
		for tokensUsed := range distanceByState[vertex] {
			distanceByState[vertex][tokensUsed] =
				unreachableTokenDistance
		}
	}
	return distanceByState
}

func shortestPathWithTokens(
	adjacency [][]tokenEdge,
	maxTokens int,
	start int,
	target int,
) (tokenPathResult, error) {
	// Compute the requested ordered or extreme result.
	if err := validateTokenPathInput(
		adjacency,
		maxTokens,
		start,
		target,
	); err != nil {
		return tokenPathResult{}, err
	}
	if start == target {
		return tokenPathResult{steps: 0, found: true}, nil
	}

	// A shortest route is simple, so it consumes at most V-1 tokens.
	tokenBudget := usefulTokenBudget(
		len(adjacency),
		maxTokens,
	)
	distanceByState := newTokenDistanceTable(
		len(adjacency),
		tokenBudget,
	)
	distanceByState[start][0] = 0
	queue := []tokenState{{vertex: start, tokensUsed: 0}}

	// FIFO order makes first discovery shortest in the product graph.
	for queueHead := 0; queueHead < len(queue); queueHead++ {
		state := queue[queueHead]
		stateDistance :=
			distanceByState[state.vertex][state.tokensUsed]
		if state.vertex == target {
			return tokenPathResult{
				steps: stateDistance,
				found: true,
			}, nil
		}

		for _, edge := range adjacency[state.vertex] {
			nextTokensUsed := state.tokensUsed
			// A consuming edge changes state as well as vertex.
			if edge.consumesToken {
				if nextTokensUsed == tokenBudget {
					continue
				}
				nextTokensUsed++
			}
			knownDistance :=
				distanceByState[edge.to][nextTokensUsed]
			if knownDistance != unreachableTokenDistance {
				continue
			}

			// Mark the full state before enqueueing it once.
			distanceByState[edge.to][nextTokensUsed] =
				stateDistance + 1
			queue = append(queue, tokenState{
				vertex:     edge.to,
				tokensUsed: nextTokensUsed,
			})
		}
	}
	return tokenPathResult{
		steps: unreachableTokenDistance,
		found: false,
	}, nil
}

func ordinaryTokenGraph() [][]tokenEdge {
	// Keep ordinary token graph in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return [][]tokenEdge{
		{
			{to: 1, consumesToken: true},
			{to: 2, consumesToken: false},
		},
		{{to: 4, consumesToken: false}},
		{{to: 3, consumesToken: false}},
		{{to: 4, consumesToken: false}},
		{{to: 5, consumesToken: true}},
		{},
		{},
	}
}

func printTokenPathResult(
	result tokenPathResult,
	err error,
) {
	// Expose token path result in logical order without changing source.
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(result.steps, result.found)
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	adjacency := ordinaryTokenGraph()
	result, err := shortestPathWithTokens(adjacency, 1, 0, 5)
	printTokenPathResult(result, err)
	result, err = shortestPathWithTokens(adjacency, 2, 0, 5)
	printTokenPathResult(result, err)
	result, err = shortestPathWithTokens(adjacency, 1, 1, 1)
	printTokenPathResult(result, err)
	result, err = shortestPathWithTokens(adjacency, 2, 0, 6)
	printTokenPathResult(result, err)

	invalidAdjacency := [][]tokenEdge{{{to: 1}}}
	_, endpointErr := shortestPathWithTokens(
		invalidAdjacency,
		0,
		0,
		0,
	)
	_, budgetErr := shortestPathWithTokens(
		adjacency,
		-1,
		0,
		5,
	)
	fmt.Println(endpointErr != nil, budgetErr != nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
4 true
3 true
0 true
-1 false
true true
```

The printed cases expose both budget-dependent answers, the zero-step
branch, exhaustion, and two invalid-input categories. Adjacency row
order controls equal-distance queue order but cannot change the
minimum step count.

##### Why it works

Define the expanded graph to contain one state `(v,u)` for every
vertex `v` and token count `u` from zero through the effective budget.
For each original edge `v -> w`, add an expanded edge from `(v,u)` to
`(w,u)` when it is free, or to `(w,u+1)` when it consumes a token and
the new count fits the budget.

Every feasible original walk maps to exactly one expanded path: track
the cumulative token count after each edge. Every expanded path maps
back to a feasible original walk because its transitions are created
only from real edges and never exceed the budget. The mapping
preserves the number of edges, so minimum steps in the expanded graph
equals the required constrained minimum.

Initially only `(start,0)` is discovered at distance zero. Suppose a
state at distance D leaves the FIFO queue. Every newly discovered
expanded neighbor receives distance `D+1` and joins behind all pending
distance-D work. If a shorter path to that neighbor existed, its
predecessor would have left earlier and discovered the same full pair
first. Thus first discovery fixes the minimum distance for a state.

Returning the first dequeued target state takes the minimum across all
its token columns. Any shorter feasible target path would map to an
expanded target state at a smaller distance and would have left the
queue earlier, a contradiction.

There are `V*(B+1)` expanded states for effective budget B. Marking
before enqueueing admits each at most once, every loop iteration
advances the queue head, and every state scans a finite row. The
search therefore terminates. If the queue empties, no expanded target
state is reachable, so no feasible original route exists.

Finally, capping B at `V-1` is safe because removing a repeated-vertex
cycle from a feasible route preserves its endpoints, removes at least
one step, and never increases tokens used. An optimal route is simple
and remains represented after the cap.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `V` be vertex count, `A` total adjacency-entry count, K the caller
budget, and `B=min(K,V-1)` the effective budget after validation. The
expanded table contains `S=V*(B+1)` possible states.

Whole-graph validation costs `Theta(V+A)`. Initializing every table
entry costs `Theta(S)`. Each reached state enters and leaves the queue
once. A state at vertex v scans all of v's outgoing edges, so one
original edge can be scanned in every token column. Worst-case search
work is `Theta(A*(B+1))`. Total worst-case time is therefore
`Theta((V+A)*(B+1))`.

For `start == target`, validation returns before table allocation, so
valid-input work is `Theta(V+A)`. For a nontrivial query, full table
initialization costs `Theta(S)` even if the target is near the start.
There is no useful average without a model for graphs, token labels,
budgets, and endpoints.

The distance table and append-only queue each use at most `Theta(S)`
space. Auxiliary space is `Theta(V*(B+1))`; the scalar result uses
constant output space. The input adjacency is not counted. Returning
an actual route would add a parent table of the same state-space order
and `O(L)` output for a path of L vertices.

In an uncapped numeric-resource variant, a factor `K+1` is
**pseudo-polynomial**: a large encoded budget can create many states
even when the input uses few digits. This implementation's `V-1` cap
makes B polynomial in V for monotone zero-or-one token consumption.
Other resources may not admit that cap. A key-set bitmask can create
`V*2^Q` states for Q keys, which is the familiar state-explosion
tradeoff.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Key visited state by `(vertex,tokensUsed)`, not vertex alone. The
  trace's `(C,1)` and `(C,0)` have different legal futures.
- "At most u" and "exactly u" describe different tables.
  This code stores exact token usage and accepts any target column.
- Mark the full state on enqueue. Marking on dequeue duplicates work;
  marking only the vertex discards valid alternatives.
- Skip a consuming edge when `tokensUsed == budget` before adding one.
  Adding first can exceed the table bound or overflow a huge input.
- Preserve the step objective. Tokens constrain feasibility; they are
  not added to distance or minimized before steps.
- Return the first target state by FIFO distance, not the smallest
  token column. A longer route that saves tokens is not a shorter
  path.
- Keep free and consuming parallel edges. They lead to different
  expanded states even when their original endpoints match.
- Self-loops and cycles are valid. A loop may change the token column,
  but the finite full-state table prevents endless enqueueing.
- Initialize every table entry to `-1`. Go's zero value is the valid
  distance of `(start,0)`.
- Validate before `start == target`. A zero-step answer must not hide
  an invalid edge elsewhere in the input.
- A nil adjacency row is a valid vertex with no outgoing edges. Empty
  adjacency has no valid start or target.
- A negative budget is invalid. A huge nonnegative budget is valid and
  is capped only because the simple-route proof applies here.
- The result `{-1,false}` means a valid but infeasible query. Invalid
  indices or budget return the zero result and an error.
- To return a path, parent identity must include both vertex and token
  count. A parent indexed only by vertex can join incompatible states.
- If using remaining tokens instead, define transitions and table
  lookup consistently. Mixing remaining and used counts reverses the
  budget test.
- Input rows are read during validation and again during traversal.
  Synchronize or snapshot them if another goroutine may mutate them.

##### When to choose it

Use state augmentation when two arrivals at the same location can
have different legal next moves or different chances of success.
Common state components include:

- coupons, obstacle removals, fuel, or remaining stops;
- parity, turn count, direction, or cooldown phase;
- which keys, switches, or objectives have been collected;
- the last value when transition legality depends on history.

Choose the smallest state that fully predicts future transitions and
goal acceptance. If only the number of collected keys matters, a count
may suffice; if door A requires key A, the state needs the actual set.
Values that affect only how the route arrived but not its future
should not multiply the state space.

Use FIFO BFS when every expanded transition has one equal step cost.
Use 0-1 BFS when expanded transitions cost only zero or one, and use
Dijkstra or A* for arbitrary nonnegative transition costs. The state
key stays augmented; only the frontier discipline changes.

When not to choose it:

Do not augment state when ordinary vertex identity already determines
all future moves and the goal. Extra dimensions then multiply time and
memory without preserving any necessary distinction.

Do not use this FIFO implementation when edge step costs differ.
Queue order follows edge count, not weighted cost; use a frontier that
matches the expanded edge weights.

This exact table is unsuitable when the relevant history is enormous
or unbounded. A set of Q independent keys has up to `2^Q` masks, and
several independent numeric resources multiply their ranges. Look for
dominance pruning, a stronger invariant, meet-in-the-middle search, or
a problem-specific compression before allocating the full product.

The `V-1` cap relies on tokens only increasing and on cycles never
improving feasibility. If transitions can refill fuel, clear debt, or
change resource values in both directions, model those values under an
explicit finite bound; do not reuse this cap without a new proof.

For general resource-constrained shortest paths with weighted costs,
multiple resources, or elementary-path requirements, this simple BFS
is only a special case. Those variants can require label dominance,
dynamic programming, or more advanced exact methods.

design.
[B.13.1 Unweighted BFS](
#b131-unweighted-bfs-queue-and-distance-array) owns the FIFO shortest-
path proof. [B.13.2 0-1 BFS](
#b132-0-1-bfs-deque-and-distance-array) and [B.13.3 Dijkstra](
#b133-dijkstra-heap-or-scan-distance-array) supply weighted frontier
alternatives for the same expanded graph.

Lee's original [path-connection algorithm](
https://doi.org/10.1109/TEC.1961.5219222) develops wave-based search
over admissible states. Beasley and Christofides'
[resource-constrained shortest-path paper](
https://doi.org/10.1002/net.3230190402) treats the broader family of
budgeted paths. NIST's [breadth-first search definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/breadthfirst.html) supplies the FIFO
neighbor-before-descendant order used by the expanded-state search.

### B.14 Dependencies and valid task ordering

#### B.14.1 Kahn's topological sort (queue and indegrees)

##### Problem and contract

A directed dependency graph says which work must happen before other
work. In this lesson, an edge `u -> v` means that task `u` must appear
before task `v`. A **topological order** is a sequence of all vertices
that respects every such edge.

A topological order exists exactly when the graph is a directed
acyclic graph, or DAG. Kahn's algorithm constructs an order by
repeatedly taking a vertex with no unmet predecessor. If no such
vertex remains before all vertices have been emitted, a directed
cycle prevents a whole-graph order.

This lesson's function accepts a directed adjacency list and returns:

- a complete deterministic order when the graph is acyclic;
- a numeric-order list of vertices still blocked when it is cyclic;
- a Boolean that distinguishes those two outcomes; or
- an error when an edge endpoint is not a vertex in the graph.

The input contract is:

- `adjacency[u]` contains the destinations of directed edges from
  vertex `u`.
- Vertices are the integer indices in `[0,V)`.
- Each stored edge occurrence is real. Parallel edges contribute
  separately to indegrees and must be removed separately.
- Self-loops, cycles, isolated vertices, disconnected components,
  and nil or empty rows are valid graph structure.
- An empty adjacency list is a valid empty DAG.

The function reads but does not mutate or retain the input slices.
Unsynchronized concurrent mutation of those slices is outside the
contract.

On a DAG, `order` and `blocked` are both non-nil. `order` contains all
vertices and `blocked` is empty. On a cyclic graph, `order` is nil so
a caller cannot mistake a valid prefix for a whole-graph schedule.
`blocked` is non-nil and contains every vertex that was not emitted.

The blocked list is deliberately not called a cycle list. It contains
vertices on cycles and vertices downstream of cycles. Identifying the
actual cyclic groups requires a strongly connected components
algorithm or another cycle-specific analysis.

Read [directed graphs and DAGs](
#a104-bipartite-graphs-and-directed-acyclic-graphs) before this
lesson.
[Queue mechanics](#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) supplies the FIFO
state.

##### Mental model

First validate every destination. Then count incoming stored edge
occurrences:

```text
indegreeByVertex[v] = number of incoming edge occurrences whose
                      sources have not been emitted
```

At initialization, no source has been emitted, so the count is the
ordinary indegree. Scan vertices in numeric order and append every
zero-indegree vertex to `readyQueue`. Those vertices have no unmet
dependency.

Use a head index rather than removing the front of the slice:

```text
readyQueue[queueHead:] = ready vertices not yet emitted
order                  = vertices already emitted
```

Repeatedly perform these actions:

- Read the vertex at `readyQueue[queueHead]` and advance the head.
- Append that vertex to `order`.
- For every destination in its adjacency row, decrement the
  destination's indegree once for that stored edge occurrence.
- When a destination reaches zero, append it to the queue.

A vertex enters the queue exactly when its last un-emitted
predecessor has been emitted. Its count only decreases, so it reaches
zero at most once and the vertex is enqueued at most once.

The ordering policy is deterministic for a fixed input encoding:

- Initial ready vertices enter in numeric vertex order.
- Vertices released by one source enter in that source's adjacency-
  row order.
- FIFO preserves the order in which vertices became ready.

This policy does not promise the lexicographically smallest valid
topological order. Use a min-heap instead of a queue when the smallest
currently ready vertex must always come next.

When the queue empties, compare `len(order)` with `V`. Equality means
every vertex was emitted and `order` is complete. Otherwise, scan the
remaining indegrees. Every positive entry names an un-emitted blocked
vertex. Return those vertices in numeric order and discard the partial
prefix from the public result.

##### Worked walkthrough

Suppose these integer vertices name tasks:

```text
0 fetch    1 parse    2 lint     3 build
4 package  5 deploy   6 docs     7 notify
```

Use this adjacency list:

```text
0: [1, 2, 2]
1: [3]
2: [3]
3: [4]
4: [5, 7]
5: []
6: []
7: []
```

The two `0 -> 2` entries are parallel edge occurrences. Vertex 6 is
isolated. Initial indegrees are:

```text
vertex:    0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
indegree:  0  1  2  2  1  1  0  1
```

Initial state: `readyQueue=[0,6]`, `queueHead=0`, and `order=[]`.

1. **Before:** vertex 0 is at the queue head and has no unmet
   predecessor. **Decision:** emit 0; decrement vertex 1 once and
   vertex 2 twice, following row `[1,2,2]`.
   **After:** indegrees 1 and 2 are zero, so the queue is
   `[0,6,1,2]`, the unread suffix is `[6,1,2]`, and `order=[0]`.
   **Known correct:** both occurrences of `0 -> 2` were removed, and
   every unread queued vertex now has zero remaining indegree.
2. **Before:** vertex 6 is next and its row is empty. **Decision:**
   emit 6 without changing any indegree.
   **After:** the unread queue is `[1,2]` and `order=[0,6]`.
   **Known correct:** an isolated task may appear anywhere permitted
   by the deterministic ready policy.
3. **Before:** vertex 1 is ready, while vertex 3 has indegree 2.
   **Decision:** emit 1 and remove occurrence `1 -> 3`.
   **After:** vertex 3 has indegree 1, the unread queue is `[2]`, and
   `order=[0,6,1]`.
   **Known correct:** vertex 3 is not ready because dependency 2 is
   still un-emitted.
4. **Before:** vertex 2 is ready and vertex 3 has one unmet incoming
   occurrence. **Decision:** emit 2 and remove `2 -> 3`.
   **After:** vertex 3 reaches zero and is appended; the unread queue
   is `[3]`, and `order=[0,6,1,2]`.
   **Known correct:** both predecessors of 3 now appear earlier in
   the order.
5. **Before:** vertex 3 is the only ready vertex. **Decision:** emit 3
   and remove `3 -> 4`.
   **After:** vertex 4 becomes ready; the unread queue is `[4]`, and
   `order=[0,6,1,2,3]`.
   **Known correct:** build is released only after parse and lint.
6. **Before:** vertex 4 is ready and its row is `[5,7]`.
   **Decision:** emit 4 and process that row from left to right.
   **After:** vertices 5 and 7 enter in row order; the unread queue is
   `[5,7]`, and `order=[0,6,1,2,3,4]`.
   **Known correct:** FIFO records the deterministic release order.
7. **Before:** only ready leaves 5 and 7 remain. **Decision:** emit 5,
   then emit 7; neither row changes a count.
   **After:** `order=[0,6,1,2,3,4,5,7]`, the queue is exhausted, and
   eight of eight vertices were emitted.
   **Known correct:** every edge source is earlier than its
   destination, so the returned order is a complete topological
   order.

Now add edge `5 -> 3`. Vertices 3, 4, and 5 form the directed cycle
`3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 3`. Vertex 7 is downstream through `4 -> 7`.

Initial state: vertices 0 and 6 are ready; vertex 3 now has indegree
3 because it receives from 1, 2, and 5.

1. **Before:** the queue is `[0,6]`. **Decision:** process 0 and 6 as
   before, releasing 1 and 2.
   **After:** `order=[0,6]` and the unread queue is `[1,2]`.
   **Known correct:** none of 3, 4, 5, or 7 is ready.
2. **Before:** vertex 3 has indegree 3. **Decision:** emit 1 and 2,
   removing their two incoming occurrences to 3.
   **After:** `order=[0,6,1,2]`, vertex 3 still has indegree 1, and
   the queue is empty.
   **Known correct:** the remaining `5 -> 3` edge prevents 3 from
   becoming ready.
3. **Before:** four of eight vertices were emitted and no ready
   vertex exists. **Decision:** stop and scan positive remaining
   indegrees.
   **After:** `blocked=[3,4,5,7]`, `acyclic=false`, and the public
   `order` is nil.
   **Known correct:** 3, 4, and 5 are cyclic; 7 is blocked downstream
   even though 7 itself is not on a cycle.

Parallel edges expose an important accounting rule. For graph
`0: [1,1]`, vertex 1 starts at indegree 2. Emitting 0 must decrement
twice, producing `2 -> 1 -> 0`. Counting both occurrences but
removing only one would incorrectly leave vertex 1 blocked. Counting
one but removing two would underflow the logical count and could
release work at the wrong time.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Kahn's topological sort (queue and
// indegrees). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

type topologicalResult struct {
	order   []int
	blocked []int
	acyclic bool
}

func validateTopologicalInput(adjacency [][]int) error {
	// Reject input outside the topological input contract before
	// mutation.
	numVertices := len(adjacency)
	for source, neighbors := range adjacency {
		for _, destination := range neighbors {
			if destination < 0 || destination >= numVertices {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %d -> %d has an invalid destination",
					source,
					destination,
				)
			}
		}
	}

	return nil
}

func countIncomingEdges(adjacency [][]int) ([]int, error) {
	// Compute incoming edges from the state without mutating it.
	indegreeByVertex := make([]int, len(adjacency))
	for source, neighbors := range adjacency {
		for _, destination := range neighbors {
			// Every stored edge occurrence contributes separately.
			if indegreeByVertex[destination] == math.MaxInt {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"indegree overflows at edge %d -> %d",
					source,
					destination,
				)
			}
			indegreeByVertex[destination]++
		}
	}

	return indegreeByVertex, nil
}

func kahnTopologicalSort(
	adjacency [][]int,
) (*topologicalResult, error) {
	// Validate before constructing any observable result.
	if err := validateTopologicalInput(adjacency); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	indegreeByVertex, err := countIncomingEdges(adjacency)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// Numeric scanning makes the initial ready order deterministic.
	readyQueue := make([]int, 0, len(adjacency))
	for vertex, indegree := range indegreeByVertex {
		if indegree == 0 {
			readyQueue = append(readyQueue, vertex)
		}
	}

	order := make([]int, 0, len(adjacency))
	for queueHead := 0; queueHead < len(readyQueue); queueHead++ {
		source := readyQueue[queueHead]
		order = append(order, source)

		// Removing source removes every occurrence in its row.
		for _, destination := range adjacency[source] {
			indegreeByVertex[destination]--
			if indegreeByVertex[destination] == 0 {
				readyQueue = append(readyQueue, destination)
			}
		}
	}

	if len(order) == len(adjacency) {
		return &topologicalResult{
			order:   order,
			blocked: make([]int, 0),
			acyclic: true,
		}, nil
	}

	// Remaining vertices include cycles and their descendants.
	blocked := make([]int, 0, len(adjacency)-len(order))
	for vertex, indegree := range indegreeByVertex {
		if indegree > 0 {
			blocked = append(blocked, vertex)
		}
	}

	// A partial prefix is not a whole-graph topological order.
	return &topologicalResult{
		order:   nil,
		blocked: blocked,
		acyclic: false,
	}, nil
}

func ordinaryDependencyGraph() [][]int {
	// Keep ordinary dependency graph in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	return [][]int{
		{1, 2, 2},
		{3},
		{3},
		{4},
		{5, 7},
		{},
		nil,
		{},
	}
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	adjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	result, err := kahnTopologicalSort(adjacency)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(result.order, result.blocked, result.acyclic)

	cycleAdjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	cycleAdjacency[5] = append(cycleAdjacency[5], 3)
	cycleResult, err := kahnTopologicalSort(cycleAdjacency)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(
		cycleResult.order,
		cycleResult.blocked,
		cycleResult.acyclic,
	)

	emptyResult, err := kahnTopologicalSort(nil)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(
		emptyResult.order,
		emptyResult.blocked,
		emptyResult.acyclic,
	)

	_, err = kahnTopologicalSort([][]int{{1}})
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
[0 6 1 2 3 4 5 7] [] true
[] [3 4 5 7] false
[] [] true
true
```

`fmt.Println` displays a nil slice and a non-nil empty slice as `[]`.
The API contract still distinguishes them: the cyclic result's order
is nil, while both empty slices in the empty-DAG result are non-nil.

The separate validation pass ensures an invalid endpoint yields a nil
result and an error before algorithm state is exposed. The indegree
increment also guards the machine `int` limit instead of allowing a
wrapped count to masquerade as readiness.

##### Why it works
