The main invariant is:

> `indegreeByVertex[v]` equals the number of incoming stored edge
> occurrences to `v` whose source has not yet been emitted.

The initial counting pass establishes the invariant because every
source is un-emitted. When source `u` is emitted, the algorithm visits
every occurrence in `adjacency[u]` and subtracts exactly those edges.
No other count changes. The invariant is therefore preserved after
each queue removal.

By the invariant, a vertex enters the queue only when no incoming edge
from an un-emitted source remains. All its predecessors are already in
`order`, so appending it cannot violate an edge constraint. Induction
over the emitted prefix shows that every edge between emitted
vertices points forward in `order`.

If all `V` vertices are emitted, that forward-edge property applies to
the whole graph. The returned slice is therefore a valid topological
order.

If the queue stalls early, every remaining vertex has at least one
incoming edge from another remaining vertex. Choose such a
predecessor repeatedly. The graph has finitely many remaining
vertices, so some vertex must repeat. The repeated segment is a
directed cycle. Thus an early stall proves that no whole-graph
topological order exists.

Conversely, a directed cycle can never be completely emitted. Before
the first cycle vertex could become ready, it would still have an
incoming edge from the previous un-emitted cycle vertex. Therefore a
graph is acyclic exactly when Kahn's algorithm emits all vertices.

Termination is bounded. An indegree only decreases, reaches zero at
most once, and causes at most one enqueue. Each queued vertex is
removed once, and each outgoing edge occurrence of an emitted vertex
is processed once.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `V` be the number of vertices and `A` the number of stored
directed edge occurrences, including duplicates.

Validation examines every row and edge in `Theta(V+A)` time. Counting
indegrees takes another `Theta(V+A)`. The queue phase enqueues and
emits each vertex at most once and processes each emitted outgoing
edge once. A DAG processes all edges. A cyclic input still had all
edges validated and counted, so total best, average, and worst time
under this full-input contract are all `Theta(V+A)`.

The indegree slice and queue use `O(V)` auxiliary space. The complete
order on a DAG or blocked list on a cyclic graph uses `O(V)` result
space. The code allocates order capacity before knowing the outcome;
on a cyclic graph that temporary backing array is also `O(V)` and is
not returned.

The head-index queue retains its processed prefix until the function
returns, so its peak backing storage is `O(V)`. This is preferable to
repeatedly shifting a slice, which would add unnecessary copying.

An invalid endpoint may stop validation at the first bad edge, so that
error path can inspect only a prefix. No result is returned on that
path.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Reverse the edge direction accidentally. Under this lesson's
  contract, `u -> v` means `u` must appear before `v`; some APIs store
  "prerequisites of u" instead and need conversion.
- Count only distinct neighbors but decrement every stored edge, or
  count duplicates but decrement once. Parallel occurrences must use
  the same multiplicity in both phases.
- Enqueue a vertex more than once. Append only on the exact transition
  from positive indegree to zero.
- Mark readiness after enqueueing without changing state. The zero
  transition itself is the one-time mark in this implementation.
- Return the emitted prefix as if it ordered the whole graph. A prefix
  can be valid even though another component contains a cycle.
- Call every blocked vertex cyclic. A vertex downstream from a cycle
  remains blocked even when it belongs to no cycle.
- Treat queue order as lexicographically smallest. Later release time
  can keep a smaller vertex behind an earlier-ready larger vertex.
- Ignore isolated vertices. They have indegree zero and belong in a
  complete order even though they occur in no edge.
- Miss self-loops. Edge `v -> v` gives `v` positive indegree forever
  and correctly proves a cycle.
- Treat nil or empty rows as invalid. Both simply mean no outgoing
  edges under this contract.
- Reject the empty graph. It has the unique empty topological order;
  this implementation returns non-nil empty result slices.
- Use a narrow counter that can overflow. This implementation uses
  `int` for slice indexing and guards each indegree increment.
- Decrement below zero. With matching count and removal passes, a
  negative indegree indicates an implementation defect.
- Mutate the input to "remove" edges when callers expect ownership.
  Separate counts preserve the adjacency list.
- Share adjacency rows with a concurrent writer without
  synchronization. Read-only intent does not make a data race safe.

##### When to choose it

Use Kahn's algorithm when all of these are true:

- The relation is directed and `u -> v` means `u` must precede `v`.
- You need one valid whole-graph order or a cycle/no-cycle answer.
- Incoming-edge counts are natural or useful application state.
- An iterative queue is preferable to recursion.
- A deterministic order based on input encoding is sufficient.

Typical uses include build prerequisites, course prerequisites,
schema migrations, data-pipeline stages, spreadsheet dependencies,
and evaluating a DAG from inputs toward outputs.

The remaining indegrees are also useful for a diagnostic blocked set.
That set answers "what could not be scheduled?" without falsely
claiming that every blocked task is itself cyclic.

When not to choose it:

Use [DFS topological sort](
#b142-dfs-topological-sort-stack-and-visit-states) when finish order
fits the surrounding traversal or when a recursion-stack technique is
needed to reconstruct a particular cycle witness.

Use [dependency layers](
#b143-dependency-layers-queue-and-level-array) when the result must
group tasks into parallel rounds rather than produce one flat order.
Use [lexicographic topological order](
#b144-lexicographic-topological-order-heap) when the smallest ready
vertex must be selected at every step.

Use strongly connected components when the caller needs the actual
cyclic groups. Kahn's blocked set can include acyclic descendants such
as vertex 7 in the worked example.

A topological order expresses precedence, not durations, worker
capacity, deadlines, or an optimal parallel schedule. Use a scheduling
model when those constraints determine the objective.

For a graph that changes after every query, rebuilding all indegrees
may be too expensive. Use an incremental dependency algorithm only
when the update frequency justifies its greater complexity.

Related material:

[A.5.1 Queues](#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) owns head-index FIFO
mechanics.
[A.10.1 Directed and undirected graphs](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) defines edge direction, and
[A.10.4 Bipartite graphs and DAGs](
#a104-bipartite-graphs-and-directed-acyclic-graphs) owns the DAG
classification. [B.12.4 Directed-cycle detection](
#b124-directed-cycle-detection-color-array) compares DFS visit
states, while [B.13.5 DAG shortest paths](
#b135-dag-shortest-paths-topological-order-and-array) uses a
topological order as a relaxation phase.

Kahn's original [topological-sorting paper](
https://doi.org/10.1145/368996.369025) presents the removal method for
large networks. NIST's [topological sort definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/topologicalSort.html) connects the
operation to partial orders.

#### B.14.2 DFS topological sort (stack and visit states)

##### Problem and contract

A directed acyclic graph can be ordered without first counting
incoming edges. Depth-first search can instead delay a vertex until
all work reachable through its outgoing edges has finished. Reversing
that finish sequence places every prerequisite before the work that
depends on it.

This lesson receives a directed adjacency list and returns one
topological order when the graph is acyclic. It uses three visit
states to reject a directed cycle encountered during the same search.
Its result contract is:

- A DAG returns a non-nil complete order, `acyclic=true`, and no
  error.
- A cyclic graph returns a nil order, false, and no error.
- An invalid edge endpoint returns a nil order, false, and an error.
- An empty graph is a valid DAG and returns a non-nil empty order.

Vertices are the integer indices in `[0,V)`. `adjacency[u]` lists
directed destinations of edges from `u`. A stored edge `u -> v` means
`u` must appear before `v` in the returned order.

Self-loops, parallel edge occurrences, isolated vertices,
disconnected components, and nil or empty rows are valid input
structure. A self-loop or any longer directed cycle makes ordering
impossible. Repeated edges are inspected in place but do not repeat a
vertex in the result.

The deterministic policy is:

- consider new DFS roots in increasing numeric order;
- inspect every adjacency row from left to right;
- append a vertex only when its row and descendants are complete;
  and
- reverse the complete finish sequence once.

This is deterministic for a fixed adjacency encoding but does not
promise the numerically or lexicographically smallest valid order.

The function validates the whole graph before search. It reads but
does not mutate or retain the adjacency slices. The returned order
owns its storage. Concurrent input mutation without synchronization
is outside the contract.

Read [graph DFS](
#b121-depth-first-search-adjacency-list-and-stack) for resumable
frames and [directed-cycle detection](
#b124-directed-cycle-detection-color-array) for cycle witnesses.
This lesson owns the distinct reverse-finish ordering result.

##### Mental model

Store one of three states at each vertex:

```text
unseen    no DFS frame has discovered this vertex
active    its frame is on the current DFS path
finished  its entire outgoing row has closed
```

Read `stateByVertex[3] == topologicalActive` as: "vertex 3 is on the
current depth-first path, and its outgoing work is not complete." A
single visited bit is insufficient because an edge to an active
vertex proves a cycle, while an edge to a finished vertex can be safe.

An explicit stack frame stores `(vertex,nextNeighbor)`. The stack
bottom-to-top is the active DFS path. For frame `(4,2)`, vertex 4 is
active, row entries before index 2 are complete, and entry 2 is next.

For each unseen numeric start, mark it active and push its initial
frame. At the top frame:

- If its row is exhausted, mark the vertex finished, append it to
  `finishOrder`, and pop the frame.
- If the next destination is unseen, advance the current frame, mark
  the destination active, and push its initial frame.
- If the destination is active, the edge returns to an ancestor on
  the current path, so reject the graph as cyclic.
- If the destination is finished, advance past the edge. That
  destination already closed safely.

Advance `nextNeighbor` before a possible push. The suspended parent
then resumes at the following entry when the child returns.

`finishOrder` is postorder, not the answer yet. A destination reached
through `u -> v` finishes before `u` when DFS descends through that
edge. If `v` was already finished, it also appears before `u` in the
finish sequence. Reversing the complete sequence therefore places
`u` before `v` in either case.

The outer root loop is necessary. One DFS tree reaches only its
directed component, but a whole-graph topological order must include
isolated vertices and every disconnected component.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use this dependency graph:

```text
0: [1, 1, 2]
1: [3, 4]
2: [3]
3: [5]
4: [5]
5: []
6: []
```

The repeated `0 -> 1` occurrence tests duplicate handling. Vertex 6
is isolated. The expected deterministic order is:

```text
[6, 0, 2, 1, 4, 3, 5]
```

Stack snapshots below run bottom-to-top. `U`, `A`, and `F` mean
unseen, active, and finished.

Initial state: all seven vertices are `U`; `finishOrder=[]`; the stack
is empty; numeric start 0 is the first unseen root.

1. **Before:** vertex 0 is unseen and its first destination is 1.
   **Decision:** mark 0 active and push `(0,0)`. Inspect `0 -> 1`,
   advance the root frame to `(0,1)`, mark 1 active, and push `(1,0)`.
   **After:** stack is `[(0,1),(1,0)]`; vertices 0 and 1 are `A`;
   `finishOrder=[]`.
   **Known correct:** the stack is directed path `0 -> 1`, while the
   second edge to 1 and edge to 2 remain unexamined.
2. **Before:** frame `(1,0)` points to unseen destination 3.
   **Decision:** advance it to `(1,1)`, mark 3 active, and push
   `(3,0)`.
   **After:** stack is `[(0,1),(1,1),(3,0)]`; 0, 1, and 3 are `A`.
   **Known correct:** every stack step is a real directed edge, and
   no vertex has been placed in finish order early.
3. **Before:** frame `(3,0)` points to unseen destination 5.
   **Decision:** advance 3's frame, mark 5 active, and push `(5,0)`.
   **After:** stack is `[(0,1),(1,1),(3,1),(5,0)]` and all four
   named vertices are active.
   **Known correct:** vertex 5 is a descendant of 3 and must finish
   before 3 can finish.
4. **Before:** vertex 5 has an empty row. **Decision:** mark 5
   finished, append 5, and pop. The resumed row of 3 is also
   exhausted, so finish and append 3.
   **After:** stack is `[(0,1),(1,1)]`; `finishOrder=[5,3]`; vertices
   5 and 3 are `F`.
   **Known correct:** every outgoing edge of each appended vertex is
   complete, and descendant 5 appears before source 3 in postorder.
5. **Before:** vertex 1 resumes at unseen destination 4.
   **Decision:** advance the frame and descend to 4. Edge `4 -> 5`
   reaches finished 5, so skip the edge and then finish 4.
   **After:** stack is `[(0,1),(1,2)]` and
   `finishOrder=[5,3,4]`.
   **Known correct:** reaching finished 5 is safe convergence, not a
   cycle; 5 still precedes 4 in finish order.
6. **Before:** vertex 1 has no remaining entry. **Decision:** finish
   vertex 1; at vertex 0, inspect the second occurrence of destination
   1, which is finished. Skip it, then descend through `0 -> 2`.
   **After:** stack is `[(0,3),(2,0)]` and
   `finishOrder=[5,3,4,1]`.
   **Known correct:** the duplicate edge creates no second frame, and
   root 0 still waits for its last child's subtree.
7. **Before:** vertex 2 points to finished destination 3.
   **Decision:** skip that safe edge, finish 2, then finish exhausted
   root 0.
   **After:** the stack is empty and
   `finishOrder=[5,3,4,1,2,0]`.
   **Known correct:** all work reachable from root 0 is finished; for
   every examined edge, its destination precedes its source in
   finish order.
8. **Before:** numeric roots 1 through 5 are finished, while isolated
   vertex 6 is unseen. **Decision:** start 6; its row is empty, so
   finish it immediately. Reverse the completed sequence.
   **After:** finish order is `[5,3,4,1,2,0,6]`; returned order is
   `[6,0,2,1,4,3,5]`; `acyclic=true`.
   **Known correct:** all seven vertices appear once and every stored
   edge points from an earlier returned position to a later one.

The isolated vertex demonstrates the tie policy. Root 6 is considered
last, so it finishes last and becomes first after reversal. The order
is valid but is not the lexicographically smallest possible order.

For a cycle, add edge `5 -> 1` to the same graph.

Initial state: all vertices are unseen and the search begins at root
0 as before.

1. **Before:** the active descent follows `0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 5`.
   **Decision:** each parent advances before pushing its unseen child.
   **After:** stack is
   `[(0,1),(1,1),(3,1),(5,0)]`; vertices 0, 1, 3, and 5 are active.
   **Known correct:** the stack itself is the current directed path.
2. **Before:** vertex 5's next edge is `5 -> 1`, and vertex 1 is
   active. **Decision:** reject immediately instead of skipping the
   visited destination or building an order.
   **After:** return a nil order, `acyclic=false`, and no error.
   **Known correct:** active path `1 -> 3 -> 5` plus `5 -> 1` is a
   directed cycle, so no whole-graph topological order exists.

Reversing discovery order is a plausible but wrong shortcut. In DAG
`0:[1,2]`, `1:[2]`, discovery is `[0,1,2]`; reversing it gives
`[2,1,0]`, which violates `0 -> 1`. Correct finish order is
`[2,1,0]`, whose reverse `[0,1,2]` respects every edge. The safe event
is completion after descendants, not first discovery.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates DFS topological sort (stack and
// visit states). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

const (
	topologicalUnseen uint8 = iota
	topologicalActive
	topologicalFinished
)

type topologicalFrame struct {
	vertex       int
	nextNeighbor int
}

func validateTopologicalAdjacency(adjacency [][]int) error {
	// Reject input outside the topological adjacency contract before
	// mutation.
	for source, neighbors := range adjacency {
		for _, destination := range neighbors {
			if destination < 0 || destination >= len(adjacency) {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %d -> %d has an invalid destination",
					source,
					destination,
				)
			}
		}
	}

	return nil
}

func depthFirstTopologicalSort(
	adjacency [][]int,
) ([]int, bool, error) {
	// Validate before creating any result or traversal state.
	if err := validateTopologicalAdjacency(adjacency); err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	stateByVertex := make([]uint8, len(adjacency))
	finishOrder := make([]int, 0, len(adjacency))
	stack := make([]topologicalFrame, 0, len(adjacency))

	for start := range adjacency {
		if stateByVertex[start] != topologicalUnseen {
			continue
		}

		stateByVertex[start] = topologicalActive
		stack = append(stack, topologicalFrame{
			vertex: start,
		})
		for len(stack) > 0 {
			topIndex := len(stack) - 1
			frame := &stack[topIndex]
			neighbors := adjacency[frame.vertex]
			if frame.nextNeighbor == len(neighbors) {
				// A closed vertex follows all its descendants.
				stateByVertex[frame.vertex] =
					topologicalFinished
				finishOrder = append(
					finishOrder,
					frame.vertex,
				)
				stack = stack[:topIndex]
				continue
			}

			destination := neighbors[frame.nextNeighbor]
			frame.nextNeighbor++
			switch stateByVertex[destination] {
			case topologicalUnseen:
				// Mark before pushing so each vertex gets one frame.
				stateByVertex[destination] =
					topologicalActive
				stack = append(stack, topologicalFrame{
					vertex: destination,
				})
			case topologicalActive:
				// An active destination is an ancestor on this path.
				return nil, false, nil
			case topologicalFinished:
				// Its descendants already precede it in finish order.
			}
		}
	}

	// Reverse postorder puts every source before its destination.
	for left, right := 0, len(finishOrder)-1; left < right; {
		finishOrder[left], finishOrder[right] =
			finishOrder[right], finishOrder[left]
		left++
		right--
	}

	return finishOrder, true, nil
}

func ordinaryDependencyGraph() [][]int {
	// Keep ordinary dependency graph in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	return [][]int{
		{1, 1, 2},
		{3, 4},
		{3},
		{5},
		{5},
		{},
		nil,
	}
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	adjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	order, acyclic, err := depthFirstTopologicalSort(adjacency)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(order, acyclic)

	cycleAdjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	cycleAdjacency[5] = append(cycleAdjacency[5], 1)
	order, acyclic, err = depthFirstTopologicalSort(
		cycleAdjacency,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(order, acyclic)

	order, acyclic, err = depthFirstTopologicalSort(nil)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(order, acyclic)

	_, _, err = depthFirstTopologicalSort([][]int{{1}})
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
[6 0 2 1 4 3 5] true
[] false
[] true
true
```

`fmt.Println` renders both a nil order and a non-nil empty order as
`[]`. The Boolean and error distinguish them: the second line is a
cycle, while the third is the empty DAG's valid empty order.

The example uses an explicit frame stack rather than Go recursion. A
long dependency chain can therefore grow heap-backed slice storage
instead of consuming one goroutine call frame per vertex.

##### Why it works

Maintain this invariant during search:

- the stack contains exactly one directed path of active vertices;
- each frame's earlier row entries are complete and its stored index
  identifies the next entry;
- every finished vertex has had its entire outgoing row processed;
  and
- `finishOrder` contains each finished vertex once, in closure order.

Starting an unseen root creates a one-vertex active path. Descending
to an unseen destination follows a real edge, advances the parent
first, and extends that path by one frame. Skipping a finished
destination completes the current edge without changing the path.
Closing an exhausted frame removes only the path's last vertex and
records it once. Each transition therefore preserves the invariant.

An edge from the top vertex to an active destination returns to an
ancestor because all active frames form one path. The path from that
ancestor to the top plus the inspected edge is a directed cycle.
Rejecting at that edge is therefore sound.

If a directed cycle exists, consider the first cycle vertex
discovered. DFS cannot finish it before processing the rest of the
reachable cycle. When a cycle edge returns toward that still-active
vertex, the algorithm rejects, unless an earlier active edge already
proved another cycle. Therefore completing every DFS tree without an
active edge proves the graph acyclic.

Now consider any edge `u -> v` in an accepted graph. When DFS examines
it, either `v` is unseen or finished; it cannot be active.

- If `v` is unseen, DFS finishes `v` and its subtree before returning
  to finish `u`.
- If `v` is finished, `v` already precedes the eventual finish of
  `u`.

Thus `v` precedes `u` in `finishOrder` for every edge. Reversing the
sequence places `u` before `v`, exactly the topological requirement.

Termination is bounded. Each vertex changes from unseen to active to
finished at most once. Each frame index advances across one finite
row, each vertex receives at most one frame, and each frame is popped
once. The outer root loop also advances through only `V` vertices.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `V` be the number of vertices and `A` the number of stored
directed edge occurrences, including duplicates.

Validation scans every row and edge in `Theta(V+A)` time. Search
activates and finishes each vertex at most once and advances once past
each inspected edge occurrence. A successful search also reverses
`V` finish entries. Because validation always reads the full valid
input, best, average, and worst total time are all `Theta(V+A)`, even
when the search later finds a self-loop immediately.

The state slice and explicit frame stack use `O(V)` auxiliary space.
On a DAG, `finishOrder` becomes the returned order in place and uses
`Theta(V)` output space. On a cyclic graph, any partial finish slice
is discarded and can have `O(V)` temporary storage. The explicit
implementation uses no recursive call stack.

A recursive equivalent has the same asymptotic `O(V)` depth bound,
but a path of `V` vertices creates `V` nested calls. The explicit
slice makes that resource visible and avoids depending on call-stack
growth for graph-depth safety.

Invalid input can return during a validation prefix. No traversal or
result slice is allocated before that pass succeeds.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Append on discovery instead of finish. Preorder does not guarantee
  that a source precedes every destination after reversal.
- Forget the final reversal. Raw finish order places destinations
  before sources and is the opposite of the required order.
- Use one visited bit. In DAG diamond `0->1`, `0->2`, `1->3`, and
  `2->3`, edge `2->3` reaches finished 3 and is not a cycle.
- Ignore an edge to an active vertex. Graph `0->1->0` would then
  produce an invalid sequence instead of rejecting the cycle.
- Mark a vertex active after pushing its child. A back edge can then
  create duplicate frames before the state reflects the path.
- Mark a vertex finished before its row is exhausted. Later outgoing
  work may need to precede it in finish order.
- Increment the neighbor index after returning. The parent would
  inspect the same child edge repeatedly.
- Return a partial finish sequence on a cycle. Vertices closed before
  the active edge do not form a whole-graph topological order.
- Search only from vertex 0. Disconnected components and isolated
  vertices must also appear in a complete order.
- Assume numeric root order yields numeric output. Three isolated
  roots finish `[0,1,2]` and reverse to `[2,1,0]`.
- Deduplicate or sort adjacency silently. Duplicates do not change
  validity, but changing row order can change the deterministic
  returned order.
- Treat a self-loop as harmless. Edge `v -> v` reaches the currently
  active vertex and correctly rejects the graph.
- Reject nil or empty rows. Both mean no outgoing edge. Nil adjacency
  itself is the valid empty DAG under this contract.
- Confuse a cyclic result with invalid input. Cycle is
  `(nil,false,nil)`; malformed input includes a non-nil error.
- Use recursion without a depth argument. A long chain can make call-
  stack resource use the practical limit even though the algorithm
  is asymptotically linear.
- Mutate adjacency while searching. The function promises read-only
  access, but a concurrent writer still creates a data race.

##### When to choose it

Choose DFS topological sort when:

- the graph is directed and must be ordered or rejected as cyclic;
- surrounding work already uses DFS entry and exit events;
- reverse postorder is useful to a later graph phase;
- adjacency row order should define a reproducible result; and
- indegree counts or a ready-task frontier are not otherwise needed.

Common applications include ordering compiler passes, dependency
evaluation, DAG dynamic programming, and graph algorithms that need
vertices after all descendants have been processed.

Explicit frames are especially useful when maximum graph depth is not
small enough to trust recursion. They also expose the exact resume
point needed for postorder.

When not to choose it:

Use [Kahn's algorithm](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) when zero-indegree
tasks are meaningful application state, when ready work may execute
in parallel, or when a blocked diagnostic set is more useful than DFS
finish events.

Use [directed-cycle detection](
#b124-directed-cycle-detection-color-array) when failure must include
an actual closed cycle. This lesson detects the same active-edge
condition but intentionally returns no cycle witness or parents.

Use [dependency layers](
#b143-dependency-layers-queue-and-level-array) when tasks must be
grouped into simultaneous rounds. Use a min-heap variant when the
smallest currently ready vertex must be chosen at every position.

Do not use topological sorting on an undirected graph or on a valid
cyclic workflow. A general directed graph can instead be condensed by
strongly connected components when its cyclic regions must be treated
as units.

For a graph updated after each query, recomputing all states may be
too expensive. An incremental ordering algorithm has a more complex
contract but can reuse work across updates.

Related material:

[B.12.1 Graph DFS](
#b121-depth-first-search-adjacency-list-and-stack) owns explicit
resume frames. [B.12.4 Directed-cycle detection](
#b124-directed-cycle-detection-color-array) owns parent-based cycle
reconstruction. [A.10.4 DAGs](
#a104-bipartite-graphs-and-directed-acyclic-graphs) defines the
structural promise, while [B.13.5 DAG shortest paths](
#b135-dag-shortest-paths-topological-order-and-array) consumes a
topological order for one-pass relaxation.

Princeton's [directed-graph chapter](
https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/42digraph/) states the reverse-
postorder property for DAGs. Tarjan's original [linear DFS paper](
https://doi.org/10.1137/0201010) develops the depth-first framework
behind linear graph algorithms. NIST's [depth-first search
definition](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/depthfirst.html)
describes following outgoing edges before remaining siblings.

#### B.14.3 Dependency layers (queue and level array)

##### Problem and contract

A flat topological order says what may come before what, but it does
not show which tasks can run together. When every task takes one
round, all prerequisites must finish in earlier rounds, and workers
are unlimited, a dependency graph can be divided into **layers**:

- layer 0 contains tasks with no prerequisites;
- layer 1 contains tasks whose prerequisites are all in layer 0;
- later layers contain tasks released after every predecessor layer;
  and
- all tasks in one layer may run in parallel under this model.

This lesson receives a directed adjacency list. Edge `u -> v` means
task `u` must finish before task `v` starts. For a DAG, it returns
both the zero-based layer of every vertex and the vertices grouped by
layer. The layer of `v` is:

```text
0                                      when v has no predecessor
1 + maximum layer among predecessors  otherwise
```

That value is the earliest round in which `v` can run. The number of
nonempty layers is the minimum number of unit-duration rounds needed
with unlimited parallel workers.

The result contract is:

- A DAG returns a non-nil plan, `acyclic=true`, and no error.
- A directed cycle returns a nil plan, false, and no error.
- An invalid endpoint or unrepresentable count returns a nil plan,
  false, and an error.
- An empty graph returns a non-nil plan with non-nil empty level and
  layer slices.

Vertices are integer indices in `[0,V)`. Self-loops, parallel edge
occurrences, disconnected components, isolated vertices, and nil or
empty rows are valid input structure. Every parallel occurrence is
counted and removed separately, although duplicates do not change the
mathematical layer.

After computing levels, the implementation scans vertices in numeric
order to build the groups. Each layer is therefore numerically sorted
even when queue release order differs. The function reads but does
not mutate or retain the input. The returned plan owns its slices.
Unsynchronized concurrent input mutation is outside the contract.

Read [Kahn's topological sort](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) first. This lesson
extends its remaining-indegree invariant with an earliest-layer
recurrence rather than repeating its blocked-set purpose.

##### Mental model

Validate every destination, then count every incoming edge
occurrence. Keep these arrays:

```text
indegreeByVertex[v] = incoming occurrences from unprocessed sources
layerByVertex[v]    = greatest candidate layer seen so far
```

Read `layerByVertex[5] == 3` as: "after all of vertex 5's
predecessors are considered, task 5 can first run in round 3." The
value may still be tentative while its indegree is positive.

Enqueue all zero-indegree vertices in numeric order. Their default
layer is 0 because they have no prerequisite. When queue processing
removes source `u`, every outgoing occurrence `u -> v` proposes:

```text
candidate layer for v = layerByVertex[u] + 1
```

Assign the candidate only when it exceeds the current value. This
maximum matters because `v` must wait for every predecessor, not only
the predecessor reached by the shortest chain.

Then decrement `v`'s indegree for that occurrence. When the count
reaches zero, all predecessors have been processed. The stored
maximum is final, so enqueue `v` exactly once.

Track the greatest processed layer. If the queue emits fewer than
`V` vertices, a directed cycle prevents a complete plan; discard all
partial levels. Otherwise, allocate one group for every layer from 0
through the maximum. Scan vertices numerically and append each vertex
to the group selected by `layerByVertex`.

This is not ordinary multi-source BFS distance. BFS remembers the
minimum edge count from any source. Dependency layering needs the
maximum predecessor chain because a merge task waits for all incoming
branches.

Processing a fixed queue batch per round is an equivalent Kahn
variant. It must snapshot the batch size before processing the round;
newly released tasks belong to the next batch, never the current one.
The explicit level array makes that boundary and every vertex's
earliest round directly observable.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use this dependency graph:

```text
0: [3, 4, 4]
1: [2]
2: [3]
3: [5]
4: [5]
5: [6]
6: []
7: []
```

Vertex 3 has a short prerequisite path `0 -> 3` and a longer one
`1 -> 2 -> 3`. It must wait for both. The two `0 -> 4` entries are
parallel occurrences, and vertex 7 is isolated.

Initial indegrees and levels are:

```text
vertex:    0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
indegree:  0  0  1  2  2  2  1  0
layer:     0  0  0  0  0  0  0  0
```

Initial state: `readyQueue=[0,1,7]`, `queueHead=0`, processed count
is 0, and maximum layer is -1.

1. **Before:** source 0 is ready in layer 0. **Decision:** process
   candidate layer 1 for destinations 3 and 4. Decrement vertex 3
   once and vertex 4 twice, once per stored occurrence.
   **After:** layers 3 and 4 are 1; their indegrees are 1 and 0;
   vertex 4 joins the queue, whose unread suffix is `[1,7,4]`.
   **Known correct:** duplicate edges used the same candidate but both
   counts were removed; vertex 4 is now fully released.
2. **Before:** source 1 is ready in layer 0. **Decision:** propose
   layer 1 to vertex 2 and remove its sole incoming occurrence.
   **After:** vertex 2 has layer 1 and joins the queue; the unread
   suffix is `[7,4,2]`.
   **Known correct:** every queued vertex has no unprocessed
   predecessor, even though release order is not numeric layer order.
3. **Before:** isolated vertex 7 is next. **Decision:** process it in
   layer 0 without changing any count.
   **After:** the unread queue is `[4,2]`; the maximum layer remains
   0.
   **Known correct:** isolated work belongs to the first parallel
   round and still appears in the complete plan.
4. **Before:** source 4 has layer 1. **Decision:** propose layer 2 to
   vertex 5 and remove `4 -> 5`.
   **After:** vertex 5 has tentative layer 2 and indegree 1; it does
   not enter the queue.
   **Known correct:** predecessor 3 is unprocessed, so vertex 5's
   earliest round is not final.
5. **Before:** source 2 has layer 1, while vertex 3 has tentative
   layer 1 from source 0. **Decision:** propose layer 2 through
   `2 -> 3`, take the maximum, and remove the last incoming edge.
   **After:** vertex 3's layer changes from 1 to 2 and it enters the
   queue.
   **Known correct:** the longer path `1 -> 2 -> 3`, not direct edge
   `0 -> 3`, determines when all prerequisites are complete.
6. **Before:** source 3 now has final layer 2. **Decision:** propose
   layer 3 to vertex 5, replacing tentative layer 2, and remove its
   last incoming occurrence.
   **After:** vertex 5 has final layer 3 and enters the queue.
   **Known correct:** merge task 5 waits for both predecessor branches
   and uses the later one.
7. **Before:** source 5 is in layer 3. **Decision:** release vertex 6
   into layer 4, then process vertex 6's empty row.
   **After:** all eight vertices are processed; maximum layer is 4;
   the queue is exhausted.
   **Known correct:** each dependency raises the destination by at
   least one layer, and no vertex remains blocked.
8. **Before:** the final level array is `[0,0,1,2,1,3,4,0]`.
   **Decision:** scan vertices 0 through 7 and group them by that
   array rather than by queue release order.
   **After:** layers are
   `[[0,1,7],[2,4],[3],[5],[6]]`; return `acyclic=true`.
   **Known correct:** every edge crosses to a later group, each group
   is numeric, and five rounds attain the longest dependency chain.

For a cycle, add edge `6 -> 3`. Vertices 3, 5, and 6 then form cycle
`3 -> 5 -> 6 -> 3`.

Initial state: vertex 3 now has indegree 3; the initial ready queue is
still `[0,1,7]`.

1. **Before:** sources 0, 1, and 7 are ready. **Decision:** process
   them, then process released vertices 4 and 2.
   **After:** processed count is 5; vertex 3 still has indegree 1 from
   vertex 6, and vertex 5 still has indegree 1 from vertex 3.
   **Known correct:** no cyclic vertex has reached zero indegree.
2. **Before:** the queue is empty but three vertices are unprocessed.
   **Decision:** reject instead of returning tentative layers.
   **After:** return a nil plan, `acyclic=false`, and no error.
   **Known correct:** the cycle prevents any valid whole-graph round
   assignment, even though five vertices were schedulable first.

Multi-source BFS gives a useful counterexample. In graph `0 -> 3`
and `1 -> 2 -> 3`, BFS from sources 0 and 1 assigns distance 1 to
vertex 3 through source 0. That is the first incorrect decision:
vertex 3 cannot run in round 1 because predecessor 2 runs in round 1.
The maximum recurrence correctly assigns vertex 3 to round 2.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Dependency layers (queue and level
// array). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

type dependencyPlan struct {
	layers        [][]int
	layerByVertex []int
}

func validateDependencyGraph(adjacency [][]int) error {
	// Reject input outside the dependency graph contract before
	// mutation.
	for source, neighbors := range adjacency {
		for _, destination := range neighbors {
			if destination < 0 || destination >= len(adjacency) {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %d -> %d has an invalid destination",
					source,
					destination,
				)
			}
		}
	}

	return nil
}

func countDependencyIndegrees(
	adjacency [][]int,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	indegreeByVertex := make([]int, len(adjacency))
	for source, neighbors := range adjacency {
		for _, destination := range neighbors {
			// Parallel occurrences contribute separate counts.
			if indegreeByVertex[destination] == math.MaxInt {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"indegree overflows at edge %d -> %d",
					source,
					destination,
				)
			}
			indegreeByVertex[destination]++
		}
	}

	return indegreeByVertex, nil
}

func buildDependencyLayers(
	adjacency [][]int,
) (*dependencyPlan, bool, error) {
	// Validate before allocating any observable result.
	if err := validateDependencyGraph(adjacency); err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	indegreeByVertex, err := countDependencyIndegrees(
		adjacency,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	readyQueue := make([]int, 0, len(adjacency))
	for vertex, indegree := range indegreeByVertex {
		if indegree == 0 {
			readyQueue = append(readyQueue, vertex)
		}
	}

	layerByVertex := make([]int, len(adjacency))
	processedCount := 0
	maximumLayer := -1
	for queueHead := 0; queueHead < len(readyQueue); queueHead++ {
		source := readyQueue[queueHead]
		sourceLayer := layerByVertex[source]
		processedCount++
		if sourceLayer > maximumLayer {
			maximumLayer = sourceLayer
		}

		nextLayer := sourceLayer
		if len(adjacency[source]) > 0 {
			if sourceLayer == math.MaxInt {
				return nil, false, fmt.Errorf(
					"layer overflows after vertex %d",
					source,
				)
			}
			nextLayer++
		}

		for _, destination := range adjacency[source] {
			// A merge waits for its latest predecessor layer.
			if nextLayer > layerByVertex[destination] {
				layerByVertex[destination] = nextLayer
			}
			indegreeByVertex[destination]--
			if indegreeByVertex[destination] == 0 {
				readyQueue = append(readyQueue, destination)
			}
		}
	}

	if processedCount != len(adjacency) {
		return nil, false, nil
	}

	// Numeric scanning gives each layer a stable internal order.
	layers := make([][]int, maximumLayer+1)
	for vertex, layer := range layerByVertex {
		layers[layer] = append(layers[layer], vertex)
	}

	return &dependencyPlan{
		layers:        layers,
		layerByVertex: layerByVertex,
	}, true, nil
}

func ordinaryDependencyGraph() [][]int {
	// Keep ordinary dependency graph in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	return [][]int{
		{3, 4, 4},
		{2},
		{3},
		{5},
		{5},
		{6},
		{},
		nil,
	}
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	adjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	plan, acyclic, err := buildDependencyLayers(adjacency)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(plan.layerByVertex)
	fmt.Println(plan.layers)
	fmt.Println(acyclic)

	cycleAdjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	cycleAdjacency[6] = append(cycleAdjacency[6], 3)
	cyclePlan, cycleAcyclic, err := buildDependencyLayers(
		cycleAdjacency,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(cyclePlan == nil, cycleAcyclic)

	emptyPlan, emptyAcyclic, err := buildDependencyLayers(nil)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(
		emptyPlan.layerByVertex,
		emptyPlan.layers,
		emptyAcyclic,
	)

	_, _, err = buildDependencyLayers([][]int{{1}})
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
[0 0 1 2 1 3 4 0]
[[0 1 7] [2 4] [3] [5] [6]]
true
true false
[] [] true
true
```

The example returns both indexed and grouped views because they serve
different callers. Direct lookup answers "which round contains task
`v`?" in constant time; the groups drive round-by-round execution.

`fmt.Println` displays a nil slice and non-nil empty slice in the same
way. The empty-DAG plan nevertheless owns two non-nil empty slices. A
cycle returns no plan at all.

##### Why it works

The first invariant is Kahn's remaining-edge fact:

> `indegreeByVertex[v]` equals the number of incoming stored edge
> occurrences whose source has not been processed.

Initial counting establishes it. Processing source `u` subtracts
exactly each occurrence in `adjacency[u]`, so no other remaining edge
is changed. A vertex reaches zero exactly after all predecessors have
been processed.

The second invariant is:

> `layerByVertex[v]` is the maximum of `layer[u]+1` over processed
> predecessors `u`; a source with no predecessor remains at zero.

The zero-filled array establishes the source case. Every processed
edge contributes its candidate through a maximum update. When a
vertex's indegree reaches zero, every predecessor has contributed, so
its stored layer is final and satisfies the recurrence in the
contract.

For every edge `u -> v`, the finalized recurrence gives
`layer[v] >= layer[u]+1`. Therefore `u` is in an earlier group than
`v`, and running groups in increasing order is a feasible schedule.

No feasible schedule can place a vertex earlier than this value.
Along a directed path of `L` edges, every next task must occupy a
strictly later round, so the last vertex needs a layer of at least
`L`. The recurrence assigns exactly the greatest such path length.
Thus every task is as early as its dependencies permit, and one plus
the maximum layer is the minimum number of unit-duration rounds.

If processing stalls early, the same finite-predecessor argument as
Kahn's algorithm proves a directed cycle among the remaining graph.
A cycle cannot receive strictly increasing integer layers around its
return edge, so no valid layer plan exists. Emitting all vertices
proves acyclicity and makes every level final.

Termination is bounded. Every vertex is enqueued and processed at
most once. Each stored edge occurrence is decremented once, and the
final grouping scan visits each vertex once.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `V` be vertex count and `A` be the number of stored directed edge
occurrences, including duplicates.

Validation and indegree counting each scan all vertices and edges.
Queue processing handles every emitted vertex once and every emitted
outgoing occurrence once. A DAG then scans all vertices to group
them. A cyclic graph still had every edge validated and counted.
Therefore best, average, and worst valid-input time are all
`Theta(V+A)` under this full-validation contract.

The indegree array and queue use `O(V)` auxiliary space. On a cyclic
graph, the discarded partial level array also uses `O(V)`. On a DAG,
the returned level array has `Theta(V)` entries. The layer slice has
at most `V` rows and stores exactly `V` vertex indices across them, so
total output space is `Theta(V)`.

The implementation retains processed queue entries until return
because it advances a head index instead of shifting the slice. Peak
queue storage is `O(V)`.

Indegree increments guard `math.MaxInt`. Layer addition is also
guarded, although any realizable simple path in a `V`-vertex DAG has
at most `V-1` edges. Invalid input may stop within the validation
prefix before result allocation.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Take the minimum predecessor level as BFS would. Merge task 3 in
  the example must use `max(0+1,1+1)=2`, not layer 1.
- Update a destination only when its indegree reaches zero. Earlier
  predecessors' candidate levels would be lost; update the maximum on
  every edge, then finalize at zero.
- Put newly released tasks in the current round. Under a batch-queue
  implementation, snapshot the current queue size before processing.
- Count duplicate edges once but decrement twice, or count twice but
  decrement once. The first can make indegree negative; the second
  can block a valid task forever.
- Enqueue on every zero observation. Append only on the positive-to-
  zero transition so each vertex is processed once.
- Return partial levels after a cycle stall. Upstream tasks may have
  valid-looking numbers even though no whole-graph plan exists.
- Group by queue order when the contract promises numeric rows. This
  example releases vertex 4 before 2, but numeric layer 1 is `[2,4]`.
- Forget isolated vertices. They have layer 0 and belong in the first
  group even though they appear in no edge.
- Treat a self-loop as a one-task layer. Its indegree never reaches
  zero, so it correctly causes cycle rejection.
- Reject the empty graph. It needs zero rounds and returns non-nil
  empty result slices under this contract.
- Confuse zero with "unset." Zero is the correct initial tentative
  level and the final level of every source.
- Assume the layer count models real elapsed time. It does so only for
  equal unit durations and unlimited parallel capacity.
- Mutate or retain input rows to save counts. Separate arrays preserve
  caller ownership and keep results independent of later input edits.
- Share adjacency with a concurrent writer. Read-only function intent
  does not make unsynchronized slices safe.

##### When to choose it

Choose dependency layers when:

- edges are hard precedence constraints in a DAG;
- tasks have equal one-round duration;
- worker or machine capacity is effectively unlimited;
- the caller needs earliest rounds or parallel batches; and
- a complete plan should be rejected when any cycle exists.

Examples include course semesters with no credit cap, build waves,
pipeline stages, spreadsheet evaluation batches, and unit-duration
project tasks. The maximum layer also reveals the critical chain
length under this simplified model.

The indexed view is useful for comparing two tasks' earliest rounds.
The grouped view is useful for executing or displaying the plan one
round at a time.

When not to choose it:

Use an ordinary [Kahn topological order](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) when one valid flat
sequence or a blocked diagnostic set is enough. Use [DFS topological
sort](#b142-dfs-topological-sort-stack-and-visit-states) when reverse
finish order fits the surrounding traversal.

Do not use multi-source BFS distance for merge dependencies. It finds
the nearest source, while a task must wait for its farthest required
predecessor chain.

For variable task durations, use weighted longest-path or critical-
path calculations in topological order. For limited workers, machines,
memory, course credits, deadlines, or mutually exclusive resources,
layers are only a precedence lower bound; use a resource-constrained
scheduler.

Use [lexicographic topological order](
#b144-lexicographic-topological-order-heap) when one smallest flat
order is required rather than maximal parallel batches. Use strongly
connected components when cycles must be reported or condensed rather
than rejected.

For frequently changing graphs, rebuilding all indegrees and levels
may be too expensive. Incremental scheduling requires an update-aware
algorithm and a more complex invalidation contract.

Related material:

[B.14.1 Kahn's topological sort](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) owns the queue and
remaining-indegree proof. [B.13.1 Unweighted BFS](
#b131-unweighted-bfs-queue-and-distance-array) owns minimum-edge
distance and explains why FIFO discovery answers a different question.
[B.13.5 DAG shortest paths](
#b135-dag-shortest-paths-topological-order-and-array) demonstrates a
different recurrence evaluated in topological order.

NIST defines the weighted [critical-path problem](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/criticalPath.html) as a longest path
in a DAG. Kelley and Walker's original [critical-path planning paper](
https://doi.org/10.1145/1460299.1460318) develops the broader project-
scheduling setting from which the unit-duration model is simplified.

#### B.14.4 Lexicographic topological order (heap)

##### Problem and contract

A DAG may have many valid topological orders. A FIFO queue returns one
of them, but its answer can depend on when a vertex became ready and
on adjacency-row order. Some callers need one canonical answer: the
**lexicographically smallest topological order** by vertex ID.

Compare two integer sequences at their first differing position. The
sequence with the smaller vertex there is lexicographically smaller.
For example, `[0,1,4]` is smaller than `[0,3,2]` because 1 is smaller
than 3 at the first difference.

This lesson receives a directed adjacency list. Edge `u -> v` means
`u` must appear before `v`. It returns the smallest sequence among all
complete sequences that respect every edge.

The result contract is:

- A DAG returns a non-nil complete order, `acyclic=true`, and no
  error.
- A cyclic graph returns a nil order, false, and no error.
- An invalid endpoint or unrepresentable indegree returns a nil
  order, false, and an error.
- An empty graph returns a non-nil empty order and true.

Vertices are integer indices in `[0,V)`, and their integer comparison
defines "lexicographic." This is not string comparison: vertex 2 is
smaller than vertex 10 even though text `"10"` sorts before `"2"`.

Self-loops, parallel edge occurrences, isolated vertices,
disconnected components, and nil or empty rows are valid input
structure. Every parallel occurrence contributes to indegree and is
removed separately. Adjacency-row order does not affect the returned
canonical order.

The function validates the whole graph before search. It reads but
does not mutate or retain the adjacency slices, and the result owns
its storage. Concurrent input mutation without synchronization is
outside the contract.

Read [Kahn's topological sort](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) for the remaining-
indegree invariant and [min-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) for
priority-frontier mechanics. This lesson owns their greedy
combination and the lexicographic proof.

##### Mental model

Count every incoming edge occurrence. A vertex is **ready** when its
remaining indegree is zero: every predecessor is already in the
emitted prefix.

Replace Kahn's FIFO queue with a min-heap. Keep this state:

```text
indegreeByVertex[v] = incoming occurrences from un-emitted sources
readyVertices       = every un-emitted zero-indegree vertex
order               = the fixed output prefix
```

Read heap root 3 as: "vertex 3 is the smallest vertex that can legally
occupy the next output position." The heap's backing slice is not
globally sorted; only its root is guaranteed smallest.

Initialize the heap with every zero-indegree vertex. Then repeat:

- Remove the heap minimum and append it to `order`.
- Decrement each destination once per occurrence in the removed
  vertex's adjacency row.
- When a destination changes from positive indegree to zero, push it
  into the heap.

A newly ready small vertex competes immediately with vertices that
were ready earlier. This is the decisive difference from FIFO. The
heap chooses by ID, not by arrival time.

When the heap empties, a complete order has length `V`. A shorter
prefix means some directed cycle prevented the remaining vertices
from reaching zero indegree. Return no partial order in that case.

The Go example adapts a named `[]int` type to `container/heap`.
`Less` defines smaller IDs as higher priority. The adapter's `Push`
and `Pop` methods are callbacks used by the package; algorithm code
must call `heap.Push` and `heap.Pop` so the package repairs its
invariant. The `any` type assertion is safe because this function
inserts only `int` vertex IDs.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use this graph:

```text
0: [1, 1, 2]
1: [3]
2: [3]
3: [5]
4: [5]
5: []
```

The repeated `0 -> 1` occurrence tests multiplicity. Vertices 0 and
4 are initially ready. Initial indegrees are:

```text
vertex:    0  1  2  3  4  5
indegree:  0  2  1  2  0  2
```

Heap snapshots below show the logical ready set in sorted braces, not
the heap's internal slice layout.

Initial state: `readyVertices={0,4}`, `order=[]`, and no edge has been
removed.

1. **Before:** ready minimum is 0. **Decision:** pop 0 and process row
   `[1,1,2]`. Decrement vertex 1 twice and vertex 2 once; push each
   when its count reaches zero.
   **After:** `order=[0]`; indegrees 1 and 2 are zero; ready set is
   `{1,2,4}`.
   **Known correct:** duplicate occurrences were both removed, and 1
   is the smallest legal second vertex.
2. **Before:** vertices 1, 2, and 4 are ready. **Decision:** pop 1,
   not the earlier-ready 4, and remove `1 -> 3`.
   **After:** `order=[0,1]`; vertex 3 has indegree 1; ready set is
   `{2,4}`.
   **Known correct:** no valid continuation of prefix `[0]` can begin
   with a vertex smaller than 1.
3. **Before:** ready minimum is 2. **Decision:** pop 2 and remove
   `2 -> 3`, changing vertex 3's indegree from 1 to 0.
   **After:** `order=[0,1,2]`; push 3; ready set is `{3,4}`.
   **Known correct:** newly ready 3 must compete immediately with 4
   rather than wait behind it by arrival time.
4. **Before:** 3 is smaller than ready vertex 4. **Decision:** pop 3
   and remove `3 -> 5`.
   **After:** `order=[0,1,2,3]`; vertex 5 has indegree 1; ready set is
   `{4}`.
   **Known correct:** choosing 4 instead would make the first
   differing position larger.
5. **Before:** vertex 4 is the only ready item. **Decision:** pop it
   and remove `4 -> 5`, releasing vertex 5.
   **After:** `order=[0,1,2,3,4]`; ready set is `{5}`.
   **Known correct:** both predecessors of 5 now occur in the prefix.
6. **Before:** ready set contains only 5. **Decision:** pop 5; its row
   is empty, so no count changes.
   **After:** `order=[0,1,2,3,4,5]`; the heap is empty; six of six
   vertices were emitted.
   **Known correct:** every edge points forward and every position
   used the smallest legal vertex, so return this canonical order.

A FIFO queue demonstrates why arrival order is insufficient. It
starts `[0,4]`. After emitting 0, it appends 1 and 2 behind 4, so its
prefix becomes `[0,4]` and its complete valid result is
`[0,4,1,2,3,5]`. The first wrong decision is keeping 4 ahead of newly
ready 1. The heap instead returns `[0,1,2,3,4,5]`, which is smaller at
position 1.

For a cycle, add edge `5 -> 3`. Vertices 3 and 5 then form cycle
`3 -> 5 -> 3`.

Initial state: vertex 3 now has indegree 3; ready set is still
`{0,4}`.

1. **Before:** the heap contains ready vertices. **Decision:** emit
   0, then 1 and 2 when they become the smallest ready choices, and
   emit 4 when it is the only ready vertex.
   **After:** `order=[0,1,2,4]`; vertex 3 retains indegree 1 from 5;
   vertex 5 retains indegree 1 from 3; the heap is empty.
   **Known correct:** neither cycle vertex is legally ready.
2. **Before:** four of six vertices were emitted. **Decision:** reject
   instead of exposing that partial prefix.
   **After:** return a nil order, `acyclic=false`, and no error.
   **Known correct:** a complete topological order cannot cross the
   mutual dependency between 3 and 5.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Lexicographic topological order
// (heap). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

type vertexMinHeap []int

func (vertices vertexMinHeap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(vertices)
}

func (vertices vertexMinHeap) Less(first int, second int) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	return vertices[first] < vertices[second]
}

func (vertices vertexMinHeap) Swap(first int, second int) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	vertices[first], vertices[second] =
		vertices[second], vertices[first]
}

func (vertices *vertexMinHeap) Push(value any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	*vertices = append(*vertices, value.(int))
}

func (vertices *vertexMinHeap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	old := *vertices
	lastIndex := len(old) - 1
	value := old[lastIndex]
	old[lastIndex] = 0
	*vertices = old[:lastIndex]
	return value
}

func validateLexicographicGraph(adjacency [][]int) error {
	// Reject input outside the lexicographic graph contract before
	// mutation.
	for source, neighbors := range adjacency {
		for _, destination := range neighbors {
			if destination < 0 || destination >= len(adjacency) {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %d -> %d has an invalid destination",
					source,
					destination,
				)
			}
		}
	}

	return nil
}

func countLexicographicIndegrees(
	adjacency [][]int,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	indegreeByVertex := make([]int, len(adjacency))
	for source, neighbors := range adjacency {
		for _, destination := range neighbors {
			// Every parallel occurrence contributes separately.
			if indegreeByVertex[destination] == math.MaxInt {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"indegree overflows at edge %d -> %d",
					source,
					destination,
				)
			}
			indegreeByVertex[destination]++
		}
	}

	return indegreeByVertex, nil
}

func lexicographicTopologicalSort(
	adjacency [][]int,
) ([]int, bool, error) {
	// Validate before constructing any observable result.
	if err := validateLexicographicGraph(adjacency); err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	indegreeByVertex, err := countLexicographicIndegrees(
		adjacency,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	readyVertices := make(vertexMinHeap, 0, len(adjacency))
	for vertex, indegree := range indegreeByVertex {
		if indegree == 0 {
			readyVertices = append(readyVertices, vertex)
		}
	}
	heap.Init(&readyVertices)

	order := make([]int, 0, len(adjacency))
	for readyVertices.Len() > 0 {
		// The heap exposes the smallest valid next vertex.
		source := heap.Pop(&readyVertices).(int)
		order = append(order, source)

		for _, destination := range adjacency[source] {
			indegreeByVertex[destination]--
			if indegreeByVertex[destination] == 0 {
				// Only this transition inserts the vertex once.
				heap.Push(&readyVertices, destination)
			}
		}
	}

	if len(order) != len(adjacency) {
		return nil, false, nil
	}
	return order, true, nil
}

func ordinaryDependencyGraph() [][]int {
	// Keep ordinary dependency graph in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	return [][]int{
		{1, 1, 2},
		{3},
		{3},
		{5},
		{5},
		{},
	}
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	adjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	order, acyclic, err := lexicographicTopologicalSort(
		adjacency,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(order, acyclic)

	cycleAdjacency := ordinaryDependencyGraph()
	cycleAdjacency[5] = append(cycleAdjacency[5], 3)
	order, acyclic, err = lexicographicTopologicalSort(
		cycleAdjacency,
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(order, acyclic)

	order, acyclic, err = lexicographicTopologicalSort(nil)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(order, acyclic)

	_, _, err = lexicographicTopologicalSort([][]int{{1}})
	fmt.Println(err != nil)
}
```

Output:

```text
[0 1 2 3 4 5] true
[] false
[] true
true
```

`fmt.Println` renders the cyclic nil order and the empty DAG's
non-nil empty order the same way. The Boolean and error distinguish
those outcomes.

The adapter clears a removed integer slot for tidy retained storage.
For pointer-bearing heap items, clearing is more important because a
stale reference can keep an object reachable until the backing array
is released.

##### Why it works

Maintain the Kahn invariant:

> The heap contains exactly the un-emitted vertices whose incoming
> edges all come from the emitted prefix.

Initial indegree counting and insertion establish it. Popping removes
one ready vertex. Decrementing exactly its outgoing occurrences makes
each count equal the number of incoming occurrences from sources that
remain. A destination enters only on its one positive-to-zero
transition. The invariant therefore survives every step.

By the invariant, the popped vertex has no un-emitted predecessor, so
appending it preserves topological validity. If all vertices are
emitted, every edge source appears before its destination.

The minimum choice is lexicographically safe. Fix the greedy prefix
before one step. Every valid continuation must choose a ready vertex
next; choosing a vertex with a remaining predecessor would violate an
edge immediately. Let `m` be the heap minimum. No legal next vertex is
smaller than `m`, and removing `m` from a DAG leaves another DAG that
still has a topological continuation. Thus any valid order differing
at this position chooses a larger vertex and is lexicographically
larger. Induction over positions proves the complete order is the
smallest one.

If the heap empties early, every remaining vertex has a remaining
predecessor. Following predecessors in the finite remaining graph
eventually repeats a vertex, proving a directed cycle. Conversely, a
cycle never releases every member. Therefore completeness is
equivalent to acyclicity.

Each vertex enters and leaves the heap at most once, and each stored
edge occurrence is decremented once. Those finite bounds prove
termination.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `V` be vertex count, `A` be stored directed edge occurrences, and
`H` be the maximum number of simultaneously ready vertices.

Validation and indegree counting take `Theta(V+A)` time. Heap
initialization is `O(V)`. Each vertex is pushed and popped at most
once, each in `O(log(H+1))` time, and every edge occurrence is
decremented once. Total time is:

```text
O(V + A + V log(H + 1))
```

The worst case is `O(A + V log V)`. A chain keeps `H=1`, so its total
time is `Theta(V+A)`. An edgeless graph starts with `H=V` and spends
`Theta(V log V)` on removals after linear heap construction. There is
no meaningful average bound without a graph distribution.

The indegree array and min-heap use `O(V)` auxiliary space. The
returned order uses `Theta(V)` output space. On a cyclic graph, the
discarded partial order can also use `O(V)` temporary storage. The
function does not copy adjacency rows.

A FIFO Kahn traversal takes `Theta(V+A)` time, so the logarithmic heap
work is the price of canonical smallest-ID tie-breaking. Invalid
input may return during its validation prefix before algorithm state
is allocated.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Use a FIFO queue and call its result lexicographically smallest. In
  the example, FIFO keeps 4 ahead of newly ready 1 and fails at the
  second output position.
- Push all vertices instead of only zero-indegree vertices. A smaller
  blocked vertex would be emitted before its prerequisite.
- Use a max-heap accidentally. Its first choice is the largest ready
  vertex and produces the opposite tie-break.
- Inspect the heap backing slice as if it were sorted. Only the root
  is minimum; use `heap.Pop` for every choice.
- Call the adapter's `Push` or `Pop` directly. Use `heap.Push` and
  `heap.Pop` so the standard package restores heap order.
- Forget `heap.Init` after building the initial slice. The package
  operations require the heap invariant before their first use.
- Enqueue when indegree is merely nonpositive. Push only on the exact
  positive-to-zero transition or duplicates can enter the heap.
- Count parallel edges once but decrement every occurrence, or count
  all but decrement once. Both break the readiness invariant.
- Assume adjacency-row order chooses ties. Once all updates for a
  popped source finish, the heap minimum makes row order irrelevant.
- Compare decimal text when IDs are integers. Numeric 2 precedes 10;
  string `"10"` precedes `"2"` under bytewise text order.
- Return the emitted prefix after a cycle. It is not a complete
  topological order and need not identify the cyclic vertices.
- Miss isolated vertices. They start ready and appear in increasing
  ID order relative to every other ready choice.
- Reject the empty graph. Its unique topological order is non-nil
  empty under this contract.
- Treat a self-loop as a heap tie. Its vertex never reaches zero
  indegree and correctly causes cycle rejection.
- Put a non-`int` into `vertexMinHeap`. The adapter's type assertion
  intentionally relies on its private integer-only use.
- Mutate adjacency while the function runs. Read-only intent does not
  make shared slices safe from concurrent writes.

##### When to choose it

Choose this method when:

- the graph is directed and must be topologically ordered;
- the smallest vertex ID defines the required tie-break;
- tests, caches, serialization, or users need one reproducible
  canonical result; and
- `O(V log V + A)` worst-case work fits the constraints.

Typical uses include deterministic build plans, judge problems that
request the smallest valid order, stable dependency serialization,
and choosing the lowest-numbered available job at every step.

For named tasks, use a heap comparison on the promised name order or
map names to stable ranks first. The comparator, not insertion order,
defines the word "lexicographic."

When not to choose it:

Use ordinary [FIFO Kahn traversal](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) when any valid order
is acceptable. It avoids heap work and can return a useful blocked set
on cycle failure.

Use [dependency layers](
#b143-dependency-layers-queue-and-level-array) when the output should
be parallel rounds rather than one flat sequence. Use [DFS reverse
postorder](#b142-dfs-topological-sort-stack-and-visit-states) when
finish events fit the surrounding algorithm and no smallest-order
guarantee is required.

This greedy method returns one canonical order, not all orders or the
number of possible orders. Enumeration needs branching over every
ready choice and can have factorial output.

Use directed-cycle reconstruction when failure must explain the
cycle. A short heap result only proves that some cyclic dependency
blocked completion; this contract deliberately discards that prefix.

For a dependency graph updated after every query, rebuilding all
indegrees can dominate. Use an incremental ordering method only when
its update complexity justifies the larger state and contract.

Related material:

[A.8.1 Min-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) owns binary-heap
representation and repair. [B.14.1 Kahn's topological sort](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) owns zero-indegree
removal and cycle detection. [B.14.3 Dependency layers](
#b143-dependency-layers-queue-and-level-array) changes the output from
one canonical sequence to parallel groups.

Kahn's original [topological-sorting paper](
https://doi.org/10.1145/368996.369025) develops the removal framework.
Go's [`container/heap` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap) defines the adapter contract and
the `Init`, `Push`, and `Pop` operations used here.

#### B.14.5 Prerequisite queries (bit sets or reachability table)

##### Problem and contract

A dependency graph may be checked once and queried many times. A
single question asks whether one vertex must precede another through
one or more directed edges:

```text
is vertex p a strict prerequisite of vertex d?
```

Running DFS or BFS for every question repeats reachability work. This
lesson preprocesses a static DAG into a packed table. Each later query
tests one bit in constant time.

The relation is **strict**. A vertex is not its own prerequisite. A
path must contain at least one edge. Thus `isPrerequisite(3, 3)` is
false even though a reflexive transitive-closure table would include
every zero-edge self path.

The representation is deliberately oriented by dependent:

```text
wordsByDependent[d] has bit p exactly when p must precede d
```

Read row 6 as "all prerequisites of vertex 6," not as "all vertices
reachable from 6." Naming the two roles prevents a common transpose
error.

The build contract is:

- A valid DAG returns a non-nil index, `acyclic=true`, and no error.
- A cyclic graph returns a nil index, false, and no error.
- An invalid endpoint or overflowing indegree returns a nil index,
  false, and an error.
- The empty graph returns a non-nil empty index and true.

Vertices are integer indices in `[0,V)`. Self-loops, parallel edge
occurrences, isolated vertices, disconnected components, and nil or
empty rows are valid graph shapes. A self-loop is valid input syntax
but makes the graph cyclic.

Every parallel occurrence is counted and removed separately. It does
not change the prerequisite relation, but inconsistent counting could
make a valid graph stall or make an indegree negative.

The builder validates the whole graph before allocating the table. It
reads but does not mutate or retain the adjacency rows. The returned
index owns its rows and exposes only a query method. Concurrent
queries
are safe after construction, provided callers do not obtain and mutate
the private storage through code in the same package.

Read [multiword bit sets](#a132-multiword-bit-sets) for packed-set
mechanics, [Kahn's topological sort](
#b141-kahns-topological-sort-queue-and-indegrees) for dependency-ready
processing, and [transitive closure](
#b129-transitive-closure-bit-sets-or-boolean-matrix) for the general
directed-graph problem. This lesson owns their DAG-specific
combination and strict-query contract.

##### Mental model

Let `W = ceil(V/64)`. Allocate `V` rows of `W` unsigned 64-bit words.
For prerequisite vertex `p`:

```text
word index = p / 64
bit offset = p % 64
mask       = 1 << bit offset
```

Each machine word therefore represents 64 possible prerequisites.
Padding bits in the final word remain zero because the algorithm sets
bits only for real vertices.

Process the graph in Kahn topological order. For every emitted edge
`u -> v`, update the dependent's row:

```text
ancestors[v] |= ancestors[u]
ancestors[v].add(u)
```

The union copies every prerequisite of `u` to `v`. The separate bit
insertion records `u` itself. Both operations are necessary: a source
has an empty ancestor row, so union alone would lose its direct edge.

The maintained state is:

```text
indegreeByVertex[v] = incoming occurrences not yet processed
readyQueue           = zero-indegree vertices waiting to emit
wordsByDependent[v]  = prerequisites contributed so far
processedCount       = emitted vertices
```

When `u` leaves the queue, all predecessors of `u` have already been
processed. Its bit-set row is therefore final. Copying it forward
cannot miss a prerequisite that will arrive later.

For each stored edge occurrence, union all `W` words, set the direct
source bit, and decrement the destination's indegree. Append the
destination only when its indegree changes to zero.

If fewer than `V` vertices are processed, a directed cycle blocked the
remaining vertices. Some rows may look partly useful, but they are not
a complete index under this contract. Discard the table and return
cycle rejection.

A query validates both endpoints, reads the dependent's row, selects
the prerequisite's word, and tests its mask:

```text
wordsByDependent[d][p/64] & (1 << (p%64)) != 0
```

For a Boolean-table implementation, the equivalent cell is
`prerequisiteByDependent[d][p]`. A table oriented as `[p][d]` is also
valid, but all build and query code must use that orientation
consistently.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use this graph. Edge `u -> v` says that `u` is a direct prerequisite
of `v`:

```text
0: [2, 3, 3]
1: [3]
2: [4]
3: [4, 5]
4: [6]
5: [6]
6: []
7: []
```

The repeated `0 -> 3` edge tests occurrence accounting. It adds no
new reachability fact.

Initial indegrees are:

```text
vertex:    0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
indegree:  0  0  1  3  2  1  2  0
```

All prerequisite rows start empty. The initial queue is `[0,1,7]`.
Queue order need only be topological; unlike lexicographic sorting,
this problem does not promise a canonical emitted order.

1. Process vertex 0.

   Before: `P2={}`, `P3={}`, and the unread queue is `[1,7]`.

   Decision: edge `0 -> 2` adds direct prerequisite 0 to `P2`.
   Both occurrences of `0 -> 3` union the empty `P0` and add bit 0.

   After: `P2={0}`, `P3={0}`, vertex 2 reaches indegree zero,
   and the unread queue becomes `[1,7,2]`. Vertex 3 still has
   indegree 1 because all three incoming occurrences count.

   Known correct: source 0 has no earlier prerequisites, so its only
   contribution across each outgoing edge is its own bit.

2. Process vertex 1.

   Before: `P1={}`, `P3={0}`, and vertex 3 has indegree 1.

   Decision: edge `1 -> 3` unions empty `P1` into `P3`, then adds
   direct prerequisite 1.

   After: `P3={0,1}` and the unread queue is `[7,2,3]`.

   Known correct: every incoming occurrence of vertex 3 has now been
   processed, so `P3` is final when 3 becomes ready.

3. Process vertices 7 and 2.

   Before: isolated vertex 7 has no edges. `P2={0}` is final, while
   `P4={}` and vertex 4 has indegree 2.

   Decision: vertex 7 changes nothing. Edge `2 -> 4` copies `{0}`
   and adds direct prerequisite 2.

   After: `P4={0,2}`, vertex 4 has indegree 1, and the unread queue
   is `[3]`.

   Known correct: path `0 -> 2 -> 4` explains bit 0, while the final
   edge explains bit 2. Vertex 4 is not ready because vertex 3 has
   not contributed yet.

4. Process vertex 3.

   Before: `P3={0,1}`, `P4={0,2}`, and `P5={}`.

   Decision: edge `3 -> 4` unions `{0,1}` into `P4` and adds 3.
   Edge `3 -> 5` performs the same update on `P5`.

   After: `P4={0,1,2,3}`, `P5={0,1,3}`, and the unread queue is
   `[4,5]`.

   Known correct: both rows contain every ancestor of 3 plus 3
   itself. `P4` also preserves the earlier contribution from 2.

5. Process vertices 4 and 5.

   Before: `P6={}` and vertex 6 has indegree 2.

   Decision: edge `4 -> 6` copies `{0,1,2,3}` and adds 4. Edge
   `5 -> 6` then unions `{0,1,3}` and adds 5.

   After: `P6={0,1,2,3,4,5}` and vertex 6 enters the queue.

   Known correct: union removes duplicate ancestry naturally. The two
   final edges preserve both branches into vertex 6.

6. Process vertex 6 and finish.

   Before: all seven earlier queue entries have been processed.

   Decision: vertex 6 has no outgoing edges.

   After: all eight vertices are processed, so the index is accepted.
   Its rows are:

   ```text
   P0 = {}
   P1 = {}
   P2 = {0}
   P3 = {0,1}
   P4 = {0,1,2,3}
   P5 = {0,1,3}
   P6 = {0,1,2,3,4,5}
   P7 = {}
   ```

   Known correct: every strict path into each dependent is
   represented,
   and no row includes its own vertex.

The example queries now answer:

```text
0 prerequisite of 6: true
2 prerequisite of 5: false
3 prerequisite of 3: false
7 prerequisite of 6: false
1 prerequisite of 4: true
```

For a cycle example, add edge `6 -> 3`. Vertices 0, 1, 7, and 2 can
still leave the queue, but vertices 3, 4, 5, and 6 remain blocked.
The queue stalls after four of eight vertices. The builder discards
all partial rows and returns a nil index with `acyclic=false`.

Bit boundaries do not change the reasoning. With at least 65 vertices,
prerequisite 63 uses the highest bit of word 0 and prerequisite 64
uses the lowest bit of word 1. Division and remainder select the two
locations without shifting by 64.

##### Implementation

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Prerequisite queries (bit sets or
// reachability table). Function comments connect each operation to
// its invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

type prerequisiteIndex struct {
	vertexCount      int
	wordsByDependent [][]uint64
}

func prerequisiteWordCount(vertexCount int) int {
	// Keep prerequisite word count in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	wordCount := vertexCount / 64
	if vertexCount%64 != 0 {
		wordCount++
	}
	return wordCount
}

func prerequisiteMask(vertex int) uint64 {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	return uint64(1) << (vertex % 64)
}

func validatePrerequisiteGraph(adjacency [][]int) error {
	// Reject input outside the prerequisite graph contract before
	// mutation.
	for prerequisite, dependents := range adjacency {
		for _, dependent := range dependents {
			if dependent < 0 || dependent >= len(adjacency) {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"edge %d -> %d has an invalid destination",
					prerequisite,
					dependent,
				)
			}
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func countPrerequisiteIndegrees(
	adjacency [][]int,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	indegreeByVertex := make([]int, len(adjacency))
	for prerequisite, dependents := range adjacency {
		for _, dependent := range dependents {
			// Parallel occurrences are separate incoming edges.
			if indegreeByVertex[dependent] == math.MaxInt {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"indegree overflows at edge %d -> %d",
					prerequisite,
					dependent,
				)
			}
			indegreeByVertex[dependent]++
		}
	}
	return indegreeByVertex, nil
}

func buildPrerequisiteIndex(
	adjacency [][]int,
) (*prerequisiteIndex, bool, error) {
	// Reject malformed edges before allocating the result table.
	if err := validatePrerequisiteGraph(adjacency); err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	indegreeByVertex, err := countPrerequisiteIndegrees(
		adjacency,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	vertexCount := len(adjacency)
	wordCount := prerequisiteWordCount(vertexCount)
	wordsByDependent := make([][]uint64, vertexCount)
	for dependent := range wordsByDependent {
		wordsByDependent[dependent] = make([]uint64, wordCount)
	}

	readyQueue := make([]int, 0, vertexCount)
	for vertex, indegree := range indegreeByVertex {
		if indegree == 0 {
			readyQueue = append(readyQueue, vertex)
		}
	}

	processedCount := 0
	for queueHead := 0; queueHead < len(readyQueue); queueHead++ {
		prerequisite := readyQueue[queueHead]
		prerequisiteWords := wordsByDependent[prerequisite]
		processedCount++

		for _, dependent := range adjacency[prerequisite] {
			dependentWords := wordsByDependent[dependent]
			// Every ancestor of the prerequisite is also required.
			for wordIndex, word := range prerequisiteWords {
				dependentWords[wordIndex] |= word
			}
			// The edge also makes this source a direct prerequisite.
			dependentWords[prerequisite/64] |=
				prerequisiteMask(prerequisite)

			indegreeByVertex[dependent]--
			if indegreeByVertex[dependent] == 0 {
				readyQueue = append(readyQueue, dependent)
			}
		}
	}

	if processedCount != vertexCount {
		return nil, false, nil
	}

	return &prerequisiteIndex{
		vertexCount:      vertexCount,
		wordsByDependent: wordsByDependent,
	}, true, nil
}
```
