- Return assignments in processing order. The contract indexes output
  by original input position, so write through `inputIndex`.
- Lose deterministic ties. Compare meeting start, end, and input
  index; compare heap end and resource index.
- Sort the caller's slice while promising preservation. Build owned
  indexed records before sorting.
- Permit concurrent writes. Copying during mutation is not a
  synchronized snapshot, although independent read-only calls are
  safe.

##### When to choose it

Use this min-heap allocation when every interval must be accepted, the
complete batch is available, identical resources can host one meeting
at a time, and callers need either the minimum count or a concrete
assignment. Meeting rooms, machines, gates, and channels are common
models when their boundaries are half-open.

Recognition clues include "minimum rooms," "assign every interval,"
and "reuse the resource that becomes free first." Start sorting plus
a heap is valuable when resource identities must survive, not only the
maximum simultaneous count.

If meetings arrive online in nondecreasing start order, the same heap
state can continue incrementally. Arbitrary out-of-order arrivals need
buffering, reordering, or a different dynamic contract.

When not to choose it:

Do not use resource allocation when meetings may be rejected and the
goal is to accept as many as possible; use [interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice). Do not merge intervals because
union coverage discards meeting identity and simultaneous demand.

Use the next [sweep-line lesson](
#b174-sweep-line-sorted-events-and-active-state) when only the maximum
active count or a timeline of load changes is required. A sweep can be
simpler because it need not construct resource identities.

This greedy method also assumes interchangeable unit-capacity
resources and meetings with one continuous interval. Different
machine skills, capacities, setup times, travel times, or assignment
costs can destroy the root-reuse proof and require matching, flow, or
richer scheduling.

Related material:

[A.8.1 min-heaps and max-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) owns the
heap invariant and logarithmic repair. [B.17.2 interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) contrasts accepting a maximum
subset on one resource with accepting all meetings on minimum
resources.

The next [sweep-line lesson](
#b174-sweep-line-sorted-events-and-active-state) computes load
from endpoint events without retaining resource identity. [B.17.5
weighted scheduling](
#b175-weighted-scheduling-sorted-slice-and-dp-array) changes the
objective to value rather than resource count.

Princeton's [COS 423 course](
https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring13/cos423/)
presents earliest-start interval partitioning, the overlap-depth
lower bound, and the priority-queue implementation. Go's authoritative
[`container/heap` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap)
defines root minimum, `heap.Push`, and `heap.Fix` behavior and costs.

#### B.17.4 Sweep line (sorted events and active state)

##### Problem and contract

Many interval problems ask how load changes over time rather than
which resource hosts each interval. Checking every time value is
infeasible when coordinates are sparse or span most of `int64`.
A sweep line visits only coordinates where the answer can change.

Given a finite `[]timeSpan`, return its maximum simultaneous load and
a canonical piecewise-constant load profile. Every span is a
nonempty half-open interval `[start,end)` with `start < end`. It
contributes one unit at every coordinate x satisfying
`start <= x && x < end`.

Each returned `loadSegment` is `[start,end):active`. Segments are
sorted, nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and have a positive active count.
Zero-load gaps are omitted. Adjacent segments with the same count are
coalesced even if input identities change at their boundary. Thus the
profile describes load, not every raw event. Load is zero before the
first segment, in omitted gaps, and after the last segment.

Duplicates contribute independently. Exact handoffs do not overlap:
`[1,3)` and `[3,5)` have maximum load one and coalesce to
`[1,5):1`. All ordered `int64` endpoints are valid. The implementation
does not subtract coordinates or invent a coordinate after an end, so
signed extremes need no special case.

An empty or reversed span returns a zero profile, a nil segment slice,
and a non-nil error. Validation completes before event allocation.
Nil and empty input succeed with maximum zero and a non-nil empty
segment slice.

The function reads but does not retain or mutate input. Events and
returned segments are owned storage. Independent read-only calls are
safe, but concurrent mutation of the input is excluded. Allocation
must fit memory.

Read [difference arrays](#a122-difference-arrays) first. This sweep is
their sparse-coordinate counterpart: endpoints are change markers,
and a running sum reconstructs load. The preceding [resource
allocation lesson](#b173-resource-allocation-min-heap) retains
resource identities; this lesson deliberately does not.

##### Mental model

Turn each span into two endpoint events:

```text
(start, +1)  the span becomes active
(end,   -1)  the span stops being active
```

Sort events by coordinate. The comparator also places -1 before +1 at
one coordinate for deterministic order, but the algorithm does not
observe tied events individually. It consumes the whole equal-
coordinate group and adds its net delta first.

After applying all events at coordinate x, `active` is the load on
the atomic interval from x to the next distinct coordinate. This is
the central invariant. End events remove spans that exclude x, while
start events add spans that include x. Grouping them makes half-open
semantics independent of their original input order.

If `active` is positive, emit `[x,next):active`. When the previous
output ends at x with the same count, extend it instead. If `active`
is zero, omit the gap. Update the maximum only for a nonempty atomic
interval, never between tied events or after the final coordinate.

The sweep needs no endpoint subtraction. It needs only coordinate
comparison, equality, and copying. Active count cannot exceed input
length, which already fits `int`; every span contributes one +1 and
one -1.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build a profile for these input spans:

```text
0:[1,5)  1:[2,6)  2:[5,7)  3:[8,10)
4:[8,9)  5:[9,10) 6:[4,9)
```

The expected maximum is 3. The canonical profile is:

```text
[1,2):1 [2,4):2 [4,6):3 [6,7):2
[7,8):1 [8,9):3 [9,10):2
```

Initial state: the caller owns seven unsorted spans. No event or
output storage exists, and active count is conceptually zero.

1. Decision: validate every span before allocation.
   After: all starts are strictly before their ends; input remains
   unchanged.
   Known correct: every later -1 has a preceding +1 for its span, and
   failure can no longer expose partial output.

2. Decision: create one +1 start event and one -1 end event per span,
   then sort and group equal coordinates.
   After: net deltas are:

   ```text
   1:+1 2:+1 4:+1 5:0 6:-1 7:-1 8:+2 9:-1 10:-2
   ```

   Known correct: summing a coordinate group preserves every unit of
   change while removing arbitrary ordering among ties.

3. Decision: apply +1 at coordinate 1. The next coordinate is 2.
   After: active is 1; emit `[1,2):1`; maximum becomes 1.
   Known correct: only span 0 contains points from 1 through, but not
   including, 2.

4. Decision: apply +1 at coordinate 2.
   After: active is 2; emit `[2,4):2`; maximum becomes 2.
   Known correct: spans 0 and 1 are active until the next event at 4.

5. Decision: apply +1 at coordinate 4.
   After: active is 3; emit `[4,5):3`; maximum becomes 3.
   Known correct: spans 0, 1, and 6 cover this atomic interval.

6. Decision: process all events at coordinate 5 together. Span 0
   ends and span 2 starts, so net delta is zero.
   After: active remains 3 on `[5,6)`. Extend the prior equal-count
   segment to `[4,6):3` instead of emitting another segment.
   Known correct: the identities change at 5, but the requested load
   function does not.

7. Decision: apply -1 at 6, -1 at 7, and +2 at 8 in successive
   groups.
   After: emit `[6,7):2`, `[7,8):1`, and `[8,9):3`.
   Known correct: each emitted count is the running sum after the
   coordinate group and before the next group.

8. Decision: at 9, two spans end and one starts, so net delta is -1.
   After: active falls from 3 to 2; emit `[9,10):2`.
   Known correct: spans 3 and 5 include 9, while spans 4 and 6 exclude
   it after ending there.

9. Decision: apply -2 at the final coordinate 10.
   After: active is zero. There is no next coordinate, so emit
   nothing and return maximum 3 with seven profile segments.
   Known correct: all spans have ended, every positive-load atomic
   interval is represented, and no zero-width tail was invented.

Counterexample to observing tied events one at a time: for `[1,3)`
and `[3,5)`, applying the start at 3 and updating the maximum before
the end at 3 creates a false transient load of 2. Neither interval
contains a common coordinate under half-open semantics. Grouping the
-1 and +1 into net zero keeps the true maximum at 1.

Counterexample to emitting at every event: the same handoff can create
zero-width pieces whose result depends on tie order. Output belongs to
the space between distinct coordinates, not to an event instant.

Focused gaps: `[1,2)` and `[4,5)` return two load-one segments; the
omitted `[2,4)` means zero. Focused duplicates: two copies of
`[-2,4)` return one segment `[-2,4):2`. Focused extremes:
`[minimumInt64,0)` and `[0,maximumInt64)` coalesce to one load-one
segment without endpoint arithmetic.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough, prints the unchanged
input, and exercises nil input. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Sweep line (sorted events and
// active state). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"cmp"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"slices"
)

type timeSpan struct {
	start int64
	end   int64
}

func (span timeSpan) String() string {
	// Format this value without changing its stored state.
	return fmt.Sprintf("[%d,%d)", span.start, span.end)
}

type endpointEvent struct {
	coordinate int64
	delta      int
}

type loadSegment struct {
	start  int64
	end    int64
	active int
}

func (segment loadSegment) String() string {
	// Format this value without changing its stored state.
	return fmt.Sprintf(
		"[%d,%d):%d",
		segment.start,
		segment.end,
		segment.active,
	)
}

type loadProfile struct {
	maximumActive int
	segments      []loadSegment
}

func compareEndpointEvents(
	first endpointEvent,
	second endpointEvent,
) int {
	// Execute endpoint events to the bounded stopping condition above.
	if byCoordinate := cmp.Compare(
		first.coordinate,
		second.coordinate,
	); byCoordinate != 0 {
		return byCoordinate
	}
	return cmp.Compare(first.delta, second.delta)
}

func buildLoadProfile(
	spans []timeSpan,
) (loadProfile, error) {
	// Build load profile in the order required by the lesson contract.
	for inputIndex, span := range spans {
		if span.start >= span.end {
			return loadProfile{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"span %d must have start before end",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
	}

	events := make([]endpointEvent, 0, len(spans))
	for _, span := range spans {
		events = append(
			events,
			endpointEvent{
				coordinate: span.start,
				delta:      1,
			},
			endpointEvent{
				coordinate: span.end,
				delta:      -1,
			},
		)
	}
	slices.SortFunc(events, compareEndpointEvents)

	profile := loadProfile{
		segments: make([]loadSegment, 0),
	}
	active := 0
	for eventIndex := 0; eventIndex < len(events); {
		coordinate := events[eventIndex].coordinate
		netDelta := 0
		for eventIndex < len(events) &&
			events[eventIndex].coordinate == coordinate {
			netDelta += events[eventIndex].delta
			eventIndex++
		}
		active += netDelta

		if eventIndex == len(events) || active == 0 {
			continue
		}
		nextCoordinate := events[eventIndex].coordinate
		if active > profile.maximumActive {
			profile.maximumActive = active
		}

		lastIndex := len(profile.segments) - 1
		if lastIndex >= 0 &&
			profile.segments[lastIndex].end == coordinate &&
			profile.segments[lastIndex].active == active {
			profile.segments[lastIndex].end = nextCoordinate
			continue
		}
		profile.segments = append(
			profile.segments,
			loadSegment{
				start:  coordinate,
				end:    nextCoordinate,
				active: active,
			},
		)
	}
	return profile, nil
}

func run(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute the requested item to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	spans := []timeSpan{
		{start: 1, end: 5},
		{start: 2, end: 6},
		{start: 5, end: 7},
		{start: 8, end: 10},
		{start: 8, end: 9},
		{start: 9, end: 10},
		{start: 4, end: 9},
	}
	profile, err := buildLoadProfile(spans)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		profile.maximumActive,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write maximum: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		profile.segments,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write segments: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, spans); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write original spans: %w", err)
	}

	empty, err := buildLoadProfile(nil)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		empty.maximumActive,
		empty.segments,
		empty.segments != nil,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write empty profile: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := run(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
3
[[1,2):1 [2,4):2 [4,6):3 [6,7):2 [7,8):1 [8,9):3 [9,10):2]
[[1,5) [2,6) [5,7) [8,10) [8,9) [9,10) [4,9)]
0 [] true
```

##### Why it works

For a span `[start,end)`, its +1 marker begins contributing at start,
and its -1 marker cancels that contribution at end. Therefore, after
all events at coordinate x are applied, that span contributes exactly
when `start <= x < end`.

More formally, let the distinct event coordinates be increasing
values `c[0], c[1], ...`. Maintain this invariant after processing the
group at `c[i]`: `active` equals the number of input spans containing
every point of `[c[i],c[i+1])` when a next coordinate exists. The
events before or at `c[i]` have been summed, and no later event can
change state inside that open stretch.

Before the first group, active is zero. No span can cover a point left
of the smallest start coordinate. At a group, every span ending there
is removed and every span starting there is added. The resulting
count therefore includes exactly spans satisfying the half-open
membership test. No endpoint lies strictly between this coordinate
and the next, so the count remains constant throughout that atomic
interval. This proves the invariant by induction.

The algorithm emits exactly the invariant's positive counts and omits
exactly its zero counts. Extending adjacent segments with equal counts
does not change the represented function. Consequently the returned
segments are canonical, and their largest count is the true maximum
simultaneous load.

Each valid span has one start before one end. Every sorted event
prefix therefore contains at least as many starts as ends, so active
never becomes negative. The total delta is zero, so active returns to
zero after the final group. The outer loop consumes at least one event
group per iteration, and the inner loop consumes at least one event,
so both terminate on finite input.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the span count, `E = 2N` be event count, `U` be distinct
event coordinate count, and `S` be returned segment count. Validation
and event construction each take `Theta(N)` time. Sorting takes
`T_sort(E)`. Grouping and sweeping take `Theta(E)`, and output writing
takes `Theta(S)`. Thus total time is
`Theta(N) + T_sort(2N) + Theta(S)`, conventionally `O(N log N)`.

The linear phases take `Theta(N + S)` in their best, average, and
worst cases. Total best, average, and worst time inherit the cost of
`T_sort(2N)`. No input distribution is assumed here. If an API
guarantees events already sorted and grouped, the sweep after
validation is `Theta(N)`. Arbitrary unsorted coordinates require
the ordering step. Merely receiving input spans in start order is not
enough because their end events can still be out of order.

Event storage uses `O(N)` auxiliary space. The returned profile uses
`O(S)` output space, where `0 <= S <= U - 1 < 2N` for nonempty input.
Sorting may use implementation-dependent stack or scratch storage.
The output can be one segment for a continuous constant load or
`Theta(N)` segments when load repeatedly changes.

If only the maximum is required, keep the running maximum and omit
segment output, reducing output space to `O(1)` while retaining `O(N)`
events. If integer coordinates occupy a small known dense domain, a
difference array can trade sorting for domain-sized storage and a
linear domain scan.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Update the maximum between individual tied events. A start before an
  end at coordinate 3 invents overlap between `[1,3)` and `[3,5)`.
  Aggregate the whole coordinate group before observing state.
- Copy closed-interval tie rules into a half-open problem. Closed
  intervals sharing an endpoint do overlap; choose semantics before
  choosing event order.
- Emit a segment at the final coordinate. There is no following
  region, so it would be empty or require unsafe endpoint invention.
- Emit zero-load gaps despite promising only positive segments. Skip
  active zero, and document that omitted regions mean zero.
- Forget to coalesce adjacent equal counts. A zero-net handoff changes
  identities but not the load function.
- Discard duplicate spans. Each input occurrence contributes its own
  unit and may raise the maximum.
- Accept `[4,4)` or `[5,3)`. This contract requires positive duration
  and rejects all invalid input before allocation.
- Subtract coordinates in the comparator. `minimumInt64` and
  `maximumInt64` can overflow subtraction; use relational comparison
  or `cmp.Compare`.
- Add one to an inclusive end. `maximumInt64 + 1` overflows. Prefer an
  explicit half-open model, or design closed-interval event ties
  without unsafe arithmetic.
- Assume sorted starts imply sorted events. Ends from long spans can
  occur after many later starts, so all endpoints still need ordering.
- Confuse event count with active count. An event is a change; the
  running sum after a group is the state on the next atomic interval.
- Sort the caller's spans while promising preservation. Sort owned
  endpoint records instead.
- Return internal reusable storage. Every successful call here owns
  its segment slice, including a non-nil empty result.
- Permit concurrent writes. Copying endpoints during mutation is not a
  synchronized snapshot; only independent read-only calls are safe.
- Preallocate with unchecked `2 * len(spans)`. Appending two events
  per span lets normal slice growth enforce representable allocation
  size without explicit integer multiplication.

##### When to choose it

Use this sweep when all intervals are available offline and the
question concerns count over time: maximum concurrency, occupancy,
coverage multiplicity, bandwidth load, or a complete positive-load
timeline. It is especially useful when coordinates are huge or sparse
but the number of endpoints is manageable.

Recognition clues include "how many are active," "maximum overlap,"
"coverage count," and "changes only at endpoints." The active state
need not be a number in other sweeps. It can be a set, heap, balanced
tree, or aggregate, provided every event has precise update semantics
and the state invariant describes the region until the next event.

The same pattern supports weighted spans by using +weight and -weight
events, but that is a different contract. Negative weights, overflow,
and whether zero or negative regions belong in output must then be
specified rather than inherited from unit active counts.

When not to choose it:

Do not use this count profile when callers need a concrete room or
machine for every meeting. Use [minimum-resource allocation](
#b173-resource-allocation-min-heap), which retains resource identity.
If intervals may be rejected, use [interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice). If union boundaries alone
matter, [merge intervals](#b171-interval-merging-sorted-slice)
returns a smaller and more direct representation.

Do not rebuild an offline event list after every dynamic update.
Coordinate compression with a Fenwick or segment tree, or another
dynamic ordered structure, is better when updates and queries
interleave. Use a dense difference array when the coordinate universe
is small enough that scanning every position is cheaper than sorting.

A one-dimensional count is also insufficient for geometric
intersection or rectangle-union problems. Those sweeps need an active
structure over the other dimension and must define degeneracies such
as shared edges. The current lesson supplies the event discipline, not
the entire two-dimensional algorithm.

Related material:

[A.12.2 difference arrays](#a122-difference-arrays) owns the dense
start-marker, stop-marker, and running-sum model. [B.6.2 batch range
updates](#b62-batch-range-updates-difference-array) applies that model
to indexed updates. [B.17.1 interval merging](
#b171-interval-merging-sorted-slice) and [B.17.3 resource allocation](
#b173-resource-allocation-min-heap) solve different interval outputs
with different retained state.

The [rectangle-union lesson](
#b305-rectangle-union-sweep-events-and-segment-tree) adds a dynamic
active structure over a second dimension. The
[sliding event counts lesson](
#b2311-sliding-event-counts-queue-or-time-buckets) handles a moving
online window rather than one offline batch.

CGAL's authoritative [surface-sweep manual](
https://doc.cgal.org/latest/Surface_sweep_2/index.html) describes the
general principle: maintain sweep status and update it at a finite set
of event points. Go's [`slices.SortFunc` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#SortFunc) defines the comparator contract
used to order owned endpoint events.

#### B.17.5 Weighted scheduling (sorted slice and DP array)

##### Problem and contract

When jobs have different values, accepting the most jobs need not
produce the most valuable schedule. One long job worth 100 can be
better than several short jobs worth 1. A permanent greedy choice no
longer has enough information; the decision depends on the best value
available before each job.

Given a finite `[]weightedJob`, return the maximum total value of one
compatible subset and the original input indices that realize it.
Each job is a nonempty half-open interval `[start,end)` with
`start < end` and a nonnegative `int64` value. Jobs that meet exactly
at an end and a start are compatible.

Returned indices are in scheduled order, not numeric input order.
The implementation sorts copied jobs by end, then start, then input
index. Its dynamic-programming tie rule prefers skipping the current
sorted job when taking and skipping have equal value. That rule makes
one optimum deterministic. In particular, all-zero input returns the
empty schedule, and equal duplicate positive jobs retain the first
input occurrence.

An empty or reversed interval or a negative value returns the zero
schedule, a nil index slice, and a non-nil error. Validation completes
before schedule allocation. Nil and empty input succeed with value
zero and a non-nil empty index slice.

If the exact optimum exceeds `MaxInt64`, return the zero schedule and
an error rather than wrapping. All ordered `int64` endpoints are
valid. Endpoint comparison and binary search perform no subtraction,
so signed time extremes are safe.

The function copies before sorting, does not mutate or retain input,
and returns owned output. Independent read-only calls are safe;
concurrent input mutation is excluded. Allocation must fit memory.

Read [binary search and bounds](
#b41-binary-search-and-bounds-slice) for insertion boundaries and
[interval selection](#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) for the
equal-value greedy case. [Grid dynamic programming](
#b165-grid-dynamic-programming-table-or-rolling-row) introduces a
table entry as the optimum for a completed subproblem. This lesson
uses that idea on sorted job prefixes.

##### Mental model

Copy jobs with their original indices and sort them by
`(end,start,inputIndex)`. End order makes the earlier jobs that are
compatible with a current job form one prefix of the sorted slice.

For sorted job j, define `compatiblePrefixByJob[j]` as the number of
earlier jobs whose ends are at or before `job[j].start`. A binary
upper bound finds the first earlier end strictly greater than the
start. That insertion index is exactly the compatible prefix length.

Read `compatiblePrefixByJob[4] == 2` as: if sorted job 4 is selected,
only the first two sorted jobs remain eligible before it. Jobs at
positions 2 and 3 end too late and overlap job 4.

Let `bestValueByPrefix[k]` store the maximum value obtainable from the
first k sorted jobs. Entry zero is zero because an empty prefix has
only the empty schedule. For current job at position `j`, compare:

```text
take = job[j].value +
    bestValueByPrefix[compatiblePrefixByJob[j]]
skip = bestValueByPrefix[j]

bestValueByPrefix[j+1] = max(take, skip)
```

Taking uses the best compatible earlier prefix. Skipping uses the best
answer before the current job was considered. These are the only two
possibilities for an optimum. Store whether take was strictly better;
an equal value records skip.

To reconstruct jobs, start at the full prefix. A skip moves to the
preceding prefix. A take records the current original index and jumps
directly to its compatible prefix. These backward jumps produce
reverse scheduled order, so reverse the collected indices once.

Because values are nonnegative, both DP operands are nonnegative.
Before addition, check
`job.value > MaxInt64-compatibleValue`. If true, the take branch is a
valid compatible schedule above `MaxInt64`; the optimum is at least
that large and cannot be represented.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use these jobs, shown as `inputIndex:[start,end):value`:

```text
0:[5,8):11 1:[1,3):5  2:[7,9):2
3:[2,5):6  4:[6,7):4  5:[4,6):5
```

The expected maximum value is 17 from original indices `[3,0]`. In the
trace, `best[k]` is short for `bestValueByPrefix[k]`.

Initial state: the caller owns six jobs. No ordered copy, compatible
prefix, DP entry, reconstruction choice, or output exists.

1. Decision: validate every interval and value before allocation.
   After: all intervals have positive duration and all values are
   nonnegative; input is unchanged.
   Known correct: every later job is a valid selectable item, and an
   input error can no longer interrupt schedule construction.

2. Decision: attach original indices and sort by end, start, then
   input index.
   After: input indices in ordered positions are `[1,3,5,4,0,2]`,
   with ends `3,5,6,7,8,9`.
   Known correct: all earlier jobs ending by a current start, if any,
   occupy one contiguous prefix.

3. Decision: initialize `best[0] = 0`. Ordered job 0 is input job 1.
   Its earlier search range is empty, so compatible prefix length is
   zero. Compare take `5 + best[0] = 5` with skip `best[0] = 0`.
   After: record take and set prefix values to `[0,5]`.
   Known correct: the best schedule using only input job 1 selects it.

4. Decision: ordered job 1 is input job 3. Its start 2 precedes end 3,
   so binary search returns compatible prefix zero. Compare take
   `6 + best[0] = 6` with skip `best[1] = 5`.
   After: record take; prefix values are `[0,5,6]`.
   Known correct: among the first two ordered jobs, input job 3 alone
   is worth more than input job 1 alone.

5. Decision: ordered job 2 is input job 5 and starts at 4. End 3
   qualifies and end 5 does not, so its compatible prefix is one.
   Compare take `5 + best[1] = 10` with skip `best[2] = 6`.
   After: record take; prefix values are `[0,5,6,10]`.
   Known correct: take combines input jobs 1 and 5, the best schedule
   ending before input job 5 starts.

6. Decision: ordered job 3 is input job 4 and starts at 6. All first
   three ends are at most 6, so its compatible prefix is three.
   Compare take `4 + best[3] = 14` with skip 10.
   After: record take; prefix values are `[0,5,6,10,14]`.
   Known correct: input jobs 1, 5, and 4 are compatible through exact
   handoff at 6 and total 14.

7. Decision: ordered job 4 is input job 0 and starts at 5. Ends 3 and
   5 qualify, while ends 6 and 7 do not, so its compatible prefix is
   two. Compare `11 + best[2] = 17` with skip `best[4] = 14`.
   After: record take; prefix values are `[0,5,6,10,14,17]`.
   Known correct: the best prefix before time 5 is input job 3, worth
   6, so taking input job 0 yields jobs `[3,0]` worth 17.

8. Decision: ordered job 5 is input job 2 and starts at 7. The first
   four ends are at most 7, so its compatible prefix is four. Compare
   take `2 + best[4] = 16` with skip `best[5] = 17`.
   After: record skip; final prefix values are
   `[0,5,6,10,14,17,17]`; compatible prefixes are
   `[0,0,1,3,2,4]`.
   Known correct: every schedule using ordered job 5, which is input
   job 2, is worth at most 16, so the 17-value optimum remains
   unchanged.

9. Decision: reconstruct from prefix 6. Its choice skips input job 2,
   so move to prefix 5. Prefix 5 takes input job 0 and jumps to prefix
   two. Prefix 2 takes input job 3 and jumps to prefix 0; stop and
   reverse.
   After: return value 17 and original indices `[3,0]`; input remains
   unchanged.
   Known correct: the recorded recurrence choices sum to 17, the two
   jobs meet at time 5, and prefix zero ends reconstruction.

Counterexample to earliest-finish greedy: on this input it selects
input jobs 1, 5, 4, and 2, worth `5+5+4+2 = 16`. The first choice
commits to input job 1, while the optimum needs overlapping input job
3 as the better prefix for valuable input job 0. Earliest finish
maximizes count, not value.

Counterexample to highest-value-first: `[0,4):10` overlaps both
`[0,2):6` and `[2,4):6`. Choosing value 10 first blocks the compatible
pair worth 12. A local value does not include the best combination.

Focused tie: `[0,1):5` is ordered before `[0,2):5`. The second job's
take and skip values are both 5, so the skip rule retains the first
job. Focused duplicates: two identical value-5 jobs likewise select
input index 0. Focused zero values return an empty schedule.

Focused boundaries: `[minimumInt64,0):3` and
`[0,maximumInt64):4` are both selected for value 7. One job worth
exactly `MaxInt64` succeeds. That job followed by a compatible
value-one job returns an overflow error because their valid total is
unrepresentable.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough, prints the unchanged
input, and exercises nil input. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Weighted scheduling (sorted slice
// and DP array). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"cmp"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"math"
	"os"
	"slices"
	"sort"
)

type weightedJob struct {
	start int64
	end   int64
	value int64
}

func (job weightedJob) String() string {
	// Format this value without changing its stored state.
	return fmt.Sprintf(
		"[%d,%d):%d",
		job.start,
		job.end,
		job.value,
	)
}

type indexedWeightedJob struct {
	job        weightedJob
	inputIndex int
}

func compareIndexedWeightedJobs(
	first indexedWeightedJob,
	second indexedWeightedJob,
) int {
	// Execute indexed weighted jobs to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	if byEnd := cmp.Compare(
		first.job.end,
		second.job.end,
	); byEnd != 0 {
		return byEnd
	}
	if byStart := cmp.Compare(
		first.job.start,
		second.job.start,
	); byStart != 0 {
		return byStart
	}
	return cmp.Compare(first.inputIndex, second.inputIndex)
}

type weightedSchedule struct {
	totalValue         int64
	selectedJobIndices []int
}

func selectMaximumValueJobs(
	jobs []weightedJob,
) (weightedSchedule, error) {
	// Reject malformed jobs before constructing any schedule state.
	for inputIndex, job := range jobs {
		if job.start >= job.end {
			return weightedSchedule{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"job %d must have start before end",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
		if job.value < 0 {
			return weightedSchedule{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"job %d has negative value",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
	}

	// End order turns every compatible earlier job into one prefix.
	ordered := make([]indexedWeightedJob, len(jobs))
	for inputIndex, job := range jobs {
		ordered[inputIndex] = indexedWeightedJob{
			job:        job,
			inputIndex: inputIndex,
		}
	}
	slices.SortFunc(ordered, compareIndexedWeightedJobs)

	bestValueByPrefix := make([]int64, len(ordered)+1)
	takeCurrentByPrefix := make([]bool, len(ordered)+1)
	compatiblePrefixByJob := make([]int, len(ordered))
	for jobIndex, current := range ordered {
		// Ends are sorted, so the first end after start is a bound.
		compatiblePrefix := sort.Search(
			jobIndex,
			func(candidateIndex int) bool {
				return ordered[candidateIndex].job.end >
					current.job.start
			},
		)
		compatiblePrefixByJob[jobIndex] = compatiblePrefix

		compatibleValue := bestValueByPrefix[compatiblePrefix]
		if current.job.value >
			math.MaxInt64-compatibleValue {
			return weightedSchedule{}, fmt.Errorf(
				"maximum schedule value exceeds int64",
			)
		}
		takeValue := compatibleValue + current.job.value
		skipValue := bestValueByPrefix[jobIndex]
		prefixLength := jobIndex + 1
		if takeValue > skipValue {
			bestValueByPrefix[prefixLength] = takeValue
			takeCurrentByPrefix[prefixLength] = true
			continue
		}

		// On a tie, retain the optimum without the current job.
		bestValueByPrefix[prefixLength] = skipValue
	}

	// Follow recorded decisions backward, then restore time order.
	selectedJobIndices := make([]int, 0)
	for prefixLength := len(ordered); prefixLength > 0; {
		if !takeCurrentByPrefix[prefixLength] {
			prefixLength--
			continue
		}

		jobIndex := prefixLength - 1
		selectedJobIndices = append(
			selectedJobIndices,
			ordered[jobIndex].inputIndex,
		)
		prefixLength = compatiblePrefixByJob[jobIndex]
	}
	slices.Reverse(selectedJobIndices)
	return weightedSchedule{
		totalValue:         bestValueByPrefix[len(ordered)],
		selectedJobIndices: selectedJobIndices,
	}, nil
}

func run(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute the requested item to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	jobs := []weightedJob{
		{start: 5, end: 8, value: 11},
		{start: 1, end: 3, value: 5},
		{start: 7, end: 9, value: 2},
		{start: 2, end: 5, value: 6},
		{start: 6, end: 7, value: 4},
		{start: 4, end: 6, value: 5},
	}
	schedule, err := selectMaximumValueJobs(jobs)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		schedule.totalValue,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write total value: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		schedule.selectedJobIndices,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write selected jobs: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, jobs); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write original jobs: %w", err)
	}

	empty, err := selectMaximumValueJobs(nil)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		empty.totalValue,
		empty.selectedJobIndices,
		empty.selectedJobIndices != nil,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write empty schedule: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := run(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
17
[3 0]
[[5,8):11 [1,3):5 [7,9):2 [2,5):6 [6,7):4 [4,6):5]
0 [] true
```

##### Why it works

After sorting, consider current job j. Every earlier job with
`end <= job[j].start` lies before the binary-search boundary and is
compatible. Every earlier job after that boundary has end greater
than the current start. It also starts before its own end, which is at
or before the current end due to sort order. The two jobs therefore
overlap. Thus the binary boundary identifies exactly the eligible
earlier prefix.

Prove DP entries by induction on prefix length. Entry zero is correct
because the empty prefix has maximum value zero. Assume all shorter
prefix entries are correct and consider the last job j in the current
prefix.

Every compatible optimum either excludes j or includes j. If it
excludes j, its value is at most the optimum for the preceding prefix,
which is the skip value. If it includes j, every other selected job
must lie in j's compatible prefix. By the induction hypothesis, the
best such earlier value is the stored entry at that prefix, so the
best include-j value is exactly take. Choosing the larger of take and
skip is therefore the optimum for the current prefix. This preserves
the induction claim.

On equality, either branch is optimal. Recording skip changes only
which optimum is observable, not its value. During reconstruction, a
skip removes no selected job. A take records j and jumps to a prefix
whose every job ends by j's start. Repeated jumps therefore construct
pairwise compatible jobs whose recorded values reproduce the final DP
value. Reversing changes only their order, yielding scheduled order.

If checked addition reports overflow, take already describes a valid
schedule whose mathematical value exceeds `MaxInt64`. The global
optimum cannot be smaller, so no exact `int64` answer exists. If the
check passes, nonnegative operands make the addition exact.

The forward loop consumes one job per iteration. Each binary search
strictly shrinks a finite candidate interval. Reconstruction either
decrements a positive prefix or jumps to a smaller compatible prefix,
because every job has positive duration. All loops therefore
terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be job count and `K` be selected job count. Validation, copied
entry construction, the DP scan, and worst-case reconstruction each
take `Theta(N)` time. Returning `K` indices takes `Theta(K)` output
work within reconstruction.

Let `S(N)` be sorting time. Each of `N` jobs performs an upper-bound
search over at most `N` earlier ends, for `O(N log(N + 1))` total
search time. The complete successful time is
`Theta(N) + S(N) + O(N log(N + 1))`. With an `O(N log N)`
comparison sort, the conventional total is `O(N log N)`.

For a fixed `N`, the DP and binary-bound phases have the same
asymptotic best, average, and worst time; no input distribution is
assumed.
Invalid input can stop during validation before allocation. A value
overflow can stop during the DP scan after sorting and state
allocation.

The ordered copy, value array, choice array, and compatible-prefix
array each use `O(N)` auxiliary storage. Sorting may use
implementation-dependent stack or scratch memory. The returned index
slice uses `O(K)` output storage. Reconstruction itself uses `O(1)`
additional scalar state and no recursion.

A quadratic version can scan backward for each compatible predecessor,
using `O(N^2)` time after sorting. Binary bounds reduce those searches
to `O(N log N)`. Enumerating all subsets takes `O(2^N)` choices before
compatibility work.

If only maximum value is needed, omit the choice and compatible-prefix
arrays used by reconstruction, but retain all `N` prefix values
because each take can refer to an arbitrary earlier prefix. Rolling
one scalar would discard required subproblem answers.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Reuse earliest-finish greedy from the unweighted problem. The main
  input returns value 16 instead of 17 because count and value are
  different objectives.
- Choose the highest single value first. `[0,4):10` blocks compatible
  jobs `[0,2):6` and `[2,4):6`, whose combined value is 12.
- Sort only by start. Compatible predecessors do not then form one
  end-ordered prefix, so the binary-bound recurrence is invalid.
- Use the first end greater than or equal to the current start. An
  earlier job ending exactly at the start is compatible; search for
  the first end strictly greater.
- Search endpoint values with subtraction. Signed extremes can
  overflow; use comparisons inside a bound search.
- Confuse a predecessor index with a prefix length. If one earlier job
  qualifies, the DP reads prefix entry 1, not job position 0 as a DP
  position.
- Include the current or future suffix in predecessor search. Search
  only positions before the current job, whose end ordering has
  already been established.
- Compare take with `best[j+1]` before that placeholder is computed.
  Skip is `best[j]`; the new answer is stored at `best[j+1]`.
- Keep only the latest DP value. Take may jump from job 50 to prefix
  7, so arbitrary earlier prefix answers must remain available.
- Reconstruct by testing values without preserving the tie rule. Equal
  take and skip values are both optimal; record the chosen branch so
  returned identities remain deterministic.
- Forget to reverse reconstruction output. Backward jumps discover the
  last selected job first, but the contract returns scheduled order.
- Add values before checking overflow. Go signed arithmetic can wrap a
  valuable schedule negative and make skip appear better.
- Treat one overflowing branch as irrelevant. That branch is a valid
  schedule, so the true optimum is also beyond `int64` even if another
  finite branch exists.
- Reject zero values or force them into output. Zero is valid, and the
  skip-on-tie rule leaves an all-zero optimum empty.
- Deduplicate equal jobs. Duplicates have distinct input identities;
  deterministic ties choose one rather than erasing both.
- Accept `[4,4)` or `[5,3)`. Both violate positive duration and fail
  before schedule state is allocated.
- Accept a negative value under this contract. Reject it during the
  validation pass instead of silently changing input meaning.
- Drop original indices while sorting. Reconstruction must map ordered
  DP choices back to caller-visible jobs.
- Sort caller-owned storage while promising preservation. Sort copied
  indexed records and return a newly allocated index slice.
- Permit concurrent writes. Copy construction is not a synchronized
  snapshot, although independent read-only calls are safe.

##### When to choose it

Use weighted interval scheduling when one resource can perform at most
one job at a time, the entire batch is known, values are additive, and
the objective is maximum total value. Profit-bearing bookings,
projects, advertisements, and reservations fit when their only
interaction is time overlap.

Recognition clues include "maximum profit from non-overlapping jobs,"
"each interval has a value," and "choose or skip each job." Finish
sorting plus a compatible-prefix recurrence is the key combination.

Keep reconstruction state when callers need selected identities. If
only the optimum scalar matters, use the smaller value-only variant
described above.

When not to choose it:

If every job has equal positive value, [earliest-finish interval
selection](#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) is simpler: one
ordered scan finds a maximum count without a DP array or per-job
binary search.

Do not use this recurrence for multiple simultaneous resources,
machine-specific eligibility, precedence constraints, setup costs, or
values that depend on neighboring jobs. Those change the state needed
to describe a remaining subproblem. Cooldowns require a different
compatibility boundary; arbitrary dependencies may require DAG DP,
matching, flow, or integer optimization.

Do not rebuild the full offline DP after every insertion or deletion
when jobs change continuously. A dynamic problem needs an augmented
ordered structure or a different update contract. Online acceptance
without future knowledge is also not equivalent to the offline
optimum.

This implementation rejects negative values. A maximum-value model
could safely skip them, but accepting them would change validation and
tie behavior. Non-additive utility, floating-point values, or
arbitrary precision totals likewise require a different numeric
contract.

#### B.17.6 Cooldown scheduling (heap and queue)

##### Problem and contract

A single processor sometimes has many copies of the same task type,
but equal types may not run too close together. Running a rare task
first can leave only one frequent type later, forcing avoidable idle
time. The scheduler must use ready work while spacing repeated types.

Given a finite `[]byte` of unit-duration tasks and a nonnegative
integer cooldown `K`, return a minimum-length sequence of task and
idle slots. If byte `X` runs at time `t`, `X` may next run no earlier
than `t + K + 1`; exactly `K` complete slots must lie between its
runs.
Input order has no scheduling meaning, but every occurrence must
appear once in the output.

A `taskSlot` stores a byte and `hasTask=true`, or represents idle with
`hasTask=false`. The Boolean keeps byte zero distinct from idle. The
result includes idle slots, so its length is the minimum elapsed time.

The schedule is deterministic. Among task types that are ready, choose
the greatest remaining count; equal counts choose the smaller byte.
Cooldown zero permits equal tasks in adjacent slots. Duplicate bytes
are separate task occurrences.

A negative cooldown returns nil and a non-nil error. Nil and empty
tasks with a valid cooldown succeed with a non-nil empty schedule. If
the minimum explicit schedule length exceeds Go's maximum `int`,
return nil and an error before output allocation. Otherwise allocation
must fit memory.

The function reads but does not retain or mutate input and returns
owned output. Independent read-only calls are safe; concurrent input
mutation is excluded.

Read [multisets and frequency maps](
#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) for remaining counts,
[min-heaps and max-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) for ready-task
priority, and [queues and circular buffers](
#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) for release order. [Character
reorganization](#b86-character-reorganization-counts-and-heap) owns
the special one-slot cooldown; this lesson generalizes it to `K` slots
and explicit idles.

##### Mental model

Count each byte. A max-heap stores one record per ready task type:

```text
(task byte, remaining unscheduled copies)
```

Read heap record `('A',3)` as: three A tasks remain and A is legal at
the current time. Greater remaining count has priority because that
type needs the most future separations. Byte order resolves ties.

A FIFO queue stores types that have run but are not ready:

```text
(task record after one execution, release time)
```

After task `X` runs at time `t`, enqueue its positive remainder with
release time `t + K + 1`. Enqueue times strictly increase because only
one task runs per increasing time slot and every type uses the same K.
The queue is therefore ordered by release time without a second heap.

At each current time:

1. Move every queue front whose release time is at most now back into
   the ready heap.
2. If the heap is nonempty, pop and run its highest-priority type.
   Decrement it and enqueue a positive remainder.
3. If the heap is empty while cooling work remains, append an idle
   slot. Time still advances by one.

Time is the zero-based index of the next output slot. The code obtains
it as the current output length, so every appended task or idle
advances time exactly once.

Releasing before selecting is essential: a type whose wait ends now is
legal in this slot. Stop only when both structures are empty.

The minimum possible length also supplies an overflow check. Let N be
task count, M the largest frequency, C the number of task types having
frequency M, and K the cooldown:

```text
minimum length = max(N, (M - 1) * (K + 1) + C)
```

N is the work bound. Each of the C most frequent types has M final
copies separated by K slots, giving the spacing bound. Checked
arithmetic computes it before allocating the explicit output.

##### Worked walkthrough

Schedule tasks `AAABBC` with cooldown 2. The deterministic minimum
schedule is `A B C A B _ A`, where `_` is idle, and its length is 7.

Initial state: no task is counted. The ready heap, cooling queue, and
output are empty; current time is zero.

1. Decision: validate cooldown 2 and count `A:3 B:2 C:1`. Here N is
   6, M is 3, and C is 1. Compute
   `max(6,(3-1)*(2+1)+1) = 7`.
   After: minimum representable output length is confirmed as 7.
   Known correct: every task occurrence is counted, and any valid
   schedule needs at least seven slots.

2. Decision: push all three positive counts into the ready max-heap.
   After: priority view is `A:3 B:2 C:1`; cooling is empty and output
   is empty.
   Known correct: every task type is initially legal, and A is the
   most urgent deterministic choice.

3. Decision: at time 0, no task is released. Pop A, append it, reduce
   its remainder to 2, and enqueue it for release at `0+2+1 = 3`.
   After: output is `A`; ready is `B:2 C:1`; cooling is `A:2@3`.
   Known correct: all unscheduled A copies are unavailable through
   times 1 and 2.

4. Decision: at time 1, queue front release 3 is later. Pop B, append
   it, and enqueue remainder `B:1` for time 4.
   After: output is `A B`; ready is `C:1`; cooling is
   `A:2@3 B:1@4`.
   Known correct: queue order matches increasing release time, and A
   and B are both cooling.

5. Decision: at time 2, neither cooling type is ready. Pop C, append
   it, and exhaust its only copy.
   After: output is `A B C`; ready is empty; cooling is unchanged.
   Known correct: C fills a separator slot without adding future work.

6. Decision: at time 3, dequeue released `A:2`, push it, then pop it.
   Append A, decrement it to 1, and enqueue it for time 6.
   After: output is `A B C A`; ready is empty; cooling is
   `B:1@4 A:1@6`.
   Known correct: exactly two full slots, times 1 and 2, separate the
   two A executions.

7. Decision: at time 4, release and run B. Its count reaches zero.
   After: output is `A B C A B`; both ready heap and all B work are
   empty; cooling contains `A:1@6`.
   Known correct: the two B executions also have two intervening
   slots.

8. Decision: at time 5, A is still cooling and no ready type exists.
   Append one idle slot rather than running A early.
   After: output is `A B C A B _`; cooling remains `A:1@6`.
   Known correct: idle is forced because every unfinished type is
   unavailable in this slot.

9. Decision: at time 6, release and run the final A. Both structures
   then become empty, so stop.
   After: return `A B C A B _ A`, length 7; input stays `AAABBC`.
   Known correct: all six occurrences appear once, every repeated byte
   has two intervening slots, and the length meets the lower bound.

Counterexample to repeatedly running the rarest ready type: it chooses
C, then B, then A. Dominant A starts its first cooldown late, and the
schedule takes nine slots instead of seven. The first wrong decision
spends a separator before starting the type that needs the most
separators.

Counterexample to ignoring the cooling queue: after running A at time
0, the heap still appears to need two A copies. Returning A
immediately would produce `A A` with zero intervening slots. Ready and
remaining are different facts.

Focused release boundary: with `K = 2`, a task run at time 0 is
illegal at times 1 and 2 and legal at time 3. Using `t+K` releases it
one slot too early. Releasing after heap selection instead of before
can insert an unnecessary idle at the exact legal time.

Focused values: cooldown zero schedules `AAB` as `A A B`. Bytes
`[0,0,1]` with cooldown one schedule as `[0,1,0]`; `hasTask` keeps
byte zero distinct from idle. Unique tasks need no cooling record, so
even the maximum `int` cooldown succeeds without endpoint arithmetic.

Two equal tasks with maximum `int` cooldown require more than maximum
`int` slots and fail before output allocation. Nil input returns a
non-nil empty schedule; cooldown -1 is invalid even for empty input.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough, prints the unchanged
input, and exercises nil input. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Cooldown scheduling (heap and
// queue). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

type taskSlot struct {
	task    byte
	hasTask bool
}

func (slot taskSlot) String() string {
	// Format this value without changing its stored state.
	if !slot.hasTask {
		return "_"
	}
	return fmt.Sprintf("%q", slot.task)
}

type readyTask struct {
	task      byte
	remaining int
}

type readyTaskHeap []readyTask

func (tasks readyTaskHeap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(tasks)
}

func (tasks readyTaskHeap) Less(
	firstIndex int,
	secondIndex int,
) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	first := tasks[firstIndex]
	second := tasks[secondIndex]
	if first.remaining != second.remaining {
		return first.remaining > second.remaining
	}
	return first.task < second.task
}

func (tasks readyTaskHeap) Swap(
	firstIndex int,
	secondIndex int,
) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	tasks[firstIndex], tasks[secondIndex] =
		tasks[secondIndex], tasks[firstIndex]
}

func (tasks *readyTaskHeap) Push(value any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	*tasks = append(*tasks, value.(readyTask))
}

func (tasks *readyTaskHeap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	oldTasks := *tasks
	lastIndex := len(oldTasks) - 1
	task := oldTasks[lastIndex]
	oldTasks[lastIndex] = readyTask{}
	*tasks = oldTasks[:lastIndex]
	return task
}

type coolingTask struct {
	task        readyTask
	releaseTime int
}

type coolingTaskQueue struct {
	slots []coolingTask
	head  int
	size  int
}

func newCoolingTaskQueue(capacity int) coolingTaskQueue {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial cooling task queue
	// state.
	return coolingTaskQueue{
		slots: make([]coolingTask, capacity),
	}
}

func (queue *coolingTaskQueue) enqueue(
	task coolingTask,
) bool {
	// Add the requested item while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	if queue.size == len(queue.slots) {
		return false
	}
	backIndex := (queue.head + queue.size) %
		len(queue.slots)
	queue.slots[backIndex] = task
	queue.size++
	return true
}

func (queue *coolingTaskQueue) front() (
	coolingTask,
	bool,
) {
	// Follow the lookup rule for the requested item without changing
	// state.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		return coolingTask{}, false
	}
	return queue.slots[queue.head], true
}

func (queue *coolingTaskQueue) dequeue() (
	coolingTask,
	bool,
) {
	// Remove the requested item while preserving the remaining
	// representation.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		return coolingTask{}, false
	}
	task := queue.slots[queue.head]
	queue.slots[queue.head] = coolingTask{}
	queue.head = (queue.head + 1) % len(queue.slots)
	queue.size--
	return task, true
}

func minimumCooldownLength(
	taskCount int,
	maximumCount int,
	maximumKindCount int,
	cooldown int,
) (int, error) {
	// Compute cooldown length from the state without mutating it.
	if taskCount == 0 || maximumCount == 1 {
		return taskCount, nil
	}

	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	if cooldown == maximumInt {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"minimum schedule length exceeds int",
		)
	}
	gapCount := maximumCount - 1
	frameWidth := cooldown + 1
	if gapCount >
		(maximumInt-maximumKindCount)/frameWidth {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"minimum schedule length exceeds int",
		)
	}
	constrainedLength :=
		gapCount*frameWidth + maximumKindCount
	if constrainedLength > taskCount {
		return constrainedLength, nil
	}
	return taskCount, nil
}

func scheduleWithCooldown(
	tasks []byte,
	cooldown int,
) ([]taskSlot, error) {
	// Keep schedule with cooldown in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if cooldown < 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("cooldown must be nonnegative")
	}

	var countByTask [256]int
	maximumCount := 0
	maximumKindCount := 0
	distinctCount := 0
	// Maintain the number of types tied at the observed maximum.
	for _, task := range tasks {
		countByTask[task]++
		count := countByTask[task]
		if count == 1 {
			distinctCount++
		}
		if count > maximumCount {
			maximumCount = count
			maximumKindCount = 1
		} else if count == maximumCount {
			maximumKindCount++
		}
	}

	minimumLength, err := minimumCooldownLength(
		len(tasks),
		maximumCount,
		maximumKindCount,
		cooldown,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	ready := make(readyTaskHeap, 0, distinctCount)
	for integerTask, count := range countByTask {
		if count == 0 {
			continue
		}
		heap.Push(&ready, readyTask{
			task:      byte(integerTask),
			remaining: count,
		})
	}
	cooling := newCoolingTaskQueue(distinctCount)
	schedule := make([]taskSlot, 0, minimumLength)
	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	for ready.Len() > 0 || cooling.size > 0 {
		currentTime := len(schedule)

		// Release every task whose fixed wait has finished.
		for {
			front, found := cooling.front()
			if !found || front.releaseTime > currentTime {
				break
			}
			released, _ := cooling.dequeue()
			heap.Push(&ready, released.task)
		}

		if ready.Len() == 0 {
			schedule = append(schedule, taskSlot{})
			continue
		}

		// Run the most frequent ready type to reduce future idles.
		current := heap.Pop(&ready).(readyTask)
		schedule = append(schedule, taskSlot{
			task:    current.task,
			hasTask: true,
		})
		current.remaining--
		if current.remaining == 0 {
			continue
		}

		if currentTime > maximumInt-cooldown-1 {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"task release time exceeds int",
			)
		}
		releaseTime := currentTime + cooldown + 1
		if !cooling.enqueue(coolingTask{
			task:        current,
			releaseTime: releaseTime,
		}) {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("cooling queue is full")
		}
	}

	if len(schedule) != minimumLength {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"constructed length %d; want %d",
			len(schedule),
			minimumLength,
		)
	}
	return schedule, nil
}

func run(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute the requested item to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	tasks := []byte("AAABBC")
	schedule, err := scheduleWithCooldown(tasks, 2)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, len(schedule)); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write elapsed slots: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, schedule); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write schedule: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(output, "%q\n", tasks); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write original tasks: %w", err)
	}

	empty, err := scheduleWithCooldown(nil, 2)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		empty,
		empty != nil,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write empty schedule: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := run(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
7
['A' 'B' 'C' 'A' 'B' _ 'A']
"AAABBC"
[] true
```

##### Why it works

At every slot boundary, each unfinished task type is in exactly one
place: the ready heap or cooling queue. A ready record may run now. A
cooling record stores the first legal future time. Running one copy
decreases exactly one remaining count, and moving records never
changes counts, so output tasks plus pending counts always equal input
counts.

Release times enter the FIFO queue in increasing order. Dequeuing all
front records due at the current time therefore releases every legal
type and no illegal type. An executed remainder returns at
`time+K+1`, so at least `K` whole slots separate equal executions.
Idle slots change only time and cannot violate multiplicity or
cooldown.

Now prove minimal length. Every schedule needs at least `N` slots for
`N` unit tasks. For any type with maximum count `M`, its final
occurrence is no earlier than position `(M-1)*(K+1)`. There are `C`
distinct types with that count, so their `C` final occurrences need
`C` distinct slots at or after that position. Every schedule therefore
has length at least `max(N,(M-1)*(K+1)+C)`.

The max-remaining choice reaches that bound. View the first `M-1`
copies of the most frequent types as cooldown frames. When two types
are ready, running the one with more copies starts one of its extra
future separations now; running the smaller count first cannot remove
any separation required by the larger count. Exchanging those two
ready choices therefore cannot make a shortest completion longer.

Applying that exchange repeatedly puts maximum remaining counts first,
which is the heap order. Other types fill frame gaps. If the heap is
empty, every unfinished type is in the cooling queue, so no legal task
can replace that idle. After `M-1` frames, the `C` final
maximum-frequency copies form the tail. Thus the algorithm inserts
exactly the idles the spacing bound requires and no optional idle,
reaching the lower bound.

The smaller-byte tie rule changes only which equally urgent legal type
occupies a slot. It does not change remaining-count balance, cooldown
validity, or length.

Each non-idle iteration exhausts one of the finite `N` task
occurrences. Each idle advances time toward the finite front release.
The checked minimum length bounds total iterations, heap repairs
traverse finite trees, and queue operations are bounded, so the
algorithm terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be task count, `U` be distinct byte count, `K` be cooldown,
and `L` be the returned slot count including idles. Here
`0 <= U <= 256`. Counting takes `Theta(N)` time. Building the ready
heap with `U` pushes takes `O(U log(U + 1))` time.

Every task occurrence causes one heap pop. Every nonfinal occurrence
also causes one queue enqueue, dequeue, and later heap push. Heap work
is `O(N log(U + 1))`; queue work is `O(N)`. The main loop visits
exactly `L` slots, so total time is `O(L + N log(U + 1))`. With a
fixed byte alphabet, this is `O(L + N)`, and writing the explicit
result already requires `Theta(L)` time.

For fixed `N` and `K`, the successful best case has enough distinct
tasks to avoid idles and `L = N`. For `N > 0`, the worst distribution
is one repeated type, with `L = N + (N-1)*K` when representable. No
task-distribution average is assumed. Negative cooldown exits in
`Theta(1)`; length overflow exits after `Theta(N)` counting and before
heap or output allocation.

The 256 counters use fixed `O(1)` storage relative to `N`. The heap
and circular cooling queue each retain `O(U)` records. Scalar
simulation state is `O(1)`. The returned schedule uses `Theta(L)`
output storage. Heap slice capacity and the queue's fixed slots remain
auxiliary.

If only minimum elapsed time is required, the checked formula computes
it after counting without a heap, queue, or `L`-slot output. The
simulation is necessary here because the contract returns one concrete
schedule. A generic unbounded alphabet would replace the counter array
with a map and make `U` no longer constant.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Reinsert a task immediately after running it. `AA` can then run in
  adjacent slots even when `K` is positive; keep its remainder
  cooling.
- Compute release as `time+K`. For `K = 2` and time 0, release 2
  leaves
  only slot 1 between runs; use `time+K+1`.
- Release after selecting a task. At its exact release time, an empty
  heap can then create a false idle; release due queue entries first.
- Choose the smallest remaining count. On `AAABBC` with `K = 2`,
  starting C can delay dominant A and produce nine slots instead of
  the minimum seven.
- Treat the heap as containing every unfinished type. Cooling types
  are unfinished but deliberately absent until their release times.
- Use a queue when cooldowns vary by type. Later executions can then
  have earlier release times; use a release-time min-heap instead.
- Assume heap slice order is sorted. Only the root follows full
  priority; use `heap.Pop` and `heap.Push` for every transition.
- Omit the byte tie key. Length can remain minimal, but the promised
  concrete schedule becomes nondeterministic.
- Treat byte zero as idle. Inspect `hasTask`; the zero byte is valid
  input and must survive multiplicity checks.
- Reject cooldown zero. It means no intervening slot is required, so
  equal tasks may run consecutively.
- Apply the spacing bound without `max(N,...)`. When many types fill
  all gaps, the frame expression can be smaller than task count.
- Evaluate `(M-1)*(K+1)+C` without checked integer arithmetic. Large
  `K` can wrap into a small capacity and later corrupt release times.
- Allocate output before proving its minimum length fits `int`.
  Reject an unrepresentable explicit schedule first.
- Append trailing idle after all tasks finish. Stop when both ready
  and cooling structures are empty; cooldown after the final copy is
  not observable work.
- Size the cooling queue below `U`. At most one record per type can be
  cooling, so `U` is sufficient and can be necessary.
- Forget to clear a dequeued circular slot. Pointer-bearing variants
  could retain stale task payloads after logical removal.
- Permit concurrent input writes. Counting is not a synchronized
  snapshot, although independent read-only calls are safe.

##### When to choose it

Use this heap-and-release-queue scheduler when unit tasks are grouped
by type, equal types share one fixed cooldown, every task must run,
and the caller needs an actual minimum-time sequence. CPU exercises,
rate-limited action batches, and repeated maintenance types can fit
this abstract model.

Recognition clues include "same task needs K intervals apart,"
"minimum time including idle," and "most frequent available task."
The heap answers urgency; the queue answers temporary eligibility.

Choose the count formula alone when only elapsed length matters. Use
the one-held-record approach in [character reorganization](
#b86-character-reorganization-counts-and-heap) when `K` is exactly one
and a compact permutation, not explicit idle slots, is the contract.

When not to choose it:

Do not use this model for variable task durations, per-type cooldowns,
release dates, deadlines, dependencies, priorities unrelated to
remaining count, or multiple processors. Release times would no longer
enter one FIFO order, and the greedy length proof would not apply.

Do not use the explicit simulation when `K` is huge and only a numeric
answer is required. A two-task input with a billion-slot cooldown has
a tiny description but an enormous explicit output; use the formula.

Do not confuse cooldown with interval overlap. Fixed jobs with chosen
start and end times belong to interval selection or resource
allocation. This scheduler chooses order and may insert idle time
among unit tasks whose only identity is their byte type.

For online arrivals, the complete frequency bound is unknown. A live
scheduler can still maintain ready and release structures, but it does
not inherit this offline minimum-length guarantee.
