[A.6.3 multisets and frequency maps](
#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) owns multiplicity invariants.
[A.8.1 min-heaps and max-heaps](
#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) owns root priority and logarithmic
repair. [A.5.1 queues and circular buffers](
#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) owns FIFO release storage.

[B.8.6 character reorganization](
#b86-character-reorganization-counts-and-heap) handles the one-turn
special case without idle output. The next [deadline scheduling
lesson](#b177-deadline-scheduling-sorted-jobs-and-heap) changes the
constraint from separation to completion deadlines.

The canonical [Task Scheduler problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/task-scheduler/) specifies unit tasks,
one shared cooldown, and minimum elapsed intervals. Go's authoritative
[`container/heap` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap)
defines root priority and heap operation contracts used here.

#### B.17.7 Deadline scheduling (sorted jobs and heap)

##### Problem and contract

Some jobs may be omitted, but every accepted job must finish by its
own deadline. Accepting jobs only until the first failure can waste
capacity: a long earlier job may be replaceable by a shorter one.

Given a finite `[]deadlineJob`, return original input indices for a
maximum-cardinality, or largest-count, subset that can finish on time.
Each job has a positive `int64` duration and a nonnegative `int64`
deadline. One machine starts at time zero, every job is available
immediately, and accepted jobs run one at a time without interruption.
A job is on time when its cumulative completion time is at most its
deadline.

Idle time cannot help because all jobs are already available and only
upper completion bounds matter. The returned indices therefore give
a gap-free execution order. They are sorted by deadline and then by
input index. Duplicate records remain distinct jobs.

When equal-duration jobs compete for removal, the later job in that
ordered sequence is rejected. This tie rule keeps the observable
answer deterministic without changing its maximum count.

Zero or negative duration and a negative deadline return a nil result
and an error. Validation finishes before allocation. Deadline zero is
valid, although no positive-duration job can meet it. Nil and empty
input succeed with a non-nil empty result.

The implementation never forms an overflowing duration sum. Every
valid `int64` duration and deadline is therefore handled exactly,
including `MaxInt64`. It copies before sorting, does not mutate or
retain the input, and returns an owned index slice. Concurrent input
mutation is excluded; independent read-only calls are safe.

Read [comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) for copied
multi-key ordering and [max-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) for
repeated longest-item removal. This lesson combines those tools in
the Moore-Hodgson scheduling algorithm.

##### Mental model

Copy jobs with their original indices and sort them by
`(deadline,inputIndex)`. This is earliest-deadline-first, or EDD,
order. The input-index key only resolves equal deadlines.

Maintain three pieces of state while scanning that order:

- `accepted` is a max-heap of tentatively selected jobs. Its root has
  the longest duration. Equal durations put the later ordered job at
  the root.
- `totalDuration` is the exact sum of jobs accepted before the current
  iteration.
- `selectedByInputIndex[i]` says whether input job `i` is currently
  accepted.

Push the current job and mark it selected. Test whether its completion
would fit without adding first:

```text
duration <= deadline and
totalDuration <= deadline - duration
```

The first comparison makes the subtraction nonnegative. The second
is equivalent to `totalDuration + duration <= deadline` but cannot
overflow.

If the job fits, add its duration to the total. If it does not, pop
one longest job from the heap and clear that job's selected bit. When
the current job is popped, the old total stays unchanged. Otherwise,
subtract the removed existing duration and add the shorter current
duration. Both operations are safe because the removed job belongs to
the old total and is at least as long as its replacement.

Before the current job, the accepted jobs form an on-time EDD
sequence. Adding only the current job can make the new last completion
late. Removing one longest duration restores feasibility while giving
up only one job and freeing as much prefix time as possible.

After the scan, filter the sorted copy by the selected bits. A heap is
not globally sorted, so iterating heap storage would not produce the
promised execution order.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use these jobs, shown as `inputIndex:(duration,deadline)`:

```text
0:(5,5) 1:(4,6) 2:(2,6)
3:(1,3) 4:(3,9) 5:(2,8)
```

The expected answer is `[3,2,5,4]`, containing four jobs.

Initial state: the caller owns six unsorted jobs. No ordered copy,
heap, selected bit, total duration, or output exists.

1. Decision: validate every duration and deadline before allocating.
   After: all durations are positive and all deadlines are
   nonnegative; the input is unchanged.
   Known correct: every later heap item is a valid job, and an input
   error can no longer interrupt result construction.

2. Decision: attach input indices and sort by deadline, then index.
   After: ordered indices are `[3,0,1,2,5,4]`, representing
   `(1,3) (5,5) (4,6) (2,6) (2,8) (3,9)`.
   Known correct: every processed prefix ends at its largest deadline,
   and equal deadlines have deterministic order.

3. Decision: push job 3. Its completion is `0+1 = 1`, which is at
   most deadline 3, so retain it and add its duration.
   After: selected indices are `{3}` and `totalDuration = 1`.
   Known correct: job 3 completes at time 1 and is on time.

4. Decision: push job 0. Completion `1+5 = 6` exceeds deadline 5.
   The longest heap job is the current five-unit job, so pop it.
   After: selected indices remain `{3}` and total remains 1.
   Known correct: the feasible earlier schedule is restored, and the
   first bad prefix necessarily rejects at least one job.

5. Decision: push job 1. Completion `1+4 = 5` is at most deadline 6,
   so accept it.
   After: selected indices are `{3,1}` and total is 5.
   Known correct: their EDD completions are 1 and 5.

6. Decision: push job 2. Completion `5+2 = 7` misses deadline 6.
   The heap root is job 1 with duration 4, so replace it with the
   two-unit current job.
   After: selected indices are `{3,2}` and total becomes
   `5-4+2 = 3`.
   Known correct: count stays two, both jobs finish by time 3, and the
   replacement creates two units of useful slack.

7. Decision: push job 5. Completion `3+2 = 5` meets deadline 8, so
   retain it.
   After: selected indices are `{3,2,5}` and total is 5.
   Known correct: EDD completions are 1, 3, and 5.

8. Decision: push job 4. Completion `5+3 = 8` meets deadline 9, so
   retain it; the ordered input is now exhausted.
   After: selected indices are `{3,2,5,4}` and total is 8.
   Known correct: every selected job is on time and no work remains.

9. Decision: filter the ordered copy by selected bits rather than
   reading heap-array order. Recheck completions `1,3,5,8` against
   deadlines `3,6,8,9`.
   After: return `[3,2,5,4]`; the input remains unchanged.
   Known correct: the result is a feasible EDD schedule, and the proof
   below establishes that no five-job schedule exists.

Counterexample to rejecting only the current late job: at step 6 that
rule rejects two-unit job 2 and keeps four-unit job 1. It later
accepts job 5 but cannot accept job 4, returning only `[3,1,5]`. Its
first wrong choice preserves avoidable duration instead of replacing
the longest accepted job.

Counterexample to globally choosing shortest duration first:
`(2,2) (1,100) (1,100)` admits all three jobs in deadline order.
Choosing both one-unit jobs first makes the two-unit job finish at 4
and appear impossible. Short duration alone ignores urgency.

Focused zero-deadline case: `(1,0)` is valid input. Its tentative
completion misses zero, so the heap immediately removes it and returns
empty. Focused exact boundary: `(2,2)` is retained because equality is
on time.

Focused tie: three jobs `(2,4) (2,4) (2,4)` can retain only two. The
heap removes the later ordered position, so indices `[0,1]` remain.

Focused overflow boundary: `(MaxInt64,MaxInt64)` fits exactly. If
`(1,MaxInt64)` follows it, the safe comparison detects that both do
not fit without evaluating their overflowing sum. The heap removes
the longer job and returns the one-unit job.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs the walkthrough, prints the unchanged
input, and exercises nil input. Save it as `main.go` and run
`go run main.go`. It uses `container/heap` as a max-heap by reversing
the `Less` priority.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Deadline scheduling (sorted jobs
// and heap). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"cmp"
	"container/heap"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"slices"
)

type deadlineJob struct {
	duration int64
	deadline int64
}

func (job deadlineJob) String() string {
	// Format this value without changing its stored state.
	return fmt.Sprintf("(%d,%d)", job.duration, job.deadline)
}

type indexedDeadlineJob struct {
	job             deadlineJob
	inputIndex      int
	orderedPosition int
}

func compareIndexedDeadlineJobs(
	first indexedDeadlineJob,
	second indexedDeadlineJob,
) int {
	// Execute indexed deadline jobs to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	if byDeadline := cmp.Compare(
		first.job.deadline,
		second.job.deadline,
	); byDeadline != 0 {
		return byDeadline
	}
	return cmp.Compare(first.inputIndex, second.inputIndex)
}

type longestDurationHeap []indexedDeadlineJob

func (jobs longestDurationHeap) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(jobs)
}

func (jobs longestDurationHeap) Less(
	firstIndex int,
	secondIndex int,
) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	first := jobs[firstIndex]
	second := jobs[secondIndex]
	if first.job.duration != second.job.duration {
		return first.job.duration > second.job.duration
	}
	// Reject the later ordered job when equal durations are tied.
	return first.orderedPosition > second.orderedPosition
}

func (jobs longestDurationHeap) Swap(
	firstIndex int,
	secondIndex int,
) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	jobs[firstIndex], jobs[secondIndex] =
		jobs[secondIndex], jobs[firstIndex]
}

func (jobs *longestDurationHeap) Push(value any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	*jobs = append(*jobs, value.(indexedDeadlineJob))
}

func (jobs *longestDurationHeap) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	values := *jobs
	lastIndex := len(values) - 1
	removed := values[lastIndex]
	values[lastIndex] = indexedDeadlineJob{}
	*jobs = values[:lastIndex]
	return removed
}

func selectMaximumOnTimeJobs(
	jobs []deadlineJob,
) ([]int, error) {
	// Validate before allocation so errors expose no partial result.
	for inputIndex, job := range jobs {
		if job.duration <= 0 {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"job %d must have positive duration",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
		if job.deadline < 0 {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"job %d must have nonnegative deadline",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
	}

	// Deadline order exposes the first prefix that cannot all finish.
	ordered := make([]indexedDeadlineJob, len(jobs))
	for inputIndex, job := range jobs {
		ordered[inputIndex] = indexedDeadlineJob{
			job:        job,
			inputIndex: inputIndex,
		}
	}
	slices.SortFunc(ordered, compareIndexedDeadlineJobs)
	for orderedPosition := range ordered {
		ordered[orderedPosition].orderedPosition =
			orderedPosition
	}

	accepted := make(longestDurationHeap, 0, len(ordered))
	selectedByInputIndex := make([]bool, len(ordered))
	var totalDuration int64
	for _, current := range ordered {
		// Tentatively accept the current job before testing its deadline.
		heap.Push(&accepted, current)
		selectedByInputIndex[current.inputIndex] = true

		// Subtraction tests the sum without overflowing int64.
		durationFits := current.job.duration <=
			current.job.deadline
		acceptedFit := durationFits &&
			totalDuration <=
				current.job.deadline-current.job.duration
		if acceptedFit {
			totalDuration += current.job.duration
			continue
		}

		// One longest removal frees the most time in this bad prefix.
		removed := heap.Pop(&accepted).(indexedDeadlineJob)
		selectedByInputIndex[removed.inputIndex] = false
		if removed.orderedPosition == current.orderedPosition {
			continue
		}

		// The removed duration is at least the replacement duration.
		totalDuration -= removed.job.duration
		totalDuration += current.job.duration
	}

	// Filtering deadline order returns a feasible execution order.
	selectedJobIndices := make([]int, 0, len(accepted))
	for _, current := range ordered {
		if selectedByInputIndex[current.inputIndex] {
			selectedJobIndices = append(
				selectedJobIndices,
				current.inputIndex,
			)
		}
	}
	return selectedJobIndices, nil
}

func run(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute the requested item to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	jobs := []deadlineJob{
		{duration: 5, deadline: 5},
		{duration: 4, deadline: 6},
		{duration: 2, deadline: 6},
		{duration: 1, deadline: 3},
		{duration: 3, deadline: 9},
		{duration: 2, deadline: 8},
	}
	selected, err := selectMaximumOnTimeJobs(jobs)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		len(selected),
		selected,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write selected jobs: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, jobs); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write original jobs: %w", err)
	}

	empty, err := selectMaximumOnTimeJobs(nil)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, empty, empty != nil); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write empty schedule: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := run(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
4 [3 2 5 4]
[(5,5) (4,6) (2,6) (1,3) (3,9) (2,8)]
[] true
```

The second line confirms that sorting did not change the input. The
final true confirms that the empty result is non-nil.

##### Why it works

First establish why EDD order is enough. Suppose an on-time schedule
has adjacent jobs `A` then `B` with `A.deadline > B.deadline`.
Swapping them makes `B` finish earlier. `A` then finishes at the old
completion time of `B`, which was at most `B`'s deadline and therefore
at most `A`'s later deadline. The swap preserves feasibility.
Repeating removes all deadline inversions, so every feasible subset
has a feasible EDD order.

Now consider the first late EDD prefix ending at job `k`. Its total
duration exceeds `k.deadline`, the greatest deadline in that prefix.
In any order containing every prefix job, whichever prefix job runs
last completes after that total duration and therefore after its own
deadline. At least one prefix job must be rejected.

Let `m` be a longest job in that first bad prefix. There is an optimal
schedule that rejects `m`. To see this, arrange any optimum's on-time
jobs in EDD order. If it already rejects `m`, the claim holds.
Otherwise the unavoidable-rejection fact supplies some other rejected
prefix job `r`.

Exchange their roles: accept `r` and reject `m`. Jobs before `k`
remain on time because the complete EDD sequence was on time before
its first failure. If job `k` remains accepted, removing `m` leaves no
more prefix duration than removing `k` because `m` is at least as long
as `k`. Jobs after `k` finish no later than before because `r` is no
longer than `m`. The exchange therefore preserves the optimum count
while making `m` a rejected job.

Before each implementation iteration, accepted and unprocessed jobs
remain in EDD order after earlier rejections. Pushing the current job
leaves every earlier accepted completion unchanged, so only the
current last job can be late. If it is late, the heap pops exactly the
longest job `m` from that first bad remaining prefix. The exchange
fact proves that this rejection is compatible with some global
optimum.

One removal is sufficient: the old total met the current deadline,
and replacing any existing longest job by the no-longer current job
cannot increase that total. Removing an earlier job shifts every later
accepted completion earlier, and the current job completes at the new
total. Unprocessed jobs retain EDD order. The scan can therefore
continue the repeated Moore-Hodgson process without restarting.

Induct over heap removals. Each removal chooses a job that some
optimum can reject, then leaves the same problem on the remaining
jobs. At exhaustion, no accepted job is late, and the number of
rejections is minimum. The number returned is therefore maximum.

The scan consumes one sorted job per iteration. Each heap repair moves
through a finite tree, and at most one pop occurs per job. Filtering
consumes the finite ordered slice, so all loops terminate.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the job count and `K` the selected count. Validation,
copied entry construction, ordered-position assignment, and final
filtering each take `Theta(N)` time. Returning `K` indices takes
`Theta(K)` output work within the filtering pass.

Let `S(N)` be sorting time. Every job causes one heap push and at most
one pop. Go documents each operation as `O(log N)`, so the successful
total is `Theta(N) + S(N) + O(N log(N+1))`. With an `O(N log N)`
comparison sort, the conventional total is `O(N log N)`.

No input distribution is assumed, so no average-case bound is
claimed. Invalid input can stop during validation before allocation.
The heap-repair path may be constant on one operation or logarithmic
when an item travels through the tree; sorting usually dominates any
isolated best case.

The ordered copy, max-heap backing array, and selected-bit slice each
use `O(N)` auxiliary storage. Sorting may use implementation-dependent
stack or scratch space. The returned slice uses `O(K)` output storage;
its capacity is `K` because the final heap length is known. The scalar
duration state uses `O(1)` space, and there is no recursion.

If only the maximum count is required, omit selected bits and output
reconstruction, then return heap length. If input mutation is allowed,
sorting indexed jobs still needs identity storage unless IDs already
travel with the records.

A direct subset search tests up to `2^N` selections and then checks
their schedules. A dynamic program indexed by the largest deadline
can be useful for variants, but its memory and work depend on the time
range. The heap method depends only on job count.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Reject the current job whenever it misses. The walkthrough then
  retains duration 4 over duration 2 and eventually returns only three
  jobs. Remove the longest accepted duration, even when it is earlier.
- Sort globally by duration. `(2,2) (1,100) (1,100)` needs the urgent
  two-unit job first; shortest-first makes it appear late.
- Use deadline order without a heap. Ordering proves feasibility for a
  chosen subset but does not identify which job a bad prefix should
  lose.
- Use a min-heap. A bad prefix must free the most time while losing
  one job, so the root must be the maximum duration.
- Pop repeatedly for one current job. The old selected total already
  met the current deadline; one longest removal restores a total no
  greater than the old one.
- Add before checking overflow. `MaxInt64 + 1` wraps. Compare duration
  with deadline, then compare total with `deadline-duration`.
- Subtract before proving `duration <= deadline`. A larger duration
  makes that subtraction negative and can misclassify the job.
- Update the total as though the current job were already included.
  This implementation delays addition; when the current job is popped,
  the old total must stay unchanged.
- Replace an existing job with a longer current job. The heap root is
  at least as long as every member, including the current item, so an
  existing removal is never shorter than its replacement.
- Treat deadline equality as late. Completion exactly at the deadline
  is valid, so the failure condition is strictly greater.
- Reject deadline zero as malformed. It is valid but cannot accept a
  positive-duration job under a time-zero start.
- Accept zero duration. This contract rejects it so every selected job
  represents real work and the proof's job-count semantics stay clear.
- Deduplicate equal jobs. They have different identities and may both
  fit; selected bits are indexed by original position.
- Depend on heap-array iteration order. Only the root has global
  priority. Filter the EDD-sorted copy to construct execution order.
- Omit a heap tie key. Count remains optimal, but the returned
  concrete subset can vary. Reject the later ordered position on
  equal duration.
- Sort caller-owned records while promising preservation. Build and
  sort indexed copies instead.
- Permit concurrent input writes. Copying is not a synchronized
  snapshot, although independent readers are safe.

##### When to choose it

Choose this algorithm when all jobs are available at time zero, one
machine runs non-preemptive jobs, every accepted job has equal value,
and the objective is to complete as many as possible by individual
deadlines. Courses with durations and last days are the standard
interview form.

Recognition clues include "maximum number before deadlines," "replace
a long accepted task," and "sort by due date, then keep durations in
a max-heap." Keep reconstruction when callers need job identities;
otherwise heap length is the answer.

Use plain EDD order without a heap when every job must run and the
objective is maximum lateness rather than rejection count. Use the
heap because this objective permits dropping jobs after seeing a bad
prefix.

When not to choose it:

Do not use this method for fixed start and end intervals. Those jobs
cannot slide earlier to fill freed time; [interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) uses earliest finish instead.

Do not use it when accepted jobs have unequal profits. Removing the
longest job may discard enormous value. Fixed intervals with additive
profits use [weighted interval scheduling](
#b175-weighted-scheduling-sorted-slice-and-dp-array); flexible jobs
with weights require a different model and are generally harder.

Release times, multiple machines, setup costs, precedence edges,
preemption, and machine eligibility invalidate the one-prefix
exchange. They require state that records availability or assignment.
Likewise, online commitment before future jobs arrive is not the same
offline problem.

Do not use the cooldown scheduler when jobs instead have arbitrary
durations and completion deadlines. [Cooldown scheduling](
#b176-cooldown-scheduling-heap-and-queue) spaces equal unit tasks and
minimizes elapsed slots; its queue and invariant solve another
constraint.

Related material:

[B.3.1 comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) owns the
copy and comparator contract. [A.8.1 min-heaps and max-heaps](
#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) owns root priority and repair costs.

[B.17.2 interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) handles fixed intervals with
equal value. [B.17.5 weighted scheduling](
#b175-weighted-scheduling-sorted-slice-and-dp-array) handles fixed
intervals with additive values. The next [coverage lesson](
#b178-interval-stabbing-and-coverage-sorted-endpoints) changes the
objective from selecting jobs to choosing points or covering spans.

The [Course Schedule III problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/course-schedule-iii/) gives the common
duration-and-last-day formulation. Cheriyan, Ravi, and Skutella's
[Moore-Hodgson proof](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.06210) formalizes the
first-bad-prefix rejection and longest-job exchange used here.

Go's authoritative [`container/heap` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap) specifies heap interface behavior
and logarithmic push and pop. The [`slices.SortFunc` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#SortFunc) specifies comparator ordering and
input mutation for the copied sort.


#### B.17.8 Interval stabbing and coverage (sorted endpoints)

##### Problem and contract

Two interval problems sound like "cover everything" but choose
different kinds of output:

- **Stabbing:** choose the fewest points so every input interval
  contains at least one chosen point.
- **Target coverage:** choose the fewest input intervals whose union
  contains every position of one target interval.

For stabbing, the input is a finite `[]closedInterval`. Each interval
`[start,end]` includes both endpoints and is valid when
`start <= end`, so `[5,5]` is a valid point interval. The function
returns a minimum-length, strictly increasing `[]int64` of stabbing
points. Duplicates remain separate requirements but may share a point.

For coverage, candidates are finite nonempty half-open intervals
`[start,end)` with `start < end`. The target is half-open and valid
when `start <= end`; an empty target needs no candidates. Return
original candidate indices in the order selected so their union
continuously covers the target. Candidates may begin before or finish
after the target.

Coverage ties prefer the smaller input index among candidates reaching
the same farthest end. If coverage is impossible, return a nil result
and `errTargetNotCovered`, not a partial prefix. Reversed bounds or an
empty candidate return a different validation error.

Stabbing uses closed intervals because a chosen endpoint must belong
to the interval. Coverage uses half-open intervals because it models a
span and gives the empty target a direct representation. Touching
coverage intervals still join: `[0,2)` followed by `[2,4)` covers
every position in `[0,4)`.

Both functions validate before allocating working storage. Nil or
empty stabbing input and an empty coverage target return non-nil empty
results. Every `int64` endpoint is valid. Comparisons never subtract
endpoints or add one, so signed extremes cannot overflow.

Both functions copy before sorting, preserve and do not retain input,
and return owned output. Concurrent input mutation is excluded;
independent read-only calls are safe. Allocation must fit memory.

Read [comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) for copied
multi-key order. [Interval merging](
#b171-interval-merging-sorted-slice) owns union normalization, while
[interval selection](#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) owns the
different goal of choosing a maximum disjoint subset.

##### Mental model

Stabbing delays each unavoidable point as far right as safely
possible. Copy intervals with input indices and sort by
`(end,start,inputIndex)`. Maintain:

- `hasPoint`, which distinguishes no point from every valid `int64`;
- `lastPoint`, the most recently chosen right endpoint; and
- `points`, the confirmed output in increasing order.

For each sorted interval, skip it when `lastPoint >= start`. End order
already guarantees `lastPoint <= end`, so that one comparison means
the point lies inside the closed interval. Otherwise, the interval is
unstabbed; choose its right endpoint.

Coverage instead extends a confirmed prefix as far right as possible.
Copy candidate intervals with input indices and sort by start, then by
end descending, then by input index. Maintain:

- `coveredUntil`, meaning every target position in
  `[target.start,coveredUntil)` is covered;
- `nextIndex`, the first candidate not yet scanned; and
- `selectedIndices`, the confirmed greedy choices.

While the target remains, scan every candidate with
`start <= coveredUntil`. An end at or before the frontier adds nothing
and is discarded. Among useful candidates, remember the farthest end,
breaking an equal-end tie by smaller input index.

If no candidate extends the frontier, the uncovered position at the
frontier proves coverage impossible. Otherwise, append the best input
index and move `coveredUntil` to its end. Previously scanned but
unchosen intervals can be forgotten: none reaches beyond the chosen
farthest end, so none can help after the new frontier.

The two rules point in opposite directions for a reason. Stabbing
chooses the earliest finishing interval's right endpoint. Coverage
chooses, among intervals already able to start the next segment, the
one with the latest end.

##### Worked walkthrough

First stab these closed intervals, shown as `inputIndex:[start,end]`:

```text
0:[1,4] 1:[2,5] 2:[7,9]
3:[4,7] 4:[10,10] 5:[8,10]
```

Then cover target `[0,10)` with these half-open candidates:

```text
0:[0,2) 1:[1,5) 2:[4,7)
3:[6,10) 4:[2,6) 5:[8,12)
```

The expected stabbing points are `[4,9,10]`. The expected coverage
indices are `[0,4,3]`.

Initial state: the caller owns both unsorted inputs. Neither function
has an ordered copy, scan state, or output.

1. Decision: validate all closed intervals with `start <= end`.
   After: all six stabbing intervals are valid, including point
   interval `[10,10]`; no allocation has occurred.
   Known correct: each later record is a nonempty closed set, and an
   error can no longer interrupt stabbing output construction.

2. Decision: sort copied stabbing entries by end, start, then index.
   After: ordered indices are `[0,1,3,2,5,4]`, representing
   `[1,4] [2,5] [4,7] [7,9] [8,10] [10,10]`.
   Known correct: the first unstabbed interval always has the earliest
   remaining right endpoint.

3. Decision: interval 0 has no earlier point, so choose its right
   endpoint 4.
   After: `points = [4]` and `lastPoint = 4`.
   Known correct: interval 0 is stabbed, and 4 is the farthest-right
   choice still inside it.

4. Decision: interval 1 starts at 2 and interval 3 starts at 4. Both
   starts are at most `lastPoint = 4`, so skip both.
   After: points remain `[4]` after the first three intervals.
   Known correct: closed endpoint 4 belongs to `[1,4]`, `[2,5]`, and
   `[4,7]`.

5. Decision: interval 2 starts at 7, beyond point 4, so choose its
   right endpoint 9.
   After: `points = [4,9]` and `lastPoint = 9`.
   Known correct: interval 2 required a new point, and every prior
   interval remains stabbed.

6. Decision: interval 5 contains point 9, so skip it. Point interval
   4 starts at 10, beyond 9, so choose endpoint 10; then stop.
   After: return stabbing points `[4,9,10]`.
   Known correct: every closed interval contains a returned point, and
   the exchange proof below shows that fewer than three cannot work.

7. Decision: independently validate the half-open target and every
   nonempty candidate, then sort candidates by start, descending end,
   and index.
   After: ordered indices are `[0,1,4,2,3,5]`, representing
   `[0,2) [1,5) [2,6) [4,7) [6,10) [8,12)`.
   Known correct: every candidate becomes eligible exactly when the
   frontier reaches its start.

8. Decision: initialize `coveredUntil = 0`. Candidate 0 is the only
   interval starting by 0, so choose its end 2.
   After: selected indices are `[0]`; target prefix `[0,2)` is
   covered; `nextIndex = 1`.
   Known correct: any cover must use candidate 0 because no other
   interval contains the target's first position.

9. Decision: at frontier 2, newly eligible candidates 1 and 4 reach
   ends 5 and 6. Choose candidate 4 because 6 is farther right.
   After: selected indices are `[0,4]`; `[0,6)` is covered;
   `nextIndex = 3`.
   Known correct: discarded candidate 1 ends before the new frontier
   and cannot improve any later continuation.

10. Decision: at frontier 6, candidates 2 and 3 reach ends 7 and 10.
    Choose candidate 3 because it reaches farthest.
    After: selected indices are `[0,4,3]`; coverage reaches 10;
    `nextIndex = 5`.
    Known correct: each selected start is at or before the preceding
    frontier, so their union has no gap.

11. Decision: test `coveredUntil >= target.end`; `10 >= 10` is true,
    so stop without scanning candidate 5.
    After: return `[0,4,3]`; both caller-owned inputs are unchanged.
    Known correct: the whole target is covered, and the stays-ahead
    proof below shows no two-candidate cover exists.

Counterexample to stabbing at left endpoints: for `[1,4] [2,5]`,
choosing 1 for the first interval misses the second and needs another
point. Choosing right endpoint 4 stabs both. The first wrong choice
spends a point before knowing how far right it can safely move.

Counterexample to earliest-end coverage: at coverage frontier 2,
choosing candidate 1 with end 5 instead of candidate 4 with end 6
forces the later choices `[4,7)` and `[6,10)`, using four candidates.
Farthest reach uses three.

Focused boundaries: closed `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` share stabbing point 2.
Half-open `[0,2)` and `[2,4)` meet without a coverage gap because the
second interval contains 2. In contrast, `[0,2)` and `[3,4)` cannot
cover `[0,4)` because every real position between 2 and 3 is missing.

A nil stabbing input returns non-nil empty. An empty target `[5,5)`
also returns non-nil empty after candidate validation. A point closed
interval is valid; a point half-open candidate is empty and invalid.

Focused extremes: `[MinInt64,MinInt64]` and
`[MaxInt64,MaxInt64]` require those two exact stabbing points. One
candidate `[MinInt64,MaxInt64)` covers the same half-open target
without endpoint arithmetic.

##### Implementation

This complete program performs both walkthrough phases, prints both
unchanged inputs, and exercises both empty results. Save it as
`main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Interval stabbing and coverage
// (sorted endpoints). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"cmp"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"slices"
)

type closedInterval struct {
	start int64
	end   int64
}

func (current closedInterval) String() string {
	// Format this value without changing its stored state.
	return fmt.Sprintf("[%d,%d]", current.start, current.end)
}

type indexedClosedInterval struct {
	interval   closedInterval
	inputIndex int
}

func compareIndexedClosedByEnd(
	first indexedClosedInterval,
	second indexedClosedInterval,
) int {
	// Execute indexed closed by end to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	if byEnd := cmp.Compare(
		first.interval.end,
		second.interval.end,
	); byEnd != 0 {
		return byEnd
	}
	if byStart := cmp.Compare(
		first.interval.start,
		second.interval.start,
	); byStart != 0 {
		return byStart
	}
	return cmp.Compare(first.inputIndex, second.inputIndex)
}

func minimumStabbingPoints(
	intervals []closedInterval,
) ([]int64, error) {
	// Validate before allocation so errors expose no partial result.
	for inputIndex, current := range intervals {
		if current.start > current.end {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"interval %d has start after end",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
	}

	// Earliest end is the farthest safe point for a required interval.
	ordered := make([]indexedClosedInterval, len(intervals))
	for inputIndex, current := range intervals {
		ordered[inputIndex] = indexedClosedInterval{
			interval:   current,
			inputIndex: inputIndex,
		}
	}
	slices.SortFunc(ordered, compareIndexedClosedByEnd)

	points := make([]int64, 0)
	var lastPoint int64
	hasPoint := false
	for _, current := range ordered {
		// Closed boundaries let a point at start hit this interval.
		if hasPoint && current.interval.start <= lastPoint {
			continue
		}

		// The right endpoint also reaches every possible later overlap.
		lastPoint = current.interval.end
		hasPoint = true
		points = append(points, lastPoint)
	}
	return points, nil
}

type halfOpenInterval struct {
	start int64
	end   int64
}

func (current halfOpenInterval) String() string {
	// Format this value without changing its stored state.
	return fmt.Sprintf("[%d,%d)", current.start, current.end)
}

type indexedHalfOpenInterval struct {
	interval   halfOpenInterval
	inputIndex int
}

func compareIndexedHalfOpenByStart(
	first indexedHalfOpenInterval,
	second indexedHalfOpenInterval,
) int {
	// Execute indexed half open by start to the bounded stopping
	// condition above.
	if byStart := cmp.Compare(
		first.interval.start,
		second.interval.start,
	); byStart != 0 {
		return byStart
	}
	if byEnd := cmp.Compare(
		second.interval.end,
		first.interval.end,
	); byEnd != 0 {
		return byEnd
	}
	return cmp.Compare(first.inputIndex, second.inputIndex)
}

var errTargetNotCovered = errors.New("target cannot be covered")

func selectMinimumTargetCover(
	intervals []halfOpenInterval,
	target halfOpenInterval,
) ([]int, error) {
	// The target may be empty, but it may not be reversed.
	if target.start > target.end {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("target has start after end")
	}
	for inputIndex, current := range intervals {
		if current.start >= current.end {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf(
				"interval %d must be nonempty",
				inputIndex,
			)
		}
	}
	if target.start == target.end {
		return make([]int, 0), nil
	}

	// Start order makes every interval eligible at one frontier.
	ordered := make([]indexedHalfOpenInterval, len(intervals))
	for inputIndex, current := range intervals {
		ordered[inputIndex] = indexedHalfOpenInterval{
			interval:   current,
			inputIndex: inputIndex,
		}
	}
	slices.SortFunc(ordered, compareIndexedHalfOpenByStart)

	selectedIndices := make([]int, 0)
	coveredUntil := target.start
	nextIndex := 0
	for coveredUntil < target.end {
		// Among all gap-free extensions, remember the farthest end.
		var best indexedHalfOpenInterval
		hasExtension := false
		for nextIndex < len(ordered) &&
			ordered[nextIndex].interval.start <= coveredUntil {
			candidate := ordered[nextIndex]
			nextIndex++
			if candidate.interval.end <= coveredUntil {
				continue
			}
			betterEnd := !hasExtension ||
				candidate.interval.end > best.interval.end
			betterTie := hasExtension &&
				candidate.interval.end == best.interval.end &&
				candidate.inputIndex < best.inputIndex
			if betterEnd || betterTie {
				best = candidate
				hasExtension = true
			}
		}
		if !hasExtension {
			return nil, errTargetNotCovered
		}

		// This choice stays at least as far ahead as any other choice.
		selectedIndices = append(
			selectedIndices,
			best.inputIndex,
		)
		coveredUntil = best.interval.end
	}
	return selectedIndices, nil
}

func run(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute the requested item to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	stabbingInput := []closedInterval{
		{start: 1, end: 4},
		{start: 2, end: 5},
		{start: 7, end: 9},
		{start: 4, end: 7},
		{start: 10, end: 10},
		{start: 8, end: 10},
	}
	points, err := minimumStabbingPoints(stabbingInput)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, points); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write stabbing points: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, stabbingInput); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write stabbing input: %w", err)
	}

	coverageInput := []halfOpenInterval{
		{start: 0, end: 2},
		{start: 1, end: 5},
		{start: 4, end: 7},
		{start: 6, end: 10},
		{start: 2, end: 6},
		{start: 8, end: 12},
	}
	selected, err := selectMinimumTargetCover(
		coverageInput,
		halfOpenInterval{start: 0, end: 10},
	)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, selected); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write coverage indices: %w", err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(output, coverageInput); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write coverage input: %w", err)
	}

	emptyPoints, err := minimumStabbingPoints(nil)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		emptyPoints,
		emptyPoints != nil,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write empty points: %w", err)
	}
	emptyCover, err := selectMinimumTargetCover(
		nil,
		halfOpenInterval{start: 5, end: 5},
	)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintln(
		output,
		emptyCover,
		emptyCover != nil,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write empty cover: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := run(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[4 9 10]
[[1,4] [2,5] [7,9] [4,7] [10,10] [8,10]]
[0 4 3]
[[0,2) [1,5) [4,7) [6,10) [2,6) [8,12)]
[] true
[] true
```

The second and fourth lines confirm that sorting preserved both
inputs. The last two true values confirm both empty results are
non-nil.

##### Why it works

For stabbing, let `I = [s,e]` be the earliest-ending interval not yet
stabbed. Every valid solution needs some point `p` inside `I`. Replace
`p` with `e`. Interval `I` remains stabbed. Any later interval that
`p` stabbed has start at most `p`, hence at most `e`, and has end at
least `e` because `I` ends first. Therefore `e` also lies inside every
such later interval.

The replacement loses no coverage, so some optimum chooses `e`.
Remove all intervals containing `e` and apply the same exchange to the
next unstabbed interval. Induction proves every appended endpoint is
compatible with an optimum. When the finite scan ends, every interval
is stabbed, so the returned number of points is minimum.

The stabbing implementation realizes removal by skipping intervals
whose start is at most `lastPoint`. End sorting guarantees their end
is also at least `lastPoint`. A new point is strictly larger than the
previous one because its interval starts beyond that previous point.

For coverage, suppose the confirmed prefix ends at frontier `x` before
the target ends. Every feasible continuation needs an interval `O`
with `O.start <= x < O.end`; otherwise target position `x` is
uncovered. The greedy scan considers every such available interval
and chooses `G` with the greatest end. Thus `G.end >= O.end`.

Replace `O` by `G` in an optimal continuation. `G` begins in time to
meet the confirmed prefix and covers at least as far right, so every
later interval that followed `O` can still follow `G` or becomes
unnecessary. The replacement does not increase the number of choices.
Induction on selected intervals proves greedy stays at least as far
right as an optimum using the same number of intervals. Greedy
therefore reaches the target in the minimum count.

If no scanned candidate ends beyond `x`, none can cover the next
target position: scanned candidates stop too early, and every
unscanned start is greater than `x`. Returning `errTargetNotCovered`
is therefore exact, not a heuristic failure.

Each stabbing iteration consumes one sorted interval. Each coverage
candidate is scanned at most once, and every successful coverage
iteration strictly increases `coveredUntil`. Finite inputs and strict
frontier progress prove termination.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `S` be the number of stabbing intervals and `P` the number of
returned points. Stabbing validation, copy construction, and scanning
each take `Theta(S)` time. Let `SortEnd(S)` be its sorting time. Total
time is `Theta(S) + SortEnd(S)`, conventionally `O(S log S)` with
comparison sorting. Constructing `P` output values takes `Theta(P)`
work within the scan.

The stabbing ordered copy uses `O(S)` auxiliary storage. Sort stack or
scratch space is implementation-dependent. The returned points use
`O(P)` output storage and may retain geometric-growth spare capacity.
The scan itself uses `O(1)` scalar state.

Let `C` be the number of coverage candidates and `K` the selected
count. Validation and copy construction take `Theta(C)` time. Every
candidate is scanned at most once, and each chosen interval advances
the frontier, so the coverage scan takes `O(C + K) = O(C)`. Let
`SortStart(C)` be sorting time. Total successful or impossible-case
time is `Theta(C) + SortStart(C)`, conventionally `O(C log C)`.

Coverage uses `O(C)` auxiliary storage for the ordered copy plus
implementation-dependent sort storage. Its returned index slice uses
`O(K)` output storage and may retain spare capacity. Scalar scan state
is `O(1)`. An empty target still validates all `C` candidates, then
returns before copying or sorting.

No input distribution is assumed, so no average-case bounds are
claimed. Invalid input may stop during validation. An impossible
cover can stop after scanning only the candidates whose starts reach
the first gap.

If input already satisfies the exact required order, each algorithm
can scan in linear time. If mutation is permitted, sorting indexed
records in caller-owned storage can avoid one copy only when identity
travels with each record and that ownership change is documented.

Brute-force verification tries point or interval subsets and grows
exponentially. Sorting exposes the exchange-safe choice and reduces
each offline problem to one bounded scan.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Treat stabbing and coverage as one rule. Stabbing chooses the
  earliest end as a point; coverage chooses the farthest end among
  intervals already eligible at the frontier.
- Stab at a left endpoint. `[1,4] [2,5]` then uses two points instead
  of the single safe right endpoint 4.
- Sort stabbing intervals by start. The first interval considered may
  end late, so its endpoint can miss an earlier-ending requirement.
- Test only `start <= lastPoint` without end order. The test is valid
  here because sorting also guarantees `lastPoint <= current.end`.
- Use `<` for closed stabbing containment. `[1,2] [2,3]` share point
  2, so equality must count.
- Reject point closed intervals. `[5,5]` is one required coordinate.
- Use a numeric sentinel for no stabbing point. Every `int64` is a
  valid endpoint; keep `hasPoint` separately.
- Choose the first coverage candidate that reaches the frontier. In
  the walkthrough, end 5 loses to end 6 and causes an extra choice.
- Choose the longest coverage interval globally. `[3,100)` cannot
  begin coverage of target `[0,10)` despite its length.
- Scan only one newly eligible coverage candidate. Every interval
  starting by the current frontier must compete for farthest end.
- Reconsider discarded coverage candidates. Once greedy reaches the
  farthest scanned end, every unchosen scanned interval ends no later.
- Accept an end equal to `coveredUntil` as progress. It covers no new
  half-open target position and can make the loop stall forever.
- Require `start < coveredUntil` for continuation. Equality is valid:
  `[0,2)` followed by `[2,4)` has no uncovered point.
- Treat integer adjacency as continuous coverage. `[0,2)` and `[3,4)`
  leave real positions between 2 and 3 uncovered.
- Return a partial cover on a gap. The contract returns nil with
  `errTargetNotCovered`, so callers cannot mistake a prefix for
  success.
- Return impossibility for an empty target. After validation,
  `[5,5)` needs zero candidates and returns non-nil empty.
- Accept an empty candidate. `[2,2)` covers no position and violates
  this candidate contract, even though closed `[2,2]` is valid for
  stabbing.
- Compare endpoints by subtraction or increment an end. Signed
  extremes are valid; use ordered comparisons only.
- Deduplicate intervals. Equal records have distinct identities, and
  coverage tie-breaking promises the smaller input index.
- Sort caller-owned slices while promising preservation. Sort copied
  indexed records.
- Permit concurrent writes. Copying is not a synchronized snapshot,
  although independent readers are safe.

##### When to choose it

Use stabbing when output items are points and each interval merely
needs to contain one: arrows through balloon spans, sensor positions,
inspection times, and representatives for acceptable ranges fit this
model. Recognition clues include "minimum points," "hit every
interval," and "one coordinate may satisfy many ranges."

Use target coverage when output items must be original intervals and
their connected union must contain a requested span: clips, radio
windows, service ranges, and replacement segments fit. Recognition
clues include "fewest intervals to cover `[L,R)`," "no gaps," and
"among starts before the frontier, extend farthest."

Keep original indices when chosen interval identity matters. If only
the minimum coverage count is needed, increment a count instead of
storing `K` indices. If only stabbing count is needed, count chosen
right endpoints instead of returning `P` coordinates.

When not to choose it:

Do not use stabbing to construct the input union. [Interval merging](
#b171-interval-merging-sorted-slice) returns maximal covered spans,
not representative points. Do not use coverage to choose a maximum
set of non-overlapping activities; [interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) deliberately prefers the
earliest compatible finish rather than farthest reach.

Open stabbing intervals need another rule because a right endpoint is
not contained. Discrete integer coverage also needs explicit
adjacency semantics; adding one to an endpoint changes the model and
can overflow.

Weighted points or intervals change the objective. The exchange may
replace a cheap choice with an expensive one, so dynamic programming,
shortest paths, flow, or general covering methods may be needed.

Multiple disjoint target spans require tracking where coverage is
actually required. Merge their union first and adapt the frontier
across gaps; do not force selected intervals to cover irrelevant
space. Dynamic insertions and online commitment need an ordered data
structure or another contract rather than repeated offline sorting.

[B.3.1 comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) owns copied
multi-key ordering. [B.17.1 interval merging](
#b171-interval-merging-sorted-slice) owns closed-union normalization,
and [B.17.2 interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) owns maximum disjoint choice.

https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/) poses both minimum
interval stabbing and minimum interval-cover problems.
The official [Video Stitching problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/video-stitching/) uses minimum interval
coverage of a target span.

Williams College's [CS 256 materials](
https://williams-cs.github.io/cs256-s21-www/) include an Assignment 3
right-endpoint stabbing exercise that requires an exchange proof. The
University of Washington's [Winter 2023 CSE 421 materials](
https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse421/23wi/) present the
farthest-reaching interval-cover rule in a section handout.

Go's authoritative [`slices.SortFunc` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#SortFunc) specifies comparator order and the
mutation behavior that motivates sorting owned copies.


### B.18 Nearest greater or smaller values

#### B.18.1 Monotonic stack (index stack)

##### Problem and contract

For every value in a sequence, find the nearest earlier and nearest
later position whose value is strictly smaller or strictly greater.
"Nearest" means the qualifying position with the smallest index
distance, not the qualifying value closest in magnitude.

`nearestNeighborIndices` accepts a slice and one relation:

- `strictlySmaller` asks for a value less than the target value.
- `strictlyGreater` asks for a value greater than the target value.

It returns two owned index slices. `previous[i]` is the largest index
less than `i` that satisfies the relation to `values[i]`. `next[i]`
is the smallest satisfying index greater than `i`. An absent neighbor
is `-1`, which cannot collide with any valid slice index.

For input `[3,1,2,2,4,1]`, strictly smaller neighbors are:

```text
previous = [-1,-1,1,1,3,-1]
next     = [ 1,-1,5,5,5,-1]
```

The relation is strict. Equal values never qualify, and duplicate
positions remain distinct. Every `int` value is valid, including its
extremes; the algorithm compares values without subtracting them.

Nil and empty input return two non-nil empty slices. An unknown
relation returns a zero result whose slices are nil and an error that
wraps `errUnknownNeighborRelation`. Relation validation happens
before output-slice allocation.

The function does not mutate or retain the input. Its two result
slices do not alias each other or the input. Independent calls may
read the same stable slice concurrently. Concurrent input writes need
external synchronization. Required allocations must fit memory.

A separate outward scan from every position is simple, but it can
inspect quadratically many pairs. The index stack remembers only
candidates that can still be nearest for an unprocessed target.

Read [A.4.2 monotonic stacks](#a42-monotonic-stacks) first. It owns
the core unresolved-candidate invariant and amortized stack argument.

##### Mental model

Run the same stack rule in two directions. A left-to-right pass fills
`previous`; a right-to-left pass fills `next`. The stack stores
indices, so a retained candidate carries both its value lookup and
the exact position needed by the output.

For a target at `index`, ask whether the value at the top stack index
has the wanted relation to `values[index]`. If it does not, pop that
index and repeat. When a wanted top remains, it is the nearest wanted
position on the processed side. Record it, or keep `-1` if the stack
is empty, and then push `index`.

For `strictlySmaller`, a candidate is wanted when:

```text
candidate value < target value
```

Popping every non-wanted candidate leaves stack values strictly
increasing from bottom to top. For `strictlyGreater`, reverse the
comparison; retained values are strictly decreasing.

The pop is a dominance decision. In a left-to-right smaller pass, if
the current value is no greater than a top candidate, current is both
later and no larger. Whenever that older candidate could be smaller
than a future target, current would also be smaller and would be
nearer. The older index can never again be the answer. The greater
case uses the symmetric argument with "no smaller" instead.

The reverse pass applies the same reasoning from the other end. Its
top is the nearest processed position to the right. Reuse the stack's
backing array after resetting its logical length to zero; candidates
from the first direction have no meaning in the second direction.
Because `len` returns `int`, empty input starts the reverse index at
`-1` and skips the loop body.

Equality belongs in the pop condition because the relation is strict.
For example, while finding smaller neighbors, an equal top is not an
answer. The newer equal position also dominates the older one for
future targets, so removing the older equal position is safe.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use input `[3,1,2,2,4,1]` and request `strictlySmaller`. Expected
results are `previous=[-1,-1,1,1,3,-1]` and
`next=[1,-1,5,5,5,-1]`. Stack snapshots show `index:value` from
bottom to top.

Initial state: both result slices contain six `-1` values. The stack
is empty. The previous-neighbor pass begins at index 0.

1. Decision: index 0 has value 3 and the stack is empty, so no earlier
   smaller value exists. Keep `previous[0] = -1` and push `0:3`.
   After: stack is `[0:3]`.
   Known correct: index 0 has no processed position to its left.
2. Decision: at index 1, top value 3 is not smaller than 1. Pop
   `0:3`; the empty stack gives `previous[1] = -1`; push `1:1`.
   After: stack is `[1:1]`.
   Known correct: neither index 0 nor any other earlier index has a
   value below 1.
3. Decision: at index 2, top value 1 is smaller than 2. Record
   `previous[2] = 1` and push `2:2`.
   After: stack is `[1:1,2:2]`.
   Known correct: index 1 qualifies and is the closest earlier index.
4. Decision: at index 3, top value 2 equals the target and is not
   strictly smaller. Pop `2:2`; top `1:1` qualifies, so record
   `previous[3] = 1` and push `3:2`.
   After: stack is `[1:1,3:2]`.
   Known correct: the duplicate at index 2 was rejected, and index 1
   is the nearest strictly smaller earlier value.
5. Decision: at index 4, top value 2 is smaller than 4. Record
   `previous[4] = 3` and push `4:4`.
   After: stack is `[1:1,3:2,4:4]`.
   Known correct: index 3 is closer than every other qualifying
   earlier position.
6. Decision: at index 5, values 4 and 2 are not smaller than 1, and
   value 1 is equal. Pop `4:4`, `3:2`, and `1:1`. Keep
   `previous[5] = -1`, then push `5:1`.
   After: stack is `[5:1]`; `previous` is final as
   `[-1,-1,1,1,3,-1]`.
   Known correct: every earlier value is at least 1, and the left pass
   has answered every position.
7. Decision: reset the stack and start the next-neighbor pass at
   index 5. No right position exists, so keep `next[5] = -1` and push
   `5:1`.
   After: stack is `[5:1]`.
   Known correct: index 5 has no position to its right.
8. Decision: at index 4, top value 1 is smaller than 4. Record
   `next[4] = 5` and push `4:4`.
   After: stack is `[5:1,4:4]`.
   Known correct: index 5 is the closest processed position to the
   right and qualifies.
9. Decision: at index 3, top value 4 is not smaller than 2, so pop
   `4:4`. Value 1 at index 5 qualifies; record `next[3] = 5` and push
   `3:2`.
   After: stack is `[5:1,3:2]`.
   Known correct: index 4 cannot answer index 3, while index 5 is the
   first smaller position to its right.
10. Decision: at index 2, top `3:2` is equal and is popped. Top
    `5:1` qualifies, so record `next[2] = 5` and push `2:2`.
    After: stack is `[5:1,2:2]`.
    Known correct: the adjacent duplicate is not accepted as smaller.
11. Decision: at index 1, pop `2:2` because 2 is not smaller than 1,
    then pop equal `5:1`. Keep `next[1] = -1` and push `1:1`.
    After: stack is `[1:1]`.
    Known correct: every position to the right has value at least 1.
12. Decision: at index 0, top value 1 is smaller than 3. Record
    `next[0] = 1`, push `0:3`, and finish the reverse scan.
    After: stack is `[1:1,0:3]`; `next` is
    `[1,-1,5,5,5,-1]`.
    Known correct: every position now has its nearest smaller index on
    both sides.
13. Decision: both finite passes are complete, so return the two
    result slices.
    After: the returned pair is exactly the expected pair.
    Known correct: every stored index is strict, on the required side,
    and nearer than any other qualifying index on that side.

Focused greater case: the same input with `strictlyGreater` returns:

```text
previous = [-1,0,0,0,-1,4]
next     = [ 4,2,4,4,-1,-1]
```

The only mechanism change is the wanted comparison. At index 4,
value 4 pops every no-greater candidate and therefore has no previous
greater index. At index 5, the retained `4:4` is immediately previous
and greater. From index 0, the reverse pass rejects values 1 and 2
until index 4 supplies the first value greater than 3.

Focused repeated-pop case: for smaller neighbors in `[1,2,3,0]`,
target 0 must pop indices 2, 1, and 0. Replacing the pop loop with one
`if` would leave value 2 on top and could report it as smaller than 0.

Focused strictness case: `[2,2]` returns `-1` on both sides for both
positions under `strictlySmaller`. Keeping an equal top by popping
only greater values would incorrectly report one duplicate for the
other.

Focused boundaries: empty input returns two non-nil empty slices. An
unknown relation returns nil result slices and the declared error.

##### Implementation

This complete program uses `errors`, `fmt`, `io`, and `os` from the
standard library. It prints both relations, the empty case, and error
identity. Only the supplied writer has an external side effect.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Monotonic stack (index stack).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

type neighborRelation uint8

const (
	strictlySmaller neighborRelation = iota
	strictlyGreater
)

var errUnknownNeighborRelation = errors.New(
	"unknown neighbor relation",
)

type neighborIndices struct {
	previous []int
	next     []int
}

func nearestNeighborIndices(
	values []int,
	relation neighborRelation,
) (neighborIndices, error) {
	// Copy and sort neighbors for deterministic output.
	if relation != strictlySmaller &&
		relation != strictlyGreater {
		return neighborIndices{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: %d",
			errUnknownNeighborRelation,
			relation,
		)
	}

	result := neighborIndices{
		previous: make([]int, len(values)),
		next:     make([]int, len(values)),
	}
	for index := range values {
		result.previous[index] = -1
		result.next[index] = -1
	}

	isWanted := func(candidateValue int, targetValue int) bool {
		if relation == strictlySmaller {
			return candidateValue < targetValue
		}
		return candidateValue > targetValue
	}

	// A left-to-right pass finds the nearest wanted index before each
	// target. Every popped index is blocked by the current value.
	stack := make([]int, 0, len(values))
	for index, value := range values {
		for len(stack) > 0 {
			topPosition := len(stack) - 1
			candidateIndex := stack[topPosition]
			if isWanted(values[candidateIndex], value) {
				break
			}
			stack = stack[:topPosition]
		}
		if len(stack) > 0 {
			result.previous[index] = stack[len(stack)-1]
		}
		stack = append(stack, index)
	}

	// Reverse direction and reuse the stack storage to find the
	// nearest wanted index after each target.
	stack = stack[:0]
	// Empty input starts at -1 because len returns int, so it skips.
	for index := len(values) - 1; index >= 0; index-- {
		value := values[index]
		for len(stack) > 0 {
			topPosition := len(stack) - 1
			candidateIndex := stack[topPosition]
			if isWanted(values[candidateIndex], value) {
				break
			}
			stack = stack[:topPosition]
		}
		if len(stack) > 0 {
			result.next[index] = stack[len(stack)-1]
		}
		stack = append(stack, index)
	}

	return result, nil
}

func writeNeighborIndices(
	output io.Writer,
	label string,
	result neighborIndices,
	err error,
) error {
	// Copy and sort neighbors for deterministic output.
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", label, err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"%s.previous = %v\n"+
			"%s.next = %v\n",
		label,
		result.previous,
		label,
		result.next,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write %s result: %w", label, err)
	}
	return nil
}

func runNeighborExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Copy and sort neighbors for deterministic output.
	values := []int{3, 1, 2, 2, 4, 1}
	smaller, smallerErr := nearestNeighborIndices(
		values,
		strictlySmaller,
	)
	if err := writeNeighborIndices(
		output,
		"smaller",
		smaller,
		smallerErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	greater, greaterErr := nearestNeighborIndices(
		values,
		strictlyGreater,
	)
	if err := writeNeighborIndices(
		output,
		"greater",
		greater,
		greaterErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	empty, emptyErr := nearestNeighborIndices(
		nil,
		strictlySmaller,
	)
	if err := writeNeighborIndices(
		output,
		"empty",
		empty,
		emptyErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	_, invalidErr := nearestNeighborIndices(
		values,
		neighborRelation(255),
	)
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"invalid relation = %t\n",
		errors.Is(invalidErr, errUnknownNeighborRelation),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write invalid-relation result: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runNeighborExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
smaller.previous = [-1 -1 1 1 3 -1]
smaller.next = [1 -1 5 5 5 -1]
greater.previous = [-1 0 0 0 -1 4]
greater.next = [4 2 4 4 -1 -1]
empty.previous = []
empty.next = []
invalid relation = true
```

##### Why it works

Consider the left-to-right pass. Before each target, stack positions
appear in encounter order, so the top is the most recent retained
position. For the smaller relation, their values are strictly
increasing from bottom to top; for greater, they are strictly
decreasing. Every removed position is dominated by a later retained
or processed position and can never be nearest for a future target.

The empty stack satisfies these facts initially. At a target, the
loop removes every exposed top that lacks the wanted relation. For
smaller, current is no larger and later than each removed candidate.
If a removed value could be smaller than a future value, current
would also be smaller and closer. The greater case is symmetric.
Thus each pop permanently removes only a candidate that cannot answer
the current target or any future target in this pass.

When popping stops, every more recent retained candidate has already
been removed as non-wanted. If a top remains, it has the wanted
relation and is therefore the nearest wanted processed position. If
none remains, no earlier position can qualify: any earlier removed
position was dominated, and there is no retained qualifying one.
Recording the top or `-1` is consequently correct.

Pushing current makes it the nearest candidate for the next target.
All nonconforming or equal tops were removed first, so pushing also
restores the strict monotonic value order. The pass invariant is
preserved.

The right-to-left pass starts again with an empty stack and uses the
same proof with left and right reversed. Its top is the nearest
retained position to the right. It therefore fills every `next`
entry with the required nearest index or `-1`.

Each outer iteration advances to a new input position. Every pass
pushes an index once, and every inner iteration pops one index
permanently, so both the repeated-pop loop and each pass terminate.
When both passes end, all previous and next entries have been proven,
which is exactly the returned contract.

Relation validation precedes allocation. The algorithm performs no
value arithmetic, so extreme integers do not overflow. Private result
and stack slices establish the ownership and mutation guarantees.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the input length. Initializing the two result slices visits
`N` entries. In each directional pass, every index is pushed exactly
once and popped at most once. The apparently nested pop loops
therefore perform at most `N` pops per pass.

Both passes take `Theta(N)` total time. Every valid input value must
be read to decide its own neighbors, so best, average, and worst time
are all `Theta(N)`. Duplicate-heavy, increasing, and decreasing inputs
change when pops happen, not their linear total.

The two returned slices use `Theta(N)` output storage. The reused
index stack retains at most `N` indices and uses `O(N)` auxiliary
space. The relation closure and scalar state use `O(1)` space.
Resetting the stack length between passes reuses its backing array.

Empty valid input takes `Theta(1)` time and returns initialized empty
slices without requiring an element backing store. An invalid relation
takes `Theta(1)` time and allocates no output slices. Runtime error
construction may still allocate.

A direct outward search uses `O(1)` auxiliary space beyond the same
outputs, but a monotone input can make it inspect `Theta(N^2)`
pairs. A specialized one-direction solution can omit one output and
one pass, but it has the same linear time and worst-case stack space.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Return neighbor values when the contract asks for indices. Duplicate
  values can occupy different nearest positions.
- Store only values on the stack. The output and distance variants
  need the retained positions.
- Treat `-1` as a real position. It is an absence sentinel and must
  never index the input.
- Use the wrong scan direction. Left to right discovers previous
  neighbors; right to left discovers next neighbors in this design.
- Replace the repeated pop loop with `if`. `[1,2,3,0]` requires three
  pops before its final target can be answered.
- Pop only `>` while asking for strictly smaller. An equal top would
  survive and be reported even though equality does not qualify.
- Pop `>=` for a non-strict "smaller or equal" contract. The correct
  duplicate rule follows the requested relation, not a memorized
  inequality.
- Report the bottom of the stack. The top is the nearest retained
  position on the processed side.
- Carry stack contents from one directional pass into the other. Reset
  logical length because the processed side has changed.
- Assume numeric stack indices are always increasing. They increase in
  the forward pass and decrease in the reverse pass; encounter order
  and value monotonicity are the useful facts.
- Compare by subtraction. `maximumInt - minimumInt` can overflow;
  direct `<` and `>` comparisons work for every `int`.
- Use an unsigned reverse index. It cannot represent the `-1` stopping
  state and can wrap after index zero.
- Return nil slices for valid empty input. The contract distinguishes
  a successful empty result from the zero result on invalid relation.
- Allocate outputs before validating the relation, contradicting the
  failure contract and doing needless work.
- Sort or overwrite input to create monotonic order. The stack, not
  the input, is monotonic, and the function promises preservation.
- Permit concurrent writes. Read-only calls share no state, but a
  writer racing with value lookups violates the stable-input contract.
- Assume linear complexity guarantees allocation success. Very large
  valid inputs can still exhaust memory.

##### When to choose it

Choose this index-stack pattern when all of these clues are present:

- every sequence position needs the nearest match on one fixed side;
- the match is an ordered strict or non-strict comparison;
- a newer value can permanently dominate older candidates; and
- the sequence is stable during the scan.

Common applications include stock spans, next-greater queries,
nearest-smaller histogram boundaries, and resolving pending events
when a later threshold-crossing value arrives. If only one direction
is needed, run only its corresponding pass.

The strict version here is a template, not a universal inequality.
For an "at least" or "at most" contract, change both the wanted test
and the equality pop rule, then re-prove duplicate handling.

When not to choose it:

Do not use this pattern for an arbitrary predicate such as "nearest
value with the same last digit." A current value may fail to dominate
an older candidate, so popping can destroy a future answer.

Do not use one static scan when values change between queries. A
segment tree or another indexed search structure may be needed to
support updates and repeated boundary searches.

Do not use a stack for a sliding-window maximum or minimum when old
candidates expire from the opposite end. A monotonic deque supports
both dominance removal and time-based expiration.

For one isolated position, a direct outward scan may be simpler and
use less memory. For arbitrary range minima or maxima, use a range
query structure; nearest-position output is a different contract.

first-out mechanics. [A.4.2 monotonic stacks](

push-once, pop-once amortized proof used here.

[B.16.10 largest rectangle](

https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1645) asks for the previous-smaller
variant. The official [Next Greater Element I task](
https://leetcode.com/problems/next-greater-element-i/) defines the
first-greater-on-the-right variant.

The Go specification's [slice types](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_types) define indexing, length, and
