beyond one word.

[B.19.1](#b191-subsets-and-permutations-backtracking-and-path)
generates the same distinct-value power set with a recursive path. The
next lesson,
[B.19.5](#b195-duplicate-aware-generation-counts-or-sorted-slice),
changes the generation rule when equal input values are allowed.

The official [Subsets task](https://leetcode.com/problems/subsets/)
defines the unique-value objective and ten-value limit. This lesson
adds explicit mask order, empty-input behavior, ownership, and
validation errors.

The Go specification defines [integer and shift
operators](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators), including
unsigned shift behavior. The standard library documents
[`bits.OnesCount64`](https://pkg.go.dev/math/bits#OnesCount64) as the
population count used to reserve exact inner capacity.

#### B.19.5 Duplicate-aware generation (counts or sorted slice)

##### Problem and contract

Given integers that may repeat, return every distinct value subset. A
subset may use at most the copies supplied by the input. Values inside
each subset are nondecreasing, and equal value sequences appear once
even when several position selections could create them.

For input `[2,1,2]`, both implementations in this lesson return:

```text
[[] [1] [1 2] [1 2 2] [2] [2 2]]
```

This is deterministic depth-first value order. It depends on ascending
values, not original positions. The input is copied or counted rather
than sorted in place, so its order remains `[2,1,2]`.

`subsetsBySortedChoices` sorts an owned copy and skips equal sibling
choices. `subsetsByValueCounts` stores each distinct value once with
its available count. They expose the same contract and return the same
order. The first is the smaller adaptation of ordinary subset
backtracking. The second makes multiplicity explicit and can shrink
duplicate-heavy search state.

Both functions accept at most 10 input values. A larger input returns
nil and an error wrapping `errTooManyDuplicateSubsetValues` before
copying, counting, sorting, or searching. The limit matches the
official Subsets II task and bounds recursion and exponential output.

Every `int` value is valid, including zero, negatives, and both
integer extremes. Nil and empty input return `[[]]` with non-nil outer
and inner slices. The outer result and every inner slice are newly
owned and independent.

The input is read-only and is not retained. Independent calls may read
the same stable input concurrently. Concurrent input writes need
external synchronization. Successful allocations must fit memory.

Read [B.19.1 distinct-input backtracking](
#b191-subsets-and-permutations-backtracking-and-path)
for choose, recurse, restore, and path ownership. Read
[B.1.3 sorted runs](
#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) and [A.6.3 multisets](
#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) for the two duplicate
representations.

##### Mental model

Duplicates change what identifies a result. With distinct input, a
chosen position set also identifies one value subset. With `[2,2]`,
position 0 alone and position 1 alone both produce the value subset
`[2]`. A correct search must distinguish available copies while
merging equivalent value choices.

The sorted-choice method copies and sorts the input. Equal values are
then adjacent. A frame remembers `firstChoiceIndex`, the first sorted
position it may use next, and `path`, the nondecreasing values
already chosen.

At one frame, equal candidate values are siblings: each would append
the same next value to the same path. Try only the first sibling:

```go
// At one depth, equal adjacent choices produce the same branch.
// Keep the first and skip later duplicates before recursion begins.
if choiceIndex > firstChoiceIndex &&
	sortedValues[choiceIndex] == sortedValues[choiceIndex-1] {
	continue
}
```

The condition is local to one frame. A child has a new
`firstChoiceIndex`, so the first equal value in that child remains
legal. For sorted `[1,2,2]`, the root skips its second 2 after
exploring the first 2 branch. The `[1,2]` child does not skip the
later 2, because that copy is the child's first candidate and is
needed to build `[1,2,2]`.

The count method builds `countByValue`. Reading
`countByValue[2] == 2` means two copies of 2 may appear in one subset.
Map iteration has no stable order, so copy the distinct keys into
`sortedDistinctValues` and sort them. `usedByValueIndex[i]` stores how
many copies of the value at sorted index `i` are currently in `path`.

A counted frame remembers `firstValueIndex`, the lowest
distinct-value index allowed next. It tries values in ascending order.
A child receives the same chosen index, so it may choose another equal
copy until the used count reaches the available count. Moving the loop
to a higher index then prevents later paths from returning to a
smaller value.

Both searches emit a copied path at frame entry. The empty root path
is therefore included. Appending a value, recursing, and restoring all
changed state produces the child subtree before the next distinct
sibling.

The two representations build the same value-level tree:

```text
[]
|- [1]
|  `- [1 2]
|     `- [1 2 2]
`- [2]
   `- [2 2]
```

The sorted method represents copies as adjacent positions and removes
equivalent siblings. The count method represents copies as a quota and
prevents use beyond it.

##### Worked walkthrough

Trace the sorted-choice method on `[2,1,2]`. A frame snapshot is
`(path,firstChoiceIndex)`, and the expected result is the six subsets
shown above.

Initial state: validation accepts three values. Copying and sorting
gives `sortedValues=[1,2,2]`; `path=[]`; the result is empty; enter
frame `([],0)`.

```text
root choices: 1, 2, (skip duplicate 2)

[1] choices: 2, (skip duplicate sibling 2)
[1 2] choice: second 2 -> [1 2 2]
[2] choice: second 2 -> [2 2]
```

1. Decision: emit a copy of the root path, choose index 0 with value
   1, and recurse with the next available index 1.
   After: result is `[[]]`; active frame is `([1],1)`.
   Known correct: the empty subset is owned by the result, and every
   child in this branch begins with value 1.
2. Decision: emit `[1]`, then choose index 1, the first 2 in this
   frame. Recurse from index 2.
   After: result is `[[] [1]]`; active frame is `([1 2],2)`.
   Known correct: `[1]` appears once, and one supplied copy of 2 is in
   the active path.
3. Decision: emit `[1 2]`. Index 2 is the frame's first candidate, so
   it remains legal even though its value equals the previous choice.
   Append value 2 and recurse from index 3.
   After: result ends with `[1 2]`; active frame is `([1 2 2],3)`.
   Known correct: the path uses both available copies of 2 without
   reusing a position.
4. Decision: emit `[1 2 2]`. No position remains, so return, remove
   the second 2, and finish that parent. Back in frame `([1],1)`,
   candidate index 2 equals the earlier sibling at index 1, so skip
   it.
   After: result is `[[] [1] [1 2] [1 2 2]]`; restore the root path.
   Known correct: every subset beginning with 1 appears once; choosing
   index 2 as the first 2 would repeat the index-1 subtree.
5. Decision: the root next chooses index 1, value 2, and emits `[2]`
   in its child. That child may choose index 2 because it is the first
   candidate in the child frame.
   After: result adds `[2]` and `[2 2]`; the root path is restored.
   Known correct: one-copy and two-copy subsets of value 2 both exist.
6. Decision: the root reaches index 2. Its value equals the root's
   earlier sibling at index 1, so skip it. No candidate remains.
   After: return `[[] [1] [1 2] [1 2 2] [2] [2 2]]`.
   Known correct: every distinct multiplicity choice has been emitted,
   and no equal sibling subtree was repeated.

Now trace the count method on the same input. Its frame snapshot is
`(path,firstValueIndex,usedByValueIndex)`.

Initial state: counting gives `{1:1,2:2}`. Sorting the keys gives
`sortedDistinctValues=[1,2]`; used counts are `[0,0]`; path and
result are empty.

7. Decision: emit `[]`, choose value index 0, and increase its used
   count from 0 to 1 before recursing with the same index.
   After: result is `[[]]`; state is `path=[1]`, used counts `[1,0]`.
   Known correct: the path multiplicity of 1 equals its tracked used
   count and does not exceed its available count.
8. Decision: emit `[1]`. Value 1 is at quota, so advance to value 2.
   Use one 2, emit `[1 2]`, then use the second 2 and emit `[1 2 2]`.
   After: the 1 branch has the same four results as the sorted search;
   restoration returns path to `[1]` and used counts to `[1,0]`.
   Known correct: every legal count of 2 after one 1, from zero
   through two, appears once.
9. Decision: restore the chosen 1, then let the root choose value 2.
   Its child can choose 2 once more before reaching quota.
   After: append `[2]` and `[2 2]`; restore path `[]` and counts
   `[0,0]`.
   Known correct: count restoration leaves no copy consumed by a
   sibling.
10. Decision: both root value indexes are exhausted, so return.
    After: the count result exactly matches the sorted-choice result.
    Known correct: the two representations traversed the same
    ascending value-level tree and reached the same stopping state.

Focused empty case: there are no sorted positions, map keys, or loop
choices. Each root still emits one owned empty path, returning `[[]]`.

Focused all-equal case: ten copies of 7 return 11 subsets, from `[]`
through ten copies of 7. The sorted method skips equal siblings at
each frame but permits one deeper copy; the count method permits used
counts from zero through ten.

Focused extremes case: `[maximumInt,minimumInt,minimumInt]` sorts and
compares directly. Both functions return the six valid subsets without
subtraction or overflow.

Focused invalid case: 11 values return nil and
`errTooManyDuplicateSubsetValues` before either representation is
built.

Counterexample to removing duplicates from the input: replacing
`[2,2]` with `[2]` removes the valid subset `[2,2]`. Merge equivalent
choices at one depth or store multiplicity; do not erase available
copies.

Counterexample to skipping every adjacent equal value: after choosing
the first 2 in `[1,2,2]`, the child must accept the next 2 to produce
`[1,2,2]`. The first wrong decision is testing only adjacency without
checking `choiceIndex > firstChoiceIndex`.

##### Implementation

This complete program uses only the standard library. It runs both
representations, compares their order, shows input preservation and
the empty identity, and reports size rejection. Only the supplied
writer has an external side effect.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Duplicate-aware generation (counts
// or sorted slice). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"reflect"
	"slices"
)

const maximumDuplicateSubsetValues = 10

var errTooManyDuplicateSubsetValues = errors.New(
	"too many duplicate-subset values",
)

func validateDuplicateSubsetSize(values []int) error {
	// Return the maintained item or subtree count.
	if len(values) > maximumDuplicateSubsetValues {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: got %d; maximum is %d",
			errTooManyDuplicateSubsetValues,
			len(values),
			maximumDuplicateSubsetValues,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func copySubsetPath(path []int) []int {
	// Create an independent copy of the requested state.
	result := make([]int, len(path))
	copy(result, path)
	return result
}

func subsetsBySortedChoices(values []int) ([][]int, error) {
	// Keep subsets by sorted choices in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	if err := validateDuplicateSubsetSize(values); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// Sort owned storage so equal choices are adjacent without mutation.
	sortedValues := append([]int(nil), values...)
	slices.Sort(sortedValues)

	result := make([][]int, 0)
	path := make([]int, 0, len(sortedValues))
	var collectFrom func(int)
	collectFrom = func(firstChoiceIndex int) {
		// Every nondecreasing path is one unique value subset.
		result = append(result, copySubsetPath(path))

		choiceIndex := firstChoiceIndex
		for choiceIndex < len(sortedValues) {
			// Equal siblings create the same next value and subtree.
			if choiceIndex > firstChoiceIndex &&
				sortedValues[choiceIndex] ==
					sortedValues[choiceIndex-1] {
				choiceIndex++
				continue
			}

			path = append(path, sortedValues[choiceIndex])
			collectFrom(choiceIndex + 1)
			// Restore the parent path before its next distinct choice.
			path = path[:len(path)-1]
			choiceIndex++
		}
	}

	collectFrom(0)
	return result, nil
}

func subsetsByValueCounts(values []int) ([][]int, error) {
	// Keep subsets by value counts in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	if err := validateDuplicateSubsetSize(values); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// Count copies, then sort only the distinct values for stable order.
	countByValue := make(map[int]int, len(values))
	for _, value := range values {
		countByValue[value]++
	}
	sortedDistinctValues := make([]int, 0, len(countByValue))
	for value := range countByValue {
		sortedDistinctValues = append(sortedDistinctValues, value)
	}
	slices.Sort(sortedDistinctValues)

	result := make([][]int, 0)
	path := make([]int, 0, len(values))
	usedByValueIndex := make([]int, len(sortedDistinctValues))
	var collectFrom func(int)
	collectFrom = func(firstValueIndex int) {
		// Used counts uniquely identify this nondecreasing subset.
		result = append(result, copySubsetPath(path))

		valueIndex := firstValueIndex
		for valueIndex < len(sortedDistinctValues) {
			value := sortedDistinctValues[valueIndex]
			if usedByValueIndex[valueIndex] == countByValue[value] {
				valueIndex++
				continue
			}

			usedByValueIndex[valueIndex]++
			path = append(path, value)
			collectFrom(valueIndex)
			// Restore both count and path before the next value.
			path = path[:len(path)-1]
			usedByValueIndex[valueIndex]--
			valueIndex++
		}
	}

	collectFrom(0)
	return result, nil
}

func writeDuplicateSubsetGroups(
	output io.Writer,
	label string,
	groups [][]int,
	err error,
) error {
	// Convert duplicate subset groups using the boundary format defined
	// above.
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", label, err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"%s = %v\n",
		label,
		groups,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write %s: %w", label, err)
	}
	return nil
}

func runDuplicateSubsetExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute duplicate subset examples to the bounded stopping
	// condition above.
	values := []int{2, 1, 2}
	sortedGroups, sortedErr := subsetsBySortedChoices(values)
	if err := writeDuplicateSubsetGroups(
		output,
		"sorted choices",
		sortedGroups,
		sortedErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	countedGroups, countedErr := subsetsByValueCounts(values)
	if err := writeDuplicateSubsetGroups(
		output,
		"value counts",
		countedGroups,
		countedErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"same order = %t\ninput = %v\n",
		reflect.DeepEqual(sortedGroups, countedGroups),
		values,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write comparison: %w", err)
	}

	emptyGroups, emptyErr := subsetsBySortedChoices(nil)
	if err := writeDuplicateSubsetGroups(
		output,
		"empty",
		emptyGroups,
		emptyErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	_, tooManyErr := subsetsByValueCounts(make([]int, 11))
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"too many rejected = %t\n",
		errors.Is(
			tooManyErr,
			errTooManyDuplicateSubsetValues,
		),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write size result: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runDuplicateSubsetExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
sorted choices = [[] [1] [1 2] [1 2 2] [2] [2 2]]
value counts = [[] [1] [1 2] [1 2 2] [2] [2 2]]
same order = true
input = [2 1 2]
empty = [[]]
too many rejected = true
```

##### Why it works

For the sorted method, maintain this frame invariant: `path` contains
values from strictly increasing sorted positions below
`firstChoiceIndex`, and those values are nondecreasing. The root
satisfies it with an empty path and boundary zero.

Choosing any position at or after the boundary appends a value no
smaller than the path's last value. Recursing from the following
position prevents position reuse. Removing the appended value restores
the exact parent path, so every transition preserves the invariant.

At a fixed frame, equal adjacent candidates append the same value to
the same prefix. Choosing the earliest copy leaves every later
position available, including all remaining equal copies. Its subtree
therefore contains every value subset that a later equal sibling could
produce. Skipping those later siblings loses no unique result and
prevents repeated subtrees.

Any legal multiset subset has a nondecreasing value sequence. Match
each copy to the earliest still-unused equal position in the sorted
input. The root chooses the first value, its child chooses the next
position, and so on until the sequence's frame is emitted. Thus every
legal subset appears. The sibling rule makes that canonical position
sequence unique.

For the count method, maintain this frame invariant: `path` is
nondecreasing; `usedByValueIndex[i]` equals the number of copies of
value `i` in the path; no used count exceeds `countByValue`; and the
next value index is at least `firstValueIndex`.

Incrementing one non-exhausted count and appending its matching value
preserves the invariant. Passing the same index permits another copy
but not a smaller value. Removing the value and decrementing the same
count restores the parent exactly.

Each distinct value subset corresponds to one count vector
`(c0,c1,...,cR-1)`, where `0 <= ci <= mi` and `mi` is the available
multiplicity. The search reaches that vector by choosing value 0 `c0`
times, then value 1 `c1` times, and so on. Nondecreasing index choices
provide no second route to the same vector, proving completeness and
uniqueness.

Both functions copy `path` at frame entry, including the empty root
path. Later append and restoration cannot change an emitted inner
slice. Sorting uses owned storage, and the count method stores integer
values rather than the input slice, so neither result aliases input.

Every recursive call increases path length by one. The maximum is
`N`, the input length. Every loop index increases within a finite
sorted slice, and each return restores state. Both searches therefore
terminate.

The two searches choose the same smallest legal next value and explore
its complete child before advancing. Their legal child quotas are
equal to the input multiplicities, so induction on the path proves
their declared orders are identical.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `N` be the input length, `R` the number of distinct values, and
`mi` the multiplicity of distinct value `i`. The number of unique
subsets is:

```text
P = (m0 + 1) * (m1 + 1) * ... * (mR-1 + 1)
```

Each factor chooses zero through `mi` copies. Let `C` be the total
number of integers stored across all returned subsets. Its exact value
is:

```text
C = sum over i of:
    mi * (mi + 1) / 2 * product over j != i of (mj + 1)
```

The sorted-choice method copies `N` integers and sorts them. In the
usual comparison model this costs `O(N log N)` time and `O(N)` owned
storage. The search creates `P` result slices, copies `C` integers,
and may inspect up to `N` candidate positions per frame, for
`O(N*P + C)` search time. Its live path and recursion use `O(N)`
auxiliary space.

The count method builds an `R`-entry map in expected `O(N)` time
under a well-distributed hash assumption. Go does not promise map
complexity. Sorting the distinct keys costs `O(R log R)` comparison
work. The search may inspect `R` value indexes per frame and copies
the same output, for `O(R*P + C)` search time. The map, sorted keys,
used counts, path, and recursion retain `O(R+N)` auxiliary space.

Both outputs retain `Theta(P+C)` slice headers and integers. Those
output costs are unavoidable when every subset must be returned.
Appending the outer result may occasionally copy slice headers;
amortized append stays within the stated upper bounds.

Multiplicity changes successful work. With `N` equal values, `R=1`,
`P=N+1`, and `C=N*(N+1)/2`. With all distinct values, `R=N`,
`P=2^N`, and `C=N*2^(N-1)`. These are useful duplicate-heavy and
distinct-value extremes rather than one input-independent best or
average case.

Nil and empty input take `Theta(1)` search work and return one empty
subset. The maximum all-distinct input returns 1,024 subsets. An
oversized input fails in `Theta(1)` time before representation or
output allocation. Memory exhaustion remains outside the successful
contract.

The example formatter writes every returned integer, so external
output work is proportional to the textual representation.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Remove duplicate input values before searching. `[2,2]` must still
  produce `[2,2]`; store both positions or the count two.
- Skip every value equal to the previous sorted position. A deeper
  frame must accept a later copy when it is that frame's first
  candidate.
- Omit `choiceIndex > firstChoiceIndex`. Then `[1,2,2]` cannot reach
  `[1,2,2]` because the child wrongly skips its first available 2.
- Compare a candidate with the next value instead of the previous one.
  The last copy can become the chosen sibling and repeat the same
  subtree.
- Skip only after recursion. The duplicate subtree has already been
  generated; test equal siblings before appending.
- Recurse from `choiceIndex` in the position method. It can reuse one
  input position indefinitely; the child boundary must be
  `choiceIndex+1`.
- Recurse from `valueIndex+1` in the count method. That forbids
  choosing a second available copy; keep the same index until its
  quota is reached.
- Increment a used count without decrementing it after the child
  returns. A sibling then sees a copy consumed by an unrelated branch.
- Range directly over map keys to choose output order. Go does not
  specify map iteration order; copy and sort the distinct keys.
- Sort the caller's slice. Both functions promise input preservation,
  so the position method must sort an owned copy.
- Save the live path without copying it. Restoration and later
  siblings can overwrite an already emitted result.
- Return `[]` for empty input. There is one legal multiplicity vector
  with no values, so the result is `[[]]`.
- Treat all-distinct input as invalid. It is the valid case where
  every multiplicity is one and the unique-subset count is `2^N`.
- Compare signed integers by subtraction while sorting. Direct ordered
  comparison handles both integer extremes without overflow.
- Accept 11 values without revisiting recursion, allocation, and
  practical output limits.
- Permit concurrent input writes. Copying or counting during a write
  is not a synchronized snapshot.

##### When to choose it

Choose sorted sibling skipping when the input is small, a copied sort
is acceptable, and ordinary boundary-based backtracking already fits
the problem. It changes one decision rule while retaining the familiar
path and position state.

Choose counts when duplicates are heavy or multiplicity is already the
natural input representation. Counts remove interchangeable positions
and make quota checks explicit. Sorting distinct keys is still
necessary when deterministic ascending output matters.

For duplicate-aware permutations, use the same principle with a
different completion rule: emit only at path length `N`, and at each
depth choose any value with remaining count. A sorted-position version
instead tracks used positions and skips an equal value when its
previous equal position is not used in the current prefix.

Use [B.19.1](#b191-subsets-and-permutations-backtracking-and-path)
when values are guaranteed distinct and original input order must
define result order. Use [B.19.4
masks](#b194-subset-enumeration-bitmasks) when positions are distinct
state dimensions and numeric mask indexing is more useful than
value-level deduplication.

When not to choose it:

Do not enumerate when the task asks only for the number of unique
subsets. The product of `(mi+1)` gives that count without constructing
paths.

Do not sort when the contract requires original relative order inside
each result. Sorting changes value order even when it happens on a
copy. An order-preserving duplicate contract needs a different
canonical rule.

Do not generate all position subsets and deduplicate complete results
in a map unless constraints and representation make that deliberate.
With ten equal values, it explores 1,024 position masks to retain only
11 value subsets, and serialized slice keys add work and allocation.

Do not use a fixed-width mask alone to solve value duplicates.
Different masks can still map to the same value sequence; the mask
identifies positions, not multiplicity-equivalent results.

Related material:

[A.6.3 multisets](#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) owns
frequency-map semantics. [B.1.3 sorting and scanning](
#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice) explains owned sorting and
equal-value runs. [B.2.4 generalized k-sum](
#b24-generalized-k-sum-sorted-slice-and-recursion) applies the
same-depth skip to fixed-length combinations.

[B.19.1](#b191-subsets-and-permutations-backtracking-and-path) owns
the basic path restoration pattern. [B.19.4](
#b194-subset-enumeration-bitmasks) contrasts position identity with
value identity.

The official [Subsets II task](
https://leetcode.com/problems/subsets-ii/) defines the
duplicate-input power-set objective and ten-value limit. This lesson
adds deterministic order, explicit failure, ownership, and two
equivalent representations.

The standard-library [`slices.Sort` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort) defines ascending ordered sorting. The
Go specification defines [map range order](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#For_statements) as unspecified, which is why
the count method sorts copied keys before searching.

#### B.19.6 Board word search (trie and visited state)

##### Problem and contract

A board contains one lowercase letter per cell. Given many dictionary
words, return every word that can be traced through horizontally or
vertically adjacent cells. One path may not use the same cell twice.

For example, search this board:

```text
o a a n
e t a e
i h k r
i f l v
```

With dictionary `[oath, pea, eat, rain]`, paths spell `oath` and
`eat`. A separate search for each word repeats the same prefix work.
A trie shares those prefixes, while recursive depth-first search owns
the temporary set of cells used by one path.

This lesson's `findBoardWords` contract is:

- The board is rectangular and contains only ASCII bytes `a` through
  `z`. It may be nil, empty, or have zero columns.
- There are at most 12 rows and 12 columns.
- The dictionary contains at most 30,000 words. Every word has 1
  through 10 lowercase ASCII bytes.
- Side adjacency is checked in up, right, down, left order. Starting
  cells are checked in row-major order, so output order is stable.
- A word is returned at most once, even if the dictionary repeats it
  or the board has several paths for it.
- Valid empty input returns a non-nil empty slice. Invalid input
  returns nil and an error wrapping `errInvalidBoardSearchInput`.
- The function reads but does not mutate or retain the board. It
  clones stored words, and the result owns its slice.

The function validates every board cell and dictionary byte before
building the trie or allocating visited state. Independent calls may
read the same stable inputs concurrently. Concurrent input writes need
external synchronization. Successful allocations must fit memory.

Read [prefix trees](#a91-prefix-trees), [flood fill](
#b163-flood-fill-and-islands-stack-queue-or-disjoint-sets), and
[backtracking paths](
#b191-subsets-and-permutations-backtracking-and-path) first. This
lesson composes their existing invariants.

##### Mental model

Build a trie from the dictionary. Every trie edge consumes one board
byte. A node's 26 child slots represent `a` through `z`. A nonempty
`word` at a node marks a complete dictionary word; intermediate nodes
represent prefixes only.

Duplicate dictionary entries reach the same terminal node. Store a
cloned word only when that terminal is still empty. No second copy or
second logical result is created.

Allocate a Boolean grid with the board's shape. Then begin a
recursive search at every cell in row-major order. A call receives a
position and the trie node for the prefix consumed before it:

1. Reject an out-of-bounds or currently visited position.
2. Follow the trie child for the board letter. If it is nil, no
   dictionary word has this path as a prefix, so stop immediately.
3. Mark the cell visited. The active recursion path now owns it.
4. If the reached node stores a word, append it and clear the field.
   Clearing the private terminal suppresses later duplicate paths.
5. Recurse up, right, down, and left with the reached trie node.
6. Clear the visited mark before returning to the parent.

Visited state belongs to the current recursion path, not to the whole
search. A cell forbidden in one path must become available to a later
sibling or starting cell. The trie terminal differs: once a word has
been reported, clearing it is safe globally because the contract asks
for that word only once.

The board remains read-only. A common in-place variant temporarily
replaces a cell with a sentinel, but a separate visited grid makes the
ownership and restoration invariant explicit and avoids choosing a
sentinel outside the alphabet.

##### Worked walkthrough

Search the displayed board for `[oath, pea, eat, rain]`. Trie paths
begin with `o`, `p`, `e`, and `r`. A state snapshot is
`(cell,prefix,visited,found)`.

Initial state: the trie is complete, every visited value is false,
`found=[]`, and the row-major scan begins at `(0,0)`.

```text
board:        oath path:           eat path:
o a a n       o -> a               t <- a <- e
e t a e            |               at row 1
i h k r            v
i f l v            t
                   |
                   v
                   h
```

1. Decision: cell `(0,0)` contains `o`, and the root has an `o`
   child. Mark `(0,0)` and enter prefix `o`.
   After: state is `((0,0),o,{(0,0)},[])`.
   Known correct: every active cell is unique, and `o` is a trie
   prefix that exactly matches the active path.
2. Decision: up is outside. Right `(0,1)` contains `a`, and trie
   edge `o -> a` exists. Mark it and enter prefix `oa`.
   After: visited is `{(0,0),(0,1)}` and no word is complete.
   Known correct: the path uses side-adjacent distinct cells and its
   bytes equal the trie prefix `oa`.
3. Decision: from `(0,1)`, right gives `oaa`, whose trie edge is nil,
   so that call stops without marking. Down `(1,1)` contains `t` and
   extends the prefix to `oat`.
   After: visited is `{(0,0),(0,1),(1,1)}`.
   Known correct: the impossible prefix did not create search state,
   while the surviving branch still matches a dictionary prefix.
4. Decision: from `(1,1)`, the visited cell `(0,1)` is rejected.
   Right would spell `oata` and stops. Down `(2,1)` supplies `h`,
   reaching terminal `oath`.
   After: `found=[oath]`, the terminal word is cleared, and the four
   path cells remain marked while deeper neighbors are checked.
   Known correct: one legal path spells `oath`, and no later path can
   append that same word again.
5. Decision: no child below terminal `oath` leads to a dictionary
   word. Return through the frames, clearing `(2,1)`, `(1,1)`,
   `(0,1)`, and `(0,0)` in that order.
   After: all visited values are false and `found=[oath]`.
   Known correct: the result remains reported, while the next root
   search receives exactly the initial availability state.
6. Decision: later row-major starts with no root child stop after one
   trie lookup. At `(1,3)`, byte `e` exists at the root; leftward path
   `(1,3) e -> (1,2) a -> (1,1) t` reaches `eat`.
   After: `found=[oath,eat]`; terminal `eat` is cleared.
   Known correct: the second word uses three distinct adjacent cells
   and appears after the first word in declared discovery order.
7. Decision: exhaust the remaining starts. No active prefix reaches
   terminals `pea` or `rain`.
   After: return `[oath,eat]` and discard the private trie and visited
   grid.
   Known correct: every board start and every trie-compatible
   continuation was considered, so no requested word is missing.

Focused no-reuse case: board `[a b]` cannot spell `aba`. After using
the only `a`, the path may move to `b`, but returning to that `a` is
rejected while it remains visited.

Focused duplicate case: board `[a a]` with dictionary `[a,a,aa]`
returns `[a,aa]`. Both `a` entries share one terminal, and clearing it
after the first start does not clear the deeper `aa` terminal.

Focused adjacency case: on rows `ax` and `xb`, `ab` is absent because
the letters touch only diagonally. Diagonal offsets are never tried.

Focused empty case: a nil board and dictionary return an allocated
empty slice. No trie or visited grid is needed.

Counterexample to a permanent visited mark: after one failed path uses
a cell, a sibling may need that cell in a different path. The first
wrong action is failing to clear the mark while returning.

Counterexample to accepting any board walk before consulting the trie:
a 12-by-12 board has many self-avoiding walks. A missing trie child
proves an entire branch cannot complete a dictionary word and must be
stopped before exploring its neighbors.

##### Implementation

This complete program uses only the standard library. It prints the
main search, duplicate suppression, empty success, and invalid-shape
rejection. Only the supplied writer has an external side effect.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Board word search (trie and
// visited state). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"strings"
)

const (
	boardAlphabetSize      = 26
	maximumBoardRows       = 12
	maximumBoardColumns    = 12
	maximumBoardWords      = 30000
	maximumBoardWordLength = 10
)

var errInvalidBoardSearchInput = errors.New(
	"invalid board-search input",
)

type boardTrieNode struct {
	children [boardAlphabetSize]*boardTrieNode
	word     string
}

type boardPosition struct {
	row    int
	column int
}

var boardNeighborOffsets = [...]boardPosition{
	{row: -1},
	{column: 1},
	{row: 1},
	{column: -1},
}

func validateBoardSearchInput(
	board [][]byte,
	words []string,
) (int, error) {
	// Reject input outside the board search input contract before
	// mutation.
	if len(board) > maximumBoardRows {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: got %d rows; maximum is %d",
			errInvalidBoardSearchInput,
			len(board),
			maximumBoardRows,
		)
	}

	columnCount := 0
	if len(board) > 0 {
		columnCount = len(board[0])
	}
	if columnCount > maximumBoardColumns {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: got %d columns; maximum is %d",
			errInvalidBoardSearchInput,
			columnCount,
			maximumBoardColumns,
		)
	}
	for row := range board {
		if len(board[row]) != columnCount {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: row %d has %d columns; want %d",
				errInvalidBoardSearchInput,
				row,
				len(board[row]),
				columnCount,
			)
		}
		for column, letter := range board[row] {
			if letter < 'a' || letter > 'z' {
				return 0, fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: cell (%d,%d) is %q; want a-z",
					errInvalidBoardSearchInput,
					row,
					column,
					letter,
				)
			}
		}
	}

	if len(words) > maximumBoardWords {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: got %d words; maximum is %d",
			errInvalidBoardSearchInput,
			len(words),
			maximumBoardWords,
		)
	}
	for wordIndex, word := range words {
		if len(word) == 0 ||
			len(word) > maximumBoardWordLength {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: word %d has length %d; want 1..%d",
				errInvalidBoardSearchInput,
				wordIndex,
				len(word),
				maximumBoardWordLength,
			)
		}
		for byteIndex := 0; byteIndex < len(word); byteIndex++ {
			letter := word[byteIndex]
			if letter < 'a' || letter > 'z' {
				return 0, fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: word %d byte %d is %q; want a-z",
					errInvalidBoardSearchInput,
					wordIndex,
					byteIndex,
					letter,
				)
			}
		}
	}
	return columnCount, nil
}

func buildBoardTrie(words []string) boardTrieNode {
	// Build board trie in the order required by the lesson contract.
	var root boardTrieNode
	for _, inputWord := range words {
		node := &root
		for byteIndex := 0; byteIndex < len(inputWord); byteIndex++ {
			childIndex := inputWord[byteIndex] - 'a'
			if node.children[childIndex] == nil {
				node.children[childIndex] = &boardTrieNode{}
			}
			node = node.children[childIndex]
		}
		if node.word == "" {
			node.word = strings.Clone(inputWord)
		}
	}
	return root
}

func findBoardWords(
	board [][]byte,
	words []string,
) ([]string, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	columnCount, err := validateBoardSearchInput(board, words)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	found := make([]string, 0)
	if len(board) == 0 || columnCount == 0 || len(words) == 0 {
		return found, nil
	}

	root := buildBoardTrie(words)
	visited := make([][]bool, len(board))
	for row := range visited {
		visited[row] = make([]bool, columnCount)
	}

	var searchFrom func(int, int, *boardTrieNode)
	searchFrom = func(
		row int,
		column int,
		parent *boardTrieNode,
	) {
		if row < 0 || row >= len(board) ||
			column < 0 || column >= columnCount ||
			visited[row][column] {
			return
		}

		childIndex := board[row][column] - 'a'
		node := parent.children[childIndex]
		if node == nil {
			return
		}

		visited[row][column] = true
		if node.word != "" {
			found = append(found, node.word)
			node.word = ""
		}
		for _, offset := range boardNeighborOffsets {
			searchFrom(
				row+offset.row,
				column+offset.column,
				node,
			)
		}
		visited[row][column] = false
	}

	for row := range board {
		for column := range board[row] {
			searchFrom(row, column, &root)
		}
	}
	return found, nil
}

func writeBoardWords(
	output io.Writer,
	label string,
	words []string,
	err error,
) error {
	// Convert board words using the boundary format defined above.
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", label, err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"%s = %v\n",
		label,
		words,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write %s: %w", label, err)
	}
	return nil
}

func runBoardWordExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute board word examples to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	board := [][]byte{
		[]byte("oaan"),
		[]byte("etae"),
		[]byte("ihkr"),
		[]byte("iflv"),
	}
	found, err := findBoardWords(
		board,
		[]string{"oath", "pea", "eat", "rain"},
	)
	if err := writeBoardWords(output, "found", found, err); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	duplicate, duplicateErr := findBoardWords(
		[][]byte{[]byte("aa")},
		[]string{"a", "a"},
	)
	if err := writeBoardWords(
		output,
		"duplicate once",
		duplicate,
		duplicateErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	empty, emptyErr := findBoardWords(nil, nil)
	if err := writeBoardWords(
		output,
		"empty",
		empty,
		emptyErr,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	_, raggedErr := findBoardWords(
		[][]byte{[]byte("ab"), []byte("c")},
		[]string{"ab"},
	)
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"ragged rejected = %t\n",
		errors.Is(raggedErr, errInvalidBoardSearchInput),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write ragged result: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runBoardWordExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
found = [oath eat]
duplicate once = [a]
empty = []
ragged rejected = true
```

##### Why it works

After validation, every board and dictionary byte has one valid
child index, every row has the same width, and all declared size
bounds hold. No invalid input can cause partial trie or result state.

Trie construction maintains this invariant: after inserting a word,
following its bytes from the root reaches one node. That node stores
exactly one cloned word. Existing prefix nodes are reused.
An empty terminal field means no unreported word ends there. Repeated
input reaches the same terminal and cannot create another copy.

For a recursive search frame, maintain this invariant: the marked
cells are exactly the distinct cells on the active path; consecutive
cells share a side; and the board bytes on that path equal the trie
prefix represented by the frame's node.

The root call begins with no consumed byte and no marked cell. Bounds
and visited checks reject illegal extensions. A non-nil trie child
matches the next board byte, and marking that cell extends the path by
one distinct side-adjacent position. The child frame therefore
preserves the invariant.

If the reached node stores a word, the invariant proves the active
path spells that whole dictionary word legally. Appending it is sound.
Clearing the private terminal cannot remove a different word because
each complete byte sequence has one trie node. It removes only future
reports of the same word, which the contract forbids.

When a child returns, clearing the current mark restores the parent's
exact set of available cells. Thus every trie-compatible legal path
from that parent is tried independently. Since the outer loops start
at every cell, any board path for a dictionary word follows the same
sequence of recursive choices and reaches its terminal. Every valid
requested word is therefore found.

Each recursive call either returns immediately or marks one previously
unmarked cell. Depth is at most the smaller of board cell count and
maximum word length. Every frame tries four finite offsets, so every
branch and the whole search terminate.

The board is never assigned. Visited marks are private and fully
restored. Trie mutation affects only private nodes, and stored words
are clones. The returned slice and strings therefore do not expose
mutable search state or retain caller-owned board storage.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `R` be row count, `C` column count, `B = R*C`, `W` the total
dictionary byte count, `L` the longest word length, and `F` the total
bytes in returned words. Here `R,C <= 12` and `L <= 10`.

Validation takes `Theta(R+B+W)` time. Trie construction takes
`Theta(W)` time and allocates at most `W+1` nodes plus cloned word
bytes. Each node reserves 26 child pointers. That is `Theta(26W)`
pointer capacity, written `Theta(W)` for a fixed alphabet.

The search checks every start. Once a path has chosen its first cell,
there are at most four first moves and at most three later moves. The
immediately previous cell is visited. A loose worst-case bound is
`O(B * 4 * 3^(L-1))` trie transitions for `L > 0`. Board boundaries,
visited cells, and missing trie prefixes usually prune much sooner.
The 12-by-12 board also caps path depth by `B`.

After trie construction, a board with no root-matching byte still
costs `Theta(B)` search time. Without a stated distribution there is
no useful average-case guarantee. Returning each found string header
costs `Theta(1)` because its bytes were cloned during trie
construction. Retained output includes `Theta(F)` word bytes plus
result headers.

The visited grid uses `Theta(R+B)` auxiliary storage including row
descriptors. Recursion uses `O(min(B,L))` frames. The private trie
uses `O(26W)` pointer capacity and `Theta(W)` stored bytes. For `K`
found words, the result retains `Theta(K+F)` space. The board is not
copied.

A per-word search avoids trie nodes but can repeat board exploration
for common prefixes. An in-place sentinel avoids the Boolean grid but
temporarily mutates the board and needs a collision-free marker.

Invalid shape or board-byte input fails while scanning the board.
Invalid dictionary input fails while scanning words. Because all
validation precedes construction, failures retain no partial result.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Reuse one cell. Check `visited` before following a path extension,
  and mark before recursing.
- Never clear a visited mark. That leaks one branch's choices into its
  siblings and loses valid words.
- Clear the mark before exploring neighbors. A descendant can then
  step back onto the same cell.
- Use diagonal offsets. The contract permits only shared sides.
- Test only terminal words. A trie path can be a valid prefix without
  ending a word, and another word can end at an internal node.
- Stop after finding an internal word. Dictionary words `a` and `at`
  require emitting `a` and continuing toward `at`.
- Append a terminal repeatedly. Clear its private word after the first
  report to suppress duplicate dictionary entries and board paths.
- Delete a shared trie node after finding one word. Longer words or
  sibling searches may still need its descendants.
- Search every neighbor before consulting the trie. A nil child proves
  that the entire suffix branch is useless.
- Subtract `'a'` before validation. Invalid bytes can underflow or
  index outside the 26-child array.
- Accept a ragged board. A first-row column count is safe only after
  every row length matches it.
- Mutate board bytes as visited state without restoring them. The
  input is read-only under this contract.
- Store caller strings without defining retention. This implementation
  clones each distinct terminal word.
- Return nil for valid empty input. Nil is reserved here for failure;
  empty success returns an allocated slice.
- Emit in map iteration order. Row-major starts and fixed offsets make
  this implementation's discovery order deterministic.
- Assume trie pruning makes worst-case work polynomial. A board and
  dictionary can preserve many prefixes, leaving exponentially many
  legal paths.
- Permit concurrent writes. Validation and search require one stable
  view of every board cell and dictionary string.

##### When to choose it

Use trie-guided board search when many candidate words share prefixes
and every legal board path must avoid reusing cells. It is especially
effective when missing prefixes cut off most board walks early.

The pattern also fits word puzzles, tile boards, and route labels.
Each state contributes one alphabet symbol and the candidate set is
known in advance. Change the neighbor offsets only when the problem's
adjacency rule changes explicitly.

Choose a separate single-word depth-first search when there is only
one word and trie construction offers no prefix sharing. Choose
breadth-first search for shortest unweighted paths. This task asks
whether complete labeled paths exist, not which one uses the fewest
moves.

When not to choose it:

Do not use this fixed 26-child representation for arbitrary Unicode.
Define the text unit first, then use rune-aware or grapheme-aware
board cells and a suitable child map.

Do not use one global permanent visited set. Word paths may overlap
across separate searches; only reuse within one active path is banned.

Do not build every possible board string and compare afterward. The
number of walks grows exponentially, while the trie can reject a path
as soon as its prefix is absent.

Do not use recursive search when a different contract permits path
depth beyond the practical call stack. Model the same enter, explore,
and restore state with explicit frames. The explicit version still has
exponential worst-case path count.

Do not clear trie branches when the caller needs every distinct board
path or occurrence count. This contract returns each word once, so
terminal clearing is intentional.

https://leetcode.com/problems/word-search/) isolates the corresponding

#### B.19.7 Exact cover (dancing links, advanced)

##### Problem and contract

An exact-cover problem has a universe of constraints and a collection
of candidate rows. Each row covers some constraints. Choose rows so
every constraint is covered exactly once.

Represent the problem as a binary matrix. Columns are constraints,
rows are candidates, and a `1` means that candidate covers that
constraint. The selected rows must contain exactly one `1` in every
column. This differs from ordinary set cover, which permits overlap
and asks only that every element be covered at least once.

`firstExactCover` receives a column count and sparse rows. Each sparse
row lists only the zero-based column indices where its matrix row has
`1`. It returns the first cover under a deterministic search:

- The column count is from 0 through 64.
- There are at most 256 rows and 4,096 listed column references.
- Every row is nonempty. Its column indices are in range and distinct.
- Equal row contents are allowed; their input row indices make them
  distinct candidates.
- The search chooses the uncovered column with the fewest remaining
  rows. A tie chooses the lower column index. Rows are tried in input
  order.
- A found solution contains selected row indices in ascending order
  and owns its storage.
- A valid problem with no cover returns a non-nil empty slice, false,
  and nil error.
- Zero columns and zero rows have one exact cover: choose no rows. The
  result is an empty slice, true, and nil error.
- Invalid input returns nil, false, and an error wrapping
  `errInvalidExactCoverInput` before the linked matrix is built.

The function reads but does not mutate or retain the sparse rows.
Independent calls may read the same stable input concurrently.
Concurrent writes need external synchronization, and successful
allocations must fit memory.

A direct Algorithm X implementation can copy or rescan a reduced
matrix at every branch. Dancing links, abbreviated DLX, represents
only the `1` entries and removes or restores them through reversible
doubly linked-list splices.

Read [doubly linked lists](#a32-doubly-linked-lists) for paired-link
invariants and [constraint search](
#b192-constraint-search-backtracking-and-sets) for choose, recurse,
and restore. This advanced lesson composes those ideas in a sparse
matrix with several interacting circular lists.

##### Mental model

Create one column header for every constraint and one data node for
every listed `1`. Four links give each node two memberships:

```text
left/right: the circular ring of 1 nodes in one candidate row
up/down:    the circular ring of available nodes in one column
```

Column headers form another left/right circular ring around a root
sentinel. Only uncovered columns are in that ring. A header's
`size` is the number of nodes currently in its vertical ring.

The links make the sparse matrix toroidal: moving far enough left,
right, up, or down returns to the starting node. Sentinels remove nil
end cases. A data node also stores its original row index and its
column header.

To cover column `C`:

1. Splice `C` out of the horizontal header ring. That constraint is
   now treated as satisfied by the current branch.
2. For every row node in `C`, visit the other nodes in that row.
   Splice each from its vertical column and decrement that header's
   size. Those rows conflict because they would cover `C` again.

The removed nodes keep their own links. To uncover `C`, traverse rows
upward and each row leftward, reversing the cover order. Reconnect
each vertical node, restore its size, and finally reconnect `C`.
Reverse order matters because a removed node's saved neighbors must
already be present when it is restored.

Algorithm X then searches:

1. If no column header remains, copy the selected row path. Every
   constraint is covered exactly once.
2. Otherwise choose the remaining column with minimum `size`. If its
   size is zero, this branch cannot cover that constraint.
3. Cover the chosen column. For each row in its vertical ring, append
   that row index and cover every other column in that row.
4. Recurse. Then uncover the row's columns in reverse and remove the
   row index from the path.
5. On success, restore the chosen column while unwinding and stop.
   After all candidate rows fail, restore it and return false.

Choosing the smallest column is the minimum-remaining-values
heuristic. It changes branch order and often reduces work, but not the
set of possible covers. Ties remain in original header order, so the
lower column index wins.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use columns `A` through `G`, numbered 0 through 6, and these rows:

```text
row 0: C E       row 3: A D F
row 1: A D G     row 4: B G
row 2: B C F     row 5: D E G
```

The expected first exact cover is rows `[0,3,4]`:

```text
row 0 covers C,E
row 3 covers A,D,F
row 4 covers B,G
```

Together they cover `A` through `G` once. A search path records
decision order, while the returned copy is sorted by row index.

Initial state: every header is linked. Sizes for `A` through `G` are
`[2,2,2,3,2,2,3]`. The selected path and solution are empty.

1. Decision: the minimum size is 2, tied at `A`, `B`, `C`, `E`, and
   `F`. Choose lower index `A`. Cover its header and hide the `D,G`
   nodes of row 1 plus the `D,F` nodes of row 3.
   After: `A` is absent from the header ring. Its vertical ring still
   supplies candidate rows 1 then 3. Other sizes are
   `B=2,C=2,D=1,E=2,F=1,G=2`.
   Known correct: every exact cover must choose exactly one current
   row containing `A`, and both such rows remain available to try.
2. Decision: try row 1 first because it has the lower input index.
   Append 1, then cover its other columns `D` and `G`.
   After: path is `[1]`; remaining headers are `B,C,E,F`.
   Column `B` has only row 2 available, so its size is 1.
   Known correct: every remaining visible row is disjoint from row 1,
   and `A,D,G` are each covered once by the selected path.
3. Decision: choose `B` and try its sole available row 2. Append 2,
   cover `C` and `F`, and recurse.
   After: path is `[1,2]`; `E` remains uncovered with size zero
   because its row 0 node conflicted through column `C`.
   Known correct: no row compatible with `[1,2]` can cover `E`, so
   this branch cannot become an exact cover.
4. Decision: the zero-size `E` column returns false. Uncover `F`,
   then `C`; remove row 2; uncover chosen column `B`; then uncover
   row 1's `G` and `D` and remove row 1.
   After: path is empty. The state matches the moment after `A` was
   covered, and its next candidate is row 3.
   Known correct: the failed branch changed no link, size, or path
   visible to row 3.
5. Decision: append row 3 and cover its other columns `D` then `F`.
   The remaining headers `B,C,E,G` each have size 1. Choose lower
   index `B`, append its sole row 4, and cover `G`.
   After: path is `[3,4]`; remaining headers are `C,E`, both supplied
   by row 0.
   Known correct: selected rows 3 and 4 are disjoint and cover
   `A,B,D,F,G` exactly once.
6. Decision: choose `C`, append row 0, and cover its other column
   `E`.
   After: path is `[3,4,0]`, and the root points to itself because no
   header remains.
   Known correct: every column `A` through `G` is covered once, and
   no two selected rows share a column.
7. Decision: the empty header ring is the success base case. Copy the
   path and sort the copy.
   After: solution is `[0,3,4]`; the live path remains `[3,4,0]` for
   restoration.
   Known correct: sorting changes only presentation, not which rows
   form the cover.
8. Decision: unwind success in reverse: restore `E`, row 0, and `C`;
   restore `G`, row 4, and `B`; restore `F,D`, row 3, and `A`.
   After: the full linked matrix and empty path are restored. Return
   `[0,3,4]`, true, and nil error.
   Known correct: the caller receives an owned solution while every
   temporary splice has its matching inverse.

Focused empty-universe case: `columnCount=0, rows=nil` begins with
the root linked to itself. It returns `[]` and true without choosing
a row. There is one way to cover no constraints: choose nothing.

Focused unsatisfiable case: with two columns and only row `{0}`,
selecting that row leaves column 1 at size zero. The result is an
allocated empty slice and false, not an input error.

Focused duplicate-row case: one column with rows `{0}` and `{0}` has
two candidate identities. The first deterministic solution is row
index 0; only one may be selected because selecting either covers the
column.

Focused maximum case: 64 rows that each list all 64 columns contain
exactly 4,096 nodes. The solver chooses column 0, tries row 0, covers
all remaining columns, and returns `[0]`.

Focused invalid case: row `{0,0}` repeats one binary-matrix column. It
returns the invalid-input error before any dance node is allocated.

Counterexample to greedy commitment: the first `A` row, row 1, leads
to an uncovered zero-size `E`. Returning failure immediately would
miss rows `[0,3,4]`; restoration must continue with row 3.

Counterexample to forward-order restoration: if `D` was covered
before `G`, restoring `D` before `G` can reconnect nodes through
neighbors that are still absent. Uncover from right to left so the
operations run in exact inverse order.

##### Implementation

This complete program uses `errors`, `fmt`, `io`, `os`, and `slices`
from the standard library. It prints a solution, a valid unsatisfiable
problem, the empty identity, and an invalid input. Only the supplied
writer has an external side effect.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Exact cover (dancing links,
// advanced). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"slices"
)

const (
	maximumExactCoverColumns = 64
	maximumExactCoverRows    = 256
	maximumExactCoverNodes   = 4096
)

var errInvalidExactCoverInput = errors.New(
	"invalid exact-cover input",
)

type danceNode struct {
	left     *danceNode
	right    *danceNode
	up       *danceNode
	down     *danceNode
	column   *danceColumn
	rowIndex int
}

type danceColumn struct {
	node danceNode
	size int
}

func validateExactCoverInput(
	columnCount int,
	rows [][]int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the exact cover input contract before
	// mutation.
	if columnCount < 0 ||
		columnCount > maximumExactCoverColumns {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: got %d columns; want 0..%d",
			errInvalidExactCoverInput,
			columnCount,
			maximumExactCoverColumns,
		)
	}
	if len(rows) > maximumExactCoverRows {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: got %d rows; maximum is %d",
			errInvalidExactCoverInput,
			len(rows),
			maximumExactCoverRows,
		)
	}

	totalNodes := 0
	for rowIndex, row := range rows {
		if len(row) == 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: row %d covers no column",
				errInvalidExactCoverInput,
				rowIndex,
			)
		}
		if len(row) > maximumExactCoverNodes-totalNodes {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: more than %d row nodes",
				errInvalidExactCoverInput,
				maximumExactCoverNodes,
			)
		}

		var seenColumn [maximumExactCoverColumns]bool
		for position, columnIndex := range row {
			if columnIndex < 0 || columnIndex >= columnCount {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: row %d position %d has column %d",
					errInvalidExactCoverInput,
					rowIndex,
					position,
					columnIndex,
				)
			}
			if seenColumn[columnIndex] {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: row %d repeats column %d",
					errInvalidExactCoverInput,
					rowIndex,
					columnIndex,
				)
			}
			seenColumn[columnIndex] = true
		}
		totalNodes += len(row)
	}
	return nil
}

func buildDanceMatrix(
	columnCount int,
	rows [][]int,
) *danceNode {
	// Build dance matrix in the order required by the lesson contract.
	root := &danceNode{}
	root.left = root
	root.right = root

	columns := make([]danceColumn, columnCount)
	for columnIndex := range columns {
		column := &columns[columnIndex]
		header := &column.node
		header.column = column
		header.up = header
		header.down = header

		// Insert headers before root in increasing index order.
		header.left = root.left
		header.right = root
		root.left.right = header
		root.left = header
	}

	for rowIndex, rowColumns := range rows {
		var firstInRow *danceNode
		for _, columnIndex := range rowColumns {
			column := &columns[columnIndex]
			header := &column.node
			node := &danceNode{
				column:   column,
				rowIndex: rowIndex,
			}

			// Insert before the header to preserve input row order.
			node.up = header.up
			node.down = header
			header.up.down = node
			header.up = node
			column.size++

			// Link all nodes for this candidate into one ring.
			if firstInRow == nil {
				firstInRow = node
				node.left = node
				node.right = node
			} else {
				node.left = firstInRow.left
				node.right = firstInRow
				firstInRow.left.right = node
				firstInRow.left = node
			}
		}
	}
	return root
}

func chooseDanceColumn(root *danceNode) *danceColumn {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	var chosen *danceColumn
	for header := root.right; header != root; header = header.right {
		column := header.column
		if chosen == nil || column.size < chosen.size {
			chosen = column
		}
	}
	return chosen
}

func coverDanceColumn(column *danceColumn) {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	header := &column.node
	header.right.left = header.left
	header.left.right = header.right

	// Remove every conflicting row node from its other columns.
	for row := header.down; row != header; row = row.down {
		for node := row.right; node != row; node = node.right {
			node.down.up = node.up
			node.up.down = node.down
			node.column.size--
		}
	}
}

func uncoverDanceColumn(column *danceColumn) {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	header := &column.node

	// Reverse both traversal directions and every pointer update.
	for row := header.up; row != header; row = row.up {
		for node := row.left; node != row; node = node.left {
			node.column.size++
			node.down.up = node
			node.up.down = node
		}
	}
	header.right.left = header
	header.left.right = header
}

func firstExactCover(
	columnCount int,
	rows [][]int,
) ([]int, bool, error) {
	// Keep first exact cover in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if err := validateExactCoverInput(columnCount, rows); err != nil {
		return nil, false, err
	}

	root := buildDanceMatrix(columnCount, rows)
	path := make([]int, 0, columnCount)
	solution := make([]int, 0)

	var search func() bool
	search = func() bool {
		// No remaining header means every column is covered once.
		if root.right == root {
			solution = append(solution, path...)
			slices.Sort(solution)
			return true
		}

		column := chooseDanceColumn(root)
		if column.size == 0 {
			return false
		}

		coverDanceColumn(column)
		header := &column.node
		for row := header.down; row != header; row = row.down {
			path = append(path, row.rowIndex)
			for node := row.right; node != row; node = node.right {
				coverDanceColumn(node.column)
			}

			found := search()

			// Restore this row's columns in exact reverse order.
			for node := row.left; node != row; node = node.left {
				uncoverDanceColumn(node.column)
			}
			path = path[:len(path)-1]
			if found {
				uncoverDanceColumn(column)
				return true
			}
		}
		uncoverDanceColumn(column)
		return false
	}

	found := search()
	return solution, found, nil
}

func writeExactCoverResult(
	output io.Writer,
	label string,
	rows []int,
	found bool,
	err error,
) error {
	// Convert exact cover result using the boundary format defined
	// above.
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", label, err)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"%s = %v found=%t\n",
		label,
		rows,
		found,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write %s: %w", label, err)
	}
	return nil
}

func runExactCoverExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute exact cover examples to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	rows := [][]int{
		{2, 4},
		{0, 3, 6},
		{1, 2, 5},
		{0, 3, 5},
		{1, 6},
		{3, 4, 6},
	}
	solution, found, err := firstExactCover(7, rows)
	if err := writeExactCoverResult(
		output,
		"solution",
		solution,
		found,
		err,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	unsatisfied, found, err := firstExactCover(
		2,
		[][]int{{0}},
	)
	if err := writeExactCoverResult(
		output,
		"unsatisfiable",
		unsatisfied,
		found,
		err,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	empty, found, err := firstExactCover(0, nil)
	if err := writeExactCoverResult(
		output,
		"empty universe",
		empty,
		found,
		err,
	); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	_, _, invalidErr := firstExactCover(
		2,
		[][]int{{0, 0}},
	)
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"invalid rejected=%t\n",
		errors.Is(invalidErr, errInvalidExactCoverInput),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write invalid result: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runExactCoverExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
solution = [0 3 4] found=true
unsatisfiable = [] found=false
empty universe = [] found=true
invalid rejected=true
```

##### Why it works

Validation establishes finite bounds and proves that each sparse row
represents a nonempty binary row: every listed column exists and
occurs once. Construction can therefore create exactly one node per
`1` without partial invalid state.

At every search entry, maintain this invariant:

- selected rows are pairwise disjoint in their covered columns;
- absent headers are exactly the columns covered once by selected
  rows;
- each remaining vertical ring contains exactly the currently
  compatible rows that cover that column; and
- every header size equals its vertical node count.

The initial structure satisfies the invariant. No row is selected,
all headers are present, and construction links every input `1` into
its row and column rings.

Covering a column removes its header. Removing every other node in
its rows hides exactly the candidates that would cover that column a
second time. All other candidates remain. Sizes decrease with the
same removals, so the invariant survives a cover.

After choosing a row from the selected column, covering all its other
columns marks every constraint in that row satisfied and removes every
row that overlaps it. The child path is therefore pairwise disjoint,
and its visible matrix contains exactly its compatible completions.

If no header remains, one selected row removed each original column.
Pairwise disjointness prevents a second selected row from sharing it,
so the path is a sound exact cover. If a remaining header has size
zero, no compatible row can cover it, so failure is sound.

For completeness, take any exact cover extending the current path.
It contains exactly one row for the chosen column. That compatible row
is in the column's vertical ring, and the loop tries it. Covering its
columns cannot remove any other row of the same solution because exact
cover rows do not overlap. Repeating this argument reaches the base
case. The minimum-size heuristic changes only which required column is
considered first, so it cannot remove a solution.

A cover splice changes neighboring links but preserves the removed
node's own links. Uncover traverses in reverse and performs inverse
assignments after later removals have already been undone. It restores
the exact prior rings and sizes. Thus every sibling starts from the
same parent state, including after early success unwinds.

Every selected row covers at least the chosen uncovered column, so a
recursive call removes at least one header. Depth is at most the
original column count. Each frame scans finite rings, and each branch
either reaches an empty header ring or a zero-size failure. The search
terminates.

Sorting the copied row indices does not mutate the live path or linked
matrix. Construction does not retain the input.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let `C` be the number of columns, `R` the number of rows, and `Z` the
number of listed `1` nodes. Let `Q` be recursive frames entered, `H`
be headers inspected while choosing columns, `T` be link removals and
restorations, and `SortRows(K)` be the time used to sort a found
solution of `K` row indices.

Validation and construction inspect every row and listed column once
and initialize every header, taking `Theta(C+R+Z)` time. Construction
allocates `Theta(C+Z)` linked nodes and headers. Sparse storage avoids
the `Theta(C*R)` cells of a dense Boolean matrix when most entries are
zero.

At one frame, choosing a column scans the remaining headers. Cover and
uncover work is proportional to the data nodes they remove or restore.
The complete search takes
`Theta(C+R+Z + H + T) + SortRows(K)` time, where `K <= C`. With an
`O(K log K)` comparison sort, the conventional total adds that term.
The `slices.Sort` API does not promise a complexity bound, so code
that requires one must own or pin the sort. Header scans give
`H <= Q*C`. The `T` term exposes sparse-matrix work rather than hiding
it behind a constant.

Exact cover is combinatorial. A coarse worst-case bound is
`O((C+Z)*R^C)`: there are at most `R` row choices at each of at most
`C` levels, and a branch can touch the sparse structure. This bound is
intentionally loose but makes clear that minimum-column selection does
not make the problem polynomial. Actual branching is limited by each
chosen column's current size and is often much smaller.

After preprocessing, an empty universe succeeds in `Theta(1)` search
time. A positive universe with a zero-size first chosen column also
fails after one header scan. A meaningful average needs a distribution
over sparse matrices; none is assumed.

The dancing matrix retains `Theta(C+Z)` storage. The selected path,
recursive calls, and result use `O(C)`, `O(C)`, and `O(K)` space,
respectively. The result is output storage; the matrix and path are
auxiliary. Cover and uncover allocate nothing.

Invalid input takes up to `Theta(R+Z)` validation time and builds no
linked matrix. A valid unsatisfiable call still builds the full sparse
structure and returns a non-nil empty result. The writer performs work
proportional to formatted output and propagates write failures.

A copied reduced matrix is easier to implement but may allocate and
copy `Theta(C*R)` state at many branches. Boolean sets or bitsets can
be faster for small dense instances. Dancing links are most compelling
when the matrix is sparse and reversible deletion dominates.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Zero columns with no rows returns `[]`, true, and nil. Treating the
  empty header ring as failure loses the exact-cover identity.
- Positive columns with no rows are valid but unsatisfiable. Their
  first chosen header has size zero.
- An empty input row is rejected. It covers nothing, would never be
  chosen by Algorithm X, and creates ambiguous no-effect candidates.
- A sparse row may not repeat a column. `{0,0}` is not a binary row
  with two separate constraints.
- Equal rows at different input indices are valid distinct candidates.
  Candidate order chooses the lower index first when both remain.
- Cover the chosen column before iterating its candidate rows. That
  prevents another selected row from covering it again.
- When selecting a row, cover every other column in its horizontal
  ring. Missing one leaves an overlapping candidate visible.
- Decrement a column size for every vertical removal and increment it
  for every restoration. Stale sizes can choose the wrong column or
  falsely report a dead branch.
- Do not clear a removed node's links. Its saved neighbors are the
  information needed to reconnect it without searching.
- Uncover rows upward and their nodes leftward. Forward-order undo can
  use neighbors that have not yet been restored.
- Restore even on early success. This implementation leaves its
  private structure consistent while the result copy survives.
- A zero-size column means failure only while some header remains. If
  no header remains, success was already established.
- Store original row indices in data nodes. Traversal positions change
  as nodes are hidden and cannot identify caller rows.
- Keep headers in original index order. Minimum-size ties depend on
  that stable order for deterministic output.
- Sort only the copied solution. Sorting the live choice path would
  break frame-by-frame restoration.
- Return a non-nil empty slice on valid failure. Nil is reserved for
  invalid input under this contract.
- Do not claim polynomial time because cover and uncover are local.
  The number of search branches can still be exponential.
- Keep all mutable nodes local to one call. Package-level matrices
  would make repeated or concurrent calls interfere.

##### When to choose it

Choose exact-cover modeling when each candidate simultaneously
satisfies several one-of constraints and every constraint must be met
once. Sudoku assignments, polyomino placements, timetable choices, and
some resource-placement puzzles have this shape.

Choose dancing links when the exact-cover matrix is sparse, the search
repeatedly removes conflicting rows, and rapid exact restoration is
worth pointer-heavy code. The minimum-column heuristic helps when
constraint sizes expose forced or nearly forced choices.

Use a simpler set-based Algorithm X first when correctness and
maintainability matter more than allocation or splice costs. Use
bitsets for small dense matrices. Use a SAT, integer-programming, or
general constraint solver when the model includes implications,
weights, inequalities, or constraints other than exactly one.

To enumerate every cover, collect a copy at each empty-header base
case and continue after restoration. That changes output size and
runtime; this contract stops after the first deterministic cover.

When not to choose it:

Do not use exact cover for ordinary set cover. If overlapping rows are
allowed and the objective is to minimize their count or cost, exact
cover's disjointness rule rejects valid set covers.

Do not use DLX merely because a problem uses a grid. First prove that
each candidate row and each exactly-once column encode the original
problem without losing or inventing solutions.

Do not choose dancing links when frequent pointer chasing and separate
allocation of data nodes dominate a small dense problem. Array or
bitset representations may be simpler and more cache-friendly.

Do not apply this primary-column implementation to optional
at-most-once constraints without changing the model. Generalized DLX
distinguishes required and secondary columns; this lesson requires
every column exactly once.

Do not rely on the first solution being lexicographically smallest by
row indices. Minimum-column branching defines the first solution; only
the row indices inside that solution are sorted for presentation.

Related material:

[A.3.2 doubly linked lists](#a32-doubly-linked-lists) owns paired-link
splicing. DLX deliberately does not detach removed nodes because their
links encode the inverse operation.

[B.19.2 constraint search](
#b192-constraint-search-backtracking-and-sets) owns recursive choice
and restoration. [B.19.3 pruned search](
#b193-pruned-search-bounds-and-partial-state) contrasts a proven bound
with the minimum-column heuristic, which only changes branch order.

Donald Knuth's original [Dancing Links paper](
https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0011047) presents reversible local operations
on doubly linked lists for exact-cover search. His official
[program archive](
https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/programs.html) includes
DLX1 and exact-cover encoders for queens, polyominoes, and Sudoku.

The standard library defines [`slices.Sort`](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort), used only on the owned result copy.
The Go specification defines [pointer types](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Pointer_types), which supply the node links;
the algorithm's ring and restoration guarantees come from this
implementation, not from the language.

### B.20 Counting and optimizing over repeated subproblems

#### B.20.1 Memoization (map and recursion)

##### Problem and contract

A recursive definition can be clear but wasteful when different
branches ask the same subproblem again. Memoization keeps the answer
from the first computation and returns it for later calls with the
same state.

The Fibonacci recurrence makes that repeated work visible. This lesson
uses zero-based indices:

```text
F(0) = 0
F(1) = 1
F(N) = F(N-1) + F(N-2), for N >= 2
```

A direct recursive call for `F(6)` asks for `F(5)` and `F(4)`.
Computing `F(5)` already computes `F(4)`, so the second branch repeats
an entire solved subproblem. Deeper states repeat even more often.

`memoizedFibonacci` has this contract:

- The input is an `int` index from 0 through 93.
- Success returns the exact Fibonacci value as `uint64` and nil error.
- Index 93 is the largest accepted value. `F(93)` fits in `uint64`,
  while `F(94)` does not.
- An index below 0 or above 93 returns zero and an error wrapping
  `errInvalidFibonacciIndex` before recursion or map allocation.
- Each call owns a new memo map. It exposes no map, retains no input,
  and has no side effect.

Independent calls are safe to run concurrently because they share no
mutable state. Successful map allocation and recursion-stack growth
must fit available memory.

Read [recursive call state](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) first. Read
[composite map keys](#a64-composite-keys-and-custom-hashes) when a
later recurrence needs several fields to identify one subproblem.

##### Mental model

The memo is a `map[int]uint64` named `valueByIndex`. Its key is the
complete subproblem state. Read this entry as a sentence:

```text
valueByIndex[4] is present means F(4) was completely computed,
and its stored value is the final answer 3.
```

Presence matters separately from value. Go returns the value type's
zero value for a missing map key, but `F(0)` is legitimately zero.
The two-value lookup `value, exists := valueByIndex[index]`
distinguishes a cached zero from an absent answer.

Seed the two base states. The recursive function then follows one
rule:

1. If the current index is present, return the stored final answer.
2. Otherwise compute the answers for the two smaller indices.
3. Add them, store the sum under the current index, and return it.

The function stores only after both dependencies finish. A present
entry therefore never means "in progress" or "placeholder." Every
cache hit can return immediately without another recursive branch.

This is top-down dynamic programming: begin with the requested state
and discover dependencies through recursion. B.20.2 builds states
bottom up in a table instead.

The memo belongs to one top-level call. That scope avoids stale values
when a recurrence has other inputs and avoids synchronization between
independent callers. Larger problems may reuse a cache deliberately,
but then the key must include every input that can change an answer.

##### Worked walkthrough

Compute `F(6)`. The expected answer is 8. A frame snapshot lists
active indices from oldest to newest. The memo shows only completed
states.

Initial state: validation accepts 6. The memo is `{0:0,1:1}`, the
active call is `F(6)`, and no nonbase state is complete.

```text
F(6)
+-- F(5)
|   +-- F(4) ...
|   +-- F(3) reused after memoization
+-- F(4) reused after F(5) completes it

each nonbase index is computed once, then read from the memo
```

1. Decision: index 6 is absent, so it needs `F(5)` first. Indices 5,
   4, 3, and 2 are also absent; each call follows its first smaller
   dependency until `F(1)` is reached.
   After: active frames are `[6,5,4,3,2,1]`; the memo remains
   `{0:0,1:1}`.
   Known correct: every suspended frame still lacks a final answer,
   and each dependency index is smaller than its parent.
2. Decision: lookup of index 1 is present, so return 1 to the `F(2)`
   frame. Its second dependency, index 0, is also present and returns
   zero. Add `1+0` and store `2:1`.
   After: the memo is `{0:0,1:1,2:1}` and `F(2)` returns 1 to
   `F(3)`.
