`0 mod 1` describes all integers, exactly the solution set of zero
constraints. Assume the current summary exactly represents all
constraints before an index. The merge proof shows that a compatible
merge returns exactly its intersection with the next constraint. An
incompatible merge proves that intersection empty. Therefore the
invariant holds after every successful iteration or justifies the
reported error.

The loop advances by one index and the finite residue slice bounds its
iterations. If it finishes, the invariant describes the entire input
system. The returned residue is canonical and its modulus is the
successive LCM, so the success contract follows.

Input validation happens before initialization and merging. Equal
lengths make every parallel index safe. Positive moduli make G and
every merged modulus positive, so `Mod` and `Quo` never divide by
zero. In particular, `N/G` may equal one for a redundant constraint;
modulo one safely yields step zero.

Every arithmetic receiver that becomes part of the result is newly
allocated. The helpers read but do not mutate slice elements or the
current result values. Arbitrary-precision operations preserve the
mathematical integers instead of wrapping. These ownership and range
facts establish the remaining API guarantees.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let K be the number of constraints. Let `B_i` be the bit length of the
LCM after processing i constraints, and let W be the final bit length.
Although each input modulus has at most 63 bits, W can reach 63K bits
and can therefore exceed one machine word.

Length comparison is constant time. The modulus-validation pass takes
`O(K)` scalar checks. The merge pass performs at most K iterations.
Each iteration performs one arbitrary-precision extended GCD plus a
constant number of big-integer additions, divisions,
multiplications, and modulus operations on values bounded by the next
combined modulus.

An implementation-independent arithmetic bound is best written as:

```text
sum over i of:
extendedGCD(B_(i-1), at most 63) + bigArithmetic(B_i)
```

The concrete cost depends on `math/big` multiplication and division
algorithms and on how quickly the LCM grows. Because the newly added
modulus has at most 63 bits, a simple word-arithmetic model charges
`O(B_i)` per merge and `O(sum B_i)`, at most `O(K*W)`, overall. For
positive K, W is at most 63K here, so this is `O(K^2)` with word-size
constants omitted. The summation is more informative when LCM growth
is slow.

Empty input is the best case after validation at `Theta(1)`. A length
mismatch also returns in constant time. A bad modulus requires checks
through its index. An inconsistent system still pays the full initial
validation scan, then stops at its first incompatible merge. A fully
compatible system performs all K merges. There is no useful average
case without a distribution over moduli and residues.

The final result retains `Theta(W)` bits. Live merge state also uses
`O(W)` big-number storage. The loop creates temporary `big.Int`
objects each iteration, so total allocation over the call is larger
than peak live storage and garbage collection may retain old backing
arrays temporarily. The input slices occupy `Theta(K)` caller-owned
storage and are not copied.

The fold is straightforward and accepts arbitrary positive moduli.
A formula that multiplies precomputed inverses can be shorter for
pairwise-coprime inputs, but it does not by itself detect compatible
non-coprime systems and can overflow fixed-width intermediates.

Production code with many repeated queries over the same fixed
moduli may precompute merge data. That trades memory and setup work
for faster queries. This implementation favors a direct, auditable
one-shot contract.

The example runner performs four fixed calls, formats a constant
number of lines, and propagates writer failure. Formatting a big
integer costs time and output space proportional to its decimal digit
count.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Reject unequal slice lengths before indexing either slice. Silently
  truncating with the shorter length drops constraints.
- Reject zero and negative moduli before `GCD`, `Mod`, or division.
  This contract uses positive periods only.
- Accept modulus one deliberately. It is a vacuous constraint and is
  also the modulus in the empty fold identity.
- Normalize negative residues with Euclidean modulus. Go's signed `%`
  alone can leave a negative value.
- Test `gcd(M,N)` against `B-A`, not against B or A separately.
  Compatibility depends on whether the two residues agree modulo the
  shared factor.
- Do not require pairwise coprimality. Shared factors are valid when
  their residue requirements agree.
- Do not multiply all moduli for the result period. Use
  `M*(N/gcd(M,N))`, the LCM, to avoid overstating the solution cycle.
- Divide the difference and next modulus by the same GCD before using
  the Bezout coefficient as an inverse.
- A reduced next modulus of one is valid. Its only canonical residue
  is zero, so the step is zero and no special inverse failure exists.
- Normalize the merged residue after `A+M*T`. A negative difference
  or coefficient can otherwise leave an equivalent but noncanonical
  answer.
- Do not calculate `B-A`, `M*T`, or the LCM in `int64`. Each can
  overflow before later conversion to `big.Int`.
- `big.Int` methods mutate their receiver. Do not reuse a receiver
  whose old value is still needed, and do not shallow-copy an `Int`.
- Return no partial solution on error. A successfully merged prefix
  does not satisfy an incompatible full system.
- Empty input is not inconsistent. It has no restrictions and is
  represented by `0 mod 1`.
- Duplicate constraints are harmless when equal after normalization.
  Conflicting duplicates are rejected by the same GCD test.
- Constraint order may change intermediate coefficients and values,
  but a compatible system has the same final canonical result and
  LCM. Order-dependent output signals an implementation bug.
- Returned `big.Int` pointers are mutable. Mutating one call's result
  is safe, but concurrent mutation of the same returned value needs
  synchronization.
- The implementation is variable-time. Do not use it for secret
  cryptographic residues when timing leakage matters.

##### When to choose it

Choose the Chinese remainder theorem when:

- several modular observations describe one unknown integer;
- independent cycles must be synchronized into one repeating cycle;
- a large computation is split across smaller coprime moduli and its
  combined residue must be reconstructed;
- compatible non-coprime schedules or congruences need one canonical
  description;
- the required result is a residue class, not one bounded integer.

Use incremental merging when moduli may share factors, inconsistency
must be reported, or the system arrives one constraint at a time. The
fold can stop as soon as an added constraint conflicts after the
initial validation pass.

Use direct search only for tiny periods where its simplicity matters
more than scale. Its work can grow with the LCM, while CRT merging
uses arithmetic whose cost grows with bit length.

Use [extended Euclid](
#b2113-extended-euclid-and-modular-inverses-integers) directly when
only one modular inverse or linear Diophantine equation is needed.
CRT repeatedly uses that tool to intersect whole residue classes.

Use [modular arithmetic](
#b215-modular-arithmetic-integers) without CRT when every operation
uses one fixed modulus. Use [Euclid's algorithm](
#b212-euclids-algorithm-integer-remainders) when only the GCD or LCM
is needed and no residues must be reconciled.

Use arbitrary-precision inputs too if the individual residues or
moduli can exceed `int64`; the merge logic already works on
`big.Int`, but this lesson's boundary API intentionally accepts
`int64` slices. Use a vetted constant-time library for cryptographic
secret reconstruction.

NIST defines the [Chinese remainder theorem](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/chineseRmndr.html) as reconstructing
a unique residue modulo the LCM of positive moduli. The standard
library documents [`big.Int.GCD`](
https://pkg.go.dev/math/big#Int.GCD), including its Bezout
coefficients, and [`big.Int.Mod`](
https://pkg.go.dev/math/big#Int.Mod), including Euclidean modulus.
The Go specification documents [slice types](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_types), including their shared backing
storage and nil behavior behind this API's nonmutation contract.

### B.22 Bits and compact state

#### B.22.1 Bit tests and population counts (integer masks)

##### Problem and contract

Many problems describe a small set of yes-or-no facts: enabled
features, selected positions, present permissions, occupied cells, or
visited vertices. When the universe has at most 64 stable positions,
one `uint64` can store the entire set. Bit position zero represents
item zero, bit position one represents item one, and so on.

This lesson evaluates one candidate mask against three rules:

- every bit in a required mask must also be in the candidate;
- no bit in a forbidden mask may be in the candidate; and
- the candidate must contain at least a minimum number of set bits.

For an eight-position universe, suppose a candidate is `00101101`.
It contains positions 0, 2, 3, and 5. Required mask `00001001` asks
for positions 0 and 3, forbidden mask `01000000` bans position 6,
and the minimum count is four. The candidate passes all three rules.

`evaluateMask` has this contract:

- `width` is the logical number of positions and must be in `[0,64]`.
- The valid positions are the half-open interval `[0,width)`. Bit
  zero is the least significant, rightmost displayed bit.
- `candidate`, `rule.required`, and `rule.forbidden` must have no set
  bit at a position greater than or equal to `width`.
- `rule.minimumSelected` must be in `[0,width]`.
- Required and forbidden masks must be disjoint. An overlapping rule
  is contradictory and returns an error rather than always rejecting.
- Invalid width, minimum, outside bits, and overlap return errors
  identified by their corresponding package sentinel.
- Width, then minimum count, then outside bits, then overlap are
  validated in that order. Every invalid call returns the zero
  evaluation and a descriptive error.
- `selectedCount` is the exact number of one bits in the candidate.
- `allRequired` is true exactly when the candidate contains every
  required position. An empty required mask is satisfied.
- `anyForbidden` is true exactly when the candidate contains at least
  one forbidden position. An empty forbidden mask finds none.
- `accepted` is true exactly when all required bits are present, no
  forbidden bit is present, and the count reaches the minimum.
- Width zero is valid only with zero masks and minimum zero. The empty
  candidate is accepted by the empty rule.
- The function uses only value inputs and returns only scalar values.
  It performs no I/O, owns no caller storage, and independent calls
  may run concurrently.

Read [packed bit vectors](#a131-packed-bit-vectors) first for one-bit
construction, setting, clearing, toggling, and point lookup. That
lesson owns the mutable data-structure API. This lesson applies the
same representation to whole-mask predicates and population counts.

##### Mental model

An unsigned integer is a row of fixed binary places. Give each place
one meaning. In an eight-position mask:

```text
position:  7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0
candidate: 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 1
meaning:       5   3 2   0 are selected
```

To name one position P, shift an explicitly typed one:

```text
oneBit = uint64(1) << P
```

For P equal to five, `oneBit` is `00100000`. A point test computes
`candidate & oneBit`. AND keeps a one only where both operands have a
one. Test the result against zero:

```text
candidate & oneBit != 0
```

The same idea tests several positions at once. `candidate & required`
keeps only required positions that the candidate actually contains.
Every required bit is present exactly when that intersection equals
the complete required mask:

```text
candidate & required == required
```

This is a subset test: the set encoded by `required` is a subset of
the set encoded by `candidate`.

Forbidden positions use a disjointness test. Their intersection must
be empty:

```text
candidate & forbidden == 0
```

The implementation stores the opposite diagnostic,
`anyForbidden`, so it tests `!= 0`.

The number of set bits is called the population count, Hamming weight,
or popcount. `bits.OnesCount64(candidate)` returns that count for all
64 storage positions. Validation ensures unused positions are zero,
so the storage count is also the logical count.

Logical width matters. For widths below 64, the allowed mask is:

```text
(uint64(1) << width) - 1
```

Width five produces `00011111`. AND NOT computes the outside bits:

```text
outside = supplied &^ allowed
```

Any nonzero outside result violates the contract. Width 64 uses an
all-one mask directly. With a runtime width of 64, the shift loses its
one and yields zero; subtracting one then wraps to all ones. Although
that final value coincides, a direct branch avoids depending on two
boundary effects.

##### Worked walkthrough

Evaluate candidate `00101101` at width eight with required mask
`00001001`, forbidden mask `01000000`, and minimum count four. The
expected result has count four and is accepted.

Initial state: no rule has been interpreted. The candidate, rule, and
width are value inputs, and the result is still the zero evaluation.

1. Decision: validate width eight. It lies in `[0,64]`, so compute
   `(1<<8)-1`, or allowed mask `11111111`. Validate minimum four;
   it lies in `[0,8]`.
   After: the logical universe is positions `[0,8)`, and the allowed
   mask names exactly those positions.
   Known correct: later shifts and counts can use a valid fixed-width
   interpretation, but no candidate decision has been made yet.
2. Decision: compute outside bits for the candidate, required mask,
   and forbidden mask. AND NOT with `11111111` gives zero for each.
   Then intersect the rule masks:
   `00001001 & 01000000 = 00000000`.
   After: all supplied masks fit the logical width and the rule has no
   position that is both required and forbidden.
   Known correct: the three predicates can now be evaluated without
   silently counting or testing nonexistent positions.
3. Decision: intersect candidate and required masks:
   `00101101 & 00001001 = 00001001`. The intersection equals the full
   required mask.
   After: `allRequired=true`.
   Known correct: positions zero and three, the complete required set,
   are both present. Other candidate bits do not affect this test.
4. Decision: intersect candidate and forbidden masks:
   `00101101 & 01000000 = 00000000`.
   After: `anyForbidden=false`.
   Known correct: forbidden position six is absent; no other position
   can make this diagnostic true.
5. Decision: population-count `00101101`. Its ones are at positions
   0, 2, 3, and 5, so the count is four. Compare four with the minimum
   four.
   After: `selectedCount=4`, and the count requirement is true.
   Known correct: the count reflects logical positions because every
   unused high bit was rejected during validation.
6. Decision: combine the three facts with logical AND: required is
   satisfied, forbidden is absent, and count is sufficient.
   After: return `{selectedCount:4, allRequired:true,
   anyForbidden:false, accepted:true}`.
   Known correct: each contract condition has been evaluated once, so
   acceptance is exactly the conjunction of all three rules.

Focused too-few case: candidate `00001001` contains both required
bits and no forbidden bit, but its population count is two. With
minimum four, the result is count two, `allRequired=true`, and
`accepted=false`. Required membership does not imply enough total
selections.

Focused missing-required case: candidate `00100101` has three set
bits but omits required position three. Its required intersection is
`00000001`, not `00001001`, so it is rejected even if a lower count
threshold would pass.

Focused forbidden case: candidate `01101101` contains all required
bits and five total bits, but its intersection with forbidden mask
`01000000` is nonzero. `anyForbidden=true`, so it is rejected.

Focused empty case: width zero produces allowed mask zero. Candidate
and both rule masks must be zero, and the only valid minimum is zero.
The empty required set is contained, the forbidden intersection is
empty, population count is zero, and the candidate is accepted.

Focused full-width case: at width 64, candidate `1<<63` is valid and
has population count one. The logical mask is built as all ones
without relying on the shift-and-underflow boundary behavior.

Focused invalid case: candidate `1<<8` with width eight uses position
eight, outside `[0,8)`. Its outside-bit test is nonzero, so the call
returns `errMaskOutsideWidth` and the zero evaluation.

Counterexample to comparing an AND result with one: candidate
`00101101` AND required `00001001` equals decimal nine, not one. The
candidate contains every required bit, so compare with the required
mask itself.

Counterexample to numeric ordering: candidate `10000000` is greater
than required mask `00000011`, but it contains neither required bit.
Integer magnitude does not express set inclusion; AND does.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program evaluates accepted, too-small, forbidden,
empty, and invalid masks. It uses only the standard library. Save it
as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Bit tests and population counts
// (integer masks). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"math/bits"
	"os"
)

var (
	errInvalidMaskWidth = errors.New(
		"mask width must be between 0 and 64",
	)
	errInvalidMinimumSelected = errors.New(
		"minimum selected count is outside the mask width",
	)
	errMaskOutsideWidth = errors.New(
		"mask uses a position outside the logical width",
	)
	errConflictingMaskRule = errors.New(
		"required and forbidden masks overlap",
	)
)

type maskRule struct {
	required        uint64
	forbidden       uint64
	minimumSelected int
}

type maskEvaluation struct {
	selectedCount int
	allRequired   bool
	anyForbidden  bool
	accepted      bool
}

func logicalMask(width int) (uint64, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	if width < 0 || width > 64 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: %d",
			errInvalidMaskWidth,
			width,
		)
	}
	// Name the full-width mask directly at the shift boundary.
	if width == 64 {
		return ^uint64(0), nil
	}
	return (uint64(1) << width) - 1, nil
}

func validateMaskWithinWidth(
	label string,
	mask uint64,
	allowedMask uint64,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the mask within width contract before
	// mutation.
	outsideBits := mask &^ allowedMask
	if outsideBits != 0 {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: %s has outside bits %#x",
			errMaskOutsideWidth,
			label,
			outsideBits,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func evaluateMask(
	candidate uint64,
	width int,
	rule maskRule,
) (maskEvaluation, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	allowedMask, err := logicalMask(width)
	if err != nil {
		return maskEvaluation{}, err
	}
	if rule.minimumSelected < 0 ||
		rule.minimumSelected > width {
		return maskEvaluation{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: %d for width %d",
			errInvalidMinimumSelected,
			rule.minimumSelected,
			width,
		)
	}

	// Validate every supplied mask before interpreting its positions.
	for _, value := range [...]struct {
		label string
		mask  uint64
	}{
		{label: "candidate", mask: candidate},
		{label: "required", mask: rule.required},
		{label: "forbidden", mask: rule.forbidden},
	} {
		if err := validateMaskWithinWidth(
			value.label,
			value.mask,
			allowedMask,
		); err != nil {
			return maskEvaluation{}, err
		}
	}
	if rule.required&rule.forbidden != 0 {
		return maskEvaluation{}, errConflictingMaskRule
	}

	// Intersections answer the two whole-mask membership questions.
	presentRequired := candidate & rule.required
	presentForbidden := candidate & rule.forbidden
	allRequired := presentRequired == rule.required
	anyForbidden := presentForbidden != 0
	selectedCount := bits.OnesCount64(candidate)

	return maskEvaluation{
		selectedCount: selectedCount,
		allRequired:   allRequired,
		anyForbidden:  anyForbidden,
		accepted: allRequired &&
			!anyForbidden &&
			selectedCount >= rule.minimumSelected,
	}, nil
}

func runBitTestExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute bit test examples to the bounded stopping condition above.
	rule := maskRule{
		required:        0b00001001,
		forbidden:       0b01000000,
		minimumSelected: 4,
	}
	eligible, err := evaluateMask(0b00101101, 8, rule)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("evaluate eligible mask: %w", err)
	}
	tooFew, err := evaluateMask(0b00001001, 8, rule)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("evaluate sparse mask: %w", err)
	}
	blocked, err := evaluateMask(0b01101101, 8, rule)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("evaluate forbidden mask: %w", err)
	}
	empty, err := evaluateMask(0, 0, maskRule{})
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("evaluate empty mask: %w", err)
	}
	_, invalidErr := evaluateMask(
		uint64(1)<<8,
		8,
		rule,
	)
	if !errors.Is(invalidErr, errMaskOutsideWidth) {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"expected outside-width error: %w",
			invalidErr,
		)
	}

	text := fmt.Sprintf(
		"eligible: count=%d required=%t forbidden=%t "+
			"accepted=%t\n"+
			"too few: count=%d required=%t forbidden=%t "+
			"accepted=%t\n"+
			"blocked: count=%d required=%t forbidden=%t "+
			"accepted=%t\n"+
			"empty: count=%d accepted=%t\n"+
			"invalid rejected=%t\n",
		eligible.selectedCount,
		eligible.allRequired,
		eligible.anyForbidden,
		eligible.accepted,
		tooFew.selectedCount,
		tooFew.allRequired,
		tooFew.anyForbidden,
		tooFew.accepted,
		blocked.selectedCount,
		blocked.allRequired,
		blocked.anyForbidden,
		blocked.accepted,
		empty.selectedCount,
		empty.accepted,
		invalidErr != nil,
	)
	if _, err := io.WriteString(output, text); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write bit-test results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runBitTestExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
eligible: count=4 required=true forbidden=false accepted=true
too few: count=2 required=true forbidden=false accepted=false
blocked: count=5 required=true forbidden=true accepted=false
empty: count=0 accepted=true
invalid rejected=true
```

##### Why it works

First establish the logical-width mask. For `1<=W<64`,
`uint64(1)<<W` has its sole one immediately above valid position
`W-1`. Subtracting one borrows through every lower place, producing
ones exactly at positions `[0,W)` and zeros above them. At W equal to
zero, the expression is `1-1=0`, correctly naming no positions. At W
equal to 64, the special all-one value names every storage position.

For any supplied mask S, `S &^ allowed` preserves exactly the bits in
S that are absent from the allowed mask. A zero result therefore means
every set bit lies inside the logical universe. Validation rejects the
opposite case before population count can include nonexistent items.

Now consider the required test. Bitwise AND keeps position P exactly
when both candidate and required have a one at P. If the intersection
equals the required mask, every required one survived and is present
in the candidate. If they differ, at least one required one was
removed because the candidate lacked it. Thus `allRequired` is exact.

The forbidden proof is similar. The candidate and forbidden sets
share a position exactly when their AND has a one. The intersection is
nonzero exactly when at least one forbidden position is present, so
`anyForbidden` is exact.

`bits.OnesCount64` returns the number of ones in the storage word.
The outside-bit validation establishes that every one is a valid
logical position. Therefore `selectedCount` is the exact cardinality
of the candidate set, and comparing it with `minimumSelected` decides
the count rule.

The final Boolean expression is true only if the three proved facts
all meet their rules. It is also true whenever all three rules hold.
Therefore `accepted` is necessary and sufficient for the declared
mask policy.

Validation checks width before constructing the allowed mask, so no
unsupported interpretation is used. It checks the minimum before
evaluation, and overlap before acceptance, so invalid policy values
cannot masquerade as ordinary rejection. Every error returns the zero
evaluation.

All loops range over one fixed three-element array. All other work is
a bounded number of fixed-width operations. The function therefore
terminates and keeps no mutable state between calls.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

The storage width is fixed at 64 bits. Constructing the logical mask,
validating three supplied masks, computing two intersections,
population-counting one word, and combining the results each take a
bounded number of machine operations. Best, average, and worst
successful time are all `Theta(1)` under this fixed-width contract.

Invalid calls also take `Theta(1)` time. They may return after width,
minimum, the first outside-bit check, or the overlap check, but the
maximum validation work is still fixed. Error formatting may allocate
diagnostic text on failure.

The function uses `Theta(1)` auxiliary space and returns a fixed-size
scalar struct using `Theta(1)` output space. The three-entry
validation array also has fixed size. No input or result storage is
retained or shared.

For a generalized W-bit integer whose width grows with input, point
tests remain constant at the word level but a full population count
takes `Theta(W/wordSize)` operations. The constant bound here comes
from choosing `uint64`, not from population count being free at every
scale.

A single word is compact, cheap to copy, comparable, and usable as a
map key. The tradeoff is a hard 64-position universe and less obvious
source code than named Boolean fields. A rule struct gives the masks
domain meaning, but callers still need one stable position-to-item
mapping.

The example runner performs five fixed evaluations, formats five
lines, and propagates writer failure. Its output work is constant for
this fixed demonstration.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Width zero permits only mask zero and minimum zero. The empty
  required set is satisfied, so the empty rule accepts the empty
  candidate.
- Width 64 uses `^uint64(0)` as its logical mask. With runtime width
  64, shifting the typed one yields zero and subtraction wraps to all
  ones. State the boundary explicitly instead of relying on both
  effects.
- Position 63 is valid only at width 64. Position 64 is never
  representable in one `uint64` mask.
- Choose an unsigned fixed-width type. Right shifts of signed negative
  integers are arithmetic in Go, and a negative value also looks like
  many selected two's-complement bits.
- Type the shifted one as `uint64(1)`. A plain `1` can acquire an
  architecture-dependent `int` type in a nonconstant expression.
- Validate a position before shifting when positions arrive as input.
  A negative runtime shift panics; an oversized shift silently moves
  the bit outside the fixed-width value.
- Test one bit with `mask&oneBit != 0`, not `== 1`. Only position zero
  has numeric value one.
- Test all required bits with `candidate&required == required`.
  Testing merely `!=0` accepts a candidate containing only one of
  several required bits.
- Test forbidden bits with intersection, not subtraction. Integer
  arithmetic does not encode set membership.
- Do not compare mask magnitudes to infer containment. High unrelated
  bits can make a mask numerically larger while required low bits are
  absent.
- Reject outside bits before counting. Otherwise a width-eight mask
  with bit 20 set can satisfy a minimum using a nonexistent item.
- Empty required and forbidden masks are ordinary identities: every
  candidate contains the empty set and intersects it nowhere.
- Reject overlap between required and forbidden masks. Treating it as
  a normal false result hides a contradictory caller configuration.
- A population count says how many positions are set, not which ones.
  Keep it separate from required and forbidden membership tests.
- Duplicate logical items must not receive different positions unless
  the domain intentionally treats their occurrences as distinct.
- Fixed-width bit operations and `math/bits` are not promised to be
  constant-time with respect to secrets on every architecture. Use a
  vetted cryptographic implementation for side-channel requirements.

##### When to choose it

Choose integer-mask tests when:

- the universe has at most 64 stable, dense positions;
- rules ask whether all, any, or none of several flags are present;
- the number of selected positions affects eligibility or a score;
- masks must be copied, compared, hashed, or passed by value cheaply;
- many repeated queries justify a compact representation.

Permissions, feature compatibility, small board occupancy, resource
requirements, and subset-state validation often have this shape. Write
down the position mapping next to the domain contract; a mask without
that mapping is only an opaque integer.

Use ordinary named Boolean fields when there are only a few unrelated
flags and source readability matters more than generic set operations.
Use `[]bool` when the width varies and direct indexing is the main
operation.

Use [packed bit vectors](#a131-packed-bit-vectors) when callers need a
mutable abstraction with set, clear, toggle, invert, and point lookup.
Use [multiword bit sets](#a132-multiword-bit-sets) when the universe
can exceed 64 positions.

Use [subset enumeration](#b194-subset-enumeration-bitmasks) when every
mask in a small power set must be visited. Use [bitmask DP](
#b207-bitmask-dp-state-table) when a table stores a result for each
selected-set mask. Those algorithms use the primitives taught here
but add exponential state traversal or dynamic-programming meaning.

The next [XOR cancellation lesson](
#b222-xor-cancellation-integer-accumulator) uses a different bitwise
law: equal values cancel in pairs. Population count and subset tests
do not provide that cancellation behavior.

NIST defines a [bit vector](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/bitVector.html) as an array of bits
that a computer word can often handle efficiently. The Go standard
library documents [`bits.OnesCount64`](
https://pkg.go.dev/math/bits#OnesCount64) as returning the number of
one bits. The Go specification defines [integer and shift operators](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators), including `&`, `&^`,
unsigned shifts, and the absence of an upper shift-count limit.

#### B.22.2 XOR cancellation (integer accumulator)

##### Problem and contract

Suppose a stream contains paired duplicate integers and one value that
has no mate. A frequency map can count every value, but the pairing
promise contains more structure than a general counting problem. XOR,
or exclusive OR, cancels equal values using one integer accumulator.

For example, `[4,1,2,1,2,4,9]` has three interleaved pairs and lone
value nine. XOR processes the slice in its existing order and returns
nine without sorting or storing a map.

The useful rule is slightly more general than "twice except once."
Every even multiplicity cancels completely. Every odd multiplicity
contributes one copy. `xorOddMultiplicityValues` therefore computes
an exact XOR signature for every input:

```text
signature = XOR of each distinct value whose count is odd
```

If exactly one distinct value has odd multiplicity, the signature is
that value. That frequency promise belongs to the caller; the
constant-space fold cannot verify it.

`xorOddMultiplicityValues` has this contract:

- `values` may be nil, empty, or contain any `int64`, including zero,
  negative values, and both signed extremes.
- The result is the bitwise XOR of every slice element in order. By
  XOR's laws, it is also the XOR of the distinct odd-count values.
- Nil and empty input return zero, XOR's identity.
- If exactly one distinct value occurs an odd number of times, success
  identifies that value. All other distinct values may occur any
  positive even number of times, not only twice.
- If several values occur oddly, the result is their combined XOR. It
  may be a value absent from the input or may be zero.
- Result zero does not prove that all counts were even. A unique zero
  or several odd values whose XOR is zero produce the same result.
- The function does not validate multiplicities and returns no error.
  Callers needing proof of the single-value promise must count or
  sort.
- Input order does not affect the result, but the function reads the
  slice in its supplied order.
- The input is neither modified nor retained. Independent calls may
  read a stable shared slice concurrently; concurrent writes require
  external synchronization.
- The function performs no I/O and uses only local scalar state.

Read [bit tests and population counts](
#b221-bit-tests-and-population-counts-integer-masks) first for Go's
fixed-width integer-bit model. This lesson changes the question from
"which positions are set?" to "which value bits have odd parity?"

##### Mental model

XOR compares two equal-width bit patterns one position at a time. A
result bit is one exactly when the two input bits differ:

```text
0 XOR 0 = 0
0 XOR 1 = 1
1 XOR 0 = 1
1 XOR 1 = 0
```

Go writes binary XOR as `left ^ right` and the update form as
`accumulator ^= value`. Four laws drive cancellation:

```text
X ^ 0 = X                 zero is the identity
X ^ X = 0                 an equal pair cancels
X ^ Y = Y ^ X             order does not matter
(X ^ Y) ^ Z = X ^ (Y ^ Z) grouping does not matter
```

Because order and grouping do not matter, equal occurrences can be
paired conceptually even when other values lie between them. Two
copies disappear. Three copies leave one because the first two cancel.
More generally, only the parity of a value's count matters: even or
odd.

The algorithm remembers one state value:

```text
signature = XOR of every element in the processed prefix
```

Equivalently, it is the XOR of the values whose counts are currently
odd in that prefix. Reading another value toggles that value's parity:
an even count becomes odd and contributes one copy, or an odd count
becomes even and removes it through cancellation.

This is a value accumulator, not a set mask. A number such as 12 is
XORed as its complete 64-bit representation; it is not used as a bit
position. Negative `int64` values use their fixed two's-complement bit
patterns and still satisfy `X^X=0`.

##### Worked walkthrough

Process `[4,1,2,1,2,4,9]`. The expected signature and promised lone
odd-occurrence value are both nine. Four low bits are enough to
display these positive values, though the code operates on all 64
bits.

Initial state: no values have been processed. `signature=0000`, the
XOR identity, and every prefix count is zero.

1. Decision: read 4, binary `0100`, and compute
   `0000 ^ 0100 = 0100`.
   After: `signature=0100`, decimal four.
   Known correct: four is the only value with odd count in prefix
   `[4]`; all unprocessed values remain unresolved.
2. Decision: read 1, binary `0001`, and compute
   `0100 ^ 0001 = 0101`.
   After: `signature=0101`, decimal five.
   Known correct: four and one each occur once, and their XOR is five.
3. Decision: read 2, binary `0010`, and compute
   `0101 ^ 0010 = 0111`.
   After: `signature=0111`, decimal seven.
   Known correct: four, one, and two are the current odd-count values.
4. Decision: read the second 1. Compute
   `0111 ^ 0001 = 0110`.
   After: `signature=0110`, decimal six.
   Known correct: the two ones cancel; four and two remain odd in the
   processed prefix.
5. Decision: read the second 2. Compute
   `0110 ^ 0010 = 0100`.
   After: `signature=0100`, decimal four.
   Known correct: both ones and twos now have even counts, leaving
   only four's contribution.
6. Decision: read the second 4. Compute
   `0100 ^ 0100 = 0000`.
   After: `signature=0000`.
   Known correct: every value in the first six positions has an even
   count, so the prefix signature is the identity.
7. Decision: read 9, binary `1001`. Compute
   `0000 ^ 1001 = 1001`.
   After: `signature=1001`, decimal nine.
   Known correct: nine is the only odd-count value in the full
   processed prefix.
8. Decision: no elements remain, so stop and return the signature.
   After: return nine.
   Known correct: the invariant now covers the whole slice, and the
   caller's single-odd-value promise lets nine be interpreted
   directly.

Focused odd-count case: `[7,7,7,5,5]` returns seven. Two sevens
cancel and the third remains; the two fives cancel. XOR needs even
counts for nonanswers, not exactly two occurrences.

Focused empty case: nil and `[]int64{}` both skip the loop and return
zero. This is a valid signature, not evidence that zero appeared.

Focused zero-value case: `[0,5,5]` returns zero because the fives
cancel and the unique odd-count value is zero. The frequency promise,
not the numeric result alone, makes that interpretation sound.

Focused signed-boundary case: `[-3,MinInt64,-3]` returns `MinInt64`.
The two negative-three bit patterns cancel exactly, and XOR cannot
arithmetically overflow.

Focused unpromised case: `[1,2]` returns three because `1^2=3`, even
though three is absent. `[1,2,3]` returns zero even though all three
values have odd counts. The signature remains correct, but neither
input permits the single-value conclusion.

Counterexample to remembering only the latest value: the last element
of `[9,4,4]` is four, while the unmatched value is nine. Cancellation
must incorporate the full prefix.

Counterexample to adding values: `[4,1,1]` sums to six rather than
four. Addition does not make equal pairs disappear and may overflow;
XOR has the required self-cancellation law.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program demonstrates a lone odd-count value, three
occurrences, empty input, signed extremes, and an input without the
single-value promise. It uses only the standard library. Save it as
`main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates XOR cancellation (integer
// accumulator). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

const minimumInt64 = int64(-1 << 63)

func xorOddMultiplicityValues(values []int64) int64 {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	signature := int64(0)

	// Each update flips the parity contribution of every value bit.
	for _, value := range values {
		signature ^= value
	}
	return signature
}

func runXORExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute xor examples to the bounded stopping condition above.
	singleOdd := xorOddMultiplicityValues(
		[]int64{4, 1, 2, 1, 2, 4, 9},
	)
	threeOccurrences := xorOddMultiplicityValues(
		[]int64{7, 7, 7, 5, 5},
	)
	empty := xorOddMultiplicityValues(nil)
	signed := xorOddMultiplicityValues(
		[]int64{-3, minimumInt64, -3},
	)
	unpromised := xorOddMultiplicityValues([]int64{1, 2})

	text := fmt.Sprintf(
		"single odd value = %d\n"+
			"three occurrences = %d\n"+
			"empty signature = %d\n"+
			"signed value = %d\n"+
			"unpromised signature = %d\n",
		singleOdd,
		threeOccurrences,
		empty,
		signed,
		unpromised,
	)
	if _, err := io.WriteString(output, text); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write XOR results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runXORExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
single odd value = 9
three occurrences = 7
empty signature = 0
signed value = -9223372036854775808
unpromised signature = 3
```

##### Why it works

Maintain this loop invariant before processing index I:

```text
signature is the XOR of values[0:I]
```

It holds initially at I equal to zero because the XOR of no values is
the identity zero. During an iteration, XORing `values[I]` appends
exactly the next element to that prefix expression. The invariant
therefore holds for I plus one.

When the loop ends, I equals the slice length, so the invariant says
the returned signature is the XOR of every input element. Now use
commutativity and associativity to regroup equal values without
changing the result. Each equal pair becomes `X^X=0`, and zero is the
identity. An even count becomes only pairs and vanishes. An odd count
becomes pairs plus one remaining X.

The final expression is therefore exactly the XOR of all distinct
odd-multiplicity values. If there is exactly one such value U, the
expression contains only U and returns U. If there are several, XOR
correctly returns their signature but cannot separate them.

The loop advances once per slice element and its finite range bounds
the work, so it terminates. XOR acts on a fixed 64-bit representation;
it neither performs signed arithmetic nor overflows. The function only
reads each element, stores one local accumulator, and returns it by
value, establishing its mutation and ownership guarantees.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the slice length. The function reads each of N elements once
and performs one fixed-width XOR per element. Successful best,
average, and worst time are all `Theta(N)` for a fixed N because data
values do not change the loop. Empty input takes `Theta(1)` time.

The function uses `Theta(1)` auxiliary space and returns one `int64`,
also `Theta(1)` output space. It allocates no growing collection and
does not recurse, copy the slice, or retain caller storage.

A frequency map can validate the occurrence promise and identify all
odd-count values, but it uses `Theta(D)` extra entries for D distinct
values and expected `Theta(N)` time under ordinary hash assumptions.
The XOR fold saves that storage by returning only a combined signature
and trusting any stronger promise.

A heapsort-style in-place comparison sort groups equal values with
`O(1)` auxiliary space and `O(N log N)` worst-case time, but it
changes input order. Other sorting algorithms have different space
bounds. Copying first preserves the caller's slice at `Theta(N)`
extra space.

The signature is mergeable: XOR partial signatures from disjoint
chunks to obtain the whole-stream signature. This supports streaming
or parallel reduction with one word per partial result, though reading
the original slice concurrently still requires stable input.

The example runner performs five fixed folds, formats five lines, and
propagates writer failure. Its demonstration output work is constant.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty input return zero through the real XOR identity. Do
  not report zero as a found input value without a frequency promise.
- A singleton returns itself because `0^X=X`.
- A unique odd-count zero also returns zero. The same result comes
  from all-even counts or from several odd values whose XOR is zero.
- Values occurring four, six, or any even number of times cancel just
  like pairs. Values occurring three or five times leave one copy.
- If every value appears three times except one, XOR does not isolate
  the exception: three is odd, so every tripled value remains. Use
  per-bit counts modulo three for that different contract.
- Multiple odd-count values combine. `[1,2]` returns three, which is
  not an input member; `[1,2,3]` returns zero.
- Negative values and `MinInt64` are valid fixed-width bit patterns.
  Do not apply absolute value first; positive `abs(MinInt64)` is not
  representable as `int64` and would also change the XOR problem.
- Go's binary `^` is XOR, while unary `^value` is bitwise complement.
  Use `signature ^= value`, not `signature = ^value`.
- `^` is not exponentiation in Go. It never raises one number to a
  power.
- Do not XOR indexes when the contract pairs values. Equal values can
  occur at different indexes and must cancel by value.
- Do not sort merely to make pairs adjacent. XOR's associative and
  commutative laws already cancel interleaved occurrences.
- Do not claim the fold validates the one-odd-value promise. It has no
  stored counts with which to distinguish zero, one, or many odd keys.
- XOR is a weak integrity checksum. Repeated or coordinated changes
  can cancel, so use a real hash or authenticated construction for
  corruption or adversarial tampering.
- The function does not mutate the slice, but a concurrent caller
  write is still a data race and can produce an incoherent signature.

##### When to choose it

Choose XOR cancellation when:

- one value has odd multiplicity and every other value has even
  multiplicity under a trusted input promise;
- paired events should toggle a parity state on arrival and departure;
- a stream needs a constant-space, order-independent parity signature;
- partial results from disjoint chunks should merge with one XOR.

The classic "every value appears twice except one" problem is the
clearest signal. The stronger fact is parity: any even count cancels,
and one odd-count value survives.

Use a frequency map when the promise must be checked, all odd-count
values must be returned, or actual counts matter. Use sorting when
comparison order is useful for later work and input mutation or a copy
is acceptable.

If exactly two values occur once while all others occur twice, the
single fold returns their XOR, not the two values separately. A second
phase can partition values by one set bit in that XOR and fold each
group. That is a different contract with two outputs.

Use per-bit counts modulo K when nonanswers occur K times and K is
odd, such as three. Use [population counts](
#b221-bit-tests-and-population-counts-integer-masks) when the question
is how many bit positions are one rather than which complete values
have odd multiplicity.

Use the later [maximum XOR trie](
#b224-maximum-xor-queries-binary-trie) when the objective is to choose
another value that maximizes an XOR result. Use an [XOR linear basis](
#b226-xor-linear-basis-basis-array-advanced) for independent
subset-XOR combinations. Cancellation alone does not optimize over
choices.

NIST defines [XOR](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/xor.html) by its
one-bit truth table. The Go specification defines [bitwise XOR](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators) for integers and states
that signed integers have fixed-width two's-complement representation.

#### B.22.3 Subset transitions (bitmasks)

##### Problem and contract

Suppose one mask names the items that are available, and an algorithm
must visit every subset of only those items. Enumerating every mask in
the surrounding universe works, but it also visits values containing
unavailable positions and then rejects them.

For example, mask `10110` selects positions one, two, and four. Its
eight submasks are:

```text
10110  10100  10010  10000  00110  00100  00010  00000
```

The transition `(submask-1)&mask` moves directly between these valid
states in descending numeric order. This lesson builds a bounded
function around that transition:

```go
// Enumerate mask's submasks from greatest to least, including zero.
// width limits which bit positions belong to the stated universe.
func submasksDescending(
	mask uint64,
	width int,
) ([]uint64, error)
```

Its contract is:

- `width` is in `[0,64]`, and logical positions are `[0,width)`;
- `mask` has no set position outside that logical width;
- a submask S is valid exactly when `S &^ mask == 0`;
- the result contains every valid submask exactly once;
- values are in strictly descending numeric order, except that the
  one-value result for mask zero has no adjacent pair to compare;
- the first value is `mask`, and the last value is zero;
- if mask has K set bits, the result length is exactly `2^K`;
- zero is included, so mask zero returns a non-nil `[]uint64{0}`;
- at most 20 set bits may be materialized, bounding output at `2^20`
  values;
- invalid input returns an error and a nil slice, never a partial
  output;
- each successful call returns newly owned slice storage.

Width 64 is supported, including logical position 63. The limit
depends on the number of selected positions, not the width. A sparse
64-bit mask can therefore be cheap to enumerate.

The function materializes its answer because its contract returns a
slice. A callback or iterator can use the same transition when a
consumer should process one state at a time instead.

This is not enumeration of every subset of an N-item universe. That
operation visits every integer from zero through `2^N-1`. Here one
fixed mask may have gaps, and the task is to visit only masks whose
ones are a subset of its ones.

##### Mental model

Interpret a mask as a set of positions. A submask may turn any set bit
of the original mask off, but it may never turn a zero position on.
With K available positions, each position independently has two
choices, present or absent, so there are `2^K` submasks.

The current submask is itself an integer. To find the greatest valid
integer below it, first subtract one. For any positive integer,
subtraction does two things in binary:

- it clears the lowest set bit;
- it changes every lower bit to one because the borrow crosses them.

Some of those new lower ones may occupy positions absent from the
original mask. AND with `mask` removes exactly those forbidden ones:

```text
next = (submask - 1) & mask
```

The result retains every allowed one made available by the borrow, so
it is not merely some smaller submask. It is the greatest valid
submask below the current value. Repeating the operation therefore
walks the valid values in descending order without testing unrelated
masks.

For current value `10100` under original mask `10110`:

```text
current       10100
current - 1   10011
mask          10110
AND           10010
```

Simple decrement would stop at `10011`, which illegally sets
positions zero and one. The AND clears position zero and keeps
position one because only the latter belongs to the original mask.

Zero needs an explicit stopping rule. Go computes unsigned
subtraction modulo `2^64`, so `uint64(0)-1` becomes 64 one bits. AND
with the original mask then recreates `mask`:

```text
(0 - 1) & mask == mask
```

A loop that performs the transition after processing zero cycles back
to the start. Append zero, test it, and break before subtracting.

The logical-width check is separate from the transition. For widths
below 64, `(uint64(1)<<width)-1` has ones exactly at valid positions.
Width 64 uses `^uint64(0)` directly. `mask &^ allowedMask` then keeps
only outside bits, so a nonzero result is an input error.

Before allocation, population count gives K. The implementation
rejects K above 20 and reserves exactly `2^K` result slots. The cap is
a resource policy, not a property of the transition.

##### Worked walkthrough

Enumerate submasks of `10110`, decimal 22, at width five. The original
mask has K equal to three, so the expected result has eight states.

Initial state: `mask=10110`, no result storage has been allocated, and
no submask has been visited.

1. Decision: with width five and mask `10110`, build allowed mask
   `11111` and compute
   `10110 &^ 11111 = 00000`.
   After: the width and every set position are valid.
   Known correct: all later values are interpreted inside one
   declared five-position universe.
2. Decision: population-count the validated mask's ones at positions
   one, two, and four, obtaining K equal to three, and
   allocate capacity `2^3=8`.
   After: the empty result has room for all eight submasks.
   Known correct: three independent present-or-absent choices have
   exactly eight combinations, within the materialization limit.
3. Decision: current submask is `10110`, the original mask. Append
   decimal value 22, then compute `10110-1=10101` and AND with
   `10110`, producing `10100`.
   After: result is `[22]`, and next current value is 20.
   Known correct: `10100` is the greatest valid submask below
   `10110`; the forbidden low one was cleared.
4. Decision: current submask is `10100`. Append 20. Compute
   `10100-1=10011`, then AND with `10110`, producing `10010`.
   After: result is `[22 20]`, and next value is 18.
   Known correct: position zero was removed while allowed position
   one stayed set, so no valid value between 20 and 18 was skipped.
5. Decision: current submask is `10010`. Append 18. Compute
   `10010-1=10001`, then AND with `10110`, producing `10000`.
   After: result is `[22 20 18]`, and next value is 16.
   Known correct: the transition remains inside the original set
   of positions and strictly decreases the value.
6. Decision: current submask is `10000`. Append 16. Subtraction
   yields `01111`; AND with `10110` produces `00110`, decimal six.
   After: result is `[22 20 18 16]`, and next value is six.
   Known correct: the large numeric jump skips only masks that set
   positions unavailable in the original mask.
7. Decision: current submask is `00110`. Repeat the transition three
   times, appending six, four, and two and obtaining successive values
   `00100`, `00010`, and `00000`.
   After: result is `[22 20 18 16 6 4 2]`, and current is zero.
   Known correct: each transition is the next smaller valid state;
   no state repeats while the value strictly decreases.
8. Decision: current submask is `00000`. Append zero, observe zero,
   and break before applying unsigned subtraction.
   After: result is `[22 20 18 16 6 4 2 0]`.
   Known correct: every one of the eight expected states appears
   once, and the loop cannot wrap from zero back to `10110`.

Focused zero case: mask zero at width zero has K equal to zero and
therefore `2^0=1` submask. The loop appends zero and immediately
breaks, returning `[]uint64{0}` rather than an empty or nil slice.

Focused singleton case: mask `1000` at width four produces `[8 0]`.
The only decision is whether its sole available position is present.

Focused full-width case: mask `(1<<63)|1` at width 64 produces four
values: both bits, only the high bit, only the low bit, and zero. The
transition is unsigned and supports position 63 without a sign bit.

Focused invalid-width case: width 65 has no representation in one
`uint64`. Validation returns `errInvalidSubmaskWidth` and a nil slice.

Focused outside-bit case: mask `10000` at width four sets position
four, but valid positions stop at three. Validation returns
`errSubmaskOutsideWidth` before allocation.

Focused resource case: a mask with 21 set bits has `2^21` submasks.
The function returns `errTooManySubmaskBits` rather than silently
allocating beyond its declared `2^20` output bound.

Counterexample to plain decrement: from `10100`, decrement gives
`10011`. That value is smaller but not a submask of `10110` because it
sets forbidden position zero. The AND projection is required.

Counterexample to a positive-only loop: `for submask != 0` visits the
nonzero states but omits the valid empty submask. Process zero inside
the loop or handle it separately.

Counterexample to transitioning at zero: unsigned zero minus one is
all ones, and AND with the original mask returns the original mask.
Without the break, enumeration repeats forever.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program enumerates ordinary, empty, full-width, and
invalid cases. It uses only the standard library. Save it as `main.go`
and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Subset transitions (bitmasks).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"math/bits"
	"os"
)

const maximumEnumeratedSubmaskBits = 20

var (
	errInvalidSubmaskWidth = errors.New(
		"submask width must be between 0 and 64",
	)
	errSubmaskOutsideWidth = errors.New(
		"mask uses a position outside the logical width",
	)
	errTooManySubmaskBits = errors.New(
		"mask has too many set bits to enumerate",
	)
)

func submaskLogicalMask(width int) (uint64, error) {
	// Return the stored logical state without mutating it.
	if width < 0 || width > 64 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: %d",
			errInvalidSubmaskWidth,
			width,
		)
	}
	if width == 64 {
		return ^uint64(0), nil
	}
	return (uint64(1) << width) - 1, nil
}

func submasksDescending(
	mask uint64,
	width int,
) ([]uint64, error) {
	// Keep submasks descending in one helper so callers use one rule.
	allowedMask, err := submaskLogicalMask(width)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	if outsideBits := mask &^ allowedMask; outsideBits != 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: %#x",
			errSubmaskOutsideWidth,
			outsideBits,
		)
	}

	selectedCount := bits.OnesCount64(mask)
	if selectedCount > maximumEnumeratedSubmaskBits {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: got %d, limit %d",
			errTooManySubmaskBits,
			selectedCount,
			maximumEnumeratedSubmaskBits,
		)
	}

	totalSubmasks := 1 << selectedCount
	result := make([]uint64, 0, totalSubmasks)
	for submask := mask; ; submask = (submask - 1) & mask {
		result = append(result, submask)
		if submask == 0 {
			break
		}
	}
	return result, nil
}

func runSubmaskExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute submask examples to the bounded stopping condition above.
	submasks, err := submasksDescending(0b10110, 5)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("enumerate ordinary mask: %w", err)
	}
	empty, err := submasksDescending(0, 0)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("enumerate empty mask: %w", err)
	}
	fullWidth, err := submasksDescending(
		(uint64(1)<<63)|1,
		64,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("enumerate full-width mask: %w", err)
	}
	_, outsideErr := submasksDescending(uint64(1)<<4, 4)
	if !errors.Is(outsideErr, errSubmaskOutsideWidth) {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"expected outside-width error: %w",
			outsideErr,
		)
	}
	_, largeErr := submasksDescending((uint64(1)<<21)-1, 21)
	if !errors.Is(largeErr, errTooManySubmaskBits) {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"expected enumeration-limit error: %w",
			largeErr,
		)
	}

	text := fmt.Sprintf(
		"submasks = %v\n"+
			"empty = %v\n"+
			"full-width count = %d\n"+
			"outside rejected = %t\n"+
			"too many rejected = %t\n",
		submasks,
		empty,
		len(fullWidth),
		outsideErr != nil,
		largeErr != nil,
	)
	if _, err := io.WriteString(output, text); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write submask results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runSubmaskExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
submasks = [22 20 18 16 6 4 2 0]
empty = [0]
full-width count = 4
outside rejected = true
too many rejected = true
```

##### Why it works

Let M be the original mask and S be a positive submask of M. A valid
submask X satisfies `X &^ M == 0`; every one in X is also a one in M.

Subtracting one from positive S clears its lowest set bit and turns
every lower position into one. Call that intermediate value T. Any
one in T at a position absent from M cannot belong to a valid submask,
so `T & M` removes it. Every one that T places at an allowed lower
position remains. Thus `(S-1)&M` is a valid submask.

Now consider any integer Y strictly between `(S-1)&M` and S. To be
below S, Y must clear a set position at or above the lowest set bit
that subtraction changes. To be as large as possible afterward, every
lower position allowed by M must be one. The transition constructs
exactly that value and clears only lower positions forbidden by M.
Therefore it produces the greatest valid submask below S.

The first state M is valid and is the greatest possible submask. Every
nonzero transition is strictly smaller, so no state can repeat and the
loop must eventually reach zero in the finite set of unsigned values.
Zero is a valid submask and is appended before termination.

Because each transition selects the immediate valid predecessor,
there cannot be an unvisited valid value between consecutive states.
Starting at the greatest valid state and ending at the least valid
state therefore visits every valid submask exactly once and in
descending order.

If M has K set positions, each valid submask chooses independently
whether each of those K positions is present. There are two choices
per position and hence exactly `2^K` valid submasks. This also proves
the exact capacity computation and the returned length.

The zero check is part of termination. Go defines unsigned subtraction
modulo the integer width. Transitioning from zero would produce all
ones before the AND, then M after the AND. Breaking first prevents the
only wraparound edge from restarting the sequence.

Width validation establishes that every original set bit has domain
meaning. For width below 64, the allowed mask contains ones exactly in
`[0,width)`. AND NOT preserves exactly any original bits outside that
set. Width 64 uses all positions directly. Thus only valid logical
masks reach enumeration.

Population count is computed before allocation. If K exceeds 20, the
function returns a nil result, so the output allocation never exceeds
`2^20` elements. At or below the limit, the mathematical count proves
that the reserved capacity is exact.

The function allocates a new slice on every successful call and never
stores it globally. It reads scalar value inputs and shares no mutable
state. Calls are independent, and changing one returned slice cannot
change another.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let K be the number of set bits in `mask`, and let R be `2^K`, the
number of returned submasks. A successful call performs one constant
amount of fixed-width work per result. Best, average, and worst
successful time are all `Theta(R)`, or `Theta(2^K)`.

That exponential time is output-optimal for a materialized result: a
function returning R distinct values must write R values. Gaps in the
logical width do not add work. A width-64 mask with three set bits
still returns only eight states.

The returned slice uses `Theta(R)` output space. Apart from that
slice, counters, masks, and errors use `Theta(1)` auxiliary space.
The implementation reserves exact capacity, so append does not need
geometric growth or repeated backing-array copies.

With the 20-bit policy, at most 1,048,576 `uint64` values are stored,
about eight mebibytes of element data. The slice header and allocator
metadata add a small fixed overhead. The limit should be chosen from
the caller's latency and memory budget, not copied blindly into every
system.

Invalid width and outside-bit calls use `Theta(1)` time and space.
The population-count rejection also uses `Theta(1)` time for one
`uint64` and allocates no result slice. Formatting an error may
allocate diagnostic text.

An iterator or callback keeps `Theta(1)` enumeration state instead of
materializing `Theta(R)` output, but total visiting time remains
`Theta(R)`. It also changes ownership and failure semantics because a
consumer may observe a prefix before stopping or returning an error.

Filtering every integer from zero through `2^width-1` costs
`Theta(2^width)`, even when K is much smaller than width. Direct
submask transitions cost `Theta(2^K)`. The two bounds are equal only
when every logical position belongs to the original mask.

When every mask M of an N-bit universe and every submask of M are
enumerated, total work is `Theta(3^N)`: each position has three roles,
absent from M, present in M but absent from its submask, or present in
both. That nested operation is substantially larger than enumerating
submasks of one fixed mask.

The example runner performs bounded demonstrations, formats five
lines, and propagates writer failure. Its output work is constant for
the fixed examples.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Mask zero has one submask, zero. Do not return an empty slice merely
  because no bit is selected.
- Include the zero submask when the contract says every subset. A
  loop conditioned on `submask != 0` omits the empty subset.
- Break at zero before calculating `(submask-1)&mask`. Unsigned
  underflow otherwise returns to the original mask and cycles.
- Do not replace the transition with `submask--`. Decrement can set
  positions absent from the original mask.
- Keep the AND with the original immutable mask, not with a changing
  copy. The original mask defines which positions are ever allowed.
- Use an unsigned fixed-width type. Signed values make the top bit a
  sign bit and obscure the wraparound reasoning.
- Width 64 needs a direct all-one allowed mask. Avoid making the
  boundary depend on a shift by the storage width and underflow.
- Validate outside bits before population count and allocation. A bit
  without logical meaning must not increase K or output size.
- Limit K rather than width when output count is the resource concern.
  Sparse wide masks can be cheap; dense narrow masks can be expensive.
- Check the limit before computing or allocating `2^K`. In a less
  bounded design, a shift or conversion to `int` can overflow.
- State whether order is promised. This transition produces descending
  numeric order, which is not Gray-code order; several bits may change
  between adjacent states.
- Numeric order is representation order, not application preference.
  Map bit positions to domain items before interpreting a state.
- A returned slice exposes owned mutable storage. Callers may change
  their copy, so do not cache and reuse it as hidden shared state.
- The function is safe for concurrent independent calls, but sharing
  and mutating one returned slice still requires caller coordination.
- If a consumer can stop early, prefer a streaming form. Building the
  entire slice wastes work and memory when only a prefix is needed.
- A callback that fails after observing values has partial external
  effects even if it returns an error. Document that difference from
  this all-or-error materialized contract.
- This transition enumerates submasks, not fixed-cardinality subsets.
  Filter by population count or use a combination-specific generator
  when exactly J selected positions are required.

##### When to choose it

Choose descending submask transitions when:

- one fixed mask names the allowed positions;
- every subset of those positions must be visited;
- gaps make scanning the entire logical universe wasteful;
- descending numeric order is acceptable or useful;
- exponential work is feasible for the number of set bits.

Common uses include splitting a selected set into two parts, trying
every available-feature combination, iterating predecessor states in
bitmask DP, and enumerating all choices restricted by a compatibility
mask.

Use [subset enumeration](
#b194-subset-enumeration-bitmasks) when the task starts with N items
and must visit every mask in the complete N-bit universe. That lesson
owns the ascending `0` through `2^N-1` traversal.

Use [bitmask DP](#b207-bitmask-dp-state-table) when each mask indexes
a stored subproblem value and transitions add or remove choices. This
lesson supplies one way to enumerate predecessor submasks but does
not define a recurrence or prove a DP state meaning.

Use [bit tests and population counts](
#b221-bit-tests-and-population-counts-integer-masks) for membership,
containment, disjointness, and cardinality without enumeration. Those
constant-size questions should not pay exponential output cost.

Use recursive backtracking when choices have richer state, pruning
depends on partial assignments, or the natural result is domain
objects rather than masks. Use Gray-code enumeration when adjacent
states should differ by exactly one bit. Use combination generation
when every output must have one fixed population count.

Prefer a callback or iterator over this slice-returning API when the
consumer processes states online, may stop early, or cannot afford the
materialized result. Preserve the same zero guard in every form.

Algorithms for Competitive Programming derives [submask enumeration](
https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/all-submasks.html), including the
descending transition, the missing-zero pitfall, and the cycle caused
by transitioning after zero. The Go specification defines [unsigned
integer overflow](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Integer_overflow) modulo the
type width and lists [bitwise AND and AND NOT](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators) among integer operators.

#### B.22.4 Maximum XOR queries (binary trie)

##### Problem and contract

Given a set of stored integers and a query integer, choose the one
stored integer that produces the greatest value after bitwise XOR with
the query. A direct scan tries every stored value for every query.
When the stored set receives many queries, those scans repeat the same
high-bit comparisons.

For stored keys 5, 2, and 12 and query 6:

```text
6 XOR 5  =  3
6 XOR 2  =  4
6 XOR 12 = 10
```

Key 12 is the answer, and the maximum XOR value is 10. A binary trie
indexes the fixed-width bit prefixes of the stored keys so each query
can discard whole groups after one bit decision.

This application uses the four-bit teaching index owned by [A.9.3
Binary tries for integer keys](
#a93-binary-tries-for-integer-keys). Read that lesson first for node
representation, insertion, exact lookup, and the complete executable
Go program.

The application inherits this contract:

- valid stored keys and queries are integers in `[0,16)`;
- every key is interpreted as exactly four bits, including leading
  zeros;
- `insert(value)` returns true for a new key, false for a duplicate,
  and an error for an invalid value;
- invalid insertion is checked before allocation and leaves the trie
  unchanged;
- `maxXOR(query)` returns the matched stored key, the resulting XOR
  value, and true for a valid query against a nonempty trie;
- an invalid query or empty trie returns `(0,0,false)`;
- each successful query chooses one stored key, never a combination
  of several keys;
- queries read the current trie and do not change it;
- later successful insertions affect later queries, so a static
  workload inserts its complete candidate set before querying;
- duplicate insertions have set semantics and do not create extra
  candidates;
- the trie owns its nodes and retains no caller collection;
- copying the trie shares descendants, and unsynchronized concurrent
  use is outside the teaching contract.

For a fixed query, two distinct keys cannot tie. If `query^left`
equals `query^right`, XORing both sides with the query gives
`left==right`. The matched key is therefore unique among distinct
stored keys.

The four-bit range keeps the trace visible. A 32- or 64-bit unsigned
version follows the same decisions but needs a wider key type, a
matching range contract, and an appropriate node representation.

##### Mental model

XOR builds its numeric result one bit at a time. At any position, an
equal pair produces zero and an opposite pair produces one:

```text
0 XOR 0 = 0     0 XOR 1 = 1
1 XOR 1 = 0     1 XOR 0 = 1
```

The most significant result bit matters more than all lower bits
combined. In four bits, bit 3 is worth eight, while bits 2, 1, and 0
together are worth at most seven. Maximization must therefore decide
from bit 3 down to bit 0.

The binary trie groups stored keys by those high-bit prefixes. At
depth D, the current node represents exactly the stored keys sharing
the D chosen most-significant bits. Its child zero contains candidates
whose next bit is zero; child one contains those whose next bit is
one.

At a query bit, first ask for the opposite stored bit because it makes
the current XOR bit one. Follow that child when it exists. Otherwise,
follow the equal-bit child; every remaining candidate is forced to
produce zero at this position.

Read one lookup state as a sentence:

```text
query prefix 01, chosen key prefix 11, XOR prefix 10
```

The chosen key prefix names the remaining candidate group. The XOR
prefix is already final: lower choices cannot change a higher bit.
After four decisions, the path reaches one complete stored key.

There are two workload phases:

```text
build once     insert every candidate as a four-bit path
query often    choose opposite bits from high to low
```

One query never changes the tree, so the next query restarts at the
root and makes its own decisions. The result of a previous query is
not a cursor, bound, or hint for the next one.

This is different from XOR cancellation. Cancellation combines every
input into one accumulator. Maximum-XOR lookup must choose the best
single stored key and therefore preserves the alternatives in an
index.

##### Worked walkthrough

Insert 5 (`0101`), 2 (`0010`), and 12 (`1100`). Then answer queries 6
(`0110`) and 15 (`1111`). Expected results are key 12 with XOR 10 and
key 2 with XOR 13.

Initial state: the trie root has no children, size is zero, and both
queries remain unresolved.

1. Decision: insert 5 by following bits `0,1,0,1` from position 3 to
   position 0, allocating each missing child and marking the leaf.
   After: path `0101` stores key 5; size is one.
   Known correct: leading zero position 3 is part of the fixed-width
   key, and one complete candidate is indexed.
2. Decision: insert 2 as `0010`. Reuse root child zero, branch at
   position 2, allocate the remaining path, and mark its leaf.
   After: paths `0010` and `0101` store keys 2 and 5; size is two.
   Known correct: the shared high-bit prefix is represented once while
   both complete candidates remain reachable.
3. Decision: insert 12 as `1100`. Root child one is absent, so
   allocate the complete path and terminal leaf.
   After: stored paths are `0010`, `0101`, and `1100`; size is three.
   Known correct: the trie contains exactly the candidate set and is
   ready for read-only maximum-XOR queries.
4. Decision: start query 6 (`0110`) at position 3. Its bit is zero, so
   prefer stored bit one. That child exists and contains key 12.
   After: chosen key prefix is `1`; XOR prefix is `1`; only key 12
   remains in the selected subtree.
   Known correct: this branch already contributes eight. Every key
   under stored prefix zero produces at most seven.
5. Decision: at position 2, query bit is one, so prefer stored bit
   zero. The key-12 subtree has no zero child, so follow its one
   child.
   After: chosen prefix is `11`; XOR prefix is `10`.
   Known correct: fallback is forced, and the optimal position-3 bit
   remains unchanged.
6. Decision: at position 1, query bit is one and opposite child zero
   exists. Follow it. At position 0, query bit is zero, opposite child
   one is absent, so follow equal child zero.
   After: reach key `1100`, decimal 12; XOR is `1010`, decimal 10.
   Known correct: all four positions are fixed, so return
   `(12,10,true)` for query 6.
7. Decision: restart at the root for query 15 (`1111`). At position 3,
   prefer stored zero, retaining keys 2 and 5. At position 2, prefer
   stored zero again, retaining only key 2. At position 1, opposite
   zero is absent, so follow one. At position 0, follow opposite zero.
   After: reach key `0010`, decimal 2; XOR is `1101`, decimal 13.
   Known correct: the four greedy decisions form the greatest
   available XOR prefix, so return `(2,13,true)`.
8. Decision: reinsert 5, try to insert 16, query -1, and query an
   independent empty trie. The duplicate reaches an existing leaf;
   16 fails range validation; -1 is an invalid query; the empty trie
   has no candidate.
   After: the original trie still stores `[2,5,12]`. The duplicate
   returns false, invalid insertion returns an error, and both failed
   lookups return `(0,0,false)`.
   Known correct: duplicate, invalid, and empty behavior cannot invent
   a candidate or disturb the three valid stored paths.
9. Decision: no operation remains, so stop.
   After: successful query results, in call order, are key 12 with XOR
   10 and key 2 with XOR 13.
   Known correct: every result came from the same three-key snapshot,
   and each call consumed exactly four bit positions.

Focused zero case: stored key zero is path `0000`, not the root.
Query 15 against only key zero returns key zero and XOR 15. Leading
zeros are data positions even when the numeric key is zero.

Focused singleton case: with only key 7, every valid query returns key
7. Opposite branches may be absent at several levels, but equal-branch
fallback always reaches the sole complete path.

Focused exact-value case: query 5 does not choose stored key 5 merely
because it is equal. Against `[2,5,12]`, key 5 gives XOR zero, key 2
gives seven, and key 12 gives nine. The result is key 12 with XOR
nine. The objective is greatest XOR, not exact membership or nearest
numeric value.

Focused invalid case: query 16 lies outside the four-bit range.
Returning `found=false` prevents the numeric zero placeholders from
being mistaken for a real key-zero result.

Counterexample to choosing the largest stored integer: for query 15,
largest key 12 produces `1111 XOR 1100 = 0011`, decimal three. Smaller
key 2 produces `1101`, decimal 13, and is the correct answer.

Counterexample to deciding from low bits first: for query 6, key 5
makes low bit zero differ and key 12 does not. Choosing key 5 for that
low-bit gain returns XOR three, while the high-bit-first path returns
XOR ten. A lost bit 3 cannot be repaired below it.

##### Implementation

The complete executable Go implementation lives in [A.9.3 Binary
tries for integer keys](
#a93-binary-tries-for-integer-keys). It is the single source of truth
for `binaryTrie`, `insert`, `maxXOR`, fixed-width validation, node
ownership, and exact output.

Run that program as documented there. Its `main` inserts 5, 2, and 12,
then executes the same queries 6 and 15 from this walkthrough. It also
exercises duplicate insertion, invalid insertion, invalid query, and
empty-trie behavior.

For a finite batch, an application adapter performs these steps:

```text
1. Validate every candidate and query against the same bit width.
2. If queries are empty, return an owned empty result.
3. If candidates are empty, reject a nonempty query batch.
4. Insert candidates; ignore duplicate false results, not errors.
5. Call maxXOR for each query in supplied order.
6. Store or stream each matched key and XOR value as required.
```

Validating the complete batch before construction gives an
all-or-error adapter. Calling `insert` directly instead gives an
incremental index: earlier successful insertions remain even if a
later independent insertion is invalid. Choose and document one
boundary behavior rather than implying rollback that the primitive
does not provide.

This application does not repeat the trie code. Keeping one primary
implementation prevents bit width, validation, fallback, ownership,
or empty-tree behavior from drifting between two copies.

##### Why it works

Insertion establishes the representation invariant. After processing
the high bits through position P, the current node represents exactly
the inserted key prefix through P. Following or creating the child
named by the next key bit extends that prefix correctly. After four
positions, the leaf represents the complete key.

Now consider a maximum-XOR query at some position P. Earlier choices
have already fixed the greatest available XOR prefix above P. If the
opposite-bit child exists, choosing it makes XOR bit P one. Choosing
the equal-bit child would make that bit zero.

A one at P contributes `2^P`. Every lower bit together contributes at
most `2^P-1`. No later choices can compensate for voluntarily choosing
zero at P when one is available. The opposite child is therefore a
safe greedy choice.

If the opposite child is absent, every stored key with the already
chosen prefix has the equal bit. Following that child is the only way
