to remain on a complete stored path, so fallback discards no better
candidate.

By induction from the most significant bit downward, every chosen
prefix is the greatest XOR prefix available among stored candidates.
After position zero, the path names one complete key and its full XOR
bit string is maximal. This proves both the matched key and returned
XOR value.

The returned key is unique among distinct stored keys because XOR by
one fixed query is reversible. Duplicates reach the same terminal path
and cannot create a second different answer.

Each insertion and query decreases the bit position from three to
zero exactly once, so both terminate. An empty-tree check runs before
traversal, and fallback always follows an existing child in a valid
nonempty subtree, so the query cannot fall off its path.

Queries perform no writes. Restarting each query at the root preserves
the trie invariant and makes results independent of call order while
the stored set remains unchanged.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let B be the fixed bit width, M the number of valid insertion
attempts, D the number of distinct stored keys, and Q the number of
valid queries. Building the trie examines B positions for each valid
attempt, including a duplicate, so it takes `Theta(MB)` time.
Answering Q queries takes `Theta(QB)` time. The complete valid
workload is
`Theta((M+Q)B)`.

The four-bit teaching implementation treats B as a constant, but
keeping B visible explains the work in a 32- or 64-bit version.
Invalid insertion or query validation is `Theta(1)` for the fixed
range and can return before path traversal.

At most one root plus `D*B` nodes are retained, so worst-case storage
is `O(D*B)`. Shared prefixes reduce the actual node count. Each
operation uses `O(1)` iterative auxiliary space beyond the retained
trie.

One query returns two integers and a Boolean, all `O(1)` output space.
If an application retains results for Q queries, its separate output
collection uses `Theta(Q)` space. Streaming results avoids that
collection but does not change query work.

A direct scan over D distinct candidates performs D XORs and
comparisons per query, taking `Theta(DQ)` time and `O(1)` retained
index space. For one query or a tiny candidate set, that simpler scan
may use less total work and memory because it avoids construction.

The trie becomes attractive when many queries amortize its
construction or when candidates arrive incrementally and future
queries should see them. Its pointer-rich nodes can consume much more
memory than the keys themselves. Packed node arrays or Patricia tries
can reduce pointer and unary-path overhead at the cost of more complex
updates and traversal.

A hash set gives expected constant-time exact membership but does not
group keys by significant bit prefixes. It still needs a scan to find
the maximum XOR partner. Sorting keys does not make XOR values
monotonic in numeric key order, so ordinary binary search does not
directly answer this objective.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- An empty trie has no candidate. Check size before traversal and use
  the found Boolean; `(0,0)` alone is also a valid key-zero answer.
- Key zero is a four-edge path `0000`. Treating leading zeros as no
  path destroys the fixed level-to-position meaning.
- Key 15 and query 15 are valid upper endpoints; 16 is excluded.
  Validate before shifting, indexing, or allocating nodes.
- Negative integers are outside this teaching contract. Signed right
  shift behavior and implicit sign extension must not leak into a
  fixed unsigned-key interpretation.
- Duplicate insertion must not increment distinct size or create a
  second terminal. Multiplicity does not improve a maximum.
- Prefer the opposite query bit, not stored bit one unconditionally.
  For query bit one, stored zero is the maximizing choice.
- Start at the most significant bit. Low-bit-first greed can sacrifice
  a larger bit for a smaller gain.
- Fall back to the equal child when the opposite child is absent.
  Absence means the current XOR bit must be zero, not that the whole
  query has failed.
- Traverse exactly B levels. Stopping at an internal prefix may return
  a value that was never inserted.
- Reconstruct the matched key from chosen stored bits. Reconstructing
  from XOR bits returns the score, not the candidate.
- Return both matched key and XOR value deliberately. Callers often
  need identity, and recomputing with the wrong query can hide an
  ordering bug.
- Do not choose the numerically greatest or nearest candidate. XOR
  order depends on differing bit positions, not ordinary distance.
- Do not carry the final node from one query into the next. Every
  independent query starts at the root.
- An insertion after earlier queries changes the candidate set for
  later queries. Build a complete immutable snapshot when all results
  must use the same set.
- Direct primitive insertions are not transactional as a batch.
  Prevalidate when an invalid later value must leave no partial index.
- Copying the trie value shares descendant pointers. Treat it as an
  owned structure rather than a deep-copyable scalar.
- A deletion-capable trie needs subtree counts before pruning shared
  prefixes. A terminal marker alone cannot prove a node is unused.
- This query chooses one key. It cannot maximize over XORs of
  arbitrary subsets; that different state space needs a linear basis.

##### When to choose it

Choose a binary trie for maximum-XOR lookup when:

- keys have one fixed, modest bit width;
- the candidate set is reused across many queries;
- the matched candidate or maximum XOR value is required;
- high-bit prefix sharing justifies retained index storage;
- incremental insertions should affect future lookups.

Network identifiers, compact feature codes, integer fingerprints, and
prefix-XOR values can produce this workload. Write down the width and
signedness before building the trie; those choices define every level.

Use a direct scan for one query, very few candidates, or a
memory-tight path where `Theta(D)` comparisons are acceptable. Use a
hash set when the only question is exact membership. Use sorting for
objectives monotonic in numeric order, not merely because the keys are
integers.

Use [XOR cancellation](
#b222-xor-cancellation-integer-accumulator) when all values should be
combined by parity rather than one partner selected. Use the later
[XOR linear basis](
#b226-xor-linear-basis-basis-array-advanced) when a query may choose
an arbitrary subset of stored values. The feasible outputs differ, so
these structures are not interchangeable optimizations.

For range-constrained queries such as "use only candidates at most
M," sort candidates and queries by M and incrementally insert only
eligible keys before each lookup. That offline layer changes the
application contract but not the trie query rule.

The foundational [binary-trie lesson](
#a93-binary-tries-for-integer-keys) remains the implementation owner.
NIST's Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures defines a [trie](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/trie.html) by shared prefixes. NIST
also defines [XOR](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/xor.html), and the Go specification
lists [bitwise XOR and shifts](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators) for integer operands.

#### B.22.5 Bitwise range aggregates (bit counts or segment tree)

##### Problem and contract

An immutable sequence of small integers receives many requests for
the bitwise AND, OR, and XOR of a contiguous range. Scanning every
requested value repeats the same per-bit work across overlapping
ranges.

For values `[13,10,7,8]`, displayed as low four-bit patterns:

```text
index:  0     1     2     3
value: 1101  1010  0111  1000
```

Range `[1,4)` contains 10, 7, and 8. Its AND is zero, its OR is 15,
and its XOR is 5. A static per-bit count index answers all three from
two stored boundaries instead of rescanning those values.

This lesson implements `bitCountRangeIndex` for immutable `[]uint8`
input. It uses eight storage positions, numbered zero through seven,
and half-open ranges `[start,end)`. Start is included; end is the
first excluded boundary.

Its contract is:

- nil, empty, and nonempty `[]uint8` inputs are valid;
- every `uint8` value contributes exactly eight bits, including high
  zeros;
- construction reads but does not retain or mutate the input slice;
- `aggregate(start,end)` accepts
  `0 <= start <= end <= len(values)`;
- the result contains the bitwise AND, OR, and XOR of exactly the
  values in that range;
- each duplicate occurrence contributes once at its original
  position;
- empty ranges return the eight-bit identities: AND 255, OR zero, and
  XOR zero;
- invalid boundaries return the zero aggregate and an error, never a
  partial result;
- a nil pointer or zero-value index returns an uninitialized-index
  error rather than panicking;
- the constructor rejects the theoretical size at which its extra
  boundary row would overflow `int`;
- allocation failure is outside the contract;
- the index owns its count rows and exposes no writable storage;
- queries perform no mutation, so concurrent read-only queries are
  safe after construction;
- each returned aggregate contains only scalar values and owns no
  shared storage.

The empty AND result is deliberate. Bitwise AND's identity for an
eight-bit value is all ones because `11111111 AND X == X`. OR and XOR
use all zeros as their identities. Another API may reject empty AND,
but it must say so rather than returning an unexplained zero.

Read [bit tests and population counts](
#b221-bit-tests-and-population-counts-integer-masks) first for bit
positions and masks. Read [prefix-sum arrays](
#a121-prefix-sum-arrays) for the boundary-prefix invariant. This
lesson stores eight prefix counts instead of one prefix sum.

##### Mental model

Treat each bit position as a separate sequence of zeros and ones. For
one position P, remember how many ones occur before every input
boundary:

```text
onesBefore[boundary][P]
    = number of values with bit P set in values[0:boundary]
```

Read `onesBefore[4][3] == 3` as: among the first four values, exactly
three have bit 3 set. The leading boundary zero contains eight zero
counts, just as an ordinary prefix-sum array starts with total zero.

For a query `[start,end)`, subtract the two counts at each position:

```text
onesInRange[P]
    = onesBefore[end][P] - onesBefore[start][P]
```

Let L be `end-start`, the number of values in the range, and C be the
ones count at one bit position. Three exact rules recover that result
bit:

```text
OR bit  = 1 exactly when C > 0
AND bit = 1 exactly when C == L
XOR bit = 1 exactly when C is odd
```

OR asks whether any range value has a one. AND asks whether every
range value has a one. XOR asks whether an odd number of ones survive
pair cancellation. Each rule depends only on C and L, so positions
can be reconstructed independently.

For an empty range, C and L are both zero at every position. The OR
test is false, the AND equality is true, and the XOR parity is even.
The ordinary rules therefore produce the three identities without a
special query branch.

The index row for the next boundary copies the preceding row, then
increments exactly the positions set in the next value. Construction
stops after every value has one row following it. A query stops after
all eight positions have been interpreted.

This static count method differs from storing prefix AND or prefix OR.
Neither operator has an inverse that can remove an earlier prefix.
Counts retain enough information to ask "none, all, or odd?" inside
an arbitrary range.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build an index for `[13,10,7,8]`, then query `[1,4)`. In low four-bit
form, the expected answer is AND `0000`, OR `1111`, and XOR `0101`.
High positions four through seven are zero in every input.

Write each count row as `[bit3,bit2,bit1,bit0]` for readability:

```text
boundary 0: [0,0,0,0]
boundary 1: [1,1,0,1]   after 1101
boundary 2: [2,1,1,1]   after 1010
boundary 3: [2,2,2,2]   after 0111
boundary 4: [3,2,2,2]   after 1000
```

Initial state: five eight-count rows are zero. Boundary zero correctly
describes the empty prefix; no input value or query bit is processed.

1. Decision: read value 13, `00001101`. Copy boundary-zero counts to
   boundary one, then increment positions zero, two, and three.
   After: low-bit count row one is `[1,1,0,1]` in displayed
   `[bit3,bit2,bit1,bit0]` order.
   Known correct: row one counts the set positions in exactly
   `values[0:1]`; later values remain unresolved.
2. Decision: read value 10, `00001010`. Copy row one and increment
   positions one and three.
   After: low-bit row two is `[2,1,1,1]`.
   Known correct: row two counts ones in values 13 and 10 without
   losing the earlier row needed by ranges starting at boundary one.
3. Decision: process value 7 by incrementing positions zero, one, and
   two, then process value 8 by incrementing position three.
   After: rows three and four are `[2,2,2,2]` and `[3,2,2,2]`.
   High-position counts remain zero in every row; construction stops.
   Known correct: every boundary now stores exact prefix counts for
   all eight positions.
4. Decision: validate `[1,4)`. Both boundaries lie in `[0,4]`, and
   start does not exceed end. Compute range length three, then
   initialize the result as the three operator identities.
   After: initialize result as AND `11111111`, OR `00000000`, and XOR
   `00000000`; no result bit has been finalized.
   Known correct: both prefix rows exist, and the initial values are
   the identities for all eight positions.
5. Decision: process bit zero. Subtract its row-one count from its
   row-four count, obtaining C equal to one. With L equal to three,
   some but not all values have a one, and the count is odd.
   After: AND is `11111110`, OR is `00000001`, and XOR is
   `00000001`.
   Known correct: result position zero is finalized as zero, one, and
   one for AND, OR, and XOR respectively.
6. Decision: process bit one with count two. It is positive, differs
   from length three, and is even.
   After: AND is `11111100`, OR is `00000011`, and XOR remains
   `00000001`.
   Known correct: bit one is zero for AND and XOR but one for OR;
   positions zero and one are final.
7. Decision: process bit two with count one.
   After: AND is `11111000`, OR is `00000111`, and XOR is
   `00000101`.
   Known correct: bit two is set in OR and XOR, while no later bit can
   change positions zero through two.
8. Decision: process bit three with count two, then positions four
   through seven with count zero. Every count differs from length
   three; bit three is positive and even; high counts are neither
   positive nor odd.
   After: AND is `00000000`, OR is `00001111`, and XOR is
   `00000101`.
   Known correct: all eight result positions now match the none, all,
   and odd-count rules.
9. Decision: all eight bit positions are processed, so return the
   aggregate.
   After: `[1,4)` returns AND zero, OR 15, and XOR 5.
   Known correct: the prefix differences cover exactly three requested
   values, and every output bit has been reconstructed once.

Focused full-range case: `[0,4)` subtracts boundary zero from boundary
four. Counts `[3,2,2,2]` produce AND zero, OR 15, and XOR 8. The odd
count at bit three is the only surviving XOR bit.

Focused singleton case: `[0,1)` has the same per-bit counts as value
13. AND, OR, and XOR all return 13, as every operator applied to one
value returns that value.

Focused empty case: `[2,2)` subtracts one row from itself. Every count
and the range length are zero, so it returns AND 255, OR zero, and XOR
zero.

Focused empty-input case: construction creates only boundary row zero.
Its sole valid query `[0,0)` returns the same three identities.

Focused invalid case: `[3,5)` exceeds the four-value end boundary. It
returns the zero aggregate and `errInvalidBitCountRange` before any
prefix row is indexed.

Counterexample to subtracting prefix OR values: for `[1,3]`, prefix OR
values are one and three. Range `[1,2)` contains only three and must
return OR three. Neither `3-1` nor `3 XOR 1` returns three. Per-bit
counts can remove the earlier contribution exactly.

Counterexample to using `C>0` for AND: range values `[0001,0000]` have
one set occurrence at bit zero, but their AND bit is zero because not
all two values contain it. Compare C with the full range length.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program builds the count index, queries ordinary,
full, singleton, empty, and invalid ranges, and propagates writer
failure. It uses only the standard library. Save it as `main.go` and
run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Bitwise range aggregates (bit
// counts or segment tree). Function comments connect each operation
// to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

const rangeBitWidth = 8

const maximumInt = int(^uint(0) >> 1)

var (
	errBitCountIndexTooLarge = errors.New(
		"bit-count index is too large",
	)
	errUninitializedBitCountIndex = errors.New(
		"bit-count index is uninitialized",
	)
	errInvalidBitCountRange = errors.New(
		"bit-count range is invalid",
	)
)

type bitwiseRangeAggregate struct {
	andValue uint8
	orValue  uint8
	xorValue uint8
}

type bitCountRangeIndex struct {
	onesBefore [][rangeBitWidth]int
}

func newBitCountRangeIndex(
	values []uint8,
) (*bitCountRangeIndex, error) {
	// Validate the request, then create the initial bit count range
	// index state.
	if len(values) == maximumInt {
		return nil, errBitCountIndexTooLarge
	}

	// Each row snapshots per-bit counts before one input boundary.
	onesBefore := make(
		[][rangeBitWidth]int,
		len(values)+1,
	)
	for valueIndex, value := range values {
		onesBefore[valueIndex+1] = onesBefore[valueIndex]
		for bitPosition := 0; bitPosition < rangeBitWidth; bitPosition++ {
			oneBit := uint8(1) << bitPosition
			if value&oneBit != 0 {
				onesBefore[valueIndex+1][bitPosition]++
			}
		}
	}
	return &bitCountRangeIndex{onesBefore: onesBefore}, nil
}

func (index *bitCountRangeIndex) aggregate(
	start int,
	end int,
) (bitwiseRangeAggregate, error) {
	// Keep aggregate in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if index == nil || len(index.onesBefore) == 0 {
		return bitwiseRangeAggregate{},
			errUninitializedBitCountIndex
	}
	valueCount := len(index.onesBefore) - 1
	if start < 0 || start > valueCount {
		return bitwiseRangeAggregate{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: start %d is outside [0, %d]",
			errInvalidBitCountRange,
			start,
			valueCount,
		)
	}
	if end < start || end > valueCount {
		return bitwiseRangeAggregate{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: end %d is outside [%d, %d]",
			errInvalidBitCountRange,
			end,
			start,
			valueCount,
		)
	}

	rangeLength := end - start
	result := bitwiseRangeAggregate{andValue: ^uint8(0)}
	// Zero, full, and odd counts decide OR, AND, and XOR bits.
	for bitPosition := 0; bitPosition < rangeBitWidth; bitPosition++ {
		onesInRange := index.onesBefore[end][bitPosition] -
			index.onesBefore[start][bitPosition]
		oneBit := uint8(1) << bitPosition
		if onesInRange > 0 {
			result.orValue |= oneBit
		}
		if onesInRange != rangeLength {
			result.andValue &^= oneBit
		}
		if onesInRange%2 == 1 {
			result.xorValue |= oneBit
		}
	}
	return result, nil
}

func formatRangeAggregate(
	label string,
	aggregate bitwiseRangeAggregate,
) string {
	// Use maintained boundaries to answer this range query.
	return fmt.Sprintf(
		"%s: AND=%08b OR=%08b XOR=%08b\n",
		label,
		aggregate.andValue,
		aggregate.orValue,
		aggregate.xorValue,
	)
}

func runBitwiseRangeExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Use maintained boundaries to answer this range query.
	index, err := newBitCountRangeIndex(
		[]uint8{0b1101, 0b1010, 0b0111, 0b1000},
	)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("build bit-count index: %w", err)
	}

	ranges := []struct {
		label string
		start int
		end   int
	}{
		{label: "range [1,4)", start: 1, end: 4},
		{label: "full [0,4)", start: 0, end: 4},
		{label: "single [0,1)", start: 0, end: 1},
		{label: "empty [2,2)", start: 2, end: 2},
	}
	for _, requestedRange := range ranges {
		aggregate, err := index.aggregate(
			requestedRange.start,
			requestedRange.end,
		)
		if err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"aggregate %s: %w",
				requestedRange.label,
				err,
			)
		}
		if _, err := io.WriteString(
			output,
			formatRangeAggregate(
				requestedRange.label,
				aggregate,
			),
		); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("write range aggregate: %w", err)
		}
	}

	_, invalidErr := index.aggregate(3, 5)
	if !errors.Is(invalidErr, errInvalidBitCountRange) {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"expected invalid-range error: %w",
			invalidErr,
		)
	}
	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"invalid rejected = %t\n",
		invalidErr != nil,
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write invalid result: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runBitwiseRangeExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
range [1,4): AND=00000000 OR=00001111 XOR=00000101
full [0,4): AND=00000000 OR=00001111 XOR=00001000
single [0,1): AND=00001101 OR=00001101 XOR=00001101
empty [2,2): AND=11111111 OR=00000000 XOR=00000000
invalid rejected = true
```

##### Why it works

For each boundary B and bit position P, maintain this construction
invariant:

```text
onesBefore[B][P]
    equals the number of set P bits in values[0:B]
```

Boundary zero contains no values and every count is zero, so the
invariant holds initially. To construct row B plus one, copy row B.
If `values[B]` has bit P set, increment that position once; otherwise
leave it unchanged. The new row therefore counts exactly the extended
prefix. Induction proves every stored row.

For valid `[start,end)`, the end count includes ones before start and
inside the requested range. The start count contains exactly the
earlier shared ones. Their difference is therefore the exact count C
inside the range. Boundary validation proves both rows exist before
either is read.

At one bit position, OR is one exactly when at least one operand bit
is one, so `C>0` is necessary and sufficient. AND is one exactly when
all L operand bits are one, so `C==L` is exact. XOR toggles once per
one operand and returns one exactly after an odd number of toggles, so
odd C is exact.

The implementation starts from each operator's identity and applies
those predicates independently at all eight positions. Reassembling
the decided bits therefore gives the exact word-level AND, OR, and
XOR of the range.

When the range is empty, C and L are both zero. The same proof yields
false for OR, true for AND, and false for XOR at every position. Those
are precisely the declared identities; no exception weakens the
invariant.

Construction advances once per input value and its inner loop advances
through exactly eight positions. A query also advances through exactly
eight positions. Both finite bounds prove termination.

Each count is between zero and N, where N is input length and already
fits `int`. The extra-boundary guard prevents `N+1` from overflowing
the allocation length. Count increments and prefix subtraction
therefore stay within `int`.

The constructor stores only new count rows and no reference to the
input slice. Queries read those immutable rows and return scalar
copies, establishing the ownership and concurrent-read guarantees.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of values, B the bit width, Q the number of
queries, and L the length of one requested range. Here B is fixed at
eight.

Construction copies and possibly increments B counts for each value,
taking `Theta(NB)` time. It retains N plus one rows of B `int` counts,
using `Theta(NB)` space. A query subtracts and interprets B counts, so
best, average, and worst successful time are all `Theta(B)` with
`O(1)` auxiliary space and `O(1)` scalar output.

Under the fixed eight-bit contract, those bounds simplify to
`Theta(N)` build time and space and `Theta(1)` query time. Across Q
queries, total work is `Theta(NB+QB)`.

A direct scan takes `Theta(L)` time per range and `O(1)` retained
index space. It can be preferable for one short query. Across many
long or overlapping ranges, the prefix index replaces repeated value
visits with a fixed eight-position query.

If only XOR is requested, one prefix XOR word per boundary is smaller.
Because `X^X==0`, range XOR is
`xorBefore[end]^xorBefore[start]`. AND and OR do not have a comparable
inverse, which is why the shared three-result index stores per-bit
counts.

The count representation grows with bit width. With 64-bit keys and
machine-sized counts, each boundary stores 64 integers before slice or
allocator overhead. If N has a proven smaller limit, narrower count
types can save space, but construction must validate that counts
cannot overflow them.

One point replacement can change a bit count in every later boundary
row, costing `Theta((N-index)B)` to repair. Rebuilding takes
`Theta(NB)`. Static prefix counts are a poor fit when updates and
queries interleave.

For dynamic data, a [segment tree](#a124-segment-trees) can store an
AND, OR, and XOR triple at every node. Combine children component by
component using the corresponding associative operator. Construction
and retained storage are `Theta(N)`; point updates and range queries
take `O(log N)` time. Its identities are all ones for AND and zero for
OR and XOR.

The segment tree uses more navigation per static query but avoids
rewriting all later prefixes after one update. A static sparse table
can also answer idempotent AND and OR ranges. Idempotent means that
combining X with X still returns X. XOR is not idempotent because
`X^X` is zero instead.

The example runner performs four valid queries, one invalid query,
formats five lines, and propagates writer failure. Its demonstration
work is constant.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input builds one all-zero prefix row. Only `[0,0)` is valid,
  and it returns AND 255, OR zero, and XOR zero.
- Empty range `[K,K)` is valid for every boundary K. Initializing AND
  to zero would return the wrong identity; start it at all eight ones.
- Full range `[0,N)` uses boundary zero and boundary N. End N is
  valid even though N is not an element index.
- End N plus one is invalid. Validate before indexing; the prefix
  slice's N plus one rows represent boundaries zero through N only.
- Start greater than end is invalid, not another empty range. Do not
  reorder or clamp caller boundaries.
- Nil and zero-value indexes have no constructed leading row. Return
  `errUninitializedBitCountIndex` rather than subtracting from nil.
- Invalid calls return the zero aggregate. Always inspect the error;
  zero is also a valid AND, OR, and XOR result for some nonempty data.
- Values zero and 255 are ordinary inputs. Zero increments no counts;
  255 increments all eight positions.
- Duplicate values increment counts once per occurrence. Deduplicating
  `[1,1]` changes its XOR from zero to one.
- OR uses `C>0`, not `C==1`. Two or more ones still produce an OR bit
  of one.
- AND uses `C==L`, not `C>0`. One missing bit makes the range AND bit
  zero.
- XOR uses odd parity, not merely nonzero count. Two equal one bits
  cancel at that position.
- Keep bit positions and value indices separate. `onesBefore[B][P]`
  selects boundary B first and bit position P second.
- Copy the previous row before incrementing. Starting each row at zero
  would store only one value's bits rather than prefix counts.
- Store a leading boundary row. Without it, ranges starting at zero
  need a fragile index-minus-one branch.
- Do not subtract prefix AND or OR words. The `[1,3]` counterexample
  shows that earlier contributions cannot be removed that way.
- Use an unsigned fixed-width value type. Signed shifts and implicit
  sign bits change which positions are considered part of the word.
- Prefix counts are immutable snapshots. Mutating the original input
  after construction does not update the index, and no update method
  is provided.
- Concurrent queries are safe only after successful construction.
  Adding mutable update methods would require synchronization or a
  new concurrency contract.

##### When to choose it

Choose per-bit prefix counts when:

- values are immutable after preprocessing;
- bit width is small and fixed;
- many arbitrary ranges ask for AND, OR, XOR, or bit frequencies;
- `Theta(NB)` retained count storage fits the memory budget;
- constant work in range length matters more than update support.

The same rows can answer how many range values contain a flag, whether
every value contains it, or how many bit positions meet a threshold.
Keep those application rules separate from the stored count invariant.

Use a direct scan for a small sequence, one query, or tight memory.
Use one prefix XOR array when XOR is the only aggregate. Use ordinary
prefix sums when values themselves are added rather than their bit
positions counted.

Use the foundational [segment-tree lesson](
#a124-segment-trees) when point updates and associative range queries
interleave. Store the exact aggregate tuple the workload needs. Use a
[lazy segment tree](#a126-lazy-segment-trees) when one update changes
a whole range and its effect can be propagated safely.

Use [static range minima](#b65-static-range-minima-sparse-table) as a
model for immutable idempotent queries. AND and OR are idempotent;
XOR is not, so overlapping sparse-table blocks cannot be combined for
XOR without accounting for duplicates.

The [prefix-sum lesson](#a121-prefix-sum-arrays) owns the boundary
subtraction invariant, while [bit tests](
#b221-bit-tests-and-population-counts-integer-masks) own single-word
position semantics. This lesson combines the two without replacing
either owner.

Algorithms for Competitive Programming documents the general
[segment tree](
https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/segment_tree.html),
including point updates and range queries. The Go specification
defines [AND, OR, XOR, AND NOT, and shifts](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators) for integer operands.

#### B.22.6 XOR linear basis (basis array, advanced)

##### Problem and contract

Given several fixed-width integers, consider every value obtainable by
XORing an arbitrary subset. Enumerating all subsets takes exponential
time. Many inputs may also be redundant: one value can already equal
the XOR of others and add no new result.

For values 10, 5, and 6:

```text
empty subset       0000 = 0
10                 1010 = 10
5                  0101 = 5
6                  0110 = 6
10 XOR 5           1111 = 15
10 XOR 6           1100 = 12
5 XOR 6            0011 = 3
10 XOR 5 XOR 6     1001 = 9
```

The maximum is 15, produced by a two-value subset. A binary trie that
chooses one stored key cannot answer this different question. An XOR
linear basis compresses the complete reachable set into at most one
independent vector per bit position.

This lesson implements an eight-bit `xorLinearBasis`. It treats every
`uint8` as a vector of eight zero-or-one coordinates. Its contract is:

- the zero value of `xorLinearBasis` is an empty, ready-to-use basis;
- `insert(value)` mutates the basis and returns true exactly when the
  value increases its rank;
- zero, duplicates, and any value already representable by existing
  vectors return false and leave the basis unchanged;
- every `uint8` value is valid, so insertion returns no error;
- `canRepresent(target)` reports whether some subset of all inserted
  values XORs to the target;
- `maximumSubsetXOR()` returns the greatest reachable unsigned value;
- the empty subset is allowed, so an empty basis returns zero;
- `rank` is the number of independent stored vectors and lies in
  `[0,8]`;
- `distinctXORCount()` returns the exact `2^rank` reachable-value
  count; `int` is sufficient because rank is at most eight here;
- multiplicity does not change the reachable set after a value is
  dependent, although it changes how many original subsets produce a
  result;
- queries return values and membership facts, not the original subset
  that witnesses them;
- `vectorsDescending()` is a display helper that returns an owned
  slice ordered by decreasing pivot position;
- displayed basis vectors may depend on insertion order and are not a
  canonical representation;
- copying the struct copies its fixed array, so later mutations of the
  copy and original are independent;
- insertion requires exclusive access, while copied or settled bases
  may be queried concurrently when no goroutine mutates them;
- a nil basis pointer is outside every method contract.

All inputs are unsigned. A wider `uint32` or `uint64` basis uses the
same method with 32 or 64 pivot slots. A full-rank 64-bit basis has
`2^64` distinct values, which does not fit `int`; a wider version
needs `math/big`, saturation, or an explicit overflow result for that
count.

Signed ordering would change the meaning of "maximum", so signed
values need a separately stated comparison contract.

Read [XOR cancellation](
#b222-xor-cancellation-integer-accumulator) first for XOR's identity,
self-cancellation, commutativity, and associativity. Read [bit tests](
#b221-bit-tests-and-population-counts-integer-masks) for fixed-width
position operations.

##### Mental model

The field GF(2) contains only scalars zero and one. Adding one-bit
coordinates modulo two is XOR. Multiplying a vector by zero omits it;
multiplying by one includes it. A linear combination over GF(2) is
therefore exactly the XOR of some subset.

The span of inserted values is the set of every reachable subset XOR.
A value is independent when it is not already in that span. A basis
is an independent collection with the same span as all inserted
values. Its size is called the rank.

The implementation stores basis vectors in an array indexed by pivot
position:

```text
vectorByPivot[P]
    = zero, or one vector whose highest set bit is P
```

Read `vectorByPivot[3] == 1010` as: this basis has one vector whose
highest one is bit 3, and it may be used to clear or toggle that bit.
No stored vector has a one above its own pivot.

Insertion resembles binary Gaussian elimination. Start with the new
value as a remainder and inspect positions from seven down to zero:

- if the remainder has zero at the position, continue;
- if its bit is one and that pivot slot is occupied, XOR the stored
  vector to clear the bit;
- if its bit is one and the pivot slot is empty, store the remainder
  there and increase rank;
- if every bit clears, the original value was already representable.

XORing an occupied pivot does not discard possibilities. It replaces
the remainder by the remainder XOR one already reachable vector. The
old and new remainders can each reconstruct the other using that same
vector.

Representability uses the same reduction without mutation. A target
that reaches zero is a combination of basis vectors. If its highest
remaining one has no pivot vector, lower pivots cannot clear it, so
the target is unreachable.

Maximum subset XOR uses another high-to-low pass. Start at zero. At
each pivot, compare the current result with the result XOR the pivot
vector. Keep the numerically larger value. That comparison fixes the
highest bit where the two candidates differ, and lower pivots cannot
change already fixed higher positions.

Basis vectors need not be original input values. They are reachable
XOR combinations chosen to preserve the span. This is compression of
possibilities, not selection of representative input records.

##### Worked walkthrough

Insert 10 (`1010`), 5 (`0101`), 6 (`0110`), and 3 (`0011`) into an
eight-bit basis. Then test targets 12 and 1 and find the maximum
subset XOR. The expected basis vectors are `[10,5,3]`, rank is three,
target 12 is reachable, target 1 is not, and the maximum is 15.

Only low four bits are displayed because every example value is below
16. Pivot positions still range from seven through zero.

Initial state: all eight pivot slots are zero, rank is zero, and only
the empty subset XOR zero is reachable.

1. Decision: insert 10, remainder `1010`. Positions seven through four
   are zero. Bit three is one and pivot three is empty, so store 10
   there and increment rank.
   After: pivot three stores `1010`; rank is one.
   Known correct: reachable values are zero and 10, and the stored
   vector's highest one is exactly its pivot.
2. Decision: insert 5, remainder `0101`. Bit three is zero. Bit two is
   one and pivot two is empty, so store 5.
   After: pivots three and two store `1010` and `0101`; rank is two.
   Known correct: 5 was not in span `{0,10}`, and combinations of the
   two pivots produce exactly `{0,10,5,15}`.
3. Decision: insert 6, remainder `0110`. Bit two is one and pivot two
   stores `0101`, so XOR them: `0110 XOR 0101 = 0011`. Bit one is now
   the highest one and pivot one is empty, so store the remainder.
   After: pivots three, two, and one store `1010`, `0101`, and
   `0011`; rank is three.
   Known correct: stored vector 3 equals reachable combination
   `6 XOR 5`; adding it expands the span without losing value 6.
4. Decision: insert 3, remainder `0011`. Pivot one already stores
   `0011`, so XORing clears the remainder to zero.
   After: insertion returns false; basis and rank remain unchanged.
   Known correct: input 3 is already represented by `6 XOR 5`, so it
   cannot create a ninth distinct XOR value.
5. Decision: test target 12, remainder `1100`. At pivot three, XOR
   `1010` to obtain `0110`. At pivot two, XOR `0101` to obtain
   `0011`. At pivot one, XOR `0011` to reach zero.
   After: `canRepresent(12)` returns true; the basis is unchanged.
   Known correct: the reduction records that 12 lies in the span; in
   original values, `10 XOR 6 = 12` is one witness.
6. Decision: test target 1, remainder `0001`. Its highest one is at
   pivot zero, whose slot is empty.
   After: `canRepresent(1)` returns false; the basis is unchanged.
   Known correct: no lower pivot exists to clear bit zero, and using a
   higher pivot would introduce a higher one that cannot cancel.
7. Decision: maximize from result zero. At pivot three, candidate
   `0000 XOR 1010 = 1010` is larger, so keep 10. At pivot two,
   `1010 XOR 0101 = 1111` is larger, so keep 15. At pivot one,
   `1111 XOR 0011 = 1100` is smaller, so keep 15. Empty slots change
   nothing.
   After: `maximumSubsetXOR()` returns 15.
   Known correct: each accepted comparison fixed the best available
   prefix, and 15 is produced by original subset `{10,5}`.
8. Decision: count three independent zero-or-one choices.
   After: `distinctXORCount()` returns `2^3`, or eight.
   Known correct: independent basis choices cannot collide, even
   though four original values define 16 subsets with duplicate XOR
   results.
9. Decision: no operation remains, so stop.
   After: basis vectors in decreasing pivot order are `[10,5,3]`, rank
   is three, and all query results are final.
   Known correct: every mutation and query inspected at most eight
   decreasing pivot positions.

Focused empty case: an empty basis has rank zero and one reachable
value, zero. It represents zero, does not represent one, and returns
zero as the maximum because the empty subset is permitted.

Focused zero case: inserting zero examines all positions, stores
nothing, and returns false. Zero was already reachable through the
empty subset.

Focused duplicate case: inserting 7 twice stores it once. The second
copy reduces against the same pivot to zero. Multiplicity creates more
original subset choices but no new XOR value.

Focused full-rank case: inserting unit values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64,
and 128 fills every pivot. Rank eight yields 256 distinct byte values,
and the maximum is 255.

Focused copy case: copy a basis containing value 2, then insert 1 only
into the copy. The copy represents 1 and reaches maximum 3; the
original still represents only zero and 2 because its array was copied
by value.

Counterexample to XORing every input: `10 XOR 5 XOR 6 = 9`, but the
maximum subset XOR is 15 from `{10,5}`. The objective chooses a
subset, not necessarily the full collection.

Counterexample to a maximum-XOR trie: querying zero against stored
keys 10, 5, and 6 chooses the greatest single key, 10. The basis may
combine 10 and 5 to reach 15. One-key and subset-choice contracts have
different feasible results.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs the walkthrough and propagates
writer failure. The basis uses only a fixed array and scalar state.
Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates XOR linear basis (basis array,
// advanced). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

const xorBasisWidth = 8

type xorLinearBasis struct {
	vectorByPivot [xorBasisWidth]uint8
	rank          int
}

func (basis *xorLinearBasis) insert(value uint8) bool {
	// Add the requested item while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	remainder := value
	// Clear occupied pivots until a new pivot or zero remains.
	for pivot := xorBasisWidth - 1; pivot >= 0; pivot-- {
		oneBit := uint8(1) << pivot
		if remainder&oneBit == 0 {
			continue
		}
		if basis.vectorByPivot[pivot] == 0 {
			basis.vectorByPivot[pivot] = remainder
			basis.rank++
			return true
		}
		remainder ^= basis.vectorByPivot[pivot]
	}
	return false
}

func (basis *xorLinearBasis) canRepresent(target uint8) bool {
	// Evaluate can represent without changing the maintained state.
	remainder := target
	// Use each matching pivot to clear the highest remaining one.
	for pivot := xorBasisWidth - 1; pivot >= 0; pivot-- {
		oneBit := uint8(1) << pivot
		if remainder&oneBit == 0 {
			continue
		}
		vector := basis.vectorByPivot[pivot]
		if vector == 0 {
			return false
		}
		remainder ^= vector
	}
	return true
}

func (basis *xorLinearBasis) maximumSubsetXOR() uint8 {
	// Compute subset xor from the state without mutating it.
	result := uint8(0)
	// A larger candidate improves the first bit where it differs.
	for pivot := xorBasisWidth - 1; pivot >= 0; pivot-- {
		candidate := result ^ basis.vectorByPivot[pivot]
		if candidate > result {
			result = candidate
		}
	}
	return result
}

func (basis *xorLinearBasis) distinctXORCount() int {
	// Keep distinct xor count in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return 1 << basis.rank
}

func (basis *xorLinearBasis) vectorsDescending() []uint8 {
	// Keep vectors descending in one helper so callers use one rule.
	vectors := make([]uint8, 0, basis.rank)
	for pivot := xorBasisWidth - 1; pivot >= 0; pivot-- {
		vector := basis.vectorByPivot[pivot]
		if vector != 0 {
			vectors = append(vectors, vector)
		}
	}
	return vectors
}

func runXORBasisExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute xor basis examples to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	var basis xorLinearBasis
	inserted10 := basis.insert(10)
	inserted5 := basis.insert(5)
	inserted6 := basis.insert(6)
	inserted3 := basis.insert(3)

	text := fmt.Sprintf(
		"insert 10 = %t\n"+
			"insert 5 = %t\n"+
			"insert 6 = %t\n"+
			"insert 3 = %t\n"+
			"basis vectors = %v\n"+
			"rank = %d\n"+
			"distinct XOR values = %d\n"+
			"represent 12 = %t\n"+
			"represent 1 = %t\n"+
			"maximum subset XOR = %d\n",
		inserted10,
		inserted5,
		inserted6,
		inserted3,
		basis.vectorsDescending(),
		basis.rank,
		basis.distinctXORCount(),
		basis.canRepresent(12),
		basis.canRepresent(1),
		basis.maximumSubsetXOR(),
	)
	if _, err := io.WriteString(output, text); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write XOR-basis results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runXORBasisExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Expected output:

```text
insert 10 = true
insert 5 = true
insert 6 = true
insert 3 = false
basis vectors = [10 5 3]
rank = 3
distinct XOR values = 8
represent 12 = true
represent 1 = false
maximum subset XOR = 15
```

##### Why it works

Maintain three invariants after every insertion:

- each nonzero slot P contains a vector whose highest set bit is P;
- stored vectors are independent;
- their span equals the span of every value inserted so far.

All slots are initially zero. The empty stored collection is
independent, and both its span and the empty input span contain only
zero, so the invariants hold.

During insertion, XORing the remainder with a stored vector clears its
highest occupied pivot. The new remainder equals the original value
XOR a combination of existing basis vectors. Therefore the original
value is reachable from the basis plus remainder exactly when the
remainder is reachable from the basis plus original value. Reduction
preserves the span that would result from insertion.

Each XOR clears the current highest one and introduces no higher one
because the stored vector has no bit above its pivot. The scan moves
strictly downward and therefore terminates.

If reduction reaches zero, the original value is a combination of
existing vectors. Adding it would not enlarge the span, so returning
false preserves all three invariants.

Otherwise the remainder reaches an empty pivot P. Existing vectors
with lower pivots cannot produce bit P. A combination using any higher
pivot has a highest selected pivot that cannot cancel because pivot
positions are unique. The remainder is therefore independent. Storing
it at P preserves the pivot invariant and adds exactly one independent
dimension. Because the original value and remainder differ only by
old basis vectors, the enlarged basis has exactly the enlarged input
span.

Representability repeats the same reductions. If a target reaches
zero, reversing the XOR steps expresses it as a subset XOR of basis
vectors and therefore of inserted values. If a highest remaining bit
has no pivot, the independence argument shows no combination can clear
it. The Boolean result is exact.

For maximization, process pivots from high to low. Before pivot P, the
current result has the greatest reachable prefix above P. XORing the
pivot-P vector changes no higher bit, so both the current value and
candidate preserve that optimal prefix. Their numeric comparison
chooses the better bit P and any accompanying lower bits. Lower pivot
vectors cannot later alter position P or above. Induction proves the
final result is the greatest value in the span.

With rank R, every basis vector has an independent coefficient choice:
zero means omit it and one means include it. There are `2^R` choices.
If two choices produced the same XOR, XORing those equations would
give a nonempty basis combination equal to zero, contradicting
independence. All `2^R` results are therefore distinct.

The fixed array stores no caller references. Read methods access it
without mutation. An ordinary struct assignment copies the array, so
pointer-receiver insertion mutates only the selected basis object.
These facts establish the ownership behavior.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let B be bit width, M the number of insertions, Q the number of
representability queries, and R the final rank. Here B is eight and
`0 <= R <= B`.

An insertion may store at the first inspected pivot in `Theta(1)`
best-case time or scan all B positions in `Theta(B)` worst-case time.
Its average depends on input values and insertion order and is
`O(B)`. A representability query may fail in `Theta(1)` best-case time
or scan B slots in `Theta(B)` worst-case time. Its average likewise
depends on queries and the basis and is `O(B)`. Maximum subset XOR
always scans B slots and takes `Theta(B)` time. `distinctXORCount`
takes `Theta(1)` time. Building from M values and answering Q
representability queries takes `O(MB+QB)` total time.

The basis retains exactly B byte slots plus rank, using `Theta(B)`
space. Insert, representability, and maximization use `O(1)` auxiliary
space. Under the fixed eight-bit contract, all single operations take
`Theta(1)` bounded work and retained storage is constant.

`vectorsDescending` scans B slots and returns R bytes, taking
`Theta(B)` time, `O(1)` auxiliary space, and `Theta(R)` output space.
Copying the basis takes `Theta(B)` work and storage in a generalized
width model.

Brute-force subset enumeration visits `2^M` subsets and performs up to
M XORs per subset without incremental reuse. Even an incremental
enumerator must produce exponentially many results. The basis reduces
construction to `O(MB)` when only span questions, rank, or an optimum
are needed.

Compression loses provenance. Returning the original indices for a
target or optimum requires tracking how each basis vector was formed.
For small M, a bit mask per pivot can record witnesses; for large M,
that adds storage and XOR work proportional to the provenance width.

The basis supports insertion naturally but not deletion. Removing one
input may invalidate a vector assembled from several inputs. Offline
deletion workloads may use rebuilding, rollback with time intervals,
or a segment tree of bases, each with a more complex contract.

A fully reduced canonical basis is useful for sorted or K-th XOR
queries. This implementation keeps only row-echelon form: unique
highest pivots with lower bits allowed. That is sufficient for
insertion, representability, rank, distinct-count, and maximum
queries, but insertion order may change displayed vectors.

The example runner performs four insertions, three queries, formats
ten lines, and propagates writer failure. Its work is constant.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty basis represents zero through the empty subset. Returning
  false for target zero forgets the additive identity.
- Inserting zero returns false and does not increase rank. Zero is
  already the XOR of no vectors.
- A duplicate value is dependent, but dependence is broader than
  duplication. In the walkthrough, 3 is dependent because `5^6=3`.
- All-zero input has rank zero and maximum zero. If a nonempty witness
  is required, that is a separate output contract.
- One nonzero value V gives rank one, reachable values `{0,V}`, and
  maximum V.
- Rank cannot exceed B. Incrementing it for a zero remainder can make
  `1<<rank` claim impossible distinct values.
- Scan pivots from most significant to least significant. Low-first
  reduction does not establish the highest-pivot echelon invariant
  used by representability and maximization.
- Store the reduced remainder, not the original input. Storing 6 at
  pivot one in the walkthrough would violate the claim that pivot one
  is its highest set bit.
- XOR with an occupied pivot instead of overwriting it. Overwriting
  can lose an independent direction already needed by the span.
- An empty pivot at the highest remainder bit means insertion is done.
  Continuing to reduce with lower vectors cannot clear that bit.
- `canRepresent` must not mutate the basis. Use a local remainder and
  read the stored vectors without changing them.
- Maximum subset XOR begins at zero because the empty subset is valid.
  Beginning at an arbitrary input can exclude better combinations.
- Compare `result^vector` with result. Unconditionally XORing every
  basis vector computes one combination, not necessarily the maximum.
- Numeric maximization uses unsigned order. Reusing this code with a
  signed type changes the meaning of the top bit.
- Internal vectors are not necessarily original inputs or canonical.
  Do not expose them as witnesses or compare snapshots across
  insertion orders.
- `2^rank` counts distinct XOR values, not original subsets. Dependent
  inputs make several subsets collide on the same result.
- Copying this array-backed basis is independent. A slice-backed basis
  would share storage and need an explicit deep-copy contract.
- Concurrent read-only queries are safe only while no insertion writes
  the same object. Synchronize mutation or query an immutable copy.
- This implementation cannot return which original values form a
  target. Add provenance deliberately rather than trying to infer it
  from transformed vectors.

##### When to choose it

Choose an XOR linear basis when:

- any subset of fixed-width values may be selected;
- the task asks for maximum subset XOR, representability, or rank;
- many original values may be linearly dependent under XOR;
- bit width is small enough for one pivot slot per position;
- exponential subset enumeration is infeasible;
- witness indices and deletions are not required, or their extra state
  is explicitly designed.

Maximum subset XOR, reachable toggle states, parity-equation rank, and
counting distinct subset XOR results have this shape. Translate the
problem to "which XOR combinations are reachable?" before choosing
the structure.

Use plain [XOR cancellation](
#b222-xor-cancellation-integer-accumulator) when every input must be
folded and only parity multiplicity matters. A basis preserves all
subset choices rather than one combined signature.

Use a [maximum-XOR trie](
#b224-maximum-xor-queries-binary-trie) when each query must choose one
stored key. A trie returns an input key; a basis may return a value
formed from several inputs and does not identify them.

Use [subset enumeration](#b194-subset-enumeration-bitmasks) when N is
small and every subset itself must be inspected or returned. A basis
answers algebraic properties without listing all `2^N` combinations.

Use ordinary Gaussian elimination when equations need arbitrary field
coefficients, multiple right-hand sides, or explicit solution vectors.
The pivot idea is shared, but this implementation is specialized to
bit vectors whose addition is XOR and whose coefficients are zero or
one.

Princeton's linear algebra appendix explains [bit vectors over F2](
https://theory.cs.princeton.edu/complexity/ab_appendixchap.pdf), XOR
addition, span, independence, basis, and dimension. Alex Li's
algorithm reference documents the [XOR basis operations](
https://algorithms.alexli.ca/xor-basis/) used here. The Go
specification defines [bitwise XOR and shifts](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Arithmetic_operators) for integer operands.

### B.23 Streaming and data-structure design

#### B.23.1 Running statistics (counters)

##### Problem and contract

A stream may be too large, too slow, or too transient to retain every
measurement. Callers may still need its count, mean, variance,
minimum, and maximum after each arrival. Recomputing from all earlier
values takes growing time and requires preserving the history.

For the stream `[2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9]`, the final count is eight, mean is
five, minimum is two, maximum is nine, population variance is four,
and sample variance is `32/7`. A running accumulator updates those
facts from a fixed amount of state per value.

This lesson implements `runningStatistics` for `float64` values. Its
contract is:

- the zero value is an empty, ready-to-use accumulator;
- `add(value)` accepts one finite value and updates all statistics;
- values may be positive, negative, zero, repeated, or unordered;
- NaN and either infinity return `errNonFiniteRunningValue` before
  mutation;
- a finite value whose update produces a non-finite intermediate or
  result returns `errNonFiniteRunningResult` without mutation;
- count is exact through `2^53`, the largest consecutive integer this
  implementation converts exactly to `float64` during division;
- adding beyond that limit returns `errRunningStatisticsLimit`
  without mutation;
- `snapshot()` returns count, mean, minimum, maximum, population
  variance, and sample-variance availability for the current prefix;
- an empty snapshot returns `errEmptyRunningStatistics`;
- population variance divides the corrected squared-deviation total
  by N and is available for every nonempty stream;
- sample variance divides by `N-1` and is available only when N is at
  least two;
- when sample variance is unavailable, its field is zero and
  `hasSampleVariance` is false; callers must inspect the flag;
- a snapshot error returns the zero snapshot, whose fields must be
  ignored;
- results are IEEE 754 binary64 approximations, not exact real
  arithmetic, and input order may change low-order rounded bits;
- snapshots contain only scalars and share no mutable storage;
- a nil receiver returns `errNilRunningStatistics`;
- methods do not synchronize access; concurrent mutation or a query
  racing with mutation is outside the contract;
- the accumulator does not retain inputs and provides no deletion,
  window, merge, or witness operation.

The first value initializes both extrema. This avoids using zero or
infinity as a sentinel that could incorrectly constrain valid data.

Read [prefix-sum arrays](#a121-prefix-sum-arrays) first for a simpler
running invariant. A prefix array retains every boundary to answer
past range queries. This accumulator retains only the current prefix
summary and cannot revisit an earlier boundary.

##### Mental model

Remember five facts after N accepted values:

```text
count = N
mean = arithmetic mean of the N values
sumSquaredDifferences = sum of (value - mean)^2 over the N values
minimum = least accepted value
maximum = greatest accepted value
```

The long third name is often shortened to M2. Read
`sumSquaredDifferences == 32` as: measured around the current mean,
the accepted values have a total squared deviation of 32. It is not
the variance yet; the requested variance chooses its divisor later.

For a new value X after N values, Welford's update is:

```text
nextCount = N + 1
deltaBeforeMean = X - mean
nextMean = mean + deltaBeforeMean / nextCount
deltaAfterMean = X - nextMean
nextM2 = M2 + deltaBeforeMean * deltaAfterMean
```

The first delta measures X from the old center. Moving the mean toward
X changes that distance, so the second delta measures X from the new
center. Their product is exactly the correction needed to transform
the old squared-deviation total into the new one in real arithmetic.

When N is zero, there is no old mean or extremum. Store the first
value as mean, minimum, and maximum, set count to one, and leave M2 at
zero. Later updates compare X with the stored extrema.

A snapshot derives both variance meanings from the same M2:

```text
population variance = M2 / N
sample variance = M2 / (N - 1), when N >= 2
```

Population variance describes the values as the whole population.
Sample variance uses Bessel's correction when these values are a
sample used to estimate a larger population's variance. The caller,
not the accumulator, decides which meaning matches the data.

Keeping `sum(value*value)` and subtracting `mean*mean` looks simpler,
but it subtracts large nearly equal floating-point values when the
spread is small relative to the values. Welford's centered update
usually loses less information. It still rounds and can overflow, so
the implementation states and checks those limits rather than calling
the result exact.

Each call performs a fixed sequence of checks and arithmetic. There
is no input-dependent loop. The example runner stops after its finite
input slice is exhausted.

##### Worked walkthrough

Process `[2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9]`. The expected final state is count eight,
mean five, M2 32, minimum two, and maximum nine. The two variances are
therefore `32/8 = 4` and `32/7`.

Fractions below describe exact real arithmetic so every update can be
replayed. The Go values are their nearest binary64 evaluations.

Initial state: count is zero, mean and M2 are zero placeholders, and
no minimum or maximum has been established.

1. Decision: add 2. Count is zero, so use the first-value branch
   instead of applying a formula that needs an old mean.
   After: count 1, mean 2, M2 0, minimum 2, maximum 2.
   Known correct: one accepted value has mean and both extrema 2; its
   distance from its own mean is zero.
2. Decision: add 4. The old mean is 2. Compute first delta 2, move the
   mean by `2/2` to 3, compute second delta 1, and add `2*1` to M2.
   After: count 2, mean 3, M2 2, minimum 2, maximum 4.
   Known correct: values 2 and 4 have deviations -1 and 1 from mean
   3, whose squared total is two.
3. Decision: add the next 4. First delta is 1. Move the mean by
   `1/3` to `10/3`; second delta is `2/3`; add `2/3` to M2.
   After: count 3, mean `10/3`, M2 `8/3`, extrema 2 and 4.
   Known correct: the first three values are summarized; no raw value
   is needed by the next update.
4. Decision: add the third 4. First delta is `2/3`. Move the mean by
   `1/6` to `7/2`; second delta is `1/2`; add `1/3` to M2.
   After: count 4, mean `7/2`, M2 3, extrema 2 and 4.
   Known correct: all three occurrences of 4 contributed separately,
   while constant repetition after the first did not change maximum.
5. Decision: add 5. First delta is `3/2`. Move the mean by `3/10` to
   `19/5`; second delta is `6/5`; add `9/5` to M2.
   After: count 5, mean `19/5`, M2 `24/5`, extrema 2 and 5.
   Known correct: the new value raises both mean and maximum; the
   centered squared-deviation total describes all five values.
6. Decision: add the next 5, then 7 using the same update. For 5,
   deltas `6/5` and 1 make mean 4 and M2 6. For 7, deltas 3 and
   `18/7` make mean `31/7` and M2 `96/7`.
   After: count 7, mean `31/7`, M2 `96/7`, extrema 2 and 7.
   Known correct: seven values are summarized, and each repeated
   update advanced count by exactly one.
7. Decision: add 9. First delta is `32/7`. Move the mean by `4/7` to
   5; second delta is 4; add `128/7` to M2.
   After: count 8, mean 5, M2 32, minimum 2, maximum 9.
   Known correct: every stream value is included once and the final
   extrema are established.
8. Decision: take a snapshot. Divide M2 by count eight for population
   variance and by seven for sample variance.
   After: return population variance 4 and sample variance `32/7`,
   with sample availability true.
   Known correct: the returned fields all describe the same accepted
   eight-value prefix; processing stops.

Focused empty case: a zero-value accumulator rejects `snapshot()`.
Zero is a valid statistic for some nonempty streams, so fabricated
zero fields would not distinguish "no observations" from real data.

Focused singleton case: after adding -3, count is one, mean, minimum,
and maximum are -3, and population variance is zero. Sample variance
is unavailable because its divisor would be zero.

Focused constant case: `[6,6,6]` keeps mean six and M2 zero after
every update. Both available variances are zero.

Focused invalid case: adding NaN or either infinity is rejected before
any field changes. A caller can inspect the same prior snapshot and
retry with a valid value.

Focused arithmetic failure: after accepting `math.MaxFloat64`, adding
`-math.MaxFloat64` makes the first delta overflow to negative
infinity. The staged update returns
`errNonFiniteRunningResult` and preserves the one-value state.

Focused count limit: a state at count `2^53` rejects one more value.
The integer count itself could grow, but the next count would not be
exact when converted to `float64` for the mean update.

Counterexample to the raw-square formula: for values
`[1000000004,1000000007,1000000013,1000000016]`, the exact mean is
1000000010 and population variance is 22.5. A binary64 evaluation of
`sumSquares/N - mean*mean` can produce -128 through cancellation.
The centered update produces 22.5 for this input.

Counterexample to updating M2 with the new delta twice: after adding
2 and then 4, the new mean is 3. Using `(4-3)^2` adds only one, but
the correct M2 is two. The update needs one distance from the old mean
and one from the new mean.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program computes the walkthrough statistics and
demonstrates empty and non-finite rejection. Updates are staged before
mutation, and the runner propagates writer failure. It uses only the
standard library. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Running statistics (counters).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"math"
	"os"
)

const maximumExactRunningCount uint64 = 1 << 53

var (
	errNilRunningStatistics = errors.New(
		"running statistics receiver is nil",
	)
	errNonFiniteRunningValue = errors.New(
		"running statistics value must be finite",
	)
	errRunningStatisticsLimit = errors.New(
		"running statistics count limit reached",
	)
	errNonFiniteRunningResult = errors.New(
		"running statistics result is not finite",
	)
	errEmptyRunningStatistics = errors.New(
		"running statistics are empty",
	)
)

type runningStatistics struct {
	count                 uint64
	mean                  float64
	sumSquaredDifferences float64
	minimum               float64
	maximum               float64
}

type runningStatisticsSnapshot struct {
	count              uint64
	mean               float64
	minimum            float64
	maximum            float64
	populationVariance float64
	sampleVariance     float64
	hasSampleVariance  bool
}

func isFinite(value float64) bool {
	// Evaluate is finite without changing the maintained state.
	return !math.IsNaN(value) && !math.IsInf(value, 0)
}

func (statistics *runningStatistics) add(value float64) error {
	// Add the requested item while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	if statistics == nil {
		return errNilRunningStatistics
	}
	if !isFinite(value) {
		return errNonFiniteRunningValue
	}
	if statistics.count >= maximumExactRunningCount {
		return errRunningStatisticsLimit
	}

	// The first value initializes extrema without sentinels.
	if statistics.count == 0 {
		statistics.count = 1
		statistics.mean = value
		statistics.minimum = value
		statistics.maximum = value
		return nil
	}

	// Stage Welford's update so failure cannot corrupt prior state.
	nextCount := statistics.count + 1
	deltaBeforeMean := value - statistics.mean
	nextMean := statistics.mean +
		deltaBeforeMean/float64(nextCount)
	deltaAfterMean := value - nextMean
	nextSquaredDifferences := statistics.sumSquaredDifferences +
		deltaBeforeMean*deltaAfterMean
	if !isFinite(deltaBeforeMean) ||
		!isFinite(nextMean) ||
		!isFinite(deltaAfterMean) ||
		!isFinite(nextSquaredDifferences) {
		return errNonFiniteRunningResult
	}

	statistics.count = nextCount
	statistics.mean = nextMean
	statistics.sumSquaredDifferences = nextSquaredDifferences
	if value < statistics.minimum {
		statistics.minimum = value
	}
	if value > statistics.maximum {
		statistics.maximum = value
	}
	return nil
}

func (statistics *runningStatistics) snapshot() (
	runningStatisticsSnapshot,
	error,
) {
	// Return a copy so callers cannot mutate stored state.
	if statistics == nil {
		return runningStatisticsSnapshot{},
			errNilRunningStatistics
	}
	if statistics.count == 0 {
		return runningStatisticsSnapshot{},
			errEmptyRunningStatistics
	}

	result := runningStatisticsSnapshot{
		count:   statistics.count,
		mean:    statistics.mean,
		minimum: statistics.minimum,
		maximum: statistics.maximum,
		populationVariance: statistics.sumSquaredDifferences /
			float64(statistics.count),
	}
	if statistics.count >= 2 {
		result.sampleVariance =
			statistics.sumSquaredDifferences /
				float64(statistics.count-1)
		result.hasSampleVariance = true
	}
	return result, nil
}

func runRunningStatisticsExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute running statistics examples to the bounded stopping
	// condition above.
	values := []float64{2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9}
	var statistics runningStatistics
	for valueIndex, value := range values {
		if err := statistics.add(value); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"add value %d: %w",
				valueIndex,
				err,
			)
		}
	}

	result, err := statistics.snapshot()
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("snapshot statistics: %w", err)
	}
	var empty runningStatistics
	_, emptyErr := empty.snapshot()
	invalidErr := statistics.add(math.NaN())

	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"count = %d\nmean = %.6f\n"+
			"minimum = %.6f\nmaximum = %.6f\n"+
			"population variance = %.6f\n"+
			"sample variance = %.6f\n"+
			"sample variance available = %t\n"+
			"empty rejected = %t\ninvalid rejected = %t\n",
		result.count,
		result.mean,
		result.minimum,
		result.maximum,
		result.populationVariance,
		result.sampleVariance,
		result.hasSampleVariance,
		errors.Is(emptyErr, errEmptyRunningStatistics),
		errors.Is(invalidErr, errNonFiniteRunningValue),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write running statistics: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runRunningStatisticsExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
count = 8
mean = 5.000000
minimum = 2.000000
maximum = 9.000000
population variance = 4.000000
sample variance = 4.571429
sample variance available = true
empty rejected = true
invalid rejected = true
```

##### Why it works

Reason first in exact real arithmetic. After N accepted values,
maintain these invariants:

- count equals N;
- mean equals the arithmetic mean of those N values when N is
  positive;
- M2 equals the sum of squared distances from that mean;
- minimum and maximum are the least and greatest accepted values.

Before any value, count is zero and there are no claimed statistics.
The first-value branch stores that value as mean and both extrema. Its
only deviation from the mean is zero, so the zero M2 is exact. The
invariants therefore hold after the first acceptance.

Assume they hold for N positive values with mean M and M2 S. For new
value X, the mean of N old values plus X is:

```text
(N*M + X) / (N+1)
    = M + (X-M) / (N+1)
```

This is exactly `nextMean`, so the mean invariant survives.

Let D be `X-M` and let `D2` be `X-nextMean`. Moving the center from M
to new mean `Mnext` changes the old values' squared-deviation total.
The old deviations around M sum to zero, so the cross terms cancel:

```text
old values around Mnext = S + N * (M - Mnext)^2
new value around Mnext = (X - Mnext)^2
```

Because `Mnext-M = D/(N+1)` and `D2 = D*N/(N+1)`, the two added
terms sum to `D*D2`. Therefore `nextM2 = S + D*D2` is exactly the new
sum of squared distances. This establishes the M2 invariant without
revisiting an old value.

Comparing X with both stored extrema preserves the minimum and maximum
invariants. Equality leaves them unchanged; a smaller or larger value
replaces only the corresponding bound.

At snapshot time, population variance is defined as the invariant M2
divided by N. Sample variance with Bessel's correction is defined as
M2 divided by `N-1`, which exists only for N at least two. The
returned values therefore follow directly from the maintained state.

The Go implementation evaluates the same recurrence in binary64.
Finiteness validation excludes NaN and infinities before comparison.
Staging every derived field and validating it before assignment means
a rejected update leaves the prior invariant-bearing state untouched.
The count limit keeps every divisor conversion exact as an integer,
though other floating operations still round.

Each method contains a finite number of branches and arithmetic
operations and no loop. The runner consumes one slice element per
iteration, so it terminates after the input length.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of accepted values and Q the number of snapshots.
Each `add` performs constant checks, arithmetic, and comparisons, so
its best, average, and worst successful time are `Theta(1)`. Each
snapshot also takes `Theta(1)` time. Processing N values and taking Q
snapshots takes `Theta(N+Q)` total time.

The accumulator retains five scalar fields and snapshots return seven
scalars. Retained, auxiliary, and output space are all `Theta(1)`.
It does not allocate per value or retain the stream.

An invalid input, nil receiver, count-limit failure, or non-finite
derived result is rejected in `Theta(1)` time. Staging uses a fixed
number of local scalars and makes the failure atomic.

Recomputing one snapshot from retained history takes `Theta(N)` time
and requires `Theta(N)` retained space. Keeping only sum, count,
minimum, and maximum also gives a running mean, but it cannot derive
variance. Keeping a raw square sum enables the algebraic variance
formula but is more vulnerable to cancellation.

Welford's recurrence improves numerical behavior; it does not make
binary floating-point exact. Results can depend slightly on order,
M2 can accumulate rounding error, and extreme finite values can make
an intermediate overflow. Higher-precision floats, decimal arithmetic,
or exact rational arithmetic trade more time and storage for a
different error contract.

This accumulator summarizes the entire prefix. A sliding window needs
to remove expired values and usually stores the window or uses a
deletable aggregate. A mergeable distributed statistic needs a
separate pairwise-combination formula and must state its rounding and
ownership behavior.

The example runner performs eight successful updates, two snapshots,
one rejected update, formats nine lines, and propagates writer
failure. Its demonstration work is constant.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty state has no mean or extrema. Returning zero fields silently
  makes it indistinguishable from the valid stream `[0]`; return the
  empty error.
- A singleton has population variance zero but no sample variance.
  Dividing its M2 by `N-1` divides by zero.
- Zero and negative values are valid. Initializing minimum to zero
  makes stream `[2,3]` report a minimum that never appeared.
- Duplicate values still increment count. Deduplicating
  `[2,4,4]` changes its mean and variance.
- NaN is unordered: both `NaN < minimum` and `NaN > maximum` are
  false. Reject it explicitly before it contaminates mean and M2.
- Positive and negative infinity are not finite measurements under
  this contract. Reject them instead of creating permanent infinite
  extrema or a NaN deviation.
- Finite inputs do not guarantee finite intermediate arithmetic.
  Stage and check the update before changing count or extrema.
- Update mean before computing the second delta. Reusing the old mean
  twice adds `D*D`, which is not Welford's correction.
- Do not update M2 before saving the old mean. Both deltas have
  distinct centers and cannot be reconstructed from only the new one.
- Population and sample variance answer different questions. Do not
  select a divisor merely because one result looks familiar.
- A negative variance from the raw-square formula is cancellation,
  not meaningful spread. Do not clamp arbitrary negatives to hide an
  unstable formula.
- Count conversion matters even when the integer field cannot
  overflow. Beyond `2^53`, consecutive `uint64` counts do not all map
  to distinct `float64` values.
- Copying the struct creates an independent scalar snapshot that can
  receive later updates. Copying while another goroutine writes is
  still a data race.
- This state cannot remove an arbitrary old value or reconstruct the
  input. Choose a windowed or history-retaining design when either is
  required.

##### When to choose it

Choose running statistics when:

- values arrive one at a time or the full collection is too costly to
  retain;
- count, mean, variance, minimum, and maximum are needed for the whole
  prefix;
- constant work and storage per arrival matter;
- approximate binary64 results meet the application's error budget;
- old observations never need removal or reconstruction;
- updates can be serialized or externally synchronized.

Telemetry summaries, sensor monitoring, online quality checks, and
one-pass file analysis often fit this contract. The decisive clue is
that each new answer concerns every accepted value, not an arbitrary
past range or only a recent time window.

Use a direct two-pass calculation when all values fit in memory and
the extra pass is acceptable; centering every squared difference
around the completed mean can be easier to audit. Use a [prefix-sum
array](#a121-prefix-sum-arrays) when arbitrary immutable range sums
are needed, because one current accumulator cannot recover old
boundaries.

Use the next [streaming-median lesson](
#b232-streaming-median-two-heaps) when order statistics rather than
algebraic moments are required. A mean cannot reveal the middle value:
streams `[0,0,9]` and `[0,3,6]` share mean three but have different
medians.

Use [sliding event counts](
#b2311-sliding-event-counts-queue-or-time-buckets) when observations
expire by time. Use a retained slice or database when callers need
deletion, quantiles, witnesses, arbitrary ranges, or exact replay.

B. P. Welford's original [corrected-sums paper](
https://doi.org/10.1080/00401706.1962.10490022) derives the online
update family. The Go specification defines [`float64`](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Numeric_types) as IEEE 754 binary64. The
standard library documents [`math.IsNaN`](
https://pkg.go.dev/math#IsNaN) and [`math.IsInf`](
https://pkg.go.dev/math#IsInf), used to enforce the finite-value
contract.

#### B.23.2 Streaming median (two heaps)

##### Problem and contract

Integers arrive one at a time, and a consumer needs the median after
every arrival. Sorting the whole prefix again repeats almost all prior
work. Inserting into one sorted slice avoids repeated comparisons but
may shift a linear number of values on each event.

For arrival order `[12,4,7,3,8,8,20]`, the exact middle pairs after
each event are:

```text
(12,12) (4,12) (7,7) (4,7) (7,7) (7,8) (8,8)
```

An odd-length prefix repeats its one middle value. An even-length
prefix returns the lower and upper middle values separately. Their
arithmetic mean is the conventional numeric median, but retaining the
pair avoids integer addition overflow and premature floating-point
conversion.

The [two-heaps lesson](#a143-two-heaps) owns the complete Go
implementation and its generic partition proof. This entry owns the
streaming application contract:

- construct a tracker with `newMedianTracker()` before use;
- every `int` is valid, including duplicates, zero, negatives, and
  both signed extremes;
- `add(value)` retains exactly one occurrence of that arrival;
- after each completed add, `middlePair()` describes all values seen
  through that event;
- odd count returns the same middle value twice and `found == true`;
- even count returns the adjacent lower and upper middle values in
  nondecreasing order and `found == true`;
- empty state returns `(0,0,false)`; the zeros are placeholders;
- arrival order determines prefix results, although two streams with
  the same final multiset have the same final pair;
- values have no timestamp or identity, so a late arrival is simply
  the next event and no earlier emitted result is revised;
- the tracker retains all accepted values in owned heap slices;
- it does not expose heap storage through the median query;
- it supports insertion and queries, not deletion, correction,
  arbitrary quantiles, or historical-prefix queries;
- a nil tracker or a tracker not created by the constructor is outside
  this application contract;
- unsynchronized concurrent access is outside the contract;
- allocation failure is outside the contract.

Read [min-heaps and max-heaps](#a81-min-heaps-and-max-heaps) before
the owning two-heaps lesson. Heap slices are not sorted; only their
roots have the extreme-value meanings this application uses.

##### Mental model

Split all retained values around the middle boundary:

- `lower` is a max-heap containing the lower half;
- `upper` is a min-heap containing the upper half;
- every value in lower is at most every value in upper;
- lower has the same size as upper or exactly one extra value.

Read `lower root = 7, upper root = 8` as: 7 is the greatest value in
the lower partition, 8 is the least value in the upper partition, and
