slice element. A two-stack variant follows the push and pop rules from
the mental model. If slices must provide a strict worst-case bound for
each push rather than an amortized bound, reserve the documented
30,000-operation limit up front or use linked nodes with a stated
constant-time allocation model.

The repository's [Min Stack practice file](
problems/medium_leetcode_0155_min_stack.go) provides the official
operation parser and cases for duplicates, increasing and decreasing
values, one item, and integer boundaries. It intentionally leaves the
exercise algorithm unsolved and is not a second reference
implementation.

##### Why it works

For paired entries, maintain this invariant: each entry's cached
minimum equals the smallest value from the bottom through that entry.
The top entry therefore holds the minimum of the complete live stack.

The first push pairs its value with itself, establishing the
invariant. For a later push, the new stack contains exactly the new
value and the old stack. The smaller of the new value and old top
minimum is therefore the new complete minimum. Pop removes one whole
pair and exposes an older pair whose prefix and cached answer have not
changed. Top and minimum only read the top pair, so all operations
preserve the fact.

For two stacks, maintain two facts: `values` is the complete push
history minus successful pops, and `minimums` contains one occurrence
for each live value that was less than or equal to every older value
at its push time. Its top is therefore the smallest live value.

Push preserves the first fact by appending the new value. If that
value is at most the old minimum, adding it to `minimums` makes it the
new minimum; otherwise the old top remains smaller. On pop, a value
unequal to the minimum top was not supporting the current minimum, so
only `values` changes. An equal value contributed the top minimum
occurrence, so removing one occurrence from both stacks reveals the
next correct minimum. Including equality makes this argument valid
for duplicates.

Each method has a fixed number of comparisons, top reads, and stack
updates. It has no size-dependent loop, so it terminates. The finite
command sequence ends after at most the documented number of calls.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the live value count, M the number of operations, and K the
number of entries in the separate `minimums` stack.

In the abstract linked-node model, push, pop, top, and minimum each
use a constant number of link operations and take `Theta(1)` time. A
linked push allocates one node; allocator and garbage-collector pauses
remain runtime costs outside that operation count. Processing M
operations takes `Theta(M)` total core work.

Paired storage keeps two integers for each of N entries, plus links or
slice overhead, so its payload is `Theta(N)`. It performs the same
small update rule for every push.

Two stacks retain N values and K saved minima, where `1 <= K <= N` for
a nonempty stack. Strictly increasing pushes give K equal to one;
strictly decreasing or all-equal pushes give K equal to N. Its total
payload remains `Theta(N)`, but it can store fewer summary integers
than paired entries for long increasing runs.

Slice append is amortized `Theta(1)`, but one growth can allocate and
copy all current elements. Reserving the known call limit removes
growth from later pushes at the cost of `Theta(30000)` reserved slots,
including unused capacity. A linked representation avoids resize
copies but pays for pointers, individual allocations, and weaker
locality.

The serialized result list uses `Theta(M)` output storage when
retained. Streaming each observation would reduce application output
storage to `Theta(1)`. All operations otherwise use `Theta(1)`
temporary storage.

Scanning a plain stack makes `getMin()` take `Theta(N)` time. A
difference-encoding one-stack variant can reduce per-entry fields, but
it performs arithmetic that needs careful overflow handling at the
documented integer extremes. Direct paired values avoid that risk.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- The judge excludes empty pop, top, and minimum. Reusable code should
  return a Boolean or error, or document a panic, instead of inventing
  a numeric sentinel that can collide with valid values.
- One pushed value is both top and minimum. Popping it must empty
  every representation, including the separate minimum stack.
- Value zero is ordinary data. Testing zero to infer emptiness fails
  for `push(0)`.
- Duplicate minima need separate support. With `[1,1]`, one pop must
  leave minimum 1; using `<` instead of `<=` in the two-stack push
  rule loses that fact.
- An increasing sequence such as `[1,2,3]` leaves one separate
  minimum. Popping 3 or 2 must not remove it.
- A decreasing sequence such as `[3,2,1]` saves every value as a new
  minimum. Each pop must expose the preceding saved minimum.
- Compare the popped value with the minimum top before discarding the
  information needed by that comparison.
- Do not scan during pop to rebuild a minimum. That moves the linear
  work instead of meeting the constant-time contract.
- Do not cache only the most recent minimum in one global field. Pop
  needs the summary belonging to the restored older state.
- Paired entries must cache the smaller of the new value and the old
  minimum, not the smaller of the new value and old top value.
- Extreme values are safe with direct comparison. Negating or
  subtracting `-2147483648` can overflow a 32-bit encoding.
- Copying a slice-backed stack can share mutable backing storage. Keep
  one owner or define an explicit copy policy.
- Concurrent operations need synchronization around the complete
  compound transition across both stacks.

##### When to choose it

Choose a min stack when:

- values enter and leave only at one last-in, first-out end;
- top and current-minimum queries are both frequent;
- every operation needs constant work with respect to live size;
- retaining one summary per state or one stack of minimum changes fits
  in memory;
- one object can own and serialize mutations.

Choose paired entries for the simplest invariant and fixed update
path. Choose two stacks when long runs above the current minimum can
make the summary stack smaller and synchronizing two private stacks
remains easy. The worst-case asymptotic memory is the same.

Use a plain stack when minimum queries are absent or rare enough that
a scan is acceptable. Use a min-heap when the smallest value, rather
than the newest value, must be removed. A heap does not preserve stack
order.

Use a balanced search tree, indexed heap, or another ordered structure
when arbitrary stored values must be updated or deleted. Cached stack
summaries above a middle change would become stale. Use a
[monotonic deque](#a54-monotonic-deques) when minima belong to a
moving window whose oldest values expire from the opposite end.

The [owning lesson](#a43-stacks-with-cached-aggregates) provides the
implementation and full cached-state invariant. The [practice
harness](problems/medium_leetcode_0155_min_stack.go) exercises the
design interface. The official [Min Stack problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/min-stack/description/) specifies the
operations, value range, valid-call precondition, call limit, and
constant-time requirement.

#### B.23.7 Queue from stacks (two stacks)

##### Problem and contract

A stack removes its newest value, but a queue must remove its oldest
value. If only stack operations are available, one stack cannot expose
the oldest value without repeatedly disturbing newer ones. Two stacks
can preserve queue order by reversing each waiting batch once.

The owning [two-stack composition lesson](#a144-two-stacks) defines
and implements the general queue. This entry applies its transfer
invariant to the standard judge interface without copying the
implementation.

The application contract is:

- construction creates one empty first-in, first-out queue;
- `push(value)` adds one integer at the queue back;
- `pop()` removes and returns the queue front;
- `peek()` returns the queue front without removing it;
- `empty()` reports whether no value is stored;
- only stack-top push, top read or pop, size, and empty checks may be
  used by the implementation;
- an array, list, or deque may simulate each stack only through those
  stack operations;
- judge values lie in `[1,9]`, and duplicate values are distinct
  arrivals;
- pop and peek are called only when the queue is nonempty;
- at most 100 calls follow construction;
- constructor and push contribute `null` to serialized output, while
  the other operations contribute their integer or Boolean result;
- the follow-up target is amortized `O(1)` time per operation, meaning
  a sequence of N operations takes `O(N)` total even though one call
  can take longer;
- the object owns both stacks, and allocation failure and
  unsynchronized concurrent use are outside the judge contract.

Read [ordinary stacks](#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks) for
last-in, first-out mechanics and [ordinary queues](
#a53-array-backed-and-linked-queues) for the required first-in,
first-out behavior.

##### Mental model

Keep an `input` stack for new arrivals and an `output` stack for the
oldest waiting batch. Stack snapshots below run from bottom to top.

- `input` stores newer values in arrival order, so its newest value is
  on top.
- `output` stores older values in reverse arrival order, so its oldest
  value is on top.

Read `input = [3]` and `output = [2,1]` as: queue front is 1, then 2,
then 3 at the back. The logical queue is `output` read from right to
left, followed by `input` read from left to right.

Push always appends to `input`. Before pop or peek, inspect `output`:

1. If it is nonempty, its top is already the oldest value. Leave
   `input` alone.
2. If it is empty, pop every `input` value and push it onto `output`.
   Reversing the batch makes the oldest input bottom become the output
   top.

This movement is often called a lazy transfer because it waits until
a front operation needs the reversal. Empty is true exactly when both
stacks are empty.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use the official sequence:
`construct, push(1), push(2), peek(), pop(), empty()`.
The expected serialized result is
`[null,null,null,1,1,false]`.

Initial state: no object exists and the output list is empty.

1. Decision: construct the queue with two empty stacks.
   After: `input = []`, `output = []`, and result is `[null]`.
   Known correct: both physical stacks represent an empty logical
   queue.
2. Decision: push 1. Put the new back value on `input`; no front
   operation needs a transfer.
   After: `input = [1]`, `output = []`, queue order is `[1]`, and
   result appends `null`.
   Known correct: 1 is the sole value and is both front and back.
3. Decision: push 2. Put it above 1 on `input` because it arrived
   later.
   After: `input = [1,2]`, `output = []`, queue order is `[1,2]`, and
   result appends `null`.
   Known correct: input bottom 1 remains older than input top 2.
4. Decision: peek. `output` is empty, so pop input top 2 and push it
   to output, then move 1 the same way. Read output top 1 without
   removing it.
   After: `input = []`, `output = [2,1]`, queue order remains
   `[1,2]`, and result appends 1.
   Known correct: the transfer changed storage direction but not
   membership or logical order; 1 is exposed as front.
5. Decision: pop. `output` is nonempty, so do not transfer. Pop its
   top 1 and return it.
   After: `input = []`, `output = [2]`, queue order is `[2]`, and
   result appends 1.
   Known correct: the oldest value left exactly once, and 2 remains.
6. Decision: call `empty()`. At least `output` contains 2, so return
   false and stop after the last command.
   After: state is unchanged; final result is
   `[null,null,null,1,1,false]`.
   Known correct: a queue is empty only when both stacks are empty.

Focused interleaving sequence: begin from the step-5 state
`input = []`, `output = [2]`, then push 3. State becomes
`input = [3]`, `output = [2]`, or logical queue `[2,3]`. Peek must
return 2 without transferring 3. After pop returns 2, the next pop
transfers 3 and returns 3. A final empty call returns true.

Focused repeated-peek case: after pushing 4 and 5, the first peek
transfers both and returns 4. A second peek returns 4 from the
existing output top with no movement or removal.

Counterexample to transferring while output is nonempty: in the
interleaving state above, pushing input value 3 onto output would put
3 above older value 2. The next pop would wrongly return 3. The first
wrong decision is mixing a newer batch into an undrained older batch.

##### Implementation

Use the complete Go program in [A.14.4](#a144-two-stacks). It owns the
two slices, lazy-transfer helper, empty handling, logical snapshots,
invariant proof, and executable output.

To adapt that owner to the judge interface:

1. Use the zero value of `twoStackQueue` for `MyQueue()`.
2. Forward `push(value)` to `enqueue(value)`.
3. Forward `pop()` to `dequeue()`, return its integer, and treat false
   as an internal contract violation because judge calls are valid.
4. Forward `peek()` to `front()` under the same precondition.
5. Implement `empty()` as `size() == 0`, or equivalently check that
   both stack lengths are zero.
6. Omit the owner's snapshot and demonstration helpers from the judge
   submission; they are diagnostic operations, not queue primitives.

The owner's slices use only their ends as stack tops: append pushes,
the last element is top, and shortening by one pops. Indexing or
removing the slice front would violate the stack-only restriction.

No separate problem file currently owns this exercise. The owning
guide program is the repository reference implementation; the
official example and focused cases here provide the application-level
checks.

##### Why it works

Maintain this invariant: logical queue order is `output` from top to
bottom, followed by `input` from bottom to top.

Both stacks start empty, so the invariant initially represents an
empty queue. Push adds a new value to the input top. That position is
the end of the input's bottom-to-top logical group, so the value
becomes queue back without changing any older position.

When output is nonempty, its top is the first value in logical order.
Peek reads it and pop removes it, so each operation returns the oldest
live arrival. Leaving input untouched prevents newer arrivals from
passing that older output group.

When output is empty, the whole logical queue is input from bottom to
top. Moving input top to output top repeatedly reverses physical
order: the oldest input bottom moves last and becomes output top.
Input then becomes empty, so output top is again the first logical
value. The transfer changes neither membership nor logical order.

Empty returns true exactly when both invariant groups have length
zero. Every transfer iteration removes one value from finite input,
so the loop terminates. Other operations have bounded local work, and
the finite command sequence ends after its final call.

For the amortized bound, charge each pushed value for its complete
journey. It is pushed onto input once, moved from input to output at
most once, and popped from output at most once. No value can be
transferred again. Therefore M calls perform `O(M)` stack operations
in total, even though one front call may move `Theta(N)` live values.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let M be the operation count, N the current queue size, and T the
number of values transferred by one pop or peek.

In the abstract constant-time stack model, push and empty take
`Theta(1)` time. Pop or peek takes `Theta(1 + T)` time. Its best case
is `Theta(1)` when output is nonempty, while its worst case is
`Theta(N)` when it transfers all current input values.

Across M operations, each value transfers at most once, so all
transfer work is linear in pushes. The total is `Theta(M)` when every
call does at least its required constant work, giving amortized
`Theta(1)` per operation. This does not promise a worst-case constant
latency for one call.

Between operations, the two logical stacks contain exactly N live
integers, so abstract payload storage is `Theta(N)`. Transfer uses one
temporary value and `Theta(1)` auxiliary storage beyond the two
stacks.

The owner uses Go slices. Appending may occasionally allocate and copy
a stack backing array, adding a size-dependent pause to that call;
repeated append is amortized under the runtime assumption explained in
the stack lesson. Empty slices can also retain old capacity, so
retained memory depends on both backing-array capacities rather than
only current N.

If serialized results are accumulated, M commands require `Theta(M)`
output slots. Streaming observations would use `Theta(1)` application
output storage. The owner's diagnostic snapshot takes `Theta(N)` time
and output space, but the judge methods do not call it.

A direct queue or circular buffer gives worst-case constant front
operations without a batch-transfer pause. The two-stack design is
valuable when stack primitives are the constraint and amortized
latency is acceptable.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Immediately after construction, empty returns true. Pop and peek are
  invalid under the judge contract; reusable code should return a
  Boolean or error rather than inventing a numeric sentinel.
- After transfer, input is empty while output may hold every value.
  Checking only input would falsely report that the queue is empty.
- Peek may transfer internal storage, but it must not remove a value
  or change logical order. Repeated peek calls return the same front.
- Transfer only when output is empty. Moving a newer input batch early
  lets its values overtake an older output batch.
- Transfer every input value. Moving only the input top exposes the
  newest arrival instead of the oldest.
- Do not move output values back to input after each read. Reversing
  repeatedly turns a linear total transfer into repeated linear work.
- Slice index 0 is the input bottom, not its stack top. Removing it
  directly simulates a queue and violates the allowed operations.
- Duplicates such as pushes `2,2` occupy separate positions and pop
  twice. Equality never identifies an occurrence.
- The judge accepts only values 1 through 9, but the owner supports
  zero and negative integers. Empty detection must use lengths, not a
  value sentinel.
- Clearing a removed slice slot prevents stale pointer retention if
  the element type later changes from integer to pointer-bearing data.
- Copying the queue struct can share either slice backing array. Keep
  one owner or define an explicit deep-copy policy.
- Concurrent calls need synchronization across the emptiness check,
  complete transfer, and final read or removal as one transition.

##### When to choose it

Choose a two-stack queue when:

- the required public behavior is first-in, first-out;
- available containers expose only last-in, first-out operations;
- amortized constant work is acceptable even if one read pauses for a
  complete batch transfer;
- values need no priority or arbitrary middle access;
- one object can own both stacks and serialize mutations.

Use a direct [array-backed or linked queue](
#a53-array-backed-and-linked-queues) when queue primitives are
allowed. Use a [circular buffer](#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers)
when capacity is fixed and predictable worst-case operation latency
matters.

Use a deque when both ends are public operations. Use a priority queue
when value rank, rather than arrival order, selects the next removal.
Use the later [stack-from-queues application](
#b2312-stack-from-queues-queues) when the available primitive and
required order are reversed in the other direction.

The [owning lesson](#a144-two-stacks) provides the complete Go program
and general invariant. The official
[Implement Queue using Stacks problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/implement-queue-using-stacks/)
specifies the stack-only restriction, operation contract, bounds,
valid-call precondition, and amortized follow-up.

#### B.23.8 Randomized set (slice and hash map)

##### Problem and contract

A hash set can insert, remove, and test membership quickly, but it has
no dense numeric position from which to choose a uniformly random
value. A slice supports direct random indexing, but preserving order
during a middle deletion would shift later values. A randomized set
combines both structures and gives up stable order.

The owning [indexed-set lesson](
#a146-indexed-arrays-with-hash-maps) defines and implements the slice,
map, and swap-delete transition. This entry applies that composition
to the standard random-selection interface without copying its full
implementation.

The application contract is:

- construction creates one empty set;
- `insert(value)` adds an absent integer and returns true, or returns
  false without mutation when it is already present;
- `remove(value)` deletes a present integer and returns true, or
  returns false without mutation when it is absent;
- `getRandom()` returns one current value, with every current value
  having the same probability on that call;
- getRandom is called only when at least one value is present;
- values range from `-2^31` through `2^31 - 1`;
- at most 200,000 insert, remove, and random calls follow
  construction;
- every method must take average `O(1)` time;
- physical and iteration order are unspecified and may change after
  removal;
- the constructor contributes `null` to serialized output, mutations
  contribute Booleans, and random calls contribute integers;
- the set owns its map, slice, and random-source state;
- allocation failure, random-source failure, and unsynchronized
  concurrent use are outside the judge contract.

Read [dynamic slices](#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) for direct
indexing and [hash maps](
#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) for expected-time lookup.
Uniform means each of N live values has probability exactly `1/N`
under the assumed uniform bounded-index source.

##### Mental model

Maintain two synchronized views of the same unique values:

- `values[index]` stores the value occupying one dense slice position;
- `indexByValue[value]` stores that value's current slice index.

Together they form a bijection, a one-to-one correspondence. Read
`indexByValue[20] = 1` as: value 20 is present exactly once, at
`values[1]`. With N values, the valid indexes are exactly `[0,N)`, a
half-open range that includes zero and excludes N.

Insertion appends an absent value at index N and records that index.
For removal, use the map to find the hole, move the last slice value
into that hole, repair the moved value's map entry, shorten the slice,
and delete the requested map key. If the requested value is already
last, shorten directly. This is swap-delete and does not preserve
order.

For getRandom, draw one index uniformly from `[0,N)` and return the
value at that index. Every live value owns exactly one possible index,
so the index distribution transfers directly to the values.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use the official sequence:
`construct, insert(1), remove(2), insert(2), getRandom(),`
`remove(1), insert(2), getRandom()`.

The official result shown is
`[null,true,false,true,2,true,false,2]`. To make this trace
replayable, assume the bounded source draws index 1 from `[0,2)` and
later index 0 from `[0,1)`. Other first draws are valid under the real
contract.

Initial state: no object exists, and the result list is empty.

1. Decision: construct an empty slice and map.
   After: `values = []`, the map is empty, and result is `[null]`.
   Known correct: both views describe the same empty set.
2. Decision: insert 1. Its map key is absent, so append it at index 0
   and record `1->0`.
   After: `values = [1]`, map is `{1->0}`, and result appends true.
   Known correct: value 1 owns the only dense index.
3. Decision: remove 2. Its map key is absent, so return false before
   reading or changing the slice.
   After: state stays `[1]` and `{1->0}`; result appends false.
   Known correct: a missing removal changed neither membership nor
   indexing.
4. Decision: insert 2. It is absent, so append it at index 1 and
   record `2->1`.
   After: `values = [1,2]`, map is `{1->0,2->1}`, and result appends
   true.
   Known correct: two unique values own the two indexes in `[0,2)`.
5. Decision: getRandom draws index 1 from `[0,2)`. Read
   `values[1] = 2` without mutating either view.
   After: state is unchanged and result appends 2.
   Known correct: index 1 was one of two equally likely valid indexes.
6. Decision: remove 1 at index 0. Last value 2 is at index 1, so move
   2 into index 0, update `2->0`, shorten the slice, and delete key 1.
   After: `values = [2]`, map is `{2->0}`, and result appends true.
   Known correct: value 1 alone is absent and the sole live index is
   dense again.
7. Decision: insert 2. The map already contains it, so reject before
   appending.
   After: state remains `[2]` and `{2->0}`; result appends false.
   Known correct: set uniqueness and the bijection are unchanged.
8. Decision: getRandom draws the only valid index 0. Return
   `values[0] = 2`, then stop after the last operation.
   After: final result is
   `[null,true,false,true,2,true,false,2]`.
   Known correct: a singleton is selected with probability one, and
   every requested observation is complete.

Focused middle-removal case: after inserting 10, 20, and 30, state is
`values = [10,20,30]` and map `{10->0,20->1,30->2}`. Removing 20 moves
30 to index 1 and records `30->1`. A following remove of 30 must find
index 1 and leave `[10]`.

Focused lifecycle case: insert 0, remove 0, insert 0, then getRandom.
The results are true, true, true, and 0. Empty and a stored zero are
distinguished by membership and length, never by a value sentinel.

Counterexample to sampling a map key directly: Go map iteration order
is unspecified, walking to a chosen key takes linear time, and the
iteration mechanism does not promise a uniform key distribution. The
first wrong decision is treating iteration position as a dense random
index.

##### Implementation

Use the complete Go program in
[A.14.6](#a146-indexed-arrays-with-hash-maps). It owns insertion,
swap-delete removal, the map-slice bijection, dense-index validation,
and executable edge cases. Its `valueAt` method is the deterministic
primitive used by random selection.

To adapt that owner to `RandomizedSet`:

1. Use its zero-value `indexedSet` for construction.
2. Forward insert and remove directly; their Boolean meanings already
   match the judge.
3. For getRandom, call a uniform bounded source with
   `len(set.values)`, then return `set.values[index]` or the
   successful `valueAt(index)` result.
4. Treat an empty call as an internal contract violation because the
   judge guarantees a live value. Reusable code should return an error
   instead of calling a bounded source with zero.
5. Keep the slice and map private so no caller can break their
   correspondence.
6. Inject a bounded draw function or seeded generator in deterministic
   tests; production code may use `rand.IntN(len(set.values))` from
   `math/rand/v2` when simulation-quality randomness is sufficient.

The repository's [RandomizedSet practice file](
problems/medium_leetcode_0380_insert_delete_getrandom_o1.go) parses
the official operations and includes duplicate, missing,
middle-removal, reinsertion, zero, singleton, and signed-boundary
cases. It remains an unsolved exercise. Its exact-output runner needs
an injected draw or a custom acceptance rule before a multi-value
random case can validate all permitted results rather than one
displayed result.

##### Why it works

Maintain this invariant for N live values: slice indexes are exactly
`[0,N)`, every slice value is unique, and
`indexByValue[values[index]] = index` for every valid index. The map
contains no other keys.

Empty construction establishes the invariant. Successful insertion
adds one absent value at new last index N and adds the inverse map
entry. Duplicate insertion changes nothing.

Successful removal gets the target's exact index from the map. When
that index is not last, moving the last value into the hole and
repairing its map entry preserves both directions for that value. All
other retained values keep their indexes. Shortening removes the old
last position, and deleting the target key removes exactly the target.
Last-element removal is the same argument without a moved value.
Missing removal changes nothing.

For any live value V, the invariant gives exactly one index
`indexByValue[V]`. A uniform draw from `[0,N)` selects that index with
probability `1/N`, so getRandom returns V with probability `1/N`.
Physical reorderings cannot change this probability while the
bijection and dense range hold.

Each structural method has a bounded number of map, slice, and
comparison steps. The random method makes one bounded draw and one
indexed read. Under a terminating bounded-source contract, every call
terminates; the finite operation sequence then terminates.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be live size, M the operation count, and D(N) the cost of one
uniform bounded draw from `[0,N)`.

Integer map lookup, insertion, and deletion take expected `O(1)` time
under ordinary Go map behavior. Slice append is amortized `O(1)`, but
one growth may allocate and copy N values. Therefore insert takes
average or amortized expected `O(1)`, not a strict worst-case
constant.

Remove performs one expected-time lookup and a bounded number of
indexed writes and map updates, so it takes expected `O(1)` time. It
does not shrink retained slice or map capacity. Hash collisions,
rehashing, allocation, and runtime scheduling can make individual
operations slower.

GetRandom takes `Theta(1) + D(N)` time and no structural mutation.
With a standard constant-expected-time bounded source, it takes
expected `Theta(1)`. A correct bounded source may use rejection to
avoid modulo bias, so a strict finite worst-case draw bound need not
follow from the average-time contract.

Across M calls, expected core work is `Theta(M)` under those map,
append, and random-source assumptions. If serialized results are
retained, they require `Theta(M)` output slots.

The live structure holds N slice integers and N map entries, using
`Theta(N)` logical storage. Backing arrays and maps may retain spare
capacity after removals, so retained bytes can follow an earlier peak
rather than current N. Each operation uses `Theta(1)` temporary
storage beyond its returned result.

Swap-delete trades stable order for fast removal. Preserving insertion
order would require shifting later slice values and repairing their
map entries, or maintaining a separate linked order with more
metadata.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty insert and remove work normally. Empty getRandom is excluded
  by the judge; `rand.IntN(0)` would panic, so reusable code must
  check before drawing.
- Duplicate insert returns false before append. Appending first
  creates two indexes for one map key and destroys uniform value
  sampling.
- Missing remove returns false before reading the last index. It must
  not change slice order or random probabilities.
- Removing the sole or last value skips the move branch. Updating a
  nonexistent moved value can recreate the key being deleted.
- Middle removal must repair the last value's map entry. Otherwise a
  later remove reads its stale old index and can access past the
  slice.
- Delete the requested map key after repairing a different moved key.
  When the target is last, skip repair so the target is not restored.
- Zero, negative values, and signed extremes are ordinary keys. Use
  map presence, not a numeric sentinel.
- Random selection must draw from `[0,len(values))`. Using the closed
  upper bound N can index past the slice.
- Applying `% N` to an arbitrary raw random integer can bias indexes
  when its source range is not a multiple of N. Use an unbiased
  bounded API.
- A fixed seed gives replayable tests but does not prove uniformity.
  Test the bijection deterministically and keep statistical tests
  tolerant enough to avoid flaky exact-count assertions.
- Returning the internal slice lets callers mutate a value without
  repairing the map. Return copies for diagnostics.
- Copying the struct shares slice storage, map state, and possibly the
  random source. Keep one owner or define an explicit deep copy.
- Concurrent operations need synchronization around the complete map,
  slice, and random-source transition.
- `math/rand/v2` is suitable for simulation, not security-sensitive
  selection. Use a cryptographic source when unpredictability is part
  of the contract.

##### When to choose it

Choose a randomized set when:

- values are unique and membership changes over time;
- insert, remove, and uniform random selection are all frequent;
- expected or amortized constant work is acceptable;
- physical order may change after deletion;
- simulation-quality randomness satisfies the requirement;
- one object can own and synchronize all state.

Use a plain hash set when random selection is unnecessary. Use a slice
alone when the collection is static or deletion cost is unimportant.
Use a linked order plus a map when iteration order must remain stable.

Use a multiset design when duplicate occurrences need separate
sampling weight. It needs occurrence indexes or per-value position
sets, not this one-index-per-value bijection. Use weighted sampling
when values need unequal probabilities; uniform index selection cannot
express weights.

Use [reservoir sampling](#b234-reservoir-sampling-sample-array) when
an unknown-length stream cannot be retained and only a fixed-size
sample is needed. A randomized set instead stores the complete live
population and supports arbitrary removal.

The [owning lesson](#a146-indexed-arrays-with-hash-maps) provides the
full structural implementation. The [practice harness](
problems/medium_leetcode_0380_insert_delete_getrandom_o1.go) exercises
the judge interface. The official
[Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/insert-delete-getrandom-o1/)
specifies the operations, uniformity, bounds, nonempty precondition,
and average-time target. Go documents the half-open range and invalid
bound behavior of [`rand.IntN`](https://pkg.go.dev/math/rand/v2#IntN).

#### B.23.9 LFU cache (hash maps and frequency buckets)

##### Problem and contract

A bounded cache sometimes needs to retain frequently used keys rather
than merely recently used keys. When a new key arrives at capacity,
least frequently used (LFU) eviction removes a key with the smallest
use count. If several keys have that count, the least recently used
one among them must leave.

The owning [frequency-bucket lesson](
#a145-frequency-buckets-with-linked-lists) defines and implements the
general cache. This entry specializes that composition to the standard
integer-key design problem without copying its linked-list and map
code.

The application contract is:

- construction receives a fixed capacity in `[1,10000]` and creates
  an empty cache;
- keys lie in `[0,100000]`, values lie in `[0,1000000000]`, and each
  live key is unique;
- `get(key)` returns the stored value on a hit and increments that
  key's use count;
- a get miss returns -1 without changing counts, recency, or
  membership;
- `put(key,value)` updates a live key, increments its count, and makes
  it most recent among keys at the new count;
- putting a live key does not change size or evict another key;
- putting a missing key at capacity first evicts one LFU key, breaking
  a frequency tie by least-recent use;
- a newly inserted key starts with count one because its put is a use;
- at most 200,000 get and put calls follow construction;
- get and put must each take average `O(1)` time;
- constructor and put contribute `null` to serialized output, while
  get contributes one integer;
- the cache owns every node, bucket, and map entry;
- capacity changes, explicit deletion, expiry, weights, loading,
  persistence, allocation failure, and unsynchronized concurrency are
  outside the judge contract.

Read [frequency maps](#a63-multisets-and-frequency-maps) for counts
and [doubly linked lists](#a32-doubly-linked-lists) for constant-time
removal of a known node. The earlier [LRU application](
#b235-lru-cache-hash-map-and-doubly-linked-list) owns pure recency
eviction and provides the closest contrast.

##### Mental model

Maintain three synchronized views of the live entries:

- `entryByKey[key]` points directly to that key's one node;
- `bucketByFrequency[count]` is a doubly linked list containing
  exactly the nodes with that count;
- `minimumFrequency` names the smallest count whose bucket is
  nonempty.

Each bucket runs from least recent at the front to most recent at the
back. Read `bucketByFrequency[2] = [1:10,3:30]` as: keys 1 and 3 have
each been used twice, key 1 was used less recently, and key 1 would
lose a tie between them.

On a hit or existing-key put, remove the node from count F, increment
it to F+1, and append it to the back of bucket F+1. If the old bucket
becomes empty, delete it. When F was also the minimum, the new minimum
is F+1 because no lower bucket existed and the promoted node now
occupies F+1.

On a missing-key put at capacity, remove the front node of the minimum
bucket and delete its key-map entry. Then insert the new node at the
back of bucket 1 and set the minimum to 1.

The key map answers where a key is. The frequency map answers which
keys tie at a count. The minimum field and a bucket's front answer
which key must be evicted without scanning either map.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use capacity two and the official sequence:
`construct, put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2),`
`get(3), put(4,4), get(1), get(3), get(4)`.

The expected serialized result is
`[null,null,null,1,null,-1,3,null,-1,3,4]`. Bucket snapshots below
list counts in increasing order and each bucket from least recent to
most recent.

Initial state: no cache exists and the result list is empty.

1. Decision: construct capacity two. Create empty maps, no buckets,
   and no minimum count.
   After: buckets are empty, size is zero, and result is `[null]`.
   Known correct: no key or eviction candidate exists.
2. Decision: put `1:1`. It is missing and space remains, so create a
   count-one node and append it to bucket 1.
   After: buckets are `1:[1:1]`, minimum is 1, and result appends
   `null`.
   Known correct: key 1 has one use and is the only candidate.
3. Decision: put `2:2`. It is also new, so append it behind key 1 in
   bucket 1 without eviction.
   After: buckets are `1:[1:1,2:2]`, minimum is 1, and result appends
   `null`.
   Known correct: both counts are one; key 1 is the older tie member.
4. Decision: get key 1. Remove its node from bucket 1, increment its
   count, append it to bucket 2, and return value 1.
   After: buckets are `1:[2:2] 2:[1:1]`; minimum remains 1; result
   appends 1.
   Known correct: key 2 has fewer uses than key 1.
5. Decision: put new `3:3` at capacity. Evict front of minimum bucket
   1, which is key 2. Insert key 3 with count one.
   After: buckets are `1:[3:3] 2:[1:1]`; result appends `null`.
   Known correct: key 2 was the unique least-frequent key and left
   before insertion.
6. Decision: get key 2. It is absent from `entryByKey`, so return -1
   before touching any bucket.
   After: state is unchanged and result appends -1.
   Known correct: a miss did not become a use.
7. Decision: get key 3. Promote it from count one to count two. Bucket
   1 empties, so delete it and advance the minimum to 2. Append key 3
   behind older key 1 in bucket 2.
   After: buckets are `2:[1:1,3:3]`; result appends 3.
   Known correct: both keys have count two, and key 1 is less recent.
8. Decision: put new `4:4` at capacity. Counts tie in minimum bucket
   2, so evict its front key 1. Insert key 4 with count one.
   After: buckets are `1:[4:4] 2:[3:3]`; minimum is 1; result appends
   `null`.
   Known correct: the recency rule resolved the frequency tie.
9. Decision: get key 1. Its earlier eviction makes this a miss.
   After: state is unchanged and result appends -1.
   Known correct: no stale map entry can reach the removed node.
10. Decision: get key 3. Promote it from count two to count three.
    Bucket 2 empties, but minimum remains 1 because key 4 is colder.
    After: buckets are `1:[4:4] 3:[3:3]`; result appends 3.
    Known correct: deleting a nonminimum bucket did not change the
    true minimum.
11. Decision: get key 4. Promote it from count one to count two. Its
    old minimum bucket empties, so advance minimum to 2 and stop after
    the last command.
    After: buckets are `2:[4:4] 3:[3:3]`; final result is
    `[null,null,null,1,null,-1,3,null,-1,3,4]`.
    Known correct: every hit, miss, promotion, eviction, and tie break
    matches the required sequence.

Focused capacity-one case: `put(1,1)`, `put(1,10)`, then `get(1)`
returns 10. The update promotes the existing node and does not evict
it. A later `put(2,2)` evicts key 1 before inserting key 2.

Focused sentinel case: `put(0,0)` followed by `get(0)` returns 0. A
missing get returns -1, which is unambiguous because judge values are
nonnegative.

Counterexample to breaking ties arbitrarily: after step 7, keys 1 and
3 both have count two, but key 1 reached that state earlier. Evicting
key 3 on the next insertion violates the LRU tie rule. The first wrong
decision is storing a frequency bucket without recency order.

##### Implementation

Use the complete Go program in
[A.14.5](#a145-frequency-buckets-with-linked-lists). It owns node
layout, list-end updates, bucket creation and deletion, promotion,
minimum tracking, eviction, snapshots, and the three-view invariant.

To adapt that owner to the integer-key judge interface:

1. Change the entry key and `entryByKey` map key from `string` to
   `int`.
2. Change the eviction-report key and key diagnostics to integers,
   including `%q` or `%s` formatting that must become `%d`.
3. Keep the positive-capacity constructor check; it matches the
   current official constraint.
4. Wrap the owner's `(value,found,error)` get. Return value on a hit
   and -1 on a miss.
5. Call the owner's put and discard its eviction report because the
   judge put method returns no value.
6. Treat the owner's frequency-overflow error as unreachable under at
   most 200,000 calls, while preserving it in reusable code.
7. Remove diagnostic snapshots from the submitted type; ordinary get
   and put never scan or sort buckets.

No separate problem file currently owns this exercise. The A.14.5
program is the repository reference implementation and executable
test of promotion, LFU eviction, LRU tie-breaking, updates, misses,
and frequency-overflow rejection.

##### Why it works

Maintain three facts after every operation:

1. `entryByKey` and all bucket lists contain exactly the same unique
   nodes, with each key in one node and one bucket.
2. A node belongs to the bucket matching its use count, and each
   bucket runs from least recent to most recent among that count.
3. When the cache is nonempty, `minimumFrequency` is the smallest
   nonempty bucket count.

Construction establishes all three facts with empty structures. A
miss changes nothing. A new key creates one matching map and list
entry at count one and most-recent position; setting the minimum to
one is exact because no valid count is smaller.

Promotion removes the one mapped node from bucket F and appends that
same node to bucket F+1, so membership and uniqueness stay fixed. Its
incremented count matches the new bucket, and the access is newest at
that count. If the old minimum bucket empties, no lower bucket exists
and F+1 now contains the promoted node, so advancing the minimum is
exact. Emptying a nonminimum bucket cannot affect the minimum.

At capacity, the minimum field selects the smallest use count. The
front node in that bucket is the least recent among all keys tied at
that count. Removing it from both the list and key map therefore
chooses exactly the contract's victim. Inserting the new count-one
node restores capacity and makes one the minimum.

Each operation makes a bounded number of map lookups and pointer
changes. It has no size-dependent loop, so it terminates. The official
call bound also keeps every frequency far below `uint64` overflow.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let C be capacity, N the live count with `0 <= N <= C`, M the number
of operations, and B the number of nonempty frequency buckets.
Integer hashing and equality inspect fixed-size values.

Get and put use a bounded number of expected-constant-time map
operations plus `Theta(1)` pointer updates. They therefore take
expected `Theta(1)` time under ordinary Go map behavior. Go does not
promise worst-case constant map operations, and allocation or map
growth can make one call slower.

A new key allocates one entry node and may allocate bucket 1. A
promotion reuses its node and allocates a destination bucket only when
that count is not already present. Eviction and promotion otherwise
reuse or detach existing nodes.

The live cache retains N nodes, N key-map entries, and B bucket-map
entries, where `0 <= B <= N`. Its logical storage is `Theta(N)`, hence
`O(C)` at capacity. Each node stores key, value, count, and two links;
this metadata is larger than an LRU node. Maps and the allocator may
retain spare capacity after entries or buckets disappear.

Across M commands, expected core work is `Theta(M)`. Retaining all
serialized results uses `Theta(M)` output slots; streaming each result
would use `Theta(1)` application output storage.

The owner's deterministic snapshot sorts B frequencies and traverses
N nodes, costing `O(B log B + N)` control work plus formatting and
`O(B + N)` output storage. Judge operations do not call it.

LFU can retain a once-popular key long after the workload changes.
Aging, decaying counts, admission filters, or periodic resets can
adapt faster, but each needs a new policy and may weaken constant-time
operations.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Capacity is positive in the judge. Reusable zero-capacity code must
  either reject construction, as the owner does, or define every put
  as a no-op; do not index a nonexistent minimum bucket.
- Capacity one makes one key both LFU and LRU. Updating it promotes
  without eviction; inserting a different key replaces it.
- Key zero and value zero are valid. Use map presence for membership
  and reserve -1 only for the judge miss result.
- A get miss changes nothing. Creating a count or refreshing recency
  on a miss can change the next victim.
- A new key begins at count one, not zero, because insertion is a use.
- Existing-key put counts as a use and becomes most recent in its new
  bucket. Updating only the value violates the official policy.
- Existing-key put never evicts because membership size does not grow.
- Promotion must remove the node from its old bucket before appending
  it to the new one. Leaving both links creates duplicate membership.
- Delete an empty frequency bucket. Keeping it can leave the minimum
  field pointing at no eviction candidate.
- Advance the minimum only when promotion empties the minimum bucket.
  Step 10 shows why deleting a higher bucket must not change it.
- After inserting a missing key, reset the minimum to one even if all
  older keys have much larger counts.
- Evict the front of the minimum bucket. Removing its back chooses the
  most recent rather than least recent tie member.
- Remove an evicted node from `entryByKey` as well as its bucket. A
  stale pointer can return a value that no longer consumes capacity.
- Frequencies do not overflow within the judge call limit. Reusable
  unbounded code should reject, saturate, decay, or widen counts
  before wraparound makes a hot key appear cold.
- Concurrent get and put need synchronization across lookup,
  promotion, eviction, insertion, and minimum updates as one state
  transition.

##### When to choose it

Choose an LFU cache when:

- repeated historical use is a useful predictor of future reuse;
- lookup is by unique key and the bound is an entry count;
- a least-recent tie rule is acceptable;
- expected constant-time get and put matter;
- extra maps, counts, and per-frequency lists fit in memory;
- one owner can serialize mutations.

Use [LRU](#b235-lru-cache-hash-map-and-doubly-linked-list) when recent
use matters more than accumulated frequency or when simpler metadata
is preferable. A scan of C+1 unique keys can pollute LRU, while plain
LFU may retain stale formerly hot entries; the workload decides which
failure mode matters.

Use a heap plus a key map when scores change by arbitrary amounts,
ordered inspection is needed, or logarithmic updates are acceptable.
Use expiry timestamps when deadlines, not use counts, choose victims.
Use weighted policies when entries differ greatly in byte size or
recomputation cost.

This structure implements eviction only. It does not load values,
suppress duplicate work, expire records, persist dirty data,
coordinate processes, or guarantee a hit rate. Those are separate
cache-system contracts.

The [owning lesson](
#a145-frequency-buckets-with-linked-lists) provides the complete Go
implementation and invariant proof. The official [LFU Cache problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/lfu-cache/) specifies capacity, counts,
tie-breaking, bounds, and the average-time target.

#### B.23.10 Time-based key store (map and sorted histories)

##### Problem and contract

An ordinary map can remember the latest value for a key, but replacing
that value destroys its history. A time-based key store must answer a
different question: what was the newest value already in effect at a
requested time?

This lesson implements the Time Based Key-Value Store contract:

- `Constructor` creates an empty store;
- `Set(key,value,timestamp)` appends one version for key;
- `Get(key,timestamp)` returns the value whose stored timestamp is the
  greatest timestamp less than or equal to the query;
- a missing key or a query before that key's first version returns the
  empty string;
- keys and values have lengths from 1 through 100 and contain only
  lowercase English letters and decimal digits;
- timestamps range from 1 through 10,000,000;
- timestamps on all `Set` calls are strictly increasing;
- at most 200,000 total `Set` and `Get` calls occur.

The global timestamp promise implies that each individual key's
versions arrive in strictly increasing order. Duplicate timestamps,
empty stored values, invalid characters, and out-of-order writes are
outside the contract and are not validated. Because stored values are
nonempty, the empty return value unambiguously means no eligible
version.

Queries may ask about any valid timestamp, including one earlier than
the latest write. Keys are independent. `Get` reads but does not
mutate the store. The constructor must be used before either method.
The store retains key and value strings. Unsynchronized concurrent
access is outside the contract.

Read [separate chaining and open addressing](
#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) for associative lookup and
[binary search and bounds](
#b41-binary-search-and-bounds-slice) for half-open boundary search.
Those lessons own map and search mechanics. This entry owns their
combination into per-key version histories.

##### Mental model

Keep one map named `historyByKey`. A key selects a slice, and each
slice element stores one timestamp and its value:

```text
historyByKey["foo"] = [(1,"bar"), (4,"bar2")]
```

Read that entry as: key `foo` had value `bar` starting at time 1 and
value `bar2` starting at time 4. The slice is ordered by timestamp.
`Set` can append because the input contract makes every new timestamp
larger than all earlier write timestamps.

For `Get("foo",3)`, exact timestamp 3 is absent. Search instead for
the first version whose timestamp is greater than 3. This is an upper
bound. The element immediately before that boundary is the greatest
timestamp at most 3 and therefore the requested version.

For a history of length H, maintain this state during search:

```text
[0,left)     timestamps are <= query
[left,right) relationship is still unknown
[right,H)    timestamps are > query
```

If the middle timestamp is at most the query, it is eligible, but a
later eligible version may exist, so move left past it. Otherwise the
middle is too new and may be the first too-new version, so move right
to it. At `left == right`, left is the upper bound. Return an empty
string when left is zero; otherwise return history element `left-1`.

Partitioning by key matters as much as ordering by time. A single
global history could find the latest write by any key, which is not
necessarily the latest write for the requested key.

##### Worked walkthrough

Run the official operation sequence:

```text
operations = [TimeMap, Set, Get, Get, Set, Get, Get]
arguments  = [[], ["foo","bar",1], ["foo",1],
              ["foo",3], ["foo","bar2",4],
              ["foo",4], ["foo",5]]
expected   = [null, null, "bar", "bar", null,
              "bar2", "bar2"]
```

Initial state: no store exists and no output has been produced.

1. Decision: construct the store. Allocate an empty map because no key
   has a history yet.
   After: `historyByKey` is `{}` and output is `[null]`.
   Known correct: every key is absent, matching an empty store.
2. Decision: set `foo` to `bar` at time 1. The key has no slice, so
   append `(1,"bar")` to its nil history.
   After: `foo` maps to `[(1,"bar")]`; append `null` to output.
   Known correct: the only stored version for `foo` starts at time 1.
3. Decision: get `foo` at time 1. Search `[0,1)`; timestamp 1 is at
   most the query, so left moves to 1. Return element zero.
   After: output appends `"bar"`; stored state is unchanged.
   Known correct: `(1,"bar")` is the greatest eligible timestamp.
4. Decision: get `foo` at time 3. The same sole version has timestamp
   1 at most 3, so its upper bound is again one.
   After: output appends `"bar"`; state is still unchanged.
   Known correct: no later `foo` version has been stored yet.
5. Decision: set `foo` to `bar2` at time 4. The timestamp is greater
   than the previous write timestamp, so append without sorting.
   After: `foo` maps to `[(1,"bar"),(4,"bar2")]`; output appends
   `null`.
   Known correct: the history remains strictly timestamp-ordered.
6. Decision: get `foo` at time 4. In `[0,2)`, middle timestamp 4 is
   eligible, so left becomes 2 and the search stops. Return index 1.
   After: output appends `"bar2"`; state remains unchanged.
   Known correct: the exact version at time 4 is the newest eligible
   one.
7. Decision: get `foo` at time 5. Timestamp 4 is still eligible and
   no later version exists. The operation stream is now exhausted.
   After: output is `[null,null,"bar","bar",null,"bar2",
   "bar2"]`; the two stored versions remain intact.
   Known correct: every operation has its required result and every
   query preserved the histories.

Focused predecessor trace: after both `foo` writes, query time 3. The
expected value is `bar`, not the current value `bar2`.

Initial state: history is `[(1,"bar"),(4,"bar2")]`, left is 0, and
right is 2.

1. Decision: inspect middle index 1, timestamp 4. Since `4 > 3`, it
   is too new, so set right to 1.
   After: candidates are `[0,1)` and index 1 is proved too new.
   Known correct: every eligible predecessor is before index 1.
2. Decision: inspect middle index 0, timestamp 1. Since `1 <= 3`, it
   is eligible, so set left to 1.
   After: the candidate interval is empty at boundary 1.
   Known correct: index 0 is eligible and every index from 1 is too
   new.
3. Decision: left equals right, so stop. Since left is not zero,
   return the value at `left-1`, which is index 0.
   After: the result is `bar` and the history is unchanged.
   Known correct: timestamp 1 is the greatest timestamp at most 3.

Focused missing case: `Get("missing",5)` selects a nil history. Its
search starts and ends at zero, so it returns `""` without indexing.

Focused early case: after storing `("x","start",5)`, querying `x` at
time 1 moves right to zero and returns `""`. The key exists, but no
version was yet in effect.

Counterexample to one latest value per key: after setting `foo` at
times 1 and 4, a plain `map[string]string` retains only `bar2`.
`Get("foo",3)` would return a future value or no history, while the
required result is `bar`.

Counterexample to one global time slice: after `(a,x,1)` and
`(b,y,2)`, a search by time alone for key `a` at time 2 can return
`y`. The map must select `a`'s history before binary search begins.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program uses the platform method names, performs the
official queries, then exercises a historical predecessor, a missing
key, and a query before the first version. Save it as `main.go` and
run `go run main.go`. The implementation relies on the stated input
contract rather than validating judge-owned bounds.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Time-based key store (map and
// sorted histories). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type timeValue struct {
	timestamp int
	value     string
}

type TimeMap struct {
	historyByKey map[string][]timeValue
}

func Constructor() TimeMap {
	// Build the requested item in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	return TimeMap{
		historyByKey: make(map[string][]timeValue),
	}
}

func (store *TimeMap) Set(
	key string,
	value string,
	timestamp int,
) {
	// Strictly increasing input keeps every key history sorted.
	store.historyByKey[key] = append(
		store.historyByKey[key],
		timeValue{
			timestamp: timestamp,
			value:     value,
		},
	)
}

func (store *TimeMap) Get(
	key string,
	timestamp int,
) string {
	// Follow the lookup rule for the requested item without changing
	// state.
	history := store.historyByKey[key]
	left := 0
	right := len(history)
	for left < right {
		middle := left + (right-left)/2
		// The answer is before the first version after the query.
		if history[middle].timestamp <= timestamp {
			left = middle + 1
		} else {
			right = middle
		}
	}

	// Insertion point zero means no stored version is old enough.
	if left == 0 {
		return ""
	}
	return history[left-1].value
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	store := Constructor()
	store.Set("foo", "bar", 1)
	fmt.Println(store.Get("foo", 1))
	fmt.Println(store.Get("foo", 3))
	store.Set("foo", "bar2", 4)
	fmt.Println(store.Get("foo", 4))
	fmt.Println(store.Get("foo", 5))
	fmt.Println(store.Get("foo", 3))
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", store.Get("missing", 5))

	later := Constructor()
	later.Set("x", "start", 5)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", later.Get("x", 1))
}
```

Expected output:

```text
bar
bar
bar2
bar2
bar
""
""
```

The first four lines reproduce the official gets. The fifth line
queries between stored versions after both exist. The quoted empty
strings distinguish the two no-result cases from blank output.

##### Why it works

Maintain the map invariant that `historyByKey[key]` contains exactly
the versions written for key and no versions written for another key.
`Set` appends only to the selected key's slice, so it preserves that
partition.

Maintain the ordering invariant that every selected history has
strictly increasing timestamps. A new store has only empty histories.
The input contract makes each new write timestamp greater than every
earlier write timestamp, hence greater than the last timestamp of its
key. Appending therefore preserves the invariant.

During `Get`, every timestamp before left is at most the query, and
every timestamp from right onward is greater than the query. Both
outside regions are initially empty. If the middle timestamp is at
most the query, sortedness proves that it and every earlier unknown
version are eligible, so moving left past middle preserves the left
fact. Otherwise sortedness proves that middle and every later version
are too new, so moving right to middle preserves the right fact.

At termination, left equals right at the first timestamp greater than
the query. If left is zero, every stored version is too new, so no
answer exists. Otherwise index `left-1` is eligible, and every later
index is too new. It is therefore the unique greatest eligible
timestamp. The map invariant makes its value belong to the requested
key.

When the search interval is nonempty, middle lies inside it. Moving
left to `middle+1` or right to middle strictly decreases its finite
width, so the loop terminates. The midpoint expression cannot
overflow because it adds left to at most the remaining distance.

`Get` copies only a slice header and reads records. It assigns to no
map entry, slice element, or retained string, proving the no-mutation
query contract.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let K be the number of distinct keys, S the total number of stored
versions, H the number of versions for the queried key, L the query
key length, and B the bytes retained by all key and value strings.
Under ordinary hash-map assumptions, locating a string key takes
expected O(L) time because its bytes must be hashed.

`Set` then appends one fixed-size record in amortized O(1) time. Its
expected amortized total is O(L). A slice growth can allocate and copy
Theta(H) records for that call, and map growth can also cause an
occasional larger operation. Go specifies map behavior, not a
worst-case constant-time bound.

`Get` takes expected O(L + log(H + 1)) time: one map lookup followed
by binary search. A missing key or empty history stops after the map
lookup. It allocates no output and returns a string header in O(1)
additional time.

The store retains O(K + S + B) logical data plus map buckets and
unused slice capacity. Each record stores an integer and a string
header; assigning strings does not copy their bytes, so the store can
keep their backing storage alive. `Get` uses O(1) auxiliary space.

A reverse linear scan has O(H) worst-case query time but is simpler
and may be competitive for tiny histories or queries usually near the
latest version. Binary search gives a reliable logarithmic bound for
long histories without changing append cost.

Supporting out-of-order writes changes the tradeoff. Inserting into a
sorted slice can shift Theta(H) records. A balanced search tree can
offer O(log H) updates and predecessor queries with greater pointer
and allocation overhead. Sorting a completed batch is appropriate
when all writes arrive before any query.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A missing key selects a nil slice and returns `""`. Do not assume a
  map lookup always yields at least one record.
- A query before the first version has upper bound zero. Check that
  boundary before reading `history[left-1]`.
- A query exactly at a version must include it. The comparison is
  `storedTimestamp <= query`, not strict less-than.
- A query between versions returns the earlier one. On timestamps 1
  and 4, query 3 returns the value at 1.
- A query after the last version returns the last value. The upper
  bound H is a valid boundary even though it is not an element index.
- Histories for different keys must remain separate. A global search
  by timestamp can return a value belonging to another key.
- Searching for the first timestamp at least the query uses the wrong
  boundary. With timestamps 1 and 4, query 3 would select future time
  4 instead of predecessor time 1.
- Stopping at the first eligible middle is also wrong. A later
  eligible version may exist; continue toward the upper bound.
- Returning the first eligible version scans in the wrong direction.
  With times 1 and 4 queried at 5, it returns the stale time-1 value.
- Appending is correct only because all write timestamps strictly
  increase. Accepting an out-of-order write without sorted insertion
  invalidates binary search.
- Duplicate write timestamps are excluded. A broader API must define
  whether a duplicate replaces, rejects, or coexists with a version.
- Empty stored values are excluded, which makes `""` a safe no-result
  sentinel. A broader value domain needs a Boolean or error result.
- Timestamp zero and negative timestamps are invalid, not special
  empty-history signals. The judge supplies values from 1 upward.
- Calling `Set` on a directly declared zero-value `TimeMap` panics
  because its map is nil. Construct the value with `Constructor`.
- Query methods do not synchronize with writes. Add a lock or external
  ownership if multiple goroutines share a mutable store.
- The 200,000-call bound limits retained versions but does not make
  this an expiry policy. No version is removed automatically.

##### When to choose it

Choose a map of sorted histories when:

- values are addressed by a discrete key;
- versions arrive in timestamp order;
- point queries ask for the latest version no later than a time;
- histories receive appends much more often than arbitrary edits;
- retaining every version fits memory.

A configuration history, price snapshot by symbol, or per-entity
status lookup can fit this pattern when its ordering and retention
contracts match. Use a plain map when only the latest value matters.
Use a reverse scan when histories are tiny. Use a balanced ordered
map, B-tree, or database index when writes arrive out of order,
deletions are common, or data exceeds process memory.

This in-memory structure does not provide persistence, expiration,
range output, cross-key snapshots, transactions, deletion, or crash
recovery. A production temporal database needs explicit contracts for
those properties rather than treating this interview structure as a
complete storage engine.

The [binary-search lesson](
#b41-binary-search-and-bounds-slice) owns the upper-bound invariant,
and the [hash-table lesson](
#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) owns associative lookup.
The official [Time Based Key-Value Store problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/time-based-key-value-store/) defines
the operation semantics, bounds, and monotone-write guarantee.

#### B.23.11 Sliding event counts (queue or time buckets)

##### Problem and contract

A lifetime counter only grows. A recent-event counter must also stop
counting occurrences when they cross a moving time boundary. Retaining
and rescanning every event repeats work, while storing only one total
loses the ages needed for expiration.

This lesson implements the Design Hit Counter contract:

- `Constructor` creates an empty counter;
- `Hit(timestamp)` records one hit at that integer second;
- several hits may share a timestamp and each counts separately;
- `GetHits(timestamp)` returns hits from the past 300 seconds;
- at query time T, included timestamps are the integers in
  `[T-299,T]`, equivalently timestamps X where `T-X < 300`;
- a hit exactly 300 seconds old is excluded;
- timestamps range from 1 through 2,000,000,000;
- timestamps across all calls are monotonically nondecreasing;
- at most 300 total `Hit` and `GetHits` calls occur.

Nondecreasing permits repeated timestamps. Operation order still
matters: a query at time 10 sees hits recorded by earlier calls, not a
later `Hit(10)` call. The counter returns only a count and retains no
event identity or payload.

The implementation does not validate timestamps or call order. Values
outside the range, decreasing time, integer overflow beyond the call
bound, and allocation failure are outside the contract. `Hit` mutates
one bucket. `GetHits` reads without mutation. The zero value is usable
as empty, though the platform calls `Constructor`. Unsynchronized
concurrent access is excluded.

Read [queues and circular buffers](
#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) for modulo slot reuse and
[fixed sliding windows](#b51-fixed-sliding-window-slice-or-counters)
for expiring one boundary while admitting another. Those entries own
the reusable mechanics. This lesson owns the online time-window
counter and the choice between a queue and timestamped buckets.

##### Mental model

There are only 300 possible integer-second positions inside any
300-second window. Keep a circular array of 300 buckets. Each bucket
stores an exact timestamp label and the number of hits recorded at
that timestamp:

```text
bucket = (timestamp, count)
index  = timestamp % 300
```

Read bucket 10 containing `(10,3)` as: three recorded hits occurred at
exactly second 10. The label is essential. Slot 10 can later represent
second 310, so its physical index alone does not identify a time.

On `Hit(T)`, inspect slot `T % 300`:

- if its label is T, increment its count;
- otherwise reset it to `(T,1)`.

Two different timestamps with the same remainder differ by a positive
multiple of 300 under monotone calls. The old timestamp is therefore
at least 300 seconds behind T and already expired when the slot is
reused.

On `GetHits(T)`, scan all buckets. Ignore an empty bucket. For a
nonempty bucket labeled X, add its count exactly when `T-X < 300`.
Monotone calls guarantee `T >= X`, so that age is nonnegative. Stale
buckets may remain physically stored; their labels keep them out of
the logical window.

A queue is the other natural representation. Store timestamp-count
groups in chronological order, remove front groups while their age is
at least 300, and maintain a running total. Buckets trade a fixed
300-item query scan for bounded storage and direct compression of a
large number of hits in the same second.

##### Worked walkthrough

Run the official operation sequence:

```text
operations = [HitCounter, Hit, Hit, Hit, GetHits,
              Hit, GetHits, GetHits]
arguments  = [[], [1], [2], [3], [4], [300], [300], [301]]
expected   = [null, null, null, null, 3, null, 4, 3]
```

Only nonempty buckets are displayed as
`physicalIndex:(timestamp,count)`.

Initial state: all 300 buckets contain zero values, so no bucket is
logically occupied and output is empty.

1. Decision: construct the counter. Zero initialization supplies 300
   empty timestamped buckets.
   After: bucket state is `{}` and output is `[null]`.
   Known correct: no recorded hit contributes to any query.
2. Decision: record time 1. Index `1 % 300 = 1` has a different zero
   label, so reset it to `(1,1)`.
   After: state is `{1:(1,1)}`; output appends `null`.
   Known correct: exactly one occurrence at second 1 is represented.
3. Decision: record time 2. Its index 2 is empty, so reset it to
   `(2,1)`.
   After: state is `{1:(1,1),2:(2,1)}`.
   Known correct: both recorded occurrences have distinct buckets.
4. Decision: record time 3 in index 3 by the same empty-slot rule.
   After: state is `{1:(1,1),2:(2,1),3:(3,1)}`.
   Known correct: the three calls contribute three total hits.
5. Decision: query at time 4. Ages are 3, 2, and 1, all less than
   300, so add all three counts.
   After: return 3 and append it to output; buckets do not change.
   Known correct: timestamps 1 through 3 all have age below 300.
6. Decision: record time 300. Index `300 % 300 = 0` is empty, so set
   it to `(300,1)`.
   After: state adds `{0:(300,1)}` and output appends `null`.
   Known correct: four recorded hits remain represented exactly once.
7. Decision: query at time 300. The hit at time 1 has age 299, so it
   is still included; the other ages are 298, 297, and 0.
   After: return 4 and append it to output; state is unchanged.
   Known correct: all four timestamps lie in the inclusive integer
   window `[1,300]`.
8. Decision: query at time 301. Time 1 now has age 300, so exclude its
   count. Times 2, 3, and 300 have ages below 300. No calls remain.
   After: return 3; final output is
   `[null,null,null,null,3,null,4,3]`.
   Known correct: exactly the hits in `[2,301]` were counted and every
   operation has its required result.

Focused slot-reuse trace: record time 1 and then time 301 in the same
counter. The expected count at time 301 is one.

Initial state: slot 1 contains `(1,1)` and all other slots are empty.

1. Decision: `301 % 300` is 1, whose label is not 301. The old hit has
   age 300 and is expired, so reset the slot to `(301,1)`.
   After: slot 1 contains `(301,1)`; the old count is gone.
   Known correct: overwrite removed only a hit outside `[2,301]`.
2. Decision: query time 301. The sole nonempty bucket has age zero,
   so include its count and finish the scan.
   After: return 1 without changing the slot.
   Known correct: the new hit is counted and the expired hit is not.

Focused duplicate case: three `Hit(10)` calls all select slot 10 with
the same label, so its count becomes three. `GetHits(10)` returns
three. At time 310, that bucket's age is exactly 300, so `GetHits`
returns zero.

Focused empty case: `GetHits(1)` scans only zero-count buckets and
returns zero. No timestamp sentinel is treated as a real hit.

Counterexample to using `age > 300` for expiry: after hits at 1, 2,
3, and 300, a query at 301 would wrongly retain time 1 and return
four. The contract excludes age 300, so the inclusion test must be
`age < 300`.

Counterexample to storing one Boolean per second: three hits at time
10 would collapse to one. Each bucket needs a count, not mere
presence.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program uses the platform method names. It performs
the official queries, duplicate-hit expiration, circular slot reuse,
and an empty query. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.
It uses only `fmt`; construction allocates no dynamic collection.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Sliding event counts (queue or
// time buckets). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

const windowSeconds = 300

type hitBucket struct {
	timestamp int
	count     int
}

type HitCounter struct {
	buckets [windowSeconds]hitBucket
}

func Constructor() HitCounter {
	// Build the requested item in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	return HitCounter{}
}

func (counter *HitCounter) Hit(timestamp int) {
	// Keep hit in one helper so callers use one rule.
	bucketIndex := timestamp % windowSeconds
	bucket := &counter.buckets[bucketIndex]
	// A different timestamp means the prior occupant has expired.
	if bucket.timestamp != timestamp {
		*bucket = hitBucket{timestamp: timestamp}
	}
	bucket.count++
}

func (counter *HitCounter) GetHits(timestamp int) int {
	// Follow the lookup rule for hits without changing state.
	total := 0
	for _, bucket := range counter.buckets {
		if bucket.count == 0 {
			continue
		}
		// Age 300 is outside the inclusive 300-second window.
		age := timestamp - bucket.timestamp
		if age < windowSeconds {
			total += bucket.count
		}
	}
	return total
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	counter := Constructor()
	counter.Hit(1)
	counter.Hit(2)
	counter.Hit(3)
	fmt.Println(counter.GetHits(4))
	counter.Hit(300)
	fmt.Println(counter.GetHits(300))
	fmt.Println(counter.GetHits(301))

	duplicates := Constructor()
	duplicates.Hit(10)
	duplicates.Hit(10)
	duplicates.Hit(10)
	fmt.Println(duplicates.GetHits(10))
	fmt.Println(duplicates.GetHits(310))

	reused := Constructor()
	reused.Hit(1)
	reused.Hit(301)
	fmt.Println(reused.GetHits(301))

	empty := Constructor()
	fmt.Println(empty.GetHits(1))
}
```

Expected output:

```text
3
4
3
3
0
1
0
```

The first three lines are the official query results. The next two
show three same-second hits before and at expiration. The last two
show safe slot reuse and an empty query.

##### Why it works

Maintain the bucket invariant: every nonempty slot labeled X stores
the exact number of recorded, not-yet-overwritten hits at second X,
and X maps to that slot by `X % 300`. Two live integer timestamps in
one 300-second window cannot share a slot, because equal remainders
would make their positive difference at least 300.

Initially every count is zero, so the invariant holds. On `Hit(T)`, a
bucket already labeled T represents exactly the earlier hits at T;
incrementing adds the new occurrence. If the label differs, any old
nonempty label X has the same remainder. Monotone calls give `T > X`,
and divisibility gives `T-X >= 300`. Its hits are expired at T and at
every later call, so resetting the slot loses no future answer. The
new `(T,1)` establishes the invariant for the new occurrence.

For `GetHits(T)`, consider any recorded hit. If its bucket was
overwritten, it was already at least 300 seconds old and cannot belong
to the current or a future monotone window. Otherwise it contributes
to the exact count in its timestamped bucket. The scan includes that
count precisely when `T-X < 300`, which is exactly the contract's
window predicate. Thus every valid hit is counted once and no expired
hit is counted.

The scan visits exactly 300 buckets and therefore terminates. Every
stored timestamp is at most the current timestamp by monotone call
order, so age is nonnegative. Both operands are between 1 and two
billion, making subtraction safe for Go's minimum 32-bit `int` range.
At most 300 calls also keep every bucket count and the total within
`int` range.

`GetHits` ranges over array values copied into local variables and
assigns only to local scalars. It cannot mutate the counter. `Hit`
changes exactly one selected bucket.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let W be the window width in timestamp units; here W is fixed at 300.
Construction zeroes W buckets in Theta(W) work and retains Theta(W)
storage inside the counter value. With the fixed contract, both are
constant bounds and require no heap allocation by the algorithm.

`Hit` computes one remainder, examines one label, and updates one
bucket, so it takes Theta(1) time and auxiliary space. `GetHits` scans
W buckets, so it takes Theta(W) time and Theta(1) auxiliary space.
For this fixed W, every query examines exactly 300 slots regardless of
hit count and is conventionally described as O(1).

The counter returns one integer and allocates no output. It retains no
event objects or strings. Under the official 300-call bound, integer
overflow is impossible. The high-volume follow-up motivates grouping
hits by second, but a real rate exceeding `int` capacity would require
a wider checked, saturating, or distributed counter.

A compressed queue stores `(timestamp,count)` groups plus a running
total. It can remove expired groups from the front. Each group enters
and leaves once, so updates and cleanup are amortized Theta(1), though
one call can remove Theta(G) expired groups, where G is the retained
group count. With cleanup on every operation, monotone integer seconds
bound G by W.

The queue scans no empty seconds and is attractive for a wide, sparse,
or configurable window. The bucket array gives deterministic storage,
no per-group allocation, direct same-second aggregation, Theta(1)
`Hit`, and a predictable W-step query. A raw queue with one entry per
hit does not scale when one second receives many hits; compress equal
timestamps before comparing it with buckets.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- An empty counter returns zero. Check bucket count before
  interpreting its zero timestamp label.
- Repeated timestamps are valid. Three hits at time 10 produce count
  three, not one overwritten occurrence.
- Calls are nondecreasing, not strictly increasing. `Hit(10)`,
  `GetHits(10)`, and another `Hit(10)` are valid in that order; the
  first query returns one and a later query at 10 returns two.
- A hit at `T-299` is included, while a hit at `T-300` is excluded.
  On queries 300 and 301, the time-1 hit changes from live to expired.
- A large time jump may make every bucket stale. The query still scans
  safely and returns zero without needing to clear all slots.
- Different timestamps can share a physical slot. Compare the exact
