  timestamp label before incrementing or time 301 would merge with 1.
- Do not clear a collision before proving it expired. The proof uses
  both equal remainders and monotone timestamps.
- Stale buckets may remain stored. Summing every nonzero count without
  checking age returns lifetime hits instead of window hits.
- Using `age <= 300` includes one second too many. The correct test is
  strict `age < 300`.
- Decreasing timestamps are outside the contract. They can create a
  negative age that this implementation would incorrectly include and
  can overwrite a still-live circular slot.
- Timestamp zero and values above two billion are invalid, not empty
  or saturation signals.
- The fixed array assumes one bucket per integer second. Finer time
  units or a different window width require a matching W and bounds.
- Copying `HitCounter` copies its complete state. Later mutations of
  the copies are independent because the representation has no slices
  or pointers to shared buckets.
- Concurrent `Hit` and `GetHits` calls race on bucket fields.
  Serialize ownership or add synchronization; individual field writes
  do not make the operation atomic.
- This count has no event identities, so it cannot retract one chosen
  hit, deduplicate delivery, or explain which hits formed the result.

##### When to choose it

Choose timestamped circular buckets when:

- the window width is fixed and reasonably small;
- timestamps use discrete units and calls never move backward;
- only a count, not event identity or payload, is required;
- many events may share one timestamp;
- bounded memory and predictable query work matter.

Use a compressed queue when active timestamps are sparse, the window
width is large or configurable, and occasional multi-group cleanup is
acceptable. Use [running statistics](
#b231-running-statistics-counters) when observations never expire. Use
an offline [event sweep](
#b174-sweep-line-sorted-events-and-active-state) when every
event is known before processing rather than arriving online.

This structure is not enough for late or reordered events, arbitrary
event-time queries, exact deduplication, durable state, or distributed
aggregation. Those systems need a lateness policy, event identities,
watermarks or ordered storage, persistence, partitioning, and an
explicit consistency contract.

The [circular-buffer lesson](#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) owns
modulo storage reuse, and the [fixed-window lesson](
#b51-fixed-sliding-window-slice-or-counters) owns rolling boundaries.
The official [Design Hit Counter problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/design-hit-counter/) defines the API;
its statement is subscription-gated. The [LeetCode Wiki mirror](
https://leetcode.doocs.org/en/lc/362/) records the example,
constraints, and high-volume follow-up used here.

#### B.23.12 Stack from queues (queues)

##### Problem and contract

A queue exposes the oldest value first, while a stack must expose the
newest value first. The task is to reproduce last-in, first-out stack
behavior while using only first-in, first-out queue operations.

This lesson implements the Implement Stack using Queues contract:

- `Constructor` creates an empty `MyStack`;
- `Push(value)` adds value as the new stack top;
- `Pop()` removes and returns the top value;
- `Top()` returns the top without removing it;
- `Empty()` reports whether no values remain;
- values range from 1 through 9;
- at most 100 total method calls occur;
- every `Pop` and `Top` call is made on a nonempty stack;
- the implementation may use only queue push-back, front peek or pop,
  size, and empty operations.

Repeated values remain separate pushes. `Push` and `Pop` mutate the
stack; `Top` and `Empty` do not. Invalid values, more than 100 calls,
and empty `Pop` or `Top` calls are outside the platform contract. The
private queue fails fast if those preconditions are violated rather
than silently corrupting state.

The implementation uses one queue, satisfying the problem's follow-up
as well as its allowance of at most two queues. Its fixed capacity of
100 follows from the total-call bound. The zero value is usable as an
empty stack, though the platform calls `Constructor`. Copying the
value copies its storage, while unsynchronized concurrent access is
outside the contract.

Read [array-backed and linked stacks](
#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks) for the LIFO contract and
[queues and circular buffers](
#a51-queues-and-circular-buffers) for FIFO order and physical slot
reuse. Those lessons own the two abstractions. This entry owns the
rotation that adapts one into the other.

##### Mental model

Maintain one decisive invariant:

```text
queue front-to-back == stack top-to-bottom
```

If the queue is `[3,2,1]` from front to back, read it as a stack with
top 3, then 2, then bottom 1. `Pop` can remove the queue front, `Top`
can peek there, and `Empty` can delegate directly.

Only `Push` needs to repair the order. Suppose N older values already
occupy the queue:

1. Save N before adding anything.
2. Enqueue the new value at the back.
3. Repeat N times: dequeue the front and enqueue that value at back.

For queue `[2,1]`, pushing 3 first produces `[2,1,3]`. Rotating 2
produces `[1,3,2]`; rotating 1 produces `[3,2,1]`. The new value has
moved to the front, while all older values retain their top-to-bottom
order behind it.

Saving the old length is essential. Rotating the new length would move
the new value once more and restore `[2,1,3]`, leaving it at the back.

The embedded bounded queue uses a circular array, but `MyStack`
accesses it only through enqueue, dequeue, front, length, and empty.
It never indexes queue storage or removes from the back.

##### Worked walkthrough

Run the official sequence:

```text
operations = [MyStack, Push, Push, Top, Pop, Empty]
arguments  = [[], [1], [2], [], [], []]
expected   = [null, null, null, 2, 2, false]
```

Queue displays below are logical front-to-back order, which is also
stack top-to-bottom order after every completed operation.

Initial state: no stack exists and output is empty.

1. Decision: construct the stack. Its bounded queue has head zero and
   size zero.
   After: queue is `[]` and output is `[null]`.
   Known correct: no pushes are pending, so the stack is empty.
2. Decision: push 1. Save old length zero, enqueue 1, and perform no
   rotations.
   After: queue is `[1]`; output appends `null`.
   Known correct: the sole value is both queue front and stack top.
3. Decision: push 2. Save old length one, enqueue to get `[1,2]`,
   then move front 1 to the back.
   After: queue is `[2,1]`; output appends `null`.
   Known correct: newest value 2 is first and older value 1 follows.
4. Decision: call `Top`. Peek at queue front 2 without removal.
   After: return 2 and append it to output; queue stays `[2,1]`.
   Known correct: observation reported the newest unpopped value and
   preserved both pushes.
5. Decision: call `Pop`. Dequeue queue front 2.
   After: return 2, append it to output, and leave queue `[1]`.
   Known correct: the newest value left exactly once and 1 became top.
6. Decision: call `Empty`. Queue size is one, so return false. No
   operations remain.
   After: final output is `[null,null,null,2,2,false]`; queue is
   `[1]`.
   Known correct: one unpopped push remains, and every operation has
   its required result.

Focused repeated-rotation trace: begin with queue `[2,1]` and push 3.
The expected result is `[3,2,1]`.

Initial state: saved old length is two; 2 is the current stack top.

1. Decision: enqueue 3 at the queue back.
   After: queue is `[2,1,3]`; no old value has rotated yet.
   Known correct: all three values are present, but the stack
   invariant is temporarily unresolved during `Push`.
2. Decision: perform the first of two rotations. Dequeue 2 and enqueue
   it at the back.
   After: queue is `[1,3,2]`; one old value remains before 3.
   Known correct: rotated value 2 will follow the new top in final
   order, while one iteration remains.
3. Decision: perform the second rotation. Move front 1 to the back;
   the saved count is exhausted, so stop.
   After: queue is `[3,2,1]`.
   Known correct: 3 is the newest top and older values 2 then 1 retain
   their prior relative order.

Focused duplicate case: push 5 twice. The second push rotates the
first, producing `[5,5]`. `Pop` returns one occurrence, and `Top`
still returns 5 for the older occurrence.

Focused empty case: a new stack returns true from `Empty`. `Pop` and
`Top` on that state are deliberately excluded by the contract.

Counterexample to omitting rotation: push 1 and then 2 would leave
queue `[1,2]`. `Pop` would return oldest value 1 instead of newest
value 2, violating LIFO at the first removal.

Counterexample to rotating until the queue is empty: each dequeue is
immediately followed by enqueue, so the queue never empties. Use the
saved finite old length as the loop bound.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program uses the platform names and one queue. It
performs the official sequence, repeated rotations, complete drain,
and duplicate handling. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.
It uses only `fmt` and allocates no dynamic collection.

The private queue's fixed array is support code. The `MyStack` methods
use only its standard queue operations; circular-buffer mechanics are
owned by the prerequisite lesson.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Stack from queues (queues).
// Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

const maximumStackOperations = 100

type boundedIntegerQueue struct {
	values [maximumStackOperations]int
	head   int
	size   int
}

func (queue *boundedIntegerQueue) enqueue(value int) {
	// Add the requested item while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	if queue.size == len(queue.values) {
		panic("enqueue into full queue")
	}
	backIndex := (queue.head + queue.size) % len(queue.values)
	queue.values[backIndex] = value
	queue.size++
}

func (queue *boundedIntegerQueue) dequeue() int {
	// Remove the requested item while preserving the remaining
	// representation.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		panic("dequeue from empty queue")
	}
	value := queue.values[queue.head]
	queue.values[queue.head] = 0
	queue.head = (queue.head + 1) % len(queue.values)
	queue.size--
	return value
}

func (queue *boundedIntegerQueue) front() int {
	// Follow the lookup rule for the requested item without changing
	// state.
	if queue.size == 0 {
		panic("front of empty queue")
	}
	return queue.values[queue.head]
}

func (queue *boundedIntegerQueue) length() int {
	// Keep length in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return queue.size
}

func (queue *boundedIntegerQueue) empty() bool {
	// Keep empty in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return queue.size == 0
}

type MyStack struct {
	queue boundedIntegerQueue
}

func Constructor() MyStack {
	// Build the requested item in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	return MyStack{}
}

func (stack *MyStack) Push(value int) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	valuesToRotate := stack.queue.length()
	stack.queue.enqueue(value)
	// Move every older value behind the newly enqueued top.
	rotationCount := 0
	for rotationCount < valuesToRotate {
		olderValue := stack.queue.dequeue()
		stack.queue.enqueue(olderValue)
		rotationCount++
	}
}

func (stack *MyStack) Pop() int {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	return stack.queue.dequeue()
}

func (stack *MyStack) Top() int {
	// Keep top in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return stack.queue.front()
}

func (stack *MyStack) Empty() bool {
	// Keep empty in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return stack.queue.empty()
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	stack := Constructor()
	stack.Push(1)
	stack.Push(2)
	fmt.Println(stack.Top())
	fmt.Println(stack.Pop())
	fmt.Println(stack.Empty())

	stack.Push(3)
	stack.Push(4)
	first := stack.Pop()
	second := stack.Pop()
	third := stack.Pop()
	fmt.Println(first, second, third)
	fmt.Println(stack.Empty())

	duplicates := Constructor()
	duplicates.Push(5)
	duplicates.Push(5)
	fmt.Println(
		duplicates.Pop(),
		duplicates.Top(),
		duplicates.Empty(),
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
2
2
false
4 3 1
true
5 5 false
```

The first three lines are the official results. The next two show
pushes 3 and 4 followed by complete LIFO drain. The final line proves
that equal values remain separate occurrences.

##### Why it works

Maintain the adapter invariant that queue front-to-back order equals
the unpopped push sequence from newest to oldest. Empty establishes it
because both orders contain no values.

Assume the queue is `[v0,v1,...,vN-1]`, where `v0` is the current
stack top. Pushing X first produces
`[v0,v1,...,vN-1,X]`. Each rotation removes the earliest remaining old
value and appends it. After exactly N rotations, X is the only value
never moved and therefore reaches the front. The older sequence
`[v0,v1,...,vN-1]` retains its relative order behind X. The resulting
queue `[X,v0,v1,...,vN-1]` reestablishes the invariant.

Given the invariant, `Pop` removes queue front, which is exactly the
newest unpopped value. The remaining front-to-back suffix is still the
remaining pushes from newest to oldest. `Top` reads that same value
without mutation, and `Empty` is true exactly when no pushes remain.

The circular queue separately maintains that its `size` logical values
occupy consecutive wrapped positions beginning at `head`. Enqueue
writes offset `size`; dequeue reads `head`, advances it, and decreases
size. These are precisely the FIFO operations used by the adapter.

`Push` saves finite N before enqueue and increments its rotation count
once per iteration, so it stops after exactly N rotations. The call
bound means N is at most 99 before a valid push, so enqueue cannot
fill beyond the 100-slot array. Valid `Pop` and `Top` preconditions
prevent the private empty-queue panics.

All adapter state is inside the receiver. A copied `MyStack` contains
its own array, head, and size, so subsequent operations cannot mutate
the original.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the stack size before an operation and C be the queue
capacity, fixed at 100 here. Constructor zero-initializes C integer
slots in Theta(C) work and retains Theta(C) storage. Under the fixed
problem bound, that is constant work and storage with no dynamic
collection allocation.

`Push` performs one enqueue plus N dequeue-enqueue rotations. It takes
Theta(N+1) time for every state of size N: Theta(1) when empty and
Theta(N) as positive N grows, with a Theta(C) worst case at capacity.
No input-distribution average is involved. It uses Theta(1) auxiliary
space and allocates nothing.

`Pop`, `Top`, and `Empty` each use Theta(1) time and auxiliary space.
They return scalar values and allocate no output. N logical values use
Theta(N) of the already retained C slots. Across P pushes without
pops, total rotation work is
`0 + 1 + ... + (P-1) = Theta(P^2)`.

A push-cheap design can enqueue in Theta(1), then make `Pop` and `Top`
move all but the newest value through a second queue in Theta(N). That
trade is preferable when pushes greatly outnumber removals or top
queries. The one-queue push-costly design favors frequent `Pop` and
`Top` after construction.

A direct slice stack provides amortized Theta(1) `Push` and Theta(1)
`Pop` and `Top`, with occasional resize copies. Queue adaptation is an
interface exercise or a response to a real queue-only dependency, not
an improvement over an available native stack.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A new or completely drained stack returns true from `Empty`. Do not
  call `Pop` or `Top` there under this contract.
- One pushed value needs zero rotations. Rotating once would move it
  from front to back, which looks unchanged only because it is alone.
- Save the old length before enqueue. Using the new length rotates X
  as well and leaves it at the back.
- Rotate exactly once per older value. Stopping early leaves an older
  value before the new top; waiting for empty never terminates.
- `Top` must peek, not dequeue and re-enqueue. The latter can change
  order unless the full repair is repeated.
- Duplicates such as two pushes of 5 are separate queue entries. Do
  not deduplicate values when rotating.
- Values are only 1 through 9. Zero is an unused cleared-slot value.
  Logical membership comes from head and size, not slot contents.
- At most 100 total method calls imply no more than 100 values can be
  stored. If that bound changes, use a growing queue or return an
  explicit capacity failure.
- The private queue panics on full, empty dequeue, or empty front.
  Valid platform calls cannot reach those branches; a broader API
  should return a Boolean or error instead.
- Queue head can wrap past physical slot 99. Always compute the back
  with modulo rather than assuming physical indexes grow forever.
- Clearing a dequeued slot is not the logical removal; decreasing size
  and advancing head define the new queue.
- Copying this array-backed stack is independent. Replacing the queue
  with a slice or linked nodes would change copy ownership semantics.
- Concurrent calls can interleave rotation and expose a temporary
  state where the adapter invariant is not restored. Serialize access
  or add synchronization.

##### When to choose it

Choose this adapter when an interface exposes only queue operations
but the consumer needs LIFO behavior, or when practicing how one
abstract data type can simulate another. Choose the push-costly form
when `Pop` and `Top` latency matters more than `Push` latency.

Use a two-queue, pop-costly form when pushes dominate. Use a direct
[array-backed or linked stack](
#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks)
whenever stack storage is allowed; it avoids the rotation cost
entirely. Use an ordinary [queue](
#a53-array-backed-and-linked-queues) when the oldest pending item, not
the newest one, must leave first.

This exercise does not provide blocking operations, thread safety,
durability, or a dynamically growing capacity. Those are separate
container or system contracts.

The official [Implement Stack using Queues problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/implement-stack-using-queues/) defines
the allowed queue operations, bounds, valid-call preconditions, and
one-queue follow-up.

#### B.23.13 Iterators and flattening (stack or cursor state)

##### Problem and contract

A nested list can contain integers, lists, and lists inside those
lists. Copying every integer into one flat slice before returning the
first value performs all work and stores all output even when a caller
stops early. An iterator should instead remember enough position state
to reveal one next integer at a time.

This lesson implements the Flatten Nested List Iterator contract:

- the top-level list has length from 1 through 500;
- each element is either one integer or another nested list;
- integer values range from -1,000,000 through 1,000,000;
- `Constructor(nestedList)` creates an iterator before the first
  integer;
- `HasNext()` reports whether an unreturned integer remains;
- `Next()` returns that integer in left-to-right nested-list order;
- repeated `HasNext` calls do not consume or skip an integer;
- the judge calls `Next` only when another integer exists.

Flattening removes list boundaries but preserves depth-first,
left-to-right order. Empty sublists are skipped. Negative values,
zero, extremes, and duplicates remain ordinary returned values.

The input is a finite, well-formed nested structure with no nil
elements or cycles. The iterator reads and retains the supplied list
slices and nodes but does not mutate them. Caller mutation during
iteration, allocation failure, and unsynchronized concurrent calls are
outside the contract. In the standalone implementation, `Next` after
exhaustion panics to expose a violated precondition.

The platform provides `NestedInteger` and its query methods. The
example defines a small compatible stand-in solely so the program can
compile and construct demonstrations; it does not claim that the judge
uses the same fields.

Read [array-backed and linked stacks](
#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks) for last-in, first-out state and
[depth-first traversal](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) for suspended parent
work. Those lessons own the mechanics. This entry owns the iterator
lifecycle: normalize to the next integer without consuming it, then
advance exactly once in `Next`.

##### Mental model

Store a stack of cursor frames. One frame contains:

```text
values     one nested list
nextIndex  first element in that list not yet handled
```

Read frame `([4,[6]],1)` as: integer 4 has been handled, and nested
list `[6]` is the next element to inspect. Frames below the top are
paused parent lists. Their indexes already point past the child list
currently being explored.

`HasNext` repeatedly normalizes the stack:

1. If the top frame is exhausted, clear and pop it.
2. If its next element is an integer, stop and return true without
   advancing the index.
3. If its next element is a list, advance the parent index first, then
   push a frame for that child and continue.

An empty child frame is immediately exhausted and popped. Advancing
the parent before descending prevents the same child from being pushed
again when the iterator returns from it.

`Next` calls `HasNext` so it is safe even when the caller omitted a
separate readiness check. It then reads the top frame's integer and
increments that frame's index. Because `HasNext` left the integer in
place, repeated readiness checks remain idempotent.

This is lazy flattening: the iterator stores a path of list cursors,
not a copy of every integer. The stack top is always the next active
depth-first list.

##### Worked walkthrough

Flatten `[[1,1],2,[1,1]]`. Call the top-level list R, its first child
L, and its final child Q. The expected output is `[1,1,2,1,1]`.

Frame snapshots run from bottom to top. `R@1` means R's next index is
1. Each loop iteration calls `HasNext` and then `Next` when ready.

Initial state: frames are `[R@0]` and output is empty.

1. Decision: `HasNext` sees list L at `R@0`. Advance R to 1, push
   `L@0`, and inspect its integer 1. Stop without advancing L.
   After: frames are `[R@1,L@0]`; `HasNext` returns true.
   Known correct: no integer was consumed, and L's first 1 is next.
2. Decision: `Next` confirms readiness, reads L index 0, and advances
   L to 1.
   After: frames are `[R@1,L@1]`; output is `[1]`.
   Known correct: the first flattened integer was returned once.
3. Decision: `HasNext` sees the second integer in L and leaves it in
   place. `Next` returns it and advances L to 2.
   After: frames are `[R@1,L@2]`; output is `[1,1]`.
   Known correct: L is fully consumed in its original order.
4. Decision: `HasNext` pops exhausted L. R index 1 holds integer 2,
   so stop there; `Next` returns 2 and advances R to 2.
   After: frames are `[R@2]`; output is `[1,1,2]`.
   Known correct: completed child L precedes its following sibling 2.
5. Decision: `HasNext` sees list Q at R index 2. Advance R to 3, push
   `Q@0`, and stop at Q's first integer. `Next` returns that 1.
   After: frames are `[R@3,Q@1]`; output is `[1,1,2,1]`.
   Known correct: the final child is active and one integer remains.
6. Decision: readiness stops at Q index 1. `Next` returns its 1 and
   advances Q to 2.
   After: frames are `[R@3,Q@2]`; output is `[1,1,2,1,1]`.
   Known correct: every integer in Q has been returned in order.
7. Decision: `HasNext` pops exhausted Q, then pops exhausted R. The
   stack is empty, so stop iteration.
   After: `HasNext` returns false; output remains `[1,1,2,1,1]`.
   Known correct: no cursor has unresolved work, so flattening is
   complete.

Focused deep trace: use `[1,[4,[6]]]`. After returning 1, the root
frame points at child A equal to `[4,[6]]`.

Initial state: frames are `[root@1]` and output is `[1]`.

1. Decision: readiness advances root, pushes `A@0`, and stops at 4;
   `Next` returns 4.
   After: frames are `[root@2,A@1]`; output is `[1,4]`.
   Known correct: A's nested child remains after its returned 4.
2. Decision: readiness advances A, pushes child `[6]@0`, and stops at
   6; `Next` returns 6.
   After: frames are `[root@2,A@2,[6]@1]`; output is `[1,4,6]`.
   Known correct: two consecutive descents preserved outer order.
3. Decision: the next readiness check pops the exhausted child, A,
   and root frames, then finds no active frame.
   After: `HasNext` returns false and output stays `[1,4,6]`.
   Known correct: every nested list and integer is exhausted.

Focused empty-list case: `[[],[[]],0]` pushes and eventually pops the
first empty child, its wrapper sibling, and that wrapper's empty child
before stopping at integer 0. It returns `[0]`. A structure
`[[],[[]]]` contains no integer, so its first `HasNext` returns false.

Focused idempotence case: on
`[[],-1000000,[[],0,1000000]]`, two initial `HasNext` calls both
return true, and the first `Next` still returns -1,000,000.

Counterexample to advancing an integer in `HasNext`: on `[1,2]`, two
readiness checks would move past both values before `Next`. Readiness
may rearrange structural frames, but only `Next` consumes an integer.

Counterexample to leaving a parent on its child index: after finishing
L in the main trace, readiness would push L again and repeat its two
ones forever. Advance the parent before pushing the child frame.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program performs both official examples, repeated
readiness, empty-list skipping, signed extremes, zero, and exhaustion.
Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`. It uses only `fmt`.

`NestedInteger` and the two builder functions are standalone support.
On the platform, remove that support and use the judge-provided type;
the iterator itself already calls only `IsInteger`, `GetInteger`, and
`GetList`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Iterators and flattening (stack or
// cursor state). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

type NestedInteger struct {
	holdsInteger bool
	integer      int
	children     []*NestedInteger
}

func (item NestedInteger) IsInteger() bool {
	// Evaluate is integer without changing the maintained state.
	return item.holdsInteger
}

func (item NestedInteger) GetInteger() int {
	// Follow the lookup rule for integer without changing state.
	return item.integer
}

func (item NestedInteger) GetList() []*NestedInteger {
	// Follow the lookup rule for list without changing state.
	return item.children
}

func integer(value int) *NestedInteger {
	// Keep integer in one helper so callers use one rule.
	return &NestedInteger{
		holdsInteger: true,
		integer:      value,
	}
}

func list(values ...*NestedInteger) *NestedInteger {
	// Expose the requested item in logical order without changing
	// source.
	return &NestedInteger{children: values}
}

type nestedCursor struct {
	values    []*NestedInteger
	nextIndex int
}

type NestedIterator struct {
	frames []nestedCursor
}

func Constructor(
	nestedList []*NestedInteger,
) *NestedIterator {
	// Build the requested item in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	return &NestedIterator{
		frames: []nestedCursor{{values: nestedList}},
	}
}

func (iterator *NestedIterator) HasNext() bool {
	// Follow the lookup rule for next without changing state.
	for len(iterator.frames) > 0 {
		topIndex := len(iterator.frames) - 1
		frame := &iterator.frames[topIndex]
		if frame.nextIndex == len(frame.values) {
			// Clear a finished frame before releasing its slot.
			iterator.frames[topIndex] = nestedCursor{}
			iterator.frames = iterator.frames[:topIndex]
			continue
		}

		candidate := frame.values[frame.nextIndex]
		if candidate.IsInteger() {
			return true
		}

		// Mark the list expanded before its child frame takes over.
		frame.nextIndex++
		iterator.frames = append(
			iterator.frames,
			nestedCursor{values: candidate.GetList()},
		)
	}
	return false
}

func (iterator *NestedIterator) Next() int {
	// Keep next in one helper so callers use one rule.
	if !iterator.HasNext() {
		panic("next called on exhausted iterator")
	}
	topIndex := len(iterator.frames) - 1
	frame := &iterator.frames[topIndex]
	candidate := frame.values[frame.nextIndex]
	frame.nextIndex++
	return candidate.GetInteger()
}

func collect(iterator *NestedIterator) []int {
	// Expose the requested item in logical order without changing
	// source.
	result := make([]int, 0)
	for iterator.HasNext() {
		result = append(result, iterator.Next())
	}
	return result
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	first := []*NestedInteger{
		list(integer(1), integer(1)),
		integer(2),
		list(integer(1), integer(1)),
	}
	fmt.Println(collect(Constructor(first)))

	second := []*NestedInteger{
		integer(1),
		list(integer(4), list(integer(6))),
	}
	fmt.Println(collect(Constructor(second)))

	boundaries := []*NestedInteger{
		list(),
		integer(-1_000_000),
		list(list(), integer(0), integer(1_000_000)),
	}
	iterator := Constructor(boundaries)
	firstReady := iterator.HasNext()
	secondReady := iterator.HasNext()
	fmt.Println(firstReady, secondReady)
	fmt.Println(collect(iterator))
	fmt.Println(iterator.HasNext())
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 1 2 1 1]
[1 4 6]
true true
[-1000000 0 1000000]
false
```

The first two lines are the official flattened orders. The next three
show idempotent readiness, empty-list skipping, all value boundaries,
and stable exhaustion.

##### Why it works

Maintain this cursor invariant: from bottom to top, frames are the
active nested-list path. In every frame, elements before `nextIndex`
have been returned if they are integers or completely explored if they
are lists. The element at `nextIndex`, when one exists, is the first
unresolved element in that list.

The initial root frame has index zero, so nothing has been handled and
the invariant holds. Popping an exhausted frame is safe because every
one of its elements is complete. Its parent was advanced before the
child was pushed, so the parent's first unresolved element is already
the following sibling.

When the next element is a list, advancing the parent marks that list
as delegated, and a child frame at index zero makes its first element
the next unresolved work. When the next element is an integer,
`HasNext` changes nothing and returns true. Repeated calls therefore
identify the same integer.

`Next` first establishes readiness, then returns exactly that integer
and advances its frame once. The invariant now marks the integer
handled. By induction, returned integers follow the recursive
left-to-right order and none is returned twice.

If the frames become empty, the root and every descendant list were
exhausted, so no integer remains. Conversely, normalization stops at
any unresolved integer before returning true, so empty frames imply
exhaustion exactly.

One normalization iteration either pops a frame, advances one
finite-list index before pushing its finite child, or returns. No list
element is expanded twice. The finite, acyclic input therefore bounds
all transitions and guarantees termination. Cyclic input would
invalidate that argument and is excluded.

The iterator changes only frame indexes and its private frame slice.
It calls read-only methods on nested nodes, so source values and list
order are preserved. Clearing a popped frame prevents that unused
frame slot from retaining its slice reference.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the total number of elements across all nested lists. This
counts both integer and list-valued elements. Let I be the number of
integers and D be the greatest number of simultaneously open lists.

Construction creates one root frame in Theta(1) time and storage. One
`HasNext` call is Theta(1) when the top already points at an integer,
but can take Theta(N) worst-case when it skips a long structure of
empty lists. A valid `Next` after readiness is Theta(1); a direct
`Next` may perform the same worst-case normalization first.

Across a complete iteration, every list-valued element is expanded
once, every frame is pushed and popped once, and every integer is
consumed once. Total iterator work is Theta(N), plus constant work per
API call. This is amortized Theta(1) per inspected structural element,
not necessarily per returned integer when many empty lists exist. No
input-distribution average is claimed.

At most D frames are active, so auxiliary storage is O(D). Slice
growth may occasionally allocate and copy existing frames; geometric
growth makes total copying amortized over pushes. Cleared popped slots
do not retain input slices, though live root and ancestor frames can
keep the remaining nested structure reachable.

The iterator stores no flattened integer output. The demonstration's
`collect` helper takes Theta(I) time beyond iterator work and Theta(I)
output storage. Its result is caller-owned. The standalone builders
allocate input nodes, but those allocations belong to demonstration
input construction, not iterator auxiliary space.

Eager flattening spends Theta(N) time in the constructor, retains
Theta(I) copied integers, then gives Theta(1) readiness and next
calls. It is attractive when every value will certainly be consumed
and steady per-call latency matters. Lazy cursors defer work, use
O(D) state, and can avoid visiting an unused suffix when a consumer
stops.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty sublists are valid structural elements. Push their frames and
  let normalization pop them without inventing a value.
- A nested structure can contain no integers even though the root list
  is nonempty. `[[],[[]]]` must make `HasNext` return false.
- Zero is a valid integer. Use `IsInteger`, not zero as a sentinel for
  a list node.
- Negative, extreme, and duplicate integers preserve their positions;
  no ordering or deduplication is part of flattening.
- Repeated `HasNext` calls must identify the same pending integer.
  Increment its cursor only in `Next`.
- Advance a parent before pushing its child. Advancing afterward can
  repeat the child or require fragile return-time repair.
- Clear and pop every exhausted frame. Leaving one on top makes
  normalization spin or index at the list length.
- A deeply nested chain has D in Theta(N). The explicit stack avoids
  recursive call-stack exhaustion but does not remove the storage
  bound.
- In Go, appending a frame may replace the slice backing array. Do
  not use the earlier `frame` pointer after `append`; this code
  advances it first and then discards it.
- `Next` after exhaustion panics in this standalone API. The platform
  promises valid calls; a general library could return `(int,bool)`.
- The iterator borrows nested slices and nodes. Mutation during
  iteration can change lengths, indexes, or values and is unsupported.
- Nil nodes and cyclic lists are malformed input. A nil dereference or
  infinite descent is not given fallback behavior.
- Concurrent readiness and next calls can race on frames and indexes.
  Serialize use or add an explicit synchronization contract.
- Clearing a frame releases only that slice header. A parent list may
  still retain the same child node through its own backing storage.

##### When to choose it

Choose a lazy cursor stack when:

- nested input is finite and ordered;
- callers want one value at a time and may stop early;
- source structure must remain unchanged;
- maximum depth is a better memory bound than total integer count;
- occasional traversal work in `HasNext` is acceptable.

Use eager flattening when all integers will be consumed, extra O(I)
storage fits, and constant per-call latency is more important than
constructor latency. Use a callback or language generator when the API
can express suspension directly. Use recursion when depth is safely
bounded and iteration need not pause between values.

The unsolved [Binary Search Tree Iterator practice](
problems/medium_leetcode_0173_binary_search_tree_iterator.go) uses
the same readiness and cursor-lifetime discipline for inorder
traversal. Its stack stores a tree path rather than list frames.

The [stack lesson](#a41-array-backed-and-linked-stacks) owns LIFO
storage. The [depth-first traversal lesson](
#b111-depth-first-traversal-stack-or-recursion) owns explicit
suspended work. The official [Flatten Nested List Iterator problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/flatten-nested-list-iterator/) defines
the judge-owned interface, flattened order, examples, and bounds.

### B.24 Array rearrangement and in-place transformations

#### B.24.1 Stable compaction (read and write indexes)

##### Problem and contract

Suppose a sequence contains values to keep and values to discard.
Stable compaction packs the kept values at the front without changing
their relative order. Repeatedly deleting one rejected value and
shifting the suffix works, but an early run of rejections can move the
same later value many times.

This lesson implements a reusable Go operation with this contract.
The `keep` function is a predicate: it returns true for a value that
must remain and false for one that must be discarded. Result
guarantees below describe a call that returns successfully.

- `values` is a finite mutable slice of any element type;
- `keep` is non-nil and decides whether one value remains;
- `keep` is called once for each original value, from left to right;
- the returned slice contains exactly the kept values in original
  order;
- the returned length and capacity both equal K, the kept count;
- `values[:K]` holds the returned sequence, while `values[K:]` is
  reset to the element type's zero value;
- the returned slice shares its first K slots with `values`;
- the compaction body allocates no second element collection.

The predicate must not mutate `values`, and no other goroutine may
read or write the shared backing array during compaction. A nil
predicate panics before mutation. If a non-nil predicate panics, that
panic propagates and earlier writes are not rolled back.

Read [fixed arrays and dynamic slices](
#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) first. That lesson owns slice
length, capacity, aliasing, and full slice expressions. This entry
owns the kept-prefix invariant that makes overwriting safe.

##### Mental model

Keep two indexes with different jobs:

- `readIndex` selects the next original value to classify;
- `writeIndex` is the first slot after the stable kept prefix.

Before reading one value, view the slice as three regions:

```text
[0, writeIndex)          kept values, final order
[writeIndex, readIndex)  processed slots no longer meaningful
[readIndex, N)           original values not yet classified
```

Always maintain `0 <= writeIndex <= readIndex <= N`. Rejecting a
value advances only the loop's read position. Keeping a value copies
it into `values[writeIndex]`, then advances `writeIndex`. Because the
destination never lies to the right of the source, a write cannot
destroy an unread value.

For example, read the state `writeIndex = 2`, `readIndex = 5`, and
`values = [1,3,2,3,2,4]` as follows: 1 and 3 are the kept values from
original indexes 0 through 4; indexes 2 through 4 are processed
scratch slots; original value 4 at index 5 is still unread.

After all reads, `writeIndex` is the kept count. Clear the remaining
slots only then, when no unread values remain. Return
`values[:writeIndex:writeIndex]`. The third slice bound makes capacity
equal length, so an append through the result cannot overwrite the
cleared tail of the original slice.

##### Worked walkthrough

Compact `[2,1,2,3,2,4]` by rejecting 2. The expected stable result is
`[1,3,4]`. The original six-slot view must finish as
`[1,3,4,0,0,0]`.

Initial state: `readIndex = 0`, `writeIndex = 0`, and no values have
been classified. The kept prefix is empty and all six values are
unread.

```text
[ kept prefix | rejected gap | unread values ]
  writeIndex ^                 ^ readIndex

start: [ | | 2 1 2 3 2 4 ]
end:   [ 1 3 4 | 0 0 0 | ]
```

1. Decision: read value 2 at index 0. `keep(2)` is false, so skip it
   and leave `writeIndex` at 0.
   After: the loop proceeds to `readIndex = 1`; the slice remains
   `[2,1,2,3,2,4]`; the kept prefix is empty.
   Known correct: original index 0 is rejected, while indexes 1
   through 5 remain unread and unchanged.

2. Decision: read value 1 at index 1. `keep(1)` is true, so write 1
   at index 0 and advance `writeIndex` to 1.
   After: `values = [1,1,2,3,2,4]`; the next read index is 2.
   Known correct: `values[:1]` is `[1]`, exactly the kept sequence
   from original indexes 0 and 1. Indexes 2 through 5 stay unread.

3. Decision: read value 2 at index 2. Reject it and keep
   `writeIndex = 1`.
   After: `values = [1,1,2,3,2,4]`; the next read index is 3.
   Known correct: `[1]` remains the complete kept sequence from the
   first three original values.

4. Decision: read value 3 at index 3. Keep it by writing index 1,
   then advance `writeIndex` to 2.
   After: `values = [1,3,2,3,2,4]`; the next read index is 4.
   Known correct: `[1,3]` preserves the order of the kept values;
   original indexes 4 and 5 remain unread.

5. Decision: read value 2 at index 4. Reject it and leave
   `writeIndex = 2`.
   After: `values = [1,3,2,3,2,4]`; the next read index is 5.
   Known correct: `[1,3]` is final for original indexes 0 through 4,
   and original value 4 at index 5 is intact.

6. Decision: read value 4 at index 5. Keep it by writing index 2,
   then advance `writeIndex` to 3.
   After: `values = [1,3,4,3,2,4]`; the next read index is 6.
   Known correct: `[1,3,4]` is every kept original value in order.
   All input values are classified.

7. Decision: the stopping check finds `readIndex == N`. Clear
   `values[3:]`, then return `values[:3:3]`.
   After: the original view is `[1,3,4,0,0,0]`; the result is
   `[1,3,4]` with length 3 and capacity 3.
   Known correct: the result has the required values and order, the
   discarded region holds zero values, and no work remains.

Focused all-rejected case: `[2,2]` performs two skips with
`writeIndex = 0`, clears both slots, and returns a non-nil empty
slice. The original view becomes `[0,0]`.

Focused no-rejection case: `[-1,0,3]` writes each value to its own
index, clears an empty suffix, and returns the unchanged sequence.
Negative values and zero have no special meaning to compaction.

Focused empty case: a nil input performs zero predicate calls.
Clearing nil is a no-op, and `values[:0:0]` remains nil.

Counterexample to replacing a rejected value from the active end:
for `[2,1,3]`, swapping 3 into index 0 can return `[3,1]`. It keeps
the correct values but violates stable order; left-to-right writing
returns `[1,3]`.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program requires Go 1.21 or later for `clear`. It
uses a generic function so the state transition is the same for any
element type. The demonstration removes integer value 2, prints the
shared backing slices, and exercises ordinary and boundary cases.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Stable compaction (read and write
// indexes). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func compactStable[T any](
	values []T,
	keep func(T) bool,
) []T {
	// Reject the missing decision rule before mutating shared storage.
	if keep == nil {
		panic("compactStable: nil keep predicate")
	}

	// The prefix before writeIndex contains the kept values seen so far.
	writeIndex := 0
	for readIndex := range values {
		value := values[readIndex]
		if !keep(value) {
			continue
		}

		// writeIndex never passes readIndex, so unread values stay intact.
		values[writeIndex] = value
		writeIndex++
	}

	// Release discarded references and prevent append from reusing them.
	clear(values[writeIndex:])
	return values[:writeIndex:writeIndex]
}

func isNotTwo(value int) bool {
	// Evaluate is not two without changing the maintained state.
	return value != 2
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	values := []int{2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 4}
	compacted := compactStable(values, isNotTwo)
	fmt.Println(compacted, len(compacted), cap(compacted))
	fmt.Println(values)

	allRemoved := []int{2, 2}
	compactedAll := compactStable(allRemoved, isNotTwo)
	fmt.Println(
		compactedAll == nil,
		compactedAll,
		allRemoved,
	)

	unchanged := []int{-1, 0, 3}
	fmt.Println(
		compactStable(unchanged, isNotTwo),
		unchanged,
	)

	duplicates := []int{1, 2, 1, 2, 1}
	fmt.Println(
		compactStable(duplicates, isNotTwo),
		duplicates,
	)

	var empty []int
	compactedEmpty := compactStable(empty, isNotTwo)
	fmt.Println(compactedEmpty == nil, len(compactedEmpty))
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[1 3 4] 3 3
[1 3 4 0 0 0]
false [] [0 0]
[-1 0 3] [-1 0 3]
[1 1 1] [1 1 1 0 0]
true 0
```

The result and input intentionally alias their first three slots in
the ordinary case. Writing `compacted[0]` would also change
`values[0]`. Appending to `compacted` cannot reuse the original tail
because its capacity is restricted to 3.

##### Why it works

Maintain this invariant before each read at `readIndex`:

- `values[:writeIndex]` equals all values kept from original indexes
  below `readIndex`, in their original order;
- `values[readIndex:]` still contains the original unread values;
- `0 <= writeIndex <= readIndex`.

Initially both indexes are zero. The kept sequence of an empty prefix
is empty, the whole slice is unread, and the index relation holds.

When the predicate rejects a value, the kept prefix and unread suffix
are not written. Advancing the read position classifies that one
value, so the invariant remains true.

When the predicate keeps a value, the invariant places
`writeIndex` at or left of `readIndex`. Reading the value before the
write therefore obtains its original value, and the assignment cannot
touch a later unread slot. Placing that value at the kept boundary
preserves stable order. Incrementing both logical positions restores
the invariant.

The range loop supplies every index from 0 through `N - 1` once. Each
iteration classifies one value, so it terminates after N iterations.
At termination, no unread values remain. The invariant then proves
that `values[:writeIndex]` is the complete stable result and that
`writeIndex` equals K.

Clearing begins only after the scan, so it cannot destroy unread
input. It changes no index below K. The full slice expression returns
exactly those K established values and gives the result capacity K.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length, K the kept count, and P the total work done
inside all predicate calls. The loop performs N reads and predicate
calls, exactly K element assignments, and `clear` zeroes `N - K`
slots. Total time is Theta(N + P), which is Theta(N) when the
predicate takes constant time. Best, average, and worst cases are all
Theta(N) under that assumption because every input value is tested.

The function stores two indexes, one value, and one returned slice
header. It uses O(1) auxiliary space beyond any state or call stack
owned by the predicate. It allocates no output elements. The result's
K visible elements occupy the input backing array, so output storage
is shared rather than newly allocated.

Clearing the tail does work that some judge contracts do not require,
but it prevents discarded pointers, maps, slices, or strings from
remaining reachable through the original backing array. Restricting
capacity prevents append through the returned view from exposing or
overwriting that tail. Other aliases to the original array remain
able to observe and change shared slots.

Repeatedly shifting the suffix needs O(1) auxiliary space but can take
Theta(N^2) time. Building a fresh output slice is stable and
simple but needs Theta(K) new element storage. Swapping with the
active end can also use constant space and linear time, but it
sacrifices stable order and can be preferable when order is
irrelevant.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil input: return nil after zero predicate calls. Do not index slot
  zero merely because a write boundary exists.
- Non-nil empty input: return a non-nil empty view. Both empty forms
  have length and capacity zero.
- All rejected: `[2,2]` yields `[]` and clears the input to `[0,0]`.
  Returning `values` instead would expose rejected elements.
- None rejected: `[-1,0,3]` remains unchanged. Self-assignment is safe
  because `writeIndex == readIndex` throughout.
- Retained duplicates: `[1,2,1,2,1]` yields `[1,1,1]`. Compaction
  filters positions; it does not deduplicate unless the predicate and
  surrounding state explicitly request that behavior.
- Rejections at either end: `[2,1,3,2]` yields `[1,3]`. The returned
  count comes from `writeIndex`, not from the last read position.
- Advance `writeIndex` only after keeping a value. Advancing it on a
  rejection leaves a hole in the claimed output prefix.
- Never write to `values[readIndex]` as the output rule. That
  preserves gaps instead of packing the result at the front.
- Copy left, not right. A destination beyond `readIndex` could replace
  an original value before its predicate call.
- Clear only after the scan. Clearing each rejected suffix immediately
  would erase values that have not yet been classified.
- A nil predicate is rejected before mutation. A predicate panic after
  earlier calls can leave a partial compacted prefix; use a copied
  input when atomic rollback is required.
- A predicate that mutates `values` can invalidate the unread-suffix
  invariant. Treat it as a decision function, not a mutation hook.
- The result aliases the input. Copy it when later mutations need
  independent ownership, even though its restricted capacity protects
  only against append reusing the discarded tail.
- `clear` requires Go 1.21 or later. On an older language version,
  assign a declared zero value across the tail explicitly.

##### When to choose it

Choose stable compaction when:

- the output is a filtered subsequence of one ordered input;
- relative order must remain unchanged;
- the input buffer may be mutated and reused;
- one left-to-right predicate call per value is acceptable;
- constant auxiliary storage matters.

Allocate a fresh result when the source must remain unchanged or the
result needs independent ownership. Use swap-with-end removal when
order is irrelevant and minimizing kept-value writes matters. Use a
linked structure when stable removals occur repeatedly at known nodes
rather than as one batch scan.

The completed [Remove Element problem](
problems/solved_easy_leetcode_0027_remove_element.go) contains stable
and unstable implementations. Its official judge permits reordered
output, so stable compaction satisfies a stricter contract. The
completed Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array problem uses the same
kept-prefix invariant with a decision based on sorted runs. Its
unsolved `II` variation permits at most two copies per run.

The official [Remove Element problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-element/description/) defines
its in-place prefix contract. The Go specification defines
[range order](https://go.dev/ref/spec#For_range),
[tail clearing](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Clear), and
[shared full slice expressions](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Slice_expressions).

#### B.24.2 Dutch national flag (three partition boundaries)

##### Problem and contract

Three categories can be grouped without a full comparison sort.
Suppose 0 means red, 1 means white, and 2 means blue. The Dutch
national flag problem rearranges one mutable sequence so every 0
precedes every 1, and every 1 precedes every 2.

Counting each color and then overwriting the slice is linear, but it
separates inspection from placement and does not generalize to
records that must be moved intact. A full sort establishes more order
than three groups need. Three moving boundaries can classify and
place one item per loop iteration.

This lesson's function has the following successful contract:

- `colors` is a finite mutable `[]int` containing only 0, 1, and 2;
- the function rearranges the same backing array in nondecreasing
  color order;
- each input occurrence remains exactly once;
- it returns `zeroEnd`, the first index after the zeros;
- it returns `twoStart`, the first index containing a two;
- `colors[:zeroEnd]` contains only 0;
- `colors[zeroEnd:twoStart]` contains only 1;
- `colors[twoStart:]` contains only 2;
- no second element collection is allocated.

Nil and empty slices are accepted and return boundaries `(0,0)`, a
useful generalization beyond the representative judge's minimum size.
Any other integer violates the precondition. The implementation
panics when it encounters one, and earlier swaps are not rolled back.
No concurrent access to the shared backing array is allowed.

Within-category order is unobservable for plain integers because all
members have the same value. A version that partitions records by a
color field is not stable: swaps can reverse records of one color.

Read [fixed arrays and dynamic slices](
#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) first for indexing, mutation,
and shared backing storage. Compare the preceding
[stable compaction lesson](
#b241-stable-compaction-read-and-write-indexes) when retained order
matters. This entry owns the four-region, three-boundary invariant.

##### Mental model

Keep the slice divided into four adjacent half-open regions:

```text
[0, zeroEnd)          established zeros
[zeroEnd, scanIndex)  established ones
[scanIndex, twoStart) unknown values
[twoStart, N)         established twos
```

`zeroEnd` is both the end of the zero region and the start of the one
region. `scanIndex` starts the unknown region. `twoStart` ends the
unknown region and starts the two region. Read
`zeroEnd = 2`, `scanIndex = 4`, and `twoStart = 6` as: indexes 0 and
1 are zeros, indexes 2 and 3 are ones, indexes 4 and 5 still need
classification, and every index from 6 onward is a two.

Initially all regions except unknown are empty:

```text
zeroEnd = 0
scanIndex = 0
twoStart = N
```

Inspect `colors[scanIndex]` and choose one of three actions:

- For 0, swap it with `colors[zeroEnd]`, then advance both left
  boundaries. If a one was displaced, it becomes the last established
  one after both boundaries move.
- For 1, it already belongs after the zeros, so advance only
  `scanIndex`.
- For 2, decrement `twoStart`, then swap the two into that boundary.
  Do not advance `scanIndex`. Either unknown is now empty, or the
  value swapped into the scan position still needs classification.

Stop when `scanIndex == twoStart`. The unknown region is then empty,
so the other three regions form the requested order.

##### Worked walkthrough

Partition `[2,0,2,1,1,0]`. The expected result is
`[0,0,1,1,2,2]`, with `zeroEnd = 2` and `twoStart = 4`.

Initial state: `zeroEnd = 0`, `scanIndex = 0`, and `twoStart = 6`.
The entire slice is unknown; all established regions are empty.

```text
[ zeros | ones | unknown | twos ]
         ^      ^         ^
      zeroEnd scanIndex twoStart
```

1. Decision: index 0 contains 2. Decrement `twoStart` to 5 and swap
   indexes 0 and 5, but keep `scanIndex = 0` because the incoming 0
   has not been classified.
   After: `colors = [0,0,2,1,1,2]`; the unknown region is `[0,5)`
   and the two region is `[5,6)`.
   Known correct: index 5 is a final two. No claim has yet been made
   about the swapped-in value at index 0.

2. Decision: index 0 now contains 0. Swap indexes `zeroEnd = 0` and
   `scanIndex = 0`, then advance both to 1.
   After: `colors = [0,0,2,1,1,2]`; zero is `[0,1)`, one is empty,
   unknown is `[1,5)`, and two is `[5,6)`.
   Known correct: the first zero and final two are established; all
   values between them remain unclassified.

3. Decision: index 1 contains 0. Its self-swap grows the zero region;
   advance `zeroEnd` and `scanIndex` to 2.
   After: zero is `[0,2)`, one is empty, unknown is `[2,5)`, and the
   slice remains `[0,0,2,1,1,2]`.
   Known correct: both zeros occupy their final category region.

4. Decision: index 2 contains 2. Decrement `twoStart` from 5 to 4,
   swap indexes 2 and 4, and keep `scanIndex = 2` to inspect the
   incoming 1.
   After: `colors = [0,0,1,1,2,2]`; unknown is `[2,4)` and two is
   `[4,6)`.
   Known correct: both twos are established, while the two values in
   the unknown region still require inspection.

5. Decision: index 2 contains 1. It is already directly after the
   zeros, so advance only `scanIndex` to 3.
   After: one is `[2,3)`, unknown is `[3,4)`, and the slice is
   `[0,0,1,1,2,2]`.
   Known correct: indexes 0 through 2 and 4 through 5 belong to their
   final regions; only index 3 remains unknown.

6. Decision: index 3 contains 1. Advance `scanIndex` to 4.
   After: `scanIndex == twoStart == 4`; the unknown region is empty.
   Known correct: `[0,2)` is all zeros, `[2,4)` is all ones, and
   `[4,6)` is all twos.

7. Decision: the loop condition `scanIndex < twoStart` is false, so
   return boundaries `(2,4)`.
   After: the observable result is `[0,0,1,1,2,2]`, 2, 4.
   Known correct: every input occurrence lies in exactly one ordered
   category region, and no work remains.

Focused repeated-right case: `[2,2,2]` never advances `scanIndex`.
Instead, `twoStart` decreases from 3 to 0, shrinking the unknown
region once per iteration. The result stays `[2,2,2]` and the returned
boundaries are `(0,0)`.

Focused missing-color case: `[1,1,1]` advances only `scanIndex` and
returns `(0,3)`. Empty zero and two regions are valid.

Focused empty case: nil input begins with all three indexes at zero.
The loop performs no access and returns `(0,0)` while the slice
remains nil.

Counterexample to advancing after a two swap: in `[1,2,0]`, swapping
the 2 at index 1 with the final 0 gives `[1,0,2]`. If the scan moves
to index 2, that incoming 0 is never moved before the 1. Keeping the
scan fixed lets the next iteration repair the order.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program uses only the standard library. The function
mutates each supplied slice and returns its two internal category
boundaries. The examples cover every branch, a repeatedly shrinking
right boundary, a missing category, and nil input.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Dutch national flag (three
// partition boundaries). Function comments connect each operation to
// its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func partitionThreeColors(colors []int) (int, int) {
	// The four half-open regions are zero, one, unknown, and two.
	zeroEnd := 0
	scanIndex := 0
	twoStart := len(colors)

	for scanIndex < twoStart {
		switch colors[scanIndex] {
		case 0:
			// Grow zero; a displaced one remains in the middle region.
			colors[zeroEnd], colors[scanIndex] =
				colors[scanIndex], colors[zeroEnd]
			zeroEnd++
			scanIndex++
		case 1:
			// The scanned one already belongs next to the zero region.
			scanIndex++
		case 2:
			// Grow two; keep scan on any swapped-in unknown value.
			twoStart--
			colors[scanIndex], colors[twoStart] =
				colors[twoStart], colors[scanIndex]
		default:
			panic(fmt.Sprintf(
				"color at current index %d = %d; want 0, 1, or 2",
				scanIndex,
				colors[scanIndex],
			))
		}
	}

	return zeroEnd, twoStart
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	mixed := []int{2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0}
	zeroEnd, twoStart := partitionThreeColors(mixed)
	fmt.Println(mixed, zeroEnd, twoStart)

	allTwos := []int{2, 2, 2}
	zeroEnd, twoStart = partitionThreeColors(allTwos)
	fmt.Println(allTwos, zeroEnd, twoStart)

	allOnes := []int{1, 1, 1}
	zeroEnd, twoStart = partitionThreeColors(allOnes)
	fmt.Println(allOnes, zeroEnd, twoStart)

	var empty []int
	zeroEnd, twoStart = partitionThreeColors(empty)
	fmt.Println(empty, zeroEnd, twoStart, empty == nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[0 0 1 1 2 2] 2 4
[2 2 2] 0 0
[1 1 1] 0 3
[] 0 0 true
```

The final boolean confirms that the empty input remains nil. Every
other printed slice is the same slice passed to the function; the
operation returns boundaries, not a newly allocated result.

##### Why it works

Before each iteration, maintain these four facts:

- every index in `[0,zeroEnd)` contains 0;
- every index in `[zeroEnd,scanIndex)` contains 1;
- `[scanIndex,twoStart)` contains every unclassified occurrence;
- every index in `[twoStart,N)` contains 2.

Initially the three established regions are empty and the unknown
region is the whole slice, so all four facts hold.

For a scanned 0, `colors[zeroEnd]` is either the scanned value itself
or an established 1. Swapping places 0 after the established zeros.
If a 1 was displaced, advancing both boundaries includes it at the
end of the one region. The unknown region loses the scanned 0.

For a scanned 1, no data movement is needed. Advancing `scanIndex`
adds that position to the one region and removes it from unknown.

For a scanned 2, decrementing `twoStart` opens the first position of
the two region. The swap fills it with the scanned 2. The incoming
value came from the final unknown position. If unknown values remain,
leaving `scanIndex` fixed keeps that value available for the next
iteration. If the scanned 2 was the final unknown value, the swap is
with itself and the loop stops.

Thus every branch preserves all four facts and decreases
`twoStart - scanIndex`, the unknown-region length, by exactly one.
That nonnegative length starts at N, so the loop terminates after
exactly N iterations on valid input.

At termination, `scanIndex == twoStart`; the unknown region is empty.
The remaining three invariant regions are adjacent, cover the whole
slice, and contain only 0, then 1, then 2. Swaps preserve occurrence
counts, so the final slice and returned boundaries satisfy the
contract.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length, and let Z and T be the counts of zeros and
twos. The unknown region shrinks once per iteration, so the function
performs exactly N classifications. Zero and two branches execute
`Z + T` swap statements, including harmless self-swaps; ones require
no swap.

For valid input, best, average, and worst-case time are Theta(N).
No input distribution is needed for that bound. The function keeps
three indexes and swap temporaries, uses O(1) auxiliary space, does
not recurse, and allocates no output collection. Its two returned
boundaries use O(1) output space.

The slice is mutated, so callers needing the original order must first
copy N elements at Theta(N) time and space. Plain integer comparisons
and swaps cannot overflow. Formatting in the demonstration is outside
the algorithmic costs.

Counting colors also uses Theta(N) time and O(1) state, then performs
N overwrite operations. It is simple when categories are exactly the
three integer values. Boundary partitioning instead moves occurrences
as records, which adapts to less-than, equal-to, and greater-than
pivot groups without a count table.

A stable three-way partition has a different contract. This swap
method may reorder records inside a category. Extra output storage or
additional data movement is usually required when that order must be
preserved.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil or empty: return `(0,0)` without indexing. Starting
  `twoStart` at `len(colors)` makes the loop guard safe.
- One 0: return `(1,1)`; the zero self-swap advances both left
  boundaries. One 1 returns `(0,1)`, and one 2 returns `(0,0)`.
- Missing zeros: `[1,1,2]` returns `(0,2)`. A boundary can equal zero
  without indicating an error.
- Missing ones: `[0,0,2]` returns `(2,2)`. An empty middle region is
  represented by equal boundaries.
- Missing twos: `[0,1,1]` returns `(1,3)`. `twoStart == N` is a valid
  empty final region.
- All twos: keep `scanIndex` fixed while `twoStart` repeatedly moves
  left. Advancing neither boundary would loop forever; advancing the
  scan would skip swapped-in unknown values on mixed input.
- On 0, advance both `zeroEnd` and `scanIndex`. Advancing only
  `zeroEnd` can place the scan inside the established zero region.
- On 1, do not move either category boundary. Only the unknown start
  changes.
- On 2, decrement `twoStart` before swapping. Using `len(colors)` as
  an element index would panic.
- Stop on `scanIndex == twoStart`. Using `<=` attempts to inspect the
  first established two or index N.
- Values outside 0, 1, and 2 violate the precondition. The defensive
  panic may occur after swaps; validate first or partition a copy when
  failure must preserve the input.
- Swaps preserve multiplicity but not record stability. Do not attach
  original-order meaning to positions within one category.
- Concurrent reads or writes to the backing array are unsupported and
  can race with swaps.

##### When to choose it

Choose the Dutch national flag method when:

- exactly three ordered categories must become contiguous;
- a mutable random-access sequence is available;
- category order matters but order within a category does not;
- one classification per occurrence and constant storage matter.

Use counting and rewriting for a tiny fixed value domain when items
are only keys and overwriting is simpler than swapping. Use a stable
partition or fresh output when equal-category records must retain
their input order. Use comparison sorting when many ordered keys need
complete order rather than three bands.

The completed [Quickselect lesson](#b33-quickselect-slice) applies the
same four regions to values below, equal to, and above a pivot, then
continues only in the band containing one requested rank. The
[Quicksort lesson](#b37-quicksort-slice-and-partition-bounds) sorts
both strict pivot bands. Those entries own selection and recursive
sorting; this entry owns the fixed three-category partition state.

The official [Sort Colors problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/sort-colors/description/) supplies the
0, 1, and 2 representation, in-place order, constraints, and one-pass
follow-up. Dijkstra's original [EWD 398 discussion](
https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~EWD/transcriptions/EWD03xx/EWD398.html)
derives the red, white, blue problem from established and uninspected
regions.

#### B.24.3 Cyclic placement (slice)

##### Problem and contract

Sometimes each value directly names the index where it belongs. If a
slice of length N contains every integer from 0 through `N - 1`
exactly once, comparison sorting ignores useful information: value 4
already says that its final position is index 4.

Such a slice is a permutation, meaning a rearrangement with no value
added, removed, or changed. Following `index -> values[index]`
eventually returns to an earlier index, so the permutation consists of
one or more cycles. Cyclic placement repairs those cycles by swapping
each encountered value directly into its home.

This lesson's function has the following successful contract:

- `values` is a finite mutable `[]int` of length N;
- it contains each integer in `[0,N)` exactly once;
- after return, `values[index] == index` for every index;
- the same backing array and multiset are preserved;
- the function returns the number of swaps it performed;
- it allocates no second element collection.

Nil and empty input are the one empty permutation and return zero
swaps. A negative, a value at least N, or a duplicate violates the
precondition. Defensive checks panic rather than indexing outside the
slice or swapping duplicates forever. Earlier valid swaps are not
rolled back. Concurrent access to the backing array is unsupported.

The final identity arrangement is unique, so stability and tie
breaking do not apply. Other aliases to the slice observe every swap.

Read [fixed arrays and dynamic slices](
#a11-fixed-arrays-and-dynamic-slices) first for indexing, swapping,
mutation, and ownership. The earlier
[missing-values lesson](#b16-missing-values-by-placement-slice)
adapts this mechanism to duplicates, irrelevant values, and the
one-based home formula `value - 1`. This entry owns the exact
permutation and cycle model.

##### Mental model

Treat each value as a destination index:

```text
value v  ->  home index v
```

For `[1,2,3,0,4]`, following destinations from index 0 gives
`0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 0`. Those four indexes form one cycle. Index 4
forms the fixed cycle `4 -> 4`.

Keep `currentIndex` at the first position not yet confirmed:

- If `values[currentIndex] == currentIndex`, that position is home;
  advance.
- Otherwise let `homeIndex = values[currentIndex]`. Swap the current
  value into `values[homeIndex]`.
- Stay at `currentIndex`, because the value displaced into it still
  needs a home.

Before using a value as an index, require `0 <= value < N`. If the
home already holds the same value while the current index differs,
the input contains a duplicate and cannot be a permutation.

Each valid swap makes at least one new home correct. A correct home is
never disturbed: another copy of its value would be required to
target it, but a permutation has no duplicates. Once the current
position becomes correct, advance and never revisit the established
prefix.

##### Worked walkthrough

Place permutation `[1,2,3,0,4]`. Its expected final slice is
`[0,1,2,3,4]`, and its four-index cycle requires three swaps.

Initial state: `currentIndex = 0`, `numSwaps = 0`, and
`values = [1,2,3,0,4]`. No prefix has been confirmed.

```text
index: 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 0
value: 1    2    3    0

one four-index cycle needs four minus one swaps
```

1. Decision: index 0 holds 1, which is in range but not home. Its
   home is index 1, which currently holds 2, so swap indexes 0 and 1
   and keep `currentIndex = 0`.
   After: `values = [2,1,3,0,4]`; `numSwaps = 1`.
   Known correct: index 1 now holds its final value 1. The displaced
   value 2 at index 0 remains unresolved.

2. Decision: index 0 holds 2, whose home index 2 contains 3. Swap
   indexes 0 and 2, then recheck index 0.
   After: `values = [3,1,2,0,4]`; `numSwaps = 2`.
   Known correct: homes 1 and 2 are fixed. Value 3 at index 0 still
   needs placement.

3. Decision: index 0 holds 3, whose home index 3 contains 0. Swap
   indexes 0 and 3 and keep the current index.
   After: `values = [0,1,2,3,4]`; `numSwaps = 3`.
   Known correct: homes 0 through 3 are all correct. The nontrivial
   cycle is completely repaired.

4. Decision: index 0 now holds 0, so advance. Indexes 1, 2, 3, and
   4 also equal their values; advance after each.
   After: `currentIndex = 5`; the slice remains `[0,1,2,3,4]`.
   Known correct: every index is its own value, and no home was
   disturbed after becoming correct.

5. Decision: the stopping check finds `currentIndex == N`, so return
   `numSwaps = 3`.
   After: the observable result is `[0,1,2,3,4]`, 3.
   Known correct: the identity permutation is complete and no work
   remains.

Focused multiple-cycle case: `[2,0,1,4,3]` contains cycles
`0 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0` and `3 -> 4 -> 3`. The length-three cycle needs
two swaps and the length-two cycle needs one, so placement returns 3.

Focused identity case: `[0,1,2]` advances at every index, performs no
swaps, and returns 0. Focused empty case: nil input performs neither
an access nor a swap and remains nil.

Counterexample to advancing after every swap: a one-swap-per-index
pass on `[1,2,3,0]` first produces `[2,1,3,0]`, then later
`[2,1,0,3]`. It ends with 2 and 0 still misplaced because index 0 was
abandoned before its displaced value reached home. Recheck the same
index until it is correct.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program uses only the standard library. It mutates
each permutation, reports its swap count, and demonstrates one long
cycle, two separate cycles, the identity, and nil input.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Cyclic placement (slice). Function
// comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func placePermutation(values []int) int {
	// A placed prefix stays fixed while one cycle is repaired.
	numSwaps := 0
	for currentIndex := 0; currentIndex < len(values); {
		value := values[currentIndex]
		if value < 0 || value >= len(values) {
			panic(fmt.Sprintf(
				"value %d at index %d has no valid home",
				value,
				currentIndex,
			))
		}

		// A value equal to its index is already in its unique home.
		if value == currentIndex {
			currentIndex++
			continue
		}

		homeIndex := value
		if values[homeIndex] == value {
			panic(fmt.Sprintf("duplicate value %d", value))
		}

		// Keep this index: its displaced value still needs placement.
		values[currentIndex], values[homeIndex] =
			values[homeIndex], values[currentIndex]
		numSwaps++
	}

	return numSwaps
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	longCycle := []int{1, 2, 3, 0, 4}
	longCycleSwaps := placePermutation(longCycle)
	fmt.Println(longCycle, longCycleSwaps)

	twoCycles := []int{2, 0, 1, 4, 3}
	twoCycleSwaps := placePermutation(twoCycles)
	fmt.Println(twoCycles, twoCycleSwaps)

	identity := []int{0, 1, 2}
	identitySwaps := placePermutation(identity)
	fmt.Println(identity, identitySwaps)

	var empty []int
	emptySwaps := placePermutation(empty)
	fmt.Println(empty, emptySwaps, empty == nil)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
[0 1 2 3 4] 3
[0 1 2 3 4] 3
[0 1 2] 0
[] 0 true
```

The final boolean proves the empty slice remains nil. Each nonempty
line prints the same slice passed to `placePermutation`; no result
slice replaces it.

##### Why it works

Maintain two facts before inspecting `currentIndex`:

- every index below `currentIndex` already holds its own value;
- every correct home anywhere in the slice remains correct forever.

Both facts hold initially because the established prefix is empty and
no home has yet been claimed by the algorithm.

If the current value equals the current index, advancing extends the
established prefix by one. No data changes, so every other correct
home stays correct.

Otherwise the value `v` belongs at index `v`. Range validation makes
that access safe. Because the input is a permutation, no other copy
of `v` exists. Its home therefore cannot already contain `v`; the
duplicate guard exposes a violated precondition if it does.

Swapping writes `v` into its unique home without touching any earlier
correct prefix position. The displaced value remains at
`currentIndex`, so rechecking that index loses no cycle member. The
swap establishes a new correct home and preserves the two facts.

Every loop iteration either advances `currentIndex` or establishes a
previously incorrect home. There are N possible advances and N homes,
and established homes never become incorrect. The loop therefore
terminates. When `currentIndex == N`, the first fact covers the whole
slice and proves `values[index] == index` everywhere. Swaps alone
also prove that the multiset is unchanged.

A permutation decomposes into disjoint cycles. A fixed point needs no
swap. Repairing a cycle of length L fixes one home per swap until the
last displaced value returns to the current index, using `L - 1`
swaps. If C counts all cycles, including fixed points, the returned
total is exactly `N - C`.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the slice length and C its number of permutation cycles.
The loop performs N advances and exactly `N - C` swaps. It therefore
executes no iterations when N is zero and fewer than `2N` iterations
when N is positive. The identity has C equal to N and no swaps; one
N-element cycle has C equal to one and `N - 1` swaps.

Best, average, and worst-case running time are Theta(N), because even
the identity must confirm every index. No input-distribution average
is needed for that bound. The algorithm stores indexes, one value,
and a counter, using O(1) auxiliary space and O(1) scalar output
space. Successful execution allocates no collection and does not
recurse.

Comparison sorting arbitrary values costs O(N log N) comparisons,
but supports inputs without direct home indexes. A visited array can
walk permutation cycles without mutating the input, at the cost of
O(N) auxiliary bits or booleans. Copying before placement preserves
the caller's order but adds Theta(N) time and storage.

The swaps are not stable, but a permutation contains no equal values
whose relative order could matter. Defensive panic formatting may
allocate only after the successful-input precondition has failed.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil or empty: return zero without indexing. The empty permutation
  satisfies the identity condition vacuously.
- One value: `[0]` is already home and returns zero swaps. `[1]` is
  out of range because its only valid value is 0.
- Identity: `[0,1,2]` performs N checks but no swaps. Do not force a
  self-swap when `value == currentIndex`.
- One long cycle: `[1,2,3,0]` needs three swaps at index 0. Advancing
  after the first swap leaves the cycle unresolved.
- Several cycles: `[2,0,1,4,3]` must resume scanning after the first
  cycle so the second one is not skipped.
- Negative or too-large values have no valid home. Check the range
  before using a value as an index, or Go will panic at an unrelated
  access.
- Duplicates break the permutation contract. In `[0,0]`, index 1
  targets a home already containing 0; swapping equal values would
  make no progress and loop forever.
- Keep `currentIndex` fixed after a swap. The incoming value has not
  been classified, even though the outgoing value is now correct.
- A direct home formula depends on the value range. Values 1 through
  N use `value - 1`, not `value`; subtract only after validating the
  range when extreme integers are possible.
- Swaps mutate every slice alias. Copy first if the caller must retain
  the initial permutation.
- A panic for malformed input may follow earlier swaps. Validate a
  copy first when failure must be atomic.
- Concurrent reads or writes can race with placement or observe a
  temporary permutation. Exclusive access is required for the call.

##### When to choose it

Choose cyclic placement when:

- each valid value maps directly to one dense home index;
- values are unique, or duplicate behavior is explicitly handled;
- input mutation is allowed;
- the result or query depends on which homes are occupied;
- linear work and constant auxiliary space matter.

Use comparison sorting when values do not provide a dense home
mapping. Use a hash set or visited array when input must remain
unchanged. Use [bounded-value counting](
#b14-bounded-value-counting-array) when counts, rather than exact
home occupancy, are the useful result.

The completed [missing-values lesson](
#b16-missing-values-by-placement-slice) applies placement to values
1 through N while safely skipping zero, negatives, and large values
and stopping duplicates. Its representative
[First Missing Positive problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/first-missing-positive/description/)
requires linear time and constant auxiliary space.

NIST's [permutation definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/permutation.html) records the
no-loss, no-addition rearrangement contract. The Go specification's
[index-expression rules](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Index_expressions)
explain why every computed home must lie in `[0,len(values))` before
it is indexed.

#### B.24.4 Rotation by reversal (slice)

##### Problem and contract

A right rotation moves a suffix to the front without changing the
order inside either moved part. Rotating `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]` right by
three steps produces `[5,6,7,1,2,3,4]`. Repeating a one-step move
works, but it repeatedly shifts values that will move again.

This lesson rotates a finite mutable `[]int` in place. Its contract
is:

- `steps` is a nonnegative `int` count of right-rotation steps;
- for nonempty length N, `shift = steps % N` is the effective move;
- a value originally at index I finishes at `(I + shift) % N`;
- order, duplicates, and every integer value are preserved;
- the slice keeps its length, capacity, and backing array;
- success returns a nil error and uses no second element collection;
