subsequence or counts of alignments rather than whether one complete
candidate fits.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty candidate and empty source return true. Do not index
  `candidate[0]` before checking whether a value is required.
- Empty candidate with nonempty source also returns true: deleting
  every source position leaves the empty sequence.
- Nonempty candidate with empty source returns false. No source
  position exists to witness its first value.
- A longer candidate returns false immediately. Equal or shorter
  length is necessary but not sufficient; order can still fail.
- Equal sequences return true by matching every position. No deletion
  is required for a subsequence.
- Duplicates require distinct positions. Candidate `aa` succeeds in
  `aba` at indexes 0 and 2, but `aaa` does not.
- Values in the wrong order stay wrong. Sorting `acb` and `abc` before
  checking would erase the contract's relative-position requirement.
- Advance the source on both matches and mismatches. Holding it on a
  mismatch loops forever; holding it after a match can reuse one
  occurrence for duplicate candidate values.
- Advance the candidate only on equality. Advancing it on a mismatch
  silently skips a required occurrence.
- A substring test is too strict because it rejects valid gaps.
  Membership or frequency tests are too weak because they lose order.
- `[]byte` and `[]rune` define different text units. Choose once and
  keep the contract, trace, and tests in the same unit.
- Rune equality does not perform Unicode normalization or grapheme
  segmentation. Visually similar text may use different code points.
- `float64` satisfies `comparable`, but NaN never equals itself. A NaN
  candidate does not match a NaN source under this `==` contract.
- If T is an interface type, comparing dynamic slice, map, or function
  values panics. Prefer concrete comparable types or validate dynamic
  values before calling.
- Pointer elements compare addresses, not pointed-to contents. Supply
  stable value keys when content equality is required.
- Concurrent input mutation can change values between comparisons and
  is a data race. Provide one stable snapshot for the call.

##### When to choose it

Choose the two-pointer scan when one or a few candidates must be
checked against a finite ordered source, equality defines a match, and
only a Boolean answer is required. It also adapts to a streaming
source by retaining `candidateIndex` between arrivals.

If callers need witness positions, append each accepted source index
to an M-element result; that changes output storage from O(1) to
Theta(M). If many candidates share one static source, use the next
[position-list preprocessing lesson](
#b252-repeated-subsequence-queries-position-lists).

Use [longest common subsequence](
#b253-longest-common-subsequence-dp-table) when neither whole sequence
is known to fit and the maximum retained length is required. Use
[exact string matching](#b72-kmp-matching-prefix-function-array) when
the candidate must occupy adjacent positions. Use [edit distance](
#b83-edit-distance-and-subsequences-dp-table) when insertion,
deletion, or
replacement cost is the objective.

Practice the bounded lowercase-string form in the unsolved
[Is Subsequence problem](
problems/easy_leetcode_0392_is_subsequence.go). Its official
[LeetCode statement](
https://leetcode.com/problems/is-subsequence/) also motivates the
many-query follow-up. NIST defines a [subsequence](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/subsequence.html) as a sequence
formed by deleting zero or more symbols without requiring adjacency.
The Go specification defines the generic
[`comparable` constraint](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Type_constraints)
and [equality operators](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Comparison_operators)
used by the implementation.

#### B.25.2 Repeated subsequence queries (position lists)

##### Problem and contract

Many candidate sequences must be checked against one stable source.
Running the two-pointer scan from source index zero for every
candidate repeats work over the same source values. Preprocess the
source once so each query can jump directly among relevant
occurrences.

`buildSubsequenceIndex` and `contains` have this contract:

- accept a finite source and finite candidates of one Go type that
  satisfies `comparable`;
- store every source index under the value found at that index, in
  strictly increasing order;
- report whether each candidate is a subsequence of the source under
  the same ordered, non-adjacent definition as the previous lesson;
- treat nil and non-nil empty candidates as matches and reject any
  candidate longer than the indexed source;
- preserve duplicates by storing every occurrence separately;
- read but never mutate the source or a candidate;
- keep a construction-time snapshot of positions, so later replacement
  of source slice elements cannot change query results;
- expose no mutation operation and require the built index to remain
  immutable while queries run.

Construction allocates a map and position slices. It does not retain
the source slice or its backing array. Map keys do copy source element
values, however, so a pointer, string, channel, or interface key can
keep referenced storage reachable. Successful construction assumes
enough memory; allocation failure is not returned as an error.

Map keys use Go equality and hashing. NaN therefore does not match
itself. If T is an interface type, construction or lookup panics when
a dynamic key is not comparable. Concurrent queries are safe only
after the completed index is published and while the index and
candidates are not mutated.

Read [single-query subsequence checking](
#b251-subsequence-checking-two-pointers) for the definition and greedy
choice. Read [binary search and bounds](
#b41-binary-search-and-bounds-slice) for lower-bound invariants. This
entry owns source position preprocessing and the repeated-query
tradeoff; it does not redefine the basic subsequence relation.

##### Mental model

Build an inverted view of the source. Instead of asking what value is
at a source position, ask where one value occurs. For source `abcba`,
the index is:

```text
value a -> source positions [0, 4]
value b -> source positions [1, 3]
value c -> source positions [2]
```

Read `positionsByValue['a'][1]` as: the second stored occurrence of
`a` is at source index 4. The outer key selects a value. The inner
offset selects one occurrence of that value. An inner offset is not a
source index; the stored integer is the source index.

Each list is already sorted because construction visits source indexes
from left to right and appends the current index. No sorting phase is
needed.

For one query, `nextSourceIndex` is the smallest source index still
legal for the next candidate value. It starts at zero. Look up that
value's position list, then binary-search for the first stored
position greater than or equal to `nextSourceIndex`.

- If the search reaches the list end, no legal occurrence remains, so
  the query fails.
- Otherwise accept the stored source position and set
  `nextSourceIndex` to one past it.

Choosing the first legal occurrence leaves every later source position
available. Each query keeps only its own integer cursor; it neither
marks nor removes positions from the shared index.

##### Worked walkthrough

Build one index for source `abcba`. Query candidate `aba`, whose
expected result is true through source indexes `[0,1,4]`. Reuse the
same index for `acaa`, whose expected result is false.

Initial state: `positionsByValue` is empty and the next source index
to preprocess is zero. No query has started.

1. Decision: inspect source index 0, value `a`, and append 0 to the
   list for `a`.
   After: the index contains `a -> [0]`; indexes 1 through 4 remain.
   Known correct: the list for `a` contains exactly its occurrence in
   the processed source prefix and is strictly increasing.
2. Decision: apply the same append rule at indexes 1 through 4: append
   1 under `b`, 2 under `c`, 3 under `b`, and 4 under `a`.
   After: the lists are `a -> [0,4]`, `b -> [1,3]`, and
   `c -> [2]`; preprocessing is complete.
   Known correct: every source occurrence appears once in its value's
   increasing list, and the index can be reused without the source.
3. Decision: start candidate `aba` with `nextSourceIndex = 0`; its
   first required value is `a`.
   After: no witness is chosen, and every source index is legal.
   Known correct: an empty candidate prefix is matched, and source
   index 0 is the earliest possible next witness.
4. Decision: lower-bound 0 in `a -> [0,4]`. The returned inner offset
   is 0, whose stored source index is 0. Accept it.
   After: witnesses are `[0]` and `nextSourceIndex = 1`.
   Known correct: candidate prefix `a` has its earliest possible
   witness, and only source indexes from 1 onward may be reused.
5. Decision: lower-bound 1 in `b -> [1,3]`. Inner offset 0 stores
   source index 1, so accept it.
   After: witnesses are `[0,1]` and `nextSourceIndex = 2`.
   Known correct: prefix `ab` is matched in order at the earliest
   possible positions; every remaining witness must be at least 2.
6. Decision: lower-bound 2 in `a -> [0,4]`. Inner offset 1 stores
   source index 4, so accept 4 rather than confusing offset 1 with a
   source position.
   After: witnesses are `[0,1,4]` and `nextSourceIndex = 5`.
   Known correct: every value of `aba` has a distinct increasing
   witness, even though the final match skipped source positions.
7. Decision: the candidate is exhausted, so return true.
   After: the first query is complete; the stored lists are unchanged.
   Known correct: deleting source indexes 2 and 3 leaves `aba`, and
   the index remains available for another query.
8. Decision: start `acaa` independently at zero and perform its first
   three lower bounds. They select `a` at 0, `c` at 2, and `a` at 4.
   After: witnesses are `[0,2,4]`, `nextSourceIndex = 5`, and one `a`
   remains unmatched.
   Known correct: these are the earliest possible witnesses for prefix
   `aca`; the earlier query did not consume any shared position.
9. Decision: lower-bound 5 in `a -> [0,4]`. The returned inner offset
   is 2, equal to the list length, so no stored position is readable.
   Return false.
   After: the second query ends without changing the index.
   Known correct: every source `a` is before 5, so no fourth
   increasing witness can complete `acaa`.

Focused empty case: an empty candidate performs no map lookup and
returns true for an empty or nonempty indexed source. A nonempty
candidate against the zero-value index fails the length guard because
that index represents an empty source.

Focused missing-value case: candidate `az` against `abcba` matches `a`
at 0, then gets an empty list for `z`. Its lower bound equals length
zero, so the query returns false without a special missing-key branch.

Focused snapshot case: build from `abcba`, then replace source index 0
with `x`. Candidate `aca` still returns true through stored positions
`[0,2,4]`; construction copied values into keys and copied indexes
into owned lists rather than retaining the source slice.

Counterexample to mixing cursor conventions: candidate `aa` against
source `aa` accepts index 0 and stores `nextSourceIndex = 1`.
Searching for the first position strictly greater than 1 wrongly
skips legal index 1 and returns false. With a next-legal cursor,
search for greater than or equal; with a last-used cursor, search for
strictly greater. Do not mix the two representations.

##### Implementation

This complete generic Go program uses `slices.BinarySearch` on source
position lists. Its returned Boolean says whether the exact target
position occurs, but the algorithm needs its returned insertion offset
even when that Boolean is false. Text call sites choose `[]rune`, so
positions count Unicode code points rather than UTF-8 bytes.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Repeated subsequence queries
// (position lists). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)

type subsequenceIndex[T comparable] struct {
	positionsByValue map[T][]int
	sourceLength     int
}

func buildSubsequenceIndex[T comparable](
	source []T,
) subsequenceIndex[T] {
	// Translate the logical location to its stored position.
	positionsByValue := make(map[T][]int)
	for sourceIndex, value := range source {
		// Appending source indexes preserves each list's order.
		positionsByValue[value] = append(
			positionsByValue[value],
			sourceIndex,
		)
	}
	return subsequenceIndex[T]{
		positionsByValue: positionsByValue,
		sourceLength:     len(source),
	}
}

func (index subsequenceIndex[T]) contains(
	candidate []T,
) bool {
	// Deletion cannot produce a sequence longer than the source.
	if len(candidate) > index.sourceLength {
		return false
	}

	nextSourceIndex := 0
	for _, value := range candidate {
		positions := index.positionsByValue[value]
		// The insertion point is the earliest legal witness.
		positionOffset, _ := slices.BinarySearch(
			positions,
			nextSourceIndex,
		)
		if positionOffset == len(positions) {
			return false
		}
		nextSourceIndex = positions[positionOffset] + 1
	}
	return true
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	source := []rune("abcba")
	index := buildSubsequenceIndex(source)

	fmt.Println(index.contains([]rune("aba")))
	fmt.Println(index.contains([]rune("acaa")))
	fmt.Println(index.contains([]rune("bb")))
	fmt.Println(index.contains([]rune("bbb")))
	fmt.Println(index.contains([]rune(nil)))

	// Construction copied positions, so this cannot change the index.
	source[0] = 'x'
	fmt.Println(index.contains([]rune("aca")))
}
```

Expected output:

```text
true
false
true
false
true
true
```

The duplicate queries show that each occurrence needs a distinct
stored position. The final line proves source-slice replacement after
construction does not alter the snapshot.

##### Why it works

After construction processes source prefix `source[:sourceIndex]`,
maintain this invariant: for every value, its map list contains
exactly the indexes below `sourceIndex` where that value occurs, in
strictly increasing order.

Initially every list and the processed prefix are empty. At one step,
the current source value belongs in exactly its own list. Appending
the current index adds the one new occurrence, and that index is
greater than every previously processed index. Other lists remain
exact. Induction proves the invariant for the whole source and
establishes the sorted precondition required by binary search.

During a query, after J candidate values have matched, maintain this
invariant: their chosen source indexes are strictly increasing, and
the chosen index for each prefix is no later than the corresponding
last index of any other witness sequence for that prefix.
`nextSourceIndex` is zero when J is zero and otherwise is one past the
last chosen witness.

The invariant is initially true for the empty prefix. For the next
candidate value, its position list contains every and only possible
source witness. Lower bound returns the earliest one at or after
`nextSourceIndex`. Appending it preserves increasing order. Any other
valid witness is the same position or later, so the earliest-prefix
property also survives.

If lower bound reaches the list end, no occurrence of the required
value is at or after the legal boundary. Every completion would need
such an occurrence, so false is correct. If all candidate values are
processed, the selected positions witness the complete subsequence,
so true is correct. This is the same safe earliest-match choice as the
single-query scan; preprocessing changes how the match is found, not
which match is safe.

The build loop advances once per source element. The query loop
advances once per matched candidate element or returns immediately on
failure. Each library binary search halves a finite position range.
All phases therefore terminate. The list-end check occurs before the
stored position is indexed, and a valid source index plus one cannot
overflow `int` because every slice index is below its representable
length.

No assignment targets an input slice. The stored map and its lists are
new allocations, so replacing source slice elements after construction
cannot affect them. Query-local state contains only integers and slice
views into the immutable index.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be source length, U the number of distinct source values, M one
candidate length, and F_j the number of source occurrences of the
candidate value processed at query step j.

The bounds below treat hashing and equality for one T value as O(1),
as for runes and ordinary fixed-width scalar keys. Variable-length
strings and large comparable arrays or structs add the work needed to
hash or compare their contents.

Construction performs a constant number of map operations and one
amortized append per source element. Under the usual expected
constant-time hash-map model, it takes expected Theta(N) time. Go
does not specify a map-operation worst-case bound, so this is an
algorithmic expectation rather than a language timing guarantee.

The lists contain exactly N logical integers in total, and the map has
U keys. Under the scalar-key model, retained storage is O(N + U),
which is O(N) because `U <= N` for nonempty input. More generally, it
stores N index integers, U key values, and any storage those keys keep
reachable. Slice capacities stay O(N) across the completed append
sequence. Empty construction returns an initialized empty map and
stores the source length.

A query that processes J candidate values performs J expected-time map
lookups. Binary search at step j takes
O(log(F_j + 1)) comparisons. Its expected total time is therefore:

```text
O(J + sum from j=1 through J of log(F_j + 1))
```

Here `J <= M`. This is O(M log(N + 1)) in the worst distribution.
An empty candidate or a candidate longer than the source returns in
Theta(1). A missing first value also returns in expected O(1). The
query uses O(1) auxiliary space, allocates nothing, and returns one
O(1) Boolean.

For Q candidates with S total candidate values, preprocessing plus all
queries costs expected O(N + S log(N + 1)) as a simple upper bound.
Repeated two-pointer scans can cost Theta(QN). The index wins when one
stable source serves enough queries to repay allocation and hashing.
For one short query, the direct scan has less setup and O(1) storage.

When the alphabet is small and fixed, a next-occurrence table can
store the next position for every source boundary and alphabet symbol.
It gives O(M) query time but uses O(N times A) storage for alphabet
size A. Position lists use O(N + U) storage and suit sparse or large
value domains, at the price of binary searches.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty source: a built or zero-value index accepts only an empty
  candidate. A missing map lookup safely returns a nil position list.
- Empty candidate: return true before any lookup, even if the source
  is empty. The empty sequence needs no witness.
- Longer candidate: return false from the length guard. Even repeated
  values cannot create more source positions than exist.
- Missing value: `positionsByValue[value]` is nil. Binary search
  returns offset zero, equal to length zero, so the ordinary failure
  branch handles it.
- Duplicates: `bb` matches source positions 1 and 3 in `abcba`, while
  `bbb` fails. Never store only the first or last occurrence.
- Inner offset versus source index: lower-bound offset 1 in `[0,4]`
  selects stored source index 4. Setting the cursor to `1 + 1` would
  break order and can reuse or skip occurrences.
- Boundary convention: this code stores the next legal source index,
  so lower bound uses `>=`. Searching with `>` rejects an occurrence
  exactly at the boundary.
- List order: do not iterate the map and reconstruct positions in map
  iteration order. Append while scanning the source left to right;
  binary search requires each individual list to be increasing.
- Snapshot staleness: later source replacement, insertion, deletion,
  or reordering does not update the index. Rebuild for an arbitrary
  new source; this API has no incremental mutation contract.
- Shared copies: copying `subsequenceIndex` copies a map descriptor,
  so both index values share the same internal lists. Read-only
  queries are fine; internal mutation would affect both copies.
- Concurrency: concurrent read-only queries can share a safely
  published index. Mutation of its map, lists, or a queried candidate
  creates invalid results or a data race.
- NaN: `float64` is comparable, but NaN is unequal to itself. A NaN
  source key cannot satisfy a NaN candidate under this equality rule.
- Interface keys: a dynamic slice, map, or function used through an
  interface key panics during hashing. Prefer concrete comparable keys
  or validate dynamic values before construction and queries.
- Reference-like keys: pointers compare identity, not pointed-to
  contents. Stored keys can keep referenced objects alive even though
  the source backing array itself is not retained.
- Text units: `[]byte` positions count encoded bytes and `[]rune`
  positions count Unicode code points. Neither performs normalization
  or grapheme-cluster segmentation.

##### When to choose it

Choose position lists when many candidates share one stable source,
exact equality defines a match, and the value domain is too large or
sparse for a dense next-occurrence table. The workload should reuse
the index enough to justify O(N) retained storage.

Use the [two-pointer scan](
#b251-subsequence-checking-two-pointers) for one or a few queries, a
streaming source, or strict O(1) auxiliary space. Use a dense
next-occurrence table when the source is stable, the alphabet is tiny,
and O(M) query latency matters more than O(N times A) storage.

This structure answers only whole-candidate membership. Use
[longest common subsequence](
#b253-longest-common-subsequence-dp-table) when the maximum shared
subsequence length is required. Use [exact string matching](
#b72-kmp-matching-prefix-function-array) when matches must be
contiguous rather than allowed to skip source positions.

The unsolved [Is Subsequence practice file](
problems/easy_leetcode_0392_is_subsequence.go) covers the base
problem. Its official [LeetCode statement](
https://leetcode.com/problems/is-subsequence/) poses the many-query
follow-up that motivates preprocessing. Go documents the insertion
offset returned by [`slices.BinarySearch`](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#BinarySearch), the valid key rules for
[map types](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Map_types), and the underlying
[equality semantics](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Comparison_operators).

#### B.25.3 Longest common subsequence (DP table)

##### Problem and contract

Two sequences may share several ordered values even when neither is a
subsequence of the other. Find a longest common subsequence,
abbreviated LCS: a maximum-length sequence obtainable from both inputs
by deleting positions without reordering the values that remain.

For first sequence `abc` and second sequence `bac`, both `ac` and `bc`
are common subsequences of length two. No length-three answer exists
because the inputs disagree on the order of `a` and `b`.

Recursively trying both possible skips at every mismatch revisits the
same prefix pair through many paths and can take exponential time. A
dynamic-programming table solves each of the `(N+1)*(M+1)` prefix
pairs once and preserves enough information to reconstruct one
optimum.

`longestCommonSubsequence` has this contract:

- accept two finite slices of one Go type satisfying `comparable`;
- return a newly allocated slice that is a subsequence of both inputs
  and has maximum possible length;
- compare elements only with Go's `==` operator;
- preserve duplicates as separate positions and preserve relative
  order while allowing gaps;
- return a non-nil empty slice and nil error when no common value is
  selectable, including when either input is empty;
- leave both inputs unchanged and retain neither backing array;
- return nil and an error before table allocation when prefix
  dimensions or their product cannot fit `int`.

Several longest answers can exist. This implementation makes output
deterministic. Equal current elements use the diagonal table state and
enter the result. At unequal elements, equal predecessor lengths drop
the current element from the first sequence. This rule does not
promise the lexicographically smallest answer, and swapping inputs can
select a different tied LCS even though the maximum length is
symmetric.

The result copies element values into new slice storage.
Reference-like elements, such as pointers, strings, channels, or
interfaces, can still keep referenced objects reachable. Allocation
failure for an otherwise valid table is outside the returned-error
contract.

Equality follows Go semantics. NaN does not equal itself, pointers
compare identity, and an interface comparison panics if a dynamic
value is not comparable. Concurrent input mutation is excluded.

Read [subsequence checking](
#b251-subsequence-checking-two-pointers) for the ordered-deletion
definition, [multidimensional arrays and matrices](
#a12-multidimensional-arrays-and-matrices) for row and column roles,
and [edit distance](
#b83-edit-distance-and-subsequences-dp-table) to contrast a table that
optimizes edit cost. This entry owns the LCS prefix recurrence and
reconstruction.

##### Mental model

Create one row for every first-sequence prefix length and one column
for every second-sequence prefix length. The table state means:

```text
lengthByPrefixes[I][J] is the maximum common-subsequence length
between first[:I] and second[:J]
```

I and J are counts, not element indexes. State `[2][3]` describes the
first two elements and first three elements. Their current final
elements, when both prefixes are nonempty, are `first[I-1]` and
`second[J-1]`.

Row zero and column zero contain zeros. If either prefix is empty, no
nonempty sequence can be common to both.

For every positive-prefix cell, inspect the two final elements:

- If they are equal, append that value to an optimal solution for the
  two shorter prefixes. Store the diagonal value plus one.
- If they differ, a common subsequence cannot use both final elements.
  Store the larger of the cell above, which drops from `first`, and
  the cell to the left, which drops from `second`.

Fill rows and columns from short prefixes to long ones. Every
diagonal, upper, and left predecessor is then final before the current
cell reads it.

The bottom-right value is the LCS length. To recover values, start
there and retrace the chosen recurrence. Equal elements are recorded
while moving diagonally. A mismatch moves to a predecessor with the
same length; a tie moves upward. These recorded equal values arrive
from end to start, so reverse them before returning.

##### Worked walkthrough

Find one LCS of first sequence `abc` and second sequence `bac`. The
expected deterministic result is `ac`, length two. `bc` is another
valid LCS, so the tie rule matters.

Initial state: both lengths are three. Dimension checks have not run,
the table does not exist, and no result value is confirmed.

1. Decision: allocate `(3+1)*(3+1) = 16` integer cells. Their zero
   initialization establishes row zero and column zero.
   After: the table contains only base values; nine positive-prefix
   cells remain unresolved.
   Known correct: every pair involving an empty prefix has LCS length
   zero, and each positive cell has its required base boundary.
2. Decision: fill the row for first prefix `a`. At `[1][1]`, `a` and
   `b` differ, so max of upper zero and left zero is zero. At
   `[1][2]`, `a` equals `a`, so diagonal `[0][1] + 1` gives one. At
   `[1][3]`, `a` and `c` differ, so left one beats upper zero.
   After: the row is `[0,0,1,1]`.
   Known correct: lengths for `a` against `""`, `b`, `ba`, and `bac`
   are final; common value `a` first becomes available at column 2.
3. Decision: fill the row for first prefix `ab`. At `[2][1]`, equal
   `b` values extend diagonal zero to one. At `[2][2]`, `b` and `a`
   differ; upper and left are both one, so store one. At `[2][3]`,
   `b` and `c` differ and both predecessors again hold one.
   After: the row is `[0,1,1,1]`.
   Known correct: both `a` and `b` are attainable length-one answers,
   but their reversed input order prevents using both together.
4. Decision: fill the row for first prefix `abc`. Mismatches at
   columns 1 and 2 keep length one. At `[3][3]`, both final values are
   `c`, so diagonal `[2][2] + 1` gives two.
   After: the complete table is:

   ```text
           ""  b  a  c
   ""       0  0  0  0
   a        0  0  1  1
   ab       0  1  1  1
   abc      0  1  1  2
   ```

   Known correct: every prefix-pair optimum is final, and the full
   sequences have maximum common-subsequence length two.
5. Decision: begin reconstruction at `[3][3]`. Final values `c` and
   `c` match, so record `c` and move diagonally to `[2][2]`.
   After: reverse-order result is `[c]`; both remaining prefixes have
   length two and their table value is one.
   Known correct: some optimal full answer ends in `c`, and exactly
   one earlier result value remains to be reconstructed.
6. Decision: at `[2][2]`, final values `b` and `a` differ. Upper
   `[1][2]` and left `[2][1]` both hold one. Apply the declared tie
   rule and drop `b` from the first prefix by moving up to `[1][2]`.
   After: reverse-order result stays `[c]`; active prefixes are `a`
   and `ba`.
   Known correct: the retained predecessor has the same optimal length
   one, so the tie choice cannot shorten the final result.
7. Decision: at `[1][2]`, final values `a` and `a` match. Record `a`
   and move diagonally to `[0][1]`.
   After: reverse-order result is `[c,a]`; the first prefix is empty.
   Known correct: the two recorded values correspond to increasing
   positions in both inputs when read in reverse.
8. Decision: stop because one prefix is empty, then reverse `[c,a]`.
   After: return newly allocated result `[a,c]`, displayed as `ac`,
   with nil error.
   Known correct: `ac` occurs at first indexes `[0,2]` and second
   indexes `[1,2]`, and its length equals the table optimum two.

Focused empty case: `""` and `abc` allocate one table row, perform no
positive-prefix comparison, and return a non-nil empty result. Empty
is the only sequence common to an empty input.

Focused no-match case: `abc` and `def` leave every cell zero. During
backtracking, mismatch moves eventually exhaust one prefix without
recording a value, so the result is empty.

Focused duplicate case: `aaa` and `aa` return `aa`. Each diagonal
match consumes one distinct position from both inputs; a third `a`
cannot appear because the shorter input has only two positions.

Focused contained case: `abcde` and `ace` return `ace`. The complete
shorter sequence is already a subsequence of the longer one, so no
common answer can be longer than three.

Counterexample to committing to the first available match: scan first
sequence `cab` against second sequence `abc` and immediately match `c`
at the second sequence's final position. No later value can follow, so
that greedy choice returns length one. Skipping the early `c` permits
`ab`, length two. Prefix DP retains both skip choices until their
final lengths can be compared.

##### Implementation

This complete generic Go program uses one flat row-major integer table
and returns actual LCS values. Text call sites convert strings to
`[]rune`, so positions represent Unicode code points. The function
does not normalize text or segment displayed grapheme clusters.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Longest common subsequence (DP
// table). Function comments connect each operation to its invariant.
package main

import "fmt"

func checkedPrefixCellCount(
	firstLength int,
	secondLength int,
) (int, error) {
	// Compute prefix cell count with an overflow check instead of
	// wrapping.
	maximumInt := int(^uint(0) >> 1)
	if firstLength == maximumInt ||
		secondLength == maximumInt {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"prefix dimension exceeds int capacity",
		)
	}
	rowCount := firstLength + 1
	columnCount := secondLength + 1
	if columnCount > maximumInt/rowCount {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"LCS table exceeds int capacity",
		)
	}
	return rowCount * columnCount, nil
}

func longestCommonSubsequence[T comparable](
	first []T,
	second []T,
) ([]T, error) {
	// Compute the requested ordered or extreme result.
	cellCount, err := checkedPrefixCellCount(
		len(first),
		len(second),
	)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	columnCount := len(second) + 1
	lengthByPrefixes := make([]int, cellCount)
	position := func(
		firstPrefixLength int,
		secondPrefixLength int,
	) int {
		return firstPrefixLength*columnCount +
			secondPrefixLength
	}

	// Each cell extends two already solved sequence prefixes.
	for firstLength := 1; firstLength <= len(first); firstLength++ {
		for secondLength := 1; secondLength <= len(second); secondLength++ {
			cellPosition := position(firstLength, secondLength)
			if first[firstLength-1] == second[secondLength-1] {
				lengthByPrefixes[cellPosition] =
					lengthByPrefixes[position(
						firstLength-1,
						secondLength-1,
					)] + 1
				continue
			}

			withoutFirst := lengthByPrefixes[position(
				firstLength-1,
				secondLength,
			)]
			withoutSecond := lengthByPrefixes[position(
				firstLength,
				secondLength-1,
			)]
			if withoutFirst >= withoutSecond {
				lengthByPrefixes[cellPosition] = withoutFirst
			} else {
				lengthByPrefixes[cellPosition] = withoutSecond
			}
		}
	}

	// Walk optimal predecessors from the full prefixes to zero.
	firstLength := len(first)
	secondLength := len(second)
	resultLength := lengthByPrefixes[position(
		firstLength,
		secondLength,
	)]
	reversed := make([]T, 0, resultLength)
	for firstLength > 0 && secondLength > 0 {
		if first[firstLength-1] == second[secondLength-1] {
			reversed = append(reversed, first[firstLength-1])
			firstLength--
			secondLength--
			continue
		}

		withoutFirst := lengthByPrefixes[position(
			firstLength-1,
			secondLength,
		)]
		withoutSecond := lengthByPrefixes[position(
			firstLength,
			secondLength-1,
		)]
		// A tie drops from first, matching the fill rule.
		if withoutFirst >= withoutSecond {
			firstLength--
		} else {
			secondLength--
		}
	}

	// Backtracking discovered equal values from end to start.
	for left, right := 0, len(reversed)-1; left < right; {
		reversed[left], reversed[right] =
			reversed[right], reversed[left]
		left++
		right--
	}
	return reversed, nil
}

func printLCS(first string, second string) {
	// Expose lcs in logical order without changing source.
	result, err := longestCommonSubsequence(
		[]rune(first),
		[]rune(second),
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("%+q %d\n", string(result), len(result))
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	printLCS("abc", "bac")
	printLCS("abcde", "ace")
	printLCS("abc", "def")
	printLCS("aaa", "aa")
	printLCS("", "abc")
	printLCS(
		"A\u00e9x\U0001f642B",
		"\u00e9\U0001f642",
	)
}
```

Expected output:

```text
"ac" 2
"ace" 3
"" 0
"aa" 2
"" 0
"\u00e9\U0001f642" 2
```

Each line contains one reconstructed sequence and its element count.
The `+` formatting flag renders non-ASCII runes with escapes so the
last line exposes its code-point result unambiguously.

##### Why it works

Maintain this invariant after each cell is filled: every cell already
visited in row-major order stores the maximum common-subsequence
length for exactly the two prefixes named by its row and column.

The base row and column satisfy the invariant because an empty prefix
has only the empty common subsequence. Assume all predecessors of a
positive cell are correct.

If the two final values differ, no common subsequence can select both
as one final value. Every candidate must omit the final first value or
the final second value, so it belongs to the upper or left
predecessor. Taking their maximum covers every candidate and stores an
attainable optimum.

If the final values are equal, an optimal answer can use both. Any
optimal answer that uses neither endpoint could append the shared
value and become longer. If it uses one endpoint matched to an earlier
equal value, remap that final selected value to the other endpoint.
Removing the shared final value then leaves a common subsequence of
the two shorter prefixes. Thus diagonal optimum plus one is both
attainable and an upper bound.

These cases preserve the invariant. Row-major order supplies the
diagonal, upper, and left facts before use, so induction proves the
bottom-right cell is the exact LCS length.

During reconstruction, an equal pair follows the recurrence that
added one and records that value. At a mismatch, moving to a
predecessor with the same stored length preserves the unresolved
optimum. The tie rule chooses one of two equally long paths without
reducing it. Therefore the reverse-order values follow one optimal
path through the table.

A diagonal move reduces both prefix lengths. Every mismatch move
reduces one. Their nonnegative sum strictly decreases, so backtracking
terminates after at most N+M moves. Reversing the recorded values puts
their source positions into increasing order in both inputs. The
result is therefore common, ordered, and as long as the bottom-right
optimum.

The fill loops advance bounded positive prefix lengths. Checked
dimensions keep every row-major position inside the allocated slice
and prevent multiplication overflow. Inputs are only read. The result
uses its own slice storage, establishing the mutation and ownership
parts of the contract.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the first length, M the second length, and L the returned LCS
length. Treat one T equality comparison as O(1), as for runes and
ordinary fixed-width scalar values. Variable-length strings and large
comparable arrays or structs add their comparison work.

Allocation zeroes `(N+1)*(M+1)` integer cells, and filling visits
every positive-prefix cell. Best, average, and worst successful time
are all Theta((N+1)*(M+1)); input equality changes cell values, not
the visited grid. Backtracking takes O(N+M), and reversal takes
Theta(L). Since
`L <= min(N,M)`, table construction dominates except at empty
dimensions where the product expression already counts the base cells.

The table uses Theta((N+1)*(M+1)) auxiliary integer storage. Flat
storage avoids per-row slice descriptors but not the quadratic cell
count. The returned slice uses Theta(L) output storage; its reserved
capacity is exactly L. Other working state and call-stack use are
O(1).

If only the length is needed, each row depends on the previous row and
its own left cell. Two rolling rows reduce auxiliary storage to
O(min(N,M)) after placing the shorter sequence on the column axis.
Discarding old rows loses direct reconstruction information.

[Hirschberg's algorithm](
https://ics.uci.edu/~dhirschb/pubs/p341-hirschberg.pdf) reconstructs
an LCS in O(N*M) time with linear auxiliary space by dividing the
alignment at prefix scores. Its recursion and tie behavior are more
involved than this full-table teaching implementation.

Dimension errors take O(1) work and allocate no table. A valid product
can still exceed available memory. The guard establishes integer
representability, not practical capacity.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Both inputs empty: return a non-nil empty result. Returning nil
  would violate this lesson's ownership convention even though both
  lengths are zero.
- One input empty: every table value is zero and the result is empty.
  Reading element `I-1` or `J-1` before testing positive prefixes
  would panic.
- No common value: `abc` and `def` return empty. Initialized zero
  cells are final answers here, not unresolved sentinels.
- Identical inputs: `abc` and `abc` follow three diagonals and return
  `abc`; skipping equality would lose attainable length.
- Duplicates: `aaa` and `aa` return two values, not three. Each
  diagonal consumes a distinct position from both sequences.
- Tied optima: `abc` and `bac` return `ac` under the upward tie rule.
  Tests expecting `bc` ignore the declared deterministic contract.
- Argument order: length is symmetric, but tied output need not be.
  Swapping the two inputs also swaps what an upward tie discards.
- Prefix count versus index: state I reads element `I-1`. Reading I
  skips the first value and panics at the full prefix.
- Flat stride: multiply a row by `M+1`, not M. The zero-prefix column
  is real table storage; omitting it overlaps adjacent rows.
- Equal recurrence: use diagonal plus one. Taking only max of upper
  and left fails even on one equal value.
- Mismatch recurrence: do not add one. Unequal final values cannot be
  one shared selected value.
- Fill order: top, left, and diagonal cells must be final before use.
  Reverse row order reads placeholders and understates answers.
- Backtracking: compare current elements and predecessor lengths; do
  not greedily search for the nearest equal pair. The `cab` and `abc`
  counterexample shows why a local match can block a longer answer.
- Subsequence is not substring. `ace` is an LCS of `abcde` and `ace`
  even though its positions are not contiguous in the first input.
- NaN: a NaN element cannot match another NaN under Go equality, even
  if their bit patterns are the same.
- Interface values: comparing a dynamic slice, map, or function
  panics. Prefer concrete comparable element types or validate dynamic
  values before calling.
- Pointer elements compare addresses, not pointed-to contents. The
  output can retain pointed-to objects after the input slices vanish.
- Text unit: `[]byte` aligns UTF-8 bytes; `[]rune` aligns code points.
  Neither representation normalizes text or identifies grapheme
  clusters.
- Oversized dimensions return an error before allocation. Ordinary
  memory exhaustion for a representable table remains outside the
  successful contract.
- Concurrent writes to either input race with table construction.
  Provide stable sequences for the call.

##### When to choose it

Choose full-table LCS when two finite ordered sequences must retain as
many equal values as possible and the caller needs one actual optimum,
not merely its length. Typical uses include sequence alignment,
deletion-based comparison, and explaining a diff's ordered common
backbone when quadratic work fits.

Use [subsequence checking](
#b251-subsequence-checking-two-pointers) when the question is only
whether one complete sequence fits inside another; its linear scan
avoids comparing every prefix pair. Use [edit distance](
#b83-edit-distance-and-subsequences-dp-table) when insertion,
deletion, or replacement costs are the objective rather than retained
length.

Use exact matching when gaps are forbidden, and longest common
substring when the shared result itself must be contiguous. Use the
[sequence-DP overview](
#b204-sequence-dp-arrays-or-binary-search-tails) or the next
[longest increasing subsequence lesson](
#b254-longest-increasing-subsequence-tails-array) when one sequence is
being optimized under an increasing-value rule rather than matched
against a second sequence.

Use rolling rows for length-only output under tight memory. Use
Hirschberg reconstruction when an actual LCS is required but the full
table is too large. Enumerating all tied LCS values is a different
output-sensitive problem and can require exponential output.

NIST defines [longest common subsequence](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/longestCommonSubsequence.html) as a
maximum-length common subsequence and distinguishes it from contiguous
substring matching. The official [LeetCode 1143 statement](
https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-common-subsequence/) supplies
the lowercase-string length-only form. Hirschberg's original
[linear-space paper](
https://ics.uci.edu/~dhirschb/pubs/p341-hirschberg.pdf) presents both
the quadratic table recurrence and linear-space reconstruction. Go
defines the implementation's [equality semantics](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Comparison_operators).

#### B.25.4 Longest increasing subsequence (tails array)

##### Problem and contract

Given one ordered integer sequence, return the greatest number of
positions that can be selected from left to right so their values are
strictly increasing. Selected positions may have gaps. Equal selected
values are forbidden.

For `[0,1,0,3,2,3]`, the answer is 4. Positions 0, 1, 4, and 5
produce `[0,1,2,3]`. Sorting the values would also produce an ordered
list, but it would erase the input-position constraint and solve a
different problem.

This lesson applies the `longestIncreasingSubsequenceTails` contract
owned by [sequence DP](
#b204-sequence-dp-arrays-or-binary-search-tails):

- accept from 0 through 2500 integers;
- accept each value from -10000 through 10000;
- preserve position order and require strict value increase;
- return the LIS length and nil error, with zero for nil or empty
  input;
- return zero and an error wrapping `errInvalidSequence` for an
  invalid length or value;
- validate length first and values from left to right before
  allocating algorithm state; and
- read but neither modify nor retain the input slice.

The function returns only a length. It does not promise selected
positions, selected values, or a tie-break among several longest
subsequences. Each call owns its working slice, so independent calls
may run concurrently when their inputs remain stable. Allocation must
fit memory.

Read [subsequence checking](
#b251-subsequence-checking-two-pointers) for the ordered-deletion
definition and [binary-search bounds](
#b41-binary-search-and-bounds-slice) for the lower-bound operation.
The sequence-DP owner contains the complete implementation and its
quadratic comparison. This entry focuses on applying the tails state.

##### Mental model

Do not retain every increasing subsequence. Group all subsequences in
the processed prefix by length, then keep only the smallest ending
value in each group:

```text
minimumTailByLength[L-1] is the smallest ending value of any
strictly increasing subsequence of length L in the processed prefix.
```

A smaller tail dominates a larger tail at the same length. Every
future value that can extend the larger tail can also extend the
smaller one. The smaller tail therefore preserves at least the same
future choices.

The retained tails are strictly increasing by subsequence length. For
the next value `V`, find the first tail greater than or equal to `V`:

- If the search reaches the end, `V` extends the longest represented
  length. Append it.
- Otherwise, replace the found tail with `V`. That length remains
  attainable with an equal or smaller ending value.

This is lower bound, the first `>= V`, not upper bound. Equality must
replace rather than append because the requested subsequence is
strictly increasing. A longest nondecreasing subsequence instead uses
the first tail `> V` so equality may extend a length.

The tails entries summarize separate witnesses. They are not
necessarily positions from one common subsequence. Only the slice
length is the LIS answer.

##### Worked walkthrough

Trace `[0,1,0,3,2,3]`. The expected strict LIS length is 4.

Initial state: validation accepts all six values.
`minimumTailByLength` is empty, so no positive length is represented.

1. Decision: lower bound in the empty slice returns index zero for
   value 0. That index equals the tails length, so append 0.
   After: tails are `[0]`.
   Known correct: a length-one subsequence exists, and zero is its
   smallest tail in the processed prefix.
2. Decision: value 1 is greater than every tail. Lower bound returns
   index one, so append.
   After: tails are `[0,1]`.
   Known correct: positions 0 and 1 witness length two, and the two
   stored minimum tails remain strictly increasing.
3. Decision: the next value is 0. The first tail `>= 0` is index zero.
   Replace that entry with the equal value rather than appending.
   After: tails remain `[0,1]`.
   Known correct: length one and length two remain attainable, while
   equal zeroes have not created a false strict extension.
4. Decision: value 3 exceeds both tails. Lower bound returns index
   two, so append.
   After: tails are `[0,1,3]`.
   Known correct: `[0,1,3]` witnesses an attainable length three.
5. Decision: for value 2, the first tail `>= 2` is index two. Replace
   3 with 2.
   After: tails are `[0,1,2]`.
   Known correct: length three still exists, now with the smaller
   ending value 2 and therefore no fewer future extension choices.
6. Decision: the final value 3 exceeds every tail. Append it at index
   three.
   After: tails are `[0,1,2,3]`.
   Known correct: input positions 0, 1, 4, and 5 witness length four.
7. Decision: every input value has been consumed. Return the number
   of represented lengths.
   After: return 4 and nil error.
   Known correct: the invariant has an entry for every attainable
   length from one through four and none for length five.

The final tails happen to spell an actual LIS in this input. That is
not part of the contract. For `[3,5,6,2]`, the states are `[3]`,
`[3,5]`, `[3,5,6]`, then `[2,5,6]`. The last list has length three,
but 2 occurs after 5 and 6, so `[2,5,6]` is not an input subsequence.
The valid length-three witness is `[3,5,6]`.

Focused empty case: nil and empty input skip the loop and return zero.
No positive subsequence length needs a tail.

Focused singleton case: `[7]` appends one tail and returns one.

Focused duplicate case: `[7,7,7]` repeatedly replaces index zero and
returns one. Equal values never extend strict LIS.

Focused decreasing case: `[5,4,3]` produces `[5]`, `[4]`, then `[3]`
and returns one. Replacements improve the tail without increasing the
represented length.

Focused signed case: `[-3,-2,-2,-1]` returns three. One `-2` may
appear between `-3` and `-1`, but the equal pair cannot both extend a
strict subsequence.

Focused maximum case: 2500 strictly increasing accepted values append
2500 tails and return 2500.

Focused invalid case: length 2501, value -10001, and value 10001 are
rejected before the tails slice is allocated.

##### Implementation

The complete executable implementation is
[`longestIncreasingSubsequenceTails`](
#b204-sequence-dp-arrays-or-binary-search-tails) in B.20.4. That
owner validates the contract, calls `sort.Search` with the monotone
predicate `minimumTailByLength[index] >= value`, appends or replaces,
and returns `len(minimumTailByLength)`.

This application deliberately links to that primary implementation
instead of copying it into a second lesson. Run its complete program
to compare the tails result with the quadratic ending-index DP result,
exercise empty and duplicate inputs, and verify wrapped invalid-input
errors. Applying the tails function to `[0,1,0,3,2,3]` returns 4 and
nil error, exactly as traced above.

When actual positions or values are required, the length-only function
is not enough. Use [DP path reconstruction](
#b2012-dp-path-reconstruction-predecessor-array) and retain source
indexes plus predecessor links. Do not attempt to reconstruct from the
final tails values alone.

##### Why it works

After each processed prefix, maintain this invariant for every
positive length L:

```text
Entry L-1 exists exactly when the prefix has a strict increasing
subsequence of length L, and that entry is the smallest possible tail
among all such subsequences.
```

The empty prefix satisfies the invariant because it has no positive
subsequence length and the tails slice is empty. Assume the invariant
holds before processing value `V`. Let lower bound return index `K`.

Every tail before K is strictly smaller than `V`. If K is positive,
an attainable length-K subsequence ending at entry `K-1` can append
`V`, so a length-`K+1` witness exists. If K is zero, singleton `[V]`
provides that witness.

If K equals the tails length, no represented subsequence is long
enough to precede a further entry. Appending `V` creates the first
witness for the new maximum length. All prior minimum tails remain
unchanged.

If K is inside the slice, old entry K is at least `V`. Replacing it
records an attainable tail for the same length `K+1` that is no
larger. The old entry was the prior minimum for that length, and lower
bound says it is not below `V`, so `V` is the new exact minimum. No
other length changes. Because the preceding tail is below `V` and the
following tail, if any, was above the old entry, the tails remain
strictly increasing.

Any new subsequence ending at `V` must extend a represented shorter
length whose tail is below `V`. Lower bound chooses the greatest such
length. No represented tail at index K or later is below `V`, so `V`
cannot create a witness longer than `K+1`. Appending or replacing
therefore records exactly the best tail for every attainable length
and preserves the invariant.

By induction, after the full input the number of entries is the
greatest attainable strict-subsequence length. That is the required
LIS length.

The outer loop consumes one value per iteration. Each lower-bound
search maintains the B.4.1 half-open interval invariant and strictly
shrinks its unresolved interval. Both loops terminate. Validation
keeps values within the declared domain, and the function only reads
the input. Local working storage and an integer result satisfy the
ownership contract.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the accepted input length and L the current tails length.
Validation reads all N values. Each value then performs one
lower-bound search with `O(log(L+1))` predicate calls and one
constant-time replace or amortized append.

Worst-case successful time is Theta(N log(N+1)), reached when the
tails length grows with N. For an all-equal or decreasing input, the
tails length remains one and total time is Theta(N), including
validation. There is no distribution-independent average without a
model for value order.

The owner reserves capacity for N integers, so successful auxiliary
space is Theta(N) even when the logical tails length stays small. The
returned integer uses Theta(1) output space. The input is neither
copied nor retained.

An invalid length is rejected in Theta(1) time. An invalid value at
index I is rejected after Theta(I+1) value checks. Both failures occur
before algorithm-state allocation.

The quadratic ending-index DP takes Theta(N^2) time and Theta(N)
auxiliary space, but it retains the best length at every input ending
position. Tails replaces those per-position facts with one dominant
tail per length. That compression enables binary search but discards
direct reconstruction and per-index explanations.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil or empty input returns zero. Do not initialize the answer to one
  before confirming that a value exists.
- A singleton returns one. Every individual accepted value forms a
  strict increasing subsequence of length one.
- All-equal and decreasing nonempty inputs return one, not zero.
- Negative integers compare normally. No offset or sentinel is
  required.
- Search for the first tail `>= V`. Searching for `> V` computes the
  nondecreasing variant and incorrectly extends duplicates here.
- Append only when the lower-bound index equals the tails length.
  Otherwise replace the found entry.
- Do not sort the input. A subsequence must preserve original position
  order; sorting destroys the problem's defining constraint.
- Do not return the tails slice as an LIS. The `[3,5,6,2]`
  counterexample shows that its entries can come from incompatible
  input positions.
- Replacing a tail does not delete the existence of the earlier
  witness. It records a better ending value for the same length.
- Preserve strict tails order. Binary search is invalid if updates can
  leave the slice unsorted.
- Return `len(minimumTailByLength)`, not its last value. Tails are
  values, while their indexes encode lengths.
- Validate all values before allocation or partial computation so an
  error cannot expose partially derived state.
- Do not use the length-only result when the caller needs positions,
  values, counts of optimal subsequences, or a deterministic
  tie-break.
- Do not call while another goroutine mutates the input. Concurrent
  read-only calls with stable inputs are safe because state is local.

##### When to choose it

Choose the tails array when one finite sequence has a total order, the
goal is strict LIS length, and quadratic pairwise comparisons are too
expensive or unnecessary. Its dominance rule is the key test: among
states of one length, a smaller ending value must preserve every
future extension available to a larger one.

Use quadratic ending-index DP from B.20.4 when the transition has
custom scores or compatibility rules, or when facts for each ending
position matter. Use [predecessor reconstruction](
#b2012-dp-path-reconstruction-predecessor-array) when an actual LIS is
required. Use the next [patience-sorting lesson](
#b256-patience-sorting-pile-tops) to connect the same lower-bound
updates to pile tops.

Use [longest common subsequence](
#b253-longest-common-subsequence-dp-table) when order must be matched
between two sequences rather than compared within one. Use a linear
scan for a longest increasing contiguous run; gaps are forbidden in
that different problem. Counting increasing subsequences is also a
different output and needs richer state than one minimum tail.

The official [Longest Increasing Subsequence problem](
https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-increasing-subsequence/)
defines strict LIS, supplies the six-value walkthrough input and the
2500-value bounds, and asks for an `O(N log N)` follow-up. The Go
standard library documents [`sort.Search`](
https://pkg.go.dev/sort#Search) as returning the first index where a
monotone predicate becomes true; the owner's `>=` predicate is exactly
the lower bound required here.

#### B.25.5 Counting subsequences (DP array or Fenwick tree)

##### Problem and contract

Count every nonempty strictly increasing subsequence of one integer
sequence. A subsequence selects input positions from left to right and
may skip positions. Two selections count separately when they use
different positions, even if their selected values are equal.

For `[2,1,3,2]`, the four singletons and the pairs `[2,3]`, `[1,3]`,
and `[1,2]` give seven subsequences. No length-three selection is
strictly increasing.

The mathematical count can grow exponentially. Both implementations
return its residue modulo `1_000_000_007`, not the exact count. They
share this contract:

- accept from 0 through 200000 `int64` values, including duplicates,
  zero, negatives, and both signed extremes;
- preserve input position order and require each selected value to be
  strictly greater than the preceding selected value;
- exclude the empty subsequence, so nil and empty input return zero;
- count position selections, not distinct resulting value lists;
- return zero and an error wrapping `errInvalidCountingSequence` when
  the input has more than 200000 positions;
- validate length before allocating algorithm state; and
- read but neither modify nor retain the input slice.

The quadratic function is correct across the full contract but is an
educational baseline, not a practical choice near the maximum length.
The Fenwick function is the intended full-scale implementation. Each
call owns its state, so independent calls may run concurrently when
their inputs stay stable. Allocation must fit memory.

Read [sequence DP](
#b204-sequence-dp-arrays-or-binary-search-tails) for ending-index
states, [Fenwick trees](#a123-fenwick-trees) for prefix sums, and
[coordinate compression](
#b66-coordinate-compression-sorted-slice-and-map) for dense ranks.
This entry owns the recurrence and the application that groups prior
subsequence counts by ending value.

##### Mental model

Every counted subsequence has one final input position. For ending
index I, remember:

```text
waysByEndingIndex[I] is the number of nonempty strict increasing
subsequences whose final selected position is exactly I, modulo M.
```

Here `M = 1_000_000_007`. The singleton containing position I gives
one way. Every earlier index J with `values[J] < values[I]` can be the
penultimate position. Append the current value to every subsequence
counted at J:

```text
waysByEndingIndex[I] =
    1 + sum of waysByEndingIndex[J]
        for J < I and values[J] < values[I]
```

The total is the sum of all ending-index states. These categories are
disjoint because a position selection has one final index.

The quadratic DP checks every earlier J. The faster version observes
that the transition needs only the sum of prior states with a smaller
ending value. Compress each distinct value to a zero-based rank that
preserves order, then let a Fenwick tree group counts by rank.

Rank R maps to one-based Fenwick position `R+1`. A prefix query with
end R covers tree positions 1 through R, which represent zero-based
ranks 0 through `R-1`. Those are exactly the values strictly smaller
than the current value. The current ending count is one plus that
prefix. Add it at position `R+1` so later positions may extend it.

Several input positions can share one rank. Their counts must be
added, not replaced, because each position supplies distinct
subsequences. Every tree cell and total stores a residue modulo M.

##### Worked walkthrough

Count subsequences of `[2,1,3,2]`. The expected result is seven.

Initial state: validation accepts four values. The DP array contains
four zero placeholders. The Fenwick representation has not yet copied,
sorted, or ranked a value. Both totals are zero.

1. Decision: DP processes index 0, value 2. There is no earlier
   position, so only the singleton ends here.
   After: finalized DP states are `[1]`; DP total is 1.
   Known correct: `[2 at index 0]` is the only nonempty subsequence
   whose final position is zero.
2. Decision: process index 1, value 1. Earlier value 2 is not smaller,
   so it cannot precede 1. Keep only the singleton.
   After: finalized DP states are `[1,1]`; DP total is 2.
   Known correct: each processed position supplies one singleton and
   no strict pair ends at index 1.
3. Decision: process index 2, value 3. Both earlier values are
   smaller. Add their counts to the singleton: `1+1+1=3`.
   After: finalized DP states are `[1,1,3]`; DP total is 5.
   Known correct: the three states ending at index 2 are `[3]`,
   `[2,3]`, and `[1,3]`.
4. Decision: process index 3, value 2. Earlier 2 is equal and earlier
   3 is larger, so neither can extend. Earlier 1 contributes its one
   singleton, giving `1+1=2`.
   After: finalized DP states are `[1,1,3,2]`; DP total is 7.
   Known correct: `[2 at index 3]` and `[1,2]` are the only states
   ending at the final position; every ending index is now complete.
5. Decision: the DP loop has consumed every position, so return the
   sum of its disjoint ending categories.
   After: return 7 and nil error.
   Known correct: the four state counts sum to seven and classify
   every nonempty increasing position selection exactly once.

Now replay the same input with coordinate compression and a Fenwick
tree. Sorting and deduplicating the private copy gives distinct values
`[1,2,3]` with ranks `1->0`, `2->1`, and `3->2`. The one-based tree
starts as `[0,0,0,0]`; position zero is unused.

6. Decision: scan input value 2, rank 1. Prefix end 1 contains only
   smaller rank 0 and currently sums to zero. Add singleton one at
   tree position 2.
   After: tree is `[0,0,1,0]`; Fenwick total is 1.
   Known correct: the tree represents the one state ending at value 2
   among processed input positions.
7. Decision: scan value 1, rank 0. Prefix end zero is empty, so its
   ending count is one. Update position 1 and its parent position 2.
   After: tree is `[0,1,2,0]`; Fenwick total is 2.
   Known correct: tree position 2 covers ranks 0 and 1 and stores both
   processed singleton counts.
8. Decision: scan value 3, rank 2. Prefix end 2 reads tree position 2
   and returns two. Add its singleton to get three, then update tree
   position 3.
   After: tree is `[0,1,2,3]`; Fenwick total is 5.
   Known correct: the three new states are the same singleton and two
   pairs recorded by DP at index 2.
9. Decision: scan final value 2, rank 1. Prefix end 1 reads only tree
   position 1, whose count is one for smaller value 1. Add the
   singleton, then add two at tree position 2.
   After: tree is `[0,1,4,3]`; Fenwick total is 7.
   Known correct: equal earlier value 2 was excluded, while tree
   position 2 now aggregates one rank-0 way and three rank-1 ways.
10. Decision: no input remains, so stop and return the accumulated
    residue.
    After: return 7 and nil error.
    Known correct: the tree invariant reproduced every DP ending count
    while grouping eligible predecessors by value rank.

Focused empty case: nil input builds no rank and returns zero. The
empty subsequence is deliberately excluded.

Focused singleton case: `[9]` returns one for its singleton.

Focused all-equal case: `[4,4,4]` returns three. Each position gives a
different singleton, while no equal value may extend another.

Focused increasing case: `[1,2,3,4]` returns 15. Every nonempty subset
of its four positions remains increasing, so the count is `2^4-1`.

Focused decreasing case: `[4,3,2,1]` returns four because only the
four singletons qualify.

Focused extreme-value case: `[MinInt64,0,MaxInt64]` returns seven.
Comparisons and ranks use order directly and never subtract values.

Focused maximum case: 200000 equal values return 200000. The Fenwick
tree has one rank; every position adds one singleton and no extension.

Focused invalid case: 200001 positions return zero and a wrapped error
before the DP array, sorted copy, or Fenwick tree is allocated.

Counterexample to reusing the LIS tails array: `[1,1,2]` has five
counted subsequences: three singletons and two distinct `[1,2]`
position selections. A tails array records only one best tail for each
length and loses the multiplicity required by this problem.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program implements both counting methods, compares
them on the walkthrough, exercises empty, equal, increasing, and
invalid inputs, and propagates writer errors. It uses only `errors`,
`fmt`, `io`, `os`, `slices`, and `sort` from the standard library.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Counting subsequences (DP array or
// Fenwick tree). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
	"slices"
	"sort"
)

const maximumCountingSequenceLength = 200_000
const subsequenceCountModulus uint64 = 1_000_000_007

var errInvalidCountingSequence = errors.New(
	"invalid counting sequence",
)

func validateCountingSequence(values []int64) error {
	// Reject input outside the counting sequence contract before
	// mutation.
	if len(values) > maximumCountingSequenceLength {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: length %d; want 0..%d",
			errInvalidCountingSequence,
			len(values),
			maximumCountingSequenceLength,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func addCountsModulo(first uint64, second uint64) uint64 {
	// Both operands are residues, so one subtraction is sufficient.
	sum := first + second
	if sum >= subsequenceCountModulus {
		sum -= subsequenceCountModulus
	}
	return sum
}

func countIncreasingSubsequencesDP(
	values []int64,
) (uint64, error) {
	// Compute increasing subsequences dp from the state without mutating
	// it.
	if err := validateCountingSequence(values); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	// Each entry counts valid subsequences ending at that exact index.
	waysByEndingIndex := make([]uint64, len(values))
	totalCount := uint64(0)
	for endingIndex, endingValue := range values {
		// The singleton containing this position is always valid.
		endingCount := uint64(1)
		for earlierIndex := range values[:endingIndex] {
			if values[earlierIndex] >= endingValue {
				continue
			}
			endingCount = addCountsModulo(
				endingCount,
				waysByEndingIndex[earlierIndex],
			)
		}
		waysByEndingIndex[endingIndex] = endingCount
		totalCount = addCountsModulo(
			totalCount,
			endingCount,
		)
	}
	return totalCount, nil
}

func fenwickPrefixCount(
	tree []uint64,
	end int,
) uint64 {
	// Keep fenwick prefix count in one helper so callers use one rule.
	totalCount := uint64(0)
	for treeIndex := end; treeIndex > 0; {
		totalCount = addCountsModulo(
			totalCount,
			tree[treeIndex],
		)
		// Removing lowbit reaches the preceding prefix block.
		treeIndex -= treeIndex & -treeIndex
	}
	return totalCount
}

func fenwickAddCount(
	tree []uint64,
	treeIndex int,
	amount uint64,
) {
	// Keep fenwick add count in one helper so callers use one rule.
	for treeIndex < len(tree) {
		tree[treeIndex] = addCountsModulo(
			tree[treeIndex],
			amount,
		)
		// Adding lowbit reaches the next block containing the rank.
		step := treeIndex & -treeIndex
		if step >= len(tree)-treeIndex {
			break
		}
		treeIndex += step
	}
}

func countIncreasingSubsequencesFenwick(
	values []int64,
) (uint64, error) {
	// Compute increasing subsequences fenwick from the state without
	// mutating it.
	if err := validateCountingSequence(values); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}

	// Sorted distinct values give dense ranks without changing input.
	uniqueValues := append([]int64(nil), values...)
	slices.Sort(uniqueValues)
	uniqueCount := 0
	for _, value := range uniqueValues {
		if uniqueCount == 0 ||
			uniqueValues[uniqueCount-1] != value {
			uniqueValues[uniqueCount] = value
			uniqueCount++
		}
	}
	uniqueValues = uniqueValues[:uniqueCount]

	// The tree groups counts from already processed ending indexes.
	tree := make([]uint64, uniqueCount+1)
	totalCount := uint64(0)
	for _, value := range values {
		rank := sort.Search(
			len(uniqueValues),
			func(index int) bool {
				return uniqueValues[index] >= value
			},
		)
		smallerCount := fenwickPrefixCount(tree, rank)
		endingCount := addCountsModulo(1, smallerCount)
		fenwickAddCount(tree, rank+1, endingCount)
		totalCount = addCountsModulo(
			totalCount,
			endingCount,
		)
	}
	return totalCount, nil
}

func runCountingExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute counting examples to the bounded stopping condition above.
	values := []int64{2, 1, 3, 2}
	dpCount, err := countIncreasingSubsequencesDP(values)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("count with quadratic DP: %w", err)
	}
	fenwickCount, err := countIncreasingSubsequencesFenwick(values)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("count with Fenwick tree: %w", err)
	}
	if dpCount != fenwickCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"counting methods disagree: DP %d, Fenwick %d",
			dpCount,
			fenwickCount,
		)
	}

	emptyCount, err := countIncreasingSubsequencesFenwick(nil)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("count empty input: %w", err)
	}
	equalCount, err := countIncreasingSubsequencesDP(
		[]int64{4, 4, 4},
	)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("count equal values: %w", err)
	}
	increasingCount, err := countIncreasingSubsequencesFenwick(
		[]int64{1, 2, 3, 4},
	)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("count increasing values: %w", err)
	}
	_, invalidErr := countIncreasingSubsequencesFenwick(
		make([]int64, maximumCountingSequenceLength+1),
	)

	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"values=%v\nDP=%d\nFenwick=%d\n"+
			"empty=%d\nequal=%d\nincreasing=%d\n"+
			"invalid rejected=%t\n",
		values,
		dpCount,
		fenwickCount,
		emptyCount,
		equalCount,
		increasingCount,
		errors.Is(invalidErr, errInvalidCountingSequence),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write counting results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runCountingExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
values=[2 1 3 2]
DP=7
Fenwick=7
empty=0
equal=3
increasing=15
invalid rejected=true
```

The displayed input still has its original order. Both successful
counts are residues, although these small examples are below the
modulus.

##### Why it works

For the quadratic method, maintain this invariant after ending index I
is processed: every state through I equals, modulo M, the number of
strict increasing subsequences whose final selected position is that
exact index.

At index zero, the singleton establishes the invariant. Assume all
earlier states are correct. Every subsequence ending at I is either
the singleton or has one unique penultimate index J. That J must be
earlier and have a smaller value. Conversely, appending `values[I]`
to any subsequence ending at such a J creates one valid subsequence
ending at I.

Different penultimate indexes describe disjoint position selections,
so adding all eligible earlier counts plus one gives the exact new
state. This preserves the invariant. Every nonempty subsequence has
one final index, so summing all finalized states returns the requested
count.

For the Fenwick method, compression preserves `<` and `=`: smaller
values receive smaller ranks and equal values share one rank. Before
processing input index I, maintain this invariant:

```text
The tree stores the sum, modulo M, of ending counts for indexes below
I, grouped by ending-value rank; totalCount sums those same states.
```

The empty tree establishes the invariant before index zero. For rank
R, the Fenwick prefix ending at R contains exactly ranks below R.
Those and only those prior values are strictly smaller than the
current value. Adding one for the singleton therefore reproduces the
quadratic recurrence without inspecting each prior index.

Adding the new count at position `R+1` includes this ending index in
the appropriate rank group for later queries. It adds rather than
assigns, so equal-valued positions remain separate counted witnesses.
The updated total includes the new final-index category. Thus the
invariant advances to the next input position, and at termination its
total is the same answer as the quadratic DP.

Modulo reduction preserves addition: reducing every state and partial
sum gives the same residue as reducing the exact final count. Every
operand is below M, so their sum is at most `2*M-2`, far below the
`uint64` maximum. One conditional subtraction is therefore sufficient
and cannot overflow.

Every outer loop advances through a finite validated slice. Sorting
terminates under the standard-library contract. A Fenwick prefix index
loses a positive lowbit, while an update index gains one and stops
before the tree boundary. Each such loop terminates. All mutation is
confined to private slices, proving the input-ownership contract.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be input length and D be its number of distinct values.
Validation takes Theta(1) time.

The quadratic DP checks exactly `N*(N-1)/2` earlier-current pairs and
performs O(1) fixed-width residue work per eligible pair. For `N>=2`,
best, average, and worst time are Theta(N^2) because value order does
not change the comparisons. Empty and singleton inputs take Theta(1).
Its state array uses Theta(N) auxiliary space; the scalar result uses
Theta(1) output space.

The Fenwick method copies and sorts N values, then deduplicates them
in Theta(N). Let S(N) be the library sort work. Every input value
performs one O(log(D+1)) binary search, one Fenwick prefix query, and
one Fenwick update. Total work is:

```text
S(N) + O(N log(D+1))
```

With the current Go comparison sorter described in
[B.3.1 comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice), worst-case
work is O(N log(N+1)). No distribution-independent average is assumed.
When D is one, the tree operations are constant-time, though sorting
and copying still remain.

The sorted copy retains N elements even after its visible length
shrinks to D, and the Fenwick tree uses D+1 counters. Auxiliary space
is O(N+D), hence O(N). Output and call-stack space are O(1). The input
is neither copied into returned storage nor retained after the call.

The maximum accepted input still makes quadratic work impractical;
the length bound defines valid data, not a timing promise for the
baseline. The Fenwick form is designed for that scale. Rejected length
takes Theta(1) function work and allocates no internal state.

Modulo arithmetic keeps every counter fixed-width and constant-space.
It deliberately loses the exact count. `math/big.Int` can preserve an
exact result, but its additions cost more as the count gains bits.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil and empty input return zero because this contract excludes the
  empty subsequence. A combinatorial problem that includes it would
  return one instead.
- A singleton returns one. Starting every ending state at zero loses
  all subsequences because no earlier state can create the first one.
- Equal values cannot extend each other. On `[2,2]`, a Fenwick query
  through the current rank returns three instead of the correct two by
  inventing an equal-valued pair.
- Duplicate positions still count separately. On `[1,1,2]`, update
  the shared rank by addition; assignment loses one of the two
  `[1,2]` selections and returns four instead of five.
- Scan the original input left to right. Processing the sorted copy
  makes `[2,1]` look like `[1,2]` and returns three instead of two.
- Rank zero maps to tree position one. Updating tree position zero
  gives lowbit zero and cannot advance.
- Query prefix end R, not `R+1`, for strict increase. Including the
  current rank changes the contract to allow equal extensions.
- Compression must sort and deduplicate. Encounter-order ranks do not
  preserve numeric order, and separate ranks for equal values make
  equality look increasing.
- Add one singleton for every input position, not once per distinct
  value. Counts classify position selections.
- Add each completed ending state to the total. Returning only the
  last state misses subsequences ending earlier.
- Reduce DP entries, tree cells, and the total modulo M. Reducing only
  the final fixed-width value allows intermediate unsigned wrap.
- The returned residue is not an overflow error and is not the exact
  count. Callers needing exact enumeration must choose another
  representation and accept output-sized work when listing results.
- Do not sort the caller's slice. Compression sorts a private copy so
  position order and ownership remain intact.
- Validate length before allocation. A rejected oversized input must
  not create a large DP array or compression copy.
- Concurrent input writes race with scanning and copying. Stable input
  is required for the duration of either call.

##### When to choose it

Choose ending-index DP when N is small, the transition rule is more
complex than one ordered value, or a simple implementation is needed
as a test oracle. Its state directly exposes the contribution of every
input position.

Choose coordinate compression plus a Fenwick tree when all values are
known before processing, only relative order matters, the recurrence
asks for a prefix sum by value, and N makes quadratic scans too
costly. Use a direct frequency array instead when the original value
domain is already small and dense. Use a balanced ordered structure
when unseen values must arrive online without rebuilding ranks.

Use [longest increasing subsequence](
#b254-longest-increasing-subsequence-tails-array) when only maximum
length matters; its dominance compression intentionally discards
counts. Counting only longest increasing subsequences is a different
problem: each state must carry both best length and number of ways.
Counting only subsequences of one fixed length needs a length
dimension or one Fenwick layer per selected length.

Use [combinatorial counting](
