the more useful implementation pattern on larger sparse networks.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- A network with no source-to-sink path returns zero, not an error.
- A zero-capacity record is stored but never traversed. Testing
  `capacity >= 0` creates false paths with zero bottlenecks.
- Parallel and opposite input edges need independent residual pairs
  and witness locations. Searching for a reverse edge by endpoint can
  update the wrong record.
- Self-loops are rejected by this contract. Same-row pair insertion
  needs different index handling, and a loop cannot improve max flow.
- Source and sink must differ. An empty path has no useful finite flow
  value under this API.
- Edges into the source and out of the sink are valid. Levels prevent
  a level path from returning to the source or leaving the reached
  sink.
- Mark a BFS vertex when enqueueing it. Marking on dequeue repeats
  work and can assign inconsistent levels.
- Reset every level before BFS and every cursor before a new phase.
  Retaining either across phases silently skips changed residual
  paths.
- Require `level[to] == level[from]+1`, not merely a greater level.
  Skipping levels breaks the shortest-path and blocking-flow proofs.
- Keep cursors during one phase. Resetting them after each push
  rescans dead records and loses the intended blocking-flow work
  bound.
- Dead-level pruning is safe only while levels remain fixed. Do not
  carry those -1 markings into the next BFS.
- Compute a path bottleneck before updating records. Partial updates
  followed by a smaller bottleneck can violate conservation.
- Update exact paired indices. Endpoint lookup is ambiguous with
  parallel or opposite edges.
- Do not delete zero-capacity records. A later reverse augmentation
  can make them positive.
- Keep flow totals and capacities as `int64`. Using `int` makes the
  supported range platform-dependent.
- A maximum witness need not be unique. Unless deterministic
  input-order tie-breaking is part of the contract, verify capacity,
  conservation, and value instead of exact edge flows.

##### When to choose it

Choose Dinic for a general directed capacity network when
Edmonds-Karp is too slow and a residual adjacency-list implementation
is acceptable. It is a strong practical baseline for sparse contest
and interview graphs, and its level graph exposes useful structure
for later variants.

Choose Edmonds-Karp when the smallest, easiest-to-audit polynomial
implementation matters more than throughput. Choose
[Hopcroft-Karp](#b282-hopcroft-karp-layers-and-matching-arrays) for
unweighted bipartite matching; its specialized phase analysis is
stronger. Choose [min-cost flow](
#b286-min-cost-flow-residual-graph-and-potentials) when the objective
also includes edge costs.

The [minimum-cut lesson](
#b285-minimum-cut-residual-reachability)
extracts the reachable side of the final residual graph. Dinitz's
original 1970 paper,
[Algorithm for Solution of a Problem of Maximum Flow in a Network with
Power Estimation](https://www.cs.bgu.ac.il/~dinitz/D70.pdf),
introduced the polynomial `O(V^2*E)` approach. Stanford's
[CS261 blocking-flow notes](
https://theory.stanford.edu/~tim/w16/l/l2.pdf) state the blocking flow
progress lemma and derive the same general bound.

#### B.28.5 Minimum cut (residual reachability)

##### Problem and contract

An `s-t` cut divides a directed network's vertices into two sides.
The source must be on the source side, and the sink must be on the
sink side. Its capacity is the sum of capacities on original edges
directed from the source side to the sink side. Edges in the opposite
direction do not add to that capacity.

Every feasible flow is at most every cut capacity. The max-flow
min-cut theorem says the greatest feasible flow value equals the
smallest `s-t` cut capacity. After a maximum-flow algorithm finishes,
one graph search in its final residual graph constructs both a
minimum cut and a checkable optimality certificate.

This lesson receives a complete flow witness rather than repeating a
max-flow solver. `extractMinimumCut` has this contract:

- Vertices are integers in `[0,vertexCount)`. `vertexCount` is from 2
  through 100000. Source and sink are valid distinct vertices.
- At most 200000 directed edges are accepted. Each capacity is an
  `int64` in `[0,10^12]`; each flow is in `[0,capacity]`.
- The supplied flow must conserve flow at every nonterminal vertex.
  The source's net outflow must equal the sink's net inflow.
- Parallel, opposite-direction, zero-capacity, and self-loop edges are
  valid and remain separate. Self-loops affect neither balance nor a
  cut boundary.
- Success returns the flow value, minimum-cut capacity, a Boolean
  source-side membership value for every vertex, and every original
  edge crossing from source side to sink side in input order.
- Crossing edges with zero capacity are included. Parallel crossing
  edges appear separately. Opposite-direction edges are not included.
- A feasible but nonmaximum flow returns an error wrapping
  `errFlowNotMaximum` because the sink is residually reachable.
- Invalid sizes, terminals, endpoints, capacities, flows, or balance
  return an error wrapping `errInvalidCutFlow`.
- A disagreement between the certified flow and cut values returns an
  internal error wrapping `errCutInvariant`.
- The function reads but does not mutate or retain the edge slice.
  Returned slices own their storage. Concurrent input mutation is
  outside the contract.

The limits keep all capacity and balance sums within signed 64-bit
range. Read [residual graphs](
#a107-reverse-adjacency-and-residual-graphs) first. A maximum-flow
witness may come from [Edmonds-Karp](
#b283-edmonds-karp-max-flow-residual-graph-and-queue) or
[Dinic's algorithm](
#b284-dinic-max-flow-residual-graph-and-level-arrays).

##### Mental model

For an original edge `u->v` with capacity c and flow f, residual
movement is:

```text
u->v has c-f residual units for sending more flow
v->u has f residual units for canceling current flow
```

Start BFS at the source and follow every positive residual record.
Store the result as:

```text
sourceSideByVertex[v] = whether residual BFS reaches v
```

Read `sourceSideByVertex[2] == true` as: vertex 2 can still be reached
from the source through changes that preserve feasibility. The source
starts true. If the sink also becomes true, the path to it can carry
more flow, so the witness is not maximum.

If the sink stays false, the Boolean values define a cut. Any original
edge from true to false must be saturated. Otherwise its unused
forward capacity would let BFS cross. Any original edge from false to
true must carry zero flow. Otherwise its reverse residual capacity
would let BFS cross in the opposite direction.

The net flow crossing this boundary is therefore exactly the sum of
capacities on true-to-false edges. That one equality certifies both a
maximum flow and a minimum cut.

##### Worked walkthrough

Name vertices `S=0`, `A=1`, `B=2`, `C=3`, and `T=4`. The last two
columns give a supplied maximum-flow witness:

```text
index   edge   capacity   flow
0       S->A       5        3
1       S->B       2        2
2       A->B       2        1
3       A->C       2        2
4       B->T       1        1
5       B->T       2        2
6       C->T       2        2
7       C->A       4        0
```

The expected certificate is:

```text
flow value = 5
source side = [S,A,B]
sink side = [C,T]
cut edge indices = [3,4,5]
cut capacity = 2+1+2 = 5
```

Initial state: balances are zero, residual rows are empty, no vertex
has been reached, and the BFS queue is empty.

1. Decision: validate edge flows and add their endpoint balances.
   `S` sends 3+2, `T` receives 1+2+2, A sends and receives three,
   B sends and receives three, and C sends and receives two.
   After: flow value is five; terminal balances are -5 and 5, while
   every intermediate balance is zero.
   Known correct: the witness is feasible, but maximality has not yet
   been established.
2. Decision: build residual records. For `S->A`, add forward capacity
   `5-3=2` and reverse capacity 3. Saturated `S->B` adds only reverse
   capacity 2. Apply the same rule to every remaining edge.
   After: useful forward records include `S->A` with 2 and `A->B`
   with 1. Two records lead `C->A`: cancellation capacity 2 for
   `A->C` and unused capacity 4 for `C->A`.
   Known correct: every permitted one-edge change is represented;
   zero-capacity records need not be stored.
3. Decision: mark S and enqueue it. Process S. Residual `S->A` has
   capacity two, so mark A and enqueue it. `S->B` has no forward room.
   After: the queue is `[S,A]`; reached vertices are `{S,A}`.
   Known correct: A has a positive residual path from S, while B is
   not yet known reachable.
4. Decision: process A. Reverse record `A->S` returns to a marked
   vertex. Forward record `A->B` has capacity one, so mark B. The
   saturated edge `A->C` has no forward residual record.
   After: the queue is `[S,A,B]`; reached vertices are `{S,A,B}`.
   Known correct: every discovered vertex has an explicit positive
   residual path from S.
5. Decision: process B. Its records to S and A are reverse records
   ending at marked vertices. Both original `B->T` edges are
   saturated, so neither has positive forward capacity.
   After: BFS exhausts with source side `{S,A,B}`. C and T remain on
   the sink side.
   Known correct: T is unreachable, so the supplied flow admits no
   augmenting path.
6. Decision: scan original edges in input order. Edge 3 crosses
   `A->C`; edges 4 and 5 cross `B->T`. Edge 7 points from the sink
   side back to the source side, so it is not counted.
   After: cut indices are `[3,4,5]` and capacity is `2+1+2=5`.
   Known correct: every counted edge is saturated, and every edge in
   the opposite cut direction carries zero flow.
7. Decision: compare cut capacity five with flow value five.
   After: return the Boolean source side and the three edge indices.
   Known correct: no flow can exceed this cut, and the feasible
   witness reaches its capacity, so both are optimal.

Focused no-path case: two vertices with no edges and zero flow return
source side `[0]`, sink side `[1]`, no cut edges, and capacity zero.

Focused zero-capacity case: edge `0->1` with capacity and flow zero is
a crossing edge. It is returned at index zero, but the cut capacity
remains zero.

Focused self-loop case: `0->0` with capacity 10 and flow 7 contributes
equal incoming and outgoing balance at vertex 0. It never crosses the
cut and does not change the answer.

Focused nonmaximum case: edge `0->1` with capacity 3 and flow 2 has
one forward residual unit. BFS reaches the sink, so the function
returns `errFlowNotMaximum` instead of mislabeling a cut as minimum.

Focused invalid case: flow one on `0->1` in a three-vertex network
with sink 2 leaves vertex 1 unbalanced. Validation rejects it before
residual storage is built.

Counterexample to collecting every saturated edge: in the main
example, `S->B` and `C->T` are saturated but do not cross the returned
partition. Saturation alone does not define a cut. The first correct
decision is residual reachability; only then can endpoint sides select
the boundary.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program extracts the main certificate and exercises
the no-path, nonmaximum, and invalid-flow branches. It uses only the
standard library. Only the supplied writer has an external side
effect. Save it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Minimum cut (residual
// reachability). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

const (
	maximumCutVertexCount = 100_000
	maximumCutEdgeCount   = 200_000
	maximumCutCapacity    = int64(1_000_000_000_000)
)

var errInvalidCutFlow = errors.New("invalid cut flow")

var errFlowNotMaximum = errors.New("flow is not maximum")

var errCutInvariant = errors.New("minimum-cut invariant violated")

type cutFlowEdge struct {
	from     int
	to       int
	capacity int64
	flow     int64
}

type cutResidualEdge struct {
	to       int
	capacity int64
}

type minimumCutResult struct {
	flowValue          int64
	capacity           int64
	sourceSideByVertex []bool
	cutEdgeIndices     []int
}

func validateCutFlow(
	vertexCount int,
	edges []cutFlowEdge,
	source int,
	sink int,
) (int64, error) {
	// Reject input outside the cut flow contract before mutation.
	if vertexCount < 2 || vertexCount > maximumCutVertexCount {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: vertex count %d; want 2..%d",
			errInvalidCutFlow,
			vertexCount,
			maximumCutVertexCount,
		)
	}
	if source < 0 || source >= vertexCount {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: source %d is outside [0,%d)",
			errInvalidCutFlow,
			source,
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	if sink < 0 || sink >= vertexCount {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: sink %d is outside [0,%d)",
			errInvalidCutFlow,
			sink,
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	if source == sink {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: source and sink are both %d",
			errInvalidCutFlow,
			source,
		)
	}
	if len(edges) > maximumCutEdgeCount {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: edge count %d exceeds %d",
			errInvalidCutFlow,
			len(edges),
			maximumCutEdgeCount,
		)
	}

	balanceByVertex := make([]int64, vertexCount)
	for edgeIndex, edge := range edges {
		if edge.from < 0 || edge.from >= vertexCount {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d source %d is invalid",
				errInvalidCutFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.from,
			)
		}
		if edge.to < 0 || edge.to >= vertexCount {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d destination %d is invalid",
				errInvalidCutFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.to,
			)
		}
		if edge.capacity < 0 ||
			edge.capacity > maximumCutCapacity {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d capacity %d is outside 0..%d",
				errInvalidCutFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.capacity,
				maximumCutCapacity,
			)
		}
		if edge.flow < 0 || edge.flow > edge.capacity {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d flow %d is outside 0..%d",
				errInvalidCutFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.flow,
				edge.capacity,
			)
		}
		balanceByVertex[edge.from] -= edge.flow
		balanceByVertex[edge.to] += edge.flow
	}

	flowValue := -balanceByVertex[source]
	if flowValue < 0 {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: source has net inflow %d",
			errInvalidCutFlow,
			-flowValue,
		)
	}
	for vertex, balance := range balanceByVertex {
		wantBalance := int64(0)
		if vertex == source {
			wantBalance = -flowValue
		}
		if vertex == sink {
			wantBalance = flowValue
		}
		if balance != wantBalance {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: vertex %d balance %d; want %d",
				errInvalidCutFlow,
				vertex,
				balance,
				wantBalance,
			)
		}
	}
	return flowValue, nil
}

func buildCutResidualGraph(
	vertexCount int,
	edges []cutFlowEdge,
) [][]cutResidualEdge {
	// Build cut residual graph in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	residual := make([][]cutResidualEdge, vertexCount)
	for _, edge := range edges {
		forwardCapacity := edge.capacity - edge.flow
		if forwardCapacity > 0 {
			residual[edge.from] = append(
				residual[edge.from],
				cutResidualEdge{
					to:       edge.to,
					capacity: forwardCapacity,
				},
			)
		}
		if edge.flow > 0 {
			residual[edge.to] = append(
				residual[edge.to],
				cutResidualEdge{
					to:       edge.from,
					capacity: edge.flow,
				},
			)
		}
	}
	return residual
}

func findCutSourceSide(
	residual [][]cutResidualEdge,
	source int,
) []bool {
	// Follow the lookup rule for cut source side without changing state.
	sourceSideByVertex := make([]bool, len(residual))
	searchQueue := make([]int, 0, len(residual))
	sourceSideByVertex[source] = true
	searchQueue = append(searchQueue, source)

	// Residual reachability defines the canonical source side.
	for nextIndex := 0; nextIndex < len(searchQueue); nextIndex++ {
		from := searchQueue[nextIndex]
		for _, edge := range residual[from] {
			if edge.capacity == 0 || sourceSideByVertex[edge.to] {
				continue
			}
			sourceSideByVertex[edge.to] = true
			searchQueue = append(searchQueue, edge.to)
		}
	}
	return sourceSideByVertex
}

func extractMinimumCut(
	vertexCount int,
	edges []cutFlowEdge,
	source int,
	sink int,
) (minimumCutResult, error) {
	// Keep extract minimum cut in one helper so callers use one rule.
	flowValue, err := validateCutFlow(
		vertexCount,
		edges,
		source,
		sink,
	)
	if err != nil {
		return minimumCutResult{}, err
	}

	residual := buildCutResidualGraph(vertexCount, edges)
	sourceSideByVertex := findCutSourceSide(residual, source)
	if sourceSideByVertex[sink] {
		return minimumCutResult{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: sink %d remains residually reachable",
			errFlowNotMaximum,
			sink,
		)
	}

	// Every original edge leaving the reachable side crosses the cut.
	cutEdgeIndices := make([]int, 0)
	cutCapacity := int64(0)
	for edgeIndex, edge := range edges {
		if sourceSideByVertex[edge.from] &&
			!sourceSideByVertex[edge.to] {
			cutEdgeIndices = append(cutEdgeIndices, edgeIndex)
			cutCapacity += edge.capacity
		}
	}
	if cutCapacity != flowValue {
		return minimumCutResult{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: cut capacity %d differs from flow value %d",
			errCutInvariant,
			cutCapacity,
			flowValue,
		)
	}

	return minimumCutResult{
		flowValue:          flowValue,
		capacity:           cutCapacity,
		sourceSideByVertex: sourceSideByVertex,
		cutEdgeIndices:     cutEdgeIndices,
	}, nil
}

func verticesOnCutSide(
	sourceSideByVertex []bool,
	wantSourceSide bool,
) []int {
	// Keep vertices on cut side in one helper so callers use one rule.
	vertices := make([]int, 0)
	for vertex, isSourceSide := range sourceSideByVertex {
		if isSourceSide == wantSourceSide {
			vertices = append(vertices, vertex)
		}
	}
	return vertices
}

func runMinimumCutExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute minimum cut examples to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	edges := []cutFlowEdge{
		{from: 0, to: 1, capacity: 5, flow: 3},
		{from: 0, to: 2, capacity: 2, flow: 2},
		{from: 1, to: 2, capacity: 2, flow: 1},
		{from: 1, to: 3, capacity: 2, flow: 2},
		{from: 2, to: 4, capacity: 1, flow: 1},
		{from: 2, to: 4, capacity: 2, flow: 2},
		{from: 3, to: 4, capacity: 2, flow: 2},
		{from: 3, to: 1, capacity: 4, flow: 0},
	}
	result, err := extractMinimumCut(5, edges, 0, 4)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("extract ordinary minimum cut: %w", err)
	}

	noPath, err := extractMinimumCut(2, nil, 0, 1)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("extract zero-capacity cut: %w", err)
	}
	_, nonMaximumErr := extractMinimumCut(
		2,
		[]cutFlowEdge{{from: 0, to: 1, capacity: 3, flow: 2}},
		0,
		1,
	)
	_, invalidErr := extractMinimumCut(
		3,
		[]cutFlowEdge{{from: 0, to: 1, capacity: 1, flow: 1}},
		0,
		2,
	)

	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"flow value = %d\nsource side = %v\nsink side = %v\n"+
			"cut edges = %v\ncut capacity = %d\n"+
			"no path = %d %v %v\n"+
			"nonmaximum rejected=%t\ninvalid rejected=%t\n",
		result.flowValue,
		verticesOnCutSide(result.sourceSideByVertex, true),
		verticesOnCutSide(result.sourceSideByVertex, false),
		result.cutEdgeIndices,
		result.capacity,
		noPath.capacity,
		verticesOnCutSide(noPath.sourceSideByVertex, true),
		verticesOnCutSide(noPath.sourceSideByVertex, false),
		errors.Is(nonMaximumErr, errFlowNotMaximum),
		errors.Is(invalidErr, errInvalidCutFlow),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write minimum-cut results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runMinimumCutExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
flow value = 5
source side = [0 1 2]
sink side = [3 4]
cut edges = [3 4 5]
cut capacity = 5
no path = 0 [0] [1]
nonmaximum rejected=true
invalid rejected=true
```

The Boolean membership slice supports constant-time side queries.
`verticesOnCutSide` exists only to print the walkthrough's vertex
lists; the extractor need not allocate both lists.

##### Why it works

Validation first establishes a feasible flow. Each edge stays within
capacity, every intermediate balance is zero, and source net outflow
equals sink net inflow. Call that shared value F.

The residual builder adds exactly `capacity-flow` units forward and
`flow` units backward for each edge. BFS therefore marks precisely the
vertices reachable by a sequence of positive feasible flow changes.
It terminates because each of V vertices is enqueued at most once.

If BFS reaches the sink, its parent-free reachability still proves an
augmenting path exists. Sending the smallest residual capacity on that
path would increase F, so the current flow cannot be maximum. The
function rejects it.

Otherwise let S contain reached vertices and T contain all others.
The source is in S and the sink is in T, so this is an `s-t` cut. For
every original edge from S to T, forward residual capacity is zero;
the edge is saturated. For every edge from T to S, reverse residual
capacity is zero; that edge carries zero flow.

Summing flow conservation over vertices in S cancels every edge whose
two endpoints are both in S. What remains is net flow across the cut:

```text
F = flow(S->T) - flow(T->S)
  = capacity(S->T) - 0
```

For any feasible flow and any `s-t` cut, the flow value cannot exceed
the cut capacity. Here equality holds. The supplied flow is therefore
maximum, the returned cut is minimum, and both have value F. The final
equality check exposes an implementation defect rather than returning
an inconsistent certificate.

Self-loops cancel within one vertex's balance and have both endpoints
on the same side. Parallel edges contribute separately to the sum.
The validated count and capacity bounds prevent `int64` overflow.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count and E be input-edge count. Validation scans V
balances and E edges. The residual graph holds at most 2E records.
BFS scans each reached row once, and the final cut scan examines all E
input edges. Every valid or nonmaximum call takes Theta(V+E) time.
An invalid call may stop earlier at its first failed check.

The returned Boolean side membership uses Theta(V) output storage.
At worst, the returned edge-index slice uses Theta(E) output storage.
Balances, residual records, and the BFS queue use O(V+E) auxiliary
storage. Reusing a max-flow solver's final residual graph can avoid
rebuilding its O(V+E) records.

The Boolean partition is compact and answers membership in constant
time. Returning input indices preserves parallel-edge identity and
lets callers recover any edge metadata. It also ties the certificate
to the original slice order; callers that reorder edges must update
the indices with them.

No average-case improvement is assumed. Even when the source reaches
few vertices, this defensive API validates every edge and later scans
every edge to construct the complete boundary.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- With no source-to-sink path, zero flow is maximum and the cut may
  have capacity zero. Do not treat an empty boundary as failure.
- A zero-capacity edge can cross the partition and is returned even
  though it contributes zero. Filtering it changes the promised edge
  set, though not the numeric capacity.
- A self-loop never crosses a partition. Its flow subtracts and adds
  at the same vertex, so it cannot change flow value or cut capacity.
- Parallel crossing edges all count. Deduplicating by endpoints loses
  both capacity and input-edge identity.
- Opposite-direction edges count only when directed from S to T.
  Adding capacities in both directions overstates a directed cut.
- Extract only after the final maximum-flow state. If the sink remains
  residually reachable, the partition is not an `s-t` cut and the
  current flow is not optimal.
- Traverse reverse residual capacity as well as unused forward
  capacity. Omitting cancellation paths can falsely declare a
  nonmaximum flow optimal.
- Traverse only strictly positive capacity. Treating zero as usable
  can mark the sink reachable without any possible augmentation.
- Validate conservation, not only `0 <= flow <= capacity`.
  Individually legal edge values may create or destroy flow at an
  intermediate vertex.
- Build residual records from the same witness being certified. Mixing
  an old residual graph with new edge flows invalidates the partition.
- Saturation is necessary for S-to-T cut edges but is not sufficient
  for membership. Determine vertex sides before collecting edges.
- Source and sink must differ. Otherwise no two-sided `s-t` partition
  satisfies the contract.
- Use `int64` for capacities, balances, and totals. Converting a sum
  to `int` makes the supported range platform-dependent.
- Minimum cuts need not be unique. This API returns the cut defined by
  residual reachability for the supplied maximum-flow witness.

##### When to choose it

Extract a minimum cut when a maximum-flow value alone is not enough:
you need a bottleneck boundary, an optimality certificate, or the
vertices still reachable from the source after all augmenting paths
are exhausted. Examples include identifying saturated transport links,
separating image regions, and reducing other selection problems to a
source-sink boundary.

Skip extraction when only the maximum-flow value matters. If the flow
solver already retains its final residual graph, search that graph
directly instead of rebuilding it from an edge witness. Use the next
[min-cost flow lesson](
#b286-min-cost-flow-residual-graph-and-potentials) when cost, not only
capacity, is part of the objective. A global minimum cut without fixed
source and sink is a different problem.

Ford and Fulkerson's original paper,
[Maximal Flow Through a Network](
https://doi.org/10.4153/CJM-1956-045-5), proves that maximum flow
value equals minimum cut capacity. Stanford's [CS261 flow notes](
https://theory.stanford.edu/~tim/w16/l/l2.pdf) give the residual
reachability proof used here.

#### B.28.6 Min-cost flow (residual graph and potentials)

##### Problem and contract

Find the greatest feasible flow from one source to one sink. Among all
flows with that greatest value, minimize the sum of `flow * cost` over
the input edges. This is **minimum-cost maximum flow**. It has two
objectives in order: maximize value first, then minimize cost.

An ordinary maximum-flow solver may choose an expensive route when a
cheap route has the same capacity. Repeatedly choosing the cheapest
unused original route is also insufficient. A later route may need a
reverse residual edge to cancel an earlier choice and reroute that
unit. The residual graph must therefore retain both capacity and cost.

This implementation uses **successive shortest augmenting paths**.
Negative input costs are allowed. One Bellman-Ford-style
initialization creates vertex potentials; later searches use Dijkstra
on nonnegative **reduced costs**.

Its input contract is deliberately bounded:

- `vertexCount` is in `2..2000`; vertices are integer IDs in
  `[0, vertexCount)`.
- `source` and `sink` are valid, distinct vertices.
- There are at most 10,000 directed edges.
- Every capacity is an `int64` in `0..1_000_000`.
- Every cost is an `int64` in `-1_000_000..1_000_000`.
- Parallel and opposite-direction edges are valid and stay distinct.
- Zero-capacity edges are valid but cannot carry flow.
- Self-loops are rejected. They cannot improve source-to-sink value,
  and paired same-row residual indices need special handling.
- The positive-capacity input graph has no negative-cost cycle,
  including one disconnected from the source.

That last restriction makes zero flow minimum-cost for value zero.
When it is false, a negative circulation could reduce cost without
changing source-to-sink flow. This implementation returns
`errNegativeCostCycle` rather than adding a cycle-canceling phase.

The result owns four values:

- `flowValue` is the maximum source-to-sink flow;
- `totalCost` is the minimum cost among flows of that value;
- `augmentations` counts shortest-path pushes; and
- `flowByInputEdge[i]` is the flow on input edge `i`.

The edge slice is read but neither mutated nor retained. The result
preserves parallel-edge identity through input order. Equal reduced
distances keep the first discovered parent. Heap ties use vertex ID,
and adjacency rows retain input order, so repeated runs are
deterministic.

The stated bounds make all arithmetic fit `int64`. Total flow is at
most `10_000 * 1_000_000 = 10^10`, and absolute total cost is at most
`10_000 * 1_000_000 * 1_000_000 = 10^16`.

Read [residual graphs](
#a107-reverse-adjacency-and-residual-graphs),
[Dijkstra](#b133-dijkstra-heap-or-scan-distance-array),
[Bellman-Ford](#b134-bellman-ford-edge-list-and-distance-array), and
[minimum cut](#b285-minimum-cut-residual-reachability) first.

##### Mental model

For an input edge `u->v` with capacity c, cost w, and current flow f,
store two linked residual records:

```text
u->v: capacity c-f, cost  w   send more flow
v->u: capacity f,   cost -w   cancel existing flow
```

Canceling one unit removes the cost previously paid, so the reverse
cost must be the negation of the forward cost. Each record stores the
index of its partner. Updating an augmenting path then subtracts from
the chosen record and adds to that exact partner. Endpoint lookup
alone would confuse parallel and opposite-direction edges.

A potential `p[v]` changes an edge's search weight to:

```text
reducedCost(u,v) = cost(u,v) + p[u] - p[v]
```

For any path from s to t, intermediate potentials cancel:

```text
reducedPathCost = originalPathCost + p[s] - p[t]
```

Every s-to-t path receives the same offset, so an original-cost
shortest path is also a reduced-cost shortest path. If every usable
reduced edge is nonnegative, Dijkstra becomes valid even when original
and reverse costs are negative.

Initialize every potential to zero, as if a super-source had a
zero-cost edge to every vertex. Relax every positive-capacity edge
for up to V passes. A change on pass V proves that some negative-cost
cycle exists. Otherwise the shortest labels satisfy:

```text
p[v] <= p[u] + cost(u,v)
```

Rearranging gives nonnegative reduced cost. This all-vertex
initialization detects a disconnected negative cycle instead of
silently ignoring it.

For each augmentation:

1. Run Dijkstra from the source using reduced costs.
2. Stop if the sink is unreachable; the current flow is maximum.
3. Add each finite Dijkstra distance to that vertex's potential.
4. Trace exact parent records to find the bottleneck and original
   path cost.
5. Push the bottleneck through every residual pair.

Only reached potentials are updated. The source-reachable residual
set cannot gain a formerly unreachable vertex after this push. The
only new positive records are reversals of path edges, and both of
their endpoints were already reached. The set may shrink when an edge
is saturated, so stale potentials outside it are never scanned later.

##### Worked walkthrough

Name vertices `S=0`, `A=1`, `B=2`, `X=3`, `Y=4`, and `T=5`:

```text
index   edge   capacity   cost
0       S->A       1        0
1       S->B       1        0
2       A->X       1       -2
3       A->Y       1        2
4       B->X       1        1
5       X->T       1        0
6       Y->T       1        0
```

The final answer is:

```text
flow value = 2
total cost = 3
flow by input edge = [1 1 0 1 1 1 1]
```

Initial state: every flow is zero. Forward residual capacities are
one, reverse capacities are zero, and all potentials start at zero.

1. Decision: run the all-vertex relaxation. `A->X` lowers X to -2,
   and `X->T` lowers T to -2. No later pass changes a label.
   After: potentials are `[0,0,0,-2,0,-2]`. Forward reduced costs in
   input order are `[0,0,0,2,3,0,2]`.
   Known correct: every usable reduced cost is nonnegative, so the
   first Dijkstra search is valid.
2. Decision: run Dijkstra. The zero-reduced-cost path is
   `S->A->X->T`; its original cost is -2 and bottleneck is one.
   After: Dijkstra distances are `[0,0,0,0,2,0]`; updated potentials
   are `[0,0,0,-2,2,-2]`. One unit is pushed, so edges 0, 2, and 5
   carry flow.
   Known correct: the flow has value one and cost -2. The new reverse
   records `T->X`, `X->A`, and `A->S` have reduced cost zero.
3. Decision: run Dijkstra again. The only augmenting path is
   `S->B->X->A->Y->T`. Its `X->A` step is the reverse of input edge 2.
   Reduced edge costs along it are `0,3,0,0,4`, totaling seven.
   After: the original path cost is
   `0+1+2+2+0 = 5`; pushing one cancels `A->X` and adds `A->Y`.
   Total flow becomes two and total cost becomes `-2+5 = 3`.
   Known correct: the witness is `[1,1,0,1,1,1,1]`; both source
   edges and both sink edges carry one unit.
4. Decision: search once more. Both residual edges leaving S have
   zero capacity, so T is unreachable.
   After: the loop stops after two augmentations.
   Known correct: no residual source-to-sink path exists, so no
   feasible flow has value greater than two.

Focused no-path case: two vertices and no edges return zero flow, zero
cost, zero augmentations, and an empty witness.

Focused parallel-edge case: two `0->1` edges with capacities two and
one and costs -1 and 2 return flow three, cost zero, and witness
`[2,1]`. Neither record is merged.

Focused zero-capacity case: a negative-cost edge with zero capacity is
ignored by relaxation and cannot create a usable path or cycle.

Focused negative-edge case: `0->1` with cost -4 and `1->2` with cost
one is accepted. Initial potentials make both reduced costs
nonnegative, and the one-unit path costs -3.

Focused negative-cycle case: a disconnected pair `2->3` with cost -2
and `3->2` with cost one is rejected. Although source 0 cannot reach
it, accepting it would contradict the contract that zero flow is
already minimum-cost for its value.

Counterexample to discarding reverse records: after the first push in
the main example, the second optimum must traverse `X->A` to cancel
`A->X`. Searching only original unused capacity cannot perform that
reroute and cannot produce the minimum cost three.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program solves the main network and exercises the
no-path and negative-cycle branches. It uses only the standard
library. Only the supplied writer has an external side effect. Save it
as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Min-cost flow (residual graph and
// potentials). Function comments connect each operation to its
// invariant.
package main

import (
	"container/heap"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

const (
	maximumCostFlowVertexCount = 2_000
	maximumCostFlowEdgeCount   = 10_000
	maximumCostFlowCapacity    = int64(1_000_000)
	maximumCostFlowEdgeCost    = int64(1_000_000)
)

var errInvalidCostFlow = errors.New("invalid min-cost flow input")

var errNegativeCostCycle = errors.New("negative-cost cycle")

var errCostFlowInvariant = errors.New(
	"min-cost flow invariant failed",
)

type costFlowEdge struct {
	from     int
	to       int
	capacity int64
	cost     int64
}

type costResidualEdge struct {
	to       int
	reverse  int
	capacity int64
	cost     int64
}

type costFlowLocation struct {
	from      int
	edgeIndex int
}

type minCostFlowResult struct {
	flowValue       int64
	totalCost       int64
	augmentations   int
	flowByInputEdge []int64
}

type costQueueItem struct {
	vertex   int
	distance int64
}

type costPriorityQueue []costQueueItem

func (queue costPriorityQueue) Len() int {
	// Report the item count required by container/heap.
	return len(queue)
}

func (queue costPriorityQueue) Less(left int, right int) bool {
	// Define heap priority, including the tie rule.
	if queue[left].distance != queue[right].distance {
		return queue[left].distance < queue[right].distance
	}
	return queue[left].vertex < queue[right].vertex
}

func (queue costPriorityQueue) Swap(left int, right int) {
	// Exchange two heap positions without losing either item.
	queue[left], queue[right] = queue[right], queue[left]
}

func (queue *costPriorityQueue) Push(value any) {
	// Append the typed item supplied by this heap owner.
	*queue = append(*queue, value.(costQueueItem))
}

func (queue *costPriorityQueue) Pop() any {
	// Remove the item already moved to the slice end.
	old := *queue
	lastIndex := len(old) - 1
	item := old[lastIndex]
	*queue = old[:lastIndex]
	return item
}

func validateCostFlowInput(
	vertexCount int,
	edges []costFlowEdge,
	source int,
	sink int,
) error {
	// Reject input outside the cost flow input contract before mutation.
	// Validate graph-wide sizes before checking individual endpoints.
	if vertexCount < 2 ||
		vertexCount > maximumCostFlowVertexCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: vertex count %d is outside 2..%d",
			errInvalidCostFlow,
			vertexCount,
			maximumCostFlowVertexCount,
		)
	}
	// Source and sink must be distinct members of the vertex range.
	if source < 0 || source >= vertexCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: source %d is outside [0,%d)",
			errInvalidCostFlow,
			source,
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	if sink < 0 || sink >= vertexCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: sink %d is outside [0,%d)",
			errInvalidCostFlow,
			sink,
			vertexCount,
		)
	}
	if source == sink {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: source and sink are both %d",
			errInvalidCostFlow,
			source,
		)
	}
	// Bound total edge work before inspecting each edge.
	if len(edges) > maximumCostFlowEdgeCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: edge count %d exceeds %d",
			errInvalidCostFlow,
			len(edges),
			maximumCostFlowEdgeCount,
		)
	}
	// Each edge needs distinct endpoints and bounded numeric fields.
	for edgeIndex, edge := range edges {
		if edge.from < 0 || edge.from >= vertexCount ||
			edge.to < 0 || edge.to >= vertexCount {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d has endpoint %d -> %d",
				errInvalidCostFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.from,
				edge.to,
			)
		}
		if edge.from == edge.to {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d is a self-loop at %d",
				errInvalidCostFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.from,
			)
		}
		if edge.capacity < 0 ||
			edge.capacity > maximumCostFlowCapacity {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d capacity %d is outside 0..%d",
				errInvalidCostFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.capacity,
				maximumCostFlowCapacity,
			)
		}
		if edge.cost < -maximumCostFlowEdgeCost ||
			edge.cost > maximumCostFlowEdgeCost {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: edge %d cost %d is outside %d..%d",
				errInvalidCostFlow,
				edgeIndex,
				edge.cost,
				-maximumCostFlowEdgeCost,
				maximumCostFlowEdgeCost,
			)
		}
	}
	return nil
}

func addCostResidualEdge(
	residual [][]costResidualEdge,
	edge costFlowEdge,
) ([][]costResidualEdge, costFlowLocation) {
	// Add cost residual edge while preserving the representation
	// invariant.
	forwardIndex := len(residual[edge.from])
	reverseIndex := len(residual[edge.to])
	residual[edge.from] = append(
		residual[edge.from],
		costResidualEdge{
			to:       edge.to,
			reverse:  reverseIndex,
			capacity: edge.capacity,
			cost:     edge.cost,
		},
	)
	residual[edge.to] = append(
		residual[edge.to],
		costResidualEdge{
			to:      edge.from,
			reverse: forwardIndex,
			cost:    -edge.cost,
		},
	)
	return residual, costFlowLocation{
		from:      edge.from,
		edgeIndex: forwardIndex,
	}
}

func buildCostResidualGraph(
	vertexCount int,
	edges []costFlowEdge,
) ([][]costResidualEdge, []costFlowLocation) {
	// Build cost residual graph in the order required by the lesson
	// contract.
	residual := make([][]costResidualEdge, vertexCount)
	locations := make([]costFlowLocation, len(edges))
	for edgeIndex, edge := range edges {
		var location costFlowLocation
		residual, location = addCostResidualEdge(residual, edge)
		locations[edgeIndex] = location
	}
	return residual, locations
}

func initialCostPotentials(
	residual [][]costResidualEdge,
) ([]int64, error) {
	// Keep initial cost potentials in one helper so callers use one
	// rule.
	potential := make([]int64, len(residual))
	for pass := 0; pass < len(residual); pass++ {
		changed := false
		for from, row := range residual {
			for _, edge := range row {
				if edge.capacity == 0 {
					continue
				}
				candidate := potential[from] + edge.cost
				if candidate >= potential[edge.to] {
					continue
				}
				potential[edge.to] = candidate
				changed = true
			}
		}
		if !changed {
			return potential, nil
		}
		if pass == len(residual)-1 {
			return nil, errNegativeCostCycle
		}
	}
	return potential, nil
}

func shortestReducedCostPath(
	residual [][]costResidualEdge,
	potential []int64,
	source int,
) ([]int64, []int, []int, error) {
	// Compute the requested ordered or extreme result.
	vertexCount := len(residual)
	distance := make([]int64, vertexCount)
	reached := make([]bool, vertexCount)
	parentVertex := make([]int, vertexCount)
	parentEdge := make([]int, vertexCount)
	for vertex := range parentVertex {
		parentVertex[vertex] = -1
		parentEdge[vertex] = -1
	}
	reached[source] = true
	queue := costPriorityQueue{{vertex: source}}
	heap.Init(&queue)

	for queue.Len() > 0 {
		item := heap.Pop(&queue).(costQueueItem)
		if item.distance != distance[item.vertex] {
			continue
		}
		for edgeIndex, edge := range residual[item.vertex] {
			if edge.capacity == 0 {
				continue
			}
			reducedCost := edge.cost +
				potential[item.vertex] - potential[edge.to]
			if reducedCost < 0 {
				return nil, nil, nil, fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: reduced edge %d -> %d has cost %d",
					errCostFlowInvariant,
					item.vertex,
					edge.to,
					reducedCost,
				)
			}
			candidate := item.distance + reducedCost
			if reached[edge.to] && candidate >= distance[edge.to] {
				continue
			}
			reached[edge.to] = true
			distance[edge.to] = candidate
			parentVertex[edge.to] = item.vertex
			parentEdge[edge.to] = edgeIndex
			heap.Push(&queue, costQueueItem{
				vertex:   edge.to,
				distance: candidate,
			})
		}
	}

	for vertex, wasReached := range reached {
		if wasReached {
			potential[vertex] += distance[vertex]
		}
	}
	return distance, parentVertex, parentEdge, nil
}

func augmentCheapestPath(
	residual [][]costResidualEdge,
	parentVertex []int,
	parentEdge []int,
	source int,
	sink int,
) (int64, int64) {
	// Keep augment cheapest path in one helper so callers use one rule.
	bottleneck := maximumCostFlowCapacity
	pathCost := int64(0)
	for vertex := sink; vertex != source; {
		from := parentVertex[vertex]
		edgeIndex := parentEdge[vertex]
		edge := residual[from][edgeIndex]
		if edge.capacity < bottleneck {
			bottleneck = edge.capacity
		}
		pathCost += edge.cost
		vertex = from
	}
	for vertex := sink; vertex != source; {
		from := parentVertex[vertex]
		edgeIndex := parentEdge[vertex]
		reverseIndex := residual[from][edgeIndex].reverse
		residual[from][edgeIndex].capacity -= bottleneck
		residual[vertex][reverseIndex].capacity += bottleneck
		vertex = from
	}
	return bottleneck, pathCost
}

func minimumCostMaximumFlow(
	vertexCount int,
	edges []costFlowEdge,
	source int,
	sink int,
) (minCostFlowResult, error) {
	// Compute cost maximum flow from the state without mutating it.
	if err := validateCostFlowInput(
		vertexCount,
		edges,
		source,
		sink,
	); err != nil {
		return minCostFlowResult{}, err
	}
	residual, locations := buildCostResidualGraph(vertexCount, edges)
	potential, err := initialCostPotentials(residual)
	if err != nil {
		return minCostFlowResult{}, fmt.Errorf(
			"initialize potentials: %w",
			err,
		)
	}

	result := minCostFlowResult{}
	for {
		_, parentVertex, parentEdge, err :=
			shortestReducedCostPath(residual, potential, source)
		if err != nil {
			return minCostFlowResult{}, err
		}
		if parentVertex[sink] == -1 {
			break
		}
		addedFlow, pathCost := augmentCheapestPath(
			residual,
			parentVertex,
			parentEdge,
			source,
			sink,
		)
		result.flowValue += addedFlow
		result.totalCost += addedFlow * pathCost
		result.augmentations++
	}

	result.flowByInputEdge = make([]int64, len(edges))
	for edgeIndex, location := range locations {
		row := residual[location.from]
		remaining := row[location.edgeIndex].capacity
		result.flowByInputEdge[edgeIndex] =
			edges[edgeIndex].capacity - remaining
	}
	return result, nil
}

func runMinCostFlowExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute min cost flow examples to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	edges := []costFlowEdge{
		{from: 0, to: 1, capacity: 1, cost: 0},
		{from: 0, to: 2, capacity: 1, cost: 0},
		{from: 1, to: 3, capacity: 1, cost: -2},
		{from: 1, to: 4, capacity: 1, cost: 2},
		{from: 2, to: 3, capacity: 1, cost: 1},
		{from: 3, to: 5, capacity: 1, cost: 0},
		{from: 4, to: 5, capacity: 1, cost: 0},
	}
	result, err := minimumCostMaximumFlow(6, edges, 0, 5)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("solve ordinary network: %w", err)
	}

	noPath, err := minimumCostMaximumFlow(2, nil, 0, 1)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("solve no-path network: %w", err)
	}
	_, cycleErr := minimumCostMaximumFlow(
		4,
		[]costFlowEdge{
			{from: 0, to: 1, capacity: 1, cost: 2},
			{from: 2, to: 3, capacity: 1, cost: -2},
			{from: 3, to: 2, capacity: 1, cost: 1},
		},
		0,
		1,
	)

	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"flow value = %d\ntotal cost = %d\n"+
			"augmentations = %d\nflow = %v\n"+
			"no path = %d %d\nnegative cycle rejected=%t\n",
		result.flowValue,
		result.totalCost,
		result.augmentations,
		result.flowByInputEdge,
		noPath.flowValue,
		noPath.totalCost,
		errors.Is(cycleErr, errNegativeCostCycle),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write min-cost flow results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runMinCostFlowExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
flow value = 2
total cost = 3
augmentations = 2
flow = [1 1 0 1 1 1 1]
no path = 0 0
negative cycle rejected=true
```

##### Why it works

The initial relaxation is Bellman-Ford from an implicit zero-cost
super-source. If pass V changes a label, a negative-cost cycle exists.
Otherwise every positive-capacity edge satisfies
`p[v] <= p[u]+cost(u,v)`, so its reduced cost is nonnegative.

Assume all residual records reachable from the source have
nonnegative reduced cost at the start of an iteration. Dijkstra then
returns correct reduced distances. The potential update changes an old
residual edge's reduced cost to:

```text
old reduced cost + distance[u] - distance[v]
```

Dijkstra's triangle inequality makes that value nonnegative for every
edge scanned from a reached vertex. Every chosen parent edge is tight,
so its updated reduced cost is zero. Augmentation may create the
reverse of such an edge; negating zero still gives zero. Those are the
only newly usable residual records.

A newly usable reverse record connects two vertices on the chosen
path, which were already source-reachable. Thus augmentation cannot
expand the reachable set. Updating only finite-distance potentials is
safe: any record a later Dijkstra search scans still satisfies the
nonnegative reduced-cost invariant.

Reduced path cost differs from original path cost by the fixed offset
`p[source]-p[sink]`. Therefore each selected residual path is also an
original-cost shortest augmenting path.

The current flow is minimum-cost for its value exactly when its whole
residual graph has no negative-cost cycle. The initial graph has none
by validation. Suppose augmentation along a shortest path created one.
Every new residual record is the reverse of a chosen path edge.
Combining the chosen path with the alleged cycle produces a unit
source-to-sink residual flow in the old graph. Decompose it into one
source-to-sink path and cycles. The old cycles are nonnegative, so
the decomposed path would be cheaper than the chosen shortest path.
That is a contradiction. Thus every augmentation preserves global
residual optimality, including components unreachable from the source.

After every augmentation, the flow is feasible and has minimum cost
among flows of its current value. Feasibility holds because internal
path vertices gain and lose the same bottleneck, while source outflow
and sink inflow increase equally. The residual update represents
exactly sending or canceling that amount.

Capacities are integers and each bottleneck is a positive integer, so
every successful iteration increases flow value by at least one. The
loop terminates after finitely many augmentations. When T becomes
unreachable, the augmenting-path theorem says the flow is maximum.
Because it remains minimum-cost for its value, it is a minimum-cost
maximum flow.

The witness is reconstructed from saved forward-record locations.
For input edge i, `capacity - remainingForwardCapacity` is exactly its
net flow. Exact reverse indices preserve this identity for parallel
and opposite-direction edges.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count, E be input-edge count, A be the number of
augmentations, and F be the returned flow value.

Validation and residual construction take `Theta(V+E)` time and
space. Initial Bellman-Ford-style relaxation takes `O(VE)` time and
`Theta(V)` space. It may stop after one unchanged pass.

One lazy-heap Dijkstra search takes
`O((V+E) log(E+2))` time and `O(V+E)` auxiliary space. Parent tracing,
potential updates, and residual mutation add `O(V)` time. The complete
bound is:

```text
O(VE + A * (V+E) * log(E+2)) time
```

Each integral augmentation adds at least one unit, so `A <= F`. A
common looser form is `O(VE + F*E*log V)` for connected sparse graphs.
This is capacity-dependent, not strongly polynomial; a large flow
split across unit bottlenecks can require many searches.

The residual graph has exactly 2E records. Potentials, distances,
parents, reachability, and heap storage use `O(V+E)` auxiliary space.
The result witness uses `Theta(E)` output space. The input is not
retained.

Pushing the full bottleneck is faster than one unit at a time and does
not change correctness. More advanced capacity-scaling, cost-scaling,
or strongly polynomial algorithms improve difficult large instances
but require substantially more machinery.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Decide the objective order. This function maximizes flow first and
  minimizes cost second; minimum-cost flow of a requested value is a
  different API.
- Add a reverse record with negated cost for every input edge. Reverse
  capacity is how a later path repairs an earlier choice.
- Store exact paired indices. Searching by endpoint fails with
  parallel and opposite-direction edges.
- Ignore zero-capacity records in relaxation and shortest paths. Their
  costs do not describe available movement.
- Do not run Dijkstra on original negative costs. Initialize valid
  potentials first, then search on reduced costs.
- Use one sign convention consistently. Here reduced cost is
  `cost+p[from]-p[to]`, so finite Dijkstra distances are added to
  potentials.
- Update reached potentials before adding reverse capacity. Chosen
  path edges become tight, making their new reversals zero-cost.
- Leave unreachable potentials unchanged. Adding an infinity sentinel
  would overflow and destroy the invariant.
- Reject a negative cycle under this contract, even if disconnected.
  Supporting it requires a minimum-cost circulation or cycle-canceling
  phase.
- Record both parent vertex and residual edge index. A vertex-only
  parent cannot select the correct parallel record.
- Relax only on strict improvement if deterministic parents matter.
  Replacing equal parents can make witness choice depend on heap
  order.
- Compute original path cost before mutating the residual records.
  Reduced distance contains a potential offset and is not the amount
  to add directly to total cost.
- Stop only when the sink is residually unreachable. Exhausting one
  cheap route does not imply maximum flow.
- Bound capacity and cost arithmetic. `int` is platform-dependent and
  unchecked `int64` products can overflow under a broader contract.
- Self-loops require special paired-index construction when both
  records share a row. Rejecting them keeps this implementation and
  its witness rule simple.

##### When to choose it

Use this approach for moderate directed networks where capacity and a
per-unit edge cost both matter: assignment through a flow reduction,
transportation, routing, or selecting several disjoint cheap paths.
It is especially useful when a flow witness per input edge is needed
and integral capacities are not enormous.

Use ordinary [Edmonds-Karp](
#b283-edmonds-karp-max-flow-residual-graph-and-queue) or
[Dinic](#b284-dinic-max-flow-residual-graph-and-level-arrays) when
only maximum value matters. Use the next
[Hungarian algorithm](
#b287-assignment-with-hungarian-algorithm-cost-matrix) for a dense
square assignment matrix; its specialized structure is simpler and
usually faster.

Use a requested-flow variant when the caller wants exactly K units and
must report infeasibility if K cannot reach the sink. Use circulation
methods when supplies, demands, lower bounds, or negative-cost cycles
are part of the valid input. Prefer cost-scaling or another mature
solver for very large or adversarial production networks.

MIT OpenCourseWare's [minimum-cost-flow notes](
https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-854j-advanced-algorithms-fall-2005/
resources/mincostflow/) cover shortest augmenting paths and scaling.
Jeff Erickson's [minimum-cost-flow notes](
https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/
G-mincostflow.pdf) derive residual optimality, reduced costs, and node
potentials. Dalhousie's [successive shortest paths notes](
https://web.cs.dal.ca/~nzeh/Teaching/4113/book/mincostflow/
successive_shortest_paths/algorithm.html) give the potential update
and nonnegative-reduced-cost invariant in detail.

#### B.28.7 Assignment with Hungarian algorithm (cost matrix)

##### Problem and contract

Suppose each matrix row is a worker and each column is a job. Cell
`costs[row][column]` is the cost of assigning that worker to that job.
Assign every row to exactly one distinct column while minimizing the
sum of selected cells. This is the rectangular **linear assignment
problem**.

Choosing each row's cheapest currently free column can fail. An early
row may take the only cheap column for a later row, even though moving
the early row to its second choice would reduce the total. The
**Hungarian algorithm** keeps a matching but permits an alternating
path to reassign earlier rows.

`minimumCostAssignment` has this contract:

- `costs` contains from 0 through 500 rows.
- A nonempty matrix contains from 1 through 500 columns.
- Every row has the same column count.
- Row count does not exceed column count, so every row can receive a
  distinct column.
- Each `int64` cost is in
  `-1_000_000_000..1_000_000_000`.
- Negative, zero, repeated, and tied costs are valid.
- An empty matrix has total cost zero and empty result slices.
- A ragged matrix, an out-of-range cost, too many rows or columns, or
  more rows than columns returns `errInvalidAssignment` and no result.
- The function reads but does not mutate or retain the matrix or its
  rows. Returned slices own their storage.

The result contains:

- `columnByRow[row]`, the selected zero-based column;
- `totalCost`, the sum of the selected original cells;
- `rowPotential[row]`; and
- `columnPotential[column]`.

The last two slices form an independently checkable optimality
certificate. For every cell they satisfy:

```text
rowPotential[row] + columnPotential[column]
    <= costs[row][column]
```

Every selected cell has equality, every column potential is
nonpositive, and the sum of all potentials equals `totalCost`.
Therefore no other assignment can cost less.

Rows are inserted in numeric order. Equal slacks keep their first
parent, and the smallest numbered tied column is chosen. These rules
make one optimum deterministic even when several assignments have the
same minimum total.

The dimension and cost limits keep selected totals and internal
potential arithmetic safely inside `int64`; `assignmentInfinity` is
`1<<60`, far above every possible finite slack. Read the
[matrix representation](
#a103-adjacency-lists-matrices-and-edge-lists),
[bipartite matching](
#b281-augmenting-path-matching-adjacency-and-match-arrays), and
[min-cost flow](
#b286-min-cost-flow-residual-graph-and-potentials) lessons first.

##### Mental model

An assignment is a bipartite matching that covers every row. The code
stores it in the reverse direction while constructing it:

```text
columnToRow[column] = matched row, or 0 when the column is free
```

Real rows and columns use one-based internal indices. Index zero is a
dummy column. At the start of one outer iteration,
`columnToRow[0] = nextRow`; this makes the new unmatched row the root
of an alternating tree without giving it a real job.

Potentials change a cell into a **reduced cost**:

```text
reducedCost(row,column) =
    cost(row,column) - rowPotential[row]
    - columnPotential[column]
```

A nonnegative reduced cost means the potential cover does not exceed
the original cell. Reduced cost zero means the cell is **tight**. The
current matching and every alternating-tree edge stay on tight cells.

For every real column outside the tree, remember:

```text
minimumSlack[column]
    smallest reduced cost from any tree row to this column

slackParentColumn[column]
    tree column whose matched row produced that slack
```

Read `minimumSlack[1] == 4` as: the cheapest known edge from any row
in the current alternating tree to real column 1 still needs a
potential change of four before it becomes tight.

Choose the outside column with least slack. Shift potentials by that
amount: add it to potentials of tree rows and subtract it from
potentials of real tree columns. This preserves tight tree edges and
makes at least one new edge tight.

If the new column is occupied, follow its matched row and expand the
tree. If it is free, follow `slackParentColumn` backward and flip the
alternating path. The new row becomes matched, while every internal
row merely changes columns.

The first shift for a newly inserted row may be negative because costs
may be negative. It establishes feasible reduced costs for that row.
Afterward all remembered slacks are nonnegative, so later shifts in
the same tree are nonnegative.

##### Worked walkthrough

Assign rows `R0`, `R1`, and `R2` to distinct columns from this matrix:

```text
        J0   J1   J2   J3
R0       1    2    9    9
R1       1  100    9    9
R2       9    9    1    2
```

The expected result is:

```text
columnByRow = [1,0,2]
total cost = 2+1+1 = 4
row potentials = [2,2,1]
column potentials = [-1,0,0,0]
```

Initial state: all real columns are free, every potential is zero,
and no alternating tree exists.

1. Decision: insert R0 at the dummy root. Its slacks to
   `[J0,J1,J2,J3]` are `[1,2,9,9]`; choose J0 and shift by one.
   After: row potentials are `[1,0,0]`. J0 is tight and free, so flip
   the one-edge path and match `R0-J0`.
   Known correct: the one-row prefix has its cheapest assignment,
   with cost one and a tight selected cell.
2. Decision: insert R1. Its initial slacks are `[1,100,9,9]`.
   Shift by one, making `R1-J0` tight. J0 is occupied by R0, so add
   J0 and its matched row R0 to the alternating tree.
   After: row potentials are `[1,1,0]`; the matching is still
   `R0-J0`. The tree contains rows R1 and R0 and real column J0.
   Known correct: no free tight column has been reached, but the tree
   represents the possible reassignment through J0.
3. Decision: scan R0's edges to columns outside the tree. The current
   outside slacks are `[J1=99,J2=8,J3=8]`. R0 improves J1 to one;
   its reduced costs to J2 and J3 are eight, so their equal slacks
   keep the earlier parent. Shift by one and choose J1.
   After: row potentials are `[2,2,0]`; column potentials are
   `[-1,0,0,0]`. J1 is tight and free.
   Known correct: all tree edges remain tight, and the parent chain is
   `R1->J0->R0->J1`.
4. Decision: flip that chain backward. Give J1 to R0, then give J0 to
   R1.
   After: `columnByRow` for the processed prefix is `[1,0]`; its cost
   is `2+1 = 3`.
   Known correct: both rows have distinct columns, selected cells are
   tight, and the dual potentials also sum to three.
5. Decision: insert R2. Its reduced slacks are
   `[J0=10,J1=9,J2=1,J3=2]`; choose free J2 and shift by one.
   After: row potentials are `[2,2,1]`. Match `R2-J2`; the final
   columns are `[1,0,2]` and total cost is four.
   Known correct: every row is assigned once, columns are distinct,
   and each selected cell equals its row-plus-column potential.
6. Decision: sum the certificate. Row potentials total five and
   column potentials total -1.
   After: the dual total is four, equal to the selected-cell total.
   Known correct: weak duality makes four a lower bound for every
   assignment, while the returned matching attains it; it is optimal.

Focused rectangular case: the unused J3 is valid. Its potential stays
zero because only occupied columns enter an alternating tree.

Focused negative-cost case: matrix `[[-5,0],[0,-4]]` returns columns
`[0,1]` and total -9. The first potential shift is negative; later
certificate checks remain unchanged.

Focused tie case: a three-by-five matrix filled with five returns
columns `[0,1,2]`. Other choices also cost 15, but strict slack
updates and lower-column tie-breaking select this witness.

Focused empty case: `nil` returns total zero with empty assignment and
potential slices. A one-row zero-column matrix is invalid because its
row cannot be assigned.

Focused malformed case: rows `[[1,2],[3]]` are ragged and rejected
before any work arrays are allocated.

Counterexample to permanent row-greedy choices: in the main matrix,
greedy assigns R0 to J0 for one. With lower-column tie-breaking, R1
then takes J2 for nine and R2 takes J3 for two, totaling 12. Taking J3
for R1 instead would total 11. The first wrong decision is refusing to
reconsider `R0-J0`. The alternating path moves R0 to J1 and frees J0
for R1, reducing the optimum to four.

##### Implementation

This complete Go program solves the walkthrough and exercises
negative, empty, and malformed matrices. It uses only the standard
library. Only the supplied writer has an external side effect. Save
it as `main.go` and run `go run main.go`.

```go
// This runnable block demonstrates Assignment with Hungarian
// algorithm (cost matrix). Function comments connect each operation
// to its invariant.
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"os"
)

const (
	maximumAssignmentDimension = 500
	maximumAssignmentCost      = int64(1_000_000_000)
	assignmentInfinity         = int64(1 << 60)
)

var errInvalidAssignment = errors.New("invalid assignment matrix")

var errAssignmentInvariant = errors.New(
	"assignment invariant failed",
)

type assignmentResult struct {
	totalCost       int64
	columnByRow     []int
	rowPotential    []int64
	columnPotential []int64
}

func validateAssignmentCosts(costs [][]int64) (int, error) {
	// Reject input outside the assignment costs contract before
	// mutation.
	rowCount := len(costs)
	if rowCount > maximumAssignmentDimension {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: row count %d exceeds %d",
			errInvalidAssignment,
			rowCount,
			maximumAssignmentDimension,
		)
	}
	if rowCount == 0 {
		return 0, nil
	}

	columnCount := len(costs[0])
	if columnCount > maximumAssignmentDimension {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: column count %d exceeds %d",
			errInvalidAssignment,
			columnCount,
			maximumAssignmentDimension,
		)
	}
	if rowCount > columnCount {
		return 0, fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: %d rows cannot fit in %d columns",
			errInvalidAssignment,
			rowCount,
			columnCount,
		)
	}

	for row, rowCosts := range costs {
		if len(rowCosts) != columnCount {
			return 0, fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: row %d has %d columns; want %d",
				errInvalidAssignment,
				row,
				len(rowCosts),
				columnCount,
			)
		}
		for column, cost := range rowCosts {
			if cost < -maximumAssignmentCost ||
				cost > maximumAssignmentCost {
				return 0, fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: cost [%d][%d] is outside %d..%d",
					errInvalidAssignment,
					row,
					column,
					-maximumAssignmentCost,
					maximumAssignmentCost,
				)
			}
		}
	}
	return columnCount, nil
}

func verifyAssignment(
	costs [][]int64,
	result assignmentResult,
) error {
	// Keep verify assignment in one helper so callers use one rule.
	rowCount := len(costs)
	if len(result.columnByRow) != rowCount ||
		len(result.rowPotential) != rowCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: row-sized result has the wrong length",
			errAssignmentInvariant,
		)
	}
	if rowCount == 0 {
		if result.totalCost != 0 ||
			len(result.columnPotential) != 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: empty matrix has a nonempty result",
				errAssignmentInvariant,
			)
		}
		return nil
	}

	columnCount := len(costs[0])
	if len(result.columnPotential) != columnCount {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: column potentials have the wrong length",
			errAssignmentInvariant,
		)
	}

	usedColumn := make([]bool, columnCount)
	primalCost := int64(0)
	for row, column := range result.columnByRow {
		if column < 0 || column >= columnCount {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: row %d has invalid column %d",
				errAssignmentInvariant,
				row,
				column,
			)
		}
		if usedColumn[column] {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: column %d is assigned twice",
				errAssignmentInvariant,
				column,
			)
		}
		usedColumn[column] = true
		primalCost += costs[row][column]
	}

	dualCost := int64(0)
	for _, potential := range result.rowPotential {
		dualCost += potential
	}
	for column, potential := range result.columnPotential {
		if potential > 0 {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: column %d potential %d is positive",
				errAssignmentInvariant,
				column,
				potential,
			)
		}
		dualCost += potential
	}

	for row, rowCosts := range costs {
		for column, cost := range rowCosts {
			coveredCost := result.rowPotential[row] +
				result.columnPotential[column]
			if coveredCost > cost {
				return fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: dual cover [%d][%d] exceeds cost",
					errAssignmentInvariant,
					row,
					column,
				)
			}
		}
		column := result.columnByRow[row]
		coveredCost := result.rowPotential[row] +
			result.columnPotential[column]
		if coveredCost != rowCosts[column] {
			return fmt.Errorf(
				"%w: assigned cell [%d][%d] is not tight",
				errAssignmentInvariant,
				row,
				column,
			)
		}
	}

	if result.totalCost != primalCost || primalCost != dualCost {
		return fmt.Errorf(
			"%w: result %d, primal %d, dual %d differ",
			errAssignmentInvariant,
			result.totalCost,
			primalCost,
			dualCost,
		)
	}
	return nil
}

func minimumCostAssignment(
	costs [][]int64,
) (assignmentResult, error) {
	// Compute cost assignment from the state without mutating it.
	columnCount, err := validateAssignmentCosts(costs)
	if err != nil {
		return assignmentResult{}, err
	}
	rowCount := len(costs)
	if rowCount == 0 {
		return assignmentResult{
			columnByRow:     []int{},
			rowPotential:    []int64{},
			columnPotential: []int64{},
		}, nil
	}

	// Index zero is a dummy column whose matched row starts each tree.
	rowPotential := make([]int64, rowCount+1)
	columnPotential := make([]int64, columnCount+1)
	columnToRow := make([]int, columnCount+1)
	minimumSlack := make([]int64, columnCount+1)
	slackParentColumn := make([]int, columnCount+1)
	columnInTree := make([]bool, columnCount+1)

	for nextRow := 1; nextRow <= rowCount; nextRow++ {
		columnToRow[0] = nextRow
		for column := 0; column <= columnCount; column++ {
			minimumSlack[column] = assignmentInfinity
			slackParentColumn[column] = 0
			columnInTree[column] = false
		}

		currentColumn := 0
		for {
			columnInTree[currentColumn] = true
			currentRow := columnToRow[currentColumn]
			delta := assignmentInfinity
			nextColumn := 0

			// Update the cheapest edge from this alternating tree.
			for column := 1; column <= columnCount; column++ {
				if columnInTree[column] {
					continue
				}
				reducedCost := costs[currentRow-1][column-1] -
					rowPotential[currentRow] -
					columnPotential[column]
				if reducedCost < minimumSlack[column] {
					minimumSlack[column] = reducedCost
					slackParentColumn[column] = currentColumn
				}
				if minimumSlack[column] < delta {
					delta = minimumSlack[column]
					nextColumn = column
				}
			}
			if nextColumn == 0 {
				return assignmentResult{}, fmt.Errorf(
					"%w: no column can extend row %d",
					errAssignmentInvariant,
					nextRow-1,
				)
			}

			// Shift dual values until one cheapest edge becomes tight.
			for column := 0; column <= columnCount; column++ {
				if columnInTree[column] {
					matchedRow := columnToRow[column]
					rowPotential[matchedRow] += delta
					columnPotential[column] -= delta
					continue
				}
				minimumSlack[column] -= delta
			}

			currentColumn = nextColumn
			if columnToRow[currentColumn] == 0 {
				break
			}
		}

		// Flip the alternating path ending at the free column.
		for {
			previousColumn := slackParentColumn[currentColumn]
			columnToRow[currentColumn] =
				columnToRow[previousColumn]
			currentColumn = previousColumn
			if currentColumn == 0 {
				break
			}
		}
	}

	columnByRow := make([]int, rowCount)
	for column := 1; column <= columnCount; column++ {
		row := columnToRow[column]
		if row != 0 {
			columnByRow[row-1] = column - 1
		}
	}
	result := assignmentResult{
		columnByRow:  columnByRow,
		rowPotential: append([]int64(nil), rowPotential[1:]...),
		columnPotential: append(
			[]int64(nil),
			columnPotential[1:]...,
		),
	}
	for row, column := range result.columnByRow {
		result.totalCost += costs[row][column]
	}
	if err := verifyAssignment(costs, result); err != nil {
		return assignmentResult{}, err
	}
	return result, nil
}

func runAssignmentExamples(output io.Writer) error {
	// Execute assignment examples to the bounded stopping condition
	// above.
	result, err := minimumCostAssignment([][]int64{
		{1, 2, 9, 9},
		{1, 100, 9, 9},
		{9, 9, 1, 2},
	})
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("solve ordinary assignment: %w", err)
	}
	negative, err := minimumCostAssignment([][]int64{
		{-5, 0},
		{0, -4},
	})
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("solve negative assignment: %w", err)
	}
	empty, err := minimumCostAssignment(nil)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("solve empty assignment: %w", err)
	}
	_, invalidErr := minimumCostAssignment([][]int64{
		{1, 2},
		{3},
	})

	if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(
		output,
		"total cost = %d\ncolumns = %v\n"+
			"row potentials = %v\ncolumn potentials = %v\n"+
			"negative = %d %v\nempty = %d %v\n"+
			"invalid rejected=%t\n",
		result.totalCost,
		result.columnByRow,
		result.rowPotential,
		result.columnPotential,
		negative.totalCost,
		negative.columnByRow,
		empty.totalCost,
		empty.columnByRow,
		errors.Is(invalidErr, errInvalidAssignment),
	); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("write assignment results: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

func main() {
	// Run the sample and print each result.
	if err := runAssignmentExamples(os.Stdout); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

Exact output:

```text
total cost = 4
columns = [1 0 2]
row potentials = [2 2 1]
column potentials = [-1 0 0 0]
negative = -9 [0 1]
empty = 0 []
invalid rejected=true
```

##### Why it works

Before row k is inserted, assume the matching is optimal for earlier
rows, every matched cell is tight, and processed-row potentials are
dual-feasible. Put row k at the dummy root. Its first minimum-slack
shift makes all of its reduced costs nonnegative and at least one
tight. Thus the invariant extends to the new row even when its costs
are negative.

During a tree search, `minimumSlack[column]` is the least reduced cost
of any edge from a tree row to that outside column. Choosing the
smallest slack delta and adding it to every tree-row potential reduces
those crossing reduced costs by delta. None becomes negative.
Subtracting delta from each real tree-column potential cancels the row
change on edges inside the tree, so tight tree and matching edges stay
tight. Edges from outside rows to tree columns only gain reduced cost.
Dual feasibility therefore survives every shift.

A zero-slack edge either reaches an occupied column and adds its
matched row to the tree, or reaches a free column. Parent entries in
the second case describe a tight alternating path from the new row to
that free column. Flipping it matches the new row. Internal rows and
columns lose one selected edge and gain one, so all processed rows
remain matched to distinct columns. Every new selected edge is tight.

Only occupied real columns can enter a tree, so every unassigned
column retains potential zero. Summing tight selected cells after the
flip gives:

```text
selected cost = sum(row potentials)
              + sum(selected column potentials)
              = sum(all row and column potentials)
```

For any other assignment, dual feasibility says each selected cost is
at least its row plus column potential. Every row appears once;
selected column potentials sum to at least all column potentials
because omitted column potentials are nonpositive. Thus every other
assignment costs at least the dual total. The returned assignment
equals that lower bound, so it is minimum-cost for the processed
prefix. Induction proves the final result optimal.

Each inner iteration marks one previously outside real column as in
the tree. It never removes a mark. Before inserting row k, only k-1
columns are occupied, while at least k columns exist. Therefore a free
column is reached after finitely many expansions. The finite outer
loop inserts every row, so the algorithm terminates.

The final verifier independently checks distinct columns, potential
signs, all dual inequalities, tight selected cells, and equality of
primal, dual, and reported totals. A broken internal invariant returns
an error instead of exposing an unverified result.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let R be row count and C be column count, with `R <= C`. Validation
and final certificate verification each inspect all `R*C` cells.

When one row is inserted, the alternating tree contains at most R
occupied columns. Each expansion scans all C columns, so one insertion
takes `O(R*C)` time and all R insertions take `O(R^2*C)` worst-case
time. For an `N` by `N` matrix this is `O(N^3)`.

If every new row reaches a free column after its first scan, the main
loop takes `Theta(R*C)` time. Input validation and certificate
checking have the same lower bound. There is no
distribution-independent average improvement.

Potentials, the reverse matching, slacks, parents, tree marks, and the
verifier's used-column set require `O(R+C)` auxiliary space. The
assignment and two potential slices use `Theta(R+C)` output space.
The caller-owned matrix occupies `Theta(R*C)` storage and is not
copied or retained.

This dense implementation scans every column even when few pairings
are allowed. Its cubic square-matrix bound is independent of numeric
cost magnitude, unlike capacity-dependent successive shortest paths.
Sparse graph representations may still make min-cost flow or another
weighted-matching implementation faster in practice.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- An empty matrix is a valid zero-row problem. Do not read `costs[0]`
  before checking row count.
- One or more rows with zero columns are infeasible. Reject
  `rowCount > columnCount` before building the dummy-root arrays.
- Every row must have the first row's column count. Indexing a ragged
  later row can panic halfway through a search.
- Extra columns are allowed and may remain unused. Do not require a
  square matrix or add fake rows unless another API needs them.
- Negative costs are valid. The first delta for a row may be negative;
  rejecting it or forcing delta to zero loses the optimum.
- Tied costs can have several optimal witnesses. Use strict slack
  improvement and an explicit column tie rule when deterministic
  output matters.
- Keep the dummy column separate from real column zero. The code uses
  one-based internals and subtracts one only when indexing the input
  or constructing output.
- `minimumSlack[c]` is the best edge from the whole tree, not only the
  most recently added row. Overwriting it unconditionally can discard
  the augmenting path.
- Store the parent column when slack improves. A Boolean tree mark
  alone cannot reconstruct which earlier matches to flip.
- Shift both sides of a tight matched edge: add delta to its row and
  subtract delta from its tree column. Updating only rows breaks
  tightness and dual feasibility.
- Flip backward from the free column. Overwriting a match before
  reading its parent loses the remainder of the alternating path.
- A large numeric sentinel is not a forbidden-assignment marker.
  Model forbidden cells explicitly; an arbitrary large cost can still
  be selected when every row must be covered.
- Transposing a matrix with more rows than columns changes which
  original side must be fully assigned. Reject it unless the caller
  explicitly wants that different contract.
- Maximization requires a carefully bounded cost transformation or a
  dedicated sign convention. Negating `MinInt64` is not safe.
- Verify totals with `int64`. Summing into `int` makes behavior depend
  on platform width.

##### When to choose it

Choose this Hungarian implementation when every item on the smaller
row side must receive one distinct item from a dense column side and
the objective is the minimum sum of pair costs. Worker-job, machine-
task, and small dense resource-allocation matrices are recognizable
cases.

Use [augmenting-path matching](
#b281-augmenting-path-matching-adjacency-and-match-arrays) or
[Hopcroft-Karp](#b282-hopcroft-karp-layers-and-matching-arrays) when
edges are unweighted and only maximum cardinality matters. Use
[min-cost flow](
#b286-min-cost-flow-residual-graph-and-potentials) for sparse allowed
pairs, capacities above one, requested flow values, or a larger
network structure.

Stable matching optimizes absence of blocking pairs, not cost sum.
The quadratic assignment problem includes interactions between pairs
of assignments and is a different, much harder problem. Scheduling
with job durations, precedence, or time windows also needs a richer
model than one static cell per pairing.

Kuhn's original paper, [The Hungarian method for the assignment
problem](https://doi.org/10.1002/nav.3800020109), develops the
assignment method from duality and matching. Munkres's
[Algorithms for the Assignment and Transportation Problems](
https://doi.org/10.1137/0105003) gives a polynomial assignment
algorithm and proof. NIST's [Munkres assignment entry](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/munkresAssignment.html) summarizes
the method and terminology.

### B.29 Dynamic graph and tree queries (advanced)

#### B.29.1 Offline connectivity (rollback disjoint sets)

##### Problem and contract

An undirected graph changes through edge additions and removals. At
selected times, answer whether two vertices are connected and how many
connected components currently exist. Ordinary disjoint sets handle
additions, but a removal may split one component and cannot be undone
from the final parent forest alone.

When the complete operation timeline is known before any answer must
be returned, solve it **offline**. Convert every edge's active
lifetime to a time interval, store that interval in a segment tree
over time, and traverse the tree with a rollback disjoint set. This
changes the order of internal work but preserves query order.

`solveOfflineConnectivity` has this contract:

- `vertexCount` is in `0..100000`; valid vertex IDs are in
  `[0, vertexCount)`.
- There are at most 100,000 operations.
- `addConnectivityEdge` activates one undirected edge.
- `removeConnectivityEdge` deactivates one active edge.
