valid because of sorted order, not because there are two pointers.

##### Implementation

Do not maintain a third copy of either implementation here. Use the
complete [hash-map complement lookup](
#b21-complement-lookup-hash-map) when the input is unsorted. Its map
stores each earlier value's earliest index, checks the complement
before insertion, guards subtraction, and returns as soon as a pair
is found. For this lesson's boolean contract, discard its two returned
indices and keep `found`.

For an already sorted input, use the complete [inward two-pointer
implementation](#b22-two-pointers-after-sorting-slice). It checks the
endpoint sum without overflow, moves exactly one endpoint after an
inequality, and returns `found`.

For unsorted input with the sorting route, first allocate a copy using
the ownership pattern in [sorting and scanning](
#b13-sorting-and-scanning-slice), sort that copy in nondecreasing
order, and pass it to the two-pointer function. `slices.Sort` mutates
the slice it receives, so copying is what preserves the caller's
order. Sorting raw values is sufficient only because the result is a
boolean; retain value-index records when original positions are part
of the output.

Both owner programs are complete command-line examples with expected
output and boundary cases. This comparison adds no executable block,
so changes to their arithmetic, ordering, or ownership contracts need
only be maintained in their primary entries.

##### Why it works

For hashing, before each current position the map represents exactly
the earlier values, and no earlier second position completed the
target. A present exact complement witnesses two distinct positions.
An absent complement proves no pair ends at the current position;
inserting the current value then preserves the prefix invariant.

For two pointers, the active interval contains every pair not yet
ruled out. If the endpoints sum below target, sorted order proves the
left endpoint also sums too low with every smaller partner. If the
sum is above target, the right endpoint also sums too high with every
larger partner. Removing the proved-impossible endpoint preserves the
active-interval invariant. Equality is a witness.

Each failed hash iteration advances one input position. Each failed
pointer comparison reduces the active interval by one. Both processes
are bounded by N and therefore terminate. Exhausting either process
means its invariant has rejected every possible second position or
every possible endpoint pair, so false is correct.

Sorting is the bridge that makes pointer elimination sound. It keeps
all occurrences, so duplicates remain distinct candidates, while
establishing the monotonic order used by both discard proofs. Copying
changes only storage ownership, not the multiset of values.

Both methods therefore decide the same existential statement. They
need not encounter the same witness. That distinction is harmless
only because the observable result is boolean; a pair-valued contract
must reconcile index identity and tie-breaking separately.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length, P be the number of examined input positions
or endpoint comparisons before return, D be the number of distinct
values stored, and Q be the number of target queries over one fixed
collection.

Hashing performs one checked complement and expected constant-time
map work per examined position. Its expected time is Theta(P), with
`P <= N`, and it retains O(D) entries. A match at the second position
can take Theta(1) work relative to N; exhaustion takes expected
Theta(N). Go specifies map behavior, but not a worst-case constant
lookup bound. Collisions and runtime policy remain implementation
concerns.

On already sorted input with N at least one, two pointers make at most
`N - 1` endpoint comparisons. They take Theta(P) time and O(1)
auxiliary storage, with Theta(1) best-case work when the initial
endpoints match and Theta(N) work on exhaustion.

On unsorted input, the sorting route must first obtain order. Copying
takes Theta(N) work and O(N) auxiliary owned storage. Under the
standard comparison-sort model, sorting adds O(N log N) comparisons
before the Theta(N) scan. The sorting implementation may need its own
temporary or stack storage. The `slices.Sort` API promises ascending
order, not a complexity bound; use an owned or pinned sorter when that
bound is part of the application contract.

If input mutation is allowed, sort the original slice and remove the
O(N) copy, but caller-visible order changes. If the input is already
sorted, two pointers avoid both the map and preprocessing. If it is
unsorted and one early answer is likely, hashing can return before
reading the suffix whereas sorting cannot.

For Q targets over one immutable collection, rebuilding a map for each
target costs expected O(QN) total scan work. Sorting once costs
O(N log N + QN) comparison and scan work. The asymptotic query term is
still linear per target, but the sorted form is reusable and avoids Q
map builds. Precomputing every possible pair sum can answer queries
faster only by spending up to quadratic time and storage.

Costs are not interchangeable with guarantees. Expected linear time
may be preferable for ordinary in-memory inputs; deterministic
comparison behavior, low auxiliary state on sorted data, or resistance
to adversarial hash distributions may justify sorting.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Nil, empty, and singleton inputs return false. Neither method may
  read an endpoint or claim a pair before proving two positions exist.
- `[5,5]` with target 10 returns true. Hash lookup must occur before
  inserting the current occurrence, and pointer indices must satisfy
  `leftIndex < rightIndex`.
- `[5]` with target 10 returns false. A set of values without position
  timing can accidentally pair one occurrence with itself.
- Signed extremes are valid. Check complement subtraction before
  evaluating it, and compare an endpoint sum safely before addition.
- Two pointers require nondecreasing order. Merely placing one pointer
  at each end of an unsorted slice gives no safe discard rule.
- Sorting bare values loses original indices. Sort value-index records
  or choose the hash route when a pair of original positions is the
  required output.
- The owner hash and pointer functions use different deterministic
  tie-breaks. Comparing their returned indices as though they shared
  one contract creates a false test failure.
- `slices.Sort` mutates its argument. A slice assignment shares its
  backing array. Allocate and copy before sorting when input order
  must survive.
- Hashing an `int` is valid, but a generalized hash key must be
  comparable in Go. Slices and maps cannot be map keys directly.
- Do not rely on map iteration order. The hash solution obtains order
  from the input scan and performs direct lookups only.
- High-cardinality input can make the map retain N keys. Low-memory
  requirements rule out that trade when no bounded direct table fits.
- Concurrent mutation can invalidate either prefix membership or
  sorted order. Both routes require a stable snapshot or external
  synchronization.

##### When to choose it

Choose hashing when the input is unsorted, there is one target, input
order or original indices matter, mutation is forbidden, and O(N)
expected auxiliary storage is acceptable. It also fits streaming
arrival: each new value can be checked against the earlier prefix
without waiting for the full input.

Choose sorting plus two pointers when the input is already sorted,
constant auxiliary state matters, or the ordered representation will
support later scans and target queries. For unsorted data, prefer it
when mutation or a copy is acceptable and comparison-based,
non-hash-dependent behavior is more important than expected linear
single-query time.

Neither is automatically right when the output changes. Use a
frequency map when every pair or multiplicity must be counted. Use a
small direct-address table or bit set when values occupy a bounded
dense range. Use nested scans when N is tiny and avoiding allocation
matters more than quadratic growth.

The decisive questions are:

- Is the input already sorted, or will ordered reuse repay sorting?
- Must original positions or a particular tied pair be returned?
- May the input be reordered, copied, or retained in a map?
- Is expected hash performance acceptable for the key source?
- Is this one early-exit query, repeated queries, or a stream?

The [hash-table lesson](
#a62-separate-chaining-and-open-addressing) explains collision and
worst-case behavior. [Comparison sorting](
#b31-comparison-sorting-slice) owns ordering contracts, and the
[data-structure comparison](
#c62-stacks-queues-heaps-and-linear-scans) demonstrates the same
workload-first selection method for evolving frontiers.

Go's [maps article](https://go.dev/blog/maps) documents map
initialization, presence checks, key rules, and unspecified storage
details. The official [`slices.Sort` documentation](
https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort) defines ascending in-place sorting.

#### C.7.2 Prefix sums versus sliding windows

##### Problem and contract

Prefix sums and sliding windows both reason about contiguous ranges,
but they remember different facts. A prefix array answers the sum of
chosen boundaries. A sliding window discovers useful boundaries while
the input is scanned. The right choice depends on whether boundaries
are supplied, must be optimized, and move monotonically.

Use one shared question for comparison. Given nonnegative costs and a
budget, return the longest nonempty half-open range `[start,end)`
whose exact mathematical sum is at most the budget. Return its start,
length, and total. If several maximum-length ranges exist, choose the
earliest start.

The executable contract matches the primary window implementation:

- input contains at most 100,000 `uint64` costs;
- each cost is at most 1,000,000,000;
- any `uint64` budget is valid;
- empty input or no affordable nonempty range returns missing;
- invalid count or cost returns a zero result and a validation error;
- the complete input is validated before result selection;
- neither route mutates or retains the input; and
- allocation failure is outside the recoverable contract.

The limits keep the greatest accepted total at
100,000,000,000,000, which fits `uint64`. For N costs, the prefix
route allocates N + 1 totals. The window route uses only scalar range
state.

Read [prefix-sum arrays](#a121-prefix-sum-arrays), [binary bounds](
#b41-binary-search-and-bounds-slice), and [window validity](
#c52-window-validity-for-sliding-windows) first. Those entries own the
boundary-sum, lower-bound, and forward-repair mechanisms. This lesson
owns the choice between their compositions for one optimization task.

##### Mental model

Let `sumBefore[b]` be the total before boundary b. A candidate range
uses two boundaries:

```text
sum(costs[start:end]) = sumBefore[end] - sumBefore[start]
```

Because every cost is nonnegative, `sumBefore` is nondecreasing.
For one fixed end, affordability can be rearranged:

```text
sumBefore[end] - sumBefore[start] <= budget
sumBefore[start] >= sumBefore[end] - budget
```

When `sumBefore[end] <= budget`, use threshold zero instead of
performing unsigned subtraction. The earliest earlier prefix at least
the threshold gives the smallest affordable start and therefore the
longest affordable range ending at end.

The prefix route materializes every boundary total. For each end from
1 through N, lower-bound search independently finds that earliest
start in `sumBefore[0:end]`. The search excludes the current end so an
empty range cannot become a candidate.

The sliding window stores the same answer frontier implicitly. Its
`left` is the earliest affordable start for the current exclusive end.
When the next cost enters, remove left costs while the total exceeds
the budget. Nonnegativity proves a removed start can never become
affordable again for that end or any later, larger prefix threshold.

Read the equivalence this way:

```text
prefix route   search earlier totals for the frontier
window route   carry the previous frontier to the next end
```

Prefix sums are a representation, not by themselves a rule for
choosing boundaries. A sliding window is a boundary traversal, not a
general replacement for range sums. In this workload, carrying the
frontier avoids repeating a logarithmic search at every end.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use costs `[3,1,2,1,1,5]` and budget 4. The expected result is
`[1,4)`, values `[1,2,1]`, length 3, and total 4. Later range
`[2,5)` also has length 3 and total 4, so the earlier start wins.

###### Prefix sums and lower bounds

Initial state: validation accepts all six costs. No prefix storage or
best range exists.

1. Decision: build one total at every boundary by adding costs from
   left to right.
   After: `sumBefore = [0,3,4,6,7,8,13]`; best is missing.
   Known correct: entry b is the exact sum of `costs[0:b]`, and the
   entries are nondecreasing because costs are nonnegative.

2. Decision: end 1 has total 3, no greater than budget 4, so threshold
   is 0. Lower bound in prior prefixes `[0]` gives start 0.
   After: candidate `[0,1)` has length 1 and total 3; record it.
   Known correct: start 0 is the earliest affordable start for end 1.

3. Decision: end 2 has total 4 and threshold 0. Lower bound in
   `[0,3]` again gives start 0.
   After: candidate `[0,2)` has length 2 and total 4; record it.
   Known correct: no longer range can end at boundary 2.

4. Decision: end 3 has total 6, so threshold is `6 - 4 = 2`.
   The first prior prefix at least 2 is total 3 at boundary 1.
   After: candidate `[1,3)` has values `[1,2]`, length 2, and total 3;
   best remains `[0,2)`.
   Known correct: start 0 is unaffordable, while start 1 is the
   earliest affordable start for this end.

5. Decision: end 4 has total 7 and threshold 3. Lower bound finds
   boundary 1, whose prefix is 3.
   After: candidate `[1,4)` has length 3 and total 4; record it.
   Known correct: every earlier start is invalid, and every later
   start produces a shorter range.

6. Decision: end 5 has total 8 and threshold 4. Lower bound finds
   boundary 2, whose prefix is 4.
   After: candidate `[2,5)` has length 3 and total 4; keep the earlier
   equal-length best `[1,4)`.
   Known correct: both length-3 candidates are known and the tie rule
   selects start 1.

7. Decision: end 6 has total 13 and threshold 9. Every prior prefix
   is at most 8, so lower bound returns no earlier boundary.
   After: end 6 has no affordable nonempty range; return `[1,4)`.
   Known correct: every possible exclusive end was considered, and
   the caller's input is unchanged.

###### Forward-window route

Initial state: validation accepts the input. Set `left = 0`,
`currentTotal = 0`, and best to missing. No right cost has entered.

1. Decision: admit cost 3 at right 0. Total 3 is affordable, so no
   removal is needed and the first nonempty range becomes best.
   After: current and best range are `[0,1)`, length 1, total 3.
   Known correct: start 0 is the earliest affordable start for end 1.

2. Decision: admit cost 1 at right 1. Total becomes 4, so the range
   remains affordable and its greater length replaces best.
   After: current and best range are `[0,2)`, length 2, total 4.
   Known correct: the carried start 0 is still the earliest affordable
   start, and both processed ends have been compared.

3. Decision: admit cost 2 at right 2. Total becomes 6, above 4, so
   remove left cost 3 and advance left to 1. Total becomes 3.
   After: current range is `[1,3)`, length 2, total 3; best is
   `[0,2)`.
   Known correct: start 0 is permanently invalid for this end, and
   start 1 is the earliest affordable one.

4. Decision: admit cost 1 at right 3. Total becomes 4, and length 3
   strictly improves the best.
   After: current and best range are `[1,4)`, length 3, total 4.
   Known correct: this is the longest affordable range ending at 4.

5. Decision: admit cost 1 at right 4. Total becomes 5, so remove left
   cost 1 and advance left to 2. Total returns to 4.
   After: current range is `[2,5)`, length 3, total 4; best stays
   `[1,4)`.
   Known correct: strict improvement preserves the earlier tied range.

6. Decision: admit cost 5 at right 5. Total becomes 9. Remove costs
   2, 1, and 1, leaving total 5, which is still too large. Remove the
   entering 5 as well and advance left to 6.
   After: current range is empty `[6,6)` with total 0; best remains
   `[1,4)`.
   Known correct: no nonempty range ending at 6 is affordable, and
   repeated repair removed each cost at most once.

7. Decision: right reaches length 6, so stop and return the best.
   After: result is start 1, length 3, total 4; input is unchanged.
   Known correct: the carried frontier produced the same candidate for
   every end as the independent lower-bound searches.

Focused zero case: `[0,0,0]` with budget zero returns the full range.
Prefix totals are all zero, so lower bound always chooses boundary 0.
The window total never exceeds zero, so left also remains zero.

Focused missing case: `[5]` with budget 4 returns missing. The prefix
threshold is 1, but the only earlier prefix is zero. The window admits
5 and then removes it, leaving an empty range.

Counterexample with signed values: for `[5,5,-10]` and budget 5, both
monotone arguments fail. Prefix totals `[0,5,10,0]` are not sorted, so
lower-bound search is invalid. A window removes the first 5 when the
partial total reaches 10, then cannot move left backward when -10
makes the full range affordable. Nonnegative costs are a correctness
precondition, not a performance hint.

##### Implementation

The complete [window-validity implementation](
#c52-window-validity-for-sliding-windows) owns this exact input,
validation, result, tie-breaking, overflow, and ownership contract.
Its `longestAffordableRange` function is the preferred implementation
for one optimization pass.

The prefix alternative deliberately composes existing owners instead
of copying their code. Use the construction invariant from
[prefix-sum arrays](#a121-prefix-sum-arrays), but store `uint64`
totals under this lesson's validated limits. For each exclusive end:

- set threshold to zero when its prefix is at most budget;
- otherwise set threshold to `sumBefore[end] - budget`;
- apply the [lower-bound implementation](
  #b41-binary-search-and-bounds-slice) to `sumBefore[0:end]`;
- skip the end when no earlier prefix reaches the threshold;
- otherwise compute start, length, and prefix difference; and
- replace the result only for a strictly longer candidate.

The type adaptation matters. The prefix owner demonstrates checked
`int64` arithmetic for signed range queries, while this contract uses
validated `uint64` costs. Do not cast a value outside `int64` merely
to reuse that example. The accepted total bound proves every prefix
addition here fits `uint64`.

This comparison adds no second copy of the full Go implementation.
Future changes to validation, result fields, or writer-error behavior
remain centralized in the window-validity owner.

##### Why it works

Prefix construction starts with zero and adds each accepted cost once,
so `sumBefore[b]` equals the exact sum before boundary b. Nonnegative
costs make these totals nondecreasing, including equal neighboring
totals when a cost is zero.

For a fixed end, a start is affordable exactly when its prefix is at
least the clamped threshold. Lower bound returns the earliest such
prior boundary. Any earlier start has a smaller prefix and is
unaffordable; any later start gives a shorter range. Thus the one
candidate found for this end is its longest affordable nonempty range.

The window maintains the same fact without storing prefixes. After an
end enters, `currentTotal` is the exact sum from left to that end.
While it is too large, removing the nonnegative left cost cannot make
the total larger. Every discarded earlier start includes the invalid
current range plus only nonnegative costs, so it is invalid too.

When repair stops, left is exactly the earliest affordable start for
that end, or it lies at the end when no nonempty candidate exists.
Therefore the window and prefix routes present the same one candidate
per end to the best-result comparison.

Both routes replace best only on strict length improvement. Equal
length candidates occur at increasing ends and therefore have
increasing starts, so the first maximum has the earliest start.

The prefix route processes N finite ends. Each lower-bound interval
strictly shrinks until empty. The window's right boundary advances N
times; left never decreases and advances at most N times. Both
terminate. At completion, every nonempty range has an end that was
represented by that end's longest affordable candidate, proving the
global optimum was considered.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of costs and Q be the number of later fixed-bound
range-sum queries over the same immutable input.

Both routes validate up to N costs first. For valid nonempty input,
prefix construction takes Theta(N) work and O(N) retained auxiliary
storage. Performing one lower-bound search for each of N ends takes
Theta(N log(N + 1)) total comparisons in the valid nonempty best,
average, and worst input shapes. The searches use O(1) additional
state, and the scalar result uses O(1) output space.

The window admits each cost once and removes each cost at most once.
After validation it performs Theta(N) more work and uses O(1)
auxiliary and output space. Valid nonempty best, average, and worst
input shapes are Theta(N) because finding the global longest range
requires considering every end. Empty input takes Theta(1); invalid
input may stop during validation.

If the prefix array already exists, the selection phase still makes N
binary searches. Its O(N log N) work can be reduced by carrying one
lower-bound position forward as ends increase. That position is the
same frontier as window left; doing so recovers Theta(N) selection but
still retains the O(N) prefix array.

Prefix preprocessing pays off for a different workload. After one
Theta(N) build, Q caller-supplied fixed-bound sums take Theta(Q) total
work, giving Theta(N + Q). A sliding window does not index arbitrary
range queries; it would need a new scan or a different maintained
state for each objective.

For several budgets over one input, the window normally runs once per
budget for Theta(N) work each. The stored prefix array can be reused,
but independent lower bounds still cost O(N log N) per budget unless
another monotone traversal is used. Reuse alone does not make the
asymptotically slower search preferable.

With signed costs, the prefix difference identity remains true, but
the prefix totals are not ordered and the window frontier can move
backward. The task then needs a problem-specific lookup or ordered
structure. Prefix storage remains useful; this particular lower-bound
and window search does not.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input returns missing. Prefix storage would contain `[0]`,
  but no pair of distinct boundaries defines a nonempty range.
- `[0]` with budget zero returns start 0, length 1, total 0. Zero
  costs make prefix totals equal and do not require strict growth.
- `[5]` with budget 4 returns missing. Including the current end in
  its prefix search would select the empty range and report a false
  candidate.
- `[0,0,0]` with budget zero returns the earliest full range. Lower
  bound must find the first equal prefix, not any equal position.
- A maximum `uint64` budget makes every accepted full input
  affordable. Compare prefixes directly; do not compute `budget + 1`.
- When a prefix exceeds budget, subtract only after the comparison.
  Evaluating `sumBefore[end] - budget` in the other branch can
  underflow unsigned arithmetic.
- Prefix arrays need N + 1 entries. Omitting boundary zero loses every
  candidate that starts at index 0.
- End is exclusive. Candidate length is `end - start`, and total is
  `sumBefore[end] - sumBefore[start]`.
- Record a window candidate only after repeated repair. Recording the
  temporarily oversized range can make an invalid range win.
- Repair with `for`, not `if`. The final cost in the walkthrough
  requires four removals and still leaves no nonempty candidate.
- Signed values are outside this contract. Casting a negative cost to
  `uint64` creates a huge positive value rather than preserving its
  mathematical meaning.
- Preserve the validation bounds that prove prefix and window totals
  cannot wrap. A nonnegative type alone does not prevent overflow.
- Neither route supports concurrent input mutation. Validate and scan
  one stable snapshot or synchronize externally.

##### When to choose it

Choose a sliding window when the task asks one longest, shortest, or
counting question over contiguous candidates and validity has a
forward-only repair rule. For this one-budget optimization, it avoids
both stored prefixes and repeated boundary searches.

Choose prefix sums when boundaries are supplied by many later queries,
when several algorithms will reuse boundary totals, or when the range
condition is naturally an exact difference between cumulative states.
Prefix sums may still need a map, binary search, deque, or tree to
discover boundaries; the array alone answers only chosen ranges.

For signed exact-sum counting, use [prefix sums with lookup](
#b53-prefix-sums-with-lookup-array-and-hash-map). For a shortest
signed range meeting a lower bound, use the [prefix-and-deque method](
#b57-shortest-signed-sum-range-prefix-sums-and-deque). Use a [fixed
window](#b51-fixed-sliding-window-slice-or-counters) when width is
predetermined, and a Fenwick or segment tree when values change
between queries.

Before choosing, ask:

- Are range boundaries given, or must the algorithm discover them?
- Does one boundary move make validity change in one direction?
- Are negative values or other reversals possible?
- Is this one optimization pass or many fixed-bound queries?
- Is O(N) retained prefix storage useful elsewhere?

NIST's [window definition](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/window.html) identifies the
contiguous aligned range at the heart of the technique. The Go
[numeric-type specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Numeric_types)
defines the `uint64` range used by the executable owner.

#### C.7.3 Backtracking versus dynamic programming

##### Problem and contract

Backtracking and dynamic programming can traverse the same choices.
The deciding question is whether different choice histories have the
same remaining problem. Backtracking keeps those histories separate.
Dynamic programming gives equivalent histories one state key and
reuses the answer stored for that key.

This lesson compares the methods on the exact Hamiltonian-path
contract implemented in [B.27.2 Hamiltonian paths](
#b272-hamiltonian-paths-backtracking-or-bitmask-dp). Given a simple,
undirected adjacency matrix with 0 through 18 vertices, return the
lexicographically smallest path that visits every vertex exactly
once.

The shared contract is:

- nil and empty matrices return a non-nil empty path;
- a valid graph with no Hamiltonian path returns `nil,false,nil`;
- a successful call returns the smallest vertex sequence and
  `true,nil`;
- malformed, asymmetric, nonbinary, or self-looped matrices return
  an error wrapping the documented validation error; and
- neither approach mutates or retains the caller's matrix.

Using one contract matters. Comparing a backtracker that returns one
path with a dynamic program that only returns a Boolean would hide
reconstruction and tie-breaking costs. Both implementations here
return the same observable result.

The choice is not "recursion versus iteration." A recursive search
can memoize states and become top-down dynamic programming. A table
can retain predecessors and reconstruct a path. Compare what is
remembered, what can be merged, and what must be emitted.

Read [B.19.2 constraint search](
#b192-constraint-search-backtracking-and-sets) for choose, reject,
recurse, and restore. Read [B.20.7 bitmask DP](
#b207-bitmask-dp-state-table) for merging histories by a chosen set.
Read [C.5.3 repeated subproblems](
#c53-repeated-subproblems-for-dynamic-programming) for deciding
whether a complete, reusable state key exists.

##### Mental model

Picture the possible partial paths first as a tree. A tree node is a
particular history:

```text
[0,2,1]
```

Its children append unused neighbors of vertex 1. Backtracking walks
this tree depth first. It carries one path and one used-vertex set.
When a child fails, it removes the child and tries the next choice.

Now ask which parts of that history affect the future. For a simple
Hamiltonian path, later choices need only:

```text
(visited vertices, last vertex)
```

The order used to reach the state no longer matters. Histories
`[0,2,1]` and `[2,0,1]` have the same visited set `{0,1,2}` and the
same last vertex 1. They therefore have exactly the same unused
vertices and legal next edges.

Dynamic programming folds the search tree into a state graph:

```text
many histories -> one (visited mask,last) state -> one suffix answer
```

The DP entry answers a suffix question:

```text
canFinish[mask][last] = can a Hamiltonian path be completed from
                        this visited set and last vertex?
```

Backtracking is history-oriented. Its mutable path is also the
candidate output. Dynamic programming is state-answer-oriented. It
stores a reusable fact, then performs a second pass to reconstruct an
output consistent with that fact.

This gives the central test:

1. Write everything the future is allowed to observe.
2. Form a key from exactly that information.
3. Find two distinct histories with the same key.
4. Prove their legal suffixes and suffix values are identical.

If step 4 fails, merging is incorrect. If distinct histories rarely
share a key, caching may add memory without avoiding much work.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use the five-vertex graph from the implementation owner. Its edges
are:

```text
0-1  0-2  1-2  1-3  3-4
```

The sorted neighbor view is:

```text
0: 1,2
1: 0,2,3
2: 0,1
3: 1,4
4: 3
```

Both methods must return:

```text
[0,2,1,3,4]
```

That is the lexicographically smallest Hamiltonian path.

###### Backtracking route

Initial state: the path is empty and every vertex is unused. Starts
and neighbors are tried in ascending order.

1. Decision: start at 0, append 1, then append 2.
   After: path `[0,1,2]`; vertices 0, 1, and 2 are used.
   Known correct: every adjacent unused choice smaller than 2 has
   already been considered at its frame.
2. Decision: vertex 2 has no unused neighbor. Remove 2.
   After: path `[0,1]`; only 0 and 1 remain marked used.
   Known correct: no Hamiltonian path begins with `[0,1,2]`.
3. Decision: from 1, append 3, then append 4.
   After: path `[0,1,3,4]`; vertex 2 remains unused.
   Known correct: the prefix is simple, but it is not yet complete.
4. Decision: vertex 4 has no unused neighbor. Remove 4, then 3,
   and finally 1 as their frames exhaust their choices.
   After: path `[0]`; only vertex 0 is marked used.
   Known correct: no complete path begins with `[0,1]`.
5. Decision: append 2, then 1, then 3, then 4.
   After: path `[0,2,1,3,4]`; all five vertices are used.
   Known correct: every consecutive pair is an edge and no vertex
   appears twice.
6. Decision: return immediately on the first complete path.
   After: the returned path is `[0,2,1,3,4]`.
   Known correct: ascending depth-first choices exhausted every
   smaller sequence before accepting this one.

This input is friendly to backtracking. It finds the answer from the
first start and stops before exploring every possible start. Its
early exit prevents some potential repeated states from being
visited at all.

###### Dynamic-programming route

Let bit `v` record whether vertex `v` is visited. The full mask is
`11111`. A full-mask state is true because no vertex remains to be
added.

1. Decision: initialize every `canFinish[11111][last]` entry for a
   valid last vertex to true.
   After: each complete state has a successful empty suffix.
   Known correct: a path that already contains every vertex needs no
   further choice.
2. Decision: process smaller masks in descending numeric order. For
   each state, try every unused neighbor of `last`.
   After: a state becomes true if at least one successor state is
   true.
   Known correct: appending that successor supplies one legal first
   edge followed by a complete suffix.
3. Decision: consider state `{0,1,2,3},3`. Its only useful unused
   neighbor is 4, and the full state ending at 4 is true.
   After: `canFinish[01111][3]` is true.
   Known correct: suffix `[4]` completes this partial path.
4. Decision: consider state `{0,1,2},1`. Neighbor 3 leads to the
   true state from step 3.
   After: `canFinish[00111][1]` is true.
   Known correct: suffix `[3,4]` works from either legal history that
   reaches this state.
5. Decision: note that histories `[0,2,1]` and `[2,0,1]` both map
   to `(00111,1)`.
   After: the suffix fact is stored once, not once per history.
   Known correct: both histories leave vertices 3 and 4 unused and
   stand at the same last vertex.
6. Decision: reconstruct in ascending order. Start 0 has a true
   state. Candidate next vertex 1 leads to a false suffix, while 2
   leads to a true suffix.
   After: the reconstructed prefix is `[0,2]`.
   Known correct: no smaller next vertex can finish the path.
7. Decision: repeat the same test from each new state. Choose 1,
   then 3, then 4.
   After: reconstruction returns `[0,2,1,3,4]`.
   Known correct: each choice is the smallest successor whose stored
   state proves completion remains possible.

The DP obtains reuse that the tree representation cannot express.
On this particular first-solution input, however, backtracking stops
before it reaches history `[2,0,1]`. Potential overlap is not the
same as overlap actually encountered before an early answer.

Focused no-path case: if vertex 4 is isolated in a graph with other
vertices, backtracking exhausts every legal prefix and restores all
state. The DP leaves every singleton-start state false. Both return
`nil,false,nil`.

Focused empty case: both implementations return a non-nil empty path
without entering a search frame or allocating a nonempty state table.

Focused state-key counterexample: a table indexed only by visited
mask would merge paths ending at different vertices. For visited set
`{0,1,2}`, ending at 1 permits edge `1-3`; ending at 2 does not. The
last vertex is indispensable.

##### Implementation

[B.27.2 Hamiltonian paths](
#b272-hamiltonian-paths-backtracking-or-bitmask-dp) owns both complete
Go implementations, their shared validator, executable examples, and
exact output. Keeping one implementation owner prevents this
comparison lesson from drifting into a second contract.

The backtracking implementation maintains:

- a length-N path buffer;
- a used-vertex Boolean slice;
- the current depth; and
- a recursive function that tries candidates, marks, recurses, and
  restores.

The bitmask-DP implementation maintains:

- one row for each visited mask;
- one Boolean entry for each possible last vertex;
- a descending-mask fill whose transitions add one vertex; and
- an ascending reconstruction pass for the lexicographic tie rule.

Read the two functions side by side. The adjacency validation and
the output contract are deliberately identical. The meaningful code
difference is whether a suffix result belongs to one path frame or
to a canonical `(mask,last)` state.

A memoized depth-first variant would sit between them. It would keep
the backtracking control flow but cache failed or successful
`(mask,last)` suffix questions. It is dynamic programming because
equivalent states reuse answers, even though recursion drives it.

Do not memoize a result under a partial key. If pruning also depends
on a budget, score, remaining capacity, or another constraint, that
quantity must be in the key unless it can be proved irrelevant to all
future choices and values.

##### Why it works

For backtracking, maintain this frame invariant: `path[0:depth]` is
a simple graph path, and `used[v]` is true exactly for vertices in
that prefix. The root satisfies it with an empty prefix. A child is
created only from an adjacent unused vertex, so appending preserves
the invariant. Marking before recursion and unmarking after return
makes every sibling start from the exact parent state.

If the depth reaches N, the invariant proves the prefix visits every
vertex exactly once and uses only graph edges. Thus every accepted
path is sound. Conversely, the candidate loops try every unused
neighbor at every prefix and every start vertex, so every Hamiltonian
path appears in the search tree. Ascending candidate order plus
depth-first traversal makes the first accepted sequence the
lexicographically smallest one.

For DP, define `F(mask,last)` as true exactly when a simple path whose
visited set is `mask` and whose final vertex is `last` can be extended
to visit every remaining vertex once. The full-mask base is true.
For a smaller mask, the recurrence is:

```text
F(mask,last) is true if an unused neighbor next has
F(mask with next,last=next) equal to true
```

Every transition adds one bit, so it moves to a strictly larger mask.
Descending mask order therefore computes every required successor
before its predecessor. Induction on the number of unvisited
vertices proves the table's meaning.

Reconstruction preserves this invariant: the current prefix is
simple, and its table state is true. At least one candidate must lead
to a true successor. Choosing the smallest such candidate preserves
feasibility and fixes the smallest possible next sequence element.
Repeating this argument returns the lexicographically smallest path.

The comparison rests on state equivalence. If two histories have the
same complete key, the recurrence exposes the same legal successors
and the same suffix result. Reusing one answer is therefore safe. If
the key omits future-relevant information, that proof collapses and
DP can discard a necessary history.

Both methods terminate. Backtracking increases depth on every
recursive call and never exceeds N. DP transitions add one previously
clear bit and cannot move beyond the full mask. All loops have bounds
derived from the validated vertex count.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the vertex count. Both implementations first validate all
N squared matrix entries, so even the empty search work is preceded
by `Theta(N^2)` validation for positive N.

The backtracker visits path prefixes. At each nonterminal frame it
may test N candidate vertices. On a favorable graph, it follows an
early successful route and uses `O(N^2)` search time after validation.
In the worst case it examines factorially many ordered prefixes, for
an `O(N*N!)` bound. Its exact time is instance-sensitive: candidate
order, dead ends, pruning, and early success all matter.

The DP has N possible last vertices for each of `2^N` masks and may
test N next vertices per valid state. Its worst-case time is
`Theta(N^2*2^N)`. The dense table has `Theta(N*2^N)` entries, so even
when many transitions fail, initialization and scanning do not gain
the backtracker's early-exit behavior.

The backtracker uses `Theta(N)` auxiliary space for its path, used
set, and recursion stack. The DP uses `Theta(N*2^N)` auxiliary space
for suffix feasibility. Both return a `Theta(N)` path on success.

These formulas do not create a universal crossover point. For the
walkthrough graph, backtracking returns quickly while the DP pays for
its table. For a dense or adversarial no-path graph, many distinct
histories may collapse into far fewer `(mask,last)` states, making
reuse valuable. Measure reachable states and repeated keys, not only
N.

Memoized DFS can avoid allocating unreachable states, but each cached
state still needs its key and value. Tabulation has predictable order
and compact indexing. Backtracking has the smallest retained state
and can stream or stop early, but its runtime can vary sharply across
inputs of the same size.

If the contract asks to enumerate all paths, output alone may be
factorial. A Boolean DP can answer feasibility or guide generation,
but it cannot avoid writing every requested path. If the contract
asks only for a count, optimum, or existence result, state merging
can remove much more duplicated work.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Decide the output before choosing the method. Feasibility,
  counting, one witness, the smallest witness, and all witnesses have
  different storage and stopping rules.
- Treat empty input according to the contract. Here it has one empty
  path representation, not a no-solution result.
- A valid graph may have no Hamiltonian path. Do not turn exhaustive
  failure into a validation error.
- A singleton graph succeeds with path `[0]`; no edge is required.
- Backtracking must undo every mutation on every failed branch. A
  leaked used mark silently removes valid siblings.
- Early return is correct for one ordered witness, but not for a
  count or complete enumeration.
- Prune only with a proof. A heuristic that merely looks unlikely can
  remove the only valid completion.
- A DP key must include the last vertex. The visited set alone does
  not determine the next legal graph edges.
- Include every budget, bound, parity, mode, or resource that can
  change the future. Equal-looking partial outputs are not
  necessarily equivalent states.
- Do not include irrelevant history in a DP key. Doing so prevents
  equivalent states from merging and recreates the search tree in a
  table.
- Give the base state its mathematical identity. A full visited mask
  has one successful empty suffix for feasibility.
- Fill or memoize dependencies before using them. A false zero value
  can mean either "computed impossible" or "not computed" unless the
  representation distinguishes those states.
- Reconstruction needs the same tie rule as the contract. A correct
  feasibility table can still produce a nonminimal witness.
- Do not call every recursive solution backtracking. Recursion with a
  reusable state cache is top-down dynamic programming.
- Do not call every table dynamic programming. A table that stores
  one entry per full history performs no state merging.
- Validate size before shifting by N or allocating `2^N` states.
- Account for the caller-owned matrix separately from auxiliary
  memory, and account for the returned path as output space.
- Independent calls are safe only while callers do not mutate shared
  input concurrently.

##### When to choose it

Choose backtracking when:

- the output is a path, arrangement, or enumeration built directly
  from choices;
- constraints reject most prefixes early;
- one early witness is enough and candidate order is useful;
- equivalent suffix states are rare or expensive to identify; or
- linear retained memory is important.

Choose dynamic programming when:

- a compact key captures everything the future can observe;
- many different histories reach the same key;
- only feasibility, a count, an optimum, or one reconstructable
  witness is required;
- the state space and table memory fit the limits; and
- a predictable bound is preferable to instance-sensitive search.

Choose memoized backtracking when the state graph is sparse or hard
to order bottom up, but repeated suffix questions still occur. It
keeps demand-driven recursion while gaining DP reuse.

Before deciding, write down:

1. the exact output and tie rule;
2. the mutable facts carried by one partial choice history;
3. the smallest complete key that determines the future;
4. the number of reachable histories versus distinct keys;
5. the strength and soundness of available pruning;
6. the memory required per key; and
7. whether early success or full enumeration is required.

If item 3 cannot be proved, use backtracking or enrich the state. If
items 3 and 4 show strong convergence, use DP or memoization. If an
early path is common and a full table is large, backtracking may win
even though equivalent states exist in principle.

The NIST Dictionary defines [backtracking](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/backtrack.html) as trying choices
and returning to a choice point after failure. It defines [dynamic
programming](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/dynamicprog.html) by
reusing cached subproblem solutions instead of recomputing them. Its
[Hamiltonian-path entry](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/hamiltonianPath.html) supplies the
graph term used by the shared example.


#### C.7.4 Greedy versus dynamic programming

##### Problem and contract

Greedy algorithms commit to one local choice and discard its
alternatives. Dynamic programming preserves the best answer for each
complete subproblem state and compares alternatives after their
values are known. The methods can examine the same choices but make
different promises about when a choice becomes permanent.

This lesson compares them on the weighted interval-scheduling contract
owned by [B.17.5 weighted scheduling](
#b175-weighted-scheduling-sorted-slice-and-dp-array). Each job has a
nonempty half-open interval `[start,end)` and a nonnegative `int64`
value. Select mutually compatible jobs with maximum total value and
return their original input indices in scheduled order.

The exact contract includes these observable rules:

- jobs meeting at one end and one start are compatible;
- nil and empty input return value zero and a non-nil empty index
  slice;
- malformed intervals and negative values fail before result
  construction;
- an optimum above `MaxInt64` returns an error instead of wrapping;
- ties skip the current finish-sorted job;
- sorting happens on an owned copy; and
- successful output storage belongs to the caller.

The tempting greedy rule is earliest finish. It is exact when every
job has equal positive value and the objective is maximum count. It
is not exact for this maximum-value contract. The dynamic program is
the correct general solution for the stated job model.

The comparison therefore has two jobs. First, determine whether a
local choice has an optimum-preserving proof. Second, if it does not,
determine whether complete subproblem answers can be stored and
combined at an affordable cost.

Read [C.5.4 safe greedy choices](
#c54-safe-permanent-choices-for-greedy-algorithms) for the
greedy-choice property. Read [C.5.3 repeated DP subproblems](
#c53-repeated-subproblems-for-dynamic-programming) for complete state
keys. [C.5.7 exchange and optimal substructure](
#c57-exchange-arguments-and-optimal-substructure) owns the proof
construction that connects these two conditions.

##### Mental model

Imagine every decision as a fork between alternatives.

```text
greedy: choose one branch now and erase the others

DP:     give each complete remaining state a name,
        solve each named state, then compare branch values
```

A greedy commitment is safe only if some optimum can be changed to
agree with it without becoming infeasible or worse. This is the
**greedy-choice property**. The proof usually uses an exchange,
cut, stay-ahead, dominance, or canonical-form argument.

For equal-value interval selection, choosing the compatible job that
finishes earliest leaves at least as much future time as any other
first choice. Replacing another optimum's first job with it preserves
both compatibility and job count. The alternatives can be erased.

Weighted scheduling changes what "worse" means. An earlier finish may
leave more time but surrender too much value. Preserving feasibility
is not enough; the exchange must also preserve the objective.

The dynamic program delays that commitment. Sort jobs by finish time
and define:

```text
best[k] = maximum value from the first k sorted jobs

p(j) = number of earlier jobs ending no later than job j starts
```

Read `best[2]=5` as: among the first two finish-sorted jobs, the best
compatible schedule has value 5. Read `p(j)=1` as: if job j is taken,
only the first earlier job lies in its compatible prefix.

For sorted job j, every optimum either skips it or takes it:

```text
skip = best[j]
take = value(j) + best[p(j)]
best[j+1] = max(skip,take)
```

This is **optimal substructure**. Once the outer take-or-skip choice
is fixed, the remaining compatible prefix must itself use an optimal
answer. Otherwise replacing it with a better prefix would improve the
whole schedule.

Greedy also often has optimal substructure. The difference is that a
greedy proof makes one branch safe before evaluating all branches.
DP keeps the branches long enough to compare their complete values.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use these jobs, written as `index:[start,end):value`:

```text
0:[0,2):2  1:[2,4):2  2:[0,4):5
```

The required maximum-value result is value 5 with selected indices
`[2]`. Jobs 0 and 1 are compatible but total only 4.

First apply the tempting earliest-finish greedy rule.

Initial state: jobs are ordered by end, then start, then input index
as 0, 2, 1. The selected list is empty and no free-time boundary
exists.

1. Decision: job 0 finishes first at time 2, so commit to it.
   After: selected indices are `[0]`; the resource is free at 2;
   accumulated value is 2.
   Known correct: the schedule is feasible, but no proof has shown
   that a value optimum can contain job 0.
2. Decision: job 2 starts at 0, before the free boundary 2, so skip
   it.
   After: selection remains `[0]`; value remains 2.
   Known correct: job 2 conflicts with the committed job, but its
   exclusion has not been proved safe for the value objective.
3. Decision: job 1 starts exactly at 2, so append it.
   After: selected indices are `[0,1]`; value is 4; no jobs remain.
   Known correct: the returned jobs are compatible under half-open
   endpoints.
4. Decision: compare the feasible result with job 2 alone.
   After: greedy has value 4, while `[2]` has value 5.
   Known correct: earliest finish is not an exact algorithm for this
   contract; its first commitment erased the optimum.

Now replay the finish-sorted dynamic program on the same input.

Initial state: sorted jobs are again 0, 2, 1. Prefix entry
`best[0]=0`; no later prefix answer or reconstruction choice has been
computed.

1. Decision: job 0 has compatible prefix zero. Take is
   `2+best[0]=2`; skip is `best[0]=0`, so record take.
   After: prefix values are `[0,2]`.
   Known correct: job 0 alone is the best schedule among the first
   sorted-job prefix.
2. Decision: job 2 also has compatible prefix zero because it starts
   at 0. Take is `5+best[0]=5`; skip is `best[1]=2`.
   After: record take; prefix values are `[0,2,5]`.
   Known correct: every schedule among jobs 0 and 2 either takes job
   2 alone or skips it and uses the best earlier prefix.
3. Decision: job 1 starts at 2. Job 0 ends at 2, so
   `p(job 1)=1`.
   Take is `2+best[1]=4`; skip is `best[2]=5`.
   After: record skip; prefix values are `[0,2,5,5]`.
   Known correct: the compatible pair `[0,1]` loses to job 2 alone.
4. Decision: reconstruct from prefix three. Skip job 1, take job 2,
   and jump to prefix zero.
   After: return value 5 and selected indices `[2]`.
   Known correct: the recorded branches reproduce the optimum and
   end at the empty-prefix base state.

The first incorrect greedy decision was not the later rejection of
job 2. It was committing to job 0 without an exchange that preserved
value. Once that decision became permanent, the later scan could not
recover.

Focused equal-value case: change job 2's value to 2. Maximum value is
then equivalent to maximum count. Earliest finish selects jobs 0 and
1 for value 4, while job 2 alone is worth 2. The exchange proof now
preserves the objective.

Focused highest-value counterexample: jobs `[0,2):6`, `[2,4):6`, and
`[0,4):10` make highest-value-first select 10, while the compatible
pair is worth 12. Replacing one unsupported local rule with another
does not establish greedy correctness.

Focused empty case: the DP returns value zero and an owned empty
selection. No prefix transition or reconstruction step runs.

Focused invalid case: `[3,3):7` is an empty half-open interval. The
owner rejects it before sorting or allocating DP state. This is an
input failure, unlike a valid batch whose best schedule is empty.

##### Implementation

Two existing entries own the executable material:

- [B.17.2 interval selection](
  #b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) implements earliest-finish
  greedy for the maximum-count contract.
- [B.17.5 weighted scheduling](
  #b175-weighted-scheduling-sorted-slice-and-dp-array) implements the
  finish-sorted take-or-skip DP for this maximum-value contract.

Do not deploy the first function as a weighted optimizer. Its code is
correct for its own objective, validation, and tie policy. Summing the
values of its selected indices would produce a feasible schedule, but
the walkthrough proves that result need not be optimal.

The weighted owner performs four phases:

1. validate interval shape, nonnegative values, and numeric rules;
2. copy and sort jobs while retaining original input identity;
3. compute compatible prefixes and `best` take-or-skip entries; and
4. follow recorded choices backward, then reverse the selected IDs.

That owner is also the executable reference for the walkthrough. The
three jobs can be passed directly as `weightedJob` values; it returns
value 5 and selected indices `[2]` without mutating the input.

The selection question belongs before implementation:

```text
Can one candidate be proved safe for some optimum now?
    yes -> commit greedily and solve the reduced instance
    no  -> retain complete states and compare required branches
```

This is not executable pseudocode. It is a proof gate. A failure to
prove one proposed greedy rule does not prove that no other greedy
algorithm exists, but it does forbid presenting that rule as exact.

##### Why it works

The counterexample disproves earliest-finish greedy for weighted
scheduling. Job 0 is the unique earliest finisher. Every schedule
containing it has value at most 4 on this input, while job 2 alone has
value 5. Therefore no optimum contains the first greedy choice. The
required greedy-choice statement is false at the root.

For the DP, sorting by finish time makes every earlier job compatible
with current job j occupy one prefix. A job before boundary `p(j)`
ends no later than j starts. A job after that boundary ends later than
j starts and, because it also begins before its own end, overlaps j.

Maintain this invariant after computing prefix length k:

```text
best[k] is the maximum value of a compatible schedule drawn from
the first k finish-sorted jobs
```

The empty prefix establishes `best[0]=0`. Consider the last job j in
the next prefix. Every compatible schedule either excludes j or
includes j; the cases are disjoint and exhaustive.

If it excludes j, its value is at most `best[j]`. If it includes j,
all other chosen jobs lie in compatible prefix `p(j)`. Replacing those
jobs with `best[p(j)]` cannot reduce feasibility and can only improve
value. The best include-j value is therefore exactly take. Selecting
the larger of take and skip preserves the invariant.

At the full prefix, the invariant gives the required maximum value.
Recorded choices reproduce that value. A skip decrements the prefix;
a take records j and jumps to its strictly smaller compatible prefix.
Those jumps preserve compatibility and eventually reach prefix zero.

This establishes the general distinction. A greedy proof must show
that all erased alternatives are unnecessary. A DP proof must show
that its states are complete, its branches are exhaustive, and its
dependencies already contain correct smaller answers.

Both methods terminate on finite jobs. The greedy scan consumes one
sorted job per step. The DP fill advances one prefix per step, and
reconstruction moves to a strictly smaller prefix on every step.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the number of jobs and K the number returned. Both owners
validate N jobs and sort an owned indexed copy. With comparison
sorting, that preparation takes O(N log N) time and O(N) owned entry
storage.

After sorting, earliest-finish greedy scans once in `Theta(N)` time
and retains only a free-time boundary besides its output. Because the
owner preserves caller input, its ordered copy still makes total
auxiliary storage O(N). Its selected-index slice has K logical items
but may retain capacity N.

The weighted DP performs one O(log N) compatible-prefix search per
job, fills N prefix entries, and reconstructs in O(N) worst-case
time. Its conventional total is O(N log N). Ordered entries, prefix
values, choices, and compatible-prefix indexes use O(N) auxiliary
space; output uses O(K).

The end-to-end asymptotic time is therefore the same for these two
owners. That does not make the greedy result acceptable for weighted
jobs. Complexity compares correct algorithms for one contract; it
cannot repair a failed optimality proof.

If jobs already have the exact required order, the greedy scan is
Theta(N). If compatible prefixes are also available, the DP fill is
Theta(N). DP still retains alternative subproblem values and
reconstruction choices that a proved greedy commitment can omit.

Across other problems, neither family has one universal bound. A
greedy algorithm may need sorting or a heap. A DP may have a linear,
quadratic, pseudopolynomial, or exponential state graph. Define the
state and transition count instead of calling DP inherently slow.

Likewise, greedy is not inherently correct or approximate. Under a
valid exchange proof it is exact. Without one it may be a heuristic,
and its approximation quality requires a separate bound.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- State the objective before the local rule. Earliest finish solves
  maximum count here, not arbitrary maximum value.
- Do not treat feasibility as optimality. Greedy's `[0,1]` schedule
  is compatible and still loses to `[2]`.
- Preserve the objective in an exchange. Replacing job 2 with job 0
  leaves more time but lowers value from 5 to 2.
- A failed greedy rule is not evidence that every greedy rule fails.
  Search for a proof or a counterexample for each proposed rule.
- A few passing examples are not a greedy proof. The equal-value case
  passes because it adds an assumption absent from the main contract.
- Do not infer DP merely because greedy failed. A useful DP still
  needs a complete state, optimal substructure, progress, and
  affordable state count.
- Do not infer greedy from optimal substructure. Weighted scheduling
  has optimal substructure but must compare take and skip.
- Make DP branches exhaustive. Every schedule either contains the
  current job or does not. Omitting either branch can miss the
  optimum.
- Keep endpoint semantics consistent. `[0,2)` and `[2,4)` are
  compatible; closed intervals would require another boundary rule.
- Preserve original indices through sorting. The state uses sorted
  positions while the caller expects input identities.
- Distinguish a job index from a prefix length. One compatible job
  means read `best[1]`, not an entry labeled by input index 0.
- Define tie behavior. Equal take and skip values are both optimal,
  but returned identities still need a deterministic policy.
- Treat zero values deliberately. Under the owner's skip-on-tie rule,
  an all-zero batch returns the empty schedule.
- Check addition before overflow. Wrapped signed values can make a
  valid high-value take branch appear worse than skip.
- Empty valid input and malformed input are different. The first
  returns an owned empty success; the second fails before allocation.
- Do not compare memory while ignoring output. Returning K identities
  requires O(K) output storage for either family.
- Do not describe a local heuristic as an exact greedy algorithm.
  State its guarantee, including "none," when no proof is known.

##### When to choose it

Choose greedy when all of these are true:

- the exact local rule is defined;
- the choice is feasible now;
- an exchange, stay-ahead, cut, dominance, or canonical-form proof
  places that choice in some optimum;
- the remainder has the same problem form; and
- a bounded measure decreases after every commitment.

Choose dynamic programming when:

- the objective decomposes after a finite outer choice;
- a complete state captures every fact affecting the remainder;
- the branches cover all valid solutions;
- state dependencies progress toward known bases;
- different histories reuse states or tabulation order is useful;
  and
- the number and size of states and transitions fit the limits.

Use this decision sequence:

1. Write the exact objective, output, and tie rule.
2. Propose a local choice and try to exchange it into any optimum.
3. Search for the smallest counterexample at the proof boundary.
4. If the proof holds, prefer the simpler exact greedy method.
5. If it fails, define take-or-skip or other complete DP states.
6. Count states, transitions, retained history, and output.
7. If DP is unaffordable, consider search, flow, approximation, or a
   problem-specific algorithm rather than using an unproved greedy
   answer.

Equal-value interval selection, Huffman coding, and minimum spanning
trees have problem-specific greedy proofs. Weighted scheduling and
zero-one knapsack retain competing subproblem values. Fractional
knapsack permits a density exchange because items are divisible;
atomic zero-one items invalidate that exchange.

Greedy and DP can also coexist. A proof may greedily remove dominated
choices before a DP, while a DP table may guide a greedy-looking
reconstruction that chooses the smallest successor preserving an
optimal value. Classify the step by its proof and stored state, not by
whether its loop looks simple.

Use [B.17.2 interval selection](
#b172-interval-selection-sorted-slice) for the exact equal-value
greedy owner and [B.17.5 weighted scheduling](
#b175-weighted-scheduling-sorted-slice-and-dp-array) for the weighted
DP owner. [C.5.7 exchange and optimal substructure](
#c57-exchange-arguments-and-optimal-substructure) develops the proof
templates in more depth.

MIT OpenCourseWare's [6.046J materials](
https://ocw.mit.edu/6-046JS15) derive earliest-finish interval
selection and show why weighted intervals require retained
subproblem values. NIST defines a [greedy algorithm](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/greedyalgo.html) by immediate local
choices and [dynamic programming](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/dynamicprog.html) by reuse of stored
subproblem answers.


#### C.7.5 BFS versus Dijkstra versus Bellman-Ford

##### Problem and contract

Breadth-first search, Dijkstra, and Bellman-Ford all propagate route
information from one source. They differ in which edge weights they
accept, when a tentative distance becomes final, and whether a
reachable negative cycle can be reported.

The common mathematical question is single-source shortest path in a
finite directed graph. A path cost is the sum of its edge weights.
For every vertex, determine whether it is unreachable, has a finite
minimum cost, or has no finite lower bound because a reachable
negative cycle can lead to it.

The least general correct method depends on the weight contract:

- equal positive edge costs permit ordinary BFS;
- arbitrary nonnegative costs permit Dijkstra; and
- signed costs in a cyclic graph require Bellman-Ford among these
  three methods.

The repository owners expose intentionally different APIs:

- [B.13.1 unweighted BFS](
  #b131-unweighted-bfs-queue-and-distance-array) returns one
  minimum-edge target path;
- [B.13.3 Dijkstra](
  #b133-dijkstra-heap-or-scan-distance-array) returns all minimum
  nonnegative `int64` costs; and
- [B.13.4 Bellman-Ford](
  #b134-bellman-ford-edge-list-and-distance-array) returns distance,
  reachability, and negative-infinity arrays.

Those output differences matter. Dijkstra's owner does not reconstruct
paths, and BFS's owner does not classify negative infinity. Choose by
both the mathematical input and the required observable result.

All three owners validate the source and every endpoint before
returning results. They accept directed cycles, self-loops, parallel
edges, and isolated vertices within their weight contracts. They read
but do not mutate or retain caller input. Dijkstra rejects negative
weights. Bellman-Ford checks both signed overflow directions.

Read [C.3.3 directed edges, weights, and cycles](
#c33-directed-edges-weights-and-cycles) for the broader method tree.
Read [C.6.1 next-item policy](
#c61-depth-first-breadth-first-cheapest-or-dependency-ready) for the
difference between FIFO discovery and minimum-cost settlement.

##### Mental model

All three methods repeatedly apply the same local possibility:

```text
route to u + edge u -> v may improve the known route to v
```

The update is **relaxation**. If the current route to `u` costs D and
edge `u -> v` weighs W, candidate cost is `D+W`. Store it when v is
unreachable or the candidate is smaller.

What changes is the schedule for those relaxations.

```text
BFS:
  every edge adds one layer
  FIFO order makes first discovery final

Dijkstra:
  every edge adds a nonnegative amount
  minimum tentative cost makes settlement final

Bellman-Ford:
  an edge may subtract cost
  scan every edge repeatedly; do not settle early
```

For BFS, `distance[v]=2` means the first discovered route from the
source to v uses two edges. A queue contains discovered vertices in
nondecreasing edge distance. With equal positive edge cost C, fewest
edges also minimizes `C * distance`.

For Dijkstra, `distance[v]=7` means seven is the cheapest route cost
known so far. The value is tentative until v is selected as the
smallest unsettled distance. Nonnegative future edges make that
selection irreversible.

For Bellman-Ford, a finite label is only the best cost found by the
completed relaxation passes. Pass k guarantees every path using at
most k edges has had its final edge considered. A later pass may still
improve the label.

Bellman-Ford also distinguishes a path from a walk. A simple finite
path uses at most `V-1` edges. If an improvement remains after those
passes, some reachable negative cycle can reduce cost again. Every
vertex reachable from such a cycle has negative-infinity cost rather
than a finite shortest path.

The methods form a generality ladder, not a speed ranking:

```text
unit weights      -> FIFO layers are enough
nonnegative       -> minimum tentative cost is enough
signed and cyclic -> repeated relaxation is necessary
```

A more general method can solve some restricted inputs, but it usually
does extra work and may expose a different output contract.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use one directed topology with source S at vertex 0 and target T at
vertex 3:

```text
0 S -> 1 A
0 S -> 2 B
1 A -> 3 T
2 B -> 1 A
2 B -> 3 T
```

Adjacency row 0 lists A before B. Change only the weights and replay
the algorithm selected by each contract.

###### Unit-weight BFS

Give every edge weight one. The required target result is distance
two and path `[S,A,T]`, or `[0,1,3]`.

Initial state: queue `[S]`; S has distance zero; every other vertex
is undiscovered.

1. Decision: dequeue S. Discover A, then B, at distance one and
   enqueue them in row order.
   After: pending queue is `[A,B]`; distances include `A:1, B:1`.
   Known correct: every one-edge destination is known, and no later
   discovery can have distance below one.
2. Decision: dequeue A. Discover T through `A -> T`, assign distance
   two and parent A.
   After: the parent chain is `T <- A <- S`; B remains pending.
   Known correct: every possible one-edge predecessor was already
   discovered in the earlier layer, so T cannot have distance one.
3. Decision: stop on target discovery and reconstruct backward.
   After: return distance two and path `[S,A,T]`.
   Known correct: FIFO layers make first discovery minimum; B cannot
   later produce a shorter path.

Dijkstra would return the same numeric costs, and Bellman-Ford would
also converge. Neither is needed because FIFO order already represents
the exact cost order.

###### Nonnegative Dijkstra

Use these weights on the same arcs:

```text
S -> A: 8   S -> B: 2   A -> T: 2
B -> A: 1   B -> T: 9
```

The required all-vertex costs are `S:0, A:3, B:2, T:5`. The cheapest
target route is `S -> B -> A -> T`, even though it uses three edges.

Initial state: S has tentative cost zero. Every other vertex is
unreachable. The minimum frontier contains only S.

1. Decision: settle S at zero. Relax its row, assigning A cost eight
   and B cost two.
   After: tentative frontier is `B:2, A:8`.
   Known correct: S is final, and B is the smallest known unsettled
   route despite appearing second in S's row.
2. Decision: settle B at two. Relax `B -> A` to three and `B -> T`
   to eleven.
   After: frontier is `A:3, T:11`.
   Known correct: the cost-three route improves A before A is settled.
3. Decision: settle A at three. Edge `A -> T` improves T from eleven
   to five.
   After: frontier is `T:5`; costs are `S:0, A:3, B:2, T:5`.
   Known correct: every finite label is a real route, and T remains
   tentative until selected.
4. Decision: settle T at five. No unsettled reachable vertex remains.
   After: return `[0,3,2,5]` in vertex order.
   Known correct: nonnegative edges prevent any later route from
   lowering a settled cost.

Ordinary BFS instead discovers T through `S -> A -> T` in two edges.
That route costs ten. Its first wrong decision is treating two edges
as cheaper than the three-edge route costing five.

###### Signed Bellman-Ford

Keep the topology but use these weights and this edge-list order:

```text
B -> A: -10
A -> T: 2
S -> B: 5
S -> A: 2
B -> T: 1
```

There is no directed cycle. The required states are finite costs
`S:0, A:-5, B:5, T:-3`.

Initial state: labels are `[0,x,x,x]`, where `x` means unreachable.

1. Decision: scan all five edges. The first two sources are not yet
   reachable. Later edges assign B cost five, A cost two, and T cost
   six from B.
   After: pass one ends at `[0,2,5,6]`.
   Known correct: every one-edge route from S has been considered;
   edge order has delayed routes that begin through B.
2. Decision: scan again. `B -> A` improves A from two to -5. The next
   edge immediately improves T from six to -3.
   After: pass two ends at `[0,-5,5,-3]`.
   Known correct: the route `S -> B -> A -> T` has three edges and
   cost -3.
3. Decision: scan a third time. No edge improves any label.
   After: stop early; the detection scan also finds no improvement.
   Known correct: another identical pass cannot create a new route,
   and no reachable negative cycle makes a finite label unstable.

If Dijkstra accepted this input, it could settle A at cost two, then
T at cost four, before processing B at cost five. The later negative
edge would improve the already settled A to -5. The owner's validator
rejects the negative edge instead of returning that invalid result.

Focused negative-cycle case: add edge `A -> B` with weight one. Cycle
`B -> A -> B` weighs -9 and is reachable from S. A, B, and T then
have negative-infinity costs. S remains finite because the cycle
cannot return to it.

Focused unreachable case: add isolated vertex 4. BFS and Dijkstra use
their documented unreachable markers. Bellman-Ford leaves its
reachability flag false; its numeric cell is not meaningful.

Focused zero-weight case: ordinary BFS cannot minimize total cost
when some edges cost zero. Use 0-1 BFS when every weight is zero or
one, rather than paying for a general heap.

Focused invalid case: an edge to vertex 4 in a four-vertex graph is
rejected before any owner indexes result storage.

##### Implementation

Use the owner matching both weight promises and output needs:

- `shortestUnweightedPath` in [B.13.1 BFS](
  #b131-unweighted-bfs-queue-and-distance-array) uses an adjacency
  list, returns one target path, and stops on safe discovery.
- `dijkstraWithHeap` and `dijkstraWithScan` in [B.13.3 Dijkstra](
  #b133-dijkstra-heap-or-scan-distance-array) use weighted adjacency
  rows and return all numeric distances.
- `bellmanFord` in [B.13.4 Bellman-Ford](
  #b134-bellman-ford-edge-list-and-distance-array) uses an edge list
  and returns all three per-vertex states.

The walkthrough uses the same vertex numbering and directed edges as
those owners. The representation changes because a plain BFS row does
not store weights, while Bellman-Ford benefits from repeated whole
edge-list scans. Convert deliberately; do not infer isolated vertices
from an edge list without its explicit vertex count.

The Dijkstra owner rejects negative weights during full validation.
The Bellman-Ford owner permits every `int64` edge weight and uses
separate reachability and negative-infinity flags, so no numeric
sentinel collides with a valid finite cost.

To make all three APIs return paths, add parent storage under each
owner's tie and failure rules. For Bellman-Ford, never return a
shortest parent path for a negative-infinity destination because no
finite optimum exists.

This comparison adds no duplicate Go implementation. The linked
owners contain the complete programs, validation, overflow handling,
early-exit rules, and executable boundary cases.

##### Why it works

BFS maintains discovered vertices in nondecreasing edge distance.
When a distance-D vertex leaves the queue, every new neighbor receives
distance `D+1` behind all pending vertices from earlier layers. If a
new neighbor had a shorter route, its predecessor would have left an
earlier layer and discovered it first. Thus first discovery is final
when every edge has the same positive cost.

Dijkstra maintains that every finite tentative value is a real route
cost and every settled value is minimum. Suppose the smallest
tentative vertex v had a cheaper route. The first unsettled vertex on
that route has a settled predecessor, so relaxation gave it a label
no greater than the corresponding route prefix. Nonnegative remaining
edges make that prefix no greater than the alleged cheaper route. This
contradicts v being the smallest tentative choice.

Bellman-Ford maintains that after pass k, each label is no greater
than any path cost using at most k edges. The preceding pass covers a
path's prefix, and the next scan covers its final edge. Any finite
minimum can be represented by a simple path after removing repeated
nonnegative cycles, so at most `V-1` passes cover it.

If an edge can still improve afterward, the improving walk beats every
simple path and must contain a reachable negative cycle. Conversely,
some edge of every reachable negative cycle remains relaxable; if not,
summing its non-strict inequalities would claim the cycle weight is
nonnegative. Forward propagation marks exactly its affected
descendants.

Each method terminates for a finite validated graph. BFS discovers a
vertex once. Dijkstra settles a vertex once, while lazy stale records
are bounded by strict relaxations. Bellman-Ford performs bounded main
and propagation passes, each over a finite edge list.

The proofs expose the selection boundary:

```text
equal cost:       queue layer proves finality
nonnegative cost: smallest tentative value proves finality
negative allowed: no local settlement proof; repeat global scans
```

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be the vertex count and A the number of directed edge
occurrences. Let R be reachable vertices and `A_R` entries in their
adjacency rows.

The BFS owner validates the whole graph in `Theta(V+A)` time and uses
`Theta(V)` auxiliary arrays. Target discovery can stop search work
early, but validation and initialization keep the documented total at
`Theta(V+A)`. A found path retains `Theta(L+1)` output vertices for
L edges.

Lazy-heap Dijkstra validates in `Theta(V+A)` time. Its worst-case
total is `O((V+A) log(A+2))`; lazy improvements can retain
`O(A_R)` heap records. The returned distance array uses `Theta(V)`
output space. Its scan variant takes `O(VR+A_R)` search time and
`Theta(V)` settled flags, which can suit dense graphs.

Bellman-Ford validates and initializes in `Theta(V+A)` time. Up to
`V-1` main passes, one detection pass, and up to `V-1` propagation
passes give `O(VA+V+A)` worst-case time. A no-change first pass gives
`Theta(V+A)` best-case work. Its three returned arrays use
`Theta(V)` result space, and the edge-scan loops use `O(1)` auxiliary
space beyond them.

No distribution-independent average is useful without assumptions
about topology, weights, reachability, and edge order. Bellman-Ford's
early stopping and Dijkstra's reachable subgraph can change concrete
work without changing their worst-case contracts.

Do not compare these bounds before checking preconditions. BFS is
fastest here only when edge count is the required cost. Dijkstra's
speed does not justify negative input. Bellman-Ford's generality is
unnecessary when a stronger weight promise enables a cheaper method.

Specialized alternatives can improve further. Zero-one weights use a
deque in `Theta(V+A)`. A DAG uses one topological relaxation pass even
with negative edges. Those structural promises are stronger than the
three-way comparison's general signed cyclic case.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Define what an edge costs. BFS minimizes edge count, not time,
  distance, toll, or another unequal numeric sum.
- Equal positive costs may be divided out and handled by BFS. Do not
  discard unequal weights merely because they are all integers.
- When converting a BFS edge count back to `cost * edges`, check
  multiplication before claiming the numeric result fits its type.
- Zero and one weights call for 0-1 BFS. Ordinary FIFO layers do not
  order zero-cost moves before cost-one moves.
- Dijkstra permits zero-weight edges and cycles. Strict improvement
  prevents equal-cost loops from producing endless heap entries.
- Reject every negative edge before Dijkstra runs. One later negative
  relaxation can invalidate a settled vertex without forming a
  negative cycle.
- A negative edge does not itself mean negative infinity. The signed
  walkthrough has finite answers because it has no cycle.
- A directed cycle is not necessarily negative. Positive cycles are
  valid for Dijkstra when all edges remain nonnegative.
- Ignore an unreachable negative cycle. It cannot affect routes from
  the selected source.
- After finding a reachable negative cycle, mark only the cycle and
  its reachable descendants. Unrelated finite branches stay valid.
- Do not represent unreachable or negative infinity with an `int64`
  value when every `int64` can be a finite answer. Use separate flags.
- Stop BFS when the target is discovered only under equal-cost FIFO
  layers. Stop Dijkstra only when the target is settled, not first
  relaxed.
- Bellman-Ford may need all `V-1` passes when edge order opposes the
  shortest path. A quiet prefix is not a quiet complete pass.
- Use strict relaxation. Equal candidates do not create a shorter
  path and should not prolong work or replace deterministic parents.
- Check addition before it executes. Dijkstra needs positive overflow
  checks; Bellman-Ford also needs negative underflow checks.
- Preserve parallel edges unless another contract proves that keeping
  only one is safe. Different weights may change the minimum.
- Self-loops are valid. A reachable negative self-loop makes its
  vertex and every descendant negative infinity.
- An empty graph has no valid source under these owners. An isolated
  valid source has cost zero while all other vertices are unreachable.
