- Concurrent input mutation can invalidate validation and later scans.
  Synchronize or snapshot shared graphs.

##### When to choose it

Choose ordinary BFS when the objective is minimum edge count or every
edge has the same positive cost. Its FIFO frontier is the cheapest
correct ordering for that promise.

Choose Dijkstra when costs are additive and every edge is
nonnegative. Use a heap for sparse graphs or a reachable subgraph, and
consider the scan form for a modest dense graph.

Choose Bellman-Ford when negative edges are allowed, the graph may
contain cycles, reachable negative-cycle effects matter, and `V*A`
work fits the constraints.

Before choosing, ask:

1. Is the objective fewest edges or minimum additive weight?
2. Are all weights equal, zero-one, nonnegative, or signed?
3. Is the graph acyclic even if some weights are negative?
4. Does the result need one target path, all distances, or explicit
   negative-infinity states?
5. When is a discovered or tentative value proved final?
6. Can path sums overflow the chosen numeric type?
7. Is this one source, one target, many sources, or all pairs?

Use 0-1 BFS for binary weights and DAG relaxation for an acyclic
weighted graph. Use A* for one target when a proved admissible
heuristic is available. For many sources, compare repeated Dijkstra,
Johnson's algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall against graph density and
weight rules.

The NIST Dictionary defines [breadth-first search](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/breadthfirst.html) and the
[Bellman-Ford algorithm](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/bellmanford.html). Dijkstra's
original [shortest-path paper](
https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390) gives the classic
minimum-selection method. Bellman's [routing paper](
https://doi.org/10.1090/qam/102435) develops the repeated routing
recurrence.


#### C.7.6 Heap versus sorting versus quickselect

##### Problem and contract

Sorting, a size-K heap, and Quickselect can all help answer ranking
questions over a finite collection. They do not produce the same
information, use the same memory, or accept the same arrival model.

Use this comparison contract. Given a finite `[]int64` and an integer
K, return the largest K values in descending order. Duplicate values
occupy separate positions. K may range from zero through the input
length. An invalid K returns an error. The input must remain
unchanged, and the returned slice owns its storage.

All three methods can meet that contract, but by different routes:

- sorting orders all N values, then reads the K values at the required
  extreme;
- a size-K min-heap retains only the largest K values seen so far;
  and
- Quickselect finds the boundary at ascending rank `N-K`, collects the
  values above that boundary plus enough equal values, then sorts only
  those K selected values for the required descending output.

The last route applies only when `0 < K < N`. K zero has no rank to
select, and K equal to N already requires ordering every output value.

This lesson owns the choice among the methods. The implementations
remain with [comparison sorting](#b31-comparison-sorting-slice),
[top-K selection](#b34-top-k-selection-heap), and
[Quickselect](#b33-quickselect-slice). Read those owners first for
their exact validation, mutation, and allocation contracts. Read
[C.6.2 stacks, queues, heaps, and scans](
#c62-stacks-queues-heaps-and-linear-scans) for the broader distinction
between a partially ordered frontier and complete ordering.

##### Mental model

Ask how much rank information the caller will observe.

```text
sorting:
  prove the relative order of every output pair

size-K heap:
  remember only the K current winners
  expose the weakest winner at the root

Quickselect:
  prove which side of one rank each value belongs on
  leave each side internally unordered
```

A sorted slice answers every rank query. Ordering two values outside
the requested top K may still serve later iteration, binary search,
grouping, or another rank query. Without such later use, that
comparison may establish information the caller never observes.

A size-K min-heap represents a moving cutoff. Once full, its root is
the smallest retained value. A new value at or below the root cannot
enter the current largest K. A larger value replaces the root. The
heap knows the winners as a multiset, but its slice is not sorted.

Quickselect represents a static partition boundary. At ascending rank
`N-K`, values greater than the boundary definitely belong in the
largest K. The boundary's equal band supplies any remaining positions.
Values below it do not belong. None of those regions is internally
ordered.

The distinction is information, not syntax:

```text
need every rank       -> sort
need K retained items -> heap
need one rank boundary -> Quickselect
```

Arrival model changes the decision. Sorting and Quickselect need a
retained batch. A heap can process values one at a time and discard
losers immediately. If K is small relative to N, it also avoids an
N-value working copy.

##### Worked walkthrough

Find the largest three values, in descending order, in:

```text
[5,1,9,3,14,8,2,14]
```

Here N is 8, K is 3, and the required result is `[14,14,9]`.
Replay all three methods against the same input.

###### Full sorting

Initial state: copy the input because the contract preserves caller
order.

1. Decision: sort the copy in ascending order.
   After: the working slice is `[1,2,3,5,8,9,14,14]`.
   Known correct: every earlier value is no greater than every later
   value, so every sorted rank is available.
2. Decision: the largest three occupy indexes 5 through 7. Read that
   suffix from right to left into new output storage.
   After: return `[14,14,9]`.
   Known correct: no value before index 5 can exceed any selected
   value, and reversing the suffix supplies descending order.

Sorting establishes more than this query needs. It also answers the
minimum, median, and every later rank without another rearrangement.

###### Size-three min-heap

Initial state: the retained heap is empty. Braces below show its
multiset because sibling order inside a heap has no global meaning.

1. Decision: retain 5, 1, and 9 while fewer than three values have
   arrived.
   After: retained values are `{1,5,9}`; root 1 is the cutoff.
   Known correct: every processed value is still retained.
2. Decision: 3 exceeds cutoff 1, so replace 1.
   After: retained values are `{3,5,9}`; cutoff is 3.
   Known correct: discarded 1 cannot enter the prefix's largest three.
3. Decision: 14 exceeds cutoff 3, so replace 3.
   After: retained values are `{5,9,14}`; cutoff is 5.
   Known correct: the removed 3 cannot outrank any retained value.
4. Decision: 8 exceeds cutoff 5, so replace 5.
   After: retained values are `{8,9,14}`; cutoff is 8.
   Known correct: these are the prefix's largest three occurrences.
5. Decision: 2 is at most cutoff 8, so discard it.
   After: retained values stay `{8,9,14}`.
   Known correct: all three retained values outrank 2.
6. Decision: the final 14 exceeds cutoff 8, so replace 8.
   After: retained values are `{9,14,14}`; the scan is complete.
   Known correct: these are exactly the full input's largest three
   occurrences.
7. Decision: pop minima 9, 14, and 14 into output positions from right
   to left.
   After: return `[14,14,9]`.
   Known correct: reverse placement turns ascending heap removals into
   the required descending order.

At no point did the heap retain more than three values. A stream could
end after any step and the same invariant would still describe its
answer.

###### Quickselect plus a selected-region sort

The boundary rank is `N-K = 5`, meaning the value at ascending
zero-based rank 5. Use B.3.3's deterministic midpoint-index pivot so
the states are replayable.

Initial state: copy the input. The active range is indexes 0 through
7, and the requested rank is 5.

1. Decision: choose midpoint index 3, whose value is 3, and perform a
   three-way partition.
   After: one valid working state is
   `[2,1,3,14,8,9,14,5]`. The bands are `[0,2) < 3`,
   `[2,3) == 3`, and `[3,8) > 3`.
   Known correct: rank 5 lies in the greater band, so indexes below 3
   never need another comparison with the requested rank.
2. Decision: continue only in indexes 3 through 7. Their midpoint
   index 5 holds 9. Partition that active range around 9.
   After: the working slice is `[2,1,3,5,8,9,14,14]`.
   The active bands are `[3,5) < 9`, `[5,6) == 9`, and
   `[6,8) > 9`.
   Known correct: rank 5 lies in the equal band, so the boundary
   value is 9. The algorithm makes no claim that either outer band is
   sorted.
3. Decision: the owner returns only boundary value 9, not its private
   partition. Scan the original input. Collect both values greater
   than 9, then one occurrence equal to 9 to reach K values.
   After: selected multiset is `{14,14,9}`.
   Known correct: exactly two inputs exceed the rank-5 value, so one
   equal occurrence fills the remaining selected position.
4. Decision: sort only the three selected values in descending order.
   After: return `[14,14,9]`.
   Known correct: boundary selection proves membership; the final
   small sort proves the output-order contract.

Quickselect alone does not meet this top-K contract. It returns one
rank value. The collection scan and selected-region sort are necessary
composition steps because the owner hides its partition and promises
ordered output nowhere.

Focused duplicate boundary: for `[7,7,7,1]` and K equal to two, the
boundary is 7. No value is greater than it, so collect exactly two of
the three equal occurrences. Collecting every boundary-equal value
would return too many items.

Focused zero case: K zero returns a non-nil empty result immediately.
Do not compute rank `N-K`, because rank N is outside the input.

Focused full case: when K equals N, every value must appear in order.
Sorting the complete copy directly avoids a selection pass that cannot
discard any output.

##### Implementation

Use the existing owner whose observable result is closest to the
caller contract:

- [B.3.1 comparison sorting](
  #b31-comparison-sorting-slice) copies and fully orders records by a
  strict comparator. For ordered integers, the analogous route is to
  copy, call `slices.Sort`, and copy the desired suffix in reverse.
- [B.3.4 top-K selection](
  #b34-top-k-selection-heap) already implements this lesson's exact
  largest-K integer contract and returns descending output.
- [B.3.3 Quickselect](#b33-quickselect-slice) copies integer input and
  returns one exact zero-based rank. To produce top K, validate K
  before computing `N-K`, select that boundary, rescan the original,
  take all greater values plus only enough equal values, and sort the
  K collected values.

The [randomized Quickselect owner](
#b315-randomized-quickselect-slice) changes only pivot selection. It
gives expected linear partition work for a fixed input independent of
uniform draws, while retaining a quadratic worst case.

Do not expose B.3.3's private working slice as an undocumented
shortcut. Its contract returns only a value and promises nothing about
the arrangement visible to a caller. An API that returns a partition
would need its own boundary, mutation, and duplicate rules.

For records, define one strict weak ordering before using any method.
The heap root must expose the weakest retained record under that same
ordering. Quickselect's comparisons and final selected-region sort
must also agree with it. If original order among equal keys matters,
include a stable tie rule or use a stable full sort; value-only top-K
selection does not preserve identity.

This comparison adds no duplicate program. The linked owners contain
the complete Go implementations and executable cases.

##### Why it works

Sorting works because its final total-order invariant states that for
all indexes `i < j`, the value at i is no greater than the value at j.
Therefore the suffix beginning at `N-K` contains exactly K
occurrences, and none of the preceding values can outrank one in the
suffix.
Reversing that suffix gives descending order.

The heap maintains a prefix invariant: after reading any prefix, it
contains exactly the largest `min(K,prefix length)` occurrences from
that prefix. Before it fills, retaining every value establishes the
claim. Once full, a value at or below the minimum retained value
cannot enter the largest K. A larger value must enter. Replacing the
minimum removes one weakest retained position. Heap repair
restores the root cutoff after either insertion or replacement.

Quickselect maintains an active-range invariant: the requested rank
lies in the active range, while discarded bands are proved to lie
strictly on the appropriate side or inside an equal band. A three-way
partition around the rank-5 value 9 proves that exactly two
occurrences are greater than the boundary. Every smaller occurrence
is outside the largest three.

More generally, let B be the value at ascending rank `N-K`. Fewer than
K values can be strictly greater than B; otherwise B would have a
higher sorted rank. At least K values are greater than or equal to B;
otherwise B could not occupy rank `N-K`. Taking every value greater
than B and enough copies equal to B therefore produces exactly the
largest-K multiset. Sorting that multiset proves the requested order.

Each method terminates. A comparison sort operates on a finite copy.
The heap scans one finite input and each repair moves through a finite
tree. Every Quickselect partition empties a finite unknown region and
then either returns or discards a nonempty equal band, strictly
shrinking the active range. The collection rescan and K-value sort are
also finite.

Validation must precede rank arithmetic. After proving
`0 <= K <= N`, handle K zero and K equal to N separately. Only then
does `N-K` denote a valid rank for the strict interior case.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the input length and K the requested output length.

Full comparison sorting takes `O(N log N)` time for the owner used
here. Preserving input requires an N-value copy, so working storage is
`O(N)`, plus `O(K)` owned output when the answer must not alias the
copy. It pays once for every rank. Later indexed rank queries then
take `O(1)` each, and ordered scans need no new rearrangement.

For positive K, the size-K heap examines all N values. Its documented
best case is `Theta(N)` and worst case is
`O(N log(K+1))`, including ordered extraction. It uses `O(K)` heap
storage plus `O(K)` result storage. K zero returns in `Theta(1)` time.
The bound is deterministic and does not depend on retaining all N
values.

B.3.3's input-preserving deterministic Quickselect always pays
`Theta(N)` to copy. Balanced partitions take `Theta(N)` total time,
but its fixed midpoint-index pivot has a
`Theta(N squared)` worst case. The randomized policy has expected
`Theta(N)` selection time and the same quadratic worst case. The
boundary rescan adds `Theta(N)`. Ordering the selected region adds
`O(K log K)`.

Thus the randomized composition has expected
`O(N + K log K)` time. It uses `O(N)` working storage under the owner
contract and `O(K)` output storage. An explicitly in-place selector
could reduce partition storage to `O(1)` beyond output, but it would
mutate input and would not implement this lesson's contract.

If only the kth value or an unordered cutoff is required, Quickselect
does not need the `K log K` final sort or K-value output. If K is
tiny, the heap's `N log K` work and K-sized storage are often
attractive. If K is near N, `K log K` approaches full-sort work and
sorting is usually simpler.

For Q independent rank queries on a static collection, sorting once
costs `O(N log N + Q)`. Repeating randomized Quickselect costs
expected `O(QN)` under these owners. Specialized multi-selection can
share partitions, but it is a different algorithm and contract.

Asymptotic bounds do not settle every case. Sorting has mature library
implementations and contiguous access. Heaps perform irregular repairs
and comparisons. Quickselect can have good locality but uncertain
latency. Measure representative N, K, comparison cost, and allocation
limits after choosing a method whose contract is correct.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Validate `0 <= K <= N`. Computing `N-K` first can turn an invalid
  request into a plausible but wrong rank.
- K zero needs no heap, sort, or selection. Return the contract's
  owned empty result without indexing a root or rank.
- K equal to N requires every value. A heap and selected-region sort
  both approach full-sort work without discarding output.
- K one asks only for the maximum value. A linear scan is simpler than
  all three general constructions when no reusable state is needed.
- Duplicate values occupy separate result positions. A set silently
  loses multiplicity.
- At a Quickselect boundary, collect all values greater than B but
  only enough equal values to reach K. Collecting every equal value
  can overfill the result.
- Quickselect returns a rank value, not an ordered top-K slice. Do not
  treat its partition as a sort.
- A heap slice is not sorted. Only its root has a global extreme
  guarantee; use ordered extraction or a final sort for ordered
  output.
- For largest K, use a min-heap so the weakest winner is exposed. A
  max-heap exposes the strongest winner and replaces the wrong item.
- Full sorting may be intentionally unstable. If equal records have
  observable identity, define tie fields or request stable sorting.
- Every method must use the same comparator. Different tie rules in
  selection and final sorting can change membership or order.
- Do not implement a comparator by subtracting signed integers. The
  subtraction can overflow; compare directly.
- A fixed Quickselect pivot can meet adversarial arrangements that
  shrink the active range by one. Expected linear time requires the
  randomized policy and its independence assumptions.
- Randomized expected time is not a deadline. Use a deterministic
  worst-case method when tail latency is part of the contract.
- Sorting and Quickselect need the complete batch under these owners.
  They cannot discard an early loser before knowing the final input.
- A heap supports a stream, but changing K later may require retained
  values that were already discarded. A sorted static copy answers
  many K values without rescanning.
- Preserving input changes memory costs. An in-place sort or selection
  is not a drop-in optimization for an input-preserving API.
- Returning a suffix that aliases working storage can retain all N
  values and lets later mutation change the result. Copy the K
  outputs.
- Concurrent input mutation can invalidate comparisons or the
  collection rescan. Synchronize or snapshot shared data.

##### When to choose it

Choose full sorting when the caller needs complete order, many ranks,
ordered iteration, binary search, or a K close to N. It is also the
simplest reliable default when N fits memory and the extra ordering is
useful or insignificant.

Choose a size-K heap when K values must be retained, K is much smaller
than N, memory should scale with K, or values arrive as a stream. Its
deterministic bound is preferable when randomized tail behavior is not
acceptable.

Choose Quickselect when one rank or partition boundary is the real
answer and a retained batch is available. Compose it with a rescan and
a K-value sort only when that expected
`O(N + K log K)` route is preferable to the heap's deterministic
`O(N log(K+1))` route and the full sort's `O(N log N)` route.

Before choosing, ask:

1. Does the caller need one value, K values, or all values in order?
2. Must the K values themselves be ordered?
3. Is the input a retained batch or a one-pass stream?
4. How large is K relative to N?
5. Will later queries reuse a complete order?
6. Must input order be preserved?
7. Do equal keys have identity or stability requirements?
8. Is expected time acceptable, or is a worst-case bound required?

For repeated updates and rank queries, move beyond these static-batch
methods to an order-statistic tree or another dynamic index. For an
unbounded stream with approximate quantiles, use a streaming summary
rather than retaining every value.

Go's [`slices` documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/slices#Sort) defines
the standard ordered-slice sort, and [`container/heap`](
https://pkg.go.dev/container/heap) defines the root and repair
protocol.
NIST defines the [kth-element selection problem](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/selectkth.html). Hoare's original
[`Algorithm 65: FIND`](https://doi.org/10.1145/366622.366647)
introduced the partition-selection family.


#### C.7.7 Fenwick tree versus segment tree versus sparse table

##### Problem and contract

Fenwick trees, segment trees, and sparse tables all summarize indexed
ranges. Choosing among them requires more than noticing the words
"range query." The update pattern, aggregate operation, query latency,
and memory limit determine which summaries can remain correct.

This comparison uses a fixed, dense `[]int64` with zero-based,
half-open ranges. It studies three nearby workloads rather than
pretending that the structures expose one interchangeable API:

- a Fenwick tree accepts point additions and answers prefix or range
  sums, including empty ranges;
- a segment tree accepts point replacements and answers nonempty range
  minima; and
- a sparse table is immutable after construction and answers nonempty
  range minima.

The owners preserve caller input, retain private state, and reject
invalid indices or boundaries before lookup or mutation. The Fenwick
owner also checks arithmetic and commits updates atomically. The
minimum owners return errors for empty ranges because their contracts
do not define an empty minimum.

The operation is part of the contract. A Fenwick range sum cancels two
prefix sums by subtraction. Minimum has no corresponding inverse. A
segment tree instead combines disjoint blocks. A standard sparse
table combines two blocks that may overlap. That is safe for minimum
because repeating a value cannot change the answer.

Read [A.12.3 Fenwick trees](#a123-fenwick-trees),
[A.12.4 segment trees](#a124-segment-trees), and
[A.12.5 sparse tables](#a125-sparse-tables) first. Those entries own
the representations and complete programs. The application owners are
[B.6.3 dynamic sums](#b63-point-updates-and-sums-fenwick-tree),
[B.6.4 dynamic minima](
#b64-range-queries-and-updates-segment-tree), and
[B.6.5 static minima](#b65-static-range-minima-sparse-table).

##### Mental model

Ask two questions before choosing storage:

```text
Can values change after construction?
What algebraic rule combines or cancels summaries?
```

A Fenwick tree stores overlapping suffixes of prefixes. Its one-based
cell i summarizes a block ending at i whose width is `lowbit(i)`.
A prefix query walks backward through disjoint stored blocks. A point
addition walks forward through every stored block containing that
point. A general range sum uses this cancellation:

```text
sum(start,end) = prefix(end) - prefix(start)
```

Subtraction is the crucial extra operation. Associativity alone does
not make that formula possible.

A segment tree stores a hierarchy of disjoint child blocks. Each
parent combines its two children. A query decomposes its range into
stored, nonoverlapping blocks and combines their summaries. A point
replacement changes one leaf and repairs its ancestors.

For minimum, read a node storing 2 over `[0,4)` as: "the smallest
current value in indices zero through three is 2." The node does not
record which child supplied 2 unless the contract asks for an index.

A sparse table spends more preprocessing to store every complete
power-of-two block. For a query of length L, it chooses the largest
power B no greater than L. One B-length block starts at the left
boundary and another ends at the right boundary. They cover the query
and may overlap.

Minimum is idempotent: `min(x,x) == x`. Therefore values repeated by
the overlap cannot change the result. Ordinary sum is not idempotent,
so the same two-block rule double-counts overlap.

These algebraic words describe concrete combine behavior:

- associative means regrouping does not change the answer, as in
  `min(min(a,b),c) == min(a,min(b,c))`;
- an identity is a neutral value used for an empty or padded block;
- an inverse removes a combined contribution, as subtraction removes
  an earlier prefix sum; and
- idempotent means combining an answer with itself leaves it
  unchanged.

The decision ladder is:

```text
point updates + invertible prefix aggregate -> Fenwick tree
updates + associative block aggregate       -> segment tree
immutable + overlap-safe aggregate          -> sparse table
```

These are sufficient conditions, not claims that a structure can do
nothing else. Specialized variants exist. Start with the least general
structure whose proof exactly matches the required operations.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use the same initial values for all three methods:

```text
[7,2,6,3,9,1,5]
```

First query half-open range `[1,6)`. Then replace index 5 from 1 with
8 and query `[1,6)` again. For sums, the expected answers are 21 and
28. For minima, the expected answers are 1 and 2.

###### Fenwick tree for dynamic sums

An assignment adapter turns `set(5,8)` into addition
`8 - currentValue = 7`, as B.6.3 requires.

Initial state: the owner copies the values and builds one-based tree
`[0,7,9,6,18,9,10,5]`. Cell 4 stores sum 18 for public range
`[0,4)`, and cell 6 stores sum 10 for `[4,6)`.

1. Decision: query `[1,6)` as `prefix(6) - prefix(1)`.
   Prefix end 6 reads cells 6 and 4, totaling `10 + 18 = 28`.
   Prefix end 1 reads cell 1, totaling 7.
   After: return `28 - 7 = 21`; the tree is unchanged.
   Known correct: the two prefix sums cancel index 0 and leave exactly
   indices 1 through 5.
2. Decision: replace index 5 by deriving addition 7. Public index 5
   maps to internal position 6. Check point value 8 and cell 6 value
   17 before committing.
   After: values are `[7,2,6,3,9,8,5]`; tree is
   `[0,7,9,6,18,9,17,5]`.
   Known correct: cell 6 is the only in-range stored block containing
   index 5; every unrelated block remains valid.
3. Decision: repeat `[1,6)`. Prefix end 6 is now
   `tree[6] + tree[4] = 17 + 18 = 35`; prefix end 1 remains 7.
   After: return `35 - 7 = 28`.
   Known correct: the answer reflects the completed point replacement
   and contains each requested value exactly once.
4. Decision: no operation remains, so stop.
   After: ordered sum answers are `[21,28]`.
   Known correct: every query observed precisely the earlier
   successful updates.

The Fenwick tree cannot use two prefix minima to answer the analogous
minimum request. It is the aggregate, not the array shape, that makes
this representation suitable.

###### Segment tree for dynamic minima

Initial state: seven values use `leafBase = 8`. Relevant nodes store
`node 4 = 2`, `node 5 = 3`, `node 6 = 1`, `node 7 = 5`,
`node 2 = 2`, `node 3 = 1`, and root `node 1 = 1`.

1. Decision: query `[1,6)` with leaf boundaries 9 and 14. Include
   leaf node 9 with value 2, node 5 for `[2,4)` with minimum 3,
   and node 6 for `[4,6)` with minimum 1.
   After: return `min(2,3,1) = 1`.
   Known correct: the three disjoint nodes cover exactly indices 1
   through 5, with no padding or outside value.
2. Decision: replace index 5 by changing leaf 13 from 1 to 8.
   Recompute node 6 as `min(9,8) = 8`, node 3 as
   `min(8,5) = 5`, and root as `min(2,5) = 2`.
   After: values are `[7,2,6,3,9,8,5]`; repaired nodes 6, 3,
   and 1 store 8, 5, and 2.
   Known correct: those are exactly the stored blocks containing
   index 5; every other node summarizes unchanged leaves.
3. Decision: repeat `[1,6)`. The same exact cover now reports node
   values 2, 3, and 8.
   After: return `min(2,3,8) = 2`.
   Known correct: disjoint block combination observes the replacement
   without rescanning all five requested values.
4. Decision: no operation remains, so stop.
   After: ordered minimum answers are `[1,2]`.
   Known correct: the root and every queryable node describe the final
   current array.

A sum segment tree could process the Fenwick workload too. Its broader
block model is useful when one implementation must later hold minima,
maxima, greatest common divisors, or richer summaries.

###### Sparse table for immutable minima

Initial state: the input is copied into length-one level 0. The table
has not accepted any query or update.

1. Decision: construct every complete power-of-two minimum block.
   After: the stored levels are:

   ```text
   length 1: [7 2 6 3 9 1 5]
   length 2: [2 2 3 3 1 1]
   length 4: [2 2 1 1]
   ```

   Known correct: each entry is the minimum of its stated block; no
   length-eight block fits seven values.
2. Decision: query `[1,6)`, whose length is 5. Choose B = 4. The left
   block `[1,5)` stores 2, and the right block `[2,6)` stores 1.
   After: return `min(2,1) = 1`.
   Known correct: the blocks cover every requested index. Their
   overlap cannot change a minimum.
3. Decision: the caller now needs index 5 to equal 8. The table has no
   update operation, so construct a new table from
   `[7,2,6,3,9,8,5]` rather than mutating one level.
   After: its length-two level is `[2,2,3,3,8,5]`, and its
   length-four level is `[2,2,3,3]`.
   Known correct: rebuilding recomputes every saved block that may
   contain the changed point; the original table remains immutable.
4. Decision: query `[1,6)` on the new table. Its length-four blocks
   `[1,5)` and `[2,6)` now store 2 and 3.
   After: return `min(2,3) = 2`.
   Known correct: the new table describes the replacement dataset,
   while the old table still correctly describes its original copy.
5. Decision: no request remains, so stop.
   After: answers across the two immutable versions are `[1,2]`.
   Known correct: no query mutated either table or affected another
   query.

Focused Fenwick counterexample: for `[2,1,3]`, prefix minima through
ends 2 and 3 are both 1. Range `[2,3)` has minimum 3, but no
subtraction or comparison of those equal prefix results recovers it.

Focused sparse-table counterexample: sum query `[0,3)` on `[1,2,3]`
uses overlapping length-two blocks with sums 3 and 5. Adding them
returns 8 because value 2 appears twice; the correct sum is 6.

Focused empty case: the Fenwick sum of `[2,2)` is zero. The two
minimum owners reject `[2,2)` before choosing a node or logarithm
level because their contracts define only nonempty minima.

##### Implementation

Use the existing owner that matches the workload:

- [A.12.3 Fenwick trees](#a123-fenwick-trees) implements checked
  point addition, prefix sum, and range sum. B.6.3 owns the conversion
  from point assignment to `newValue - currentValue`.
- [A.12.4 segment trees](#a124-segment-trees) implements point
  replacement and range minimum with power-of-two leaf storage.
- [A.12.5 sparse tables](#a125-sparse-tables) implements immutable
  range minimum with power-of-two levels and deep snapshots.

Those owners use `int64`, zero-based indices, and half-open ranges.
Their programs contain construction, validation, expected output,
ordinary cases, boundaries, and defensive ownership checks. This
comparison does not duplicate them.

For another aggregate, define its combine operation before adapting a
structure:

- a segment-tree combine must be associative, and padding needs an
  identity that cannot change a real answer;
- the overlapping sparse-table query additionally needs repetition to
  be harmless, as it is for minimum, maximum, or greatest common
  divisor; and
- a general Fenwick range query needs a commutative prefix aggregate
  that can be canceled with an inverse, as addition is canceled by
  subtraction.

If combine order matters, a segment-tree query must accumulate left
and right blocks in their original order. The minimum owner is
commutative, so its single running minimum does not expose that extra
requirement.

Ordinary segment trees and the owners here perform point updates. Use
a [lazy segment tree](#a126-lazy-segment-trees) when one operation
changes a whole range and its update can be summarized safely. Use a
prefix array for immutable sums; it is simpler and smaller than all
three dynamic or logarithmic-level structures.

##### Why it works

The Fenwick invariant says cell i stores the aggregate of the block
ending at i with width `lowbit(i)`. A prefix walk selects disjoint
cells that exactly cover `[0,end)`. A point update visits exactly the
stored blocks containing its position. Therefore both prefix sums are
correct after every successful update, and subtraction cancels the
common prefix `[0,start)` from a range query.

The segment-tree invariant says each leaf stores one current value and
each parent stores the correct combination of its two child blocks.
A point replacement can affect only its leaf and ancestors, so
repairing that path restores every changed summary. A query selects
disjoint stored blocks whose union is exactly the requested range.
Associativity makes their grouping irrelevant, so combining their
correct summaries returns the range aggregate.

The sparse-table invariant says level k stores a correct summary for
every complete block of length `2^k`. Each larger entry joins two
adjacent correct half-length entries, establishing the invariant by
induction over levels.

For a query of length L, let B be the largest power of two no greater
than L. The left and right B-length blocks lie inside the request.
Because `2B > L`, they touch or overlap, so their union covers the
whole range. Idempotence makes repeated overlap irrelevant. Combining
their two correct summaries therefore returns the requested minimum.

The update distinction follows from those proofs. Fenwick and segment
tree updates repair every stored summary affected by one point. A
sparse table stores that point in many blocks at many starts across
its levels; its owner exposes no bounded repair path. Rebuilding
restores the complete level invariant, while changing only one entry
leaves other containing blocks stale.

All traversals terminate. Fenwick positions move by a positive lowbit
toward zero or beyond N. Segment-tree positions move to parents until
they meet or reach the root. Sparse construction has finitely many
levels and starts, and a valid query performs a fixed number of reads.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let N be the value count, U the number of point updates, and Q the
number of range queries.

The checked Fenwick owner builds in `Theta(N)` time. Each update or
range sum visits `O(log(N+1))` cells, although some operations touch
only a constant number. A complete dynamic-sum workload takes
`O(N + (U+Q) log(N+1))` time. The retained values and tree use
`Theta(N)` space. Atomic updates temporarily stage `O(log(N+1))`
changes; queries use `O(1)` auxiliary space.

The segment-tree owner builds in `Theta(N)` time and retains
`Theta(N)` values and nodes. A point replacement takes
`Theta(log N)` for N greater than one. A range query can take
`Theta(1)` for one exact stored block and `O(log N)` in the worst
case. A dynamic-minimum workload takes `O(N + (U+Q) log N)` time.
Updates and queries use `O(1)` auxiliary space in the iterative owner.

The sparse-table owner builds in `Theta(N log N)` time and retains
`Theta(N log N)` block summaries for N at least two. Every valid
query takes `Theta(1)` time and `O(1)` auxiliary space. A static
workload takes `Theta(N log N + Q)` time. Each changed dataset needs a
new `Theta(N log N)` build under this immutable contract.

These bounds expose the trade:

```text
Fenwick: O(N) storage, compact dynamic prefix algebra
segment: O(N) storage, broader dynamic block algebra
sparse:  O(N log N) storage, immutable O(1) queries
```

For immutable sums, a prefix array builds in `Theta(N)`, uses
`Theta(N)` storage, and answers in `Theta(1)`, so a sparse table is
unnecessary. For a few short queries, direct scanning may beat every
index because it pays no preprocessing. Let W be the total number of
values scanned across all queries; the direct route costs `Theta(W)`.

Concrete performance also depends on constants and layout. Fenwick
uses one compact tree array plus the checked owner's value copy.
Segment-tree power-of-two padding can reserve nearly twice as many
leaves as values. Sparse-table levels multiply memory traffic and may
dominate cache capacity. Measure representative N, U, Q, and range
lengths after the required operation contract is satisfied.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty input gives the Fenwick owner an unused cell zero, and empty
  sum ranges return zero. The minimum owners reject every query
  because no nonempty range exists.
- On one value `[4]`, every valid structure answers its supported full
  range. Fenwick and segment updates touch no higher in-range block;
  the sparse table contains only level zero.
- Public ranges are half-open. Full range is `[0,N)`, and singleton i
  is `[i,i+1)`. Treating end as inclusive drops or overreads a value.
- Fenwick public index zero maps to internal position one. Starting an
  update at internal zero gives `lowbit(0) == 0` and never advances.
- Assignment through a Fenwick tree must add
  `newValue - currentValue`. Adding the replacement itself turns a set
  into accumulation and makes every later sum too large.
- Fenwick checked arithmetic can fail at the point, a stored block, a
  prefix total, or the final subtraction. Stage all update changes so
  one overflow cannot leave partial state.
- Minimum has no prefix inverse. On `[2,1,3]`, equal prefix minima
  hide the fact that suffix `[2,3)` has minimum 3.
- A segment-tree leaf update is incomplete until every ancestor is
  repaired. The first skipped ancestor makes any covering query stale.
- Segment-tree padding must use the aggregate identity. Padding a
  minimum tree with zero incorrectly wins when every real value is
  positive.
- Associativity is required for regrouping segment blocks. An
  operation whose result depends on parentheses needs additional state
  or a different structure.
- For noncommutative associative operations, preserve left-to-right
  block order. Combining right-side blocks in discovery order can
  reverse part of the requested sequence.
- A standard sparse table cannot accept a hidden point update.
  Changing level zero alone leaves larger blocks containing that
  point stale.
- Sparse minimum queries need `floor(log2(length))`. Using the ceiling
  selects a block extending outside the request.
- Sparse overlapping lookup is wrong for ordinary sum, product, or
  concatenation. The repeated overlap changes the answer.
- Duplicate minima need no tie rule when only the value is returned.
  If an index is required, define whether the leftmost or rightmost
  minimum wins and store that identity consistently.
- Range-wide updates are not point updates. Repeating point repair
  over a long interval can cost `Theta(N log N)`; use lazy
  propagation or an offline difference method when its contract fits.
- A fixed dense index domain is assumed. Compress sparse coordinates
  only when removed gaps carry no information needed by a query.
- Returning internal slices would let callers corrupt summaries.
  Preserve ownership with copies, and synchronize mutable structures
  before mixing updates with concurrent queries.

##### When to choose it

Choose a Fenwick tree when point changes and prefix or range sums
interleave on a fixed dense index domain. It is especially attractive
for cumulative frequencies, inversion counts, and other workloads
where the needed inverse exists and compact iterative storage matters.

Choose a segment tree when updates interleave with range queries but
prefix cancellation is unavailable, or when each block must retain
richer state. Dynamic minima, maxima, greatest common divisors, and
maximum-subarray summaries have this shape.

Choose a sparse table when values are immutable, queries are numerous,
the aggregate tolerates overlapping blocks, and constant worst-case
query time justifies `Theta(N log N)` preprocessing and storage.
Static minimum, maximum, and greatest-common-divisor queries are the
classic examples.

Before choosing, ask:

1. Are values immutable, point-updated, or range-updated?
2. Is the aggregate associative?
3. Does it have an inverse for canceling two prefixes?
4. Is it idempotent, so overlapping blocks are safe?
5. Are ranges empty, half-open, or inclusive at the public boundary?
6. Is `O(log N)` query latency acceptable?
7. Can memory hold `Theta(N log N)` summaries?
8. Do results need a value, an index, or richer tie information?

Use a prefix array for immutable sums, a direct scan for a small
workload, a lazy segment tree for compatible range updates, and a
persistent tree for historical versions. A disjoint sparse table can
serve immutable associative operations whose overlap is unsafe, but
its query mechanism is different from this standard sparse table.

Fenwick's original paper introduces the
[`binary indexed tree`](https://doi.org/10.1002/spe.4380240306).
LeetCode supplies the dynamic-sum workload in
[problem 307](https://leetcode.com/problems/range-sum-query-mutable/).
CSES supplies authoritative dynamic and static range-minimum workloads
in [task 1649](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1649/) and
[task 1647](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1647/). The linked A.12
owners provide the complete checked Go implementations used here.


#### C.7.8 DFS versus disjoint sets for connectivity

##### Problem and contract

Depth-first search and disjoint-set union can both answer whether two
vertices belong to the same undirected connected component. They keep
different evidence and fit different update histories.

Use a fixed vertex set `[0,V)` and an ordered stream containing:

- `add(u,v)`, which adds an unweighted undirected edge; and
- `connected(u,v)`, which returns whether a path exists after all
  earlier additions.

The common walkthrough has no deletions. Self-loops, duplicate edges,
and reversed repeats do not change connectivity. Invalid endpoints
must be rejected before changing adjacency or component state. An
isolated vertex is a one-vertex component and is connected to itself.

The DFS route stores reciprocal adjacency entries. Each query starts
a fresh traversal from u and returns true if it discovers v. It can
also retain parents to reconstruct one actual path. Its result is
about the current graph snapshot.

The disjoint-set route begins with one group per vertex. Each edge
unions its endpoint groups. A query compares representatives. It can
report component size and count, but it does not retain graph edges or
an actual path.

The exact repository owners expose related but different APIs:

- [B.12.1 DFS](
  #b121-depth-first-search-adjacency-list-and-stack) accepts a
  directed adjacency list and one start. It returns discovery order
  and reachability. Reciprocal rows model this undirected workload.
- [A.11.1 disjoint sets](#a111-parent-and-size-arrays) owns online
  `union`, `connected`, representative, size, and count operations.
- [B.12.3 component merging](
  #b123-component-merging-disjoint-sets) validates a complete edge
  batch and returns merge and count timelines plus final sizes.

This lesson owns the choice between current-graph traversal and a
maintained partition. Read [A.10.1 graph direction](
#a101-directed-and-undirected-graphs) first. Directed reachability is
not an equivalence relation and cannot use ordinary DSU.

##### Mental model

DFS answers a question by looking for present evidence:

```text
Start at u.
Follow current edges.
If v is discovered, the followed parents form a path.
If all reachable work ends first, no path exists now.
```

Its `reached[x]` bit means x has been discovered during this query.
The explicit stack stores the active depth-first path and each frame's
next unexamined neighbor. A later query normally needs fresh reached
state because edges or endpoints may differ.

DSU answers by maintaining a compressed summary:

```text
parentByVertex[x] -> next step toward x's component root
sizeByRoot[r]     -> component size when r is a root
```

Read `parentByVertex[3] == 0` as: "vertex 3 currently belongs to the
component represented by root 0." Equal roots answer connected true.
Different roots answer false.

Undirected connectivity is an equivalence relation:

- every vertex is connected to itself;
- if u is connected to v, then v is connected to u; and
- routes u-to-v and v-to-w can be joined into a route u-to-w.

DSU stores exactly that partition into equivalence classes. Adding an
undirected edge either joins two classes or changes nothing when its
endpoints already share one. Union by size keeps parent trees shallow;
path compression shortens routes to a root.

The information difference drives the choice:

```text
DFS keeps edges and can produce a witness route.
DSU keeps only which vertices have been merged.
```

For a static graph with many connectivity queries, a third useful
shape combines these ideas: run a DFS forest once, assign one
component label to every vertex, and compare labels in constant time.
DSU is most distinctive when additions and queries interleave.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use vertices 0 through 6. Process these additions and questions:

```text
add 0-1
add 2-3
connected 0 3   -> false
add 1-2
connected 0 3   -> true
add 4-5
connected 0 5   -> false
add 3-4
connected 0 5   -> true
```

Vertex 6 remains isolated. Reciprocal adjacency rows preserve edge
arrival order. Both methods must return query results
`[false,true,false,true]`.

###### Repeated DFS on the current graph

Initial state: seven empty adjacency rows exist. No query-specific
stack, reached slice, or parent array exists yet.

1. Decision: add edges 0-1 and 2-3 in both directions. For query
   `connected(0,3)`, mark 0 and push its frame. Inspect `0 -> 1`,
   discover 1, then inspect `1 -> 0` and skip the reached endpoint.
   Both frames become exhausted and pop.
   After: this query reached `{0,1}` and returns false; components
   `{2,3}`, `{4}`, `{5}`, and `{6}` were never entered.
   Known correct: every edge leaving the reached set was examined, and
   none leads to vertex 3.
2. Decision: add reciprocal edge 1-2. Clear the previous traversal
   state and query `connected(0,3)` again. Descend through
   `0 -> 1 -> 2`. Row 2 examines earlier neighbor 3 before neighbor 1,
   so discover the target and stop.
   After: return true with parent path `[0,1,2,3]` if parents are
   retained.
   Known correct: every consecutive pair in that path is a current
   edge, so it is a witness for connectivity.
3. Decision: add edge 4-5. Start a fresh query from 0 to 5. DFS visits
   0, 1, 2, and 3, skipping reciprocal edges when their endpoints are
   already reached. It exhausts that component before seeing 4 or 5.
   After: return false; query reached set is `{0,1,2,3}`.
   Known correct: no current edge crosses from that exhausted set to
   component `{4,5}`.
4. Decision: add reciprocal edge 3-4 and restart the query from 0.
   DFS descends `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5` and discovers the target.
   After: return true with that six-vertex witness path.
   Known correct: the newly added bridge joins the two earlier
   components, and every parent edge is present in adjacency.
5. Decision: no operation remains. Discard the last query's stack,
   reached bits, and parents, but retain adjacency if future graph
   inspection is needed.
   After: query results are `[false,true,false,true]`; vertex 6 is
   still an isolated adjacency row.
   Known correct: each answer describes the graph at its own stream
   position, not only the final graph.

The repeated visits to 0, 1, 2, and 3 are the cost that DSU avoids.
They are also what lets DFS produce a route and inspect current edges.

###### Incremental disjoint sets

Initial state: parents are `[0,1,2,3,4,5,6]`, every root size is one,
and component count is 7. No adjacency list is stored.

1. Decision: union 0 with 1, then 2 with 3. Both pairs have equal
   singleton sizes, so each first root wins its tie.
   After: parents are `[0,0,2,2,4,5,6]`; roots 0 and 2 have size 2;
   component count is 5. Query 0 and 3 compares roots 0 and 2 and
   returns false.
   Known correct: the parent forest represents exactly the two added
   edges and three remaining singleton components.
2. Decision: add edge 1-2. Find root 0 through 1 and root 2 directly.
   Their sizes tie, so attach root 2 below root 0 and set root 0's
   size to 4. Query 0 and 3 follows `3 -> 2 -> 0` and compresses 3.
   After: parents are `[0,0,0,0,4,5,6]`; component count is 4; return
   true.
   Known correct: edge 1-2 joined exactly components `{0,1}` and
   `{2,3}`; path compression changed representation, not membership.
3. Decision: union 4 with 5. Query 0 and 5 compares roots 0 and 4.
   After: parents are `[0,0,0,0,4,4,6]`; root 4 has size 2;
   component count is 3; return false.
   Known correct: `{4,5}` is still a different equivalence class from
   `{0,1,2,3}`.
4. Decision: add edge 3-4. Finds return roots 0 of size 4 and 4 of
   size 2. Attach root 4 below root 0. Query 0 and 5 follows
   `5 -> 4 -> 0` and compresses 5.
   After: parents are `[0,0,0,0,0,0,6]`; root 0 has size 6;
   component count is 2; return true.
   Known correct: vertices 0 through 5 now share one root, while 6
   remains a singleton root.
5. Decision: no operation remains, so stop.
   After: query results are `[false,true,false,true]`; final component
   sizes are six for vertices 0 through 5 and one for vertex 6.
   Known correct: the maintained partition matches the final
   undirected graph, although it stores none of the witness edges.

Focused static case: on the final graph, one DFS forest can label
vertices `[0,0,0,0,0,0,1]`. Any later static connectivity query is
one label comparison. Re-running a traversal per query would repeat
work even though the graph cannot change.

Focused directed counterexample: with only arc `0 -> 1`, DFS says 0
can reach 1 but 1 cannot reach 0. Unioning 0 and 1 makes both queries
true. The first wrong decision is treating one-way reachability as a
symmetric component relation.

Focused deletion counterexample: add 0-1 and 1-2, then remove 1-2.
DFS on the current adjacency says 0 and 2 are disconnected. Ordinary
DSU still gives them the same root because it has no split operation.

##### Implementation

Use the existing owner matching the required output:

- [B.12.1 depth-first search](
  #b121-depth-first-search-adjacency-list-and-stack) implements full
  adjacency validation, deterministic stack frames, discovery order,
  and a reachability slice. For an undirected graph, store each edge
  in both endpoint rows.
- [A.11.1 parent and size arrays](
  #a111-parent-and-size-arrays) implements validated union, connected,
  representative, component size, count, union by size, and path
  compression.
- [B.12.3 component merging](
  #b123-component-merging-disjoint-sets) applies the same DSU rules to
  a complete ordered edge batch.

B.12.1 does not return parents. To return a witness path, add an owned
`parentByVertex` slice, assign a parent exactly when a vertex is first
discovered, and follow parents backward from the target. Reversing
that chain produces a valid start-to-target path. This is an API
extension, not an existing owner result.

To label every component of a static undirected graph, keep one
reached slice across an outer vertex loop. Start the owner traversal
from each still-unreached vertex and give all discoveries the current
component label. Increment the label only after that traversal
finishes.

For a long-lived graph service, validate an added edge before
inserting either reciprocal adjacency entry. The exact B.12.1 owner
instead validates the entire supplied adjacency list before each
standalone call. Do not claim its narrower traversal-only cost while
retaining its full-validation contract.

Neither implementation is safe for unsynchronized concurrent updates.
DFS queries need an immutable adjacency snapshot while running. DSU
finds may compress paths even during a logical read, so `connected`
also mutates representation and needs synchronization.

This comparison adds no duplicate Go program. The linked owners
contain the complete implementations, validation paths, and
executable cases.

##### Why it works

For DFS, maintain that every reached vertex has a current graph path
from the start and every stack frame represents one vertex on the
active path. A discovery follows a real adjacency entry, so assigning
its parent extends a valid path. Marking before pushing prevents
cycles from producing duplicate frames.

If DFS exhausts its stack without reaching the target, every outgoing
entry of every reachable vertex has been examined. If an unreached
target had a path from the start, the first unreached vertex on that
path would have a reached predecessor whose connecting edge was
examined. That contradiction proves a false result is correct.

For DSU, maintain that the parent forest partitions vertices exactly
like the connected components of all processed undirected edges.
Initially both partitions contain V singletons. If an added edge has
equal endpoint roots, an earlier route already connects them and the
partition stays correct.

If the roots differ, no processed route crosses between their two
components. The new edge creates routes between every vertex on one
side and every vertex on the other. Linking exactly those roots merges
exactly the graph components. Union by size changes only tree shape,
and path compression points vertices to the same root, so neither
optimization changes membership.

Therefore DFS and DSU agree after any prefix of undirected additions:
DFS finds a route exactly when DSU gives equal roots. DFS derives that
fact from stored edges at query time; DSU preserves it inductively as
each edge arrives.

Both methods terminate. DFS advances a finite row position, discovers
a vertex once, or pops a frame on every transition. A DSU find follows
a finite acyclic parent path to a self-parented root. The operation
stream is finite, so all traversals and unions finish.

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let V be vertex count, E the number of currently stored undirected
edges, Q the number of connectivity queries, and M the total number of
DSU unions and finds.

The exact B.12.1 DFS owner validates all V rows and 2E reciprocal
entries before traversal, so one call takes `Theta(V+E)` total time.
In a long-lived service that validates each edge on insertion, one
query traversal takes `Theta(R+A_R)`, where R vertices and `A_R`
adjacency entries are reachable from its start. Its worst case remains
`Theta(V+E)`.

Running DFS independently for Q interleaved queries can therefore cost
`O(Q(V+E))` at the final graph size, while earlier prefixes may cost
less. Retained adjacency uses `Theta(V+E)` space. Each query uses
`O(V)` reached and parent storage plus up to `O(V)` active frames. A
returned path uses `O(L)` output vertices for path length L.

For a static graph, one complete DFS forest takes `Theta(V+E)` time
and stores `Theta(V)` labels. Q later connectivity queries then take
`Theta(Q)` total time. This is often the fair comparison to DSU when
there are no updates.

DSU construction takes `Theta(V)` time and retains two V-element
arrays. With union by size and path compression, M intermixed finds
and unions take `O(M alpha(V))` total amortized time for positive V.
The inverse Ackermann function `alpha` grows extremely slowly. Union
by size also bounds one parent path by `O(log V)`. Operations use
`O(1)` auxiliary space.

The batch B.12.3 owner additionally validates E edges and materializes
per-edge flags and counts plus V final sizes. Its output alone is
`Theta(V+E)`, so its complete best case is already
`Theta(V+E)`. A long-lived DSU that returns one Boolean per query need
not retain those timelines.

DSU's smaller storage and near-constant amortized operations come from
discarding adjacency. That saving is invalid if a caller later asks
for a route, neighbors, bridges, cycle edges, or deletion repair. DFS
keeps the evidence needed for those tasks.

No probabilistic average is involved. Concrete costs still depend on
allocation, graph density, query endpoints, and how quickly a DFS
finds its target. Choose by observable outputs and update rules before
comparing constants.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- With V zero, DSU is a valid empty partition. B.12.1 has no valid
  start, while a static DFS-forest wrapper can return empty labels
  without starting a traversal.
- An isolated vertex such as 6 is connected to itself and to no other
  vertex. Omitting vertices absent from the edge list loses this
  component.
- A self-loop and a duplicate undirected edge do not change the
  partition. DSU must not decrement component count for equal roots;
  DFS must still prevent repeated discovery.
- Undirected adjacency needs both `u -> v` and `v -> u`. Storing one
  direction can make DFS depend incorrectly on which endpoint starts.
- Directed reachability is not symmetric. Never union endpoints merely
  because an arc exists.
- Mark a DFS vertex when discovered, before pushing. Marking after pop
  lets a cycle schedule duplicate active work.
- A recursive DFS can overflow the Go call stack on a deep graph.
  Explicit frames make retained depth visible and bounded by V.
- Clear query-specific reached and parent state before a new DFS.
  Bits from a different source can invent connectivity; after an
  addition, skipping an old reached vertex can miss a new bridge.
- One DFS start does not label a disconnected graph. An outer loop
  must start from each still-unreached vertex, including isolated
  ones.
- DSU representatives are implementation names, not minimum vertex
  labels. Equal-size tie direction can change a root without changing
  connectivity.
- Find roots before unioning. Assigning `parent[u] = v` directly can
  detach a subtree or create a parent cycle.
- Decrement component count only after linking different roots. A
  self-loop, duplicate, or already-connected edge changes no count.
- Ordinary DSU cannot delete an edge or split a component. Keeping
  its old root equality after a bridge deletion returns stale
  connectivity.
- DSU cannot reconstruct a graph path. Parent links are compression
  metadata and need not correspond to input edges.
- Validate both endpoints before adjacency insertion, path
  compression, or union. Otherwise a bad second endpoint can leave
  partial mutation.
- Concurrent adjacency mutation can invalidate a DFS row during a
  query. Concurrent finds and unions can corrupt a DSU parent forest.
  Snapshot or synchronize according to the API contract.

##### When to choose it

Choose DFS when the graph snapshot is static or changes arbitrarily,
query volume is modest, adjacency already exists, or the caller needs
an actual route or edge-sensitive analysis. DFS also supports directed
reachability, where ordinary DSU is invalid.

Choose DSU when vertices are fixed, undirected edges are only added,
and additions interleave with many connectivity, component-size, or
component-count questions. Kruskal's algorithm and incremental network
merging have this shape.

For a static undirected graph with many queries, label components once
with DFS or BFS, then compare labels. This matches DSU's cheap query
phase while preserving adjacency for later graph work.

Before choosing, ask:

1. Are edges directed or undirected?
2. Are edges only added, or can they also be deleted?
3. Is the graph one snapshot or an interleaved operation stream?
4. Does the caller need only a Boolean, or an actual witness path?
5. Are component sizes, counts, or merge events required?
6. Is adjacency already stored for other graph operations?
7. Can preprocessing answer all later static queries?
8. Must concurrent reads avoid hidden representation mutation?

Use BFS instead of DFS when a returned unweighted path must have the
fewest edges. Use strongly connected components for mutual directed
reachability. For deletions, consider recomputing a traversal, offline
reverse processing, rollback DSU, or a fully dynamic connectivity
structure according to the operation schedule.

NIST defines [depth-first search](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/depthfirst.html) and
[connected components](
https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/connectedComponents.html).
Tarjan's original [set-union analysis](
https://doi.org/10.1145/321879.321884) establishes the near-linear
sequence bound behind union by size or rank with path compression.


#### C.7.9 Trie versus hashing versus string matching

##### Problem and contract

A string problem is not defined merely by having string inputs. The
required relation decides the useful index:

- exact dictionary membership asks whether a whole key was stored;
- prefix lookup asks which stored keys begin with a query; and
- substring matching asks where a pattern begins inside a text.

Choosing by input type alone can produce an efficient answer to the
wrong question. A hash set, a trie, and a string matcher all compare
text, but each preserves different information.

This lesson chooses among those tools for immutable byte strings. A
dictionary contains D keys with S total bytes. A query has L bytes.
A searched text has T bytes, and one pattern has P bytes. Results must
be exact: a fingerprint may filter candidates, but it must not create
false matches.

The examples use lowercase ASCII so byte order and displayed letter
order agree. A production contract must separately decide whether its
unit is bytes, Unicode code points, or grapheme clusters; whether case
and normalization matter; how duplicates behave; and what an empty
key, prefix, or pattern means.

Read [membership tracking](#b12-membership-tracking-hash-set),
[trie dictionary lookup](#b74-prefix-and-dictionary-lookup-trie),
and [KMP matching](#b72-kmp-matching-prefix-function-array) first.
They own the complete implementations. This lesson owns the choice
between their contracts.

##### Mental model

Ask what must remain visible after preprocessing.

A hash set remembers whole-key equality. Conceptually, hashing sends
the complete key to a bucket, then equality distinguishes keys in that
bucket. It deliberately forgets useful ordering between different
keys. Knowing that `ant` exists says nothing directly about all keys
whose first three bytes are `ant`.

A trie remembers prefix structure. The root is the empty prefix, one
edge consumes one input unit, and a node represents the path prefix.
A terminal marker distinguishes a stored word from a path that exists
only because a longer word uses it. Descendants of the `ant` node are
exactly the stored words beginning with `ant`.

A string matcher remembers alignment state while scanning a text. KMP
stores how much of one pattern matches the suffix of text processed so
far. Aho-Corasick generalizes that idea to many fixed patterns. These
states answer "what ends here?", not "what dictionary keys descend
from this prefix?"

The word "hashing" can name two different tools:

- a hash table indexes complete stored keys for lookup; and
- a rolling hash fingerprints consecutive, equal-length text windows.

Rabin-Karp uses the second meaning. Its rolling fingerprint avoids
rehashing every window, but equal fingerprints do not prove equal
strings. Exact verification remains necessary under this lesson's
contract.

Use this first question:

```text
What relation must one query reveal?

whole key equals a stored key       -> hash set or map
stored keys begin with this prefix  -> trie or ordered index
pattern occurs inside this text     -> string matcher
```

Only then compare workload, memory, output order, update frequency,
and worst-case requirements.

##### Worked walkthrough

Use this dictionary:

```text
["an", "ant", "ante", "anthem", "banana"]
```

Also search text `bananana` for pattern `ana`. Three similar-looking
questions now need different preserved relations.

Initial state: the immutable dictionary is loaded into both a hash set
and a trie. No query result exists. The text and pattern remain
unchanged, and no prefix table or match range exists.

First ask whether exact key `ant` was stored.

1. Decision: give the complete bytes `ant` to a hash set lookup.
   After: lookup reports true.
   Known correct: exact equality is the entire requested relation;
   no order or prefix enumeration is needed.

2. Decision: ask the same set whether `ana` was stored.
   After: lookup reports false.
   Known correct: `ana` occurring inside `banana` is irrelevant to
   dictionary membership, and no dictionary key equals `ana`.

Now ask for every dictionary word beginning with `ant`.

3. Decision: follow trie edges from root through `a`, `n`, and `t`.
   After: the current node represents prefix `ant` and is terminal.
   Known correct: `ant` itself is stored, and every longer answer must
   lie below this node.

4. Decision: inspect the terminal before descendants, then visit child
   edges in byte order. Emit `ant`, descend through `e` to emit
   `ante`, then backtrack and descend through `h`, `e`, `m` to emit
   `anthem`.
   After: results are `["ant","ante","anthem"]`.
   Known correct: all and only paths below the prefix node begin with
   `ant`; terminal-before-child order places a word before extensions.

5. Decision: try to answer the prefix query with only the hash set.
   After: exact lookup of `ant` finds one answer but exposes neither
   `ante` nor `anthem`; finding them requires scanning the dictionary
   and testing every key's prefix.
   Known correct: a hash table stores equality access, not prefix
   adjacency. A full scan can recover the answer but loses the index's
   intended query advantage.

Finally ask where pattern `ana` occurs in text `bananana`.

6. Decision: preprocess KMP pattern `ana`. Its prefix-function array
   is `[0,0,1]`: the full pattern's longest proper border is `a`.
   After: matching begins with zero pattern bytes matched.
   Known correct: the table records which matched prefix can remain
   useful after a mismatch or a complete occurrence.

7. Decision: scan text bytes `b`, `a`, `n`, `a`. The first byte does
   not extend the pattern. The next three grow the matched length from
   zero to three.
   After: report half-open range `[1,4)` and fall back to matched
   length one rather than zero.
   Known correct: `text[1:4] == "ana"`; its final `a` is also the
   first byte of a possible overlapping occurrence.

8. Decision: consume the next `n`, `a` pair. The retained `a` plus
   those bytes completes another match. Repeat once for the final
   pair.
   After: ranges are `[1,4)`, `[3,6)`, and `[5,8)`.
   Known correct: every overlap is preserved, and every reported slice
   equals the pattern.

9. Decision: consider using the dictionary trie for this text search.
   After: its root path does not automatically begin at text indexes
   1, 3, and 5. A plain trie search would need to restart from many
   text positions or gain failure links.
   Known correct: trie ancestry indexes prefixes from one known start;
   arbitrary substring starts require matching state such as KMP or
   Aho-Corasick.

The first wrong choice in each counterexample is asking a structure to
recover a relation it discarded. A hash set discarded prefix order. A
plain trie did not encode arbitrary text alignments. KMP preprocessed
one pattern, not a dictionary of changing prefix queries.

##### Implementation

Do not combine all three tools into one universal string index. Route
each operation to the smallest owner whose contract matches it.

For whole-key membership or associated values, use the complete
[hash-set scan](#b12-membership-tracking-hash-set) or the relevant
map value type. A dictionary set normally uses `map[string]struct{}`;
a frequency or payload requirement uses a map value instead.

For exact and prefix queries over one reused dictionary, use the
complete [dictionary trie](
#b74-prefix-and-dictionary-lookup-trie). Its terminal marker, ordered
child traversal, duplicate policy, validation, and output ownership
are part of the implementation contract.

For every occurrence of one pattern, use the complete [KMP matcher](
#b72-kmp-matching-prefix-function-array) when deterministic linear
work matters. Use the [Rabin-Karp matcher](
#b73-rabin-karp-matching-rolling-hash) when rolling fingerprints are
central and exact candidate verification is retained.

For many fixed patterns scanned through one or many texts, build the
[Aho-Corasick matcher](
#b77-multi-pattern-matching-aho-corasick-automaton). It augments trie
paths with failure and output links; a plain dictionary trie is not a
drop-in substitute.

The routing logic can be written before any data structure:

```text
if query is exact whole-key lookup:
    choose a hash table unless ordered or prefix work also matters
else if query begins at the key's root and follows a prefix:
    choose a trie or another ordered prefix index
else if query may begin at any text position:
    choose a string matcher
else:
    restate the operation before selecting storage
```

That final branch is important. Fuzzy matching, wildcards, regular
languages, suffix queries, and edit distance need contracts not owned
by these three choices.

##### Why it works

The choice is correct when the index's invariant is the relation the
query needs.

For a hash set, maintain that a key is present if and only if an equal
whole key was inserted. A successful lookup therefore proves exact
membership. It proves no prefix relationship between unequal keys,
because that information is absent from the invariant.

For a trie, after consuming I query bytes, the current node represents
exactly `query[:I]`. If an edge is missing, no stored key has that
prefix. If the full prefix path exists, every terminal descendant adds
only suffix bytes, so it is a completion. Conversely, every stored
completion follows that path before its suffix, so it lies in the
subtree. The final node's terminal marker separately proves exact
membership.

For KMP, between text bytes, the matched length is the longest pattern
prefix equal to a suffix of processed text. Equality extends it. A
mismatch follows a border to the next viable alignment without moving
the text backward. Full pattern length proves one occurrence. Falling
back to the full pattern's longest border preserves overlaps.

For verified Rabin-Karp, the rolling invariant says the maintained
fingerprint belongs to the current P-byte window. Unequal hashes rule
out equal strings. Equal hashes only select a candidate; byte equality
proves the reported match. The verification is what turns a possibly
colliding fingerprint into an exact result.

Each owner's termination measure is also different. A hash lookup is
bounded by its table operation. A trie path consumes one query unit,
and finite subtree traversal completes or reaches its result limit. A
matcher consumes text positions; every KMP fallback strictly reduces
the matched length before that scan advances.

Thus the decision is not "which string algorithm is fastest?" It is
"which invariant proves the requested answer, then which qualifying
implementation best fits this workload?"

##### Costs and tradeoffs

Let D be dictionary key count, S their total byte count, and L query
length. Under the usual hash-table assumption, building a string set
takes expected Theta(1+D+S) time and O(D+S) retained key storage if
the index owns key bytes. An exact query takes expected Theta(1+L)
time because hashing and possible equality inspect the query bytes.
Go specifies map behavior but does not promise a worst-case lookup
time.

A fixed-alphabet trie also builds in Theta(1+D+S) time and creates at
most S non-root nodes. It can answer exact membership or locate a
prefix in Theta(1+L) time. Completion is output-sensitive: after the
prefix path, it visits subtree nodes and copies returned words. Array
children give predictable selection but can reserve many nil pointers;
child maps save sparse slots but add hashing and ordering work.

The two indexes can share the same asymptotic exact-query bound yet
have very different constants. A hash table usually has fewer nodes
and is the direct fit for equality only. A trie pays per-prefix-node
overhead to make prefix traversal and shared-prefix enumeration
available. Shared prefixes reduce duplicate edges, but do not make a
pointer-heavy trie automatically smaller than retained strings.

Using a hash set for prefix enumeration requires testing all D keys.
The work is at least proportional to the keys inspected and returned
bytes; no hash-bucket rule groups a prefix's answers. A sorted static
array can instead locate a prefix range with binary searches and may
be more compact than a trie.

For text length T, pattern length P, and K matches, KMP preprocessing
and scanning take Theta(1+T+P) time. Its prefix table uses Theta(P)
auxiliary space, and returned ranges use Theta(K) output space. Best,
average, and worst successful scans share the linear asymptotic bound
because this all-match contract consumes the full text.

Verified Rabin-Karp uses O(1) auxiliary state beyond results and rolls
across all equal-length windows. Let V be the bytes examined during
exact candidate verification. Its time is Theta(P+T+V) when P fits
the text. Collisions or many real matches can make V large and yield
Theta(T*P) worst-case time. KMP retains its deterministic linear bound
by storing a pattern table instead.

For many fixed patterns, separate KMP scans repeat text work. The
Aho-Corasick owner builds shared trie, failure, and output state, then
scans one text in expected O(T+K) time under its Go-map transition
assumption. The retained automaton and construction are worthwhile
only when pattern or text reuse repays them.

No average case should be quoted without a distribution over keys,
prefixes, texts, patterns, and hash behavior. Measure representative
data after the contract and worst-case requirements rule out invalid
choices.

##### Edge cases and mistakes

- Empty string has different meanings. It can be a dictionary key,
  the root prefix, or a pattern occurring at every chosen boundary.
  State each contract rather than sharing one accidental behavior.
- A trie path is not necessarily a word. After inserting `anthem`,
  path `ant` exists even if its terminal marker was never set.
- A word can also be a prefix. Emit terminal `ant` before descendants
  such as `ante` when lexicographic completion order is required.
- Duplicate keys may collapse in a set or Boolean-terminal trie.
  Frequency maps and pattern IDs require a different stored value.
- Go map iteration order is unspecified. A hash set cannot promise
  lexicographic output without separately sorting results.
- A child map in a trie also has unspecified iteration order. Sort
  child labels or use ordered child slots when output order matters.
- A plain trie answers prefixes from its root. Restarting it at every
  text position can become quadratic and is not Aho-Corasick.
- KMP for pattern `ana` must retain border `a` after a match.
  Resetting to zero loses the overlaps at starts 3 and 5 in
  `bananana`.
- Rolling-hash equality is not string equality. Verify candidates if
  false positives are forbidden.
- A hash table and a rolling hash solve different subproblems. Calling
  both "hashing" without naming the indexed object hides the choice.
- Pattern longer than text has no nonempty match. Check lengths before
  slicing the first window in a rolling matcher.
- Byte indexing can split UTF-8 encodings. Rune indexing still does
  not equal user-perceived grapheme indexing.
- Case folding and Unicode normalization can change length and
  equality. Normalize at a declared boundary, not inside one owner
  while leaving the others byte-based.
- Prefix completion can return far more data than the prefix length.
  Include output volume and an optional limit in the contract.
- Untrusted inputs can target fixed public fingerprints or consume
  trie memory. Exact verification preserves correctness, but resource
  limits and deterministic bounds are separate requirements.
- If the dictionary changes often, include update and deletion costs.
  A terminal deletion may require pruning; a static sorted index may
  require rebuilding; an automaton may need full reconstruction.
- Do not choose from asymptotic lookup alone. Ownership, build cost,
  reuse count, memory layout, output order, and witness requirements
  can decide between otherwise valid structures.

##### When to choose it

Choose a hash set or map when queries ask for exact whole-key
equality, prefix order is irrelevant, and expected hash-table behavior
is acceptable. Common examples are intern tables, deduplication,
counts, and key-to-record lookup.

Choose a trie when one dictionary serves many prefix operations, such
as autocomplete, prefix counts, lexicographic completion, or longest
stored-prefix queries. Prefer a sorted slice or compressed radix tree
when static data, compact storage, or long unary paths dominate.

Choose KMP when one exact pattern must be found anywhere in a text and
deterministic linear worst-case work matters. Choose verified
Rabin-Karp when rolling equal-length windows are already central or a
fingerprint is a useful candidate filter. Choose Aho-Corasick when
many fixed patterns share each text scan.

Before implementing, answer these questions:

1. Is the query about a whole key, a key prefix, or an arbitrary text
   position?
2. Is there one pattern, many fixed patterns, or one fixed text with
   many changing patterns?
3. Must results be exact, ordered, bounded, or accompanied by ranges?
4. Are duplicates identities, counts, or collapsed set entries?
5. What is the matching unit and normalization policy?
6. How many queries repay preprocessing and retained memory?
7. Are deterministic worst-case bounds required for hostile input?
8. Can the index be immutable, or must updates and deletions be cheap?

If one workload needs exact lookup and prefix completion, a trie may
serve both. If it also needs arbitrary substring search, build a
separate matcher or an automaton whose contract explicitly supports
that operation. One data type need not own every query.

Fredkin's original [trie paper](
https://doi.org/10.1145/367390.367400) introduces trie memory. The
[KMP paper](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0206024) establishes
matching time proportional to combined string lengths. Karp and
Rabin's [fingerprint paper](https://doi.org/10.1147/RD.312.0249)
develops randomized pattern matching, while the original
[Aho-Corasick paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/360825.360855) presents
multi-pattern finite-state matching. The official [Go specification](
https://go.dev/ref/spec#Map_types) defines map semantics without an
algorithmic lookup-time guarantee.

#### C.7.10 Exact versus randomized or approximate algorithms

##### Problem and contract

An algorithm can use random choices and still return an exact answer.
Another algorithm can be fully replayable and still return only an
estimate. "Randomized" describes how work or evidence is chosen;
"approximate" describes what the result promises. Treat them as
separate axes.

This lesson chooses among four broad contracts:

- a deterministic exact algorithm returns a valid exact answer on
  every accepted input without random choices;
- a randomized exact algorithm returns a valid exact answer for every
  valid random path, while its work may vary;
- a Monte Carlo algorithm fixes or bounds work but permits a stated
  probability of error or returns a statistical estimate; and
